consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a betrothed husband who contracted betrothal by words of present consent with Titia and received one hundred from her under the title of dowry, if she dies before the consummation of the marriage, gains half of the dowry.
2. Whether a marriage by present consent alone is a true marriage.
3. Whether an agreement to gain a certain part of the dowry in the event of death takes effect when one of the spouses enters religion.
4. The word nuptials is taken in multiple senses in law.
5. Betrothal is commonly said to be by words of present consent.
6. Statutes ought to be brought back to the ius commune as far as possible.
7. A law consists of intention and words.
body: THE factual contingency is as follows.

† A certain A contracted betrothal by words of present consent with a certain B, and received from her one thousand under the title of dowry. It happened that before the woman thus betrothed was led to his house, or the marriage was otherwise consummated, she departed this life. Now it is asked whether the said betrothed man gains half of the dowry, in view of the statute written below, namely: "If any woman shall die without children by the man to whom she was married, at the time of her death, let half of her dowries remain with the husband, not computing in the said half the profit of the donation on account of marriage, of which part the husband cannot be deprived," etc. Afterwards, certain additions were made to the said statute, in which mention was always made of existing children or not. And invoking the names of Christ and His mother, it is argued first, so that the truth may shine forth more brightly, for the affirmative side as follows: The statute, in conferring this gain upon the husband, requires only two things, namely, that the woman be married, and that she die without children by her husband. But these two things occurred in the proposed fact, as I will immediately prove; therefore he ought to have half of the dowries. The consequence is sufficiently evident of itself; and the major premise is also proved. For it is true to say that this woman died without children by her husband, since no one appears, and facts are not presumed, as in c. in praesentia, de prob. and c. Raynutius, and c. Raynaldus, extra de testa. and in c. cum in iure, de of. del. with similar texts. That she was married, I prove most aptly by a very notable text, in my judgment, in l. cum fuerit, ff. de cond. & dem., where it is most clearly proved that she is called married even though she was not carnally known. And what is more, even if she had not been led home; and it is enough that present consent to marriage intervened, which alone makes a marriage, and not carnal commingling, as is proved there at the end of that law, and the gloss and Bar. hold this more extensively there. Secondly, it is proved by l. 3, ff. de don. inter ui. & ux., joined with the gloss on the word concubinae, where notably it is called a marriage, and they are called husband and wife, merely by contracting betrothal by words of present consent, even though carnal intercourse has not intervened. And so the gloss concludes there that just as a gift between husband and wife is prohibited during the marriage when the marriage is consummated, so too when the marriage is not consummated, once present consent has intervened. And although it says there that this holds in canon law, I say the same of civil law, as is proved in Auth. de nupt. § nuptias, and there is a good gloss, and that text makes excellently for that side: where it is proved, especially joined with the gloss, that nuptials are contracted by the sole consent of both, namely of the man and the woman, even if nothing else has intervened. 2

† Thirdly, I prove it by many canon laws, which commonly say that a marriage is true marriage from present consent alone, even if nothing else has intervened, to such an extent that by a second marriage, even with intercourse, the first is not undone, because it already had its essence from its consent, as is proved in c. si. de spon. duo. and 27 q. 2 c. sufficit, and c. cum nunciatus, with many following texts to the same point, c. unicum, de uoto, lib. 6, and as noted by Host. in c. ex publico, de conuer. coniu. For the definition of marriage, which is posited and declared in 27 q. 2 in prin. and Inst. de nup. in prin., where there is a good text with the gloss, supports this. Fourthly, see this at first glance from the case, especially joined with what Bal. says there on l. Deo nobis, C. de epis. & cle., where it is said to be proved that 3

† a pact concerning gaining a certain part of the dowry in the event of death takes effect when one of the spouses enters religion; and yet it is certain that after the consummation of the marriage it is not lawful for one of the spouses to enter religion, de conuer. coniu. c. cum sit, and c. ex publico, with many similar texts. Thus that text seems to be understood when one enters religion after the marriage has been contracted and not yet consummated: because then it is lawful even against the will of the other, as in c. ex publico, and c. 2 eo. ti. And according to this, that text seems to prove that the said pact concerning gaining a certain part of the dowry in the event of death claims its place even when death intervenes after betrothal by words of present consent has been contracted, the marriage not yet being consummated, as happens in our case. And what is read in l. non sine, C. de bo. quae lib. supports these points. But notwithstanding these points, I consider the contrary to be true in law, namely, that the said man gains nothing under pretext of the said statute. And first, as a foundation, I lay down two presuppositions. The first is, 4

† that the word "nuptials" is taken in multiple ways in law. Sometimes it is taken for the very pure essence of marriage, which is taken when present consent alone intervenes, as is proved in the said l. cum fuerit in the said § nuptiae, and c. omne nuptiarum bonum, 27 q. 2, with similar texts. Sometimes it is taken for the carnal commingling itself that intervenes after marriage has first been contracted, as is proved in c. causam, and is proved clearer than daylight in c. genuit, especially joined with the second gloss, which holds this most clearly, in the same causa and quaestio, and there something by Archi. Sometimes it is taken for the preparation and festivities that occur at the time when the wife is led to the husband's house, as is proved in c. nostrates, and c. foeminae, 30 q. 5; and thus it is taken in the Gospel, where it is said that "nuptials took place in Cana of Galilee," when Jesus made wine from water there. And this last exposition seems more proper and conforming to the common speech; whence in the vernacular of certain places it is called, as is said there, "le noze"; and so thought Gasp. de Cald. on the rub. de sponsa. The second presupposition is that the word "matrimony" or "marriage" is sometimes verified in a marriage contracted by words of present consent, carnal copula not yet having intervened;

† and in the vernacular they are called sponsalia by words of present consent, and thus they are accustomed to be designated, the woman not yet having been brought into the man's house, as appears most clearly in c. sicut ex literis, and the preceding chapter de sponsa, and more clearly in c. tertio loco, de praesum., with similar texts. Sometimes the word "marriage", or the word "wife" and "husband", is only verified in a marriage consummated by carnal copula, as is proved in c. debitum, de biga. in princ. and in c. ex publico, de conuer. coniug., and more elegantly proved in c. si quis desponsata, 27 q. 2, where it is said: "If anyone uses a woman betrothed to him and delivered to him, it is duly called a marriage." To the same effect is c. quapropter, above, in the same causa and quaestio. Whence this diversity arises can be sufficiently gathered from what is read and noted in the said c. quapropter, by the said c. debitum, and by the gloss in the often-cited said c. ex publ. Having presupposed these things, I infer toward the decision of our question, and in this manner: Since the word "wife" and the word "husband" are verified and found to be verified after marriage is consummated, and not before, and especially the word "married woman" (nupta), which is properly applied at least to her who is solemnly led home, therefore this written interpretation must be made in our case. The antecedent was fully proved above. Moreover, I prove the consequent most clearly thus: A just cause for restricting a statute exists when, if it were understood simply and broadly, someone would improperly take a gain, or another would suffer a loss. The first notable point is proved in l. ut gradatim § sed et si lege, ff. de mu. & ho. and c. Abbate, de uerb. sig. The second is proved in l. 2 and l. adigere § quamuis, de iure pat. and l. fi. § in conputatione, what is noted there, C. de iu. delib., and both far better than elsewhere are proved in c. cum dilectus, de consue., where a proved custom does not prejudice the ius commune; where the words of the statute are not only restricted to an understanding that is in some way extraneous, but also one very remotely adaptable to the words; whence the word "election", referred to certain persons, is taken for confirmation. And Bart. also confirmed this doctrine in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu. To the same effect, wherever statutes are penal—and they are sufficiently called penal from the fact that they diminish someone's patrimony, as noted by Io. And. in the said c. 1 de ele. lib. 6—the words ought to be restricted so that they do not take that understanding which they would take according to the broad signification of the words; this is proved in c. cum in cunctis, de ele. joined with c. si compromissarius, eo. ti. lib. 6, and by Io. An. in reg. odia, de reg. iu. lib. 6 in Mercu.; what he himself notes in c. statutum, de ele. lib. 6 supports this. But since in our case not only distributively but collectively all these aforementioned things concur, therefore the aforesaid restriction ought to be made, which is evident. For this man would unlawfully, and with no just cause demanding it, take half of the dowries here, although he has not consummated the marriage, nor solemnly led the betrothed to his house. Likewise, the heirs of the girl would suffer a grave loss from that broad interpretation. Likewise, prejudice is done to the ius commune, since upon the dissolution of the marriage the dowry ought to return to the woman, as in c. 1 de do. post diuor. resti., with many similar texts; and on this ground alone the narrower understanding ought to be adapted to the statute, since every departure from the ius commune is odious and therefore to be restricted, as in c. 1 and 2 de fil. presb. lib. 6 and the said c. cum dilectus. To the same effect is the notable statement of Inn. in c. cum dilecti, de do., where he says that privileges, insofar as they touch the rights of those granting them, we interpret broadly, as there in c. olim, de uerb. sig. and l. fi. de consti. prin.; but insofar as they touch the rights of others, strictly, as in c. ex tuarum, de autho. & usu. pal. And the same Io. An. in the said c. olim; and I adduce the text in l. 2 § si quis a principe, ff. ne quod in loco publ. Therefore this statute, since it is of such kind, even if it is privileged, ought to be understood strictly to the prejudice of the girl's heirs; and especially if we consider the cause, this statute will be judged exceedingly odious without cause according to that vague understanding with respect to the disparity between the betrothed man and the betrothed woman, or husband and wife. Since when the man dies first, especially before the leading home and the consummation of the marriage, the woman obtains no gain; nor did the man bear any burdens of the marriage, entirely contrary to the mind of l. fi. C. de do. ante nup. and c. fi. de do. inter uirum & uxo. Secondly and principally, what moves me to this opinion is the intention of the statute, which is gathered in many ways. First, from its very beginning, when it says: "shall have died without children," etc., which are referred to those words, "at the time of her death shall have died without children." Which is clear of itself, and from the doctrine of Bart. in l. ex facto, ff. de uul. & pup., where he says that a quality added in any sentence is understood according to the tense of the verb to which it is added; for this see the notable gloss in c. statutum, in prin. on the word canonicus, at the end, which ought thus to be understood, de rescrip. lib. 6. From which words, assuredly, the makers of the statute seem to have understood a woman who was in the state and power of producing children at the time of her death. For these words "without children," etc., include in themselves the privation of children, and include in themselves the capacity and power of the act, or the state of having children. And this is notably proved at the end in l. 1, ff. de suis & legi., where see Bar. on the word intestatus. But in our case this woman at the time of her death was not in such a state and power, since she had not yet been led into the house of the husband. Therefore it is most clearly evident that those words of the statute are not verified in her, especially since it was not through her that she was not led home, ar. c. sicut ex litteris, de sposa. It must also be observed that in all the additions made to that statute concerning the mention of children, the intention of the statute-maker is evidently presumed from conjectures, l. licet, ff. de leg. 1. Thirdly, I principally weigh those words: "By the man to whom she was married," etc. For properly, according to common usage of speech, he who contracted betrothal by words of present consent, before he leads the woman to his house, is not called the husband of that woman, except by the custom of certain places, as is proved in c. genuit, 27 q. 2, where Jerome says: "When you hear Joseph called the husband of Mary, let not the suspicion of nuptials, that is, of carnal union, steal upon you, but remember the custom of the scriptures, that betrothed men are called husbands, and betrothed women wives"; and below he clearly holds, where Jerome also says, that one contracting by words of present consent, just as the Blessed Virgin contracted with Joseph, is properly called a betrothed man rather than a husband, since she has not yet been led home; but Joseph was called husband on account of the custom of the scriptures; for this see that c. sicut ex litteris, and c. ult. de spon., where they are called sponsalia de praesenti. And by the fact that before the leading home one may enter religion against the will of the other and dissolve the marriage, as I said above. Therefore he cannot strictly be called her husband, namely in the proper meaning. That, however, is true in the circumstances; and this word "husband" and "wife" are often used for one who has consummated marriage, and especially by the common custom of our time; therefore this meaning ought to be taken restrictively in our mind through those things which I said above, and by reg. odia restringi, de reg. iu. lib. 6.

† And because statutes ought to be reduced to the ius commune as far as can be done, as is proved in c. cum dilectus, de consue. and l. 2, C. de noxa., as noted by Inn. in c. causam, quae, de rescr. and Bar. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu. Likewise, the statute says "nupta" (married woman), and I have spoken most fully about this word above in the beginning. Likewise, it says "with the husband" (apud maritum), etc. But in many places and writings he is called "sponsus" before he leads her home, and not "maritus", as fully alleged above and in the said c. genuit, and especially attentive to the custom of this city and of almost all places in which I have been, according to which he is called "sponsus" even on that day on which he solemnly led her into the house, until he should consummate the marriage. And common usage of speech must be observed even in statutes, because in any disposition common usage of speech is preferred to the proper signification of the word, even in a restrictable matter, as noted by Io. An. in c. fundamenta, de elec. lib. 6, and Bart. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iur., Innocent in c. olim, de uerb. sig., and the gloss in c. nonnulli, de rescrip. I do not allege the laws proving this, because they are copiously alleged in the said places. Lastly, I adduce a beautiful motive which I derive from the statements of Petrus and Cynus, principally on l. non dubium, C. de legi., and what Baldus notes there supports it, and in l. scire, ff. de excusatio tutor. and in l. si quis seruo, C. de furt. & ser. corrup. and by Dyn. in reg. fin. de regu. iur. lib. 6. Which motive is as follows: We ought not only to depart from the words of the law and preserve the intention where the intention is expressed, but also where the intention or reason is not expressed in the law, provided that that pre-defined reason is natural, and can naturally and commonly be proved by analogy, by which reason, even if the law were contrary, the contrary could be imagined; and it can be notably proved by l. scire oportet § sufficit, ff. de excu. tut., where the text says there, "from natural justice itself," etc. To the same effect is l. mulier, joined with the gloss, ff. solu. matrimo., where the intention is conjectured against its words. To the same effect, de uerbo. significa. chapter intelligentia, and 1 quaestio 1 chapter Marchion, and l. scire leges, ff. de legib.

† For Baldus also notably says: just as man consists not only of soul, but also of body, so the law consists of intention or reason, and words; and the words are as the body and the surface, while the reason is as the spirit and the soul; and this ought rather to be restricted than the surface of the words, as in the said l. scire, with similar texts. Moreover, to conjecture the reason of the law where it is not expressed, we ought to conjecture for what purpose a wise man would have acted, or by what reason he would have been moved, since the legislator is presumed to be such. For the law ought to be reasonable, distinctio 4, cap. erit autem; and to the jurist and the judge has been given the power of interpreting the law, l. una, C. de profe. qui in ciuita. Constan. lib. 12, as noted by Innocent in cap. cum speciali, de appella. But certainly in our case it cannot be presumed that the cause of the gain was the marital affection, or the remnants of the betrothal by present consent: because by the same reasoning it would have extended a similar gain to the woman, since husband and wife ought not in these matters to be judged unequally, capit. gaudemus, de diuor., and better as to the matter proposed in c. fi. de do. post diuor. resti. and l. ult. § penulti. C. de dona. ante nup. Nor can we conjecture that the reason was that the husband is the head of the woman. For this reason does not suffice, as appears in the said cap. fin., and what the gloss notes in l. deo nobis, C. de episco. & cler. and clem. nullam. Therefore, what other good and efficacious reason can we conjecture for this diversity between husband and wife, unless because the husband, in leading her to his house and in sustaining the burdens of marriage, incurs many expenses? For he expends almost the entire dowry on adornments and the feast, so that if he wished to sell those adornments, he would not find half of what he expended. Likewise, the expenses incurred in an extraordinary banquet, as by analogy, the husband in no way recovers. Lest the husband remain burdened with expenses, the statute wished to provide for him in the gain of half of the dowries; so by analogy the law provided in the restitution of dowry in l. alia, ff. solut. matrimo. In the wife, however, these reasons cease; deservedly, the statute did not confer a gain upon her. Since therefore this and no other is the reasonable and sufficient reason of the statute, it ought not to have place in our case, where the reason of the law ceases. And although perhaps he had incurred some expenses, he nevertheless did not incur those excessive ones that are accustomed to be made in a solemn leading home. For small matters are not to be cared for, l. scio, ff. de in integ. restitu. and chapter 1, eodem titu. For the bride also incurs some expenses among kinsmen, and at least to honor herself for the first time, in which nonetheless the statute does not appear to have had consideration. From these things it is most clearly inferred for the decision of this case that the said husband gains nothing by virtue of the said statute. It remains now to answer the first and last motive, because to the others the answer is sufficiently evident from what has been said. And first to l. cum fuerit: for I say, as I said above, that the word "nuptials" is sometimes verified in a marriage contracted by consent alone, but sometimes not, as I have fully proved above. For in the said l. cum fuerit it suffices to contract by consent alone for this reason: because there we are in wills, in which a broad interpretation is made, as in chapter cum dilecti, de donatio.; deservedly that broad sense is taken. But in our case we are in a strict matter; deservedly the other, stricter understanding ought to be taken. Nor is this unusual, that the same word is taken one way in a broad matter and another way in a strict matter; indeed it is expressly proved that this can and ought to be done, in capit. cum dilectus, de consuetu. and in chapter statutum, joined with what is noted there by Ioan. And., de elec. lib. 6; what Bart. notes in l. 4 § ait praetor, ff. de damn. infect. supports this; and we use this daily. Likewise in the said l. cum fuerit the intention of the legislators was satisfied, as I said above. It remains to answer l. Deo nobis, C. de episco. & cleri., to which I reply simply: First, that it is in no way gathered there that the marriage was not consummated, nor does it avail that after consummation one can enter with the consent of the other, as in chapter cum sis, and chapter uxoratus, and chapter ad apostolicam, de conuer. coniug., and that law can be understood in such a case. Secondly, I reply, and more subtly, that there the pact of gain was common to the husband and the wife, as there in the text and gloss; to such an extent that if there were any disparity, it is reduced by disposition of law to parity, as there according to the understanding of the gloss; in which case it cannot be said that the gain is conferred there on account of expenses or the burdens of marriage, because it would not claim its place in the woman according to the aforesaid, if by that parity a burden is necessarily understood, but that that gain yields on account of marital affection, which affection arises from the sole essence of marriage, de conuer. coniu. chapter ex publico, de uo. eodem titulo lib. 6; therefore it claimed its place even before the leading home and the consummation of the marriage, especially since each can be in gain and loss there, and thus the same disposition of law applies. So it is in our case: because the reason of the statute ceases, the disposition of the statute ought to cease, by commonly known laws. See the good gloss on a similar point in the replication of fraud, which is sometimes granted and sometimes denied, the same reason always remaining, as noted in chapter dilecte, de excep. To l. non sine, C. de bon. quae libe., I say that it does not stand in the way, because it speaks in a favorable disposition, but it is otherwise in an odious one, as commonly noted there, and especially by Baldus, who seems to contradict what he thought in the said l. Deo nobis. And assuredly, all bias ceasing, I deem this opinion to be most true. Nor ought the opinion of perhaps some single jurists move the judge to the contrary, because either in their terms all the aforesaid points do not concur, or, as evidently refuted by the aforesaid points, it is not to be followed, since it is sometimes evidently false or can be overcome by probable arguments, as a good judge of the sharpest intellect will assess according to de feriis c. capellanus, alleging to this the text noted in l. 1 § sed neque ex multitudine, C. de uete. iur. enu. And let these things suffice. Summary of the following consilium: While a matter of dispute was pending between a certain Master Giovanni on the one side and a certain Guglielmo de Castellione on the other side on the occasion of a loan, at the urging of the podestà of the said place they finally submitted to arbitration before a certain Gaspare as arbitrator and amicable compounder. Gaspare immediately in the palace of the podestà, where the submission was made, having heard the petitions of the said Master Giovanni, the plaintiff, and the answer of the said Guglielmo, and certain of their proofs, promulgated an award and arbitral judgment condemning the said Guglielmo to pay the said Master Giovanni 15 florins, but on the other matters acquitted him from the claim of the said Master Giovanni. Master Giovanni immediately, before leaving the palace, approved the said award. After the expiration of the office of the said Lord Podestà, Master Giovanni lodged a complaint, seeking that the arbitration be reduced to the equity of a good man, saying that he had suffered an enormous injury, since he ought to have had a far greater sum from the said Guglielmo. He also said that that approval and confirmation of the award did not bar him, because he had made it under the intimidation of the lord podestà, who enjoined upon him that he should by no means leave the palace unless he approved the said award, because the podestà was formidable against those resisting him. The said Guglielmo, having been thus summoned, answered that the entire award was iniquitous and unjust, since he was bound in nothing to the said Master Giovanni; whence it was evident that the entire award should be annulled and cancelled, etc. Finally they came to proof: on behalf of Master Giovanni's side two witnesses were produced concerning the loan, and two after the deadline, who nevertheless took an oath within the time given for proving. The first two deposed concerning a confession of the said loan made by the said Guglielmo; they were, however, singular in their depositions, since they deposed about different confessions. The other two witnesses seemed sufficiently to prove the order of the podestà made to the said Master Giovanni in the aforesaid manner. On behalf of Guglielmo, however, some witnesses were produced, who were also singular in their statements, deposing concerning the confession of the said Giovanni that he had received many and certain quantities of money in repayment from the said Guglielmo, etc. It was asked what the duties of the judge were in this case.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The petition for reduction to the arbitrament of a good man is as it were a kind of appeal.
2. One seeking reduction on the grounds of iniquity must prove the iniquity itself.
3. The judge ad quem, if upon inspecting the old or new records he does not see that the sentence is justified, ought to retract it.
body: Having invoked the names of Christ and of his Mother, I have advised that the judge ought to retract and annul the entire award and arbitrament, and declare that the said Guglielmo is bound in nothing to the said dominus Giovanni, and impose silence upon him, and absolve the said Guglielmo from the suit of the former, and condemn him in the expenses incurred in this cause. And although in this matter a bare counsel ought to have sufficed, since it was sought by the judge, and thus it was decisive, and not by the parties—just as is observed in rendering a sentence according to the counsel of a doctor, in capitu. sicut, de iud., by Ioan. And. in additio. in titu. de senten. prola. §. qualiter, versi. cæterum, and note what the advisers [state]—nevertheless, lest perhaps out of the bareness of the counsel the mind of anyone might be weighed down into scandal, I have briefly inserted some points moving my mind to this judgment; and for an evidential basis I premise several things.

† First, that the petition for reduction to the arbitrament of a good man is as it were a kind of appeal, l. 1. C. de arbitr., with the notes there; nevertheless it removes the presumption of the award, as noted in a similar case regarding an appeal from excommunication, which, although it does not suspend the excommunication, as in capitu. pastoralis, de appella., nevertheless suspends the presumption of justice and of process, and devolves the cause to the superior, as noted by Innocen. in capitu. bonæ, il 1. de electio., and in capitu. quoniam contra, de proba.; what the gl. notes in capitu. ad reprimendam, de offic. ord., supports this. Likewise I also premise,

† that one seeking reduction on the grounds of iniquity must prove the iniquity itself and the grievance; which iniquity or grievance he can prove either from the old records or from new ones, according to, however, the distinction of Barto. in l. si societatem. §. arbitrorum, ff. pro socio, and more perfectly in consi. 275, and in Specu. de arbit. §. ultim. versi. sed nunquid, and see Ioan. And. in addi. Specu. eodem titul. §. præallega. versi. item quid si compromissum, and by Anto. But. in capitu. Quintavallis, de iureiurand. It is not, however, because from this there is a strong presumption in favor of the arbitrator’s statement, according to what is noted in capitu. post cessionem, de proba., but because this is the intent of the plaintiff seeking to have the award rescinded. Thirdly, I premise that although an appellee who approved the sentence cannot on his own behalf seek the confirmation of the sentence, de re. iud. cap. quod ad consultationem, nevertheless if the appellant insists against the sentence, the appellee can ask that something be added to or subtracted from that sentence, and that it be formed thus or otherwise, because the appeal, although interposed by only one party, suspends the whole sentence, l. 1. ff. ad Turpil., and cap. venientes, de iureiurand., with similar texts; whence on the basis of the other's person the appellee obtains what he could not obtain on his own behalf; and a similar point is found in c. autho. Martini, de concef. pręben. lib. 6., and in l. petendę, C. de tempo. in integ. restitu. Cap. Raynutius and ca. Raynaldus, de testam., and l. omnem honorem, C. quando prouo. non est neces. support the aforesaid. And the lords of the Rota hold this notable conclusion, decisi. 358, and they say it was thus obtained in the Curia. Anto. de But. follows in c. cum Ioannes, in fi. de fide instrumen. And this is supported by the fact that the judge of the appeal succeeds to the place of the judge a quo, and thus he ought to do all that which the judge a quo could and ought to do; a good text in ca. cum causa, de sen. & re. iu. Fourthly, I premise,

† that if the judge ad quem, having inspected the old records or the new ones, does not see that the sentence is justified, he ought to retract it, in c. cum ad sedem, de rest. spo., noted by the doctors in c. in pręsentia, de renun., and noted in l. per hanc, C. de temp. app. These things having been premised, I infer for the decision of the present matter: since from the matters now argued in this judgment of reclamation it clearly appeared that the said dominus Giovanni did not have full proof regarding the loan, as the witnesses were singular, to whom credit is not given, as in capitul. cum dilecti, de elect., and c. licet, de proba., especially considering the proofs of the other party, it is inferred that the said arbiter or arbitrator unjustly and iniquitously condemned the said Guglielmo to 15 florins. Therefore, the judge of the challenge, who succeeds to the place of the arbiter or arbitrator, ought wholly to absolve the said Guglielmo from the claim of that plaintiff, just as that arbiter ought to have done from the beginning. To this effect is what is noted in the said §. arbitrorum and the said cap. cum ad sedem; what Barto. notes in l. 1. ff. de leg. 3. and Innocen. in cap. statutum, de rescrip. lib. 6. (and formerly it began præsenti) supports this, where they singularly state that an appeal cannot be made from this judge of reclamation, just as neither from a good man, since he succeeds to his place. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that this Guglielmo approved the rendered award; because he is seen to have approved it to the extent that the other party wished to approve and admit his approval; as the gloss notes in a similar case in cap. 3. de eo, qui mit. in poss., and as I have said above regarding an appellee, who obtains from the person of the other what he cannot obtain from his own person. Likewise, it supports this that the parties undertook a dispute concerning the injustice and iniquity of the entire award, and it was established by that very fact, which made it clear that no right pertained to the aforesaid Giovanni; therefore the judge ought to retract the entire award; just as Innocent notes and states in a similar case in capitu. cum dilecti, de elect., and capitu. cum Bertoldus, de re iud., where he intends the same in a sentence that has passed into res judicata. It can also be said that that deposition of witnesses made outside the term given for proving was invalid, since within the term he did not apply any diligence so that the witnesses might be examined. And Barto. notably says this, refuting But. in the said l. damni. §. Sabini, ff. de dam. infect., and what the lords of the Rota note in decisi. 7 supports it, and so I held writing on cap. licet, de proba., where I pursue this more fully; and let these things suffice, as I said before, and let this be a decisive counsel, and thus quasi-sentence, etc. Praise be to Almighty God.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Wherever the common utility of clerics is concerned, the burden ought to be common to both.
2. The goods of churches are assigned to public spiritual use.
body: The case upon which counsel is sought is as follows. A certain powerful lord, at the petition of certain subjects of his, decreed to build, or have constructed and cause to be built, walls in a certain village situated within his territory for the protection of the men dwelling therein, or wishing to dwell there, so that they may live there more safely on account of hostile incursions. However, since a certain solemn monastery possesses there certain properties and houses, which are cultivated and inhabited by the men of the said village, the lord urges, especially at the demand of the inhabitants in the said village, that the monastery ought to contribute pro rata to the expenses to be incurred in the building of the said walls. The monastery resists, alleging ecclesiastical immunity granted by divine and human law. It is asked, what is the law? Having first implored divine aid, whose honor is at stake, it seems at first that the said monastery is bound pro rata.

† For wherever the common utility of clerics and laics is concerned, the burden ought to be common to both; to this effect is the text in c. pervenit, de immuni. ecclesia., where men of the church undergo watch-duties of the walls against enemies just like the laics, so that with all watching, the custody of the city may better be managed, as the text says in the said c. pervenit. If therefore they are bound to personal burdens when common utility is present, all the more so to real burdens, since clerics are more easily excused from personal than from real burdens, because in the former they are drawn away from divine offices; arg. 33. quaestio. 8. c. reprehensibile, and in l. placet, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi. Secondly, there is notably adduced l. ad instructiones, C. eodem titul., where the text says that even venerable houses or churches are held to the construction of roads or bridges; by parity of reason they ought to be held to the building of walls, since public utility and piety are involved on both sides. Therefore the poor dwelling there; which certain authors held, as Cyn. reports there. Thirdly, l. ad portus, C. de ope. publi. supports this, where express provision is made regarding the building and repairing of walls; and it is added that no one is to be excused by privilege of dignity. Fourthly, the reason is given: it is certain that the goods of churches are exposed to piety, yet the common piety of the poor; whence for feeding its poor, defending them from oppressions, and redeeming captives, even the ownership of the ecclesiastical property itself can be laid open and alienated, as in c. aurum, and in c. sacrorum, 12. quaestio. 2., and there on this in summa. But in our case, the matter concerns rescuing and relieving the poor living there so that they are not taken captive. Therefore churches ought not to be immune from the oppressions of tyrants and enemies, and so that they are not taken captive. Therefore churches ought not to be immune from other assessments. And this opinion was held by certain moderns in c. non minus, de immu. eccle., after the gloss, and there Hostien., who seems to follow the gloss there; which nevertheless does not speak expressly of the building of walls. Hostien. himself, however, clearly held the contrary in summa, as I will subjoin among the points that I first advance. But notwithstanding these, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer, which I shall prove by several reasons and by the authorities of the foremost doctors. And first I advance c. non minus, cited above, where the construction of ditches is treated, which indeed concerns the defense of the city and the public utility of clerics as much as of laics; and nevertheless it is decided that no contribution ought to be exacted from clerics; rather it is prohibited under pain of anathema, unless the bishop has examined both the necessity and the utility, and without any coercion deems that subsidies should be offered through the churches to relieve the common utilities or necessities, where the resources of the laics do not suffice. And weigh that word, 'common utilities,' etc., joined with c. adversus, eodem titulo. From which it is clear that even when the common utility of clerics and laics is pressing, clerics are not bound to confer anything unless they wish to do so voluntarily, with the approval of the bishop and clergy, and where the resources of the laics do not suffice; and today, by c. adversus, cited above, clerics cannot in the aforesaid case pay voluntarily without consulting the Roman Pontiff. And that was decreed on account of the imprudence of certain persons, who often alleged such necessity or utility. Secondly, to the same effect is adduced the notable text in Auth. Item nulla communitas, C. de episcop. & cleric., where it is generally prohibited that anyone dare to exact from churches collections, taxes, angariae, or perangariae; all of which are exacted on account of public utility for the defense of the commonwealth, in which the utility of laics and clerics is included. To the same effect also c. 1, de immu. ecclesi., in VI°, and c. quamquam poena, eodem titu., and Clem. praesenti, eodem titu., and c. fin., de vita & honesta. cle., and l. placet, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi., l. 2, C. de episco. & cler., 16. q. 1. c. generaliter, with countless similar texts, which exempt churches and their goods from all collections, gabelle, exactions, and the like. It is proved, fourthly, by this reason:

† the goods of churches are dedicated to public spiritual use; 12. quaestio. 1. c. videntes; 16. quaestio. 1. c. quoniam, de praebend. c. ratio, and the said l. placet. This is stated by the text in c. nulli liceat, 12. quaestio. fin., that everything that is consecrated to the church, whether it was an animal or a field, is made the holy of holies and pertains to the right of the priests. Therefore they ought not to serve a worldly and public use, because what is once dedicated to God ought no longer to be transferred to human uses, as in the rule, semel Deo dicatum, de regu. iur., in VI°. For public law also consists in priests; 1. distinct. c. ius publicum. Since, therefore, laics are worldly and principally derive utility from the worldly commonwealth, they ought to undergo the burdens of the worldly commonwealth; but the goods of churches, which belong to God, ought to serve the spiritual commonwealth. We see something similar in persons: for secular soldiers war for the world, but heavenly soldiers war for God; and thus the former in temporal affairs, the latter in spiritual affairs, as in c. reprehensibile, and c. quo casu, 23. quaestio. ultim. Rightly, therefore, did the text state in the said c. non minus that as long as the resources of the laics suffice, even voluntarily the church ought not to give anything, lest goods be withdrawn from spiritual use. Hence the notable text in Clem. quia contingit, de religio. domi., says that things assigned to a certain use by the bounty of the faithful ought not to be assigned to another use, the authority of the Roman Pontiff alone excepted. Hence the text in the said c. non minus says that these public burdens are of the laics, as is clear there: 'These, however, their public burdens,' etc., although in what follows they treat of common necessity or utility. But it said they belong to the laics because they fall upon them for the reasons aforesaid, although some also wrongly understand that text through that word, 'their,' etc., as speaking solely of the necessity of the laics; which certainly is not true, and because it did not subsequently repeat about the laics, but says concerning common burdens; and it says the same in the said c. adversus, and especially de propria, where it says that it is in their interest to provide for common utilities. It therefore understands this of the utility of clerics and laics. This opinion is also proved by the common theory of the doctors of both laws, concerning which see the canonists in c. fin., de vi. & ho. cle., and in c. 1, de immu. eccle., in VI°, in Clem. praesenti, de censi., by Ioan. de Lig., by Barto. in l. rescripto, ff. de mune. & hono., in l. placet, C. de sacro. san. ecclesi., and in similar places. For they say that the goods of churches are not held to any worldly burdens unless they had first been made tributary or subject to census before coming to the church, so that they had paid a certain tribute or census. Otherwise, however, they are not held, even though the prior possessors had previously paid certain collections or levies in time of necessity or utility; to this effect are many laws cited above. This opinion, precisely with respect to our case, namely in the repair of walls, is held by the subtle glossator in the Decretum, 16. quaestio. 1. c. generaliter, § novarum, where the gloss expressly says this through the said l. ad instructiones. Most clearly of the same view was that mirror of canon law, Io. An., in the said c. non minus, upon the gloss, where he says that clerics are not held, because by no law of the Digest, nor of the Code, nor by any statutory authority could the immunity of churches be restricted. This same opinion was followed by the most renowned glossator of civil law on the said l. ad instructiones, where he affirmed that churches are not held to the repair or construction of walls. Barto. there, the illuminator of civil law, says the same, stating that the said l. ad instructiones is partly corrected by the Auth. Item nulla communitas, cited above. He distinguishes real burdens from those that are imposed on persons on account of things by reason of property, such that churches are held to the former, but not to the latter. Whence, for the repair of bridges and walls, burdens are imposed on persons on account of things. For by no law is it provided that possessions are obligated to these burdens. Why say more? Hostien. himself seems to have corrected his opinion that he held in c. non minus, most recently in his Summa, tit. de immunita. ecclesi., § a quibus, versic. ad extraordinaria, where he says that today churches are immune from all those burdens concerning either public or private utility through the said Auth. Item nulla communitas, with similar texts. And thus that today the provision of the said l. ad instructiones does not proceed entirely; and thus he coincides with the opinion of Bartol. Many other ancient doctors have also followed this opinion, whom I do not dwell upon, since on behalf of this opinion we have the illuminators of the law, such as the glossators of both laws, and Ioan. Andr., and Hostien., and Bartol. Who, therefore, would dare to advise the opposite, especially against religion, since it is no small reason that makes for religion; l. sunt personae, ff. de religi. & sumpt. fune.? And indeed, if anyone weighs the gloss on the said c. non minus, it does not support the opinion adduced in the beginning; rather, it seems to hold the opposite. For that gloss is placed there upon an excepted case, when the bishop and clergy have inspected the common necessity or utility and the resources of the laics do not suffice; and then, without any coercion, they may give bountifully. Whence the gloss there intended rather to provide an example of common utility or necessity than to establish an excepted case from the disposition of that chapter. And this is clear enough when it says, 'for they ought to contribute,' etc. And thus, through the word 'for' (enim), it connects itself to the text. For if it had intended to establish an excepted case, it would have said, 'yet they ought to contribute' (conferre tamen debet), or would have spoken through similar words. And whatever it meant, this opinion recited above is sufficiently supported by laws, reasons, and authorities. Wherefore I conclude that the said monastery ought not to be held to undergo these burdens, unless the disposition of that c. non minus were observed, namely with the Roman Pontiff having first been consulted, as is stated in the said c. adversus. And this was observed on another occasion when a commission was made to that excellent doctor of both laws, dominus Anto. de Rosellis, and to me by the powerful lords priors of the commune of Siena, specifically in a question of fact that was pending with the magnificent and most devout monastery of Santa Maria of Monte Oliveto, and the clause, although by bare word and succinctly we made our report at that time. The contrary arguments formulated above do not stand in the way of this conclusion. And first, I reply to c. pervenit: for it has various interpretations. First, indeed, it is understood in lands subject in temporalities to the church. Secondly, it is understood according to those times in which that city of Troyes was oppressed by infidels, and a sudden and unforeseen fear was threatening, as Innocen. notes there. Item, it is also understood not of clerics, who are not to be withdrawn from divine services (23. quaestione. 8. c. reprehensibile), but of the men of the church, who otherwise enjoy the said immunity (l. 2, C. de episco. & cleric., 12. quaestio. 2. c. ecclesiarum servos), unless there were most urgent necessity, as Hostien. notes in summa, eodem titul., in the said § a quibus, versicu. vere etiam personalia. Item, fourthly, it does not speak of fruits and goods to be alienated, but of a certain custody for the necessary defense of the city, which is not pressing in our case. Item, assuming that there were such great necessity, the tenor of c. non minus and c. adversus ought to be observed, since there is no danger in consulting the Roman Pontiff. To l. ad instructiones cited, sufficient answer has been made above. And l. portus does not stand in the way, because it does not speak of the church, as the gloss clearly intended on the said l. ad instructiones. Item, that law, according to one solution given there in the gloss, can be adduced in favor of this opinion of ours, since it says that graduates, on account of the public good that they foster, are privileged from those burdens; by stronger reason churches ought to be exempt on account of the spiritual public good, and through the other reasons cited above. To the fourth motive, I reply that those points proceed for redeeming captives or feeding the poor, in which cases the church distributes its own goods; it is otherwise in this case, where no utility reaches the church, and the lord of the castle will receive the whole benefit. For he who feels the benefit ought also to feel the burden, as in the rule, qui sentit, de regu. iur., in VI°. Item, necessary expenditures ought not to be withdrawn from divine worship, and from the poor, and from other religious persons, to be expended on a cause not so necessary, and where piety is not so directly favored; and if necessity is strongly pretended, let that be observed which is contained in c. non minus and c. adversus. For I see that churches are not bound to assist temporal lords, except insofar as they wish; and thus let divine worship be altered in nothing, as in the said l. placet, and Auth. Item nulla communitas; all the more is it not held to contribute to the building of walls. I extend myself no further, since the favor of religion, supported by the authority of so many most renowned men, seems abundantly sufficient in this matter, to the praise of the undivided Trinity, amen.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Coerced will in misdeeds does not excuse from sin.
2. Whether a community excommunicated through fear incurs the penalty of excommunication.
3. Pope Marcellinus was deposed because he sacrificed to idols, although coerced by fear of the Gentiles.
4. Fear excuses a woman more than a man.
body: The contingent fact is as follows. A certain woman, having been accused of adultery by her husband in order to gain her dowry and effect a divorce with respect to bed; the woman, having been known by another as pregnant, alleges that violence was inflicted upon her by a certain man in magistracy in a place of abstinence, and she proves it by sufficient conjectures. It is asked whether on this account she ought to escape the penalty of the law? And it seems first that she should not;

† because a coerced will in misdeeds does not excuse from sin, nor in turn from the penalty of sin. 2. q. 1. capitu. in primis. 23. quæstio. 6. capitu. item ne. where it is said that one ought rather to suffer all evils than consent to evil. The reason for this statement is that conditional force does not take away consent. capitu. maiores, de baptis. & capitu. merito. 15. quæstio. 1. & l. si mulier, ff. quod met. caus. Secondly, this is proved by analogy in capitu. in sacris, quod met. cau.

† where a community, having communicated under fear, incurs the penalty of excommunication just as he who communicates voluntarily. The reason is given there: because although fear mitigates fault, it nevertheless does not entirely exclude it. Thirdly is adduced capitu. nunc autem. 22. dist.

† where it is evident that Pope Marcellinus was deposed because he offered incense to idols, although he had done so induced by fear of the Gentiles. Therefore, since this woman about whom inquiry is made prostrated herself to the lust of another, and thus violated her husband's bed, she ought not to escape punishment on account of fear, by virtue of the laws alleged above and many others that are omitted for the sake of brevity. But these notwithstanding, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer in law, moved by the below-written reasons and by the authorities of many. For either this woman suffered absolute violence; and in case of doubt it must be said that she ought not to suffer punishment; nay rather, she did not even contract any stain of sin; indeed she merits from the chastity of her heart, unless the contrary is proved. 22. quæstio. 5. capitu. 1. & 2. & in said capitu. in sacris, the violence or fear was conditional. And therefore, although she contracted some sin and is worthy of penance because there was present at least some sort of consent, nevertheless she ought not to suffer the penalty of adultery; and thus she ought not to be deprived of her dowry and of the cohabitation of her husband, since this is a penalty of adultery. This is expressly proved in l. uim passam, and in l. uxor. §. si quis planè, ff. de adult. & l. fidelissima, C. eod. titul. & l. 1. §. remoueri, ff. de posthum. And the reason is that adultery with respect to the law is not committed without dolus, although some fault was present or intervened, as is noted and proved in l. penult. ff. de adult. the text joined with gloss. fina. 34. quæsti. 2. c. in lectum, & 15. quæstione 1. capitu. inebriarunt. And the laws proceed even in conditional fear, as the gloss most clearly intended or holds in two places, 32. quæstio. 5. capitu. proposito, otherwise beginning Lucretiam. In support of this: because dolus is craftiness or machination to deceive, etc., l. 1. ff. de dolo, which things also cease when fear intervenes, even if conditional. And it must be noted,

† that dread or fear excuses a woman more than a man, on account of her imbecility, as the notable gloss says in capitul. cum locum, de sponsa. For it is considered that not only fear inflicted by that man must excuse the woman from the penalty of adultery, but also shame and a certain modesty, which the woman feared to incur by crying out, since she was seen, but especially at nighttime, since she could particularly be killed by the man. The reason is that there dolus ceases, which is required to incur the penalty of adultery, as I have said above. This is very notably proved in capitu. proposito. §. Lucretiam, previously alleged, joined with the gloss, cum ueritas facti contingat. For that Lucretia, noble and modest in the city of Rome, in order to avoid this ignominy and disgrace exposed herself to the lust of the son of King Tarquin; nor was she judged an adulteress by Augustine, a most holy and learned man; rather, she was commended for chastity of mind, as the gloss there understands, and rightly so. Because although toward God she may not have been unstained from adultery by virtue of the laws alleged above in the beginning, nevertheless with respect to the penalty of the law she was excused from adultery, since it is not committed without dolus, as I have said above. I conclude, therefore, this matter: that she ought not to suffer the below-written penalty of adultery. To the laws alleged to the contrary, response could be made in multiple ways. But a single general response suffices for all: by saying that where dolus is required to incur a penalty, culpa does not suffice. l. 1. C. ad legem Cornel. de sica. noted in l. in actionibus, ff. de in lit. iur. & instit. de suspec. tuto. §. suspectus, & l. quod Nerua, ff. de posi. Moreover, to incur the penalty of adultery, dolus is required; which is excluded through fear, as has been most fully proved above. And so Bartolus seems to confirm in l. quod Nerua, previously alleged; and also with respect to a pecuniary penalty, gross fault is not equated with dolus where the law expressly requires dolus; and the notable gloss says the same in l. magna negligentia, ff. de uerborum signifi. And although action is not brought here criminally toward the penalty of adultery, nevertheless since action is brought toward a penalty, that culpa without dolus does not suffice, especially since action is brought here toward a severe penalty, namely that she lose her patrimony. For the dowry of women is deemed patrimony, l. 4. ff. de mino., and that she be separated from her husband, and thus be deprived of the right of seeking the conjugal debt and passively of the support of maintenance, and how grave this is, anyone can discern. And let these things suffice, etc.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One cannot pay rent for one's own property.
2. Although a contract does not appear usurious from its form, it is nevertheless judged usurious on account of the intention of the contracting parties.
3. One who sells a thing for more than it is worth is deemed usurious.
casus: Sempronius leased a certain house of his to Titius for a term of eight years, a rent of six florins having been fixed. In the year immediately following the said lease, he sold the said house to Titius the lessee for the price of one hundred gold florins; which price indeed he confessed to have received from the said Titius the buyer, not under hope of future counting [of the money], and he renounced the exception of uncounted money (exceptio non numeratæ pecuniæ). After this, the said Titius the buyer, notwithstanding the aforesaid confession regarding the receipt of the price made by Sempronius, [acknowledged himself debtor] and payer [?] to the said Sempronius the seller in the amount of the said one hundred gold florins for the price of the said house, which one hundred gold florins the said Titius promises to give and pay at the term of eight years, and meanwhile promised each year six gold florins under the name of rent according to the pact of the aforesaid lease, with the pact that if the said Titius should offer any part of the said one hundred florins to the said Sempronius, Sempronius himself ought to receive that part and reduce proportionally the rent of the said six florins. It happened that within the term of eight years no part of the said one hundred florins was paid to the said Sempronius by the said Titius; but he paid him six florins [each year]. When the said term of eight years had elapsed, Sempronius brings an action against Titius for the payment and recovery of the said one hundred florins. Titius himself alleges and says that he has already paid 48 florins, and offers himself ready to pay 52 florins for the remainder of the said sum, saying, namely, that he bought the house, as is evident from the instrument of purchase, and therefore was not bound to pay rent, and that what he paid was for usury on the aforesaid one hundred florins, and that it was stated in fraud of usury that he should pay under the name of rent, and thus what was paid ought to be computed toward the true principal of the said one hundred florins. Sempronius replies that although he sold the house and confessed to have received [the price], nevertheless in truth he received no price, which ought to be inferred from the confession and obligation made immediately afterward by Titius the buyer, and thus, the price not having been paid, ownership of the said house was not transferred to the buyer; therefore, rent is owed to him until he should pay the whole price of the said house, and thus the said 48 florins paid under the name of rent ought not to affect [?] the said price of 100 florins, and thus the price of the house must be paid in full. It is asked what the law is, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.
body: Having invoked the names of Christ and His mother, omitting the arguments that could be rather frivolously made in favor of the said seller, I shall thus reach the substance of the matter itself. For I say, always saving a better judgment, that the said Titius, the buyer, is not bound to pay beyond 52 florins, and thus the 48 florins paid under the name of rent ought to be credited toward the true price of the said house; which I prove in multiple ways. First, thus: namely, by the very fact that the said lessor sold the house to the buyer, the price having been received, or at least credit having been extended for the price; and this was a perfected contract, and the ownership of the house passed to the buyer, and there was a departure from the contract of lease. This is most openly proved in l. si quis, ff. de acquir. possess., and Inst. de rerum diui. §. interdictum, §. uenditæ. And that credit for the price was at least extended to him is most clearly evident from the confession of the seller himself, which, even if it were fictitious, nevertheless sufficiently indicates that he intended to deliver the thing presently by reason of the sale, credit having been extended for obtaining the price in the future, as is also sufficiently inferred from the obligation and confession made afterward by the said Titius, the buyer. Therefore, since the ownership was transferred to the said buyer, and there was a departure from the contract of lease, as has been proved above clearer than day, he could not afresh execute that subsequent confession, and the contract of lease could not be revived, nor could there be a departure from a perfected contract of sale and purchase, the matter no longer being intact, C. quando lic. ab empt. disc. l. 1. & 2. Thirdly, because they were not doing this; on the contrary, they intended the contract of purchase and sale to remain in its firmness, as is clear from the words of the purchase or confession. It is evident therefore from the premises,

† that that payment made under the name of rent was invalid, since no one can pay rent for his own property, as in the said l. qui rem propriam. Whence, even presupposing that no fraud of usury intervened, nevertheless he who paid what was not owed can set it off against the true debt to be paid, l. etiam, ff. de compensa., de fide instrumen. capitu. cum Ioannes, to which add l. cuius per errorem, ff. de regu. iur., and capitu. fina. de solu., with the glosses noted there. Nevertheless, I think that the seller himself can also on another ground credit those 48 florins toward the true price; because if all the transactions are carefully weighed, this rent was established in fraud, and thus it would be usury for the deferred payment of those one hundred florins, concerning which [it is usury] above with respect to the contiguity of the contract. For if he intended to sell immediately, and did sell, and confesses that he received the price, to what purpose was it necessary to premise a contract of lease, since there is no presumption that someone wishes to depart immediately from his prior purpose, l. non ad ea, ff. de condi. & demonstra., and de baptis. capitu. maiores? And from those things that occur immediately, a presumption of fraud arises, in capitu. officii, with the glosses noted there, de electio., and things done immediately seem to be inherent, l. lecta, ff. si certum pet. Secondly, fraud is presumed from the fact that the seller previously confessed to having received the price, not in the hope of future counting, but rather renounced the exception of non-counted money; and yet afterward the buyer confessed that he was a debtor for one hundred florins on the occasion of the price of that house; and from these contradictions there results a presumption of fraud, in capitu. ut nostrum, ut ecclesi. benefic. Thirdly, a presumption arises by reason of the presumption of the payment to be made for rent contrary to the nature of that contract of sale which had preceded. To this, what is read and noted in this case from that appended pact: that if within the time of eight years he should pay any part of the said one hundred florins, a pro-rata reduction of the rent ought to be made. For if the ownership of the house was not transferred to the buyer, as the seller alleges, why would that pro-rata reduction be made, when ownership would still be with the seller? For it cannot be said that ownership passes in part as the price is paid in part, l. traditionibus, C. de pactis. Therefore, it is clearly concluded therefrom that the said rent was established as a fee for the payment of the said one hundred florins, so that, a part of the debt having been discharged, the burden of the rent or fee ought likewise to be discharged. For from all these very abundant conjectures and presumptions, such a contract ought to be judged to have been executed in fraud of usury, according to what is stated and found in capitul. ad nostram, de emptio. & uenditio., and that capitu. uos, de pig. And if you should say, how ought this to be presumed and judged here, since a loan did not intervene, without which usury is not committed, as is evident from the definition of usury? For it is profit from a loan, etc., as is fully noted by Ioan. And. in regu. peccatum, de reg. iur. lib. 6. in Merc., to which adds c. consuluit, de usu.

† I reply that although from its form it does not appear to be a usurious contract, nevertheless on account of the intention of the contracting parties it must be judged usurious. For since that seller was to receive that profit from the deferred payment of the price, the law feigns that the buyer paid the money to the seller, and that the seller loaned it to him, and willed that profit as a fee. Nor let this seem strange, because it is an express case in law on similar terms in c. in ciuitate and in c. nauiganti, de usu.

† Where it is said, according to the common understanding, that that seller must be judged usurious who sells a thing for more than it is worth because he defers the payment of the price; and thus it is not a usurious contract from its form, because a true loan is not made there, but it is feigned in the aforesaid manner on account of the intention of the contracting parties. Therefore, usury is committed, whether it be a true loan or a feigned one in the aforesaid manner; and so it is commonly noted in the previously cited legal authorities. From all of which I conclude that on a twofold ground this buyer can obtain his intention: either because he pays, or because however usury may be understood, it can be deducted in set-off against the price of the one hundred florins, as in the said capitu. illo uos, with the glosses noted there, and capitul. cum contra, de pig., de iureiuran. capitu. debitores, with similar texts. And let these suffice, etc.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The burdens of a community are incumbent upon laymen, and not upon clerics.
2. Gabelles and duties are paid on one's own property [?].
body: The case upon which arguments were requested. A certain Lord Francis, canon of Massa, sold from his patrimonial goods wine, corn, grain, pigs, and similar items, and is said to trade in them; and he has certain animals which he wishes to send to the common pasture lands of Massa without any payment, which the citizens there commonly make for the alleviation of the burdens of the community; nor, even with respect to his patrimonial goods in which he is said to trade, does he wish to be subject to the statutes of the city by paying gabelles, duties, tolls, and the like, excusing himself on two grounds: first, by reason of his clerical status; second, from a certain pact entered into especially between the community itself and the bishop and chapter of the church of Massa, that it should be lawful for the bishop and the chapter, without any payment, to send their animals to graze in the pastures of the community. It happens now that there is doubt on two points. First, whether Lord Francis ought to pay for pasture, to which he frequently sends his own animals to the said lands of the community, according as the other citizens pay according to the form of the statute of the community. To the first point it must be said, that if the pasture lands have been accustomed to belong to, and are of, the corporate community of the laity, then I think the said Lord Francis can be compelled to pay according to the form of the statute and laws of the community, if he wishes to send his animals to those lands of the community. The reason for this is that in this case the community is not said to impose a law upon clerics, nor are they said to levy collections on clerics, or to exact duties or gabelles from them; but they are said to sell the use or the usufruct of the property of the community, which they may do without injury to anyone. For in his own property everyone is the lawful moderator and arbiter, as in l. in re mandata, C. manda. and capitu. de his, de sepultu. For although clerics are found to be privileged so that they do not pay gabelles or duties on their own property, as in capitul. quamquam, de censib. in Sexto, and in clement. praesenti, eod. titu., and as I shall say more broadly in the subsequent argument, they are not found to be privileged so that they may, for themselves and their animals, use the property of the community of laymen. Indeed, on the contrary, by divine law they had no share of the Promised Land under the law, but that was granted by divine disposition solely to the laity, while to clerics were reserved only the tithes and certain other appurtenances, as is found in Numbers 18 and noted in capitu. 1, de deci. in Sexto. If, therefore, they wish to use the property of the community of laymen, they ought to pay, just as if they wished to graze their animals in private places. For a community acts with respect to its own property just as a private person does with respect to his own, on the argument in capitu. licet, de probatio. and capitu. conquestus, de foro competen.; and the clergy is separated from the people, for the clergy is one thing and the people another, said cap. si sententia, de sen. excom. lib. 6 and 12 q. 1 cap. duo sunt genera. Likewise I see,

† that the burdens of the community fall upon the laity and not upon the clerics, as is noted in capitu. non minus, and capitu. adversus, de immuni. ecclesi. Since, therefore, they are unwilling to feel the burdens of the property of the community of the laity, they ought not to feel the advantages. For those who wish to take the profits and advantages and are unwilling to undergo the burdens are not to be tolerated: C. de cadu. tollen. l. 1 § pro secundo, and in regu. qui sentit onus, de regulis iur. in Sexto. And if you should say that clerics are bound to these things, and not to the payment of a gabelle or duties, I answer,

† that gabelles and duties are paid from one's own property; whence, since the persons are exempt, so too is their property, because it follows the condition of the persons, as noted in the said capitu. praesenti, de censi. and capitu. quamquam, eod. titu. in Sexto. Therefore, the laity cannot exact this from non-subject and exempt persons. But in our case they do not pay for the property of the clerics themselves; rather, those who lease property of the community, or buy the use or usufruct from the private person of the community, are justly bound to pay, just as if they were leasing or buying the use or usufruct of a private person; capitu. 1 de in integr. restitu. supports this. If, however, these pasture lands had been for the use of the community of both clerics and laity, and were thus common to clerics and laity, then they would not be bound. Dominus Federicus says that clerics are not bound to pay by statutes of the laity, both because statutes of the laity do not affect clerics, in capitu. bonae quidem, 96 distinct., capitu. ecclesia sanctae Mariae, de constitu.; and because in common property the laity alone cannot enact anything to the prejudice of others having a right in the property, wherefore, what touches all must be approved by all, capitu. quod omnes, de regu. iur. lib. 6 and capitu. ad haec, de offic. archid.; and because in common property the condition of the one prohibiting is stronger, regu. in re communi, de regu. iur. libr. 6 and l. Sabinus, ff. communi dividun., and an equal has no authority over an equal, capitu. innotuit, de electio. The agreement made with the bishop and the church of Massa, that it should be lawful for them to have their animals in the pastures of the territory of Massa, does not stand in the way of the aforesaid, because that was granted to the chapter, not to individual persons of the chapter. It will therefore apply to the episcopal animals, but not to the animals of individual canons; for the chapter is one thing, and the individual members another. An indulgence granted to the chapter, therefore, is not extended to the individual members of the chapter, in capitu. qui manumittitur, 12 quaestio 3, and in capitu. fin. de praeb. lib. 6, and in l. sed et si § qui manumittitur, ff. de in ius vocan. Indeed, that pact rather works against the said Lord Francis, because it tacitly indicates that those places were not common to clerics and laity, but belonged to the laity; and this as to the first doubt. As to the second doubt regarding this matter, I say that on the aforesaid items they are not bound to pay gabelles or duties, because clerics of the church are exempt from these together with all their goods. For they are not bound to pay the laity, to whom they are not subject, nor do they fall under their statutes, as is very clearly proved in the said capitu. quamquam and the said clemen. praesenti, by Specu. de immuni. eccle. in fin. and Feder. de Senis, consi. 200. Nor is it true that by selling wine, corn, oil, and the like from his own goods, he is said to trade, so that cap. fin. de vita & hone. cle. and similar laws to be cited would apply. For he is properly said to trade who buys a thing in order to sell it intact for the sake of profit; not he who buys a thing in order to reduce it to some form, or if he sells wine or corn harvested from his own possessions, as is proved in c. eiiciens, 88 dis., noted by the Doctors on our subject in the said cle. praesenti and the said c. quamquam, and by Fed. in the said consi. 200. I concede, however, that if he bought a thing in order to sell it intact for the sake of profit, he would be bound to pay according to the statutes of the country if, having been warned a third time by the bishop, he does not desist, as is proved in the said c. fin. de vita & hone. cle. But prior to a warning, he is not bound to a toll, as in the said c. quamquam and the said cle. praesenti. By an a contrario reading it is noted by Fed. in the place previously cited, and Spec. ubi supra; and in this case the laws do not seem to make mention of a warning, perhaps because the laity may refuse to permit those things to be brought in without the payment of the due gabelle or toll. And let these remarks suffice for the arguments. For a full discussion, see the subject matter in the said clementi. praesenti, and the said capitu. quamquam, and capitu. fina. de vita & hone. clerico. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument: 1. Whether a judge is bound to express the ground in a sentence, if several grounds could be deduced from a general sentence.
body: I was asked in a matter of fact,

† whether a judge is bound to express the ground in a sentence, if several grounds could be deduced from a general sentence? I answered by way of counsel that if prejudice could be generated to a party from the diversity, the judge ought then to express the ground. For example, if it could be doubted whether the defendant was absolved from the claim of the libellant; whether because the plaintiff did not prove it, or because of a defect of instance; or because the defendant was not in possession; or something similar. This seems to be proved in l. properandum, C. de iudi. and the express gloss there at the verse ideò; it is also according to the opinion of the doctors in cap. sicut, de re iud. and Specu. in the title de senten. prola. §. qualiter, at the verse verum si rationes, and Ioan. Andr. in cap. finem, de dolo & contu. and Butr. in c. examinata, de iud. and Spe. in the title cited above, where they set down certain cases in which the ground must be expressed, where no other reason for those cases can be elicited, except to avoid ambiguities; not, however, to the prejudice that it might impose upon a party, or otherwise in any way. The same is held by Bartol. and certain others in l. 2. §. ignominiae, ff. ex qui. cau. infa. irro. I also proved this by another reason: wherever several and diverse actions can be deduced from what is narrated in the libel, the judge ought to compel the libellant to express the name of the action; or deny a hearing to one refusing to do so, in order that uncertainty may be avoided, as is noted in l. edita, C. de eden. and l. 1. ff. eod. by the canonists in cap. dilecti, de iud. And Innocen. says in c. 2. de ordi. cogn. that a judge is foolish who receives a libel otherwise. Behold, therefore, that although otherwise the action itself need not be expressed in the libel, as is noted in 9. distin. cap. quo iure, and said c. dilecti, and said l. edita; nevertheless, for the aforesaid reason the judge compels him to express the ground. With stronger reason, therefore, ought the judge himself to express the ground in the sentence (in order to avoid that uncertainty), since a sentence ought to be clearer than a libel, insti. de act. §. curare; noted by Inno. in c. tanta, de exces. prael. I think, however, that the sentence does not fall from the omission of the ground, but we interpret altogether the reason of the congruent ground. And if it is manifold, we interpret that which is of lesser prejudice. To this, what is noted by Innocen. in c. 2. de ord. cog. and Spe. in the title de off. iudi. §. deseruit, verse in sententiae and following, where he says that when a defendant is simply absolved, the exception of res judicata does not bar the plaintiff wishing to sue again, and according to him he will be able to prove that the petition was inept, and he ought to be admitted by the judges and counselors of the case, by the argument in l. 3. ff. de susp. tu. I think that even if proofs are lacking, we will interpret the ground of lesser prejudice, by the argument in the aforesaid l. 3. and from what is noted by Inn. in c. 2. de ord. cogni. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument: 1. Whether the religious order instituted by the blessed Bridget is said to be contrary to canonical sanctions.
casus: It is asked whether the religious order instituted by the blessed Bridget, which was confirmed by the pope and subsequently called into doubt by his successors in the papacy, is said to be contrary to the decrees of the holy fathers or canonical sanctions, especially because in such a religious order priests or brothers are also to be instituted who must serve the same nuns in divine offices.
body: Having invoked the protection of Christ, of His mother, and of the same Bridget whose deed is at issue.

† First, arguing on the affirmative side (as is customary), it seems that the said religious order is contrary to the decrees of the holy fathers. And first, it seems to be proven by capitu. monasteria, 18. quæstio. 2, where it is expressly said that monasteries of maidens are to be established far from monasteries of monks on account of the snares of the devil or the slander of men. But in the said religious order of Saint Bridget, priests or brothers are established in the monastery of maidens, at least under a general clause; therefore it is expressly contrary to the prohibition of the law made for a most honorable cause. Secondly, to the same effect is adduced capitu. in nullo, the same causa: monks and nuns ought not to cohabit in one monastery; rather, even double monasteries are prohibited by law, or where there are two colleges of monks and nuns, as in the said capitu. in nullo and capitu. diffinimus.
