If, therefore, we say that there is a single monastery in which brothers and sisters are present, or whether there are diverse colleges and diverse monasteries, they seem prohibited by law, at least on account of proximity and familiarity; and this seems especially proven in capitu. in decima, 18. quæstio. 2, where the familiarity of those monks who were to correct those nuns is prohibited. Likewise, if those laws alleged above are well weighed, the rationale of the prohibition is twofold: first, on account of the crime of incest, which could arise from the proximity and familiarity of those cohabiting, etc.; the second rationale is on account of evil repute and on account of the slander of men. But these two rationales urge and militate against the said religious order of Saint Bridget; therefore the same prohibition ought to apply, and where the same rationale exists, the same law is to be established, as in capitu. translato, de constitutio. and capitu. cum dilecta, de confirma. util. uel inutil. Likewise, among other things contained in the said Rule, it is provided in capitu. 7 that the abbess of the monastery must be the head and mistress of the monastery; and the general confessor, on account of the judgments of the brothers and the preservation of the order, shall do nothing at all without the counsel of the abbess, but the abbess herself, as the head of the monastery, is to be consulted concerning the ordering of the business and property of the monastery; and thus the abbess according to the same Rule seems to be the head of all, both men and women. Which sounds absurd, since according to the Apostle the man ought to be the head of the woman, and not the reverse; and the same is held in capitu. hæc imago, and capitu. cum caput, and capitu. est ordo, 33. quæstio. 5. Likewise relevant is that which is objected by several people, namely, that since the brothers are bound to obey the confessor and not the abbess, and the sisters the abbess herself, as in capitu. 12 of the same Rule, there will be two chapters, and commonly two monasteries and two convents. Lastly, it seems that one should dwell on this no further, since our present Lord Pope Martin the Fifth expressly asserts in his revocatory letters that by that Rule double monasteries are established contrary to the law of prohibition; and one must stand entirely by the words of the pope, seeing that he bases his intention upon them, as in clemen. literis, de probatio. But these things notwithstanding, I consider the opposite to be true in law. And first, I am moved by that which is found in the said Rule, capitu. 10, where it is said that the sisters to be instituted in the monastery shall have clerics who will canonically chant the Mass and the office for them, and that the clerics themselves are to be entirely separated from the monastery of the sisters, having of their own a curia in which they shall dwell, and from the curia an entrance into the church and the lower choir, whereas they [the sisters] shall have a choir raised above, so that they may be able to see the sacred rites and hear the office, etc. From which words I weigh first that the intention of the blessed Bridget was not to place together or institute two monasteries, namely of men and of women, nor to institute males and females in one monastery, but only to institute nuns, or a college of nuns; and that these clerics, or brothers, were not there as forming a college, but as individuals and servants in divine matters. Which is clearly evident from those words when it says 'they shall have clerics.' Likewise from other words, while it says in the same chapter that these clerics shall have one curia of their own so that they are entirely separated from the monastery of the sisters. Which words signify that these clerics or brothers do not of themselves form a monastery, nor is there anything other than one monastery of the sisters, since it is said that they are entirely separated from the monastery of the sisters. But 'curia' also signifies a place of habitation, just as we see happening today in all monasteries of nuns, who are not able of themselves on account of the defect of their sex to celebrate Masses and preach, as in capitu. noua, de pœni. & remis.; they have priests and seculars near the monastery celebrating and preaching for them, for which observance capitu. dilecta, de exces. prælat. and capitu. fina. de statu. regu. are relevant; and the brothers, or clerics, are substituted in their place; and since all are presumed holy on account of the many austerities that they promise to observe, they are to be presumed more honorable, or more holy, 16. distin. cap. nulli, and capitu. doctos. For since the sisters cannot be without priests ministering divine rites to them, it is better that they have these more suitable, or more holy men, chosen and instituted by so most devout a saint, than that they have others, through whom perhaps they might more easily come to evils. Nor does it stand in the way if objection is made against them concerning familiarity and cohabitation; because I answer that if the words of the Rule recited above are well weighed, these clerics, or brothers, must remain entirely separated from the monastery of the sisters; and I weigh the word 'entirely' [omnino] that is used, which denotes continuous separation and not just slight distance. Likewise, in capitu. 22 of the Rule it is said that the confessor or any of the priests or brothers may never enter the monastery of the nuns, except when the sacraments are to be administered to the sick, or a deceased sister is to be buried; in which cases it would be permitted even to secular clerics, nor is all familiarity and cohabitation avoided, so much so that in the said chapter of the Rule it is also contained that in the said monastery there will even be appointed gratings; but when the sisters confess, they can indeed be heard, but by no means seen. Secondly, I am principally moved to this opinion by that which is found after the beginning of the same Rule at the end of the prologue, in the chapter that begins 'hanc igitur,' etc.; there it is said that to the honor of the Blessed Virgin she wished to found this religious order through women first and principally, and no mention is made of the brothers; rather, more is said in capitul. 13, that these priests ought to devote themselves only to the divine office, study, and prayer, and entangle themselves in no other business or other offices; which words sufficiently indicate that the monastery is not common, nor are they there as a college, but as servants in divine matters. And so the words of the preceding chapter intend, where it is said that the abbess is always to be consulted regarding the business and property of the monastery. This is also understood while it is said in the said chapter that the general confessor of the monastery must receive from the bishop of the place the power of binding and loosing, of correcting and reforming all priests, brothers, etc.; by which words it is also argued that the brothers are not there as an enduring college. For if they were as a college, they would elect for themselves a prelate, who from the election alone and the subsequent confirmation of the bishop would obtain the said power of binding, loosing, and correcting the other brothers, as in capitu. 1. de elect. 18. quæst. 2. capitu. 1. and capitu. Abbas, and c. nulla, de off. ord. c. cum ab ecclesiarum. Thirdly, I principally adduce the said cap. in decima, 18. quæst. 2, which I adduced above to the contrary, by adducing it in another manner, it serves the matter very well; for there it was decreed by a general council with the common consent of all that the monasteries of virgins in the province of Baetica should be governed by the administration and protection of monks. And it is added there: 'We only approve—that is, grant—wholesome things to virgins dedicated to Christ when we choose such spiritual fathers by whose governance they can not only be protected, but also be edified by their teachings,' etc. From which words we can very well argue that the said Rule is not against the sayings of the holy fathers, since there, by an entire general council, monks were deputed to rule and govern monasteries of nuns; so in our case, without any violence to the law, the said priests or brothers can be deputed to administer divine rites to the said sisters. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that in the said capitu. in decima familiarity of monks and nuns is entirely prohibited, so that it is not permitted to approach familiarly even to the vestibule, that is, to the parlor; because in the said Rule of Saint Bridget, if the words adduced above are well weighed, the opposite is not said, but rather almost the same, since, as I said above, those priests or brothers must remain entirely separated from the monastery of the nuns, and they can never proceed to the parlor, except rarely for the most honorable causes, such that not even in hearing confessions can they see them. If, therefore, the words of the Rule and all the aforesaid are weighed, it cannot be said that they have double monasteries; nor that they dwell in one monastery, since the brothers must remain entirely separated from the monastery of the sisters, nor is there familiar access to them. Whence at least we cannot deny that this way of living has not hitherto been prohibited by law, nor ought we to extend the subject matter in this odious act with the suppression of so many monasteries, especially considering that Saint Bridget was a most noble saint, so much so that, her works demanding it, she was canonized by the Supreme Pontiff; and she with such solemnity asserted that the revelation of this religious order was made to her from heaven by Christ the Lord. Added to this are the points noted by Innocen. in cap. ne innitaris, de constitu., where he says that the sayings of the saints are to be followed entirely, so long as they are not found to be openly reprobated. Likewise, from reprobation many monasteries would then be condemned, since the said priests, or brothers, do not have, nor can they have according to that Rule, a monastery or college of their own, but are deputed there as servants in divine matters; whence it would be necessary to give them a new and good rule whence they might live, since the sisters are not bound to this, since all the property belongs to the monastery of the nuns themselves, and the said brothers have no common share in it, as is sufficiently clear in cap. 10 and cap. 14 of the same Rule. And thus the division of goods, of which mention is made in it and by the Lord Pope in the said revocatory letters, has no place. And as I said above, since we are now dealing with an act capable of retraction and the revocation of that which was repeatedly approved by Roman Pontiffs, we ought to apply the strictest interpretation to the said laws that seem to stand in the way, by argument in the rule odia, and the rule in pœnis, de regu. iur. lib. 6, and l. penulti. ff. de pœnis, and what the gloss notes in cap. decet, de immuni. eccle. lib. 6. I conclude therefore, always saving a better judgment and especially that of our Lord [Pope], that the said religious order of Saint Bridget is not in any way to be violated on the ground that the monasteries are said to be double, or that males and females dwell in the same monastery. Now I respond to the arguments framed above for the contrary side. And first, cap. monasteria does not stand in the way, because it speaks of when two equally principal monasteries are to be founded; for then, since no necessity compels nor utility advises it, they ought to be placed at a distance from one another so that evil in fact and in repute may be avoided. But if the said Rule is well considered, the case seems to be altogether different, since there is only a single monastery of the nuns, but the priests or brothers, as deputed only to serve in divine matters, have only a certain habitation entirely separated from the monastery of the nuns, as is contained above in the said Rule. Cap. in nullo does not stand in the way, because, as I said above, the brothers and sisters do not dwell together in one monastery, as was said above, nor do they have a monastery of their own, but a certain curia or habitation, so that they may more easily serve the sisters in divine rites, and thus they cannot be called double monasteries, as I also fully stated above. To c. in decima I have sufficiently responded above. The twofold rationale of prohibition of the said laws does not stand in the way; I concede, nevertheless, that where monks form a college and rule of their own, they ought to be established farther from the monastery of the nuns, because then no necessity or utility underlies it, but they could fall into evil in fact or in repute. And therefore it is no wonder if the laws prohibited it, since on one side there is danger and on the other evil, by argument in c. cum ab omni specie, de uita & hone. cler. But in our case there underlies a rationale of utility and necessity, since they have to serve them in the said offices, so that, if they stayed farther away, they could not easily come daily into the said monastery, especially since it is not becoming for the said brothers, and as most devout brothers dedicated to God, to go out daily at all hours through the streets and squares of the city, ar. 16. q. 1. c. si cupis. Nor is it to be cared that the mouth of those speaking speaks iniquity, provided that we do not depart from the path of truth; but it is to be said just as Christ said of the Pharisees scandalized by Him: 'Let them alone; they are blind and leaders of the blind,' as is held in c. magnæ, de uoto. Nor does the other motive stand in the way, namely that according to one of the chapters of the Rule concerning the Abbess, since she is a woman, she seems to be the head, whereas the contrary ought rather to be the case. For these things proceed given equality between man and woman. But in our case the abbess, by reason of her dignity, has jurisdiction over the said monastery, and she could have jurisdiction over secular clerics, although in our case she has no jurisdiction over the brothers, as in the said c. dilecta, de ma. & obe. and de exces. præla. c. dilecta; indeed, a woman by reason of succession in a realm could have the fullest jurisdiction over all subjects, as in c. deuotissimam. 12. q. 2. and in c. dilecti, de arb. The penultimate motive does not stand in the way, because in our case there are not two equally principal heads of the same body; on the contrary, the Abbess is over her monastery and her nuns, just as by law she ought to be. The general confessor, however, is over the brothers in the place of the bishop, since he receives power and authority from the bishop, as the Rule says. And thus they are not diverse heads of the same body, but of diverse persons and in a diverse respect, and in these cases one is subordinate and subject to the other, just as we see in a bishop, and in several prelates and inferiors. The last argument from cle. literis, de probat., that one must stand by the words of the pope, does not stand in the way, because the contrary proceeds when the pope bases his intention upon his own act; otherwise if upon the act of another. For then at least proof to the contrary is admitted, since the pope could easily err regarding the act of another, as the gloss notably says in the said cle. literis. But in our case the pope says in the said revocatory letters that in the said Rule of Saint Bridget it is among other things expressly provided that a monastery of this order to be founded and constructed for the habitation of brothers and sisters must be double, which in fact is false; because, if the words are well inspected, these monasteries cannot really be called double, but of the nuns, as I said above. But the Lord Pope could thus plausibly have been deceived by a false reason, since the said Rule consists in fact and not in law, by argument in cap. 1. de consti. lib. 6. And let these stated things suffice. After this consilium I saw the bullate letters of the Lord Martin confirming the aforesaid religious order according to the decision of this consilium. Praise be to God and to Saint Bridget. Abbot Nicolaus.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether the Friars Minor are bound to pay the tithe from their gardens?
2. If an unprivileged thing passes to privileged persons, it takes on their privilege.
casus: The convent of the Friars Minor of the town of San Ginesio had a certain garden for their necessities. Wherefore they acquired a certain land contiguous to their garden, which they converted into a garden, and thus out of that newly acquired land and their garden made one garden, and they obtained from the community of the town of San Ginesio that they should not be bound to pay anything for the tax (libra) or assessment formerly imposed on the said parcel of land. It happens at times that they have the said garden worked by a sharecropper or métayer, at times by a tenant farmer hired for a wage, or by a servant of the monastery who is maintained from the goods of the monastery. The tithe is demanded both from the friars and from the tenant farmer. Likewise, it is demanded from the tenant farmer that he pay for the aforesaid land according to the tax formerly imposed. To the contrary, the friars allege the privilege granted to them concerning not paying tithes from their gardens and shrubberies. Likewise, with respect to the tax or assessment [?], they allege the immunity granted to them by the said commune. It is asked what the law is, etc.
body: Having invoked the name of Christ, amen. Here arise four doubtful points. First, whether the friars are bound to pay the tithe to the parish priest for that parcel of land newly acquired. Second, what concerning the tenant farmer? Third, whether the friars are bound to pay the tax assessment (aestimum) formerly imposed on the said parcel of land before it came into their hands. Fourth, what concerning the tenant farmer? And touching upon these very briefly, and deciding rather than insisting on behalf of the parties, regarding the first I think that, if the privilege was granted to them simply,

† as is alleged, namely that they are not bound to pay the tithe from their gardens, they could not be compelled to pay from that parcel of land which has been reduced to a garden; therefore also upon their gardens, following the excellent argument in c. quia circa, de priui. Nor ought one and the same thing to be judged under a different law, de serui. l. eum qui. Nor does any reason appear why they should be more bound to pay for the said parcel of land newly acquired than for the original garden, since not every land is subject to the burden of tithes; whence, for that reason by which they do not pay from the first parcel, so neither from the one reduced [to a garden]. What is held in a similar case in l. generaliter, ff. de fideiusso. and by Ioan. Andr. in c. cum olim, de re iudica. and in regula, is qui in ias, de regul. iur. lib. 6 supports this. And if a thing

† not privileged passes to privileged persons, it takes on their privilege, as in c. uno, de iure pat. li. 6, and as noted there in the Novella, and in c. dilectus, de praeb.; what is noted in auth. quas actiones, C. de sacrosan. eccle. also supports this. And an absurdity would follow from the contrary. For imagine that from the beginning they had had no garden, or an exceedingly modest one; shall we say that they could not acquire a new one without the burden of tithes? Certainly let this be absent, since their privilege would be of no benefit to them, contrary to c. in his, de priui. Nevertheless, I understand the aforesaid to be true unless their garden were so large that they caused it to be cultivated and the garden produce to be sold for a price. For this is not permitted, as in cle. exiui de paradiso, de uerbo. significa.; for this is repugnant to their rule, as in the said clemen. exiui; and then I would think the tithe ought to be paid, because the privilege does not extend itself to this case, as in the said clem. exiui, §. licet. And this concerning the first doubt. To the second concerning the tenant farmer, thus: either he cultivates for money wages, or at the expense which he receives from the monastery, and he is not bound to pay the predial tithe, because that gain comes from the land, which whether it produces or not, he always has his wage, as noted in c. tua, de deci.; or he is a sharecropper, or a métayer. And then the words of the privilege of the friars themselves must be inspected. For if the garden is exempted from the burden of tithes, then the tenant farmer is not bound to pay the predial tithe, because the land is privileged and exempt from the burden of tithes. Or the friars [personally] are exempt, as because it is said in the privilege that the friars are not bound to pay, or cannot be compelled, or [pay] an excise tax (sisia), and then such a tenant farmer is bound to pay from his portion, because that portion comes from land that is not privileged. But the persons of the friars are privileged, and the obligation of the lord is one thing, and that of the tenant farmer another, as in c. a nobis, and c. tua, de dec., and likewise there Pau. and the doctors commonly. And this concerning the second point. I come to the third, in which I say that the friars are not bound to pay anything for the tax assessment (aestimum) or the pound-tax (libra) formerly imposed, both on account of the immunity that they had from all burdens of the said land, which they cannot revoke according to what is noted by Inn. and others in c. nouit, de iudi., and in the rule, quod semel placuit, de re. iu. li. 6, and l. si, de decr. ab or. fa.; and also because I think they are exempt by common law, since a fixed and remarkable burden was not attached to the said land, according to what is noted by the doctors in c. fin. de uita & hon. cle., c. peruenit, de censi., notwithstanding the theory of Bart. in l. rescripto, ff. de mune. & hono. To the fourth, I think the tenant farmer is bound to pay from his portion, because he receives that portion as gain for his labor, but not as lord or possessor of the garden, by the argument in l. male agitur, C. de praescri. 30. ann.; this proceeds especially in our case, where the tenant farmer has no possession of the said garden, but burdens that are paid for possessions are only patrimonial burdens, as in l. munerum, §. personalia, ff. de mun. & hono., and therefore they ought to be imposed on the owners or possessors of things, which this gardener is not, as I have said above. And let these very brief remarks suffice. Nico. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A release occurring in the one ought not to be referred to the other.
2. Where there are two servitudes with respect to the same thing, the remission of one does not exclude the remission of the other.
3. A sentence rendered on the pretext of false instruments, or by a judge not one's own, is to be annulled.
body: Invoking the names of Christ and His mother: In the cause and dispute pending between the clergy of Pisa of the one part, and Matteo, hospitaler of the new hospital of the said city of Pisa, in the name of the hospital itself, of the other part, in order to spare prolixity, I shall pass over the arguments which are commonly made by many for the parties, and I shall come down decisively to the resolution of the doubtful points. For four things are alleged against the clergy.

† First, the instrument of deliberation and release made by the presiding officers, or Captains, of the said clergy. Second, the instrument of release made by dominus Calanus, syndic and chamberlain of the said clergy. Third, another instrument of nearly the same effect drawn up by mandate of the said syndic. Fourth, the sentence rendered by the honorable Podestà of Pisa, delegated in this matter by the magnificent Priors of the city of Florence. All of these certainly do not stand in the way of the intention of the said clergy, if they are all thoroughly examined on their merits. And following the order, I come to the first, which is the foundation in our whole matter, namely to the release made by the said Captains. For I say that it does not bar the clergy of Pisa, nor does it presently relieve the said hospitaler with respect to the burdens newly imposed on the occasion of the interest and provisions to be paid for the principal long since acknowledged. For the clergy and the said hospitaler were equally and primarily bound to two things: namely, to paying the capital itself already imposed for distribution, and to paying the interest or provision on the principal already lent to them. Therefore, things done by the said Captains with respect to the amount already imposed and distributed ought not to be extended to any amount that was not yet imposed nor distributed, even if this amount arose on the occasion of the first amount, with respect to which the said hospital was released for three hundred pounds by the said Captains. This is proved in §. non solum, joined with the gloss in l. et eleganter, ff. de dolo, and l. 3. §. idem Iul. ff. de eo quod cer. loc., and by what is noted in l. 3. C. deposi., and by Bartolus in l. centum Capuæ, ff. de eo quod cer. loc., for this reason: because an inference is not made from separate things, de transl. præal. capitul. fin.; cap. dilecti, de foro compet. and capit. peruenit, de fideius. support this, where therefore someone is primarily compelled to pay interest, just as the debt itself primarily;

† a release occurring in the one ought not to be referred to the other; this is especially to be said in our case, in which the Captains of the clergy, with the intention of making a gift, made that remission of the principal for one hundred pounds; wherefore, since this gift redounds to the prejudice of another, namely of the entire clergy, it ought to be restricted, according to what is noted by Innocentius in c. dilecti, de don. and by Ioannes Andreæ in c. olim, de uerbor. signific.

† Second, it is principally clear in a similar case: where there are two servitudes with respect to the same thing, the remission of one does not exclude the remission of the other, as in l. si domus, ff. de ser. ru. præd. and cap. ex tuarum, and de auth. & usu pal. Therefore, the same is to be said in the case where the remission was made to the hospital only with respect to the portion affecting the hospital from the entire principal previously imposed. And that this release was made only with respect to the principal is most plainly gathered from the wording of the said conferral and release. For he released the hospital from all debt contained in the books by reason of the impositions or dispositions already made. But this imposition of nine thousand florins, which is being made now, had not yet been imposed at that time, nor was it entered into the books of the clergy; and consequently those general words of release are not extended to this case: because the words cannot be adapted to this case, and one must not depart from the words unless the intention of the disposer is expressly apparent, l. non aliter, ff. de leg. in capitul. fin. de uerbor. significat. Also because general words are restricted to those matters only which were expressly treated, as in l. qui cum tutoribus, and l. cum Aquiliana. ff. de transatio. and noted in capit. 1. extra eodem titul. l. qui Romæ. §. duo fratres, ff. de uerbor. obligatio. noted by Bartolus there, especially at the end. And on these points, however much it was dealt with from the words of the release itself and of the other instruments, in which mention is always made of all things already imposed in the past and distributed, but not of those to be imposed and distributed beyond the principal, even if on its occasion. The words afterwards added in the margin by another hand, which seem to extend also to things to be imposed on the occasion of the principal amount, do not stand in the way: because I say that if we are willing to take good notice, they rather make against the hospital than for it; because since they were written down by another hand, and they concern the substance of the business at issue, the instrument is rendered defective and suspect, and thus they do not provide proof, as is clearly proved in capit. cum uenerabilis, de regio. domi. and in cap. inter dilectos, de fide instrumento. And if the notary had added it, or had caused it to be added, by the consent of the parties, he ought at least to have stated at the end how he himself added it, or caused it to be added by another, and the cause, and then at least it would have provided proof; otherwise it is different, as is gathered from capit. cum inter, de sentent. & re iudica. and from those things which are read and noted in the said capitul. inter dilectos, and more clearly in l. 1 and l. cancellauerat, ff. de his, quæ in testa. delen. and by Bartolus in the said l. 1. and Archidiaconus in capitul. cleri. 30. quæstio. 9. Whence, since the said forgery appears to have been made by the hospital or at its petition, it appears to have doubted its own right, and thus, as to the genuine instrument, it does not extend to this case, argum. capitul. cum olim, de officio delega. and capit. olim de rescrip. and by Bartolus in the said l. 1, unless by favor of religion we say otherwise according to those things which are read and noted in capitul. uenerabilis, de excep. And let these things suffice to remove the objection of the said release made by the said Captains of the clergy. I come now to the second and third points, and I shall dispatch them together: because they are of the same effect and from the same person, namely the syndic, and are said to have emanated from him, or to have been drawn up at his disposition; and I say that for many reasons they can be rescinded and invalidated. Both for the aforesaid reason: because the words concerning the effect of this present business were added by another hand, and thus they do not create belief, but rather establish a ground of forgery against the hospital, as I said before in the preceding remarks. Secondly, because that syndic was not acting to release anew, but to do all things according to the release, or deliberation, of those Captains of the clergy, which is expressly clear where he said 'according to the deliberation,' etc. And thus they induce nothing beyond what is contained in that deliberation of the Captains, since it was made after the likeness of it, although more things are contained in these, according to what is noted by Innocentius and by Ioannes Andreæ in cap. inter dilectos, de fide instrumento. Likewise he was deceived by the false words added in the said deliberation, wherefore I argue, first, that where the principal does not hold, consequently neither does the accessory, nor all that which proceeded from it on that account, as is the text noted in a similar case in cap. inter dilectos. §. cæterum. præal. Thirdly and more strongly it operates: because the said interlineation, or writing made in the margin, even if it had not made mention of the said deliberation, still also for another cause stated in the instrument of release, the syndic could not release the hospital: because, since the hospital was bound to contribute together with the rest of the clergy in the imposition to be made with respect to interest and provision, the release having been made by the Captains of the clergy only with respect to the principal, the release made by the syndic of the clergy was not valid to the effect that nothing could be demanded from the hospital even on the occasion of that principal: because that is a kind of donation, which an administrator cannot make, since he does not have free administration; nor can he donate unless he has a special mandate to donate, in capitul. fin. de officio uica. lib. 6. l. contra iuris, ff. de pac. l. filiusfa. ff. de don. and l. præses, C. de transat. And the said syndic did not have a mandate to donate: because those instruments are of no avail with respect to that which is now demanded from the hospital, therefore it cannot be of avail. And first, because a sentence was rendered, and as I may now touch upon whether the sentence seems to absolve, namely from everything that can accrue on the occasion of the principal: I say nevertheless that for many reasons the sentence does not avail the hospital.

† And first, because it was rendered on the pretext of false instruments; and therefore it can be annulled according to those things which are read and noted in capitul. licet, de probat. and C. si ex fal. instr. throughout, and l. Diuus, ff. de re iudica. and l. si prætor §. Marcellus. ff. de iudic. Secondly, because it was rendered by a judge not its own, de iud. cap. at si clerici, C. si a non compe. iudic. throughout. Thirdly, because at the time of the release obtained there was no dispute between the clergy and the hospital; and thus the rescript was not valid toward future matters, since there was no circumstance present to which it might apply, according to those things which are read and noted in capitul. fin. de rescrip. From these points it is concluded that the laws alleged on the part of the hospital itself do not avail to defeat the claim of the clergy; and thus the hospital is bound to contribute the portion assessed for the payment of the interest, or provision, to be made on the occasion of that principal, etc. And let these things suffice. Praise be to Almighty God. NICOLAUS ABBAS.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The solemnity of human law ceases in a disposition to pious causes.
2. Things moved by the Spirit of God are not under the law.
body: IN the case pending between the hospital administrators of Santa Maria della Misericordia of the city of Arezzo on the one side, and Francesco and Accursio, sons of the late Gregorio, on the other side, concerning the inheritance of the late Lazzaro, merchant of Arezzo, I shall proceed by stating the judgment of my own mind rather than arguing for the parties in the customary manner, because the arguments on both sides have already been sufficiently treated by others. And for a clearer resolution of the question, I shall examine two limbs. First, whether the first will, in which the said brotherhood was instituted heir, is valid even disregarding the second alleged nuncupative will, in which the said Francesco and Accursio, nephews of the said testator Lazzaro (namely sons of the said Lazzaro's brother), are said to have been instituted heirs. The second limb: assuming the validity of that will, it is asked firstly about the validity of the instruments themselves—namely, which of them is to be preferred? And because the matter has been sufficiently discussed by others, I shall proceed succinctly. Regarding the first, I say that the will is valid in itself, because it possesses all its requisite solemnities, especially since in a disposition to pious causes the solemnity of human law
† ceases, and the sole solemnity of natural and divine law suffices, as in c. relatum, de test. and the notes there, and in l. 1 and there by all, C. de sacros. eccl.
† For those things that are moved by the Spirit of God

† are not under the law, de reg. c. licet, and 19 q. 2 cap. duo sunt. Nor do those words of the testator, uttered after the lapse of ten years—that he did not wish that will to be valid—stand in the way, so that the will would seem annihilated through l. sancimus, C. de test. For if those words of the testator are weighed carefully together with the words and deeds uttered and performed by him, we are most clearly outside the case of that law. For that law speaks only of when a testator says simply that he did not wish his will to be valid, and thus departed entirely from his prior intention with the lapse of ten years; but in our case he did not say simply that he did not wish that will to be valid, but restrictively: namely, in that manner and form in which it had been made, and thus that he had the intention of adding or subtracting something; which was clearly evident from subsequent events. For after those words, he revoked the legacy made to the church of San Francesco, and wrote this in the copy, or in the margin of the copy of that will, and thus brought to effect the prior words uttered by him in general terms; nor does he seem to have wished to depart from the prior will in any other way, the argument being l. praecipimus, in fi. C. de ap. For obscure words are clarified by preceding and following circumstances, l. si servus plurium, and l. qui filiabus, ff. de lega. 1. For if he had wished to alter more, he would have written more, just as he did in revoking the legacy made to the friars. For that revocation of the legacy specially made would have been pointless if he had wished to invalidate the will entirely. Thus, therefore, in its existence it admits of limitation only in what was expressly stated, as in cle. exivi, de verb. sign., and especially because, when afflicted with illness, he said that he had made a will, and this could not be understood except of this one, since it appears that he had made no other at that time, arg. in l. 2, C. de autho. praestan. and what is noted there; and these things are especially true in a will made for pious causes. For just as one made among children is proved by any indications whatsoever, as is the notable text in l. fin. C. fami. ercis., so must it be said of a will made for pious causes, especially when the testator's children do not stand in the way. For this disposition is not less privileged than that made among children, as Bart. notes in d. l. 1, C. de sacros. eccl., and 19 q. ult. c. si qua mulier supports this. For the soul is to be loved above all things, 12 q. 1 c. praecipimus, and especially at the end of life, when there is no longer room for repentance: because as each person departs from here, such will he appear or be represented in judgment, dist. 15 c. qualis. Likewise, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that by those words previously uttered the testator wished to depart from the prior will in such a way, nevertheless, because when in extremis he said that he had made a will, he seems, as it were, to have embraced anew that intention as his last, since he is not found to have made any other will previously, as I have said above. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that those were enunciative words uttered for another reason, namely by way of a reason, which do not fully prove a last will, although it is otherwise in enunciative words uttered principally for their own sake, in accordance with what is read and noted in l. ex hac scriptura, ff. de do. For I say that this applies to last wills not for pious causes. For regarding pious causes, a last will is proved by words enunciatively uttered, even by way of a reason, as is the text directly on point in c. fin. de succes. ab intest., and Host. and Io. An. hold this there, and Bar. in d. l. 1, and d. l. fi. C. fami. ercis. supports it, since it can be proved by any indications whatsoever, as I said above, and especially in this case, where the will previously made is evident, upon which those words set forth above are verified; and thus they will work a renewal of that intention, presupposing that he had departed from it, ar. insti. de mili. testa. § sed et si quis. And presupposing that those enunciative words did not prove fully, but half-fully, as in d. c. fi. according to another interpretation that is not so common as the preceding one, nevertheless this would suffice to infer what I said above, that he did not have the intention of departing entirely from the first will; which is gathered from many subsequent circumstances, as is clear from the premises and from the statement of the case. Wherefore I conclude as to the first limb that the said will, in which the brotherhood was instituted, is valid and firm. Now I come to the second, which is more difficult: which of the two prevails over the other? And I think that it is the one in which the brotherhood was instituted; and omitting many arguments that can be brought forward, the foundation is this: wherever anyone has presumption and probability against him, he is burdened with a heavier burden of proof than is ordinarily required by law in such an act, whence the proofs must be crystal clear, and such witnesses concerning whom there is no probable suspicion that they would perjure themselves; this is proved in the text and gl. in l. non est verosimile, ff. quod met. cau., and in c. quia verosimile, de praesump., and in c. super hoc, de renun. But in our case there are many presumptions that openly show that the second will was not probably made, at least by those words asserted by the party; therefore the adverse party is burdened with proving the will itself. The first presumption is that the testator seems to have had the intention of changing the first will only upon the birth of natural children, and yet he is said to have changed it afterwards and to have made no mention of the prior will, l. si quis, in princ. ff. de leg. 3. And especially in our case mention was to be made, since he had first tested for pious causes for his soul, and afterward he is said to have tested among collateral agnates and to have left nothing to pious causes, upon which he had previously poured out almost his entire estate; which certainly is not probable, because he would at least have made some mention of the prior will, and would have left something to pious causes, especially since he was a merchant, who was easily burdened with debt and with things acquired through an unlawful cause, de poeniten. distinct. 5 capitul. qualitas, and distinct. 88 capitul. eiicies and capit. quoniam. What is read and noted by Cyn. in auth. hoc inter liberos, C. de testam., arguing from a disposition among children to pious causes, as I said above, supports this excellently. And that dissimilarity ought especially to hold force in our case, in which the pious cause does not compete with the testator's children, but with collaterals; capitul. cum olim, de re iudica. also supports this, where it is clear that if a prince says he will provide for a certain specific matter, and if he afterward provides without making other mention, he is presumed to have acted not out of liberality, but rather having been circumvented; what Bartol. notes in l. quod iussit, ff. de re iudica. supports this. But in our case the testator in the prior will reserved to himself only the intention to change the will upon the supervening of children; therefore, he does not seem to have wished afterward by simple words to depart from the prior will without having made mention of it. The second presumption is that the witnesses in the second alleged will were not requested; whereas in every will requested witnesses ought really to be brought for this purpose, as l. haeredes palam § in testamento, ff. de testamen., in l. hac consultissima, C. eodem, even if it is a soldier's will, as in l. divus, ff. de testamen. milit., though there is a special rule in it when he is pressed by death, according to what is noted in d. l. Divus, and l. miles, C. eodem. For frequently these words, 'I leave you as heir,' are uttered to please someone; therefore they do not produce proof unless the witnesses were requested, as in d. l. divus. L. hac consultissima § si quis does not stand in the way, where the presence of five witnesses would suffice when those succeeding on intestacy are instituted, to the point that they take from an imperfect revoked will where strangers had been instituted, and they come at least on grounds of intestacy. For I say that that law does not apply in our case, where the soul of the testator himself, or God Himself, was instituted, so to speak, Who is honored in the persons of the poor, Whom we ought to love above all things with all our strength and all our mind. For this pious cause is more favored than those succeeding on intestacy, especially since they are not among his children, as is noted in d. l. 1, especially by Bar. And the rationale of that law ceases. For a less solemn will for pious causes invalidates an earlier solemn one, according to what is held similarly in d. l. hac consultissima § ex imperfecto, noted in d. l. 1; a fortiori, if it was solemn, it ought not to be overcome by a second, less solemn will, as in authen. multo magis, C. de episco. et cle. and c. cum in cunctis, de elect. And by this I say that in the aforesaid second will five witnesses ought not to suffice, because we are outside the case of that law; and these two presumptions seem entirely to invalidate or render ineffective the alleged second will. The third presumption is that, having been questioned several times, he always replied that he wished to stand by the prior will, in which, as I have said, he had poured out almost his entire estate for pious causes. Whence it is not probable that the testator wished to depart entirely from a good purpose, and to recoil from a prior intention so often confirmed, at least by leaving nothing to pious causes, especially since, when a notary arrived after the alleged nuncupative will, he would never answer; on the contrary, he turned on his side, and he did the same when two other notaries arrived afterward, as it were at the very end of his life. For from these extremities we ought to presume about the middle, namely that he did not have the intention of departing from the prior will, according to the notable gloss in c. accedens, de conver. coniu. The fourth presumption arises from the said wife, who says that she always stood at her husband's side and never heard that he wished to change his prior intention and make a will anew. Nor does the fact that she is a legatee stand in the way of the prior will, because it at least creates a presumption, according to what is fully noted in c. insuper, de test. by Ioan. And. and others, since she would perhaps in any event obtain her legacy because there was a codicillary clause in the prior will, which I do not examine at present. Which presumption is clear because almost all the witnesses are relatives of those nephews whose advantage is primarily at stake; and although by law it seems that such persons can be employed as witnesses to a will, since only the heir's father and brothers who are in the same power with the heir are excepted (because then a common matter seems to be transacted, as is proved in inst. de testa. ord. § in testibus with the following, and l. qui testamento, ff. eodem supports this), nevertheless, since no notary was employed here, so much credit does not seem to be given to them, since the entire testimony in this case originates from them, especially where there are so many presumptions against the said will; the notable gloss in c. in literis, de testi. supports this. Nor is any account to be made of those women, since they cannot be witnesses to a will, l. haeredes palam, cited above. I conclude therefore that, since in our case there are so many presumptions against the second will that it cannot be believed to have probably emanated at least from a deliberate will of the testator, the nephews ought to prove it by crystal-clear proofs, far greater than those required by law, as I said above. But they cannot prove this; rather, they do not even have the other required proofs, at least with the due solemnities, as I have fully stated above; therefore they must fail. Likewise, given a doubtful state of facts, judgment must be given in favor of a pious and salutary cause for the soul of the deceased, concerning the worship of God and the relief of the poor, as all laws proclaim and natural reason urges. Likewise, given a contradiction and conflict of proofs, one must always stand with what is more probable, as Inn. notes in c. 1 eod. ti. li. 6, and with what accords more with the nature of the matter in question, l. 3, ff. de testi. and 4 q. 3 c. si testes. And let these things suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A father is compelled to endow a daughter by the office of the judge.
2. Whether a statute is valid whereby a penalty is imposed on one contracting marriage with a daughter under paternal power without the consent of the father.
3. Marriage belongs to the forum of the Church.
4. A statute by which marriage would be impeded for a time is not valid.
5. Any administrator is bound by the action on management of affairs to render an account of administration.
casus: The case is as follows: The magnificent Lord John, Duke of Arra., took to wife the magnificent Lady Timbor de Capraria, daughter of Lord Bernard de Capraria, the said Lord Bernard being unwilling to consent, but resisting as much as in him lay, yet with the consent of all the blood-relatives and affines. No dowry had been constituted for her except the promise made by the same Lady Timbor to the said Lord John, in place of a dowry, of all actions belonging to her against her father or another in the name of dowries or of the legitime in the paternal and maternal goods. Then Lord Bernard John de Capraria, legitimate and natural son of the said Lord Bernard, exceeding the twentieth year of his age while his said father was still living, promised the said Lord John to give and assign in the name of his sister's dowry 18,000 Aragonese florins, both before his father died and after he should have obtained his inheritance, and concerning this promise he made a writing written with his own hand and confirmed by the subscription of three witnesses, by the oath, and by the seal of the same Lord Bernard John. Afterwards the said Lord Bernard, the father, died; the son obtained the inheritance and was formally called upon to pay and assign the dowry promised to his sister according to his promise; but he refused to pay, alleging two or three reasons. First, because the said Lady Timbor, his sister, lost every right belonging to her concerning a dowry, since she married against the will of her father. Second, because, since the said Lady Timbor formerly, while her father was living, held and administered for a certain time a county of the Kingdom of Sicily, receiving the revenues and proceeds of the said county, she ought before all else to render an account of administration for what was received. Third, with respect to his own obligation, he answered that he had been a minor and deceived. All things are denied by the adverse party, and it is asked what sort of right belongs to the said Lady Timbor against her said brother. It is asked moreover whether she has any right in the maternal dowry, since the mother died intestate, leaving behind three children, namely the said Lord John Bernard, and the said Lady Timbor, and a certain other Lady Sabena.
body: The patronage of Jesus Christ the Savior and of His pious Mother having been humbly invoked, so that the matter of the present theme may clearly appear, I elicit eight doubts. First, whether the said Lady Timbor, by marrying against the will of her father, lost the capacity to demand a dowry. The second doubt, presupposing that she did not, whether that demand, or imploration of the judge, which was available against the father, is available today against the brother, who succeeded the father in the county. The third, whether the said Lady Timbor can demand the legitime due to her in the father's goods by natural law, and in which goods, understanding that she wishes to desist from the demand for the establishment of a dowry out of the paternal goods. The fourth doubt, what concerning the maternal dowries. The fifth doubt, whether she can demand the legitime of natural law together with the dowry promised to her by her brother, and thus whether the brother is bound out of his own goods by reason of his obligation to pay the aforesaid dowry. The sixth, whether the said Lady Timbor is bound to render an account of administration concerning the revenues of the county, seeing that the father did not demand an account during his lifetime, and it was necessary for her to maintain men-at-arms for the defense of the said county. The seventh doubt, if the legitime does not suffice for the establishment of a dowry according to the dignity of women, presupposing that the brother is not bound by his obligation because he was a minor, whether he can be compelled to endow her according to the dignity of the lady herself because the brother succeeded in the county. The eighth and last, whether the said Lord John is able in effect to liberate himself from his sworn obligation by virtue of minority, by seeking at least absolution from the oath. Once these are discussed, it will be clearly evident and seen what sort of right belongs to the Lady Timbor against her brother. I come to the first, and it seems firstly that she cannot demand a dowry, since by marrying without the father's consent she became so ungrateful to the father himself that she could be disinherited by him: C. de inoffi. test. in auth. & si post, in the body, whence it is taken, as in auth. ut cum de app. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum, ver. si vero. And this civil law seems in effect to have been approved by canon law, as in c. honorantur, 32, q. 2, where it is said that it is not of virginal modesty to seek a husband, but this must be left to paternal care, especially since by this provision is made for the women themselves, who often struggle against their own interests on account of the infirmity of their sex. Nor can she complain about the father because he had not given her in marriage, seeing that she had not then exceeded 25 years of age, as in the said auth.; and it seems most especially that she cannot demand a dowry because, since the father is not bound to endow a daughter except by the provision of civil law, as in l. qui liberos, ff. de ritu nupt. and l. fi. C. de dot. promis., he could, for certain most honorable causes, withdraw that right, gain, or provision introduced by it, even in things accessory to marriage: to this point is the notable gloss in c. cum secundum leges, de haer. in 6.

† Item, the father is compelled to endow the daughter by the office of the judge so that she may find someone whom she can marry, as in the said laws noted by Bart. in l. obligamur, ff. de actio. & obligatio. Therefore, seeing that she is married, the remedy of demanding a dowry fails her, since the reason of the law ceases, as noted by Bar. after others in the said l. obligamur, ff. de actio. & obligatio. To the same point, both reason and the laws compel the father to constitute a dowry for the daughter because no remedy belongs to the daughter in the goods of the father while the father is living; which reason ceases once the father is deceased, since she has or can have the legitime by natural law, of which she could not be deprived by the father without cause: l. scimus and l. quoniam in prioribus, C. de inofficio. testament. and de testa. c. Raynut. and c. Raynald., and in authen. ut cum de appel. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum, pre-alleged. But notwithstanding the aforesaid, I think it should be stated thus: that either the said Lady Timbor married after 25 years of her age, and she can be marked with no ingratitude under civil law, in auth. pre-alleged; or before that age, and the father did not expressly disinherit her on this account, but tolerated her, even pretermitting her in the will, and still ingratitude cannot be objected against the daughter by the heir; rather, she can void the will on account of preterition, concerning which, however, it must be stated as is read and noted in l. omnimodo, C. de inoffi. testa. and in the said auth. ut cum de app. cog. §. si autem haec observata non fuerint. But a doubt arises: what if the father expressly disinherited her for this cause? And in this case I deem that cause not to be sufficient, since by canon law marriage ought to be free from all coercion and penalty: c. cum locum and c. requisivit, de spon. in c. Gemma, with what is noted there, de spon. and in c. pe. and ult. and what is noted thereon, de sec. nup. By the provision of the civil law, not only is the freedom of marriage impeded in waiting for paternal consent, but indeed an occasion is provided to women for committing fornication, since they cannot be joined matrimonially, at least up to 25 years, without the judgment of ingratitude. And for this, the notes of Jo. And. in the said c. statutum, de haere. in 6., where he forms the question, serve exceedingly well.

† Whether a statute is valid by which a penalty is imposed upon one contracting marriage with a filiafamilias without the father's consent. And after many things, he concludes that it is not, because by this statute marriage is intimidated and the free capacity to contract it is impeded.

† Item, because marriage and its cause, as well as its dependencies, pertain to the ecclesiastical forum, since it is a sacrament, especially in the Church: c. debitum, de biga., c. tuam, de ord. cog., and c. lator, qui fil. sint legi.; therefore the civil law or a statute of laymen could not make disposition over it: arg. in l. fi. ff. de iuris. om. iu., c. ut animarum, de consti. li. 6. For we see that on this account many civil laws have been corrected: 30, q. 2, c. uno, and what is noted thereon, and by the doctors in the said c. pen. & ult. de secun. nup.; and by Fed. de Sen. consi. 35, where he says that since marriage is one of the seven sacraments, it ought, together with its accessories and dependencies, to be governed and disposed of by divine and canon law, and not civil law. Nor do the laws hold which require the consent of the father, or that the governor of a province cannot contract with a provincial, or a guardian with his female ward, and the like. To the same point is the notable gloss in c. de puellis, §. quibus verbis, 36, questio. 2, which says that one must not abide by the laws that prohibited marriages from being contracted between a ravished woman and her ravisher. Nor is the law to be obeyed, because since under canon law marriage is lawfully contracted between such persons (de rap. c. cum causam), the legal prohibition and every penalty attached ought to cease. And if anyone should examine rightly, he will say that this is not contrary to the civil law. For in these spiritual matters of this sort and their accessories, those laws are to be understood which say that the laws do not disdain to imitate the sacred canons: in c. clerici, de iudi., and in Auth. ut clerici apud pro. Episcopos, §. pe. col. 6; therefore the disposition of the law is seen to revoke its own opinion if the canon says the contrary: to this point what is noted in the rule possessor, de reg. iu. li. 6, and by Joan. And. in reg. sine culpa, eod. ti., and in the Mercuriales. What more? Concerning this there is the Ordinary Gloss on c. fi. 30, q. 2, and on c. de raptoribus, 36, q. 1, and in both places they maintain that although a daughter married without the father's consent, the father is nonetheless bound to endow her through the said law and through some of the aforesaid reasons, at least where the daughter did not choose someone unworthy of herself; Arch. and others also maintained this there, and Bar. in the said l. obligamur. Limit this, however, to when the daughter promised a dowry, not being able to marry otherwise; because if she found someone whom she married without a dowry, the provision of the law ceases. And maintaining this limitation of Bart., we still attain our purpose in our case, since the Lord John, Duke of Aragon, was unwilling to receive her without a dowry, but rather received the promise or cession belonging to the same lady in this regard, as is set forth above in the narration of fact. Therefore, in this doubt, the said Lady Timbor, from the contract of marriage—especially with the necessary consent having intervened, even though the father resisted—did not lose the right belonging to her to the legitime after the death of the father, as I shall say below, nor the dowry to be demanded from the father, or from another according to the permission of law, since she married a person most worthy in dignity and morals, namely the said Lord John. The contrary law alleged above does not stand in the way. For sufficient answer has been made above to the civil laws. To c. honorantur, it is answered that it speaks of propriety and not of necessity, as noted there in c. 2, the same causa and quaestio, by the gloss and doctors in c. 1, de spon. in prin. For in these spiritual matters, the father's consent is not of necessity to be required: in c. si annum, de iud. lib. 6, and in the said c. sufficit.

† Nor is a statute valid by which the freedom of marriage would be impeded even for a time: in the said l. pe. & ult. de sec. nup. For there also it is evident that the law could not impede marriage, even within the year of mourning, although a most honorable cause underlay it, as there, nor does the penalty attached hold, as there; all the more so ought it not to hold in our case, where it impedes by attaching a penalty or by delaying marriage through the penalty of ingratitude from the time of puberty, that is, from 12 years up to 25, as in the said §. aliud, ver. si vero. The gloss in the said c. cum secundum does not stand in the way, because either it did not speak well, and the gloss of the Decretum holds the contrary in the said §. quibus verbis; or it proceeds only when it takes away only a gain conferred by law, and thus it speaks properly; but in our case a penalty is imposed, since a dowry in a woman is deemed her patrimony, as in l. 3, ff. de minor., and succeeds to her in place of maintenance, according to what is noted in c. cum haberet, de eo, qui duxe. in matrimo. Item, the legitime is owed by natural law, whether the amount or the quota is determined by civil law, according to what is noted in chapter Raynaldus, de testamen., and by Dyn. in the rule in dubio, de regulis iuris, in the sixth book. Therefore, if it were lawful for a father to disinherit a daughter and deny a dowry on the grounds that the daughter married without permission, he would now be imposing a very great penalty; and thus, through fear of this penalty, the freedom of marriage would be taken away, at least for a time. But the imposition of a penalty is not valid in this matter, as that very gloss maintained. To the last contrary argument, it could sufficiently be said that if the permission given to her is sufficient to establish a dowry for her according to her dignity, she cannot sue against her brother as the father's heir to establish a dowry for her, because in this case the reason of the law ceases. For it compels the father to endow the daughter so that she may find someone whom she can marry, according to the notes by Barto. in the said l. obligamur; which reason ceases once the father is dead, since the right of the legitime belonged to her, and she can establish a dowry for herself. For the extraordinary remedy ceases from the moment an ordinary one belongs to her. Nor ought she to have both dowry and legitime out of the paternal goods, as in authen. ex testamento, and l. filiae, C. de coll. And this as to the first doubt, from the examination of which the second remains declared. I come to the third: whether the said Lady Timbor can demand the legitime, and in which goods. And I say briefly that she will be able to demand the legitime if nothing else stands in the way, as is clear from what I said in the first doubt. But there is a doubt out of which goods it is owed, since her father had counties, and other castles, and movable goods. This question is sufficiently decided from the notes by Jo. An. and others in c. licet, de voto. For it must be known that a Kingdom, Duchy, Marquisate, and County are not divided among the sons of the deceased, but are devolved in order of primogeniture on account of the public good, so that there may be one prince. For a multitude of princes is harmful, as the Philosopher attests, and by the order of nature there ought to be one prince: 7, q. 1, c. in apibus. Nor are dignities divided, since they are indivisible. It remains, therefore, that they ought to devolve in direct order to the firstborn, to the exclusion of the other children, as is proved in c. licet; and this is approved by custom and by divine and human law, and is fully noted there by Old. cons. 97. To the same point is what is found in lib. feu. de feu. proh. alie. in c. imperialem, §. praeterea, where it says that the aforesaid dignities ought not to be divided; therefore the said Lady Timbor ought not to be endowed out of the counties, or have a legitime, but ought to leave them to the firstborn in place of his legitime. For a kingdom or county is devolved by hereditary right, as Old. fully disputes and concludes in the aforesaid cons. But out of the remaining movable and immovable goods, she ought to have her legitime together with the other sister; and this legitime will be distinguished according to law based on whether he made a will or not: in auth. novissima, C. de inoffi. test., and l. quoniam in prioribus, and l. scimus, eod. tit. Nor is a distinction to be made in these goods between male and female children, as in l. maximum vitium, C. de lib. praet. in auth. de haere. ab intest. From these things, an inference is drawn for the fourth doubt, what concerning maternal dowries. The answer must be concerning the maternal dowries: for under the common law, all three children ought to succeed equally to their common mother; nor ought the said Bern. John to have preference, because, as I have said, the difference of sex is today removed in this matter, and all succeed equally in the aforesaid rights, as in authen. in successione, C. ad Tertu. To the fifth doubt, whether the said Lady Timbor can demand the legitime owed by natural law and the dowry generously promised to her by her brother, without dwelling much upon allegations, I believe that she can. I am moved by the notable text in l. una, §. accedit, with the following, C. de rei uxo. act., where it says that if a stranger promises or delivers a dowry for a woman, he is deemed to endow her out of his own patrimony. And any person who does not have the woman to be endowed under his power is called a stranger as far as this is concerned, as is singularly held there. Which would proceed even if he is otherwise a debtor of the woman, provided the woman does not manage his affairs, as Bar. notably says after the gloss in l. fi. C. de do. promis. Since, therefore, the said Lord John Bernard, the brother of the said Lady Timbor, his sister, was not managing her affairs at the time the dowry was promised, nor was the said Lady Timbor under his power, he is seen to have promised the dowry from his future patrimony with the intention of making a gift; and this interpretation is especially to be made in the case of one who was alone to succeed to the paternal counties, with the sisters excluded. What is noted in a similar case in l. cum quid, ff. si cer. pe., supports this, because it is characteristic of nobles and counts to give gifts, as noted in cap. 2, de supplen. negli. praela. in 6., and in cap. 1, de dona., especially to their relatives and kin: 86 distinctio, cap. non satis, cap. & si quaestiones, de simo. She can, therefore, demand the dowry from her brother as given to her, and the legitime in the paternal and maternal goods by her own right. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said Lord Bern. John promised the dowry when he had acquired the paternal inheritance, and thus the effect of the promise was destined for the time when he would be managing his sister's affairs; therefore, it ought to be just as if he had promised it then, as in l. quod sponsae, and what is noted there, C. de dona. ante nup., and cap. de uxore, de sepul. For I say that it is necessarily inferred that after the father's death he would have to manage and administer the goods belonging to his said sister, since a brother cannot against his sister's will take all the common goods of the father; and thus that which happens to be absent does not prove this to be the case: l. neque natales, C. de proba., and in c. 2, de transla. praela. Therefore he is not deemed to have felt this when he had possession of the county, because at the time of the promise he had nothing, since he was a filiusfamilias. And if it should be said that this man could not obligate himself since he was a minor filiusfamilias, or at least he can seek restitution in integrum, answer as I shall state below in the last doubt. But l. filiusfamilias, ff. ad Maced., seems to stand against this conclusion, where it is said that where a filiusfamilias receives borrowed money to marry off his sister, an action de in rem verso is brought against the father, because an action for the dowry is acquired for the father upon dissolution of the marriage, and thus it means that the son is not deemed to have given of his own. But I answer that that law speaks of when the son gave the dowry acting in the business of the father. But here that reason ceases, since he promised to give the dowry after the death of the father, and thus he is deemed to have promised it after the death of the father, because the effect of the obligation was deferred to the same time, as in the said l. quod sponsae. I now take up the sixth doubt, whether the said Lady Timbor is bound to render an account of administration, etc.

† And it seems firstly that she is, because any administrator in an actio negotiorum gestorum is bound to render an account of his administration, as in l. 1, §. officio, and there noted, ff. de tute. & ra. distr. To the contrary makes the fact that a daughter is quasi-owner during the father's lifetime: §. sui, Insti. de haere. qua. & diffe., and in l. suis, ff. de libe. & posthu.; therefore she ought not to be bound to render an account like a stranger administrator: arg. in l. 2, ff. re. amota. What shall we say? I indeed consider three cases in this doubt. The first, when it is certain that something from the revenues of the county was with her at the time of the father's death; and certainly that which will come into the division of the father will come into the division of the inheritance to be divided, seeing that she does not prove it was left to her by the father. Nor is it sufficient that the father said nothing during his life, because, since it arises from the paternal estate, it comes to division unless it is proved to have been left. This is proved in l. filiae licet in sacris, C. de col., and l. cum oportet, after the beginning, and especially joined with the gloss, C. de bo. quae lib., l. certum, C. fami. erciscund. And it is excellently proved by the argument a speciali in the said l. cum oportet, §. sin autem res, where in adventitious goods, the usufruct of which is acquired by the father, if the father was unwilling to possess them, but willed them to be in the hands of the son, whose the property is, and said nothing during his life, the father's heirs cannot raise a question against the son concerning the usufruct of those things, since from that long-continued forbearance the father is deemed to have gifted the usufruct to the son, as there. Therefore, in other goods that are not adventitious, but paternal, it is otherwise: to this effect what the gloss notes there after the beginning, and in the said laws alleged above. The second case is when it is proved that a certain thing reached the said Timbor, but it is established that it was consumed during the father's lifetime; and then she is not bound to deduct it in the division, because it ceased to be peculium; for this, the said l. filiae licet in sacris, joined with the last gloss. The third case, when it is proved that a certain thing reached her during the father's lifetime, whether it is presumed to have been present at the time of the father's death, so that she would thus compute it into her legitime, can well be doubted. For I think it sufficient that if she alleges consumption, she is bound to show for what cause she consumed it: an excellent argument in the said l. cum oportet, ver. sed in hac specie, where a special rule is established in the father who administers the adventitious goods of his son, whose usufruct is acquired by him, that he is not bound to render an account. It is otherwise, therefore, in the son, who does not make the usufruct his own, so that he ought to render an administration in paternal goods. If, therefore, there is a special rule there in the father, and on account of the free administration which he had in adventitious goods, it is otherwise, therefore, in the son with respect to paternal goods. To the same point is the said §. sin autem res, arguing also by the argument a speciali, as above; to this point makes l. tres fratres, ff. de pact., and l. si soror, C. de coll. I think, however, that that strict accounting is not to be demanded from her as from a stranger, by reason of consanguinity, but it is enough that she show generally how much she could plausibly have expended on mercenaries; item, for her household and similar things; nor is she bound to show specifically how much she spent per day on dogs or similar things, for the aforesaid reason. Nor is it necessary to produce witnesses, but it suffices that she plausibly incurred expenses, as noted in a similar case by Innocen. in cap. cum & plantare, de privileg. The seventh doubt was: if the legitime does not suffice to endow the said Lady Timbor according to her dignity, whether the said Lord Bernard John is bound to endow her, because he is a brother, and because of his succession to the county? The presumption is that he is not bound by his obligation. In this doubt I conclude briefly for the affirmative part, namely that he is bound by a twofold bond. First, because he is the father's heir; for he takes the county by hereditary right, as I said above; just as, therefore, the father himself was bound to this, as I said in the first doubt, so also his heir: to this point, l. postulante, and what is noted, ff. ad Trebelia., and l. quaedam sunt personae, §. nihil interest, de eden., and l. veteres, C. de contrahen. & commit. stipu. To the same point is what is noted by Joann. Andr. and Hostiens. in capitul. licet, de voto, where he says that although the firstborn alone succeeds in the county, yet other children ought not on this account to beg, but as much is to be granted to them by the firstborn as that from which they may live: an argument in l. 1, ff. de tute. & ra. distra. post principium. If, therefore, he is bound to maintain them, therefore also to endow a woman, since the cause of dowry and that of maintenance are equal, as noted by Cyn. in l. non omni, C. de admi. tuto., and noted in l. si quis a liberis, ff. de liber. agno. The said Bern. John is therefore bound to endow the said Lady Timbor as the father's heir, if her legitime does not suffice, and if she does not have goods from elsewhere. Under the second head, he is bound as a brother; and this insofar as the said Lady Timbor did not have the means from which to endow herself, as is read and noted in l. cum plures, ff. de admi. tuto., and by the gloss and Cy. in the said l. non omni. It is more useful, therefore, for the said Lady Timbor, insofar as her legitime does not suffice, and in the case where the said Lord Bern. John is not suitable, that she sue as against the father's heir rather than as against a brother for the aforesaid reason. The last doubt was whether the said Lord Bernard John is able in any way to liberate himself from that obligation of paying the dowry, by seeking at least absolution from the oath. And certainly this article could be much doubted, on account of those things which are held and noted in cap. cum contingat, de iureiur., and in auth. sacramenta puberum, C. si adver. ven., and in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideius., and I have spoken most fully in a certain disputation of mine which begins stante statuto etc. But here I will pass over it lightly, touching upon this article only decisively. And first, I say the said Lord Bernard John is bound by that promise of his. First, through l. filiusfamilias, ff. de act. & obli., and ff. ad Maced. l. si filiusfamilias, §. 1, where it is clear that a filiusfamilias is regularly bound by a contract or quasi-contract provided he does not receive borrowed money, and especially in this case, where the effect of the contract was related to the time when he would be sui iuris: l. in tempus, ff. de haered. instituen. Nor did minority stand in the way, because the oath represented him as an adult, as in the said authen. sacramenta puberum, and capitul. 1, de deli. puer. Nor can he seek restitution in integrum by reason of minor age, because he is not deemed a minor once the oath has intervened, as in the said authen. sacramenta puberum, with the notes; both because restitution is not available there against one's own oath, although absolution from it is sometimes granted, as Innocen. remarkably says in capitul. 2, de iureiurand., but against the oath of another restitution in integrum is indeed given to a minor, as in l. nam & postea, ff. de mino. Whether, however, upon requesting it, he ought to be absolved from that oath, many things could be alleged pro and contra. But in this case I believe he is not to be heard, since this oath contains no turpitude on the part of the one swearing, or on the part of the recipient. For it is not shameful that he who was to succeed in two counties should promise a dowry of 10,000 Aragonese florins for his sister. Nor does the sister receive the obligation shamefully, since she is excluded from succession to those dignities, as I said above; and because it is characteristic of nobles to give gifts, especially to their own kin and household, as in the laws pre-alleged. Therefore, this oath must necessarily be observed by him; and the Pope could not absolve from an oath lawfully taken when a known cause subsists, since an oath is of divine law, as noted by Innocen. in capitul. cum in contemplatione, de reg. iuris, and the gloss and doctors in capitul. autho. 15, quaest. 6; the gloss in capitul. non est, on the word authoritate, de vot., and the text in capitul. & si Christus, de iureiurand., support this. There is no deceit here, especially in the matter itself or by design, such that it also concludes what is presumed: argument in l. omnes, §. Lucius, ff. de his, quae in fraud. cre., and l. creditor, §. Lucius, ff. mand., and l. qui testamentum, de probat., and l. si quis cum aliter, ff. de verbo. oblig. In which case, by reason of minor age and enormous lesion, absolution from the oath could perhaps be sought, as noted by some in the said capitul. cum contingat, and in capitul. 2, de pact. in 6., and capitul. 1, de iureiuran., supports this. I say, however, that here there is no such deceit, but none at all, if one considers the quality of the promisor and of her to whom the promise was made, and the time of the promise, and the closest kinship between them, which things are to be considered in every donation, as in c. & si quaestiones, de simo., and capit. magnae, de voto; l. si servus communis, ff. de dona. inter virum & uxo., and what is noted in the said l. cum quid, ff. si cer. pet., support this.
