Whether, however, that exception—that she first render an account of the administration of the paternal goods—ought to stand against this demand for a dowry? I believe that it does not, since in this case proceedings are not conducted by the action familiae erciscundae, in which case l. filiae, licet in sacris, C. de colla., has a place, but from the earlier promise of the Lord Bernard John himself, and between what is liquid and what is not liquid there is no set-off: l. fin. C. de compen., with what is noted there, especially since this question concerning administration could not be resolved within as much time as that in which the said promise was to be executed, according to what is noted by Bartol. in l. aufertur, §. qui compensationem, ff. de iure fisci. Nor does it stand in the way that the obligation was reduced to a private writing. For it is sufficient that proof can be made that it was of the said Lord Bernard John, according to the matter of l. comparationes, C. de fide instrumento., and l. scripturas, C. qui pot. in pig. hab., especially since this is his seal, as by Innocen. in c. 2, de fide instrumento., a case in c. tertio loco, de proba., and especially in our case, where a favorable matter is at issue: arg. l. 1, §. accedit, C. de rei uxo. act., with what is noted there. From all the aforesaid, therefore, I conclude that the said Lady Timbor can demand a third part in the paternal goods, or a third part according to the aforesaid definition, whether the will made by the father is valid or not. Item, the dowry promised to her by her brother. Item, that in the event that her said brother is not found to be bound in his own name, and the legitime belonging to her in the paternal goods does not suffice to endow her according to the condition of her person, she can sue against the brother as against the father's heir to make up the dowry, just as the father himself was bound; he can also be compelled as a brother where all remedies fail her, as is fully clear from the aforesaid.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument: 1. Equity must always be observed in doubtful matters.
body: The case is this: A certain woman, having at the same time a male and a female child by her predeceased husband, married a second husband, by whom she bore two daughters. While he was surviving, she closed her last day, having first made a testament in which, in all her goods, both in pre-legacies and in instituting heirs, she made all the children, both of the first and of the second marriage, equal, except in a fourth part of her goods; for she had previously conferred this inter vivos upon the daughters of the second marriage. After the death of the said lady, all the daughters and the male son intermeddled together in the inheritance in good harmony, collecting many hereditary debts, and selling certain goods, each receiving a portion pro rata according to the institution and the pre-legacy. Now the son of the first marriage wishes to exclude from the succession his pre-legatee sister and full blood-relative by virtue of the statutes, concerning which a legal dispute arises. And first, it seems that only the son ought to succeed to the whole of the said mother, the sister being excluded; which seems to be proved by joining two statutes: namely, that under the rubric "That women having etc.," which begins "If any woman endowed by her father"—such as was the said sister against whom the action is brought—cannot succeed to her mother intestate, even though a male son survives from her. But this deceased mother seems in effect to have died intestate in respect of three parts of her goods, as is gathered from the second statute cited above, where it is said that a woman having sons or daughters cannot leave or donate beyond the fourth part of her goods, but may dispose of the fourth part to the prejudice of the male son. The rubric of that statute supports this; and it is lawful to argue from the rubric, since it does not openly contradict the black letter, as is fully noted by Io. An. in addi. Spe. in tit. de dispu. & alle. in fi., and by gl. de pœ. dif. 1. § hæc autem uerba, and C. etiam ob chiro. pe. pi. re. po. super rub., and C. ne fideius. dot. den., and l. una, C. de prose. qui in urbe Constan. li. 12, with many similar texts. Item, the rationale of the statute excluding dowered daughters from succession was that the dignity of agnation might be preserved; to this effect l. 1. § sed si seruus, ff. de uen. inspi., and by Bar. in l. 2. C. quæ sit lon. consue. But certainly this same rationale does not seem to have been present in the second statute, that a woman cannot dispose beyond a fourth part, and that the remaining three parts be divided among the children pro rata: therefore it is sufficient that the woman disposed inter vivos of the fourth part. Of the three parts, therefore, she could not dispose of anything, as in the rubric of the statute, and consequently she seems to have died intestate regarding them, ar. in l. 1. ff. de hær. insti. But notwithstanding these points, which if well weighed do not stand in the way, I think the contrary is truer in law. And first, this sister has her intention grounded for her out of the testament with the foundation of the ius commune, in Auth. ut cum de ap. cog. § aliud quoque capitulum, and C. ad Orfi. l. si qua illustris. Let us see therefore now whether the aforesaid statutes intend to exclude her. And for the negative part I first bring forward almost all statutes which speak of the inheritance of one dying intestate and reserve the voluntary disposition of the father or mother; therefore, the woman herself having made disposition, the daughters could succeed with the males, ar. in l. cum prætor, ff. de iud., 25. dist. c. qualis, de præsump. c. nonne, and l. commodissimè, ff. de lib. & posth.; and especially because ancient laws ought not to be corrected so far as they may be found compatible, C. de ap. l. præcipimus. Nor through implications ought a correction of the law to be introduced, as is noted by glo. in c. cupientes, § cæterum, de ele. li. 6. Whence statutes, lest the ius commune be corrected, ought to be understood most strictly, and restricted as much as possible, de iureiu. c. in nostra; c. 1. & 2. de fil. presb. li. 6 is to the point. Nor ought they to be extended through similarity of rationale, l. quod verò contra rationem, ff. de legi., by Bar. in auth. quas actiones, C. de sac. san. ec. Nor does that statute cited above stand in the way, which seems to take away from the woman the power of disposing of the three parts, because if well weighed, it does not stand in the way. For it says that a woman having sons, or daughters, etc.; thus it willed to provide not only for male children, but also for females. Item, it does not simply take away the power of disposing of the three parts, but with the limitation: if by her disposition the children should be deprived. And so she cannot dispose, except of her own part, when the children would be deprived of the succession, so that those three parts would not come to them. The statute therefore willed to prohibit only an inofficious or indiscreet maternal will or disposition, but it did not will to take away a just disposition conforming to the laws, when she disposes equally among her children. It is no objection if it be said that the statute mentions only males when it said "so that the sons [filii] would be deprived etc.," because in those words females are comprehended: both because the masculine comprehends the feminine in this almost favorable conclusion, according to what is noted in l. 1. ff. de uer. sig., and by Arch. in c. si quis suadente, 17. q. 4, and by Cy. in l. quicunque, C. de ser. su.; and because since at the beginning it made mention of daughters, the word "sons" [filii] comprehends also the daughter, an excellent argument in l. qui filiabus, ff. de le. 1. It is no objection that the rubric similarly says that women having sons should not leave beyond the fourth part, because when in these words the dispositive part speaks more generally and more specifically and by assigning the cause, the rubric must be supplemented and understood according to the black letter, as is the notable gloss in l. 1. C. etiam ob chiro. pe. pi. re. po., and there noted, and noted in auth. ad hæc, C. de usu. in gl., and by the doctors in the prologue of the Decretals. And five considerations favor this understanding. First, because through this understanding favor is shown to the testament, which is exceedingly to be favored, as here in c. cum dilecti, de don., and l. 1. C. de sacros. ecc., and de re iud. c. ult., where the text is excellent. Second, there is less departure from the ius commune, and we ought always under a title to restrict the words of a statute so that they harm the ius commune less, when they can, especially where prejudice is involved, as is the notable text in c. cum dilectus, de consue., and the said c. in nostra, and the said l. quod verò, ff. de legi., supports this. Third, not so great a distinction is made between male and female, and thus we offend less against l. maximum uitium, C. de lib. potest. Fourth, daughters will not be excluded to such an extent from maternal goods; and thus on their part there is favor, on the part of the son there is odium, since the daughters themselves are striving not to lose this quasi-natural right, and the son is striving to acquire a right, and capturing gain and losing what has been acquired are not on a par nor of the same rationale, l. si sponsus, § si maritus, ff. de do. inter ui. & uxo.

† Fifth and finally, because in doubtful matters we must always follow equity, l. placuit, C. de iud., and tran sa. c. ult., ff. de eo, quod cer. lo. l. quod si Ephesi, in fin. The statute, therefore, intended to provide for the children upon intestacy. It is otherwise, therefore, when the mother herself wishes to dispose of her goods equally among all the children, etc., as is clear from the aforesaid; notwithstanding what I said above about preserving the right of agnation, etc., because in truth there is not the same rationale when she has died intestate as when she wishes to make a testament, because the greatest prejudice would be done to the woman by taking away from her the power of testating, as in l. 1. C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi. Item, the reasons cited above stand in the way. And let these things suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If an exception is raised against an appellant that he appealed in cases not granted by law, the judge must take cognizance of this before all else.
2. Wherever jurisdiction is denied through the raising of a declinatory exception, the judge must before all else pronounce upon it tacitly or expressly.
3. If declinatory exceptions are true, the proceedings on the principal matter do not hold, and why.
4. Where a judgment gives rise to an exception in one cause, it ought not to be accumulated at the same time in another.
body: IN the name of the undivided Trinity, amen. In the cause or question pending between Andrea di Antonio of Arezzo on the one part, and Lazzaro di Tommaso of Consuma on the other part, concerning the petition for the reduction of a certain award rendered between them to the judgment of a fair-minded man: having examined all things produced before me, I conclude upon this point, and briefly upon that alone which was inquired into, namely: whether, if the said Lazzaro was aggrieved, he can have recourse through the judge in that—when the same Lazzaro excepted that there was no room for reduction to the judgment of a fair-minded man, and that the said judge could not hear the aforesaid Andrea on many grounds and especially because a municipal law stood in the way—the said judge fixed a term for the said parties to substantiate the aforesaid matters, and thus pronounced that they should proceed to the further merits of the cause, saving however and reserving to each party all and singular their exceptions and oppositions, and those of either of them, which ought to be reserved and are to be reserved, and can be reserved to the parties themselves and to either of them, as is gathered more fully from the said acts, which are here taken as expressed insofar as they touch upon this point. And it seems first that no grievance was inflicted upon the same Lazzaro from that interlocutory decision or fixing of a term alone; which is proved thus. Upon any incidental exception, the judge must pronounce either tacitly, namely by proceeding to a further act contrary to the exception, or expressly through his interlocutory decision, according to what is read and noted in c. 1 de ord. cog. and l. 1 C. de ord. iud. Nor does it matter whether the judge pronounces upon it expressly or tacitly by passing on to further matters, as is proved in cap. ex parte M. de appell. and there by the doctors, and Ioan. And. in c. dilecti, under the same title, and Bart. in l. a procedente, C. de dila. And for that reason there is need to appeal if the party feels himself aggrieved by the preterition, or else the act passes into res judicata, as is fully noted in the places alleged above. But in our case, the judge, by setting a term upon the merits of the cause, seems to have rejected the exception of the adverse party and thus to have issued an interlocutory decision upon it; therefore the law has been satisfied. Nor can he be said to inflict a grievance solely from the fact that he rejected the exception, since the power of rejecting or admitting an exception which seems to him ought to be rejected is granted to the judge; nor does he inflict a grievance solely from the fact that he rejected a probable exception, because he could have been moved by a just cause not to admit it. Innocen. expressly notes this in cap. post electionem, de concess. præbend. near the end, and Ioan. And. in cap. super eo, il. 1. de appella.; this is proved in capitul. interposita, under the same title, where it is clear that an appeal interposed from the rejection of a probable exception is not justified merely by proving that a legitimate exception was raised and not admitted, but it is necessary that the truth of the exception itself be proved; and there it is expressly said that this arises from no other reason than the aforesaid rationale. So I shall say in the proposed matter: unless the truth is proved—that is, that there was no room for reduction to the judgment of a fair-minded man—the grievance is not proved from that pronouncement alone. Secondly, it seems to be proved more clearly thus: this judge reserved to the parties, and to each of them, the proposed exceptions; therefore he prejudiced no one, since each one's right remains preserved, and that he was able to do this is found in the text in c. ad dissoluendum, de despon. impu.; c. Cumana, de elect. with the notes there supports this; therefore, etc. But notwithstanding these points, which truly do not stand in the way, I think the contrary. And first I adduce the text in c. Roma. § si uero, with the two preceding paragraphs, de app. lib. 6, where it is said,

† that if it is excepted against the appellant that he appealed in cases not granted by law, the judge must before all else take cognizance of this: whether, an appeal having been interposed in this way, jurisdiction has devolved upon him. To the same effect is what is held in the preceding paragraph. But in this case jurisdiction was denied. Indeed, the exception was that recourse had been made to the judge in a case forbidden by a statute of the city, and thus jurisdiction is denied; therefore this ought to have been inquired into before he made a transition to the merits of the cause. For this petition for reduction is a species of appeal, as in l. non distinguemus, § cum quidam, ff. de arb., noted in l. societatem, § arbitrorum, ff. pro soc., and in c. Quintauallis, de iureiuran. Secondly it is proved thus:

† wherever jurisdiction is denied by the objection of a declinatory exception, the judge must before all else pronounce upon it tacitly or expressly, as noted by Io. An. and others in c. 1 de ord. cog. Nor ought a transition to the merits of the cause be made beforehand, even with exceptions reserved. This is proved in c. si clericus laicum, de fo. compe.; l. si, C. de excep. supports this; noted in c. inter monasterium, de re iud. and by Bar. in l. quidam consulebat, ff. eod. tit.; and it is proved in l. si quis ex aliena, ff. de iud. and in l. 2 si quis in ius uoc., noted in both places, and by Inn. in c. super literis, de rescrip., and the gloss in c. 1 de off. dele. li. 6, and in c. Romana, de pœnis, eod. li. But in our case such an exception was raised, by which the jurisdiction of the judge was declined; therefore the judge inflicted a grievance by not pronouncing upon it beforehand. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that he pronounced tacitly by passing on to further matters, because he did not pronounce even tacitly here, since he reserved the exceptions to the parties; and thus that reservation harmed rather than helped. For if he had pronounced expressly by rejecting the exceptions of Lazzaro, or tacitly by passing on to the act of hearing without that reservation of the exception, then, to see whether he inflicted a grievance, it would be necessary to consider the statutes and all the arguments alleged, according to what I said above. But in our case it is not necessary to examine this, because by that very fact he inflicted a grievance, that he wished to hear the merits of the award before having pronounced whether jurisdiction belonged to him; and this I declare thus: For either he wished to hear those declinatory exceptions and the merits of the cause together, simultaneously and at once, and a certain contradiction results—for regarding the declinatory exception he says they must proceed, and in proceeding to further matters he says the contrary, and this is directly against the text of c. exhibita, de iud., and c. tuam, de ord. cog., and c. lator, qui filij sint legit., and Fed. consi. 221 touches upon this; or he wished first to proceed upon the merits of the award and afterwards upon the declinatory exceptions, and the order is perverted and preposterous, from which perversion either the process is rendered null, because it is a perversion of the order of the same cause according to what is fully noted in l. prolatam, C. de sen., or at least it gives the ability to appeal according to l. 1 C. de appel. and the notes in c. 2 de ordi. cogn. For he inflicts no small grievance upon the parties.

† For if the declinatory exceptions are true, the process on the principal matter will not stand, since the judge did not first pronounce upon his jurisdiction, as fully noted by Inn. in c. præterea, de dila. and by Io. And. on the rule sine possessione, de reg. iur. lib. 6 in the Mercuriales; the parties would therefore be found to have litigated in vain, and how grievous this is, everyone has felt. Likewise, and thirdly, the matter of joinder stands in the way, concerning which see l. edita, C. de eden., and l. fundi, l. fundum, and l. sed & si, ff. de exce.

† For wherever a judgment on one cause produces an exception in another, they ought not to be joined together, as in the laws alleged above. But so it was in our case; for if it is pronounced that the statute stands in the way of the exception for reduction to the judgment of a fair-minded man, or that the agreement has no place, the exception stands in the way of the hearing or the clearing of the award; therefore, etc. And by this the first contrary arguments remain resolved. For I say that the judge did not pronounce upon those exceptions even tacitly, on account of the reservation of the exception. Likewise, although he did not inflict a grievance by not rejecting the exceptions, he nevertheless inflicted a grievance in that he wished to make a transition to the merits of the cause before the declinatory exceptions were discussed and examined. Anto. de But. expressly held this in c. exhibita, in the first column, where he says that such a transition ought not to be made with exceptions reserved. And all hold this, although there was variation among the doctors as to whether the process stands if an appeal and exception have not been interposed; which I pursue more fully there, but do not touch upon here, because it is not relevant to the purpose. I conclude, therefore, that this Lazzaro was aggrieved by that pronouncement, and consequently in all other acts subsequent to it concerning the merits of the award. And yet by this I do not conclude that the said Andrea maintains an injustice on the principal matter; for it was not entrusted to me to advise whether reduction of that award to good equity could be sought, but solely whether the said Lazzaro was aggrieved by the pronouncement of the judge; and I have said that he was, by the aforesaid matters, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A contract is to be judged by the principal intention of the contracting parties, when in one and the same contract two kinds of contract intervene, or two things proportional to different contracts.
2. Usury does not arise from a true contract of lease, but only from a pure contract of loan.
3. Usury is gain owed by agreement, or exacted, from a loan.
body: IN the name of Jesus Christ, and of his Mother. The question is asked whether the aforesaid contract is usurious, since beyond the lease the lessor bound himself to lend ten Florins for the period of six years during which the lease is to endure, and thus in executing the obligation he actually lent them; and it seems at first that it is. For whatever is joined to a loan by a preceding agreement or a subsequent action, whatever that may be, is usury, 14. q. 3. c. 2. & 3.; indeed, the mere hope of obtaining something from a loan, followed by the giving, makes a man a usurer, as in the Gospel of Luke: “Lend, hoping for nothing thereby,” and derivatively in c. consuluit, de vsu. But in our case an estimable real advantage arises from that loan, since otherwise that lessee would not have bound himself to establish so great a rent. Therefore it is a usurious contract, since whatever is added to the principal on the part of the recipient is usury, as in the aforementioned laws. Likewise, it was agreed, while the loan was to be gratuitous, yet with the intention of having a higher rent; therefore, etc. To the same point makes c. si quis obiecerit, 1. q. 3, where it says that if I sell one of two things, without which the other does not come about, the other is also deemed sold. But in our case so great a rent would not have been established with respect to the lease, unless the loan had intervened. Therefore, the whole contract can be called usurious. But notwithstanding these points, which seem to stand in the way, I think the contrary is true in law. And first, it must be subtly considered.

† That wherever from one and the same contract two kinds of contracts, or two things proportional to different contracts, intervene, the contract is to be judged by the principal intention of the contracting parties; where the intention is not apparent, one must have recourse to conjecture; and this Io. And. expressly maintained in c. ad quæstiones, de re. pmu., and Bart. in l. Arist., de dona.; Cyn. held this in l. cum te, C. de pact. inter emp. & uen.; and it is proved in l. tenetur, C. de act. emp., and in l. si tibi, ff. si cert. peta., and l. quicquid, de acq. re. do., and in the said c. ad quæstiones. There it is clear that a contract of exchange is not judged to be of another kind, regard being had to the specific thing that intervened, but rather a sale, regard being had to the money and the principal intention of the contracting parties, insti. de emp. & uen. §. pretium. So conversely, if I exchanged my property for yours, and because mine was worth more you added a certain quantity of money, it is not judged a purchase on account of the price which comes accessorily, but an exchange on account of the specific things exchanged and the principal intention of those wishing to exchange, as is proved in the said c. ad quæstiones, and noted by Bart. in the said l. Arist. So I say to the purpose: in that contract in which two things having a diverse nature intervened, namely letting and hiring, much is conjectured from the agreement. We ought therefore to judge this contract according to the intention of the contracting parties as a letting and hiring, and it clearly appears from the words of the contract, although the loan enters accessorily to serve the lessee himself, so that he may better inhabit the leased property. Therefore, the profit proceeding therefrom ought not to be attributed to the loan, but to the lease. But even presupposing and not conceding that here the intention of the contracting parties is not apparent, nevertheless this is gathered evidently by conjectures. First, because before the obligation of the loan was submitted, the lessee had already bound himself from the contract of the lease of the vineyard to that farm-rent or rent for the vineyard alone. Nor is anything said to be by reason of the loan. Likewise, the leased property itself is far more valuable than the quantity of the loan. Likewise, that it was agreed that he could return the loaned money at any time, nor is anything thereby diminished from the rent established by reason of the lease. And this is the greatest conjecture: because the rent was not established with respect to the loan; otherwise, it would have been agreed that upon repayment of the loan the rent would be diminished, at least proportionally. Likewise, that lessor could not demand the return of the loan at any time during the duration of the lease. Therefore, it was made by reason of the lease; otherwise, he could have demanded it back at any time, as is of the nature of a loan. So much so that it can be said that it is not altogether a true loan, or it does not have all its incidentals or naturals of the contract. To this point, see what is noted by the Gloss in l. si pœnam, ff. de uer. obl., in the said l. si tibi, ff. si cer. pe. What further? Let the custom of the region be looked to, in which to a sharecropper something is almost always provided, so that he may better manage himself; to this point, de pig. c. illo uos, and l. quia semissem, ff. de usufr., and ff. de ædil. edi. l. quod si nolit, §. quia assidua, and what Bart. notes in l. nemo est, qui nesciat, ff. de duo. reis.

† Furthermore, usury does not arise from a contract of lease, but only from a pure contract of loan, as in c. eijciens, 88. dis. Fully noted by Io. An. in regula peccatum, de reg. iu. li. 6. in Mercu. The fact that a loan intervened does not stand in the way. For by a stipulation one can bind oneself to lend, as in the said l. si pœnam, ff. de uer. obl.; whence this man bound himself, so that the other might more easily manage himself in the leased property. This same point is proved in the previously cited c. ad quæstiones, joined with what is noted there by Inn., where it is clear that one church with its possessions can be exchanged for another church and its possessions; and if one abounds in possessions, money may lawfully be refunded by the other party. Nor by this is it said to be given for a spiritual right, but rather for the estates, provided that the contracts are separate, at least as to nature, as Inn. says there, since they do not intend to mix money with spiritual matters, but for temporal matters. So I say to the purpose: since the rent is not established for the loan itself, but for the leased property, as is clearly gathered from the contract and the aforesaid words of the contract. The intervention of the loan does not stand in the way, since I can give you money with the condition that you lend it to me, said l. si tibi. So I can establish for you a certain rent from your property leased to me, with the condition that you give me a certain quantity. Nor do I intend to establish the rent from the loan, but I want this prerogative and advantage from you; for with that money I can do many good things, even with the leased property, and gather far more abundant fruits. Likewise and lastly, in our case the definition of usury is lacking; therefore, the thing defined is also lacking, as is noted on the rub. de sum. tri. and insti. de ob. in princ.

† For usury is profit owed or exacted from a loan by agreement, as is noted in the said regula peccatum. But here the profit does not proceed from the loan, but from the lease itself, as appears in the contract and from the aforesaid; therefore, it is not usury. Moreover, to judge a contract usurious, as in the contentious forum, the form of the contract must be looked to, as in c. ciuitate, de usur. But this contract by its form is of letting and hiring. The contrary arguments alleged above do not stand in the way: because I deny that the rent is established here by reason of the loan, but rather by reason of the leased property. Nor is anything given here principally on the occasion of the loan, but all is attributed to the lease, even though the lessee wished for this advantage from the lessor, so as to make there some advance to endure during the time of the lease, perhaps so that he might buy oxen, implements, or the like. I conclude, therefore, that the contract is not to be judged usurious by its form, but of letting and hiring, etc. Nico. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Two witnesses suffice in proving any matter.
2. A notary testifying upon any case does not create greater faith than one witness.
body: Invoking the name of Christ, for a clear decision of the present doubt three things must be examined. First, whether the said Donatus is held to the commune of Castilione as an institor of the commune itself, or of the said Andreas. Second, whether at least he is obligated by reason of his promise, which he is said to have made to the said commune according to the confession of the aforesaid deponents; which is to ask whether the statements of those witnesses fully prove the said fact. Third, whether at least, with all else failing, Donatus is held by reason of the sequestration which is said to have been made against him by the chancellor of the commune of Castilione. A fourth could be added: whether, if the aforesaid are not sufficient distributively to prove the intention of the said commune, they prove it at least collected into one. And first with respect to the first point, it seems that the said Donatus would be obligated as an institor. For an institor is obligated from contracts managed by him, even after his office has expired, since that office is voluntary; just as we say in the case of a procurator and the like, as noted by the glo. and Bar. in l. procurator quod, C. de proc., where the text seems to say this, and in l. seruum Titij, ff. mand., although certain authorities held the contrary. But the first seems to be the common opinion; and this the glo. seems to hold in c. sicut, 48. dist. But the aforesaid Donatus was an institor of the commune or of the said Andreas; which is proved. For an institor is one who is placed in charge of another's profit-making business, as in l. institor, and l. quicunque, ff. de instit., fully by Inn. in c. quod quibusdam, de fideiuss. But the said Donatus was placed in charge of the salt business by the said Andreas, and thus was his institor, and consequently stands obligated to the community of Castilione, and to anyone else by reason of the contract, l. 1, ff. de exerci. It can be said that he was an institor of the community of Castilione, insofar as he conducted its business and sold salt in its name. But notwithstanding these things, which truly do not stand in the way, I think the contrary is true in law. For an institor is not held, nor does that actio institoria arise, against him, or against the principal, except with respect to a contract entered into by him within the office assigned to him. Hence when either element is lacking, the said action ceases; and so in our case it ceases. For the said Donatus was only placed in charge of selling salt at retail, but not of buying it, nor of receiving salt from the commune of Florence or from any other person. Therefore he cannot be held as an institor from a contract made by Andreas, his master; this is express in the previously cited l. quicunque, ff. de instito., in § non tamen omne, where it is said that if someone was placed in charge of selling, he is only held insofar as he sold, but not if he bought; and likewise vice versa. Item, an institor is not obligated except insofar as he himself contracted within the office assigned to him, as in l. 1, de exerci., but not from every circumstance. But in our case the said Donatus did not contract with the commune of Castilione, nor could he contract with it by virtue of his office, since he was only placed in charge of selling salt at retail, and he did not sell salt to the said commune, nor did he buy from it, nor could he have bought as an institor, since he would have exceeded the scope of his office. Therefore only the said Andreas will be obligated, insofar as he himself contracted as an institor by selling salt, and thus from the office over which he had been placed. Nor can it be said that he was an institor of the said commune, since he was not placed in charge of any business by the commune itself. Therefore he was not its institor, d. l. institor, and l. quicunque. Nor did he manage the business of the commune, but only that of Andreas himself. Nor can he be said to be obligated to the commune on the ground that the salt belonged to the commune itself, because by the sale and delivery made to Andreas himself, ownership of that salt was acquired by Andreas, l. traditionibus, C. de pac. But presupposing, though not conceding, that the salt itself had remained in the ownership of the said commune, nevertheless the money proceeding therefrom is not the commune's, but rather his who sold it, or in whose name he sold it, l. si pecunia, C. si quis alteri, vel sibi. Hence Donatus more rightly paid the money to the said Andreas, nor is he held in anything to the said commune. For he is obligated to Andreas by reason of the contract even from the delivery of another's property, l. si urbana, ff. de cond. ind., Innocen. in c. in literis, de testi., where he notes by d. l. that one who pays the lessor of another's property is released, since he is held to the said lessor by reason of the contract. Nor can he be sued by the owner of the property, because he made no contract with him. Secondly, principally relevant are the notes by the doctors and the glo. in c. Michael, de vsur. It is concluded by the common opinion that a mere minister for exercising usury is not obligated to restitution, since he was solely appointed to lend and receive profit; therefore beyond that which he manages an obligation does not arise, although the gl. in d. c. sicut held otherwise, basing itself on the fact that he managed a matter condemned by the law. But in our case it does not seem to agree with the intention of the law that this Donatus be held, since he conducted a lawful matter, and was a mere minister to sell salt at retail, because neither tacitly nor expressly, but only for this was he appointed; nor did he conduct anything with the commune. Therefore he ought not to be obligated to the commune for the price of the salt, or for the payment of the gabelle. From the contrary it would follow as to the second point that a mere minister would be obligated in those matters which he conducted with his master outside the office appointed above, contrary to l. in omnibus negociis, ff. de act. & obl. And this as to the first, and as to the second, whether he is obligated by reason of the asserted promise. But whether the asserted promise is proved by the statements of those witnesses, it seems that it is. For realistically in proving any matter two witnesses suffice, even by divine law, as in the Gospel, in the mouth of two or three, etc. And it is found in the law in many places, in c. licet, lo primo, de testi., and 2. q. 4. throughout, and the laws on this are quite familiar, but in our case there are not only two witnesses, but far more. For there are four, who were then among the priors of the said town, who can testify in a case of the community, as is proved in c. insuper, and c. cum nuncius, de testi., and cap. & si Christus, in fi., de iureiu., and 14. q. 2. super prudentia, and especially in business matters that are transacted within the community itself, ar. tex. in l. consensu, C. de rep., in favor of which is in l. parentes, C. de testi., and c. veniens, il 2., de testi., in c. tertio loco, de proba. Item, there are present here two other witnesses, who heard the said Donatus saying that he was obligated to the said commune and to the aforesaid Andreas; they do not fully prove by themselves, because they depose concerning enunciative words uttered on account of another matter, in c. si papa, de priuil. li. 6., noted in l. ex hac scriptura, ff. de dona., and in c. fi., de suc. ab intest.; nevertheless they introduce a presumption, which greatly aids the statement of the other witnesses, in favor of which is a good text with gl. in c. illud, de præsump., and in c. cum olim, de censi., and it is proved in d. c. fi. Item, there is present, or concurs, the statement of the chancellor, who says that he often heard the said Andreas, the principal, in the council-hall, [saying] that the said Donatus should pay the commune. But notwithstanding these things, I think that it is not fully proved from the statements of those witnesses that the said Donatus obligated himself to the commune. For the said men, who were among the priors at that time, can be rejected from testifying in multiple ways. First, because wherever individual members of a corporation depose in favor of the corporation in an act that subsequently turns to the favor of the advantage or disadvantage of the individual members of the corporation, they are not suitable witnesses, because in effect they would be deposing regarding their own deed, and they obtain an advantage. This is proved by natural reason. For we must look to the effect of the matter, as the doctors most clearly hold, and especially Ioann. Andr. in the previously cited capitul. cum nuncius, and in dict. l. parentes, where he says that if a community contends over the pastures of the community itself, where the pastures of the individuals are located, those of the corporation are not suitable witnesses. And this applies most especially in a secular corporation. For individual members are not devoid of affection toward the corporation itself, whence they do not prove as fully as others, nor is only the advantage of the corporation treated, as noted by Archi. in prin., but in our case there is treated not only the advantage and favor of a secular corporation, but by consequence the prejudice of the individuals, because if the said proof fails, a tax must be levied on the individuals to satisfy the burdens of the commune, and in support of this is what Bart. notes in l. deferre, ff. de iur. fisc., and in l. omnibus, C. de testi., where he says that a procurator for business is not a suitable witness when, if the matter itself were lost, he would remain obligated. Item and secondly, the said former priors are rejected from testifying by reason of the suspicion of harm threatening them, since by not finding suitable sureties they are themselves liable in subsidium, ff. de magist. conue. throughout. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that they received the said suretyship out of superabundance, not out of necessity. For although it is not found expressly enacted in the statute of the commune, nevertheless since there is a most ancient custom in the said commune that the priors receive sureties from the buyers of the aforesaid gabelle, by the very fact that these men were elevated to the office of the priorate, they are seen as obligated to perform what was customary to be done by others. In support of this appears the text in c. ecclesiasticum, and in c. his, 11. distin., and well supports the text in l. quod si nolit, in § quia assidua, ff. de ędil. edi., in support of which is what Bar. notes in l. nemo est qui nesciat, ff. de duob. re., and there he says that in a contract that which is customary to be done is tacitly included, and therefore the said former priors are not suitable witnesses in this matter, since in avoiding loss they would readily depose regarding the said promise. Item and thirdly, they are not suitable witnesses, because wherever officials, even after resigning their office, wish to depose concerning an act performed before them or by them, from the performance or omission of which praise or blame could be ascribed to them, they are not suitable witnesses, and it is noted by the doctors in c. cum nobis, de testi., by Inno. in c. 3, de arbi. But in our case blame or ignorance could be ascribed to them, as if they had not provided for it nor acted as other predecessors did. Therefore etc. These three considerations, even considered individually, seem to suffice, and much more strongly where they all concur, as in our case. Nor does the statement of those two witnesses stand in the way. For first, as I said before, they depose only concerning enunciative words uttered on account of another matter, nor do they create a presumption, because they are singular; for they depose regarding different confessions, and not regarding the same matter. Hence, although a true witness creates a presumption when he deposes regarding the very fact in question, it is otherwise when he deposes regarding an indicium. For it is necessary that two witnesses at least prove an indicium, nor does one witness suffice; thus the glo. remarkably holds, and more clearly Barto. in l. fina. ff. de quæstio. But in our case those enunciative words only create an indicium, since they had been uttered on account of another matter, nor are they proved by two witnesses, and therefore they do not relieve the burden, nor do they assist. And in support of this, capit. cum dilecti, de electio., cap. tam literis, de testibus, especially in the absence of the party, l. certum, § si quis absente, ff. de confess., and what is noted in c. fin. eod. tit. Nor does the statement of the chancellor stand in the way, who was not sworn, nor did he depose in the form of testimony, as will be discussed more broadly in the following member. Item, it does not necessarily conclude an obligation that followed, but only says that Andreas said he would see to it that Donatus paid the commune. Whence it does not follow that he did so, especially since Andreas himself afterwards deposed that the said Donatus never obligated himself. And by this it is clear what must be said on the second point, and the response to the contrary is sufficiently clear as to the third, whether he is obligated by reason of the sequestration. And not lingering on words, I say first that since the sequestration does not appear through letters of the chancellor drawn up afterwards at the request of the lords, in no way is it proved that a sequestration was possible, even if the chancellor were now to attest that the sequestration had been made in the fullest form; and this is proved most clearly, first, because a notary's live voice is not to be believed, as noted by Host. in cap. post cessionem, de proba.; indeed his writing does not make proof, even when conceived concerning an act, unless it has the inscription of witnesses, as in auth. de hære. & fal. § si uero absunt, and in auth. de tabell., and in auth. de fi. instr.; but in this case even the writing of the notary does not appear, because these letters of the chancellor, merely testimonial, attesting to a deed of price, were neither writings at the time at which he is said to have been requested, nor is it in his protocol; therefore they make no proof, as is read and noted. Item, a notary deposing regarding any case does not make greater proof than one witness, but is counted in the number of witnesses, as l. Domitius labeo, ff. de testa., and more clearly in c. cum Ioan. de fid. instru.; and in our case they do not have the force of one witness, because they do not depose under the form of an oath, nor after citing the party, nor having taken an oath, and therefore his statement is worth nothing, as is proved clearly in cap. tua, de cohabi. cleric. & mulie., and in c. insuper, in cap. tuis, de testi. Item, presupposing that he were to come now and swear in the form of testimony, he would not make full proof, because one witness is not sufficient, even if he shines with episcopal dignity, as says the text in c. licet ex quadam, de testibus. And by this I infer as to that which I said regarding the fourth doubt, whether all these proofs or presumptions ought to be joined together to make full proof according to the rule, 'things that do not profit individually, help when many,' in cap. cum causam, de testi., and in l. 3, ff. eod.; and very briefly I say that they ought not to be joined, because wherever presumptions of diverse kinds concur, they are not joined to make full proof, because since they are not committed into one, they cannot be mixed together; this is the theory of Bartol. in l. admonendi, ff. de iureiur., and of Ioan. Cald. and others in d. c. cum causam. But so it is in our case. For the sequestration is one deed in itself, separate from the asserted promise; therefore it cannot be joined, nor does it assist the statement of those witnesses, who, since they were priors, the statement of the two in no way relieves, as I said above. Wherefore, with the aforesaid considered, I conclude that the said Donatus is not in any way obligated to the municipality of Castilione; therefore etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument: 1. If a woman having only sixty in her property donated it to someone so that he would maintain her, and for this did not consult the judge of the place nor her grandson, it is asked whether prejudice is done to the grandson?
body: Standing a statute of the following tenor, namely: if any woman having legitimate sons or daughters, one or more of whatever sex, shall make a testament, or codicils, or donations, she may not leave, give, sell, or alienate; so that her children who remained after her could be deprived of her property, except for reason of necessity, or sustenance; saving that she may dispense at her own discretion, or dispose of, the fourth part of her property, notwithstanding the disposition that had first been made; afterwards an addition was made, so that it says there, ‘having children,’ it also says ‘grandchildren descending from her,’ and those words were deleted, namely ‘shall make a testament, or codicils, or donations,’ and there was added at the end, ‘the remaining three parts shall be divided pro rata.’ Likewise, it was provided by another statute that no interpretation be made or ought to be admitted upon any chapter of the statutes, but as the words lie, they are to be understood simply and commonly without any interpretation.

† It happened in fact that a certain woman, having perhaps sixty [florins] in property, having no other means whereby she might live, donated that property to certain relatives on the condition that they ought to govern [care for] her; nor for this did she seek the judge of the place, nor the grandson, the son of her daughter. It is asked, is prejudice done by this to the said grandson with respect to the three parts? For the sake of brevity, I judge that it is; so that her said relatives will have that property just as was agreed between them. I am moved first because the aforesaid statute excepted the case of necessity from its provision, nor did it otherwise qualify the excepted case. Therefore, it is left purely under the disposition of the common law, by that which is noted on exceptions by the Gloss on the rubric de regu. iur. lib. 6; this is supported by capit. susceptum, de regulis iuris libro 6, and l. commodissime, ff. de libe. & posthu. But under the common law, ascending parents can freely dispose of their property without consulting children or grandchildren, nor judges, provided they do not act in fraud of descendants, as noted in l. hæreditati, ff. de bo. auc. iud. poss., where by Bartol. in cap. Raynutius, de testa.; and thus the children will have nothing after the parents' death, as there stated. Therefore, observing the common law, it was permitted to this woman to contract as she did, without consulting the grandson or the judge. Secondly, and the same is proved thus: wherever a statute issues against the disposition of the law, it must be understood most strictly, and departure from the terms of the common law must be as little as possible, as in l. 1. §. hæc autem uerba, ff. de neg. gesto., l. si uero §. de uiro, ff. solu. matr., in cap. in uostra, de iniur., noted by Innocen. in cap. cum causam, de rescript., and Bartol. in l. omnes populi, de iusti. & iur. But in our case, this statute is against the common law, in that a mother cannot dispose except of a fourth; therefore, insofar as it excepted the cause of necessity, it ought to be reduced to the common law, so that in the case of necessity she may freely dispose of all property, just as she can under the common law even when necessity ceases. For the statute works sufficiently against the common law since it works prejudice outside the case of necessity. In the case of necessity, therefore, common interpretation and addition ought to cease. Wherefore recourse cannot be made to the judge or the grandson without injury to the common law, which must not necessarily be done, because a statute ought to be restricted so as to be reduced to the terms of the common law, in capitu. cum dilectus, de consuetu., and l. 2. C. de noxa. Therefore, it ought not to be amplified and broadly understood so as to depart from the free power of the common law, as would happen in our case if there were need to have recourse to the judge or the grandson. Likewise, from that contrary understanding it would follow that the woman would be bound to receive maintenance perhaps from someone from whom she would not wish, which was never the intention of the statute; rather, it only intended to restrain the illicit and unbridled disposition of a woman in prejudicing her descendants. Likewise, and fourthly, the statute in its beginning says really that a woman cannot alienate, and afterwards it simply excepts the case of the necessity of her sustenance. Therefore, she can then alienate without the requisition of the grandson or the judge, for otherwise it would not say she ‘cannot’ simply; for he is not simply said to be able who must have the consent of another, or observe some solemnity, l. tutor qui repertorium, ff. de admi. tuto., and C. de prædi. mi. sine decre. throughout; for we are said to be able to do that which we can lawfully do, c. facit homo. 22. q. 2, and l. filius, ff. de condit. instit. And especially she is not bound to go to a judge, by the excellent argument in l. fin. C. de prædi. mino. sine decre. non ali. lib. 10, where it is evident that a decree thus permissive regarding a certain species of alienation against the disposition of the law is not extended to another unprovided case. So it must be said in our case. And if you should say that she is not said to act out of necessity of sustenance, because necessity is when she has no other means of relief, in c. quanto, de consuetu.; but she had a remedy by asking from the grandson; I say that the statute did not intend that a woman should go begging for her sustenance even by the hands of her children or grandchildren, but only that she should leave it outside the case of necessity. For the statute would well have known how to state this also if it had wished, arg. de deci. c. ad audientum; for it burdened her sufficiently outside the case of necessity, whence [it did not intend] to take away the provision granted by law in the case of indigence, since affliction ought not to be added to the afflicted, de cleri. ægro. throughout; nor is she properly said to be without necessity if she must seek sustenance through begged suffrages, because we are not said to be able where honesty resists, d. l. filius, and it is a disgrace to beg, 93. dist. c. diaconus. Furthermore, there appears on this a case in auth. contra rogatus, C. ad Trebel., where it is said that he who is asked to restore whatever remains of an inheritance is bound to preserve at least a fourth for the fideicommissary, unless he alienates for the necessity of his sustenance; and thus it simply concedes alienation for cause of sustenance. Nor does it require that he first have recourse on this to the fideicommissary in whose favor the alienation was prohibited, because neither is it fitting that he go to a judge, as noted in a similar case by Bart. in auth. res, quæ. C. communia. de leg. Therefore, a fortiori it was not necessary in our case to go to a judge or to consult the grandson, where the woman's own property is at issue, and where if it were otherwise understood, there would be a departure from the common law, and without fault the woman would be so severely prejudiced, contrary to what is noted by Barto. in l. omnes populi; and especially must this be said in our case, where modest property is concerned, in which solemnity ceases under urgent necessity even as brought about by law, as is proved in cap. terrulas, joined with c. sine exceptione. 12. quæstio. 2. And this truly I believe must be held, although on the contrary we consider there to be the theory of some doctors; but it cannot hold in our case, where the common law would be injured and women would be so bitterly prejudiced. Wherefore I conclude that the said agreement made with the said relatives was valid, since in truth she made it out of the necessity of her sustenance, as is sufficiently gathered from the tenor of the agreement itself, although she did not otherwise approach a judge, nor consult the grandson himself. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a donation made between husband and wife is valid.
2. A testament once made is not revoked except by another solemnly executed.
3. The last will is ambulatory until death.
casus: A certain lady Dominica, wife of a certain Ambrosius, after having made a will without her husband's knowledge, instituted an outside co-heir. Afterwards, without mention having been made of this will, she solemnly entered into a certain settlement with her husband, to the effect that if she predeceased him, certain goods of the woman would pass to the husband with a certain charge for pious causes, and those goods comprised almost the greater part of the woman's goods; and if on the contrary the husband should die first, the goods belonging to the husband ought to pass to her, also with certain charges for pious causes. Finally, without having otherwise revoked the said will, the said woman died. It is now asked whether the settlement is prejudicial to the will, since no mention was made of it, or vice versa.
body: Invoking the names of Christ and His Mother, it seems at first that the said settlement was invalid. First, because it seems to take away the freedom of testating, or of changing the will while the settlement subsists, when all the goods of the woman would be included, which is contrary to l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, ff. de uerb. obli.; for it is contrary to good morals that anyone should have an heir against his free will, which ought to be ambulatory until the very end of life, l. 4, ff. de adi. leg., and c. cum Marthae, de cele. mis. Nor does it stand in the way that an oath was appended to this settlement, because, as Bar. notes in the said l. stipulatio, it does not bind; c. non est obligatorium, de re. iu. in 6., and this seems especially to proceed on the part of the husband, to whom the wife promised all her goods by a solemn stipulation.

† Secondly, it is proven thus: a donation made between husband and wife is not valid, as in de dona. inter ui. & uxo. l. 1. & 2., and c. fi. eo. ti. But this was a certain donation, since it proceeded from mutual conjugal love; therefore, etc. And according to certain authorities, such a donation is not confirmed by an oath, because it is seen as contrary to good morals if they despoil themselves out of mutual love, as noted in c. cum contingat, de iureiur., and in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiuss., and l. Seius & Augerius, ff. ad l. Fal.

† Thirdly, it is relevant that a will once composed is not revoked except by another solemnly executed, l. sancimus and l. hac consultissima, C. de testa. But the will was not revoked expressly, nor tacitly by this statement, according to what is held and noted in the said laws; therefore, it ought to remain firm and take precedence over the aforesaid settlement. But notwithstanding these points, which do not stand in the way nor urge against the settlement, I judge that the said settlement is valid, and that it takes precedence over the will regarding the matters contained therein. And first I cite the text in l. rem legatam, ff. de adimen. leg., where it is clear that what was bequeathed in a will, the testator granted to another out of pure liberality.

† Likewise, the last will is ambulatory until the end of death, as in the laws previously cited. Nor can anyone establish a law for himself in a will from which it would not be permitted to depart, even if he had sworn, as is fully noted by Ioan. Andr. in regula quod semel, de regu. iur. in 6., in Merc., not. 13, quaest. 2, c. ultima uoluntas; the text is seen in l. si quis, in princ., ff. de lega. 3; whence a testator can freely dispose of his goods by contracting both in a will and after a will, as in l. haeredes palam, ff. de testa., and the said c. cum Marthae. It was therefore lawful for the said Dominica to dispose of her property even after the will, even without making mention of the will, especially by contracting, as she did, as is sufficiently proven in the previously cited laws. It only remains, therefore, to see whether the said settlement in the aforesaid manner was valid, and especially between husband and wife; and thus a reply is made indirectly to the contrary, and I say that it was. For if the words of the settlement are well inspected, the freedom of testating, or of changing the will, was not taken away therein from either of the spouses, nor was derogation made by them to the institution of the heir made in the will; for the said lady Dominica did not promise to make the husband her heir, nor vice versa, nor did she give all her present and future goods—in which case the points noted by Bar. in the said l. stipulatio, and by Cy. and others in l. fi., C. de pac. might apply. But the wife disposed only of certain particular things, and the husband disposed of present things, but not of future things; in which case the stipulation is valid according to the Gl. and Bar. and all in the said l. fi. and l. stipulatio. Since they can testate concerning things to be acquired in the future, the will of the said Dominica remains valid regarding things and rights not included in the said settlement while the will subsists; that nothing further remained at the time of death, however, cannot stand in the way. For it is enough that something could have remained, and that at present the heir can enter upon the inheritance, since an inheritance exists even without assets, as it is a legal term [nomen iuris], l. haeredis appellatio, ff. de uer. sig.; and this is gathered from the words of the said settlement, for the observance of which they did not bind themselves to take away the free power of testating, but bargained only concerning certain goods; nay, rather, I say that if the heir entered upon the inheritance from that will, he is held and bound to the husband to observe the said settlement, according to l. ueteres, C. de contrahen. & commit. stip., and what is noted in c. 1, de test. And further I say that if they had donated all present and future goods, the donation would be valid, especially with the intervention of an oath, notwithstanding the opinion of Bar. which more modern authorities have not followed, since one can become a testator without particular assets, because an inheritance is a legal term, as I said before; and Bar. himself thought this in auth. ingressi, C. de sac. san. eccle. Nor does the said l. stipulatio stand in the way, because there the power of instituting an heir was directly removed, which does not happen in our case; whatever the situation may be with our case, nevertheless the opinion of Bar. does not stand in the way, but agrees, since present and future goods were not included in this settlement, nor did they promise to institute each other as heirs, but rather intended the contrary, as I said before; and by this the first and the last arguments are removed. The point concerning the prohibited donation between husband and wife does not stand in the way for multiple reasons: first, because it was confirmed by death, which can happen, c. fi., de dona. inter uir. & uxor., as in l. donationes, C. eod. tit. Likewise, because it was not a donation inter vivos, but causa mortis, which is not prohibited between husband and wife, since thereby the other is not made poorer, as in l. in donationibus, C. ad l. Fal., and l. si causa mortis, ff. de donat. Likewise, the contrary can be said: that it was not a donation, but a certain settlement, like a mutual pact to gain certain goods once the marriage is dissolved by the death of the other, which can lawfully take place between spouses, as in the said c. fi., de dona. inter uir. & uxor., and l. Deo nobis, C. de episco. & cleri. For that cannot be called a simple donation which is made with the intention of obtaining something else or of remunerating, as in the said l. hoc iure, in fi., ff. de donat., as noted by Bar. in the prologue of the Digest, such as this one was. I conclude therefore that the will of the said Dominica remains valid, and the settlement made by her with her husband is to be observed in all respects, especially by reason of the oath and the disposition made for pious causes, arg. c. relatum, § 1, de testa. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A statute, as far as can be done, ought to be reduced to the terms of the ius commune, even through the improper use of words, if that is expedient.
2. A husband who is bound to give a share of those things which he had to the children of the first marriage is not compelled before the lapse of a year to restore a dowry that consists of immovable property.
casus: A certain woman promised three hundred as dowry for her daughter to the husband, who received and stipulated for himself and in his own name, with this added among other things in the contract itself: that if the marriage were dissolved otherwise than by the death of her daughter, the said dowry ought to be returned to her. Afterwards, children having been born of the said marriage, the husband died, and thus, the stipulation having taken effect, the dowry was restored to the said woman. Finally, as the said daughter entered into a second marriage, the said woman, her mother, promised three hundred as dowry to the second husband, with this added among other things: that if the marriage were dissolved by the death of her daughter, with children of that marriage surviving, then the dowry should remain with the husband himself, holding it in the name of those children, so that the dowry would accrue to those children only; and to this end she obligated herself and her heirs by a solemn stipulation. Lastly, the said daughter dies, to whose succession come the children of the first marriage, claiming that they ought to succeed to the said dowry together with the children of the second marriage, especially by reason of the local statute in which it is provided, among other things, that if any woman enters into a second marriage and dies intestate leaving children from the first marriage and from the second or any other, then in that case the children of the first marriage, and of the second, and of any marriage whatever, shall succeed intestate to their said mother in equal portion, both in the dowries of their mother, from wherever she had and derived them, and in any other goods of hers whatsoever, notwithstanding any pact added in the dowry instrument of the mother herself, etc. The second husband raises an exception based on the aforementioned stipulation. It is asked what the law is, etc.
body: Invoking the names of Christ and His Mother. For its clear decision, it must first be considered what should be said according to the ius commune; secondly, whether the disposition of the ius commune is varied in this matter by virtue of the said statute. In the first inquiry, omitting the arguments usually made by the parties, a distinction must in my opinion be drawn as follows: either the mother dowered the daughter from her own proper goods, or from the goods of the daughter herself; and this is deduced from the administration of the goods of the daughter herself. For if at the time of the promise the mother was administering the daughter's goods, then the mother is deemed to have conferred the dowry from her own, as is gathered from what is read and noted in l. fin. C. de dot. promiss. and l. una, C. de rei uxor. act. §. accedit. In the first case, since she conferred the dowry out of her own estate, she was able, even to the prejudice of future children, to stipulate that the dowry be returned to herself, just like any third party, as in d. §. accedit and l. quoties, ff. solu. matri.; and thus, when giving the dowry to the second husband, she could lawfully attach a pact excluding the children of the first marriage, since in her own property she was able to attach any pact whatever, C. man. l. in re mandata, and c. de his, de sepul. In this case, therefore, with the children of the first marriage excluded, the dowry itself belonged solely to the children of the second marriage. In the second case, since the mother dowered from the daughter's goods, the pact attached to the prejudice of the children of the first marriage was not valid; for just as the mother herself could not directly exclude the children of the first marriage from her succession, l. cum aliis, C. de secun. nupt. and in Auth. ut cum de appel. cogan. §. aliud quoque capitulum, so, and indeed a fortiori, she could not, when dowering from the daughter's goods, attach a pact excluding the children of the first marriage, by the argument in l. nemo potest, de leg. 1. and l. ius agnationis, ff. de pactis. But in this case it would be judged that the grandmother herself is bound to make up the shortfall to the second husband out of her own estate, since she obligated herself and her heirs, and obligated herself to the fulfillment of everything that came into the contract. Therefore, as much as is taken away from him on account of the children of the first marriage, so much must be made up to him by the said grandmother out of her own estate, since she was able to obligate herself to this, by the argument in l. rem alienam, ff. de contrahen. emptio. and l. eleganter §. qui reprobos, ff. de pigno. actio. and l. ex empto, de actio. emptio.; and it is well supported in a similar matter by c. inter cætera, de præben. These considerations hold good looking at the disposition of the ius commune. But now it must be examined what is to be said looking at the words of the municipal censure.

† And it seems first [that it should not apply]: for the said statute must, as far as possible, be reduced to the terms of the ius commune, even through the improper use of words if expedient, as in c. cum dilectus, de consuetu. and l. secunda, C. de noxa, by the Doctors in c. causam quæ, de rescript. Let the said statute therefore be understood as meaning to invalidate a pact attached to a dowry originating from the daughter herself or from her father; otherwise if from a third party, as is the mother in this case, who, since she is not bound to dower the daughter, must [not] be prohibited from contracting that the dowry be returned to her, contrary to many laws alleged above and similar ones. For it is a just cause that a statute be restricted when someone would suffer damage without fault, as noted by Barto. in l. omnes, ff. de iustitia, & iure. But since the words of the statute seem sufficiently clear and general in this respect—for they exclude any pact attached in the dowry instrument, from wherever the mother had the dowry or the dowry itself originated—the statute therefore includes a dowry originating from the mother, since it says, 'from wherever it originated,' etc.; for general words are to be understood generally, 19. distin. c. si Romanorum, 30. q. 1. c. si dormierit; and in support of this is what Barto. notes in a similar case in l. 4. §. prætor ait, ff. de damn. infect., where he says that if it is provided by a statute that the defendant is to be cited in person or at his house, it suffices that the citation be made personally or at the house, nor should it be reduced to the terms of the ius commune so as to be understood that it must first be in person, if he can be found, and then at the house; because according to this interpretation the statute would add nothing to the ius commune. Therefore, since in our case the words are clear, providing concerning the maternal dowry, from wherever it originated, they are to be understood generally; c. in his, de priuileg. is applicable. And that this was the intention of the legislators is clearly gathered from the addition: where she stipulates to the prejudice [of the children] that the dowry be returned to her, it is provided that in a certain case the dowry remains there in the hands of the dowered woman and her heirs, and this proceeds especially since the daughter dowered by the mother is excluded from the succession of the mother, etc., as is more broadly contained there. Thus the legislators in this case appear to have intended to prejudice the dowering party, so that, notwithstanding any pact whatever attached in the dotal instrument, the children of the first and of the second marriage must come to the succession of the mother. I conclude therefore in our case that, whether the said dowry originated from the estate of the dowering mother, or from the goods of the daughter herself, all the children, of the first as well as of the second marriage, come to the maternal succession equally and in virile portions, as is contained in the said statute; and d. l. cum aliis is applicable. But the mother herself, who obligated herself in her own name to the second husband, was bound to make up out of her own property as much as was taken away from him by the children of the first marriage, as in the laws previously alleged.

† As to when, however, the husband was bound to give the portion of those things which he had to the children of the first marriage, I say that the husband is not really compelled before the lapse of a year to restore a dowry that consists in immovable property, as in our case, as in l. una. §. exactione, C. de rei uxo. act. The grandmother, however, in respect of her portion, is not found to be privileged in this regard; whence she is bound to deliver within a time to be determined by the arbitrament of a good man, according to what is noted in l. 2. and l. 4. ff. de re iu. and l. 2. C. de usu. rei iu. and the like. And let these remarks suffice. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whence territory is named.
2. Whence district is named.
casus: Upon the question pending between the commune or men of Piancastagnaio on the one part, and the notary of the wool guild on the other part, namely whether the statute of the commune of Siena prohibiting cloths from being transported into the Sienese territory, etc., as is fully and broadly contained in the said statute, which begins, 'Veduto che grande quantità', etc., applies in the said constitution [?] of Piancastagnaio, and especially with respect to foreigners of the clergy [?], who, the gabelle concerning which it is contained in the said statute not having been paid, introduced a certain quantity of cloths into the said castle, etc.
body: IN the name of Christ, amen. Having implored the aid of Christ, it seems at first that it is so, whether we consider the disposition of the common law or the contents of the chapters long since entered into between the magnificent commune of Siena on the one part, and the commune and men of the said castle on the other. For by common law it was lawful for the said community of Siena to impose gabelle on transported goods throughout its entire territory or district, and to prohibit the importation of certain goods, since it exercises the rights of a prince throughout its entire territory, and the said city of Siena has exercised these rights for so long a time that there is no memory to the contrary, as in cap. super quibusdam, de uerbo. sign., in l. infamem, in fin. ff. de pub.; to which is relevant what Innocent notes in cap. cum te, de re iud. and in c. cum P. tabellio, de fid. instru. And thus l. uectigalia, ff. de pu., does not stand in the way, which prohibits gabelle from being imposed by one inferior to the emperor. It is certain that the said castle of Piancastagnaio is of the territory, or district, of Siena.
† For territory is named from "terrorizing" (a terrendo),

† and district from "distraining" (a distringendo). Therefore, wherever anyone has the power of terrorizing or distraining, all that is said to be of his territory, or district, as in l. pupillus, §. territorium, ff. de uerb. sign., by Bartolus in l. non dubito, ff. de cap. & postli., and what is read and noted in cle. ne Romani, de elec. Whence, although it might be disputed whether the said castle is of the county of Siena, especially by that which is contained in the 20th chapter of the said pacts, nevertheless it cannot be denied that it is of the territory, of the jurisdiction, and of the district, as is clearly gathered from the premises joined with the submission made by the men of the said castle, as appears most clearly from the tenor of the submission. Therefore, the said statute concerning the entire territory and district of Siena extends its binding force and power to the said castle. Wherefore, from the non-payment of the gabelle, the said cloths incurred forfeiture, as in c. cum secundum legem, de hære. in 6. and in l. fin. ff. de pub. with similar texts. Nor are the chapters or pacts entered into by the city of Siena and the said castle able in any way to impede the force of the said statute, or the penalties of forfeiture arising from it. For, if properly weighed, they do not take away from the commune of Siena the power of statuting and punishing in the said castle. For three chapters appear to bear upon the matter, namely the second, the ninth, and the twentieth. For those chapters seem only to exempt the men and commune of the said castle from gabelle and other burdens. For they do not grant the power of bringing forbidden kinds of goods from other places, especially with respect to foreigners, who are not found to be privileged. Nor is a privilege granted to one to be extended to another, nor is a personal law to be extended to other persons, 29 dist. through the whole. But the said pacts, as having been entered into, have the force of law, as in l. Cæsar, ff. de pub.; the men of the castle of Acquapendente, who brought cloths to the said castle of Piancastagnaio contrary to the tenor of the said statute, cannot defend themselves by virtue of the said pacts. But these notwithstanding, which in my judgment do not stand in the way, I think that by virtue of the said pacts the said statute does not claim application for itself in the said castle of Piancastagnaio, not even over foreigners bringing cloths to the said castle. And first, through the said second chapter of the said pacts, in which among other things it is contained that not only the men, but the commune of the said castle, ought to be exempt and free both in general and in particular from all taxes, tolls, gabelle, and any other real burdens whatsoever for the term of the twenty years then next following. But it is certain that if, from the importation of cloths—even those imported by foreigners—the gabelle contained in the said second chapter were paid for entry into the aforesaid castle, the said castle would not be immune from gabelle, or free and exempt, since the men and the commune of the said castle would indirectly be taxed and assessed gabelle, since they would either have to lack the said cloths if foreigners did not bring them, or they would buy them for more than usual, since the importers would sell more dearly on account of the burdens of the gabelle; to this effect is l. fundi partem, ff. de contrahen. emp.; relevant is c. quanto, de priui. and c. fin. de immu. eccl. in 6. Likewise, holding the contrary would directly offend against the said ninth chapter of the said pacts, in which chapter it is provided that all revenues, ordinary and extraordinary returns of the said town of Piancastagnaio, of whatever condition they may be, of the civil benches, and condemnations of penalties, etc., are and ought to belong to the community of the men of Piancastagnaio for the said term of twenty years. Nor can it be denied that a gabelle or a penalty imposed in the said place is against the immunity and the good of the said castle, at least by a certain consequence. Therefore, etc. And consequently I conclude that the said statute does not claim application for itself in the said castle, nor even over foreigners bringing cloths to the said castle, etc. Niccolò de' Tudeschi, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether the bishop's vicar is to be preferred to the archdeacon.
2. The bishop's vicar is associated with him in jurisdiction.
3. The bishop's vicar holds a dignity as long as he is in office.
4. A custom contrary to propriety is not valid.
5. What the first degree of humility is.
body: Having invoked the names of Christ and His mother. Having examined the doubtful matter concerning which it is asked: whether the vicar of the lord bishop is to be preferred to the lord archdeacon of Bologna, and vice versa.

† And first it seems that it must be said that the lord archdeacon is to be preferred, since his office is perpetual, while the office of the vicar is temporal. Whence things that remain perpetually are more worthy than temporal ones; moreover, the archdeacon is said to be the vicar of the bishop, as noted by Io. An. in c. 1, de of. arch. Yet notwithstanding these things, which truly do not stand in the way, I think the contrary is truer. And first I advance this: because he who is in greater jurisdiction, in doubt is to be preferred there to the lesser in seating, as in c. statuimus, 17. dis., §. fi., & c. seq. The archdeacon, however, has no power over the bishop's vicar.
