Nor does he have contentious jurisdiction in anything by the common law; but rather he bases his claim by the common law solely upon two express matters in c. ad haec, in §. in quadam, de of. arch.; they proceed rather according to the various customs of places than by the common law, as noted by Io. An. in d. §. in quadam. To the same effect is the good

† gloss in c. ad haec, de exces. prael. Also and secondly, the vicar of the bishop is said to be associated with the bishop in jurisdiction, as the text states in c. in noua actione, 16. q. 7. Therefore, after the bishop, he is to be preferred to all diocesans, arguing from c. recolentes, de sta. reg., and c. cum in tua dioecesi, de spon. Also and thirdly, the better the persons over whom someone presides, the greater and more honorable he is, as the text says in auth. de defen. ciui., in §. nos igitur. But the bishop's vicar presides over better persons, such as the archdeacon and everyone in the diocese, as was said above, and he has ordinary jurisdiction, whereas the archdeacon has no contentious jurisdiction by the common law, as I said above. He is therefore far greater than the archdeacon himself, and therefore to be preferred to him. Also and fourthly, the bishop's official general constitutes the same consistory with the bishop himself, and participates in the jurisdiction of the bishop himself, as in c. 2, de consue., lib. 6, and in c. Romana, de app., eo. tit. Therefore he is to be honored above all others except the bishop, just as we say regarding the Pope, who constitutes the same consistory with God, as noted by Inno. and Host. in c. 4, de transla. prela.; therefore, after God,
† he ought to be honored above all others. To the same effect is the good text in c. fin., 93. dist.

† The contrary arguments formulated above do not stand in the way. And first, to the first it is answered that the bishop's vicar holds a dignity as long as he is in office, even though, according to some, it is extinguished upon his death, or if he is removed, or if he is removed by someone being appointed, as noted in cle. et si principalis, de rescr., and in d. c. quoniam Abbas; and it is enough that it can be perpetual, that is, held for his life if he is not removed by another being appointed, according to what is noted in d. cle. et si principalis. Likewise, it is enough that, while he holds the vicariate, he has ordinary jurisdiction above the archdeacon himself, and therefore he is to be preferred, and the dignity of the vicariate is proper to it, whence they rightly treat separately of the office of the vicar. And although the jurisdiction proceeds from the jurisdiction of his bishop, it is nevertheless held from the law, and not immediately from the bishop himself; otherwise it would not be ordinary, according to what is noted by Inno. in c. cum ab ecclesiarum, de offi. or., and l. quia, ff. de iur. om. iu. To the second argument it is answered that the archdeacon is said to be the vicar of the bishop because those two matters that belong to him, of which mention is made in d. §. in quadam, formerly belonged to the jurisdiction of the bishop, as noted by Io. And. in c. 1, de offi. Archi.; but the official general of the bishop is vicar in the entire jurisdiction, subject however to those things contained in c. licet, de offi. uic., lib. 6. And he constitutes the same consistory with the bishop, which the archdeacon does not. The third argument, which says that he holds the place of the bishop, does not stand in the way, because from the fact that he is said to hold the place of the bishop, his jurisdiction is said to be the same as the jurisdiction of the bishop; it is not said in the sense that he has power solely in the presence of the bishop; on the contrary, he also has it in his absence, as I said above, whence he is said to be joined with him in administration, as in d. c. noua actione. The last argument does not stand in the way, namely that the archdeacon is said to be greater after the bishop's officials, because he himself ought to be honored like the bishop, as I said above, since he has the jurisdiction of the bishop over the archdeacon. But he is called greater with respect to the other clerics of the diocese. For, as I said above, the vicar constitutes the same consistory with the bishop; whence, positing the bishop, by consequence the vicar is posited. And let the aforesaid suffice. It was asked of me subsequently: whether a custom is valid in the above-written case which is contrary to all law: first, divine law, as is gathered sufficiently from chapter ad haec, 88. distinctio; secondly, the natural order, as gathered from chapter est ordo, 33. quaestio. 5; likewise canon law, since the greater in administration is to be preferred, as was fully alleged above; likewise civil law, as gathered from l. ut gradatim, ff. de muneri. & honori., and l. 1, ff. de albo scrib.; therefore it is imprescriptible, and is called a plague rather than a custom, according to the things contained in a similar matter in chapter ad nostram, in text and gloss, de probat.

† Likewise, a custom contrary to honesty is not valid, as in chapter cum decorem, de uita & honesta. clerico. And no wonder, since the principal thing required in a law is honesty itself, as in 4. distin. cap. Erit autem lex honesta, etc. If, therefore, those things that proceed from express consent are not valid without reason, as is stated there, how much less valid is a custom that is introduced by tacit consent? And regularly, tacit consent works less than express consent, according to the note in c. dilecti, de consue., and in l. 2, C. quae sit lon. consue., and 8. di., c. mala autem consuetudo, and cap. consuetudo. But this custom is contrary to reason, as is clear from the aforesaid. For it seems to have proceeded only from a certain madness and ambition, or foolishness, as the text intimates in cap. legimus, in prin., 93. distinct.; therefore it is not valid; and what lacks reason must necessarily be extirpated, 68. dist., c. cor episcopi, in fi.; and especially this custom, which is rather a corruption, must be entirely extirpated, because it is contrary to the first necessary degree of humility.

† For the first degree of humility is to defer to the greater, and not to prefer oneself to an equal, as the notable gloss notes in clemen. 1, de relig. domi., upon the word humilitatis, which pursues the other degrees, and c. de Constantinopolitanis, 22. di. is to the point. Hence it is that the law provides against those who obstinately wish to prefer themselves to the more worthy, that as a penalty they hold the last place, as expressly in c. fi., 93. di.; that such a custom is not valid is the meaning of the text in d. c. legimus, where the practice of places is rejected in which deacons wished to prefer themselves to priests, to whom they were nevertheless not subject with respect to jurisdiction; all the more is it not valid in this case, where the vicar has jurisdiction over the archdeacon, as was said before; 93. di., c. illud is to the point. And although a certain privilege is alleged in favor of the archdeacon, wherein among other things it is provided that the archdeacon himself ought to hold the first seat after the bishop, nevertheless, such a privilege speaking generally, in my judgment, ought to be understood with respect to other clerics not having jurisdiction over the said archdeacon. For a privilege speaking generally ought to be understood and restricted so that absurdity may be avoided, as is the notable text in similar matter in c. ex ore, de priuile.; for it would be absurd that the archdeacon ought to precede the vicar of the bishop, as is clear from the aforesaid. Likewise, the privilege gives the first seat after the bishop. But between the bishop and his vicar in his diocese no degree is to be given, since he represents the same tribunal and consistory, in c. 2, de consue., lib. 6, and in c. Romana, de ap., eo. lib.; he is therefore said to hold the first seat after the bishop, and immediately follows the bishop. For the vicar shines forth from the rays of the bishop, and his jurisdiction is his, just as in a similar case we say of a wife, who is ennobled from the lineage of her husband, l. fin., C. de incol., lib. 10. And let these things suffice. Nico. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A manifest usurer is proved by repute and arguments.
2. In invalidating the will of a manifest usurer, to what canon law had regard.
body: In the name of the Savior and of His mother, amen. Although the consultation, for greater clarity as I see it, deduces four doubts from the stated facts, nevertheless they can in effect be reduced to one: namely, whether the will of a minor under twenty-five and over fourteen years of age is valid when security was not first furnished according to the form of cap. quamquam, de usur. lib. 6, since it is not proved that he overtly and formally practiced usury, or openly and publicly sold goods or merchandise at a higher price because of deferred payment of the price than when the price was paid on the spot. And it seems, first, that the said will was valid. For the aforementioned c. quamquam invalidates solely for lack of security not furnished the will of a manifest usurer; hence it is not enough that the testator was a usurer, unless he was also a manifest one. Therefore, the will cannot be attacked on that ground. The consequence is plain. The major premise is proved in the said c. quanquam; but the minor premise is proved by this reason: usury is not committed except in a contract of mutuum, as is evident from its definition, for usury is gain from a mutuum, etc., as fully noted by Ioan. And. in regula peccatum, de reg. iu. lib. 6. in Mercu. and 14. q. 3. almost throughout; de usur. c. consuluit. In a contract of purchase and sale usury is not committed, even if one party is enormously injured, as appears in c. cum dilecti, extra de empt. & uendi. But the aforesaid minor only sold merchandise at a higher price; therefore he did not commit usury. Likewise and secondly on this point the text in c. in ciuitate, de usu., seems to apply, where it is expressly stated that a contract of this kind cannot by such form be deemed usurious, although the sellers incur sin, unless there is doubt whether that merchandise will be worth more or less at the time of payment. Therefore the said minor can be excused, even from sin, on account of the probable doubt whether at the time of payment the said merchandise would be worth more. Likewise, granting that he sinned once the doubt regarding variation of price ceased, he nevertheless does not incur the sin of usury, since no mutuum intervened, as the text indicates in the said c. in ciuitate. Likewise and thirdly, granting that he in effect committed usury by contracting in such a manner, he nevertheless cannot be called a manifest usurer, since such a contract does not appear usurious from its form, as the text states in the said c. in ciuitate. But that is manifest which is clearly evident and cannot be concealed by prevarication, as in c. manifesta, and the said c. de manifesto. 2. q. 1. and c. euidentia, de accusa. Fourthly, granting that manifest usury results against the person of the said minor from the said contracts entered into publicly, nevertheless that effect cannot be produced, since it is provided by municipal ordinance that a minor cannot contract without a certain form, which in the said contracts was not observed. For the said contracts were contrary to law, as in l. non dubium, C. de legi. and in regula, quæ contra ius, de regu. iur. lib. 6. For he does not seem to have contracted with respect to legal effect. But notwithstanding these points, which in true judgment do not stand in the way, I consider that the contrary opinion should be followed. And first, the very clear text in c. nauiganti, de usu., where it is stated that one contracting otherwise is only then excused from the crime of usury when it is plausibly doubted whether the merchandise sold would be worth more or less at the time of payment. Nor is even this doubt sufficient, unless at the time of the contract the seller giving the merchandise for a lower price would not have sold for a lesser price then offered; on the contrary, whoever offered the price immediately, he sold to him for a lower price than he would sell to those who deferred payment over time, as is most clearly proved through his account-books, which establish proof, in cle. unica, de usur. This was also the intention of the gloss in the said c. in ciuitate, at the verse uenditores, which explains that text: while stating that contractors of this kind incur sin, it expounds the statement concerning usury through the said c. nauiganti, and says that the said c. in ciuitate is to be understood according to the provision of that c. nauiganti. And in this the gloss speaks very well, because one law must be interpreted according to the provision of another, since laws are to be harmonized with laws, in capitu. cum expediat, de elect. libr. 6, in l. unica, C. de inoffic. do. And since he made these contracts openly and publicly, and kept a shop set up for this purpose, it is sufficiently called manifest usury, according to what the gloss notes in cap. primo and 2. de usur. lib. 6, Bar. in l. fur. ff. de fur., and what is noted in cap. 2. de usur. Likewise and secondly, the qualification “manifest” which is required in the said capitu. quamquàm ought not to be taken for notorious, but as manifest is a species distinct from notorious; for this is the proper meaning of this word, because that is manifest which can be proved, as the gloss notes in cap. uestra de cohab. cleri. & mu. And it holds an intermediate position between secret and notorious, or at least manifest is called both well-known report and common and certain knowledge, and arising from certain grounds; but in our case the said contract could be proved, and there was public fame and common opinion concerning the wickedness of those contracts during the life of the said minor. Therefore, it can sufficiently be said that the said minor was a manifest usurer. Thirdly, these matters are proved by the notable text in capitu. cum in diœcesi, de usur., where

† it is held that someone is proved a manifest usurer by reputation and presumptions, and in our case there are not only presumptions, but true proof of the usurious contracts. Indeed, what is more, I find it was advised by Bartol., Gas. de Cal., and the Lord Cardinal of Florence, that although one does not publicly practice usury during life, if it can nevertheless be proved that he was a usurer during the time of his life, it is sufficiently proved that he was a manifest usurer, even to the effect of changing his testament, because that offense was manifest which could be proved, although Federic. in his consilia seems to deviate from this last point. The contrary arguments formulated above do not stand in the way. And first to the first, it must be admitted that the said contracts by their formality do not appear usurious, since they are of purchase and sale, and so the said capitu. in ciuitate speaks as to form and appearance. But in the particular case and in the other circumstances, especially that one because he sold similar merchandise to others for a lower price when payment was made immediately, the contracts are sufficiently proved usurious, as the text in the said capitu. nauiganti openly indicates. Nor does it stand in the way that no mutuum intervened here; because I say that indeed a fictitious mutuum intervened. For the fair price seems to have been due to the buyer on the spot, and to have been immediately granted to him by the seller for a time with the increase of that excess which he paid for the deferred payment, as the doctors note in the said capi. in ciuitate and in capitu. nauiganti. For laws are not imposed on words, but on the effect of things, in capitu. commissa, de electio. lib. sexto; and if we were to say the opposite, a way would be open to evade it, and matter would be promulgated against usurers that ought not to be said, as is evident in capitulo ad nostram, de emptio. & uenditio. and in that capitulo uos, de pigno.; capitulo quanto, de priuileg. and capitulo gaudemus, de diuor. support this. Capitulo manifesta does not stand in the way, for there “manifest” is taken for “notorious” and not in its proper meaning; for one must not depart from the proper meaning of words when a contrary intention is not evident, as in l. non aliter, de le. 3. and in c. fi. de uer. sig. Likewise, this man could be called a notorious usurer, since he notoriously kept a bench set up for selling merchandise in such manner; to this effect notes the gl. in the said cap. 1. & 2. de usu. lib. 6, joined with c. nauiganti; for if the said contracts make him a usurer, as proved above, and were publicly practiced by him, as is presupposed in the case, therefore it cannot be denied that he was a public and manifest usurer. The final motive does not stand in the way, namely that by obstacle of the statute he could not contract. For I reply twofold. First, that a contract is deemed prohibited to a minor insofar as he is bound to another, but not insofar as another is bound to him, as is proved in l. Iulia. §. pe. ff. de actio. emptio.; l. non eo minus, C. de probatio. supports this; and the same is held similarly concerning the church in 12. quæstio. secunda, capitu. si qua de rebus, and by the gloss in capitu. primo, ne se de uacan., and by the doctors in capitu. primo and capitu. tuæ, de his quæ fiunt a præla. Therefore the statute was no obstacle to his increasing his estate in that manner.

† Secondly, I reply that canon law, in invalidating the testament of a manifest usurer, had regard to the hatred of the man, and not to the validity of the contracts, which is manifestly clear from this, that contracts regarding the payment of usury are null by operation of law, wherefore no obligation is acquired by the usurer, as in c. debitores, de iureiuran., and what has been paid can be recovered, as in the said capitulo debitores, and de usur. capitu. cum tu. Hence I presuppose that even if the minor could not contract, nor was the contract valid, he nevertheless, as far as in him lay, contracted the crime of usury; as in an obligation which is contracted from an agreement, the act itself is considered, as in the said capitu. debitores, joined with capitu. quanquam; capitu. nuper, de biga. and l. obligamur, ff. de actio. & obliga. support this. Nor does minority stand in the way; because where a penalty is imposed by law ipso iure, the person committing the prohibited offense falls into that penalty, although in some respect he should be punished more mildly, as Barto. notes in l. secunda. ff. de recepta. But the said capitu. quanquam invalidates the testament ipso iure; therefore the minor is bound by the penalty of the statute, and to this capitu. primo de delic. pue. and capitu. secundo under the same title, which seems to stand in the way, but must be restricted according to that reading and according to that theory of Bartol. in the place previously cited. The general custom of the merchants of the city does not stand in the way; because what in itself is sin is not excused by a general custom, or rather corruption, of the whole world, as in capitulo adulterij malum, and the rest, and cap. flagitia. 22. quæstio. secunda, just as men would not be excused if they directly, openly, and publicly practiced wicked usurious lending. For it makes no difference what is done out of equivalent things, in capitulo licet ex quadam, de testi., and in contracting a crime not the form but the effect is looked to, as in capitulo ea quæ de simo. For a good name does not excuse an evil, nor does a custom to the contrary avail, as there; and to this effect is that good text with the gloss. And let these things suffice as to the first three questions. I come to the last question, to which, because it is fairly easy, I reply briefly. For I say that the right to invalidate the testament belongs to the sisters, who succeed as upon intestacy under the ius commune to their brother equally with their mother, as in the authentica de hære. quæ ab intesta. defer. For capitu. quamquam only changes the testament, but does not exclude those coming upon intestacy; it supports this, as is held today in the authentica bona damnatorum, C. de bon. proscrip. Before which judge, moreover, this question of nullity must be litigated, I say that it must be before the ecclesiastical judge, through what is noted in the clementina compendiosam, de iudic., and in capitulo cum sit generale, de foro competen. And on the point that is asked concerning the sequestration of the fruits, which must be made while the question is pending, I say that sequestration can sufficiently be made if there is plausible fear of waste, if the possessor of the goods is not [solvent], he can be compelled to give satisfaction for the fruits to be gathered in the meantime in the case of purchase, according to what is noted in capitulo secundo and fin. de sequestratio. possessio. & fruct.; and I think otherwise if the possessor is capable of giving satisfaction, because then the mere fear of the waste of the fruits does not suffice for the sequestration of the fruits through the said capitulum finale, l. imperatores, ff. de appellatio., where it sets forth a special case after an appeal. In every case, however, the goods and fruits may be inventoried according to the theory of Barto. in l. unica. C. de sequest. And let these things suffice. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a security for paying the judgment has force before other judges.
2. The obligation of a surety ceases when the obligation against the principal has really ended.
casus: At the petition of Petrus Bartholomaei, a sequestration of a certain amount of money was executed on the 21st day in the year of the Lord 1333 in the hands of Franciscus Ioannis against Hieronymus Antonii by the officials of the Mercanzia of the city of Siena. Thereafter, on the 30th day of the same month, a certain Antonius appeared in his own and private name, and as procurator of Hieronymus, as he stated appeared by the hand of the notary Ioannes Mattheus de Asano, and offered to submit to law, and to answer at law, and to satisfy the judgment, and caused the said Petrus Bartholomaei to be cited by Dominicus del Dota, the messenger of the court. Which messenger reported that he had cited him at the house of the customary residence of the said Petrus, and upon the non-appearance of the said Petrus, the officials caused the sequestered money to be restored, with the said master promising, standing surety, obligating, renouncing, and swearing. These words are found written thus generally by the notary in the acts of the said court. Finally, after many months had elapsed and the said Hieronymus had died, an action was brought on behalf of the said Petrus Bartholomaei in the year of the Lord 1336 against the said Antonius. An exception is raised by the said Antonius that he is not bound, most especially because these are not the officials before whom he made the promise, since they have completed their term of office. It is asked what the law is.
body: Having invoked the protection of Christ and His mother. It appears that the said Peter is not bound in any respect; for he is not held as procurator, since his office expired by the death of the said Hieronymus while the matter was still intact (re integra), l. mandatum, C. manda. and cle. fina. de procu., and consequently he ought not to be held for things previously done in a procuratorial name, just as we say in the case of a tutor whose office has ceased, as in l. post mortem, ff. quando ex facto tut., to the same point l. fin. ff. de insti., he is not held once his office has ceased; nor ought he to be held in his own name as a surety not of a contract, but of appearance in court (de iudicio sisti), nor did he make any writing concerning this with his own hand; he was freed, since within two months the said Peter di Bartolomeo did not pursue the business of the trial, as is the notable text in l. fideiussor, C. de fideius. Nay more, he not only did not sue within two months, but rather several months have elapsed; therefore in that regard the said Antonius does not seem to be bound to respond for the said Hieronymus.

† Thirdly it stands in the way that a security, even for paying the judgment (de iudicato soluendo), has no force before other judges, or in another instance, l. cum apud and l. cum lite mortua, ff. iud. solu. But in our case these are not the officials before whom the promise was made; therefore the security is extinguished. But notwithstanding these points, which in my judgment present no obstacle, I hold the contrary opinion to be true. And first I say that he is held in his procuratorial name by the express text in l. procurator qui pro euictione, ff. de procu., where it is proved according to the reading of Bartolus and almost all authors that a procurator who has bound himself is held to answer even after his office has ended; to the same point l. seruum Titij, ff. mand. But this Antonius expressly bound himself, even in his private name, as is clear from the narration of fact; therefore he remained bound after the death of the said Hieronymus. Nor does the lapse of several months or a year stand in the way, because, since there is an action arising from his promise against him, especially a personal one, it is not extinguished except by a space of thirty years, l. sicut, C. de præscriptio. triginta annorum; nay, prescription does not seem to run, bad faith standing in the way by the disposition of canon law according to what is commonly noted by the Moderns in cap. fina. de præscrip., although Bartolus thought otherwise in l. sequitur, §. si uiam, ff. de usucap. But I do not dwell on this situation, because it is not necessary with respect to our case, since so much time has not elapsed that prescription can be said to be complete against this person. But it appears that this Antonius was bound under the name of surety, for the officials in the absence of the said Peter could, upon the revocation of the sequestration, take a surety in favor of the said Peter, as in cap. pe. de eo, qui mit. in pos., and this is the ordinary gloss in c. 1. eo. titu. in the verse parati, and Speculator holds it in tit. de primo decre. §. iam de effectu, the penultimate verse; which obligation indeed did not expire through the lapse of a year or two years while the principal obligation against Hieronymus endured; this I prove as follows. The obligation of a surety is not dissolved in reality while the principal obligation endures, except in cases in which he can press the principal to release him from the suretyship, as I have read and noted in ca. fin. de fideius. and in l. si pro eo contra quem; nor can he compel the adversary to sue for the purpose of obtaining release, as in l. fideiussor, ff. eod., noted in ca. constitutus, eod. titu.

† But the obligation of a surety in reality ceases once the obligation against the principal is ended, as in l. græcè, in sim. ff. de fideius. From this, however, we find an exceptional case in the said l. si fideiussor, where he is freed by the lapse of two months; which case, since it departs from the rules of law, must there be understood strictly, and not extended to an unexpressed case, arg. in l. præcipimus, in fin. C. de appella. But in our case we are outside that case of l. si fideiuss.; therefore we must judge concerning it according to the aforesaid rule. And that we are outside the case of that law is proved: for that law speaks of one who became surety only for producing someone in court. But in our case matters proceeded further, because he promised to stand to the law, and to answer, and to pay the judgment, and at the end he simply bound himself and became surety for Hieronymus; this is evident in the writing contained in the acts of the court. Whence it must be noted that the said l. si fideiussor properly speaks when, upon a lawsuit being commenced, someone provides a surety for appearing in court. Whence, since the plaintiff is bound to contest the suit within two months, and thus provides security, in 3. quæstio. 3. cap. Inducię §. libellum, and in auth. generaliter, C. de episco. & cleri., if the plaintiff does not prosecute within two months, he seems to have receded from his intention; fittingly the law introduced the rule that the surety is released, since that party seems to be in fault in not prosecuting, and it seems tacitly agreed to contest the suit within two months. And this seems the true ratio decidendi, and very notable for that law, which Hostiensis adopts in his summa, eo. ti. §. qualiter sit fideiussor; on this ground therefore, and by the tacit agreement of the parties, that law in that case departed, swerved from the common rules, freeing the surety upon the lapse of that modest period of time. Hence it is that a surety for appearing in court is freed by an event supervening upon the person of the defendant, as in l. sancimus, C. eod. But in our case all the aforesaid cease. For here, with one party a lawsuit was not commenced, nor was there hope of commencing it in the near future, but sequestration was made because the said Hieronymus was suspected. Likewise, suretyship was provided for standing to the law in a private name, and at the end, upon the renunciation of the sequestration, he bound himself simply by becoming surety. Whence it must be noted that that writing, which is among the acts of the court, is an abbreviation made in the manner of notaries, which must be extended according to their custom, pursuant to the notes in cap. cum P. tabellio, de fide instru. and in l. Gallus, ff. de lib. & posth. And if it is weighed diligently, it has two parts: for in the first part, at the beginning of the appearance, he bound himself in his own and even private name, and as procurator of the said Hieronymus, to stand to the law and answer the judgment, nor had he yet obtained that the sequestration be revoked, but he had the said Peter summoned; and upon the latter not appearing, he obtained that the sequestration be revoked, and anew promised for the said Hieronymus, and bound himself, and became surety simply, nor was it said regarding appearance in court. And that that new obligation was made after an interval is evident after the first obligation, concerning which at the beginning of that writing it says that he had the said Peter summoned, and that the messenger reported that he had summoned him at his house; and thus an interval had to intervene, and afterward, when that man did not appear, he obtained the revocation of the sequestration by becoming surety for the said Hieronymus simply, just as must be done in a revocation of sequestration, pursuant to what is noted by Cino in l. una, C. de prohi. sequest. and by the canonists in cap. 2. eod. tit.; therefore the said obligation endures at present, and he can be sued effectively, since the said Hieronymus or his heir is incapable of paying, pursuant to the matter of the auth. præsente, C. de fideiusso. Finally, on another ground, suretyship was furnished here in order to avoid sequestration, pursuant to the theory of the doctors in the said texts of law, and by Bartolus in l. litibus, C. de agric. & censi. lib. 11. and l. fideiussor, ff. qui satisd. cogan. and in l. senatus, de off. præsi.; it ought therefore to savor of the nature of sequestration, as in capit. ecclesia quæ, ut lit. pend. and in l. si rem & pretium, ff. de peti. hæredi., Innocentius in c. ex ratione, de appel. But the nature of sequestration is that it endures until the lawsuit receives its end, pursuant to what is noted in cap. examinata, de iudic. and in l. si oleum, ff. de dolo; therefore the suretyship as well, through which the sequestration is avoided, ought to endure until that time; and this appears most clearly from the intent of the text in the said l. litibus and l. si fideiussor and l. senatus. And if we should speak to the point, that remedy of suretyship would not be sufficient to avoid sequestration. Therefore this suretyship does not savor of the simple nature of a suretyship for appearing in court. Nor would this surety be freed by the death of the principal, just as he is freed when he bound himself to present the defendant in court, since the plaintiff would not be sufficiently satisfied. The arguments alleged above to the contrary do not stand in the way. For a mandate is dissolved while the matter is intact. But here the matter was not intact, since he had bound himself for the principal. Likewise, here he bound himself in his own and private name, and it was a voluntary office, and thus the contrary in l. post mortem ceases; for there the institor did not bind himself, as is said in the text, but in our case, yes. To l. fideiussor sufficient answer was made above. To l. cum apud and l. cum lite, I say that they apply to a surety for appearance in court, or for paying the judgment; but here he was a simple surety upon the revocation of the sequestration having been made, as I said above. Likewise, those laws apply when someone promised simply to pay the judgment without expressing the proper name of the judge; for then he is held upon the promise before the judge who is the successor of the same tribunal, because it is deemed the same judge, l. deponebatur, ff. de iudi., and Speculator clearly holds this in ti. de leg. §. excipi. verse sed quid si plures, and more clearly Bartolus in l. cum apud; and so it was in our case. Wherefore from all the aforesaid I conclude that the said Antonius is bound to answer and pay the judgment according to the aforesaid. And let these things suffice for the present article, etc. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Remission is not made according to the custom of Italy.
2. The judge of the crime ought to purge the province of evil men.
body: Rodulphus, a citizen of Corneto having his domicile in Viterbo, while he was in Corneto, ordered or persuaded that Martinus, a citizen of Corneto, be killed, which was done in that same place, while Rodulphus himself was residing in Viterbo. After some days, the governor of both cities, possessing all-encompassing power as a legate de latere from our Lord the Pope, coming to Corneto and having heard the ill repute of the said homicide, upon his return to the city of Viterbo ordered the said Rodulphus to be arrested in the city of Viterbo and caused him to be placed in the hands of the podestà; an investigation is now being conducted in Corneto, and proceedings are being drawn up against the said Rodulphus for homicide; the podestà of Corneto requests that he be remitted to the place of the crime, to Viterbo, since Viterbo and Corneto are under the same president, and petition is made to the governor or president that he order the podestà of Viterbo that Rodulphus be remitted to the place of the crime committed. Doubt is now raised on four points. And first, whether at the requisition of the podestà of the city of Corneto the governor or president is bound to order the podestà of Viterbo to remit him; and whether at the order of the governor the podestà of Viterbo is bound to remit him. Secondly it is asked, whether the aforesaid Rodulphus can be punished in Viterbo, where he is detained under arrest, for the homicide committed in Corneto, by reason of the domicile which he has in Viterbo, especially since the said cities are under the same governor? Thirdly it is asked, whether the remission ought to be made before the beginning of proceedings against the said Rodulphus, or after? Fourthly, whether the aforesaid governor, having the full power of a legate de latere, could cause the said Rodulphus to be detained in the said city of Viterbo by reason of the crime committed in Corneto, to the end that he may be punished there, or whether he is to be remitted to the place of the crime. I come to the first; and it seems that the governor or president is not bound to make the remission or to order it to be made, but rather to release that prisoner or to cause him to be released: because the crime was consummated outside the territory of Viterbo, whence even presupposing that the order had been to commit the homicide in that very city of Viterbo, and that the crime had ensued not there, but only in Corneto, he cannot on that account be sued in Viterbo, according to what is noted by Barto. in l. si ut proponitur, ff. de fideiusso. and in l. non solum. §. mandato. ff. de iniur.; the text seems [to support this], joined with the gloss in clemen. pastoralis, de re iudic. in the clause necnon procedendo, and noted by some in c. fina. de foro competen.; therefore the remission ought to be made to the place of the crime: because before his capture he was not contumacious in the place of the crime, therefore he could not be arrested in the said city of Viterbo for the purpose of a remission being made, according to what is noted in l. 1. C. ubi de crimi. agi opor. and the text in Auth. ut nulli. §. si uero quis comprehensorum, colla. 9 seems [to support this]. Likewise, presupposing that he could have been arrested in Viterbo, it seems that the governor is not bound to order the podestà of Viterbo to remit him: because remission to the place of the crime seems rather a matter of courtesy than of necessity, arg. of the said clemen. pastoralis, in the clause de more; noted by Barto. in l. si cui, ff. de accu.

† Likewise, more strongly, custom holds throughout all Italy that remission is not made, as noted by Barto. in l. sepulchri, ff. de sepul. uiola. Therefore he is to be released. For he cannot be punished in Viterbo, because he did not commit an offense there, nor can he be remitted to Corneto, because custom is contrary to remission. Likewise he had not been contumacious in the place of the crime; therefore etc. Likewise for this makes the fact that the said Rodulphus has his domicile in Viterbo, as is presupposed in the statement of the case, whence presupposing that the crime had not been committed in the territory of Viterbo, nevertheless by reason of domicile he could be accused and investigated concerning a crime committed elsewhere, and on this account be restrained by the due penalty, on which the case in c. cum contingat, de foro competen. seems [relevant]; so holds Ioan. And. in c. 1. de rapto. and Barto. following Cyn. in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. tri. and Ioan. de Lig. in the aforementioned clem. pastoralis; the text with the gloss seems [to support this] in l. 1. & 2. & in auth. qua in prouincia, C. ubi de crimi. agi opor.; expressly the same Ioann. And. in the additions to Specu. following Odof. in the title de compe. iud. adi. §. 1. in the clause 6. ratione criminis; yet he seems there to maintain that under civil law this statement holds when one proceeds by way of accusation: otherwise where it is solely by way of inquisition, because the judge acts for vengeance, and it is not of his interest, since he offended outside his territory. For in the place of domicile he can be sued not because he offended, but because he acquires forum, and thus he ought to hear the accuser under this head, and he can punish him if the crime is proved. But an inquisition into the present crime concerns an offense which does not happen to belong to the judge if it was committed outside his territory. And as to the canon laws, which broadly permit inquisition, he says that they apply in their own forum. But lord Archi. says in c. si. de foro compe. that also under civil law one can proceed by right of domicile by way of inquisition concerning a crime committed elsewhere. For the reason why he can be accused in the place of domicile, although he offended elsewhere, is that wherever an offense is committed he is subject to the judge of domicile; and this reason has place whether one proceeds by way of accusation or of inquisition.

† Likewise, just as it is of interest to the judge of the crime to purge his province of evil men, as in l. congruit. ff. de off. præsi., so it is of interest to the judge of domicile to chastise his subjects and purge his province of such men, although they offended elsewhere; the said l. congruit, and l. præses. under the same title; and I find that Barto. held this in l. cunctos populos. de sum. trin. & fid. cath., which seems truer, and in our case it matters greatly: because in the lands of the Church we observe the canon law, as in c. si duobus, de app. and noted in c. quod clericis, de fo. compe. Likewise, if the case is weighed well, it is not expedient on another head to discuss this much: because the governor or president has jurisdiction not only in the place of domicile, but in the place of the crime; thus he can throughout his entire province cause him to be arrested, as in the said §. si uerò quis comprehensorum, and in c. nouit, de offi. deleg., where there is a good text in a similar matter. For the entire province is for him one territory; and thus the crime was committed in his territory, and the capture made within his territory was permissible; therefore also the governor or president could and ought to have caused him to be arrested in any part of his territory, since he offended within his territory, even if he had been a foreigner, as in the said l. præses. and de offic. deleg. c. 2. For the president or legate properly has in the province decreed to him jurisdiction which any ordinary, whoever he may be, can exercise in the place, and he is greater than all after the prince, as in l. ex omnibus. with the following, ff. de offi. præsi.; noted by Spe. in the title de leg. §. nunc ostendendum. in the clause legatus. and the following, and in §. superest. in the first clause, under the same title; it is read and noted in the said c. 2. and c. 1. under the same title in the antiqua. Therefore he could cause him to be arrested and delivered to another so that justice might be done, according to c. fin. ne cle. uel mona. lib. 6. From the aforesaid I infer for the decision of the last doubt, and conclude affirmatively, that the lord governor not only could, but ought, even out of the duty of his office, to cause the said Rodulphus to be arrested in the said city of Viterbo. It remains now to examine the first three doubts together, whether Rodulphus can be punished in Viterbo, and whether he can be remitted to Corneto, or must of necessity be remitted thither. Omitting for the sake of brevity the arguments that can be made for both sides, I say conclusively that where remission is not requested by the judge of Corneto, in case of doubt he can be punished in the place of domicile, as in l. 1. C. ubi de crimi. agi. oport., and there this was held by Bart., Bald., and Ioan. Cal. in c. 1. de rapto; it seems proved in the said c. cum contingat. and the said l. 1.; and if we were to say the contrary, in vain would we deal with the forum of domicile, since anyone is always sued either by reason of crime, or contract, or property. For the forum by reason of domicile is more general than the others, whence one can be sued there concerning property existing elsewhere, as noted in l. si. C. ubi in rem act. and in c. si. de fo. comp. Likewise concerning a contract made elsewhere, as one reads concerning a crime committed elsewhere, as in the laws cited above. And especially in our case, in which we presuppose that the governor has jurisdiction also in the place of the crime. If, however, remission is requested by the judge of Corneto, I deem that it is not of necessity to be made, but he could be punished in Viterbo. I am moved first, because the §. si uerò quis comprehensorum speaks of when the offender has left the province of the crime and betaken himself into the territory of another president, which did not happen in our case, since he is under the same president. Likewise the president is greater than the judge of Corneto, and he can take cognizance of and punish all things that occur in the province, as in the said l. præses. and l. ex omnibus. For also in the place of the crime the president, as I have said, is greater than the podestà of Corneto. Therefore he cannot be requested by him to remit him to him, according to the said laws. Likewise and secondly, remission is not of necessity to be made, because the common custom of Italy does not necessitate remitting according to what Bar. noted as above; but Cald. treats these matters more openly and more fully in the said c. j. de rapto. and concludes that if the offender were not in the place of domicile, or if the custom were to prevail because through this the public utility would be harmed, which requires that crimes not remain unpunished, such a custom would be burdensome; therefore it does not prevail by custom, c. j. and c. fin. But a custom by which the judge of domicile does not remit to the judge of the crime, or vice versa, would well prevail, provided that the other of the aforesaid, in whose territory he lives, were willing to punish offenders, because then the aforesaid reason would cease, and according to this distinction I deem the statement of Bar. to be restricted. To the point, therefore, since the offender was arrested in the place of domicile and proceedings are underway so that he may be punished there, that custom of not remitting can sufficiently be observed; and this reason concludes that even if the judge of Viterbo had arrested him without the authority of the governor, he is not bound to remit to the place of Corneto, but it can be defended under a third head that remission not be made, by holding the opinion of Ioan. Calde. in the said cap. j. de rapto. For the doctors divided themselves on the matter of remission, some asserting that it must be made of necessity unless there was a custom, because it is of courtesy, and fully noted by the gloss in clemen. pastoralis. in the clause de more. Ioan. Calde., taking a middle course, distinguished that either the criminal lives under the judge of domicile who intends to punish him, and the opinion holds that remission is made from courtesy alone; or he lives under another judge of domicile, or the judge of domicile does not care to punish, and that opinion holds that it is of necessity to be made; therefore under multiple heads it can be defended that remission need not be made of necessity, as is evident from the aforesaid. But can he voluntarily be remitted to the place of the crime? I would say that either the will of the governor and of the podestà of Viterbo concurs, and then undoubtedly it could be done, because justice is more fittingly exercised in the place of the crime to the terror of others, so that scandal may cease there, in cap. 1. de rapto. 2. quęst. 7. cap. j. and l. capitalium. §. famosos. ff. de pęnis. with many similar texts. For although custom holds that the judge of domicile is not compelled to remit, it does not however hold that he cannot remit, since that is purely of faculty. If however the governor wishes to remit to the podestà of Viterbo, appointing him his delegate, he could remit him against his will; because the podestà today holds in the city the place of the president, according to what is noted by the gloss in l. j. C. de pręscrip. long. tempo. and by Bar. ff. de dam. infect. Whence, although the governor is greater than he, just as he is greater than a bishop, as in the laws alleged above, nevertheless he cannot without another reasonable cause extract a prisoner from the hands of an ordinary, since there is room between them for prevention with respect to cognizance; for there a case is to be ended where it was begun, l. ubi cęptum. ff. de iudic., to which what I have read and noted in c. ex tenore. de rescrip. contributes. And since in this case remission is voluntary, the third doubt need not be discussed, because remission can be made before and after the beginning of proceedings; but in that case in which remission would have to be made of necessity, some summary cognizance ought to precede, where the crime was not notorious, but infamous, concerning which see the gloss in the said clem. pastoralis. and Bar. in the said l. 1. C. ubi de cri. agi opor. And let these suffice as to the doubts. I conclude therefore that the said Rodulphus could be arrested in Viterbo, and can be judged and punished there, nor must he of necessity be remitted to the city of Corneto, although he could voluntarily be remitted according to the aforesaid distinction. And the contrary arguments formulated above remain sufficiently resolved; for the first would proceed where he was not sued in the place of domicile. Likewise the governor has jurisdiction in both places, as I said before; for all things are declared and qualified according to the aforesaid, therefore I do not respond otherwise specifically for the sake of brevity.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether an archpriest has jurisdiction of the contentious forum over canons.
2. Whether theft is called a great crime.
casus: A canon regular who had expressly professed the rule of the blessed Augustine in the cathedral church of Perugia, in the cloister of the said church on the night of Wednesday of Holy Week, while the canons were at matins, stole one hundred florins from a certain canon who had been deputed as collector by the clergy of Perugia to collect a certain quantity of money to make a certain gift to our lord the Pope. This theft is proved both by confession and also by a cleric of his who accompanied him while the aforesaid moneys were taken by the said [canon]. The vicar, in the absence of the archpriest of Perugia, having a mandate for this from the bishop, proceeded against the said [canon] up to the definitive sentence exclusively. Three doubts arise. First, whether these proceedings were valid, since it is claimed by some that they were not, because the proceedings ought to have been conducted not by the bishop's vicar, but by the archpriest or his lieutenant. Second, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the jurisdiction belonged to the archpriest or his lieutenant, whether this defect can be supplied by the governor of Perugia having the full power of a legate de latere. Third, with what penalty this canon is to be punished, and whether he can be deprived of the portion that they call a procuration of the cathedral church of Perugia, since there are no distinct prebends, but the chapter has assigned to each canon a certain portion, which they call a procuration, so that each canon may thus be more diligent in working to make his procuration, and each year, the chapter having been convoked, each canon renders an account of the administration of the procuration, and on account of the assignment of this portion they do not live in common, but in the same cloister separately in their own chambers, from which it follows that de facto each of them holds private property; likewise it is also presupposed that this canon in question has a certain parish church, which is accustomed, however, to be conferred upon canons regular, etc.
body: The aid of the Savior and of His mother having been humbly invoked, I shall touch upon these doubtful matters conclusively, omitting arguments for the opposing sides to avoid prolixity. And following the order, concerning the first I say,

† that the archpriest does not have jurisdiction of the contentious forum, especially over canons, but it belongs to the bishop: 11 q. 1 c. de persona; de off. or. in c. 1; de fo. comp. c. si quis contra clericum; de iudi. cap. at si clerici; the legal texts on this are almost infinite. And he was indeed able to delegate this jurisdiction regarding the act of inquiring to his vicar: in c. licet de off. vica. lib. 6. Therefore, by common law, the proceedings framed by the vicar were valid. If, however, by custom it belongs to the archpriest—which can be the case, according to c. irrefragabili § excessus de off. ord.—then it must be noted that, since that prescription is contrary to the common law, it is necessary that a colorable title and a period of 40 years concur, or, failing a title, a period of time of whose beginning memory does not exist is required, as in c. non est de consuetu. lib. 6. And that it belongs to the jurisdiction of the bishop is proved in c. cum ab ecclesiarum and c. pastoralis de off. ordi. And, presupposing that these matters are proved, it must then be examined whether those proceedings framed by the vicar were valid. For at first sight it seems that they were not, because they were conducted by a judge not his own, as in the said cap. at si clerici and C. si a non compe. almost throughout. But notwithstanding this, I say that this canon, having been investigated or summoned before the bishop's vicar, did not except on grounds of incompetence, nor did he state that the jurisdiction belonged to the archpriest; whence he is seen to have prorogated the jurisdiction of the vicar or of the bishop, and thus the proceedings will be valid; on this there is the text with the glossa in l. 1 C. ubi de cri. agi opor. and according to Bar. and Bald. For in criminal cases prorogation has a place before a judge possessing by his own right a similar jurisdiction, as is noted there by the glossa and Bar., and by Inn. in c. de causis de off. dele., and by the glossa in l. 1 C. de iur. om. iu. But it is questioned whether this applies in the case of a cleric without the license of his own judge, which did not intervene here; and it seems that it does not, through c. significasti de foro compe. But notwithstanding this, the contrary can be maintained in this case, since the jurisdiction of the bishop, which is natural and ordinary, is prorogated. For a matter easily returns to its own nature: 35. distinc. c. ab exordio and l. si unus ff. de pact.; it is otherwise where the jurisdiction of another is prorogated by a subject of the bishop without the bishop's license, for then the prorogation would not be valid; and so speaks the said c. significasti. And in doubt it is approved in our case, in which this canon held neither orders nor a benefice from the archpriest, whence he is subject to him only with respect to the bare exercise of jurisdiction; whence the same reasoning that applies to that cleric who prorogates without the license of his own judge applies to this cleric as to our case, according to the note in the said c. significasti and by Barto. in l. 1 ff. de iud. And this as to the first doubt. I come to the second doubt: presupposing that the said proceedings were not valid, namely because the jurisdiction belonged to the archpriest and prorogation did not intervene in the aforesaid manner, can the defect be supplied by the governor? And I say briefly that it cannot. Because, since the judicial acts in this case would be null, not even a legate de latere can supply such a defect; for that would be to act against the solemnity of judicial proceedings—devised through many vigils and labors—contrary to clement. ne Romani de elec. and c. inferior 21. distin. And this Specu. clearly maintained in titu. de lega. § nunc ostendendum, verse 18, where he says that this supplying belongs only to the Pope; and this proceeds especially in our case, where it is not merely supplying a defect concerning the solemnity of judicial proceedings, but giving jurisdiction to one who does not have it, to the prejudice of the proper judge, and thus depriving another of his right, which a legate cannot do. For it belongs to the prince alone to give the right of one to another, according to the note in c. constitutus de religio. domi., 25. q. 2 c. visam. Nay rather, the glossa doubts with respect to the Pope whether he can give away the right of one church to another without cause, as noted in c. 1 distinc. 22 upon the verse in instantiam, on which see Specu. in titu. de lega. § praeal. verse 67. To the aforesaid contributes the notable glossa in c. pen. de haere. lib. 6, which by disputation concludes that a legate cannot commit a cause that is by its nature plenary to be handled without the noise and form of a trial, because that would be to take away the solemnities of judicial proceedings; and so Specu. in titu. de lega. § superest, verse nunquid potest cognoscere. What Innoc. notes in a similar matter contributes to this, in c. prudentiam de offic. delega., where he maintains that acts done before a judge not one's own cannot be ratified by the proper judge, even if they were done in his name, because they collapse from a defect of the solemnity of judicial proceedings, the free disposition of which does not depend on the power of the proper judge, but of the prince; and that opinion the doctors commonly follow there; what is noted in glossa 9. q. 2 in summa also contributes. Now I come to the third doubt: with what penalty this canon ought to be punished. Regarding this, it must be noted that canon law makes a distinction in the quantity of the penalty according to the manner of proceeding. As a rule, it imposes deposition for a serious crime if it is established by way of accusation; but by way of inquisition the penalty is lesser, so that regarding deposition the penalty seems discretionary; yet he can be deprived of benefices or afflicted with another penalty, unless they are such offenses as impede the execution of holy orders even after penance has been performed, such as simony and homicide; and of this there is text in c. inquisitionis and in c. qualiter el. 2 de accus. and c. dilectus 2 de simo., although civil law does not seem to make a distinction: l. 4 C. de sepul. vio., in l. ordo ff. de publ. iudi., in l. ea quidem C. de accusat.; Barto. holds this in l. 2 § 2 de adulte. and l. 3 § praeterea de suspe. tuto. But regarding canonical suspension there are found certain penalties of civil law which hold that one condemned by way of inquisition for a notorious crime avoids infamy on account of the mode of proceeding; so notes the glossa in the said § praeterea de suspe. tuto and l. 3 and l. fina. C. eo., and there by Cyn. and l. 1 C. de modo mul. Barto., however, holds otherwise in l. infamem ff. de publi. iudi., and fully by Bald. in l. etiam de fur., by Specu. in titu. de sent. § 1 verse qui de insti.; and these things serve to know whether, if this man is condemned by way of inquisition, he will be rendered infamous. On this I do not dwell further, because the question is not about this, but solely about the penalty to be imposed. I say therefore, answering the first, that if this man was accused of this theft, he must be punished with the ordinary penalty, which is the penalty of deposition from office and benefice; the text is in c. cum non ab homine de iud.; noted by Hosti. in summa de fur. under the rubric; and he says further there that after deposition he ought to be thrust into a monastery to perform penance, through c. tuae de poenis. But it must be observed that that c. tuae does not speak of simple theft, but of robberies, which amounts to more than theft, as in auth. sed novo iure C. de ser. fugi. and in the body from which it is taken, in authen. ut nulli iudi. at the end, and l. capitalium § famosos latrones ff. de poenis. But because the text in the said chapter adds that for great crimes the penalty of thrusting away and deposition is imposed, it would have to be examined whether this theft is called a great crime; on which see the notable glossa in l. ad ea ff. de regu. iur., by Barto. in l. non solum § si mandatum ff. de iniur., something noted in l. 1 C. de requir. re.; and the common conclusion is that if it is in a matter of great value, it is called a serious offense. Whence in our case, having regard to the circumstances,

† it can well be called a great crime: both because it was in a religious place, and because it was in moneys designated for the honor of the prince; and also by reason of the time, because it was in Holy Week while Matins were being sung; and, what is worse, committed by a religious who sinned against his vow and the essentials of the Rule by wishing to have personal property, and especially by theft. All these things aggravate the offense: 40. distin. c. homo Christianus and cap. cum quidam de iureiur. and what is noted in them. Thus I conclude that the penalty of the said c. tuae can well be inflicted in our case. But there is a doubt in our case, because this man is a regular, whether he ought to be expelled from the church and deprived of that procuratorship which he holds in the church of Perugia; and this is specifically asked in the presupposed case. I say that on this there is the specific doctrine of Inno., Hostien., and other commentators in the said c. dilectus 2 de simo., where it is said that through deposition he is not freed from the regular yoke, but he shall not have a voice in the chapter, nor will he be summoned to common acts, nor to receive the common prebend, but provision will be made for him in confinement; so says literally Joann. And. following Innocen. and Hostien. Therefore, through deposition he is deprived not only of a prebend or individual portion, but also of the common one, so that he does not eat with the others, nor is he treated in the usual manner, but in a close place, according as it shall seem fit to the superior, provision will be made for him in the necessities of life. c. fin. de reg. and what is noted there supports this; and thus he can be deprived even of a parish church, notwithstanding that he held it from the Apostolic See, through what is noted by the glossa in c. 1 de confir. uti. The superior will also be able, dispensing with him, to punish him less; this is proved in c. at si clerici § de adulter. de iudi.; what is read and noted in l. quid ergo § poena gravior ff. de his qui not. infam. supports this; and these things proceed when proceeding was done by way of accusation. If, however, it was done by way of inquisition, then there is greater doubt according to what was said above. But I say that he can be deprived of that procuratorship, and also of the parish church, through the said c. qualiter & quando el. 2 de accusatio., where the text says that if a serious offense is proved by way of inquisition, although the offender is not degraded from his order, he is nevertheless removed from administration; although certain persons have said that that chapter speaks of a prelate, whereas in inferior clerics the penalty is discretionary; and thus they understand c. inquisitionis 1. responso, under the same title, as noted in them. But nonetheless it must be said that the superior, using discretion, can deprive the offender of all ecclesiastical administration, especially regular, as in c. inquisitionis in the glossa on the word aliquando. But whether in this case he can be deposed from the office of orders, it seems not from the above; but to the contrary is the notable and singular statement of Innoc. in cap. qualiter & quando, where he says that when a crime is established by confession, the mode of proceeding is not looked to, but the ordinary penalty, however severe, can be imposed, because there is then no room to doubt that he was convicted through false proofs. And the lord Anto. de But. follows the statement of Innocen. in cap. dilectus, cited above, and cap. fina. de celebratio. miss., and the case seems to be there in cap. 2 de poen.; and what Barto. notes in l. si confessus ff. de custod. reorum supports this. Since therefore in our case the crime is established by his confession, he can be punished just as if proceeding had been conducted by way of accusation; whether proceeding was conducted against this regular canon by way of inquisition, he can be deposed from office and every benefice and administration; but in nothing does he remain a canon, and provision will be made for him in some close place according as it seems fit to the superior, especially attentive to the disposition of cap. fina. de regu. It must be noted, however, that where the proceedings were found to be null for the stated reasons, proceedings could be initiated anew not only by the archpriest, if the jurisdiction were his, but also by the governor, since he has the power of a legate, because a legate together with any ordinary, whoever he may be, is greater than anyone after the prince, as is read and noted in cap. 1 de offic. legat. and in cap. secundo under the same title in the sixth book, and by Specula. in titu. de lega. § nunc ostendendum verse si legatus and following, and there fully, and in § super. And the said canon is compelled to persist in his confession, according to what is noted in cap. at si clerici de iudic. and by Innocen. in cap. per inquisitionem de elect., through the glossa and Barto. in l. capite ff. de adulte., and it must be maintained as is more fully noted in the said legal authorities. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Laymen may enact statutes concerning their own property not yet transferred to the Church.
2. Whether statutes of laymen are valid providing that movable goods cannot be alienated to those not subject to the jurisdiction of those enacting the statute.
casus: Certain officials of the town of San Gimignano, asserting that they had the power to make an ordinance from the entire people of the said town, enacted and ordained in effect that, concerning all movable and immovable goods to be bequeathed or transferred in any way whatsoever by lucrative title, whether in a last will or inter vivos, to any place whatsoever, even if they are hospitals, whether they are subject to the said community or not, the said places or their rectors are bound to assign and pay for their return and income to the said town of San Gimignano and to the benefit of the sacristan of San Gimignano two denarii per pound, according to the value of the said goods. And they willed that this ordinance be extended even to past bequests or gifts in which execution had not yet intervened; this in sum is what that ordinance contains regarding the matter for consultation, although many other words are contained therein and are extended to other persons. Now it happens to be doubted whether a certain hospital founded in the said town of San Gimignano, subject to the most distinguished and most famous Hospital of Santa Maria della Scala of the city of Siena, is bound to the observance of the said statute, etc.
body: The aid of Christ Himself and of His mother, whose cause is here treated, having been humbly implored, it seems that it is so. For although laymen may not enact statutes over the property of the Church, as in the chapter bene quidem, 96 distinctio, and the chapter ecclesia Sanctae Mariae, de constitutionibus,

† nevertheless, no one can with an unabashed face deny that they are able to enact statutes concerning their own property not yet transferred into the church, since all peoples possess the power of enacting statutes by law, as in the law omnes populi, ff. de iustitia et iure, and the law cunctos populos, C. de summa trinitate, and in his own property everyone is the lawful controller and arbiter, l. in re mandata, C. mandati, and c. de his, de sepulturis; hence Bartolus in l. rescripto, ff. de muneribus et honoribus, gives the theoretical rule of how goods to be transferred into the church can be affected and obligated through the statutes of laymen, so that they pass into the church afterwards with that burden of paying tributes and levies; so it seems must be said in the matter at hand.

† For these officials enacted statutes concerning their own goods to be transferred into any person whatsoever, and not concerning the goods of the Church, since they were not yet the Church's, but their own. For just as any private individual could have bequeathed to the hospital with that burden of paying two denarii per pound, by the argument in c. cum dilecti, de donationibus, and c. verum, de conditionibus appositis, so also the entire community will be able to establish this; wherefore, what can be done by contract ought to be able to be done by a law or statutes, as the notable Gloss says in C. de decretis decurionum super rubrica, book 10, by Bartolus in the aforementioned l. omnes populi, on the word iuxta praedicta. But these things notwithstanding—which, if weighed properly, truly do not militate in our case—I think the contrary must be said in law. And first, I bring forward for this question, almost as a parallel case, c. finale, de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, where it is said that laymen cannot make statutes concerning mortuaries, nor generally concerning other things that are annexed to a spiritual right; and that word, 'annexed,' is to be weighed: therefore, they are prohibited from making statutes not only concerning purely spiritual matters, but also concerning annexed matters and concerning mortuaries; and this proceeds openly there, on account of what is noted there by the doctors in the exposition of that word, which sufficiently resolves this question, so that we may say that bequests made to a pious cause are said to be annexed to spiritual things because they are designated for a special use, just as we say concerning mortuaries, that is, concerning those things which are brought with the funeral or bequeathed on the occasion of funerals; and consequently, such a statute, insofar as it encompasses an established hospital and other pious places, is invalid as having been enacted by those lacking the power to enact statutes. Secondly, I allege a clear case in c. requisisti, book 1, de testamentis, where the text lays down the general rule (although the question there was spiritual concerning the number of witnesses) that bequests made to pious causes ought not to be decided and handled according to civil laws, but according to the statutes of the decretals; which means that if such things, since they are arranged for a pious use, are not subjected to the dispositions of laymen, even of emperors, but to the Church alone—and so Bartolus says in his repetition on l. 1, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, in the penultimate or last column, that that text is understood; and the canonists in the said c. relatum; for in these things the people ought to be taught and not teach, and have recourse to the Church, which is the mother of all; and they ought not to put a sickle into another's harvest, as in chapter docendus, 62 distinction, and in c. si imperator, in the same distinction. And thus ought the dictum of the emperor to be understood, that the civil law does not disdain to imitate the sacred canons, as in the Authentica ut determinatus sit numerus clericorum, and in the Authentica de ecclesiasticis titulis, and in transcription in chapter clerici, de iudiciis. Thirdly, Bartolus most clearly appears to hold this in the said l. 1, where he says that a statute of laymen, even of the emperor, is invalid over matters pertaining to a pious cause, since this is not of their jurisdiction, but of the Church's, as he proves through the statement of the Apostle and many other things, very elegantly and at length. Fourthly, I cite what was noted by Johannes Andreae on c. finale, de immunitate ecclesiarum, in the Sext, in his Novella, where he poses the question whether a statute of laymen is valid which provides that immovable goods cannot be alienated and transferred to persons not subject to the jurisdiction of the enactors. And he concludes that it is not valid with respect to churches and pious places. He is moved, among other things, elegantly by the fact that pious places are privileged by princes so that gifts may be made or sales made to them freely, l. prima, and l. illud, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis. Therefore, a contrary statute is invalid for a twofold or threefold reason: First, because inferior laymen cannot take away the laws and privileges granted by a superior, especially to the Church, as in chapter cum inferior, de electione, and by Bartolus in the said l. omnes populi, and 25, q. 2, almost throughout. Secondly, because this would be against the liberty of the universal Church, and consequently the authors of the statute are ipso facto excommunicated, and subjected to the other penalties of civil law, concerning which in Authentica cassa, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, and Bartolus also in the said Authentica cassa. Thirdly, because the power of making laws granted to inferiors through the aforementioned l. omnes populi appears to have been granted without prejudice to the privilege granted by the emperor himself, because a genus is derogated by a species, as in c. veniens, de praescriptionibus, and the rule
† generi, de regulis iuris, in the Sext, by Bartolus in the said l. omnes populi, on the said word.

† Fourthly, in accordance with the aforesaid notes, I say thus on the matter at hand: since the privilege has been left to churches and pious places that anyone may freely bequeath to them, according to the said l. 1 and l. illud, the said statute is not valid, since freedom in donating and acquiring is impeded when one must pay upon the donation, and especially since it is said in the aforesaid provision that for the revenue of the said land of San Gimignano, though for the utility of the sacristy, two denarii per pound are to be paid, and thus they wish to make an alms from another's property; to whom, or against whom, it can be said that the alms of one is the sin of another, nor ought one altar to be uncovered that another may be covered, especially by one lacking the power, as in c. cum causam, de praebendis; and it is a species of theft to serve or make an alms from another's property, l. si pignore, ff. de furtis, and 1, q. 1, c. non est putanda eleemosyna, and 14, q. 5, c. forte, and c. multa. Fifthly, to the same effect I cite l. sancimus, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, canonized in 23, q. 8, c. in qualibet civitate, § sancimus, where it is sufficiently gathered that nothing can be exacted from churches even from those things which they acquire by lucrative or onerous title; to which what Cino notes in l. deo nobis, C. de episcopis et clericis, contributes, and the text there in the beginning contributes; and especially the aforesaid things are indubitably true regarding bequests or donations made in the past, even if execution has not yet occurred, in which the enactors, so to speak, do not appear to have had even the color of law. For from the sole title of the bequest or gift, ownership and right was acquired by the hospital, as in l. finale, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, although execution has not been made; in which case that which they presumed to enact to the prejudice of the hospital seems incapable of being conceived on any ground, for directly against it are the above-cited c. ecclesia sanctae Mariae, de constitutionibus, and c. quae in ecclesiarum, under the same title, and c. finale, de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, and the said c. bene quidem; indeed, what is more, such cases ought to be decided even in the secular forum according to the canons and not according to the laws, as is noted in c. 1 and c. ecclesia, de constitutionibus. The motives alleged in the beginning do not stand in the way. For I admit that laymen can make statutes concerning their own goods by obligating those goods or imposing a perpetual burden. But in our case those goods are not obligated to those burdens, but rather they have disposed concerning the places to which it might happen that those goods are transferred, and they cannot do this, as I said before. In support of this is what the doctors note on c. finale, de vita et honestate clericorum, in c. praesenti, de censibus. Furthermore, it is one thing to obligate goods simply so that they are transferred, and especially to a pious cause, contrary to all the laws cited above. Furthermore, in this statute not all consent, since women and wards do not, etc., and yet they could not freely bequeath to the hospital. Furthermore, it is one thing when someone donates or bequeaths and wishes to impose a burden, since by this the freedom of donating to the church is not restricted, nor is the privilege granted to the church violated, and thus speak the laws cited to the contrary; it is another thing to make a statute or law taking away the free power of bequeathing and donating as each person wishes. Furthermore, as I have said, the people cannot enact statutes even concerning property to the prejudice of those things that are specially enacted and reserved to princes, and especially above a privilege granted to the Church, as I have said above, and as Bartolus notes in the said l. omnes populi. I conclude therefore that the said provision or statutes of the said land of San Gimignano must not in any way prejudice the said hospital, especially since it made specific mention of the hospital according to the doctrine of Bartolus in l. cunctos populos, C. de summa trinitate. And let these remarks be abundantly sufficient. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. When a legacy is made to a church, ownership is acquired ipso facto from the day of the testator's death.
2. Favor to the church is not to be granted to such an extent that we do injury to others.
casus: CASE. A certain Lady Gemma made her will, and among other things disposed as follows, etc.: “I bequeath and by right of legacy leave to my below-written heirs this house of mine in which I live, situated etc., under these conditions and agreement, namely, that my said below-written heirs be bound and obligated to sell it and transfer it to Michael and Gabriel, full brothers and sons of the late Nicolaus, for 100 florins of good and pure gold, etc. Which 100 florins, in the event that it is so sold, shall be expended and converted by my below-written heirs into the restoration of the church of Sant'Agostino of Massa, which is said to be newly built or repaired, and this insofar as the aforesaid church is newly built or repaired. And in the event that the said church is not newly built and repaired, I bequeath the house and by right of legacy leave and will it to belong to the said church, and to be sold by my below-written heirs, and also the price [to be expended] on the works or repair of the said church.” Many years having elapsed, the churchwardens of the house of San Pietro of Massa demand that the said heirs be compelled to hand over the aforesaid house to be converted to the fabric of the said church, and if that cannot be done, to another pious use in order to satisfy the will of the said testatrix. On the part of the heir many things are objected, and especially among others, that the said church of Sant'Agostino is not being newly built [?], nor is it being repaired, nor is it in a state in which it can be newly built or repaired; nor ought it to be converted to another pious use, because this was not of the tacit or express will of the testatrix. The question is what the law is.
body: IN the name of Christ, amen. It seems, in the first place, that if it can be converted to the repair of the said church, the matter admits of no doubt that it should be done as the churchwardens demand, namely, that it be sold and the proceeds converted to the repair of the church, just as the testatrix disposed, as in c. nos, de test. 13. q. 2, c. ultima uoluntas, and in auth. de test. almost throughout; the legal authorities for this are commonplace.
