If, however, it is not sufficient for the repair, or the church is not repaired, then it seems that it ought to be converted to another pious use, because a bequest to pious causes does not lapse, but, if it cannot be used or is not sufficient for the designated use, it must be converted by the superior, after summoning the heirs, to another pious use, as in said c. nos, and as noted there; but better in l. legatum, ff. de usufr. leg., and fully there by Bart. in l. pater, §. tusculanus, ff. de leg. iij., and in l. legatam, ff. de admi. re. ad ci., per Io. de Lig. in cle. contingit, de reli. domi., and in cle. exiui de paradiso, de uerb. sig.; for in these cases that rule applies: "if what I do is not valid as I do it, let it be valid as it can be valid," de despon. impu. c. 1. lib. 6.

† Likewise, when a bequest is made to a church, ownership is acquired ipso facto from the day of the testator's death, l. si, C. de sacr. san. eccle.; therefore the church can dispose of the bequeathed property, either for the designated use, if it can be done, as in the aforesaid cle. quia contingit, or it may be converted to another use if it cannot be done, as in the places cited above. But notwithstanding these points, which indeed do not stand in the way, I consider the contrary to be true in law. And first, I lay down as a foundation that the aforesaid bequest made to the church is not unconditional, but is under a suspensive condition, namely, "insofar as the said church is newly built or repaired," which condition is twice repeated in the will, and it is of the nature of this condition to suspend the effect of the disposition pending the event, so that beforehand no action lies, as in l. cohæredi, ff. de condi. & demon., as noted in c. uerum, de condi. appo., and in l. j. C. de condi. quæ sub modo. From which I infer that, before the occurrence of the said condition—namely, that the church be newly built effectively and not in fraud—the aforesaid bequest has no effect. Nor does said l. si stand in the way, because it speaks of an unconditionally made bequest. But, as it appears, the said church is not being newly built, nor can it be newly built; therefore, the bequest designated for one use cannot be claimed, nor indeed ought it to be converted to another pious use, because the contrary opinions apply when the bequest was made unconditionally out of contemplation of a pious cause alone, and when the testator did not provide otherwise in the event that it could not be converted to the designated use, as noted by Barto. in said l. legatum, ff. de usufructu legato, and so speaks c. nos, de testamen. But since in our case the bequest was left under a condition, because he did not wish the heir to be bound unless the said church were newly built or repaired; and thus there is no bequest before the condition is fulfilled; and consequently we treat of commutation in vain, since commutation presupposes an unconditional bequest, by the argument of capit. ad dissoluendum, de despon. impub., and in l. decem, de uerbo. obliga. Second, a case on this is likewise seen in l. pater, §. Tusculanus, ff. de lega. 3., where a testator bequeathed a hundred to Sempronius and wished it to be given to the college of a certain temple; it is said there that, when the college is dissolved in the meantime, the bequest remains with the legatee, nor does commutation to another use take place, because the testator seems to have had only that college in mind; so too, and all the more strongly, in the present matter, by repeating the condition, he did not wish the heir to be bound otherwise. Third, commutation of a bequest to another use takes place on account of the tacit will of the testator, as in said l. legatum; hence it is that if the testator disposed otherwise in our case, so that it cannot be converted to the use designated by him, commutation ceases, as is the fine case in l. liberto, §. lucius, ff. de annu. lega., noted by Barto. in said l. legatum. But the testator most clearly wished the said house to remain with the heir if the said church were not newly built, which is clear from the condition twice repeated. The distinguished doctor Lord Fede. de Sen. in consi. 170 seems to hold this sufficiently in a similar question. Nor must one depart from the words of the testator unless something else is evident regarding his intention, l. non aliter, ff. de lega. 3. To the aforesaid points also makes cap. cum dilecti, with the notes there, de dona.; and although

† favor is owed to churches, it is nevertheless not so great that we ought to do injury to others, by the argument in c. ex tenore, de fo. comp., and 17. q. 4. in fin., where it is clear that a donation made to a church, even unconditionally, is revoked by a tacit condition, as noted in c. fi. de don.; all the more strongly is the effect impeded, and not from the fulfillment of the condition. And because this case seems to me very clear, I have therefore decided not to dwell on a multitude of words. For someone might perhaps from this deem it to be doubtful. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A public official obliged to render an account satisfies the edict if he delivers his codex or parchments to be read or copied.
2. An appeal reduced to writing is valid, even though the appellant does not read it, provided he presents it to the judge.
3. That is said to be certain not only which is certain in itself, but also by reference to another certain thing.
4. A notification of an act [?] can be made not only by word, but also by deed.
casus: An edict was solemnly issued, or a provision was solemnly made by one having authority, that the notaries of the city of Siena should report all contracts, testaments, and the like which they had drawn up from the beginning of their office up to that day, the reporting to be made within the time limit contained in the provision; otherwise, anyone acting to the contrary would incur ipso facto a certain penalty contained in the statute. Subsequently, certain notaries reported many contracts specifically, and, being unable easily to report all acts summarily and compendiously, they brought all their writings and presented them to the official deputed over these matters, making one general report in addition to that specific one, saying that they also reported everything contained in their codices or parchments, and for the space of a month and a half they left all their writings with the official. In the course of time, one of the said notaries is accused of not having reported a certain donation of which he had been requested to draw up the instrument two years before the decree. The notary excuses himself on the grounds that that donation was contained in the writings produced by him, and thus it was sufficiently reported. It is replied that such a general report does not suffice. It is asked what the law is.
body: Having invoked the protection of Christ and His mother, omitting the allegations that are commonly made by some on behalf of the parties, I think I will address the matter itself. For I say that the said notary satisfied the edict, and consequently incurred no penalty. And first, I cite, as it were by way of an exact case, l. argentarius, § edicto, ff. de eden., where it is proved

† that a public official, bound to render an account, satisfies the edict if he delivers his codex or parchments to be read or transcribed. Therefore, by identity of reason, the same must be said in our case. For the said Ser Mariano sufficiently reported the contracts concerning which he had previously been requested, if in the aforesaid manner he delivered all his parchments to the official in place of a reporting. For he reported by act, even if not by word; and no less, indeed even more, does a notification or reporting avail which is made by an indubitable act in the aforesaid manner, namely by the delivery of the writings, than that which is made by word, as in c. dilecti, de app., and c. ad audientiam, eodem tit. Secondly, this seems to be approved in c. appellatio, de appellat., lib. 6, where it is said

† that an appeal is valid if the appellant presents it reduced to writing to the judge, even though he does not read it; he is deemed sufficiently to read it and to appeal if he refers himself to the writing presented to the judge. If, therefore, in an appeal, which is a provocation from an inferior judge to a superior, this suffices, it ought all the more to suffice in our case, since such a reporting is required in order to certify the official concerning the contracts, testaments, and similar transactions executed. Which certification indeed is more strongly and certainly gathered and disclosed from the delivery of the originals than from a bare and verbal reporting, as in c. quoniam contra, de probatio. Thirdly, I adduce c. qui ad agendum, de procura., lib. 6, where it is held that cases requiring a special mandate are included when certain cases are expressed and followed by a general clause; to the same effect is l. sed & si quis, § quæsitum, ff. si quis cau., and what is there noted by the Glossa and Bartolus. But in the present matter a specific reporting of many contracts was made, and a general clause was added, namely, that he would subsequently report all other contracts; therefore, he seems to have reported all. Fourthly, I adduce this reason:

† that is said to be certain not only which is certain in itself, but also by reference to another certain thing, in c. cum venerabilis, de religio. domi., and de excep., c. cum venerabilis, and what is noted in both places; l. certum, ff. si cert. petat. supports this. But in our case the notary referred himself to certain writings which he had, in which no doubt could fall. Therefore, he cannot be said to have reported unclearly and without certainty; and especially because the officials accepted those writings and kept them in their possession for a month and a half. And the statement of Bartolus in l. eos, ff. de fal. supports the same, where he gives counsel to a witness who is recalled concerning that about which he previously testified, that he should not testify specifically, lest by chance through forgetfulness he fall into the crime of forgery, but should refer himself to his first statement, saying: ‘I said all things when I was previously examined, wherefore I refer myself in all things and concerning all things to those which are contained in the prior acts,’ and from this it will be held just as if he had testified specifically. Returning therefore to the proposed matter, all contracts and other matters concerning which he was requested, as contained in these parchments, ought to be held just as if he had specifically reported all and singular contracts, especially in a penal matter, as ours is, in which a strict interpretation must be made so that punishment may be avoided: the rule odia, and the rule in pœnis, de reg. iur., lib. 6; and words do not take that broad meaning which they could have from the proper and broad significance of the words; which is greatly to be attended to and noted in the present matter. These are the words of Johannes Andreae on the rule odia, previously cited, in the Mercuriales, and it is proved in c. cum in cunctis, de electione, and in c. si compromissarius, eodem tit., lib. 6. Lastly, there can be adduced l. de pupillo, § meminisse, joined with the Glossa, ff. de noui ope. nuncia., where it is proved

† that the notification of a new work can be made not only by word, but also by deed, for example by the throwing of a stone, provided the intention of the one wishing to notify is apparent. 11, q. 3, c. existimant, and c. cum solum, with the concordances noted there in the Glossa, support the aforesaid. To the same effect is l. 3, C. de sen. quæ sine cer. quanti., and what is there noted by Bartolus and Johannes Andreae in the Speculum, in the title de sen. prola., § qualiter, verse sed pone iudex, and Innocent in c. 2, de lib. ob. For although an uncertain sentence is invalid, l. 1, C. de sen. quæ sine cer., and 2, q. 6, c. ei qui, § diffinitiua, nevertheless it is sufficient that it can be made certain through the acts, especially when the judge has referred himself to the acts, the same l. 3, and what is noted in the places cited before. So it must be said in our case, that the reporting ought sufficiently to be called certain, since it was made through references to the parchments in which the matters to be reported were contained. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A prince is said to be the arbiter in his own affair.
2. Whether the effect of a denomination is proved through a mention made incidentally in any writing.
casus: The case upon which counsel is sought is submitted in the following terms. The castle of Monte Spoleti in the territory of Siena exists as exempt, as is presupposed, from all jurisdiction of the bishop of Arezzo, and immediately subject to the ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the lord abbot of the monastery of Saint Anthony. It happened that the men of the said land, wishing to look after their hospitals, had supplication made to our Lord Pope Martin V that it be permitted to them to place a rector there without waiting for the confirmation of any superior. Likewise, that regarding bequests left to the said hospitals, the rectors of the said hospitals should not be bound to pay the canonical portion to the abbot or to anyone else. Our Lord Pope granted them letters with leaden seals in the manner of the Roman Curia, in which he narrates among other things that a petition had been presented to him on behalf of the men of the said land, in which it was contained among other things that the men of the said castle in past times had appointed rectors to those hospitals without the lord bishop of Arezzo contradicting it in the least. Likewise, he commanded the commissioner that, having summoned the bishop and the abbot and others who ought to be summoned, he should diligently inform himself concerning the contents of the petition, and if he finds the assertions of the men to be true, and the assent of the aforesaid bishop is added to this, he ought by apostolic authority to grant to them what is requested, as is more fully contained in the said letters. Now it is doubted whether by the aforesaid words making mention of the bishop of Arezzo any power or jurisdiction is in any way acquired for the said bishop, or at least proved to be held by him, so that at least in the future any prejudice could be generated against the said lord abbot regarding the episcopal jurisdiction that he has in the said castle or over the men of the said castle, since they claim that they are exempt from the said lord bishop and immediately subject to the said lord abbot, etc.
body: The aid of Christ and His mother having been invoked, I firmly consider that no prejudice ought to be generated by the said words against the said lord abbot or the men of the said land regarding the exemption or episcopal jurisdiction owed to the said lord abbot. I am moved first by that general argument: that which happens to be absent from something does not prove it to exist, de transla. præla. cap. 2, and in l. neque natales, C. de proba., and what is noted there. But once all jurisdiction on the part of the person of the bishop is removed, the men of the said land can insist that they appointed rectors to the said hospital with the lord bishop by no means contradicting it, because in truth he never contradicted it, neither de facto nor by alleging any legal obligation. Likewise, that the Lord Pope wished to grant this favor with the consent of the said lord bishop; for he perhaps wished in this to honor his person and dignity. For just as he could in the concession of a favor append any other condition, so he could wish, without prejudice to another, that the consent of the said lord bishop be provided, arg. in l. j. ff. de leg. 2.

† For everyone is the lawful controller and arbiter in his own property, and especially a prince, l. in re mandata, C. manda., cap. his, de sepul., and c. bonæ, in fi. de postu. præla.; therefore the aforesaid words do not prove that any jurisdiction belongs to the said lord bishop in the said castle. Secondly, it is proved thus: the men of the said castle do not possess or have any jurisdiction; on the contrary, they are quasi-possessed by the lord abbot. Therefore, their possession could not prejudice the lord abbot, l. fi. C. de acqui. poss., l. 3, §. quod seruus, ff. eo. ti., and what is noted by Innocentius in c. olim, de resti. spo., where he says further that, presupposing that subjects of someone actually obey another prelate as their superior, yet if their own prelate contradicts it and excommunicates them for this transgression, no prejudice concerning possession is generated against him in this, because incorporeal rights are not lost without the knowledge or sufferance of the possessor, l. 2, C. de serui. & aqua., as noted by Innocentius also in c. bonæ, de postu. præla., and in c. conquerente, de offic. ord., and c. cum dilectus, de religio. domi., and in many places. And this applies most especially in our case, in which, on the part of the men, there only intervened bare words uttered enunciatively on account of something else, and thus they induce no disposition, l. ex his uerbis, C. de test., and in c. si Papa, de priuile. libr. 6., and in cle. si Romanus, de sent. excom., as noted by Bartolus in l. ex hac, ff. de do. not., and in capitu. fin. de suc. ab intesta. And our case seems to be proved by many legal texts. First, in the said c. olim, according to one interpretation, as is clear: that if men subject to one person endure and observe an excommunication fulminated against them by another, they do not through this appear to wish to obey him as a superior, nor is any possession of jurisdiction acquired by the one excommunicating, because they could have observed the excommunication with the intention of deliberating, or because it is characteristic of good minds to fear fault where no fault is found, as in c. 2, de obserua. ieiu. So, and even more strongly, it must be said in our case, where it is presupposed that they assert in their petition that the lord bishop of Arezzo does not contradict it; they do not by this confess that the same lord bishop has any jurisdiction over them; indeed, I say that they rather appear to confess the opposite, since from his silence something seems to have been written against him as the diocesan. For since these words are introduced to exclude the bishop’s right, they ought not to produce a contrary effect against the intention of those who utter them; in support of this in a similar matter is a good text joined with the gloss in c. si iudice, de appel. lib. 6. Thirdly, it appears to be proved in l. non epistolis, and the following law, C. de proba.,

† where it is clear that by a naming made incidentally in some writing, the effect of that denomination is not proved. To the same effect is l. epistola, ff. de pactis, and l. neque professio, C. de testa., and very well l. interrogata, C. de libe. cau., joined with the gloss there on l. iubemus, C. eod., where it is clear that an express confession made against one's liberty outside of a trial concerning free status does not prejudice the confessing party. Therefore, the same applies in our case, and all the more strongly because the said words do not imply any acknowledgment against liberty. In support of the aforesaid is what is read and noted in c. cum olim, de testi. Likewise, with respect to the other words in which the Lord Pope requires that the consent of the lord bishop intervene for the granting of the favor, one can reply in many ways. First, as I said above, that perhaps the Lord Pope wished to honor the person of the said lord bishop, or perhaps, trusting in his diligence, wished that he be consulted, and this proceeds most especially after weighing two things. First, because it is not required that he consent as diocesan. Second, because in the same letters it is said that the said land, with respect to the ecclesiastical forum, pertains to the said lord abbot; which words sufficiently show that the Pope by these words did not wish to grant any jurisdiction to the said lord bishop in the said castle, since—indeed, and I say further—that even if the Lord Pope had called the said lord bishop the diocesan of that castle, he is not thereby presumed to have wished to confer anything anew upon the said lord bishop, as is proved in the said cle. si Romanus, and in c. si Papa, because these words were uttered enunciatively on account of something else, as I said above. Hence the Lord Pope in case of doubt is not presumed to wish to prejudice the right of a third party, as in c. super eo, de off. dele., and in l. 2, §. si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in loco pub. And let these things suffice, and far fewer would have sufficed, since this seems to me to be held without doubt, so that the trepidation of the petitioners might be satisfied more than the instituted doubt deserves. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. An appeal can lawfully be lodged when a grievance is inflicted in the execution of a sentence or of a precept.
2. Doubtful statutes ought to take an interpretation according to the law, so that they impair the ius commune as little as possible.
casus: HAVING SEEN the acts conducted both in the instance of the principal cause and of the appeal between Antonius Dominici on the one part, and Nicolaus Ioannis Martini on the other part, concerning a certain augment of the dowry of Lady Angela, mother of the said Antonius, consisting of one hundred and fifty florins, and concerning the execution of a precept made to the said Nicolaus to pay, and most recently concerning the validity of the appeal interposed from the lord podestà of the territory of Chianciano to the honorable syndics of the said territory by the said Nicolaus concerning the remainder of the payment of the said silver.
body: Having first invoked the help of our Savior and of his Mother, I shall proceed very succinctly. For a multitude of acts and allegations generates confusion, such that one must feel compassion for the lords syndics themselves, upon whom the burden presently rests. And for a clear decision of this matter, it must be observed that it is solely inquired by the lords syndics, judges of appeals, what their duties are in pronouncing judgment; and thus one need only distinguish concerning the validity of the appeal interposed to them by the said Nicolaus, who, in his libel of appeal produced before them, complains of the execution of the precept made against him by the lord podestà of the said territory, and in effect petitioned that it be sententially pronounced, decreed, and declared by the said lords syndics and their office that the said execution made against him, being unjustly, inequitably, and improperly made against the person of the said Nicolaus, be annulled and be of no efficacy and moment, because it was made besides and against the form of law and of the statutes of the said territory; and that it be pronounced and decreed that a copy of the petition and of the precept concerning the said execution be given to him, Nicolaus, with a term for objecting against the said precept, which term the said podestà refused to grant him, etc. On the part of the said Antonius, however, appellee in this article, it is excepted that the said appeal is not to be admitted, because it is against the form of law and of the statutes of the said territory speaking of execution to be made, as can be gathered especially from the form of the exceptions produced by the said Antonius. It only remains to be seen whether an appeal could be lodged by the said Nicolaus from the execution made personally by the said lord podestà. And omitting for the sake of brevity the arguments that could be made, rather frivolously, on the part of the appellee, I conclude that the said appeal is just, and consequently to be admitted. And I am moved to this opinion by several considerations, both from the disposition of the ius commune and from the statutes of the said territory.

† For wherever a grievance is inflicted in the execution of a definitive sentence or precept, an appeal is lawfully made even under the civil law, since no other definitive sentence is awaited in whose appeal the aggrieved party could be relieved from the grievance, as is read and noted in l. ab executione, C. quorum appel. non reci., and in c. quod ad consultationem, de re iud.; to which makes what is noted in l. 2, ff. de app. reci. uel non, and auth. habita, C. ne fi. pro patre, and 2, q. 6, c. sunt quorum ab executore. But in our case the podestà aggrieved the said Nicolaus by executing that sentence or precept; therefore he could appeal. That he aggrieved him is clear, because he denied him a copy of the petition produced by the said Antonius, nor did he wish to give him a term to object, when by law many things may be objected against the execution of a sentence, as is read and noted in l. 3, § condemnatum, and in l. a diuo Pio, ff. de re iud., and in both places by Bar.; in c. de caetero, eod. tit., de offi. del. c. pastoralis, § quod uero, and what is there fully noted, especially by Inn. in the said c. de caetero; and especially the aforesaid things proceed in our case, where execution was not sought upon adjudicated things, but in a personal action against the person and goods according to the form of the statute, in which case a citation must be made and the opportunity of defending oneself must be given to the party, as in l. a diuo Pio, cited above, at the word in uenditione, and there Bar. clearly maintains this, which Inno. also holds in c. cum super, near the end, de re iud. Nor does the statute of the city of the said territory, upon which the appellee grounds himself, stand in the way of this opinion—the statute placed under the rubric on the execution of an instrument with a clause of guarentigia, in the words in fine, where among other things it is provided that sentences and precepts not complained of or suspended by the remedy of appeal ought to be ordered into immediate execution, nor may anything be objected except that which can be objected against an instrument of guarentigia, etc., as is more broadly contained in the said statute—because I say that if the end of that statute is diligently weighed, that statute proves the opposite more clearly than light and grounds the position of the appellant. For there at the end is placed the following clause, namely: 'observando però la forma e sopra data secondo la forma del presente cap. e come ne li instrumenti guarentig.' And thus the end of that statute clearly intends that, in the execution of such a sentence or precept, the manner and form of the preceding chapter be observed, and so it is observed in an instrument of guarentigia; but in the present chapter it is provided that the podestà and his vicar are held and bound to assign a term of three days to the defendant to receive a copy of the petition and of the instrument of guarentigia and to object against it. Therefore it is clearly gathered that in our case as well the said term of three days ought to have been given to receive a copy of the petition and to object, even though he could not object anything except that which can be objected against an instrument of guarentigia; and since the podestà, though humbly requested, did not do this, the said Nicolaus could well appeal, through the things I have stated above. For that clause placed at the end of the statute, 'observando', qualifies the preceding provisions, as in c. inquisitioni, and c. 2, requiris, de ap., and as is read and noted especially by Bart. in l. talis scriptura, ff. de leg. 1. To the same effect is what is read and noted in l. Titio, ff. de uerb. ob., and in c. apostolicus, 34, q. 7, in gl. fi.; and this is also proved by another consideration.

† Doubtful statutes ought to take their interpretation according to the law, so that they impair the ius commune as little as possible, as is proved in c. dilectus, de consue.; in l. 3, C. de noxa; noted by Inn. in c. 1, de rescr., and Bart. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu., and l. 1, ff. ad leg. Fal. But by the ius commune, in the execution of a sentence or precept, at least in a personal action, a citation ought to be made, such that the party can object and defend himself, as in the said § in uenditione, and there Bar., and by Inn. in the said c. cum sup.; and it is proved similarly in c. a multis, de test. And because the said statute—presupposing that it were doubtful at its end, which in truth it is not—ought to be understood according to the ius commune, so that, as above, a citation is required and the ability to defend oneself is given to the party; and especially because natural laws urge this, so that it is lawful for anyone to defend himself; nay, defense is not denied even to an excommunicate, as in c. cum inter, de exce.; and the laws proclaim that nothing is to be attempted against an unheard party, in c. 1, de cau. pos. & proprie., and in Clem. pastoralis, de re iu., 3, q. 10, c. caueant, and in c. omnia; to which makes l. de unoquoque, de re iud. Likewise, it cannot be denied that, a doubt having arisen concerning the meaning of the statute, the lord podestà ought to have had recourse to the consilium of a sapiens, according to what is provided in the statute of the said territory; for this see l. et post rem iudicatam, ff. de cond. indeb. Wherefore, at least on this ground, the appeal of the said Nicolaus was just. It is no objection if it is said that the said Nicolaus was not to be heard because he did not observe the form of another statute concerning payment to be made according to the amount of the claims; because, if it is well noted, that does not apply to our case, since the statute speaks of those who claim something from a defendant, nor does it say that if payment is not made he is in no way to be heard so that the process is not valid. But in our case the said Nicolaus was claiming nothing for the present, but was only excepting by requesting a term to object and a copy of the petition, and thus we are outside the case of that statute. For I see that an excommunicate, who can claim nothing in court, can nevertheless defend himself if he is sued, as in the said c. cum inter; so in the present matter, although the said Nicolaus would not have been heard when demanding where payment was not made, nevertheless he ought not to have been excluded from defense against the petition of the said party. For otherwise an innocent person would often be condemned, which is absurd, as in the said c. cum inter. From all of which I conclude that the lords syndics ought to pronounce that the appeal of the said Nicolaus was and is just and legitimate, and to declare that the said execution made against his person by the said podestà was and is null, and insofar as it might be of any effect, to retract it as iniquitous, and to decree that a copy of the said petition made before the said lord podestà concerning the execution to be made be given to the said Nicolaus, assigning him a term of three days to object against the said execution sought, and to condemn the said Antonius to the said Nicolaus in the expenses incurred in this cause of appeal, because he litigated rashly; and finally the said syndics ought to proceed in the cause just as the said podestà would have proceeded, since they succeed in his place, de appel. c. ut debitus, with the similar chapters. And let these things suffice as to the present article. N. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A prelate alone without other solemnity can repudiate an inheritance of long standing made to the church, even of immovable property.
2. Hospitals constructed without the authority of the diocesan cannot be called religious places, nor strictly pious.
3. Lepers staying in a place not founded by the authority of the bishop are not bound to episcopal rights.
casus: The factual situation is as follows: In the city of Massa there is a certain fraternity of laymen which is called the fraternity of the Holy Cross, and they assemble in a place of the Order of St. Francis in a certain chapel under the title of the Holy Cross; which fraternity indeed undertook many works of piety, both from the substance of the brothers themselves and from bequests made to the said fraternity. To this fraternity a certain man devoted to God left many goods to be distributed to pious causes, and it was specifically added that something should be given to the lord Bishop of Massa; yet he did not burden them as to the quantity, leaving it to the conscience of the members of the confraternity. This fraternity gave 12 florins to the lord Bishop, and also had and received from him an acquittance and a free and complete release concerning the said bequest. At length, upon the Bishop's death, it is claimed in the name of his successor that the said release was not valid for so small a quantity, and the full quantity is demanded, both of that bequest and of the others. On the part of the confraternity they allege that the said release was valid, and that the said fraternity is not bound to the canonical portion, especially because there is no memory that it had ever paid it, although many bequests had been made to it. The question is, what is the law?
body: The aid of Christ the Savior and of His most devout Mother having been implored, for the clear decision of all the aforesaid matters three questions must be examined. First, whether the said discharge can be revoked by the successor. Second, whether the said fraternity is bound to pay the canonical portion to the local bishop from the bequests made to it. Third, assuming that it is bound by law, whether by virtue of custom or prescription the said confraternity can excuse itself. Concerning the first, I will not insist much, since it does not seem to me to contain great doubt, as it is clearer than certainty that the said lord bishop was able to make that discharge. For either the fourth was not owed from the bequest—which in truth was not owed, as will appear from what is to be said below, and the case is indubitable, because that same bishop could not demand more than the quantity that had been left in their conscience, according to what is held and noted in cap. statutum, § assessorem, de rescrip. in Sexto; and the notable gloss in clementi. prima, de iure patro.—or because, assuming that something more was owed to the bishop, the bishop, since he had the free administration of revenues according to what is noted by the gloss in 12. quaestio 1. cap. duo sunt genera, and is proved in cap. cum nobis, at the end, de elec., could make a remission of the remainder, especially since everything was to be converted to a pious cause. For a bishop is bound to convert superfluities to a pious cause, 83. distin. cap. 1, and 12. quaestio 1. cap. uidentes; and whatever clerics have belongs to the poor, 16. quaestio 1. cap. solite. Therefore, he was able to leave not merely a part, but the whole to the fraternity to be distributed to pious causes; for a prelate, not only in acquiring, but indeed from what is already acquired, can make a fitting alms, as in cap. ad haec, and cap. relatum 2. de test.; moreover, he may give modest gifts to anyone, as in cap. caeterum, de dona. Likewise I say, for the aforesaid reasons, that if the fourth had been owed, and especially because here it was a matter of losing something to be acquired, a bishop can make the condition of the church worse, as is noted in 16. quaestio 6. § fin., where there is a good gloss, and by Innocent in cap. fraternitatem, de dona.; and the things noted by the doctors in cap. quoniam, de deci. serve excellently. Hence Federicus de Senis notably said in consil. 9, and Baldus follows him in l. pupillorum, C. de repu. haer.,

† that a prelate alone without other solemnity can repudiate an inheritance of long standing made to the church, even of immovable property, because it is one thing not to acquire, and another to alienate things already acquired. But in our case there is not such great doubt, because he left the bequests to be converted into a pious work, and because, as I shall say below, in the truth of the matter the fourth was not owed. I conclude therefore that the successor cannot rescind the said discharge made by his predecessor. I come to the second, which is more doubtful: namely, whether the said fraternity is bound to the bishop on account of the canonical portion. And it seems at first that it is, because not only from churches, but also from monasteries and other pious places do the laws will that the bishop can exact his canonical portion, as is proved in c. requisisti and c. fin. de testa. But the said fraternity is a pious collegium, as in c. si quis, 62. dist., and there by Archidiaconus; l. 1 and what Bartolus notes there in ff. de col. illi. supports this; and this is clear by reason of its exercise. For it exercises works of piety, therefore it is pious; for a place is called pious from the fact that works of piety are exercised there, as Johannes Andreae notes in c. Joannes, de testa., and Speculator in the title de instru. editio. § nunc uero aliqua, at the verse & scias, near the middle. What more? Dom. Petrus de Perusio expressly held this in his treatise on the fourth. But these notwithstanding, I think the contrary proceeds by law, especially in our case. I am moved first because this fourth is owed from bequests made to pious places subject to the bishop, but not from a personal bequest, even if it was made to a cleric. This is proved in c. requisisti, and c. fin., and 10. q. 1. de his, and c. antiquis, il 2, and noted by Johannes Andreae after Hostiensis in c. 1. de sepul. But in our case it is not left to the said fraternity, but the legacy is made to a place, because the fraternity is not assigned to a place, but is a personal collegium and a certain fictional represented body, as in l. mortuo, ff. de fideiusso., noted by Bartolus in l. si, ff. de colleg. illi.; for it can assemble wherever it wishes, by the argument in cap. si quis; therefore the fourth was not owed. For when it is left to such a fraternity, respect is not had to the place where it assembles, but to the fictional and represented body itself. And if anyone wishes stubbornly to persist there, saying that it is made to the place, I say that it is all the more clear that the fourth is not owed, because the said fraternity is in an exempt place, which is not bound to the bishop for the canonical portion, as the doctors commonly note in capitulo officium, de testamen.; Federicus, consil. 116. Second, I am principally moved by the ceasing of the rationale for why this fourth is owed to the bishop. For the fundamental rationale is the very communion that exists between the bishop and the clerics subject to him, by reason of which common bond all goods were common between the bishop and inferior places. But because common things are accustomed to generate scandal, l. cum pater, § dulcissimis, ff. de lega. 2, and what is read and noted in capitulo si quis, de uita & honesta. cleri., and in capit. ex tenore, de senten. excommu., canons were issued decreeing that the fourth is owed to bishops; these things are clearly gathered from the said capitulo requisisti, and from the sayings of Johannes Andreae there. This rationale of community ceases between the bishop and the said fraternity. For there is no communion by reason of the place—both because the place does not belong to the fraternity, and because that place is exempt—nor by reason of persons, since they are pure laics, and thus are of another kind than the bishop, and there are two kinds of Christians, one of clerics, the other of laics, as is held in capitulo duo sunt genera, 12. quaest. prima; and thus there is no communion between them, indeed there ought not to be, since the life of clerics ought to be separated from the life of laics, in capitulo laicos, and the following chapter, 2. q. 7. Nor by this fraternity do they cease to be under the jurisdiction of the secular judge, since this is proved by no law, but rather the opposite is noted in clemen. prima de religiosis domi. And if anyone should wish to say that there is another rationale for this fourth, namely on account of the episcopal burden which the bishop undergoes in the collation of orders, and consecration, and administration of sacraments, as the said Petrus thinks in the said treatise; Hostiensis in Summa, de sepul. § licitum, alias § uetus, at the verse naturalibus; I say that this rationale entirely ceases in this confraternity, since the bishop does not undergo these things toward this confraternity either by reason of place or of persons; therefore the statutory disposition ought to cease, as in capitulo cum cessante, de appel., 16. quaest. prima, capit. generaliter. Third, I introduce this reason: the bequest to the confraternity is not made by reason of place, nor by reason of the persons of the confraternity, but by reason of the poor; hence this confraternity seems chosen as a distributor and dispenser for pious causes, as is clear from the intentions of the testators and is gathered from the sense of the said cap. si quis. But from a bequest made to the poor a fourth is not owed to the bishop, as in capitulo 2. de sepul., even if it is to be distributed through another or through the bishop himself, as in l. nulli and in l. si quis ad declinandum, C. de episco. & cleri.; therefore neither from a bequest made to the said fraternity. Nor does a saying of Johannes Andreae stand in the way, set down in capitulo dudum, de conuer. con., where he says that if a bequest was made to the poor of a certain place, the fourth is owed, by the argument in the said cap. requisisti. Because, although that saying is true, nevertheless it does not oppose our conclusion. For when a bequest was made to the poor of a certain place, the bequest seems to be made not only in contemplation of the persons, but also of the place, because the bequest is acquired for the pious place itself, concerning which it can dispose at will; hence since the pious place is subject to the bishop, deservedly by reason of the common bond and the episcopal burden such a bequest ought to be shared with the bishop. But in our case the bequest is in no way acquired for the place—and assuming that it were acquired, which is nonetheless false, the rationale would cease, since that place is exempt—rather the bequest is personal, and made principally on account of the needy. Hence no reason appears why this fourth should be owed to the bishop. And if the ancient laws are weighed well, this fourth was introduced on account of the poverty of the bishop; hence it seemed honorable that the pious places subject to the bishop should succor him from all things that came in, since the bishop is the ruler and head of such pious places, and the administrator in many things, and undergoes many burdens in contemplation of them, as is held in 10. q. 3. capitulo 1 & 2. Which rationale indeed ceases in these laics, who are not under the jurisdiction of the bishop, but only assemble so that they may exercise works of piety, as I said above. The laws speaking of this fourth commonly speak of bequests made to churches and pious places, but not those made to collegia approved by law, and thus the foundation of those holding the opposite ceases. Nay rather, Baldus, a most excellent doctor, and two other doctors with him, advised against the bishop in broader terms, namely, that from a bequest made to a hospital not constructed by the authority of the bishop, the fourth is not owed, because the laws speak of pious places, and thus of religion, which are subject to the bishop.

† But such hospitals without the authority of the diocesan cannot be called religious, nor strictly pious, since they can be dissolved at the will of the builder, as in capitulo inter dilectos, and what is noted there by Innocent, de dona., and capitulo de Xenodochijs, de re. domi.; for since such a place is private, it does not seem capable of receiving a bequest, and thus the bequest seems made rather to the poor than to the place. This must be said all the more strongly in our case, and precisely on our terms in favor of the fraternity and against the bishop; Bartolus determined this after lengthy words in l. si quis ad declinandum, C. de epi. & cleric. Likewise, it at least cannot be denied that the case is doubtful; but in doubt one must stand by custom, which is the best interpreter of laws, as in capitulo dilecto, de consuetu., and l. si de interpretatione, ff. de legi. But the custom in the said city of Messina, and commonly in other places, is that the fourth is not exacted from the said fraternities; therefore it ought entirely to cease. And to this argument I now see no answer. Federicus also seems to hold this, consil. 225, where he says,

† that lepers dwelling in some place not founded by the authority of the bishop are not bound to episcopal rights, since their place is private and not religious. I conclude on the second article that the said fraternity is not obligated to the fourth from bequests. I come to the third: assuming that it is bound by law, whether by virtue of prescription or custom it can defend itself. And this question is found formulated by the doctors regarding churches, whether by this right they can prescribe

† against the bishop. And I find three opinions. The first, that it can be prescribed in quantity, but not as a whole. The second, that notwithstanding custom, at least the fourth is owed. The third, that it can be prescribed as a whole; this is noted in cap. requisisti and cap. officij, de testa., and in cap. certificari, de secul. That it cannot be prescribed as a whole, as Johannes and Vincentius and Hostiensis maintain in the said cap. requisisti, and likewise Innocent there, although Hostiensis reports that Innocent later changed his opinion in a question of fact and said that the fourth was owed notwithstanding custom, yet this does not appear in Innocent's lectura. Likewise, Hostiensis himself, discussing this matter most broadly in his Summa, title de secul., in § an litium, alias under metus, at the end of that §, concluded that, notwithstanding that he was a bishop, a custom diminishing the portion is valid, but not one taking it away entirely, since it seems irrational; but prescription is valid according to him if the title is against the law, as in c. de quarta, de praescript. The gloss very clearly held the same in c. 1, de sta. reg., and Johannes Andreae clearly agrees there, alleging in corroboration of that gloss c. de quarta, and many moderns follow this in the said c. requisisti. And so this seems to be the common opinion, that it can be prescribed as a whole. And this opinion has always pleased me. And our case is squarely in point in the said cap. de quarta, where it says that a priest can defend himself against the bishop over the fourth of tithes and the oblation of the dead by prescription. But in our case there is a prescription of such time that there is no memory of its beginning. And such a prescription supplies the defect of title and is valid against the common law, as in cap. 1. de praescript. in Sexto; therefore one must stand by this prescription, and it fully takes away this fourth, as in cap. officij, de testa.; therefore also prescription. For prescription is valid against these immovable things of the church, as in cap. auditis and in c. cum olim, de rescrip., and more strongly against things to be acquired, and especially in our case, where by law it is not clear that this fourth is owed. I conclude that this fraternity can defend itself by prescription, even assuming that it was bound by law. From these things the first article remains clearer. For the bishop received those twelve florins by reason of the bequest, and not by reason of the fourth, and thus the successor cannot say that the fourth was not paid in full. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A hundred-year prescription only runs in bequests made to religious places.
2. Knowledge is not presumed in the act of another.
3. The Church is granted restitution against judicial acts.
casus: Circumstances of the case: A certain man, now deceased, while he was alive, disposed among other things in his testament as follows: 'First of all, I direct that my body be buried at the house of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis of Siena, where I choose my burial; in which place I direct, will, and command that my below-written executors make or cause to be made a chapel dedicated to the blessed apostle Bartholomew in that spot which shall seem fit to my said executors. On which chapel, together with the ornaments of the church and vestments and other things necessary for the same, two hundred gold florins shall be spent from my goods, so that the divine office may be celebrated in it in perpetuity for my soul and the souls of my parents.' And the said testament or legacy was made in the year of the Lord 1255, and thus 80 years have already elapsed during which nothing was ever executed by the said executors or by anyone else. Now it is asked whether prescription stands in the way of claiming the said legacy; and, assuming that it does stand in the way, whether against it the benefit of restitution in integrum can be implored, etc.
body: The aid of Christ and of His Mother having been humbly implored: It seems in the first place that it must be said that prescription does not apply in this case, because prescription does not run against one who is legally unable to sue, as in l. 1, C. de anna. excep., where prescription does not run against a son during the father’s lifetime who has the usufruct of his property, because while the parent is living he cannot sue for those things, l. non solum, C. de bon. quę libe. To the same effect is l. in rebus, C. de iur. do., where it is said that prescription does not run against a wife during marriage with respect to dowry goods, because during marriage she cannot sue for them, as in l. doce ancillam, C. de rei uen. To the same effect is cap. quia diuersitatem, de conces. pręben. But it is the case that the Friars Minor cannot appear in court for temporal matters, and thus cannot sue, as in clemen. exiui de paradiso, de uerbo. significa.; therefore prescription does not run.

† Furthermore and secondly, in bequests made to religious places only a hundred-year prescription runs, as in l. ut inter diuinum, C. de sacro sanct. eccle. But in our case so much time has not elapsed; therefore the church's right is intact, and especially if it is considered that that entire period of 80 years to be reckoned from the opening of the testament ought not to be computed in the prescription; because since prescription does not run without good faith, de prscrip. cap. uigilanti, and cap. fin., and in the rule possessor mal fidei, de regu. iur. lib. 6, and an outside heir is presumed to know the contents of the testament, at least that time ought to be deducted from which the goods remained in the hands of the heir himself, from which time prescription cannot begin because bad faith stands in the way. For he was in bad faith from the moment he had knowledge of this legacy, 34. q. 2. c. si uirgo, which knowledge he is presumed to have had for the reason aforesaid. Likewise and thirdly, the friars were ignorant of the bequest; indeed, it was generally unknown,

† nor is knowledge to be presumed in the act of another, as in the rule prsumitur ignorantia, de reg. iur. lib. 6; therefore prescription does not run, which was primarily instituted out of hatred for the negligent, as in cap. uigilanti, de prscrip. But these points notwithstanding—which in truth are not conclusive in our case, as will appear below—I say that two things must first be examined: first, what sort of right was acquired by the friars from that bequest; second, it must be considered against whom the action is brought for the execution of the said bequest. As to the first, I say conclusively that no right was acquired by the aforesaid friars, since they cannot appropriate anything to themselves, as in the said clemen. exiui de paradiso, but the right was acquired by the church itself of the friars. Whence, although in other religious orders and colleges this is the case, that they themselves have a right in the church, and that which is granted to the church is deemed granted to the college; nevertheless in the case of the Friars Minor these things cannot be said, because they have no right in the church, but only a simple use of fact. Whence the church and the pious place are deemed to use by precarious right. These are the words of Barto. in the tractate on the Minorites, which begins ‘Si aliquis in suo testamento,’ where he reports that, although the friars are incapable of inheritance, as in the said clementi. exiui, this nevertheless is not to be referred to their church, because they cannot be instituted heirs as another ecclesiastical college can, l. j. C. de sac. sanct. eccl., because through such a bequest nothing is acquired by the friars. The same and even more forcibly must be said in the case of a bequest made to a church; therefore, for divine worship the right acquired by the church shall be exercised, or the thing bequeathed shall be claimed, as Barto. concludes in the place cited above in the following chapter, through the syndic of the Roman Church, since the Supreme Pontiff is the rector of the churches of the Friars Minor themselves, while the friars themselves have simple use, as was said above. The friars themselves, however, can nominate a syndic by virtue of the privilege granted to them by Pope Martin IV, which with respect to bequests made to the church has not been revoked, as Barto. notes more fully in the said tractate. But if the said syndic cannot be had, because the friars are unwilling to nominate him, or it has been forbidden to them, he says that the bishop will be able to pursue such matters by reason of the pious cause, by the argument in l. nulli, and l. si quis ad declinandum, C. de episc. & cle., notwithstanding that the church is exempt, just as if the bequest concerned some pious cause outside the diocese. For the bishop can intervene by reason of the testator himself, if he were under his cure, as in the said l. nulli, and what is noted there. If, however, the bishop does not act, or is negligent, the city in which the church is established can intervene, because the church there pertains to the honor and benefit of all citizens; l. j. ff. de publi. iudi. is relevant, and l. ciuitatibus, ff. de lega. j. is exceedingly relevant; and Bartolus speaks when the church of the friars has been instituted heir, as in our case, where the testator ordered a chapel to be built. I adduce the clear text in authen. de eccle. titu. col. 9, where it is said that causing execution belongs not only to the bishop, but also to the civil judge, so that there is room for prevention; thus I say that the citizens deputed here at Siena by the general council were able to take cognizance of this cause. I conclude therefore concerning this first point that from such a bequest no right was acquired, nor is any held in the hands of the friars themselves, but rather in the hands of the church, to be advanced nevertheless through the aforesaid persons. Now, for the solution of the principal question, the second inquiry must be examined, which is now at issue, through which it will appear what sort of right belongs to the church, and whether it is prescribed, and by how much time. In which it must be observed that either the action is brought against the heir, and he cannot defend himself by prescription because he is presumed to be in bad faith, as I said above—and the same seems to be said of the heir’s heir, even if he himself was in good faith, because since he is deemed the same person, the bad faith of the deceased harms the heir, and this is very clear in civil law, as is proved in l. cum hęres, ff. de diuer. & tempo. pręscrip., although according to canonical equity the contrary seems to hold, so that an heir who has good faith may by equity begin prescription, as Din. thinks in the rule possessor, de regu. iur. lib. 6; what is read and noted in cap. de quarta, de pręscrip., and cap. cura, de iure patro., supports this; but since the action is now brought against a layman, the civil law is to be observed, by the argument of the things noted in cap. 2 de ar. lib. 6 and cap. de clericis, de foro compe.—or the action is brought against an outside possessor of the goods of the said testator, which can happen by bringing the hypothecary action according to l. j. C. communia de leg., and then, if indeed he possesses by title of heir and now alleges the prescription of the hypothecary action, and in doubt, for prescription to be completed, it is required that he has possessed with good faith for 40 years, because a shorter time does not prescribe against the church, de pręsc. c. de quarta, and cap. cum olim, and almost throughout, and in authen. quas actiones, C. de sac. sanct. eccle., and in the body, de eccle. ti. . pro temporalibus; and the same seems in this case to apply against a private person, because the hypothecary action is not prescribed in a shorter time, as in l. cum notissimi, C. de prĖscri. 30. uel 40. anno.; or this third party possesses without title of heir, indeed he alleges prescription against the heir, and consequently against the church, and then a period of 40 years with title seems to suffice by the text in l. prima and secunda, C. si aduer. hĖre., for the hypothecary action is primarily directed against the church. But it is the very ownership of the heir that I say is prescribed by lapse of time, as in the previously cited legal authorities, unless we say that there is a special rule in the rights of the church, so that they are in no way prescribed in a time less than 40 years, as in the said . pro temporalibus, where the text also speaks of bequests for pious causes and clearly provides that recovery is not prescribed in a time less than 40 years. From these things the solution to the principal question can be grasped, whether the prescription is valid or complete. Nor do the arguments formulated above to the contrary stand in the way. And first, to the first, I admit that the Friars Minor themselves could not and cannot sue, but others could sue, such as the syndic of the Roman Church, or the bishop of the place, and the city where that church is; whence through the negligence of administrators prescription runs against one who cannot sue, as is clearly seen in a bequest made for the redemption of captives and the feeding of the poor, who cannot plead the case because the captives are uncertain, but because of the negligence of the bishop prescription runs; such is the text with the gloss in the said l. ut inter diuinum, noted by Federic. de Senis, de consti. capitu. 1. What is said concerning the son of a family and concerning the wife does not stand in the way, because the husband does not possess as administrator of the wife, but by his own right which he has in those things, and the same in the father. Likewise no church can sue, since it is an inanimate body, but because of the negligence of the possessors and administrators prescription runs against it, as in de pręscri. throughout. The second argument concerning l. ut inter diuinum, where in such bequests only a prescription of one hundred years is admitted, does not stand in the way, because I say that that law was corrected in this respect by authen. quas actiones, which immediately follows there and appears more clearly in the body from which it is taken, namely de eccle. tit. . pro temporalibus; so holds the gloss in c. si. 16. q. 4; whence today only the Roman Church enjoys the privilege of one hundred years, as in c. 2 de prscrip. lib. 6, and in c. cum nobis, eod. titu., and the said authen. quas actiones. The third principal argument founded upon ignorance does not stand in the way, because prescription runs even against the ignorant, as is proved in l. fin. C. de prscrip. long. tempo., and the said c. 2, and cap. uigilanti, de prscri.; for they are seen in a certain way to be negligent in that they do not seek out what is incumbent upon them and pertains to them, arg. in cap. quamuis, de regu. iur. I come now to the second principal question: presupposing that the prescription is complete, whether restitution in integrum ought to be granted to the church against that prescription; and this is an elegant and subtle doubt, in which the ancient glossators and writers intermingle diverse opinions, and Ber., the first glossator, varied greatly on this in capitu. auditis, de prscript., turning now toward one opinion and now toward the contrary, but nevertheless he adhered to the opinion of Joan. and Vincen., who agreed that restitution is to be denied, moved by the fact that the laws intended churches to be prejudiced in prescriptions, in cap. placuit 16. q. 3, and in the same cause, qust. 4, capitu. uolumus. Likewise because, if restitution were available, the laws of prescription speaking against the church would have been issued in vain. Gossre. held the same in sum. de in integ. resti. in the 2nd column, saying that he never found a church restored in usucaption so that the periods of time were removed from the midst, as in capitu. 1 de rescrip.; in judicial prescriptions the church is equated to a minor. This opinion is shared by the gloss in cle. prima de integr. resti., saying that that clementine speaks of restitution against prescription against which restitution is granted, remitting to the note in the said capitu. auditis, introducing nothing new; but more numerous in number and more elegant in intellect agree on the contrary opinion: first Accur., the glossator of the civil law, in the said authen. quas actiones, and more clearly in auth. de eccl. titu. . pro temporalibus, where he said this is commonly held. Secondly, Joan., the glossator of the Decretum, held this in capi. placuit, col. 2, 16. qust. 3. Pope Inno., a most subtle doctor, in cap. 1 de in integ. resti. Pau. de Leaza. and Joan. de lig. followed this opinion in cle. 1 de in integ. rest., cited above, c. auditis. And there almost all moderns in cap. contingit, de transac., and Hostien. in suma, de in integ. rest. . 3 near the end; Bal. and Bart. held this in the said auth. quas actiones, where they poorly and unfaithfully recite the opinions of the canonists. This opinion is proved by reason: prescription runs against a minor, yet he is restored, C. si aduer. usu., and in l. fi. in qui. cau. in integ. rest. non est neces., noted by the gloss in l. sicut, C. de prscr. 30. anno.; therefore the same must be said of the church, which enjoys the right of a minor in restitution, as in capit. primo, and cap. auditis, de in integ. resti., and in cap. 1 and 2, eo. tit. lib. 6, and in cle. una, e. tit. Nor is it valid if it is said that those laws speak of contracts and judicial prescriptions, because no reason appears for so restricting them. For if restitution is granted against a contract, through which, delivery having followed, ownership is transferred, therefore it is even more forcibly to be granted against prescription, since contract is of the ius gentium, l. ex hoc iure, ff. de iusti. & iure, and the consent of both parties intervenes, l. sicut, C. de act. & obli. Prescription, however, was invented by civil law, and caused independently of the consent of the parties. If therefore the stronger bond is dissolved, much more forcibly is the less strong, argu. in auth. multo magis, C. de epis. & cle., and cap. cum in cunctis, de elect. Likewise judicial acts, in order that they may hold, are very favorable, and thus they are the end of lawsuits, in c. finem litibus, de dolo & contu., and l. quidam Ėstimauerunt, ff. si cer. pe.; hence elsewhere a noted gloss said that the wrongdoing of a prelate harms the church in judicial matters, but not in contracts, as is noted in the rule delictum prlati, de regu. iu. lib. 6.

† But against judicial acts the church is restored, even against a judgment, as in cap. j. de in integ. resti. lib. 6, and in cap. auditis, cited above; therefore much more forcibly against extrajudicial prescription. Furthermore, the said clementine speaks indistinctly that the church may not be restored against the lapse of time, therefore against prescription, which is caused by the running of time. And this side I judge to be truer, especially in view of the ignorance of this legacy. For in legacies, as Bartol. singularly maintained in l. 1 . si quis autem, ff. de iti. actuque priua., an adult is to be restored against prescription when ignorant, by the argument of that law; I adduce to the same effect the notable gloss which held this in l. P. Antonius, ff. de acquir. hĖredi. That the laws intended to prejudice the church by prescription does not stand in the way, because the same is found in a minor, and nevertheless restitution is granted; nor does it follow that the laws are thereby rendered futile, because this is false, since restitution must be sought within a four-year period, which having elapsed, if no other just cause appears, the prescription remains firm, as in cap. 1 & 2 de in integ. restitutio. lib. 6. That this is not expressly provided in the law does not stand in the way, because it is enough that it is included under general words; for the laws generally will that the church be aided by the benefit of restitution, as in the laws cited above. But there now remains another point no less strong: for presupposing that restitution is to be granted, nevertheless it must be obtained within a four-year period from the time of injury, and not beyond, as in the said cap. 1 & 2 de in integ. restitutio. lib. 6, and in clemen. 1 eod. titu., and l. fin. C. de tempo. in integ. restitut. But in our case it is impossible according to what I said above, because not only the time of completed prescription, and thus of the injury, and thus the four-year period, but a greater time has elapsed; therefore, such a case occurring, this benefit is not to be granted. To this I reply in two ways: First, that that period of four years is from the beginning available time (tempus utile), whence it does not run against one who is ignorant; the text is in cap. 2 eodem titu. lib. 6, where it says: ‘if anyone has negligently omitted,’ etc. But one who is ignorant does not act negligently, as is proved in cap. 2 joined with capitu. quia diuersitatem, de concessio. pręben. To the same effect is the gloss in capit. qum sit, de electio. libr. 6, on the word ‘distulerit’; and this opinion was singularly held by Zen. and Joan. de lig. after him in the said clemen. una, on the word ‘continuum’; this is supported by the fact that this four-year period succeeds in place of the available year (annus utilis) which formerly applied, as the text says in the said l. fin. C. de tempo. in integ. restitu.; it ought therefore to be available (utile) from the beginning, so that it thus smacks of the nature of that in whose place it is substituted, arg. cap. ut ecclesia, ut lit. penden. Secondly, I reply no less effectively: the text in the said cap. 1 says that the church is not to be heard after the four-year period unless some reasonable cause underlies, which ought to move the superior to grant this benefit; but if all circumstances in our case are well weighed, a reasonable cause is very easily found. Here, first, there was ignorance of the legacy, which is a just cause for restoring even an adult, as I said above. Secondly and better, here the right of that church is at issue which for promoting this matter does not have a special and proper administrator, without whom the affairs of the church cannot be conducted, and the Pope is very remote, and cannot bestow care in these matters, and the bishop does not care, since on account of ecclesiastical exemption they are less accustomed to care. To this effect is what Innocen. singularly noted in the said cap. olim, col. 2, de restitu. spolia., where he says that if an inferior church lacks a legitimate and immediate administrator, prescription does not run against it, although the bishop could act on its behalf, and this on the ground that there is no one who takes special care; the same therefore, and more forcibly, should be said, so that here at least that four-year period does not run, given probable ignorance, which here is sufficiently to be presumed, etc. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The ordinary must obey the delegate in the act of executing a sentence.
2. A sentence of excommunication, whether just or unjust, is to be feared.
3. The appeal of a manifest despoiler is not to be admitted.
4. Many things are said to be notorious which are not.
casus: The case in effect is such: A judge deputed by the Apostolic See cited a certain absent person by edict, perhaps being unable to cite him personally, and upon his finally not appearing, he fulminated sentences of interdict and excommunication against him, and thus at last commanded that he be publicized through the churches and avoided. Afterward, that man thus excommunicated appeared in those churches in which he had been publicized, and produced proof of an appeal of his interposed before those sentences were passed, with just causes apparent in it, and especially that cause, that he had been cited to a place notoriously suspect to him and unsafe, saying that he ought no longer to be avoided, especially because the judge to whom the appeal was made admitted it and issued an inhibition against proceeding further while the appeal was pending. Likewise because certain statutes are found in the cathedral church of that place which seem to concede communion in the aforesaid case. But the judge from whom the appeal was made, who pronounced the excommunication, insists that he be avoided, saying that the appeal is null, especially because those sentences and censures were passed for a notorious excess; the defendant, however, wholly denies this. It is asked whether, matters standing thus, he ought in the meantime to be avoided in divine offices and other matters.
body: The protection of Christ and of His Mother being humbly invoked, it appears at first that he ought to be avoided, through what the glossa notes on cap. dilectus, de appella. in fin., which says that if it is doubted whether the appeal holds, he is rather to be avoided than that one should in doubt communicate with him; argu. de elect. extra in cap. fina., and more to the point is cap. illud in the same title, where in our subject-matter the text says that in doubtful matters the safer path is to be chosen, namely that the excommunication be rather observed. To the same effect serves in argu. cap. iuuenis, de spons. cle. exitu, de uerbo. significa., where it says that in doubtful matters that path is to be chosen which is without danger, but in the case of avoidance no danger underlies, and in the other case there is, assuming the validity of the excommunication; therefore, etc. To this also serves cap. 1 and the glossa noted there, de scruti. Secondly and principally, Innocent appears to hold this in cap. ad præsentiam, de appella., where he says that although an excommunicated person after an appeal is not bound to conduct himself as excommunicated if he is confident of his appeal, he is nevertheless to be avoided by others; cap. per tuas, de senten. excommunica., where the text seems to intimate this in versic. nos igitur.

† Thirdly serves capit. pastoralis, § quia uero, de offic. delega., where it is said that even the ordinary must obey the delegate in the act of executing a sentence, even if he knows his sentence to be unjust. Therefore, since the delegate in our case insists, it seems that his precept ought not to be resisted.

† Fourthly, because a sentence of excommunication, whether just or unjust, is to be feared, 12 q. 3, c. sententia pastoris, and a subject in doubt is bound to obey and comply with his superior, 23 q. 5, c. quid culpatus, and 11 q. 3, c. quod ergo.

† Fifthly, there is a case on this in cap. cum sis Romana, in fin., de appel., where it is said that an appeal of a manifest despoiler is not to be admitted, and that for a notorious crime the Apostle excommunicated the Corinthian while absent and without having summoned him; to the same effect serves 2 q. 1, cap. de manifesta. But notwithstanding these things, which in my judgment do not stand in the way, I say on this point, saving a better judgment, that the case falls under c. solent, in fi., de sen. excommu. in 6., where it is said that if anyone objecting that he was excommunicated after a probable appeal demands to be admitted to prove it, he ought only to be avoided in judicial matters, and not in other, extrajudicial matters; wherefore he is to be admitted to elections and to other spiritual matters or divine offices during the appeal, and this is clearly the opinion there of Inn. and Io. And., who say that even before proofs are admitted as to whether the causes of the appeal are true or not, he ought to be admitted to the aforesaid matters, at least with a protestation. Wherefore it is enough according to them that the excommunicated person appears and says that he had appealed before the sentence. And in favor of this opinion I cite a text that in my judgment openly proves this, in c. licet, in the same title in 6., where it is said that if anyone asserts that he was excommunicated after an appeal, and has prosecuted the appeal within the time established by law, he ought to be pronounced and denounced as excommunicated, so that he may be avoided, and not only in judicial matters, but also in extrajudicial and other lawful acts, until he has proved that the excommunication was not lawful or has otherwise shown its nullity. Behold therefore, most clearly, that before any prosecution of the appeal he ought not to be avoided, provided that he asserts that he appealed, and thus within the time for prosecution established by law. And thus in those two chapters the case of this question is seen to consist. Another chapter quite remarkable on this subject I introduce to the same effect, namely capitulu. dilectis, in fin., de appella. previously cited, where canons communicating with excommunicated persons after an appeal and after the denunciation of the archbishop are judged blameless, because they preferred to defer to the appeal interposed to the Pope rather than to the denunciation of the archbishop. And the reason for all the aforesaid can be that, since a lawful appeal has the effect of suspending the jurisdiction of the judge, and thus of impeding the validity of an excommunication afterwards pronounced, as in capitulu. per tuas, de sen. excom. and capitulu. cum contingat, de of. del. and the said c. licet, the injustice of the appeal ought not to be presumed with so great a prejudice to the appellant; and because on the other hand it is not to be presumed entirely against the judge, a sort of middle way is taken, so that in judicial matters, which are more odious, the excommunicated person ought to be avoided while the appeal is pending, but otherwise in extrajudicial matters, lest his right be so greatly prejudiced. Although Innocent concedes in the said capitulu. solet that in private familiarity he may be avoided in secret, if this can be done without scandal, but not in public, unless it were notoriously evident that the appeal was unjust, because such an appeal does not defend, by the said capitulu. cum sit Romana and capitulu. cum appellatio, de appella. in 6. But in our case this cannot be said. First, because the judge ad quem received the appeal, and did what he could not do unless he had first received the appeal as made on a probable cause and not against what is notorious, as is proved in capit. Romana, § si uero, with § seq. and capitulu. non solum, de appella. in 6. Likewise, since the citation was made to a place notoriously not safe, he was able to appeal immediately even in the absence of the judge, as in clemen. pastoralis, § & pristina, and the gloss there, de re iudi., and what is read and noted in capitulu. ex parte, de appel.; to which serves capitulu. si iustus, in the same title, and what Innocent notes in the said capitulu. dilectus. Nor is it valid if it is said that he was notoriously occupying unjustly the property of the church, because this is denied by the adverse party, and a probable title for possessing was alleged, and thus the matter is rendered doubtful, as is the gloss noted in capitulu. fin., de offic. delega. in 6.; to which serves l. 3, C. quibus ad liber. procla. non licet.

† Moreover, many things are called notorious which are not, in capitulu. consuluit, de appella., and it is sufficient that he could have had some just cause of possession; therefore he ought not to be excommunicated before his defenses were heard, a good argument in capitulu. licet episcopus, de præben. in 6. Likewise, the text in capitulu. sacro indistinctly forbids anyone to be excommunicated without a canonical warning preceding, no matter how notorious the act is said to be; because an excommunication is pronounced by man not on account of the delict, but on account of contumacy, as the gl. notes in c. episcopi, 11 q. 3. But it is equivalent not to cite someone or to cite him to a place notoriously not safe, argu. in the said laws, and c. si duobus, de appel. The contrary arguments do not stand in the way. And first, the gloss in the said cap. dilectis; for it must be understood and determined according to the new laws cited above, or it can be saved in private and secret familiarity, as I said above, or in judicial matters. To the second, concerning the statement of Innocent in cap. ad præsentiam, de appel., it must be said that it must be understood and limited as he himself notes in the said cap. solet. For he is moved there by capitulu. per tuas, de appel., which today receives a limitation through cap. solet and cap. licet, previously cited. To the third, concerning cap. pastoralis, I say that it proceeds when the sentence is of some effect, even if unjust. But in our case the precept of the judge regarding avoidance is void by law itself, since it is against the laws cited above. Therefore such a precept can be disregarded; to this effect what Innocent notes in cap. si quando, de offic. deleg.; for the law is more to be obeyed than the mandate of a delegate, 11 q. 3, c. Iulianus, and c. dominus, and cap. qui resistit. The fifth argument does not stand in the way; for it proceeds when the excommunication holds, as because it is just. But in our case it is presupposed to be void. To the last, the said cap. cum sit Romana, it has been sufficiently answered; for it is denied that the act is notorious, and a just cause of possession is alleged. Likewise, the Apostle had frequently admonished the Corinthian, and the act was notorious, which could by no subterfuge, etc.; which does not occur in our case. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Movables are usucapted in three years, immovables in ten, actions in 30 years.
