2. Who is called a manifest usurer with respect to the annulment of a testament.
3. Whether account-books of usury make anyone a manifest usurer?
4. Singular witnesses do not suffice to prove the truth of an offence.
casus: The FACT from which the below-written doubts arise is proposed as follows. A certain lay merchant appointed a certain monastery of monks as his universal heir; upon his departure from life, the monastery entered upon the inheritance and behaved in all respects as heir, both in court and out of court, by taking hereditary goods, alienating some of them, etc. At length it was found in the debt-books of the testator that this same testator, and his predecessor in the same inheritance during their lifetime, had received from diverse persons, at the rate of eight or ten per cent, a certain sum of twenty thousand florins, and many debts of similar condition left to the said monastery by the said testator were recovered and spent on the common uses of the monastery. A scruple of conscience arose because the monastery made many expenses by reason of the inheritance itself by paying legacies and many other debts, by litigating both in the Roman Curia and outside it, and by building in the monastery and incurring other expenses by reason of the inheritance to such an extent that, in order to make satisfaction for the usury according to the testator's book, the things that remain of the aforesaid inheritance would scarcely suffice together with the remaining goods of the monastery; and on account of the servitude of Christians and for the instruction of the simple, an inquiry was made concerning four doubts regarding the premises. The first doubt: whether the said testator is undoubtedly to be deemed a usurer from the said contracts. The second: whether the said monastery is fully bound to make satisfaction for the usury of the testator according to the sums contained in the book of debts. The third: whether other goods of the monastery, if the goods remaining from the said inheritance do not suffice, ought to be exposed and alienated for the satisfaction of debts of this kind. The fourth: whether the Pope can by law, or otherwise canonically or lawfully, succour the said monastery without danger of destruction by dispensing, and further in the premises, etc.
body: The aid of Christ and His Mother having been humbly invoked, I shall touch, according to the order previously touched upon, upon the first doubt, which is very clear in law. For whatever accrues to the principal from sin is usury, however small it may be, whether it consists in counted money or in another species, as is proved in 14 q. 3 throughout the entire question; nay rather, the sole intention of the lender makes him a usurer, once the handing over of a gift beyond the principal has ensued, if he would not otherwise have lent in the absence of hope of gain, as is proved in the Gospel of Luke: ‘Lending, hoping for nothing thereby,’ and as a borrowed argument in the chapter consuluit, de usur. For those are foolish who think it lawful to receive 10 or another smaller amount for a hundred, since even to receive small gifts by agreement is usury, in cap. 2, 14 q. 3; the text in c. per vestras, de do. post divor., makes for this, and Bart. in l. divus, ff. ad l. Fal., and Jo. An. in reg. peccatum, de reg. iur. lib. 6 in Mercu. These things briefly as to the first point. I come to the second: whether the monastery is bound to make full satisfaction. On which I say attention must be paid to whether the testator was a manifest usurer, or an occult one. For if he was manifest, the testament did not hold, the security having been neglected of which mention is made in c. 2 de usur. lib. 6. For that text annuls the testament of a manifest usurer indifferently if security for the restitution of the usuries has not been furnished by him, nor the disposition reserved to pious causes, according to that which is noted by Bar. and Bal. in l. 1, C. de sac. san. ec.; and consequently the monastery would be bound to restore all the hereditary goods that reached it; it could nevertheless defend itself by prescription, since it possessed in good faith and had a title as heir, inasmuch as the time has elapsed which suffices for prescription.

† For movables are usucapted in three years, immovables in ten, and actions in 30 years, as is read and noted in l. pro haerede, ff. de pet. haere., and in l. 1, ff. pro haerede. But in our case, since the matter concerns the exclusion of intestate successors, a time of 30 years would be required, because the right of accepting the inheritance is prescribed in no lesser time, as is noted by the gl. and Bar. in l. licet and l. cum antiquioribus, C. de iure deli. I consider the aforesaid true, unless it was notorious that the testator was a usurer; for then the monastery is plausibly presumed to have known, by the arg. in c. 2 de postu. praela. and in c. qui dictis, 16 dist., and could not have prescribed, because either it knew the testament was invalid, and was in bad faith, 23 q. 2, or if it believed it to be valid, it was in error of law, and an error of law hinders prescription, as in l. nunquam, ff. de usuca., and l. quemadmodum, C. de agri. & censi. lib. 11, and is read and noted in c. apostolicae, de dona., and c. dudum, de deci. In the restitution suit, however, an accounting of expenses would have to be held, since the monastery was in good faith, even though it erred in law. Likewise it is not bound to the restitution of consumed fruits, because it made them its own on account of good faith, as is the noted text in l. sed si, § scire, ff. de peti. haeredi., by Bar. in the said § scire and in l. ex diverso, ff. de rei ven., by Di. in regula, possessor, de reg. iur. lib. 6, by the doc. in c. gravis, de resti. spo. And concerning this matter of fruits it must be spoken as is fully noted in the said c. gravis and the said l. ex diverso.

† Who, however, may be called a manifest usurer as to the annulment of a testament when security has not been provided, is stated in various ways. For if he kept a bench publicly prepared for lending at usury, in doubt he is called manifest and notorious, as the gloss notes in 2 quaestio 2 manifesta, and it is the better glo. in cap. 1 de usur. lib. 6, which posited many other modes of publication, for instance if he confessed in court, or was convicted, etc., as there; another mode the glo. posits in the said cap. 2, when he confessed this crime before a priest and witnesses, handing over his usurious books. Likewise according to Barto., if he lent in his chamber to all coming to him, in l. fur est, ff. de fur.; a notable mode is gathered from the glo. in c. cum in dioecesi, de usur. Likewise if during his lifetime there was public fame concerning this, sufficiently with some indications; and many worthy men have so advised, although Fed. consi. 62 seems to hold that that does not suffice for this, namely that a testament made is void, even though the bishop could have published him from such proof, and only after publication would the testament have been void; and this dictum has equity, lest someone be punished by mere fame with indications without having first been given the opportunity of purging it, and lest the testament be invalidated ipso facto. Likewise he can be called public if it can easily be proved, for instance through his books, as Archi. notes in the said c. 2 in prin.; nevertheless, the glo. on c. sane, 24 q. 2, which is on the word librorum, well opines the contrary, which says that if his accounts or instruments are found through which it is evident that he was a usurer, he cannot receive communion unless he has made satisfaction, if this was occult—as if it meant to say that through this alone he is not proved a usurer; and Archi. says there that many great men have followed this dictum, unless other indications appear, and this dictum seems to be contrary to what Archi. says in chapter 2. Someone says: concerning this a case is seen in cle. pe. de usur., where books or accounts prove against a usurer. But it can certainly be replied that here we are outside the case of that Clementine, since there it was established that they were usurers; here, however, it speaks when it was not established except through the showing of the books. Certain moderns in c. cum in tua, de usur., say that usurious account books suffice; nay more, they say that even if after death it can be proved through witnesses that the deceased was a usurer, the testament will not be valid, because it sufficiently appears that he was manifest, since he could be proved a usurer; and thus they recount that it was advised by some. But I find that Bal., Lau. de Pun., Bart. de Saly. advised the opposite, as do. Pet. de An. reports in repe. cap. canonum, de consti., concluding that for the annulment of a testament it is required that the usurer was manifest or notorious. Whence the word ‘manifest’ in the said cap. 2 is taken for ‘notorious’; wherefore fame does not suffice, nor that he is proved a usurer through two or three witnesses; nay rather, they say that a bishop’s constitution is invalid which provides that fame suffices, or two witnesses of the truth, to prove someone manifest, because the bishop could not alter the provision of the law to the prejudice of usurers and misuse the terminology of the thing, since appellative nouns are immutable, l. si quis in fundi vocabulo, ff. de leg. primo; and thus they advised in Bologna, where there was such a constitution. Bald. himself seems to hold the same in l. prima, C. de sacrosanc. eccle., where he says it is not sufficient that three prove that someone was a usurer, even with usurious account books appearing, unless public acts or common opinion are proved, because the text in the said chapter 2 bases itself upon ‘manifest’ in the invalidation of the testament. I believe it can safely be said that since that chapter 2 imposes a new penalty and imparts quite a lot, since it in effect deprives one of the capacity of testating, which is partly of the ius gentium and partly of the civil law, according to the notes in l. qui testamento, ff. de test., and they do this for a most just cause, both in favor of the commonwealth and on account of the danger to the souls of the usurers themselves, as in c. usurarum voraginem, de usur. lib. 6, and cap. quanto, under the same title, the words ought to be understood and taken in their proper signification, so that they should neither be expanded less nor restricted less, arg. of those things noted in gl. in l. quemadmodum, C. de agric. & censi. lib. 11. But ‘manifest’ in its proper signification imports less than ‘notorious’, and more than ‘fame’; whence everything notorious is manifest, as in chapter cum olim, de verb. signi., and chapter vestra, and chapter si, de coha. cle.; but it is not convertible, because not everything manifest is notorious, as the doc. commonly note in the said c. vestra, and is noted in c. quia suspecti, 3 quaest. 6. ‘Manifest’, however, is commonly defined, especially by Joan. And. in the said c. vestra, as public or famous intimation or proclamation, and common and certain knowledge proceeding from certain authors; and in this last point it has more in it than fame, which proceeds from suspicion alone and an uncertain author, as Jo. And. notes there; but Joan. Cald. in the said cap. vestra adds to the said definition ‘that it can be proved’, which pleases domino An. there; he means to say that manifest is that which can be proved beyond that public or famous intimation, and I quite believe this was the mind of Joan. And. For if the truth could not be proved, it would not differ from fame, and for this cap. de hoc, de simo., and cap. porro, de divor. Therefore, he is called a manifest usurer as to the invalidation of a testament who can truly be proved a usurer, and beyond this the common fame of the place proves it.

† From which I infer that the usury books alone do not make him manifest, but with fame they suffice, or if the judge has declared him public by a sentence, for it passes into the notorious, which is more. And thus I take a middle path, whence I do not necessarily require the notorious, nor do I think that mere proof of the delict suffices.

† Likewise I say that to prove the truth of the delict single witnesses do not suffice, as Fede. fully notes in consi. 72, even if a bishop’s constitution contained this; that which the same Fede. notes in consi. 26 makes for the aforesaid, where he holds that an extrajudicial confession of usuries does not suffice for him to be called manifest thereby. Chapter cum in dioecesi, cited above, does not stand in the way of the aforesaid, where fame with some arguments seems to suffice; for it can be answered that it does not speak as to the invalidation of a testament, but as to executing the penalty of cap. quia in omnibus, de usur., which, since it is of slight prejudice, the words are not taken so strictly, as noted by Federic., consilio 72 cited above. Or I say that it is understood of arguments that suffice along with fame to prove someone a usurer, since they cannot easily be convicted, argu. cap. illo vos, de pigno., cap. ad nostram, de emptio. & vendi., and what is read and noted in cle. i. de usur. For arguments or indications sometimes prove fully, l. indicia, C. de rei vedi. [sc. vendi.], and l. sciant cuncti, C. de proba., and as noted in c. tertio loco, de proba.; and thus it agrees with the aforesaid. And through this it is determined whether the testament was null, and whether the said inheritance is in a case of restitution or not, assuming that it is not in a case of restitution, for example because he was not a manifest usurer in the aforesaid manner. It is asked, returning to the principal doubt, whether the monastery is bound to make satisfaction for all usuries contained in the aforesaid books? And I say briefly that either the monastery entered upon the inheritance with the benefit of inventory, and in case of doubt is not bound beyond the assets of the inheritance, as in l. fina. C. de iure deli.; insofar, however, as the inheritance suffices, deducting reasonable expenses, I think the monastery is bound to restitution, as the usuries are gathered from the books of the testator. For in this they produce proof, because regularly books produce proof against the writer, as in l. quidam, § numularios, and what is noted there, ff. de eden., and in l. exemplo, and l. rationes, and l. instrumenta, C. de probatio., and in cap. 2 de fide instru.; and also because in our case the action is to unburden the soul of the deceased, very exact proof ought not to be required, as in cle. j. de usur. and what is noted there; and this restitution ought to be made to those from whom they were extorted or to their heirs, if they survive, as in cap. cum tu, de usur., or they are to be distributed as uncertain to the poor, as in the said cap. cum tu; and as to practice there is a good glo. in cap. 2 de usur. lib. 6 on the word satisfieri, and more broadly by Fede. cap. j. And these things proceed even if the deceased commanded nothing about restoring the usuries, as in cap. tua nos, de usur., joined with the said cap. 2 in the gl. on the word mandaverunt. Or the monastery did not draw up an inventory, and then, although at first sight it seems to be bound even beyond the hereditary assets by l. fina. C. de iure deliberan. and by that which the glo. holds regarding the church in cap. j. de testa.; nevertheless I say that on a two-fold ground it is not bound beyond what reached it: first, because the church as heir is not bound through the omission of an inventory beyond the hereditary assets, as Barto. notes in l. j. C. de sacr. sanct. eccle., arg. auth. sicut, under the same title, because an inheritance ought not to be deferred to it except insofar as it is lucrative, as in the said auth. sicut; and Bal. in the same l. fi. C. de iure delib. is moved by l. 1, ff. de iu. fis., and because the church ought not to enjoy a lesser privilege than the treasury, as noted in c. 1 de in inte. resti. Secondly, because it is not bound because the usuries are sought from the delict of the deceased; and thus by civil law the heir would not be bound except insofar as reached him from the delict, since issue was not joined with the deceased, as in l. ut debitum, C. ne ex deli. defun.; but the final law C. de iu. delib. only binds through the omission of an inventory him who could not pay in solidum, but by civil law this claim did not lie. For by canon law the heir is not bound from the delict of the deceased beyond the assets of the inheritance, as in c. in literis, de rapto, and in similar cases; and thus in our specific terms Fede. advised, consil. 21, and do. Anto. holds in c. debitores, de iureiur., by Joan. Andr. in c. 2 de usu. lib. 6 in the novella; the glo. holds in c. fi. on the word mandaverit. I conclude therefore thus on this second doubt: that the monastery is bound insofar as the assets of the inheritance permit, so that from the proper goods of the monastery they are not bound to expend anything, except as I shall immediately say in the third doubt. I come now to the third doubt: whether, if the goods of the inheritance are insufficient, the monastery is bound to expend the goods of the monastery? On which I say that if all hereditary goods were extant, the monastery would not be bound to expend anything of its own, as was stated quite fully above. But since, as appears from the narration of the case, the monastery consumed much for its own utility, I judge that the monastery is bound to make satisfaction from its own property insofar as reached it from the goods of the inheritance, because in those things the monastery can be said to have been made richer, since it would have had to make from its own those expenses which it made from the hereditary goods, as in l. pupil., ff. sol.; it is bound therefore to make satisfaction according to the hereditary assets, and to satisfy the debt the church is compelled even to sell immovable goods, as in auth. hoc ius porrectum, 10 quaestio 2; and this concerning the third. As to the fourth: whether the Pope can lawfully dispense regarding these things, lest the desolation of the monastery follow upon the alienation of the goods; I believe that regarding certain usuries, that is, those that are owed to those from whom they were extorted, or their heirs if they survive, the Pope does not lawfully dispense, because he cannot take away money from specific lay persons and give it to the monastery, by the arg. of those things noted by Innoc. in cap. quae in ecclesiarum, de consti., and cap. inquisitioni, de sent. excom.; that which is found in clem. pastoralis, de re iud., makes for this, and what is noted by the legists in l. fi. C. si contra ius vel util. pub., especially since usuries can be sought by the condictio indebiti, as noted in cap. Michael, de usuris, and cap. debitores, de iurei., and 16 quaest. 6 c. si episcopus. But over uncertain usuries, in case of doubt the Pope can dispense, since they are at the disposal of the church; nay rather, I say that even the local bishop could make this concession, as Joan. Andr. expressly notes in cap. 2 de testa. lib. 6; and thus it was formerly disputed and concluded, as noted there by him; and Bal. holds the same in similar terms in l. si quis ad declinandum, C. de epis. & cler. I also think it can be maintained that if that monastery was in need at the time of the testament, that testator could give all uncertain usuries to the monastery as to the poor, as in cap. cum tu, and what Jo. And. notes in the said cap. 2; and thus it would not be bound to seek a Papal or episcopal concession, because it is lawfully received from him who has the power of giving to the poor; and an indigent monastery is sufficiently poor, as is noted in the places cited above, and l. privilegia, C. de sacrosanct. eccle., and cap. diaconi, 93 dist., and 16 q. 1 cap. fi. make for this. It could also be said that if at the time of the testament the monastery was not in need, at least in so great an amount, yet if today it should become indigent from the distribution of uncertain usuries, the chapter of the monastery itself could distribute these uncertain sums to their church and monastery, since in this no ambition is noted. We see a similar thing in the bishop, who is the dispenser of the goods of the church, 2 q. 2 c. videntes; nevertheless he can take for his own necessities, 12 quaest. 2 c. Episcopus. It is more cautious, however, to have the authority of the Bishop or the Pope, especially on account of those holding the opinion that the distribution of uncertain usuries belongs to the local Bishop and not to the heir, concerning which it is noted in the said capit. 2 de testamen. lib. 6 and cap. cum sit nimis absurdum, de Judae. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A constitution solemnly enacted binds everyone without distinction after the lapse of two months.
2. Laws are instituted when they are promulgated.
3. The ignorance of private persons ought not to prejudice the community.
casus: The factual situation is this: in the city of Siena, it was provided by statute that those selling bread for sale were bound and had to pay by way of gabelle eight quattrini per stama. Then, with the passage of time, with a certain scarcity and impending high price of wheat, a public proclamation was made in the name of the commune or of the officials deputed for this purpose, containing in effect that it was permitted to anyone to make bread for sale without the payment of any gabelle. In view of this proclamation, many bakers were induced to make bread for sale, and they continued this for two years without any demand or payment of any gabelle. Finally, it was intimated to them that the remission regarding the bread had not been unconditional, but suspended only for a period of 18 months [?], and thus they began to pay the said gabelle for the future. However, after a period of four years had elapsed, the notary of the gabelle proceeded against the said bakers, claiming that they were liable for the payment of the gabelle for the period of six months during which they made bread after the lapse of the aforesaid 18 months. It is also asserted by the said official that they are bound to pay the penalty for defrauded gabelle contained in the statutes of Siena, on the grounds that during that period of six months they did not pay the said gabelle at all. On the part of the bakers, ignorance of the said provision is alleged, since the proclamation had been made unconditionally concerning the remission of the gabelle. It is asked what the law is, etc.
body: The aid of Christ and His mother having been invoked in all things, it seems at first that the said bakers are bound to pay the gabelle of those six months and to the penalty for defrauded gabelle, by the notable text in l. interdum, § licet, and § diui, ff. de publi., where it is clear that error does not excuse one from the property being confiscated on account of unpaid toll.

† Secondly, it is proved otherwise. A constitution solemnly enacted binds all persons without distinction after the lapse of two months, so that after that time ignorance is not presumed, as in auth. ut factae nouae constitu. in the rubric and the black letter, and noted in cap. ij, de constitu., and this is when the constitution is enacted by the prince. But if it is by an inferior, not so much time is granted, but a lesser time to be determined by a good judge, taking into consideration the size of the territory, which is distinguished by the said statute; since it is not equitable that as much time be assigned for the constitution of an inferior, which sometimes extends its effect over a small area, as is assigned in the law of a prince, which distinguishes the whole world, as noted by Host. in summa, de consti. § quando, and Ioan. And. super data lib. 6, who are commonly followed in the aforesaid c. ij, de consti. But in our case, at the time of the reform made in the general council, not only had two months passed, but 18; therefore they cannot allege ignorance, especially since it was not a new statute, but a certain suspension of the old one; and just as the old statute bound after 18 months, so too the new one, as in l. cum precario, ff. de preca. Thirdly, c. 1, de postu. praela. makes for the same conclusion, where it says that after a constitution has been solemnly enacted and publicly promulgated, everyone is presumed to have knowledge of it, nor is one pretending ignorance easily heard; indeed Inno. said in the aforesaid c. ij that one alleging ignorance is not heard unless he proves it clearly, as in ca. quod dicitis, 16. distin., and c. proposuisti, 82. distin. But these notwithstanding, the contrary is true in law. I am moved first by the decisive text of this question in the said cap. 1, de postu. praela., where two things are required for anyone to be bound to the observance of a constitution: that the constitution be solemnly enacted, and that it be publicly promulgated.

† To the same effect is the text in the said auth. ut factae nouae consti. and 4. dist. c. in istis, § leges, where it is said that laws are instituted when they are promulgated, and not upon being dated, as below. But in our case that reform of the suspended gabelle was not promulgated, but only solemnly enacted; therefore it did not bind those acting contrary to it. On the contrary, the proclamation was made unconditionally without the pre-fixing of any time, and thus it ought to be presumed to be both perpetual and unconditional, by the argument in l. seruus, C. de poenis, and c. eos, 1. q. 1, and what Inno. noted in c. ex literis, de constit. Nor were the bakers bound to investigate anything else, since a statute ought not to be presumed to have been made otherwise than as it was proclaimed, as in l. Labeo, ff. de supel. leg.; indeed, the part which is not published cannot be called a statute for the effect of binding another, by the argument in the said § leges, and because one and the same matter ought not to be judged under a duplicate law, such that one part is published and another not, as in cap. cum in tua dioecesi, de deci. and 12. q. 2. c. cognouimus. To the same effect is l. quidam haeredem damnauerat, ff. de tri. ui. & oleo lega., where by bequeathing wine simply, the testator is deemed to have bequeathed all the wine he had, since an indefinite term is equivalent to a universal one, as in c. ut circa, de elect. lib. 6. But in our case the proclamation was made simply and unconditionally; therefore it is to be observed purely as such, and not otherwise. Secondly, as my main argument I make the following point: through that proclamation a quasi-contract appears to have arisen between the commune and the bakers, just as Bart. notes in a similar case in l. pe. ff. de decre. ab ordi. fa., where he says that if a commune makes a statute that whoever goes to live in a walled city is exempt from payment of the gabelle, the commune and those going to live there are deemed quasi-contracting, so that the immunity once granted cannot be revoked, since it has passed into a contract or quasi-contract. If, therefore, there was a general quasi-contract with these bakers or oven-keepers, the reform was not valid, at least so that the oven-keepers could be compelled to pay the gabelle, and much less to the penalty for defrauded gabelle, since no fraud was committed here by them, as is clearly proved by the similar case in l. sed si pupillus, § proscribere, together with the two preceding paragraphs there, ff. de instit., where it is clear that if someone has publicly appointed an agent (institor) over some business, it does not suffice simply to revoke him to prevent contracts made with him, but it is necessary that it be publicly proclaimed, so that others may be cautious and desist from entering into contracts with such an agent, lest under that pretext and indiscriminately they might easily be deceived. For every thing ought to be dissolved by the same means through which it arises, in the rule secundum naturam, de reg. iur. lib. 6. Thirdly, it is principally proved on another ground: even presupposing that that suspensive reform enacted in the general council had bound without any publication, nevertheless it did not affect those who were probably ignorant, as in l. pe. ff. de decr. ab ordi. fa., and l. iubemus, C. de testa., and in c. ut animarum, de consti. lib. 6, and as is read and noted in the said c. proposuisti, 82. dist. But no one can doubt that these millers or bakers had a probable cause of ignorance, since knowledge of the constitution ought not to be presumed in our case as in other cases, seeing that here, after the reform was made, a proclamation was issued without the fixing of a time, and thus otherwise than the act was proposed in the general council. And so they could remain secure without any further inquiry, since, as I said above, it was not to be presumed that it had been published otherwise than it was enacted; and especially because after that period of 18 months, nothing was extorted from them in the name of the gabelle. Nor can proof of ignorance be made in our case except by their oath, since it concerns their conscience; this is what the singular gloss says in c. proposuisti: reliance must be placed on the oath of the one alleging ignorance of a statute, and especially in our case, where that urgent presumption of ignorance concurs on account of the publication that was made. And these points apply above all with respect to the penalty for defrauded gabelle, which is imposed with respect to fraud and deceit—which reason ceases here on account of ignorance, as in the said c. ut animarum, and Cyn. in l. si quis non dicam rapere, C. de epi. & cle.

† Likewise someone might object, saying: it does not seem that the ignorance of private persons ought to prejudice the commune, nor is this matter concerning a penalty, but about paying a debt to a superior. I say that in our case it is otherwise because of the preceding quasi-contract between the commune and these bakers. For if they had been certified about the payment, perhaps they would not have made bread for sale anymore, or not so much, or not from such material, or in such a manner; therefore they ought to enjoy the benefit of the proclamation until it has been announced to them in a legitimate manner, lest they be deceived by the prince's benefit, since one ought not to be deceived, but rather aided by a benefit, as in c. 1, de priuile., and the said l. si pupillus supports this. The contrary arguments alleged above do not stand in the way: to the first, regarding l. interdum, I say that it speaks there of gross and supine ignorance, as Bart. notes there; it is otherwise if it is probable, as in our case, as noted there and in the legal authorities alleged above. The other two contrary arguments are sufficiently resolved by what was seen above, for they apply when the constitution was publicly promulgated, and when probable ignorance has not been alleged by the opposing party. But in our case that suspensive reform was not published, because in the publication nothing was said about the fixing of a time. Likewise, probable ignorance is alleged here, which is caused by the aforementioned facts. I conclude therefore that the said bakers cannot be constrained to pay the gabelle for the said six months, and still less to the penalty for defrauded gabelle, especially if they swear to their ignorance of the suspension. And let these things suffice. Nicholas, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Under the appellation of sons, females are included in favorable matters.
2. Male and female are said to be correlatives.
3. The word "son," by its proper signification, does not comprehend a daughter.
4. The common usage of speech ought to be observed in last wills.
casus: A certain Andreas, a citizen of Siena, made a will. In which, among other things, this clause is found: "Likewise, if it should happen that his sons die at any time without legitimate and natural children, or that of them only one son of the said testator remains, having no children, in that case, in which only one male remains, he bequeathed, adjudicated, and left that from his estate they should give each year in perpetuity to the monastery of the Friars Minor of Siena two salmae of wine for celebrating the sacrifice in their said church." After his death it happened that all the male and female children died except for one female, from whom they now claim the said legacy. It is asked whether it is owed.
body: The protection of Christ and of His name having been humbly invoked, it seems at first that it is so, on this ground: a legacy conditional from the beginning can be claimed upon the occurrence of the condition, as in cap. Raynutius and in capitulum Raynaldus, de testa., and l. cedere idem, ff. de uerb. signifi., with many similar texts. But in our case the condition occurred, since only an only daughter remained without legitimate sons, the others having died also without children; therefore, etc. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the testator made mention solely of a son, and not of a daughter, whereas now a daughter survives, and not a son, and thus the condition does not appear to be fulfilled; because under the appellation of "son" a daughter is also comprehended, as in l. filii appellatione and l. quisquis, ff. de uerb. sign., read and noted in l. 1, eodem titulo, and in l. si ita, ff. de lib. & posth. It is clearly proved in l. legati, in l. qui duos, and l. seruus, and l. Lucius, §. quæsitum, ff. de leg. 3, where it is evident that by bequeathing mules [mulos] one is deemed to have bequeathed female mules [mulas] as well, and when male slaves [seruis] are bequeathed, female slaves [ancillæ] also pass, and when male children [pueris] are bequeathed, female children also pass. Likewise, under the appellation of "brothers" sisters also pass, even in the matter of a legacy, as is read in the said §. quæsitum, and is noted in l. tres fratres, ff. de pact.; which is for no other reason than that the masculine comprehends the feminine, as in the said legal texts, and in l. si ita scriptum, ff. de leg. 2, and in c. si quis suadente, 37. quæst. 4, joined with c. mulieres, de sen. exc.

† Likewise and thirdly, the common opinion of the doctors of both laws is that in legacies and other favorable matters, females pass under the appellation of "sons," and that the masculine includes the feminine, as noted by Bartolus following the doctors in the said l. 1, ff. de uer. signi., and l. si quis in tantam, C. unde ui, and l. quicunque, ff. de fer. fug., through Cynus, and by Archidiaconus sufficiently fully in the said c. si quis suadente, and Johannes de Lignano in cle. 1 de elec., by the gloss in c. generali, de electio., lib. 6, by Hostiensis in c. Raynaldus, de test., and Speculator in the title de dispu. & alleg., §. post autem, at the final verse, ubi masculinum. But these notwithstanding, which do not truly stand in the way in our case, I say that the contrary is true in law. I am moved first because, if the words of the testament are weighed well, in the condition mention is made not only of a son, but subsequently he adds, of a male son [de filio masculo]. For although it is found in the law that a daughter is comprehended under the appellation of "son," as in the laws previously cited, it is nevertheless nowhere found that under the appellation of a "male son" a female is comprehended; indeed, on our subject, Hostiensis, Goffredus, and Johannes Andreae clearly intended the contrary in the said c. Raynaldus, where the testator thus substituted a son "if he should die without male children [filiis masculis]," etc. And the aforesaid doctors say that if that word, "male," had not been added, it would have sufficed to have had female daughters, because the masculine, etc. And thus they most clearly maintain that the masculine comprehends the feminine when the word "male" has not been added, but it is otherwise when it has been, as occurred in our case. And Bartolus says the same in l. cum auus, ff. de condi. & demon. And beyond their reasoning, there can be another rationale for the difference. For the word "male" [masculus] properly applies to males and not to females; for it is a diminutive, and is derived from "mas, maris" with "-culus" added, as Papias says. For appellative nouns are unchangeable by man; hence it is that an error in them invalidates a legacy, as is read and noted in l. si quis in fundi uocabulo, ff. de lega. primo. And thus a female does not pass under the appellation of a male, since this appellative "male" denotes something different from a female: l. quæritur, ff. de sta. & ho., and cap. si testes, 4. quæstio

† 3. §. hermaphroditus. Likewise, male and female are correlatives, because one is called male in respect to a female, just as husband and wife, father and son; whence, since they are entirely different, the one does not comprehend the other, just as if I were to bequeath to a husband, the wife would not be comprehended, or if I bequeath to a father, the son does not pass; but it is otherwise where mention is made only of a "child/son" [de filio]. For "son" and "daughter" are not correlatives, and "filius" is derived from "philos," which is love, l. liberorum, at the end, ff. de uerbo. sign., which word indeed, on account of its etymology, applies to both, male and female. Secondly, I prove this principally by another reason: words in any disposition ought to be understood in such a way that they effect something, as in cap. si papa, de priuile., in 6., and l. si quando, C. de inoffic. testam. But in our case, if the testator had wished to comprehend a female daughter, he would have made mention of males in vain, and thus that addition, "males," would effect nothing—which must not be said, pursuant to the aforesaid texts; and had he intended otherwise when he said "male," he would have said "son or daughter," arguing from cap. ad audientiam, extra de deci., and that text is very helpful; for we ought not to depart from the proper meaning when the intention does not appear otherwise, as there, and c. si, de uerb. signific., and l. non aliter, ff. de leg. 3.

† Thirdly, it supports this that the word "son" [filius] comprehends a daughter not by its proper meaning, but through interpretation and extension, as in l. pronunciatio, in principio, ff. de uerb. signi., and the note of the gloss in the said l. 1, ff. de uerbo. signifi., and the said l. qui duos, de leg. 3. But if the word "male" [masculus] were also to comprehend a female, two extensions and improper usages would concur in the same case, which must not be said, in l. 2, C. de dotis promiss. Fourthly, I cite l. si ita, ff. de liber. & posthu., joined with the gloss which Bartolus follows there; for Bartolus says there that under the appellation of "son" [filii] all sons and daughters pass, for the gloss says that this is true unless a proper noun had been added, because by that addition he is seen to have narrowed himself to a single son. So in the present matter, by adding this quality, "male," beyond the word "sons," he appears to have restricted it to a male son, and not to a female. Fifthly, it is proved by clear reason: that which of its nature effects an exclusion ought not to induce an inclusion, arguing from c. si necesse, de do. post diuor., and c. si, de uerbo. signi. But the word "male," when added to the word "son," is placed to exclude the female, since it is a quality exclusive of the female sex; therefore it ought not to work her inclusion. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the testator in the beginning made mention of a son simply; because since in the same clause and disposition he made mention of a male son, he is seen always to have meant a male. For preceding doubtful words take their meaning from subsequent ones. And this clearly seems to be proved in a similar case in l. qui filiabus, ff. de lega. 1, and l. fin., §. cui dulcia, ff. de uino triti. & oleo lega., and l. si seruus, at the end, de leg. 1.

† Sixthly and lastly, it is proved unconquerably: in any disposition, and especially in last wills, the common usage of speech ought to be observed, even against the proper meaning of the words: l. filiorum, §. quod tamen Cassius, ff. de lega. 3, and l. cum delanionis, §. asinam, ff. de fund. instru., and l. Labeo, ff. de supel. leg., and there fully through Bartolus, through the gloss in c. nonnulli, de rescript., and through Innocent in c. olim, de verbo. sig. But it is a case surer than certainty that under the appellation of a male son no one understands a female; indeed, it would be downright foolish to say the opposite; therefore, etc. And this last point ought to suffice for the victory of this cause, and by these points the arguments formulated for the contrary party are removed. Nor does it stand in the way if it were said that the father wished to burden the male son, or rather that he appears to have wished to burden the female, since agnation is preserved through the male, l. 1, ff. de uen. inspi., and what is noted in l. 2, C. quæ sit lon. consuet.; because I say there is another reason regarding a female so far as this case is concerned. For a female does not know how to earn a livelihood, and she must be married, nor would she easily find a husband for herself with this perpetual burden. But a male is the master of the house, and thus he can engage in business, nor is he so burdened by this charge. And whatever the case may be, it is enough that the testator spoke of a male, and not of a female, wherefore it suffices that it is written: l. prospexit, ff. qui & a quibus, and 6. q. 3. c. ita scriptura. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Monasteries are said to be exempt with respect to the diocesan law.
2. Where an office is removed, the reward of the office is also removed.
casus: A certain diocesan of Volterra left one hundred to the monastery of Monte Oliveto. The bishop of the place demands the canonical portion from such a bequest; the aforesaid monastery contradicts, alleging exemption, and also prescription of such a long time that there is no memory of its beginning. It is asked what the law is, etc.
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of Christ and His mother, three points are to be examined for a clear decision. First, whether monasteries of religious, in the absence of a special exemption, are bound to this canonical portion. Second, positing that they are, whether a special exemption defends this monastery and others of the same order, since the whole Order of Monte Oliveto is said to be specially exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop. Third, presupposing that the exemption does not avail, whether at least by reason of prescription, of the beginning of which there is no memory, the lord Bishop can be excluded from demanding this from the monastery. And first, as to the first doubt: it seems that all monasteries are free from the payment of this canonical portion, because all monasteries are exempt with respect to the diocesan law, as in 16. q. 1. c. cum pro utilitate, and c. dilectus, de offi. ordi. with similar texts. But the payment of this portion belongs to the diocesan law; therefore, etc. The minor premise is proved from the theory of the gloss in the said c. dilectus, 10. q. 1. in summa, where it notes that everything consisting in receiving—such as the cathedraticum, the fourth of tithes, of fraternities, and the like—belongs to the diocesan law. But notwithstanding this, I say that the contrary proceeds from law, as is openly proved in c. requisisti, and c. officii, de testa., where it is clearly evident that monasteries and other pious places are bound to this kind of fourth; Innocent holds this in c. 1. de stat. mona. and Hostiensis in summa de sepult. in §. a quibus, and commonly all writers follow this. Nor is that theory of the gloss in the said c. dilectus true, as is clearly proved in the said legal authorities; and concerning these two laws, the diocesan law and jurisdiction, I refer to what is fully noted in the said c. dilectus, and by Innocent in the said c. 1. de stat. mon. So I conclude that that general exemption granted to all monasteries with respect to the diocesan law does not suffice regarding this payment of the canonical portion. I come therefore to the second doubt: whether at least a special exemption avails this monastery. And it should be known that Hostiensis was of the similar opinion that it does not; he held this in §. et a quibus, unless the church were specially exempt from this fourth, and a certain Cardinal of Todi is said to have held the same in a certain treatise of his. Their motive is that this fourth is owed to the bishop by all churches of his diocese, as in c. conquerente, de offic. ordi. But certainly, whatever they say, all other doctors, both ancient and modern, hold the contrary—namely, that if a church is exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop, it is not bound to him for this fourth; and Hostiensis himself seems to hold this in c. officii, de testa., where Innocent holds this, and more clearly in c. in nostra, de sepul., and more broadly Johannes Andreae in the said c. officii, and on the rubric. And the same there lord Antonius de Butrio, the lord Cardinal of Florence, Petrus and Paulus, and all the writers. And so advised Federico of Siena, a most excellent doctor of the Decretals, as appears in his consilia, consi. 96. Lord Baldus follows him in l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de episc. & cler., and I have always held this opinion in lecturing and advising. The foundation of this opinion is that this portion is owed to the bishop by the churches of his diocese likewise by reason of his episcopal jurisdiction and the care he undertakes in the said churches, as is proved in the said c. requisisti, and noted by the doctors in the said pre-alleged places, and especially in c. officii, and on the rubric. But between the bishop and exempt churches that rationale ceases, nor does he undergo labor in them concerning episcopal rights, since they are immediately subject to the Roman Pontiff, as is clear in 16. q. 1. c. frater noster. Whence we say that the Pope is the bishop of the exempt, as the gloss notes in the said c. nulla, 93. distin. and in c. authoritate, de priui. in 6. And perhaps on this account Petrus said, as Johannes Andreae recounts in the said c. requisisti, that exempt churches ought to pay this canonical portion to the Pope. Second, this also seems to be proved in cle. dudum, de sepul., where the Friars Preachers and Minors pay only one fourth, namely to the parish church, if the deceased was buried with them, and silence is imposed upon all others regarding further portions or deductions to be made—under whose designation of 'all' bishops are included; de iudici. c. 1; for this see what the gloss notes there on the word quartam.

† Furthermore, where the office is removed, the reward of the office is also removed, ff. de excu. tut. l. tria onera, with similar texts, and l. Seio, in prin. ff. de an. le.; and from whom the care is removed, the reward of the care is also removed, l. alumnæ, ff. de adimen. leg.; but from the bishop the care and office of episcopal jurisdiction are removed through exemption; therefore also this reward of the canonical portion is removed. Nor does c. in nostra, de sepul. stand in the way, where the exempt pay a fourth, because, as Johannes Andreae well says in the said c. officii, that chapter speaks of the other fourth which is paid to the parish church from a legacy made to a church by reason of burial by its own parishioner; that is owed by every church, however exempt, provided the parishioner was buried with it. The reason is that that is paid on account of the sacraments and divine offices which it provided to the parishioner during his life; whence in recompense the laws willed that the testator leave a fourth part to the church, and if he did not leave it, they grant in subsidy an action against the legatee church, so that in this exemption does not avail the exempt, as in c. 2. de sepul. and the said clem. dudum. But the fourth which is owed to the bishop is paid by the legatees themselves on account of episcopal burdens and the communion he has in them, all of which cease in the exempt. Whence I conclude that the church is not bound to pay the canonical portion of funerals to the bishop, but to the parish church. So also here, if his parishioner was buried with that exempt church. By which it is concluded that the monasteries of Monte Oliveto, since they are exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop, are not bound to this kind of fourth, unless they should have a non-exempt people. For then, by reason of the non-exempt people, they have communion with the bishop, and the bishop is burdened regarding episcopal law, by the argument of c. ex ore, de priuil. Thus Innocent singularly limited this opinion in the said c. in nostra; which is quite pleasing, and this concerning the second doubt. I descend to the third: presupposing without prejudice to the truth that this exemption did not avail (which in truth does avail), can the said monastery protect itself by reason of prescription? And I briefly conclude that it can; the text is open in c. de quarta, de præscr.; the ordinary gloss holds this in c. 1. de sta. mo., and likewise Johannes Andreae there by the said c. de quarta, incidentally after Federico of Siena, and the Younger in c. requisisti, de testa., although Hostiensis says there that the same later spoke otherwise. But this does not appear in the lecture of Innocent himself; Hostiensis himself nevertheless feels the first opinion in c. certificari, de sepul., and he undertook to dispute this matter more broadly in summa, under the same title, in §. an licitum, otherwise under §. uetus; and there at the end he concludes that a custom totally absorbing this fourth is not valid, but in part it is; nevertheless prescription can absorb it, but title is required, since it is against law. But in our case there was the title of exemption. For since the opinion is common that an exempt church is not bound, as is clear from the points discussed in the preceding article, even presupposing that it were false, it would at least have furnished a legitimate cause for prescribing, by a very good and virtually express argument in c. cum dilectus, de consue. Likewise, even granted that every title ceased, there is nonetheless here the lapse of so much time, of whose beginning memory does not exist, which has the force of a title, as is clear in c. 1. de præscri. in 6. And that prescription is valid was held by Johannes and Vincentius in the said c. requisisti, and commonly by more modern writers, nor is it necessary to press much on this, since it is openly proved in the said c. de quarta. To the same effect is c. officii, de testa., where it is clear that a privilege is valid in this matter, and therefore so is prescription, since these commonly walk hand in hand. Nor is it any wonder, since through prescription rights already acquired by a bishop are taken away, as in c. cum olim, and c. auditis, de præscri., and all the more so rights that were to be acquired, by the argument of 16. q. 1. §. fi. I conclude therefore that the said monastery can be protected against the lord bishop regarding the exaction of this canonical portion, namely by reason of exemption and of prescription. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. An appeal cannot be made before a definitive sentence.
2. When an arbiter takes cognizance in the place of a judge, an appeal lies from him.
3. The judge of reduction ought to arbitrate according to good equity.
casus: The case in effect is as follows. Two citizens of Volterra, on the occasion of a certain debt contracted between them, chose certain appraisers of certain goods to be given in payment for the said debt, giving them the power of appraising, and they promised to abide by their appraisal under a certain penalty. Finally, the said arbitrators or appraisers appraised and rendered an award according to their judgment; and while one of the parties approved this award, the other disapproved it and had recourse to the lord podestà of the place, requesting for certain reasons that the said award be pronounced null or inequitable. The said lord podestà, having cited the parties, prefixed a term to prove the matters incumbent on the case, within which the plaintiff proved his claim, while the defendant proved nothing within the same term, nor did he allege an impediment. After the said term had elapsed, the plaintiff requests that the depositions of his witnesses be published, while the defendant objects and requests that a term be appointed for him to prove his claim. However, the podestà, notwithstanding the objection of the defendant, published the statements of the witnesses, from which publication an appeal was interposed by the said defendant, alleging principally two causes for the said appeal. First, that a term for proving ought not to be appointed simultaneously to both parties, namely first to the plaintiff, secondly to the defendant [?]. Second, because the said defendant had been cited to see a term appointed for the plaintiff, and thus at that proceeding a term could not be prefixed for the defendant himself. But after this appeal was rejected as frivolous, the podestà in due time pronounced the said award null; from which pronouncement an appeal was again taken by the said defendant, and before the judge of appeal he produced, in proof of his right, certain articles directly contrary to the articles produced before the lord podestà. The other party, namely of the appellee, alleges that there is no place for an appeal, nor can the said contrary articles be produced. It is asked what is the law.
body: Having invoked the protection of Christ and of His Mother, three matters are to be investigated for a clear elucidation. First, whether the first appeal interposed from the interlocutory decree was valid. Second, whether an appeal could be taken from the definitive sentence rendered by the same lord podestà. Third, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the said appeal should be admitted, whether articles directly contradictory ought to be admitted in the appeal case. Coming to the first in order, omitting for the sake of brevity the arguments that can be made for the affirmative side, I say that the said appeal from the interlocutory decree was not valid.

† First, because the rule of civil law maintains that an appeal cannot be taken before a definitive sentence when the grievance is reparable through an appeal from the definitive sentence, as in l. ante sententiae tempus, C. quorum appel. non recip., and in l. ij, ff. de appe. recip. uel non, and there fully by Barto. in l. intra utile, ff. de mino., where he restricts what he had noted in the said l. ante sententiae; and l. generaliter, § ij, C. de iureiur., and c. super eo, el. ij, de app., support this. But this pretended grievance was of such a nature, since he could have made proof in the appeal from the definitive sentence; therefore, the said appeal was not to be admitted. Also, and secondly, and better: since the lord podestà had prefixed a term for both parties to produce proof, he was not bound, nor ought he, to appoint a term anew when no impediment was alleged or proved by the adverse party, because every dilatory proof is understood to be peremptory; the text is open in c. licet, de proba., and there by the doctors, and in l. si and l. oratione, ff. de feriis; Archi. holds this in c. iudicantem, 30, q. 6, and Bar. in l. 1, C. de dila., § uidendum, at the word 'quid si data'. Nor do the grounds of the adverse party stand in the way: for this case is summary, as appears in the statutes of Volterra, and the podestà could simultaneously and once for all appoint a term for both parties; the text is in cle. saepe, de uer. sign., and there this is commonly held by the doctors. The other ground does not stand in the way, namely that the citation was made to appoint a term for the plaintiff and not for the defendant himself: for this would have been vitiating if the cited defendant himself had not been present at the appointment made to him. Thus do I understand the text and Bar. in l. aut qui aliter, ff. quod ui aut clam. But in our case, since the said defendant was present at the appointment of the term, another citation was not necessary. For citation is made so that the party may be present, but once presence is given, citation is not necessary, as noted by Io. And. in c. fi., de elec., lib. 6; l. si ut proponis, 2, C. quomodo & quando iud., supports this, where it is gathered a contrario sensu that if a judge cited to one place and afterwards proceeded in another with the party present, the act holds, although it would be otherwise if the party had been absent, as is noted there and by Bart. in l. fi., ff. quod ui aut clam. Thirdly, that which is immediately subjoined in the second article militates against that appeal. From these points I conclude that the said appeal from the interlocutory decree was not valid, and consequently did not suspend the jurisdiction of the lord podestà, as in c. non solum, de appe., li. 6. I pass to the second article: what of the appeal from the definitive sentence? And this is a beautiful and subtle article, and in effect it must be asked whether an appeal can be taken from the aforesaid judge concerning the reduction of an arbitrament to equity, on which I find principally two opinions. The first is that of But. in l. si societatem, § arbitrorum, ff. pro socio, who held that an appeal can be taken, since he pronounces as a judge. And An. de But. followed this opinion in c. Quintauallis, de iureiur. Io. And. holds the contrary opinion in addi. Spe. in the title de appel., § in quibus, at the word 'quid si conuenit', where he recounts that an ancient doctor, Rusticanus, disputed this question and concluded that an appeal cannot be taken. The principal ground is that from an arbitrament no appeal lies; therefore, neither from the sentence which is rendered upon it. Likewise, the judge does not take cognizance in this case as a judge, but as an upright man (bonus vir), as in the said l. si societatem, at the end; and it is regarded just as if he had been assumed for it not as a judge. Whence, since the judge in this case is subrogated into the place of an upright man, just as no appeal lies from an arbitrator who is an upright man, so neither from this judge, who, being subrogated into the place of another, assumes the nature of that other; ff. si quis cau., l. si eum, § qui iniuriarum, and in c. ecclesia, ut lite pen. Thus we see in the converse case: for when an arbiter takes cognizance in the place of a judge, an appeal is taken from him as from a judge, as in l. cum spiritualis and l. apertissimi, C. de iud., and de of. dele., c. arbitro, ff. qui satis. cog.

† It also supports this that, if we were to say the contrary, the parties would fall into the labyrinths of litigation through a first and a second appeal, and on account of this the doctors shrank from that opinion. The opinion that pleases me I find held by Bart. in l. 2, at the end, ff. de leg. 2, where he reports that Inno. held the same in c. praesenti, de rescrip., lib. 6 (which today begins 'statutum'), where he seems to state the noble rule that wherever a judge arbitrates something as an upright man, an appeal is never taken from him; for Bart. says that not even a reduction to the arbitrament of an upright man can be sought, and he cites Iac. But. in the said § arbitrorum. Lord Zab. the Cardinal also followed this opinion in cap. exposita, de arb., where he reports that Lord Bart. de Sali. advised the same; and Bartol. agrees in l. fin., C. de contrahen. emp.

† It also makes for this opinion that the judge of the reduction does not have to render a sentence in the manner of the original arbitrator, but has to arbitrate according to equity, as noted by Bartol. in the said § arbitrorum, and thus it cannot be said that he takes cognizance as a mere judge. And these points militate against the appeal from the interlocutory decree about which I spoke above, and it ought not to have been admitted, just as it would not have been admitted before an arbitrator. From these points I conclude that the said appeal is not to be admitted. I also allege another principal cause from another head invalidating the said appeal: for wherever an appeal from an interlocutory decree is manifestly frivolous, an appeal is not valid, nor from a definitive sentence, as having been interposed by a manifestly contumacious person; the text is notable in clem. unica, de dolo & contu. But the first appeal was manifestly frivolous, as appears from the aforesaid; therefore, no appeal could be taken from the definitive sentence, and through this the third article remains superfluous. But presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the said appeal were to be admitted, would articles directly contradictory have to be admitted? And this question depends on the first article, whether the publication of the attestations causes harm; and say that if it was not legitimately made, it ought not to prejudice the party, as noted by Io. Andr. in cap. fraternitatis, and cap. constitutus, il 2, de test. If, however, it was legitimately made, it ought not to be admitted because of the danger of subornation of witnesses, as noted in the said cap. fraternitatis. And such is today the text in cle. 2, de test.; Bart. holds this in l. per hanc, C. de tempo. appell., and in l. peremptorias, C. sen. resc. non pos. In our case the publication was legitimately made, since the adverse party had not legitimately alleged the contrary, as appears from the aforesaid; therefore, etc. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Although a guardian cannot remit a liquidated debt of a ward, he nevertheless can remit an unliquidated one.
2. An oath binds Jews, just as it does Christians.
casus: The CASE upon which counsel is sought is in the following terms. A certain Bonaventura, a Jew, received on loan from a certain Deodatus 1,200 florins, as is said to be established by a private writing in the hand of the debtor himself. With the lapse of time, a certain person named Genitus, an unemancipated son of the said debtor, without consulting his father, subscribed himself upon the same chirograph in this form: “I, Genitus, confess to have had and received out of the above-written 1,200, which I promise to trade with, and to render a good account to the said Deodatus.” After the aforesaid events, the creditor himself died, leaving surviving him a certain niece under the age of puberty, yet near to puberty, whom he instituted as his universal heir, and he made five legatees, and instituted each of them in a fifth part of his goods. And then the local judge gave to the above-written girl under puberty a guardian for business, lawsuits, and causes, one of the above-written legatees; which guardian, having diligently examined the accounts of the said deceased and the release made by him concerning the said Bonaventura, released and acquitted the said Bonaventura and his heirs from the said debt of 1,200 florins, with an oath interposed both by the said guardian and by the aforesaid pupil heir. Now it is asked whether the aforesaid Genitus, who subscribed himself in the manner and form mentioned above, is acquitted by virtue of the said release, and whether that guardian could release him and his father, and this without consulting the other legatees, etc.
body: The aid of the Divine Name having been humbly invoked, two questions must be subjected to examination. First, whether the son of the said Bonaventura has been released. Second, what is the case regarding the father. Concerning the first, omitting for the sake of brevity the arguments usually made for the parties, I say that the said Genito cannot be sued on two grounds by the heirs of the said Deodatus, the former creditor. First, he himself was never bound to the said Deodatus, because he either in truth had the said 1200 florins, or he did not. If he had them, such money was lent to the father, and thus passed into the ownership of the father, since from a loan made, money passes into the borrower's ownership, l. ij. ff. si cer. peta., and the profit proceeding therefrom is common to the father himself and to Genito the son, according to what is noted by Bart. in l. cum oporteat, C. de bon. quæ libe. and in l. j. ff. pro socio. Nor could the son, without consulting the father, novate the father's obligation so that in respect of those 1200 florins he himself would be bound in place of the father, so that the money would thus be his own and he would traffic and do business in his own name for his own benefit and that of the first creditor; on the contrary, he did not effect any novation, but simply confessed that he had received from the money lent to the father, to this effect l. j. & l. ij. C. de nouat.; whence he promised unduly and through error to traffic and render an account to the said Deodatus, since he had received nothing from him nor from his money. And thus such a writing, or bond unduly made, ought not to prejudice him, as in cap. si cautio, de fide instru. and l. cum de indebito, in fin. ff. de probat. If, however, the said Genito received no money, which seems truer and seems sufficiently gathered from the tenor of the release made, then it would be clear that the said Genito is not bound, since a real obligation cannot be contracted without a thing intervening, as in l. si tibi. x. de pactis, and l. rogasti, si cert. peta. and l. Hactenus, de constitu. pecu. Secondly, on that ground the said Genito cannot be sued by virtue of the absolution and release made by the said guardian and the ward herself, who expressly released the said Bonaventura and his sons both in respect of the principal of the said 1200 florins and in respect of the profit, as is clear from the tenor of the said instrument of release; whether this was entirely valid I shall examine immediately in the following article. I come therefore to the second article, namely whether the guardian could release the said Bonaventura and his son, namely Genito, presupposing that Genito himself was bound. And it seems first that he could not, through l. pactum curatoris, C. de pact. and l. Lucius Titius. §. fi. ff. de admini. tut., where it is clear that the pact of a curator or guardian can benefit a minor in exacting, but not harm him in remitting. For a guardian is held in the place of an owner when he administers well, and not when he does so unlawfully, as in l. qui fundum, ff. pro emp. But notwithstanding this, the contrary seems to be affirmed on a twofold ground of law. First, from the common theory of the Doctors in l. si præses, C. de transa. and the said l. pactum curatoris, where the Gloss, Bart., and commonly the other Doctors

† maintain that although a guardian cannot remit a liquidated debt of a ward, it is otherwise, however, when the debt is not liquidated. For we see that a guardian alone can compromise, as in l. si pignore, in fi. and l. interdum, ff. de pact., which holds that although a son having the administration of a peculium cannot remit or agree not to sue with the intention of making a gift, it is otherwise, however, if it is done without the intention of making a gift, as for instance because he distrusted the proofs; for then a remission made by one having administration is valid, even though he obtains nothing in exchange for its being made. But in our case that debt of 1200 florins was not only not liquidated, but indeed it expressly appeared from the books of the deceased that it had been satisfied, as is stated by the guardian himself in the said instrument of release; the said guardian could therefore lawfully release the said Bonaventura and his son by acknowledging good faith, especially since in this he was following the judgment of the deceased, as was evident from his books, in which case even in the alienation of immovable property a decree of the governor is not required, C. quando decre. opus non est, throughout; in point as an argument for the aforesaid are l. peto, in princip. ff. de lega. 3. and l. pater, de lega. 2. Secondly and principally, it makes for the aforesaid release that the female ward swore an oath, especially with the authority of the guardian, and promised not to contravene it. Whence, since she was older than an infant, and thus capable of deceit, the oath had to validate the contract or release, even if it had otherwise been invalid, so that she is bound inviolably to the observance of the oath, as in the authentica sacramenta puberum, C. si aduer. uen., which, although it speaks of a person with puberty, the Doctors of both laws commonly hold that it also applies to one below puberty who is capable of deceit, because just as by sinning and committing perjury one can bind oneself to the Devil, so also to God, as in cap. 1. de deli. pue. And this is commonly held by Bartolus and others in the said authentica sacramenta, and commonly by the canonists, and especially Hostiensis in c. cum contingat, de iureiuran.

† Nor does it stand in the way that they are Jews, because an oath is of divine law and binds even by the disposition of the Old Testament according to that saying, 'perform your oaths to the Lord,' as is quoted in cap. & si Christus, de iureiur. Moreover, the Mosaic Law indeed binds Jews, as in cap. gaudemus, de diuor., to such an extent that they can be compelled by the Roman Pontiff to observe it in matters of natural law, as noted by Innocent in cap. quòd super his, de uoto; to the aforesaid points c. mouet. 22. quæstio. 1 makes. Wherefore I conclude that even if the son had been bound—which however I do not believe, through what I said at the beginning, since that money had been made the father's by the intervention of the loan, whence he could not promise it to another or traffic for another, according to l. contra iuris. ff. de pactis, and l. filiusfami. ff. de donatio.—nevertheless the subsequent release made by the guardian and the ward, especially with an oath intervening, had to absolve them, since an oath removes the defect of age, as in the said authentica sacramenta puberum. Nor does it stand in the way that the other legatees did not consent, since they did not have the administration of the ward's property. I concede, however, that this release does not prejudice them for the share of the inheritance deferred to them, since the compromise of one heir does not prejudice another, since an unfair condition ought not to be brought upon one by another, l. j. C. de transact. For inherited active and passive actions are divided by operation of law among the heirs according to their hereditary shares, l. ea quæ, C. famil. ercisc. And let these things suffice, etc. Nicolaus, Abbot. Case of the following consilium. The contingency of FACT is as follows. The noble and distinguished Enrico, son of the late Federico da Crisino of Vicenza, having at that time no legitimate and natural male son or sons, solemnly made a will in which he left a dowry to certain of his daughters, and instituted them heirs in that dowry, ordering that they be silent and content. Which testator, since he had a pregnant wife, universally and equally instituted in the said will as legitimate and natural heirs the son or sons, if any he should have in the future by his pregnant wife, one or more. But if the said testator should not have at the time of his death a legitimate and natural son or sons, or legitimate and natural male descendants from the said sons, or should have them and his said natural male sons and the legitimate and natural descendants from them should die without legitimate and natural male sons and legitimate and natural male descendants from them, he vulgarly, briefly, compendiously, and by fideicommissum substituted, and willed and ordained to be heir and successor in his goods and inheritance, the notable man Federico, son of the late Passo da Crisino, nephew of the said testator, if at the said time the said Federico should survive him. And in the event that the said Federico should not be living and should not survive, he substituted in his goods and inheritance the legitimate and natural male descendants from the said Federico. And if the said Federico or his legitimate and natural male descendants should not be in the nature of things, he pupillarly, vulgarly, and by fideicommissum substituted as heir and willed to be successor in his goods and inheritance Lionello, son of the late Bartolomeo del Nevo of Vicenza. And if the said Lionello should not be living, he substituted vulgarly, pupillarly, and by fideicommissum the legitimate and natural male descendants of the said Lionello. And if the legitimate and natural male descendants of the said Lionello should not be living, the said testator ordered that his inheritance and goods should devolve to the next of kin of the said testator. After this solemn will was made, the said testator, surviving for some years, at length died, his will unchanged. Federico, however, his nephew substituted as above, there being no legitimate and natural male sons from the said testator, by virtue of the aforesaid substitution or institution solemnly entered upon the aforesaid inheritance of the said Enrico, testator and his uncle, with no one speaking against it. Finally, after some time had elapsed, at the petition of the said Lionello, the said Federico was summoned by the vicar of the podestà of the place, and at his instance a deadline was fixed by the said vicar for the said Federico for the execution of certain bequests made to pious causes. Which Federico, seeing himself burdened with debt from the said inheritance or on the occasion of it, approached the Bishop of Vicenza and obtained a prolongation of the deadline for a two-year period, and within the prolonged deadline, not having the money for the satisfaction of the said bequests, he assigned for their execution certain properties of the said inheritance to the said Lord Bishop, who accepted and received them. Now doubt happens to arise concerning three main points. First, whether, if the said Federico happens to die without male children, Lionello, the substitute, or even, failing him, his legitimate and natural male children, are admitted to the said inheritance by virtue of the aforesaid substitution, or whether every substitution was terminated by the entry into the inheritance by the said Federico, the testator's nephew. Secondly, whether the said Lionello, positing that he or his sons are admitted, can demand from Federico that he give security for preserving and not diminishing the assets of the inheritance and for restoring them when the case of the aforesaid substitution occurs, since it is alleged that the said Federico is misusing his estate, although Federico himself alleges that he alienated those things which were alienated for the sake of satisfying debt and the hereditary creditors. Likewise, positing that he ought to be held liable, since no one is found who is willing to act as surety and be personally bound, whether his simple bond suffices. Thirdly, it is doubted whether the said Federico is deprived of the said inheritance because he did not satisfy the pious causes legally within the year fixed by the judge, and is not preserved unharmed by the said prolongation and consignment of goods made in the aforesaid manner. And positing that he is deprived, whether the said inheritance or its goods ought to devolve to the said Lionello or his substituted sons, and to the Lord Bishop of Vicenza as father of the poor and of the pious cause, etc.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A substitution made under a condition vanishes in the event of the condition.
2. One must not depart from the words of the testator.
3. An argument based on the topic from the specific is valid in law.
4. A judge, upon examining the cause, can alter a time limit established by law.
5. The strictest interpretation must be made in the case of penalties that are imposed ipso iure.
body: The aid of Christ and His mother having been humbly invoked, I come to the first doubt. And it seems first that, upon the death of the said Federicus without legitimate and natural children, the said Leonellus as substitute, or upon his death his children, ought to be admitted to the said inheritance; which is shown thus: in testaments recourse must be had rather to the intention of the testator than to the words of the testament itself, l. si mihi & Titio, ff. de condi. & demon., even contrary to the proper meaning of the words, in l. Labeo, ff. de supel. lega. But by conjecturing the testator's intention, the said Leonellus, or his children, appears to be substituted in the event that Federicus does not exist without legitimate and natural male children. Therefore, upon the occurrence of the condition, they are to be admitted, as in c. Raynal., de testa. The minor premise is proved from the tacit intention of the testator; for the testator is not presumed to have loved more a nephew by a brother—who is not properly called a grandson [nepos], as in l. iurisconsultus, § nepos, ff. de gra. affi.—than his own legitimate and natural sons, since paternal love overcomes all affection, l. si, C. de cur. fur. But the said testator wished simply to institute his sons, or grandsons by his sons, who are truly grandsons, said § nepos, and who are loved as sons, as in l. liberorum, in fi., ff. de uer. signi. But he substituted Federicus for them in the event that they should die without legitimate and natural offspring, as appears in the statement of the case. Therefore, it is all the more strongly to be presumed that he did not intend to substitute the said Federicus simply, but tacitly burdened him with the duty of restoring to the said Leonellus or his children if he himself should die without legitimate and natural issue, even though he did not expressly provide for this; to this effect is the notable text in l. cum acutissimi, § fideicommi., and l. generaliter, § cum autem, C. de institut. & substituti., where it is evident that although the father in the substitution of a natural son made express mention of grandchildren, he is nevertheless tacitly presumed to have thought of them to the exclusion of the substitute, because the testator is not to be presumed to have wished to prefer a stranger to his own offspring, as the text says there. To the same effect is the notable text in l. cum auus, ff. de condict. & demonstra., where children from a grandson are seen to be tacitly called even to the exclusion of the substituted paternal uncle, lest he seem to have loved a surviving son more than the offspring of a predeceased son; and that is a notable case.
