So in the present case, since the testator wished to grant to his own offspring the power of disposing of the hereditary goods at will in the event that they died without legitimate posterity, but substituted for them the said Federicus, his nephew, much more strongly is the same to be presumed to have been willed in the person of Federicus, since he is presumed to have been loved less, both by natural reason, as in said l. liberorum, in fin., and from the institution, since he called in the first place the sons descending from them. Second, principally, another and different reason operates: that the said burdens imposed on the instituted heir seem to be repeated in the substitute, as in l. illud, ff. de lega. 1, and l. non iustam, C. ad Trebel.; l. unica, C. de cadu. tollen., operates to the same effect. But he substituted to his own sons in the event of a lack of children. Therefore, he seems to have repeated the same in the substituted nephew, and this is tacitly to be conjectured all the more strongly as he is seen to have loved his sons more than a nephew by a brother. But these points notwithstanding, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer. I am principally moved by l. Lucius, ff. de hæredit. institut., where a testator instituted his brother, and if he should die before having a son or a daughter, he substituted two of his slaves; the instituted heir entered upon the inheritance, but did not have children. It was asked whether the said substituted slaves ought to be admitted as substitutes, or at least in some part as adjecti; and it is viewed there by the jurist that they ought to be admitted neither as adjecti nor as substitutes, since the testator wished the instituted brother, and also the children, to be preferred to them. And thus, solely by the aditio of the inheritance, the substitutes are excluded, even though in the substitution mention was made of children, since the brother was instituted simply and not under the condition 'if without children.' So principally it seems must be said in our case, because Federicus was instituted in the second degree simply, although mention of children was made in the event that Federicus himself should not exist; since, however, he himself exists and accepted the inheritance, the substitution entirely vanished, however much he might not procreate children, and should die with none existing, as in the said l. Lucius.

† To the same effect is that a substitution made under a condition vanishes upon the non-occurrence of the condition, l. prima, C. de conditio. inser., with similar laws. But Leonellus and his children were substituted under a condition, in the event that the said Federicus or his descendants should not exist in the nature of things; which must be understood of existence at the time of the testator's death, as appears from what was said in the first degree of institution. For subsequent words are clarified and determined by preceding ones, l. si seruus plurium, in fin., ff. de lega. 1, and l. qui filiabus, under the same title, where there is a good text. But Federicus existed at the time of the testator's death, and accepted the inheritance; therefore the substitution made concerning Leonellus and his children vanished, assuming that Federicus dies without children, because when mention was made alternatively of him and of children, it does not suffice for its purification that the other part exist, as in the rule in alternatiuis, de regulis iuris, lib. 6, and cap. inter cætera, de rescript.; and as to our matter, the text seems to be in l. is qui ducenta, § utrum, ff. de rebus dubijs.

† Third, it principally operates that one must not depart from the words of the testator unless it is clearly evident that there was a contrary intention, l. non aliter, ff. de leg. 3. But in our case the testator simply substituted Federicus, and if he were not extant, the children, and if neither were extant, Leonellus; but here the other party, namely Federicus, exists. Therefore the substitution vanished most clearly from the words. Now in the response to the contrary arguments formed above it will be seen whether he meant that from the words. Whence, to the first contrary argument, I reply that by no laws are children understood so that the testator would seem, contrary to the duty of piety, to have loved a stranger more than the posterity of his sons, or a survivor more than the offspring of a predeceased son, contrary to what is held in Instit. de hær. quæ ab intesta. defe., § cum filius. But in our case, if it is well considered, this reason entirely ceases, and every absurdity would apply, because the reason does not hold for disposing thus as the testator disposed. For in the substitution of the sons the reason was that a paternal uncle is in the place of a father; whence if the sons died without issue, the testator did not wish his nephew, who is in the place of a son, especially for the preservation of the agnation, to be excluded. Rather, he wished Federicus, his nephew by his brother, to be called, lest the sons have an opportunity to alienate those goods outside the family, especially with Federicus excluded. Whence he called him whom he deservedly ought to love in preference after his sons; but in the second part of the institution, which he made concerning Leonellus, this reason did not operate, since Leonellus himself was not of the agnation and family, nor was he related to him in that degree by which he ought to be loved in the place of a son. Whence he deservedly wished him to be excluded simply by the existence of Federicus or of his children; and it is enough that we are outside the case of the said laws. For it cannot be denied that the said l. cum acutissimi and l. generaliter, previously cited, are grounded upon the greatest equity, as appears in them. But law grounded upon the greatest equity against the rules of law ought not to be extended, arg. l. quod uerò, ff. de legibus; indeed, Ioan. Andr. in cap. primo and secundo, ut lit. pend., lib. 6, maintained that such law is not to be extended even on the basis of identity of reason. Here, however, there is no parity of reason, but indeed complete dissimilarity, as appears from the preceding. Likewise, in those laws the words are not entirely distorted, but an implied condition 'if he should die without children' is superadded in favor of the instituted heir to the exclusion of the substitute. But in our case the greatest distortion of words would occur, as appears from what has been said, against the instituted heir, who was so preferred by the testator, and in favor of the substitute, who was not so loved by the testator. To the second contrary argument I say that it does not apply to bequests made ab intestato, or to burdens enjoined upon the instituted heir, which are seen to be repeated in the substitutes in order that the testator's will may be satisfied. But in our case we are not dealing with bequests or burdens enjoined upon instituted heirs, but with a certain qualification attached to those instituted in the first degree, which was not repeated concerning those instituted in the second degree; l. Iulius Paulus, ff. de conditio. & demonstratio., supports this. Likewise, and better, things attached and stated in the institution are seen to be replicated in the substitution, unless a contrary intention of the testator is elicited from conjecture, as the text notably says in l. illud, de legat. 1. But in our case the contrary intention of the testator is most clearly evident, since in the first degree he pronounced one law, and in the second degree another. For no one is presumed to have said what he did not first turn over in his mind, l. Labeo, previously cited. Nor is it likely that he instantly forgot or contradicted himself, argu. l. non ad ea, ff. de condi. & demonst. And if he had wished to dispose regarding Federicus as regarding his sons, he would well have known how to express it, and not substitute alternatively, as in a similar case the text says in c. ad audientiam, de decim. And this as to the first doubt, by the decision of which the second seems to be removed; for security is not to be provided if the substitution vanished. But, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that there were a substitution, what is to be said? Certainly the case seems indubitable that sufficient security must be provided, as is the case joining glo. 1, ff. ut lega. not. For it is special in a father who is requested to restore an inheritance to a son that he is not bound to give security, in l. iubebus, C. ad Trebel. Therefore, it seems otherwise among other relatives; for

† an argument from the special case is valid, as I read and is noted in capitul. præsenti, de præbend., lib. 6. But in this case the one asked to make restitution alleges inability to provide sufficient security. Certain laws in other settings seem to maintain that in the case where sufficient security cannot be provided, that security which can be provided should be provided, at least promissory security [cautio iuratoria], as in Auth. generaliter, C. de episcop. & cler., and in Auth. ut nulli iudicum, § si verò, and in capitul. per vestras, qui fil. sunt legit., and in Auth. de litigiosis, § ad excludendas. This question can be readily adapted to the similar question that arises regarding a usufructuary, who is bound to give sufficient security to the owner to use the property according to the judgment of a good man, and to restore it once the cause of the usufruct is ended, in capitul. fin., de pigno. & in aliis causis, and in l. usuffruct., C. de vsusfruct., and in both places by the glossa and the doctors of both laws. And on this there are many opinions, but there are two principal ones, which seem sufficiently to agree in effect. One is that of Hostiensis, Ioan. Andr., and their followers in the said capitul. fin., that promissory security suffices; but if he should in any way act against the oath, or begin to dissipate his goods, he would lose this privilege, argum. de deci., c. suggestum. The other is that of Bartolus in said l. ususfruct., that if the person is suspect, a sequestration should be made; otherwise, one stands by promissory security; and thus the contrary opinions yield to harmony. For our precise matter I cite the text joined with the notable gloss in l. postquam, § in præsenti, ff. ut leg. no. c., where it seems to be intimated that a sequestration should be made concerning this with an upright man, who would answer for the fruits to the heir himself, or at least it ought to remain with the heir if he were not suspect—I understand this, provided promissory security is furnished—and thus Bartolus's opinion seems to be proved there. Concerning poverty, one may sufficiently stand by the oath of Federicus, argum. in said Auth. generaliter, where this seems to be proved; cap. nulli, de elect., lib. 6, supports this. And this as to the second point. I address lastly the third question: whether the said Federicus is deprived of the aforesaid inheritance? It seems first that he is; even a secular judge can impart his office so that bequests for pious causes are carried into execution, as is notably proved in Auth. de ecclesi. titu., § si quis ædificationem. Therefore, since the admonition was made by his judge, and within a year from the day of admonition it was not obeyed, Federicus the heir was ipso facto deprived, and immediately by disposition of law Leonellus as substitute became heir ipso iure, as seems to be proved in Auth. hoc amplius, on the word 'excluditur eo, quòd præter', C. de fideicomiss., and better in the body of the text whence it is taken in § omnibus, de hære. & fal., and the gloss most openly seems to hold in the same Auth. de hęred. & fal., § si quis autem non implens, on the word 'auferri'. Indeed, the notable gloss joined with the text in capitul. si hæredes, de test., seems to maintain even more: that the heir not fulfilling the deceased's will in bequests for pious causes is ipso iure deprived, even of the due subsidy of goods, and Hostiensis says the same there; the text joined with the gloss in capitul. Siluester, 11, quæstio prima, supports this. But these points notwithstanding, I think the contrary is true in law as to our case. I am principally moved by the notable and singular text on this subject in c. nos quidem, de testa., on the word 'neglexerit', where it is evident that the heir is deprived when he has neglected to fulfill it for a year; it is otherwise, therefore, if he was prevented by a just cause; and Hostiensis intimates this there, and more openly Federicus de Senis, consil. 124, that Auth. hoc amplius applies when out of contumacy or negligence the heir delays execution beyond a year. Bartolus agrees there, and the text joined with the gloss in the word 'distulerit', Instit. de actio., § item mista, seems to show this; and that gloss is quite notable for our subject, and what the gloss notes in capitul. quam sit, on the word 'distulerit', de electio., lib. 6, supports it. But this Federicus, about whom the inquiry is made, did not neglect it, nor did he delay beyond a year without cause; rather, he approached the local bishop, and satisfied the burdens of debts incumbent upon the inheritance, which must be cleared first, l. si uniuersæ, C. de leg., and l. 1, ff. ad l. Falc.; and thus he had an extension of the deadline. Moreover, that the bishop could extend the deadline upon cause shown is sufficiently proved from the said capitul. nos quidem, de testam., and from the said consilium of Federicus. For he is principally the judge and party in these bequests for pious causes, and has greater power than a secular judge, as is sufficiently gathered from l. nulli and l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de episcop. & cleric., and better in Auth. de ecclesi. titu., § si autem, qui hoc facere, and in capitul. sua, and capitul. si hæredes, and capitul. Ioannes, de test.

† Moreover, a judge can regularly alter a deadline established by law upon cause shown, as is fully noted by Bartolus in l. 1, ff. de re iudica., by canonical authorities in capitul. quod ad consultationem, under the same title, in capitul. cum sit Romana, de appella., and especially in our case, where the laws weigh negligence, as I said above. And the bishop is presumed to have been moved by a just cause to extend the deadline, argum. in l. 1, and what Bartolus notes there, C. de prædijs mino. sine decret., libr. 10; and whatever the case may be, it is enough for avoiding the penalty that this man did not neglect it, nor delay without cause, as in the laws previously cited.

† For in penalties that are imposed ipso iure, we must make the strictest interpretation, as in the rule in pœnis and the rule odia, de regu. iur., libr. 6, and what is noted there by Ioann. Andr.; l. penult., ff. de pœnis, supports this. And as to whether he is now freed from the execution of those bequests by the consignment of those bequests and goods made to the lord bishop, it can sufficiently be argued that he is, through a singular statement of the Speculator in the title de instrumen. edict., § nunc aliqua, verse 'quid si executor in potestate iuris', where he says that the one who has to execute a pious will has the period of a year running against him even if impeded, not, I say, as to the penalty, but as to the devolution of the execution to be made to the lord bishop; and his statement can be supported by the notable gloss in capitul. statutum, de præbend., libr. 6, on the word 'numerandum', which holds that where time is appointed not to the detriment but in favor of someone, then it runs even against one who is ignorant and not negligent. And l. genero, ff. de his qui not. infam., supports that gloss. Since therefore the power in executing those bequests seems sufficiently to have satisfied as much as lay in it, since it assigned the hereditary goods to the bishop who accepted and received them; in favor of this is a good text in l. fina., § & si præfatam, C. de iur. delibe., and l. si necessariis, § omnis, ff. de pig. act. And through this there remains resolved that about which it is ultimately asked: whether the devolution of the inheritance goes to the lord bishop or to Leonellus the substitute. For there is no place for devolution, as appears from what has been said. But, in order to satisfy all doubts, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the said Federicus were deprived, it seems first that the said Leonellus as substitute was made heir, as in Auth. de hære. Fal., § in omnibus, and § si quis autem non implens, in the gloss on the word 'auferri', and in the said Auth. hoc amplius. On the contrary, in favor of the lord bishop, there appears the notable text in Auth. de eccl. tit. 1, § si autem qui hoc facere, where it is said that if the heir does not fulfill pious bequests, the bishop can claim everything, even with the profits of the intermediate time; and that text at first sight is very adverse to the said Auth. de hær. & Fal. and the said Auth. hoc amplius. I find that a certain doctor, who was of outstanding intellect, reduced them to harmony, so that in bequests to non-pious causes the substitutes succeed, but in pious bequests the bishop succeeds, which is quite pleasing, and thus according to this interpretation the previously cited capitul. si hæredes can be understood. And according to this, the devolution in our case would be made to the lord bishop and not to the said Leonellus. Nor does it stand in the way that here a double admonition did not intervene, which seems to be required in the said § si autem qui hoc facere, because that section applies when the year is not waited for, but the penalty is remitted to him immediately; but if the lapse of a year is awaited, a single admonition suffices, as in § si quis autem non implens, and in Auth. hoc amplius, previously cited. And thus Bartolus understood in the said Auth. hoc amplius, and the gloss in the said § si quis autem non implens. And let these things suffice, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. An alienation made of the properties of a monastery in a case not permitted is null, no matter how much the form was observed.
2. Everyone is presumed to exercise his office diligently.
3. Every solemnity is deemed to be remitted by the commission and indulgence of the Pope.
4. The Pope can lawfully donate the goods of a church to someone, and he is presumed to be moved by a just cause.
5. A privilege granted to a non-subject cannot be revoked.
body: Having implored the aid of the Savior and of His most pious Mother, it must in effect be examined whether the said cousin brothers, about whom the statement of fact treats, were secure regarding the purchase of the monastery's properties against the Abbot and Convent of San Maurizio. In the examination of which, indeed, it is necessary to declare and discuss five items presented to me: namely, first, the blessing granted; second, the confirmation of Pope Boniface; third, his own general revocation; fourth, the confirmation of Pope Innocent; fifth, the revocation of John. And first, the said sale appears to contain very many errors in itself. For there was no formal inquiry into the cause, which by the ius commune ought to occur in the alienation of ecclesiastical property, 12 q. 2 c. sine exceptione, and especially with a preceding discussion, as noted by Innocen. in cap. 1 de reb. ecclesi. non alie. lib. 6 in verbo tractatus, at the end, and by Fede. de Sen. consi. 137; nor was the inquiry into the cause taken away by the Pope's mandate, but rather augmented, since he commanded that diligent inquiry be made concerning the alleged causes for making the alienation; whence the said sale falls, both from the omission of the solemnity of law and from the bypassing of the form of the mandate, as in the said legal authorities, and in capitul. cum dilecta, de rescript. and capitul. Pisanis, de restitu. spolia. To this makes the notable dictum of Barto. in l. diem proferre, §. stari, ff. de arbi., where he says that if a submission was made to an arbitrator with this expressly stated, that he pronounce according to law, if he pronounces contrary to it, the award is invalid, because it is contrary to the form of the submission, even though otherwise that form did not express his dictum, although contrary to law it could have been reduced to the arbitrament of a good man, as in l. si societatem, §. arbitrorum, ff. pro socio, and capit. per tuas, and capitu. dilecti, de arbit. So in the matter at hand, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that by ius commune the said sale would have been valid, nevertheless, because the Bishop of Verona, the papal commissioner, gave the license without having first verified the causes contained in the rescript, the granting was not legally valid. Clemen. 1 de reb. eccle. non alie. serves excellently for the aforesaid, where it is evident,

† that an alienation made of the properties of a monastery in a case not permitted is void, no matter how much the form was observed; which is also the opinion of the gl. and Io. Cal. in capitu. 1 de in integrum resti. and Archid. and Ioan. And. in c. 2 de re. ecc. non alie. lib. 6 and Bal. in auth. qui res iam dictas, C. de sacrosan. eccl.; and the cause must be known and evident, nor does it suffice that a necessity of alienation should arise, as is notably proved in cap. 1 de rebus. ecclesi. non alie. lib. 6. To this makes what is noted by Barto. in l. si forte, ff. de castre. pec. and l. secundum, ff. de verbo. signifi. and in authé. si quis in aliquo documento, C. de eden., which is not established here, even though it was also commanded in the commission. Secondly, there is a defect because the alienation cannot be made to relatives of the prelate. For there is a presumption of law that on their account the church would be unduly burdened; this seems to be proved in authen. quibuscunque modis, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi., and this Bartol. and Bald. seem to hold; 10 q. 2 capitul. hoc ius porrectum helps; the text with the glo. in capitul. peruenit, 1 q. 3 serves excellently, where the glo. says that bishops are blind regarding their nephews and other relatives. Thirdly, there is a defect because here it is not proved that the price was paid down, and consequently the ownership of the things sold does not seem to have been transferred. For wherever a sale is permitted by reason of a cause, faith cannot be given concerning the price, nor does an acknowledgment of the price received suffice, unless it appears paid or committed to the cause on account of which the sale was permitted, as is notably proved in l. a diuo pio, §. sed si emptor, ff. de re iudica., and there Bartho. expressly holds this; to the same effect is l. si procurator, ff. de iure fisci, and what is noted there by the same author. But in our case the Pope permitted the alienation of the properties of the monastery up to the value of one thousand florins on account of certain and express causes in the commission. Therefore, the Abbot, in selling, could not acknowledge having received the price, since it is not otherwise established that it was committed to the causes by reason of which the sale was granted. For it is one thing to acknowledge having received the price, and another to have truly received it, as in l. si ex cautione, and what is noted there, C. de numera. pecun. And by this is removed the objection that can be framed from the notable dictum of Innocent. in capitul. 1 depo., where he states it to be special in a loan that it is necessary to prove the use, but otherwise in a contract of purchase; and to this makes what is noted in l. ciuitas, ff. si cert. peta.; for it ought to be understood where it is established that the prelate received the price. And thus an argument can also be gathered from C. de quadri. præscript. l. 2, §. final., where it is clear that although the procurator of the fiscus cannot be believed regarding the price, as in the said l. si procurator, nevertheless if he acknowledges having received the price, the purchaser is secure, which Bar. also notes in the said l. si procurator; for it ought to be understood when the alienation was permitted simply, but otherwise if so that the price should be applied to a certain cause, as in our case, as I have said above. The confirmation of Boniface, made from certain knowledge, does not stand in the way of the aforesaid, because he himself revoked it, which he could do, since he granted it without legitimate cause to the grievance of the church, as in capitul. si quis presbyterum, de rebus ecclesi. non alie.; and the revocation of things wrongfully done is of great wisdom, 22 q. 3 capitul. magna, and in capitul. non liceat papæ, 12 q. 2, which Archi. notes, where he says that the Pope sins mortally if he alienates the goods of the church to give them to relatives or friends. To the same effect is what he himself notes in cap. non debet, 12 distinct., where, following blessed Thomas, he says that the goods of the church are in the power of the Pope as administrator, but he does not have true ownership or true possession of them, for these belong to God, as in capitul. cum ex eo, de elect. lib. 6, and by Innocent. in capitul. cum super, de causa posses. & proprie. Nor does the confirmation of Innocen. stand in the way, because John, his successor, revoked it, for a Pope can revoke the acts of his predecessor where he finds a just cause for revoking, as in capitul. sententiam, 35 q. 9, and capitul. tum ex literis, de in integ. restit., which also proceeds in the alienation of church property, by the argument of those things which are read and noted by Inno. in c. cum sit generale, de fo. comp.; the text in c. quia sancta, §. verum, 63 di., serves excellently. And although Bar. was so plausible that he seems to conclude in this respect, nevertheless I consider the contrary opinion to be true; and if we are willing to consider everything well and diligently, the said sale is found to have been legitimately made. For Boniface first commissioned the Bishop of Verona to inform himself of the contents in the petition, and if he should find them true, to give that abbot the license to sell, etc. From which words it is clearly evident that this was not a mandate to the Bishop as a judge or to proceed judicially, since there was no contention with an opposing party, but as a good man, that he might inform himself extrajudicially; whence the Bishop was not bound to compile witnesses on this and publish the process, though it would have been useful, provided he informed himself extrajudicially; and this is openly seen in a similar case according to the mind of Innocent. in capitu. dudum, de præsumptio., in the last column; although in truth, if true causes did not exist, the act would be void if the lack of causes were proved in the future, capitu. cum contingat, de rescript. It is also proved by reason: in the alienation of church property, it is not necessarily required that witnesses be received by the ordinary, or that he interpose a decree, but it is enough that an inquiry into the cause take place with the interposition of the required solemnities, as noted by Innocen. and the glo. in capitu. 1 de reb. ecclesi. non alienan. lib. 6. Likewise, it appears to have been commanded as to a commissioner; for since the Pope himself could proceed extrajudicially and inform himself, so also could his commissioner, by the argument of capitu. super literis, de rescriptis. For that reason which moved the delegating authority ought to move the delegated authority, as there, and by Innocent. in the said capitu. dudum. But in our case it is to be presumed that the bishop commissioner made a diligent inquest and found the causes true, which is evident from the fact that he subsequently gave the license to alienate after auctions were held. For from the consequent a presumption arises concerning the antecedent, l. illud, de acquirend. hæred., and capitu. præsentiam, and capit. præterea, de offic. delega.

† For everyone is presumed to exercise his office diligently, in capitu. ad audientiam, de præscrip., and capit. deputati, de appel., by Cyn. in l. si quis decurio, C. de fal., especially, however, if this was asserted, as it is presupposed in the narrative that the bishop commissioner applied an inquiry into the cause. The noted glo. in l. 1, C. de fid. instrum. & iure hastæ fis. lib. 10, makes for this, and what is noted by Innocen. in capitu. quoniam, de proba. Whoever, therefore, wishes to say that the stated causes were not true must prove this, since the presumption is in favor of the authority of the judge intervening afterwards, by the argument in l. 1 and what Barto. notes there, C. de prędiis decu. sine decre. non alie. lib. 10, which Innoc. sufficiently endorses, if it is well weighed, in the said cap. dudum; nor was it necessary that another discussion be prefixed, because the discussion which is committed to the commissioner is held in place of a discussion.

† Likewise, every solemnity seems to have been remitted by the commission and indulgence of the Pope, and it is sufficient to observe the words of the rescript; whence the abbot and convent, having obtained the license of the Bishop, could legally alienate goods up to the value of one thousand florins purely without other authority and solemnity. This seems to be singularly proved by the text in capit. ad audientiam, 11 [c. 2], de eccle. ędi., joined with the glo. and the dicta of the doctors there. And Arch. opines so in cap. antepe. 12 q. 2. By this also is removed the objection that is made that these purchasers were relatives of the abbot. For alienation to relatives is prohibited because of the presumption of fraud, which fraud entirely ceases here, since the alienation was made to them by the authority of the Bishop. When fraud ceases, however, an alienation can be made even to relatives, as Fede. notably says, consil. 273. And Barto. opines so in the said authen. quibuscunque modis, at the end. I also say, beyond others, that that authentica speaks of a relative of an oeconomus, and not of a prelate. For an oeconomus does not have so full a right as a prelate, as is noted in 5 q. 1 c. 1 in gl. Likewise, it is more easily presumed against an oeconomus than against a prelate and the whole convent. Nay rather, I cite the notable text that a prelate can alienate and give goods of the church to his own people if he contributes as much to the church from his own patrimony, so that it is not necessary that the church be made better off, but it suffices that it not be made worse off, as is very notably proved in c. si quis qualibet, with the preceding §, 12 q. 2, and more expressly in the same causa, q. 5, cap. si episcopus, and by Innocen. and Ioan. And. in cap. cum in officiis, de testa. A fortiori, therefore, could he sell to his own people for a just price and for the necessity of the church, since even a guardian himself can openly buy property of the ward, l. pupilli, ff. de autho. tuto. Likewise, the civil law could not prohibit this; whence it is enough that it is not found prohibited by the canons. For when canon law delivers a certain form in the alienation of church property, one must not run to what the civil law decrees, as Innocen. and the glo. notably state in the said capitul. 1 de re. ecclesi. non alienan. lib. 6. The only doubt that remains, therefore, is whether the acknowledgment of the receipt of the price was valid, which is sufficiently doubtful on account of the things said above. For the said l. 2 in fin. C. de quadri. præscri. makes sufficiently for it to be valid, and proves it, since the fiscus and the church proceed on par, as noted in cap. 1 de in integ. restitu. Likewise, here there intervened the acknowledgment of the prelate and of the entire convent, who have great power regarding counted money. A good text for this is in cap. quod quibusdam, de fide instrumen., and to this makes what is noted by the glo. in cap. 2 de ord. cog. and the gl. in c. delictum, de reg. iu. lib. 6. And what Ioan. And. notes in cap. quia clerici, de iure patro., where it is commonly noted that the act of a prelate, with the counsel of the chapter shared, prejudices the church. Moreover, presupposing that some doubt arises over this, nevertheless the confirmation of Boniface and of Innocen. so solemnly made causes us to presume that the entire price was paid down, or converted to the utility of the church. A good text for this, joined with the glo. and the dicta of the doctors, is in cap. constitutus, de relig. do., and in cap. ad hæc, de rescript., and clemen. 2, eod. titu., at the end. And it is akin to sacrilege to doubt whether that is lawful and worthy which the prince has established and confirmed with cause, 17 q. 4 c. si quis suadente diabolo, §. qui autem, ff. ad l. Iul. pen. l. sacrileg., 19 distinct. cap. 1 helps, and l. quidam consulebat, ff. de re iud., especially

† since the Pope can freely donate some goods of the church to someone, and he is presumed to be moved by a just cause, 12 q. 2 c. cum redemptor, in c. ea nobis, de deci., and there by Hostien.; what is noted de pręscript. cap. causæ makes for this; the legists legitimately note this in l. 1, C. contra ius uel utilit. pub., and in l. scripta, and l. præscriptione, C. de prec. impera. offeren.; and presupposing that a legitimate cause was not underlying, nevertheless he who received it is sufficiently safe with respect to the church militant, since no one can rebuke the Pope in this matter. To this is the noted gl. in capitu. non est, de uoto, & uoti red., nor may anyone judge of his act, 9 q. 3 cap. nemo, and cap. aliorum. It does not stand in the way that Pope Boniface himself revoked it, because if it is well observed, the revocation does not extend to our case, since he only revoked concessions made by him of non-alienable church properties; but in our case he not only donated, but even confirmed from certain knowledge the sale, which could sufficiently be sustained, at least from the subtlety of law without any confirmation, as appears from the things said above; and it is one thing to confirm, another to grant anew or donate, as is quite clearly gathered in capitul. inter dilectos, de fide instrumen., for which reason an investigation of it is not frequently to be made, capitul. 2 de translatio. prælato., and l. neque natales, C. de proba. Likewise, it could not undeservedly be urged that since he donated spontaneously, and from certain knowledge, and of his own motion, and the privilege came to the knowledge of the privileged person, he himself or another could no longer revoke it where fraud does not appear, if immediately after it came to the knowledge of those brothers it had its effect, as is read and noted in the glo. in capitul. 1 de conces. præbend. lib. 6. To this makes what Innocen. remarkably maintains in capitul. nouit, de iudic., Ioan. And. in capitul. constitutus, de relig. domi., and Arch. in c. quicunque, 6 q. 1, where they maintain

† that a privilege granted to one not a subject cannot be revoked, and what is noted by Barthol. in l. penul. ff. de decre. ab or. fa., and especially in this case, where ownership was acquired instantly, and thus it had a consummated effect, and passed into the ius gentium. Hence it is said that a perfected donation cannot be revoked, l. perfecta, C. de donatio. quæ sub mo., so that God Himself, nothing else appearing, would not revoke it, 22 q. 2 capitul. non tantum; nor is a layman subject to the Pope in patrimonial matters, as noted by Innocent. in capitul. inquisitioni, de sentent. excommun.; capitul. si duobus, de appellat., at the end, helps. But those goods, after the sale, and the confirmation in the donation that followed, became the patrimonies of those laymen. And it would be ridiculous to say that the Pope could donate and afterwards revoke at will, nothing else appearing; and perhaps a cause will be presumed in him with respect to laymen who are not subjects; and whatever the case may be, it is also sustained on another ground, namely from the subsequent confirmation of Innocen. solemnly made. Nor does the revocation of John stand in the way, both because he does not seem to be able to revoke to the prejudice of laymen, no other legitimate cause appearing, especially when two supreme pontiffs had confirmed and donated—for the act was consummated, as appears from the things said above—and because that revocation was openly surreptitious, since no mention was made of the ratification of the arbitral award. For an arbitral award is a kind of transaction or compromise, in authent. ut diff. iu., and in authen. si uero contigerit, C. de iud. But a grant is not valid where no mention is made of a preceding settlement, as is the clear text in capitul. ex multiplici, de deci., and more expressly in our very terms it seems to be proved in capitul. cum olim, de præscript. Likewise, every concealment which, had it been expressed, would have led the grantor to refuse, or even to grant with greater difficulty, must invalidate, as in capitul. postulasti, and there expressly by Hostiensi., de rescript. But it is surer than certainty that if the abbot had stated that the arbitral award had been ratified by both parties, he would not have obtained the letters of revocation, or at least not so easily. Therefore, etc. And this alone suffices for the annulment of the letters, and through all these points I conclude that the said brothers can legitimately defend themselves against the Abbot and Convent of San Maurizio, and the contrary points framed above are sufficiently shown to be distinguished and resolved by the premises, etc. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. How someone is proved a heretic.
2. Whether a bishop's statute is valid by which it is provided that someone is proved a usurer through four singular witnesses.
3. Witnesses are always singular with respect to the sense through which an act is perceived.
body: Out of many matters argued in court, this is what is asked in effect: whether an heir is to be compelled by ecclesiastical censure to exhibit his father's account-book, since it is asserted by the opposing party that usury received by the deceased is contained therein, and the loan is proved, as well as that the deceased was a usurer. But this last point is proved only by singular witnesses who depose that they received a loan from the deceased under usury, and each speaks of his own fact. The heir, on the other hand, says that he is not bound to exhibit the book, alleging moreover that he firmly does not have it. And first, it seems that the heir ought to be compelled in the aforesaid manner by the notable text in clemen. vnica, de usu. §. cęterum, where it is said that a usurer is to be compelled to this when usury is at issue; and the gloss there on the word "ipsos" says the same concerning his heirs, whether proper or extraneous, by argument in cap. tua nos, de usur., and c. Michael, and ff. de eden. l. si quis ex argentariis, §. 1. Nor is it sufficient for the usurer or heir to say that he lost the book, even under oath, unless he proves the circumstance of the loss, by argument in c. cum olim, de priuileg.; because when the prejudice of another is at stake, reliance is not to be placed on an oath alone, especially in our case, where it is established that the deceased had that book, since he refers to it in another book of his produced in court in this case. And this is maintained through many arguments by the gloss on the said clemen. una, on the word "compellendi", and the commentators there generally agree. Nor does it avail if it is said that it is not established that the deceased was a usurer, on the ground that singular witnesses do not make proof, as in the laws cited below: because where the proof of some universal that has successive parts is at issue, diversity in time and in the parts of the whole does not vitiate it. It vitiates it only when that which is unfolded in a single continuous context must be proved; for then diversity in time implies diversity of facts, and then the witnesses are truly singular. For example, if the proof of a will is at issue, and one witness says that it was executed on Monday, another that it was on Tuesday; for either those witnesses are false, or they depose concerning different wills, and thus they ought not to make proof, since each deposes concerning one single will. But where they depose concerning something successive having distinct parts and diverse in time, the diversity does not vitiate, because it does not imply diversity of fact with respect to the whole that hangs to be proved: an example is in proving possession. For if one deposes that Titius possessed for five years, and another speaks of five years, possession of ten years seems to be proved, because they depose upon the same possession. This seems to be the mind of the gloss in l. ob carmen, §. fina., ff. de testibus. And some cite there for the present l. quidam, C. de hæred. To the same effect is what Iacob. Butr. notes in l. ecclesia, C. eod., where he says,

† that if I wish to prove someone a heretic, it suffices for one witness to say that he heard him say that he did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, and another that he said he did not believe Christ to be the Son of God. So it seems should be said in the present case, since the proof of a specific contract is not at issue. Rather, in this universal—that the deceased was a usurer—diversity in time and in the contracts of the usurer cannot vitiate the testimony. To this opinion three examples can be adduced which Innocen. sets forth in capitu. qualiter & quando 2, de accusat.: when the proof of common fame, or of jurisdiction, or of the collection of tithes is at issue, it is not necessary for the witnesses to agree in time; rather, it suffices that they agree on the whole, namely that he is infamous, or that he exercised jurisdiction, or that he collected tithes, because they agree sufficiently on that which it is incumbent to prove. But notwithstanding these points, I consider that the contrary opinion prevails as to our case. And first, I am moved because the said clemen. una does not claim a place for itself in our case. For it founds itself upon the usurious quality; for it says that usurers are to be compelled, etc. Therefore, it must first be established that the deceased was a usurer: because where a disposition of law founds itself upon some quality, it is necessary that it first be proved as the foundation of the disposition; this is sufficiently proved from those things that are read and noted in cap. 1, de offic. deleg., lib. 6, and capit. accusatus, §. sanè, de hæred., eod. lib. 6, and what is noted in clem. una, de sequestra., in the final gloss, and more fully and elegantly touched upon by Barto., joined with the gloss and text in l. 1, ff. quod ui aut clam; especially since that Clementine introduces something new deviating from the common rules of law. For no one ought to be compelled to exhibit his books that he kept privately in his house for the maintenance of his household, as noted in the said clem. una, in the gloss on the word "rationum"; it is otherwise if he kept books in public, as do those manifest usurers, to whom there seems to be a tacit mandate to write, and thus must the text and what Bar. notes there in l. quædam, in prin., ff. de eden., be understood. Whence that cle. una, in §. cæterum, emanated solely out of hatred for usurers, so that thus secret usurers, or those who keep private books, might be compelled by a new provision to produce their books. Therefore, it must be established that the deceased was a usurer. Which certainly in our case has not been proved by those singular witnesses. And first, I will adduce the authorities that I find on the matter. Secondly, the general laws. Thirdly, sufficiently urgent reasons. Fede. de Sen., who conducted himself most subtly in his consilia, openly holds this in our precise terms in consilio 62, where he says that someone is not proved to have been a usurer by singular witnesses, especially when they depose about their own deed, just as in our case, since similarity excludes from testimony, as in capitu. personas, de testibus.

† Likewise, and even more strongly, he himself confirms this in consilio 17, where he further says that an episcopal statute is invalid which provides that someone may be proved a usurer by four singular witnesses, since this is contrary to law, which a bishop cannot decree, according to what is noted in capitu. super his, de maior. & obedien., and 25. quæstio. 2. capitu. institutionis, and capitu. igitur, fully by Ioan. And. in capitu. fina. de offic. archid. Dominus Anton. de Butr., having rejected the opinion of Iacob. Butr., holds this opinion on our precise terms after many arguments in capitu. cum oportet, de accus., where among other things relevant to the issue he says that sometimes a diversity is given in the causes of the statements, which relate to the matter to be proved as divisible parts of a whole, and the witnesses do not make proof. Whence, if one witness says "I know that he prescribed, because I saw him possess", he does not make proof. Sometimes the parts relate as indivisible parts of the same whole, and they do make proof, as if I wish to prove a Mass, and I produce two witnesses, one of whom says he heard the Epistle, the other the Gospel; and on this there is the notable gloss in capitu. nihilominus, 4. quæstio. 9. The same holds, according to him, if the parts are divisible, yet each relates to the whole, as if I wish to prove a tithe, and one says that he saw me receive the tithe of wheat, another the tithe of barley; or if I wish to prove jurisdiction by one witness that I exercised a certain jurisdictional act, and by another I prove the exercise of another act, and thus he saves the examples of Innocen. in the said capitu. qualiter & quando. If, however, the causes do not relate as parts implying the whole, but as causes multiplying the same whole in species, they do not make proof according to him. For example, if I wish to prove someone a saint; for it does not suffice that some depose concerning one miracle, and others concerning another, as Archidia. notably says in capitu. nouit, 25. quæst. 5, which is contrary to that statement of Iacob. Butr., through which he infers on our precise terms that if one deposes that Titius is a usurer because he lent to Caius, the witnesses do not prove him a usurer. And it should be noted that through the example he considers this to hold even if the witnesses were not deposing concerning their own deed; it is otherwise, he says, if I wish to prove someone a notorious usurer, and one says he heard it from others than the other does, because this diversity does not obstruct proving fame, according to what is noted by Innocen. in the said capitu. qualiter, and capitu. cum oporteat, and by Barto. in l. de minore, §. tormenta, ff. de quæstio. The singular gloss in the said capitu. nihilominus, 3. quæst. 9, seems to want this same opinion, namely that in our case singular witnesses do not make proof; which gloss seems to give the rule that singular witnesses never make proof, even if they are brought to prove a universal or a whole, unless when the fact was successive and indivisible, and the witnesses depose upon indivisible elements of the whole: an example in the proof of a Mass, if one deposes concerning the Epistle and the others concerning the Gospel. It is otherwise if they depose upon divisible things, as if one speaks of the Gospel and the other of Vespers, or if I wish to prove the payment of a tithe, and one says wheat was paid and the other beans; and thus that gloss which speaks of the proof of jurisdiction or a tithe clearly holds that they do not prove someone a usurer when they depose upon divisible acts, nor is the fact indivisible or successive. Pet. and Cyn. after him seem openly to hold this same thing in l. 2, C. quæ sit long. consuetu., where they say that to prove custom, and thus something universal or a whole, it is not sufficient for witnesses to depose upon diverse acts from which the custom is induced, unless they are co-witnesses who saw those acts together, which Arch. seems sufficiently to approve in a similar case in the said c. nimirum. Innoc. seems to approve this same opinion in cap. licet ex quadam, de testi. For although he first gathers an argument there that if I wish to prove that I used jurisdiction or some servitude, and one speaks of one act and another of another, they do make proof, nevertheless immediately thereafter he says he believes it is safer to say that each witness heard from the same two persons and at the same time; otherwise they will be singular in their statements. For they falsely cite supra de elect. capitul. cum dilectis; and he says that it is noted concerning this in the said capitul. qualiter & quando. And thus Innocen. stands on the latter opinion, that in proving some whole that has divisible parts successively, singular witnesses do not make proof, although some wrongfully cite Innocent. for the contrary opinion. And it should be noted that by that statement his statement in the said capitul. qualiter & quando is clarified. And thus Innocent. stands on the latter opinion. For Innocent. does not say there simply, as some wrongfully cite, that in proving jurisdiction or the payment of a tithe witnesses deposing singularly concerning diverse acts suffice; on the contrary, he first put forward that statement, and immediately put forward the contrary opinion, saying that others speak against him, asserting that wherever one might be bound to prove something, unless the witnesses agree on place, time, persons, and all other things, they are not held as multiple witnesses (he cites the said capitul. nihilominus), and that they are altogether singular in their testimonies (he cites the said capitul. cum dilecti). Whence those authors hold, as he reports, that even in proving fame witnesses ought to agree, so that they say, "on such a day we heard such rumor or infamy, and in such a place, and from such persons." Innocent. impugns that latter opinion in another way, and Ioann. Andr. passes over it there simply, reciting almost according to the context. But by the statements in the said capitul. licet, Innocent. seems to approve this latter opinion as safer, and an urgent reason, which I will subjoin below, supports him. Specul. also in two places notes on the gloss of Innocent. in the said capitul. qualiter, reporting singularly the contrary opinions, as I have said above, and approves neither, as is evident in titu. de testib., §. iam de interrogatorijs, versi. item de tempore, and in titu. de inquisi., §. nunc verum, quòd si negauerit; indeed, he recites there the opinion of Vicen. in cap. illud de præscrip., which says that if one witness deposes concerning fame in one part of the city and another concerning another part, fame is not sufficiently proved, because the witnesses are singular. The glossa ordinaria in the said cap. licet ex quadam seems to approve this opinion, which says that in proving consanguinity it is not sufficient that some depose on one side and others on the other. And thus, far more strongly, it does not want it to suffice if each witness was singular in his statement. And let these suffice with respect to authorities. Now I prove it by introducing the laws. And first, many laws speaking generally, without distinguishing between a successive act and a momentary one, say that singular witnesses do not make proof, as in the said c. nihilominus, and c. tam literis, de testib., and capitul. cum dilecti, de elect., and capitul. bonę [memoriæ] ii, de elect., versi. licet, with similar texts; nor is any text found that proves the contrary opinion. Rather, it was the bare interpretation of certain men, who often destroy the text by their own headstrong opinions; and against them militates singularly that c. cum dilecti. For there the canons wished to prove that they had not consented to that person elected by the compromissaries, and each deposed that he had not consented, nor was multiplicity of an act inferred thereby; and nevertheless the Pope says there that they do not make proof, because they are singular, since each deposes concerning his own consent, which is openly contrary to the mind of the gloss in the said l. ob carmen, §. 1. To the same effect is the said c. bonæ, where the canons wished to prove that they had not been summoned; nor does it avail if each says that he was not summoned; and yet they come to prove that universal proposition, that the chapter had not been summoned; nor is a chapter constituted except of each and every one being unaware, by argument of what the gloss notes in c. si capitulo, de conces. præb., lib. 6.

† I prove it lastly by an effective reason: in every matter upon which witnesses depose, the witnesses are always singular with respect to the sense by which the act is perceived. For if you and I saw Titius strike Sempronius, you perceived it through your sense, and I through mine, and your sense is not mine, nor vice versa. To this is what Bartol. notes in l. 2, ff. quemadmo. test. aper. Whence, when it is required in this respect that they be co-witnesses, namely with respect to the object upon which they depose, they must be co-witnesses if they presented themselves at the same time to the senses of the witnesses themselves; whence an approach to the sense made at the same time makes them be co-witnesses, and this is clear to anyone subtly considering this matter. For what reason, moreover, it is required that they be co-witnesses in this, and thus that they perceived together at the same time, is certainly for no other reason than because one witness is not believed to the prejudice of another, as in the common laws. But when they agree together in all things, that rule of divine and human law has place: "In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand", in the said capitul. licet vniuersis, and 2. quęstio. 4, in princip. Moreover, this reason has place even when the proof of something in general is at issue, if the witnesses depose upon diverse acts. For how can it be concluded in our case that Titius was a usurer, unless each witness is believed by himself deposing upon one contract? And thus it is necessary to say, holding the contrary opinion, that one witness is believed, which is contrary to the laws cited above. And if you should say, if the article is general, that he was a usurer, and the witnesses depose upon this universal proposition in which all seem to agree, I answer that they are not concordant in the rendering of the cause. Whence they must also be co-witnesses in the particular act by which they are moved to depose upon the universal. For they do not perceive that usurer through their sense, but only those particular acts upon which they depose; moreover, witnesses are permitted to depose concerning those things that were done in their presence, as in capitul. testes, 3. quęstio. 9, and l. testium, C. eod.; and in the act of prescription through sense it is required that the witnesses were present together, as in the said capit. nihilominus. Wherefore I hold with the singular gloss of that capitul. nihilominus, so that we say that regularly witnesses do not make proof unless they saw that upon which they depose together at the same time, unless the fact is successive and indivisible, and they depose upon indivisible parts of the whole: an example is in the proof of a Mass, or when through a hole one immediately after the other the witnesses saw certain persons committing adultery, as noted there by Cyn. in the said l. testium. Nor is there any text that says the contrary. l. quidam, C. de hęre., which some cite, does not stand in the way, because it proves nothing; nor is even the gloss in the said l. 1, ob carmen proved by law, nor do the doctors in the said law simply approve it, and Barto. himself reports it in the said l. ob carmen; and on our precise terms there are several contrary authorities, as is clear from the preceding. And let these things suffice, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The word "lawsuit" comprehends every action, both in rem and in personam.
2. That is said to be able to be done which is according to law.
3. The word "goods" comprehends actions in itself.
4. The intention of the contracting parties is regarded more in contracts than the words.
casus: A certain Lord Antonius, the brother of a certain woman, namely Lady Petra, a widow, spontaneously and of certain knowledge constituted a certain dowry for his said sister when she entered upon second nuptials; for the safeguard and security of the second husband receiving the dowry from the said Lord Antonius, the father of the said woman promised the said husband by a solemn stipulation under a certain penalty to keep him and his heirs indemnified from every claim, lawsuit, and controversy that could be moved, or might be moved at any time, by the children of the first marriage, or in their name, both on the occasion of the dowry, and generally of all goods that could pertain to the children of the first marriage, or in their name, both on the occasion of the dowry and on the occasion of the said Lady Petra, their mother. It happened that the said woman died, leaving children of the first and second marriage. Then the son of the second marriage died, and a lawsuit is commenced against the second husband by the children of the first marriage on the occasion of their mother, saying that they ought to succeed equally together with the son of the second marriage. It is asked whether the second husband is bound to restore to the said children of the first marriage a part of the dowry, according to what the statute of the city provides? Does the said husband have recourse, or can he have it, against the father of the said woman on the occasion of the aforementioned stipulation, especially since the father himself spontaneously swore to have and hold all and singular the aforesaid things firm and ratified forever, and in no way to act or go against them by himself or another, de iure or de facto, in court or out of court, for any reason, device, right, manner, or cause?
body: Having sought the aid of Christ and of His most pious Mother, it appears at first that in the prescribed case no right belongs to the said second husband against the father of the said Lady Petra; for he promised to keep the said husband and his heirs indemnified from every claim, etc., and thus so that they would be without loss. But loss is properly a diminution of patrimony, as in l. 3, ff. de dam. infect. Yet in our case the patrimony of the said second husband is not diminished, since succession belongs by law to the children of the first marriage, namely in the maternal goods proportionately, as in l. cum aliis, C. de secund. nuptiis. Therefore the said stipulation is not incurred. For that which is done by law merits no penalty, l. Gracchus, C. de adult. and 22. quaestio. 4. capitulum qui peccat, and no one does an injury who exercises his own right, l. 1. §. denique, ff. de aqua plu. arcen. Furthermore, the said stipulation is invalidated on another ground: namely, because he could not promise the act of another, as in l. stipulatio ista, in principio, ff. de verbo. obliga. and Institu. de inutil. stipul. §. si quis alienum. But the said father promised the act of the children of the first marriage; therefore the stipulation was not valid. But notwithstanding these points, I consider that the contrary opinion must prevail. I am moved first by the text that as it were expressly decides this case, joined with the gloss in the said l. stipulatio ista. §. sed quatenus, and the following §. hi qui; and it is maintained there that if I stipulate that it be permitted to me to hold a certain thing under a certain penalty, the stipulation is incurred whether that thing is evicted from me by law or de facto: because, as the text there says, one is not permitted to hold if something has diminished from him out of the right that he had. So in the matter at hand, this second husband cannot be said to be indemnified if a part of the dowry is taken away from him or from his son, however much it may be taken away by law through the children of the first marriage; and what is found in the said l. stipulatio ista. §. quaesitum supports this, where it is expressly said that even concerning another's property that stipulation—to be permitted to hold—is valid, provided a penalty is added below, as in our case. For let us imagine that Titius donates another’s property to me, and promises to keep me indemnified from every lawsuit, and controversy, etc.; who doubts that, however much it may be evicted from me by law, Titius is bound to me for the interest, according to what is held and noted in l. 1, C. de euict. and l. Aristo, ff. de dona.? Whence, although this agreement may not be valid to the prejudice of the child of the first marriage, l. si unus, ff. de pactis, because it is an act done between others, l. 1, C. de transact. and capitulum inter dilectos, de fide instrumen., nevertheless it prejudices the father himself who promised indemnity, so that at least the penalty attached to the stipulation is incurred, as in the said §. quaesitum, and §. 1. Secondly, in the principal matter, the words of the aforesaid stipulation are strongly persuasive because they are very general, inasmuch as indemnity was promised from every claim of suit and controversy that could be brought or might be brought, etc.; wherefore one weighs first those general words, 'from every claim and controversy', as much in law as in fact. For whoever says 'every' excludes nothing, as in cap. solitae, de maio. & obed. and 19. dist. capitulum Ramanorum; and c. Caynaldus, de test. strongly supports this, where a penalty added by agreement is incurred, although he may be sued lawfully. Second, that word 'lawsuit' etc. supports this.

† For the noun 'lawsuit' (lis) encompasses every action, both in rem and in personam, as in l. litis nomen, ff. de verbo. sig.; and an action is a right, Insti. de actio. in principio. Therefore, by this word he promised to keep this husband indemnified from every legal action to be brought against him by the children of the first marriage, whether in rem or in personam. Likewise, weigh those words, 'which could be brought or might be brought', etc. For those words 'might be brought' ring of fact; but those 'which could be brought' ring of law, which is clear from the word 'could' (posset).

† For that is said to be able to be done which is done by law, as in c. faciat. 22. q. 2. and l. filius, ff. de condi. insti. Beyond those words, therefore, he intended to keep him indemnified, whether the children of the first marriage should sue him by law or in fact. Thirdly, in the principal matter, this opinion appears to be proved by that general clause added in the stipulation, namely: 'And generally on the occasion of all goods which could pertain to the children of the first marriage on the occasion of the said Lady Petra', etc. Whence first I weigh the words, 'of all goods'.

† For the word 'goods' is extremely general, including within itself even actions, as in l. bonorum, ff. de verbo. signifi. Likewise, weigh those words, 'which could pertain', etc. For they are not said to be able to pertain unless they pertained by law, which that word 'could' (possent) denotes, according to the things said above. And thus it is most clearly inferred that also with respect to a claim in court he willed to keep him indemnified. Furthermore, those general words that follow support this, namely, 'on the occasion of the said Lady Petra', etc. For it cannot be denied that they claim part of the dowries on the occasion of their mother, dict. l. cum aliis, C. de secund. nupt.; therefore there is room for the stipulation. Fourthly, the form of the oath of the said promisor affords a great argument for the aforesaid things in that he swore not to contravene the said promise by law or in fact, by any reason, scheme, right, manner, or cause, etc. By which words we can sufficiently argue with respect to the preceding words that he wished to bind himself for indemnity with respect to the claim of the children of the first marriage, whether it be claimed by law or in fact. For preceding general words are explained by the subsequent ones, in l. si seruus plurium, ff. de legat. 1. and l. qui filiabus, and l. si cui dulci. ff. de vi. tri. & oleo lega. and in capitulum sede with the notes there, de rescript. Fifthly, in the principal matter, I advance such an argument:

† In contracts the intention of the contracting parties is to be looked to more than the words, as in l. in conditionibus, ff. de conditio. & demonstratio.; and this intention is indeed elicited from conjectures, so that an intention about which there is certainty through conjectures is said to be evident, as the text remarkably implies in l. licet, ff. de lega. 1. But if we wish carefully to conjecture the intentions of the contracting parties, the said security or promise was made for no other cause than that the dowry assigned to the second husband might remain in its entirety with the children of the second marriage. For on account of the children of the first marriage, who succeed equally with the children of the second in the dowry, as in the said l. cum aliis, widows will rarely find a husband with the same dowry, since they cannot transfer the intact dowry to the children of the second marriage. Hence it is that this promise was made solely with respect to the children of the first marriage concerning the dowry assigned by the brother, who is deemed to donate by the very fact that he does not stipulate that the dowry be returned to him, l. vnica. §. in extraneis, C. de rei vxo. act. For the children could bring no action during the lifetime of their mother, but only upon her death, since children have no legitimate claim during the lifetime of their parents, l. 1. §. fin. ff. de colla. bono., Barto. in authen. ingressi, C. sac. sanct. ecclesi., and l. 1. §. nec castrense, ff. de colla. bono. Security was therefore taken with respect to the claim that they could lawfully bring after the death of the mother, as well by the common law as by the rigor of the statute. And that this is true is clear beyond the aforesaid points. For if the husband had only wished to look ahead [to a claim in fact] and not by law, he would have received the promise generally with respect to anyone who brings a question against him; but here he restricts himself to the children of the first marriage, which cannot be said to be for any other reason than because they could succeed by law together with the children of the second marriage. And it strongly supports the aforesaid that he promised to keep indemnified not only the husband, but also his heirs. From which it is inferred that even after the cause of the dowry had ended, the said promise of maintaining indemnity endured; whence it seems to have been tacitly agreed that the entire dowry should remain with the children of the second marriage, and that which is tacitly agreed is held as expressed, l. cum quid, ff. si certum peta. That word 'whenever' placed in that promise also greatly assists this understanding, by which word it is inferred that Antonius was to be kept indemnified even from a claim to be made after the death of the said Lady Petra, especially joining those words, 'on the occasion of the said Lady Petra'. l. quae dotis causa, with its subject matter, ff. solut. matrimo., supports the aforesaid by way of argument. From all these things I conclude, the aforesaid conditions standing, that the said second husband has recourse against the said father, the promisor, for that part which he had to restore to the children of the first marriage, so that in this and in other respects there is room for the said stipulation. And through the aforesaid things the response to the contrary arguments framed above is sufficiently clear. For the patrimony of that husband would be sufficiently diminished—since by agreement the entire dowry ought to remain with him—if a part were evicted from him. Nor does it stand in the way that he promised the act of another, both because a penalty was attached, in which case the stipulation is valid, as in the said legal authorities, and because he promised his own act rather than another's, namely, undertaking the suit upon himself and keeping him indemnified. And let these things suffice, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A woman is so subject to her husband that she is presumed to have been summoned by him.
2. Whether a simple extrajudicial renunciation prejudices.
3. An arbitrator ought to examine the dispute diligently.
4. A statute deviating from the common law ought to be restricted as far as possible.
body: In the present question there are two principal doubts. First, whether the said arbitral award was null. Second, presupposing its nullity, whether this exception of nullity ought to be admitted against the petition for execution, notwithstanding the said statute by which the exception and defense of nullity seem entirely prohibited. And concerning both I shall proceed in a highly conclusive manner, since the matter has been sufficiently weighed by the first consulting counsel. For it seems to me that the said award is null ipso iure on two grounds: on the side of the woman, and from the path entered into on the part of the husband. In favor of the woman there first militates the authentic. Si qua mulier, C. ad Velleian. For according to the interpretation which Odofred. places there, in whatever way husband and wife contract in the same instrument, the wife is not bound ipso iure unless the money is proved to have been converted to the benefit of the woman herself, as is stated there at the end. The reason is that, in doubt, the woman is always presumed to have been brought in to intervene for her husband.
† For the woman is so subject to the husband that she is presumed to have been summoned by the husband himself. Nor is it an obstacle

† that the woman herself might be said to have renounced by the third preceding argument, both because a simple extrajudicial renunciation does not prejudice the woman herself, as Bartol. notes on l. generaliter, C. eodem titul., and because in the case of that authentic a renunciation is not valid, even if a judgment were rendered, as the text and note state there; and it is a special rule in the case of that authentic when she truly or presumptively intervenes for her husband in the same instrument. And it militates in favor of both, namely the wife and the husband, that the said arbitrators did not resolve the whole question, and thus they do not appear to have pronounced an award, as is the text in l. dicere and l. non distinguemus, §. quaesitum, ff. de arbit.; for an arbitrator ought to pronounce in such a way that the entire dispute is departed from; otherwise the sentence is not valid, as in the laws cited above. And there is a good gloss on said l. dicere. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the submission was made to the consuls of the wool guild, both present and future, because this must be understood to mean that if the present ones did not decide within the term, their successors could arbitrate, but it ought not to be understood that they might decide in part, contrary to l. in hoc iudicio, with what is there noted, ff. famil. erciscun., and by Innocen. in capitu. cum inter, de re iudic.; or that they might deliver an uncertain award, contrary to 5. quaestio. 6. capitu. ei qui, §. diffinitiva, and by Innocen., capitu. cum venerabilis, de exceptio., on the word "autem". For a sentence is not valid that is not certain in itself or does not have reference to an act, as Innocen. notes there, and more fully by Joan. Andr. in addit. Specu., in titu. de senten. prola., §. qualiter, verse "sed pone iudex". And this seems to be proved in l. 4, C. de senten. quae sine cer. quantita.

† For an arbitrator must diligently discuss the dispute and impose a final end to the controversy, as in l. si de meis, §. recepisse, ff. de arbit. From all of which it is clear enough what must be said on the first doubt. Concerning the second, which seems more doubtful—whether, notwithstanding the statute, this exception of nullity ought to be admitted—the theory of Bart. on l. prima, ff. quod vi aut clam, strongly supports this, where he says among other things that if a statute removes all exception and defense, there is no remedy except for the party to pay and afterwards claim restitution, if he has a just cause for raising an exception and, because of the statute's prohibition, was not admitted; unless he wishes to raise an exception by removing that quality upon which the statute is founded. As, for example, if it says that against a public instrument no exception or defense may be admitted, I can raise the exception that the instrument is not public; or if it says that against an arbitral award no exception may be admitted, they can raise the exception that those persons were not arbitrators, as the gloss in clemen. unica, de sequest. properly speaks in this case, which says that if an exception cannot be opposed against a sentence, I may oppose the defect of jurisdiction; the reason is that if he did not have jurisdiction, it cannot be called a sentence, de re iudica. clemen. pastoralis, and noted in l. 2, C. communia utriusque iud.; and thus through this exception the quality upon which the statutory provision is founded is removed. But in our case this cannot be said, since they were arbitrators, nor through this exception of nullity does it cease to be an award of arbitrators; and capitu. ex parte. 2, de offic. delega., together with the gloss, seems to speak excellently to this, where it is held that if in a legal provision exceptions are expressly removed, they cannot be opposed even if they are reasonable. But these points notwithstanding, I think the contrary must be said in our case on two grounds. First, because when exceptions are removed generally, a notoriously legitimate exception does not appear to be removed, since no mention is made in the statute of the quality of notoriety. This is excellently proved by analogy in the said cle. pastoralis, de ap., joined with c. ex conquestione, in its gloss, de res. spo.; for it is said in c. pastoralis that by the clause "appeal being removed" all appeal is removed which is not expressly granted by law, and yet if one is notoriously aggrieved, although that case is not expressly determined by law, an appeal is admitted, as in the said c. ex conquestione, with the gloss. And this the doctors commonly hold there. To the same effect serves c. inter caetera, de re iu., and what is noted in cle. pastoralis, cited above, in the gloss on the word "non habebat". This same point I prove secondly by his own theory on l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iure, and l. non dubium, C. de legi., where he says that there is a legitimate cause for restricting a generally worded statute when someone would suffer loss unduly, l. adigere, §. quamvis, ff. de iure patronat., or when someone is unjustly admitted to a gain, as in l. ut gradatim, ff. de mu. & hono.; cap. abbate, de verbor. significatio makes for this; or if, in the case of restriction, the rationale that moved the legislator ceases, as in the said §. quamvis; capitu. cum dilectus, de consuet., and l. 2, C. de nox. support the aforesaid. But in our case, not merely one of these reasons, but all of them militate. For if this exception of nullity is not admitted, this husband and wife would unduly suffer loss, and these creditors would obtain an unjust gain, as is clear from what follows. Likewise, given the said notoriety of the exception, the general rationale of the statute ceases. For no rationale could have moved the legislator to remove exceptions except that there is fear of malice and fraud on the part of those raising objections, seeking to delay the trial: an excellent argument in said capitu. ex parte. But this rationale ceases when the exception is notorious, an argument from 8. distinct. cap. veritate manifesta. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that no rationale is expressed in the statute, because it is lawful to conjecture the rationale that could have moved the lawmaker, etc., and according to that conjecture it is lawful to restrict or amplify the statute, as Cyn. and others note on said l. non dubium; what the gloss notes on 1. distinct. capitul. consuetudo makes for this. Likewise, a statute deviating from the common law must be restricted as much as possible, so that it may impair the common law as little as it can, as is notably proved in the said capitul. cum dilectus, and said l. 2, C. de noxa. And that this exception is notorious is evident, because it is clearly gathered from the acts; and that which is apparent from the acts can be called notorious, as is the text in capitu. cum olim, de verbo. significa., and the lords of the Rota note in decisio. 439, and Innocen. notes in cap. ex insinuatione, de appell. Under the second head they ought also to be admitted, because the statute removes exceptions against an arbitral award, but it cannot be called an award when the controversy is not decided, but a referral is made to others, as is proved in said l. non distinguemus, §. quaesitum. I say, therefore, that this exception removes the quality upon which the statute is founded, and consequently it ought to be admitted, as in said l. 1 and what is there noted, quod vi aut clam, and by the gloss on said l. una, de sequestra. And let these things suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A prelate can donate modest amounts from the property of the church.
2. A bishop has bare administration of the property of the bishopric.
casus: CASE. A certain Lord Bartholomaeus, formerly bishop of Massa, solemnly granted to certain persons, by title of lease for nine years then next following under an annual rent of 125 florins, a certain fortress of his episcopal right together with the houses and other appurtenances of the said fortress, with this being specifically and solemnly agreed between the said parties among other matters, namely that the lessees themselves are bound, during the said term of the lease, to maintain the said fortress and its houses at their own expense in the condition in which they were, or in a better one, and, the said term of the lease having ended, to restore them to the aforesaid bishopric. It happened that through the carelessness, negligence, or inadvertence of the lessees themselves, the houses of the said fortress partly fell into ruin, to such an extent that the bishopric suffered damage of nearly 200 florins. Finally, the term of the said lease having ended, the aforesaid bishop of Massa, at the excessive insistence of the lessees, freely and gratuitously absolved and released them from every obligation; and upon this bishop having departed this life, his successor in the bishopric seeks that the damage be made good, alleging that the said release is null. It is asked, what is the law? And because the case does not seem to contain great doubt, I shall proceed briefly.
