body: The aid of Christ and of His Mother having been humbly invoked, it seems to me quite clearly that the said release was not valid to the prejudice of the bishopric. For to remit gratuitously is the same as to donate, l. quin etiam, ff. de calum. and c. ueniens, li. 1, joined with the gloss, de testi. But a bishop cannot donate the rights and revenues of his church without legitimate cause; and if this should happen, such a donation is revoked, as is proved in c. si quos, and in c. de seruis, 12, q. 2, and in c. fraternitatem, de dona., where it says that a bishop is the procurator of ecclesiastical property, and not the owner; therefore he can make the condition of the church better, but ought not to make it worse, as the text there says. Secondly, to the same effect makes c. caeterum, de dona., where it is held,

† that a prelate can donate modest amounts from the property of the church, if custom holds this, as if he could not make a great donation, even if custom so holds, because a custom that is greatly injurious to churches is not valid, as in c. 1, de consuetu. But in our case, having weighed the loss and the revenues of that same bishopric, the donation appears quite immense, especially since from it the church remains ruined and without hope of repair; therefore the said release was not valid. Thirdly, it seems to be proved by c. episcopus, in which it is clear,

† that a bishop has bare administration of the property of the bishopric, and he cannot dispose of movable or immovable property, or of revenues, at his pleasure: but according to God; if he acts otherwise, he incurs damnation; to the same effect, 1, q. 3, c. peruenit. Fourthly, it is proved by an argument from a specific case in c. episcopus, and c. bonae, 12, q. 2, and in c. apostolicae, de donationi., in which laws it is granted by special privilege to a bishop that, by building a monastery anew, or magnifying a church for his own burial, he may give a hundredth, or a fiftieth part of the revenues of his church: with this limitation, however, that he does not inflict grave damage upon his church thereby; whence if he inflicts grave damage from this, it is not valid by law, even in those privileged cases, as is noted there. But in our case, not only are we outside the said special cases: but also damage was inflicted on the church from that gratuitous release, regard being had to the slightness of the revenues of the said bishopric, and to the damage inflicted on the said fortress, or its houses. Fifthly, it makes for this that whenever anyone has free administration, he does not thereby acquire the power of donating, or of making a gratuitous agreement, as in l. contra iuris, ff. de pac., and l. filius, ff. de dona., and l. praeses, C. de transac., and c. fraternitatem, de dona.; although, therefore, a bishop is said to have free administration in the property of the bishopric, as in c. cum nobis, in fi., de elect., he could not, however, to the prejudice of the church make a release gratuitously, as in the laws previously cited. And to this makes exceedingly well what Hostiensis and Johannes Andreae note in c. 1, de postu., where they say that by sheer law it is not permitted to a prelate to renounce gratuitously a useful defense belonging to the church, as above, de pac. l. contra iuris, C. de transac. l. praeses. To the same effect, C. de pact. l. pactum curatoris, and ff. pro emp. l. si quis fundum, § si tutor, with similar passages, in which it is clear that a tutor, or curator, or administrator of a city, and the like, however much they have free administration, cannot gratuitously remit a right of a ward, or of a minor, or of a city; this is clear and indubitable. Nor is it an obstacle if you should say that a prelate, especially a bishop, has greater administration than the aforesaid have, as is clear from the gloss noted in 5, q. 3, c. si, and by Innocent in c. ueniens, de rescrip. For I confess this to be true, yet not so much greater that he can donate at pleasure, or remit rights of the church or of the bishopric with grave damage, as is proved in the laws cited above, and by Innocent in the said c. ueniens, and c. accedentibus; and these things suffice. NICOLAUS ABBAS.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A husband and wife can make new agreements different from those that were made regarding the primary dowry for an augment of dowry.
2. A woman cannot augment the dowry unless the husband augments the donation propter nuptias by an equal increase.
3. A woman having property, if she marries, is deemed tacitly to give all her property as dowry.
body: Having prayed for the aid of Almighty God, I elicit three doubts presented to me. First, whether under the standing statute providing that a husband gains half of the dowry, Nicolaus son of Ioannes Martini of the district of Anghiari, surviving his late wife Lady Angela, ought to gain half of the one hundred and fifty florins which he confessed he had received as an augment of the dowry of the said Lady Angela from ser Leonardo di Pietro, the father of the said Lady Angela. The second doubt, whether Nicolaus gains half of certain properties of the said Lady Angela, which he says were assigned to him as dowry and of which the said Nicolaus had the administration during the life of the said Lady Angela, although it cannot be expressly proven by an instrument or witnesses that the said properties were given as dowry; indeed, the son of the said Lady Angela from another marriage, succeeding to his said mother intestate, asserts that those were the paraphernal goods of his mother. The third doubt, since the said Nicolaus bought certain goods from the said Leonardo for himself, and for the said Lady Angela his wife, and their heirs, whether Antonius son of Dominicus Laudi of Anghiari, the son of the said Lady Angela by another husband, ought to succeed his said mother in half of those goods in the aforesaid manner. And let this proceed conclusively upon these doubts, since counsel is requested by arbitrators jointly chosen by the parties regarding the positions to be adopted by them. Regarding the first, I say:

† that in an augment of dowry, husband and wife can make new agreements different from those that were made regarding the primary dowry, as is the text in l. si constante, C. de do. ante nupt.; and if nothing was newly agreed, one stands by the prior agreements and conventions, so that the statutes and agreements concerning the dowry apply to the augment of the dowry, since the augment is part of the dowry, and one and the same matter ought not to be judged under different law; supporting this is the good text in c. cognouimus, 12, q. 2; and this opinion on our precise terms is held by the Gloss and Cy. in the said l. si constante, and an express text is seen in l. inter socerum, § cum inter, at the end, ff. de pac. dota. And so I conclude that if that augmentation of dowry had been valid, the said Nicolaus would gain half of that augment, since new agreements did not intervene. But you may say that that augmentation of dowry is not valid, because although by law either party could augment the dowry or the donation propter nuptias on either side, as in the said l. si constante, yet today under the law of the Authentics

† a woman cannot augment her dowry unless the husband augments the donation propter nuptias by an equal increase, lest the woman be deceived, as is the text in auth. sed iam necesse, C. de dona. ante nupt., and in the body from which it is taken, it is contained more broadly, in Auth. de aequa. dot. § 2. I therefore conclude regarding this first point, that if the said Nicolaus equally augmented the donation propter nuptias, he gains half of the augment, just as half of the dowry. But if he did not give an increase, he will gain nothing from the augment, because it was not valid to the prejudice of the woman. I come to the second doubt, in which I say briefly that the said Nicolaus gains a half share of those properties, because when no other assignment of dowry appears, it is to be presumed that those properties were assigned to him as dowry; this I prove in multiple ways. First,

† because if a woman possessing goods marries, she is seen tacitly to give all her goods as dowry, as noted by the Gloss in l. mulier bona, ff. de iure dotium. Bart. follows this, and more clearly and extensively in l. si constante, ff. solut. mat. Likewise, since the father of the said Lady Angela after the fact confesses a dowry, as was said above, he therefore previously constituted a dowry for her, because there could not be an augment of dowry without a dowry, arg. in c. cum Marthae, de cele. missa, and c. ad dissoluendum, de despon. impu., and l. decem, ff. de uerb. ob. Therefore, in doubt, we ought to presume that those goods were given as dowry, both because the husband had the administration of them, and because they had been given to the first husband, as is gathered from his will, and a father ought not to diminish the dowry of a daughter entering a second marriage, as in auth. sed quamuis, C. de rei ux. act. Thence it ought to be presumed that he gave those goods to him as dowry, because when someone is bound by law to an act, and that act is found to have been done, it is presumed to have been done by him who was bound to this by law, as in l. 2, C. de alim. pupil. praestan., and in l. cum seruum, ff. de uer. ob., and as noted by Bar.; and this concerning the second point. Regarding the third and last point, I say that the said Antonius, if he wishes to succeed to half of those goods bought by the said Nicolaus in the aforesaid manner, ought to contribute half of the price to the said Nicolaus, because in doubt, since Nicolaus alone then bought for himself, his wife, and their heirs, he is presumed to have bought with his own money, and to have managed the business of his wife and the heirs in this. If therefore the wife or the heirs wish to ratify the said purchase, they ought to pay half; this seems to be proved in l. 3, C. pro soc., and Bart. expressly holds this there, and takes the same view in l. si patruus, C. communia utriusque iud., and in l. quae dotis, ff. so. ma.; l. si ego, and l. penult., ff. de ne. gest. support this. For a donation ought not to be presumed, as in the aforesaid laws; nor indeed would it have been valid between husband and wife while marriage lasted, ff. de don. inter ui. & ux. throughout, and in c. si., of the same title. Furthermore, it does not appear from the instruments that the wife paid part of the price from her own assets; and this concerning the third point. From all the aforesaid, I say that the role of the arbitrators in this case is that they should pronounce that the said Nicolaus ought not to gain anything from the augment of the dowry, unless, as I said, it were proved that he equally augmented the donation propter nuptias. Likewise, that he ought to gain part of those properties, as dotal. Moreover, that the said Antonius ought to pay half of the price of those bought goods, if he wishes to have half of them by ratifying the purchase made by the said Nicolaus. And let these things suffice. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A blind man is prohibited from aspiring to a new magistracy, yet he can retain one already begun.
2. A blind man can succeed a father who is a baron or holds another jurisdiction, even though such a dignity cannot be conferred upon him anew.
3. An election is made by citizens to duties which one necessarily undertakes; by it alone a right is acquired for one who is absent and unaware, even against his will.
4. One nominated to an office must appeal immediately; otherwise he cannot refuse it.
casus: Nicolaus, son of messer Spinellus de Picolominibus, being sound in all his senses, was nominated, elected, and placed into the electoral pouch for the office of the priors. In the course of time, however, he was by misfortune deprived of both eyes, and lacking this sense at the time of the drawing, he was chosen for a certain office of podestà. He indeed accepted this magistracy. But it was objected by some that he was disqualified for this magistracy by reason of the defect. It is asked what is the law.
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of Christ and of his mother: It seems at first that the said Nicolaus would be disqualified, and thus not to be admitted to the said office of the podestà, by the express text in l. 1, §. casum, ff. de postu., where after many points it is concluded

† that a blind man is prohibited from aspiring to a new magistracy; but he can retain one already begun; but the aforesaid Nicolaus had not begun to administer the said office of the podestà before his blindness; therefore he must be accounted disqualified for it. To the same effect, secondly, makes the gloss in l. cæcus, ff. de iud., which says that that law is to be understood when a blind man was not already a judge beforehand; then he is not prohibited from performing the office of a judge; otherwise if he was not before, as in our case. For by election alone one does not attain a dignity, but acceptance and entry upon office are required, as seems to be proved in l. pupillus, ff. de con di. & demon. and l. ex eo, ff. de milit. testa., and in both places by Bartolus, especially in the said l. ex eo; there is the gloss in l. priuatorum, C. de iurisd. omn. iud., which says that by election alone one obtains the right of dignity, though not the administration. Thirdly makes c. nulli, de elect. in Sexto, where it is clear that after an election even the electors can raise a supervening defect; and thus capacity at the time of election does not suffice unless it is also present at the time of confirmation or acceptance. But these notwithstanding, I think the contrary proceeds according to law. I am moved principally by the text in the said l. 1, §. casu, de postula., where the text says that one is prohibited from aspiring to a new magistracy, which words, if well weighed, clearly prove that the said Nicolaus is capable. For first it says ‘to a new’, etc.; but it cannot be called a new magistracy, since he was elected and placed into the electoral pouch long before his blindness, by argument in c. consuluit, de iudi. Likewise, one must weigh the word ‘to aspire’, which clearly intends to repel this defect at the outset of the appointment; but in our case it cannot be said that a blind man aspired to this magistracy, since he had already been declared at a time when he had all his senses intact. Secondly, to the same effect makes what Bartolus noted in the previously cited l. cæcus, where he says

† that a blind man can succeed his father who is a baron or who holds another jurisdiction, even though such a dignity could not be conferred upon him anew, as if it suffices that he was capable at the time when he had the hope of succeeding; whence supervening blindness does not deprive him of that hope; yet there is an argument that a son, during the father's lifetime, has no administration in the father's goods, nor any right of claiming the legitim, but only a hope, as in l. 1, §. impuberem, ff. de col. bo., noted by Bartolus in l. 1, §. nec castrense, and auth. ingressi, C. de sacros. eccle.; what is read and noted in §. sed sui, Inst. de hære. quali. & diffe. also supports this. Whence supervening blindness not only deprives one of administration already held, but also of a hope acquired before the blindness. But in our case, through election and being placed in the ballot-bag, a stronger right than a bare hope was acquired by the said Nicolaus; because through election the right of dignity is acquired, even if not its exercise, as says the notable gloss in the said l. priuatorum, although it is wrongly criticized by Bartolus in the said l. ex eo; for the opinion of that gloss is held by the notable gloss in the Decretum, dist. 63, c. quanto, and the Doctors in c. transmissam, de ele.; and especially this is indubitable in the case where after election no other confirmation is required, as in our case, in which case Bartolus's objection ceases, as he himself meant in l. absenti, ff. de dona., where he saves the gloss that he wrongly criticized in the said l. ex eo. For in the case of the elected person himself, he says in the said l. absenti, where

† an election to public duties is made by citizens, which duties one necessarily undergoes, from that election alone a right is acquired by an absent and ignorant person, even against his will, as in l. illud, with the following law, ff. de tu. & cu. da. ab his; although the right of administering is not acquired except after he is decreed to that office, by the argument in l. fi. C. arbi. tu.; nor against his will can another be appointed to that office, C. quando arb. tu. throughout, according to him in the said l. absenti. Since therefore this office is of such a nature, and no other confirmation is required, immediately a right was acquired by the said Nicolaus, that is, at the time of the election and appointment; therefore blindness does not have to deprive him of a right already acquired, since it cannot be called a new magistracy, as in the said §. casum and the said l. cæcus. To the same effect also is c. cum percussio, 7, q. 1, and de cle. ægro. c. 1, where it is said that a supervening disability ought not to deprive one of a right already acquired, even in ecclesiastical dignities, lest affliction be added to the afflicted and anyone be thus deprived of their right without fault of their own, contrary to c. satis peruersum, 7. di., since pity should rather be shown to the blind, and assistance given to them by way of gift, as in c. licet, de censi. Furthermore, the text makes for this in l. qui ad scribendum, and l. qui ad ciuilia, C. de ap., where it is said

† that he who is nominated to any office must appeal immediately; otherwise he cannot refuse it, as if a right is immediately acquired by him such that he can no longer appeal; therefore he cannot be deprived of it by supervening blindness either; and on this is the text in the said l. cæcus, where it is simply said that a blind man performs the office of judging. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that, since a judge must deliver a sentence in writing in person, as in l. 1 & fi., C. de sen. ex peri. reci. and c. fi., de re iudi. in Sexto, but a blind man cannot read, therefore etc.; because even though he cannot deliver it in person, he will nevertheless be able to deliver it through his vicar; for the podestà is among the higher magistrates, who can deliver a sentence through another, as the gloss and Bartolus note in the said l. fi. And Bartolus says this concerning a blind man in the said l. cæcus; for unlettered men are also taken into these offices, who deliver sentences through others, as in l. certi, C. de iud. Likewise, a supervening necessity operates to this effect, by reason of which many things otherwise prohibited are permitted, as in de cleri. ægr. throughout, and l. si longius, ff. de iud. The other counter-arguments framed above do not stand in the way, for the answer is clear enough through the aforesaid points; for they proceed when a right was not yet acquired at the time of the supervening blindness; but here full right was acquired, and only the exercise was lacking, since in our case neither confirmation, nor acceptance, nor entry is required, but a right is acquired even by an unwilling person, since this is a public duty which the person elected is necessarily bound to undergo, as I said above. And let these things suffice. I conclude, therefore, that the said Nicolaus, although he is now found to be blind, ought not to be deprived of the said office of the podestà, since at the time of the election and placement in the ballot-bag he did not suffer from this defect. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument: 1. The hope of marriage ought not to be violated.
casus: The case is as follows. A certain Franciscus Tucii, having a blood sister named Lena, promised by private writing to give her as a bride to a certain Ioannes. And to this they agreed on 5 April 1425. Then on the following 5 May, for the greater validity of the thing promised, Leonardus and Ioannes, maternal uncles of the said Lena, promised by public instrument to the said Ioannes under a certain obligation that they would bring it about and see to it that the said Lena would contract marriage by words of the present tense with the said Ioannes, who received from him the same obligation of contracting marriage with the said Lena. When these things had been concluded, Franciscus, the brother of the said Lena, wishing to begin to fulfill the promise made by him to the said Ioannes of contracting marriage with the said Lena, caused a certain quantity of money to be given to the said Ioannes in two banks as part of the future dowry. After this, the said Ioannes sent certain jewelry according to the custom of the region to the said Lena as his betrothed, all of which she received as his betrothed, and there was also public talk among the people that she was the betrothed of the said Ioannes; and the said Ioannes very frequently visited her as his betrothed, both in the house of the father of the said Lena and in certain other places to which the said Lena was invited as his betrothed. Finally, a date for contracting marriage de praesenti was very frequently set by the aforesaid parties, but it was always missed because of the said Ioannes, who, alleging fictitious and feigned occasions, always delayed contracting, being shamefully enamored of a certain low woman whom he kept in the place of a concubine for no short time, and is said to keep even today. Provoked by all these things, the said Lena, seeing herself thus spurned by the said Ioannes, refuses to have him as a betrothed and wishes to contract marriage with another and to depart from the said Ioannes, who now resists and says that he is ready to contract marriage with the said Lena. Now it happens in law that several points are doubted. And first, whether betrothals de futuro were contracted between the said Lena and the said Ioannes, since the said Lena never expressly consented to the said Ioannes. Second, presupposing the bond of betrothal, whether the said Lena may lawfully withdraw from the said contract of betrothals and be joined in marriage to another. Third, whether the said quantity of money paid as part of the dowry by the said Franciscus can be reclaimed from the said Ioannes, seeing that the said Lena refuses to contract marriage with him. Fourth, whether the said Leonardus and Ioannes, maternal uncles of the said Lena, and Franciscus, her blood brother, remain in any way bound to the said Ioannes by force of the said promises, since it does not rest with them that marriage does not follow between him and the said Lena, but solely with Lena herself, etc. It is asked, what is the law?
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of Christ and His mother, I shall address each of the doubtful points in the order written above. And first, regarding the first point, setting aside all superfluity, it must be said here that betrothals de futuro were contracted between the said Giovanni and the said Lena. For although a brother, or an uncle, or indeed not even parents are able to bind an unwilling or unknowing woman to contracting marriage, but the free consent of the woman herself is necessarily required, as is proved in cap. uno. in fi. de desponsa. impube. lib. sexto, and 32. quæst. 2. c. ubi non est consensus, and noted in cap. 1. de despon. impu., which is supported by cap. si annum. de iudic. lib. 6; nevertheless, if kinsmen make a promise in the name of an absent woman, and she, afterwards being informed, consented expressly or tacitly—such as by receiving jewelry as a betrothed woman, or if the betrothed man turns aside to the house of the woman herself as a betrothed man—the said betrothals are sufficiently validated from that moment, and this seems clearly proved in cap. literas. joined with the gloss, de despon. impube., and more expressly in cap. 1. de matrimo. contracto contra interd. ecc. in glo. in uer. tanquam in uiris. in fine; and Ioan. And. very clearly holds this in cap. unico. de desponsa. impube. lib. 6. upon the gloss in his Novella, saying that between parents and other kinsmen there is this difference: because children are bound by the contract of their parents if they are present and do not contradict, whence presence alone is held for consent, and thus the text properly speaks in the said cap. uno; but in the contract of other kinsmen presence alone does not suffice, but it is required that the woman, being informed of the betrothals contracted by them, consent tacitly in the aforesaid manners or similar ones, as in the laws cited above. And that which is noted in cap. sicut. de spon. supports this; for consent alone suffices to contract betrothals or marriage, 27. q. 2. cap. sufficiat, and de sponsa. c. cum locum, nor does it matter in whatever manner it is had, provided it is established, according to what is noted in c. tuæ. and c. cum apud. de spon. Since, therefore, it sufficiently appears from those things that were stated in the narrative concerning the consent of the said lady Lena, wishing the betrothals made by her blood brother and uncles to be ratified, I would say that betrothals de futuro were contracted between the said Giovanni and Lena. I come therefore to the second point, namely, whether the said lady Lena can at least withdraw with impunity from the said betrothals, the betrothed Giovanni being unwilling and resisting? And it seems at first that she cannot, by the clear text in cap. præterea. and cap. requisiuit. and c. ex literis. with many similar chapters, de sponsa., in which laws it is evident that the said Lena can be compelled by the ecclesiastical judge to contract marriage de præsenti. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said Giovanni delayed the completion of the said marriage for a long time through his own fault. For the said Lena is not thereby freed from the contract of betrothals. For she ought at least to have waited for the said Giovanni for a period of two years; upon the lapse of which she could freely have coupled herself to another, whereas before she cannot do this without fraud, as is expressly proved in l. 2. C. de sponsa. and there fully by Cyn.; nay rather, it is not said there that the betrothals are entirely dissolved by the lapse of two years through the fault of the betrothed man, but that if the woman has married another, it is seen as being without fraud, because she did not suffer her wish to be mocked for so long a time by the man; but in our case, before the lapse of two years, the said Giovanni wished to contract with the said Lena, nor did it stall through him, but through the said Lena. Indeed, as he says, it could be maintained that even after the two years have elapsed she is bound to contract with him, if the betrothed man wishes to complete the marriage while matters are intact, since the ground of the said l. 2 then ceases, nor can she take from the lapse of the said time a just excuse for contracting with another; l. mancipiorum, ff. de opti. leg. makes an argument for this. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that a day was often set for contracting the marriage, and it failed through the said Giovanni, whence it would seem that the said Lena was freed from her promise, as in c. sicut, de spon. noted by Ioan. And. in c. de illis, under the same title. For surely that text and Io. And. speak of when he was bound from the beginning with respect to a certain day. But in our case the betrothals were from the beginning contracted unconditionally, although afterwards they agreed simply upon a day for contracting the marriage; for by this agreement they did not restrict the obligation previously contracted unconditionally, as is sufficiently gathered from the text of the said l. 2. in fi., where it considers that the wishes of the woman were often mocked by the betrothed man, and the text in the said c. sicut clearly intimates this, while it requires the fixing of a term at the time of the contract of the betrothals; l. Celsus, ff. de arbi. and c. cum dilecti, de do. & contu. support the aforesaid. But notwithstanding these points, on another ground I say that the said lady Lena is in no way bound to contract marriage with the said Giovanni, but can freely withdraw from the said betrothals and contract marriage with whatever man she prefers, through the clear text, to which no answer can be made, in c. quemadmodum, de iureiu., where it is said that even if betrothals were sworn to, nevertheless if one of the betrothed parties afterwards did not practice continence and was sexually active contrary to the law of betrothal, the other is not bound to complete the marriage, because for this cause a person already married can be divorced, and therefore a fortiori one yet to be married, because, as the text says there, it is more shameful to cast out than not to admit, etc. Nor does the oath stand in the way, because the condition is understood: if the other party has not sinned contrary to the law of betrothal, or unless something else worse should happen, such as if one of the spouses should become a leper, or lose a nose, or something similar, as is said there.

† For just as it is not permissible to violate a marriage lustfully, so it is not permissible to violate the hope of marriage, as in l. si uxor. §. diuus, ff. de adult. and de iniu. l. apud Labeonem §. sponsum. and noted in the said c. quemadmodum, in glo. in uer. non admittere. But in our case it is presupposed that the said Giovanni, after the contract of betrothals, lustfully fell in love with a certain low woman, and kept her for no small time as a concubine, and mocked his said betrothed at various times by postponing the contract; therefore the said lady Lena can lawfully and with impunity withdraw from those betrothals, even if they had been sworn to, and contract with whatever man she prefers. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said c. quemadmodum speaks of a betrothed woman fornicating, and not of a male, because I say that in this matter the reasoning is the same regarding a betrothed man fornicating, as is openly proved in c. apostolus, 32. q. 7; what is read and noted in capitu. 1. ut lit. non contest. supports this. For as to these matters they are not judged unequally, de diuor. capitu. gaudemus, and 32. q. 6; what is read and noted in capitu. 1. 2. 3. 4. and the end supports this; and this as to the second doubtful point. Concerning the third point, whether the money delivered by way of dowry can be recovered from the said Giovanni, the said Lena refusing to contract marriage with him for the said cause, I say it is certain that it can, because it was delivered for a cause, namely of contracting marriage, which not having followed, it can be recovered, as in l. si mulier, and l. si extraneus, with the following law, and l. quod Seruius, ff. de condi. cau. da. and l. si ego, and l. licet. §. quoties, with similar laws, de iure dot., in which laws it is commonly said that if a woman, or another on behalf of a woman, gave something to a future husband by way of dowry, it can be recovered if the nuptials do not follow; and most clearly in our case Bar. holds this in the said l. quod Seruius, where he says that it is not necessary that the woman first marry another, but it suffices that she has renounced the betrothals in order for recovery to be made, and the end of that l. quod Seruius sufficiently intimates this. But I turn now to the question: by whom must this recovery be made, whether by the said Francesco, the brother of the said Lena, who paid the money, or by the said Lena, in consideration of whom it was paid? And in this I say it must be considered that either the said Francesco paid out of his own funds, and then he himself has an action in his own name, because although a brother, or any other person who does not have the woman under parental power, by giving a dowry is considered to donate it to the woman unless he stipulated that the dowry be returned to him, as in l. una. §. accedit, and §. extraneum, C. de rei uxo., this is true, however, when the nuptials have followed; but when they have not followed, the payor himself has the recovery, as if the cause did not follow, as in l. si ego, and l. licet, §. quoties, ff. de iur. dot. and in the previously cited l. si extraneus, according to one reading which Barto. expressly approves there; or the said Francesco paid out of the woman's goods, and then the lady Lena herself, if she approves this, at least tacitly, will be able to recover it, on the argument of l. qui se debere, ff. de condi. cau. da. and l. penul. ff. de nego. gest., where there is a good text and it seems to prove that even if the woman was unaware, nevertheless, by now ratifying the act of her brother, she will be able to recover the money. But the question is: is Francesco seen as having paid out of his own funds with the intention of making a gift, or rather out of the woman's goods? In which I say that in case of doubt it must be presumed to be out of the woman's goods; but it would be otherwise if he had not administered them, as noted by the gloss and Barto. in l. fine. C. de dot. promissi; what is read and noted in l. Nesennius, ff. de nego. gest. and l. alimenta, C. under the same title, where in a similar case Barto. agrees, supports this; and this proceeds especially with regard to the statute of this city of Siena, by which it is provided that a woman dowered by her brother has no recourse against the paternal estate, whence the said Francesco seems to have wished to free himself from this burden, and not to deliver from his own funds, on the argument of those things which are read and noted in l. 2. C. de ali. pup. præstan. and better in l. si cum dotem. §. si pater, ff. solu. matri. From all of which I conclude that both the lady herself will be able to recover by approving the payment made by her brother, or Francesco himself can recover if she does not approve it, since she is not compelled in this to ratify the act of her brother; what is read and noted in the said l. qui se debere, joined with the gloss in the verse nomen te, de cond. cau. data, strongly supports this; and this concerning the third point. I come down to the fourth and last point, namely, whether the said Leonardo, and Francesco, and Giovanni remain bound in anything to the said Giovanni from the said promise; and I say briefly that they do not: both because the contract of betrothals between the contracting parties themselves contained a tacit condition, namely if the other party did not sin against the law of betrothals, as in the said c. quemadmodum, de iureiur. and as I have said more extensively there, so that when one sins, the other is released from all obligation; and a fortiori the same must be said regarding those who promised accessorily to induce that lady Lena through the contract, since an accessory stipulation takes on the nature of that to which it is accessory, as in l. si eum. §. quæ iniuriarum, and what is noted there, ff. si quis cau., just as in a similar matter l. quòd relicta says that legacies left by an instituted heir are seen as repeated by a substitute heir, l. licet, ff. de leg. 1. and l. non iustam, C. ad Trebel. Furthermore, one who abandons an agreement for a just cause is not seen to act against a promise, even a sworn one, as in l. qui iurato, ff. qui satisd. cog. and 22. q. 2. c. ne quis, and c. beatus. But the aforesaid cause of lust with another woman gives the power of withdrawing from the obligation of contracting marriage, as in the said c. quemadmodum, and c. apostolus. 32. q. 7; therefore the aforesaid persons are not seen to have acted against the obligation, especially because, since the said Giovanni by his own fault gave cause for this repudiation, the promisors are nevertheless seen to have fulfilled their promise, since through the said Giovanni it failed to take effect, on the argument in l. iure ciuili, and l. Iulianus. ff. de condi. & demon. and in reg. imputari ei non debet, de regu. iur. lib. 6. Furthermore, on another consideration the aforesaid are not bound to any penalty promised: because since marriage ought to be free, a penal obligation is not valid between the betrothed themselves, or their parents, as in c. Gemma, de spons. and l. Titia. ff. de uerbo. oblig. And the same applies to related persons, when the girl would probably not incur a penalty, or the male would be induced to contract: because the same reason seems to apply that exists in the case of parents, on the argument in l. hæres meus, in fi. ff. de cond. inde.; Io. An. holds the same in the said c. Gemma, in fi. and Bar. in l. Titia, in prin. And whatever the case may be, nevertheless in our case it is most certain that the said Giovanni can claim nothing, since he by his own fault provided the cause for this repudiation, on the argument of c. si. de iniu. & dam. dato. And let these things suffice. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The low amount of the price provides a strong argument for the simulation of a contract.
2. Although by civil law repairs fall upon the lessor, nevertheless by special pact they can pertain to the lessee.
casus: The state of the facts is as follows. A certain Massitarius bought a small house by public instrument from a certain compater of his for the price of 25 florins purely and absolutely, and the said seller gave the buyer power to enter possession at will; in the meantime he constituted himself as possessing precariously from the said buyer. Finally, the sale having been perfected on the same day and hour, the said seller leased the said house from the same buyer for the price of two florins under title of lease, with an added pact that the lessee should repair the said house at his own expense during the time of the lease. Later the buyer dies, and in his will he disposed, among other things, by title of legacy, that if the said seller should give to his heirs throughout the entire month then current 25 florins, which he had paid out for the price of the said house, the said house should be given to him, and that he should be held to give and pay nothing for past times on account of the rent of the house. Within this month the seller delayed fulfilling the condition; indeed, he or his heirs paid eight florins in the name of rent to the heirs of the said buyer. Most recently, a dispute is raised by the heirs of the said seller against the heirs of the buyer, saying that that contract was a contract of pledge and made in fraud of usury under the name of a sale, and in effect they raise four proofs of this fraud and simulation. First, that immediately after the sale the seller leased the house and remained in possession of it. Secondly, that it was sold for a low price. Thirdly, they say this is to be presumed from the addition of that pact, that the repair of the house should pertain to the lessee. Fourthly, because the aforesaid house was never assessed among the goods of the buyer according to the statutes and customs of that city, but remained in the tax roll of the seller himself, and he always bore the burdens for it. Lastly, the will of the said testator is adduced, who seems to have wished to discharge his conscience concerning the aforesaid by bequeathing in the aforesaid manner. Everything having been discussed, it is asked what the law is, etc.
body: Having invoked the aid of Almighty God. It seems firstly from the aforementioned that simulation is sufficiently proven. For since the seller was in possession, simulation is presumed, as in l. sicut, § supervacuum, and what is noted there, ff. quibus mod. pig. vel hypo. sol., where Bartolus says that the presumption of simulation is not excluded even though the seller declares that he possesses in the name of the buyer. For actual and corporeal possession is required according to him. Likewise,

† secondly, the low amount of the price affords a strong argument of simulation, as in c. ad nostram, de emp. & ven.; what the gloss notes in c. conquestus, de usuris, supports this. Thirdly, the addition of that pact makes for it, namely that the repairs should pertain to the lessee. For it is of the nature of a lease that the repairs pertain to the lessor himself, as in l. si merces, ff. locat.; therefore such pacts induce a presumption of fraud, as in the said cap. ad nostram, and what is noted there. Fourthly, the presumption arising from that tender and disposition of the testator makes for it. But notwithstanding these points, I think that solely from the aforesaid the said contract ought not to be judged to be simulated. I am moved firstly by the form of the sale itself, which appears defective in no part; for one must stand by the form of the contract until the contrary is proved, as in c. in civitate, de usur., and c. Ioannes, de fide instru., de praescrip. c. ad audientiam, and l. cum precibus, de proba. Let us examine, however, whether the aforesaid conjectures are sufficient. First, indeed, it is no obstacle that the seller leased the house in the very same instrument. For this is not disapproved by law, but rather expressly permitted, in l. quaedam mulier, ff. de rei vend., where the text and Bartolus note this; on the contrary, the text there holds that by an act of lease of this kind possession is transferred to the lessor, and thus such an act is not only not disapproved, but to such an extent approved that possession is transferred through it to another; therefore, it does not induce a presumption of simulation, because what is done with the permission of the law is free from defect, l. Gracchus, C. de adult., and 23. q. 4. c. qui peccat. To the second point concerning the low amount of the price, I reply that that allegation is not true, as was verbally explained to me. Hence it is that the said house was afterward sold for the same price; and if indeed there was any deception in the price, it was very slight, which is not to be cared about, l. in causae, § in pretio, ff. de mino., and l. 2, C. de rescin. vendi., and c. cum dilecti, and c. pen., de emp. & vendi.

† The third point does not stand in the way, because although by the common law the burden of repair lies on the lessor himself, nevertheless by a special pact it can pertain to the lessee. For this is not contrary to the nature of the contract itself, but beyond it; whence such a pact is not disapproved by the law, but rather approved, l. qui insulam, § si, ff. locat. For pacts placed beyond the nature of a contract are valid, as in c. uno, de commo., and c. bona fides, de depo., and l. 1, ff. eo. tit. Hence the rule of law states that contracts are known to receive their law from agreement, as in reg. contractus, de reg. iu. in 6. Furthermore, a burden enjoined in a contract is seen as part of the price, as in l. fundi partem, ff. de contrahenda emp.; that burden could therefore be converted so as to take the place of part of the rent, especially since in the statement of facts it is proposed that the said house was leased for a modest rent. To the fourth point I say that that release does not relieve the heirs of the seller himself, because this arose solely from his own act; for this did not enter into the pact, and this act followed after the sale was perfected. The fifth point concerning the testament of the buyer does not stand in the way: because from it a conjecture of simulation of the contract cannot be gathered, since in no part of it did he say that the contract was one of pledge. On the contrary, he calls it and says that he paid out the price for that property; whence one rather gathers the contrary, since at the end of life one is not presumed to be unmindful of one's salvation, 1. q. 7. c. sancimus. For we see that someone sometimes bequests a release to his debtor, ff. de libe. leg. throughout; so this man could bequeath to that seller, who was his godfather, the rents owed for the past time. Likewise that he might have the opportunity of recovering that house, which he had perhaps sold out of necessity. For if it had been a usurious contract, he would not have bequeathed with a time limit of one month, and he would at least have remitted the rents unconditionally, which he does not do, but conditionally, if he paid 25 florins within a month. Nor is it novel that a legacy is made with some attached burden of making a payment, as in l. Lucius, and l. iure civili, with countless similar laws, ff. de condi. & demon. From all of which I conclude that in consideration of the premises, the said contract cannot be said to have been usurious. The contrary points alleged above do not stand in the way. For the § supervacuum speaks of when it was not evident that a sale had intervened; therefore, since he who says he sold is found in possession, he is presumed not to have sold, as is noted there. Likewise that text speaks when the prejudice of a third party is at issue, but here it is only a question of the prejudice of the contracting parties. Furthermore, as Bartolus says there, when the rent has been paid, every presumption of simulation ceases, especially since here it was paid for ten years. The other points have been sufficiently answered above. And let these things suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Acts done in a summary proceeding do not provide proof in a plenary proceeding.
2. Where the manner of proceeding varies from summary to plenary, the cumulation or reopening of the same matter is not prohibited.
3. A judgment rendered upon the whole does not impede a proceeding to act upon a part.
body: IN the name of the Lord, amen. Concerning the question pending between the lady Lucia, daughter of the late [N.], on the one part, and Angelo, a servant of the same land, on the other part, I shall touch upon nothing concerning the merits of the principal case, upon which judgment has already been rendered, since that was not entrusted to me; but I shall examine only whether a new trial could be instituted according to the form of the libel produced by the said lady Lucia, notwithstanding the judgment rendered against her and the appeal lodged from it. And the entire thrust of the question depends on this: whether the first and the second proceedings are so related that an absolutory judgment rendered in the first creates a plea of res judicata in the second. For if the appeal was admitted by the judge ad quem, as is alleged by the said lady Lucia, or if she tacitly renounced the appeal by approaching the judge a quo, the first judgment remained firm, de appel. c. personas, and c. cum sit Romana, cum tsi. If, however, the said appeal is said to be pending, the same question still arises, which must be examined, namely whether, while the first proceeding is pending, it can be cumulated. Secondly, it must be examined whether the first proceeding is such that an absolutory judgment rendered in it creates a plea of res judicata in the second. For when the first proceeding produces such an effect, the cumulation of a second is not permitted, being barred by an exception, as is proved in l. fundi, and l. fundum. ff. de except., more clearly in the matter of cumulation fully examined by the Glossa, Cynus, and Bartolus in l. edita, C. de eden., and by the Canonists in c. 2. de lib. obl. Let us therefore see whether the first proceeding is such that its absolutory judgment creates an exception of res judicata in the second newly instituted by the said lady Lucia. And it seems first that it does not: because that which is examined summarily is not
† prohibited from later being brought into court plenarily, as in l. pen. ff. de his qui sunt sui uel alie. iud.

† Hence it is that acts done in a summary proceeding do not provide full proof in a plenary one, as in c. ueniens, de test. What Innocent notes in c. 2. de ord. cog. near the end supports this, where he says that if I pleaded my dispossession as an exception against a plaintiff and was defeated, I can nevertheless bring that dispossession by way of accusation. Secondly, and principally, the notes of Bartolus in l. qui Romae. §. duo fratres. in verse 5. opp. de uerb. oblig. support this, where he says to the point that if a ruling is made upon an exception in a case where the examination was summary, res judicata is no bar if that same matter is later brought to court principally, by the argument of de re iudic. l. a diuo Pio. §. si super rebus. If, however, it is examined plenarily in the case, and then a ruling is made against the plaintiff, another accessory proceeding somewhat dependent on the first cannot be cumulated, in the said §. duo fratres. Or the other proceeding is more principal, or equally principal, and again it may be revived notwithstanding the exception of res judicata, as in l. sed si ante, de excep. But in our case the second proceeding is more principal, or equally principal, and the first was principal, and the second was summary; therefore it can preserve the exception of res judicata, or in judging, the appeal notwithstanding. To the same effect is
† what Antonio de Butrio notes in c. aduersario de excep., where he says

† that where the mode of proceeding varies from summary to plenary, the cumulation or renewal of the same matter is not prohibited, according to what is noted in l. 1. C. de condi. indeb. and in l. si quis a liberis, ff. de lib. agna. But notwithstanding these points, which in truth do not stand in the way in our case, as will clearly appear below, I consider that the contrary opinion must prevail, namely that that new proceeding cannot be cumulated by the said lady Lucia, being barred by an exception. First, I am moved by the indubitable rule of law that wherever at least three things concur in the second proceeding that concurred in the first, the exception of res judicata always stands: first, if the same body or the same quantity is sought; second, if the right or cause of action is the same; third, if the condition of the persons is the same; this is proved in l. cum quaerit, with the two following laws, ff. de exce. rei iud., and noted in the said c. aduersario. But in our case these three things are present in the second proceeding: because the same quantity is now sought that was sought in the first proceeding; the cause of action is the same, for she was seeking restitution of the dowry from the said Angelo as heir of his brother, and now she says the same thing; and it is the same cause, and the condition of the persons is the same. Therefore, the absolutory judgment rendered in the first creates the exception of res judicata in the second. Furthermore, and secondly, wherever the end of the action is entirely the same, it cannot be brought by way of exception, as is the noted text in l. duobus. ff. de excep. rei iudi. But in our case the end of the action in the second is entirely the same as was in the first. For the said lady Lucia intended nothing other, nor intends, in the first and second proceedings, than that the dowry should be restored to her by the said Angelo as the heir of her former husband; therefore, the joining or renewal of the second proceeding ought not to be admitted, and especially so in our case, where first it was pursued by way of action, and now the exact same thing is renewed. Also, and thirdly, the contrary would result in the same Lord Podestà being able to render a directly contrary judgment, revoking the first rendered by him, contrary to the letter and spirit of l. 1. C. senten. rescinde. non poss. Fourthly,

† because a judgment rendered upon the whole bars an action upon a part, and conversely, one rendered upon a part bars a renewal upon the whole, as in l. si quis cum totum. in the beginning and §. fin. ff. de excep. rei iudi.; all the more strongly, therefore, it ought to bar in our case, where the exact same thing is sought and the cause is the same. Fifthly and lastly, the elegant remarks of Innocent in c. suborta. de cau. poss. & proprie. are relevant, where he says further that if the parties take up an argument upon an issue raised incidentally or by way of cause, and prosecute it fully just as the principal matter itself, the judgment rendered upon the incidental issue creates the exception of res judicata just as if it had been principally litigated, which Antonio de Butrio follows more clearly to our purpose in the said c. aduersario. But in our case the parties not only took up a full argument upon the rights of the said lady Lucia, but the said lady Lucia also presented her entire right by way of choosing. For although she acted generally without naming the person, nevertheless, since the said Angelo thereafter appeared at the general citation and opposed the lady Lucia, and began to contest fully with her in court concerning the restitution of dowries, and judgment was solemnly rendered in favor of the said Angelo, absolving him from her claim, the said lady Lucia ought not to be able to repeat that same matter in effect against the said Angelo, or to cumulate it while an appeal is pending, assuming it is pending; since an absolutory judgment rendered in the first creates the exception of res judicata in the second. For it is an ordinary proceeding when someone appears upon a general citation, taking upon himself the regular proceeding, according to the notes by Innocent in c. 1. de ele. and Bartolus in l. si. ff. de quaestio. at the beginning and end. The arguments alleged above for the contrary party do not stand in the way. And first, to the penultimate law, the answer is that it speaks when something was brought into court not principally, but incidentally, and such an incidental matter was examined summarily with respect to proofs, as when alimony is sought from a son; for filiation is examined incidentally and summarily; then, notwithstanding the judgment rendered on alimony, the matter can be litigated principally regarding filiation, since it was not plenarily examined, but it would be otherwise if it had been fully examined, as the Glossa and Bartolus note there, and as is clear from what is noted in l. j. C. de ord. iud. But in our case the first proceeding was not incidental, but rather principal, nor was it summarily examined, but rather plenarily, so much so that recourse was had to the counsel of a jurist (consilium sapientis), and it was solemnly pronounced by the counsel of a jurist. Nor does c. ueniens stand in the way, because, as the text says there, the first action was for one thing, and the second for another. Likewise, in the beginning the proceeding was summary with respect to proofs, because he only had to prove that he had an interest in acting. But in our case the action is for the same thing in the first and the second, and each is plenary with respect to proofs, although the first was summary with respect to the mode of proceeding on account of the instrument of guarantee (guarentigia); but this is nothing to us, because by this privilege it ought not to be permitted to repeat the same thing in another proceeding contrary to all the rules of law. Nor does the saying of Innocent in c. 2 stand in the way, because he speaks when the dispossession is brought for a different effect in the second proceeding than in the first. For in the first it was brought to repel, in the second to obtain; and thus one of the three things I mentioned above is lacking, namely that the same cause of action or the same end does not exist. Nor do the notes by Bartolus and the said Antonio stand in the way, because they apply when a pronouncement was previously made upon an exception or upon an incidental matter proposed, as appears from the laws cited there, and thus it was not the end of the action. But in our case a pronouncement was made upon the direct petition of the lady Lucia herself, which in effect contained the same thing as the second petition. For she wanted nothing other in both the first and the second except that the dowry be restored to her by the heir of her husband, and a ruling was made against her for lack of proofs, as appears from the judgment to which reference is made. Likewise, Bartolus himself maintains in the said l. j. C. de ord. iud. that even if a pronouncement was made upon an exception, that cannot be brought by way of action if the end of the exception is entirely the same. Wherefore, from all the aforesaid, I conclude that this second proceeding cannot be instituted, whether the appeal was not admitted, or has lapsed, or is pending.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Parties can remit the oath to witnesses.
2. Under the appellation of books there do not come small private writings, or booklets, which merchants make for the security of a creditor.
3. The word "only" is taxative, and implies in itself a negative with respect to other proofs.
4. If witnesses add to an instrument, the instrument is not thereby said to be disproved.
casus: The factual contingency of the case is in effect this. A certain Master M. consigned certain sums of money to a certain moneychanger Esau for a share of lawful profit, and at various times caused other moneys to be assigned to that moneychanger in the aforesaid manner, and sometimes received some moneys therefrom. And concerning the said receipts, the said moneychanger, in addition to the book which he kept at the bank, wrote and made a certain codex or small book, which remained continuously in the possession of the said Master M., in which booklet it is also contained that an account had been taken between them at various times for certain periods, and the capital liquidated, and how the said moneychanger acknowledged that the said Master M. ought to have certain sums of money by reason of the profit accruing up to that time of the account taken; and this happened at various times. However, for four years before the death of the said Master M. it does not appear that any account was settled between them. Finally, shortly before his death, the said Master M. made his testament, in which among other things he disposed as follows, namely: "Likewise, the testator himself considering that he has had, and has to make, certain accounts and reckonings with Esau, etc., and trusting entirely in Esau himself, willed, declared, and mandated that concerning the said contracts and reckonings of accounts one should stand by and give credit to, and ought to stand by and give credit to, the proper book or books of the said Esau, etc." Finally, upon the death of the testator, the said Esau, in rendering the account, produces his books which he kept in his shop or house; in which, although the entire capital of the said Master M. and several other entries of reciprocal receipts and payments are contained, nevertheless of the entries or capital profits only two or three are contained, whereas in the booklet which he himself had written and which was preserved in the possession of the said Master M. far more are contained. Now it turns upon doubt whether one ought to stand by and give credit to the said books which the said Esau presently produces, in which not all the said entries of the said provisions and profits are written; or whether one ought rather to stand by and give credit to the said booklet written in the hand of Esau himself, which the said testator kept in his possession, in which booklet or private writing there appear, as I said above, accounts both calculated and settled up to the year of the Lord 1403 and 1404, so that up to the said times one ought to stand by the said booklet or private writing, and after the said years until the death of the testator, during which time it does not appear that an account was calculated, one ought to stand by the books which the said Esau newly produces and exhibits. It is asked, what is the law.
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of Christ and His mother, it seems first that one must abide by the books concerning the entire account which the said Esau shall produce, and not by that notebook which the said testator was keeping in his possession. For although one must stand by a private writing to the prejudice of the writer once it is established that it was drafted by his hand (l. rationes, and l. exemplo, and what is noted thereon in C. de probat., and l. scripturas, C. qui po. in pig. hab., per Barto. in l. nuda, ff. de dona., arg. l. quaedam, §. nummularios, ff. de eden., and l. admonendi, ff. de iureiu., and in authen. Et si contractus, C. de fid. instr., per the gloss and the doctors in c. 2, de fid. instr.), nevertheless, since the testator willed that faith be given to the proper books of Esau himself, one must stand by the disposition of the testator. For the testator could have disposed that one should stand by the simple word of Esau himself, as in l. Theopompus, and what is noted there, ff. de do. praele., because anyone is the lawful moderator and arbiter in his own property, l. In re manda., and in c. de his, de sepul.

† Hence it is that they can remit the oath to witnesses, as in c. tuis, de testa.; to which pertains what Barto. notes in a similar case in l. si, ff. de accep. For the last will is to be observed as law, 13, q. 2, c. ultima voluntas, as in authen. de nupt., §. disponat. Secondly, this is proved in multiple ways through the words of the said testator: for first he said, "trusting entirely," etc. And thus one must abide by his books not only in part, but even in the whole; which would not be observed if one were to stand in part by the notebook, or private writing. Secondly, he said that one should stand by the proper books of the said Esau. Whence I weigh the word "books," and the word "proper."

† For under the appellation of "books," at least from the common usage of speech, there do not come those small private writings, or booklets, which merchants commonly make for the security of a creditor, and those which merchants keep at the bank; to this effect is what is read and noted in l. librorum, in principio and in §. quod tamen Cassius, ff. de lega. 3, and l. Labeo, ff. de sup. leg. Furthermore, those are said to be proper books of which one has the ownership and disposes of them at will, l. Quintus, ff. de aur. & argen. lega., and l. 1, ff. de pecu.; to this pertains what is noted in c. 2 and in c. cum ad monasterium, de statu mona. But the said private writing, or booklet existing in the possession of the said testator, was not of this kind, since it belonged to the master himself. Therefore, the testator did not understand this booklet; and thus it seems that one must stand solely by the books of Esau himself. Thirdly, those words seem to constrain greatly: for since he said that one must stand by the books of Esau "only," he seems to have excluded other kinds of proving to the contrary.

† For the word "only" (tantum) is taxative, and implies within itself a negative with respect to other proofs, as in c. cum ecclesia Sutrina, de cau. possessio. & proprie., and there per Ioan. An. following Gotfre. on the verse tantum. Fourthly and principally, the theory of Iac. de Aret. in l. 1, C. si adver. lib. is relevant, where he says that if by statute one must abide by the word of someone denouncing, one must never depart from his statement through other proofs; but the word of the testator has the force of law in matters depending upon his will, as I said above. Therefore, since the testator willed that one must abide by the proper books of the said Esau, one must not depart from them through the said writing, especially a private one, which is proffered by the heirs. But notwithstanding these points, which if weighed correctly do not stand in the way, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer in law. And first, I am moved by the words of the aforesaid disposition, when the testator said that since he has certain accounts and calculations to settle with Esau, and "trusting," etc. From which words it is clearly gathered that he chose the faith of the said Esau and of his books with respect to accounts and calculations not yet made, in which trust and faith properly fall, but not with respect to those that are already discharged and finished, concerning which it was clearly established through Esau's own writing. Whence even a settlement (transactio) is impeded regarding them; to which l. eleganter, §. si quis post transactionem, ff. de condi. indebi., l. post rem iudicatam, de transact., and c. exposita, de arbi., with what is noted there, excellently apply. For we judge a disposition and its effect toward the limits of perfection, so much so that the words are even restricted so that they may conform to perfection, as in l. cum pater, §. dulcissimis, ff. de lega. 2, and l. fin., ff. de haered. insti. Let one stand, therefore, by the books of the said Esau with respect to that time in which no settled and balanced account appears. Secondly and principally, I introduce this reason: the testator willed that faith be given to the books of the said Esau. But in our case, no less faith is given to his books if, where something is missing in them, it is supplied by another writing, especially Esau's own. For this does not directly go against the faith of the said books, although sometimes certain things are omitted through forgetfulness, 23. distinct., c. praeterea; and in support of this is the notable gloss in c. cum Ioannes, de fide instrum., on the verse quodlibet instrumentum, in c. si., which says,

† that if witnesses add to an instrument, the instrument is not on that account said to be reproved. Hence we see that no less faith is given to the evangelists concerning the deeds of Christ, although one is supplied by another, as is read and noted in c. periculose, de verbo. signifi. Thirdly, I weigh those words of the testator, "trusting in the said Esau," etc., by which words it sufficiently appears that the testator did not intend through those words to make a legacy to him, but merely to choose his faith and fidelity. But through this and similar words, no matter how general, fraud (dolus) is never seen to be remitted, as in l. creditor, §. Lucius, ff. manda., and l. Lucius, de his quae in frau. credi. But in our case, the said Esau appears to be in fraud if he does not wish to stand by his own writing, since no one ought to be presumed so indolent, simple, and foolish as to write down a transaction, or money assigned for profit, that was not transacted or assigned, as the text remarkably states in a similar case: "it is exceedingly unjust that anyone should be ignorant of what he has protested in a clear voice," etc., as in c. per tuas, de probat., and l. generaliter, C. de non nume. pecu. Moreover, a writing produces greater faith than a confession, because one errs more easily in confessing impulsively than in writing, as Innocen. notes in c. cum olim, de censi., and c. cum venerabilis, de excep. Fourthly, I weigh those words, "his own proper books." By which words indeed the testator seems to have chosen the faith of Esau's writing rather than the physical volumes of the books. But the small book remaining in the possession of the testator himself can be called Esau's by reason of his handwriting, since instruments are often called true not by reason of the material, but of the contents within them, as noted in c. 1, de proba., and c. 1, de fide instrumen.; therefore, etc. Fifthly, I cite what is noted in c. continebatur, de despon. impu., joined with c. per tuas, de probat.: for although it is disposed by law that faith is to be given to a husband asserting his wife [to be of age], notwithstanding the contrary, as in said c. continebatur, and c. si quis uxorem, 32. q. 2, nevertheless the wife is heard when wishing to prove the contrary by the appearance of her body, as in said c. per tuas. So in the present matter: although the testator said that faith should be given to the books of Esau because he trusted in him, it does not therefore follow that the contrary cannot be proved, especially through Esau's own writing; which is especially to be maintained in our case, where that writing does not reject the book of Esau, but is rather supplied, as I said above. With this opinion Iac. But. and Bald. in said l. 1, C. si adver. rem iudi. seem to agree, where regarding that previously cited saying of Iac. de But. they say that although the statute says faith must be given to the words of the denouncer, nevertheless if it appears through other proofs that the denunciation is false, the judge ought not to believe him, arg. l. divus, ff. de fal. Sixthly, I cite the theory of Barto. in extravag. Ad reprim., on the verse legibus, where he remarkably says that if after a general law a special one emanated (an example in l. sciendum, ff. qui satisda. cog., joined with auth. Offeratur, C. de lit. cont.), the special does not abolish the general except insofar as it is expressed in it, unless it is said in the new law, "notwithstanding any law whatsoever which would conflict with this in whole or in part," arg. l. nam & posteriores, de legi., and l. praecipimus, in fi., C. de app. So it seems one must say in the present matter: for although the testator said that one must stand by the books of the said Esau, he did not by this intend to exclude the faith of Esau's own writing, especially since through it the books of Esau are supplemented, and they can be brought into harmony, so that over things settled and calculations made one stands by the books, but over other matters already balanced other proof may be adduced. And in favor of this interpretation is the theory of Bart. in l. non dubium, C. de legi., and l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iure, where he notably says that a sufficient and just cause for restricting a disposition is when, the words being so understood, one party would obtain a profit without legitimate cause and the other would suffer a loss, as in l. gradatim, ff. de muner. & honor., and l. 2, C. de noxa; ca. cum dilectus and what is noted there, de consuetud., and cap. abbate, de verborum significatio, apply excellently. From all of which I conclude that one must stand by the said small book or private writing of Esau himself regarding those entries and profits assigned to the said master M. concerning which nothing is said in the books of the said Esau, and generally in all things that supplement the books of the said Esau; the contrary arguments alleged above do not stand in the way. For to the first it is sufficiently clear that an answer has been given, since, as I said above, the will of the testator is no less preserved if a supplementation is made through another writing of Esau himself. To the second, I say that one sufficiently stands by his books in the whole, insofar as they are contained in them. Likewise, it does not take away proof through contrary evidence, as I said above. The word "proper" and the word "books" do not stand in the way, for the response is sufficiently clear from the aforesaid. To the third principal argument, which seems to press more regarding that word "only" (tantum), I say that that word operates to the effect that, whereas otherwise faith would not be given to the books of that Esau insofar as they concerned his own favor, but there would be need of another adminicle, as in l. exemplo, and l. rationes, C. de probatio., and per the gloss and Bartol. in said §. numularios, and in authen. Et si contractus, because of these words faith is extended even in his favor. The testator therefore willed through those words that faith be given to those books only, in the sense that other proof is not to be demanded from him. And equity securely supports this interpretation, lest he obtain a gain without cause, and lest he be admitted when wishing to go against his own writing, which all laws abhor: C. de non. numera. pecu., authen. Contra qui., and de fide instru., l. si cautio, and l. cum de indebito, ff. de probat.; and the other authorities introduced above also support this, for it is enough that those words effect something, even against ordinary law. Whence they ought not to be interpreted so broadly that many laws are injured, arg. opti. in l. si quando, C. de inoff. test., and l. 2, C. de noxa, and said cap. cum dilectus; or at least let them be understood as intending to exclude a private writing [of third parties], but not the writing of Esau himself through which his books are supplemented; or they can be understood as applying when proof to the contrary is not offered through the aforesaid. To the last, a sufficient answer has been given above in the fifth reason for the affirmative side. And let these things suffice. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument: 1. If a witness first said one thing out of court and says the contrary in court, even under oath, credit is not given to the second statement, but he ought to be punished for forgery. Whether the wife and sister of a guardian can be witnesses in a testamentary case?
casus: A certain man, afflicted with illness, made a testament, and having instituted his sons as heirs, disposed among other things as follows: "Likewise, he willed and commanded that the said heirs and their guardians be bound and ought to distribute and expend for the love of God, for the soul of the testator himself, that which shall be declared to them by Lady Mariana, his wife, whose conscience he burdened, since he related to her certain secrets of his soul, etc." Subsequently, upon the death of the testator, the said Lady Maria, his wife, seeking counsel in the forum of conscience from two most upright men, said that the said testator had charged her to cause a certain illegitimate daughter of his, who was staying at the hospital of Santa Maria, to be removed from the said hospital and nurtured in the house of the testator himself, and to be married with a dowry of 100 florins, the said Lady Mariana adding that nothing else had been enjoined upon her by the said testator. She said the same thing in substance on another occasion in the presence of two ladies, of whom one is the wife and the other is the sister of one of the guardians of the said sons, and a carnal brother of the said testator. Afterwards, when nearly three years had elapsed from the death of the said testator, the said Lady Mariana, disturbed and angered for certain reasons with the said guardian, went voluntarily to the vicar of the lord Bishop of Siena and asserted, an oath having first been administered to her, that the said testator had willed that 70 florins, which the father of the said testator had formerly wrongfully extorted from certain persons, should be restored by his heirs to those persons who are established in the books of the testator's father. Likewise, since the said testator during his lifetime had vowed to visit the church of Saint Anthony of Vienne and could not fulfill it, he willed that one person be sent at the expense of the heirs of the said testator. And she says that this will of the said testator had been declared to the same Lady Mariana. Finally, when the heat of ill will subsided, certain persons approached Lady Mariana, saying that they marvelled at the things she had said, [to which she replied] that if she could, she would revoke them. Now it is asked whether, on the basis of that confession thus made in the presence of the lord vicar, the heirs could be compelled to execute the things thus declared, notwithstanding the contrary confession made before and afterwards.
body: Having humbly invoked the protection of Jesus Christ and of His most pious Mother. It seems at first that one must abide by the declaration made in the presence of the lord vicar, concerning which the case seems clear, and as noted in l. Theopompus, ff. de dote praele., where it is evident that one must stand by the statement of the single person whom the testator chose for his trust and approved in this matter, and especially because she took an oath, according to the theoretical doctrine of Bartolus in the said l. Theopompus. Likewise, the first and last statement were without an oath, whereas the declaration made in the presence of the lord vicar was made under oath. But a sworn statement must be preferred to an unsworn statement, as in c. j. de consan. & affi.; l. iusiurandum, C. de testi., canonized in 4. q. 2. c. iusiurandi, supports this. Thirdly, since she is treated in this case in the place of a witness, inasmuch as she deposes concerning the intention of the testator, her statement was not valid without an oath, according to the opinion of Bartolus in the said l. Theopompus. But notwithstanding these points, I deem that the contrary opinion prevails. First, I am moved by the notable doctrine of Bartolus in l. eos, ff. de fal., where he says,

† that if a witness first said one thing outside of court, and afterwards says the contrary in court, even under oath, credit is not given to the second statement; indeed, he can be punished for forgery. Therefore, he himself advises one who fears the wavering of witnesses to have them interrogated beforehand outside of court, so that if they subsequently say the contrary in court, faith is not lent to them; and this opinion of Bartolus is followed by Antonius de Butrio in the chapter cum in tua dioecesi, de testi., in the last column. Following that dictum, this case would be decided. And although that dictum can be criticized to some degree, nevertheless, on account of many other factors concurring here, I think that, without distinction, the said lady Mariana is not to be believed. First, because while she was seeking counsel in secret, where all fear and desire to please a party ceased, she asserted the contrary, saying that it had merely been enjoined upon her that that girl should be rescued from the hospital, and so it was done. For no one is presumed to speak falsely when seeking counsel for his soul, because one is not presumed unmindful of his own salvation; 1. quaestio. 7. capitu. sancimus, and capitu. literas, de praesumptio., and cap. significavit, de homicid. And in such matters one stands by the statement of the priest, at least for the purpose of refuting a contrary confession, to which point the gloss and doctors note in the said capit. testimonium, de testi.; especially because the second statement arose out of anger, and thus it ought not to prejudice, as is the text with the gloss noted in capitu. literis, de divor.; and at the first time, when she seemed inflamed with zeal for God, as in the said capitu. literas, de praesump., where the very notable text implies that, through the said qualities, one should rather stand by the first unsworn statement, or at least the presumption of the second statement is removed by the first statement, so that one may simply stand by it. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that those who depose concerning the counsel of the soul are single witnesses, because they were not present together. For I say that, on account of the subject matter, she ought to be believed, since counsel is not given in public, according to what is noted in capitu. testimonium. Likewise, she asserted that very same thing in the presence of two women, who can perfectly well testify in a civil cause, as I have read and as is noted in capitu. forus, de verbo. signi., and 15. quaest. 3. capitu. ex eo.
