† Nor does it stand in the way that one is the wife, and the other the sister, of the guardian, because the cause is not that of the guardian, since the advantage or disadvantage does not pertain to him; 2. q. 6. capitu. biduum, at the verse palam. Likewise, a sister and a wife can be witnesses in a civil cause, even if it were their own, although perhaps less credit is given to her than to others, according to what is noted by the gloss and by Innocent in capitu. in literis, de test., and by the Speculator under the same title, §. 1, and by the gloss on 4. q. 5. capitu. 1; the text with the gloss in the said capitu. literas supports this, where it is evident that a brother can be a witness for a brother. But in our case there is no doubt, since the cause does not pertain to the husband, but to the sons of the said testator and of the said lady Mariana herself. Moreover, here is another very probable conjecture, in that, after the deposition made before the lord vicar, she said the opposite outside of court, agreeing with the earlier statement; wherefrom the statement before the lord vicar is weakened, so that it alone is not to be believed, which Antonius de Butrio clearly held in the said capitu. cum tua, in the last column, where he says that if a witness afterwards says outside of court the contrary of what he said in court, and sentence has not yet been rendered, one must not stand by his statement. Innocent seems to hold this same view notably in capitu. praeterea, de testi. cog. And in our case several factors concur here, because not only afterwards, but also beforehand on various occasions she said the opposite, and she went to the said vicar in a state of agitation. Likewise, because she is a woman, whose testimony is variable and changeable, as in capitu. forus, de verb. sig. Likewise, this same thing seems to be presumed from the quality of the statements. For to what purpose would he have said in secret that someone should be sent to visit the church of St. Anthony? Likewise, since he was not the sole heir of the father, to what purpose would he have burdened himself in solidum to make restitution for things unlawfully taken by his father, since he was not liable except for his hereditary portion; l. 2, C. de acqui. haere. But the first statement has verisimilitude, since it would be shameful for the said testator, who was a nobleman, to have left his daughter, albeit illegitimate, lying unknown at the hospital; rightly did he say this secretly to his wife, in whom he wished to confide; and where the statements are in doubt, the statement that is more probable is to be embraced, as in 4. quaest. 3. capitu. si testes omnes, noted by Innocent in capitu. auditis, de praescri.; the text in capitu. licet, de proba., supports this; and let these points suffice. Therefore, I conclude that one must stand by the earlier statement, which had execution, and not by what was asserted before the lord vicar, especially since deceit and inconsistency are condemned by the law, in cle. cum illusio, de regu. iur. The contrary arguments do not stand in the way; for they proceed when other factors do not concur to the contrary, as is evident from the aforesaid. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The property of churches is not bound to the burdens and levies of laymen, both under canon and under civil law.
2. Oblates of religious orders, who have dedicated themselves and their property, also enjoy in the property which they hold in the name of the monastery all the privileges of that religious order.
3. The serfs of churches are not bound to the burdens of laymen.
casus: A certain Andreas Petri and Ioanna his wife, of the city of Massa, offered, gave, and dedicated themselves and all their property and that of each of them, movable and self-moving, rights, actions, and claims in any way belonging to them and to each of them, to Almighty God, and to the order and convent of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine of Massa into the hands of the prior of the convent of the same place, who received them in the name of the entire convent and the aforesaid friars; the said Andreas and Ioanna retain certain of the aforesaid property, or perhaps all of it, receiving therefrom the support due to nature. It is now asked concerning the aforesaid property, whether it ought to pay collections and other burdens, just as the other laymen of the same city pay? And whether their persons can be burdened with the civic duties or burdens of the city, like the other citizens and inhabitants of that city, etc.
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of Christ and of His mother, I shall proceed succinctly and decisively, because the aforesaid matters do not seem to me to present great doubt. And first concerning the property, that it is entirely exempt from the burdens and levies of laymen.

† For it is certain that church property is not bound to these burdens, both under canon and under civil law, as is proved in c. non minus and c. aduersus, de immunita. eccle., and in l. placet, C. de sacrosanc. eccle., canonized in 16. quæstio. 1. capitu. placet. But the aforesaid property of the said Pietro and Giovanna was purely donated and offered to the church of Saint Augustine; therefore, immediately, even without tradition, ownership of it passed to the aforesaid church on a twofold ground. First, by the privilege of l. fina. C. de sacrosanct. eccle. Second, from the status of those persons who offered themselves. For by an offering purely made, they passed into the power of the church, so that they are, as it were, the church's, as the gl. notably says in cap. ut lex continentię. 27. quæstio. 2. Therefore, by a certain consequence, both the ownership and the possession of that property passed to the church by l. si adoptauero, ff. de priuileg. and l. si arrogator, ff. de adop.; Ioan. Andr. holds this in cap. in pręsentia, de proba. and noted in 19. quæstio. 3. cap. si qua mulier, and Bartol. expressly holds this in our exact terms in authenti. ingressi, de sacrosanct. eccle.; and thus the church is said to possess this property, albeit through them, just as a master is said to possess through a slave, as in l. j. C. si per uim uel alio modo and l. fin. C. de acquiren. possessio. and in cap. cum dilecta, de rescript. And the text in cap. fin. qui cleri. uel uouen. according to the reading of the gl. and of Innocen., which is commonly held by other writers, seems to support the aforesaid. It is certain that the property of laymen bestowed upon churches is exempt from the burdens of laymen, such as collections and the like, unless they were specific burdens perpetually annexed to the things themselves, for then they pass to the church with their encumbrance. This is the common conclusion of the doctors of both laws, and noted by Cano. in cap. fin. de ui, & honesta. clerico. and cap. 1. de immu. eccle., and in clemen. pręsenti, de censi., and Barto. in l. rescripto, ff. de mune. & hono. Second, principally for the aforesaid conclusion, an open text appears along with the gl. in cap. j. de deci. in fi., where it is clear

† that the oblates of religious orders, who have dedicated themselves and their property, also enjoy in the property which they hold in the name of the monastery all the privileges of that religious order; and that text together with the gl. serves exceedingly well. As to the second doubt, whether the said obligati enjoy ecclesiastical privilege in their persons: and I say that they do, since they are fully oblates; and they are called fully oblates since they have dedicated themselves and their property, as in the said cle. j. in fin., joined with the gl. To the same effect is the gloss on the said cap. ut lex continentię, which says that those oblates are, as it were, slaves of the church.

† And it is clear that slaves of churches are not held to the burdens of laymen, as in capitu. ecclesiarum seruos, 12. quæst. 2., and the text speaks there of wholly lay slaves. Much more forcefully must the same be said of these persons who, beyond church servitude, are religious persons, by the argument in capitu. non dubium, de senten. excomm., and 12. q. 1. capitu. duo sunt genera; to which tends what Inno. notes in capitu. cum monasterium, de electio., and Archi. in capitu. uno, de exces. præla., libr. 6., and Ioan. de Lig. in clem. per literas, de præben. Nay rather, it was the opinion of some that even those serving clerics, since they are within the household of the church or of clerics, enjoy this immunity in their persons, as noted in the gl. in capitu. eos, 32. dist., and by Archid. in capitu. clericum, 11. quæst. prima. Some, however, take the contrary view on this last point, which nevertheless I do not intend to dispute at present, since it does not bear on our proposition; but I introduce it chiefly as an argument, because if there are divergent opinions concerning the aforesaid servants and hired men, what is to be said of these concerning whom inquiry is made, who offered themselves and their property to the religious order? Certainly I have no doubt regarding them that they are ecclesiastical persons and enjoy the privilege of the church even in their persons. As to their property, moreover, there is no room for dispute, since they possess no property, inasmuch as it was bestowed by them upon the church. Wherefore I conclude that both the persons of the said oblates and the property bestowed by them upon the monastery are free and exempt from all burdens of seculars, just as other church property and ecclesiastical persons are. Afterward, however, it was reported to me that a certain reform was enacted by the citizens of Massa, in which it is contained among other things that no subject person may bind himself or his property to any church, even to the prejudice of the order, invalidating all subjections and alienations made within the past ten years. But this obligation, or donation, was made before that reform, within the prescribed ten-year period. But I say that this reform is not valid to the prejudice of a right already acquired by the church, as in capitu. quæ in ecclesiarum and capitu. ecclesia, de consti., and capitu. si, de rebus eccle. non alie., and 6. dist. capitu. bene quidem; nay rather, it cannot even impede a disposition to be made in the future, because it would be contrary to the privilege granted to the universal Church, concerning which in l. prima, C. de sacrosan. eccle., and more fully by Ioan. And. in capitu. fin., de immu. eccle., unless the precaution of Bart. were observed, of which in the said l. rescripto, which was not observed here. Likewise, this concerns property already previously acquired for the church, in respect of which a provision of laymen to the contrary is not valid, as Barto. himself expressly admits in the said l. rescripto, de muneribus & honoribus. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The right of patronage is acquired either from construction, or from foundation, or from endowment.
2. Possession of patronage is proved by presentation followed by institution.
3. If a church has been constructed, and it is not clear in whose diocese it is, it belongs to that bishop who proves that he exercised some episcopal right.
4. The right of patronage of a church passes also to extraneous heirs.
casus: The factual occurrence of the case is as follows. A certain Iacobus, money-changer, son of the late Ghinus Pucii Grassi of Arezzo, disposed in his will among other things as follows: Item, he disposed, ordered, and mandated that the chapel of Saint Matthew, built in the pieve of Santa Maria of Arezzo by the testator himself and Simone his brother, be endowed from the common property of the said Iacobus and Simone and the heirs of their said nephews, namely from certain goods and possessions held in common with the aforesaid Simone and his nephews, namely the sons of the late Cecilius and Petrus, former brothers of the said testator and of the said Simone; and he specifically expressed in the will the possessions to be assigned for the dowry with their boundaries, directing that the said possessions must serve as the dowry of the said chapel, and their fruits must in perpetuity come into the hands of the present and future chaplain for his sustenance and necessities. Also after this the said testator died, survived by a son and heir, a certain Duccius, who later died, leaving only two legitimate and natural daughters, namely the ladies Francischina and Christofora. Which ladies, as heirs of their father, together with a certain lady Matthaea, daughter of the late said Simone, presented a certain Don Bartholomaeus, canon, as rector of the said chapel, which was then vacant. Within the term of the edicts an exception was raised that they were not patronesses, but rather that the right of patronage had belonged fully to a certain Franciscus Ghini; which Franciscus instituted certain extraneous heirs, etc. It is asked whether from the said will those ladies are proved to be patronesses, nothing else having been proved to the contrary, especially since in a certain exchange formerly made concerning the said chapel it is stated in the instrument of the said exchange that the said chapel had been endowed by the said Simone Ghini, brother of the said testator Iacobus, the said instrument and other acts and proceedings in this case before the lord vicar of Arezzo having been examined, etc.
body: The assistance of Christ and of His Mother having been humbly invoked: It seems first that, by the said will or other acts in this case, the patronage is not proved to belong to the said women,

† because the right of patronage is acquired in one of three ways, namely from construction, foundation, or endowment: 16 q. 7 c. filiis, vel nepotibus; c. decedet, de imm. eccl.; and c. quicunque, and c. Fulgentius, and c. piae mentis, and there the excellent gloss on this matter; and through Ioan. Andr. in rub. de iurepat.; c. nobis and what is noted there, eod. titu., supports this; and whether prescription can be acquired, is noted in capitu. querelam, de electio., and fully by Ioan. Andr. in regul. quod alicui gratiose, de regul. iur. libr. 6. But in our case it is not necessarily proved by the said will or by another act that the said lord constructed, founded, or endowed the said chapel; therefore, etc. The inference is clear: in the said will only the words of the testator are contained, but his statement is not accepted in his own favor and to the prejudice of another, as in l. rationes defuncti, and l. exemplo, and l. instrumenta, C. de proba.; 12 q. 2 in princi. supports this; nor does the instrument of the said exchange prove that the said Simone endowed that chapel, because those words were uttered for another purpose and incidentally, and thus they do not furnish proof, as in capitu. si papa, de priuile. libr. 6, and in capitu. fin. de succes. ab intest., and C. de proba. l. non epistolis, and l. non nudis, and fully through Bar. in l. ex hac scriptura, ff. de dona., and through the Canonists in d. capitu. fin. and cle. unica, de proba., especially since that recital was not of the substance of the exchange that was being transacted; on the contrary, even if that recital had been of the substance of the exchange, nevertheless, since the validity of that exchange is now at issue, the right of patronage is not proved, nor that asserted endowment through the instrument of exchange, since the question now principally turns upon the challenged instrument, as is proved in c. illud, de praesum., and the gloss intended to note this in l. optimam, C. de contrahen. & commit. stipu. Likewise, thirdly and more strongly, through the instrument of exchange it appears that Francesco, the late Simone Ghini's son, was alone in possession of the patronage of the said chapel, which is evident not from that bare narrative of the donation made by Simone, the father of the said Francesco, but from the fact that Francesco alone, as patron, consented to the said exchange. For in an exchange there intervenes a resignation, and an express or tacit presentation, and a following institution by the superior, according to what is noted by the gloss in cle. una, de re. permu., and by Fede. in trac. de permuta.

† But by presentation, followed by institution, possession of the patronage is proved, as in cap. consultationibus, de iure pa., and cap. querelam, de electio., cap. cum olim, de cau. pos. & proprie, and fully through Innocen. in cap. 2 de in integ. restitu., cap. in literis, de restitu. spolia. Therefore the presentation ought to be admitted at that time through the heirs of the said Simone, even if the ownership of the patronage pertains to another; because presentation is a kind of fruit of the right to be rendered, and therefore it pertains to the possessor in good faith, and not to the owner, as is read and noted in cap. querelam, and cap. consultationibus, previously alleged; indeed, Innocen. maintains more, noted in d. cap. in literis, that when two presentations are made, one by the owner and the other by the possessor, that one is rather to be confirmed or admitted which is made by the possessor, by d. cap. querelam, and cap. consultationibus; what he himself noted in d. cap. 2 de in inte. resti., and cap. querelam, de ele., supports this. But the said ladies are not proved to be in possession of presenting, but only the said Francesco, nor is it even proved that ownership pertains to them; therefore they must be entirely turned away from their petition. But these things notwithstanding, I say that in this case it must be subtly observed that the said late Jacopo Ghini, the present brother of the said Simone, asserted in his will that that chapel of Saint Matthew had been constructed by him and the said Simone his brother, and also mandated that that chapel be endowed from the common property of the same Jacopo, and Simone, and of their nephews through predeceased brothers, as appears in the will of the said Jacopo, and he made and appointed the said Simone his brother as executor of the will. Now, however, the said chapel is found to have been constructed and endowed by lord Simone, executor of the said will, out of the property asserted in the will; which is proved thus: wherever anyone is bound to do something in which expense is required, if that subsequently appears to have been done, it is presumed to have been done by him upon whom this necessarily devolved; this is notably proved in l. 2 C. de alimen. pup. praestan., and there Hugo most clearly holds this, in l. cum seruus, ff. de uerbo. obliga.; but upon the said Simone, as executor of the will, this devolved; therefore, another patron not appearing, it is to be presumed that the said Simone endowed the said chapel from the common property concerning which mention is made in the will. For this it also makes that chapels are not born, but necessarily require a builder and an endower, whence at first sight it is presumed to have a patron, as noted by Ioan. And. on reg. quod alicui, de regu. iur. lib. 6, in Mercu., near the end. But another patron not appearing, it must be presumed that the heirs of Jacopo, and Simone, and of their nephews (from whose goods it is to be presumed that the said chapel was endowed) are the patrons. Secondly, to the same effect cap. 1 de reli. domi. serves very well, where it is proved, especially joined with the things noted by the doctors,

† that when it does not appear in whose diocese a basilica was built, something in that place is presumed to belong to that Bishop who proves that he exercised some episcopal right in that place, although he does not prove the exercise of all episcopal rights, as if a slight presumption suffices, since the right of another is not established. So in this matter: since it is not established that another endowed the said chapel in the will of Jacopo, when he had ordered it to be endowed from the common property, it must be presumed, since it now appears endowed, that it received the endowment from that common property, as is disposed in the will. And because the donation appears in the aforesaid manner, the same must be presumed concerning the construction, since it does not appear to have been constructed by another; the argument of d. capit. 1. Thirdly, it is proved from those narrative statements contained in the said exchange, in which it is contained that that chapel had been endowed by the said Simone Ghini, which indeed, where a great prejudice is not treated, furnish full proof, especially in ancient matters, where proof cannot easily be had, as is the singular gloss in c. cum olim, de censi., which says through that text that if in any public writing something is contained concerning the boundaries of any bishopric, it must be relied upon when other evidence concerning the boundaries does not appear, although that writing was executed simply for another purpose, as there; indeed at least it cannot be denied that those words create a not inconsiderable presumption, as is proved here in the text; and it is a good text with the gloss in c. series, de testi., and c. illud, de praesum., and c. fin. de succes. ab intesta., and the gloss in d. l. opti. C. de contrahen. & commit. stipul., which, however, I say, ought in a will to provide full proof, by the argument in c. 2 qui matri. accus. pos. and c. cum causa, de proba. Nor does it hinder if it is said that in the said writing mention is made only of Simone, and not of Jacopo or the other nephews, because I say that Simone did this in the name of all as the executor of the will, which he as executor was bound to do; therefore it is so to be presumed according to what is noted in d. l. 2 C. de alimen. pup. praestan.; for it is not said that he did it in his own name, and writings are to be reconciled with one another, since this can be done: de fide instru. cap. inter dilectos, § caeterum; de uerb. signifi. c. nihil; c. cum expediat, de elec. lib. 6, and l. unica, C. de inoffi. do., support this. For this it also makes that Francesco, son of the said Simone, consented in that act of exchange as patron. Nor does it hinder if it is said that he alone was patron and in possession of presenting, as I said above in the last argument of the first part. For this does not hinder if it is carefully and subtly weighed. For wherever the right of presenting pertains to several patrons together, although it appears that only one of them presented, and at their presentation the superior instituted the person presented, since it does not expressly appear that those patrons presented with the intention of despoiling the others of their possession, no prejudice is caused to the other patrons in subsequent acts, neither regarding ownership nor regarding possession, because one who is negligent in one act does not create a prejudice for himself in a subsequent one. This is clearly gathered from what is subtly touched upon by Innoc. and Compostel. in c. querelam, de elect., and more clearly Federicus de Senis sets it forth in our terms, consil. 97 in ulti. articu.; on the contrary, I say that through the presentation of Francesco, who was one of the patrons on the father's side, the possession of all patrons is preserved, as is gathered from the places previously alleged. Since therefore the said chapel was endowed from the common goods of the said Jacopo, and Simone, and of the nephews from predeceased brothers, I say, as I said above, that all their heirs are patrons, and the heirs succeed in this right of patronage by stirpes, and not per capita. Whence all the heirs of Jacopo hold the place of one; as to the heirs of those nephews who represented two brothers of the said Simone and Jacopo, they hold the place of two; whence four patrons concur here from the beginning, just as the dowry of the chapel emanated from the goods of all four brothers, and thus all descendants from them, or their heirs, hold the place of four patrons. This is proved today in clem. secunda de iure patro. And it must be noted,

† that the right of patronage of a church also passes to extraneous heirs, and not to sons only, as noted by Innocen. super rub. de iure patro. in fin., and Ioa. And. in c. cum seculum, eo. tit.; the gloss touches upon it in c. considerandum, and c. cum filiis, 16 quaest. 7. And this is the common opinion of Inno., although some say the contrary, but the former is truer. For if it passes with the universality of an estate to an extraneous purchaser, in c. ex literis, and in c. cum seculum, eo. titu., more strongly does it pass with the inheritance to an extraneous heir. What, however, if there are some heirs in equal portions? See through the gloss and the doctors in c. 1 eod. titu., where this is fully noted. And from these things I conclude for our case, that since those two daughters of the said nephew through the son of the said Jacopo, namely Franceschina and Cristofora, were universal heirs of the said Jacopo, no other extraneous heir appearing—by the argument in l. in suis, ff. de libe. & posthu., and l. prima, C. de his qui ante aper. tabu.—since they assert that they are heirs—by the argument in l. gerit, and l. pro haerede, ff. de acqui. haeredit.—they themselves ought to hold the place of one patron, namely of Jacopo, the paternal heir; and if others do not appear who can legitimately show that they are co-patrons, presentations by these ladies ought to be admitted; because it is to be imputed to those not legitimately appearing, by the argument in cap. dilecti, and cap. cum nobis, and c. scriptum, de elect., and through Ioan. And. in d. cap. querelam; and thus if they do not appear and show concerning their right, and they present another, he is to be instituted who has more voices of the patrons, computing the patrons by stirpes and not per capita in the aforesaid manner, and who is supported by greater merits, concerning which it must be spoken as in d. cap. 3 and cap. cum autem, de iure pa. Of lady Matthea, daughter of the said Simone, no serious special mention was made, because she had a male brother, whence I do not know whether she was equally heir to her father with the said Francesco. Whence if they were heirs of the father, at least in part of the property, she ought to be admitted as a patroness, because all the children of Simone hold the place of one patron, as appears through the aforesaid, nor is a distinction to be made between male and female. And if a female is an heir, she succeeds in the right of patronage just as a male; the same if she constructs or endows, as noted by Ioan. And. in cap. nobis, de iure pa., and Ioan. de Lig. in clemen. 2 eo. tit., through Fed. consi. 16; cap. si, de conce. praeben., supports this. It must be said otherwise if the said lady Matthea was not an heir of the father or the brother. From these things it clearly appears what must be said in this entire question, etc.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A corporate body that is not approved by law cannot acquire.
2. Civil and canon laws disapprove of public begging without an evident cause of necessity.
3. A perfected donation is not revoked, nor does it admit conditions ex post facto.
4. Corporate bodies of mercy, of disciplinati, and of those helping the oppressed are approved by law.
5. If the prince grants someone permission to transfer domicile, knowing that he is a guardian in that place, he is deemed to have released him from the guardianship.
6. Whatever a proctor does beyond what is contained in the mandate is not valid.
body: ON the question that is pending between the friars of Saint Francis, on the one hand, and those poor men commonly called the inhumati, on the other, concerning a certain estate or certain lands donated to both in solidum for an oratory and for sustaining divine services therein, as more fully appears from the instruments drawn up regarding the said donations, it seems first that the said inhumati have no right in them. Which is proved first as follows: the donation of those lands was made to their society, as appears from the instrument drawn up concerning this; but their society is not approved by law, rather it is disapproved; therefore no right could be acquired for them. The consequence is clearly proved in l. collegium, C. de hære. instit., and l. j. §. deinde, and in c. 1 de reli. do. lib. 6, joined especially to the notes by Ioan. An. there, in all of which it is stated in effect

† that a corporate body which is not approved by law can acquire nothing. The minor premise, however—namely, that these inhumati do not constitute an approved society or corporate body—is proved in many ways. First, by the said cap. 1 de relig. do. lib. 6, where the text expressly reproves those who invent a new order or religion not approved by the law or by the Roman Pontiffs; therefore, etc. And at least it cannot be denied that they wear a new religious habit, for they wear a certain habit in contempt of the world, and that is called a certain habit which is distinct from others by rule or constitution in color and form, as the gl. notes in cle. 1 de elec. But the habit of these inhumati is distinct from others in both, namely in color and in form; therefore they have a certain and determinate religious habit contrary to the provision of that chapter; and to this effect serves the notable gl. in the said c. 1 on the word habitum, which says that that text does not prohibit an individual person who does not invent sects and who lives apart from donning a new habit for himself, for this 41. d. c. parsimoniam; and thus it expressly meant that several persons living in this corporate body cannot invent and wear a certain habit so as to appear in a state of religion; whence the text in the said c. 1 speaks alternatively in its prohibition, as neither to invent a new religion nor to wear a certain or new habit, etc. Whence, presupposing that they did not invent a religion along with their corporate body, at least on this account, because they invented a certain and new habit without the license of the Roman Pontiff while living together. To the same point cle. 1 de reli. do. serves excellently, where the Pope, reproving the state of certain women living together under a certain veil, protested that by that prohibition he did not intend to inhibit faithful women from being able, having promised continence or without promising it, honorably to do penance residing in their own dwellings and to serve the Lord of virtues in a spirit of humility, etc.; whence weigh those words, in their own dwellings, because in a dwelling or corporate body it is not permitted to live under a certain shadow of religion, even for the sake of penance. Thirdly serves c. indemnitatibus, near the end, de elect. libr. 6, where the Pope expressly protests that by that constitution he does not intend to approve the state, order, or rule of certain women who neither renounce their own property nor make a regular profession, just as in secular churches secular canons, etc. Behold, therefore, that it is not permitted to assemble together for the sake of religion—even though those assembling do not renounce their own property nor make a regular profession—under a certain shadow and veil of religion; which seems contrary to the understanding of Bartol. in l. 1 ff. de colle. illici., who says that cap. fin. de rel. do. proceeds when several assemble into one for the sake of religion in such a way that they become ecclesiastical persons, but he says it is otherwise if they remain laymen. For this seems contrary to that text where those women remained lay, and yet he did not wish to approve their state, even though they assembled for the sake of religion. Nor does l. 1 ff. de colle. illici., upon which Bar. bases himself, stand in the way, which can proceed when they assemble together, yet do not constantly live under the same roof, nor assume for themselves a new habit; whence subsequent canons have in many ways limited that on account of the confusion and scandals that arose on this account in the church of God, as in the said c. fi. and in the previously cited chapter. Fourthly, contrary to this seems the case in the said c. fi. de rel. do., where the Pope expressly prohibited not only inventing a new religion, but also founding a religious house anew, unless the rule and institution are taken from those that are approved. But these inhumati daily build religious houses anew for themselves; indeed, in this very land concerning which the dispute arises, they wish to build a religious house for themselves; therefore this is not lawful, and thus that donation was void. Indeed, the case seems to fall under the extravagante of John XXII that begins Sancta Romana, which expressly, unless one cavils, seems to reprove their state, especially in that it expressly intimates that these de facto collegiate persons ought not to beg publicly, lest their state appear approved. And concerning this it must be observed

† that civil and canon laws expressly reprove public begging without evident cause of necessity, as in l. unica C. de emend. uali. lib. 11, and 93. dist. capitu. diaconi § nunc autem, joined with the gl. and the following chapter; but if there is no necessity, since they could seek food with their hands and not take away the relief of the needy poor, therefore their state is disapproved by both laws. From all of which it is concluded that if the donation made to their society was invalid, the donation made in the second place to the friars of Saint Francis, whose order is approved by the Church, as in the said c. 1 de reli. do., was valid; and in acquiring this place they had a special license from the Lord Pope Martin, and thus c. 1 de exces. præla. lib. 6 does not stand in their way. By these arguments what is objected is removed, namely, that the said friar Antonius Ioannis did not have full mandate to resign and donate those places; because there was no need for a resignation by the inhumati themselves, because if ownership was not acquired for them on account of their incapacity, therefore ownership remained with the donor, and thus he could freely donate to others, as in l. nec utile ff. de acq. re. do., and as noted by the gl. and Bar. in l. quod meo § a furioso ff. de acq. pos. Secondly, principally against the rights of the inhumati serves the fact that Biancus Saboni and Antonius Ioannis, both inhumati, receiving the donation of those lands, could not acquire ownership for the society, since they did not have a mandate for this from their society, and through a free person ownership is not acquired for us, Inst. de inu. stip. § si quis ali., and per quas personas nobis acquiritur § ex his itaque. Thirdly serves the fact that, presupposing that ownership thereof had been acquired, nevertheless by the free renunciation of their procurator they lost it, as in cle. j de renun., and c. super hoc eod. tit., and l. si quis ui § differentia ff. de acq. pos. Fourthly, all else failing, the concession of the friars of Saint Francis from the Lord Pope Martin ought to suffice, who in these spiritual matters and churches and pious dispositions has free faculty, in cle. quia contingit de reli. do., and c. innotuit de elec., and c. proposuit and c. cum nostris de conces. præben., for which serves the notable gl. in c. principalem 9. quæstio. 3, and Specul. in the title de leg. § nunc ostendendum, verse 57, and better in verse 89 § nunc breuiter, before the end, and Io. And. upon the said verse 57; also the gl. in c. constitutionem de relig. domi., and 25. q. 2 in summa serves this. But notwithstanding these points, I deem the said inhumati to be stronger in the said donated properties. The argument for this conclusion is sufficiently ascertained: for they were prior in the donation and in the delivery of possession, and thus ownership was transferred to them, l. traditionibus C. de pac., Inst. de re. diui. § nihil tam naturale, l. quoties C. de rei uendi.

† Now it is established that a perfected donation is not revoked, nor does it admit conditions ex post facto, as in l. 3 C. de reuo. do. and l. perfecta C. de dona. quæ sub modo; nor is there underlying, nor is there alleged, any cause of ingratitude, and thus we are outside the case of c. fi. de dona. and l. j C. de reuocan. dona.; therefore the donation made in the second place to the friars of Saint Francis was not valid, since ownership had already been transferred to the inhumati, and no one gives what he does not have, c. quod autem de iure pa., and j. q. 7 c. Daibertum, in c. nuper de do. post diuor. resti., and l. traditio ff. de acquir. re. do., and it is proved most clearly in our case in the said l. quoties. Wherefore, to fortify the right of these inhumati, nothing remains but to respond to the contrary points framed above. And first, to the laws that seem to press hard against the state of these inhumati, it can be said that they speak in other cases. For these inhumati, as they say, do not have a certain habit by law, or constitution, or otherwise, but use it at will, and can assume other garments both in form and in color, and use diverse habits at the same time, since that law or constitution does not compel them to the contrary; and thus they cannot be said to have a certain habit. Likewise, they say that they are pure laymen and have no superior, and assemble together for the sake of devotion, just as the Apostles and other blessed Christians did in the primitive Church, who had one heart and one soul, and all things were common to them, according to the saying of the Psalm: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity. And in favor of the aforesaid a good text seems to be in c. dilectissimi 12. q. j. They also deny that their house is religious, but rather purely profane, inasmuch as it is dedicated without the authority of the bishop and without a church; for they have only an oratory, which it is lawful for anyone to have in his own house for the sake of praying, as in c. unicuique with the two following chapters, de cons. dis. j, by Inno. in c. inter dilectos de dona., where there is a good text according to his reading. To the same effect serve the notes by Bar. in l. fi. ff. de coll. ill., where he says

† that these corporate bodies of mercy, and of the disciplinati, and of those helping the oppressed are approved by law through l. j ff. eod. tit. And properly Anto. de Butr. seems to approve the state of these inhumati in chapter secundo de foro competen., where he says that these inhumati, since they live regularly, are ecclesiastical persons, even though they do not make a profession, and that they ought to enjoy ecclesiastical privilege; he alleges the text with the gl. in c. indemnitatibus de electio. lib. 6 in fin., and what is noted in 11. quæstio. ulti. capitu. fin. de maio. & obe. c. dilecto. Likewise, according to him, since such persons bind themselves with many disciplines and walk barefoot, they can be said to be in the state of penitents, who are under the Church, 11. quæst. 1 c. aliud, which state is approved by the Church; and such persons are subject to the Church, even though there is no approved rule, because they cannot be called regulars since they do not have perpetual vows; yet their state of living is not disapproved according to him; for this he adduces the extravagante of John XXII that begins Ratio recta, which removes the penalties of cle. 1 de reli. do. even with respect to those women who are called Beguines, provided that they live honorably and do not involve themselves in preachings; and thus from the authority of so great a man the response to the contrary points ought to suffice. And as to what is said concerning begging, it can be said that they work insofar as they beg on behalf of them, which is not disapproved by law, 82. dist. cap. 1 and 42. dist. c. qui istam; and whatever may be said in the subtlety of the law, upon which I do not intend to dwell at present, that which especially moves me to this opinion is that our Lord Pope Martin granted certain indulgences of his certain knowledge to the houses of these inhumati, by which he seems to tolerate their state, by the argument of those things noted by Innoc. in capitu. ueniens de fil. presby., so that at least that saying proceeds in the prince, by the argument of l. Barbarius ff. de offic. præto. To the same effect is the good text in l. sed in hoc § fin. ff. de excu. tut., where it says

† that if the prince grants someone a license to transfer his domicile, knowing that he is a guardian in that place, he seems to have absolved him from the guardianship; so too the Lord Pope, by granting these indulgences, seems to approve their state. For if they were in a state of sin, an indulgence—which is granted to those truly penitent and confessed—would not benefit them, concerning which see de pœni. & remis. capitu. quod autem and capitu. quod quidem; and a license or indulgence or dispensation is extended to those things which necessarily follow from the dispensed act, as the notable gl. says in cap. quia in tantum de præben. and cap. quia non potest eod. titu. lib. 6 and cap. si quis in clero 7. q. 1, fully by Ant. de But. in cap. at si clerici § de adul. de iud. And for the aforesaid serves the excellent text with its subject-matter in capitu. quia circa de consan. & affi., where it is clear that the Pope tolerated or dissembled in the specified case, where he says that he wishes to dissemble, which induces a dispensation, as there; all the more strongly, therefore, where he grants indulgences, since a passive act operates more strongly than neglect, as in capitu. ex ore de his, quæ fiunt a maio. par. ca., joined with cap. decimas de rest. spo. lib. 6. Likewise, in a doubtful case we have recourse to custom, in capitu. cum dilectus de consue. and l. si de interpretatione ff. de legi.; all the more strongly must recourse be had to the judgment of the Pope alone. For it cannot be denied that the state of these inhumati is doubtful; the Pope, therefore, by granting an indulgence, seems to declare their state not disapproved by law; these men can therefore be defended either by pure law, or from the tacit judgment of the Pope, or by his dispensation, as is sufficiently gathered from the aforesaid. And by these arguments the points extensively alleged against their society are removed. To the second principal motive response is made in multiple ways: First, that those men, Biancus and Anto., receiving that donation, were not strangers to that society, but rather of the very body of the society; and what is donated to one member of the body in consideration of that body is acquired as donated for the body, as in capitu. requisisti in fin. de test.; to which serves what the gl. notes de mona., Insti. de inuti. stipu. § si quis alij. Likewise and secondly, presupposing that they had been entirely strangers, from the fact that they received it in the name of the society of the inhumati, and those inhumati afterward ratified it by building there and dwelling there, they acquired that ownership, ff. de neg. gest. l. si ego and l. penulti., as noted by Barto. in l. qui mihi donatum ff. de do.; indeed, although one cannot stipulate for another, yet if he stipulates in the name of another, the stipulation is valid if the other afterward ratifies it, the said l. penul., as noted by Bartol. in l. stipulatio ista § alteri, de uerbo. obligatio. The third motive concerning the renunciation of the procurator of these inhumati does not stand in the way, because, as appears in the form of the procuration, he did not have a mandate for this. For a special mandate is required in this matter; otherwise the donation is not valid, no matter how much he had full administration, and in l. filiusfamil. and there by Barto. ff. de donatio. and in l. contra iuris regulas ff. de pact. For one is not presumed, by appointing a procurator generally, to wish to throw away what is his, l. cum de indebito ff. de probat.; to which serves capit. qui ad agendum de procura. lib. 6.

† Moreover, whatever a procurator does beyond what is contained in the mandate is invalid, as in capi. cum olim, the first, de offic. delega., and l. diligenter ff. manda.; especially when it concerns the alienation of property of a community, which ought not to be alienated without the greatest discussion; indeed, it might be doubted whether the authority of the bishop ought necessarily to intervene, concerning which see by Hostien. in capit. nulli de rebus eccle. non alienan., and l. iubemus C. de sacrosan. eccle., joined with l. omnia priuilegia C. de episco. & cleri., where all privileges granted to churches are extended to pious places; for it is called a pious place where pious acts are performed, concerning which see by Specu. in the title de instru. edit. § nunc uero aliqua, verse & scias, quod inter legata ad pias causas. To the fourth and last point it must be responded that that concession of the Lord Pope is of no weight, as being surreptitious, since it was falsely narrated that those donated goods belonged to another and that he wished freely to confer them upon the friars themselves, which was false, since ownership had already been irrevocably transferred to these inhumati, as I said above. Now princes never intend by their letters to cause prejudice to a third party when no mention is made of him, in capit. super eo de offic. delega. and l. 2 § si quis a principe ff. ne quid in loco publi. Likewise, a privilege obtained by surreption is null and void by operation of law, as noted in cap. ad audientiam de rescrip. and in c. 1 & 2 de filiis presby. lib. 6 and in cap. inter dilectos de fide instru. From all of which I conclude that these friars, or poor men who are called inhumati, are stronger in the ownership of those lands concerning which there is at present dispute. And let these remarks suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A monastery cannot alienate immovable property without the consent of the diocesan, nor can it bind itself through a compromise.
2. A prelate cannot, through a compromise made without the consent of the superior, generate a perpetual prejudice to the church.
casus: The circumstance of the case is as follows. A certain Candor, a citizen of Lucca, syndic and proctor of the monastery of the nuns of San Carbone of Lucca of the Cistercian Order, in the said name of syndic and with the will and consent of the ladies abbess and nuns of the said monastery, on the one part, and a certain Lambert, son of the late Coluirnus, a citizen of Lucca, for himself and his heirs, on the other part, compromised upon a certain archpriest of Lucca as arbiter, arbitrator, and amicable compounder for the said parties concerning all and singular causes, lawsuits, questions, controversies, and disputes of law pending between the said parties, so that those lawsuits and questions upon which a judgment had been rendered should also be understood [to be included], etc., as is fully established from the instrument drawn up concerning this. By virtue of this compromise, the said archpriest pronounced, among other things, that the lady abbess, chapter, and convent of the said monastery are bound and ought, between now and the next eighteen months, whenever at the request of the said Lambert, to sell, give, deliver, and execute a legally valid sale to the aforesaid Lambert of certain immovable properties of the said monastery specified in the arbitral award for the price of one hundred and fifty florins. The said Candor, syndic of the said monastery, approved this arbitral award, and the said Lambert subsequently, in his own name, within the period of the eighteen prescribed months caused the said abbess and nuns to be cited and required before the lord vicar of the bishop of Lucca, offering himself ready to buy and demanding that the abbess and convent ought to sell him the goods included in the arbitral award, and requested that they be compelled to this end. But when they, namely the abbess and nuns, alleged the nullity of the arbitral award in that part and declined the bishop's court as being exempt, the said Lambert, by mandate of the vicar, deposited the said price of one hundred and fifty florins with a certain Dominicus. Nor does it appear that any sentence was otherwise pronounced upon the aforesaid exceptions, but so much time has elapsed since the deposit was made that recovery of the said deposit seems impossible or difficult, especially under a certain statute in force in the city of Lucca that introduces a prescription of ten years among present parties and twenty among absent parties against every debt, as appears more fully therein. It is now asked upon whom the risk of that deposit or its pursuit falls, etc.
body: Having humbly invoked the help of Christ and His mother, it seems first that the risk belongs to the monastery by the clear text in l. si a te, C. de pac. inter emptio. & uendit., joined with l. acceptam, C. de usu., and what Bar. notes there, where it is evident that even to acquire an action it is sufficient for the buyer to tender and consign, or deposit, the price by order of the judge, so that such consignment has the force of payment, and the risk of the money belongs to the seller. But in our case the aforesaid Lambert tendered, and by order of the vicar consigned it. Therefore, the risk or the pursuit of the money belongs to the monastery, as in the said laws; nor can the abbess and nuns allege the nullity of the arbitral award, since their syndic expressly homologated the award, and thus they can be compelled to observe it, as in cap. per tuas, de arbit., and l. penul., C. eod. titu. Nor was the power to enter into a compromise lacking, since it was not a question here of the liberty of the monastery—in which case the compromise would not have been valid without the Pope's license, if the monastery were exempt—but it concerned other matters, as appeared from the determination, as is proved in cap. cum tempore, de arbi. Nor were the matters alleged by the exempt nuns themselves able to impede the validity of the consignment or deposit, because the consignment was made before the proof of exemption; indeed, it does not appear that the exemption itself was ever fully proved. Wherefore, not being proved otherwise, the bishop's vicar was to be regarded as the competent judge, 18. quæstio. 2. cap. monasteria, and cap. abbate, and de re li. do. cap. cum uenerabilis, and de offic. uica. cap. licet; thus we are within the terms of cap. acceptam, cited above. But these notwithstanding, I judge that the contrary prevails in law. To this contrary opinion I am principally moved by the nullity of the arbitral award itself; which being given, it is most certain that that consignment did not produce any legal effect, and that that award was null, insofar as it constantly directed the monastery to the alienation of immovable property, as is proved.

† Just as a monastery cannot alienate immovable property without the consent of the diocesan, 12. quæst. 4. c. in uenditionibus, so neither could it bind itself to this by a compromise, because what is directly prohibited ought not to be permitted indirectly, in c. tuae, de procu., and c. cum quis una uia, de reg. iu. lib. 6. So Host. remarkably maintained in c. 3. de arbit., and Ioan. An. after him,

† that a prelate cannot, through a compromise made without the consent of the superior, generate a perpetual prejudice to the church; therefore, an alienation cannot result from a compromise, otherwise a path would be opened to make an alienation, and so Lap. held in his allegation 2. Fed. clearly held the same in consi. 89, where he says that a transaction made by a prelate of a church is not valid, even with the consent of the chapter, unless the consent and authority of the diocesan has intervened, when from it follows the alienation of an immovable thing of the church itself or another perpetual prejudice; for this is the text in l. cum hi. § si cum lis, and § si uni, ff. de transac., and there he answers to c. contingit, de transac., saying that there inquiry is made solely concerning the right of the chapter, and the answer is given saving the right of the diocesan; just as in a similar case the gloss notes in cle. 1. de re. eccle. non alien., and the matter well returns to its own nature, so that agreements and transactions are not valid without the authority of the superior. To the same effect is what Bart. notes in l. nulli, ff. de transac., where he maintains the same regarding a prelate; for a compromise is a kind of transaction, in Auth. ut dif. iudi. § si uero. Item, that award was contrary to the form of law, inasmuch as it compelled the selling of ecclesiastical goods outside the cases permitted by law and the prescribed form, just as is handed down in capitu. exceptiones, 12. quæstio. 2., and in the summa of the same question; therefore here it was null, as in capitu. examinata, de confir. uti. If, therefore, the award was not valid, consequently that consignment and deposit were not valid at all, as being made from a cause that was null and disapproved by law; and thus we are outside the authorities alleged above, since the monastery was not bound under that award to sell, and consequently not bound to receive the money, and thus that risk was not transferred to the monastery, nor could such consignment operate any effect, since it was not made lawfully. For this is the text joined with the gloss in l. 2. C. de usu., and what Barto. notes in the said l. acceptam. And if they should say that that monastery is exempt, and thus the lack of the diocesan's consent ought not to be an obstacle, I say that in exempt matters the Pope takes the place of the diocesan, and thus a direct or indirect alienation must be made by his authority, as noted in c. authoritate, de priuile. lib. 6., and 24. dist. capitu. nulla, and cap. cum dilecta, de confir. uti., and there is a clear gloss on our very point in clem. prima de re. eccl. non alie. on the word proprij. Furthermore, even assuming without prejudice to the truth that the aforesaid did not stand in the way—which in truth are conclusive—nevertheless, on another ground the risk of the money did not belong to the monastery, because for a consignment to have its effect, it is necessary that it be done by the authority of a competent judge, as in the said l. acceptam, and l. 2. C. de usur., and what is noted in them. But it is notoriously established that the bishop's vicar is not the competent judge of religious of the Cistercian Order, since that order is exempt and immediately subject to the Pope, as noted in capitu. cum ordinem, de rescrip., and has long been and is in peaceful possession of the exemption, and thus the alleged ignorance of fact is removed. Item, since this was disputed, he ought not, before it was established that he was the judge, to have made the deposit at his command, arguing from l. nimis propere, C. de execu. rei iudi., and in capitu. super literis, de rescri., with similar texts, and better, de iudi. capitu. exhibita; and by this the answer to all the motives alleged above is clear. I conclude, therefore, that the risk or the pursuit of that deposited money belongs to the said Lambert, but not to the monastery. And let these things suffice. Case of the following consilium: From the underwritten apostolic letters, the tenor of which was transmitted and presented to me as follows, namely: 'John, Bishop, etc. For a future memorial of the matter, etc.' And after many things disposed and ordained by the lord Pope himself, there follows in the said letters, law, or apostolic constitution: 'And to the end that divine worship may be increased to the extent that the said church has been adorned with a greater number of canons and chaplains, we decree that the Bishop and chapter of the said church for the time being, together with the said consuls, as often as it shall seem expedient to them, may newly create and also establish, beyond the accustomed number, new canons and canonical prebends and portions for those chaplains in that number and quantity from time to time, as they shall deem to be fitting for the honor and utility of the said church. Provided, however, that from the prebends presently existing, or from that which is distributed from the mensa of the said chapter to the provost and canons or chaplains who are now or shall in the future be instituted in the benefices that are now in the church mentioned, nothing may or ought to be subtracted or diminished in any way, and also because future prebends and portions of this kind to be instituted or decreed in the same church are not, nor ought to be, of less fruit, rent, and revenue than the principal one existing. If, however, the chapter itself should refuse to be present at the aforesaid creation and institution, or at any one of them, or should contradict, or refuse to consent without cause to agree with the bishop and consuls themselves, then in that case the bishop with the consuls themselves may and can by all law create the canons and chaplains, and institute canonical prebends, and also make such portions, etc., in the premises, which they could have made with the said chapter, anything notwithstanding, they may have and be deemed to have by the authority of the present letters, etc.' And near the end of the said constitution of the lord John in the said letters, these words are also placed, namely: 'By the aforesaid things also or any one of the aforesaid, let no prejudice be understood to be, or be capable of being done to any privileges or indults granted hitherto by the Apostolic See regarding the premises, or any of them, to the aforesaid consuls or to the operarii of the mentioned fabric.' Now, therefore, the underwritten doubts are raised: First, whether, regarding the ordination and creation of the prebends, and ultimately the election of the canons, having regard to the words of the said apostolic letters, we ought to say that there are three voices, namely one of the bishop or archbishop, another of the chapter, and the other of the consuls, or ought we to say that there are two, namely one of the bishop and chapter, and the other of the consuls? And what if the bishop agreed with the chapter or consuls, and concurred with the bishop and chapter, but not the majority of the consuls? And what if the consuls agreed with the chapter, or the majority of the chapter, with the bishop dissenting: whether the canons and chapter must be summoned, such that if they were not summoned, they could sue for contempt? And may the canons who are present, or the majority of them, contradict or withhold consent from the aforesaid ordinations and institution made by the archbishop and consuls, such that by their contradiction or failure to grant consent, the creation and also the institution made by the archbishop and consuls is impeded or annulled? Second, it is principally doubted, since in the aforesaid constitution of the said Lord John it is said that the future prebends to be created are not, nor ought to be, of less fruit, rent, and revenue than the principal existing ones, wherefore, since in the said church there are prebends of greater fruit, middling, and lesser, it is asked in what quantity these new prebends ought to be created? Third, it is principally asked whether by the lords consuls, or at least together with the bishop, in the creation of such prebends and the ordination of the prebends themselves, certain burdens or observances or qualities can be imposed upon those to be received and promoted to the said canonries and prebends, and what these might be, such as that those to be received must be priests, or that they are bound to be promoted within a time limit, or that they are bound to reside and maintain continuous residence, or to celebrate such a mass at such a time, and the like? And whether, for those not doing so, it can be ordained by the lord bishop, with the chapter and the consuls, or at least with the consuls if the chapter refuses, that those not observing such things may be removed, and that those not performing them incur the penalty of the loss of the fruits of the prebends and other emoluments, or that at least the said revenues or part of the said prebends can be withheld from them by the said consuls? Fourth, it is principally asked, since it is the case that such prebends were properly ordained and created from the revenues and goods of the operaria, and consequently of those deputed to the governance of the said operaria, and thus of the consuls of the wool guild, and so they seem to acquire the right of patronage from the endowment, whether the said right is said to be acquired in this way, and thus in the aforesaid creation it can be ordained by the bishop and by the aforesaid consuls that, in consideration of the aforesaid donation, henceforth in the future the consuls of the wool guild for the time being are the patrons of the aforesaid prebends, so that, when those prebends are vacant, the presentation belongs to the consuls themselves and the confirmation to the said archbishop, so that the chapter does not have to intervene in the confirmation, etc.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If in an election a prelate has a third part, the chapter another third, and some university another third, then votes are not judged by heads.
2. Where the consent of the chapter and of the bishop is required, they are not joined so that it suffices to have the greater part.
3. When several bodies are joined together, not as constituting one body, but as diverse, in order that an act may be said to be done by all [?], or by the greater part, it is necessary that the consent of each body intervene.
4. One who promises a craftsman is understood to promise an average one.
5. In doubt, a papal rescript is drawn to the ius commune.
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of Christ, and of His Mother, and of the glorious Virgin Agatha, I shall address each doubt on its own for the clearer information of the consultation. And first, following the order of the interrogation, I will undertake the first doubt, to which many doubts are incidentally connected. And first it is argued that the archbishop and chapter stand in the place of one person, so that they have only one vote in this matter; whereas the consuls stand in the place of the other, and thus have the other vote, so that all together constitute two votes. This seems at first sight to be proved in l. si, C. de impub. & alijs substit., where it is held that a testator instituted heirs thus: "Let Titius together with his sons, and Sempronius, be my heirs." From such an institution of the father with the sons—who are joined together, and by nature are almost the same person—they ought to have a half, and thus Sempronius alone would have as much as the father and sons who were joined together. So it seems should be said in the present case: for since the bishop and chapter are joined together, it seems that they are only in the place of one. The consuls, however, who are summoned by themselves, ought to be in the place of the other; to the same effect, l. si quis in fundi, ff. de insti. & substi. Secondly, it is principally supported by what Ioan. And. notes after Hostien. in capitul. scriptum, de electio.,

† where he says that if in an election a prelate has a third part, the chapter another third, and some other university another third, the prelate alone has as much as the whole chapter or the other university, nor are votes counted by heads. So in the present matter, since the bishop and the chapter are joined together, and also by law make one body, as in capitul. nouit, and capitul. quanto, de his quæ fi. à præla., although they are more in number than the consuls themselves, they have together only as much of a vote as the consuls themselves. But notwithstanding these points, which truly do not stand in the way, I consider that the contrary opinion prevails: that all the aforesaid are in the place of three persons, notwithstanding that the bishop and chapter are joined by the copulative word "and". An open case regarding this seems to appear in a similar situation in l. si quis Titio, ff. de usufruct. accre., where it is evident that the testator says thus: "I leave the same thing to Titius with my heirs, and to Maevius." From this bequest three parts are made, of which one is owed to Titius, another to the testator's heirs, and the third to Maevius; and the text adds there that it makes no difference whether it is said, "I leave to that one and that one, and to Maevius," or "to that one and that one with Maevius," for there are always three shares. Behold, therefore, that when two are joined by the word "with", all are called equally; l. Titiæ textores makes for this, and what is noted there, ff. de lega. 3. All the more must the same be said when they are joined by the word "and"; for this word "and", by which the bishop and chapter are joined here, causes each item to enter principally, so that neither can be called an accessory to the other, as the gloss has it in cap. querelam, de simo. The gloss ff. de iur. & fac. igno. super rubr. holds the same. Secondly, the text in l. si quis ita stipulatus, ff. de uerbor. oblig. seems to support the same, where it is proved that if two are joined in a disposition by the word "and", both must intervene. But if the bishop and chapter were joined together into a single vote, the pope's disposition would not be verified. For imagine there are twenty canons: if the bishop is joined with them, they would be twenty-one. Suppose also that ten canons and the bishop agree for one side, and the other ten for the other side. Now, according to the contrary opinion, did those eleven represent everyone, or constitute a majority of all? And thus it will not be true to say that the chapter consented here, as is required by the form of the mandate: because the chapter is not present here on any side, since a majority of the chapter is not found on any side; for ten make half of the whole. To this purpose c. 1. de his, quæ fi. a præla. and l. quod maior, ff. ad muni. and a good text in c. ecclesia, de elec., where it is clear that there is no chapter to be recognized unless at least a majority of the whole is given, and not a minor part by comparison with a minor part. Likewise, suppose another case under the said terms: that out of twenty canons, fifteen consent for one side, and the archbishop with the remaining five for the other side. According to the contrary opinion, those fifteen constituted or presented that entire vote belonging to them; and thus they went against the form of the mandate, since the consent of the archbishop did not intervene here—who nevertheless ought to be principal in authorizing, as is evident from the form of the mandate. Therefore, so that these absurdities may cease, let us say that the bishop must consent by himself, and the consuls by themselves, according to that dictum of Io. And. and Host. in said c. rescriptum, which fits our case well. Thirdly, this principally supports it: the bishop and chapter are summoned here by appellative and collective names in a single respect, and not as individuals. Therefore, in order to satisfy the rescript of the pope, it is necessary that the bishop consent, and the chapter by itself. For the chapter is a body distinct in itself from the bishop, and to such an extent that under the designation of the chapter the bishop is not included, as appears from the diversity of titles: for the title de his quæ fi. a præl. & maio. par. cap. is one thing; and although they fictively constitute one body, as in said c. nouit and c. quanto, nevertheless the bishop is the head, and the canons are the members. But the head differs from the members; the notable gloss formulated this opinion in cle. ut hi, de æt. & quali. Fourthly, we see

† that where the consent of the bishop and of the chapter is required, they are not joined together such that it would suffice to have a majority by head count; but the bishop must consent by himself, and the chapter by itself, so that at least the consent of the majority of the chapter is obtained, as read and noted in c. uno, ne sed. vac. and in the good gloss there, and fully and faithfully by Io. An. in c. a collatione, de ap. li. 6. Fed. also gave counsel, having first consulted Io. An., as he himself reports in his consilia, consi. 1, and fully by Cal. in c. postulasti, de conces. præb., although Hos. thought otherwise there. But all the moderns there follow the first opinion, which also proceeds when the consent of the bishop and chapter is required by the form of a mandate, as in our case, on which there is a notable gloss in c. si propter, de rescr. li. 6. Fifthly, it is proved from the tenor of the aforesaid rescript. For if the bishop and chapter constituted one vote, they would not distinguish at the end of the rescript, where it says notably that if the chapter does not consent, the bishop could ordain with the consuls, etc. The meaning of any disposition ought to be single and uniform, nor should the tail be separated from the head so that there is one meaning in the first part and another in the second. For if they were joined, they would always remain joined; to this purpose a good text with the gloss in c. maiores, de bapt. on the word cæterum, joined with the gloss on the word authoritas; and preceding matters take their understanding from subsequent ones, in l. si seruus plurium, and l. qui filiabus, ff. de leg. 1. Sixthly and lastly, I say that in effect it does not matter much to discuss this doubt, because from the form of the mandate it is clearly gathered that the consent of the archbishop and consuls is always required, but the contradiction of the chapter does not harm. This is proved thus: the exclusion of one operates the inclusion of the other, as in c. cum renunciatur, 32. q. 1, and l. cum prætor, in prin. ff. de iudi., and 25. dist. c. qualis, de præsump. c. nonne; just as in the rescripts it is said that if the chapter should wish to consent or be present, or if it should contradict, then the bishop with the consuls themselves can and may without the chapter, etc. Therefore, since he excluded only the chapter, he seems openly to have intended that without the consent of the archbishop and consuls that creation cannot take place. For to what end would he have excluded only the chapter in the case of contradiction, if the same held when the archbishop or consuls contradicted? He willed, therefore, that in every case the archbishop and the consuls must consent; and this seems conformable to the common law. For the archbishop could not do it without the consuls, since the consuls must provide the endowment, and spiritualities cannot exist without temporalities, 1. q. 3. c. si quis obiecerit; nor can the consuls do it without the archbishop, because laymen cannot establish benefices, but this pertains to the bishop, 18. q. 1. c. quidam, de conse. dist. 1. c. nemo, and c. postulasti, de iure pa. The chapter, however, in the case of contradiction, is rightly excluded, because without just cause it cannot impede those things which are justly ordained by the bishop, as noted by Ioan. And. and Arch. in c. 1. de const.; what is read and noted in c. 1. 65. dist. supports this. From the aforesaid I conclude that the archbishop, the chapter, and the consuls make three votes; nevertheless, the contradiction of the chapter does not have to impede the act, whether they wish to be present, or contradict, or wish to consent, since this matter has been approved by the pope; but it is otherwise if the consuls, or a majority of them, or the archbishop should contradict; and I speak with respect to those things which are contained in the letters of John. And through these points many other consultations contained in the first doubt remain decided. And first, whether the bishop with the chapter without the consuls can proceed regarding that ordination and election concerning which it is treated in the letters of John. And it must be said that they cannot, as was evident from the aforesaid. Second, what if two or three of the consuls were agreed? I say that it does not suffice, because the consuls are summoned here by appellative and collective names, that is, as a university and college, not as individuals. Therefore the consuls cannot be said to consent unless a majority of them consents; said l. quod maior, and c. ecclesia, and c. 1. de his quæ fi. a præla., and l. refertur, ff. de regu. iu.; for this the good gloss in c. cum inter canonicos, de elect., and the text in c. apostolica, 56. dist. The decision of the third consultation is also evident, namely, what if the consuls should agree with the chapter, or the majority of the chapter, with the bishop dissenting? I say that this does not suffice, as is evident from the aforesaid, because the consent of the archbishop and of the consuls is necessarily required both from the form of the mandate and by common law. To the fourth consultation, whether the canons and chapter must be summoned, such that if they are not summoned, they can sue for contempt, I say that if they are not summoned, the act would not hold by virtue of the papal letters, because this power was given jointly to the bishop, the chapter, and the consuls. If, therefore, the chapter is not summoned, the act falls through lack of power and from breach of the form of the mandate, as in c. venerabilis, de offi. deleg., and c. cum dilectus, de rescrip., and l. diligenter, ff. mand. For wherever power is given to three, what two do, without the other being summoned, does not hold, because the exercise belongs to them proportionally, de offi. deleg. c. vno delegatorum, and c. causam matrimonii, and what is noted in c. prudentiam, eod. tit., where by the gloss and Bar. in l. 1. §. si plures, ff. de exer.; c. si duo, de procu. lib. 6. supports this, and what is read and noted in l. si interest, ff. de arb., and c. 2. eod. ti. lib. 6. Nor does cap. sicut, de elect. stand in the way, where the act seems to hold notwithstanding the contempt of some, although an action for contempt may lie; because I say that there one does not err in form nor in power, since by law the power of a university rests with two parts of the university, l. nulli, and l. planè, ff. quòd cuiusque vniu. nomi., and l. nominationum, de decre. ab ordi. fa. But in our case there is a lack of power, which is given here to all together. Likewise, an offense is committed against the form of the rescript. I say, however, that their contradiction does not vitiate it, as is clear from the rescript. For the chapter is summoned because, perhaps by good counsel, it will be able to draw the others back from their opinion, as is read and noted in cap. cum in veteri, de elect., in cap. cum olim, de arb., in said cap. 2. eod. titu. lib. 6. Moreover, the decision of the last consultation, namely of the aforesaid first doubt, is evident: for I say that the contradiction of the chapter does not have to stand in the way of the ordination of the archbishop and consuls in those matters which are contained in the letters, through the aforesaid; and to the aforesaid I add the notable text in cap. pastoralis, de rescript., and what is noted there,

† where it is evident that when several bodies are joined together, not making one body, but as diverse bodies, in order that an act may be said to be done by all, or by the majority, the consent of each body must intervene. By these points I say it does not suffice that the bishop with some of the consuls makes a majority so that it is said to be done by the consuls and by the bishop or archbishop; but the bishop must consent by himself, and the majority of all the consuls by themselves, and the same must be said in that case, because their consent would be distributed; and by this the first doubt remains resolved along with all its accessories. Now I respond to the contraries formulated above in the beginning. And first, to l. si, C. de impu., the response is clear through what is noted there by the first gloss, and by Bart. in said l. si quis Titio. To the dictum of Host. and Ioan. And. in c. rescriptum, I say that it proceeds when it is certain that some joined together have a certain part in an election. But in our case, since all are summoned equally by appellative names, each body has by itself a third part in the disposition of the act, and thus in our case what is noted there can be observed, save for what is said of the chapter: because its contradiction does not stand in the way, and that of the others does, by the special form of the rescript, as is evident from the aforesaid. Nor is it an objection if it should be said that the said consuls are not summoned to the creation and institution of the prebends as principals, but rather as having the power to give consent, as seems to be gathered from the beginning of the rescript, where it is said that the bishop and chapter together with the consuls, etc. For these things are diverse in themselves: that three together have to carry out an act among themselves, or that two do so with the consent of the third. For in the first case, all are authors in the deed; in the second case, there are only two, and the third provides consent, as read and noted in c. 1. ne sede vac. lib. 6. For I say that this is false, namely that the consuls are not summoned as principals. For if the words of the rescript are well weighed, the act of swearings and institution refers to all equally, as is clear there: "as often as it shall seem good to them to create anew." Likewise and more clearly at the end of the rescript, where it is said that, the chapter refusing to consent or be present, the bishop with the consuls themselves can and may by full right create canons, etc. And if they are principals in the creation and institution in this case, since the act of disposition refers equally to all, it is just as much to say "that one and that one" as "that one with that one"; and this is the proper case of the said l. si quis Titio. For the bequest referred to all equally, therefore the word "with" joins principally; and this is what Feder. meant in the said consil. 1. I come now to the second principal doubt, namely: when the ancient prebends are found to be of unequal value and income, and the new ones according to the form of the rescript ought not to be of lesser value than the ancient ones, in what manner shall they be conformed to the ancient ones? It seems first that the new ones ought to be made in the likeness of the middling ones. For in doubt the author seems to have considered the mean, by the argument in l. legato generaliter, ff. de lega. 1; because under this species variety is found, not the highest, nor the meanest, but the middling.

† Likewise, if it is said: "If I promised you an artisan," it is not understood of the highest, nor of the entirely unlearned, but of a middling one, as in l. sciendum. §. item sciendum, ff. de ædil. edic. Likewise, there are many things in law which in doubt choose the middle way, in c. quærenti, de off. deleg., and 45. dist. c. disciplina, de rest. spol. cap. literas, according to that saying: "For a greater grace resides in middle things." Concerning waiting for this mean, many texts are alleged in ca. scientes, de censi.
