But notwithstanding these points, I think otherwise in our case, through the notable text in capitul. cum olim, de consuetu., where it is notably proved that where something is to be done in the likeness of another, if that other is varied, that is chosen which is more reasonable, consonant with common law, and less prejudicial to the other party; and Anton. de Butr. notes this more clearly there. Whence in our case I say that the new prebends ought to be made in the likeness of those ancient ones which are more reasonable and conformable to common law, whether they be richer, or middling, or lowest: because in doubt the pope seems to have thought of reasonable prebends, deeming that in so famous and flourishing a chapter, and in such a city, the prebends ought to be according to the disposition of the common law.

† For the rescript of the pope ought in doubt to be brought back to the common law, even if it were necessary to transpose clauses of the rescript, lest something absurd follow, as is proved in c. cum causam, de rescrip. And for this is the rescript of Gregory, who commanded prebends to be created at that value so that the canons to be instituted could live decently and pay the episcopal dues; and what the gloss notes in c. 1. 21. q. 1 makes for this. And better regarding prebends makes the text 12. q. 1. §. fin. a.; for otherwise an absurdity could follow. For suppose that the middling ones on account of wars or the negligence of the canons have been so diminished that they do not suffice to provide for individual canons: shall we say the pope understood concerning those? Certainly not at all; arg. in c. 1. de consuet., in c. nemo, de consecr. dist. 1., and c. ad audientiam, il 1. de eccl. ædifi. And this concerning the second principal doubt. I come to the third question, namely whether the said consuls by themselves, or at least together with the bishop, can make statutes regarding the new prebends and those newly to be instituted in them, etc. It seems that they can. First, from the rescript of Gregory, who seems to grant this to them, at least that the bishop should do so with the consent of the consuls. Likewise, by a certain consequence this same thing seems to be lawful from the rescript of John: because to whom anything is granted, all that seems granted without which the former cannot conveniently be exercised, l. ad rem mobilem, and l. ad legatum, ff. de procur., and in c. prudentiam, and c. prætereà, de offi. dele.; and to whom the principal is granted, the accessory also seems to be granted, ar. in c. ex parte, il 2. de deci.; the rule accessorium, de regu. lib. 6. supports this. But the institution and creation of canons and prebends cannot conveniently be done without the ordination and institution of those things which the ones to be instituted must do, arg. in c. significantibus, de præben. Therefore, since the power of creating was given to the consuls and the bishop, the power of ordaining seems given. Nay more, it seems that from the right of patronage the consuls can make statutes by themselves, because in the transfer of one's own property one can attach a burden, in c. de monachis, de præb., noted by the gloss in c. generali, de elect. lib. 6., and in cap. cum Bertold. de re iud. But I consider that the consuls neither by themselves nor together with the bishop can establish this so that they themselves are called authors in those ordinations and statutes. I am moved principally because by common law laymen are not allowed, even in the transfer of their own property which they make to churches, to attach spiritual conditions or modes; so Inn. elegantly posits in c. quoniam, ne præla. uices suas: because laymen are not allowed to make statutes concerning spiritual things, even regarding an endowment that they give to a church, 10. q. 1. c. decernimus, de consti. c. ecclesia S. Mariæ, and 96. distin. c. bene quidem. But regarding temporal things they may well attach some pact at the beginning; thus the authorities alleged above in the first part ought to be understood. But the remedy is that the archbishop confirm those statutes at the petition of the consuls; which he can do even by departing from the disposition of common law. The notable text in capit. cum dilectus, de consuetu. proves this, there, "at the petition of the patrons," etc. To the same effect is what the doctors note in cap. ad audientiam, de cleri. non resi., where Hostien. and Ioan. And. say that a constitution can be made against non-residents, even if there is a custom in the church to the contrary, provided it is made principally for the utility of the church—which is to be noted, and what is noted in c. cum omnes, de constitu. supports it; for there that constitution against ancient custom was rejected because the vice proceeded from its root and it was not common to all, as noted there. For the bishop can make statutes aiding the common law by the imposition of a penalty, as noted in the gloss in clem. ne Romani, de elect., fully by Ioan. And. in capit. fin. de offi. archi.; and the bishop ought to do this at the petition of the patrons, since the statutes are honorable, as is proved in said c. cum dilectus; chapter præterea. 2. de iure patro. supports this; and the bishop in this ought to seek the counsel of his chapter, de his, quæ fiunt a præla. c. nouit, and cap. quanto; yet their contradiction does not stand in the way, since the statutes are otherwise reasonable, but they ought to be held as consenting, as noted by Ioan. And. and Archi. in c. 1. de consti. lib. 6. The allegations made on behalf of the consuls at the beginning of the doubt do not stand in the way. For the rescript of Gregory did not permit this to the consuls, but to the wardens (*operarii*); but a disposition is not extended from person to person, de priuil. cap. sanè, and 7. quæst. 1. c. petisti, just as not from case to case, in c. tua, de præbend. lib. 6. And even if he had granted it equally to the consuls, it is nevertheless enough that he granted it to them, as noted on a similar point in said c. tua; for the consuls do not proceed by virtue of the rescript of Gregory, but of John. What I said concerning the rescript of John does not stand in the way, that that power comes by a certain consequence: because I deny that without new statutes the creation of prebends and of new canons cannot take place. For they can be left to the disposition of the law, as noted in c. susceptum, de rescript. lib. 6. Likewise, since we are in a matter subject to dispensation and restriction, namely that laymen should dispose of spiritual things, we must make a most strict interpretation, not only that things not specifically granted should not be included, but also that those things which can be comprehended from the proper meaning of the words should not be included, as is notably read and noted in c. quod dilectio, de consan. & affi., and in c. 1. & 2. de fil. presby. lib. 6., by Io. An. in regula, odia, de reg. iu. li. 6. in Mercu., and c. olim, de ver. sig., by Bar. in l. beneficium, ff. de const. prin. And this concerning the third doubt. Finally, descending to the fourth doubt, in effect containing whether the presentation of the canons to be instituted to the new prebends belongs to the consuls, since the prebends were endowed from the property of the works (*operaria*), which the said consuls oversee. It seems first that it does; because the right of patronage belongs from a donation, 16. q. 7. c. piæ mentis, and what is noted there, in c. filii, and c. decernimus, ea. cau. & q., with many similar texts; which also proceeds in the donation of prebends created in a collegiate church, as noted by Inno. and more clearly by Io. And. in c. nobis, præal., although the gloss said otherwise, and less well, in c. 1. eo. tit. Nor does the dictum of Ho. in said c. postulasti please, where he says that deputation to prebends belongs to the patron in a collegiate church if the patron specially reserved it to himself, otherwise not; and so the gloss wished to limit it in said c. postulasti. But that dictum is proved by no law. For the laws generally, in the creation of any benefices whatever, reserve the right of patronage of presenting, provided the patron does not specifically change the right, as in c. significauit, de testi., and 26. q. 7. c. filiis piæ mentis, c. decernimus, with many similar texts; what the gloss notes in c. si quis basilicam, de conse. dis. 1. supports this; then Io. And. says in regula, quod alicui gratiose, de reg. iu. lib. 6. in Mercu. that a bishop does not today found his intention by common law upon the free collation of benefices, but only upon institution, because churches are not born [free], but one is presumed to have a patron to whom presentation belongs, through the general laws alleged above. From that general disposition of the laws, however, only the election of a prelate in a collegiate church is found excepted, and nothing is said of canons, as in said cap. nobis. Therefore the prebends remain under the general disposition, by the argument in l. præcipimus, in fi. C. de app., and in l. commodissime, ff. de lib. & posthum., and in c. susceptum, de rescript. lib. 6., l. cum prætor, ff. de iud., and c. qualis, 25. dist. And thus the dictum of In. and Io. An. in said c. nobis simply pleases me. But to the contrary, that presentation cannot belong to the said consuls, I prove thus. The works (*operaria*) or fabric of a church is not a true body, but a fictive one, nor does it have a college in itself, but they are certain revenues assigned to the fabric of the church, and consequently they belong to the church itself. For if I give or leave to the fabric or works of a church, I give or leave to the church itself; whence ownership is acquired for the church whose benefit the bequest or donation concerns. For it does not matter with whom the testator speaks, but one must consider into whom the benefit of the disposition is transferred, as in l. cum pater, §. donationis, ff. de leg. 2., and l. 2. §. biduum, ff. quando appel. sit., and 2. q. 1. c. biduum. For the fabric, since it consists of certain revenues of it, cannot have ownership of other revenues, nor is the utility of the church itself granted away; l. collegium, C. de hære. insti. supports this. That things assigned to the use of the fabric are in the ownership of the church is sufficiently gathered by the aforesaid reasoning, and 10. q. 3. imo, and 12. q. 2. c. quatuor, and c. concessis, with similar texts. But the right of patronage is acquired by him from whose property the thing proceeded, not by him who was the author of the endowment; whence if out of the property of one church another church is established or endowed, the right of patronage is acquired by the principal church, as is proved in c. apostolicos, in fi. with the joined gloss, 2. q. 2., and c. ad audientiam, il 2. de eccl. ædifi. Therefore, in the present article, I consider this to be the very truth: that we should distinguish thus, that either the ownership of the works remains with the commune until it is expended on the fabric itself, perhaps from an ordinance thus made at the beginning when the property is donated to the works, so that the free disposition of the property belongs to the commune of Florence; and then the first allegations proceed, so that the patronage is thence acquired by the community from whose property the endowment of the said prebends proceeded, and consequently the presentation will belong to the consuls, since the free administration of the rights of the works was granted by the community to the consuls themselves; or the ownership of that property belongs to the church, as because the property was given purely to the bishop; and then the church itself will have the right of patronage of those prebends, as in said c. apostolicos, in fi. with the joined gloss; what the gloss notes in c. unico, de iure patrona. lib. 6. and c. quia clerici, eo. tit. supports this. But under the name of the church in this case the bishop with the chapter will be included: because the bishop is in the church, de testa. c. requisisti, arg. 7. q. 1. c. scire debemus. And in this case the allegations in the second part proceed; and by this let all the doubts be satisfied. And he who wrote otherwise considered the aforesaid subtleties, etc. Praise be to God. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. To whom predial tithes are owed, to the baptismal church or to the parish church, and throughout the whole consilium.
2. Under the designation of obventions and proceeds come all tithes, and whatever can proceed.
body: IN the question which is contested between the plebanus of San Giusto in the diocese of Volterra, on the one hand, and the men of the commune of Antignano and the commune of Personato of the same diocese, on the other hand, concerning predial tithes arising from estates situated within the parish of the church of San Bartolomeo lying within the boundaries of the plebanatus of San Giusto—to which plebs the parishioners of the church of San Bartolomeo have recourse solely on account of the sacrament of baptism, while they receive the remaining sacraments in the church of San Bartolomeo—it is asked in law

† whether predial tithes are owed to the baptismal church, which is seen as the mother of the other chapels, or to the parish church where the estates are situated and where the men receive the other sacraments. And this doubt is certainly not slight in law, since the laws speak variously on this case. For the doctors have leaned towards various and diverse opinions; and so that the difficulty of the question may be clear, I will first argue for the parties. Secondly, I will set forth the opinions which I find on our case. Thirdly, I will conclude what seems to me consistent with law. That they are owed to the plebs of San Giusto, which is baptismal, is shown first by the clear text in capitulo de decimis, 16. quaestio. 1, where it is said that it seemed good to all the ancients that tithes should be given only to the plebes, where the sacrosanct baptisms are administered. To the same effect are cap. statuimus and capit. in sacris, in the same causa and quaestio, where it is held that he is to be excommunicated who wishes to pay tithes outside the baptismal church without the knowledge of the bishop. The text of 14. q. 1. cap. ecclesiis, §. in dioecesi seems to mean the same thing. Secondly and primarily, the text in cap. ex transmissa, de praescrip., along with the penultimate gloss, supports this, where it is evident that the mother church, namely the baptismal church, vindicates for itself all tithes from the men of the chapels, excluding the clerics of the chapels themselves. Thirdly, it is supported according to one interpretation that the gloss places there on c. ad audientiam, 1, de eccle. aedifi., where it is evident that although a chapel is constructed within the boundaries of any parish on account of the necessity of the men, nevertheless the ancient church remains the mother, and some honor is owed to it from the chapel, lest predial tithes be withdrawn from it. The same must therefore be said in our case, for these chapels were built after the fact within the plebanatus of San Giusto; wherefore that plebs remained parochial in many rights. And in favor of this last point are c. ecclesiae and c. quicunque, 16. q. 1, where it is said that ancient churches ought not to be deprived of their rights, especially tithes, on account of newly built churches. Fourthly, it cannot be denied that the baptismal church is the parish church of all the chapels, since otherwise this sacrament of baptism—which is the chief and the foundation of the other sacraments, in c. si, de presb. non bapti.—could not be administered to them by its own right; wherefore it seems absurd not to preserve its parochial right. For it is sufficient that the chapels have personal tithes and other parochial rights; for anciently the plebes alone possessed all parochial rights, but on account of the increase of people, chapels were later constructed and parishes assigned to them; the plebes nevertheless remained parochial, at least in the sacrament of baptism. Whence, both by reason of this sacrament, and because they ought not to be entirely deprived of their right on account of new churches, and to avoid the enormity of prejudice, we must say that at least the predial tithes have remained with them, as those cap. 16. q. 1 and c. quicunque seem to indicate. On the contrary side, that they are owed to the church of San Bartolomeo, which is the parish church of those of Antignano, many laws are adduced which state that predial tithes pertain to the parish church where the estates are situated, as in cap. quoniam, c. cum contingat, and in cap. cum in tua dioecesi, de deci., and the text in capit. ad decimas, de restitu. spo. lib. 6 seems clear enough. Secondly and primarily, I adduce the good text in cap. pastoralis, de his quae fi. a praela., where it is said that by the authority of the diocesan, parishes were delimited so that the revenues of individual parish churches would yield to the uses of the church and the stipends of the ministers, etc. Behold, therefore, that all revenues arising from spiritualities within the parish of any church yield to that church; therefore predial tithes from estates situated in the parish, since they are spiritual revenues, de praescrip. cap. causam quae. Thirdly, it seems proved by not quibbling with the letter in capitulo ad audientiam, 1, de ecclesi. aedific., but by adducing it otherwise than above. For there, on account of the excessive distance from the parish church, a chapel was built within the boundaries of the parish, and a certain village was assigned there to the parish, and the Pope decreed that all obventions and revenues of that village should yield to the sustenance of the rector to be instituted therein. Now, it has been said

† that under the appellation of obventions and revenues fall all tithes and whatever can lawfully accrue to a church, as in capit. transmissae and c. cum inter, de verbo. fig., and c. dilecto and c. cum inter, together with the gloss on the said c. ad audientiam, and c. non solum. If therefore the Pope solemnly decreed this there, it must be said that the law is the same in a similar case, and in doubt that it was so done from the beginning, as in capitul. consanguinei, de re iud. Fourthly, I adduce the good text in cap. fin. de iure patro., where it is proved that predial tithes are owed to that church in whose parish the estates are situated, even if the owners of the estates reside elsewhere and receive no sacrament from the parish church. All the more, therefore, are they owed there when the owners of the estates, as in our case, reside there, or the cultivators are parishioners of the predial church, as is the church of San Bartolomeo in our case. Fifthly, it is argued thus: since the church of San Bartolomeo is a parish church having a delimited parish, distinct from the church of the plebs of San Giusto, it ought therefore to have all parochial rights, as de parochia almost throughout, and 13. q. 1. c. 1. But tithes belong to parochial right: because, since the estates are on parochial land, by common law the tithes pertain to the parish church, as in cap. fin. de paroch. and the said c. ad decimas, de resti. spol. lib. 6. These arguments having been examined, I will introduce the opinions that I find on the matter, the first of which holds that on this point one must abide by custom as to whether they are owed to the baptismal church or to the chapel, per cap. ad apostolicae, de deci., and this was what Innocent meant there in the gloss on c. cum contingat, under the same title, and Raymond in his Summa, under the same title; and from this opinion no one departs. For by custom or prescription they can be owed to that church which has no right in them, as in cap. cum contingat and in c. cum in tua, de deci. The second opinion is that, in the absence of custom, they are owed to the baptismal church; this opinion is held by the gloss on the said c. cum contingat and on c. statuimus, 16. q. 1; Innocent on the said c. ad apostolicae; Tancred on c. nuncius; and Johannes Andreae follows it in the Speculum under the same title, §. 2, post principium. It is said, however, that in three cases they can be owed to the chapel. The first is when custom so dictates, as I said above. The second is when, in the delimitation of a new chapel, since souls could not otherwise be provided for, the bishop, with the consent of his chapter, assigned to that new chapel the predial tithes or delimitations of its parish; the said c. statuimus supports this, and what is noted on the said c. ad audientiam and c. constitutus, de reli. domi.; otherwise, unless he had expressly assigned them, predial tithes would not pass (according to him), per the said c. quicunque and c. ecclesiae. The third is when in some large territory there were many churches and none was baptismal, and newly one of them is chosen as a plebania and baptismal church, or newly a plebs is established there with baptism; for then the reasons adduced above in favor of the plebs cease, indeed they resolve in favor of the chapels according to him; and these cited laws must be weighed carefully, because they seem to qualify his opinion, so that it proceeds when it is certain that the chapel was built within the boundaries of the plebs, as if then the ancient church ought not to be so enormously harmed by the construction of the new church. The third opinion is that predial tithes are owed to the predial church in whose parish the estates are situated, even if it is not baptismal. Archidiaconus holds this opinion on c. 1, 13. quaestio. 1, saying that this is proved in the said c. ad decimas, by which he says this controversy was put to rest, and he reports that Laurentius, Vincentius, Goffredus, Bernardus, and Philippus hold this very thing on cap. fin. de paroch., as well as the gloss on the said cap. 1, 13. q. 1 and c. ad apostolicae, de deci., and Roffredus and Johannes de Deo, who notes thus in his Summa de decimis, §. sed quibus, saying that the canons indicating the contrary speak according to ancient times, but today according to Roffredus they must be given to the parish church by common law, even if it is not of baptism; to this effect is 13. q. 1, in fine, and de mune. et hono. l. 1 and 2 supports it. Huguccio and Laurentius also approve this view, and Archidiaconus says in the place cited above that Raynerius also approves it, as he notes in his Summa de decimis, in the beginning; and Hostiensis also holds it in capitul. cum homines, de deci., and in the Summa on the same title, §. cui dandum; and most recently, against Johannes Andreae, Calderinus, his adoptive son, broadly pursues and holds it, founding himself much upon the said c. ad audientiam, adducing it as above. Nor does the gravity of the prejudice stand in the way, upon which Johannes Andreae founds himself heavily, for otherwise it must be understood that this chapel was constructed by the bishop with the requisite consent of his chapter, which can be prejudiced, nor can and ought it to be done otherwise; the things noted in capitul. constitutus, de reli. do. support this. Also according to him, with due respect to Johannes Andreae who attempts to answer the said capitul. ad decimas, upon which Archidiaconus founds himself, it has not been sufficiently answered by him, because although that church of San Nicola which was suing is not a plebs, as Johannes Andreae says, nevertheless the text principally founds itself there on the fact that the tithes arose from the aforesaid lands which were claimed there and were situated within another parish. And by this it is there inferred that those tithes pertained to that church. And thus it openly implies that predial tithes are owed to the church within whose parish the estates are situated; if the estates about which inquiry is now made are within the parish of San Bartolomeo, they are therefore owed to it. Furthermore, the moderns have followed this opinion, and especially Antonio de Butrio on capit. cum contingat, who, harmonizing the opinions, says that either the new parish does not have special boundaries, and then all are in agreement that predial tithes are owed to the baptismal church, because they arise within its parish—and Johannes Calderinus specifically holds this, and in this case the ancient canons preferring the baptismal church to the chapel apply; or special and distinct boundaries have been assigned to the chapel, and then either necessity compels it because the baptismal church does not suffice on account of the vastness of the parish, and all obventions must be assigned to the chapel itself by mandate of law, as in the said capitul. ad audientiam (nor is a prejudice then said to be inflicted upon the ancient church, since the law does not perceive it, and in doubt it must be presumed that this mandate of the law was followed; and to the contrary laws he responds that they must be understood of a case where the chapel was constructed without great necessity); or it is doubtful which was more ancient, the parochial or the baptismal church, and in doubt he says they must be given to the parish church, per capitul. cum contingat and capitul. ad decimas; for the rationale of capitul. quaecunque and ca. ecclesiae, 16. q. 1, now ceases. And this opinion I deem truest, and it leads to a clear decision of our question. For I say that on a two-fold ground this church of San Bartolomeo ought to prevail. First, because it has a certain and delimited parish, and it must be presumed that it was built out of necessity according to the disposition of the law, since it is far distant from the church of the plebs of San Giusto, and thus that the bishop from the beginning awarded to it all the obventions of that parish, following the disposition of the law set forth in the said capit. ad audientiam. Likewise on another, lesser ground: because it does not appear whether the plebs of San Giusto is older than the church of San Bartolomeo; therefore it has a well-founded claim by common law, since the estates are found in its parish, and in this case all the arguments of Johannes Andreae fail, nor does he himself hold the contrary in this case, since it could not be said that the chapel ought not to have been built with grave prejudice to the plebs, when it does not appear to have been built afterwards. But even granted that it does so appear, nevertheless they would be owed to it, since a parish was decreed to it and nothing appears concerning any condition; all these things seem sufficiently clearly proved by those things which I alleged in the second part. Now it remains to answer the contrary arguments founded in the first part. And first, to c. de decimis, and c. statuimus, and c. in sacris, 16. q. 1, I reply twofold: first, that they speak of tithes situated within the parish of the plebs, because in many parts there are no other parish churches besides the plebes; that this is true I openly prove by the said capit. in sacris, where it is said that the peoples received all sacraments in the baptismal church, and thus it implies that it is otherwise if the estates were outside the parish of the plebs. Secondly, they can be understood of when the plebs alone has a parish, while chapels without boundaries have the care of certain persons; and thus also can cap. ex transmissa, de praescript. be understood, as is clearly implied by that text. To the third argument concerning c. ad audientiam, I say that sufficient answer was given above, for it rather supports the contrary opinion, because the Pope commanded that the obventions and revenues of the parish be assigned to the chapel itself, as I said above. In the second part of the arguments, to c. ecclesiae and c. quicunque, a twofold response is evident from the foregoing. First, they can be understood of when it is established that the chapels were built afterwards within the boundaries of the plebs, and certain parishes were not assigned to these chapels. Secondly, that they apply when new chapels are built not out of the necessity of the people, but solely out of will; for then ancient churches ought not to be deprived of their rights on account of newly built ones; but it is otherwise when it is out of the necessity of the people, as is proved in the said c. ad audientiam. To the fourth and last argument, I say that, presupposing that the plebs is in some respect parochial to the men dwelling in the chapels, at least by reason of baptism, nevertheless the revenues arising within the parish of the chapel are assigned by law to the chapel itself, as in the said c. ad audientiam, nor are predial tithes owed by reason of sacraments; yet a certain honor is reserved to the baptismal church according to the assessment made in the beginning, or the custom of the place, pursuant to those things which are noted in the said c. ad audientiam. Tithe revenues, however, ought not to be withdrawn, as is stated there, and the aforesaid things apply above all in our case, in which it does not appear, as I said before, which church is older. I conclude therefore that by common law the predial tithes in question are owed by law, saving custom to the contrary, to the church of San Bartolomeo, and not to the plebs of San Giusto, etc.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If a testator says to a stranger, "I commit my will to your disposition", he is deemed to have instituted him as heir so that he may distribute the inheritance to pious causes.
2. In case of doubt, a substitution ought rather to be interpreted as direct than as fideicommissary.
3. The Trebellianic portion ceases in legacies to pious causes.
4. An executor is properly one who exercises the office of execution.
body: Having inspected the will of the late Colinus, my friend from Campagnatico in the county of Siena, in which among other things a posthumous child was instituted, he disposed as follows: "Likewise he willed, ordered, and mandated that if the said posthumous child or children, one or more, son, daughter, or sons, heir or heirs instituted above, are not born or should not be born and do not come into the light of day, or should die within the age of pupillarity, then and in that case, upon the occurrence of such condition, all his movable and immovable goods, things, and actions shall be given, granted, and distributed by his commissaries written below to the poor of Christ for the love of God and to pious places for the remedy of his sins, in the building of pious places, making chapels, repairing doors, roofs, and walls of churches, just as and how it shall seem fit and pleasing to his fideicommissaries written below, etc." Subsequently, after the testator died, his wife gave birth to a daughter, who died within the age of pupillarity. Inquiry is now made concerning three matters. First, whether the mother of the said female ward can seek the legitime due to a mother by the law of nature from the goods of her daughters, and what is to be said regarding the Trebellian portion. Second, whether the bishop of the place may interfere within a year in the execution of that will. Third, whether after a year the execution devolves to the lord bishop with respect to matters not executed by the fideicommissaries. Regarding the first, it seems that the mother can deduct her legitime, because a mother succeeds to her daughter intestate, C. ad Tertul. throughout; nor can she be expressly deprived by the children, just as neither can the daughter herself, in Auth. ut cum de appel. cog. § aliud quoque capitulum. Likewise, the same seems to be said regarding the Trebellian portion: for the said substitution to pious causes seems to have been fideicommissary, since it was not made in direct words, but in oblique ones, as is clear there: "shall be given and distributed, etc.," according to what is noted in l. verbis civilibus and in l. centurio, ff. de vulg. & pup., c. si pater, de test. li. 6. Therefore, the daughter can deduct the Trebellian portion in the restitution: because although the Falcidian portion ceases in legacies made to pious places or to pious causes, as in auth. similiter, C. ad l. Falc., the Trebellian portion does not so cease, as the glossa notes in the said c. si pater. And since the daughter was not requested to restore purely, but upon the occurrence of a condition, namely if she should die within pupillary age, she could legitimately deduct two fourths, one owed by the law of nature, the other from the Trebellianum, according to those things that are held and noted in c. Raynutius and c. Raynaldus, de testa., noted by the gl. in l. Papinianus § meminisse, ff. de inoffi. test., which is supported by what is read and noted in l. quanquam, C. ad leg. Fal. But these things notwithstanding, I say that in our case the mother can claim nothing for herself by law, because the substitution made to the impubes was direct pupillary. This is clear from the fact that these fideicommissaries receive the inheritance from no one, but from themselves; and to those words, "shall be given, and distributed, etc.," these words are understood, namely that the fideicommissaries "shall receive, sell, etc.," as in Auth. de eccl. tit. § si quis autem; this is supported by what is read and noted in l. alio, de ali. & ciba. lega. Bar. disputes this broadly in our terms, and follows it in l. centurio, in repetitio, ff. de vulga. & pup. and in l. fundi Trebatiani, ff. de usufruc. lega., and there he reports having so advised four times; and c. cum tibi, de testa., makes for this, where the case is seen almost according to the common reading; for there it is clear

† that if a testator said to a stranger, "I commit my will to your disposition," he is deemed to have instituted him heir so that he may distribute the inheritance to pious causes. So it must be said in our case, that these fideicommissaries are heirs and directly substituted to the pupillus for pious causes; which is especially indicated by those words: "all his goods, etc.," and thus he called these fideicommissaries to all his goods; this is supported by what is read and noted in l. quidam testamento, ff. de vulg. & pup.

† Likewise, in doubt we must always interpret so that a substitution is direct rather than fideicommissary, especially when the substitution is made to pious causes, as in c. 1, de test. lib. 6. This being presupposed as most true, it is inferred that the mother can claim nothing. For although the son from his own person cannot exclude the mother, as I said above, nevertheless the father, by testating for the son, can. For that will is the father's, or rather a part of the father's; and this is most clearly decided in the said c. si pater, and it seems also to have been of the law of the Digest, as in l. Papinianus § meminisse, de inoffi. testa. Through this also the Trebellian portion ceases, which has no place in a direct substitution, said c. si pater. Likewise, under another head the Trebellian portion has no place here:

† because for pious causes the Trebellian portion ceases, just like the Falcidian portion, as is today the common opinion of the doctors, as held by more modern jurists in c. Raynaldus, de testa., by Bar. in l. Marcellus, ff. ad Trebel., where he answered to the gloss of the said c. 1 which I alleged above to the contrary, by Bar. in l. id quod pauperibus, C. de epi. & cle. It seems express in Auth. de eccl. tit. § si autem haeres, and l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de epi. & cle.; and thus I have seen it advised many times by the most outstanding men, and through this the answer is clear to all the contrary arguments formed above. I come to the second doubt, whether the bishop of the place may interfere in the execution within a year, or seek anything from the said inheritance. And first I say that in the present case he can seek nothing: because the bishop does not take a fourth, except from bequests made to the poor or to other pious causes, as in c. requisisti, de test., joined with the gl. in c. 2, de sepul., and in l. nulli, and in l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de epi. & cle.; the reason is clear from the things noted in c. officii, de test. If these fideicommissaries give anything to churches or pious places, the bishop will be able to demand a fourth from those pious places, if custom holds this: because they are seen to receive these goods from the testator himself, since he himself is said to do this through his fideicommissaries, ar. c. sane, de of. dele., and c. si apostolicae, de preb. li. 6; unless he gives it to some privileged cause for the fabric or for other things concerning perpetual divine worship; as for instance, that a chapel, or an altar, or a prebend, or something similar be constructed in a church. For from these a fourth is not deducted, as is read and noted in cap. fi. de test. I also say that within a year the bishop cannot interfere concerning the execution of those goods, because they are not wrongfully taken and uncertain; and thus the things noted in c. 2, de testa. lib. 6, and c. cum sit nimis, de Iudae. cease to apply, since they are the goods of that testator who willed them to be distributed to pious causes for his soul and the remedy of his sins, as shall seem fit and pleasing to his fideicommissaries; and thus the execution must be carried out by them, not by bishops, as in c. tua, and in c. Ioannes, de testa., and the said l. si quis ad declinandam, and l. nulli. Nevertheless, the bishop can interpose his office so that all things proceed according to the will of the deceased, as in the said c. tua, and c. Ioannes, in Auth. de ecc. ti. § si quis aut aedificationem; and this as to the second matter. I come to the third, whether after the lapse of a year he can supply the execution in matters not executed by the fideicommissaries? I say conclusively yes: because by common law after the lapse of a year the power of executing devolves to the bishop, as in c. nos quidem, and c. si haeredes, de test., and in Auth. de ecc. ti. § si quis aut aedificationem. Nevertheless, this year does not run except from the day of admonition, as is expressly gathered in the said c. nos, and the doctors commonly hold there, and it is more clearly gathered in auth. hoc amplius, C. de fideic., and in the body of the law from which it is drawn, as Fed. holds, consi. 114. I also say that the lawful year does not run except against the negligent, as is expressly gathered from the said c. nos quidem, on the word "neglexerit." And Ho. opines there, and more clearly Fed. in the place previously cited. Bart. also opines in the said auth. hoc amplius, and the text joined with the noted gl. is seen in Insti. de auct. tu. § item, on the word "distulerit"; that which is noted in c. quam sit, de ele. lib. 6, on the word "distulerit," also supports this. For if they are prevented from executing within the year from a legitimate cause, certainly the power does not devolve to the bishop, because time does not run

† against one unable to act, in c. quia diversitatem, de conces. pb., and in l. contra maiores, C. de inof. test. I would say the same if they could not do so conveniently, because we are said to be able to do that which we can do conveniently, as in l. Nepos Proculo, ff. de ver. sign., 22. q. 2, c. faciat homo. Nevertheless, bishops are accustomed to have statutes in which it is provided that this year runs for those having execution from the day of the testator's death, and thus without waiting for any warning that might be valid, as Fed. opines in the place previously cited. For bishops can make statutes, with the aid of the common law, as in c. 2, de constitu. lib. 6, where the glo. notes in clem. ne Romani, de ele., more fully by Io. And. in c. fi. de offi. archi. But I say that that statute claims a place for itself among mere executors, but not among these commissaries of whom we treat here: because these are not called mere executors, since they have to choose and discern for what cause and in what manner those goods are to be distributed,

† for an executor is properly one who exercises the bare office of execution: as if a testator had commanded that they should give a hundred to such a church, ar. in l. executorem, ff. de exec. rei iu. Notably says Bar. in l. quidam, ff. de leg. 2. It is necessary therefore that they first be admonished, unless the statute also provides concerning these persons having the power of choosing, whence the words of the statute must be inspected. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A mandatary, or surety, can sue the mandator, not only for the principal sum when he has paid on his behalf, but also for damages and interest.
2. A surety can pay for interest to be paid on the basis of a simple pact.
3. A surety is bound to propose the exceptions available to himself or to the principal, when he can.
4. Debtors of a city, if they pay a tyrant, even on his simple mandate, are discharged from the city.
5. One who calls someone to a just war is bound to him by the action on mandate for the reparation of all damages.
body: Since the matter has been discussed sufficiently abundantly by the excellent doctor dominus Antonius, the first consultant, I will be content with the addition of certain things beyond what was previously said, which seemed to me to conclude most clearly in this matter. And first, for an easier conclusion, I premise that the said Ioannes was truly, both civilly and naturally, obligated to the said Count Rolandus by the suretyship made by him, since, being placed in prison, he wrote to him that he should be surety for him, and also, after his release, he approved it and anew promised to preserve the same Count Rolandus indemnified from that promise. For one placed in prison, provided he does not become a slave, just as that Ioannes was not, according to the note in l. hostes, ff. de captiu. & postlim. reuer., especially by Bartolus, and Innocentius in cap. olim. 1. de restitu. spol., can appoint a procurator and obligate himself to another, particularly as to the one detaining him for his own liberation, as is notably proved in l. metum, § sed licet, ff. quod met. cau., and l. Papinianus exuli, ff. de mino., noted by Innocentius in c. cum locum, de sponsal., and Bartolus in l. qui in carcerem, ff. quod me. cau. Secondly, I premise,

† that a mandatary, or surety, can sue the mandator, not only for the principal sum when he has paid on his behalf, but also for damages and interest, as is proved in c. peruenit, and c. constitutus, de fideiussoribus, and in l. inter causas, § impendia, and l. quae mutuum, in fi., ff. mand.; indeed Innocentius maintains in c. sicut, 2, de iurei., that he can sue the mandator even for damages which he suffered by an unforeseen event (casus fortuitus), if they were plausibly expected to happen, and Ioannes Andreae follows him in regula accessorium, de reg. iur., lib. 6, in Mercurialibus. Thirdly, I premise thus: regularly, all defenses (exceptiones) competent to the principal are competent to the surety, and he is bound to raise them; if he omits them, knowing that they are competent to the debtor, and pays, he has no action on mandate, on the ground that he paid out of hatred for that debtor; and although an ignorance of fact may excuse, an ignorance of law does not. These things are proved in l. omnes exceptiones, ff. de excep., and in l. si fideiussor, ff. manda. Fourthly, it being presupposed that if the surety did whatever he could, nor was there any failure on his part to have the defenses competent to the defendant or to himself admitted, but he was compelled by force to pay without his own fault, even if this occurred through the injustice of superiors, he can nevertheless sue the mandator. This is proved according to the letter a contrario sensu in the said l. exceptiones, and Bartolus follows this there, as well as Ioannes Andreae in the said regula damnum; I adduce for this a most open text joined with the gloss on the word *iudicium* in l. nam & seruius, ff. de nego. gest. These premises having been set down, I say that on manifold grounds the said Count Rolandus has recourse against the said Ioannes, both for the principal sum paid and for damages and interest. And first, because he paid for him pursuant to a preceding mandate, and on the occasion of the default (mora) of the said Ioannes he suffered those damages, as in the legal authorities alleged above. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that he ought to have raised the defenses competent to the principal, especially since the principal notified him, and thus he could not pretend ignorance, said l. si fideius. For to this I respond manifoldly, even assuming that those who caused the delay had been true procurators, and even assuming the justice and truth of those defenses: for I say that a surety is not bound to raise defenses with any shame (pudor) to himself, although by the rigor and subtlety of law he might have raised them. On this there is a very notable text in l. Quintus, ff. mand., where it is said,

† that a surety for the payment of interest arising from a simple pact can pay, nor is he bound to raise the defense that it was not contracted by stipulation from the fiction of a naked pact—which is observed among practical men—because he is not bound to consult another's interest, namely the principal's, with shame to himself, as is notably said there. So to the purpose: since that count had promised to pay that Sempronius, even at the time when he was a rebel against the Church, it seemed unseemly for so great a man to allege religion, or another defense which did not most clearly conclude against the justice of the claimant, since from this the good faith and reputation of lords is wont to be diminished among their own people and strangers, especially because it seems shameful to reprobate customs which one previously approved: 32, q. 5, c. horrendus, and in l. creditores, ff. de pri. cr., noted by Bartolus in l. fi., C. de spon., and in c. quemad., de iureiur. Secondly, just as a surety is not bound to raise defenses with any shame of fact, said l. Quintus, so and with greater reason, neither with great danger to his own goods. For that Sempronius was far more powerful than he, as the outcome showed, whence from the denial of the principal sum and the raising of those dishonorable defenses he could deservedly and justly fear the destruction of his status, or the loss of his goods or the greater part thereof. He is therefore excused if, led by that fear, he did not raise them, as is excellently proved in l. nouissime, ff. quod cum fal. tu.; for fear regarding all one's goods, or the greater part of them, excuses, as in c. Abbas, quod met. cau., and c. frequens, de resti. spo., lib. 6. Thirdly, it is proved most clearly by another reason:

† a surety is bound to raise the defenses competent to himself or to the principal when he can, as because he is before a competent judge; but where he cannot on account of the power of the adversary, whom he is not able conveniently to resist, he is not bound; nay rather, if he pays, he has recourse against the principal. This is proved most clearly in the said l. nam & Seruius, joined with the gloss on the word *iudicium*, ff. de neg. gest. For there those about whom the text speaks promised in prison to their captor, and thus a defense was competent to them by l. pe., ff. quod me. cau., because they were slaves, and thus could not be civilly obligated; and yet, because that defense would not have benefited them in fact if they had raised it, they have recourse against the third party for whom they paid, because it was not to be imputed to them, as it says there; and although that happened through an injustice not done to them, nevertheless, as the gloss says there—which Bartolus notes remarkably there—because that injury occurred by the act of that principal who did not return, it is not imputed to them. Whence they sue for damage against the principal. Thus it happened precisely in our case. For this Count Rolandus did not have a competent judge, at least easily, against that Sempronius, nor would those defenses have profited him, but rather they would have provoked Sempronius to worse things against him; and thus he was justified in remaining silent, even if they had been true: said l. nam & Seruius, and 11, q. 3, c. si quando. Nor did the said Rolandus pay spontaneously; rather, he waited for the invasion and devastation of some of his goods, and the said Count Rolandus often required the said Ioannes, by law and in fact, to relieve him from that danger and not to leave him long obligated under that suretyship, as in c. fin., de fideiuss., and l. si pro eo, C. man.; whence at least from this delay, because he ceased for a long time to free him from his suretyship, he is bound to relieve him from all damage and interest, because whatever arises from his delay ought to be imputed to him: l. necessario, ff. de peri. & con. rei uen., and the said c. peruenit, and c. dilecta, de for. compet., especially since the damage was inflicted out of hatred of Ioannes himself, and thus it ought to be turned back upon him, as is notably said in l. si merces, § certe, ff. loc. Fourthly, what is noted by Bartolus in tract. de tyranno makes excellently for this, where among other things he says,

† that if debtors of a city pay a tyrant, even if upon his simple proclamation, they are freed with respect to the city, because, led by just fear, they paid the tyrant, nor could they plausibly plead defenses without great danger, and especially when that command was made out of hatred of the city; and for this he alleges the said l. nouissime, and l. Paulo Callimacho, ff. de leg. 3, with many similar laws. So in the matter at hand, the lord Count Rolandus, the surety, is excused if he paid without having raised the defenses, even if true; for he paid rather wishing to provide for his own danger and to leave the burden of recovery to Ioannes, the principal. What is noted in a similar matter by Ioannes Andreae in the said regula damnum, in Mercurialibus, regarding a surety who paid undue usuries, supports this. If, therefore, payment is justly made to a tyrant who has no right when fear is pressing, so also to that Sempronius, even if he had been a rebel against the Church. For, as Augustine says regarding heretics, we sustain some whom we unwillingly tolerate: 23, q. 1, c. quisquis, and 14, q. 7, c. quicunque. Likewise, with respect to damages, the dictum of Innocentius in the said c. sicut makes most clearly for this, where he says that one who calls another to a just war is bound to him by the action on mandate for the reparation of all damages, even if he suffered unjust damages, because this is of the nature of mandate, even if those damages happen by an unforeseen event, provided that that unforeseen event could plausibly happen. So it must be said here: since this man suffered damage on the occasion of the mandate, even if unjustly, he ought nevertheless to have recourse against the mandator. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that he was excommunicated because he pursued a Cardinal with hostility. For one can respond to this manifoldly. And first, that for our own utility, especially that we may avoid damage and the slaughter of men, we may refrain from avoiding excommunicates, at least in the case of a simple canon, as was true in our case with respect to a momentary payment, as seems to be singularly proved in c. si uere, de sent. excom.; and Innocentius agrees there in the beginning. Whence, lest that Sempronius should invade the entire land of the said Count Rolandus, as he had begun, he could justly make payment to him. Likewise, payment is not made to his men, but to his servant, who lawfully communicates with his excommunicated master: in c. qui multos, 11, q. 3. Likewise, as I seem to understand, that Cardinal was not of the obedience of Ioannes, as Sempronius himself was, and thus as toward him he did not enjoy the privilege of the Cardinalate: arg. c. licet, de electio., and 23. dist., c. in nomine Domini. Moreover, according to many, a debt is lawfully paid to an excommunicate, as Innocentius maintained in c. ueritatis, de do. & contu., and the gloss of Ioannes, 15, q. 6, c. nos sanctorum, and Archidiaconus there; whence, although some say the contrary, nevertheless, taking into account that the point is doubtful and there was danger in delay, it is lawfully paid: said c. si uere. For excommunication ought to harm the excommunicate himself, and not a third party; communication is withdrawn to his own detriment, and not that of a third party. Whence, lest the devastation of the territory of Count Rolandus himself should follow from this, he justly paid, even on the premise that he was truly excommunicated and also a heretic. For if communication with an excommunicate is permitted for his sustenance, lest he perish: said c. quoniam multos, in fi., it is permitted with greater reason in favor of the subjects of the said Count Rolandus, lest from the invasion of Sempronius they should perish most violently. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If a sentence was rendered between present parties, it is presumed that the judge had jurisdiction, because it passed into res judicata.
2. A legate, even de latere, cannot take away a right acquired by another.
3. The prince alone can take away a right acquired by another.
4. Possession of jurisdiction is acquired through a single act that is not accustomed to be granted out of grace.
5. The March of Ancona pertains in spiritual and temporal matters to the Church.
6. A fact is not called ancient before the lapse of twenty years as regards impugning a sentence for nullity.
7. Knowledge of the possessor is required [?] in the acquisition of incorporeal rights.
body: Having invoked the protection of the Savior and of His mother Mary: In the cause and dispute which is presently pending between the community or corporation of Monte Santa Maria in Cassiano on the one side, and the community or corporation of Montefano on the other side, in the province of the March of Ancona, concerning the nullity of the sentence rendered by masters Bartolomeo of Cremona and Antonio de Civolis of Trent, doctors of laws, then commissioners of the magnificent and potent lord Pandolfo de' Malatesti, as well as concerning certain boundaries of those same communities, as is most clearly evident from the acts had in this cause before various judges, I shall touch briefly upon certain principles of the matter, since I have not had time to review all the acts because of the haste of the party seeking this consilium. It is presupposed to me in fact that all things are true which are related in the consilium of the excellent doctor, Master Matteo de' Feliciani. And first, it seems that the said community of Montefano sustains a most just cause, since the sentence was rendered in its favor by the said commissioners now 15 years ago; and although an appeal was made from it by the other party, it was nevertheless not prosecuted within the due time, and thus the sentence remained valid; thus it passed into res judicata, as in c. personas, and c. si Romana, and cap. oblatae, with many similar texts, de app., which creates law between the parties even if it contained injustice in itself, as in l. res judicata, ff. de re. iur., and l. ingenuum, ff. de sta. ho., and c. cum inter, de re iu., and c. quod ad consultationem, eo. ti., and in auth. ei qui ap., C. de temp. appe., and in cle. sicut appellationem, de ap. The defect of jurisdiction alleged in the delegator with respect to the community of Monte Santa Maria does not stand in the way. For this is answered in multiple ways. First, through the notable and singular statement of Inn. in c. cum in iure, de off. dele., and Io. Cal. is of the same view in c. quoniam contra, de proba. For Inn. says,

† that where a sentence was rendered between present parties, it is presumed that the judge had jurisdiction, because it passed into res judicata; hence the burden of proof rests on the one alleging the defect of jurisdiction, and many have said the same if it was rendered contumaciously against an absent party, especially when the fact is ancient, as noted in the said laws, especially by the more modern authorities; and to this effect makes l. Pomponius, §. rati, ff. de procur., and what the gloss notes in c. 1, de ele., lib. 6. For it is clear that after litis contestatio, a defect of mandate is not objected so far as to require the proctor to speak concerning his mandate, since the other party seems to have consented to him. Item, and all the more strongly is this to be said in the case of one who appealed from the judge, or appealed and did not prosecute, and especially since the fact here is sufficiently ancient. For the magnificent lord Pandolfo could have had delegated jurisdiction, or perhaps his jurisdiction was prorogued, and thus in doubt it must be presumed from silence for so long a time. To the same effect is what is noted in the said cap. cum in iure, and c. bonae, the first of that name, de ele.; for it says that one must presume in favor of the sentence after it has passed into res judicata, as in the laws previously cited. Secondly, it is argued from a sufficient enumeration of the parts: either the said lord de' Malatesti had jurisdiction in the said castle of Monte Santa Maria, or none. In the first case, in doubt that sentence is valid, because a delegate discharges the office of the delegator, as in c. sane, de officio & potest. iudi. delegat., against which the Governor of the March could not commit the cause anew, because

† a delegate, even de latere, cannot take away an acquired right from another, in cap. fin., de confirmat. utili., and alter the order of law, as the gloss says following Spec. in cap. fin., de haeret., lib. 6.

† For it belongs to the prince alone to take away an acquired right from another, according to what is noted in c. constitutus, de relig. domi., and in the rule indultum a iure, de regu. iu. in 6., and 25. quaest. 2., in summa. If, however, the said lord did not have jurisdiction, it seems it should be said that either by litigating before his delegates appointed in this matter, those men of Monte Santa Maria prorogued the jurisdiction of that lord de' Malatesti—I do not say of his delegates, as some have inconsiderately alleged in this cause. For that dispute does not apply here as to whether the jurisdiction of a delegate can be prorogued; for that inquiry has a place when the delegate wishes to take cognizance beyond the matters included in the rescript, according to what is noted in capitu. cum olim, the first of that name, and capitu. P. & G., and capitu. de causis, de offi. deleg. But since in our case these delegates took cognizance only of the cause, and between the persons, concerning which they were given the commission made to them, it is inquired in vain whether delegated jurisdiction can be prorogued, because these commissioners completely discharged the office of that lord de' Malatesti, as in the laws cited above; and thus it seems rather that the jurisdiction of that lord was prorogued, who, since he was otherwise an ordinary, could by his own right have his jurisdiction prorogued, and by virtue of the prorogation commit the cause, as in l. 1, ff. de iud., and l. 3, C. de iur. om. iu., l. ex consensu, C. de epis. aud., and c. significasti, with what is noted there, de fo. comp. For a prorogued jurisdiction is of that nature of which the principal jurisdiction is, as noted in c. P. & G., and it is clear in the said l. 2; whence just as he could commit his own jurisdiction, l. una, C. qui pro iurisdi., so too a prorogued one. Moreover, in the prorogation of jurisdiction, at least an ordinary one, the tacit consent of the parties suffices, by the argument in l. 1, C. de iurisdict. om. iud., and l. 2, ff. de iudi., noted by Bar. in l. 1, ff. eo. tit., and Inno. in c. ad petitionem, de accu., in princ.; but this was notorious to the communities themselves, that their syndics were litigating before the delegates of that lord; therefore the tacit consent of their communities ought to suffice. And thus many things alleged by some seem to be refuted which emphasize that the syndic of Monte Santa Maria did not have a mandate to prorogue jurisdiction, because the syndics, but rather the communities themselves, seem to have prorogued it by suffering those syndics to litigate before them; and to this effect is the notable text joined with the gloss in the said c. cum olim. Or, failing prorogation, one must say that this lord de' Malatesti acquired jurisdiction in his own right by exercising this jurisdictional act upon that community. For to delegate a cause is an act of jurisdiction, as in l. imperium, ff. de iurisdi. om. iud., in fi., noted by the gloss in c. si a subdelegato, de of. dele., lib. 6.

† Moreover, by a single act which is not accustomed to be granted out of favor, possession of jurisdiction is acquired, as noted by Inno. in c. cum ecclesia Sutrina, de cau. pos. & prop., and in c. bonae, the second of that name, de postu. praela., and in c. dilectus, de cap. mo., Bart. in l. 1, §. hoc interdicto, ff. de itine. actuque priu., by reason of which those things which the possessor exercises are valid, as noted by the doctors following Inn. in c. cum dilectis, de reli. do., and c. olim. 2, de resti. spo.; to which makes c. constitutionis, de iure patro., and c. querelam, de elect. Thirdly, there makes principally what the gloss notes in c. significasti, de fo. comp., which says that a party litigating knowingly before a judge who is not his own, even though he could not have prorogued his jurisdiction, as in the case of a cleric with respect to a layman, nevertheless cannot go against the sentence, at least as a pact; just as an ineffective acceptilatio, ff. de pact., l. si unus, §. penul., and ff. de accep., l. si acceptilatum; to which makes l. 2, C. communia utriusque iudi., where there is a good text. Fourthly, it makes because I hear it is notorious that the magnificent and potent lord Carlo de' Malatesti at the time of that sentence was exercising all manner of jurisdiction in the said castle of Monte Santa Maria, who also committed the cause generally to Master Bartolomeo, one of the said commissioners. And thus at least on this ground the sentence ought to be valid, even presupposing that the said Carlo had not had jurisdiction there by law. For by reason of public utility, since he is reputed as lord, the things done by him are proved to be valid, l. Barbarius, ff. de offi. praeto., and 2, q. 6, §. veruntamen.

† Fifthly, lord Pandolfo was, and is, lord of Montefano. But in the action for establishing boundaries, each party is plaintiff and defendant, as in c. ex literis, de proba., and ff. fami. ercis., l. inter cohaeredes, §. qui fami. ercis.; therefore the said lord was able to commit the cause, insofar as the dispute was brought against his subject, because the plaintiff follows the forum of the defendant, de for. comp., c. cum sit generale. But these things notwithstanding, I judge that the contrary opinion prevails, and I say that that sentence is null for multiple reasons. First, because it was rendered by him, or by the authority of him, concerning whom it is notoriously evident that he had no jurisdiction in this cause.

† For the whole province of the March of Ancona belongs in spirituals and temporals to the jurisdiction of the Church, as is proved in the Extravagante of John XXII which begins Dierum excrescente malitia, Romana ecclesia, and today at the present time it exercises all manner of jurisdiction. Therefore lord Pandolfo could not delegate this cause to those doctors. For no one gives what he does not have, l. traditio, ff. de acquir. re. domi., and c. de multa, 1, q. 7, and c. quod autem, de iure patro.; wherefore the sentence rendered by those men as lacking jurisdiction does not stand with legal force, C. si a non compe. iudi., throughout, and c. at si clerici, de iud., and c. uno, de offi. deleg.; wherefore, notwithstanding the desertion of the appeal, the said community of Santa Maria can sue for nullity, as is the text in l. si expressim, ff. de ap., and the text joined with the gloss in c. licet, de sent. excom., lib. 6, through the doctors in clem. saepe, de appel. To the aforesaid makes the very notable gloss in cap. cum iure, de offi. delega., which says that one ought to preserve the instrument of the judge's power, because otherwise there is no presumption in favor of the sentence, and this is discussed more fully there. Secondly, the said sentence is null because one of the compromise-commissioners committed the cognizance of the cause to his co-delegate, which he could not do, since he was a delegate not from the prince, as in cap. cum causam, de appel., and l. a iudice, C. de iud.; for although a delegate from an inferior prince can subdelegate a non-jurisdictional article, according to the notable statement of Innoc. in c. cum Bertholdus, de iudic., for which the text makes according to one interpretation, and the notable gloss of civil law takes the same view in authen. de defen. civi. near the end, he nevertheless cannot commit a jurisdictional article, as in the laws cited above. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that he committed his powers to a colleague: the same reason of prohibition exists in a colleague as in a stranger, and the laws speak in this matter without distinction; for this makes the gloss in c. is cui, de offi. deleg., lib. 6, and the said c. cum causam. It is therefore just as if Master Bartolomeo had proceeded alone, in which case it is undisputed that a process conducted before one of two delegates is invalid, as in c. causam matrimonii, and in c. uno delegatorum, de off. deleg. Thirdly, the said sentence falls because of a defect of judicial order: because it is said that the suit had not been contested. Item, the lord de' Malatesti, since he recognizes a superior, could not commit the cause simply and plainly, without noise and form of trial, and thus remove the solemnities, because this belongs only to the prince or to one having the rights of a prince, according to what is noted by the gloss in cap. fin., de haere., lib. 6, and Spec. follows this in ti. de leg., §. superest, ver. sed nunquid. Fourthly, it makes that wherever the party in whose favor a sentence was rendered takes up the dispute before a competent judge concerning the justice or injustice of the sentence, if the judge finds the sentence unjust, he ought to retract it, notwithstanding that it passed into res judicata, as Innocent notedly states in capitul. cum dilecti, de rescript., and capitul. cum Bertoldus, de re iudica. But in our case, as I am told, that community of Montefano took up this dispute; therefore, if the judge rejects it as unjust, he ought to have retracted it, as he did. Fifthly, I prove this by a subtle reason: jurisdiction over the community of Monte Santa Maria never pertained, neither by law nor by fact, to lord Pandolfo. But at the time of that commission and litigation, lord Carlo was exercising jurisdiction de facto in the said territory; whence lord Pandolfo did not commit that cause simply to those doctors, but only insofar as it pertained to him, as if on the part of the community of Montefano, which community pertained and pertains to him; whence he said that that community was his; he did not speak thus of the community of Monte Santa Maria, as if placing hope that lord Carlo, although in general, committed the cause to Master Bartolomeo, one of those two commissioners, but they were the said commissioners of lord Pandolfo alone, who had no jurisdiction over the said community of Monte Santa Maria; therefore by law itself the sentence was null, especially because, as I said, the said lord Pandolfo did not intend to commit it alone; for this makes capit. cum super abbatia, and what is noted there, de offi. deleg., and c. ex parte Astensis, de conces. praeben., and what Barto. notes in l. si is, ff. de acqui. haere. Now I come to the response to the contrary arguments, which seem at first glance to urge strongly. And first, to the first point, I say that it does not appear that the parties were present here at the sentence; and presupposing that the parties had been present, I say that a defect of jurisdiction is sufficiently proved here on the part of the community of Monte Santa Maria. For the common law is in their favor, as well as the notoriety of fact, from which it is evident that full jurisdiction in the said community pertains to the Roman Church; therefore, someone else exercising it is presumed to have usurped it, unless he shows a title or a colorable possession, as they hold in a similar matter in c. ad decimas, de rest. spol., lib. 6; 100. dist., c. contra morem makes to this effect. Item, as I said just above, lord Pandolfo did not intend to commit the cause except with respect to Montefano. Nor does the fact being ancient stand in the way.

† First, because there is a notable opinion that before the lapse of 20 years a fact is not called ancient as to impugning a sentence for nullity, even with respect to order, as Joan. Cal. maintained in the said c. quoniam, de proba. Item, it is otherwise concerning forgery, because it can be objected within 20 years, as in c. cum venerabilis, de exce., and l. querelam, C. de fal.; therefore, the same must be said all the more strongly regarding the nullity of a sentence from a defect of jurisdiction; c. super eo, and what is noted there, de fal., makes to this effect. Item, the antiquity of the fact relieves, unless the defects are openly proved, for a presumption ceases where the truth openly appears. It is also evident that lord Carlo restored the said community to the Roman Church as its lady, as is presupposed to me in the fact; nor did lord Pandolfo ever have anything to do there, because he did not have jurisdiction there, nor did that party intend to prorogue his jurisdiction, which is evident from the fact that lord Carlo, who de facto exercised jurisdiction there, committed this cause, whence that community of Monte Santa Maria was litigating by virtue of the commission made by lord Carlo; for prorogation ought not to be presumed, since the contrary is established from conjectures, because it is not easily presumed to have occurred, as in c. cum in iure, de offi. deleg., and l. unica, C. de man. princi. Nor is it plausible that anyone would wish to prorogue jurisdiction into a non-lord, since the one who conducts himself as lord committed that cause to him. From this I also say that lord Pandolfo did not intend through that commission to acquire possession of jurisdiction, which he did not intend; this is evident from the words of the commission, by the argument in l. fi., ff. quemadmo. ser. amit., and what Innocen. notes in the previously cited c. bonae. Nor could he even have acquired it, because in the acquisition of these incorporeal rights the knowledge of the possessor is required, which is not proved here, neither truly nor presumptively, l. 2, C. de servi. & aqua, noted by Innoc. in the said previously cited c. bonae, and in c. conquerente, de off. ord., and by Bart. in l. 1, ff. de aqua plu. arc., and in l. si publicanus, §. in vectigalibus, ff. de publ. To the third argument I answer that that gloss is not simply true, nor is it commonly approved there by the doctors. For a null sentence has the force of a pact when, after it has been rendered, it is approved with certain knowledge by the parties, and thus is understood l. 2, C. communia utriusque, as noted there, and in l. unica, C. qui pro sua iurisd., and l. licet, C. de iud., by Anto. de But. in the said c. significasti, which does not happen here. To the fourth argument it is answered first as I have said, because although the said lord committed it, nevertheless the commissioners proceeded as delegates of lord Pandolfo alone, as is evident from their sentence. Item, since lord Carlo had or would have had no title there, whatever he did was worth nothing, according to what is fully noted by Innocen. in cap. nihil est, de elect., by Bartol. in the tractate De tyranno; to which make cap. alienationes, 12. quaestio. 2, and cap. 1, de schisma., and l. decernimus, C. de sacrosanct. eccl. Law Barbarius does not stand in the way: for it is sufficiently answered by Innocen. in the said c. nihil est. To the last argument I say that if the words of the sentence of the said delegates are well inspected, one of the community of Montefano initiated the claim before the said delegates; although each party is plaintiff and defendant in these shared actions, nevertheless he holds the place of plaintiff who first summoned the other to judgment, as in l. in tribus, de proba. I conclude, therefore, that the role of the apostolic judge in this cause will be as lord Matteo Feliciani concludes in his consilium, if those things which he relates in the fact are true, etc.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A prelate without the authority of a superior, and especially without the consent of his chapter, cannot submit to arbitration concerning the rights of the church.
2. A prelate alone, by making a compromise (transactio), does not bind his successor.
3. A judgment and a contract entered into in the person of a prelate in the name of the church effectively pass to the church, if no alienation of the rights of the church is entailed.
4. The presumption of fraud ceases from the quality of the judge and of the persons.
body: Having implored the aid of Almighty God, the question of law is asked: whether, upon viewing the compromissum and the award following thereupon entered into between the reverend father, the late Lord Bartolomeo, former bishop of Massa, on the one part, and Bartolomeo di Stephano da Castronuovo, on the other part, and also having weighed the confirmation of the said award or sentence subsequently made by the Lord John, then Pope XXII, any remedies, and what ones, are available to the same Bartolomeo di Stephano or to his successor against and toward the successor of the Lord Bartolomeo, bishop, and the bishopric, or toward the bishop of Massa. And first, it seems that no remedy is available. For the pronouncement does not stand as a sentence of an apostolic delegate, because, since he was a layman, the delegation made to him by the Supreme Pontiff, especially by word of mouth (oraculo vivae vocis), collapsed by operation of law, per cap. statutum, de rescrip. lib. 6. Nor did it stand as an arbitrament by virtue of the compromissum.

† For a prelate, without the authority of a superior, and especially without the consent of his chapter, cannot submit to arbitration concerning immovable property or concerning the rights of the church, at least so far as that the obligation should pass to the church, at least through the death of the one submitting to arbitration. For just as he alone cannot directly alienate church property, or perpetually bind his church, 12. quaestio. 2. capitu. sine exceptione, and capit. 1. de his quae fi. a praela., so neither can he do so indirectly, namely by submitting to arbitration, as in capitu. pervenit, de arbi., and there Hostiensis and Speculum explicitly hold this, eod. titu. §. restat, ver. sed nunquid clericis, and §. finitur, ver. sed nunquid praelatus, and Federicus consi. 20, and Lapus in allegatione 10. Another proof is offered

† by reason: it is certain that a prelate alone, by making a compromise (transactio), does not bind his successor, but the compromise is deemed strictly personal, as is proven in c. veniens de caetero, de transact.; therefore the same must be said of a compromissum made to someone as an arbitrator, and of the award following thereupon. For it is a kind of transactio, as is read and noted in authen. si verò contingerit, C. de iud., and in the body from which it is drawn, in tit. ut diffe. iud., and noted by Innocent in capitu. Quintavallis, de iureiurand., and Bartolus in l. societatem. §. arbitrorum, ff. pro socio. And secondly and principally, the said award is invalid because it contains in itself usurious wickedness in that it condemns the bishop to pay six florins for each hundred until he pays the principal contained in the said condemnation; for although usury is not deemed to arise except from a contract of loan (mutuum), as in c. consuluit, de usu., fully through Jo. And. in regula, peccatum, de reg. iur. lib. 6. in Mercu., nevertheless a true or fictitious loan suffices, as is read and noted in c. in civitate, and c. naviganti, de usu.; it is clear in the case of one who sells merchandise for more than it is worth because he defers payment of the price. For there is not a true loan there, but a fictitious one, because the buyer is feigned to pay the true purchase price and to receive it back as a loan from the seller, and to give for usury that excess over what is owed, as is noted in the said texts of law. And so by equal reason it seems must be said in the matter at hand, that the bishop is feigned to pay those 200 florins, and subsequently to receive a loan, and to pay six per hundred, which is unlawful, as per tot. ti. de usu., especially in d. c. in civitate, and c. naviganti. And thirdly, the confirmation made by John, then pope, does not stand in the way of the aforesaid, because it was not made in common form, but conditionally, or under a condition; for he confirms all things 'as they reasonably proceeded, etc.' Which confirmation indeed confers no new right, but confirms an old right, if any right existed; hence it accomplishes little or nothing, as in c. examinata, de confir. uti., and in c. quia diversitatem, joined with the gloss, de conces. praeben.; hence it does not cause a personal compromise to become real, as is the noted gloss which all follow in d. c. veniens. But notwithstanding these points, which in truth, if subtly weighed, do not stand in the way, I judge that the contrary opinion prevails. And first, I say that to the said Bartolomeo, or to his successor, the remedy of claiming the said 200 florins is available, because they are under obligation by virtue of the said sentence and award, although the successor or the bishop of Massa may pay six per hundred and avoid the payment of the two hundred florins, as is contained in the award. I am moved because, although a prelate cannot by contract or compromissum alienate immovable property of the church without solemnities, as in the cited laws, he can nevertheless compromise and contract in the name of the church in such a way that the obligation effectively passes to the church, if there is no alienation of the rights of the church, as is proven in cap. dilecti, de for. compet., and c. 2. de preca., and c. 1. de so., and cle. j. de reb. eccle. non alie., noted by Hostiensis in c. contingit, de transact.; it is proven in a similar case: a tutor transacts concerning the property of a ward, l. interdum. §. qui tutelam, ff. de fur.; therefore also a prelate, who is deemed the tutor of the church, 16. q. j. c. in canonibus, noted by the gloss in c. auditis, de in integ. restit.
