Likewise an administrator of a city, as l. praeses, C. de transact.; therefore also a prelate, who has broader power, in c. cum nobis, in fin. de electio.; what is read and noted in cap. fin. v. q. iij. supports this. Likewise a procurator having general and free power compromises, as in c. qui ad agendum, de procu. lib. 6; therefore also a bishop, who has general and free power, as does any other prelate, d. cap. cum nobis, and d. ca. fin. v. q. iij., which is a good text joined with the gloss in l. nulli, ff. de transact., where it says that a prelate alone can compromise regarding the property of the church, if the property about which there is dispute remains with the church by reason of the compromise, and the church is obligated to give or do something; for then no alienation follows, but rather the condition of the church is made better. In which case the consent of a superior or of another is not required, as l. cum hi. §. quid ergo, and what the gloss notes in §. si uni, ff. de transact., which principally occurs in our case. The compromissum was therefore valid, at least by virtue of the approval subsequently following, since it was a kind of compromise made regarding the alienation of church property, and the church was made better off. And even presupposing that it had been harmed, it must be imputed to the church if it did not seek restitution in integrum, at least from the guardian of the said Lord Bartolomeo, according to what is held and noted in d. c. 1. de in integr. restitu. lib. 6. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that an alienation of the rights of the church rather follows, because the church is obligated to give six per hundred annually under the obligation, which a prelate alone cannot do, d. cap. de caetero. For I say that that annual payment is not an obligation, but lies in the faculty of paying. For only the payment of the two hundred florins is under an obligation of paying, and thus the church can, if it wishes, discharge itself by a single payment, as is clear from the form of the award and sentence. In support of this is what is read and noted in l. miles. §. decem, ff. de re iudi. And most especially the aforesaid things proceed because the said Chetius was not a mere arbitrator, but also an apostolic delegate, and he proceeded both as delegate and as arbitrator, as is clear from the tenor of the sentence, which he could do; this is proven in c. nisi, de praebend.; what Innocent notes in c. cum ex officii, de praescript. supports this. And thus, since there was no appeal from his sentence, it passed into res judicata, de re iud. c. quod ad consultationem. And the sentence of a delegate passed to the church and to the successor, although only the prelate was in judgment, as noted in c. edoceri, de rescript.; d. c. dilecti, de for. compe. supports this. For the said Lord Bartolomeo approved the apostolic delegation and the compromissum and the award following thereupon, and acted in the name of his bishopric; and the church never dies, 12. q. 2. ca. liberti,

† and thus the judgment and contract in the person of the prelate in the name of the church pass effectively to the church, since no alienation of church rights is inflicted, and so the said award, especially after approval followed, since it is a kind of contract, as I said above; for it was thus quasi a purchase of the rights of the said Bartolomeo, which purchase indeed the prelate can sufficiently make in the name of the church, since he acquires for the church; cap. 2. de dona., and c. aurum, 12. quaestio. 2., and c. quicunque suffragio, ea. causa & quaestio support this. From which it can be inferred that even without the apostolic confirmation, the obligation arising from the said award and sentence passed effectively to the church, especially since no ambition or fraud is to be presumed from the quality of the person of the delegate and arbitrator, who was in this city of Siena a man of the highest repute.

† For from the quality of the judge and arbitrators the presumption of fraud ceases, as is a good text in c. nisi, de praeben. And thus that transactio must be called real, d. l. praeses. Nor does the said c. veniens, and cap. caeterum, de transactio. stand in the way, where a transactio is said to be personal and not real without the confirmation of a superior. For it can be answered in a two-fold way. First, that those texts of law apply when, by occasion of it, perpetual prejudice is caused to the church, as because its goods or rights are alienated, and thus those texts speak properly. But in our case no alienation follows, but rather the acquisition of the rights of the said curia, about which there was dispute, and that annual payment of six florins per hundred is in the faculty of the church itself, and not in obligation; whence the Church of Massa can discharge itself by a single payment of two hundred florins, as I said above; whence, just as other contracts and judgments pass to the church and successor, as in the laws cited above, so also these which are under discussion here. Secondly and principally, that presupposing without prejudice to truth that the aforesaid did not stand in the way, nevertheless by apostolic confirmation the aforesaid things are rendered valid, and pass to the church and successor. For by apostolic confirmation made from certain knowledge (ex certa scientia) a confirmed act is validated if it had been invalid, and is made real if it was previously personal, as is proven in cap. 1. de transact. with what is noted there, and in cap. 1. and 2. de confir. uti. To such an extent that no one short of the Roman pontiff can take cognizance of the validity or invalidity of that act, as there. To the second, that the act is made real and passes to the successor through apostolic confirmation, I allege the express case in d. c. veniens; that this confirmation was indeed made ex certa scientia is proven from the tenor of the acts in the statement of facts. For as often as those things which are confirmed are specifically expressed in the confirmation, the superior is said to confirm ex certa scientia, because those words which are accustomed to be inserted in a confirmation, namely, 'as and in what manner they proceeded, etc.', stand not conditionally, but causatively; whence those words 'as reasonably' are expounded as 'because reasonably,' as is proven in c. pen. de confir. uti. and the text and doctors there. In our case, all things that are in the principal matter are expounded in the confirmatory letter. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the annual payment of those florins per hundred is not specifically contained therein, because I say that it was confirmed no less, if it is said to have been made ex certa scientia, because, as has often been mentioned above, that payment is not in obligation, but only in faculty; whence there was no need to narrate it specifically. For what is principal in the matter and turns upon the obligation is narrated, namely the condemnation in two hundred florins and the adjudication of the rights of the church. Nor does the said Bartolomeo or his successor wish or intend to claim anything beyond 200 florins; and beyond the aforesaid, this is sufficiently gathered from the clause therein at the end, 'supplying any defects which might perhaps have intervened in all the premises'; concerning the virtue and power of which enough is had through Spec. titu. de leg. §. nunc ostendendum, ver. 18., and through Archid. in c. Cenomanense. 62. dist., through the text and doctors in clem. pastoralis, de re iu.; which clause is never appended when the confirmation is made in common form, since that gives no right, but simply affirms an old right, as I said above. I conclude therefore that the premises are valid on three grounds: first, by virtue of the delegation; second, from arbitral power and subsequent approval; third, from the apostolic confirmation. From which is proven the first point mentioned above. Therefore, the said Bartolomeo or his successor can sue the bishopric of Massa or the successor of the said Lord Bartolomeo in the bishopric for the said two hundred florins, while the bishopric or successor has the faculty of paying six per hundred. And the response to the contrary arguments alleged above is clear, except as to two, to which I respond. I say that the delegation was certainly valid, although he was a mere layman, because it was made ex certa scientia of the pope, since he knew him to be a layman and committed that cause to him present before him by word of mouth (oraculo vivae vocis), as is clear from the words of the pope contained in the said confirmation; and thus the commission is not vitiated, as Innocent wishes in what he notes in said cap. statutum, de rescri. li. 6., where in the beginning what Joan. Andr. notes in c. nonnulli, de rescrip. supports this. Nor is it necessary that it be expressed ex certa scientia, as some have maintained, and as at first glance Joan. Andr. seems to hold in said cap., as the gloss says in clemen. 2. de re judica. For it is enough that from what is expressed therein the certain knowledge of the pope is gathered. And so Joan. Bu. maintained in said cap. nonnulli, and so his gloss in d. clem. 2. ought to be understood; and so it happens in our case: for Pope John had knowledge of Chetius, and calls him in his confirmatory letter simply 'Chetius', nor does he call him a cleric, nor a master, nor established in any dignity, as is commonly done by style. Likewise, presupposing and not conceding that the said commission had not been valid, nonetheless by virtue of the compromissum the aforesaid conclusion would stand, since the said Chetius chose the way of a good man rather than of a judge, as is clear from the tenor of the said sentence and award, and willed that the pronouncement be valid in the best manner in which it can be valid, and thus the pope also confirmed it. Likewise, the pope at the end of the confirmation supplied every defect; by which clause indeed all defects regarding solemnities of law omitted are purged, as in Spe. and Archi. in the places cited before, which is much to be weighed in our case both regarding the consent of the chapter and of the superior, if by law it ought to have intervened, although I do not believe it to be necessary from what I said above. I come to the other contrary argument, and I say that if all things are well weighed, no usury results in the said award except from a true or fictitious loan, and from an agreement of the parties, as noted in the said regula, peccatum, by Jo. Andr. But in our case there is no true or fictitious loan, nor an agreement of the parties, but that provision proceeded entirely from the arbitrament of the judge and arbitrators; for the said Bartolomeo did not lend anything to the bishop truly or fictitiously. Nor can he demand the principal debt, and thus it is contrary to the nature of a loan, and thus consequently that evangelical saying ceases, 'lend, hoping for nothing thereby', de usu. c. consuluit; and that the judge could do this from arbitral power is proven in cap. nisi de praebend.; what Innocent notes in cap. in civitate, de usu. supports this. Likewise this was done in compensation for the fruits to be gathered by the said curia before the payment of the two hundred florins, which, since they pertained to the said Bartolomeo, the arbitrator willed to be handed over to him in compensation, before the payment of those two hundred florins, at six per hundred; in support of this is what Bartolus notes in l. fistulas, in fi. ff. de contrahen. emp., l. Julianus. §. officii, ff. eod., and l. fi. ff. de fund. do., and in place of interest, even if something is shared from the debt, if there is truly an interest, as noted in c. conquestus, and in l. curabit, C. de act. emp., by Inn. in c. sacrosan. de sen. exc.; l. 2. in fi. and what is noted there, ff. de eo, quod cer. lo. supports this. Lastly, I say that if all the aforesaid things were to fail, which in the truth of law subsist, it cannot be caviled against that, if the Church of Massa or the bishop does not wish to recognize that sentence or transactio as anything more than personal, they are bound to restore all things which by virtue of that sentence or award they obtained, because an award ought not to be valid on the church's behalf and against the canons. In support of this is capi. 1. and what is noted there, de in integ. resti., and cap. cum olim, de censit., and l. quod si minor. §. restitutio, and l. intra utile, ff. de mino.; what the gloss notes in cap. 1. de in integ. restit. lib. 6. supports this; and this is another and unfailing remedy available to the said Bartolomeo or to his successor; l. cum precibus, C. de praescript. ver. supports this beyond the aforesaid. And let these things suffice, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Statutes and customs against ecclesiastical liberty are null and void by operation of law.
2. A general provision ought not to be extended to unlawful matters.
3. A statute of a city or of a lord providing that no one may donate or sell immovable property to anyone not belonging to the jurisdiction of those enacting the statute does not include a donation or sale to the church.
4. When the law simply defers certain property or a certain quota of property to someone out of the property of another, the person thus burdened cannot, even for pious causes, make a testamentary disposition of the property deferred to the other.
5. When someone's property is confiscated on account of a crime, the person thus deprived cannot make a testamentary disposition, even for pious causes.
6. A son under paternal power cannot, even for pious causes, make a testamentary disposition of adventitious property.
7. A law or statute can prohibit someone from making a testamentary disposition, at least concerning certain things in favor of another.
casus: In view of a certain constitution of the late Emperor Frederick, which he gave to the men and people of Massa of the Kingdom of Sicily of the tenor written below, namely: all goods of husband and wife, from whatever source they come, upon the birth of children are merged and form one mass, and if the husband and wife wish to divide with the children, a third part of the goods is held for the father, another for the mother, and the remaining third for the son or sons. But if the father or the mother predeceases intestate, and the son or sons are living, with the father or mother surviving, the third part of the predeceased parent falls to the sons or son, and thus the same sons have two parts, one owed to them by natural law, the other that of the predeceased parent. But if his father predeceases testate, his testament shall stand, provided that in the same testament he recognizes his sons with respect to the third. But if the mother predeceases, she may make a testamentary disposition at will concerning the movables of her third portion. Immovables, however, upon her death, fall to the sons. If, however, there are no movables, she can make a testamentary disposition concerning immovables up to half the value of the same immovables according to a fair valuation. A certain lady having sons, and movable and immovable goods, being in marriage, having fallen ill, made a testament and, having made several legacies of movables, bequeathed a certain immovable property for pious causes. It is asked whether, by the words of the said constitution, in favor of a pious cause, the said legacy is valid.
body: The aid of Christ and of His Mother having been humbly invoked, it seems first that the said legacy is not valid.

† For all statutes and customs against ecclesiastical liberty are null and void by operation of law, as in c. nouerit and c. grauem, de sentent. excommu., and in authen. cassa, C. de sacr. san. eccle. Those statutes, moreover, are against ecclesiastical liberty which tend against things that have been granted by the prince or by the Pope to the universal Church, as noted by Inno. in the said c. nouerit, and Bar. in the said auth. cassa. But the constitution about which the paragraph deals, if extended to pious causes, is of such a kind; therefore either it ought not to be extended, or it is null by operation of law as being against ecclesiastical liberty. This is proved in this manner: the Emperor granted a privilege to the universal Church and to every single member of the Church itself concerning donations, legacies, and heirs, so that anyone might have the free capacity of donating and bequeathing to an ecclesiastical corporate body, as in l. illud, l. j., and l. fina., C. de sacr. san. eccle. Moreover, he privileged the Church so that, with regard to delivery, ownership was acquired from title alone, d. l. fina. But by this constitution the free capacity of bequeathing their own goods to churches would be taken away from women having children; therefore it is contrary to the privilege granted to the universal Church, and consequently against ecclesiastical liberty. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that authen. cassa and cap. nouerit and capit. grauem speak of particular statutes, whereas this constitution, which is at issue in our case, was enacted by the Emperor, who could limit his own constitution, l. princeps, ff. de legibus; because once the Emperor granted a privilege to the Church, he could no longer revoke it, because once he granted it to a non-subject, it passed into a contract, as Innocen. expressly held in capi. nouit, de iudic., and Ioannes Andr. in cap. constitutus, de rer. do., and Archi. in cap. quicunque, xj. q. j. Likewise, the Pope privileged the Church in bequests of this kind, to the extent that in them he remitted all legal solemnity, as in capit. relatum, de testa. Wherefore it is better and safer to say that the said statute, speaking generally, is not extended to pious causes,

† because a general provision ought not to be extended to unlawful matters, as in cap. primo, de iureiur., lib. 6. Supporting the aforesaid is the question posed by Ioannes Andr. in c. fin., de immu. eccle., lib. 6, where he asks

† whether a statute of a city or of a lord providing that no one may donate or sell immovable property to anyone who does not belong to the jurisdiction of those enacting the statute, or who is not under the common protection or that of the lord, includes a sale or donation to the Church; and he finally concludes that it does not, or, if it were said otherwise on account of the intention of the enactors against ecclesiastical liberty, that it is null, being moved by the aforesaid and other reasons. Secondly and principally thus: an unreasonable constitution does not bind, for it does not possess the essentials of law, concerning which see iiij. distincti., c. sit autem, lxxj. distin., consuetudo, as noted by Barto. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iustitia, & iure. But this constitution, about whose force the question is raised, is unreasonable if it were extended to pious causes; therefore either it ought not to be extended, or, as unreasonable, it is not valid. The minor premise is proved: the law wills that one ought to count the church or monastery at least in the number of one's children, as in authen. si qua mulier, C. de sacr. san. eccle. But this constitution does not forbid this, yet extends its force to pious causes; therefore it is unreasonable. For if the contrary is reasonable, then this is unreasonable, for it is of the nature of contraries that if one is good, the other is evil, xxxij. quæstio. ij., cap. hospitiolum, and c. intellecto, de iureiuran. Likewise, one ought to love one's soul more than one's children, as is clear in the Gospel, and cap. Iacobus, de simo., and xij. quæstio. j., c. præcipimus supports this; hence Barto. says in d. l. j. that a disposition for pious causes is more favored than one between children. But this constitution would produce the contrary if it extends its force to pious causes; therefore it is unreasonable. A third unreasonableness is that in the portion to be conferred upon children it makes a distinction between father and mother, against l. maximum uitium, C. de liber. præte. Thirdly and principally it supports this that the said constitution does not state that a woman cannot testamentary dispose of immovables at her will, and from an affirmative statement concerning certain things the negation of other things does not follow which are otherwise conceded by law. This is proved in cap. ut commissi, de hære., lib. sexto, together with the gloss, and in clementi. ij., eod. titu., and there the good gloss on the word ipsorum commiss. Moreover, by the common law parents are granted the free capacity to testate as well in immovables as in movables, and it is sufficient to institute the children in something however modest, although they can afterwards bring an action for the supplement of the legitime, l. omnimodo and l. scimus, C. de inoffi. testamen. And the aforesaid proceed most especially if they wish to testate for pious causes. We say, therefore, that the intention of the constitution was that a woman can testate at will concerning movables, even leaving nothing to the children, but not so freely concerning immovables. But notwithstanding these points, which in right judgment do not stand in the way, I consider that the contrary opinion prevails, which I demonstrate manifoldly as follows. And first thus:

† wherever the law simply confers certain goods or a certain quota of goods upon someone out of the goods of another, the person so burdened cannot testate, even for pious causes, out of the goods conferred upon the other, nor ought the church to receive such goods, as is clearly proved in c. fi., 17. q. 4, where Augustine says: Whosoever wishes to make the Church his heir having disinherited his son, let him seek another who will accept it, not Augustine; God willing, he will find no one, etc., as there. Moreover, it is certain that the portion is owed to the son not by the law of nature, but by legal disposition, since by natural law only maintenance is owed to the son, as in cap. ius naturale alimenta, 1. distin. For a certain portion cannot be owed to a son by natural law, since by that law all things were common, 8. dist., c. quo iure, 12. q. 1, c. dilectissimus. And thus the law, by conferring a certain portion upon the son in the goods of the father, deprives the father of the power of testating concerning that portion, even for pious causes. So it must be said in the proposed case, since the said constitution confers the immovable goods of the predeceased mother, even with a will, upon the children themselves; therefore the mother cannot testate concerning them, even for pious causes. That the said constitution could do this, moreover, is clear: for the portion owed to children out of the goods of their parents cannot be increased or diminished by law or statute, as is the opinion of Dy. on the regula indultum, de reg. iu., lib. 6, and in c. Raynutius, de testa., and he says there that elsewhere it is not so well proved as it is there. For custom is observed in the deduction of the legitime; so holds Cy. in l. sancimus, C. de nupt., and Bartol. in d. l. Titio, §. Titio genero, ff. de cond. & demon., and Bald. in l. cum Leoniana, C. de epis. & cle. This is proved by reason of natural law, as I said above: to children only maintenance is owed. But by positive law a certain portion was conferred upon them; and first it was a fourth, afterwards increased to a third and a half according to the number of children, as is proved in l. cum quæritur, joined with auth. nouissima, C. de inoffi. test. Whence, just as it could increase it to a third and a half, so it could be enacted that the immovables pass to the children, movables being reserved to the free maternal disposal, and if movables are lacking, a half of those immovables should pass, as in the said constitution; an excellent argument in l. cum ratio, ff. de bo. dam. & eorum quæ leg., and as noted in l. nam & si, ff. de inof. test. And because father and son are deemed the same person, as in auth. iure, a mo. præ., §. 1, and in l. fin., C. de impu. & aliis substi., and 35. q. 3, c. contradicimus by this authority; hence ownership is continued in the son, l. in suis, ff. de li. & post. Since therefore this statutory portion succeeds into the place of the portion owed by the common law, it ought to be deemed by the same law, because that which is subrogated must savor of the nature of that into whose place it is subrogated, de bapt., c. maiores, and c. ecclesia, ut li. pen.; what Inn. notes in c. ex ratione, de appel. supports this. Just as therefore concerning that portion owed by the common law the father or mother cannot testate, even for pious causes, as in the said c. fi., so neither can they concerning this statutory portion, because it is moved by the same reason; most especially because the said constitution was enacted by the Emperor, and thus it is common law as to them. And I would say the same where the city itself had enacted this, because in this it has power from the common law, as in d. l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu. Secondly and principally, what Io. And. notes in c. 2, de usu., lib. 6, and Bal. in l. 1, C. de sac. san. eccl. supports this, where he held

† that in the case where the goods of someone are confiscated on account of a crime, that person so deprived cannot testate, even for pious causes, because it would be disposing of another's property, supra c. filius, de testa. And Io. An. holds there that in the goods of condemned persons, which today are not confiscated, but are conferred upon agnates, as in auth. bona damnatorum, C. de bo. proscrip., from that case where the law confers them upon agnates and deprives the person of the power of testating, he cannot testate for pious causes; because since the law simply provides, and the contrary is not found in our law, the legal provision must be maintained, in cap. 1, de no. ope. nunc., and when the law speaks generally, it ought to be observed generally, 19. dist., c. si Romanorum, and c. solitæ, de maio. & obe. Likewise, since the goods are conferred upon others by the law, that which is given by him who by law cannot donate is held as not given, 1. q. 7, c. Daibertum, and l. traditio, ff. de acqui. re. dom., and c. quod autem, de iure patro. Nor does the favor of a pious cause stand in the way, because it applies when the testator bequeaths what is his own; otherwise if he bequeaths what is not his own, as in our case, nor on account of the favor of such legacies ought an injustice to be done to another, de fo. compe., c. ex tenore, de dona. inter uir. & uxo., c. nuper, de pœnis, c. sacram; 1. q. 1, c. non est putanda supports this. If therefore the aforesaid points hold where the law confers goods upon another on account of a crime, a fortiori the same must be said where it confers them out of natural equity and the favor of filiation, since favors ought to be amplified and odious things restricted, as in the rule odia restringi, de re. iur., lib. 6. Thirdly, I cite the good text in cap. quæsitum, 17. quæst. 4, at the end, where it is expressly gathered that the Church ought to surrender gifts conferred upon it which it cannot retain when natural equity urges otherwise, although by strict law it could retain them; but in our case all equity resists. For it is sufficient that the mother can testate concerning movables, or if these are lacking, concerning immovables up to one half, as is provided in the said constitution, which seems in effect to agree, or to differ little in sense from the said authen. nouissima. Therefore the Church ought not to accept these goods conferred upon it; nay rather, if by strict law it could retain them, nonetheless by the law of heaven they ought to be restored to the daughter. Fourthly, I cite what is noted by Bartol. and Bald. in l. 2, C. de sac. san. eccle.,

† where he held that a son under paternal power cannot, even for pious causes, testate concerning adventitious goods by the general disposition of the law, which forbids a son under paternal power from testating in favor of the father, as in l. penul. & fina., C. qui testa. face. poss. And this seems to be most clearly proved in cap. licet pater, §. fina., at the end, de sepultu., libr. 6. Whence Bartol. establishes as a rule in l. 1 that wherever the law prohibits someone from testating in favor of another, that prohibition is never deemed to be relaxed in favor of a pious cause; which is clearly proved in the said capit. licet. So it is punctually in our case, as is clear from the aforesaid.

† The law or a statute can therefore prohibit someone from testating, at least concerning certain property, in favor of another, since this is custom, by the argument in l. uenditor, ff. commun. prædio., and l. dubium, C. de contrahend. emptio., and l. mercatores, C. de merca. & merc., and what is noted there; and these proceed most especially holding the singular gloss on l. illa institutio, ff. de heredita. institutio, which says that the capacity to testate is granted as a favor, since by strict law one cannot testate, because the effect of a will is referred to that time at which one will not be owner, and thus it is just as if it had been established at an ineligible time, l. quod sponsæ, C. de donatio. ante nupt.; capitulum de uxore, de sepult. and l. in tempus, ff. de acquiren. hæredita. support this, for it is easily taken away, as noted in clemen. 2, de offi. ordina., and capitulu ab exordio, 25. distinctio supports this, especially when cause suggests it, as in our case. I conclude therefore that the said legacy of immovable property, although made for pious causes, was not valid. The contrary arguments formulated above do not stand in the way. And first, to the first I say that the statute is not against ecclesiastical liberty, neither directly nor indirectly. For the prohibition is not made in hatred of the Church, nor are men generally prohibited from donating to the Church, but the constitution increases the portion owed to the son. Concerning the portion thus increased, testating is prohibited, just as is clear in the portion owed by the common law; nay, if it be subtly considered, it is conformable to divine law. For one can honor the Church in movable goods, or in immovables if movables do not exist, according to the tenor of the constitution, and in the rest of the goods provide for the children so that they do not suffer from poverty, since God Himself commands that the poor must be helped, and the Church is bound to provide for the poor out of its goods, xvj. q. j., c. enim, xij. quæst. ij., c. aurum; a fortiori it ought not to take away from them goods conferred by the law. Otherwise, if we were to say the contrary, it would follow that the law could not deprive someone of his goods for cause, against l. si uerberatum, ff. de rei uendi., and what is noted by Bart. in l. fin., C. si contra ius uel uti. publi., and Cyn. in l. præscriptione, C. eod., and by Inno. in c. quæ in ecclesiarum, de consti., and against the text in c. 2, de usuris, lib. 6, and c. cum secundum leges, de hære., eo. lib., with countless similar passages. What Bar. notes in a similar matter in l. rescripto, ff. de muneri. & honori. supports the aforesaid. But it would be otherwise where someone were simply prohibited from alienating to the Church directly or indirectly to the prejudice of another, on the ground that the goods are conferred upon others, and thus proceeds the question which Io. And. poses, of which mention was made above in the contrary. To the second contrary I respond that this constitution is not unreasonable, on account of the identity and unity which exists between father and son, as I said above; and the contrary speaks where someone enters a monastery without having made a will, for then on account of the burdens monasteries are to be computed in the number of children, but it is otherwise where he testated beforehand, as noted in auth. si qua mulier, C. de sac. san. eccle., and c. in præsentia, de probat., if in no way he enters a monastery, because then he is not bound to leave anything to the Church, saving the legitimate portion, concerning which see c. 2 and c. 1 with similar chapters, de sepul. Likewise I admit that one ought to love one's soul more than one's children, but one ought not by this to deprive the children of the portion conferred upon them by the law, on account of the Church. For in other ways too one can provide for one's soul, most especially because one can honor it according to the tenor of the said constitution. What is said concerning the difference between father and mother does not stand in the way, because in many matters there is a difference, most especially under the law of the Twelve Tables, according to which the mother was excluded from the succession of children by the agnates of those children. Likewise, this was to restrain maternal judgment, because women act against their own interests and are easily deceived, l. si pater, C. de sponsalibus. To the last contrary I respond that the said constitution does not speak simply affirmatively, granting the capacity of testating concerning movables, but proceeds further by conferring the immovable goods themselves upon the children, and thus consequently prohibits testating concerning them, as I said above. It is proved in a second way in the clause autem, where it permits testating concerning immovables up to a half if movable goods are lacking; therefore, a contrario, if movables exist, it prohibits testating concerning immovables, by the argument in l. inter socerum, §. cum inter, ff. de pactis, by Bal. in l. conuenticula, C. de episcop. & cleri.; otherwise, if she could testate concerning movables at will, those words of the constitution would be superfluous, against c. si Papa, de priuile., lib. 6, and in l. si quando, ff. de inofficio. testamen. Thirdly it is proved from the fact that the clause si uerò præmoriatur comes adversatively to the clause si uerò pater, where the father is permitted without distinction to testate provided he recognizes the children with respect to their portion; therefore in the clause si uerò præmoriatur it intended to establish a different law in the mother, for the reason noted in c. at si clerici, de iudi. And let these things suffice, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. When a submission to arbitration is made to three, the pronouncement of two is not valid if the third was unconsulted.
2. If an arbitral decision is contrary to God, it is not to be obeyed.
3. An award is a kind of transaction, which at first sight is presumed just and equitable.
4. Arbitrators are not bound to draw up writings, but it suffices to inform themselves extrajudicially.
5. Although an ordinary judge ought not to pronounce on the last day of his jurisdiction, yet if he pronounces, it is valid.
6. A cause of nullity does not impede the execution of a sentence in the case where that sentence was twice confirmed by competent judges.
7. An instrument is taken for any document containing transactions between the parties.
casus: In the name of God, amen. Having seen the submission to arbitration and the award following thereupon, and the objections against them, and the petition regarding nullity, and the replies made thereto, and the other matters pleaded between E., citizen of Vicenza, on the one part, and A. of the same city; having weighed the statutes making provision on this subject-matter; it happens concerning two matters: that the submission is impugned, having regard especially to the things objected concerning the private writing, and that the submission and award were made regarding usuries, and that two out of three delivered the award while the other remained unconsulted. Secondly, whether the objections are of such kind and of such great efficacy that, pending the said cause of nullity, the judge can or ought by law to inhibit the said E. from making any innovation against the said A. pending the said cause, or ought not to inhibit, having regard to the replies and the aforesaid statutes, etc.
body: Having repeated the name of Almighty God, I come to the first matter, and I shall take up from the objections those which seem somewhat to sting at first glance. For first, the said award seems null, because it was delivered on the last day of the term. For the submission was made in the month of August, and the power of pronouncing was granted throughout that entire month, but the arbitrators pronounced on the last day of August, and on a day on which they were not going to be arbitrators in the future, contrary to l. eum, in fi. ff. de iurisdi. omni. iudi.

† Secondly, wherever a submission is made to three persons, the pronouncement of two is not valid if the third was unconsulted, l. si in tres, with l. seq. ff. de arbit. and what is read and noted in c. 2. eo. tit. lib. 6. and in c. uno delegatorum, de offi. deleg. But in our case two judged, or made the award, without the third having been consulted; therefore the award is null from defect of power, and especially does this apply in our case, in which the third was not present at the time of examination. And thus we are of the opinion of Inno. concerning which in c. Raynaldus, de test. although Bar. speaks better in l. duo ex tribus, ff. de re iudi. that whether they were present at the time of examination or not, the sentence of two would not be valid unless all have pronounced, and this from defect of power, because all together have the power of pronouncing, d. l. duo, which d. c. uno and c. causam matrimonij, eo. tit. support. Thirdly, there contributes to establishing the nullity of the award and of the submission the quality of the case concerning which pronouncement was made, because it was concerning usury, of which even an ordinary secular judge cannot take cognizance; all the more neither an arbiter, especially a secular one, can have power from the parties. The first proposition is proved from what is read and noted in cle. dispendiosam, de iudi. and in c. cum sit generale, de for. compet. in c. illo uos, de pigno. and c. ad nostram, de emptio. & uendit. by Bar. in l. Titia, ff. solu. matri. and l. ij. de iurisdi. omni. iudic. Likewise pronouncement was made concerning church rights, and concerning these spiritual matters a submission cannot be made to a layman, especially by laymen, as in c. contingit, and ca. per tuas, de arbit. joined with c. ecclesia Sanctæ Mariæ, de constitut. and c. bene quidem. 96. distin. and c. si. de rebus eccle. non alie. Fourthly, the nullity of the award is evidently gathered because it was expressly delivered contrary to law, especially divine law, in which case the arbitrament or award collapses by operation of law, as is the open text in cap. examinata, de arbitr. Moreover, that this award was of such a kind is clear from this: because the arbiters ordered not only the payment of usuries, but also usuries of usuries, which is not only against divine and canon law, as throughout the whole title de usuris, but also against civil law, as in authen. de eccle. tit. and in l. sancimus, C. de usur. rei. iudic. and especially with respect to the church, because they wanted to make the church in a certain manner usurious. For no arbitral precept binds to sin, as Hostien. notes in c. Quintauallis, de iureiur. where he says,

† that where an arbitral decision is contrary to God, it is by no means to be obeyed, no matter how much a penalty or oath has intervened, citing what is noted de tempo. ord. c. ad aures. I say this holds not only in the decision of arbitrators, but of any judges whatsoever, as in c. dominus, and c. Iulianus, and c. qui resistit. 11. q. 3. Fifthly, the award seems null from this: because from a general submission these arbitrators pronounced concerning liquidated matters by virtue of the statute of Vicenza, namely concerning a deposit, concerning which there appeared a private writing having by that municipal law ready execution, just like a guaranteed instrument [instrumentum guarentigiatum], and concerning matters decided and liquidated through a settlement and division previously made between the parties, contrary to c. exposita, de arbi. and what is read and noted in l. eleganter. §. si quis post transactionem, ff. de condict. indeb. and l. post rem iudicatam, ff. de transact. For just as a transaction cannot be made regarding liquidated matters, as in the said laws, so neither can a submission, since a submission is a kind of transaction, as noted in Authen. ut diffe. iudi. in prin. and in authen. si quando C. de iudi. noted by Innocen. in cap. Quintauallis, de iureiur. and Barto. in l. societatem §. arbitrorum, ff. pro socio. Nor does that general clause inserted in the submission help, that concerning all things upon which an award was made, a lawsuit and dispute &c. should be understood; because through general words the power of pronouncing over already liquidated matters about which there was no dispute does not seem to have been granted, from the rule in generali, de regu. iur. lib. 6, and cap. fina. de officio iudi. eodem lib. and cap. primo. de iureiuran. eodem lib. and capitu. cum uenissent, de institut. Here, however, Angel. de Perus. notably said in a certain consilium which begins 'uiso compromisso prorogato', that through that clause the power of pronouncing is not granted over those matters concerning which a transaction is prohibited by law, by the argument in l. cum hi. §. sed cum lis, ff. de transactio. and what Bartol. notes in authen. si quis in aliquo documento, C. de eden. and in l. & si forte, ff. de castr. pecu. Sixthly, the said award seems null, or at least most inequitable and fraudulent, because, taking into account all the things narrated in the award, A. was a creditor of E., yet from this award he remains a debtor in the amount of nineteen hundred florins; wherefore at least by reason of inequity it does not deserve execution, but ought to be reduced to the judgment of a good man, even if it had been sworn and promised not to seek reduction to the judgment of a good man, as Din. and Ioan. Andr. note in regula scienti, de regu. iur. libr. 6. and Hostien. in cap. Quintauallis, de iureiuran. and there especially by Anto. de Butr. and Bar. in d. §. arbitrorum. For that pact ought to be understood if they have arbitrated equitably, and if as good men and amicable compounders, by the argument in l. quæro. §. inter locatorem, and there by Bartol. ff. loc. and said cap. Quintauallis, and fully by Cyn. where cited above. But notwithstanding these points, I think that unless something else is proved, the said award cannot be called null, nor inequitable, but is to be presumed valid and equitable. The foundation of this conclusion is because an award is at first sight to be so presumed, and the burden of proving falls upon the one asserting it to be inequitable or null.

† The reason is that an award is a kind of transaction, which at first sight is presumed just and equitable, and upon the one asserting the contrary rests the burden of proof, and it does not suffice to prove that the party was defrauded beyond half of the whole taking into account the true debt, as is remarkably proved in l. Lucius. §. fin. ff. ad Trebel. So too an award is presumed just to such an extent that it does not suffice to prove that the party was defrauded, taking into account the true debt, nor that by law pronouncement ought to have been made otherwise, as Bartol. notes in the said §. arbitrorum; the reason being that arbitrators are not bound to judge according to law, but can for the sake of concord deviate from the law and give that which belongs to one party to the other, as l. si de meis, ff. de arbi. and the good text in c. nisi. de pręb. Wherefore, in order to perceive the inequity of an award, it is necessary to consider the state of the suit, and the standing of the persons and the compromitants, and why they came to submit, and the amount of the deception. And if, having considered all these things, the arbiters are found not to have pronounced as a good man would have done, then inequity—I do not say nullity—is inferred, as noted by Bart. in d. §. arbitrorum, clear from the things that are read and noted in d. l. Lucius, at the end, and l. 2. C. de rescinden. uendi. and c. penult. de emp. & uend. And that the burden of proving inequity rests upon the one alleging it is maintained by Ioan. Andr. following the ancients in the additions to Specul. under the title de arbi. §. sequitur, at the word 'item quid si compromissum', and Bartol. openly holds in the said §. arbitrorum, and Feder. consil. 274, Anton. de Butr. in the said capitu. Quintauallis; l. ab ea parte, and l. uerius, and l. ei incumbit, ff. de probatio. support this.

† Likewise because arbitrators are not bound to make written records, but it is enough for them to inform themselves extrajudicially, as Innocent notes in the said capitu. Quintauallis, and Bartol. in the said §. arbitrorum. Hence it would be absurd to say that there is no presumption in favor of the justice of the award, since according to this almost no award would stand, since the exactitude could not be proved. Therefore, one who says he has been harmed by a contract always has to prove it, as in l. 1. C. de fide instru. & iu. hast. fisc. lib. 10. and cap. 2. eod. titu. in the ancients; but the one standing for the contract does not have to justify the contract. So it must be said regarding an award, since it is a kind of contract, as I said above. It also supports this that there is a presumption in favor of intrinsic formalities, d. l. ab ea parte, in fin. and insti. de fideiusso. in fine, and in c. præsentia, de proba. noted by Innocen. in cap. innotuit, de eo, qui fur. or. and Bartol. in l. sciendum, ff. de uerbo. oblig. and by this the position of the one standing for the award is grounded. And beyond the premises there contributes the solemn promise of the compromitants themselves, who promised not to appeal from the award to be rendered, nor to allege nullity, nor to oppose inequity, nor to seek that it, or anything contained in it, be corrected in whole or in part, amended, or reduced to the arbitrament of a good man, but to hold and observe perpetually firm and ratified that submission and the award resulting therefrom, and all things contained in it, and in nothing to act against or contravene it, &c. And thus I do not see with what countenance he now alleges nullity. For nothing is contained in the award itself which could not be expressly approved by the parties; therefore the pact made from the beginning not to allege nullity was valid, and the acts ought to have at least the force of a pact where other remedies might fail, by the argument of what is noted by the gloss in cap. significasti, de foro compe. l. una. C. qui pro sua iurisdictione, and l. 2. C. communia utriusque iudi. And although some cases are excepted when the pleading of nullity is prohibited by law, according to the notes in clem. 1. de re iudi. l. 1. ff. de tabu. exhib., nevertheless with respect to a party who renounces or solemnly promises, that does not seem to have place, by the argument of cap. quàm periculosum. 7. q. 1. and because he who says 'all' excludes nothing, in c. solitæ, de ma. & obe. 19. dist. c. si Romanorum. And the reason for the distinction can be this: for when the law prohibits the pleading of nullity, it does this not because it wishes to confirm a null act, but because of the presumption of fraud, which presumption ceases if proof is offered immediately—thus proceed the notes in d. l. 1—or when nullity is alleged with respect to defect of jurisdiction. For then the exception is admitted because that quality is removed upon which the law founds itself in taking away the power of calling a sentence null, because it is not a sentence if the judge lacks jurisdiction, to which purpose Bart. notes in l. 1. in fi. ff. quod ui aut clam, and thus proceed the notes in cle. unica, de seque. pos. But when a party solemnly promises not to object concerning nullity, he does this because he wishes it to be entirely valid in the strength of a pact, and thus he without distinction closes to himself the avenue of alleging nullity, whose validity depends upon his consent, to which purpose is noted in c. cum inter P. & C. and c. ex transmissa, de renun. and in l. nemo potest, ff. de leg. 1. and d. c. quam periculosum, and d. l. una. C. qui pro sua iuri. Now it remains to examine whether the objections are of such efficacy that, the aforesaid notwithstanding, the said award can be called null or most inequitable, and I say that they are not. And first to the first in order I say, that if the time assigned in the submission and the day of the delivery of the award are properly inspected, it cannot be said that the award was not delivered within the term, as the other party incorrectly alleges. For it was delivered on the last day of the term, which in doubt could be done, as is expressly proved in cap. consuluit, de offic. delegat. where it is said that a delegate can pronounce on the last day of the term; therefore all the more the same must be said of an arbitrator, whose award is rather a kind of transaction or contract than a sentence, as noted in the laws cited above. The contrary does not stand in the way, for that speaks of an ordinary judge, whose successor has arrived. For he blushes at the abdication of jurisdiction, but it is otherwise in a delegate or arbiter, in whom this reason ceases, as Ioan. And. notes in d. c. consuluit.

† Likewise in an ordinary judge, although he ought not to pronounce on the last day of his jurisdiction, yet if he does pronounce, it is valid, as the gloss notes in c. & si Christus, de iure. on the word 'seruando', and noted in l. meminisse, ff. offic. procon. Therefore on this ground the award cannot be said to be null. I come to the second objection, to which I respond that it proceeds in doubt if nothing else had been expressed in the submission, but power had been simply given to three, even to two in the absence of the third and without him having been consulted, which can be done; for power can also be given to delegated judges so that all, or two, or one alone can pronounce, as in c. cum plures, de offic. deleg. lib. 6; therefore the same and more strongly in arbitrators, who assume power unto themselves from the compromitants themselves, for the parties can remit even substantial formalities of judgments to arbiters, as l. diem proferre. §. si quis litigatorum, ff. de arbit. noted by Bart. in d. §. arbitrorum. And that this clause, that one or two may pronounce, can be attached, and not be joint and several [in solidum], is expressly proved in l. non distinguemus. §. cum in plures, ff. de arbit. and in c. uno delegatorum, de offic. deleg. lib. 6. And thus the second objection is entirely removed. To the third objection, which seems more doubtful, I respond that a usury case is then spiritual or of the ecclesiastical forum when there is doubt whether the contract is usurious, in which case cognizance belongs to the ecclesiastical judge alone, and in this case the contrary authorities properly proceed, as Barto. notes in d. l. ij. & l. Titia, cited for the contrary, and c. cum sit generale, de for. competen. in clemen. dispendiosam, de iudi. But in our case there was no submission on whether the contract was usurious, nor did the arbitrators pronounce the contract to be usurious or not usurious; rather, nothing was said concerning usuries, but merely a condemnation was made at eight per hundred, reducing those eight at the turn of the year by reason of damages and interest, which provision indeed draws strength from a two-fold head: First, by reason of the agreement of the parties and the power granted to the arbitrators themselves by the same parties, as appears in the award in the clause that begins 'Item saluo' &c. For although from the beginning an agreement to give a certain amount per hundred is not valid, as in c. debitores, de iureiur., yet after the fact, when the anxiety of seeking or finding a loan ceases, the agreement is well valid, because it seems a kind of liberality and recognition of services and reparation of damages; for a creditor can after the fact receive something liberally offered to him, as noted in c. consuluit, de usur. and 14. q. 3. c. 1; c. quàm pio, in fine, il 2. and c. tua, de simo. support this. We see something similar in the pact of the lex commissoria, which is disapproved in pledges if it intervenes at the time of the contract, but otherwise if after the fact, when that anxiety of finding a loan ceases, as is read and noted in l. j. C. de pact. pigno. and there Cyn. and Barto. report through the canonists in c. significauit, de pigno. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the arbitrators themselves are not to be believed, even though they assert this, as in c. quoniam contra, de probatio. where it is clear that a judge is not believed except insofar as it appears through the acts. Nor does the argument in l. pen. C. de arbi. stand in the way; for it can be said that it is otherwise with arbitrators, because they are not bound to make written records as I said above, wherefore they seem to be believed in those matters which concern the fact, since they are fully informed, and the parties chose them as suitable, at least if they depose these same things before a judge, as Bartol. singularly maintained in the said §. arbitrorum. Likewise, in this the arbiters themselves seem to be believed since it concerns moderate prejudice, since they themselves could have done this on their own without this agreement of the parties, as I shall say immediately. For in those matters which are of moderate prejudice, one stands upon enunciative words, even of a notary, as is the gloss noted in ca. olim. de censi. and the same there Inno.; what the gloss notes in l. optimam. C. de contrahen. & commit. stipu. supports this. Furthermore, the said provision was valid from the second head, namely from the power of the arbiters themselves and the disposition of the law. For even where money has been delivered under an obligation, regard can be had to interest, by reason of emergent damage and lost profit from the time of default, noted by Inno. in c. sacro. de senten. ex commu. and the gloss in c. conquestus. de usur. and l. cum allegas. C. de usur. and in l. curabit. C. de act. emp.; l. 2. in fin. ff. de eo, quod cer. lo. and what Bar. notes in l. una. C. de sen. quæ pro eo, quod interest, support this. Likewise, the arbiters themselves ought to inform themselves fully concerning greater interest of the creditor himself than the condemnation was made for; and this is plausibly to be believed in merchants. Nor ought the other party to complain of this, since from that money paid in his name he received or could have received each year a certain profit from the monte. Likewise by reason of his deposit his adversary was condemned to him at the same rate; wherefore, as I said above, it is to be believed that all things were lawfully weighed and treated in our case by these arbitrators, unless the contrary is proved by the opposing party. Likewise, these were arbitrators, who for the good of peace can somewhat exceed the bounds of law and condemn one of the parties to give something to the other for money already retained, as is proved in a similar case in cap. nisi. de præben. And thus the objection concerning usuries and usuries of usuries entirely ceases, since the whole was done in lieu of interest, unless the contrary is proved and enormous lesion should follow therefrom, according to what is noted in the said capit. quintauallis and said §. arbitrorum. Nor does what is said concerning the church stand in the way, because the submission or award here was not concerning a spiritual right, in which case the contrary authorities proceed, but concerning those monies designated by the parties themselves for the repair of the church, a portion of which is in the possession of the parties themselves, upon whom as heirs rests the burden of repairing the church and upholding it in necessities; wherefore the award in this part rather concerns the private prejudice of the parties themselves and of the heirs than of the church. Whence we ought not to look to the church being named in the award, but to whom the effect of the words is directed, as in l. cum pater. §. donationis. ff. de le. 2. And from the aforesaid the third argument also remains resolved. I come to the fifth objection, to which I say that the arbitrators did not pronounce upon the deposit to its prejudice, or contrary to the private writing executed concerning it, in which case the contrary would militate in favor of the depositary himself, but upon disputes newly arisen, namely upon damages and interest arising from the non-restitution of the deposit. Likewise, that what was received by the depositary on that occasion ought to be restored; all of which no one doubts can fall into a submission, as is the case in d. c. exposita. de arb. Likewise I say further that even if they had pronounced expressly contrary to the deposit, nullity of the award itself would not follow on that account; because, since that chapter is separated by itself, it does not have to infect the other chapters of the award, because as many as there are chapters, so many are the sentences, as in l. uirum. §. 1. ff. de mino.; what Inno. notes in ca. fraternitatis. de hære. and the rule utile per inutile and what is noted there de reg. iur. lib. 6 supports this. The sixth and last objection does not stand in the way. For it is very general and superficial. For A. was a creditor of that E. in a certain respect, namely of the deposit. Likewise that E. was a debtor beyond the deposit by reason of inheritance. Now, however, from a different cause he is made a creditor, namely because he paid an entire quantity of money for that A., so that even with the deposit compensated he remains a creditor, especially with regard had to damage and profit, not to the payment of the resulting debt. Nor is this absurd, since he could be a debtor in a certain respect in a small quantity, and a creditor in another respect in a large quantity. For an inference is not made from diverse and separate matters, as in c. 2. de transla. præla. and in l. neque natales. C. de proba.; wherefore from this alone neither inequity nor enormous lesion is proved, especially since concerning this new debt it clearly appears through the books of the monte. From these points, therefore, I conclude to the first doubt that by reason of the objections neither nullity nor inequity of the award is proved, and that the award must be stood by, unless the contrary is proved. I come to the second principal doubt. And it seems first that the said inhibition ought to be made pending the suit of nullity through the text in cle. 1. de re iudi. arguing by the locus from the special.

† For as is clear there, a cause of nullity does not impede the execution of a sentence in that case where that sentence was confirmed twice successively by competent judges. It is otherwise, therefore, where only a single sentence rendered is found, as noted there in the gloss; and especially in our case, where the execution of an award or arbitrament is dealt with, which is not of such strength as a sentence itself, l. 1. and what is noted there, C. de arbi. Secondly, to the same purpose contributes l. 4. §. condemnatum, de re iudi. where it is said that someone does not seem condemned where the sentence is null by operation of law, nor can a null sentence be called a sentence, as there; therefore the one objecting concerning nullity detracts from the quality of the act upon which the law bases itself in the execution of a sentence, and deservedly ought to delay its execution according to what is noted by Barto. in l. 1. ff. quod ui aut clam; to the same purpose l. iudicati, C. si ex fal. instru. and l. si prætor. §. Marcellus, ff. de iudi. and c. de cætero, de re iudi. To the contrary makes l. fin. C. de ordi. cogni. where it is clear that an exception of nullity does not impede the execution of a sentence. This was expressly maintained by Innocen. in c. cum in iure, de offic. deleg. where he says that he nowhere finds touched upon that an exception of nullity impedes the execution of a sentence, citing c. suscitata, de in integ. resti. and the same the gloss there on the word 'effectum sententiæ', unless proof were produced immediately, arg. c. literas, de restit. spol. Nor would it be admitted then, according to those glosses, if a presumption of chicanery [calumnia] were against the exceptor; in which case the sentence ought first to be ordered to execution, and finally he ought to be heard by way of action. Likewise and thirdly, as to our case, the statute of Vicenza expressly seems to state under the rubric on the general execution of awards, where in effect it is provided that an award or arbitrament is to be ordered to execution, just like a guaranteed instrument [instrumentum guarentigiatum], with every appeal of nullity, inequity, reduction to the judgment of a good man, objection, contradiction, exception, or disagreement removed and rejected, &c., where it is more broadly contained. Since therefore the statute expressly removes the pleading of nullity to impede the execution of an award, the inquiry whether it ought to be remitted is made in vain; what shall we say? Certainly, setting aside the statute, under the ius commune I consider a distinction must be made, as Bart. distinguishes after Spe. and Imo. in l. 4. §. condemnatum, previously cited, whom Io. de Lig. in cle. 1. de re iudi. and l. 1. ff. de tribu. follows in all respects. And the conclusion is that if a defect of power asserted is alleged, execution is impeded, and I understand this when the denial is probable: otherwise it seems vexatious and not to be admitted, as Inn. notes in c. tua, de cohabi. cler. & mulie.; what is noted in l. post rem iudicatam, ff. de transac. supports this. And certainly in our case it does not seem probable, since the power of these arbiters is expressly established, as appears from the form of the submission, and from the things which I have said above. Or nullity proceeding from elsewhere is alleged, and then if it is established, or can be established immediately, or within the time that is given for the execution of the sentence, it ought to be admitted, and execution is impeded; otherwise it is different, and thus the laws cited above for and against ought to be reduced to harmony. But in our case the situation seems clearer at first glance, since the statute expressly takes away the power of pleading nullity, and a statute seems to be understood and interpreted so as to add something to the ius commune, according to what is noted by Barto. in l. 4. §. prætor ait, ff. de dam. infect. Nevertheless I think that where the nullity was clear, or could be proved on the spot, and all presumption of fraud ceased, it would have to be admitted, and execution of the sentence impeded notwithstanding the statute; because the mind of the statute was not to wish to order a null award to execution with such prejudice to the party, but rather to remove malicious objections of nullity, or to avoid excessive delay: all of which cease if manifest nullity is given, or with manifest fraud ceasing on the spot, an excellent argument for this being c. literas, de restitu. spolia. and by the gloss noted in l. 1. §. si autem, de tabu. exhiben. and by Bal. in l. data opera, C. qui accus. non pos. and by Old. consi. 45. For a general statute also is to be interpreted according to the ius commune, as Innocen. notes in c. causam quæ de rescri. And it is enough that it produces a new right of action or exception, according to what is noted by Barto. in l. 1. ff. ad l. Falc.; what is read and noted in c. ex parte, de uerbo. sign. supports this. Although the statute does not express the cause previously alleged, but speaks generally, yet we can and ought to conjecture the natural reason of the statute, and according to that reason thus conjectured extend and restrict the disposition of the statute, as Cyn. elegantly notes in l. non dubium, C. de legi. In the previously cited statute, however, no other good reason of the statute besides the aforesaid can be alleged. Nor is it to be presumed that the law is without reason. I say, however, that through those things which were objected against the award as stated before, I do not see a present nullity, nor one to be proved on the spot, through the things which I have said more extensively above. Therefore let the discreet judge consider the things objected and to be objected, and according to the aforesaid he will inform the motion of his mind for making the inhibition or denying it. And in the event that according to the aforesaid he should admit the cause of nullity before execution, let him cause to be observed the statute situated under the rubric 'how to proceed when an instrument is usurious', &c. For that statute was issued to avoid frauds, a good argument from what is read and noted in c. lator, qui fil. sint legi. and excellently in c. statutum, de rescrip. lib. 6. §. præferendo, and c. constitutus, de fideius. For the said statute speaks generally of every instrument, and any other whatsoever; to this purpose what Barto. notes in l. si quis legatum, ff. de fal. where he declares the meaning of this word 'instrumentum'.

† For it is taken for a document containing the transactions between the parties, and as more broadly there by him. Likewise the speaking words of that statute contribute, which are broader and discretionary. And these suffice with respect to the ius commune and the statute; since both parties expressly promised not to object against the award concerning nullity, it does not seem to be admitted, as I said above in the beginning, unless at least enormous lesion concurs in the nullity, so that he may not seem to have thought of such nullity, by the argument of what is read and noted in c. ueniens, and c. Quintauallis, de iureiu. and by Dyn. in said regula scienti, and by Barto. in §. arbitrorum, or something else concerning which he would plausibly not have thought, arg. c. fi. de offi. uic. lib. 6. and regula in generali, de reg. iu. lib. 6. And let these things suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If brothers, by remaining in common ownership, have tacitly contracted a partnership by sharing with one another the profits of their business dealings which they carried on, such a partnership nevertheless does not extend to other profits that are entirely separate.
2. A mother, by donating a house to one of the brothers, indirectly deprives the son and grandsons of the due support of the goods.
casus: The factual situation is as follows. Petrus de Mazolinis of the city of Bologna died, leaving two sons, namely Mathæus and Petronius, and a wife named Agnesina. After their father's death, Petronius and Matthæus stayed together and lived together, no division having been made, nor any other new partnership formed. While they were living thus, Agnesina, the mother of the aforesaid, donated to Petronius one of her houses. While they were moreover living thus, Matthæus dies, leaving two sons, Petrus and Bartholomæus, who, coming to division with Petronius their paternal uncle, want half of the said house donated to Petronius by their grandmother. Petronius on the contrary says that it is entirely his from the donation made to him by the mother, and that it does not enter into division. It is asked what the law is.
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of Christ the Savior and of His Mother, I shall touch upon the decision of this doubtful matter very briefly on the basis of the facts presented, omitting the arguments on either side, lest I seem to have deemed this doubtful question difficult, since the case appears clear to me.

† For I say that the said Peter and Bartholomew cannot, on their own behalf or on behalf of their father, claim a share of that house donated to the said Petronius by their common mother, but rather that that house belongs exclusively and in its entirety to the said Petronius and does not enter into the division of the said inheritance. For this point I first allege the clear text in l. cum duobus, §. papi., or which begins l. si fratres, ff. pro soc., where it is stated that brothers kept their parents' inheritances undivided so that they would share the profit and loss therein, yet whatever they acquired from elsewhere was not reduced into common ownership. And thus, whatever one acquires from whatever source, since they did not enter into a partnership, as is presupposed in the facts, he is not bound to share with the other. The same holds if one has suffered a loss outside the common property: for example, because he was condemned for a delict; for he must impute what he paid to his own share, nor is the one bound to suffer the other's loss in other debts which he contracted in his own person, as if he provided a dowry for a daughter, or did something similar, as in l. ex parte, §. filius, ff. fa. er., fully by Spec. in ti. de iudi., §. sequitur, ver. quid si duo fratres, and ver. quid si isti; by Bar. in l. Titium & Meuium, ff. de admi. tu., and l. si patruus, C. com. utriusque iud., and l. 1, §. si quis hoc interdicto, ff. de iti. actuque priu., and the said l. si fratres; in which places he says further that even if the brothers, by remaining in common ownership, tacitly contracted a partnership by sharing with one another the profits of the commercial dealings they carried on, such a partnership nevertheless does not extend to other profits that are entirely separate, or to goods otherwise acquired, such as from purchase and the gift of legacies, and the like, because a tacit partnership does not extend beyond the practice through which it was contracted, ar. d. l. 1, §. si quis hoc interdicto; to this makes what is noted at the end by Inno. in c. dilectus, de cap. mo.; to the same effect makes c. auditis, and c. cum olim, de præscr., and 2, q. 1, c. manifesta, and ca. causa, q. 4, c. 1; and it seems to be proved more clearly in l. coiri, with the two following, ff. pro so., where it is clear that even if a partnership is expressly contracted, if it was not differentiated, but contracted simply, it extends only to everything that enters into the contract. Moreover, gain is understood to be that which derives from each person's labor, as there in l. quæstus; but inheritances, legacies, donations causa mortis, or inter vivos do not enter, because these do not come from gain, but generally fall to one through personal merit, as is said there. All the more strongly, therefore, in our case do they not enter, where not even a partnership was contracted. For it is not equitable that a brother should be bound to share with another brother, or with nephews, that which falls to him by the favor of fortune, argum. inst. per quas personas, §. 3, and §. præterea; makes l. filiæ, and what is noted there, ff. fam. ercis. I say, however,

† that if the mother, by donating that house to the other of the brothers, indirectly deprived the other son, or the grandsons, of the due support of her estate—for instance, because she had nothing else among her assets, or nothing else remained to her that would suffice for the other son, or the grandsons descending from him, for the legitim owed by natural law—then those grandsons will be able to revoke that donation as inofficious up to the portion owed to them by natural law, as is read and noted in cap. Raynaldus, de testam., and l. si liqueat, de legat. 2; but Petronius is not simply bound to share it with the grandsons. I conclude, therefore, that if the mother is still alive, these grandsons can claim nothing, because while the parents are living no right to the legitim belongs to the sons or grandsons, as in l. j, §. si impuberi, ff. de colla. bono. Nay rather, according to Bart. in authen. si qua mulier, C. de sac. san. eccle., it is owed to sons or grandsons only through natural death, and not civil death. If, however, the mother, or grandmother, is dead, then either that donation was not inofficious in the manner aforesaid, and is in no way revoked, but simply remains with Petronius himself; or it was inofficious, and is revoked up to the legitimate portion owed to the other son, or to the grandsons, by natural law. For the other son, or the grandsons succeeding in the son's place, ought to have a third in the assets of the mother or grandmother, because a third is owed to both sons, as in authen. nouissima, C. de inofficio. testamen., noted in the said c. Raynaldus. And let these things suffice, etc. Nicolaus, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether usury can be deduced from the aforesaid contract set forth in the case above.
2. Ownership is not transferred by sale alone.
3. Wherever a burden is imposed in a contract of sale, it is regarded as part of the price.
4. Contracts take their law from agreement. § 1.
casus: HAVING SEEN a certain instrument, in which it is contained in sum that Galeatius, son of the late Thechus of Lord Teglius of Pisa, residing in Castrum Consultorum, solemnly sold to the syndics of the commune of Monte Guidi of the community of Siena, buying on behalf of the said commune, lands, houses, and possessions which the said Galeatius held in the said castle of Monte Guidi, for the price and under the name of the price of four hundred gold florins; which price indeed by mutual consent the said syndics promised to pay to the said Galeatius within four years, it being expressly agreed between them that as long as the said buyers in the names as above should not pay and should defer paying the said price of four hundred florins to the said Galeatius, the ownership and property of the said possessions and houses should be and be understood to remain with the said Galeatius and his heirs. And for the rent and lease-hire of the reservation of the said ownership and property, the said syndics in the name as above promised and agreed to give and pay to the said Galeatius, receiving for himself and his heirs, 90 florins at the end of the time of the said payment due at one year. These things having been thus solemnly transacted between the said buyers and sellers, payment of the said 400 florins was made on behalf of the said commune. For it seems to the said buyers that they are not bound to the payment of those [florins], both because it seems to be usurary depravity [?], since the promise of those 90 florins was made on account of the delay of the price, and because it seems contrary to all equity that the said seller should have rent from a thing sold to another. It is asked, what is the law, etc.
body: Having humbly invoked the help of Christ and of His Mother, two matters are to be examined for the clear decision of the aforesaid subject. The first is whether the said contract can be noted for usurary depravity. The second, presupposing the lawfulness of the contract, whether at least the said buyers can be assisted by any remedy, lest they seem to have paid part of the price and the full rent of those things, just like any third-party lessee.

† Concerning the first, I briefly think that no usurary depravity can be noted from the form of the said contract. For if the words of the contracting parties are juridically weighed, the ownership of the things sold remained with the said seller until the debt was paid in full, since the seller is not bound to deliver the thing before full payment has been made to him, as in l. Iulianus. §. offerri, ff. de actio. emptio. Indeed, even if it is delivered, ownership is not transferred unless credit has been given for the price, Institu. de rerum diui. §. uenditæ.

† Nor is ownership transferred by the sale alone, as in l. traditionibus, C. de pactis. But in our case credit was not given for the price. Rather, the contrary was expressly agreed between the contracting parties, namely that ownership should remain with the seller until he was paid the price in full, nor was the thing delivered except under the title of lease. Rightfully, therefore, could the said seller lease the said things sold to the said buyers, or to anyone else, until the price was paid in full to him. For just as before full payment of the price the seller properly collects the fruits, d. §. offerri, so too can he in the meantime lease the thing itself to anyone. Nor does it matter whether the seller himself remains in possession of it, or hands it over to another in order to receive rent, as is the text in l. cum antiquitas, C. de usu. & habi. Furthermore, if the buyer himself, the price not having been paid, had collected the fruits without any other title, he would be bound to the seller for damages, because if he wished to collect the fruits, he ought not to have deferred the payment of the price, as in l. curabit, C. de actoi. empt. From these points it is clearly concluded regarding the first issue that usury can in no way be noted in the said contract, which only arises from a true or fictitious loan, as in j. c. consuluit, and in c. in ciuitate, and in c. nauiganti, de usur. and fully by Io. An. in regula, peccatum, de reg. iu. li. 6. in Merc. Which indeed in no way intervened here, but rather a true and pure contract of lease and hire intervened within the time for paying the price. And this holds especially when considering that this sale could not be called complete in all respects, since the price was not payable purely at present, nor was the seller then bound to deliver the thing, according to what is held and noted in l. necessario, C. de pe. & comm. rei uendi. I come now to the second, more doubtful issue; and it seems that no remedy is available to the said buyers before they make the full appointed payment. It is certain, as is clear from the aforesaid, that ownership of the said things sold lawfully remained with the said seller until the full price was paid. Likewise, that he could lawfully lease those things in the meantime to anyone, as concluded above. Therefore he can lawfully demand the rent, d. l. cum antiquitas; otherwise the said buyers would seem to use force, to invert possession, and to possess as robbers, l. si ex stipulatione, ff. de ac. pos., l. nec ex uera, and l. cum nemo, C. eo.

† Secondly, it is proved thus: wherever any burden is attached to a contract of sale, it is deemed part of the price, as in l. fundi partem, ff. de contrah. emp. Therefore, also by this consideration that rent can be demanded, even if part of the price was paid each year, since he perhaps sold for less precisely in order to obtain the said 90 florins over and above the said price.

† Thirdly, it is owed by the pact solemnly made between the said parties; for contracts take their law from agreement, as in regula, contractus, de reg. iu. lib. 6. and l. 1. §. si conueniatur, ff. depositi; thus it is a serious matter to break faith, l. 1. ff. de pac. But notwithstanding these points, I consider that a remedy is available to the said buyers, so that a deduction or discount from the rent may be made pro rata with the price paid.
