This is proved in l. fi. ff. de fun. do., where it is proved that if the buyer [v. venditor] pays part of the price, he does not acquire ownership in part, as in l. fistulas. §. qui fundum, ff. de contrah. emp. and d. §. offerri; yet once the price is paid in full, he can claim the fruits pro rata with the price he paid; and this is held there by Bar. in l. fistulas, pre-alleged, and d. §. offerri, which seems supported by all natural justice, from which an argument can be drawn even if positive law were lacking, as in l. scire oportet. §. sufficit, ff. de excusa. tuto. and extra de app. c. secundo requiris, in fin. no. glo. 1. di. c. consuetudo. For it does not seem equitable, indeed it is inequitable, for the seller to collect the entire rent and part of the price. Which would occur especially in the third year, in which the seller had three parts of the price, if he were nevertheless to have the entire rent here; to which d. l. Iulianus. §. offerri greatly contributes, where the text says that the seller must either have full payment of the price, or hold the thing sold as a pledge for the price. Therefore it is most equitable that up to the limits of the price paid he restore the fruits, or remit part of the rent, which is the price of the fruits, according to the note by Bart. in l. si merces. §. uis maior, ff. locati, and in l. cotem ferro. §. qui maximos, ff. de publ. For he ought to retain the fruits for himself only insofar as it concerns his interest, and not otherwise, just as is observed in the person of the buyer himself, who, if he held possession by virtue of the sale and paid only part of the price, is obligated for interest with respect to the unpaid part alone, and not with respect to the entire price. So too, in our case, a remission of the rent ought to be granted to the buyers for the part of the price paid, and only to the extent that it concerns the seller's interest, namely with respect to the unpaid part; nor ought he to be enriched to another's loss; to which what is read and noted in a similar matter in cap. suam, de pœnis greatly contributes. Likewise l. fructus, with l. pen. C. de act. emp., where it is evident that the fruits of a thing sold after a perfected sale belong to the buyer even before delivery of the thing, as do the risk and disadvantage of the thing itself, l. necessario, ff. de peric. & commo. rei uen. The seller, on the other hand, can only claim the price with interest or damages when the price has not been paid. Nowadays, moreover, the exaction of interest having ceased, damages can be claimed, even under canon law, as the gloss notes in d. l. curabit, C. de act. empti. and in c. conquestus, de usu. And thus it seems that the said Galeazzo ought only to have the rent with respect to the unpaid part of the price, but not the remaining part of the interest, since with respect to that part he cannot claim interest. And although it might be objected that this applies in a perfected sale, which does not seem to have been the case here, since the price was not payable purely at present, nor was the thing then to be delivered according to what is held and noted in d. l. necessario, nevertheless I consider the intention and reasoning of the law, which was to provide for the seller with respect to his interest, but not that he should have the fruits and part of the price, especially the greater part, as occurs in our case. The arguments alleged for the opposing party do not stand in the way. And first, to the first, I say it must be admitted that before the entire price was paid the said seller was permitted to collect the fruits and to lease to anyone; nevertheless, after full payment he is bound to restore or deduct pro rata with the price paid, as Bar. maintained and is clear from the aforesaid. To the second counter-argument, I say that the contrary would apply where a burden were simply attached with respect to the sale. But in our case it was expressly agreed and stated that they should pay that rent by reason of the reserved ownership. For it was possible that these buyers would not have paid even part of the price within those four years, and yet would have owed the said rent in full without any deduction and remission. But once partial payment was made, the rent is owed, but a remission ought to be made pro rata with the paid price, as is clear from the aforesaid. And in this way the third argument is also resolved; for I say that the pact must be understood in the aforesaid manner, lest that man be enriched to the loss of another, etc.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A custom that someone need not reside in his canonry, even without keeping a vicar, is valid.
2. When it is known that a cleric is absent, and he cannot be suitably cited [?], he ought not to be cited by a general edict, but personally, a term for appearing having been fixed for him.
3. A custom that the reception of canons pertains solely to the chapter is valid.
casus: The Bishop of Lucca deprived two canons, who had already been absent for several years and not residing in the church of Lucca, of their revenues on account of their absence, a general edict at the cathedral church only, with a certain term, having nevertheless first been issued; five months or thereabouts having elapsed after the said deprivation, he caused it to be denounced orally to the chapter—to which the reception of the said [canons] pertains by ancient custom—that they ought within the legal term to elect two canons in place of those already deprived and present them to him to be confirmed by him, asserting that that right of confirmation pertains to him. In relation to the aforesaid, several questions are asked by the chapter of the said church. And first, whether the bishop could deprive the said canons, at least in the manner in which he deprived them, especially in view of the statute of the said church confirmed long ago by the chapter and observed over a long time, in the following terms, namely: 'Likewise they statuted and ordained that the revenues and profits that exist for the time being in the chapter of Lucca shall by no means be divided except among those residing throughout the entire continuous year. If, however, such residents happen to be absent for only three months, nothing at all shall be deducted from their annual prebend on this account, but they shall be counted as residents. But if they remain away beyond this, only a portion prorated for the time shall be assigned to them, provided that in each year they have already been present for at least six continuous months, or else in the meantime they shall receive nothing from the prebend, etc.' Secondly, it is asked whether the six-month period prescribed by law for the chapter to elect canons began to run from the time of the deprivation of the said canons, presupposing the validity of the deprivation, or from the time of the notification? And whether the said notification was valid, since it was made by word of mouth without writing? The third doubt is whether the right of confirmation pertains to the bishop, notwithstanding a custom to the contrary, according to which the bishop for the time being confirms no one elected by the chapter, but the free election or reception of canons has pertained to the chapter itself. Fourthly, it is incidentally asked whether statutes of the chapter confirmed by the Bishop and observed by his successors can be abolished by a newly created Bishop, or violated with the chapter objecting, etc.
body: The protection of Christ and of his mother having been humbly invoked, descending [to the matter] in due order: and first, it seems that the said deprivation can be impugned on many grounds; and first, from a defect of cause; secondly, from a defect of the order not having been observed. In respect of the cause: because since by custom the canons of Lucca did not require residence (which custom indeed seems approved, a constitution having been tacitly subjoined, and by law, as is the case in c. cum omnes, and there the gloss and doctors, de consti., and better through Io. And. in c. extirpandae, § qui vero, de praeben.,

† where he maintains that a custom is valid that one need not reside in one's canonry, even without keeping a vicar; yet if the church is in need, he can be compelled to serve through a vicar, arg. c. pe. de cle. non residen.), could the lord Bishop simply, with the custom and statute standing to the contrary, deprive them, since he alone cannot abolish custom and ancient statutes of the church already confirmed by the Bishop, as in c. cum consuetudinis, de consue., and what Io. And. notes there? And thus this Bishop, if he saw that the custom of the church was burdensome, ought first to have called the chapter and set a time for the canons regarding the residence to be performed, which he can do according to the note in c. cum omnes, and through Io. And. in c. ad audientiam, de cler. non resi., and, a statute having been made against the ancient custom, intimate the statute to the absentees and recall them to residence. Since he did not do this, but simply proceeded to the deprivation without regard, or at least without the counsel of the chapter, the said deprivation can deservedly be called null, as in c. novit, de his, quae fiunt a praela., without the consent or at least the counsel of the said chapter, said c. novit, and c. quanto, eo. tit., noted by Io. And. in c. 1. de consti. lib. 6. All the more can he not do this by going against ancient custom and the statute of the church, since there are then two impediments, said c. cum consuetudinis. Likewise, presupposing that the lord Bishop could have proceeded alone against the absentees, nevertheless, since they were defended by custom, the Bishop ought not immediately after the term to have proceeded to deprivation, but, proceeding more leniently, first cause the church to be served through a vicar, the revenues being withheld from those absentees, and if in the course of time they persevered in contumacy, proceed to deprivation, as is noted in a similar case in c. pe., joined with the gloss, de cler. non residen. Likewise, the said deprivation collapses from a defect of the order not having been observed.
† For where it is known that

† an absent cleric is, and he can be suitably cited, he ought not to be cited by a general edict, but personally, a term for appearing having been fixed for him, as in c. ex parte, and c. qualiter, and c. inter quatuor, with similar texts, de cler. non residen. There is a notable gloss to which recourse is had daily, in c. quoniam frequenter, § si vero, de cle. non resid., which is a gloss directly on point in the sacred canons, which says that a sentence of deprivation made otherwise does not hold, and the doctors commonly follow it. Likewise, if it is not known where he is, three citations ought to be made successively in the church, after the lapse of which the absentee ought to be waited for through six months, as is proved in c. ex tua, de cleric. non residen.; and therefore three are required successively, because a single one, even peremptory, does not suffice, as Io. An. fully pursues and establishes properly on our point upon the rubric de cler. non residen. in additio. Specu. in the last question. And the law established this so because this citation is not made to the person, nor to the house, but in the church; whence such a canon who will report to the absentee will be made more certain in the second or third citation, who was unaware in the first. To the same effect makes what the gloss notes in a similar case in clemen. 1. de vita & honest. cle., on the word tertio. But in our case these things were not observed against these canons, since it was intimated to me by word that of one of them it was known where he was, nor is he so far absent that he could not be conveniently cited, nor was he cited personally; all the more, if it was not known where he was, nevertheless he was not sought out with three citations having been made successively, nor waited for through six months after their lapse. From which I conclude that the said deprivation is not valid, both from a defect of cause, and from a defect of the order not having been observed. From these, as superfluous, the second doubt could be left aside; but so that those inquiring may be satisfied as to what should be said, the validity of the deprivation being presupposed, I speak thus: that notice of the deprivation either likely reached the canons through capit. quia diversitatem, at the end, de concess. praeben., and cap. licet, de supplen. neglig. praelato., nor is intimation of the deprivation necessary, because one who is certain ought not to be certified, as in the rule eum, qui certus, de reg. iur. lib. 6., and in l. 1, ff. de act. emp., and fully through the lords of the Rota, decis. 25 and 1191. And this briefly concerning the second point. As to the third, I say
† that a custom is valid that the reception of canons pertains solely to the cha-

† -pter. Thus the bishop cannot, notwithstanding the custom, claim for himself the right of confirming: the text is in c. cum ecclesia vulterrana, de elect., and c. postulasti, de concess. praebend., and cap. unico, ne sede vacan. lib. 6; the text joined with the gloss in c. fin. de reg. iur. eod. lib. makes to this effect. And this is commonly held by all doctors; nay rather, provision could also be made by individual canons concerning a custom to be observed, as in cap. fin. de praeben. lib. 6; c. cum in ecclesia, eod. titu. & lib., makes for the first point. To the fourth, I say that the bishop cannot abolish reasonable and ancient customs and statutes without the chapter, nor conversely the chapter without the bishop, as in said cap. cum consuetudinis; nay rather, if they are honorable to the church, they ought not to be abolished even by the bishop and the chapter together, as Inno. notes in c. accedentibus, de privileg. If, however, they tend to the grave prejudice or dishonor of the church, the bishop ought to abolish them with the counsel of the chapter; but if the chapter does not wish to consent, the bishop alone can assemble [or: proceed], even if an oath had intervened, as in c. j. de his quae fi. a maio. par. cap.; what the gloss notes in cap. in his, xj. distinct., makes to this effect. If, however, the act were indifferent, then I think the consent of the chapter is required through the said capit. consuetudinis, and what Ioan. And. notes there after Abb. And from these things it is clear what must be said on the points of our question, as was stated more specifically above. And let these things suffice, etc. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The penalty for unpaid gabelle passes to the heirs.
2. He is said to commit fraud who, for the deception of another and for his own advantage, either keeps silent about the truth or expresses what is false.
3. Statutes must be understood according to the proper meaning of the words.
4. A professed friar left the order and took a wife; whether an inquisitor can proceed against him.
5. A tax farmer who leased tolls from the fiscus, if he delays paying at the appointed time, can be compelled to make satisfaction, but nevertheless does not incur the penalty.
casus: In a certain Sienese statute it is provided among other things as follows: 'We also ordain that no one, against anyone, shall presume not to pay gabelle by any direct or indirect manner, for which he was bound to pay gabelle, or indeed in any other manner; and whoever acts to the contrary shall be condemned, for each that he was bound to pay, in one hundred denarii, etc.' While this statute was in force, a certain master of cups, who by a certain ordinance of the city was bound to pay in the name of gabelle one hundred Sienese pounds for every year in which he worked or caused cups to be worked, paid the gabelle for a certain time. Finally, after one year had passed in which he had caused work to be done for a short time, he paid for the following year, making no mention that he had worked in the preceding year; he did not, however, say the contrary, but simply paid for that year. Proceedings are subsequently brought against this master by an official of the gabelle submitting that he had defrauded the gabelle and incurred the penalty of the said statute. It is said on behalf of the said master that, from the fact that he did not pay, he committed no fraud, because he did not delay payment with the intention of defrauding. It is asked what the law is.
body: IN the name of Christ, Amen. It appears at first that the said master has incurred the penalty because he neither paid nor declared himself bound to pay, which is shown as follows. For those things that are paid to the prince are called either a toll (vectigal), or a tribute, or a public function, or a tax, as noted by the Gloss and Bartolus in l. 1, ff. de pub. But from the non-payment of any of these at the due time, a penalty is incurred ipso facto by reason of the unpaid tribute, nor is it confiscated ipso facto, as in l. Imperatores, and what is noted there, ff. eod.; and by reason of a toll, the whole thing from which the toll was to be paid is confiscated.

† So much so that this penalty also passes against the heirs, as in l. fraudati, and l. commissa, ff. eo., which occurs especially because such persons, by not paying, appear to intend to defraud the prince or the gabelle, d. l. fraudati. Therefore, the said master, by not paying for that year, nor otherwise declaring himself a debtor, as a defrauder of the gabelle ought to have incurred the penalty of the statute ipso facto. And for this, in the same direction, serves the Gloss in l. 1, C. de uect. & commis. and in d. l. commissa, which says that if someone declares that he is bound to pay the gabelle, yet does not pay, he does not incur the penalty, but is only obliged to the due payment, as in d. l. 1 according to one interpretation. If, however, he neither pays nor declares, as a defrauder he incurs the penalty ipso facto. Secondly, it is principally proven because otherwise the aforementioned statute punishes anyone defrauding the gabelle directly or indirectly; but the said master com-

† mitted a fraud against the gabelle; therefore. The minor premise is proven: he is said to commit a fraud who, for the deception of another and for his own advantage, either keeps silent about the truth or expresses what is false; this is proven from what is read and noted in l. iurisgentium, §. dolo malo, §. sed si fraudandi, ff. de pact. and l. 1, §. dolum malum, ff. de dolo. But the said master kept silent about the truth, namely that he was obligated for the preceding year, and paid for the following year, as if no obligation had preceded. Therefore, from this conjecture he seems to have intended to deceive the commune and defraud the gabelle, since fraud cannot exist without malice (dolus), which cannot be proved except by conjectures, l. dolum, de dolo, c. præsumitur, de reg. iur. lib. 6. And in unlawful acts malice is presumed, de præsump. c. 1; hence Innocent says there in c. 1 that where one inflicts evil or harm, a bad intention is always presumed, unless a contrary presumption prevails, citing l. si obstetrix, §. fin. and l. ita uulneratus, ff. ad l. Aquil. But this master committed harm and fault by not paying at the due time, nor otherwise declaring the debt, but passed on to the payment of the other year, as if he were obligated for nothing at present; therefore he ought to be presumed to have acted with a bad intention, and a culpable person is presumed to act fraudulently, as in l. magna negligentia, ff. de uerb. sig. But these notwithstanding, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer. The foundation of this my opinion is that wherever the law, in imposing a corporal or pecuniary penalty, expressly or tacitly requires malice (dolus) or fraud, or speaks through words implying malice or fraud, to incur that penalty it is required that the person was truly in malice or in fraud, so that it does not suffice for him to be in fault, even gross fault (culpa lata). Hence gross fault in these cases is not equated to malice, as is proven in c. si quis suadente, 17, q. 4, joined with c. si uerò, ti. 2, de sen. excom. and l. 2, §. hæc actio, ff. ui bo. rap. and l. 2, §. si quis ideo, ff. ne uis fiat ei, and what is noted in d. l. magna negligentia; and it is a notable theory of Bartolus in l. 1, ff. si quis testa. lib. esse ius. sue., and what he notes in l. quod Nerua, ff. deposi., l. 1, ff. de legi. and in l. aut qui aliter, ff. quod ui aut clan. supports this. But the statute of which mention is made above speaks through words implying fraud; therefore there is no place for that penalty unless the said master was in fraud, nor does it suffice that he was in fault, even gross fault. In favor of which also serves l. 1, §. lege and l. 3, ff. ad l. Iul. de sica. and l. 1, C. eo. tit. This most true foundation having been established, it remains to examine whether the said master was in fraud by withholding payment for one year and paying for the following; and certainly I find him in no fraud. For first, the rule of law is in his favor, which does not presume anyone to be malicious; but the burden of proof is given to the one asserting malice, as in l. quoties, §. qui dolo, ff. de proba. Secondly, it is proven from the proper meaning of the words.

† For statutes must be understood according to the proper sense of the words, as Baldus notes in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu. For fraud is the same according to the interpretation that Bartolus places there, or it inheres in malice as a species according to the more principal interpretation, which seems more pleasing to the Gloss there, so that fraud does not exist without malice; but malice according to this interpretation can exist without fraud; for fraud occurs when I wish to deceive and mislead someone without my own advantage; and whichever of these interpretations holds, it is not of great concern; as to the proposition, it is commonly held that fraud is not committed without malice, which is proven in l. fraudis interpretatio, ff. de reg. iur. But in malice there is all craftiness, scheming of deceit applied to circumvent, mislead, and deceive another, as d. l. 1, §. dolum malum, and d. l. iurisgentium, §. dolo malo. But certainly, if this master was indebted to the commune for two consecutive years, and paid only for the latter, he applied no deceit or craftiness to deceive the community or defraud the gabelle, for he does that which is permitted to him by the ius commune. For wherever someone is indebted to a creditor for diverse debts, he can, in paying, specify to which cause he wishes to pay, as l. Paulus, §. Paulus, ff. de solu. Nor is he said to commit fraud in choosing the recent debt and not paying for the older cause, as there; for fraud ceases in that which is done by permission of the law, l. Gracchus, C. de adult. and c. qui peccat, 23, q. 4. Nor is it provided by any law that by choosing the more recent cause the debtor is bound to mention all preceding debts. The gabelle of one year, however, is entirely separate from the gabelle of another year, so that there are as many debts as there are payments, as l. cum notissimi, and what is noted there, C. de præscrip. 30. uel 40. ann. Thirdly, I prove it thus: wherever someone can be moved to an act from a malicious and fraudulent cause and from a licit and honest cause, or at least a non-malicious one, we ought never in doubt to presume the fraudulent cause, as is the text in l. merito, ff. pro soc.; chapter estote misericordes, de regu. iur. supports this. But the said master could have omitted the payment from inability to pay, or from forgetfulness, because in that year he had caused work to be done for only a short time on account of the plague that supervened, for which cause he absented himself for a long time from the city, as is presupposed to me in the fact, and two years elapsed before he paid anything; therefore in this doubtful fact we ought rather to presume one of these honest causes than to presume fraud and malice, since we ought to presume good concerning anyone, as in cap. fi. de præsum., and we are taught by experience that debtors defer payment beyond the due time rather from inability to pay than with the intention of defrauding the creditor; and in doubt the argument from what commonly happens is valid, as noted in ca. 1, de cleri. non residen. Also, the presumption of fraud is excluded on another ground, namely that he exercised his craft notoriously, and a writing was made concerning all payments; hence it is not likely that he would have notoriously wished to deceive his community, for the presumption of fraud and malice ceases in a notorious fact, according to what is noted by Iacobus Butrigarius in l. 2, C. de summa trini.; in addition to this, the texts in l. non existimo, ff. de admini. tuto., and l. qui sine, de neg. gest., and l. fin., de ritu nupt. Hence Butrigarius concludes

† as above, regarding a question that was de facto: a certain professed friar left his order and took a wife. It was asked whether the inquisitor could proceed against him, and he concluded thus: that either he married the wife secretly, and is presumed to be in malice and not in error, and therefore the inquisitor ought to investigate; or he took her openly, and is not presumed to be in malice, but to err. So I say to the purpose at hand: if this man had had the intention of defrauding, he would not have worked publicly as he did, but in secret, because he who does evil hates the light, de off. deleg. ca. consuluit. Moreover, from the omission of one year and the payment of the following, a presumption is not inferred that he paid for the other; hence he lies neither expressly nor tacitly. Therefore all craftiness and deceit, which is required to commit fraud, ceases. To this serves the good text and what is noted there in l. quicunque, C. de apoc. lib. 11.

† See further that if a tax-farmer (publicanus), who leases tolls from the fiscus, defers paying the stipulated price to the fiscus at the due time, he does not incur any penalty, but can be compelled or forced to satisfy it with interest of a modest time, l. uectigalia, §. fi., ff. de publi.; therefore the same must be said regarding this master, who seems to be bound to the fiscus from a certain quasi-contract entered into with the community. For this master did not conceal the thing from which the gabelle was to be paid, from which fraud would be presumed, l. fraudati, ff. de public.; nor was he bound to pay tribute from his own property, in which case the property would fall into forfeiture (commissum), and so speak the laws cited above; but he was bound to pay from a quasi-contract entered into with the commune, according to what is noted at the end by Bartolus in l. fi., de decr. ab or. fac.; nor was he bound to show any thing, since payment was not to be made for transporting goods, in which case the laws that speak of declaration and payment apply; but he was bound to pay from the cause that he was working. Hence, if he did not pay, he is in fault, yet not in malice. Nor in this case ought we to presume malice, on account of those things that I have set forth more extensively above. And through this let there be an answer to the contrary points formulated in the beginning. I conclude, therefore, that the said master has not incurred the penalty of the said statute, especially because in doubt we ought to interpret on the more favorable side, l. hæ causæ, ff. de suspec. tuto., and l. interpretatione, ff. de pœnis, and the rule in pœnis, ff. de regu. iu. lib. 6; what is noted by Bartolus in l. 1, ff. de effrac. supports this. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus de Tudeschis (Abbas Panormitanus).

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A buyer, when a dispute is raised against him concerning the purchased thing, if he voluntarily submitted to arbitration and was defeated, has no recourse for eviction against the seller.
2. One is not said to have peaceful possession if a dispute is immediately raised against him concerning it.
3. One who has suffered a second decree can, by benefit of the law within a year, tender the debt to the creditor and recover his goods given in satisfaction to that creditor.
casus: In effect the case is as follows. It is provided, among other things, in a certain Sienese statute that if anyone has received in satisfaction and payment by authority of the court or of any judge any immovable property, by a first and second decree, or otherwise for the execution of a sentence, arbitral award, or other public instrument in cases in which, by a second decree or in whatever manner, it was adjudicated or delivered to him by authority of the court or judge, etc., so that the ownership, property, or possession of such thing is transferred, then in the said cases the recipient alone is bound to pay the full gabelle of such thing, namely eight denarii per pound; and after some words it is added: so that once a part has been alienated, it suffices that the gabelle of such property be paid once. While this statute was in force, a certain Nannes domini Angeli held by virtue of a first decree, on the occasion of a certain debt, certain immovable goods of his debtor, and with the passage of time obtained a second decree over the same, through which those goods were delivered to him in satisfaction and payment. From this sentence or interposition of the decree an appeal was made by the adverse party, and while the appeal was pending, a submission was made to common friends [as arbitrators], who among other things invalidated and annulled the aforesaid second decree, so that the said Nannes restored the said immovable goods by virtue of the pronouncement of the arbitrators. Now it is asked whether by virtue of the said statute he is bound to pay the said gabelle, etc.
body: The aid of Christ and His mother having been humbly invoked: It seems, first, that it should be said that he is liable. For there must be no departure from the words of a statute unless the intent is otherwise evident; l. non aliter and l. ille aut ille, ff. de leg. 3. [cited as 4] and c. fin. de uerbo. significa. But the statute binds one who receives immovable property by virtue of a first and second decree to the payment of the gabelle, and this Nannes obtained those goods by virtue of a first and second decree; therefore, he is bound to pay the gabelle. For immediately upon receiving the goods under the first and second decree, the right to the gabelle accrued; l. cedere diem, ff. de uerb. sign.; and he is bound to pay even if the goods were afterward to perish in his hands, since it is enough that the provision of the law was once operative, just as the law says in a similar situation that it suffices that a condition was once fulfilled, even though it did not endure; l. si quis hæredem, C. de insti. & subst. And this applies especially from the subsequent words in the statute, insofar as they only require for the payment of the gabelle that ownership or possession be transferred to the recipient; and in our case, not only ownership or possession, but indeed both possession and ownership were transferred to the said Nannes by the interposition of the second decree. For since by the first decree the detention of those goods was with the said Nannes, so that by the second decree, through which those goods were given to him in payment and satisfaction, he immediately acquired ownership and true possession, inasmuch as he already held those goods in his detention, so that that judgment immediately carried execution with it; a good text for this is in l. fi. C. de iu. do. impe. and Instit. de rerum diui. §. interdum with the following §, and what Bartolus notes in l. si finita, §. Iulianus, ff. de dam. infe. Nor does it stand in the way if it be said that those goods did not remain with him, so that the said Nannes cannot be excused by this; for since he lost them by his own voluntary act, it is to be imputed to him, for he ought not to have submitted to arbitration, but to have pursued the appeal. A good text for this is in l. si dictum, §. 1, ff. de euic., where it is said,

† that if a buyer, when a dispute is raised against him over the purchased property, voluntarily submitted to arbitration and was defeated, he has no recourse for eviction against the seller. For he ought to have awaited the judge's sentence and thus proceeded by a necessary act; l. utique, ff. de iud. For just as he would not have avoided the gabelle if he had transferred those goods to another by a compromise or another contract—because it is sufficient that the right to the gabelle accrued once; an argument in l. commissa and in l. fraudati, ff. de pub. and l. continuus, ff. de uerb. obl.—so he ought not to avoid it if he lost those goods through a submission to arbitration; because a voluntary submission to arbitration is a kind of transaction (compromise), as is read and noted in Auth. si uerò contigerit, C. de iud., noted by Innocent in c. quintauallis, de iureiuran., and by Bartolus in l. societatem, §. arbitrorum, ff. pro socio. And this seems the stronger argument, and at first glance it seems to conclude according to rigor, especially considering the text in l. cum hi, §. si cum lis, ff. de transact. But these notwithstanding, I consider the contrary opinion to be truer, to which I am moved by several most equitable and natural reasons. And first, because an act cannot be said to have been done, especially in an odious matter, when the act does not endure, as in c. nam & ego, de uerb. sign., with the concordances noted there in the Glossa; just as, in granting an action against a father, money is not said to have been turned to his benefit when the benefit does not endure; ff. de in rem uerso. And the word 'to receive', like the word 'to have', must be understood effectively and not superficially, as in c. relatum, de præben., so that the disposition of the statute may have a permanent effect; de pœn. distinc. 1, c. hæc autem uerba, and l. 1 and 2, ff. quod quisque iur., and 1, quæst. 1, ca. Marchion. Therefore, the aforesaid statute binding one who receives goods by virtue of a first and second decree to the payment of the gabelle must be understood as referring to one who receives with effect, such that the transfer of ownership or possession held and endured. For an act cannot be said to have taken place if its effect is immediately extinguished or obstructed; an excellent argument in c. commissa, de elect. in Sexto, and what is noted there, where it is clear

† that one is not said to have had peaceful possession if a dispute is immediately raised against him concerning it. For it was not the intention of the enactors of the statute to bind and obligate anyone to the payment of the gabelle without benefit and a real acquisition, since this is contrary to natural reason, according to which no one ought to be enriched to the loss of another; as in the rule locupletari, de reg. iu. in Sexto, and l. nam hoc natura, ff. de cond. indeb., and especially since the fiscus is then deemed to abound when it has wealthy subjects; in Auth. ut iudic. sine quoquo suffragio, §. cogitatio; and especially because gabelles are odious; l. 2, C. noua uectig. insti. non po., and l. uectigalia, and what Bartolus notes there, ff. de publica. But in our case the effect of the second decree did not endure, since it was immediately extinguished by the appeal, and thus by a lawful act without any fault of this Nannes, as is proved in l. 2, ff. de pœ. and l. 1 at the end, ff. ad Turpil. And although there have been different opinions as to whether a sentence is extinguished or suspended by an appeal—since the texts of canon law commonly say that it is suspended, as in cap. uenientes, de iureiuran., and c. pastoralis, §. præterea, de off. delega., and the civil laws say that it is extinguished, in said l. 1 at the end—nevertheless, it is sufficient for our purpose that the effect of that sentence was thereby immediately removed for the present by the appeal, which applies even to a sentence that carries execution with it, as is proved in l. furti, ff. de his qui not. infam. By these laws it is proved that, an appeal having followed, this Nannes cannot be said to have ownership or possession of those goods; therefore, he is not bound to the payment of the gabelle. Nor does it hinder that he submitted to arbitration, because by this submission alone he did not lose the ownership and possession of those goods, since through the appeal he did not have ownership and possession by virtue of the first and second decree, nor ought he to incur that penalty through the act of submission, since in submitting to arbitration he made use of a legitimate legal path, as in Clementin. quandiu, de appella., and in Auth. si tamen, C. de tempo. appell. And just as he was defeated before the arbitrators, so could he have been defeated before the appellate judge. Likewise, this Nannes seeks nothing from another on the ground that he was defeated—in which case the provision of l. si dictum, cited above, would apply—but the gabelle is sought from him, to which he is not bound, since he did not obtain the effect of the second decree, nor was it through him that he failed to have it. Second, it is principally and elegantly relevant

† that one who has suffered a second decree may, by benefit of the law within a year, tender the debt to the creditor and recover his goods given to that creditor in payment; an excellent argument in l. fi. C. de iure dot. impe., as Bartolus notably says in said §. Iulianus. If therefore the debtor, while the appeal was pending, came to terms with this his creditor through the intervention of arbitrators and recovered his goods, it ought not to be imputed to this man; for without any submission to arbitration he could have done this according to the aforesaid. And to this reason I see no answer, at least no sufficient one; for this man ought not to be compelled to pay to the public revenue that which in effect he did not have. Third, it works principally for this Nannes that in a doubtful matter judgment is to be rendered against the fiscus, as is a notable text in l. non puto, ff. de iur. fis., especially in our case, in which the fiscus contends for capturing a gain and the said Nannes for avoiding a loss, since from that second decree he obtained no benefit, and the fiscus suffered no harm; and this has the greatest equity, lest the fiscus be enriched contrary to all natural justice and good equity, and with the loss of its subjects. For natural justice can be alleged in their dispositions; l. scire oportet, §. sufficit, ff. de excu. tut., and l. secundò requiris, in fine, de ap.; and equity is to be preferred to rigor; l. placuit, C. de iudi.; and the judge ought to have the highest equity before his eyes; l. quod si Ephesi, in fine, ff. de eo, quod cer. lo., c. fi. de trans. And through these things the answer to the authorities cited above is clear, for they apply in cases different from ours. I conclude therefore that the said Nannes is not bound to the payment of the gabelle. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus de Tudeschis, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If one who holds a benefice is infirm, and is bound to appoint a vicar, if the benefice does not suffice for the sustenance of the lives of both, who will have to provide.
2. When two causes concur, of which one is natural and the other accidental, the natural one then prevails.
3. Whether anyone can obligate a benefice.
casus: A certain canon of Massa has long canonically held certain chaplaincies in the same church of Massa, which he cannot now serve, as those benefices require, on account of old age or a worsening illness. The lord bishop of Massa is pressing him to maintain a chaplain there at his own expense, or at least to contribute to the expenses of a chaplain placed there. The said canon replies that the revenues of his benefices scarcely reach the sum of 25 florins, so that he could not be sustained from them and bestow a portion upon the chaplain to be instituted. It is asked what the law is, etc.
body: The protection of Christ and of His loving Mother having been humbly invoked. It seems at first that the said canon is bound to give a competent portion to the chaplain, even though he could not live without penury out of the remainder, according to c. de rectoribus, de cle. ægro., where the text states that if the rector of a church is unable on account of the disease of leprosy to serve the church, a coadjutor must be appointed, who is to receive a suitable portion from the resources of the church; and the gloss there seems to decide our case.

† For it asks: what if the church cannot suffice for both? And it answers that the one serving the church shall have the revenues, and the bishop shall provide for that infirm man; it cites di. 82, c. 1 and 2. Likewise and secondly, it does not seem lawful for anyone to hold several chaplaincies in the same church, especially if he is a canon, as in our case: just as in the same church it is not permitted to hold several prebends; indeed, through the acquisition of a second, the first becomes vacant ipso facto, as in c. literas, and what is noted there, de conces. præben., and in clem. fin. de præben.; so it is not fitting for anyone to hold multiple similar offices or benefices in the same church: because the status of the church is disfigured and it is defrauded of its due service, since one cannot serve except for one; this is supported by what Ioan. And. notes in the said c. literas. But these notwithstanding, I judge that the contrary opinion prevails in law. I am moved first by the said c. de rectoribus, where a certain portion is given to the coadjutor; therefore all the revenues remain there with the prelate; and thus a richer provision is made for the rector than for the coadjutor. Therefore, if the revenues do not suffice for both, provision must first be made for the sick rector, as the more worthy and having a richer right, arg. in c. dilectus, and c. uolentes, de offic. delega., especially because the sick man is deemed to be serving. Whence the law states that sick servants whom we care for are understood to be serving us, as in l. 4, § Stichus, ff. de statulib., and l. in rebus, ff. commod., by which laws and c. 1 de cle. ægr., together with what is noted there, it is proved that the church is bound to support a sick rector; and if during the time of illness sustenance were denied to clerics, others would be deterred from the clerical state, and none would be found willing to soldier in the Church of God, as the text states in the pre-alleged c. 1. Hence it is that daily distributions are given to the sick, which are not given except to those serving and being present at the divine offices; as in c. 1 de cler. non resi. lib. 6, by which it is clear that the sick are to be held as serving; which I understand to apply when the illness was the proximate cause of not serving; otherwise, if he was not serving before the illness, because then he does not enjoy the benefit of a sick man, as noted in the said c. 1, and as Innocent held in c. ad audientiam, de cler. non resi.

† Furthermore, when two causes concur, of which one is natural and the other accidental, the natural prevails, l. qui habet, ff. de tutel.; this is supported by what the gloss notes in clem. 2 de offi. ordi. Provision must be made by priority to the infirm rector, who has the title and is deemed to be serving, rather than to an extraordinary chaplain or coadjutor who has not been instituted; and if the church suffers a deficiency in ministers, the bishop of the parish must provide for the chaplain; a very good argument to similar effect lies in those matters which are read and noted in c. 1 and c. de his, de eccle. ædifi., where it is clear that a beneficed cleric is not bound to repair the church except from those things that remain to him as a surplus. Whence he must first provide for himself, and afterwards for the fabric; and if the fabric does not suffice for itself, the people or the bishop must come to its aid, as is more fully noted there.

† To the same point: for at the time of illness, another person who has not wherewithal to live could well encumber the benefice by contracting debts, as Ioan. And. notes in c. ex præsentium, de pig., and as is noted in c. 1 de solu. The contrary arguments adduced above do not stand in the way. For the gloss in the said c. de rectoribus truly does not prove it, because the laws which it cites say only that the bishop is bound to provide for those who cannot seek their livelihood with their own hands; nor do they speak more of clerics than of laypersons. But in our case this canon has benefices, which at the time of illness he is deemed to serve; and thus he must be sustained from their revenues. And against that gloss, Vincentius there openly holds this, whose opinion the doctors cite and pass along with him, nor do they reject it; nay rather, an eminent doctor advised in a question of fact according to that opinion of Vincentius, namely Dom. Franciscus, Cardinal of Florence, as I heard from his own mouth, and he sets it forth in the said c. de rectoribus. To the second contrary argument, I answer that c. literas and the Clementine cited above speak of two prebends, not, however, of other inferior benefices of the same church. Nay rather, Federico of Siena advised in consi. 115 that a canon can by episcopal dispensation hold a chapel in the same church, since with a dispensation from the same bishop one can hold a canonry, a prebend, and a dignity or personatus and an office in the same church, as in c. 1, joined with the gloss, de consuetu. lib. 6. And today, by common custom, one may retain several simple benefices, especially when they do not require residence, or the one does not suffice for the sustenance of the beneficiary, as is fully noted by the gloss in capitu. gratia, de rescrip. libr. 6, and cle. gratiæ, eod. titu., and in capitu. dudum, § 2, de electio., and by Innocent there and in capitu. iam dudum. And whatever may be the case in law or custom, nevertheless in this matter of fact it is presupposed that the said canon lawfully possesses the said chapels, nor is the legitimacy of the title disputed; therefore I do not dwell further on this. It is concluded, therefore, that the said canon is not to be compelled to provide for the chaplain, or to contribute, if, after his necessities have been deducted, nothing remains to him. Nic. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A statute presuming fraud and simulation in certain contracts, especially of minors, is valid.
2. If a woman renounces the Velleianum in the same contract out of court, it is not valid.
3. A statute providing for a contract does not apply to a quasi-contract.
4. A statute of laymen is not valid concerning things pertaining to ecclesiastical jurisdiction.
5. An oath has the force of the clause: if what I do is not valid as I do it, let it be valid as it can be valid.
6. A minor can stand in court without a curator in spiritual matters.
7. A minor corporally swearing that he is of age, absent fraud on the part of the adversary, is excluded from the benefit of age introduced by the common law.
8. A fiction falls upon what is certain, a presumption upon what is uncertain.
9. An oath cannot be remitted without legitimate cause, even by the Pope, to the prejudice of another.
casus: In this cause, which is presently pending between Iacobus, son of the late Matthæolus de Fabricano, on the one part, and Nicolaus Cane on the other part, concerning the validity of certain contracts and oaths, and their relaxation, in order to reach a lucid decision, etc.
body: Having invoked the help of Christ and His mother, I shall set forth five doubtful points to be examined. First, whether by the oath taken during his minority by the said Iacobus, in that he first swore that he was of age and afterwards swore to the observance of the contract, he incurred any bond, given the statute of the province in which a certain formality is prescribed for contracts of minors, which, if disregarded, the said contracts are decreed to be presumed and fictitiously held to have been made deceitfully, and to retain no validity, and nonetheless those contracting with minors contrary to the form of the statute are to be punished at the discretion of the judge. The second doubt: assuming the invalidity of those oaths and of the contract from the defect of statutory formality, whether the said contract entered into with the said minor Iacobus can be sustained on the basis of a ratification by the same Iacobus, confirmed by oath during his majority, while implying that he was deceived in that contract beyond half the just price. The third doubt: assuming the validity and bond of those oaths, or of either of them, ought the said Iacobus to have been heard when seeking absolution from the lord bishop. The fourth doubt: whether the lord bishop and his vicar acted lawfully both in pronouncing and in relaxing the said oaths. The fifth and last: what the role of the judge of appeal is and ought to be. I reply to the first: and first to the negative side, that no bond inheres in the said oath.

† For according to all, a statute is valid that presumes fraud and simulation in certain contracts, especially of minors, to such a degree that oaths sworn in them are rendered of no effect, as if extorted by fraud and simulated; for this, l. si mulier, and in auth. si qua mulier, C. ad velle., l. principalibus, ff. si cer. pe., and l. unica, C. de contra. iud. Note on our precise point Bar. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iur., in the 8th or 9th col., where he says that either the statute simply annuls the oath when the formality is not observed, and it is not valid, or it provides that a contract entered into otherwise is presumed fraudulent, or that minors are presumed to be induced by fraud, and it is also valid to the extent of annulling the oath. He is moved by the reason that a statute can presume fraud, and an oath extorted by fraud is not valid, as in c. cum contingat, de iureiu., and c. 2, de pac. in 6., and auth. sacramenta puberum, C. si adver. ven. Bal. thinks more broadly in the said auth. sacramenta puberum; for he says that even if the statute does not feign fraud and simulation and iniquity—for instance, because the malice of the men of that place was prompt to deceive minors—statutes annulling oaths are valid, and since they have equity and natural reason, they cannot be called contrary to law; he admits it to be good caution, which is observed in many places, that contracts contrary to statutes are presumed to have been entered into through fraud or fear. The same Bal. touches upon this matter more fully in l. non dubium, C. de legi.; nevertheless, as regards our case, he seems to mean that an oath without the formality of the statute being observed is not valid. For he says in effect, as to our proposition, that either the reason for the statutory prohibition is founded upon natural equity, and the oath is not valid, as for instance when the statute is founded upon fraud and simulation, as in our case; or it is founded upon a certain positive equity, and it is valid, and in this case those texts can be understood which are found in c. 2 and c. cum contingat, and the auth. sacramenta puberum cited above. And if someone should say that this applies with respect to an oath interposed concerning the observance of the contract, and not when he swore beforehand that he was of age: I reply that if that oath was taken in the same contract, it ought to be presumed extorted just as the contract itself, because an oath is not presumed to have been taken of one's own will, which is almost always from evil, as the text says in c. super hoc, de renun., since with the same ease with which minors are induced to contract, they can be induced to swear that they are of age. And if we were to say the contrary, such a statute would be of no effect, since minors induced to contract would easily swear that they were of age. For this there is a good text in the said l. si mulier; hence Bar. in l. si, C. ad velleia., says,

† that if a woman renounces the Velleianum out of court in the same contract, it is not valid, because with the same ease with which she is induced to obligate herself, she can be induced to renounce, and thus the law would be made a mockery. The same is noted on a similar matter in l. si ex cautione, C. de non nu. pec., where it is said that a renunciation made in the same contract is not valid when someone confesses that he has received loaned money. To the same effect is what he himself notes in l. nemo potest, ff. de leg. j., where he says that a renunciation of the defense of simulation in the very contract which is alleged to be simulated is not valid, because everything in the same instrument ought to be presumed simulated if the contract is proved to be simulated. So it seems should be said in our case, since by the statute, when the formality is not observed, the contract is presumed to have been extorted by fraud; everything then done, as accessories and preambles, ought to be presumed extorted by fraud. This is supported by the rule accessorium, de reg. iur. in 6., and l. oratio, ff. de spon., and c. prudentiam, and c. praeterea, de offic. dele. But these points notwithstanding, I consider the contrary opinion to be truer. I am moved first because the said statute ought not to be extended to an oath previously taken, since he swore before any contract that he was of age, for since a statute deviates from the rules, it ought in no way to be extended to a case similar to a fiction, as in l. 3, § haec autem verba, ff. de neg. gest., noted by Bar. in l. non dubium, cited above; this is supported by what I have read and noted in c. in vestra, de iureiu., and by Io. An. in the rule pro possessore, de reg. iu. in 6., in Mercuriales, and c. statutum, de electio. in 6., and l. quod vero contra rationem, ff. de legi. Nay more, what is greater,

† a statute providing regarding a contract has no place in a quasi-contract, as Bar. expressly notes in l. apud Iulianum, ff. ex qui. caus. in pos. ea., and in l. si minor, ff. de acquir. haere. Just as, conversely, a statute concerning a quasi-contract has no place in a true contract,

† as the gloss intended to note in c. decet, de immu. eccle. in 6., where it says that the provision of that chapter annulling a judgment held in a church is not extended to contracts. So it seems should be said in the present case: that this statute, providing regarding a contract, ought not to be extended to the prior oath concerning majority, since that is neither a contract nor a quasi-contract, as is proved from what is found in l. Labeo, l. a 2., de verb. signi., and l. omnem obligationem, ff. de iudi., with the notes there. Nay, even more: that even if the statute had expressly wished to include that oath, it would not have been valid, because it does not belong to laypersons to decide concerning an oath, any more than concerning another spiritual right, as Host. notes in c. quemadmodum, de iureiu.; this is proved in c. venerabilem, de elec., and noted by Fed. de Senis, consi. 91 and consi. 95, where he says generally

† that no statute of laymen is valid concerning matters belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction. For this, c. si imperator, dist. 90, where it is said that for spiritual matters even the emperor must have recourse to the Church; c. novit, de iudi., supports this. It is proved by an unassailable reason: for if a layman cannot take cognizance of the validity of an oath or another spiritual act, as in c. tuam, de ordi. cog., and c. lator, qui fil. sint legi., and c. si iudex laicus, de senten. exc. in 6., and noted by Bart. in l. Titia, ff. so. mat., and l. 1, de iur. om. iu., therefore, with greater reason, he cannot enact statutes concerning it, since a statute takes its force from the power of the lawmaker, de senten. excom. c. a nobis, and l. fi., ff. de iur. om. iu., and c. ut animarum, de consti. in 6. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that it was taken upon the contract, because the statute presumes fraud, since this oath, as I have said, preceded the contract and cannot be called part of the contract. Whence, even granting that the contract collapsed entirely, the oath would nonetheless remain valid, and thus it ought not to be judged according to the nature of the contract; for this, l. etiam, ff. de mino., and l. scire debemus, ff. de verbo. obli.; this is supported by what Inno. notes on a similar point in c. fi., de resti. spo., saying that it is sustained even though the judgment collapses, and it is proved in cle. constitutionem, de elec. For an oath subsists by itself, nor does it even accede to the contract; whence it can be taken even upon a null contract, as in c. debito res, and what is there noted, de iureiur. Furthermore, one is presumed to approach an oath more deliberately, as a spiritual act and one perilous to the soul, than a contract concerning temporal matters; therefore one ought more easily to be presumed induced by fraud regarding a contract than regarding an oath; for this, what I have read and noted in l. cum quis, § codicillis, ff. de leg. 3, and in authen. de iureiur. a maio. praest., by Bart. in l. sciendum, ff. de verb. obli., and l. 2, C. de rescin. ven.; the text, with the gloss there, in l. cum pater, § filius matrem, ff. de leg. 2, supports this excellently. Hence we say,

† that an oath has the force of the clause: 'if what I do is not valid as I do it, let it be valid as it best can be valid', as there, and it is proved in c. ad nostram, in l. 3, de iureiu. Hence it is also provided by law

† that a minor can in spiritual matters stand in judgment without a curator, and not so regarding temporal matters, as in c. si annum, de iudi. in 6., joined with the gloss on l. clarum, C. de aucto. praestan. From these points it is concluded that the first oath is valid, by which he swore that he was of age, since it is not proved that the same Iacobus was induced by fraud to take the oath, nor is the statute extended to this case by the things said above, and the argument formed above to the contrary ceases through this. Nay, I say further that it must be presumed that Iacobus himself swore fraudulently that he was of age, since he himself then knew that he was a minor, as he himself narrates in his libel, which must be believed against him, as in l. cum precum, C. de lib. cau., noted by Bar. in l. certum, § si quis absente, ff. de confes.; whence at least in this case fraud ought to be presumed, since he knew he was a minor, and the gloss in l. si alterius, C. si mi. se. ma. di., and Ioan. And. after Nico. de Ma. in addi. Spec. in tit. de sen. prola., § ut autem, after the beginning, ought to proceed in doubt; although Barto. says otherwise in the said l. si alterius, yet they can be harmonized: namely, if it is not proved that the older one knew he was a minor, not fraud, but simplicity is presumed, as Bar. intended; but if it is proved that he knew, let fraud be presumed, as in the gloss and by Io. And. For by swearing knowingly contrary to the truth, nothing other than fraud can be presumed. For this, l. quid enim, ff. de dolo; c. illud, and what is there noted, de praesum., supports this. And this concerning the first oath. I come now to the contract itself and the oath placed upon it: if it is proved that the contract is valid and holds, the statute ought to be judged and regarded just like the common law, and must take its interpretation from it, as in cap. cum dilectus, de consuetu., and l. 2, C. de noxa, noted by Innocen. in cap. causam, de rescrip., and Barto. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iure.

† But a minor swearing corporally that he is of age, where fraud on the part of the adversary is absent, is excluded from the benefit of minority introduced by the common law, as in the said l. si alterius, C. si mi. se. ma. di. Therefore he ought also to be excluded from the benefit of the statute, which Ioan. And. and Nico. de Mata. also meant in the aforesaid addition. This is supported by the fact that because a minor acts fraudulently, he ought not to enjoy the benefit of minority, l. 1, § pupillum, ff. depositi, and l. auxilium, ff. de mino. But this man swore that he was of age, as has been proved above, therefore he ought not to enjoy the benefit of the statute as a minor. Furthermore, I say that even in the absence of the first oath, the sale ought nevertheless to be valid on account of the oath placed upon it to observe it; because although a statute is valid as to breaking an unsworn contract, it is otherwise, however, where an oath has intervened, because a statute of laymen cannot, to the prejudice of an oath, presume fraud, for otherwise a way would be opened to laymen to invalidate all instruments of minors and women, namely by presuimg that—to wit, fraud or simulation—and that which is prohibited by one path ought not to be admitted when introduced by another, capitu. tuae, de procura., and the rule cum quid una via, de regul. iur. in 6. And therefore lord Anton. de Butr. elegantly said on this passage in the capitu. cum contingat, cited above, that either a legitimate cause for presuming fraud or simulation appears in the contracts of minors, and the virtue of the oath is impeded, or a legitimate cause for presuming does not appear, and the oath is valid, even if the statute specifically annulled the oath. But I examined this article more broadly in a certain disputation of mine, and most recently in the lecture on that cap. cum contingat, and there I then concluded, and now also conclude anew, that since no specific and probable conjecture appears for presuming fraud or another illicit cause, the statute does not suffice to empty the oath; because where an urgent cause does not appear, an obligation to be rendered to God neither ought to nor can be impeded, ar. 25, quaestio. j., c. sunt quidam, and what Innoc. notes in cap. quae in ecclesiarum, de constit., and better in cap. quia plerique, at the end, de immu. eccle., and by the legists in l. fin., C. si contra ius vel uti. publi. For such a statute would be a cause of bad faith and perjury contrary to l. j., C. si adver. ven., and contrary to the canonical laws, nor ought faith to be lent to the enunciative words of the statute, since such words are not to be believed when the matter does not depend upon the mere disposition of the enactors, according to the note by Barto. in authen. si quis in aliquo documento, C. de eden., and in l. si forte, ff. de castren. pec., and in l. sciendum, ff. de verbo. obliga. Rather, it is necessary that the cause be proved extrinsically, for instance because in the place of the statute minors were accustomed to be led on by fraud, which is proved extrinsically. And this is supported by cap. 2, de pact. in 6., where the text says that such oaths are by all means to be observed, and the text in authen. sacramenta says 'inviolably,' etc., unless they are proved to have been extorted by fraud or fear, which is not proved here. Nay, if the words of that statute are well weighed, the enactors seem to have doubted concerning true fraud in that it is said in the statute that the contract is presumed and feigned to have been extorted by fraud; wherefore I weigh the word 'feigned.'

† For fiction falls upon what is certain, and presumption upon what is uncertain and what can be true, as noted in l. una, C. de rei uxo. acti., § accedit, on the word 'praesumatur', and by the canonists in c. is qui, de spon.; and thus the enactors wished to feign fraud where it did not exist, which they could not do to the prejudice of an oath. From this word I clearly argue that they did not have sufficient cause to presume fraud; otherwise they would not have used the word 'feigned'. Furthermore, if laymen cannot take cognizance even incidentally and accessorily of the validity of an oath or another spiritual act (the said c. tuam, de ord. cog., and c. lator, qui fil. sint legi.), so much the more can they not enact statutes in a doubtful matter, even incidentally and necessarily. I conclude therefore that the said contract was and is valid, and was confirmed by oath, according to what is noted by Bart. in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiu., and by the canonists in c. cum contingat, cited above; and the dictum of Bart. in the said l. omnes populi, and Bal., applies when from the beginning he did not swear that he was of age, and when it is proved that the enactors had a probable cause for presuming fraud; and through this the arguments formed to the contrary are removed. And this conclusion is especially to be maintained by those things which I shall subjoin below in the following doubt. I proceed to the second, in which, to avoid prolixity, I shall proceed conclusively. And I say that that ratification, if it was made in majority, imposes without any scruple all end and silence upon this dispute, so that without any doubt no deceit could now be alleged, even if it were proved beyond half the just price, even when an oath intervened, which has the effect of excluding the remedy of l. 2, C. de rescin. ven., and as noted there by the gloss and Bar., and by the gloss and doctors in l. pe., de emp. & vendi. Both because this Iacobus said that, having been made certain of the true price of the thing sold, that it was worth more, he made a gift of it, which suffices according to Bar. in the said l. 2; l. si quis donationis, ff. de contrahen. emp., supports this. And although the said Iacobus uttered these words in the first contract when he was a minor, nevertheless, since he afterwards ratified and approved it, he is seen to have uttered them and contracted anew, l. 1, C. si ma. factus. This is supported by what Bar. similarly notes in l. Theopompus, ff. de dote praeleg., and l. eos, ff. de sal., and what is noted in cap. cum in tua, de testi. Likewise, one unassailable consideration supports this: for since he who confesses the same seems excluded from every benefit, so that he may be considered to have donated through error that which is worth more, and it ought especially to be presumed from the span of the intervening time that he truly knew the real value of the thing; for this there is an excellent text in l. si mulier, and in l. unica, near the end, C. de plus peti., noted by Bar. in l. cum scimus, de agri. & censi. lib. 11. And this is primary in this matter, even though the first confession or donation was made at an incompetent time, as is proved in the said l. si mulier. I come to the third, and I shall proceed both in this and in the following points conclusively, to avoid excessive prolixity. And I say that the said Iacobus ought not to have been heard when seeking absolution, as appears from the aforesaid, since no deception intervened, even if the value of the thing were proved to be beyond half of the price paid; for he freely donated what he could, since he was of full age at the time of the ratification, the said l. si quis donationis; and thus, even if he were de facto absolved from the oath, the contract would nevertheless remain firm and irrevocable, since it is of the ius gentium, l. ex hoc iure, ff. de iusti. & iure, to such an extent that even the Pope could not revoke it; for this, what Inno. notes in c. 2, de confir. uti., and in c. inquisitioni, de sen. exc., for those things which are of the ius gentium cannot be taken away by the prince, in cle. pastoralis, de re iudi., and Inst. de legi. agna. tute. at the end, and de iure naturali, gentium, & ciui. § sed naturalia, by the legists in the said l. fi., C. si contra ius, vel uti. pu. And even assuming that the said ratification had not intervened, he still ought not to have been heard, because lesion beyond moiety is not proved, nor indeed any lesion, if the statements of the witnesses are well weighed, as appears from their depositions, and from the notes of Bar. in l. pretia rerum, ff. ad l. Falci., and the said l. 2, de rescin. ven., and by the gloss in cap. cum causa, de test.; and therefore, when lesion beyond moiety does not subsist, the minor ought not to be heard; supporting this is the said auth. sacramenta, which commands oaths to be inviolably observed, and the said c. 2, de pact. in 6., where it is said 'let them by all means be observed', etc. Through that text Archi. hints there against Nico. in c. cum contingat, de iureiuran., where he said that the woman could in that c. 2 urge that she be absolved; for this is false through the said laws, and lord Ant. holds this in the said c. cum contingat, and I have always held it, and pursued it very extensively in the said disputation. For if absolution could be sought indifferently against those laws, they would serve almost as wind, which must not be said, since they emanated with such solemnity. Nor is there any text in the world that grants this absolution in this case. Nor does c. 1, de iureiur., and the note in c. debitores, under the same title, stand in the way, because there an usurious creditor, by not making restitution, is therefore compelled to relax the oath, or is heard when seeking absolution. Which does not occur in our case, since deceit is not proved; and in doubt this must be so held, whatever others may have thought. From these points I infer with respect to the fourth doubt, in which I say that the said bishop and his vicar in this matter, with due respect to them, did not proceed well: first, because they absolved the said Iacobus when no injury had been lawfully proved against the oath. Likewise, because he had ratified that contract; and if the said goods were worth anything more, he had donated this to the buyer, and the donation was perfected, as c. si, de don.,

† and an oath cannot be remitted without legitimate cause, even by the Pope to the prejudice of another, especially when judgment has been rendered, as noted by Inno. in c. cum inter, de renun., the gloss, and commonly the doctors in capitu. quanto, de iureiu., from which it can be said that that absolution was not valid, because it was made by one lacking power. Likewise, because the said Iacobus in the first contract had knowingly and deliberately declared by swearing that he was of age, and thus he ought not to obtain the benefit of absolution against the second oath, because he in vain invokes the aid of the law who transgresses against the law, de usur. c. quia frustra. Likewise, they pronounced and absolved upon matters not sought, contrary to all common rules of law, and especially in that judgment was pronounced upon the contract itself, whereas they were only approached concerning the accessory, namely concerning the oath; for concerning the contract, they ought to have preserved the case for its proper judge, as in capitu. sator, and capitu. causam, cited above, and what is noted in capitu. de prudentia, de do. post divor. resti., and c. causam, qui fil. sint legi., and c. novit, de iudi. From all these things I infer with respect to the last: namely, that the office of the judge of appeal consists in pronouncing that it was well appealed and badly judged, and in absolving, to declare that the contract is valid, etc. Nic. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A settlement made with some among several having the same right is not extended to the others.
2. An agreement that an emphyteuta cannot be expelled on account of cessation of the payment of the canon is valid.
3. Any custom against the church is not always null.
body: Invoking the name of Almighty God: in the matter of Guido Pauli of Urbino concerning emphyteutic right, two questions must be examined for the clarification of the entire subject matter. First, whether the articles entered into between the commune of Urbino and the chapter of the church of the same city regarding emphyteutic right extend to the property of a certain abbey situated in a foreign territory. The second doubt is, presupposing that the said articles are not to be extended to this case, whether the said Guido Pauli can at least be defended on the basis of the custom observed there, according to which the property of any church whatsoever situated in the territory of Urbino cannot be taken away from the emphyteuta by reason of a failure to pay the canon, but an action may only be brought for the payment of the rent itself, etc. In the name of our Christ, amen. Regarding the first, I briefly state that the said articles ought by no law to be extended to the property of the said abbey. First, from the lack of power of the enacting parties, for laymen could not make statutes to the prejudice of churches, even with respect to property situated in their territory, as is expressly stated in capitu. quae in ecclesiarum, and c. ecclesia sanctae Mariae, de const. and 96. di. c. bene quidem, and c. fi. de reb. eccl. non alie.; the auth. cassa, C. de sac. san. eccl. supports this. Secondly, even granting the power of the enacting parties, an extension ought not to be made to the property of that abbey, because, as is clearly evident from the words of the last article through which the extension is made, that extension ought to be directed to persons, as stated there: 'by all syndics, and proctors, or under whatever other name, and all managers of whatsoever churches, abbots, monks, etc.' Therefore, it does not encompass the property of those who are not from that territory, even if it were otherwise property subject to the jurisdiction of the enacting parties, as is clearly evident from the note by Inno. in capitu. postulasti, de fo. compe. and Bart. in l. cunctos populos, de sum. tri.; what is noted by Ioan. And. in c. cum secundum leges, de haeret. lib. 6 supports this. For although the articles with the canons appear to be drafted in rem, nevertheless the extension, which is relevant to our purpose, is conceived in personam. For it was not said that those articles should apply to all property situated in the territory of Urbino—in which case we would say the law was given with respect to things and not persons—but it was said that the persons ought to observe those articles and cause them to be observed, and thus they cannot encompass abbots from a foreign territory, arg. in l. 1. ff. de tuto. & cur. da. ab his. Nor on the grounds that the canons consented are the abbots bound to observe them, because an agreement is not extended to outside persons or property, l. si unus. §. ante omnia, ff. de pact.

† Indeed, a compromise made with some among several persons who have the same right is not extended to the others, l. j. C. de transactio. I also say that even if the bishop and the chapter had consented, an extension still would not be made to that abbot, per capitu. vestra, and what is noted there by Inno. de locato. From these points it is clearly concluded regarding the first question that by virtue of those articles, or of the extension, the said Guido Paulus cannot defend himself. I come to the second question: whether he could defend himself at least by force of common observance and custom. And first it seems that he cannot, because such a custom would be harmful to churches; therefore it is invalid, as in c. 1. de consue. Secondly, it seems that it is contrary to the substance of the emphyteutic contract, since it is of its nature that, if the rent is not paid within two years, the emphyteuta can be evicted by the lord, as in cap. potuit, de loca. and in l. 2. C. de iure emph. and institu. loca. §. adeo (I speak of the emphyteuta of a church, for in private law the statutory time is required, as in said l. 2); but a custom contrary to the substantial elements of an act is invalid, as in c. 2. joined with the gl. de consue. lib. 6; l. per servum, ff. de usu & habi. supports this. Likewise I see that if an agreement is made in which it is stated that he cannot be evicted, it is nevertheless understood provided that he has paid the rent; whence, if he ceases to pay for two years, he can nonetheless be evicted, even notwithstanding the agreement, as is the notable text in l. quaero. §. inter locatorem, ff. loca. Therefore, what an agreement cannot do, custom ought not to be able to introduce, according to what is noted by the gl. C. de decre. decu. super rub. lib. 10. But notwithstanding these points, I consider the contrary opinion to be truer in law. I am moved first because an agreement

† is valid that an emphyteuta cannot be evicted upon the cessation of the payment of the canon, as the gloss notably determines, which Bartol. follows in the previously cited l. 2. C. de iure emphy. Therefore, custom ought to be valid, since it is stronger than an agreement of private parties, as is proved in capitu. fin. de consue.; what the gloss notes super rubri. previously cited, and what Bartol. notes in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iur. support this. Nor is that agreement contrary to the substantial elements of the contract; rather, it would be contrary to the substantial elements if an agreement or custom were made that, with no rent paid, the contract would hold, because a lease or emphyteusis does not stand without a price or rent, l. si merces, ff. loca. and said §. adeo. But that an action be brought for the rent, and no eviction take place, is not contrary to the substantial elements, but contrary to the accidental elements, since those things are of the substance without which an act cannot stand, institu. de emptio. & venditio. §. pretium, as noted by Bartol. in l. prolatam, C. de sent. & interlo. omni. iudi. It is established, however, that an emphyteutic contract stands without eviction, said capitu. potuit; for, in the absence of an agreement and custom, the owner is able not to evict the emphyteuta, but to sue for the rent, as in said cap. potuit, and what is noted there, and in said l. 2; therefore the agreement is valid, l. 2. §. convenerit, ff. deposi. and capitu. uno, de commoda. and regula, contractus ex conven. de reg. iur. lib. 6. Furthermore, the Pope commands that cases of ecclesiastical persons and clerics be decided according to the custom of the country, as in capitu. 3. de eo, qui mit. in posses.; capitu. constitutus, de in integ. restitu. and the text a contrario sensu in capitu. cum causa, de re iudi. and what is noted by Bartol. in said l. cunctos populos support this. And I understand this—so that every objection may cease—when there is a common custom of both laymen and clerics, as happens in our case. For here a custom could not have been introduced without the tacit consent of the clerics; and a custom is introduced from non-use when the use contains in itself a tacit act contrary to the disposition of the common law, according to what is fully noted by Ioan. And. in capitu. Ioannes, de emptio. & venditio. and Cyn. in l. 2. C. quae sit longa consuetu. and is proved in said cap. Ioannes, understanding it, however, according to what is noted by Cy. in the place previously cited. A custom cannot give law to all property existing in a territory, whosesoever it may be, as in l. rebus, ff. de censi. and l. munerum. §. patrimoniorum autem, ff. de mune. & hono; 8. dist. c. quae contra, and 12. dist. c. illa, and l. illud, and what is noted by Inn. in said c. postulasti, and Bar. in said l. cunctos populos support this.
