And relevant to the matter is what Federicus posits in consi. 146, and Io. And. following Archidiaconus in c. 1. de immu. eccl. lib. 6, where they inquire about the property of an abbey existing in a territory other than where the abbey itself is located. The contrary arguments cited above do not stand in the way. To the first I say that this custom is not very harmful to churches; for it is already sufficient to be able to obtain the appointed rent, and this has equity, which the church ought to observe above others, as in c. suam, de poenis.

† For not every custom against the church is null, but that which brings great prejudice and is supported by no reason; for this, capitu. cum dilectus de consuetudi. and c. cum ecclesia Sutrina, de cau. possessio. & proprieta., cap. 2. de consuetu. lib. 6, and c. abbate, de verb. signi. with many similar texts. To the first point above, sufficient answer has already been given. To the fourth and last, I say that it applies when it was simply agreed that an unwilling tenant farmer or tenant should not be evicted; for the tacit condition is understood, 'provided he has paid the rent,' as stated there; but we are speaking where the custom expressly provides that the emphyteuta cannot be evicted, even if the canon has not been paid for more than two years, but that an action can be brought so that it may be paid. In which case I think that the custom is valid against a church, even one situated elsewhere, since the property is in the territory; in support of this is that a contract regarding a thing seems to be entered into according to the custom of the place, even if it has not been expressly stated, as in l. quod si nolit. §. quia assidua, ff. de aedili. edicto; Bar. notes this in l. nemo est, qui nesciat, ff. de duobus reis; l. fina. in fine, C. de fide instrumentorum supports this. And let these things suffice. Niccolò de' Tudeschi, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One can confess against oneself, but by no means in one's own favor.
2. Presumption must be made in favor of a sentence after it has passed into res judicata.
3. A judge cannot render a sentence under a resolutive condition.
casus: In the dispute which is pending between Laurentius, called Pallo, and his partners on the one part, and Balthasar Gentilis on the other part, concerning the capture and detention of the said Balthasar on the occasion of a paternal debt, having examined a certain booklet presented to me, in which are contained only certain statutes and reforms of the renowned city of Florence, and also a sentence rendered by the officials of the Mercanzia against the said Balthasar in favor of the said Laurentius and his partners, and certain simple executions alleged on behalf of the said Balthasar.
body: The aid of Christ and of His Mother having been humbly invoked, it appears at first that the said Balthasar is unjustly punished and unduly detained, and consequently ought to be released, both by common law and under the municipal statutes. For by the common law this seems most clear, since a son, whether of full age or a minor, is permitted to abstain from his father’s inheritance and avoid the hereditary creditors, as in l. necessariis, ff. de acq. haered. and Inst. de haeredum quali. et diffe. § sin autem, and similar texts; nor can a son be sued in the name of his father, C. ne filius pro patre, in the rubric and the black letter, especially in l. patris nomine. But the said Balthasar has abstained from the inheritance of Gentile, his father; therefore, he cannot be sued or detained on account of his father’s debts. The same must seemingly be said upon inspecting the provisions of the statutes: for sons are bound thereby when their parents have absconded (cessaverunt), or committed fraud or deceit, as is clear from the statute under the rubric ‘On sons and other descendants, and on fathers and other ascendants, and on brothers who abscond, and of fugitives, etc.’ and the statute under the rubric ‘On factors and apprentices of any partnership, etc.’ But from the premises it is not established before me that the said Gentile, the father of the said Balthasar, absconded, fled, or committed fraud or deceit in his agency or business. Therefore, by virtue of those statutes he is not bound, and consequently, since that case is not provided for in the statutes, it ought to be left to the disposition of the common law, de rescri. c. susceptum, li. 6, and l. commodissime, ff. de lib. et posthu. Nor does it impede this that this is stated to be contained in the libel of Lorenzo, where it is narrated that the said Gentile absconded, fled, and committed fraud and deceit; because the statements narrated in a libel certainly prove against the libelant, as is the notable text in l. cum pretium, C. de lib. cau., noted by Bartolus in l. certum, § si quis absente, ff. de confe., and the Canonists in c. 1, eodem titulo, but not in favor of the libelant:

† because although one may confess against oneself, one can by no means confess in one's own favor, 14, q. 2, in prin.; on the contrary, he must clearly prove those things that he sets forth in his libel, otherwise a doubtful proof does not relieve, as in c. in praesentia, de proba. Nor does the sentence rendered in favor of the said Lorenzo stand in the way: because that sentence can be said to be null, since it was pronounced under a resolutive condition. For at the end it was reserved to him that if the said Balthasar should prove his right throughout the entire month then fixed, the said sentence would be null and of no effect. But this the officials could not do: because no judge can rescind his own sentence or that of his predecessor, even if the innocence of the defendant should appear afterward, as in C. sen. rescin. non pos. l. 1 & 2, and l. divi, ff. de poe., and l. 1, § fin., ff. de quaest., and c. in literis, ff. de of. dele.; and notably on our exact point, Bartolus in l. iudex, ff. de re iud.; by the aforesaid laws, they conclude that a judge cannot render a sentence under a resolutive condition. Therefore the sentence ought not to stand, as being rendered contrary to the customary and due order of law, l. prolatam, C. de sen. et interlo. om. iu., and 2, q. 6, c. ei qui, § diffinitiva. But truly, unless something else is shown to me, it does not at all appear, as I deem it, that the said Balthasar ought on the aforesaid grounds to be released. First, there openly militates against him the sentence pronounced against him by the officials of the Mercanzia, from which it does not appear that an appeal was taken, but rather that it was confirmed by the lapse of time, which creates law between the parties, even if it had been unjust from the beginning, as in cap. cum inter, de re iud., and l. ingenuum, ff. de statu ho., and l. res iudicata, ff. de regul. iur. And there is a presumption in favor of this sentence both with respect to its justice and to its procedure, as in capitul. in praesentia, de renun., and cap. bonae, de elect., and cap. causam quae, de re iudic.; noted by Innocent in cap. cum in iure, de offi. deleg., and cap. quoniam contra, de proba., and the said cap. bonae, de elect., where he says

† that there is a presumption in favor of a sentence after it has passed into res judicata, because it is harsh to continually re-examine the proceedings; and it is fully noted by Giovanni Calderini in the said cap. quoniam contra. Whence, since in the libel it is said that the said Gentile absconded, fled, and committed fraud and deceit, and proofs on these matters were adduced on both sides, as is narrated in the sentence, and the officials rendered their sentence, approving and confirming the arrest of the said Balthasar, and pronouncing that he, as a son in paternal power, was bound and would be liable for the act of his father to the said Lorenzo and his partners; which sentence, having not been rescinded or suspended by any law or remedy, certainly created law between the parties, so that the said Balthasar can no longer complain of an unjust sentence. For by not appealing he is deemed to have acquiesced to that sentence, as in c. quod ad consultationem, de re iud., which applies both in civil and in criminal matters, even where the penalty of ultimate punishment is to be imposed, as in l. non tantum, ff. de app., and the said l. 1, § fin., de quaestio., and the said l. divi; to which is relevant what is noted by Bartolus in l. qui ultimo supplicio, de poenis. Nay rather, if after an unsuspended sentence the innocence of the defendant should become evident, perhaps from newly discovered proofs, only the prince could grant him restitution, as is notably proved in the said l. divi, and l. 1, § fi., cited above, and in both places by Bartolus; to which relates cap. suborta, cap. inter monasterium, de re iud., and l. sub praetextu, C. de transact. Nor should credence be given to the bare words of the said Balthasar now alleging that his father had not committed deceit: because credit must rather be given to the sentence than to him, and let him impute it to himself why he did not show this before the officials, or why he did not appeal. Moreover, this allegation of Balthasar—that his father did not commit deceit or fraud—even if it were true, does not establish the inequity of the sentence or that his arrest was unjust; because if the statutes alleged above by me are well weighed, they provide not only against factors who employ fraud or deceit, but also against absconding fugitives or those refusing to render an account to their masters and partners, or failing to restore to them what they owe. All of these things were alleged by the said Lorenzo, and proofs were introduced regarding them; consultations were held with various doctors, and finally it was advised and pronounced against the said Balthasar, against which sentence nullity is alleged by him. Whence, nothing else appearing, I conclude that justice does not favor the said Balthasar against his arrest and detention. Nor does it impede that the narrations in the libel of the said Lorenzo are not to be believed in his own favor. For it must be admitted that upon that narration the judge ought not to have based the sentence; but since it appears that the sentence was rendered, it is presumed that it was promulgated on the basis of true and just proofs, as in the laws alleged above, especially since it is narrated therein that the officials had first examined the depositions of witnesses and other documents or letters. The contrary does not stand in the way.

† For I admit that a judge cannot render a sentence under a resolutive condition. But the sentence rendered does not fall on this account: rather, that part concerning the resolution is held as not added, and the sentence remains unconditional (pura), as Bartolus notably maintained in the said l. iudex; to which is relevant what is noted in l. dicere, with the following law, ff. de arb.; and in support of this is that the valid ought not to be vitiated by the invalid when the valid can be separated from the invalid, as in the rule utile per inutile and what is noted there, de reg. iu., li. 6, and in l. 1, § Trebatius, with the following, de aqua quot. et aest.; to which relates l. 1, § biduum, ff. quando app. sit. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The lord can demand from the emphyteuta that he exhibit the emphyteutic instrument.
2. An emphyteusis of a church does not pass to extraneous heirs.
3. An emphyteuta cannot donate, or bequeath, or otherwise transfer the property to an extraneous person.
4. An emphyteuta cannot exchange the property without asking the lord.
casus: Certain citizens of Siena paid annually for thirty years and more a certain sum of money to the rector of a certain church on the occasion of certain squares or houses, which they claimed to hold in emphyteusis from that same church. It happened afterwards that certain citizens did not pay the customary ground rent for very many years. Some indeed transferred the said squares or houses to extraneous persons by way of legacy, or institution of heir, or donation, without the said rector having been requested at all. Concerning the aforesaid, it is asked what the law is, etc.
body: The protection of Jesus Christ and of His mother having been humbly invoked, two principal matters are to be examined regarding the aforementioned premises. First, whether through the aforesaid payments the direct ownership of the Church is proven, since no authentic document regarding the owner or the emphyteutic grant appears. Second, presupposing that the ownership of the Church and the emphyteutic grant are proven, whether through the said grants or alienations made without requesting the rector of the Church, the said citizens have forfeited their right from the Church, so that those goods have freely reverted to the right of the Church. Although these are several fine doubts, and it could be argued at length pro and contra, nevertheless, for the sake of brevity, I will proceed conclusively, submitting in summary what I judge in them. And first, regarding the first point, I think that through the said payments the direct ownership of the Church is sufficiently proven, so that the said citizens can no longer withdraw themselves from the said payment, nor deny that the Church is the lady and patron of those squares or houses; this clearly appears in l. cum de in rem verso, ff. de vsur., and Bartolus sufficiently affirmed this there; indeed, payment for ten years suffices, provided it was made in contemplation of those squares, which Bartolus confirms there, and especially through the moderns in capitul. peruenit, de censib.; l. fin. and l. ius emphyteutici, C. de fun. pa. lib. 11 makes for this; Speculator most clearly holds it directly in point in the title de loca. § nunc aliqua, verse 64. And a dictum of Baldus in l. praetor ait, § 1, ff. de edend. makes extraordinarily for the aforesaid, where he concludes,

† that the lord can demand from the emphyteuta that he exhibit the emphyteutic instrument, and Speculator also holds this in the said § nunc aliqua, verse 124. And if he does not exhibit it, Baldus says that the emphytheusis is presumed extinct and ended, and thus the emphyteuta can be evicted, on the argument there, since the lord has a claim grounded on a civil and emphyteutic matter, while the emphyteuta himself proves nothing concerning his own right. Whence, since the Church has a grounded claim, they appear able to be evicted according to the aforesaid. However, I do not believe that this dictum is true as stated, at least in that case where it is proved that they paid for forty years, through the notable text in l. benigne, C. de fund. pat. lib. 11. Speculator clearly holds in our case, when an instrument does not appear, in the said verse 147; and the said conclusion especially proceeds in our case, since the ancient books of the Church do not appear concerning the aforesaid. Even if these are not authentic, they nevertheless provide no small proof according to what is noted in capitul. cum causam, de probatio. Regarding the second point, I say that those who did not pay for a two-year period, nor purged default, have forfeited their right through capitul. potuit, de loca., and they lose whatever they spent under the title of improvement, as in auth. qui rem huiusmodi, C. de sacrosanct. eccle. and 10, q. 2, c. hoc ius porrectum, verse qui rem. A doubt arises concerning those who made gifts inter vivos and in a last will. For Speculator held in the said § nunc aliqua, verse 95, that they do not incur any penalty, and he holds the same in verse 107 and following. Johannes Andreae holds the same after Innocent and the gloss in the verse multos alios, in the said capitul. potuit, and Accursius and Cynus in l. 3, C. de iure emphy.; yet Accursius and Cynus speak of a private emphyteuta, but Speculator and others speak specifically of an emphyteuta of the Church. For they say that capitul. potuit speaks of an alienation which takes place by means of a price, because affection is then directed toward the price, and therefore it makes no difference whether he obtains it from a stranger or from the lord; therefore the laws intended that the lord should first be requested, in case he should wish to buy; but in a donation or legacy this reason ceases, since these are made on account of affection held toward the person of the donee, legatee, or heir, which does not attach to the person of the lord: thus the reason of that capitul. potuit ceases. But Bartolus most clearly holds the opposite both in the case of a private person and in that of the Church, in l. fin., C. de iure emphyt., and more extensively in l. si domus, § fin., ff. de lega. 1, where he says that without the license of the lord it cannot be donated, nor left in a last will. First, because the text in the said l. fin. prohibits alienation. Likewise because the lord would not be sufficiently secured, since through that transfer his right would be made worse, because he would have no action for the rent against the successor, but it would be necessary to proceed by vindication of the thing, which is dangerous; and in the case of an emphyteuta of the Church he says this is express in l. 2, C. ne rei do. uel temp. [and] capitul. potuit, de loca. Finally, it appears that without requesting the Church it ought not to be done, but if she is requested, it may; nevertheless, through this intervening consent of hers no prejudice can occur to her. Yet, as Johannes Andreae reports, Guilelmus simply holds what Bartolus holds, and what Johannes Andreae himself notes in capitul. in praesentia, de proba. and in the additions to Speculator in the said § nunc aliqua, verse 103 makes for this, where he says that

† an emphyteusis of the Church does not pass to extraneous heirs, by virtue of what is contained in authen. de non alie. aut permu. § emphyteusim, through which many have said that that paragraph was amended; which Bartolus held in authen. perpetua, C. de sacrosan. ecclesi., fully through the said Speculator in the said verse 115, because, according to Johannes Andreae, although it was amended with respect to the title of successors, it was not, however, with respect to their qualities, as if he meant that, although it can be granted in perpetuity, as in § licentia, it cannot, however, with respect to an extraneous heir, as in the said § emphyteusim. And consequently it would seem must be said,

† that the emphyteuta cannot donate the thing, or bequeath it, or otherwise transfer it to an outsider; whence in this, if I conceive correctly, Johannes Andreae was somewhat contradictory to himself. Bartolus, however, in the said auth. perpetua, C. de sacrosan. eccle., held without distinction that that § emphyteusim was amended, although he thought otherwise incidentally in l. si tibi, ff. de pact. and l. Gallus, ff. de libe. & posthu. Baldus in the authentic si quas ruinas, C. de sacrosan. eccle. holds that the custom of the place must first be inspected, namely whether ecclesiastical property is customarily granted only up to the third generation, or in perpetuity, but not with respect to outsiders, and then that custom must be observed. If, however, there is no evidence of a custom, then, looking to pure law, the grant can be made simply in perpetuity, since the utility of the Church requires this, as in the said authentic si quas ruinas. I myself held simply in capitul. praesentia, de proba., that since alienation of direct and beneficial ownership is permitted for cause of necessity or utility or another cause, all the more can the thing be granted in perpetual emphyteusis, where only beneficial ownership is transferred; capitul. 2, de rebus eccle. non alie. lib. 6 and capitul. nulli, under the same title in the ancient [decretals], with what is noted there, make for this. And what Speculator notes in the said § nunc aliqua, verse 7, and what Archidiaconus and Johannes Andreae note in the said c. 2 in sum., and 10, quaestio 2, cap. perpetua, also make for this. What, then, is to be said in this so diverse matter? I would conclude that either the emphyteutic instrument appears, and it must be stood by, if the grant appears to have been made from a legitimate cause, 12, quaest. 2, in summa, with the others cited above, during the emphyteusis, unless the custom of the region is contrary, a donation made inter vivos or in a last will is valid, even to an outsider, even without requesting the consent of the lord, through the general rule that anyone can transfer his right to another if he is prohibited by no law; for this c. nuper, de do. post di. rest., and Inst. de re. diui. § per traditionem, and l. nihil tam naturale, ff. de regu. iur. Likewise, it is evident in cap. potuit, by an argument from a special case. For if an emphyteuta of the Church is prohibited from selling without requesting the lord, on account of the above-stated reason, therefore he is not prohibited from making other contracts of alienation, as in c. nomine, de praesum., and l. praetor, ff. de iud., at least by lucrative title, and in a non-lucrative contract l. fin., C. de iure emphy. could be understood, where it prohibits selling or transferring to another, which I understand as when he can obtain from the lord that very same thing which he is about to obtain from the other. Therefore, Speculator in the said § nunc aliqua, verse 121, and more clearly there Johannes Andreae in the additions, elegantly held,

† that the emphyteuta cannot make an exchange without requesting the lord, but must do so with him if he can obtain from the lord that which he could from the outsider, because exchange is a kind of purchase, l. 1 in fi., ff. de rerum permu.; it is otherwise if he cannot obtain from the lord that which he could from the outsider. Furthermore, the text in l. fin., C. de fun. pa. lib. 6 seems to prove my conclusion, where the emphyteuta of the fisc can donate an emphyteutic property, saving the right of the fisc, and the donation is valid. Therefore the same applies in the Church, since the Church and the fisc are equated, l. 2, C. ne res do. uel tem., noted in capitul. primo, de in inte. resti., because by this the ownership of the Church is not alienated without solemnity, because, as Johannes Andreae says in the said capitul. potuit, through this donation the direct ownership, which was in the power of the Church, is not alienated, but the beneficial ownership, which was in the power of the emphyteuta. And that this was the intention of Bartolus I prove, because he was moved to hold the contrary by a false reason. For he says it is one thing in the case of the fisc than in that of a private person or in the Church, because property of the fisc passes to any other person with its encumbrance, so that it does not have necessity of proceeding against the new possessor, but according to him it is otherwise in a private person, because he has need to bring an action for vindication of the thing; but this is false, although Speculator held this last point in the said § nunc aliqua, verse 108, because the property passes with its obligation to any other person, as is proved in Auth. de non alie. § scire, and Baldus singularly noted that text in the said authentic si quas ruinas; therefore, the dictum of Bartolus falls with the fall of its reasoning, l. cum pater, § dulcissimis, ff. de lega. 2. Likewise, there is also another remedy against a successor who does not pay; for he forthwith falls from his right, whoever he may be, since the property is thus conditioned; for this purpose, si de feu. fue. controuer. capitul. uasallus, and what the same Bartolus notes in l. cum ratio, ff. de interdi. & re., makes for this, and Baldus expressly holds it in the said auth. si quas ruinas. But on account of the diversity of opinions it would not be bad to say that if the grant is to someone and his heirs, it ought simply to be understood of children, and not of outsiders; and thus Speculator could be saved, who held this in the said § nunc aliqua, verse 108; but in our case it is doubtful, since no instrument appears, and I would think that the custom of the region should be regarded in this matter, by the argument in l. quod si nolit, § quia assidua, de aedi. edic., and in l. an in totum, C. de aedi. priua., and in l. circa locationes, C. locati; what Bartolus notes in l. nemo est qui nesciat, ff. de duo. reis makes for this. Whence, if in that place it is customary for a grant to be made to the recipient and his heirs, even outsiders, a disposition made to another will be valid; otherwise not. The said l. 2, C. ne re. domi. uel temp., which Bartolus cited, does not stand in the way of the aforesaid; for that law speaks no more of the Church than of the prince, but property of the prince can be donated, saving his right, by the said law; therefore also the emphyteutic property of the Church. To that l. 2 it can be said that it speaks of when someone alienated that property as his own, so that he intended to transfer the beneficial and direct ownership; it is otherwise, however, when the emphyteuta intends only to donate his improvements. Likewise, if the emphyteuta could not donate to another indifferently on account of the reasoning of Bartolus, he would now not be able to sell when the lord is unwilling to buy. For if the lord does not wish to buy, prejudice ought not to be brought upon him, so that by this he could make a sale to another; which, however, is false, as in the said l. 2 and capitul. potuit. Therefore the law intended to prefer the lord in alienation only in that case where no prejudice arises from that preference which the emphyteuta has attained. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The mother, as nearer in degree, excludes the nearest grandfather.
2. A case omitted by a statute or by man is left to the disposition of the ius commune.
3. A statute prohibiting an implied meaning in statutes is deemed to prohibit an argument a contrario sensu.
4. A statute excluding the mother from the succession of an intestate child in favour of agnates does not claim application in the case of an infant who could not make a will.
5. A statute in favour of agnates up to the fourth degree excludes the mother from the entire succession due to her under the ius commune.
6. A statute, if it excludes a female daughter from succession in favour of a male, also excludes a granddaughter.
7. The reason and mind of the law are related to the law as the soul is to the body.
8. An argument a contrario sensu is derived from the law, or from its mind.
9. Common usage of speech is preferred to the proper meaning of a word.
casus: A certain person died in infancy, leaving behind his mother, a paternal grandfather, and paternal uncles. The question is asked concerning the manner of succeeding to his property, since the municipal enactment here in Siena is in force under the following terms, namely the rubric of the statute: 'In what measure ascendants from the paternal line succeed'. The text of the statute provides as follows: 'Item, if any person dies intestate without legitimate children and ascendants from the paternal line, and with no surviving brother or sister, without a son or daughter of a brother or sister of the deceased person himself from the same father at the time of his death, the mother, grandfather, or grandmother [?] of such deceased person, or on the part of the mother, is not admitted, [or] can come at most to a fourth part of the legitimate intestate succession of all movable and self-moving and immovable things, except for the houses and castles formerly belonging to such deceased person. But the other property of such deceased person the male relatives on the part of the father and of the paternal grandfather up to the fourth degree of the nearer order shall have; and if there survive to such deceased person a brother or sister without children, or a daughter of a brother or sister, then the mother, grandfather, or grandmother on the part of the mother shall succeed in nothing, etc.'
body: Having humbly invoked the help of Christ and of His Mother. First, one must consider the manner of succeeding after inspecting the ius commune, and municipal law according to the first manner. The case seems clearly decided by the text and gloss in authenti. defuncto, C. ad tertullia. and in the body of the law from which it is taken, de succes. quæ ab intest. defe.

† For the mother, as closer in degree, excludes the nearest grandfather, just as the father would exclude the maternal grandmother, as the gloss expressly notes in said authenti. defuncto; but a difficulty, and no small one, turns upon the understanding of the municipal statute, in which I shall pursue two main heads. First, whether the mother, by virtue of the statute itself, is excluded by the paternal grandfather. Second, presupposing that she is defeated by that grandfather, whether the mother at least ought to obtain the legitime due to her by natural law. Regarding the first, it seems that it must be said that the mother is to be entirely preferred to that grandfather, looking solely to the ius commune. And the first argument runs as follows.

† A case omitted by a statute or by man is left to the disposition of the ius commune, as in l. si cum dotem, in princip. ff. solu. matrimo. and in cap. suspectum, de rescript. lib. 6. But the statute provides for the exclusion of the mother, either in whole or in a certain part, in only two cases. The first case is when someone dies intestate without legitimate children and ascendants from the paternal line, and with no surviving brother or sister, or son and daughter of a brother and sister of the deceased himself. In which case it does not permit the mother to be admitted except to a fourth part of the legitimate intestate succession of all the goods, and in this we are outside the terms of the statute, because the said infant did not die without ascendants, but left behind a paternal grandfather. The second case of the statute is when someone dies intestate, leaving surviving him a brother or sister, or a son or daughter of a brother or sister; and in this case it makes provision, and the mother is excluded in whole, and in this too we are outside the statute, because he died with none of the aforesaid surviving; therefore recourse must be had to the ius commune, according to which the mother excludes the grandfather. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that, a contrario sensu, the grandfather, as an ascendant, is presumed to have to exclude the mother, since the argument a contrario sensu is very strong in law, as in cap. cum apostolica, de his quæ fiunt a præla. and 25. distinct. cap. qualis, and l. cum prætor. ff. de iudic. and l. j. ff. de offic. eius, cui man. est iur. Because in this case said argument does not seem to have a place, since in the contrary case a decision of the ius commune is found; and the common rule seems to be that an argument a contrario sensu has no place where the ius commune is to the contrary, as is proved in capitu. a nobis, the second, de senten. excom. noted by the gloss in cap. significasti, de electio. or if an absurdity arises, l. 2. C. de condit. inser. noted by the doctors in cap. publicato, de elec. In our precise terms, Bartolus expressly holds this after Iacobus Butrigarius in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iur. and Baldus in l. apud antiquos, C. de furt. where they say that an argument a contrario sensu does not proceed in statutes where the ius commune is found to the contrary, as is true in our case. Secondly, to the same effect is what Baldus notes in said l. 2. C. de conditio. inser. where he says,

† that if a statute prohibits an understood sense in statutes, it seems to prohibit an argument a contrario sensu, which is called an implied understanding. For it does not come from the words, but from interpretation, as Bartolus fully notes in said l. omnes populi, to which I allege the notable text in said cap. cum apostolica, in fin. where it is given to be understood indirectly; from which it is plainly gathered that that which comes through the contrary sense is gathered indirectly. But it is certain that a correction of the laws ought not to be introduced through implied understandings, as the gloss notes in cap. cupientes. §. & si per uiginti, de elect. lib. 6. at the verse petere; therefore, a correction of the laws ought not to be introduced by an argument a contrario sensu. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that, from identity or a fortiori reason, the grandfather ought to exclude the mother, at least in the three legitimate intestate successions, and in houses and castles; because if more remote relatives up to the fourth degree exclude the mother, as the statute provides, therefore all the more does the grandfather, who is closer, as seems to be proved in l. 3. C. de bo. mat. For to this, in favor of the mother, the answer is made that a correction of the law ought not to be introduced by identity or a fortiori reason, as Bartolus notes in authenti. quas actiones, C. de sacrosanc. eccle. Baldus established the same thing there, at least in that case where the reason is not expressed in the constitution; and to this c. constitutionem very well contributes, together with the gloss at the word prorogamus, de regu. iu. lib. 6. and what Ioannes Andreæ notes on the rule in pœnis, de reg. iur. lib. 6. in his Mercuriales. Fourthly, it makes very well for the mother that under another head we are outside the terms of the statute. For the statute speaks of one dying intestate; now, he is called intestate who died without a testament, yet had the faculty and power of testating; whence an infant is not properly said to die intestate, as in l. prima. in princip. ff. de suis & legi. And in our precise terms Bartolus plainly confirms this in titu. de success. feu. cap. primo. where he says,

† that a statute excluding a mother from the succession of an intestate son in favor of agnates does not claim a place for itself in the case of an infant who could not make a will, because we are in an odious matter and one against natural equity, and the mother is excluded from the succession of her son contrary to l. nam & si parentibus. ff. de inoffic. testamen. and the words must be understood properly and strictly, nor, according to him, should one heed the common usage of the vulgar, upon which Bartolus founds himself in said l. prima, because according to him statutes are made by learned men, and thus they seem to have used proper words. He says it is otherwise where there is no question of odium and the exclusion of the mother, but of how agnates ought to be admitted to the goods of an intestate deceased. For then those who are not able to testate would indeed be included; and by this and the aforesaid, the paternal uncles of the said deceased also seem to be excluded, since we are outside the terms of the statute by the aforesaid: and it is certain by the ius commune that they exclude paternal uncles, since only brothers of the deceased concur in succession with the parents, according to the said authen. defuncto. But although the aforesaid might seem at first glance very pressing, I nevertheless judge the contrary opinion to be truer, namely that the paternal grandfather excludes the mother and the paternal uncles. And first this is proved by the beginning of the statute, a contrario sensu and by the tacit intention of the statute itself. For

† the statute in favor of agnates up to the fourth degree excludes the mother from the total succession due to her by the ius commune, and admits her only to a fourth; and the remaining three parts, and the houses and castles, it defers to those agnates. Nor does it admit the mother unconditionally to that fourth, and the other agnates to those three parts, but only if the son died without legitimate children and ascendants from the paternal line, and with no surviving brother or sister, or son or daughter of a brother or sister of the deceased himself: therefore, with these or any one of them surviving, the mother ought to be excluded, not in whole, by an argument a contrario sensu and by the tacit intention of the legislators. For that which would come from the tacit intention is seen in the statute, as is proved in l. his solis. C. de reuocan. donatio. and Baldus in l. non dubium. C. de legi. And that this is of the intention of the statute is proved from the fact that it calls more distant agnates up to the fourth degree to three parts, and to the houses and castles, with the mother excluded; whence all the more does it seem to have wished to exclude the mother when there are surviving ascendants, of whom it makes mention tacitly and through the contrary sense in the beginning, for it calls more distant agnates in default of ascendants and descendants, and brothers and their children. For if in contemplation of them it admitted more distant agnates, and those more remote in degree, to the exclusion of the mother, it acted all the more forcefully by tacitly excluding the mother entirely when ascendants survive; for this there is an excellent text in a similar matter in l. tertia. at the verse nam licet. C. de bonis mater. where the text, even in corrective matter, makes such an argument, that what is disposed to the prejudice of sons should have place in the case of grandsons, lest sons be found to be in a worse condition than grandsons; to this effect Baldus notably adduced that text in l. penultima. otherwise fina. C. de in ius uocand. where by that text he says,

† that if a statute excludes a female daughter from succession in favor of a male, it also seems tacitly to exclude a granddaughter, namely the daughter of a daughter, because more ought not to be granted to a granddaughter than to a daughter. For the reason of the statute does not permit this: said l. tertia. And Bartolus intended the same in a similar matter in l. secunda. at the verse sed si forte. ad Tertullia. where he says that if in favor of agnates the mother is excluded from the succession of her son, the statute seems to exclude the maternal grandfather and other more remote ascendants through the maternal line; so I say in the case at hand. It is not likely that the statute wished to place ascendants in a worse condition than collaterals up to the fourth degree; therefore we ought to say that in the beginning ascendants and descendants are tacitly called to all manner of legal succession; and if we said the contrary, an absurdity would follow, that since the children and parents of the deceased are not called directly to the succession in any part of the statute, the children of a brother and sister would be in a better condition than the proper children and parents; which is proved from this: for the statute in the aforesaid part expressly and directly calls them, in the words & si supersint, it expressly calls a brother and sister, or children born of them: it would follow, therefore, that these would exclude ascendants and descendants. Moreover, the statute in the beginning equated ascendants, descendants, brother, sister, and their children, namely to this effect: that other collateral relatives are admitted to the three parts; since it afterwards made mention of brother, sister, and their children for the total exclusion of the mother and other agnates, it seems all the more forcefully to have called the children and ascendants of the deceased himself, of whom it had tacitly made mention in the beginning. For it is not to be believed that the statute-makers were so negligent that they wished these collaterals to be preferred to ascendants and descendants. For as often as certain persons are equated in a certain part of a disposition, that which is disposed in the one seems disposed in the other, even in penal and corrective matter, as is the text together with the gloss in c. quamuis, in fi. de elect. lib. 6. noted by the gloss in auth. quas actiones, cited above; l. fin. C. de indic. uidu. supports this, and the gloss in c. 1. in fin. C. de postu. præla. to the same effect, l. qui filiabus, ff. de leg. 1. Why, moreover, the statute did not make express mention of them, as it did of brothers and sisters and their children, I believe is because it held that to be beyond doubt. For if these exclude the mother entirely, all the more do those who are closer: because if I defeat the one who defeats you, therefore I defeat you, as in c. quia cunctis, and what is there noted, de conces. præb. lib. 6. And from these conjectures it is concluded that the intention of the statute is evident toward the inclusion of the grandfather and the exclusion of the mother. For that which is established through conjectures is called evident, as is notably noted in l. licet, ff. de leg. 1. And consequently it is concluded that an argument a contrario sensu has place in our case, and that a case omitted by express words ought not to be left to the disposition of the ius commune, but ought to be said to be tacitly provided for and expressed: said l. his solis, where it is notably proved. For the mind of the law is the law itself; so that where the mind and reason of the law have place, the law itself ought to have place, whether it be penal or corrective. For he offends against the law who, while embracing the words of the law, goes against the virtue of the law: l. non dubium, C. de legi. and c. fin. de reg. iur. lib. 6. and there by Dynus; for the law itself is regulated by the reason and intention of the law, which is the same as the reason of the law, as Dynus notes in said rule fi. and Baldus in said l. non dubium, and it is regulated just as the body is by the soul itself. For, as Baldus notably says in l. scire, ff. de excu. tut., just as man consists of soul and body, so the law consists of words and mind, or reason.

† For the reason and the mind stand in relation to the law just as the soul to the body. For the body is said to exist from the disposition of the soul; so the law from the disposition of reason. And thus, in whatever matter we are, where the mind of the law has place, the law itself ought to have place, as Baldus clearly intended in said authen. quas actiones. And although in corrective matter it is required that the reason be expressed, nevertheless elsewhere he notably limited this, saying that although the law does not express the reason, nevertheless, if no other than a single, natural, and indubitable reason can be drawn and presumed from the statute, an extension ought to be made because of the boundaries of reason, as if the reason itself were expressed; otherwise where the reason is doubtful, in which case the opinion of Bartolus in said authen. quas actiones might proceed. Baldus notably meant this in l. maximum uitium, C. de lib. præte. alleging l. milites agrum, in princi. ff. de re. mil. and l. nominati, under the same title. And Iacobus Butrigarius determined this same thing in a similar question, as he himself relates. For regarding a statute excluding a daughter from the succession of her father in favor of a son, he said in a certain disputation that under the appellation of 'son' a grandson is included, even though the matter was corrective: because he says that the same reason exists in a grandson through a son as exists in the son himself: l. liberorum, in fi. ff. de verb. sign. For there could be no other reason for the statute than that the dignity of the agnation and family be preserved: l. 1. ff. de ven. insp. noted by Cynus in l. Publica, C. de adul. But in our case the mother is excluded from three parts, and from houses and castles, in favor of the agnation, as is clear from the words of the statute, when it calls male relatives from the line of the father and grandfather up to the fourth degree. Likewise she is excluded entirely in favor of a brother and a sister, and their children; which cannot be except in favor of the agnation, and because they succeed in the place of agnates, as are the children of sisters; therefore, all the more ought this to have place in the case of the paternal grandfather, who is an agnate and closer than the others, and in default of whom other collaterals are called beyond brothers and their children, as is clear from the form of the statute, in which that and an even greater reason concur; nor can any other natural reason of the statute be alleged for the exclusion of the mother. Cynus originally intended the same as Baldus, following Petrus in l. non dubium, C. de legi. and in l. 1. C. quæ sit lon. consue. What the gloss notes in l. tale pactum, in fin. ff. de pact. serves excellently, where it notes that although the reason is not expressed in the law, nevertheless that reason is to be conjectured which could move a just and wise prince. And Baldus intended the same in said l. scire. Finally, in our precise terms, though not so clearly, Baldus intended this in l. conuenticulam, C. de episc. & cle. where he says that this question occurred de facto in Florence: it was provided by statute that any woman should succeed to her mother intestate if male children do not exist: it was asked whether, a contrario sensu of the statute, when males exist, the daughter would be excluded? And he concludes that female daughters ought to be excluded by brothers who claim the maternal succession, because the statute seems to intend this a contrario sensu, as in l. qui testamento. §. mulier, ff. de testa. and what is there noted by Cynus on the rule factum, de reg. iu. lib. 6. Likewise, according to him, an argument a contrario sensu is taken in pacts, as is notably proved in l. inter socerum. §. cum inter, ff. de pact. dot. therefore the same applies in a statute, which is a kind of tacit agreement, as is noted on the rubric C. de decr. decu. lib. 10. Moreover, the statute seems to intend this, having weighed the reason of the final cause, which always inheres in the disposition, as is noted in ff. de cond. & demon. l. cum tale. §. falsam. Nor does l. commodissimè, cited above, stand in the way according to him, where an omitted case is left to the disposition of the ius commune: because that proceeds when an omitted case cannot be held as expressed from any conjecture; but where it can be held as expressed, it is otherwise, as under the same title l. si ita. For an evident will is gathered expressly or through conjecture: said l. licet. But in the aforesaid case the will of the legislators is of such kind, therefore etc. And he relates that Cynus holds the same in his consilia, adding that said Bartolus noted through the aforesaid that the case in said §. cum inter serves better for this than any other law. And said Petrus de Ancharano followed this opinion of Baldus in his solemn commentary on c. canonum statuta, de consti. If, therefore, Baldus held this with correction of the laws in the aforesaid question, where many conjectures did not concur, far more forcefully must this be said here, where so many conjectures concur for the exclusion of the mother by the paternal grandfather. But where conjectures do not concur, the argument a contrario sensu with correction of the laws ceases to apply; and in this case proceeds the opinion of Bartolus and Iacobus Butrigarius and others, and of Baldus himself, who is usually alleged in this argument to be contrary to himself by what is noted by him in said l. apud antiquos, C. de fur. and in said l. qui testamento. §. mulier, ff. de testa. But in truth he does not contradict himself, but rather limits all contrary statements, as is clear from the response which he makes to l. commodissimè. Nor is it true to say that an extensive interpretation is made here: because, since the mind is established through so many conjectures, it is not called extensive, having respect to the mind, but rather intensive, and intrinsic, or declarative: because it does not extend beyond its proper bounds, which are rooted in the mind; in support of this is l. fi. C. de indi. vid. where there is an excellent text, and in l. liberum, §. senatus, ff. de ritu. nup. where, nevertheless, from identity of reason the disposition of the law is extended to the prejudice of the free faculty of contracting marriage, and thus with derogation of the ius commune; the same Bartolus after Cynus intended this in said l. non dubium.

† Likewise, the argument a contrario sensu is gathered from the law, or from its mind, as is proved in 15. q. 3. c. ex eo, and in c. qualis. 25. dist. Therefore, one should not care about the correction of the laws, if from the mind drawn through conjectures the will of the law is apparent, which has the same force, inst. de iure nat. gen. & ciui. §. sed quod principi. And through this the response is clear to all contrary points formed above in favor of the mother, except for the last; to which I answer that although properly and strictly speaking he is not called intestate, but intestable, who from defect of reason cannot make a testament, said l. 1. ff. de suis & legit. nevertheless, from the common usage of speaking, such a one is called intestate. And the jurisconsult approves this sense, said l. 1. in prin. and Bartolus expressly holds it in said law in our precise terms, when a statute excludes a mother from the succession of an intestate son.

† For the common usage of speaking is preferred to the proper signification of a word: l. librorum. §. quod tamen Cassius, ff. de leg. 3. l. Labeo, ff. de supel. leg. l. cum de lanionis. §. asinam, ff. de fun. instru. Nor does what Baldus says stand in the way, namely that since they are made by learned men, it must be presumed that they used proper words; because I say that statutes here in Siena are not commonly made by learned men, but by those ignorant of the laws. Therefore Bartolus notably says in l. stipulatio ista. §. hoc quoque, ff. de verbo. oblig. that if a statute contains any word having two significations, one proper, the other according to the common usage of speaking, we ought to take that which the common usage of speaking has according to the quality of the persons enacting the statute, since they are not legal experts; to this effect is that text with its gloss. Likewise I say that even laws made by learned men ought to be understood according to common usage, because a law ought to conform to the locality; so noted the gloss in c. nonnulli, de rescriptis. Innocent also says in c. olim, de ver. sig. that in the interpretation of a disposition, whether it be a law, a privilege, or anything else, recourse must be had to the common usage of speaking: l. si de interpretatione, ff. de legi. and as to statutes, Bartolus expressly intended this in l. omnes populi, cited above. From all these things I conclude as to the first point that the paternal grandfather excludes the mother and the paternal uncles of the deceased himself. Now I descend to the second: whether the mother ought to be excluded even from the legitime due by natural law; and it seems not: because just as a son cannot be deprived entirely, since this portion is due to him by natural law, as in l. cum ratio naturalis, ff. de bonis dam. so it seems that neither can parents be deprived, since in like manner the inheritance of children is due to them, as in l. nam & si parentibus, ff. de inofficio. testamen. For this reason the burden of support falls equally upon parents and children, as in ff. de lib. agno. l. 1. and l. si quis a liberis. But these notwithstanding, I say that although there are opinions whether children can be deprived of the legitime by statute, nevertheless the more common opinion is that they can, provided there is at least a legitimate cause, and a legitimate cause is the favor of males and of the agnation; whence commonly in Tuscany female daughters and the mother are excluded in favor of agnates. Baldus expressly holds this in l. cum l. Leoniana, C. de episc. & cler. and Bartolus in l. Titio. §. titio genero, ff. de cond. & demonstratio. and Cynus in l. sancimus. C. de nup. and Dynus on the rule indultum, de regu. iu. lib. 6. according to Ioannes Andreæ in capitul. Raynutius, de testamen. For it is not true that this portion is of natural law, since by that law all things would be completely in common, 8. distin. in prin. and 12. q. 1. cap. dilectissimi; but the provision of support is indeed of natural law, 1. dist. capit. ius naturale; but this portion of a fourth, or a third with a half, of which in auth. nouissima, C. de inoffi. testam. and in the body of the law from which it is taken, de trien. & semif. §. 1. is of positive law, therefore it can be diminished, changed, and entirely removed by positive law: because nothing is so natural, etc. l. nihil, ff. de reg. iur. and in c. 1. under the same title, and insti. de legi. agn. tu. in fi. But the very right of support, where necessity arises, cannot be taken away, since it is of natural law, and in this case the contrary opinion is to be understood; and thus the dictum of the lords of the Rota in decis. 18 and of those who held that it cannot be diminished entirely can be preserved; but in our case such necessity does not fall upon the mother. Wherefore I conclude that the statute entirely excluding the mother in favor of agnates is valid; which Bartolus also seems to intend in l. 1. ff. de suis & leg. This being presupposed, I say that in our case the mother is excluded in whole, because the statute intended this, if it is well weighed. For if the son died without ascendants and descendants, etc., it admits the mother only to a fourth part, and thus diminishes her legitime, since that by the ius commune is a third when other closer relatives do not exist, just as they did not exist here, as noted by the gloss in auth. de trien. & semis. §. 1. and Bartolus in said auth. nouissima. But when ascendants and descendants through the male line, or a brother and sister, do exist, the statute says that the mother shall succeed in nothing, and thus it wished to deprive her of the legitime entirely; otherwise it would add nothing to the preceding case, and he who says all excludes nothing, de maio. & obe. c. solitæ, by the argument of 19. dist. cap. si Romanorum, with its likes. I conclude therefore from all the aforesaid that the said paternal grandfather, having regard to the mind of the said statute, excludes the mother in whole. And the theory of Bartolus in l. 2. §. sed fortè, ff. ad Tertul. makes for the aforesaid, where he says that where a mother or daughter is excluded in favor of others, those others seem to be tacitly called: because that gain is to be applied to them. The notable statement of Bartolus also makes for the aforesaid conclusion in auth. itaque, C. communia, de succes. where through that text and in l. 2. C. de bo. quæ lib. he says that where parents are called to succession, parents on the father's side are preferred in goods acquired from the father's side, whereas parents on the mother's side are preferred in goods acquired from the maternal line, which is a notable and singular statement. And although it could be said that that statement of Bartolus was to be restricted to when parents concur in equal degree, as the laws cited above seem to intend, which does not happen here, since the mother is closer; nevertheless I say, looking to the reason and equity of that statement, that the same seems to be said in our case, having regard to the mind of the statute. For the goods in question were acquired from the father's side. And these things suffice. Nicolaus, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The quality of a contract is presumed from the quality of the price.
2. When a pact of reselling is not free, there is a presumption that it is made for the sake of gaining the fruits of that intervening time.
3. A statute speaking on a matter of law ought to be understood according to the ius commune.
4. One is said to be in bad faith who has consciousness of another's property.
5. An heir is bound to satisfy the soul of the deceased.
body: In the present consultation, the protection of Christ and of His Mother having been humbly invoked, three things are succinctly to be examined. First, whether the sale that initially appears to have been made concerning the whole house is to be presumed simulated and executed in fraud of usury. With that presupposed, it will consequently have to be seen what the role of the judge ought to be in rendering judgment in this matter. Second, presupposing that the first sale cannot be proved simulated in lieu of a pledge, whether the heirs of the buyer are bound to pay the rent for the half of the house which he subsequently resold to the seller himself, having received fifty florins from him under the name of price, notwithstanding the pact agreed upon between them. Third, whether the heirs of the creditors, or buyers, can defend themselves against the claimant by prescription by virtue of the statute of Siena providing that whoever has possessed any immovable property for the space of ten years with title prescribes it. I return to the first point, in which I will not linger by arguing the sides in the accustomed manner, lest I seem to have treated an unquestionable matter beyond what is necessary; for both in my judgment, and to speak more truly, in all our written law, a direct case on this question, which can in no way be caviled at, is seen in cap. ad nostram, de empt. & ven., where a contract entered into under the form of purchase and sale is judged to be of the nature of a pledge from two conjectures alone: first, because a pact of reselling was made in favor of the seller, yet not at any time whatsoever, but from seven up to nine years, that is, within seven and nine years, so that he wished freely to gain the fruits of seven years; second, because the smallness of the price had intervened, taking into account the true value of the property. For from the quality of the price the quality of the contract is presumed, l. per diversas,

† C. man., in capit. & si quæstiones, de simo., noted by the gloss in l. 1, ff. de superficie, and Bartolus in l. cotem ferro, § qui maximos, ff. de pu. Likewise, when a pact of reselling is made that is not free—such as because the recipient does not wish to be bound until a certain time—there is a presumption,

† that he does this for the sake of gaining the fruits of that intervening time in lieu of usury; and this presumption is strengthened by the smallness of the price. For often a presumption that is not conclusive and does not of itself suffice for a judgment passes into a violent presumption through another intervening presumption, so that it suffices for a judgment, as is the noted gloss in c. insinuatum, de simo., and the text is seen in c. cum contumacia, together with the gloss, de hære. lib. 6. But in our question not only did the aforesaid two circumstances intervene, but there are also many other supporting indications; and so far more strongly ought the contract in our case to be judged usurious. For here, to begin with those two, first, a pact of reselling was had, not purely, but after the feast of St. Michael next following, from one year in the future to three years then in the future, so that he wished to be able freely to gain the usufruct of that house for a year and seven months by occasion of those one hundred florins. Second, the smallness of the price intervened, which clearly appears from this: because Antonius himself before the said contract paid by way of rent for the said house sometimes ten, sometimes eight florins; whence it is not likely that a house in the city of Siena yielding a revenue of 10 or 8 florins would not be worth more than one hundred florins, since commonly in the city property yielding a revenue of four or five florins is accustomed to be sold for one hundred; what is noted by Bartolus in l. pretia rerum, ff. ad leg. Fal. and in l. 2, C. de rescin. vendi. makes to this point. Furthermore, the smallness of the price is gathered from the writing of that creditor. For he promised that in the event the seller, or debtor, did not redeem the house within the three-year period, he would give him 25 florins beyond the price of one hundred florins originally assessed. And thus it is not likely that from the beginning the true price of the thing intervened. Likewise and thirdly, from this promise of 25 florins it is evidently presumed that this contract from the beginning was not one of true purchase and sale, but rather of the nature of a pledge; because it seems contrary to the nature of the contract of sale that after the act, when the other wishes to buy back, a greater price must be given; whence it does not appear that from the beginning there was a perfected sale, in l. necessario, ff. de peri. & commo. rei ven.; and from such pacts contrary to the nature of the contract intervening, the contract is rather presumed to be of the nature of a pledge, as in c. illo vos, and what is there noted, de pig.; what is noted by Bartolus in the said § qui maximos makes to this point. The fourth conjecture is from the fact that he willed in the pacts that the resale be made to him, and that the debtor ought to pay every tax, and the remaining expenses to be incurred concerning notaries for the share falling to both contracting parties; so that that fictitious seller was unwilling to incur any expense, but simply and absolutely to gain the usufruct of the said house, at least for the time of those months. The fifth conjecture is gathered from the subsequent contract, in that he willed that, upon the sale of a moiety of that house held in common having been made, he should not be bound to any rent beyond two years on account of the delay in buying back the other half of the house. And thus he openly makes the contract usurious. Whence from this the quality of the price can more easily be presumed, as in l. qui semissam, ff. de usur. and in c. illo vos, at the end, de pigno. and in cap. ex studiis, and in ca. mandata, de præsumpt. Moreover, that the second contract contained in itself usurious wickedness will be evident from what is to be said below under the second principal doubt. And from all the aforesaid, it is concluded with respect to the first doubt that we may clearly say that that contract made under the form of purchase and sale is simulated and executed in fraud of usury, and is in truth of the nature of a pledge, since there concur supporting indications beyond what is necessarily required in the said c. ad nostram. And no wonder, because even in a more doubtful case it is commonly concluded that the contract is to be presumed usurious, namely, when there is simply a pact of reselling and a low price intervened; this was clearly the opinion of the Glossa Ordinaria in c. conquestus, de usu., and of Archidiaconus in c. plerique, 14, q. 4, and of dominus Antonius in c. illo vos, de pig.; and so for many other reasons have I advised, and maintained while lecturing. Nor do the remarks noted by Jac. de Aren., as Cynus relates in l. 3, C. plus valere, quod agi., stand in the way of the aforesaid, where he said that three things joined together do not prove a usurious contract, namely, a pact of reselling, the smallness of the price, and that the buyer was accustomed to practice usury. For his statement is false and is not approved by law, and he attempts to answer the aforementioned c. ad nostram, but by no means answers it; on the contrary, he erred in the understanding of it and in his response, as Johannes Andreæ expressly attests in the said c. illo vos. From these points it is concluded what the role of the judge ought to be in pronouncing judgment. For I say that he ought to pronounce that the rents of the house which that creditor received or could have received be computed into the principal debt, and the remainder ought, together with the house, to be handed over and assigned to the debtor, as is proved in ca. 1 & 2, de usur. and in l. cum contra, C. de pign. act. The agreements made in the second place do not stand in the way: because all things were done in fraud of usury, and the accessory follows the principal, regula accessorium, libro 6. I come to the second point, namely, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the said contract is not proved usurious by the aforesaid, whether at least by virtue of the second agreement he is bound to pay the rents for half of the house from the time at which the said fifty florins were paid. And although it is not necessary to examine this point, since from what was said above it appears that the said contract was usurious, nevertheless, to comply with the consultee's wish, I say very briefly that the heir is bound to the payment of those rents. For it is certain that from the second agreement a sale of a moiety of the house held in common was made, and ownership and possession were transferred to that first seller by the second buyer; which is clearly gathered from this, that half of the whole price having been paid, he promised to pay him three florins under the name of rent for the said moiety up to a certain time then next following, and promised to make for him an instrument of sale; through which ownership and possession of the moiety held in common were sufficiently transferred to him, as is proved in l. quædam mulier, ff. de rei ven.; l. quod meo, ff. de acquir. poss. makes to this point. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that, although he promised to make an instrument of sale, it nevertheless does not appear to have been made; because I say that he did not promise to sell, but to make an instrument of sale for the purpose of proof to be made; whence I say that he did sell at the present time, which is evident from the fact that he then promised to pay rent; l. sicut datam, C. de li. cau. and c. ecclesia sanctæ Mariæ, ut lit. pendent. makes to a similar point; for the instrument is not of the substance of the contract, but is made for the proof of the contract, l. consensu, ff. de actio. & oblig. and l. pactum, C. de pa. These things having been premised, it is clearly evident that he is obligated to the payment of the rent constituted for the half of the house. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that an agreement was entered into between them after the two years then next following, during which he would not be obligated to the payment of any rent if the remainder of the moneys owed were not restored to him; because I say that such a pact, as containing usurious wickedness, is not valid, as in capitul. debitores, de iureiurand., for he wished to retain those rents because the payment of the debt was being delayed, contrary to capitul. consuluit, de usur., and the notes in capitul. dilecti, de arbit. And it should be subtly noted: because from these words contained in this second agreement it is clearly evident that the first and the second contract were usurious. For he says that he sold him a moiety of the house held in common, and afterwards he says that unless he restores to him the remainder of the money which he ought to have, he is not bound to pay. Whence he does not say that he wished to resell to him the other moiety, but that he ought to have the money; and thus in truth no true sale intervened, but the whole contract was of the nature of a pledge, and drawn up in the form of a sale in fraud of usury. Lastly, I come down to the third and final point, in which I say that no prescription can be alleged here:

† because a statute speaking in a matter of law ought to be understood according to the common law, namely where good faith intervenes, as in cap. cum dilectus, de cle. non resi.; l. 2, C. de noxa. makes to this point, and in cap. cum dilectus, de consuetu.; and if it were understood otherwise, the statute would not be valid, because it would induce sin, as in capitul. final., de rescript., noted by Bartolus in l. omnes populi, ff. de iustit. & iure, in l. fin., C. si contra ius. vel uti. publ.; as in our case the creditor was in bad faith, from the fact that he contracted in fraud of usury, 34, quæstio 2, cap. si virgo. For he is said to be in bad faith who has awareness of another's property, as there,

† and thus on the part of the creditor fictitiously buying, or unlawfully agreeing, no prescription can be alleged. I say the same with respect to the person of his heir by a twofold consideration: first, because the bad faith of the deceased harms the universal heir, as l. cum hæres, ff. de diver. & tempo. præscript.; second and better, because the heir is bound to make satisfaction for the soul of the deceased, as in capitul. a nobis, at the end, de sen. excommu., and in capi. literis, de rapto, and capit. fin., de sepul.; and from these things it is clear that prescription does not benefit the heir. And let these remarks suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Partners can agree among themselves that one [?] shall have two parts of the profit.
2. In order for a partnership to be lawful, it is necessary that losses and profits be shared in common.
casus: A certain Franciscus is said to have consigned one hundred gold florins to certain wool-workers, under a pact and agreement confirmed between the said parties, namely that the said wool-workers should have, hold, and trade with the said one hundred florins in their trade and craft of wool, and in such a way that the said florins should stand in the said trade at loss and at profit, with this expressed: that the said Franciscus should not be bound to undergo loss in the said capital beyond ten florins in a year, nor should he even be admitted to profit beyond ten florins, so that the said Franciscus wished neither to experience loss nor profit beyond ten in a year. It is asked whether the pact is lawful, etc.
body: With the help of Christ and His mother humbly invoked, it seems at first that it is so. For although when one contributes money and the other labor, with nothing else expressed, the losses and profits ought to be common according to the note by the gloss which Bar. and commonly the doctors follow in l. 1, C. pro socio, and as seems to be proved in l. si non fuerint, ff. eod., they can nevertheless by agreement remove this disposition of the law and agree that one partner shall bear a greater share of the profit than the other, as in the said l. si non fuerint, § 1, with the following law; and there is a good text in § de illa institutione, of the same title,

† where it is said that partners can agree among themselves that one shall have two parts of the profit. And no wonder, for contracts take their law from the agreement, as in the rule contractus, de reg. iur., in the Sixth. And an agreement against the accidentals or naturals of a contract is fully valid, as in ff. de postula. l. 1, § si convenerit, and in l. pacta conventa, C. de contrahen. empt., and l. pacisci, and l. iurisgen. § si paciscar, de pact., and in the single chapter, de commo., with many similar texts. Thus the agreement between the said parties ought to be upheld, especially taking reason into account, since it seems fair enough, given that each can stand equally toward profit and toward loss. For just as the wool-merchants could lose ninety with respect to the said capital, so they could have gained ninety if they had made a profit of one hundred in the year; whence at least in a case of doubt the contract ought to be sustained, based on the argument in chapter in civitate and chapter naviganti, de usu. Secondly, on the principal issue, the case in Inst. pro socio, § & adeo, seems almost to support this, where it is said that it can be agreed that one may experience profit but not loss; and thus it appears that the risk to the capital can, by agreement, belong to the other alone. This seems to be the view of Hostiensis in his Summa, de usu., § an aliquod, at the verse quid si periculum, and of Ioan. Andr. in chapter per tuas, de dona. post divor. resti., where he says that a dowry collected from a husband heading toward insolvency is deposited with a merchant who will give security that, the capital being preserved safe, he will account to the woman for a share of an honest profit. If, therefore, it can be agreed that the risk of the entire capital belongs to the recipient, all the more does the agreement hold valid in our case, in which that Franciscus was willing to bear up to ten of the loss in any year, and prepared himself in equal manner regarding profit. Thirdly, to the same effect: it is certain that a partnership was contracted between the aforesaid, and not a loan, since the said Franciscus was willing to stand to both profit and loss, at least up to ten; therefore usury ceases, since usury does not occur except in a contract of loan, as in chap. consuluit, de usu., and chapter eiciens, 87th distinction, and fully by Ioan. Andr. in the rule peccatum, de reg. iur. in the Sixth, in the Mercuriales. But notwithstanding the aforesaid, I deem that the said contract was in no way lawful. First, I shall prove this by authorities, so that faith may more easily be lent; second, by legal rules and reasons. For this seems first to be held by the ordinary gloss in the Decretum, 14, question 3, c. plerique, where it asks: May anyone lawfully give his money to a merchant, so that he may buy merchandise therewith and give him a share of the profit? And it says that he may not, if the risk pertains to the recipient, because it seems to be a kind of loan contract. But if they contract a partnership such that the risk pertains to both, it says it is lawful for one partner to give money and the other to supply with labor what is lacking in money; said l. si non fuerint, with the text cited above. Goss. held the same view in his Summa, de usu., and in c. naviganti, of the same title, saying,

† that for a partnership to be lawful and for all sin to cease, it is necessary that losses and gains be shared in common. Hostiensis ultimately adopted this same opinion in the said § an aliquod, at the verse est tamen veritas. Azo and the ordinary gloss of Accursius in the said l. si non fuerint concur in this opinion, where they say that if one partner does not contribute more to the partnership than the other, an agreement introducing disparity between them is invalid; which is very much to be noted. Likewise Io. Cal. seems to intend this in c. naviganti. But in our case there was disparity between them without any just reason; therefore no partnership was contracted between them. This, beyond the aforesaid copious and solemn authorities, is proved in this manner: Partnership contains within itself a certain right of brotherhood, as the text expressly says in l. verum, in the beginning, ff. pro soc.; therefore, a pact introducing this disparity between them without reasonable cause is against the substance of the contract, since it breaks the very right of brotherhood: for it is of the nature of brotherhood that all things be common. Hostiensis alleged this reason as above, and by it departed from his prior opinion, saying that between partners it is not valid for one to bear the risk of the capital alone. Nor does it stand in the way that in other contracts an agreement is valid whereby one bears the risk where otherwise he is not bound by law, as in deposit, loan for use, and the like; because, according to him, in others the agreement is against the accidentals of the contract, but in our case it is against the substantials on account of the right of brotherhood that exists between partners, said l. verum. Secondly, I prove this by the said l. si non fuerint, and the said § de illo, with the following text, where it is expressly said that between partners losses and gains ought to be equal, and inequality can be introduced by agreement when one has contributed more industry or money, and thus for cause; otherwise, however, the agreement is seen to be broken as contrary to the substance of the partnership. But in our case no legitimate cause underlies why the said Franciscus ought not to bear the risk in the capital equally, just like the said wool-merchants, but wished to stand safe so as not to lose more than ten; which is repugnant to the law of partnership and brotherhood. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that he equally refused to share in the profit beyond ten: because disparity does not cease through this; on the contrary, it increases. Likewise and better, it is not likely that in a year those wool-merchants could have gained more than twenty, or a little more; and thus the said Franciscus would likely have had his entire principal, and profit. But it is indeed much more easily contingent that the whole capital, or some other part, be lost, and the said wool-merchants would have had a double loss: for they would have lost their labors, and would have borne the whole risk of the capital beyond ten. The said Franciscus, however, could alone suffer a single and modest loss. And thus no one can reasonably deny that there would be a great disparity between them without a reasonable cause. For by law the said Franciscus ought alone to bear the loss in the capital, even in whole; the wool-merchants, however, only in their labors, as is the singular gloss which Pet. and Cyn. follow in the said l. 1, C. pro socio, which says that once the money which the one contributed is lost, the partnership is dissolved, and he who provided the labor is not held; and through this notable consideration the baseness and disparity of the aforesaid contract clearly appears: for the wool-merchants could lose their labors and bear the risk of the capital, ten florins excepted. Likewise and thirdly, the laws nowhere admit a disparity in the entire loss of capital without a concurrent reasonable cause, as in the said § si non fuerint, and in the said § de illo. Nor does § adeo, Instit. pro socio stand in the way: because it is answered in many ways by Host. and Ioan. Cald. in the places cited above. But I am accustomed to answer more clearly, and, as I believe, more truly: for I say that that text must be understood of an agreement conforming to the common law, namely when it was agreed that he who contributes labor should not bear the loss of capital, but should share in the profit. And this is because he bears sufficient loss in his labors. For his labor is worth as much as the other's money, as is said there; deservedly it is enough that he lose his labor, and the other alone bear the loss in the capital, and so the text seems to mean if the end of that paragraph is referred to the preceding parts, which must be done, by the argument in l. si ita stipulatus, § Chrysogonus, ff. de ver. obli. But I would not admit that an agreement would be valid whereby the one giving the money would not feel loss, but only profit. For this partnership would be quasi-leonine, and contrary as it were to the right of brotherhood, contrary to said l. si non fuerint and said l. verum, because he would have the loss of the labor from the money, and the other would feel no loss. Likewise, it would in effect be a contract of loan: because he would experience profits and no loss, as the gloss says in said c. plerunque. And through this, answer can be made to the third opposing argument formed above.
