For although a partnership may seem to be contracted, nevertheless, because the risks were not common, but rather such great disparity existed, it seems rather a certain presumed and feigned or simulated contract of loan, and thus it would contain usurious depravity, by the argument in said c. in civitate and c. naviganti. Likewise, presupposing that it were not a usurious contract, at least it was not a lawful partnership by the aforesaid; therefore it cannot be claimed by reason of partnership, nor can profit, when it is claimed in fact, because profit does not arise from money when partnership ceases, as in said c. eiciens. To the authority of Io. And. in c. per tuas, I say that it is not proved by law, as Io. Cal. also says in the said chapter naviganti. Yet certain persons wishing to save that saying said that it proceeds in favor of the dowry; which nevertheless does not please me, because an agreement ought not to be committed in favor of a dowry, as in c. super eo, de usuris. From these points, all the contrary arguments formulated above remain resolved. And an inference can be made for the resolution of the other doubt, concerning which it is asked whether the statutory prescription has a place in the case: it seems indeed that it does, because that money remained purely as a debt, and not in partnership; therefore the same must be said of it as in another debt, from identity of reason, de confirmatio. util. c. cum dilecta and c. translato, de const. and l. illud, ff. ad legem aqui.; and let these things suffice. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If an accusation or inquisition was made concerning an assault committed with weapons, or concerning a striking with effusion of blood, and afterwards a simple assault without weapons, or a striking without effusion of blood is proved, an acquittal ought to be made.
2. Rashness alone is sufficient for someone to be condemned in expenses.
body: Having examined the entire proceeding held in the accusation instituted against Venturello, son of Manuel Sabbatini, a Jew and inhabitant of the land of Monte Spoletano, by a certain Nicola, son of the late Bartolomeo of Cortona, an inhabitant of the said land, three matters are to be very briefly examined for a clear decision on the facts. First, whether the said Venturello, or his father appearing in his name, should be acquitted or condemned. Second, presupposing that he is to be acquitted, whether the said Nicola should be condemned for calumny to the penalty of retaliation (poena talionis). Third, presupposing that he ought to avoid the penalty of calumny, whether he ought at least to be condemned in the expenses incurred in the said accusation. As to the first, omitting argumentation on either side for the sake of brevity, since this is a decisive consilium, I say that the said Venturello, or Manuel his father appearing in the name of the said Venturello his son, ought to be acquitted of the said accusation. I am moved by the fact that if the words of the above-written reformation, by whose provision the said Venturello is impugned, are weighed, they contain two principal parts. The first is that all and singular retailers of wool cloth, linen cloth, etc., are wholly bound and obliged to come, stay, and exercise their crafts in the place of the said merchandise, etc. The second part is that elsewhere wool cloth, linen cloth, etc., cannot be retailed shop-fashion (apothecaliter), under and upon a penalty of 100 florins upon anyone contravening, etc. If, however, the statements of the witnesses produced against the said Venturello are carefully weighed, he is proved to have fallen under neither part of the said reformation. It is clearer than light that he has not fallen under the first, because it is proved by none of the witnesses that the said Venturello is a retailer and exercised the craft of retailing outside the place of merchandise, as the reformation requires; rather, the witnesses produced in the second place instead prove the opposite, in that they unanimously state that the said Venturello had been a retailer or had kept a retail shop until the said reformation was made prohibiting it in the manner aforesaid; and thus by limiting themselves to that time they seem tacitly to intimate and testify that after the said reformation he did not exercise the said craft, argum. in l. cum praetor, ff. de iud. and in l. ex eo, ff. de testib. and in cap. nonne, de praesump. and dist. 25, cap. qualis. And to avoid the penalty it is enough that the contrary is not proved, since facts, and especially delicts, are not presumed, l. una, C. de mand. princ. and capitul. cum in iure, de offic. deleg., since everyone is presumed good unless the contrary is proved, in cap. fin. de praesumpt. and in cap. uno, de rescript. For retailing may be called what the common people call such, since we do not have this defined in law, for which there is a good text in l. sciendum, §. illud sciendum, ff. de aedili. edic. and as Barto. notes in the prooemium to the Digest. But it was not in the least proved that he was a retailer after the law, or that he exercised the craft of retailing outside the place of merchandise, since it is not proved that he was regarded as such in the said land, or that he exercised the said craft, at least by admitting everyone wishing to buy cloth from him by way of retail without distinction; which seems necessary for one to be said to exercise a craft, following what is read and noted in l. palam, ff. de rit. nup. and what Cy. notes in l. 1, C. de episc. aud.; to this also contributes what Barto. notes in l. semper, ff. de iure immu. and in the said prooem. ff., where he says that he is properly called a merchant who has the greater part of his fortune in merchandise, in which one must abide by the common appellation of the populace, argumentum in d. §. item sciendum, and in l. cum delanionis, §. asinam, ff. de fun. instru. et instru. leg., l. Labeo, de supel. lega. Against the said Venturello, however, nothing of the aforesaid has been proved. From which it is clearly concluded that he must be acquitted on the basis of the first part of the said reformation. The same, it seems to me, must be said with respect to the second part; for that, if well weighed, requires one thing with a certain qualification, namely that cloth cannot be retailed shop-fashion (apothecaliter) outside the place of merchandise, etc. Whence that adverb apothecaliter must be considered, which determines and qualifies the verb retaliari, according to what was noted by Bartol. in l. ex facto, ff. de vulg. et pupil.; wherefore to incur the penalty it is not sufficient to prove that one retailed cloth, unless it is proved that he did this shop-fashion: because when something is to be proved with a certain limitation or qualification, it does not suffice to prove it without the requisite qualification or determination, as in l. Fulcinius, and there by Bartol., ff. ex quibus cau. in poss. ea., and by the same in l. divus, ff. de re iudicat.; and here it is not proved that he sold cloth shop-fashion. For none of the witnesses deposes that he saw the said Venturello retail that cloth, at least shop-fashion, as the statute requires; on the contrary, they rather prove the opposite, since one says that he heard from the said Venturello that he retailed that cloth in the merchandise market. Likewise, other witnesses simply say that they saw the said Venturello deliver three braccia of wool cloth to the said Nicola. From this it cannot be concluded, even if it were true that the said Venturello delivered the said cloth, that he retailed cloth shop-fashion; it imports the same as 'as a retailer', as the preceding words of the statute clearly intimate, which must be observed for the declaration of those that follow, as in l. si servus plurium, in fin. de lega. primo, and in l. nummis, ff. de legat. 3. But it is not in the least proved that he sold the said cloth as a retailer. And therefore it is not sufficient for the condemnation of Venturello, especially having regard to the quality of his person, since by the pacts entered into with the exalted Commune of Florence it is lawful for him to sell expired pledges. And he also has in his pacts that no statute can be made to the prejudice of his pacts; whence it could be that he sold the said cloth not shop-fashion as a retailer, but as a moneylender who holds it for expired pledges; for an accusation must be proved in full, so that the proof accessorily concludes it, as in capitul. in praesentia, de probat.; to this contributes what Barto. notes in l. non solum, §. sed et reprobari, ff. de nov. oper. nuncia.; hence the gloss noted on l. 2, C. de proba.: that if an accusation

† or inquisition was made concerning an assault committed with weapons, or a striking with the shedding of blood, and afterwards a simple assault without weapons or a striking without the shedding of blood is proved, an acquittal must be made, because the quality of the act adduced in the accusation is not proved, for which see l. denunciasse, §. quid tamen, ff. de adulte., and l. 2, ff. vi bonorum rapto., with the like. So I say in the present case. From these things I conclude that the said Venturello is not proved to have fallen either under the first or under the second part of the said statute; and thus he must be acquitted: because when the accuser does not prove, the defendant must be acquitted, as in the common texts of law. I come now to the second question, whether the said Nicola, the accuser, is to be punished for calumny; and on this a long question could be examined, which exists in law, whether the accuser is said to act calumniously by the very fact that he fails to prove. Concerning this question, it is noted fully in l. 1, ff. ad turp., and there by Barto.; in l. athletas, de his qui not. infa.; and in cap. 2, de calum.; and 2, quaest. 4, capitul. qui non probat, and §. notandum, with many similar texts. But not insisting on words, the common conclusion is that an accuser who fails in his proof is excused from the penalty of calumny if he has on his side some evident indications, such as common report, or having heard it from trustworthy persons, or something similar, as is noted in the laws cited above, especially in the said §. calumniator, and cap. 1, in fi., de elect., serves excellently. But from the statements of the witnesses produced in this case it can be conjectured quite evidently that the said Nicola was not guilty of calumny, so that he could plausibly have believed that the said Venturello, by that act, had contravened the aforesaid reformation. Calumny, however, consists in the intent, and requires dolus, which is not without craftiness and fraud, l. 1, ff. de dolo, and l. iurisgentium, §. sed si fraudandi, ff. de pact., in which the said Nicola does not seem to have been. From which I briefly conclude on the second point, namely that the said Nicola is not to be condemned for calumny to the penalty of retaliation. As to the third, namely what regarding expenses, I judge that the said Nicola should be condemned in them: because although he was not guilty of calumny, nevertheless he rashly persevered in the accusation, since he ought first to have examined and consulted more experienced persons as to whether the accusation to be instituted against the said Venturello would be proved by that act; which since he did not do, he is found in temerity,

† which alone suffices for someone to be condemned in expenses, as in capitul. calumniam, de poeni., and there by the doctors, and it is more fully noted in capitul. finem, de dolo et contumacia, and in l. eum, quem temere, and there by Barto., ff. de iudi., and in l. 1, ff. ad turpil., by the same; whence ignorance of the law does not excuse from condemnation in expenses; so hold the glossa and doctors in the said capitul. finem, and Barto. in the said l. 1, ad turpil., and Specu. in the title de expen., §. fi., vers. ex praemissis. The duty of the judge in this accusation will therefore be to acquit the said Venturello, or Manuel appearing in the name of his son, from the said accusation, and to condemn the said Nicola in the expenses which the said Venturello, or the father for him, has reasonably incurred in this case. Concerning the expenses of the present consilium, however, since the Podestà sought it ex officio, to whom it belongs, I say that one must stand by custom, according to what is noted by Spe. in the title de sala., §. 1, vers. consuetudo, and by the glossa in cle. statutum, de elect., in the absence of which the ordinary judge can claim nothing for salary; whence if he acted, he can obtain it at his own expense, since for these incumbent burdens a salary is instituted for him, according to what is noted by Ioan. An. in c. cum ab omni, de vita et honest. cle.; he can nevertheless by civil law seek sportulae and certain gifts, which, however, are not determined by law, but one must stand by the custom of the law, as in auth. offeratur, on this by the gl. and Bar. in the said auth. offeratur. And let these things suffice. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One bound to the restitution of a universal or particular fideicommissum is regularly bound to give security with sureties.
2. A brother's son is improperly called a grandson.
3. A father requested to restore to his son is regularly bound to restore.
body: That which is inquired concerning the law is whether a son is compelled to restore the inheritance to his paternal uncle—namely, the brother of the testator—if he should die without children, and whether he is bound to give security with sureties for making the restitution upon the occurrence of the condition or restitution. And I say briefly that this doubt depends upon the understanding of l. iubemus, C. ad Trebellia. For this is of undoubted law,

† that one bound to the restitution of a universal or particular fideicommissum is regularly bound to give security with sureties, as is the text joined with the gloss in l. semper, ff. ut lega. nom. caue., and is more expressly proved in l. si quando, under the same title. Likewise by an argument from a special case in l. filius, under the same title. For if there it is a special rule in the case of a newly emancipated son or a manumitted slave, that the father or master is relieved by furnishing security under a hypothec of his goods; therefore in other cases, with stronger reason, security—even under a hypothec of goods—does not suffice; indeed, even if he were unable to provide suitable security, a bare promise, even with a hypothec of goods, would not suffice, but one must proceed in accordance with those things that are notably held in l. postquam, §. imperator, under the same title. The difficulty therefore arises, as I have said before, when the son is requested to restore. For he seems privileged, so as not to be bound to this furnishing of security, as in the said l. iubemus. And although that text speaks of when someone is requested to restore the inheritance to his own son, the grandson of the testator, or great-grandson, and so forth, nevertheless certain authorities who were considered moderns in the time of Cynus said the same when the son is requested to restore to a stranger, from an identity or greater force of reason, lest a stranger be more ungrateful than a son, or grandson, or related person. For if I overcome the closer in degree, with stronger reason I overcome the more remote, as in l. 4, at the verse sed licet, C. de bon. mat. And this argument made Cynus vacillate in l. iubemus, at the end; nevertheless, he himself seems finally to settle in the contrary opinion, so that that text is not extended beyond the persons expressed therein, because the text in the said l. iubemus, at the end, expressly prohibited this, where this contrary conclusion is most clearly proved; and there Odofredus clearly held this, saying that that special rule had been introduced among descendants lest discord arise among them. For a certain mistrust seems to arise from the demanding and furnishing of this security. I adduce a similar point in the furnishing of a surety for the restitution of a dowry, which is prohibited between husband and wife for the aforesaid reason, but otherwise in a stranger receiving a dowry for another, as is read and noted in the rubric and black letter of C. ne fideiuss. dot. dent., and especially in l. et in dotibus, C. de dona. cau. non nu. Likewise, the text in the said l. iubemus speaks of a grandson and great-grandson; properly, however, according to the canons and laws, such a person is called the son of a son, or of a daughter, and the son of a grandson; ff. de gradibus, l. iurisconsultus, §. secundo gradu, at the end, and 35, q. 6, c. 1, and 2, and 3.

† A brother's son, however, is improperly called a grandson according to the common manner of speaking, as is noted by Johannes Andreae in c. fundamenta, de ele., in the Sext, and more fully by Federico de Senis, consi. 28. But laws, especially ancient ones, ought to be understood properly, and not according to an improper manner of speaking, especially a modern one, because the most expert lawmakers do not use the words of the vulgar, as Baldus notably stated in c. 1, de succes. feu.; to which makes what Bartolus notes in l. stipulatio ista, §. hi qui, ff. de uerbo. obli. Why say more? For this understanding of ours, I adduce, beyond the others, two notable glosses of the civil law. One is in l. 1, ff. ut lega. nom. caue., at the verse semper, where it first stated that the children of a testator do not give security by virtue of the said l. iubemus, and immediately after it adds that that is a special rule when a son is requested to restore to his own son. Secondly, a more notable gloss is in l. filio, under the same title, which restricts the said l. iubemus even further, saying that it applies if the son was requested and the fideicommissary was in the power of the one requested, which does not happen in our case; and Bartolus intended the same there.

† Furthermore, a father requested to restore to his son is regularly bound to give security, as is proved by an argument from a special case in the said l. filio; therefore, with stronger reason, one is bound to restore to a paternal uncle. And thus I conclude in our case that surety must be given to the paternal uncle. Nor is the said l. filio corrected by the said l. iubemus, as the gloss notes in the said l. filio, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If usuries are owed to absent persons, they ought to be sent to them.
2. As long as restitution can be made to the one who paid, that money ought never to be given to the poor, or converted to another pious cause.
casus: Between the magnificent commune of Siena on the one hand, and Raynerius Toscanus of Milan on the other, a certain formal agreement was entered into on the occasion of the usuries to be restored, which Zeno ordered to be restored at the end of his life, and to the restoration of which the said Raynerius obligated himself in the manner written below. The words of the agreement, however, are these: 'That the usuries must be fully restored over the course of six years, each year a certain amount, which restitution must effectively begin and be made for the first year on the calends of January, and so thereafter continue from January to January, especially of the said six years, returning first to citizens, then to country-dwellers and subjects, according as they were written down in order, and then to those who should be found or were foreigners; likewise let the restitution of all the moneys be made in this manner: that a depositary be chosen from those present to hold and return the said moneys of the usuries, that is to say, to those where the persons themselves, or their heirs, are found; as for the others, that they come to devolve [?] upon the House of Wisdom.' It is asked whether, etc. Now it is presupposed that certain persons, both citizens and foreigners, did not demand their sixth part at the first deadline, and the administrators of the House of Wisdom demand it as an uncertain debt. It is asked whether they can do so, etc.
body: Having humbly invoked the protection of Christ and of his Mother, I briefly conclude that if it can be established to whom the said moneys are owed, the administrators of the House of Wisdom cannot claim them, neither under the ius commune nor by virtue of the said agreement. For under the ius commune it is clear that so long as those from whom they were extorted, or their heirs, survive, they ought not to be distributed to a pious cause as being uncertain, as is the clear text with the gloss in c. cum tu, de usu. and in c. sicut dignum, § res, de homi. Indeed, the gloss in c. cum tu says one thing,

† namely that if those to whom they are owed are absent, they ought to be sent to them. Therefore, no action for claiming those moneys belongs to the House of Wisdom, on the presupposition that by law uncertain moneys are owed to it, because, as I have said, they cannot be called uncertain through what the gloss noted in c. 2, de usu. lib. 6, at the word 'satisfactione', and by Federicus de Senis in consi. 150. For the said Raynerius is bound to make restitution to those to whom it is clear they are owed, from whose obligation he would not be relieved, even if he made restitution to the poor, or to any others whomsoever, in the said c. eos, because a debt is not remitted, but increased when it is improvidently paid to anyone, when it is due to another out of debt, as the text says in c. ea te, de iureiur., and ff. de sol., l. vero procuratori. Nor is he bound to pay, even if the House of Wisdom were willing to furnish him with security to keep him indemnified; for that alone does not cause someone to be bound to pay to one to whom he does not owe, even if he were a relative of the person entitled to receive, as noted by the gloss and Bartolus in l. vero procuratori, cited above, and l. qui hominem, under the same title. Nor also by virtue of the above-said agreement is the said Raynerius bound to pay, because he was obligated to pay the House of Wisdom under a condition, namely in the event that moneys were found, and because it were unknown or those to whom they are owed, or their heirs, cannot be found. For, as the gloss says in the said c. cum tu,

† as long as restitution can be made to the one who paid, that money ought never to be given to the poor, or converted to another pious cause; and if it were improvidently paid to a pious use, the said Raynerius would nevertheless be bound to pay again to those entitled to receive, pursuant to the laws cited above and the remarks of Federicus, where cited above, and Antonius de Butrio in the said c. cum tu. Therefore, before the condition of uncertainty exists, it cannot be claimed, because the day of the payment to be made is not said to have arrived (cessisse dies), as in l. cedere diem, ff. de verb. sig., and in c. prudentiam, and by Innocent in de offic. deleg.; for while the condition is pending, only a hope is in the obligation, instit. de verbo. obliga., § ex conditionali, and what is owed on a future day, although it may be paid beforehand, yet cannot be claimed, in l. continuus, § eo quidem tempore, ff. de verbo. oblig., and in c. unico, de plus peti. I therefore conclude that, while those persons or their heirs to whom the money is owed are still extant, it cannot be claimed as uncertain by the administrators of the House of Wisdom, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The dowry is called the woman's own patrimony.
2. Probable conjectures suffice to prove knowledge of a fact.
3. A father can institute a daughter in her dowry.
body: Having implored the aid of Almighty God, it seems firstly that the said Catherina is in no way barred from being able to seek the said dowry of 800 florins from the heir of her husband. For whether we say that that dowry was common to father and daughter, or of the daughter alone, one paying the father alone is not released, as in l. ij. ff. solu. matr. and l. qui hominem. §. si gener, ff. de sol. And in our case I say more strongly that one paying the father is not released, because that dowry belonged to the daughter alone, since at the time when the father married off the daughter, she was emancipated. For if a dowry is consolidated into the person of the daughter alone if she is emancipated after the fact, as in l. unica. §. uideamus, C. de rei uxo. act., this occurs more strongly if she was emancipated from the beginning, as noted by Bar. in said l. ij.

† For the dowry is the woman's own patrimony, as in l. iij. §. si igitur, ff. de mino.; therefore the daughter has a well-founded claim against the husband's heir, nor can other things that intervened afterwards prejudice the daughter herself. For the second constitution of a larger dowry when she was given in marriage a second time is no obstacle, because she did not receive the money of the first dowry collected by the father, but rather the maternal dowry, which is inferred from the quantity of both dowries, namely the maternal one and that of the daughter herself, and this is more clearly drawn from the release and discharge which the said Catherina, as heir of her mother, made to her father, there where it says, “and she did this because she confessed to having had from the said Bernardo the said dowry of my lady, etc.”; for although from the beginning the dowry of 1400 florins had been constituted simply by the father, nevertheless it is evident from subsequent events that he intended to give, and she to receive, that maternal dowry. For subsequent events explain preceding ones, as in l. si seruus plurium, in fi. and l. qui filiabus, de leg. 1. and l. nummis, de leg. 3. Moreover, the general release and discharge which she made to her father cannot stand in the way of the said Catherina, because that does not refer to things unknown by the said Catherina, as in l. tres fratres, C. de pac. and l. si soror, C. de coll. and l. nec ignorans, C. de do.; relevant is what is read and noted in l. qui Romæ. §. duo fratres, ff. de uerbo. obli. Also because the discharge was made with respect to those things which she could claim from her father, but the said Catherina demands nothing from the father, nor from his heir, or from her creditor; therefore, etc. And by the same consideration another ground is removed that can be drawn from the father's testamentary disposition and the discharge of the heir that subsequently followed. But these notwithstanding, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer, and I say that the heir of the husband was completely released from the obligation by which he was bound to the said Catherina. I am moved first because release occurs by payment made to the father, whether the father demanded it from the beginning with the daughter knowing and not contradicting, as in l. ij. §. uoluntatem, ff. sol. mat., or she knew after the fact and did not contradict, at least with some positive act intervening, as in l. Paulus, ff. rem ra. ha. and cle. j. de procu. and a good text in l. filiusfa. absente patre, ff. ad Mace.; relevant is what is noted by Bar. in l. cum tabernam. §. idem quęsijt, ff. de pig. and in l. quo enim, ff. rem ra. ha.; and this occurs most especially in l. si seruus communis, ff. de do. inter uir. & uxor., where by reason of the union between brothers, one who is silent is regarded as consenting, even where a loss to the family property is involved; for this, what is noted by Cyn. in l. inuitus, C. de proc. and Bar. in l. quæ dotis, ff. sol. matri through the Canonists in c. nonne, de præsumpt. Moreover, that the daughter knew, or performed some positive act approving after the fact the payment that had been made, seems sufficiently elicited and proven from the merchants' account-books, in which he made the said Catherina the creditor of the said amount, and he asserts that he paid various amounts to diverse persons for her at various times. For although in law merchants' books do not create full proof in their own favor, as in l. exemplo, and l. rationes, C. de probatio. and in cap. 2. and what is there fully noted de fi. instrumen., nevertheless to the prejudice of a third party and in favor of another than the merchant himself, at least where it concerns the presumed knowledge of a third party, they make full proof according to what is noted in l. quædam. §. nummularios, ff. de eden. and l. optima, C. de contrahen. & commit. stipu. and in c. illud, de præsump.; relevant is what is noted by the gl. and Inno. in c. cum olim, de censi. To the same effect is what is noted by Bar. in l. Celsus, ff. de usucap., where he says bad faith, and thus awareness of another's property, is proven by the reputation of the place and other conjectures.

† Whence, to prove knowledge of any fact, probable conjectures suffice, since otherwise it cannot easily be proven. Moreover, a specific act intervened here by causing payment to be made to others from the said money, as is sufficiently gathered from the merchant's book, to which full faith is given especially by the judgment of the city. Secondly, this same point is proven from the general discharge which the said Catherina gave to her father; for since she knew, as appears from the foregoing, that her dowry had come to her father, and she universally discharged him with certain knowledge, she can therefore claim nothing further by reason of the said dowry, according to what is fully noted by Barto. in said §. duo fratres; and said l. tres fratres, in fin. a contrario sensu, de pac. is relevant. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the said Catherina made the release and discharge only concerning monies which the said Catherina could have sought from her father, since he had not had a mandate from him in seeking it, nor does she even then seek it from him, but from the heir of the husband; because I say that from the fact that he sought the daughter's dowry, and thus by the act and deed itself conducted the business of the daughter, the said daughter—even had she been ignorant at the beginning—could, by ratifying the father's deed and seeking the dowry from the father himself, as is read and noted in l. si absentis, C. si cer. pet. and in l. si mater, C. de rei uend. and l. 2. C. pro soc., therefore be seen to have released him from that amount of the first dowry, since she could have claimed it from him. For those words of the release, “could have claimed,” etc., are very general and merely denote the ability to claim, according to what is noted in c. si. de restitu. spol.; whence by so releasing her father from it, she is seen to ratify the payment made to her father and to release the father himself, an excellent argument being in l. 3. ff. rem ra. hab., where the principal, by appealing from the sentence of the procurator, approves. To the same effect is what is noted in a similar case by Bartol. in l. 1. C. de arb. Thirdly, and lastly, what strongly and most powerfully supports this side as the principal point is what the gl. notes in said l. 2. ff. sol. ma. in the versicle adempta, and the text in l. si cum dotem. §. si pater, eod. tit., where it is said that although the father alone demanded the dowry without the daughter's consent, nevertheless, since the father left to her in his will as much as the dowry was, and the daughter accepted what was bequeathed, she immediately precluded for herself the avenue of seeking the dowry from the father's heir or from a third-party creditor. And it should be noted that the text and gloss cited above in no way weigh the daughter's knowledge, but only the conjectured intention of the father, that since he alone received the dowry, he is seen to have made the bequest to the daughter with the intention of set-off against the dowry received by him. Nor indeed does it matter whether it is claimed from him or from a third party, because it is sufficiently claimed from the father, or from his heir, since if an action were effectively competent against the husband's heir, it would in effect be claimed from the father himself, or his heir, because of the recourse they have against the father's heir; for this, an excellent text in a similar matter is in l. fin. C. de usu. rei iud. Indeed, the text in said §. si pater, if properly weighed, expressly denies an action to the daughter against the third party, and the gloss cited above meant this more clearly in said l. 2. on the word adempta. And this must be said most especially in our case, where we have what amounts to the express will of the testator in this matter. For he left to the said Catherina by right of institution eight hundred florins, and thus the amount of the first dowry received by him, in lieu of all legitime that the said Catherina could claim in the estate of the said testator, and in lieu of all and the whole of that which the said Catherina could claim on any other ground, for whatever other cause, etc. And he commanded that she give a release to his heir, as above more fully, etc. From which words it is gathered quite clearly that the father, who knew he had received the dowry, had the intention of setting it off.

† For a father can also institute a daughter in her dowry, as noted by the gl. and Bar. in l. 3. ff. de mino.; c. Raynutius, de testa. and what is noted there are relevant. On this ground one must not be concerned about the knowledge or ignorance of the said Catherina. Rather, it is sufficient to conceive this effect: that she received as much from the father's testament as was that which the father received on the occasion of the dowry from the person of the daughter. From all of which I conclude that an action regarding the eight hundred florins must be denied to the said Catherina, whether against the father's heir, or the husband's heir, or anyone else on the aforesaid occasion; and the response to all the arguments alleged above to the contrary is clear. And let these things suffice, etc. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One can prescribe against the emperor, so that he is not acknowledged as prince.
2. An argument drawn negatively from the etymology of a word is valid.
3. The Empire today depends upon the Church.
4. The emperor does not acknowledge the empire from the Roman people, but from the Church.
5. A title is presumed from conjecture.
6. Vassals are properly called faithful.
7. The entire diocese is the bishop's territory.
8. Ascendants do not succeed to a fief.
9. A brother succeeds a brother in an ancient fief.
10. A vassal can make the condition of a fief better, but not worse without the lord's will.
11. A surety has no action against the principal if he paid without raising the exceptions available to the principal.
body: Having implored the aid of the Creator of all things, although in these doubts much and eloquent argument and counsel have been put forward, nevertheless, in order to comply with the request of the petitioner who seeks my judgment in specific terms, I shall specifically touch upon each of the aforesaid doubts by introducing certain points barely touched upon by others; and when through the decision of one matter the resolution of the others can be attained, one must begin from that as the more principal, according to what is held and noted in c. pastoralis, § 1, de rescrip., and c. prudentiam, de offi. dele., with its like. Therefore, I shall first begin to examine whether the cities and castles concerning which there is dispute are feudal property, or rather the proper and patrimonial property of the grantors themselves. And it seems firstly that they are proper, and ought to be acknowledged by no one, at least in respect of the useful and direct lordship: possession from a time of whose beginning there is no memory has the force of a title, even in prescribing against the common law, as is the case in c. 1, de præscri., li. 6, and l. hoc iure, § ductus aquæ, de aqua quoti. & æsti. But these noble ancestors of these disputants, namely of Titius and Anselinus, possessed that city and the castles as lords for so long a time; therefore they prescribed in them a free and whole lordship and jurisdiction. For whether we say that these goods pertained to the Roman Church, or to the Empire, prescription can always be alleged: because although against the Roman Church prescription does not run in respect of the supreme power, nor against God, whose place it holds, yet in temporal rights, as in the possession of some city, castle, or village, prescription does indeed run, as in c. ad audientiam, and what is noted there, de præscr.; so Innocen. elegantly stated in c. bonæ, part 2, de postu. prælato., in the 2nd column; and the same is to be said even more strongly regarding the things belonging to the Emperor. For against those things belonging to the Emperor prescription lies, even if they are such things as were reserved as a mark of special privilege, as is the text noted in c. super quibusdam, de verbo. sig., and in l. si publicamus, § in vectigalibus, and there by Bar., ff. de publ.

† Nay more, many have held that one can prescribe even against the Emperor, so that he is not acknowledged as prince; concerning which it is fully noted in c. per venerabilem, qui filii sint leg., where Inn. held this, and by others in cle. Romani, de iureiu., in prin., by Io. de Lig., and by Bar. in l. 1, ff. de aqua plu. arcen., and in l. hostes, de ca. & postli. re., and in l. infamem, in fi., ff. de pub. iud.; and it seems most true, at least when it is prescribed passively, so that he may be subject to the Pope, as Hos. held in the said c. per venerabilem. Secondly, it is principally proved thus.

† An argument drawn negatively from the etymology of a word is valid in law, as is proved in l. 2, § appellata, ff. si cert. peta. Likewise it is valid taken affirmatively, if it does not contradict the definition, as Barto. notes in l. 1, de test. But a fief (feudum) is named from fidelity (fidelitas), which the vassal ought to render to the lord by oath, as the text says in cap. 2, per quos fiat inue.; but this Titius and Anselinus, or their ancestors, never rendered or promised it as vassals; therefore it cannot be said that they held it in fief; nay rather, if it had been a fief from the beginning, by the passage of so much time it would have been prescribed, according to what is noted by Ioan. Andr. in titu. de præscript., in addit. Specul., in the penultimate and last columns, by the gloss in cap. 1, de capi. qui cu. vendi., and there by Bald.; and it seems to be proved in cap. si diligenti, and cap. ad audientiam, de præscript. Thirdly, to the same point it is shown thus: if within a year the vassal does not seek investiture from the heir or successor of the lord, he falls from the right of the fief, as in cap. 1, de cap. qui cu. vend., as is read and noted in c. veritatis, de iureiu.; but in our case there is no memory that investiture was ever sought, either by the heirs who first held that city and the castles, or from any successor in the papacy or empire; therefore it is not likely that it is a fief; what is read and noted in c. longinquitate, 12, q. 2, supports this. But notwithstanding these things, I think the contrary opinion prevails, to which in the first place I bring forward that it is surer than sure that the Roman Pontiff has a grounded claim in matters of jurisdiction over the city of Rome and its entire territory, not only from the donation of Constantine made to the person of blessed Sylvester, but also from the approval and disputation of Emperor Louis, as in c. ego Ludouicus, 63 dist., and c. Constantinus, 96 dist., and in clem. Romani, de iureiuran. Nor does it depart little from error to call into doubt the validity of that donation, since the text in ca. fundamenta, de elect., lib. 6, says that it was divinely made for most just causes; this Bald. himself says on proœ. rubr. feu.; Bald. ultimately holds this in proœm. ff. vete.; fully by Ioan. de Lig. in the said clemen. Romani. And this seems today to be proved by exquisite reason,

† namely, the empire today depends on the Church, in which is both powers: 22 distinct., cap. 1 and 2; c. nouit, de iud.; and in c. causam, qui filij sint legi.; and by the gloss noted in clem. aduersus, de hære.; Bar. held this in l. 1, de requi. reis. And so to believe is of the necessity of salvation, as is decided in the Extravagant of Boniface which begins Unam Sanctam, and the note of the gloss in the said cle. aduersus.

† Whence today the Emperor does not hold the Empire from the Roman people, who acquired it through force without any color of justice, but from the Church, by which he is confirmed, crowned, and deposed when there is need, as in c. venerabilem, de elect., and c. ad apostolicæ, de re iudica., lib. 6; and he swears fidelity and obedience to the Church, as in the said cle. Romani, and through the Pope the Empire is transferred from nation to nation, d. c. venerabilem; whence Constantine conferred nothing new upon the Church, but rather restored what was its own, as notes Ioann. de Lig. in cle. Romani. And thus the argument is of no force for attacking that donation which maintains that the Emperor cannot diminish the rights of the Empire, concerning which see the gloss in Auth. quo modo opor. epis., § 1. From all of which it is sufficiently concluded as the first presupposition that the Roman Pontiff has a grounded claim over the City and its whole territory, in temporal and spiritual matters, as in the said capitul. fundamenta. Therefore it is necessary to infer that whoever has jurisdiction in that territory can pretend to a right only from special law, since the Pope succeeded in that place to the Emperor, who alone had jurisdiction there. For with the Emperor alone was the fountain of jurisdiction; and from him, as from a fountain, powers flowed into others. For inferior powers proceeded from the munificence of the Prince himself, as in authent. de exhiben. reis, § æquissimum, and capitul. quis dicatur dux, colla. 10; and this Bald. notes there, and better in capitu. 1, de natura feu., and in capitul. vno, de pact. iur. fir., where he says that all jurisdiction and district belongs to the Emperor by common law; whence supports 7, quæstio 1, capitul. in apibus, and what is noted by Ioan. de Ligna. and by others in clement. pastoralis, de re iudica., and in the said clemen. Romani. And since it is not established in our case by what special right the ancestors of these parties held the said places, and a title must be presumed from tacit long duration, as in the said capitul. 1, de præscript., lib. 6, and by Bartol. in l. cum de in rem verso, ff. de vsu., and by Ioan. And. in the said capitul. peruenit, de censib.,

† it is necessary to presume a title from conjecture, according to what is noted in the said l. cum de in rem verso, and in capitul. constitutus, de relig. domi., and l. si tibi pecuniam, ff. si cer. pet.; and by Bartol. in l. cotem ferro, § qui maximos, ff. de publi., and the gloss noted in l. 1, ff. de superfi., which says that the price and the quantity of rent serves to distinguish a buyer from a tenant. To the same point is a good text and what is noted in l. si filiusfamilias, C. de petit. hæred., and in capitul. peruenit, de empt. & vendi. It is certain that if we wish in our case to judge of the title from conjectures, it must necessarily be said that a feudal title underlies: because, as is clear from the factual situation, nothing else can be legitimately gathered and judged, owing to usurpation, which is not to be presumed; for here it is presupposed that the ancestors of these parties called themselves the faithful and servants of the holy Roman Church and of the Roman Pontiffs for the time being. Furthermore, it is presupposed that a certain one of their ancestors, upon coming to death, who had three parts in those goods, commanded in his last will that the said lands be held in obedience and reverence to the Roman Church, from which he asserted that he and his own had received many goods; which words most clearly indicate and infer that those goods are feudal.

† For vassals are properly called 'faithful' (fideles), as in capit. de forma, 22 quæstio 5, and in capitul. vno, de forma fide., colla. 10. And although anyone may be faithful, because faith or fidelity is more engaged in that contract than in another, as Bald. says in the prooemium to the Feuds, the lord in a certain manner commits his person—namely, his honor and goods—totally to the vassal; therefore a fief (feudum) is called from faith (fides) or fidelity (fidelitas). And these things especially apply since he commanded in his last will that those goods be held in obedience and reverence to the holy Roman Church, from which he asserted that he and his own had received many goods; nor does it appear that they held other goods from the Roman Church besides these; moreover, to hold goods in obedience to someone belongs more to the nature of a fief than to any other special title. To this is a good text in the said clement. Romani. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that those words—that they were faithful, etc., that they were held in obedience to the Roman Church, etc.—were spoken out of a certain devotion which good Christians are accustomed to have toward the Church; because I say this is not likely: for those things which are not usually said out of donation and goodwill, and which can redound to greater prejudice, are not presumed to have been said out of affection, but rather on the basis of a right belonging to another, according to what is elegantly noted by Innocen. in the said capitu. bonæ, de postula. prælato., and by Bartol. in l. 1, ff. de itine. actúque priua. In support of the aforesaid is the Authentica item si quis liberos, C. de natu. lib., where it is said that if one having natural children, he is seen to legitimate them. Likewise, a confession repeated rather often makes proof, although it does not have all its substantial requirements, according to the text noted and there by Barto. in l. cum satis, C. de agrico. & censi., libr. 11; the text in l. unica, C. de plus peti., and capitu. per tuas, de probat., with what is noted there, also supports this. For we ought not here to presume prescription, because there is no supporting evidence of prescription, nor ought it easily to be presumed; for we would be presuming negligence in the Roman Church, where there is such great vigilance, in capitu. de offic. delega., libr. 6. Nor a privilege containing a pure gift, because it is not to be presumed that the Church gave away its goods, against capitu. non liceat papæ, 12 quæstio 2, and l. cum de indebito, ff. de probat. Nor is it to be said that they themselves caused the city and those castles to be built: because in fact the contrary is presupposed. But even granting that it were so, nevertheless, although the property of the building could belong to the builder, yet jurisdiction does not; because it resides in the territory, just as a servitude does in an estate, whence it belongs to him whose the territory is, as capitu. 1, ver. ad hæc, and there by Bald., de pac. iur. firman.; what is found in l. pupillus, § territorium, ff. de uerbo. signi., and what is noted there, supports this.

† Hence we say that the whole diocese is the territory of the bishop, 16 quæstio 7, capitu. omnes basilicæ; and although another bishop may build a church there, nevertheless jurisdiction belongs to that bishop in whose territory it is, 16 quæst. 5, capit. 1. Let us therefore presume a fief, which is more probable, and is very often constituted by the Roman Church, and does not carry the greatest prejudice. For an argument drawn from things that commonly occur is valid, in capitu. 1, and what is noted there by Ioan. Cald., de cle. non resi. And in obscure matters we look to what is more probable and what is commonly accustomed to be done, as in the rule inspicimus, de reg. iur., lib. 6. And in doubtful cases the least is to be followed, as in the rule in dubiis, in the same book. And this is especially to be said in favor of the Church, lest it lose the direct lordship belonging to it by law, by the argument in l. sunt personæ, ff. de reli. & sumpt. fune. From these points I conclude that it must be presumed that these goods are feudal goods of the Roman Church, either by a grant made of old, or by prescription of so much time. For since these men held those goods as faithful subjects of the Church, they appear, if a title did not precede, to have acquired that feudal right from prescription, which can occur according to what is read and noted in capitu. ad audientiam, de præscript., and by Barto. in l. cum de in rem uerso, in fin., ff. de usu., and in l. quemadmodum, C. de agrico. & censi., lib. 11; l. si, and l. emphyteuticum, C. de fun. patri., and similarly the notable gloss in l. 2, C. de iure emphy., on the word repellere, at the end, support this. What was alleged above to the contrary does not oppose this conclusion; for those points apply when there is sole possession of the longest time without other accompanying circumstances indicating another contract, as is clear from what was said before. To the second I answer that, although the oath of fidelity is to be rendered by the vassal, this is true unless it was remitted from the beginning, which can be done, as is the text noted in the said capitu. 2, in titu. per quos fiat inuest. And although this is not presumed—nay rather, unless special pacts are proved, the fief is to be presumed to have been committed according to common custom and the common rules of fiefs, as is the text noted in capitu. 1, in fin., in the title quid si inuesti., column 10, where Bald. notes this—yet from the lapse of so much time the oath is to be presumed to have been remitted: the said l. filius, and c. peruenit, previously alleged. Likewise, such a fief could remain frank and free, so that they were bound by oath only to those things contained in c. de forma, de forma fideli., previously alleged, as Ioan. And. thinks in addit. Spe., in the title de præscrip., in the penultimate and last column, against which it does not appear that they ever contravened; and through this the answer to the third point is clear. For it seems prescribed that they are not bound to seek investiture, but are bound to fidelity solely from confession; for just as this seeking of investiture can be remitted by privilege, as is remarkably proved from what is read and noted in c. ueritatis, de iureiuran., so also from prescription, especially of so much time, from the beginning of which no memory exists, since that has the force of a constitution, the said c. 1, de præscript., lib. 6, and l. hoc iure, § ductus aquæ, ff. de aqua quoti. & æsti. Likewise it could be said that, presupposing that they had been deprived, yet the Pope seems willing to grant them indulgence, since this was introduced in favor of lordship, whence it is not excluded by this that it is a fief; and what was established to the detriment of vassals ought not to be turned to their advantage and favor, as in c. 2, de transla. præla.; for it is enough that they once held these goods as faithful subjects and servants of the Roman Church, and in obedience and reverence to it, as I have said above. To the aforesaid add the notable text, with the comments noted there, especially by Inno. in c. 1, de relig. domi., where it is said that if it is not established in whose diocese a church is, or at least it is doubted, through the exercise of one act performed by a certain bishop it is presumed that that church pertains to him in whole, since it is not established that it pertains to another. And thus through one act an extension is made to others; since it is already established that these goods are in the territory of the Pope and that their ancestors held them as faithful subjects of the Church, it ought to be said that by the whole right of the fief it belongs to the Roman Church, and thus that they are bound to the Pope for those things contained in the said c. de forma; and that text is sufficiently notable in our subject matter. From these points it can most clearly be inferred toward the solution of the other doubts. And first, whether a judgment rendered by the Senator of the City in favor of the mother succeeding in the person of predeceased sons against Anselinus the surviving son is valid: I say that if the mother brought that case to court as a feudal matter, saying that she ought to succeed in the person of the predeceased sons for the shares concerning them, the judgment is not valid; because when a cause is between vassals concerning a fief, jurisdiction belongs to the lord of the fief, and not to the ordinary of the place. For the law grants this jurisdiction to the ordinary exclusively and extinguishingly as to the jurisdiction of the ordinary, as is a good text in capit. cæterum, de iudic., and there Innoc., Hostien., and the other following doctors clearly hold this, at least when the lord of the fief summons the vassals before the ordinary; to the same effect is l. imperialem, § prætereà, de prohib. feu. alie. per Feder., where see the gloss and Bal. Nay rather, the vassals cannot, even by express consent, prorogue the jurisdiction of another, bypassing the lord of the fief without his consent, as the gloss and Bald. note in the said § prætereà; Barto. in l. j, § & post operis, ff. de noui oper. nunciatio., and in l. j, ff. de iudic.; and the canonists in the said capitu. cæterum; and there seems to be a text on this in cap. transmissa, de foro competen. This judgment is therefore found to have been rendered by one not having jurisdiction, and so it ought to be of no effect, as in capit. at si clerici, de iudi., and capit. si a non competen. iudi., through the whole. Or the mother brought this cause not as feudal, but as proper and private, and I say that the judgment held to the prejudice of Anselinus, because in this case a defect of jurisdiction is not given; for the law gives jurisdiction to the lord of the fief when it is established that the disputants are vassals and are disputing about a fief, as in the said c. cæterum, and in the said § prætereà, previously alleged. Furthermore, just as prescription runs against a vassal, although it does not harm an ignorant lord, as in c. 1, de cap. contra., where see the gloss and Bald., and by Ioan. And. in tit. de præscript., in the addition previously alleged, and by Bal. in the said § prætereà, at the word quæro pono, so it must be said that a judgment ought to harm the vassal who neglected to plead the peremptory exception arising from the feudal covenant, but not the lord, at least an ignorant one; cap. suborta, de re iudi., and capi. cum dilecta, de confir. util., and what is noted in the said capitu. ad audientiam support this. From these things it is clear what must be said regarding the validity of the first judgment. Now I enter upon the other doubt, namely, whether against the said lady mother of those predeceased sons seeking the execution of that judgment rendered against Anselinus the son, Titus, brother of the said Anselinus and his co-vassal, can oppose himself and impede that execution? And although at first glance it might seem to be said that he cannot, by the theory of Innocen. in cap. ueniens, part 2, de testi., which Bartol. cites and approves in the said l. a diuo Pio, ff. de re iudica., in that he says that if execution is sought on goods possessed by another, a third party cannot impede execution for his own interest, since he can afterwards sue against that new possessor just as he could have sued against the third party, for which l. is a quo, ff. de rei uendi., is relevant; so in the present case, since the said Anselinus possessed, against whom the mother brought suit, it does not seem that Titus, by opposing himself as a third party, can impede the execution. To the same point is another notable statement of Innocen. in capitu. cum in iure, de offic. delega., where he says that an exception of nullity is not so great for anyone as to impede the execution of a judgment, for which capitu. suscitata, de in integrum restitutione, serves. Notwithstanding these points, however, it seems to me that it must be concluded otherwise; and first, for the understanding of what is to be said, I premise that the said lady can have, or has, no right in the said goods, since, as they are feudal, and the fief is paternal or ancestral of those progenitors of Anselinus and Titus, the mother could in no way succeed to the sons: both because a woman does not so succeed in fiefs unless shown by special grant, even if she is the daughter of a vassal—which is more—as is proved in cap. 1, de succes. feud., and in cap. 1, de alie. feu. paterni, colla. 10; if therefore a daughter is excluded, then a mother is excluded, as in authent. in successione, C. ad Tertul., because if I conquer the one conquering you, etc., as in c. authoritate, de concess. præbend., lib. 6. Likewise the mother is excluded on another ground,

† because ascendants do not succeed in a fief; it is otherwise in descendants, as is proved in capitu. primo, de natura success. feud., where the text is notable. She is excluded on a third ground, which concerns agnates; whence, since the fief is paternal, it cannot pass to cognates; nay rather, in default of agnates it reverts to the lord, as in cap. 3, de feu. mar., and in cap. 1, de succes. feu. These things having been premised, with respect to the principal question I say that the said Titus has many remedies against the demand of the said lady. For first he can oppose by way of a peremptory exception, saying that no right belongs to that lady by the aforesaid points; for it is in his interest to oppose, lest the nature of the fief be altered to his prejudice. For if the said Anselinus should die without children, the fief would pass to him, even against the will of Anselinus himself, because a vassal cannot dispose of a fief in a will to the prejudice of the children or agnates who are to succeed in the fief.

† For a brother succeeds a brother in an ancestral fief, as in the said cap. 2, de feud. mar., and ca. 1, de succes. feu., previously alleged, and there by Bald. Likewise he can oppose by impeding the execution of the judgment, because, as I said, it is in his interest that execution not take place; since the said lady does not come, nor can she come, as a vassal, but as a stranger, and tends to alter the nature of the fief, it is in the interest of each of the agnates who could succeed the said Anselinus intestate that execution not take place, by the excellent argument in l. 1, 2, and 3, ff. de libe. cau., and better in l. a sententia, ff. de appel.; the notable text in capitu. 1, de inuesti. rei alie., which says,

† that a vassal can make the condition of the fief better, but not worse without the will of the lord or of those agnates to whom it can pass through succession, supports this; with which the text in cap. 1, de alie. feud. pater., seems to agree; and thus the said Titus sufficiently claims an interest lest an alteration of the fief occur. Therefore the theory of Inno. fails. Likewise, since the mother possesses undivided, if the claim of the said lady were admitted, she would possess only for a part. For in the division of common property an alienation occurs; hence it is that a minor can be challenged, but cannot challenge to a division: l. penulti., C. de prædiis mino. ¶ Nor does the other theory of Innoc. in cap. cum in iure stand in the way, because it applies unless the excipient wishes to prove nullity within a non-lengthy time, as is fully noted by Ioan. de Lig. in clementi. 1, de re iudi., and the text there seems so. For if there is a special case in which the exception of nullity does not impede the execution of a judgment, therefore otherwise it has to impede it, by the argument in cap. præsenti, de præbend., lib. 6; and these things especially apply if nullity arising from defect of jurisdiction were pleaded, according to the notable and common gloss in clem. 1, de seq. pos. & fruc., and what Bartol. notes in l. 1, ff. quod ui aut clam. Furthermore, it can be said that unless Titus opposes for his own interest, it is enough at once superficially to prove his interest so that he may be admitted and execution suspended. ¶ Afterwards, however, he can prove it fully and within the due delays, as is the singular text in the said cap. ueniens, part 2, de testi., and there by Innocent. But as to whether a declinatory exception can be opposed against the senator on the basis of privilege by objecting that the cause is feudal: Bal. in the said § præterea holds that it can, but yet he does not firmly establish it; but I am pleased by one theory which can be gathered from the words of Inn. in the said c. cæterum, where he notably says that either the plaintiff sues generally, so that a feudal cause can be comprehended in the libel, and then it can be excepted that that cause pertains to the lord of the fief, since it is feudal; or it expressly appears that the cause is not brought as feudal, and then it cannot be opposed by way of a declinatory exception, because, since suit is not brought concerning a fief as a fief, nor does the plaintiff call herself a vassal, the jurisdiction of the lord is excluded, since the laws make him judge only when the question is between vassals concerning a fief; so say the laws previously alleged. It is otherwise if between a vassal and a third party, as the gloss notes in the said capitu. cæterum, and there Anton. de Butr. and the gloss in the said § præterea openly hold. It must therefore be opposed in the aforesaid manners. A defect of her right can also be opposed against the said lady by way of a declinatory exception to prevent joinder of issue (litis contestatio); because where it is concluded through an exception that no right belongs to the plaintiff, as happens in our case, one can so decline, because no one sues without an action: l. si pupilli, § uideamus, ff. de nego. gesto, and cap. examinata, de iudi.; Barto. notably held this in l. cum quærebatur, ff. iudi. sol. And through this that doubt seems dispatched, namely whether it could be objected concerning the ineptitude of the libel. Likewise, division of the city and castles is sought. For in vain do we inquire concerning ineptitude, since no right belongs to her by the aforesaid. If, however, these goods were not feudal, or this lady were to be admitted by some special right, then I would not consider the libel inept on this account. For if they are feudal, they can be divided, since the law only provides that a fief which sounds in the name of a dignity, such as a duchy, marquisate, and the like, cannot be divided. It is otherwise concerning other fiefs, as is proved in § præterea ducatus, in c. imperialem, de prohi. feu. ali. per Fede., and there Bald. openly holds this; and to that distinction ought to be reduced the statement of Bar. in l. si inter, ff. de admi. tut., and l. si uni, otherwise beginning Pomponius, ff. de re iudic. What is read and noted in c. licet, de uoto, supports this. I, however, notably say one thing which I do not find weighed by others: that although in the division of other property it suffices for one of the partners to demand it, because no one is compelled to remain in common ownership, as C. commu. diui. throughout, yet in the division of feudal property all co-vassals must agree and concur, otherwise division cannot be made; this the singular text intended, if properly weighed, in the said § præterea ducatus, on the word si consortes uoluerunt, and the chapter. Therefore the consent of the others is required; to this is the text joined with the gloss in c. sæpe, de uer. sig., at the end. For since that text permits division against the nature of a fief, it must be understood in its strict terms, nor must one depart from the words of the text, as in l. non aliter, ff. de le. 3, and in c. fi., de uerb. sig. If, however, the goods are not feudal, then I do not see what impedes the division of the castles, since they can be sold separately, as they do not consist in a certain dignity, and therefore can also be divided; but with respect to the city, which is a single place, it can be more doubted, since this division occurs to the prejudice of the commonwealth, whose interest it is not to have several lords, and that its territory not be divided; l. fi., C. si contra ius, uel utili. pub., supports this. And it is in the interest of the citizens not to change lords, as Inno. notes in c. auditis, de præscrip., and c. inter quatuor, de maior. & obed.; whence it could even be attempted that the city come into the action for dividing common property, just as other goods come which cannot commodiously be divided; and one must then proceed as is provided in l. ad officium, C. communi diui., and insti. de offi. iudi.; and Bal. in the said § præterea ducatus thinks that it can be divided so that one has up to a certain place, the other the remainder, etc.; yet what I said first is more equitable. I come to the other doubt, namely whether this Anselinus has fallen from his right because he fraudulently alienated by not excepting against the mother. And in this statement it must be observed that if we hold those goods to be feudal, the disposition of the testator prohibiting alienation under a penalty operates nothing in this, because a vassal cannot dispose in a will regarding a fief, as in the said c. 1, de succes. feu. Likewise there is the prohibition of law as to feudal property in c. 2, de uasal. qui contra consti. Lotha., and in § præterea, with its like; whence we ought to decide this case according to the laws of fiefs, and hold that he ought to lose the fief, or that he has ipso facto fallen from his right, at least with respect to the part fraudulently alienated; allege the fine text in c. 1, § callidis insuper machinationibus, de prohi. feu. alie. per Fede.; nay rather, one ought to be punished more when he alienates in fraud of the law than when done against an act in fraud of man, and there Bald. notes this; and for this is noted also a good text in a similar matter in l. si libertus minorem, ff. de iure pat. For it appears from conjectures that Anselinus maliciously did not plead an exception, since he had exceptions so ready against the mother, as is clear from the aforesaid; l. j, ff. ad Turpi., supports this; whence just as he alienates who suffers prescription against himself, as in l. alienationis uerbum, ff. de uerb. sig.—to such a degree that the notable gloss in c. placuit, part 2, xvj, q. iij, says that against a bishop who has allowed prescription to run against the Church, the Church can sue so that he may keep it indemnified out of his own property—so also he who has not pleaded the due exceptions, and all the more strongly when in our case he appears to have acted in fraud. For that which is gathered from conjectures is evident, as in l. licet, ff. de leg. 1. And it is the same thing to remit as to give: l. quinetiam, ff. de calum., in c. ueniens, part 1, de test. Hence it is,

† that a surety has no action against the principal if he paid without pleading the exceptions available to the principal, l. si fideiussor, ff. manda. The same seems to be said if the goods are not feudal: then he incurs the penalty of the testator, since, as I said above, one who alienates in fraud ought to be punished just as if he had alienated by a direct route: the said § callidis, and in l. non dubium, with what is noted there, C. de legib. And by these considerations all the doubts remain resolved in effect, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A statute is said to be against ecclesiastical liberty if on account of it clerics are rendered more timid.
2. A statute of laymen does not hold even in favor of the churches.
body: The present doubt in effect consists in whether a statute of laymen, wherein among other things it is contained that no one, under a certain penalty, may dare to apprehend or take possession of any benefice or hospital without the express license of the secular lords, and that no notary or witness may take part, is against ecclesiastical liberty. In which case it can very easily be inferred toward the decision of other doubts, and I say that the said statute is not valid. For that statute is said to be against ecclesiastical liberty which tends against those things that have been granted to the universal church, generally or singularly, by God, the Pope, or other secular princes. This is the common theory of all the doctors: c. nouerit, de sen. & re iudi., and Bar. and Bal. approve it in auth. cassa irrita, C. de sa. san. eccl.

† Adding that it is also said to be against ecclesiastical liberty if, by a statute of laymen, clerics are rendered more timid and laymen more audacious, through l. 1. §. quæ onerandæ, ff. qua rum rerum ac. non da. And concerning the privileges granted to the church by God Himself, they give the example thereof in the said chapter nouerit, in the privilege that the church alone may administer ecclesiastical property, as in c. si imperator, 96. distinct., de reb. eccl. non alie. c. si. Likewise, that to the church alone belongs the right of enacting statutes concerning spiritual things and rights, as in c. denique and in c. cum ad uerum, 96. di.; to which serves 12. q. 1. c. duo sunt genera, and c. ecclesia, de const., and c. bene quidem, 96. dist., 33. q. 1. c. quodcunque ligaueris. Hence it is that a statute of laymen concerning matters of this kind is said to be a destitution rather than a constitution, as in the said c. si. Therefore, it remains manifestly to conclude that the present statute, since it disposes of spiritual and ecclesiastical matters whose administration and jurisdiction thereover belong by privilege to the universal church itself and its administrators, as has been proved above. Likewise, it is contrary to the privilege granted to the universal church by the Roman Pontiffs in their canons, namely that recourse must by no means be had to seculars concerning matters of this kind, as appears in c. 2. de officio Archi., cap. ut nostrum, and c. ad hoc, and the said c. bene quidem, to such an extent,

† that a statute of laymen does not hold even in favor of the churches, which provides by disposing, commanding, or adding a penalty according to those things that are fully noted in the said cap. ecclesia, de consti., and by Io. An. and Host. in c. si. de sol., and Ioan. de Lig. and Ant. de Butr. in c. quo clericis, de foro competen. Furthermore, this statute violates the supreme and principal grant bestowed by Christ Himself upon the Roman Pontiffs, namely, 'Whatsoever thou shalt bind upon earth,' etc., in the said cap. quod cunque, which Inno. expounds in c. quanto, de consuet., saying: 'whatsoever thou shalt bind,' that is, through statutes or precepts and in matters concerning the soul, unless they be against the faith, etc. But this statute is contrary to the mandate of the Pope made in spiritual matters and those concerning the soul, since the Pope mandates the execution of his grace so as to send the impetrant into possession, which he cannot deliver for fear of the penalty; therefore it is also inferred from this that clerics are made more timid by this statute, and laymen more audacious in legislating. And thus under multiple grounds this statute can be said to be against ecclesiastical liberty. And c. quoniam, de immu. ecc. li. 6, serves the aforesaid most excellently. From these points I infer with respect to our case that, under a twofold ground, neither those otherwise lawfully apprehending possession, nor the witnesses taking part, nor the notaries requested concerning the apprehension of possession, incur the penalty of the statute. First, from the disposition of the ius commune. For the statute is not valid, nor is the penalty attached, especially since such statutes are null and void, as in the said auth. cassa and the said c. nouerit and c. grauamen, eo. ti. What is noted in cap. signifi. de offi. dele. and in l. pacta quæ contra, C. de pact. serves this point. Nay rather, those enacting and those causing the statutes themselves to be observed are ipso facto excommunicated, as in the said laws, beyond the penalty treated in the said authen. cassa. Nor are they excused under the pretext of the statute placed at the end of the statutes by which it is provided that statutes against ecclesiastical liberty are to be held as void, because the laws will that they cause them to be erased from the book of statutes, lest they ever be observed de facto, as in the said laws, as Bart. and Bald. expressly confirmed in the said authen. cassa. Under the second ground, the statutory penalties cease in the aforesaid matters from the form of the other statute, by which it is provided that if any statute should be found against ecclesiastical liberty, it shall be void and null, etc.; therefore the premise statute has no force, even having considered the mind of the legislators in the said authé. cassa, and especially having regard to the reformation of the statutes made afterward, in which nearly the same is contained, etc. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Although the prince from certain knowledge can take away from me those things that are of civil law, he cannot nevertheless take away those things that are of the law of nations.
2. A freedman must be restored to freeborn status by the emperor with the consent of the patron.
3. If a publicly banned person is restored in full by the emperor, that restitution must not be extended to goods alienated by the prince at another intervening time.
4. The prince has the fullest power over positive law.
5. If the prince from certain knowledge approves something or inserts it into his privilege which is not valid under the common law, it will be firm.
6. The emperor can restore a freedman, even without the patron's consent or without him being summoned.
7. Although the prince cannot without cause issue a rescript against divine law, if he nevertheless issues a rescript, a just cause is presumed in him.
casus: In sum, this question of law is asked: Whether a donation inter vivos exceeding the sum of five hundred florins, without lawful filing intervening, with the intervention of a confirmation of the emperor made from certain knowledge, is valid after the death of the donor, in such a way that prejudice is caused by it to those who ought to succeed intestate, etc.
body: The help of Christ and His mother having been humbly invoked: It seems first that the said donation, in so far as it exceeds the sum of five hundred gold coins, is of no effect, and is to be held as not written, as is proved in l. sancimus, joined with l. si quis pro redemptione, C. de dona., by which law l. si tamen in donatione inter vivos seems to be amended, of which sort this was, as no one doubts, since such a gift requires filing (*insinuatio*) for its validity in so far as it exceeds five hundred gold coins, as in the laws previously cited. Nor can the confirmation made benefit it, even by the notable gloss joined with the text in l. quoties, C. de preci. impe., where it is noted

† that although the prince from certain knowledge can take away from me those things that are of civil law, such as actions, he cannot nevertheless take away, even from certain knowledge, those things that are of the law of nations, such as the ownership of property, because those things are immutable, insti. de iure natu. §. pe. and de legi. agna. tu. in fi. and v. dist. in prin. Innocent meant the same in c. quae in ecclesiarum, de consti. But it is certain that by the death of the donor prior to the emperor's confirmation, a right was acquired for these nephews as the closer relations in the inheritance of Lord Anselinus their paternal uncle, at least the right of entering upon his inheritance, as in auth. de success. ab intest.; and the notable gloss in l. omnium, C. de testa. supports this, which says that through a testament a full right is given as to the acquisition of ownership, a fuller right through death, and the fullest right through entry; but in this respect an intestate succession is equated to a testament, since it defers the inheritance to the closer relatives, as in auth. post fratres, C. de leg. haere. Therefore that right, already acquired and inhering in the bones of these closer relatives, namely the nephews, could not be taken away without cause after the emperor's confirmation, even when made from certain knowledge; for that which is ours cannot be plucked away from us without our own act, l. id quod nostrum, ff. de reg. iur., c. ab eo, de ele. lib. 6., and what is read and noted in l. Iulianus, ff. de condi. indebi., and in l. 3, ff. pro socio, and in cap. 1, xxij. distinct. in the gloss on the word *iustitiam*. Bartolus seems to have meant the same in l. si, C. si contra ius, uel utilit. publi., where he says that the prince cannot take away my property without cause, because since he holds his power from God, as in authen. quomodo oportet episcopos, God did not give him the power to sin or to take away the property of another; to this effect xl. distin. cap. 1 and cle. pastoralis, de re iudi. Secondly, principally against this confirmation I advance the excellent text in l. fi. ff. de nata. resti., where it is said

† that a freedman is restored to his freeborn status by the emperor with the consent of the patron, because the right of the patron is lost through this restitution; and through that text the doctors have commonly said that the prince, when making a legitimation, ought to summon the agnates who were to succeed on intestacy, and make the legitimation with their consent, at least in that case where a son seeks to be legitimated after the father's death; which the canonists held in cap. per uenerabilem, qui fil. sint leg., and Bartolus in l. Gallus §. et quid si tantum, ff. de liber. & posthu., and Baldus in prooemio C., where for this reason he said that the emperor cannot legitimate in the lands of the Church, because he has to cite the agnates, over whom, since he has no jurisdiction in those lands, he cannot decree a citation or in any way prejudice them as non-subjects. But in our case these nephews were not called to this confirmation, nor did they consent, etc. And by this I proceed to the third attack against the said confirmation. For these properties are said to be in the city, county, and district of Bologna, in which the emperor has no jurisdiction, but the full right in temporal and spiritual matters belongs exclusively to the Pope, as in cap. fundamenta, de elect. lib. sexto, and in c. ego Ludouicus, lxiij. distinct., in cap. Romani, de iureiuran., and in the said capi. per uenerabilem. Nor is it necessary to dispute about the donation made to the Church by Constantine, since it was confirmed and approved by many emperors and by the Church, as in the said clem. Romani and other laws cited above, especially in cap. fundamenta, cited before, where it says that it was made by divine inspiration. Whence it would not be far from heresy to hold the contrary, especially considering what is contained in the Extravagant of Boniface which begins *unam sanctam*. And for its validity stands Baldus in prooemio digestorum in fi.
