Therefore, the emperor could not dispose over those properties, as in the said clementi. pastoralis; the text in l. fin. ff. de iurisdictio. omni. iudi. supports this. Fourthly, principally relevant is the text in c. quamuis and cap. si pro te, de rescript. lib. sexto, where it is held that a restitution or a new grant is not given retroactive effect with prejudice to him to whom a right was acquired in the meantime, by reason of which Johannes Andreae says in the rule *sine culpa*, de regu. iur. lib. sexto, in the *Mercuriales*, that under a special law providing that the firstborn succeeds to the whole, a natural firstborn who was legitimated by a subsequent marriage ought not to be preferred to a legitimate and natural second-born, because that legitimation effected by subsequent marriage ought not to be drawn back with prejudice to the second-born, since the right of primogeniture had already been acquired previously. To the same effect is what the gloss and Bartolus note in the said §. et quid si tantum, and better in l. fina. C. de senten. pass., where he says

† that if a publicly proclaimed outlaw is restored *in integrum* by the emperor, that restitution ought not to be extended to property alienated to another by the prince in the meantime, using an argument in l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadrien. praescriptio. But these things notwithstanding, I deem the contrary opinion to be truer in law. And first, for a foundation, I say that the emperor concurs in the exercise of jurisdiction with any inferior lord having jurisdiction, just as the Pope concurs with any prelate. For the emperor is called the lord of the world, l. deprecatio, ff. ad legem Rhod. de Iaco. and the said l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadrien. praescriptio, and viij. quaestio prima, capi. in apibus. For God made two great luminaries in the world, one to rule the day, the other to rule the night: namely, the emperor in temporal affairs, and the Pope in spiritual affairs, as the text says in c. solitae, de maio. & obe. and 96. di. c. si imperator, and c. cum ad uerum. Whence, just as recourse can be had to the Pope throughout the whole world in spiritual matters, so to the emperor in temporal matters, as in the said laws. And Baldus meant this very thing in c. 1, qui seu. da. pos., and elsewhere he said that all jurisdiction and district belongs to the emperor by common law, as noted in c. 1, de na. succes. feu. and in c. 1 uno, at the word *ad hoc*, de pa. iura fir.; what the doctors note in cle. pastoralis and in clemen. Romani, cited above, supports this. These things having been premised, I prove that the said confirmation ought to be valid and hold to the prejudice of these nephews. And first I allege the text joined with the singular gloss in clement. 1, de immunita. ecclesia., where it is said that so great is the prince's power regarding positive law, that things done can be held as not done, as to every effect of law; so that he causes it to look back, as if it had never emanated.

† Hence it is concluded there that if someone incurs excommunication by virtue of a constitution, if the Pope wills to hold that constitution as not done, that person does not need any absolution, but it is just as if he had never been excommunicated. For the prince has the fullest power over positive law, as in c. proposuit, de conces. praeben., and in l. princeps, ff. de legi., and l. digna uox, C. eod. titulo. The entire title *de capti. & postlimi. reuer.* extraordinarily supports the aforesaid, where the prince fictions against the truth and retroactively applies many things, as if they had never been done; so much so that one recovers a lost right, and many other things, and this is held most fully there, and especially in l. postliminium est ius, under the same title. Since therefore in our case the right of entry was acquired for these nephews and closer relatives by the disposition of the civil law, and by that same law the said donation collapsed through a defect of filing (*insinuatio*), as in the said l. sancimus; and since by natural law or the law of nations this filing is not required, but the will of the donor suffices for the validity of the donation itself, as in §. per traditionem, institu. de rerum diui., but it was introduced by civil law, at least so that men would not be defrauded, according to what is fully noted by Bartolus in l. Modestinus, ff. de dona.; the emperor, as lord over this positive law, was able to hold that law as not done as to every effect of law; and thus the donation would be just as valid as if that law had never emanated; thus also he was able to apply the said donation retroactively and supply the defect of law regarding that formality of filing, as if the filing had occurred at the beginning; what is read and noted in l. omnium, C. de test. excellently supports this. For here the emperor expressly willed that that donation be retroactively applied, as if it had been filed at the beginning; and he did this from certain knowledge, and thus from the plenitude of power. For this is what the said clause imports, as the notable gloss indicates in cap. ad haec sumus, de rescriptis. To the same effect, the final gloss in cap. ex multiplici, de deci., joined with the text, contributes much to our matter. Likewise, the emperor here expressly supplied every defect, if any had intervened in the said donation, which supplying at least operates with respect to the formality of law according to the notes by Speculator in the title *de leg.* §. nunc ostendendum, verse 18, and by the Archdeacon in c. Cenomanen. 56. dist.; the text and what is noted there in cle. pastoralis, de re iudic., and in cap. 1, de transac. support this, and what is

† noted there by Hostiensis, where Innocent also says: if the prince from certain knowledge approves something, not yet confirming it, but only inserts into his privilege that which is not valid by law, it will be firm; just as a statute of laymen concerning churches is valid and is held as confirmed if the Pope approves it in his letters, arg. ff. de pign. l. fideiussor §. fi. and de const. cap. ecclesia sanctae Mariae, 96. distinct. cap. bene quidem, with similar texts. Since therefore the said donation collapses from a defect of formality introduced by the civil law, the emperor was well able to supply that defect, and to decree as if it had intervened at the beginning, through the aforesaid, notwithstanding that in the meantime the right of entering had been acquired by those nephews, because this right came to them through the disposition of the civil law, concerning which, as I said before, the emperor was able to dispose, holding it as not done as to every effect of law. Nor did the emperor here principally dispose regarding the private right of those nephews, but by a certain consequence. For he principally disposed concerning the civil law, by supplying the formality required by it. For many things are permitted by consequence which are not allowed principally, as in l. prima, ff. de autho. tuto. And especially since this right had been acquired by the nephews not from their own contract or act, but from the disposition of the civil law; whence we see in a similar case that the prince admits a petition (*supplicatio*) against a judgment from which there could be no appeal, even though it had already created law between the parties, as in l. res iudicata, ff. de regu. iur., and l. ingenuum, de sta. homi., and c. cum inter, de re iud., as is clear in auth. quae supplicatio, C. de preci. impe. offe.; and he grants restitution *in integrum* against it, as in c. tum ex literis, and c. auditis, and c. ex literis, de in integ. restit., and where and before whom, l. appellationem, l. prima, ff. a quibus appel. non licet, and c. super quaestionum, de offic. deleg.; and by restoring a minor *in integrum* against a contract, he also prejudices him to whom it came in the meantime through a contract made with the buyer of the minor, as in l. causae, la prima §. si, de mino. Likewise, he restores *in integrum* against prescription, through which by authority of law the fullest right had been acquired, according to what is noted in l. si, ff. rem rat. habe., and in c. ad aures, de praescri. The aforementioned c. auditis and clem. una, de in integ. restit., support the aforesaid. Secondly, principally I cite the notable text in l. 2, ff. de na. rest. at the end, where the text said that emperors are not easily accustomed to restore a freedman to freeborn status unless the patron consents, since the patron could not afterward come to the freedman's succession. And yet, as the text there intimates,

† the emperor could restore a freedman without the patron consenting and without his being summoned, although he is not easily accustomed to do so. Therefore, he can do it from certain knowledge if he wills, because that which is rarely done is nevertheless done, as in c. 2, de cogna. spir. li. 6., and what Innocent notes in c. nisi cum pridem, de renun., where he says that a superior in whom resides the power of dispensing can grant a dispensation even without summoning those who are prejudiced; and through the text of that l. 2, Bartolus notably said in the said l. Gallus §. et quid si tantum, that if the emperor wishes to legitimate someone without summoning the agnates to whom the inheritance was deferred, he can, provided he does this from certain knowledge; and thus by these authorities our case seems clearly decided. For *a fortiori* he will be able in our case to supply this defect of law to the prejudice of these nephews, to whom the right of succeeding had been deferred on intestacy, arising from a slight defect of formality, according to what is noted in the said l. Modestinus, de dona. For it is a weightier matter to legitimate and to feign someone as legitimately born, or to restore him to his ancient freeborn status, than to supply a defect of formality with respect to filing (*insinuatio*); and in both cases prejudice is caused to those to whom an inheritance had been deferred on intestacy. Thirdly, principally I cite the things noted by Cinus in l. rescripta, C. de preci. impe. offe., which are commonly approved by the other modern legists and canonists in c. quae in ecclesiarum, de consti.; he says

† that although the prince cannot issue a rescript contrary to divine law without cause, nevertheless, if he does issue a rescript *de facto*, a cause must be presumed in him. Whence, if the prince orders someone to be killed or deprived of his property, he must be obeyed, because he would judge according to conscience, nor is he presumed corruptible, and a cause is always to be presumed in him; cap. in memoriam, 19. distinctio, and c. quid culpatur, 33. q. 1, and c. quid ergo, 11. quaest. 3, support this. Since therefore the emperor is said here to have confirmed from certain knowledge, a legitimate cause ought to be presumed for him, especially because in the public interest the prince can deprive someone of his property, as in l. item si uerberatum, de rei uendi., noted by Bartolus in the said l. fin. C. si contra ius, and in l. Antiochensium, ff. de priuil. credi., and in the said l. rescripta; and the prince seems to assert this in the preamble of that confirmation, since public law is concerned in his person. For public law consists in sacred rites, priests, magistrates, and clerics, as appears from his enunciative words, upon which it must be believed that he based himself, as in clemen. j. de probat.; what Bartolus notes in l. ambitiosam, ff. de decre. ab ordi. facien., supports this. Much more strongly, therefore, we necessarily have to say that the said confirmation was valid, since through it prejudice is not caused to a right acquired from the act of a party, but from the mere disposition of the civil law. And by this I conclude that the said confirmation was valid, and prejudices those nephews. And through this, to one who observes subtly, the counterarguments adduced above against the confirmation remain resolved. For they proceed when the emperor principally wishes to dispose contrary to the law of nations, by taking away a right acquired by the act of man alone, whether truly or presumptively ceasing; but we speak of a right acquired by authority of the civil law. And when the prince principally disposes by supplying a defect of positive law, or by restoring that which is lacking, a cause must be presumed, as I have said. To the second counterargument, the answer is also sufficiently clear above from the aforesaid. For l. fi. speaks of ordinary power, but not of absolute power, as l. ij. under the same title speaks, which intervened here through that clause, *ex certa scientia*, etc. To the third, I say that here it is not presupposed that the donor or these nephews are from the territory, whence I presume that they are of the jurisdiction of the empire; and thus, presupposing that the goods are in Bologna, nevertheless, because it is presumed of the empire, that donation thus corroborated extends to goods wherever situated, as in a similar matter Bartolus notes in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. tri., especially in that question whether a testament made in a certain place according to the special statutes of that place ought to be extended to goods existing in a place not subject to the maker of the statute; and it is concluded that it does, as there most fully by him, and l. j. C. de testam. with similar texts supports this. To the last counterargument, I say that in those laws a true restitution *in integrum* did not intervene, as the gloss notes there. Likewise, it was not apparent concerning the will of the Pope that he had wished the act to be retroactively applied with prejudice to another, otherwise it would be different, as the text openly says there; here, however, it expressly appears concerning the will of the emperor. And in the same way it can be answered to the authority of Johannes Andreae in the said rule *sine culpa*, although also many most eminent doctors held against his opinion, as he himself relates there; but here, as I said, the clear will of the prince is established, who was able to dispose in this matter, as is gathered from the aforesaid. And let these things suffice, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The common opinion must be held, unless it is notoriously mistaken or reasonably refuted.
2. A conditional legacy is not transmitted to an heir.
3. No one can impose upon himself in a will the rule that he may not depart from an earlier one.
4. The relative pronoun "quis" or "qui", joined with a verb of the future tense, denotes a condition.
5. He is called a son who is born of a husband and a wife, and whence the term is derived.
6. The son of a first-born can be called first-born.
7. A cleric is immediately deprived and stripped of every clerical privilege, and is subjected to the court of the secular judge, when bigamy supervenes.
8. If a layman was forestalled by a secular judge, and while the case is pending becomes a cleric, the case is not thereby exempted from the secular forum [?].
body: In the present question, having implored the aid of almighty God, two things—in order to comply with the petitioner's custom—I shall add from the opinions of others and from the reasons alleged on both sides; and since it has been sufficiently argued on both sides, with other matters omitted, I shall touch upon them briefly, since, as is most beautifully stated in l. j, C. de uete. iure enuclea., one must not judge by the multitude of authorities, since the opinion of lesser authors can perhaps surpass both many and greater in some respect. Hence Io. And. in c. 1 de constitu. was perhaps moved to say:

† That the common opinion must be followed unless it is notoriously mistaken or is reasonably refuted, which a good judge of the sharpest intellect will discern. The first doubt will be whether the first-born son ought to be preferred to the paternal uncle in the mayorazgo granted to a certain noble man, Pedro de Assa, a Spaniard, having regard especially to the words of the concession made to the same by the illustrious prince, the King of Castile, in which among other things relevant to the purpose are contained these words, namely: "And that after his death, one of them, as has been said, namely the elder son whom he had had of lawful marriage, and the other sons and daughters and heirs who have descended from him or from you from our line of lawful marriage, or who has been legitimated as the law requires, shall succeed and inherit the said half of the said first-named shops, namely after the death of the other by degrees, and it shall always be conferred upon the elder, etc." The second doubt is, when the uncle, as one constituted in minor orders, was convicted by the nephew in the Roman Curia, and the process there was declared null by the lord, whether by the supervention of bigamy, which the said uncle is said to have incurred, the said cause is exempt, or ought to be exempted from the Roman Curia, and remitted to the secular judge. I come therefore to the first, concerning which I say it must be observed that since sons and grandsons are called to this succession by royal disposition and privilege, the words of the privilege are to be weighed more than the ruling of the ius commune disposing of the succession of an uncle and grandsons in the property of a grandfather or father. For there it is principally treated concerning the efficacy and comprehensiveness of the privilege, and the words of the privilege itself are to be attended to and weighed, as in c. porro, and in c. recepimus, de priuileg., in Auth. de manda. prin. § si quis autem; and truly, if the aforesaid words of the privilege or concession, in which the full force of this question consists, are observed with the heart, it will become most clearly apparent that the said nephew is to be preferred. I am moved first to say this because immediately after the death of the father, to whom the concession was principally made, the first-born is called by royal disposition. And thus the first-born attains this right of succeeding not from his father, or from the common law, but from the special royal disposition, according to what is noted by Bar. in d. l. ut iusiuran., ff. de ope. libe., and by Bal. in auth. si quas ruinas, C. de sac. san. eccle., to which makes the text with the things noted there, especially by Bal. in c. una, de succes. feu. coll. x. Therefore, he attains this right of succeeding immediately when the first-born comes into the light, in habit and expectation; and it is a firm and unalterable expectation, since it cannot be taken away by the father or by another, lower son, since it has passed into a contract, as in c. 1 de proba., and by Io. And. in c. significasti, de for. compe.; to this makes the text in c. 1 de feu. sine cul. non amit., and what is noted by Bal. in c. 1 de succes. feu., and by Bar. in l. fi. alias pe. ff. de decre. ab ordi. fac. And even presupposing that the prince could have revoked it, so that it depends on the power of the prince alone, it is said that it cannot be done, as in l. apud Iulianum, in fi. ff. de leg. 1, and as Dy. notes in the rule semel deo, de regn. iur. lib. 6. Therefore, the first-born confirmed this expectation and transmitted it irrevocably to his son; this is proved from the identity of reason, just as a father transmits to his son an expectation belonging to the father from a conditional contract, as in § ex conditionali, Institu. de verbo. obliga., which occurs from nothing else than because that firm and irrevocable expectation, with a power easily reducible to act, is held as the act itself, as in c. Pisanis, and what is noted there, de restitut. spolia.; so too this firm and unalterable expectation, as belonging by virtue of the king's privilege, ought to be capable of being transmitted to the son. Nor does the text in l. una § sin autem, C. de cadu. tol. stand in the way of this motive, where it is said,

† That a conditional legacy, because from it there belongs only an expectation, is not transmitted to the heir before the event of the condition; because the reason for the difference can be twofold: one which the gloss alleges in the said § ex conditionali, saying that in a conditional contract there intervenes the act of the contracting party himself, who wishes to provide for himself and his heirs; but in a legacy no act of the legatee intervenes, and it is principally intended to provide for the person of the legatee, whence, since it has not taken root in the person of that legatee, it is not transmitted to the heir; wherefore I hold rather to the reasoning of that gloss than to the words. For since in our case there intervened a royal concession, providing not only for the person of the first-born himself, but also for his sons, as is clear from the words alleged above, therefore this expectation is transmissible to the son. For if contracting parties can do this, all the more can a private law, that is, the prince, by the argument in l. non impossibile, ff. de pact., especially in this case, where the special disposition of the prince here openly intended to provide not only for the person of the first-born, but also of his son, as is clear from the words of the concession: "and the other sons and daughters and heirs who have descended from him or from you, etc." And this consideration, in my judgment, is the best. To this makes what is read and noted on a similar matter in l. Lucius, la 2, ff. de hæredit. institu., and noted by Bal. in l. 1, C. de his, qui ante apertas tabu. The second reason for the difference between the aforementioned § ex conditionali and § sin autem is that in contracts the will or expectation is firm and fixed, because contracts are voluntary from the beginning, but of necessity ex post facto, l. sicut, C. de actio. & obli.; it is otherwise in last wills, because what is left is not so firm, since it depends on the will of the testator, as in cap. cum Marthæ, de celebra. miss.

† For no one can lay down that law for himself in a testament such that he may not depart from it, as says the text in l. si quis, in princ. ff. de lega. 3; but since in our case this right is owed to the first-born by benefit of a special law, which it is judged impossible to take away, as I have said before, therefore it approaches the nature rather of a contract than of a last will, so that transmission is made to the son; nor must it be minded that here the act of the son did not intervene, because that is not a necessarily concluding reason, but rather that which I have set forth, namely that the expectation is certain and firm. Ioan. Andr. notably perceives this reason in c. licet, de uoto, and in additio. Specu. in titu. de feu. in the 6th column. For it cannot be denied that a stronger right is acquired here by the first-born from a royal concession purely made, especially when mention was made of the sons, than from a conditional contract, since if the condition fails, the whole contract falls, by the said § ex conditionali. But the said concession always endures, and is pure and firm, except in the case where no one should be found of the agnation of this Pedro Assa, as is clear from the privilege; therefore, all the more must this expectation be transmitted—since a right belongs at least in habit at present—than that fragile one depending on a future event which belongs from a conditional contract. For an argument from an identity of reason, or from a fortiori, is valid, as in the common legal texts. Moreover, that the first-born is here called principally after the death of Pedro is openly proved by those words: "That because after your death, etc." For if they were not understood of the first-born, those words would truly be superfluous, since in the following words mention is made of other sons descending from this Pedro, and it is disposed that the conferral be made always upon the elder. For a disposition ought to be understood so that words are not superfluous, but effect something, as in capitu. si papa, de priuileg. libr. 6, and l. si quando, C. de inofficio. testamen. And words must always be reduced to the doubtful case, as l. prima in fine, ff. de administratione tuto. and l. Labeo ad Carbon. Secondly, it is proved from the allusion of the term: for since it calls the elder son of this Pedro, therefore the first-born, since the first-born is elder by nature. For one is called a brother or younger by reason of birth, as in cap. licet, de uoto; to this makes what the gloss notes in cap. consuetudo est, 1. dist. Secondly, I am principally moved to this opinion by another consideration, because if the words are well weighed, the first-born seems called under a condition, namely if he shall survive at the time of the father's death; this is gathered from those words there: "your elder son whom you have had, etc."

† For the relative pronoun "whoever" or "who" or "whom," joined to a verb of future tense, denotes a condition, as is proved in l. Sticus, qui meus erit, ff. de leg. 1, and by Bart. there; whence those words, "your elder son whom you have had, etc.," import this, that is, "if you have had any," and in default of the first-born; I observe that it calls the sons of this Pedro, [and] calls first the sons of the first-born; therefore the elder of them is to be preferred; which is proved thus: for wherever it is a matter of an honor or a burden to be applied to certain persons, and it cannot be applied except to one person, at least at the same time, and it is not apparent which person the disposer meant, one always abides by the order of the writing, so that the one named first is deemed called first, as is proved in l. generaliter § quid ergo, with the following, ff. de fideicom. lib., and l. quoties, de usufr., l. hæredes mei § peto, ff. ad Trebel., and in c. pen. de elect. lib. 6, and c. mandato, de præben. eo. lib., with similar texts noted by Barto. in l. 2 § prius, ff. de uulg. & pupil. But here, in default of the first-born, all descending from him are called, with the addition that one have it after the death of the other; therefore, the elder son of the first-born is to be preferred to the paternal uncle, since he is named first. Nor is it an obstacle if it be said that this doctrine does not have place when well-ordered affection contradicts it, according to what is noted in d. l. hæredes mei, since a father is presumed to love his own son more than a grandson. And first, since a grandson is more remote from him than a son.

† Hence properly, namely from philos, which is love, we call that person who is born of husband and wife; but a grandson is improperly called a son, as is notably proved in l. filium, ff. de his, qui sunt sui uel alie. iu., and by Bar. in l. liberorum, ff. de uerbo. signifi. For I say that those words were not uttered by the father, and thus the presumption of well-ordered affection ceases; but they were uttered by the King, who intended rather to provide for the lineage of this Pedro than for the persons. Likewise, doubtful things ought to be understood according to the custom of the speaker, as l. si quis seruum, de leg. 1, and l. nummis, de leg. 3, and l. cum delanionis § asinam, ff. de fun. instru., and l. Labeo, de supel. leg., with similar texts. But the kings of Castile have been accustomed to honor and prefer the son of the first-born to the other sons, because he represents the person of the first-born, as is clearly evident from the words of certain constitutions of that kingdom; therefore we ought to presume that the King of Castile in that concession seriously made mention of the sons of the first-born before the other sons of Pedro himself. To the same makes that where affection between persons does not apply, the one named first is more powerful. For this there is an excellent text with its matter in l. si communis seruus ita stipulatus, ff. de stipul. seruo., by which law Bart. said there, and as is noted by the moderns in c. quoniam abbas, de offi. deleg., that if a case is delegated to someone with both his proper and appellative name expressed, other conjectures ceasing, we shall say the disposition is personal or real from the order of the words. For if the appellative precedes, it is deemed real; if the proper, personal. And through it ceases the contrary that can be formulated from l. si uiua, C. de bonis ma. For this proceeds from the special disposition of the prince, who is not more affected toward the uncle than toward the nephew, but had regard to the right of primogeniture, which is very frequently observed among princes, especially of Spain, as I have said before, as is clear from the constitutions of the kingdom of Castile. Nor does it stand in the way, on that account, if it be said that between the sons of the first-born and the uncles the elder is called, as is evident from that clause set down above: "and let it always be conferred upon the elder, etc.," which seems to determine all the preceding things, as in c. inquisitioni, and in c. 2 requiris, de appel., fully by Bar. in l. talis scriptura, ff. de leg. 1, and l. prætor ait, ff. ui bo. rap. For I say that that clause refers to the preceding things in successive order, so that the sense is that among the sons of the first-born the elder is always preferred; and so, upon their failing, among the other sons of the said Pedro. For just as the sons of the first-born are called by themselves, and the other sons of the said Pedro are called secondarily by themselves, and the aforesaid ought to be preferred to the latter; so the subjoined clause receives its understanding from the preceding things, so that, just as in the persons all seem to be called in successive order, so too that clause qualifies the sons of the first-born and of Pedro also in successive order, by a good argument from those things which are read and noted in l. hæredes mei § peto, ad Trebel., and in c. olim, and c. abbatem, de rescr., and by Bart. in l. Gallus, ff. de lib. & posthum. All the aforesaid considerations urge that this understanding be followed, and lest the prince by those general words seem to have departed immediately from the right of primogeniture already conferred, contrary to l. non ad ea, ff. de cond. & dem. Other considerations also urge this, because the person of the father is said to be represented by the son, and he is said also to be and to stand there, l. cum antea, C. de agrico. & censi. lib. 11, and the voice of the son is said to be the father's, Insti. de inutil. stipu. § eodem uero, and they are said to be almost the same person, C. de impube. & aliis substitu. l. fina., and one flesh, 35. quæst. 3 c. hac authoritate. Likewise, the father remains in the son; hence it is said that the father loves
† The son more than vice versa, as is noted in d. l. si liberorum, in fin.

† Whence the son of the first-born can be called first-born, and not entirely fictitiously, but in part truly, since in him is the substance and flesh and part of the first-born himself; and thus that which is objected from de lega. tertio § hæc autem uerba, ff. de nego. gest., ceases; and all the more so in our case, because the King in the concession made mention not only of the first-born, but also of the others descending from him, whom by placing them before in this way he seemed to have wished to prefer to his uncles, as in the said l. Lucius. It seems to be excellently proved according to one interpretation which Bald. follows in the said l. prima, de his, qui ante apertas tabu. Moreover, many other considerations urge this which Ioan. And. made in the aforementioned additions to the Speculum, where he supports this opinion, even where mention of the sons of the first-born had not been made. And the same does Oldrad. in his consilia, consi. 200. But in our case doubt seems groundless by the aforesaid. Furthermore, cap. licet, de uoto makes excellently for this, where a nephew is preferred to an uncle in a kingdom. And although there the kingdom was rooted in the person of the first-born, since the father cannot dispose of it at will according to what is read and noted especially by Bald. in cap. primo, de success. feud. in the proem of that book of the Feuds; but rather it is disposed that the first-born son represents the first-born himself; and in my judgment this is a good and new consideration. And by these things the motives of Cyn. and Bald. in l. secunda, C. de bonis matern. and l. cum antiquioribus, C. de iure deliberan. and of Barto. in authen. post fratres, C. de legit. hæred. seem greatly to cease, where he says that where the succession of a fief is treated, the nephew does not succeed in place of the father, because that succession is not derived from law, but from the lord's concession—which truly seems contrary to the texts in cap. primo, de success. feu., and in cap. primo, de natura success. feu., and in cap. primo and 3, de feud. mar. collatio. 10, where the nephew succeeds with the uncle in a fief, holding the place of his father, and there by Bald. in l. tertia, ff. de interdict. & relega. Nor does it stand in the way if it be said that there the uncle is not excluded, but succeeds equally with the nephew, because the same reasoning that applies to part with respect to part militates in the whole with respect to the whole, l. quæ de tota, ff. de rei uend., and cap. pastoralis § item cum totum, de off. delega., for this said capit. licet, de uoto. Nor does the nephew exclude the uncle by his own person, but by the person of his father, whence he is constituted from his own person, similar in cap. maritus, de concess. præbend. libr. sexto, and excellently to the point in l. prima § fin. and l. si nepotes, ff. de colla. bono., and de coniungen. cum emancip. libe. l. 1 § si filius, ad finem; through which it is clear that although an emancipated son by common law does not collate, nevertheless an emancipated son collates to an emancipated grandson by a brother constituted in power at the time of death, which is for no other reason than because he represents the person of his father, as in the said l. si nepotes, where it is said that collation is made to grandsons as to a brother, and they are all deemed to be one, just as the father was; therefore grandsons succeed per stirpes in place of the father, as in l. secunda, C. de suis & legiti. hæred. Nor does it stand in the way if it be objected from l. prima, alias secunda, § si impuberi, ff. de coll., where it is held that the expectation of succeeding to an adoptive father does not come into collation of goods, and thus is not deemed to be firm in the person of the son, because I say that that proceeds because only that comes into collation which the son would have acquired for the father if he had not been emancipated; but that expectation he would not have acquired for the father, therefore it does not come into collation. Nor also does it stand in the way if it be said that the fourth owed to an arrogated son is not transmitted by the son to his descendants if the son dies during the lifetime of the arrogator, because that text does not prove this; on the contrary, it rather implies the opposite, since in the beginning it simply said that it is transmitted to the heir, which Ioan. Andr. seems to hold in the aforementioned additions. Likewise, holding the other interpretation, that he does not transmit, it could be answered that that is so because by death that filiation and every consequence of it is entirely dissolved. But it is not so in our case, both because of the concession of the kings, which not only called the elder son, but also the descendants from him, and because here natural rights concur, which are more powerful than civil rights, l. qui habet, ff. de tutel., and in § sed naturalia, Institu. de iure natur. Furthermore, the right of primogeniture is alienable to a special successor, as in capitu. quam periculosum, and what is noted there, 7. quæst. prima; therefore all the more transmissible to a son and universal successor; and this concerning the first doubt. I come now to the second, in which it seems first that this uncle would be exempt from the jurisdiction of the ecclesiastical judge by the supervention of bigamy, truly or fictitiously, as because he contracted with a widow or a deflowered woman while he was in minor orders, as in capi. uno, de bigamis, lib. sexto, where it is said,

† That upon the supervention of bigamy, a cleric is immediately deprived and stripped of every clerical privilege, and is assigned to the forum of the secular judge. But notwithstanding this, I think the contrary to be truer in law. For a supervening privilege does not have the effect of exempting a cause from the power of the prior judge, because he anticipated him through the act of citation while he was of his jurisdiction, as in l. si quis postea, ff. de iudic., and l. cum quædam puella, ff. de iuris. om. iu.; to this makes l. si quis decurio, C. de sal., and c. proposuisti, de foro comp. All the more in our case the defendant, already anticipated, is bound to answer before the ecclesiastical judge, since he changed forum not by privilege, but as a penalty; for that which was enacted to his detriment ought not to be twisted to his advantage, as in c. 2 de transla. prælat., and in auth. si necesse, C. de don. inter uir. & uxo.

† Furthermore, the common opinion holds that if a layman, anticipated by a secular judge, becomes a cleric while the cause is pending, the cause is not thereby exempted from the secular penal forum, as is noted by Io. And. and commonly by the doctors in c. uno, de obli. ad rati., and Spec. in tit. de reo, post prin., followed by Bar. in l. 1, ff. de pœnis. Therefore, all the more the cause of a cleric ought not to be exempted from the hands of the ecclesiastic who has already anticipated, on account of the stripping and deprivation of ecclesiastical privilege. For if a supervening clerical status is not capable of effecting this exception—although it not only changes the forum by divine law, but also changes the condition of the person, and by reason of his order he is made greater than any secular person, since no secular dignity is comparable to the priesthood, 96. dist. c. duo sunt, and ea. denique—all the more a change of forum on account of delict or disqualification will not have the effect of inducing this. The aforementioned c. j, de bigamis does not stand in the way, because it must be understood of causes to be initiated after bigamy has been contracted, but otherwise of those already initiated, by the aforesaid. And let these things suffice, Nic. Ab.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One legitimated at the instance of his father must in all respects be treated just like one legitimately born.
2. If a father, having previously made a testament, causes his son to be legitimated, the testament is broken.
body: Having implored the aid of Almighty God, on the question pending between Giuliano, son of Ser Matteo, on the one side, and the woman Antonia, legitimate and natural daughter of Stefano, full brother of the said Ser Matteo, on the other side, concerning the inheritance of the late Maria, paternal aunt of the said Giuliano and Antonia and full sister of the said Ser Matteo (father of the aforesaid Giuliano) and of the said Stefano—which inheritance, as is asserted, consists solely of the dowry of the said Maria—as to who should be preferred in the said inheritance, since Ser Matteo was alive at the time of Maria's death, and during his lifetime had the said Giuliano, with his consent, legitimated by an imperial Count Palatine, although at the end of his life he made the said testament, pretermitted the said Giuliano, and instituted Giovanni, his grandson by the said Giuliano: I say that, looking to the ius commune, the case is clear and plain enough. For since the said Maria died intestate without ascendants or descendants, and her property devolved upon the said Ser Matteo, her full brother, as to one half, and upon the said Antonia as to the other half, since she succeeded into the place of her father Stefano, who was also a full brother of that deceased Maria. (For where the succession to a grandfather, paternal uncle, or paternal aunt is concerned, children succeed into the place of their father, and succeed by roots [per stirpes] together with the surviving brother, their uncle, as is the case in auth. post fratres, and there by Barto. C. de legi. hære. and insti. de hære. quæ ab intest. defe. §. cum filiis, and in the body of the law; which half indeed the said Ser Stefano transmitted to his heir, since during his lifetime he conducted himself as heir to the said Maria by claiming her property, as in l. pro hærede, and in l. gerit, ff. de acquir. hæred.) And although the said Ser Matteo instituted his grandson through his son, that institution was nevertheless void for the reason that he pretermitted his own son who had been legitimated at his instance, namely Giuliano; Giuliano may deservedly assert that the testament is null and take his father's property upon intestacy, as in Auth. ut cum de appel. cogn. §. aliud quoque capitulum, and as is read and noted in l. filio præterito, ff. de iniust. rup. & irri. test.

† For one legitimated at the instance of his father must in all respects be treated just like one legitimately born, as in Auth. quibus modis natura efficiuntur sui, §. illud. Nor should that which is openly objected against that legitimation stand in the way, namely that the mother of the said Giuliano did not petition for or consent to the said legitimation: because nowhere is it proved that the mother must consent, for it suffices that the father alone, into whose power he passes, consents, together with the one to be legitimated himself, who passes into the power of his natural father; whence even if the mother is dead, the father can cause the son to be legitimated. These points are proved in the said §. illud; and noted by Barto. in l. Gallus. §. & quid si tantum, ff. de lib. & posthu.; and Bald. in proœmio. C. and in l. rescripta, in fi. C. de preci. impe. offeren.; and Ioan. And. and the Doctors following him commonly in c. per uenerabilem, qui filii sint legitimi; and once the consent of the father is given, the legitimated person succeeds even to agnates and cognates, at least in that case where the one legitimating so expresses it, as the Count did with respect to the said Giuliano, as Iac. de Bel. maintained in disputation in auth. quib. mo. na. effic. legi. coll. 6, and more fully by Ioan. And. in addi. Specu. in titu. de succes. ab intest. §. 1. uersi. ex facto. And another disputation of dominus Iaco. de Bel. in Auth. quib. mo. na. effi. sui, coll. 7, is relevant to our matter, where he says,

† that if a father, after having previously made a testament, causes his son to be legitimated, the testament is broken just as by the birth of a posthumous child: because if a fictive surviving son breaks a testament, such as the monastery into which the father entered, according to the note in auth. si qua mulier, C. de sacrosanct. eccle. and 19. quæstio. ultima. cap. si qua mulier, then a fortiori this legitimated son, who has the concurrent cause of naturality, on the basis of the argument in l. filio, ff. de liber. & posthum. Likewise, if a son subsequently arrogated breaks a testament, as in the said l. filio, then a fortiori this legitimated son, who is a natural son, does so. And in support of this I cite the notable text in the said §. illud, where it is said that after legitimation he differs in nothing from other sons. By this text it is clearly concluded that a testament previously made is broken, just as it would be broken if he had been born at that time. Likewise, that a testament drawn up subsequently, in which this legitimated son was pretermitted, is null by operation of law, just as would happen if he had pretermitted a legitimately born son. From these points it is concluded that, looking to the ius commune, Giuliano, as heir of Ser Matteo his father, ought to have one half; and if the said Antonia is mentally incapacitated, then her curator lawfully appointed will be able and ought to petition for the possession of goods [bonorum possessio]. And if she should subsequently die in that state, that portion ought to devolve upon the said Giuliano, because it would have devolved upon his father if she had not been mentally incapacitated in the intermediate period following Maria's death; this is proved by the notable text in l. fina. uersicu. tale, C. de curato. furio. But now it must be examined whether, looking to any special law, Giuliano ought to be preferred for the whole in the person of his father. And I say that this is so in the castro of the Abbey, where there is a statute providing that, while males are extant up to a certain degree, females do not succeed, or something similar; then without doubt the said Antonia was excluded by the said Ser Matteo. If, however, there is no statute regarding the inheritance, it must be examined whether he can be aided with respect to the nature of the dowry, since it is presupposed to me orally that the late Maria was dowered by the said Ser Matteo. Regarding which, it must be said that if the said Ser Matteo made an agreement at the time of delivery that the dowry should revert to him upon the dissolution of the marriage, then without doubt it belongs entirely to the said Giuliano, through the text in l. unica. C. de rei uxo. act.; l. inter socerum. §. cum inter. ff. de pact. doti. is relevant. The same applies in the absence of a pact if there is a statute in the castro of the Abbey, as is presupposed to me, that upon the death of the woman the dowry ought to return to the donor; for the provision of a statute succeeds in place of the provision of a man, according to the said l. una. §. accedit. And by this I draw the inference as to the second question, whether the other sisters of Ser Matteo could transfer to others their dowries, which they received from the said Ser Matteo. For it must be said that they could not, if Ser Matteo made a pact, or if a statute underlies it, providing that the dowry revert to the donor upon dissolution of the marriage, as in the said §. accedit; otherwise it is different, unless, having pretermitted Ser Matteo, her full brother, she had instituted a disreputable person, as in l. fratres. C. de inofficio. testamen. &c. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Prelates can seek restitutio in integrum, even without a mandate from the church.
2. The office of a delegated judge is not extinguished by the sentence alone, unless it has been executed.
casus: The lord Abbot of the monastery of San Michele di Passignano, of the Vallombrosan order, acknowledged and confessed extrajudicially to a certain Florentine citizen, who had managed the affairs of the monastery for a long time, that he was bound to the said citizen in the name of the monastery for five hundred and thirty florins, which the aforesaid citizen said he had spent and converted to the utility of the monastery; and indeed the general syndic of the monastery ratified and approved this confession. Later, the said citizen obtained an apostolic rescript against the said lord abbot, and before the delegated judge sought that the lord Abbot be condemned; the latter immediately confessed before the delegate that he was bound in the said amount, and the general syndic of the monastery did the same. By virtue of this confession, the said delegate rendered sentence against the said lord abbot for the said amount, from which no appeal was made; on the contrary, he paid part of the debt. Finally, within a year from the time of the condemnation, the said delegate, at the instance of that citizen, strictly commanded the abbot to comply with the condemnatory sentence. It is asked whether, in view of the aforesaid, any remedy is available to the said lord Abbot against that sentence and against his own confession and that of the syndic, etc.
body: Having humbly invoked the help of Christ and of His Mother, I say that there is one most prompt and unquestionable remedy available, namely, to seek restitutio in integrum in the name of the monastery against the said sentence, and also against the confession, which it ought to obtain without hesitation, since it is within the four-year period from the time of the sentence and confession. Through this restitution, indeed, it ought to be restored to the former state in which it was before the sentence and confession; the text is most clear both as to a sentence and as to a confession in l. 1. & 2. C. de tempo. in integ. resti.

† And it is certain that an abbot and other prelates, as legitimate administrators, can seek restitutio in integrum even without a mandate from the church, as noted by Inno. and others after him in c. suscitata, de inte. resti. For prelates are bound by virtue of their office to manage the affairs of their churches, as in c. edoceri, de rescrip., and what is noted there. But concerning this a doubt arises: before whom, or from whom, ought restitution of this kind to be requested? And certainly, there is no doubt that restitution can be obtained from the Roman Pontiff himself, or from another delegate of his by specially petitioning him on this matter; d. c. suscitata, and c. tum ex literis, and almost throughout the entire title, de in integ. resti., and especially in l. pen. & l. fi. C. ubi & apud quos. However, it cannot be obtained from the ordinaries of the places, such as a bishop or an archbishop, nor even from a general legate of the Pope, by the text in c. 2. de offi. dele., and more expressly by the notable text in l. aduersus sententiam, C. si aduer. rem iudic. The doubt therefore remains whether this restitution could be obtained from the said delegate who rendered the aforesaid sentence. And it seems at first that it cannot, by the notable text in d. l. aduersus, where it is said that against one who has judged in the place of the prince, only the prince can grant restitution; and on the basis of that text, Bart. and Bal. held this there, and the same Bart. in l. si. C. ubi & apud quos. But the same Barto. seems to hold the contrary in l. iudex, ff. de re iud., where he says that if the sentence has not yet been executed, since the officium nobile remains with the judge, he will be able by virtue of that same office to grant restitutio in integrum, just as he can execute the sentence and impose fines, as is clear in c. ex literis, and c. significasti, and c. quærenti, de offic. delega.

† For the office of a delegated judge is not extinguished by the sentence alone, unless it has been executed, or at least a year has elapsed from the time of the sentence, as in c. proxi. allega. And thus can be understood the text and statement of Bar. and Bal. in d. l. aduersus, when the delegated judge has entirely fulfilled his office—as because no execution remains, since the sentence was declaratory of acquittal, and thus brought execution along with it; or if it was condemnatory, it was committed to execution. It is otherwise, however, where execution is imminent and remains to be carried out, nor has the period of a year elapsed from the day of the sentence, as happens in our case. And in support of this I cite a very notable gloss, and Innocen. in c. suscitata, de in integ. resti., where they say on the basis of that text that a proctor can without a special mandate seek restitutio in integrum against a sentence rendered against him: because he is said to seek it incidentally, and not principally, since the sentence has not yet been committed to execution, in c. penul. eod. tit. For according to Inno., a mandate of jurisdiction is similar to a proctorial mandate, as in l. & quia, ff. de iurisdi. omn. iudi.; and thus he clearly holds by this reasoning that restitutio in integrum is sought against a sentence not yet committed to execution. In which case, namely when it arises incidentally, a delegated judge appointed generally over a case can grant restitutio in integrum, as in d. c. penul. de in integrum restitutio, and l. fin. C. ubi & apud quos; and understanding it thus, the opinion can be upheld which the gloss relates in d. l. aduersus, because it regards it with disfavor; therefore the law was changed by d. l. fin., where it is held that a delegate can do so; let us understand it, upholding it in the aforesaid manner, such that while execution, and consequently jurisdiction, is still pending, he can do so, otherwise not. Equity fosters this opinion, so that the labors and expenses of the parties may be spared, as in c. cum te, de offic. deleg. Furthermore, we see that when a delegate reserves execution to himself and commits the hearing and deciding of the cause to others, recourse is always had to him if it happens that an appeal is taken from the subdelegate, as in c. si delegatus, de offic. deleg. lib. 6. For it cannot be denied that this restitution is said to arise incidentally in the case committed to him, since his officium nobile still endures; therefore he can grant it to him and hear the cause anew, so that the burden of proving the debt legally falls upon the one against whom this restitutio in integrum is directed; l. diuus, and what is noted there, ff. de in integ. restitu., and 2. q. 3. §. notandum. And restitutio in integrum can also be sought by way of an exception against the petition for restitutio in integrum; l. postea, §. si minor, ff. de iureiur. Nor does it stand in the way that the lord Abbot paid part of the condemnation: because by this the way is not barred from asserting that the entirety was not owed, nor does payment of a part not owed obligate one to pay what is not owed, as in l. fin. C. ne uxor pro marito; on the contrary, through that restitution he ought to be restored to the former state; and thus that citizen should be compelled effectively to restore whatever he received by virtue of the sentence, unless he proves the debt anew; to this point l. in causæ, ff. de mino., and l. uideamus, §. in Fauiana, ff. de usu., and l. cum prætor, ff. de uerb. signifi. For the word "restitution" encompasses every advantage of the plaintiff, as stated there. Nor ought the sentence to be put into execution in the meantime, while this cause of restitution is being treated, as in l. una, C. de integ. resti. pos.; nor is there any suspicion of malice against the said lord Abbot who seeks it, since his single petition is clearly supported, as in d. c. 1. & 2. de in inte. resti. lib. 6. And thus the special provision ceases of which mention is made in c. suscitata, de in integ. resti. I also think that, presupposing that the said delegate does not have the power of granting restitutio in integrum against the sentence, it nevertheless seems proper to say that he can pronounce that it ought to be granted, that execution should be stayed, and that he can remit the case to the Roman Pontiff, by the argument of what is read and noted in c. de cætero, de re iudi., and in c. biduum, 2. q. 6. versic. siquidem, where the gloss says that although an archbishop cannot depose a bishop, he can nevertheless pronounce that he ought to be deposed; and the Doctors say the same regarding a legate in c. 1. de offi. le.; so it seems it should be said in the matter at hand. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Laws speaking of slaves with respect to acquisition apply to monks.
2. An abbot can vindicate his monk.
3. A monk cannot possess private property.
4. It is not permitted for monks to have privileged portions.
5. A monk ought not to depart for any studies unless permission has first been sought from the prelate.
6. Study is appropriate to religious life.
casus: The factual contingency is presented thus: In the church of Catania, a certain custom among regular monks has prevailed from a time whose beginning is beyond memory, that fifty gold coins are given to each of the monks for his necessities by the bishop of the place, who receives all the revenues of the church. All the monks, however, live with common board, and that which is left over from the said provision is assigned pro rata to each for clothing and other necessities. For the bishop is not bound to other burdens of the monks. It happened that, while the bishop was in distant parts, one of the monks, who is now a doctor, dominus P. Ioannes de Massaro, having been licensed by the vicar of the bishop with the faculty of receiving the said provision in all respects [?], betook himself to general studies, the time of his stay not being determined by the vicar. Nor was it expressly arranged to which studies or branches of knowledge he ought to devote himself. Subsequently, over several years, with the knowledge and consent of the bishop who had afterwards returned, the said provision was answered for in full to the said dominus Ioannes or to another in his name. But now, some years having elapsed, the bishop of the place, or the vicar during the bishop's absence, ceased to answer to him, especially taking the occasion that the said dominus Ioannes prolonged his stay in study beyond five years, is now at present a doctor, and thus the cause of study has utterly ceased. It is now asked whether the said dominus Ioannes can claim the said pension from the time of cessation up to the present day, especially since he is absent, etc.
body: Humbly invoking the aid of Almighty God and Mary His Mother. It seems that the said dominus Ioannes should by no means be heard in his petition. And first, this is shown from a defect in the person of the plaintiff. For just as a slave is not permitted to bring an action against his master, as in l. vix certis ex causis, ff. de iudic., so neither is a monk against his prelate; for he is deemed a slave of the monastery. And although this is a spiritual servitude, it is nevertheless considered stricter than secular servitude, as is proved in cap. multos, 54. distinctio; and he is deemed dead to the world and to live unto God, 16. quaestio prima, capit. placuit. Hence it is said that a monk has neither willing nor nilling, but depends entirely upon the judgment of his superior, whom he placed above his head in God's stead: 12. quaest. prima, cap. nolo, and c. non dicatis; and in c. si religiosus, de elect., in Sexto; and cap. secundo, de test., in the same book; to which corresponds what is contained in the authen. de mona., colla. prima. Secondly, this is proved from the absence of an obligation, which is the mother of an action, l. licet, in fin., ff. de procur.; and without an action no one can properly sue, l. si pupilli, ff. de nego. gest., and l. tutor, C. eod. And although under canon law it is not necessary to formulate the specific name of an action, de iudi., c. dilecti, there must nonetheless underlie a right to sue, which arises from a civil obligation, if weighed properly, as is fully noted in the said cap. dilecti; and there is a notable gloss on 10. di., c. quo iure, and as Bartolus notes on l. j., ff. de eden. Hence it is that if one thing is under an obligation, and another is discretionary, and someone sues as if both were alternatively under the obligation, he loses even under the simplicity of canon law, as is the notable text in cap. cum dilecti, de emptio. & vendi. But between master and slave, even when contracting, no obligation arises—at least none capable of founding an action, as in l. interpositas, C. de transa.—therefore neither does it between prelate and monk, as Federico notes, consi. 252, and Archidiaconus in c. cum pastoralis, 2. q. 7; especially since in the person of a monk no obligation actually falls, but whatever he acquires passes immediately and without any delay to the monastery; for which see what is noted by Innocentius and others in c. in praesentia, de proba., and in cap. cum olim, de privile., and by Bartolus in l. si communis servus, ff. de stipula. servo. And in these two last citations Innocentius and Bartolus correctly held

† that the laws speaking of slaves with respect to acquisition apply to monks. Strongly supporting the aforesaid is l. placet, ff. de acquirend. haeredita., where it is said that whenever an inheritance or anything else is acquired by someone under another's power, it is immediately acquired by the one in whose power he is, so that it cannot reside even for a moment in the person of him through whom it is acquired. To the same effect are l. si adoptavero, ff. de procurato., and l. arrogato, ff. de adopt. And it is certain that a monk is under the power of a superior: 18. quaestio secunda, cap. abbates, and the said cap. nolo, and cap. non dicatis;

† for an abbot can claim his monk back, as is noted in l. 1, ff. de rei vendi. If, therefore, an obligation does not reside in the person of a monk, he consequently cannot sue, as by the laws cited above. Thirdly, it is proved from a defect of capacity;

† for a monk cannot possess property. For the renunciation of property is one of the three substantial elements of monasticism, as in c. cum ad monasterium, and in c. 2, de statu regu. And it is called private property because he wishes to possess something against the will of, or secretly from, his superior, in the said c. cum ad monasterium, and there by Ioannes Andreae. Therefore the petition of the said dominus Ioannes manifestly appears inept and consequently to be torn to pieces with teeth, as Innocentius notes in c. 1, de offi. vicar., and as is proved in c. sacerdotibus, 11. q. 1. Indeed, a monk cannot, even before entering the monastery, agree that it be lawful for him to have the usufruct of goods once his own so that he could hold them in the future against the abbot's will; for to retain this itself by an agreement would be property and would indicate that he had a willing and nilling, as is noted by the legists in auth. ingressi, and in the authen. si qua mulier, C. de sacrosan. eccle.

† Item, nor is it lawful for monks to have privileged or separate portions, as Innocentius notes in c. dilectus, 1 & 2, de praeben., nor private cells, unless they lead a solitary life, 20. q. 4, c. monachum. Fourthly, it is shown by another path:

† for it is not lawful for monks to depart for any literary studies unless permission to go has first been granted to them by their prelate with the counsel of the chapter or of the greater part, as is proved in c. 2, ne cler. vel mona., in Sexto. But the said dominus Ioannes by no means had permission from the bishop, who in the said church of Catania stands in the place of the abbot with respect to the monks themselves, according to what is read and noted in c. causam quae, de Iud. Nor was the counsel of the chapter sought; therefore such departure was unlawful, and consequently was not to be rewarded, but punished. Nor can it be done with the license of the vicar, because the vicar's power by no means extends to such things, as is sufficiently gathered from c. licet, de offic. vicar., in Sexto. What is read and noted in c. fraternitatem, 71. distinct., is most pertinent. Fifthly, it is relevant that he did not study in the faculty of theology, by reason of which those privileged might receive the fruits of benefices in absence, as in c. 1, de magi., and as Hostiensis notes there, and by him in summa eod., § fin., where he says that students in other faculties do not enjoy the same privilege. If, therefore, secular clerics do not enjoy such a privilege when studying in other sciences with respect to their own benefices—in which, after collation is made to them, they acquire a right and can say that those benefices are their own, as in c. si tibi absenti, de praeben., in Sexto, and c. penul., eod. titu., and c. si, de conces. praeben., in the same book—all the more so monks do not in the goods of the monastery, in which they do not have such a right, but rather are possessed by the monastery and are called sons of the monastery, as in c. sicut, de simonia. Sixthly, because even assuming that students in other sciences ought to enjoy that privilege, they still ought not to enjoy an ampler privilege, by an argument a minori, and this is sufficiently proved by the argument of c. super specula, de privileg.; but that chapter grants the capacity to receive fruits only for a five-year period, which length of time the said dominus Ioannes is said to have already received. Therefore, beyond that, no right belongs to him, especially since he is not a doctor and the reason for study ceases. Hence, even if he had had a license for a longer time, since the cause of the indulgence ceases, the extension of time ought to cease; to this effect is the good text on a similar point in l. a filia, § 1, ff. ad Trebel., and in cap. cum cessante, de appel., and l. generaliter, C. de episco. & cleri., canonized in 16. q. 1, c. generaliter. What is noted in c. cum ex eo, de elect., in Sexto, and by Bartolus in l. Lucius, ff. de leg. 2, is highly applicable. But notwithstanding these points—which, as will become clearly evident from what is to be said below, do not in law apply to our case—I judge the contrary opinion to be truer. And first, I take as my foundation that a monk is permitted by the holy fathers and by law to devote himself to literary study. Jerome, a most Christian man and one of the four doctors of the Church, invites monks to study, writing to the monk Rusticus, saying among other things: 'Learn for a long time what you may later teach,' 16. quaest. 1, cap. sic vive. And elsewhere to the same man: 'If the desire for the clerical state allures you, learn what you can teach. Offer a reasonable sacrifice to God, lest you be a soldier before being a recruit, lest you be a master before being a disciple.' And shortly after: 'It pleases me that you have the fellowship of the saints, and that you do not teach yourself nor enter without a teacher upon a path you have never entered before.' The same causa and quaestio, cap. si clericatus. A despiser of knowledge is a member of the devil rather than of Christ, as in cap. finale, xxxviij. distinctio.

† And that study is appropriate for religion, Ioannes Andreae fully proves and pursues in capit. sane, de regu. Hence canon law provides that in a monastery there should be a master to instruct the monks in the preliminary sciences, so that the opportunity to progress in knowledge is not lacking to them. And thus, at the expense of the monastery, monks ought to be instructed not only in the preliminary sciences such as grammar, but also in the other principal sciences; this is proved in the Clementine ne in agro, at the end, de statu regu., and a prelate negligent in this regard must be compelled by an inferior, as is noted there. To the same effect is the said capit. secundo, ne cler. vel monac., in Sexto, where it is proved that with the prelate's license they can leave monasteries and go to general studies; and cap. non magno, under the same title in the ancient collections, agrees, where it is forbidden for monks to go to studies to learn secular law or medicine; therefore, if they apply themselves to theology or the canons, this is permitted to them, especially where they have a cure of souls or are in a cathedral church, as in our case, and as is noted in the said cap. non magno, and capit. super specula, under the same title, and by Ioannes Andreae in cap. secundo, ne cle. vel mona., in Sexto. Indeed, it is doubted whether, against the will of the abbot, a bishop can give license to a monk to go to study at the expense of the monastery. And there were various opinions among the commentators, as noted in the said cap. 2 by Ioannes Andreae and Archidiaconus. And it is the common conclusion of the doctors that a monk who is at study with the superior's license—unless something else was agreed upon in the granting of the license—will be able to bind the monastery for the necessities of study, because once license to study is given to a monk, all things seem to be granted without which he cannot comfortably exist at study, as noted in ca. ex parte, de accus., and by Archidiaconus in the said c. 2, ne cleri. vel monac., in Sexto, and in the said cap. pastoralis. From which foundation, indeed, the claim of the said dominus Ioannes appears at first sight well founded, since he is a monk of the church, and had a license lawfully, as will appear below, nor was it agreed that he should provide for his expenses otherwise, but rather that he should live from the said annual provision, as is clear from the tenor of the letters drawn up by mandate of the vicar regarding the payment to be made to him. It remains, therefore, only to respond to the opposing arguments formulated above, from which response the claim of the said dominus Ioannes and this affirmative rule will be elucidated. Nor does the first contrary argument stand in the way. For although a slave regularly does not sue his master, a monk nevertheless can sue, at least by imploring the office of the superiors, in order to receive from the monastery what is necessary for him, to which the monastery is bound through its superior in the name of the church, as in cap. olim, and in cap. ex parte, and what is noted in them, de accus., and in c. cum ad monasterium, de sta. regu., and c. si., de regu. What Ioannes Andreae notes in c. cum singula, de praeb., in Sexto, is applicable. Just as a son also sues his father for maintenance, as in l. si quis liberis, ff. de libe. agnoscen., and a slave against his master, as in l. 1, § quod autem, ff. de off. praefe. urbis, and Inst. de his, qui sunt sui vel alien. iur., § sed hoc tempore; and he who denies maintenance is deemed to kill, l. necare, ff. de lib. agnoscen. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that this applies by reason of future maintenance, but differently in past maintenance, where the reason of necessity ceases. Similarly as to what is contained in l. de alimentis, C. de transactio., and what is noted in l. cum hi, ff. eodem, a settlement is permitted without the authority of superiors for past maintenance, and not for future, because I say this applies to a monk who would receive all necessities from the monastery. But since in our case the bishop does not provide for the monks except from the said annual pension, by very ancient custom, as I said before, this annual provision takes the place of necessities; hence from that provision, whether past or future, he must buy for himself books, clothing, and other necessities. For if he had had the other provision at the proper time, he would have provided for himself the necessities which he now cannot provide from future provision; and this is especially to be allowed in the person of the said dominus Ioannes, who by an unexpected accident lost his books and other utensils in a fire. Furthermore, during this intermediate time in which he did not have his annual provision, he contracted many debts, to which I can attest, for the payment of which he can undoubtedly demand that provision from the bishop, and for this purpose he must implore the superior's office. For he was able, for the sake of study, to obligate the monastery up to the sum granted to him for the purpose of study, as Archidiaconus notes in capit. cum pastoralis, 2. quaest. 7, and Speculator in the title de solutio., § fina., verse monachum. And through these things the solution to the second contrary argument is inferred. For it may happen that a formal action does not belong to a monk against his prelate. But on account of the annual provision denied to him, which takes the place of necessities, as I said before, he can have recourse to the bishop's superior, imploring his office, just as a slave does against the cruelty of his master in impiously denying him necessities, as in the laws cited above. What Ioannes Andreae sets forth in the rule non est obligatorium, de regu. iur., in Sexto, in the Mercuriales, strongly supports the aforesaid, where he concludes that a statute of an abbot and convent made for the sake of avoiding grumbling and scandal is valid, allowing each of the monks to have property for clothing and other necessities, since these appropriately take the place of necessities, and thus are governed by the same rule with them: by the argument of cap. ecclesia, ut lite penden., and in l. si rem & pretium, ff. de peti. haered. And a monk is said to hold property only when he retains something secretly, without the knowledge of his superior, disposing of it at his own pleasure, as Ioannes Andreae notes in the previously cited capit. cum ad monasterium. But it is otherwise if he retains it for a just cause with the superior knowing and tolerating it, and especially expressly ordering it, as noted by him there. And this is excellently proved in capitulo insinuante, qui cleric. vel monac., where there is a notable text, where the gloss, Innocentius, and the doctors generally there held this very thing clearly. For even a slave is said to have if the master permits it, nor is he thereby said to have private property, but the administration of a peculium, as in l. quam Tuberonis, ff. de pecu.; c. 2, de sta. regu., and what is noted there, is to the same effect. Hence, so long as the bishop permits that ordinance of the ancient church, that fifty is owed to each for necessities, each properly and without sin takes that provision by administering it well, and can demand it, since the bishop does not provide the monks' necessities as he ought by law, since he stands in the place of the abbot, as I said before. And by this the third contrary argument formulated above is solved. I come to the fourth contrary argument, in solving which I say that it must be readily admitted that a vicar, from a general commission of office, does not have the power of granting this license to a monk to depart for studies, by the laws adduced to the contrary. But in our case, dominus Ioannes can defend himself on a threefold ground. First, on account of the absence of the lord bishop in remote parts, in which case the power of the vicar himself then extends more broadly. To this effect is the notable text in c. cum nullus, de tempor. ordi., in Sexto, where it is held that when the bishop is staying in remote parts, his vicars can have the power to grant license to a cleric to take orders, which they could not grant in the bishop's presence, as there; hence, lest the utility and necessity of the church be hindered, the laws expand the power of the vicar in the bishop's absence. So in the present matter, since in our case it concerned no prejudice to the church or bishop, but rather an honor and a desirable thing toward which the bishop ought constantly to strive, so that he may have learned men at his disposal—especially because he ought to transact all business of his church with the counsel of the chapter, as in c. novit, and c. quanto, de his, quae fiunt a praela., and 12. q. 7, c. episcopus nullus—it can sufficiently be admitted that the vicar's license sufficed; nor is there question here of making a donation or alienation, but rather of acting for the welfare and honor of the church. For at study he obtains only the provision that he used to have in the church. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that in the meantime divine worship is withdrawn from the church or diminished: because one who devotes himself to study is said to promote the utility of the church, not only particular, but universal. For the church needs literate men for its governance, as in c. cum ex eo, de elec., in Sexto. For which cause power is given to the bishop of dispensing with those promoted to the governance of parish churches so that they are not bound to be promoted to the priesthood within seven years, as in the said c. cum ex eo. If, therefore, for the sake of study the service of the principal rector is withdrawn in a church with cure of souls, this must all the more be allowed in our case, where other monks remained behind. To the same effect is the notable text in c. super specula, de magistris, where divine service is expressly diminished in the church with respect to teachers and learners. Secondly, he can defend himself from the broader power which I surmise the said vicar had, since the lord bishop, being at the Curia, sent him to take possession of the bishopric; hence it is probable that he gave him the broadest power. This, however, can be understood from an examination of the mandate. For if he gave him the power of doing whatever the bishop himself could do in person, as is commonly accustomed to be inserted in mandates, the vicar sufficiently had the power of giving that license, because through those words free power is given; hence the vicar can do all things, and even alienate, provided it does not contain a mere donation. This is read and noted especially by Bartolus in l. procurator, cui libera, ff. de procu., and in l. creditor, § Lucius, ff. manda. Likewise, according to Bartolus in the said l. procurator, if the bishop promised that he would hold ratified whatever the vicar himself did. The same must be said if in the mandate certain cases requiring a special mandate were expressed, with a general clause subjoined, as in c. qui ad agendum, de procurato., in Sexto; what is read and noted by the gloss and Bartolus in l. sed & si, § quaesitum, ff. si quis cau., is applicable. Thirdly, dominus Ioannes can ground his position unassailably: because the lord bishop, coming to the church, consented that the annual provision be given to the said dominus Ioannes, who was then absent. Hence, presupposing that the said vicar had not had the power, yet because he gave it as vicar of the bishop, and thus in the name of the bishop, and the bishop, later informed, not only remained silent but willed that the annual payment be made there, he is sufficiently said to have approved the act of the vicar; this is clearly understood from the doctrine of Bartolus in l. quo enim, ff. rem ra. habe., where he treats at length whether, if an act concerning me is performed in my absence, I am later seen by knowing and remaining silent to approve or disapprove. And he distinguishes: that either that case concerns my benefit and advantage, and then by the very fact that I know and do not disapprove I am seen to approve, as in l. si absentis, C. si cert. peta.; what is read and noted in the rule qui tacet, de regu. iur., in Sexto, is applicable; or it concerns my prejudice, and then, if knowledge supervenes, I am not seen to approve, l. procurator, ff. rem rat. habe. If, however, knowledge intervenes along with some positive act, such as because I received letters or an instrument concerning that act and did not object, then I am seen to approve it; to this effect is the notable text in clemen. 1, de procurato., and l. si filius, C. ad Maced. And on this last point, the same Bartolus notes the same in l. cum tabernam, § idem quaesiit, ff. de pig., and in l. Titius Seio, ff. de consti. pecu.; cap. ex ore, with what is noted there, de his, quae fiunt a maio. parte capit., is most applicable. To the matter at hand, therefore, since in our case it was a matter of a desirable and honorable thing, that the church should have worthy monks, the mere knowledge of the lord bishop himself is taken as ratification.
