Likewise, presupposing and not conceding that this act had redounded to the prejudice of the lord bishop himself, yet since beyond simple knowledge a positive act intervened, namely the paying of that provision, it can in no way be denied that such an act ought to be taken as ratification; especially since otherwise the lord bishop himself would be called negligent and slothful for having permitted a monk to wander without a license. But in doubt we ought to presume so as to exclude sin, as in c. estote, de reg. iu. For he could not properly have paid him unless he had approved the cause of study, and thus the remarks noted by Bartolus in l. Paulus respondet, ff. rem ra. ha., cease to apply. Nor does what I said in the counter-argument stand in the way, that the counsel of the chapter was not had, unless it be presupposed by word of mouth that the chapter consented, but no writing was drawn up from it. Item, the chapter granted him in his absence a share of the mortuaries, and thus not only consented, but showed him favor. And from this also consent is sufficiently inferred, according to what Ioannes Andreae notes on the rule qui tacet, in the Mercuriales, in Sexto, and by Bartolus in l. cum pater, § libertus, ff. de leg. 2, and Baldus in l. si filius, C. de peti. haered. And in these matters tacit consent suffices, as in c. 2 & 3, de his quae fiunt a praela., and as noted in c. j., de reb. eccle. non al., in Sexto. The fifth contrary argument does not stand in the way, for a manifold reason. First, because although according to one opinion the law automatically privileges only students in theology, as in the said c. si., de magi., it is nonetheless not ruled out that by special license of the bishop one studying in other disciplines can receive revenues in absence, as is openly proved in c. cum ex eo, de ele., in Sexto, and noted by Hostiensis in summa de magist., § j., in the middle. But dominus Ioannes had a special license, as I said before. Secondly, the custom of the church is relevant; for commonly the monks of that church are accustomed to study in canon law and to receive that annual pension, in which case the revenues would be owed, as the same Hostiensis notes in the place previously cited. And although in the granting of the license it was not specified in which faculty he ought to study, nevertheless on account of the custom of the church it sufficiently seems to have been granted that he could study in canon law: a very good argument in l. quod si nolit, § quia assidua, ff. de aedil. edi., and in l. si, C. de fideiuss., and what Bartolus notes in l. nemo est qui nesciat, ff. de duob. reis; c. ex literis, de const., and c. causam, de rescr., are applicable. Thirdly, because even setting these aside, I think it quite clear that even under the common law students in other sciences, provided they are not prohibited, can receive the fruits of benefices in absence, because by studying they promote the utility of the churches; and therefore they ought to be regarded as present, as in the said c. cum ex eo. For if those who are in the service of the bishop receive fruits in absence, who ought not to be called absent, as in c. ad audientiam, de cle. non resi., all the more so must the same be said of students. Item, the reasoning of c. cum dilectus, under the same title, must be weighed, where it is said that members of the Pope's household enjoy fruits in absence because they render themselves serviceable to all, and sometimes promote the business of the church. The same, therefore, must be said of students: by the argument of that c. cum ex eo. And Archidiaconus held this opinion in c. 2, de privi., in Sexto, and in cap. de quibusdam, 37. distinctio; and on cap. fin., de magist., he supplies 'especially'; and several moderns, out of favor to studies, held the same in cap. tua, de cle. non residen. But I, following that opinion, answer differently to that c. fin., namely, that with respect to students in theology it intended to remove customs and church statutes to the contrary, as is clear at the end; and thus it wished to privilege only them in the receiving of fruits, because by the tacit intention of the law all are privileged. Hence if one weighs capitulum cum ex eo, which speaks generally of every science, the dispensation is only that those appointed to parish churches are not bound to be promoted to the priesthood, as if with respect to the receipt of fruits no indulgence is required; however that may be under the subtlety of sound law, the said dominus Ioannes can sufficiently defend himself from the aforesaid. I come to the sixth and final contrary argument, in which I say that a license simply given, as was the case here, is understood to last according to the nature of the discipline in which the licensee is to apply himself. But specifically in the study of canon law a seven-year period is required, as the text joined with the gloss in the said c. cum ex eo shows; therefore the license seems to have been given for that length of time. And although canon law was not expressed in the granting of the license, nevertheless, as I said before, it is understood on account of the church's custom. For although by sharpness of intellect that time can be anticipated—because intellect makes up for time, and for those who study well and vigorously, as the gloss notes in c. tum ex literis, de in integ. restit.—nevertheless this does not commonly happen, especially because of the multitude of lectures today; and would that in seven years they were well skilled! For experience, which is an effective mistress of things, sufficiently proves this, de elect., cap. quam sit, in Sexto. Indeed, I think further that if, because of a lack of money occurring because the bishop did not provide for him at the due time, dominus Ioannes was unable to return to his homeland once the seven-year period had ended, and thus had to contract many debts, as in truth happened to him, to which I can attest, he will be able to demand the provision beyond seven years, at least to satisfy his creditors; for a monk ought to live from the goods of the monastery, nor is it to be imputed to him why he did not return, since he could not comfortably return without fault of his own. And by this reasoning the objection raised concerning the supervening doctorate is removed; for he was able to contract debts up to the sum assigned to him for his necessities, as is noted by Archidiaconus in the said c. pastoralis. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus de Tudeschis, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A libel must be evaluated according to the force of its prayer, and not of its narrative.
2. If proofs are de facto admitted against a sentence, by which proofs that sentence appears less legitimate, the judge must adhere more to the proofs than to the sentence previously rendered.
3. Proof to the contrary through the confession of the one in whose favor the law presumes is admitted against a presumption of law and of right (iuris et de iure).
4. A notoriety arising from a sentence is a notoriety of presumption.
5. Prescription is of greater efficacy than a bare sentence.
6. The principal defense belongs more to the lord than to the subjects.
7. If a bishop brings an action against a monastery seeking episcopal rights there, and he who previously exercised episcopal rights there does not defend the monastery, he prejudices himself with respect to possession.
body: Humbly entreating the aid of Jesus Christ the Savior and of His most loving Mother: In the question which is presently pending between the city of Iesi on the one part, and the castle of Belvedere on the other part, or between the universitates of both places, it seems first that judgment should be rendered in favor of the said city. For since previously a sentence was rendered against the men of the said castle in favor of the said city, containing in effect that the said castle of Belvedere was formerly and is a fortress with its territory and district and with its appurtenances and county of the said city of Iesi, and that the nobles of Buscareto had retained and possessed it unlawfully, and were condemned to restore and release it to the community of the said city of Iesi; and it condemned the said universitas of the said castle to allow itself to be recovered by the said city; and pronounced that the said universitas must be compelled to withdraw itself from the power and jurisdiction of the said nobles, etc. Nor does it appear that this sentence has been or is rescinded or set aside by any remedy; therefore, judgment must now be rendered according to it, even if witnesses or instruments to the contrary now appear. For a sentence, provided it is not rendered expressly contrary to the ius commune, even though it may be rendered contrary to the right of the litigants, ought not to be rescinded even under the pretext of newly discovered proof. For a sentence establishes law between the parties; these matters are clearly proved in c. cum inter, de re iudica., where the text, which is very notable, seems to intend this to apply even if it now appears that the proofs upon which the sentence was rendered do not necessarily establish the claim of the party for whom it was rendered. To the same effect are c. suborta, and c. inter monasterium, eod. titu., and l. imperatores, ff. de re iudica., and l. sub praetextu, C. de transac., and l. ingenium, ff. de statu ho., and l. res iud., de regu. iur. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that what was contained in the said sentence is not now being sought, since it has now only been sought that it be pronounced and declared that the universitas and men of the said castle are held and bound to pay in the future real, mixed, and personal burdens according to their share of those which are imposed from time to time for the governance of the said city, just as other universitates and men of the castles and vills of the county of the said city bear them, etc.

† Moreover, the libel must be evaluated according to the force of its prayer (conclusio), and not of its narrative. For the prayer of the libel is not broadened by the variety and multiplicity of the narrative, as is read and noted in cap. ex parte B., de foro competen., and c. literae, de dila., and c. finale, de iudi., and by Feder. de Senis, consil. 23; because I say that what is now being sought is sufficiently contained in effect in that sentence already rendered. For if it was pronounced that that castle of Belvedere belongs to the district and county of the said city, and that the nobles of Buscareto retain and have retained it unlawfully and unjustly, and were condemned to restore and release it to the said city of Iesi: therefore it is concluded that the men of the said castle must pay the burdens imposed or to be imposed by the said nobles; nor can they any longer name them as their lord, or defend themselves under their pretext. For they must blame themselves for why they did not appeal at that time; therefore, they must now answer to the said city, just as other castles that belong to the district and county of the said city do, since in effect such an outcome results from that sentence. For wherever a castle has no jurisdiction, but the entire jurisdiction resides in the city, they are bound to obey the commands of the city and to bear its burdens, and they are called citizens of that city. All these things are proved from what is noted by Barto. in l. 1, ff. de dam. infect., and l. 1, ad muni., and l. non dubito, ff. de cap. & postli. reuer. Furthermore, l. qui ad iura, ad munici., and l. incola, with the following law, de mune. & hono., and what is noted by Ioan. And. in c. 1, de immu. eccle., lib. 6, support this. Therefore, the proofs now made by the universitas of the said castle—that for 56 years and within that time the said nobles possessed all manner of jurisdiction in the said castle, and that they paid burdens and taxes pursuant to their impositions—ought not to relieve the said universitas; because it was already pronounced against the said universitas that the said nobles possessed that castle unlawfully and unjustly, and thus unjustly in that case imposed burdens, as in c. licet, de probat., and what is noted by Innocen. in c. literis, de resti. spo., and c. 2, de in integ. resti., from which sentence no appeal was taken, as I said before. And thus this proof now made does not relieve them, but that sentence must now be ordered for execution according to the petition, as in c. cum super, de re iudi., and in the other legal authorities cited above. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said castle could proceed by the benefit of restitutio in integrum under l. res publica, C. ex qui. cau. maio., because according to the gloss there, that law has no place in vills and castles. And even presupposing that it ought to be observed in populous castles, as some have said and Bart. follows there, nevertheless that benefit ceases now, since a four-year period has elapsed from the time of the sentence: l. fin., C. de tempo. in integ. restit. peten., noted by Bar. in d. l. res publica. Nor can it be objected if it is said that the said nobles, who possessed the subjection in the castle, ought to have been sued, and not the men of that castle, who were possessed, as in c. inter quatuor, joined with the gloss, de maio. & obe., and c. auditis, de praescr.; because I say that subjects, too, for their own interest, and because they themselves cause the plaintiff not to possess, can be sued, at least so that the sentence to be rendered may prejudice them, as is proved in c. cum inter, and c. cum super, de re iud., noted by Inno. in d. c. auditis, and c. inter quatuor. But these things notwithstanding, I deem the contrary opinion to be truer: namely, that a twofold remedy can be applied to impede the intention of the said city of Iesi and to assist the said nobles. First, because although that sentence is found to have passed into res judicata, nevertheless, since objection was made against it contrary to law and proofs were made to the contrary—as it appears then by lawful proofs that the said nobles lawfully prescribed all manner of jurisdiction in the said castle—since the judge must pronounce upon the matter of which he has taken cognizance, as in l. de qua re, ff. de re iudi., and cap. cum super, de causa possess. & propriet., he ought to pronounce against the said city, and absolve the said castle from its suit on the matter newly petitioned, and thus pronounce that the universitas of the said castle lawfully appealed. To this effect is the most notable statement of Inn. in c. cum dilecta, de rescr., and c. cum Bertoldus, de re iud. And he thinks the same in cap. fraternitatis, de frigi., and c. ex ratione, de appell. For Inno. says in the cited places,

† that if proofs are admitted de facto against a sentence, by which proofs that sentence appears to be less lawful, the judge ought to adhere more to the proofs than to the sentence previously rendered. Dom. Anto. de But. expressly confirms this opinion in d. c. cum dilecta, saying that once proof has been made, it passes into notoriety; therefore the effect of the presumption arising from the sentence is removed, just as it is removed by the confession of a party, which similarly induces notoriety, as the same Inn. notably brings out in d. c. cum dilecta: that if he for whom the sentence was rendered confesses that it is unjust, the judge ought to retract it. To this effect is what is noted by Cyn. and other doctors in authen. sed iam necesse, C. de donat. ante nupt., where they say,

† that against a presumption of law and by law (iuris et de iure), proof to the contrary is admitted through the confession of the one in whose favor the law presumes, which proceeds from nothing other than that a confession passes into notoriety. The same applies to proof already made after the conclusion of the case, as in cap. olim, de uerb. sig., and noted by the lords of the Rota, decis. 403. Relevant is what is noted by Inn. in c. constitutus, de fil. presby., where he says that although against a plaintiff in a possessory action proofs regarding a defect of ownership ought not to be admitted, as in cap. in literis, de rest. spo., and cap. fin., de ord. cogn., nevertheless, if by his confession and the admitted proofs the defect of ownership were established, then restitution would not be made to him against what is notorious. And if it is said that notoriety also arises from the prior sentence, and thus ought not to be removed by a subsequent notoriety, since the first is equally powerful, it is answered according to Dom. Ant.

† that the notoriety arising from a sentence is a notoriety of presumption; and since this case concerns prescribing jurisdiction against the said city of Iesi, and not against the Roman Church, ordinary prescription suffices, so that if it is with title, a period of 10 years between present parties and 20 years between absent parties suffices. For this prescription of long time has place even in these incorporeal things, as is proved in l. fin., C. de praescrip. longi temporis, and l. 1, C. de serui.; and if it is without title, a period of 30 or 40 years suffices, as in 16, q. 3, c. dilectio, § potest. And directly to our case is the text joined with the gloss on the word "principaliter" in ca. ad audientiam, de praescr., and the good gloss in c. uolumus, 16, q. 4, and in c. dilectus, de capel. mona. To the same effect is what is noted by Barto. in l. publicanus, § in uectigalibus, ff. de publi., in which legal authorities it is gathered and noted that prescription can run against one holding the rights of the prince by common law, if it is only a question of prescribing and provided that the prince is preserved unharmed. Since, therefore, it is now most clearly established by lawful proofs—and, as is presupposed, admitted in court—that the said castle is subject to the said nobles of Buscareto by lawful prescription, this proof ought to prevail over the sentence already rendered,

† since prescription is of greater force than a bare sentence, as is gathered from the comments on l. finali, ff. rem ratam haberi, and on l. obligationum, § placet, ff. de action. & obligation., joined with what is noted on l. Iulianus, ff. de condictio. indebi.; capitulum ad aures, de praescrip., is relevant, where the text states that prescription excludes absolutely every action; and what is noted by Io. An. in regula possessor, de reg. iu., lib. 6, in Mercurialibus, joined with the comments of Inn. in d. c. quia plerique. Hence it is that if someone confesses a sentence to be unjust, even after it has passed into res judicata, or if it afterwards appears unjust through admitted proofs, the sentence ought to be retracted, as I stated above following Inn.; it is otherwise, however, if after prescription is complete it is established that the thing belonged to another, according to the common opinion of the canonists, as noted by the gloss and the doctors in c. uigilanti, de praescri., and Io. And. fully pursues and holds under the said regula possessor. And in this case it ought to be presumed that the said nobles of Buscareto prescribed in good faith, since before that sentence they possessed for more than thirty years; for from the length of so much time, a just title is presumed, even in incorporeal things, as Inn. intended in c. 2, de integ. resti., and Bar. in l. fi., C. unde ui, at the end. Nor could the sentence rendered prejudice the nobles themselves, as I shall presently state in the second remedy. And it remains certain that the said castle could allege the right of the nobles, as in c. cum olim, tit. 2, de priuile., and c. cum personae, eo. titu., lib. 6, noted by Inno. in c. auditis, de praescrip. And from this remedy I say that in this case it must be pronounced by the judge of appeal that it was well appealed, and he ought to absolve the universitas of the said castle from the suit of the said city of Iesi, because the first judge ought to have done this if this prescription had been proved before him, as is proved in capitulum Raynaldus, and cap. Raynucius, de testamen.; what is noted by Bar. in l. cum apud, ff. iudi. sol., supports this. This remedy, however, is somewhat doubtful with respect to the subjects themselves: because since it was previously pronounced with them litigating that the said nobles had possessed unjustly, they cannot now allege their possession, since in prejudice of themselves it must be presumed just, given that no appeal was taken by them from that sentence. Therefore, it is safer that the nobles themselves appear and put forward their right, as is set forth in the following remedy. The second remedy for effectively impeding the claim of the universitas of Iesi is that the said nobles appear for their interest, which they can do, as in capitulum ueniens, tit. 2, de testi., and capitulum cum super, de re iudi., and l. si suspecta, ff. de inoffic. test., and in l. ad execu., and in l. a sententia, ff. de appella. And if they wish to impede the execution of the sentence in the event that it should happen to be rendered against the universitas of the castle, it is sufficient to plead concerning their right; and this is beyond doubt if at the time of the first sentence they were ignorant that the suit was being conducted against the universitas of the castle, since they possessed the jurisdiction, as is proved in d. capitulum ueniens, and there by Inn., and in l. saepe, ff. de re iudi., noted by Inn. and commonly by other doctors in c. cum super, and c. penul., eo. titu. And if they wish judgment to be pronounced in their favor, they must present at least some sort of petition, as noted by Host. and Ant. de Butr. in capitulum cum super, cited above; although Inn. there took the view that without distinction that lord appearing for the right which he has in the subjects must be heard without another petition, and can use the proofs made by the subjects. But the preceding opinion pleases me more, because just as proof made by the subjects does not harm an absent lord, as I shall say below, so neither ought it to benefit him, by the argument of those things noted in cap. causam, de testi.; and they are sufficiently presumed to be ignorant if they were in the age of infancy, by the argument of c. fi., qui matrimonium accusare possunt. But presupposing that they were aware that the suit concerning subjection was being conducted by the universitas of the castle and remained silent, was prejudice inflicted upon them? It is somewhat doubtful; and I premise that it is certain that subjects may be sued by a third party concerning the right of subjection, both because it is in their interest not to change lordship, and because they themselves seem to prevent the third party from possessing by not submitting, as I said above. This is proved in c. cum super, de re iud., and c. cum inter, eo. ti., noted by Inn. and commonly by the doctors after him in c. auditis, de praescrip., and c. inter quatuor, de maio. & obe., and d. c. cum super; however, Inno. said in d. cap. auditis that some hold,

† that although the subjects are admitted to defense and can be sued, nevertheless the defense in the first place belongs to the one who possesses the subjection. He reports that others say, and better according to him, that the defense does not pertain more principally to the lord than to the other, but fully to both. But principally the defense belongs to the subject and to the one possessing the subjection; he cites l. principaliter, C. de lib. causa, and the doctors commonly agree with this second statement. But the doubt now is whether a sentence rendered against the subjects harms the lord, or the one possessing the subjection, if he knew the dispute was being litigated and kept silent, and did not afterwards appeal from the sentence. Inn. in c. suborta, de re iudi., takes the view that it does; he requires, however, that the lord knew the dispute was being conducted and was not ignorant that a right belonged to him over the litigating subjects; he also takes the same view in d. c. auditis, because the sentence of one does not prejudice others unless he knew and did not defend, because then it does prejudice; he cites c. quamuis, de re iud., l. saepe, § pen., ff. eo. He held the contrary, however, in c. cum super, de re iudi., where he holds that there is no prejudice to the lord as to ownership (proprietas), but only as to possession, nor is there execution for the one who obtained the sentence concerning subjection when the lord knew and was silent; and the case there seems to concern this. He holds the same in d. c. quamuis, where he says, on the argument of what is said concerning a freedman in d. l. saepe,

† that if one bishop sues a monastery claiming episcopal rights there, and he who first exercised episcopal rights does not defend the monastery, it prejudices him as to possession; and this opinion—that no prejudice is done as to the ownership of the bishop in the lordship, even though he knew and did not defend—is held and approved by Ant. de But. and commonly by the other canonists in d. c. cum super, and in d. c. quamuis, and it seems clearly proved in d. c. cum super. Nay more, Dom. Franc. de Zabarellis, formerly Cardinal of Florence, in lecturing held in d. c. cum super that there is no prejudice to the lord himself even as to possession, if he is in possession; and as to c. cum super, the answer is that it is understood when the lord was not in possession. For whereas previously he could have impeded execution about to take place on vacant property under pretext of his right, as is read and noted by Inno. in d. capitulum ueniens, de testi., and by Bartol. in l. a diuo Pio, ff. de re iudi., he will not be able to now, since he was aware and did not undertake the defense. But if the lord himself were in possession, he ought not to be deprived of his possession on account of a sentence rendered against subjects, because this would be directly contrary to the meaning of that chapter, where it says that a sentence rendered against a monastery in favor of a bishop must be ordered for execution without prejudice to the other bishop, who said that that monastery was subject to him. And the text adds there: the reason is because acts done against the monastery ought not to prejudice a bishop claiming subjection, although he knew and did not appeal, since a matter handled between others regularly ought not to harm others according to canonical and civil constitutions. Whence two points must be particularly weighed from that text: First, because it says that without prejudice to the bishop claiming subjection that sentence must be ordered for execution; for if he were deprived of possession, it would not take place without his gravest prejudice, since the advantage of possession is great, for often ownership itself is lost due to a defect of proof concerning ownership, as in c. saepe, de resti. spol., and the burden of proving falls on the non-possessor: l. si, C. de rei uen., and c. ex literis, de proba., and Instit. de interdic., § commodum. Let that text, therefore, be understood of whatever prejudice is generated for a silent lord, since execution is on vacant property, for he would have prevailed more easily if no one had possessed: d. capitulum ueniens; and Innocen. seems to have tacitly adopted this interpretation in capitulum quamuis, cited above, at the beginning. Secondly, the reasoning of that decision must be greatly weighed when it says that a matter handled between others, etc. And thus in an exceptional way that text intends, and I do not know where else, that the lord is called an entirely different person in this regard, so that no prejudice—at least no grave prejudice—is done to him from acts conducted with those subject to him, and that that rule, res inter alios acta, has place in his case, and consequently it is inferred that l. saepe and c. penul. have place regarding the lord as to the rule stated there, and not as to the excepted cases. I prove this: First, through the reasoning of Inn. himself in d. c. auditis. For there he said,

† that defense, when subjection is at issue, pertains principally and equally to the lord and to the subjects, because just as it is in the lord's interest not to lose subjects, so it is in the subjects' interest not to change lord; d. l. principaliter supports this. Therefore, the sentence of one ought not to harm the other, even if he knows of it; which I prove through the said l. saepe and d. c. pen. For then the sentence of one harms the other when he to whom the action belonged in the first place permitted the subsequent party to proceed, when he could have repelled him from the court, as is stated there. But if it pertains equally to both, the lord could not have removed the subjects from the court. Likewise, why is this to be imputed to the lord, when the subjects litigate for their own interest? And thus the sentence will have effect against the subjects, so that by reason of their interest they can no longer contradict it, but not against the lord, since no matter ought to exceed its own effect and pass to other persons: de his quae fiunt a maio. par. cap., c. quaesiuit, and l. sancimus, C. de poenis. Someone will say: this seems contrary to the text in d. l. saepe, in § nam & si libertus, where it is said that a freedman litigating concerning his status, when he obtains an adverse sentence, prejudices the lord himself concerning his right of patronage. For to that text a twofold answer can be given. First, that that text has two interpretations. The first is that it is understood when the lord intervened in the court; and this the text seems to suggest when it says, "me interueniente", etc. And Ioan. An. held this interpretation, and Inn. approves it in d. c. cum super. For Io. said, and well according to Inno., that if someone claims rights that I possess in a certain thing, with my knowledge, and obtains them, it does not however prejudice me unless I defend it; and he explains the words of d. l. saepe, namely, "intervening and defending"; and thus it appears according to him that if he offers himself for defense, he must prove his right, otherwise prejudice would be done to him. These are formally the words of Inno. in d. capitulum cum super. The second interpretation was that of Rodolphus, that knowledge alone suffices; and although Bartol. holds this interpretation in d. l. saepe, Inno., however, and Io. Andr. say that the pope seems to reject that interpretation in d. capitulum cum super. But if we wish to reconcile the interpretation of Io. An. and Bar., let us say otherwise, and thus: that either we are speaking of a freedman litigating, and thus prejudice is done to the knowing lord, as in d. § nam & si libertus; or we are speaking of a subject litigating, and prejudice is not done to the lord, even if he knows, unless he intervened in the court and offered himself for defense; and so we speak of d. capi. cum super; and Dom. Anto. de Butr. presents this interpretation in d. capitulum cum super. And in my judgment it appears to be the intention of Bart. in d. § nam & si libertus. And if his reasoning is well weighed, the reason for the distinction is because the freedman obtained freedom from the lord, and thus seems to have had permission to litigate concerning lordship, and consequently concerning the right of patronage by permission of the lord himself; deservingly is prejudice done to the knowing lord, just as by the same reasoning it is said regarding a creditor litigating concerning the ownership of pledged goods in bringing a hypothecary action, so that he causes prejudice to the knowing debtor. For he obtained that obligation by the act of the debtor, and he seems to have given him permission to litigate concerning ownership, as noted by Bar. in d. l. saepe. In a subject, however, this reason ceases, since he has nothing by the act of the lord, but is merely possessed. If therefore he litigates concerning subjection, he appears purely for his own interest and his own act; therefore it ought not to prejudice the lord; nay rather, as to his right the lord is deemed an entirely different person, as the text in d. c. cum super clearly intended; and with this explanation c. suborta and the statement of Inn. there can be understood. For he is speaking of an exempt person litigating concerning a right of exemption. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One who promises under a certain penalty that he will cause and see to it that Titius contracts marriage with Sempronia is not bound to the penalty if he did whatever he could.
2. If a legacy has been made to a woman if she marries Titius, she is deemed to be prohibited from marrying another, but only with that Titius.
3. If someone has been ordered to stay with someone or to contract, if that person refuses, or if he cannot conveniently or honorably stay or contract with him, the legacy is due, and the obligation is extinguished.
body: Concerning the first doubt, having first implored the aid of the Savior, it seems that the sureties, who promised that they would do and see to it that masters Petrus and Antonius, in accordance with their promise, would build and construct the warehouse in the town of Liminio under a certain penalty, are bound and obligated principally to the act, that is, to the construction of the warehouse itself, and also to the promised penalty, since the work was not completed within the promised time, namely 18 months, notwithstanding the event of death occurring in the person of master Petrus before the completion of the work. And that they are bound to the principal act itself seems to be proved by l. nemo est, qui nesciat, ff. de duo. reis, and l. si quis pro te, together with the gloss, ff. de fideiuf., in which legal authorities it is proved that sureties can intervene in obligations and be obligated to the principal act itself to which the principal promisor was bound. For through the intervention of a surety it seems to be tacitly agreed that the skill of the principal promisor is not deemed to have been exclusively chosen, but that the work can be done through sureties or others who possess the same skill as in the promise. That they are obligated to the penalty is evident because before the death of the said master Petrus the penalty was incurred, since within the period of 18 months in accordance with the promise the work was not completed; therefore, death supervening after the penalty has been incurred does not release the sureties: the text is in l. si decesserit, ff. qui satisd. cog. Nor are they relieved if they say that after the lapse of the time prescribed for doing the work the Florentine officials appointed over that work, together with the lord and the priors of that city, assigned money to the said masters for completing the work, and by accepting that act they seem to have tacitly departed from the penalty, so that they can at least be released by way of an exception, as in l. 2. ff. si quis cau., because that applies when a penalty was simply attached; but when the clause was added, 'the pact remaining ratified,' then an extension granted after the penalty was incurred for completing the work does not release from the penalty already incurred: the text is noted in l. cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo, ff. de uer. ob., and there by the gloss and Bar.; in favor of this is a good gloss in c. dilecti, de arbi. in fi.; l. pe. and what is noted there, de transact., is relevant. But notwithstanding these points, I deem that the contrary opinion prevails, if other contingent matters in this affair are rightly weighed. And first I shall discuss whether the said sureties remained obligated to the principal act; secondly, whether to the penalty. Concerning the first, I say that they are not, because these sureties did not promise the principal act, which is the case spoken of in the said l. nemo est, qui nesciat, but had obligated themselves that they would do and see to it that the masters would perform according to the promise; in which case they are not themselves obligated to the principal act, since they did not promise it, but rather that they would do and see to it that those men perform, as noted by Bar. in the said l. si quis pro eo; and what the gloss notes there supports this; to this effect is the text in l. stipulatio ista §. si quis dolum, ff. de uerbo. obli., and institu. de inut. stipu. §. si quis alium. For an obligation takes its effect from the intention of the contracting parties, l. in conuenientibus, ff. de uerbo. signi. And this must especially be maintained in our case, since they are not of the same skill as the principal promisors, as noted in the said l. si quis pro eo and the said l. nemo est, qui nesciat, and this is completely clear. I come to the second point, namely whether they are obligated to the penalty, and I conclude that they are not, because the penalty was not incurred before the death of the said master Petrus; and thus, since it was not through their fault that they did not see to it and bring it about that those masters complete the work, the stipulation of the penalty is not incurred, because a supervening difficulty or impossibility prevents the incurring of the penalty: the text is noted in l. Si uehenda, ff. ad legem Rhod. de iac., noted there more broadly by Bar., and more clearly in l. continuus. §. illud, de uerbo. obli. And Fede. de Senis, after holding counsel with Io. Paglarensis, gave counsel in the same sense in more difficult circumstances than ours, as he himself relates in consilio 117, where he says,

† that if someone promised under a certain penalty that he would do and see to it that Titius would contract marriage with Sempronia, if he did whatever he could, he is not bound by the penalty, because he satisfied the obligation as far as in him lay, and difficulty prevents the penalty from being incurred, as in the said l. si uehenda. But in our case not only did difficulty supervene, but also impossibility, because it was impossible after death to see to it that that master Petrus would complete the work; therefore, on account of the person of the said master Petrus dying before the penalty was incurred, the sureties are not held. Nor did that obligation pass to the heirs of the said master Petrus, because an act inherent to the person of the deceased does not pass to the heir: the said l. si decesserit, and there by Bar., through which he says that if someone promised that he could be taken personally for a debt, that obligation does not pass to the heirs. To the same effect is l. una §. fin autem, at the end, C. de cadu. tollen. Furthermore, that the penalty was not incurred before the death of the said master Petrus, notwithstanding the lapse of the 18 months prescribed for completing the work, is proved by the fact that, as is presupposed in the facts, they contracted for the work to be done within that time, with the condition that they would build upon a certain ancient wall; but eventually it was subsequently discovered by the officials that that work so to be built would not endure, and they leased anew to the said master Petrus that he should build that wall anew, and they appointed a new wage for him for that, setting a time of three months for the construction of that wall. And if work was added to the second stipulation that was not included in the first promise, whence there was a tacit departure from the time first prescribed, so that they are at least protected by force of an exception, nor is the penalty incurred within the time previously agreed; to this effect is what the gloss notes in l. fi. C. de noua., and by Bar. in l. pe. ff. de pacto. stipula., and by the same and the gloss in l. 2. ff. de noua. Highly relevant to the aforesaid is l. & ideo haesitatur, and what Bar. notes there, ff. de uerb. ob., where it is said that if someone promised to build an apartment building within a certain time, and then some part of the built apartment building collapsed from fire, it is said that the promisor must have a whole time for building on account of the supervening impediment; and so it seems must be said in our case, since when the work is changed, diligence is impeded, and consequently the time ought to be increased, since nothing else was expressed: argument in l. Seio, 1. responso, at the end, ff. de an. leg.; and the first stipulation sometimes receives an extension, as if time were tacitly included, as in l. interdum, ff. de uer. ob. And if I promise simply to give one hundred, nevertheless a time within which it can be paid by me is tacitly understood. And that this was the intention of the contracting parties is sufficiently shown because, after the 18 months first prescribed had elapsed, the aforesaid officials raised nothing concerning the penalty; for from the things that follow, presumptions are made as to the preceding things, as in l. si seruus plurium, at the end, and l. quae filiabus, ff. de lega. 1. And this especially holds if that clause, 'the pact remaining ratified,' was not appended, as noted in the said l. cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo, and in l. 2. si quis cau. The same is true, however, even if it was appended, in view of the aforesaid, especially because this is presupposed: namely, that the said work with the construction of the wall anew could not conveniently be done within the time previously prescribed; l. Nepos Proculo, ff. de uerb. sig., is relevant. Moreover, if there had not been a departure from the time previously prescribed, to what end would a time of three months have been appointed for constructing the new wall, since that wall was to be built solely on account of the construction of the warehouse? Whence the time appointed over the whole was sufficient, since by reason of the whole the part was being treated: argument from the things noted in c. auditis, de procu., and in c. cum dilecti, de dolo & contu. And from these points I infer with respect to the second doubt, whether the sureties are at least obligated from the person of the surviving master Antonius; and I say that they are not, both by the aforesaid, and because master Antonius did not obligate himself together with the said master Petrus so that they would be two co-debtors, and thus l. 1. C. de duobus reis, and l. reos, ff. eo. with similar laws—where it is clear that two co-debtors seem to be obligated in solidum, although today it is otherwise through auth. hoc ita, C. eo. tit.—cease to apply. But master Petrus was the principal promisor; that master Antonius, however, obligated himself to do his part together with the said master Petrus, and thus he chose the skill and industry of the said master Petrus, who was the more outstanding master, and perhaps without him he would not have obligated himself to so great a work. Whence, since on account of the death of the said master Petrus he cannot build together with that master Petrus, he is released from that obligation, nor is he bound to build with another: a good argument in §. cum autem, and in c. is cui, de officio delega. lib. 6, and what Inno. markedly says in c. fin. de offi. dele.; l. cum ita legatum, ff. de condit. & demonstra., is relevant,

† where it is said that if a legacy was made to a woman thus, 'if she marries Titius,' she is deemed forbidden to marry another, but only with that Titius. So in the present matter, if master Antonius obligated himself to build together with master Petrus, if he cannot work with him, he is not bound without him or with another. For this is what the words of the obligation import, from which there must be no departure when a contrary intention is not established: l. non aliter, ff. de leg. 1; and especially in our case, because in doubt words are to be interpreted against the stipulator. For those officials ought to have framed the words more broadly when it was in their power, as the text expressly says in l. quicquid astringendae, de uerb. obli. To the same effect is l. 1. C. de insti. & sub., and l. Caio, ff. de ali. & cib. leg., and l. meuia, ff. de ann. leg., and what Bartol. notes in them, where it is evident

† that if someone is ordered to dwell with someone or to contract, if that person refuses, or if he cannot conveniently or honorably dwell or contract with him, the legacy is due and the obligation is discharged. From these points it is inferred that if the said master Antonius did not remain obligated after the death of the said master Petrus, neither are his sureties bound to the penalty, because they promised that they would do and see to it that those men would perform in accordance with the promise made by them, and the promise was qualified by that condition of fact, that he was to build the said warehouse together with master Petrus; also because a defense available to him by reason of coherence is also available to the surety, as in l. exceptiones, la. 2. ff. de exceptio.; indeed, it is imputed to him if he knowingly omitted it, as l. si fideiussor, ff. manda. From all of which it is concluded that neither from the person of master Petrus nor from the person of master Antonius are the said sureties in any way obligated. Nic. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. When different penalties are alternatively imposed by the law, and the words of the law are directed to the judge, the choice is not given to the party, but to the judge alone.
2. Many benefits are conferred upon the unwilling, when provision is made for their advantage, not their will.
3. A potentiality easily reducible to an act is held as an act.
4. If a wealthy sick person forbids any medicines to be given to him, nevertheless, if a physician treats him and gives him medicines, he can afterwards recover [their cost].
5. A provision of the law is more favorable than a statute.
6. A judge can by virtue of his office remove a curator already appointed and designate another.
7. When two actions are available, one under the common law and the other by benefit of the praetor, once one has been chosen, the other remains excluded.
8. The power is given to the judge of moderating the penalty of the law from the beginning.
9. A minor cannot at his pleasure remove himself from the power of a tutor by will alone.
body: Having besought the aid of almighty God: As to the first doubt, namely whether, under the aforesaid statute, a curator is to be given to an unwilling minor who otherwise has no curator, it seems at first that he is not. For it is provided by law that a curator is not given to an unwilling minor except for litigation, as in Inst. de cura. § item inviti, and elsewhere it is said that he ought not to be given except to one who is present and stipulating, as in l. qui habet, ff. de tute. Moreover, it is elsewhere provided by law that another cannot petition for a curator for a minor, but he must petition for himself, as in l. divus, § curatores, ff. quod

† pet. tut. vel cura. Therefore, since the present statute, by which it is provided that relatives may petition for a curator for a minor, deviates from the disposition of the common law, it ought to be strictly construed, so that it may conflict as little as possible with the common law, l. 3, § haec autem verba, ff. de neg. ges., c. in nostra, de iniur., c. j. & 2, de fil. presby. lib. 6; to which makes what Inn. notes in c. causam, de rescrip., and Bar. in l. omnes populi, ff. de ius. & iur., and l. j. ff. ad leg. Fal., and Io. And. in the rule pro possessore, de reg. iu. lib. 6 in Mercu. That statute therefore provides that relatives are admitted to petition for a curator where otherwise they were not admitted, as I said before, and it is not to be understood that one is given to an unwilling minor, lest the common law be corrected in another respect, especially since this is not expressed in the statute, and without this the statute can have its effect; to this makes l. si vero, § de viro, ff. so. ma., and c. statutum, de elec. lib. 6. But notwithstanding these things, I deem the contrary opinion to be more worthy of approval. First, through the words of the said statute where it says that if they shall come and nominate a curator or curators, and swear that they make the said petition in good faith and for the benefit of the minor, and will nominate the better persons, the aforesaid curator or curators shall be given to the same minor within fifteen days after the petition and the aforesaid oath. Whence I weigh first the word "shall be given" (dentur), which word is mandatory upon the judge, inducing necessity, just as in a similar case is held in c. si diligenti, de fo. comp.,

† and c. j. de iniur. lib. 6, and c. de multa, § is quoque, de praeben.; which words, since they are impersonal, are directed to the judge alone, and thus do not require the will of the minor or of another, but solely denote the act and office of the judge. To this is what in a similar matter is found in Clem. j. de re iudi. joined with the gloss on the word "admittatur", which is notable. To the same point is another notable gloss in l. si soror, C. de colla.; to this makes what Cy. notes in l. quicunque, C. de ser. fugi., where he says

† that if different penalties are imposed alternatively by the law, and the words of the law are directed to the judge, the choice is not given to the party, but to the judge alone, so that the ministry of the judge alone suffices. The same holds when the words are uttered impersonally, because in doubt they are directed to the judge, as is the text joined with the gloss in c. a crapula, de vita & ho. cleri., and in c. fraternitatis, 34 dist., and c. sicut, de iudi. Secondly, it makes to this that one must not depart from the words unless it is openly established that the intention was otherwise, as in c. si [propter demerita], de verb. sign., and l. non aliter, ff. de legatis 3. But the words of the statute in our case are most clear and

† certain, since they say that nomination must be made by the relatives, nor do they require that the minor be summoned or that he consent; therefore they ought to be understood without distinction, so that whether the minor wishes it or not, those nominated must be appointed for him, observing however the form of the statute. For when the words are clear, extraneous interpretation ceases, l. ille aut ille, ff. de leg. 3, and in c. estote, de reg. iur.; for the lawmakers would well have known how to state, had they wished, that the minor should be summoned and should consent. Since therefore they did not say so, one must not heed whether the minor resists; for this is a good text in a similar matter in c. ad audientiam, de deci., and 19 dist. cap. si Romanorum, and c. solitae, de maiorita. & obe., and l. de pretio, ff. de publ. Thirdly, it makes to this that if he were not given to an unwilling minor, but to a consenting one only, the statute would not require that solemnity that the relatives swear that they make the said petition in good faith and for the benefit of the minor, since without this he ought to be given if the minor concurred by consenting to the petition; arg. l. si filius, and what Bal. notes there in l. cum pater, § libertus, ff. de lega. 2. Furthermore and fourthly, if this were true, that statute would provide for nothing or for very little, because the minor would have nothing to do but contradict, and thus he would impede the petition of the relatives and render void the nomination and the oath of the relatives and the provision of the statute founded upon his benefit, which is not to be said; an excellent argument in cap. in his, de privileg., cap. si papa, de privile. lib. 6, and l. si quando, C. de inoffic. testa. Nor in this case must one heed the contradiction of the minor, since the statute intends to provide for his benefit and not his will, as appears in those words, "for the benefit of the minor," etc. To this is cap. qui emendat, 45 distinct., where the text says

† that many good things are bestowed upon the unwilling when provision is made for their benefit, not their will, because they are found to be enemies to themselves. To the same point is 33 q. 4 c. displicet, and cap. ipsa pietas, and what Bar. sets down as noted in l. 4, § praetor ait, ff. de dam. infect., where he says that if it is provided by statute that citation be made to the face or to the house, it ought not to be understood as an alternative of order—and thus first to the face, and in default thereof to the house—even though the words of the law are so understood and expounded, as in l. scire oportet, ff. de excusa. tuto.; but the alternative words ought to be understood as imposed so that citation either to the face or to the house suffices, in order that the statute may effect something. Nor does the argument framed above stand in the way, namely that it could operate so that relatives are admitted to petition; because that defect would be slight and virtually useless, since by the sole contradiction of a minor who is perhaps undisciplined that provision would be utterly annihilated, and thus words would have been set upon words rather than upon things, which ought to be the contrary, as in c. commissa, de elect. lib. 6, and l. 2 in fin. C. communia de leg., and the words of the law ought to be understood with effect, in cap. relatum, de cleri. non resi., and l. j. § haec autem verba, ff. quod quisque iuris. Nor ought the interpretation of any disposition to be made so harshly that its effect depends on the judgment of another, as is notably seen in the text in cap. pisanis, de restitu. spolia.

† For a potency easily reducible to an act is held for an act, as there; whence just as we see that the law provides for an unwilling prodigal through the giving of a curator, l. j. ff. de cura. furio. and l. is cui bonis, ff. de verbo. obli., until he has recovered sound morals, as in said l. j., and for a woman who lives luxuriously, in l. & mulieri, ff. eod., so the statute in this case wished to provide for the minor. For it presumed a curator to be necessary for him from the fact that the relatives are admitted to petition and swear that they seek a curator to be given in good faith and for the benefit of the minor; to this are ll. 1, 2, and 3, ff. de libera. causa, and the judge ex officio ought to provide for a minor, as is noted in l. 4, § hoc autem iudicium, ff. de dam. infec. Furthermore, since the relatives are presumed to be moved by good zeal, as in the laws just alleged, and petition and swear that they do so in good faith and for the benefit of the minor, if the minor himself is contradictory, he seems unsound in his conduct, and his dissent ought not to offer an impediment; to this is the notable gloss on c. 1, 83 dist., which notably says

† that if a wealthy sick person forbids any medicines to be given to him, nevertheless if the physician cures him and gives him medicines, he can afterward recover [his fee], notwithstanding l. si, C. de nego. gest., because in so resisting he is presumed not to be of sound mind, whence the physician can cure an unwilling person; so I conclude on the present doubt that, the solemnity of the statute being observed, a curator can be given to an unwilling person by the judge. I come to the second doubt, which in my judgment is more difficult: whether, a proceeding having been commenced by the relatives regarding the petition for a curator, with the solemnity of the statute observed, the giving of the curator afterward petitioned for by the minor himself, made by the judge before whom the question was pending, was valid. And at first it seems so. For it is certain that a curator is to be given to the minor himself upon his petition by the magistrate by provision of the common law, as in said l. divus, § curatores. Which provision of the law is not deemed in doubt to be abrogated by the provision of the statute, but both remedies concur, so that one can be given at the petition of the relatives and also at the minor's own petition. For an ancient provision of the law is not deemed abrogated by a lesser one, but both concur, unless it is expressly provided in the new law, as in l. quoties and l. nunquam, ff. de actio. & obliga.; to this makes l. fin. C. de dona., and what Barto. notably lays down in l. j. ff. vi bono. rapto., and the gloss in c. quod olim, de iudaeis.

† Moreover, the provision of the law is more favorable than the statute, because in that which departs from the common law it is odious, as in the laws alleged above in the first part. Since therefore at that time the provision of the common law concurred, especially with the will of the minor, it seems that the aforesaid appointment is valid; arg. in the rule odia restringi, de regu. iur. lib. 6, and l. quod vero, ff. de legi., and cap. cum dilectus, de consuet.; to this makes l. 2, C. de noxa, and excellently in l. praesens, in fi. ff. de poenis; and elsewhere the text says that where a natural and an accidental cause concur, the natural is to be preferred, l. qui habet, ff. de tute. But the provision of the law, that a curator be given to a petitioning minor, is natural and more favorable than the provision of the statute, that one be given to an unwilling person at the petition of relatives; therefore it is to be preferred. Secondly, l. quoties, C. de rei vendi., makes to this, where it appears that if I sell a thing to two persons, he is preferred to whom the thing was first delivered. And thus in an equal cause he is preferred who first arrived at the consummation of the act; to this makes c. tibi, qui, de praescrip. lib. 6. But in our case, with the petition of the relatives and that of the minor pending, the curatorship was first decreed at the petition of the minor; therefore he is preferred, especially since the rationale of the statute now ceases. For the intention was to provide for a minor who is in need of a curator, as appears from the words of the statute, there: "for the benefit of the minor," etc. But now the minor has curators against whom nothing is improperly objected; therefore the extraordinary provision of the statute ought to cease, arg. in c. cum cessante, de appel., and excellently makes l. ex facto, ff. de vulg. & pupilla., and what Bar. notes there in l. generaliter, C. de episco. & cleri., canonized in 16 q. j.; and to one who has a curator another curator is not to be given, as in l. curatorem habenti, C. qui da. tuto. vel cura.

† Furthermore, the judge himself can ex officio, for cause, remove a curator already given and depute another, l. 3, § praeterea, ff. de suspectis tuto. A fortiori, therefore, he was able not to admit the curator petitioned for by the relatives and to depute another at the petition of the minor, since one is more easily not admitted than removed, as in capit. quemadmodum, de iureiurando: "It is more shameful to be cast out than not admitted," etc., as there. Likewise, capitulum pastoralis, de iure patronatus, makes very strongly in a similar matter, where it is held that if a patron presents first one person to a vacant church, and the bishop without legitimate cause delayed to institute him, and if the patron presents another and the bishop institutes him, the institution made of the second is valid, even though the bishop is punished who without legitimate cause delayed to institute the first. Much more a fortiori, therefore, in our case ought the giving of the second person to be valid notwithstanding the preceding first petition of the relatives, since in the meantime a second petition of the minor himself intervened and was admitted by the judge; for in such a case the bishop can institute the first or the second without any fear of penalty, as in c. cum autem, eod. ti. To the same point makes well in a similar matter l. relegatorum, § ad tempus, ff. de interdic. & releg., where it is said that the judge ought not to take away the property in whole or in part from him whom he relegates; yet it adds that if he took it away, the sentence will not be invalidated; to this makes what is read and noted in l. quid ergo, § poena gravior, ff. de his qui no. in fa., where it is held that from the provision of the law the judge can depart by mitigating the penalty from the beginning, and it is said there, even if the penalty is imposed by statute, and Bal. says in l. non dubium, C. de legi., that in doubt he is seen to have departed from the penalty of the law or statute for cause. And these things seem to press strongly on the part of the minor himself, especially because suspicion seems to lie against the relatives so intruding themselves, arg. in l. quae omnia, ff. de procura. But notwithstanding these things, always saving a better judgment, I deem that the opposite prevails. And first, I am moved because the statute of the Commune of Florence, from which the judge received power, commands the judge himself to give a curator under a certain form, of which mention is made in the said statute. And since the said judge did not observe that form, the curatorship decreed by him in the second place was not valid, or at least it must be nullified; just as an election made against the form of a statute is nullified, as in c. cum dilectus, de consuet. To this makes cap. abbate, de verbo. signi., especially since in our case the statute was made by the Florentine people, and thus can be called civil law, as noted by Bar. in l. fi. ff. de poenis and l. 4, ff. de verbo. obli., especially since the Florentine city, not recognizing an emperor, has as much power in its territory as the emperor has in his, as noted by Barto. in l. hostes, ff. de capti. & postli. rever., and to this makes c. per venerabilem, qui fil. sint legi. For the aforesaid I introduce a very notable gloss in Clemen. 1 de iure patro., which says that if an order is given to one who otherwise does not have power to do something under a certain form, even though he be an ordinary, if he does it without observing the form, the act is not valid; to this make c. cum dilecta, de rescrip., and c. fi. de resti. spolia., and cap. venerabili, de off. delega., and said l. diligenter, ff. mandati; it is otherwise if an order is given to one who otherwise had power, because then an act not observing the form afterward given holds, although the transgressor is to be punished; and so speak cap. dilectus, ii 2, de praeben., and c. soli, in prin. de conces. praeben. lib. 6, with similar texts. To the point, therefore: since by the power from the Florentine statutes it is provided, among other statutes, that upon curators being petitioned for and nominated by the relatives, those nominated shall be given within fifteen days, and the cathedral judge, transgressing the form of the statute, did not give those nominated within fifteen days, nor afterward, but others, that giving of a curator ought not to hold; l. non dubium, and what is noted there, especially by Bal., C. de legi. But whenever a certain and special form of a statute is given, not only is that annulled which is done contrary to the form, but also that which is done outside the form, as is notably proved in c. prudentiam, there: "ille quippe", de offi. dele., and c. si cui, de elec. lib. 6. Nor ought the judge to be moved by unwritten equity against written law, as in l. 1, and by the gloss and the note of Bar., C. de leg., and as noted in l. placuit, C. de iud., and in l. fi. C. de trans. Nor ought the judge to wish to appear more clement than the law, as the text says in auth. de iud. Likewise and secondly, where two parties concur in a disposition, the one first attempted and presented prevails, since both cannot have effect, as in c. fi. de rescrip. lib. 6, where it is said that if two have obtained a similar favor under the same date, the one presenting first is preferred. Moreover, l. quod in haeredem, § eligere, ff. de trib., and c. ut quis duas, de elect. lib. 6, and l. praetor edixit, § 1, ff. de immu., make to this. So to the point, presupposing that the minor also could petition, since the relatives anticipated and attempted the provision of the statute, and the nomination was already made by virtue of the statute, the minor was not permitted afterward to attempt the provision of the law, unless by legitimately objecting against those nominated by the relatives; for the said path was closed to him, said l. praetor edixit, and said c. ut quis duas, de elec. lib. 6. Likewise excellently makes l. 1 and what is noted there, ff. vi bo. rapt., and auth. qui semel, C. quomo. & quando iudex. For the presumption is that the minor is not moved by good zeal, since he did not petition earlier, but only after the petition was made by the relatives. If we were to say the contrary, fraud could also be contrived, because to exclude those nominated by the relatives, the minor himself would easily nominate persons agreeable to his own ways, and thus he would evacuate the provision of the statute, which is not to be said. For fictions and frauds must be resisted, in c. quanto, in fi. de divor. For it is to be presumed that relatives advanced in age and discretion, especially since they have taken an oath on this, make a better choice than the minor himself, who does not yet have right judgment and might, enticed and seduced, petition for curators from whose care he might suffer a sad outcome; and minors, like women, often struggle against their own interests, as the text says in l. si pater, C. de sponsa; to this makes l. si vero non remunerandi, § si adolescens, ff. mandati, with similar texts. For the statute would have known how to say, had it wished, that those nominated by the relatives ought to be given unless the minor himself petitions; but it provides simply and without distinction that those nominated by the relatives be given. Hence we see that in many places statutes flourish providing that without their consent they cannot bind themselves. For they observe that that age is exposed to many deceptions and subjected to the snares of many, as the text says in l. 1, de mino. But through the intervention of the relatives, especially with an oath, the suspicion of fraud is removed, arg. in l. transactione, C. de transactionibus. Likewise, the presumption is against the minor who does not wish to acquiesce in the counsel of his relatives, argument in c. ex studiis suis, de praesum. Furthermore, the interdict of the pope can be anticipated by the ordinary through an act of citation, as in c. ut debitus, de appel., and a delegate by a delegate, as is fully noted there in c. 1, and c. si autem, and c. plerunque, de rescr.; and through citation one is anticipated, so that a change of domicile does not profit afterward, l. si quis postea, ff. de iudi., and l. cum quid, ff. de iuris. om. iud., and c. proposuisti, de fo. compe.; and thus conflicting collations by the pope and the ordinary concerning the same benefice, the one first made is preferred, in c. si a sede, de praeben. lib. 6; and in the jurisdiction of a bishop and an inferior prelate there is place for prevention, as Io. An. notes in c. pastoralis, de offi. ordi., and Inn. opines in c. quanto, eod. ti.; to this makes l. fin. C. de iurisdi. om. iud. So it must be said on the matter at hand, that where the legal and the statutory provisions concur, the first provision attempted is to be preferred; to this makes 32 q. 1 c. cum renunciatur, and what Inno. notes in c. 1 de collu. dete., where it is said

† that where two actions are available, one under the common law and the other by benefit of the praetor, one being chosen, the other remains excluded; to this make said l. quod in haeredem, § eligere, and l. ita in fi., and l. licet, ff. nau. cau. stab. From these things the answer to the points alleged above on behalf of the minor is sufficiently clear. For I admit that while the matter is intact both provisions are available; yet because the relatives anticipated the statute being commanded so that those nominated by the relatives be given, the minor subsequently attempts the legal provision as one already anticipated, as in the laws previously alleged. The second argument concerning l. quoties does not stand in the way, because that case is that by the sale the seller is only personally bound to the completion of the contract. But by delivery subsequently made ownership and possession are acquired, l. traditionibus, C. de pactis; therefore the thing becomes the second party's, and the seller is liable to the first for damages, just as he was previously bound by the nature of the contract, as noted in l. 1 and l. ex empto, ff. de actio. empti., and he can be sued for fraud, as is the notable text in l. qui duobus, ff. de falsis. It is otherwise, however, if a right in the thing had been acquired first, because then he is preferred notwithstanding the delivery made to the second party; whence if the seller had made a constitutum and had delivered, the first would nevertheless be preferred through the notable text in l. certe, ff. de preca., concerning which see Io. An. in addi. Spe. de emp. & vendi. § 1, ver. & hoc scias, Cy. in said l. quoties, and Bar. in l. si is qui pro emptore, ff. de usucap. So it must be said in the present case: for by the nomination and petition of the relatives the judge is bound to present those nominated, and the provision of the law is deemed excluded, and a right, which is now present, is deemed acquired by the nominees; to this makes what is held in the second statute alleged above, and l. severiter, C. de excusa. tuto., and it seems to be a right attaching to the thing by the sole petition, since the judge is bound to give them; to this makes what Inn. notes in c. dilectus, de of. lega. Whence the provision made concerning another ought not to be valid, both because it was contrary to the form of the statute and because the provision of the law ceased once the statutory provision was attempted, through the aforesaid. The argument from l. tutor, ff. de suspec. tuto., does not stand in the way, because I say that the judge cannot ex officio remove a tutor unless it is clear to him from the most obvious proofs that he is suspect, as the text says in the said case, which does not happen in our case; for the judge ought not to proceed according to what seems good to him, even though it may seem equitable, since a certain and determinate way of proceeding has been set forth by law or statute, as Inn. notably says in c. 1 de consti. and Bar. in l. 1, C. de legi. The fourth argument concerning c. pastoralis and c. cum autem, de iure patro., does not stand in the way, because c. cum autem proceeds by reason of the power granted to the patron so that he may vary by adding before institution; whence, parity being given between the presented candidates, the choice belongs to the bishop, as is noted there. To c. pastoralis I say the same by the same rationale: for since the lay patron is given the faculty of varying, a right is acquired by the second presenter just as by the first; therefore the institution made of the second is valid. But if the bishop, prior to the presentation of the second, spurned instituting the first without cause, he is liable in that he refused without cause to institute him before the presentation of the second; but in our case this does not occur, because the statute, trusting in the lawfulness and oath of the relatives, precisely commands that those nominated by the relatives be appointed, and thus the right of petitioning for a curator was taken away from the minor, since the matter is not intact; rather, he was anticipated by the statutory provision. The fifth argument concerning l. relegatorum, § ad tempus, does not stand in the way, because the law there proceeds further by sustaining, as appears in c. ita, so that it did not stand within the mere boundaries of the precept; and so Bald. answers that law in said l. non dubium. To l. quid ergo, I say that it speaks of a sentence;

† for the power is given to the judge of mitigating from the beginning the penalty of the law, as there, and in l. 1, ff. ad Turpillia., where see Bartol. on this, and ll. 2 and 3, § notandum, since the mind of the judge can be informed from various proofs; nor is it necessary to express the cause in the sentence, as in capitulum causam and capitulum sicut, de re iudi. If, however, the judge departs without cause in his sentence, he is punished by the penalty provided by the law, as Bart. notes in said l. 1; to this makes l. si filius, ff. de iudi., and C. de poena iudicis, throughout. But outside of a judgment the power is not so given to a judge of departing from the provision of the law or statute when no cause appears; rather, he is to be punished as a transgressor of the law, as Bald. notes in said l. non dubium, and it seems to be proved in capitulum dilectus, de tempo. ordi.; to this makes what Innocent notes in capitulum innotuit, de eo, qui fur. ordi. rece. Nor does l. quae omnia, ff. de procur., stand in the way, because I say that it ought not to be presumed against the relatives, since they do not appear to assume the curatorship for themselves, but urge that good curators otherwise nominated be given to the minor, and that the solemn provision of the city be observed; for it redounds to the ignominy of the relatives if a minor relative were reduced to poverty through bad care, arg. in l. 1 in fi. de lib. causa. From all of which I conclude that the appointment of the second curator made by the judge at the petition of the minor, after the petition and nomination of the relatives was legitimately made, is not valid, no other legitimate extrinsic cause appearing, but those nominated by the relatives are to be given, unless something is legitimately objected against them according to law. I come now to the third and last doubt, namely: whether the curator or curators given at the petition of the relatives by virtue of the above-alleged statute can be revoked at any time at the will of the minor, or must endure until the minor's full age. And in concluding briefly on this, and to avoid prolixity, I deem that they endure until lawful age. Nor are they to be revoked at the will of the minor. First, I am moved because a minor having a curator is equated to a pupil or a prodigal who is interdicted from his goods, as is read and noted in l. si curatorem habens, C. de in integ. rest.;

† but a minor cannot at his pleasure tear himself away from the power of a tutor by sole will, as is express in l. 2, C. quando tuto. vel cura. esse desic. Thus, therefore, neither can a minor tear himself from the bonds of a curator, arg. in l. illud, ff. ad l. Aquil., and capitulum cum dilecta, de confirma. uti., and capitulum translato, de constitu. Secondly, I am moved because the appointment of a curator endures to the limits of the cause by reason of which it is given; the text is in l. 1, ff. de cu. furio., where it says that if a curator is given to a madman or a prodigal, the curatorship endures as long as the madman recovers sanity and the prodigal sound morals, as in said l. 1. But since in the matter at hand a curator is given on account of defect of age, and the statute simply commands curators to be given to a minor, the curatorship ought to endure until he arrives at full age, namely twenty-five years. For within that age a minor is always exposed to the snares and deceptions of others, as the text says in said l. 1, ff. de mino. To the same point, and thirdly, makes the reasoning of l. ex facto, ff. de vulg. & pupil. Fourthly, it makes to this that if we said the opposite, the provision would be frustrating; because the minor would have nothing to do but petition for the curators to be removed, and thus the law would be without effect, and verbal rather than real, against all laws, natural reason, and all equality. Fifthly makes l. j. C. quando tut. vel cura. For it is special there that curators cease upon the arrival of puberty, because they were joined to tutors, and thus are deemed under the same law with them; whence the office of him to whom he is joined ends, as that text notably proves according to Bar. there; it is otherwise, therefore, where curators are not joined to tutors, nor given to pupils, but to adolescents, because then they endure until complete age, arg. there by the argument from a special case. Furthermore, just as the office of guardianship endures until complete age, that is, puberty, because it is given to pupils, as in said l. j. C. quando tu. vel cura., so also the office of curatorship ought to endure until full age, because it is given to a minor on account of defect of age, which defect endures until twenty-five years, as in ff. de mino. throughout, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A sentence rendered without citation and a peremptory decree, especially in a criminal matter, is of no moment.
2. The consent of private persons cannot cause a sentence that is null by disposition of law to stand.
3. No one short of the prince can retract his own sentence in its entirety.
body: Having invoked the name of Christ, against the sentence rendered against Domenico Consti, a citizen of the district of Magliano, by the lord captain presiding at that time over the aforesaid district, ex officio of the inquisition, it is asked whether any remedy is available. And I briefly state, having inspected the records presented to me concerning the said inquisition, that the said sentence is null by operation of law, and ought to produce no effect; the principal reason that moves me is that the said sentence was rendered while the said Domenico was absent and not cited, although at that time he was in prison. For that is most certain,

† that a sentence rendered without citation and without a peremptory decree, especially in a criminal case, as in our case, is of no moment, as is proved in cle. pastoralis, de re iu., even if it were rendered by the prince, as is held there; because, since defense is of natural law, that citation, which is made so that the accused may come to defend himself, cannot be abolished, as the text says there; inst. de iure nat. gen. & ciui. §. sed naturalia supports this, and what Bar. notes in l. cum mulier, ff. sol. mat. To the same point, l. j. §. item cum ex edicto, ff. quæ sen. sine app. rescin. and in c. cum ecclesia, de const. and 3. q. 9. c. omnia, de maio. & obe. c. inter quatuor, and in c. 1. de cau. pos. & proprie. with infinite similar authorities. Nor could it be validated by the omission of an appeal, as in l. si expressim, ff. de appel.; nor could he even expressly approve that null sentence, although he might ratify it after the fact, as in l. 2. C. communia utriusque iud.; nevertheless that applies so that it may be valid as a kind of contract entered into by mutual consent between the parties, but not as a sentence, as Bar. notes in the said l. 2. and in l. una, C. qui pro sua iurisd. And the reason is,

† because the consent of private persons cannot cause a sentence that is null by disposition of law to stand, since private individuals cannot dispose contrary to law based upon public utility, ff. de leg. j. l. nemo potest, and l. priuatorum, C. de iur. om. iud. But in our case the said null sentence could not be ratified as a contract for two reasons: first, because nothing was done by way of contract, as is noted in l. j.
