C. de pac.; likewise, because, since the sentence was rendered to the mutilation of a member unless he paid a pecuniary condemnation contained within a certain time in the sentence, the said Domenico could not approve the said null sentence even by agreement, because no one is the owner of his own limbs, l. liber homo, ff. ad legem Aquil., and as is expressly proved in l. non tantum, ff. de appel., where it is clear that in a corporal penalty one cannot approve a sentence through a legal remedy; c. contingit, li. j. de sen. excom. and c. si diligenti, de so. comp. support this. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the captain of the territory afterwards caused that part containing the amputation of the hand to be canceled; because I say that he could not do that after the sentence was rendered,

† because no one short of the prince can retract his own sentence in whole or in part, even if he sees it to be unjust, and this holds both in a civil and in a criminal matter, as in l. iudex, ff. de re iud. and C. senten. rescin. non pos. l. 1. and l. moris est. §. & si fortè, ff. de pœnis, where the text is most evident in our case. And this most true and undoubted conclusion can thus clearly be proved from an inspection of the records: that the sentence was rendered while the party was neither cited nor present; for this proof—namely, that it is not found in the records—suffices, as in c. quoniam contra, de prob., and there Io. Cal. expressly holds this, at least in a matter that is not very ancient, as in our case, and Io. An. in addi. Spe. in ti. de sen. §. iuxta, ver. & not. But there is a doubt: what if nothing appears except the sentence, in which nothing is said concerning the presence or citation of the party, as happens in our case; would it be a sufficient challenge on Domenico's part so that he is thus relieved by saying, 'I was not cited, nor does the sentence contain this'? The doubt is a fine one, since the time for appealing has lapsed. For if he had appealed, there would be no doubt that the burden of proving citation would fall upon the judge, as is proved in c. quoniam contra, and there commonly by the doctors, de proba., and Spec. maintains in the place cited above; on which doubt there are indeed various opinions, as Spec. recounts in the place cited above, and he seems to hold there that after a sentence has passed into res judicata, the presumption is in its favor unless the contrary is proved. But Inno. examines this article more fully in c. cum in iure, de offi. dele., and seems to incline more toward not presuming that the party was present unless this is at least expressed in the sentence, and Ioan. An. in the aforesaid addition seems to hold this position. Indeed, he relates that Guil. argued that even if the judge says in the sentence that he cited the party peremptorily and that he pronounced judgment upon that party's failure to appear, etc., it is not thereby proved that a peremptory decree preceded, because credit is not to be given to the judge, as in the said c. quoniam contra, nor to the notary writing it down, especially since it is an attestation concerning the past, as Inno. notes in c. quoniam contra, and through Bart. in auth. si quis in aliquo documento, C. de eden. It is otherwise, Io. An. says there, if it were stated in the sentence that the party was present, because then credit is given to the reporting notary, since the attestation is concerning the present. Fede. de Sen. follows this same opinion in consi. 165, where he says that a party can raise an exception against the first and second decree that a peremptory summons did not precede, and the burden of proving the contrary falls upon the adversary, because here there cannot be a presumption in favor of the sentence, since it is not established that the party was present, but rather the party denies it; and thus the things noted by Innoc. in c. innotuit, de eo, qui fur. ordi. rece. and the said c. quoniam contra, and c. cum in iure do not apply, which say that the presumption is in favor of the sentence and the process when the sentence was rendered against a person present and no appeal was taken. For it is presumed that all things were done rightly and properly, given that the party was present and did not appeal. Which reasoning ceases when it does not appear that the party was present, and this opinion pleases me as being in conformity with law and equity. For if we were to say the opposite, an unjust judge would have only to condemn an absent, uncited, and undefended party, and after the lapse of ten days the party would have no defense, since, with no other acts appearing, the presumption would be in favor of the sentence, because the time prescribed for appealing had lapsed. Likewise, if the sentence was rendered against one who was not cited, it cannot be said that it passed into res judicata after the lapse of ten days, because, since it is null, it cannot produce that effect, as in the said l. si expressim, and l. 1. & 2. C. quando prouo. non est necess. and 2. q. 6. c. ei qui. §. diffinitiua, and c. 1. de re iudi. And thus falls the opinion of Spe., who bases himself upon the passage into res judicata so that the presumption would be in favor of the sentence. And this applies most especially in our case, in which the said Domenico was in prison at the time of the sentence, and thus the sentence was rendered against an absent person, nor is lawful citation established. From all of which I conclude that, since it does not appear that the said Domenico was present at the sentence, nor that he was lawfully and peremptorily cited to it, especially since nothing is said in the sentence about citation, the said sentence ought not to be ordered for execution against the said Domenico, nor produced to any effect, unless it first be established that a peremptory citation preceded, or that he was present, etc. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. When a disposition is conceived in the name of a dignity, the successor always takes cognizance.
2. If a podestà is elected for the next six months, if during this time he cannot exercise the office, he cannot claim his office for another six months.
3. A person deputed to elect can purge the former delay after the time has elapsed.
4. Successors are bound to do those things that their predecessors were bound to do.
casus: By a statute of the city of Grosseto it is provided regarding the election of a physician in this manner: 'Because attention must chiefly be paid to the preservation of bodily health for the sick (for nothing better can be done than to restore them to health), by this special law we provide that each year in the month of January the priors of the city of Grosseto shall be bound to elect a good and qualified physician, with a salary and terms that seem to them suitable, who must reside continuously in the city of Grosseto to treat persons, from which he cannot absent himself without the permission of the priors; and if indeed he absents himself without the permission of the priors, he shall then lose his salary. And if by chance the aforesaid priors were negligent in the aforesaid matters, they shall be punished in the sum of 40 Sienese.' And it happened that the priors in office in the month of January did not elect a physician, as they were bound to do according to the form of the said statute. Wherefore the priors in office in the month of May, seeing that the election of the physician had been omitted by the said priors of the month of January, wish to elect a good and qualified physician with a salary and terms that seem suitable to them, according to the form of the statute, for the time ending on the calends of January next following. It is asked whether they may do so, etc.
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of the Savior Jesus Christ and of His most pious Mother, two matters are principally to be examined. First, to whom the election of the said physician belongs: whether to the currently existing Priors, or rather to the Priors who served in the month of January, or to the council of the people by which the aforesaid statute was enacted, or to no one, such that that power is extinguished since the form of the statute was not observed at its proper time. Second, presupposing that this power continues in some of them, whether the hiring can be made for an entire year, or only for the remainder of the time until the month of January. Regarding the first, it seems that that power for this remainder of the time belongs to no one by virtue of the aforesaid statute, because when a statute cannot be observed in all its form, its disposition ceases. For wherever many elements concur for the operation of a law, if any of the concomitant requirements fails, the disposition of the law ceases, as is proven in cap. quoniam frequenter, §. porro cunctis, and §. si vero, extra, ut lite non contesta, and l. liberorum, ff. de his, qui not. infa., and l. adigere, §. quamvis, ff. de iure patro. For it is said in the said chapter that in a matrimonial case one can proceed lite non contestata against an absent and contumacious spouse; but if the contumacy ceases, as because he is absent without fault of his own, one cannot proceed, for the things upon which the disposition of the law is founded do not concur. So it seems should be said in the present case: that since the statute requires two things—that the election be made by the Priors, and in the month of January—which cannot concur in this remainder of time, the disposition of the statute ought to cease. For it cannot be made by the council by virtue of that statute, because both requirements apply to the person of the council and both fail; for the election cannot be made in the month of January, nor would it be made by the Priors, which the statute requires. For this power was not given to the council, but to the Priors, and one must not depart from the words when the intention is not otherwise evident: l. ille aut ille, and l. non aliter, ff. de lega. 3, and c. fin., de verbo. significa. And the former Priors of the month of January cannot do it, both because it would not be done at the time required by the statute, and because this power was not conferred upon persons, but upon the office and dignity of the priorate. For the commission was made by the express name of the office and dignity, and not under the expression of persons, but remains in the dignity, as in c. quoniam abbas, de offic. deleg., and c. si gratiose, de rescri., lib. 6, and l. annua, §. j, ff. de annuis leg. To this purpose Innocen. said in the said c. quoniam abbas,

† that when a provision is formulated in the name of a dignity, as because it was committed to the Bishop of Siena, the successor always takes cognizance, and if the one who was then bishop transfers to another dignity, he relinquishes the delegation to his successor; in support of this is c. pastoralis, §. præterea, de offi. ord., and ff. de iudi., l. mortuo. For the rule is that a successor is bound to that to which his predecessor was bound: de sol., cap. 1; 11, q. 3, cap. si episcopus; 12, q. 2, cap. hæc huius placiti; 18, q. 2, cap. dubium; C. de servo corru., l. furti. By the currently existing Priors, however, it cannot be done, because it cannot be done at the time required by the statute; and wherever something is commanded under a certain form or qualification, the act is not valid unless the mandate is fulfilled in that form or qualification, as in cap. fin., de resti. spo., and l. diligenter, ff. manda., and c. cum dilecta, de rescrip.; to which makes the notable gloss in cle. j, de iure patro. For a disposition varies according to time; therefore the law said that if a usufruct is bequeathed to me for a continuous two-year period from the death of the testator, and it was the heir's fault that it was not given, I cannot seek the usufruct of the following two-year period, because a future usufruct is one thing and a past one another, but I shall seek the valuation, as in l. si ususfructus, ff. de ususfruc. leg. To the same effect is l. si non sortem, §. libertus, ff. de condi. inde. Hence it is said that if a podestà is elected for the next six months, and during this time he cannot exercise the office, he cannot seek the office for another six months, because that which is in the obligation varies according to time by the said legal authorities closely alleged, and which is read and noted in c. fi., de iudi., and by Bar. in l. et ideo, ff. de verb. obli., and the said §. libertus. But notwithstanding these points, which in truth, as will appear from what is to be said below, by no means stand in the way in our case, I think that the Priors existing for the time being can make this election. And for the first point I allege a good text in l. cum quidam, ff. de leg. 2, where it is clear

† that one deputed to choose can, after the time, purge the former default, so that an execution is made by man or by the law; for there the legatee was bound to make a good choice within the time, as is read and noted at the end of that law. And although an action is available to the fideicommissaries on account of default, nevertheless before the petition and litis contestatio, etc., he can, by choosing after the time, purge the default; and by that law Bar. says there that if a testator left certain things to be distributed among the poor whom certain persons should choose, they can, after that year has elapsed, choose and purge the default, and thus the power of choosing the poor will not devolve upon the bishop through the lapse of a year, because one appointed to choose by man or by the law can, according to him, purge the default before execution has been made by man or by the law; it is otherwise if execution has been made, as in l. si is cui, ff. commo., and what is noted there. Secondly, there also appears the text in l. mancipiorum, ff. de optio. lega., where a very notable text says that if an option is given to someone, the judge can set him a time limit for opting; and even if he wishes that, if he did not choose within the time limit, the action on the legacy should not belong to him, nevertheless it is said there that if he did not choose within the time limit, he can choose after the time limit, if the heir will not suffer loss from this, on account of which the judge made the decree. So in the matter at hand: although the time for choosing a physician was predetermined in the statute, nevertheless, since through the lapse of time the reason and cause of the statute do not cease—indeed, they militate all the more strongly—the power of choosing ought not to be excluded. For I give great weight to the preface and proem of the statute, from which one may argue when the intention of the disposer is gathered, as in l. fi., de hære. institu., and l. cum pater, §. dulcissimis, de leg. 2, and in c. ubi periculum, and there by Io. An., ne cleri. vel mona., li. 6, by Bart. in l. eum qui certarum, ff. de verb. obl., and l. ambitiosa, ff. de decre. ab or. fa. For the reason of the statute was to preserve health and to provide for the sick; which reasons certainly do not cease after the month of January, but rather increase, because the more it is deferred, the more delay will bring danger, and therefore the disposition of the statute ought not to cease. For a law must be limited, restricted, and extended according to its reason, even against the words of the law itself, as in the said §. dulcissimis, and l. 2, ff. ad Tertul., by Bar. in l. item quæritur, §. qui impleto, ff. loca., Din. in the last rule de reg. iu., lib. 6. Therefore the Priors can be censured and punished for negligence because they did not choose, but the power nonetheless endures, since that which is principally in the obligation does not vary with time. For a physician is no less beneficial if he was elected in the month of January than if he is elected now; to this effect is the good text and what Bart. notes there in the said l. et ideo, ff. de ver. obl., where it is clear that if a certain time was appointed for building an insula and part of the insula collapsed, another time for building is given, because, as Bar. notably says there, those things that vary with time must be distinguished, and in the others it endures even after the time; for since the building of the insula is principally involved in the obligation, it does not matter as to the execution of the obligation whether it is done now or afterward: said l. ideo, and the good text in l. servus, qui testamento, §. primo, ff. de sta. libe. And it serves the aforesaid points exceedingly well that near the end the statute commands the negligence of the Priors in the aforesaid matters to be punished if they have not chosen at the due time, or if they have permitted the physician to be absent, etc. For only those two things were set out before in the statute. And thus that clause punishing negligence cannot refer to anything other than those, since it speaks in the plural. From which it follows that, since it only commands negligence to be punished and does not take away the power, it seems to leave the power to them after the time; just as we say in a similar case when a statute prohibits something and afterward imposes a penalty on the one who acts against it. For by the imposition of a special penalty it seems to intend to preserve the act, as noted by Bald. following Cyn. and Joan. in l. non dubium, C. de legi. Thirdly, it is principally relevant that wherever someone is commanded to do a certain thing at a certain time, two commands are seen to exist: one, that he do it, and the other, that he do it at a certain time; and if he cannot fulfill it in time due to an impediment or negligence, he is bound to execute it after the time: the text is in capitulo cum dilecti, de dolo & contuma., l. celsus, ff. de arbi. But the Priors are commanded to choose a physician each year in the month of January; therefore, if they did not choose in time, and thus cannot fulfill the mandate in time, they are bound to execute it after the time, as I have said above. For if the words of the statute are considered, this is not granted to the Priors as a privilege, but they are necessitated to do this, as is clear from those words of the statute, "they shall be bound to choose," etc.; they ought to obey the law in the best manner they can. For this provision refers to the Priors in general, and thus the command is made not to the persons, but to the office; it therefore follows the Priors existing at any time.

† For successors are bound to do those things that their predecessors were bound to do, as in cap. adversus, at the end, de immun. eccle.; to which makes de sent. excommu., cap. gravem, and c. noverit, and the said cap. 1, de solut., along with the other legal authorities alleged above. Fourthly, there is c. si tibi absenti, at the end, especially joined with the gloss, de præb., li. 6, where after the fixed time limit for accepting, one can accept. Likewise, when the laws prescribe a time limit for electing or conferring, if they wish the power to devolve upon others after the predetermined time, they express this; otherwise, however, devolution does not occur after the time, as in c. quia propter, de elect., and c. 1, de conces. præben., and auth. hoc amplius, C. de fideicom., and c. 2, de testamen. Therefore, since in our case the statute does not provide that after the month of January devolution should be made to others, but only commands negligence to be punished, the power therefore remains, and the negligence is punished. I conclude, therefore, that the Priors existing for the time being can make this election of the physician, and I think that they will be able to hire him for an entire year, because it is principally provided by the statute that the election should take place every year, and thus each election ought to last for a year. And although the year was to be begun in the month of January, nevertheless, since it cannot be begun at that time, the year can end at a subsequent time, because that which is principally in the obligation ought not to be deferred on account of a variation of time, since time is not considered principally, but incidentally, for well-being, and perhaps because the beginning of the year is then. Well suited to the aforesaid is the text in l. servus, qui testamento, §. 1, ff. de statulib., and in the said l. et ideo, and in l. domum, ff. de contrahen. empt.; for the omission of a slight formality is not to be cared for, as in l. j, at the end, ff. de ven. inspic.; so for a trivial matter restitution in integrum is not granted: l. si ex causis, ff. de mino., and l. Seio, ff. de in integr. resti., and c. penul., de rebus eccle. non alien.; and through this the answer to the second question is clear. The contrary authorities alleged above do not stand in the way. For they speak of when something is purposely commanded to be observed as a substantial form, such that the act cannot stand without the form. For that is of the substance of the act which, being posited, the act is posited, and which, being removed, the act is removed, as noted by Bart. in l. prolatam, C. senten.; to which makes what is noted by the gloss in c. 2, de consuetu., lib. 6, and ij, q. j, c. manifesta, and what is noted in l. universa, C. de precib. impe. offe. But in our case the time was not added so as to be of the substance of the election, but rather for well-being, as is clear from the reasons set down in the statute and from the things I have said above. Likewise, in an election default can be purged after the time unless it is provided otherwise by law or by man, as has been said above. But in our case nothing is provided to the contrary, nor does the election of a physician vary with time, as I have said above. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A custom contrary to law is not valid, unless it is reasonable.
2. One church can prescribe tithes in the parish of another church.
casus: A certain church without cure of souls, for a time whereof there is no memory of its beginning, did not contribute at all with the other churches of the city to the burdens commonly incumbent [upon them], but, while the others paid pro rata according to the assessment and distribution of the whole [body], it paid nothing at all to those deputed over these matters for that church, except that within the last twelve years it is proven to have paid once, and to have contributed together with the others when the Commune of Siena imposed, by permission of the Supreme Pontiff, a certain collect for the acquisition of a certain castle. Now, however, the syndic of the whole clergy brings an action against the rector of the said church, requesting that the said church contribute together with the others to the common burdens, and make satisfaction for past ones. It is asked what the law is, etc.
body: The assistance of Jesus Christ the Savior and of His most pious Mother having been implored, it seems firstly that the said church cannot free itself through prescription either from past or from future burdens. For by common law it is certain that, since burdens fall upon all, they ought to be borne by all superiors, to which even religious are bound on behalf of their chapels and churches, as in cle. ij. §. sunt nonnulli, de censi. The rule works in favor: that which touches all, de regu. iur. lib. 6. And Innocent says in c. 1. de statu regu. that it is by diocesan law that individual churches contribute to the common affairs of the entire diocese, xij. q. ij. c. nobis. x. q. iij. c. unio. Nor does it seem that custom can relieve the aforesaid church,

† because a custom contrary to law is not valid unless it be reasonable, as in c. fi. de consue. But this custom cannot be reasonable, because shameful is the part that does not agree with its whole, as in c. fi. de spon. duorum; and it is consonant with nature that those who embrace the advantages of things should not refuse the burdens, as in cle. j. de consti.; and thus such a custom seems contrary to natural equity, and therefore imprescriptible. Nor can prescription be of avail, because although in the name of another one can allege prescription—as if it were subject to another, and bound to bear burdens at that other's command, as in c. auditis, and c. cum olim, de præscr., and noted by Io. An. in c. cum uenerabilis, de censi.—nonetheless in its own name it cannot allege this prescription, because it could not prescribe against obedience, nor separate itself from the body and from the head, as in c. cum non liceat a capite, de præscri. lib. 6. And at first glance the case in c. accedentes, de præscr. seems to bear on this matter, where the canons of a cathedral church were compelled, at the petition of the whole clergy, notwithstanding prescription, to contribute together with the rest of the clergy to providing procuration to the legates and nuncios of the Apostolic See; and the decisive reasoning of that text must be weighed, for it says 'to willing persons', and 'what hangs over all should be borne by all, etc.', and it removes prescription even of the longest time; and thus it seems from the general reasoning of that text that against common burdens prescription cannot be made by particular churches, even over the longest time. But these things notwithstanding, I hold the contrary to be truer in our case. And first, I allege for this the case joined with the gloss on the word 'legitima' in cle. j. de censi., where it is proved that prescription is of avail in avoiding these burdens—in those things, however, which are prescriptible according to the gloss there; and perhaps it added that limitation because it is doubted whether prescription runs against the cathedraticum. For the gloss in c. quicunque xvj. q. vij. held that although prescription runs as to quantity, yet it does not run entirely so that nothing is owed; however, Archidiaconus thought otherwise in c. 1. de præben. lib. 6., and more fully on this by Ioan. And. in c. cum uenerabilis, that a church cannot in its own name allege prescription. And likewise in procuration by reason of visitation, as in c. cum ex officij, de præscri.; likewise in the procuration of legates and nuncios of the Apostolic See, said c. accedentes. Some things are therefore imprescriptible, but in other ordinary burdens prescription runs, as Io. And. holds in said c. cum uenerabilis. For we see that in the fourth part of tithes and of mortuaries prescription runs even against the bishop, as in c. de quarta, de præscri., noted by the gloss in c. de statu regu.

† Likewise, one church prescribes tithes in the parish of another church, as in c. 1. de præscrip. lib. 6. and c. ad apostolicæ, de decimis. Furthermore, it is certain that by privilege some churches can be exempt from common burdens, as in said cle. j. and in c. cum uenerabilis, previously alleged; therefore also by prescription. For privilege and prescription are equated, as in c. duo simul, de offi. iud. ord., especially when it is of such length of time that no memory of its beginning exists. For in that memory it is held as a title or grant, as in said c. 1. de præscr. lib. 6., and clear in l. hoc iure. §. ductus aquæ, ff. de aqua quoti. & ęsti. and l. j. in fin. de aqua plu. ar.; for it is to be presumed that it was exempted from some lawful cause, since it did not pay for such a long time. For we see this apply in the prescription of services and census, such that it suffices to allege such time as the cause of prescription, as noted by the gloss in c. nullus episcopus j. q. j., and Io. An. in c. peruenit, de censi., and Bar. in l. cum de in rem uerso, ff. de usuris. A fortiori this must be admitted in the prescription of liberty, which is more favorable, as Io. de Lig. singularly stated in c. accedentes, previously alleged; because although in the procuration of legates and nuncios of the Apostolic See prescription does not run against the legates and nuncios themselves—in which case he understood that text—nonetheless against the remainder prescription does indeed run, so that the remaining clerics or churches are bound to the entire procuration of the legates and nuncios. For in this case nothing is detracted from the legates and nuncios, because prescription runs solely against the remaining churches; and this was a subtle consideration, although the text in my judgment somewhat resists this interpretation. It is no objection if it is said that the text in said c. accedentes admits legates of the Apostolic See, but rejected prescription, and thus prescription does not effect what a privilege does. For the answer can be threefold. First, that it speaks where prescription is not introduced with the knowledge of him who can grant a privilege; otherwise it is different, as Ant. de Bu. holds there. Second, it can be said that it does not speak of prescription of such time that there is no memory of its beginning; for that has the force of a grant, as in the laws alleged above. Third, it can be answered that it speaks in the special case in favor of the provision of legates and nuncios of the Apostolic See, just as it is special in procuration owed by reason of visitation that prescription does not run against it, said c. cum ex officii; whence that text can be adduced for this opinion by an argument a speciali, in that the text there says: 'since in such matters prescription cannot claim a place for itself', therefore it is otherwise in other, unprivileged burdens. Finally, it supports this that, just as one church prescribes against another church in its own rights, as throughout the entire title de præscriptionibus, so a fortiori the prescription of liberty against all churches ought to be admitted, which specially operates against a particular church, as Innocent notably stated in c. cum dilectus, de consue. I conclude therefore from the aforesaid and from what was noted by Io. An. in said c. cum uenerabilis, de censibus, that with the exception of procuration by reason of visitation, and of legates and nuncios of the Apostolic See, and charitable subsidy, or cathedraticum according to some, the aforesaid church can in its own name defend itself from other burdens, and even from the aforesaid, by alleging prescription against the remaining churches according to that notable opinion of Io. de Lig. It is no objection if it is said that it is now twelve years that it contributed with the others; because it would be answered in two ways. First, that tax was imposed by special right on the authority of the Supreme Pontiff on the exempt as well as the non-exempt. Likewise and secondly, presupposing that it had been imposed simply by the clergy, nevertheless, since prescription had already been completed at that time, a single act could not take it away. For a time sufficient for prescription is required, and thus forty years, since for a lesser time prescription does not run, said c. de quarta, and in authen. quas actiones, C. de sacros. eccl. In support of this is the notable gloss in l. temporalis permutatio, otherwise est. §. nemo alienæ, ff. de uerb. sign., which says that although prescription is interrupted by a single act while it is in the process of becoming, yet after it has been established, a single contrary act does not suffice to prevent it from being prescribed in the due time; on this there is a text according to one interpretation, and noted by Ioan. in c. fi. de consue. in the treatise on custom, on the fifth chapter. Nor do the other things alleged above stand in the way, because from the lapse of such time a reasonable cause is presumed, as I said above. Likewise, that church will avail itself of prescription, and not of custom; for strictly speaking it is prescription, since the right of liberty is not acquired in common, but precisely for this church. To this point, see the note in c. fi. de consue., where it is noted in what respect prescription differs from custom. And let these things suffice to the praise and glory of Almighty God. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. At the time of a transfer, the original institution is not to be considered, but the actual observance.
2. Whether the rule of canons regular is stricter or slacker than the monastic rule.
casus: A certain canon regular of the Order of St. Augustine, having expressly professed that order in a monastery in which he lived under regular observance, left the monastery out of a certain levity of mind, license having neither been sought nor obtained from his superior. And when he had wandered for some time, with that levity of mind with which he had left [?], [entering] a monastery of St. Dominic, in which life was lived not under regular, but cloistral observance according to the common manner of speaking, he again made profession in that same place. Now it is asked whether the second entry into a religious institute was valid, license having neither been sought nor obtained from his superior, but indeed with all formalities omitted, and without informing the prelate who received him into the Order of St. Dominic about these matters? Also, whether it is lawful for him on his own authority to resume his first habit and remain in his first Order of St. Augustine?
body: In the name of God, and of His glorious virgin Mother, and of the blessed Jerome, and of the entire triumphant heavenly court, amen. In the present consultation, proceeding in brief words and touching only upon the true conclusions of the doctors without any dispute of arguments, I will nevertheless endeavor to set forth the truth briefly. For the elucidation of which I premise, that if someone has professed in any of the approved religious institutes, and wishes, having left that religious institute, to transfer to a stricter or harsher religious institute or order, he ought first to seek license from his superior, as is the tex. and the glo. in c. licet, de reg., and there Ioan. And. and other doctors; and there is a glo. in c. cum singula, at the word Canonicae, de praeben. in VI. And although concerning this matter—namely, in what manner, and what is required for a religious to be able to transfer from his religious institute to another, or from his monastery to another monastery—the doctors speak variously in different places, and Spec. in the same title, §. nunc quoque, verse 24, touches upon something, and through Ioan. in c. fin. de renun., and Io. And. after others in c. non est, on the first glo., de reg., and on the gloss at the word praelatum, through the doctors in cle. j. de elect., and through Inno. in c. sicut nostris, de iureiuran., and through the gloss, Inno., and other doctors in c. significatum, de reg., and through the gloss in c. cum singula, de praeben. in VI, and there Io. Mona., and through Archi. in c. si religiosus, de testa. in VI, and through the same Archidiaco. xviij. q. ij. c. alienum, §. sed subaudiendum, and xx. q. j. c. monachum, and fully through Butr. in the gloss and the doctors in the said c. licet, de regu., in which places it is fully treated: what if a religious transfers to an equal religious institute; what if to a slacker one; what if to a different place of the same religious institute; what if to a stricter religious institute? Nevertheless, the true and indubitable conclusion of all is that if he wishes to transfer to a stricter religious institute, he ought to ask license from his superior; and then, once license has been sought, even if not obtained, he can lawfully transfer, through the laws cited above and through the doctors in the places previously named. Secondly, I premise that regarding whether one rule is stricter than another—for the purpose of preventing someone from transferring from one to a stricter one—regard is had not to the time of the rule's institution, but to the time at which he transfers, whether that to which he transfers is stricter in terms of actual observance than that from which he transfers, even though the latter was stricter from the institution of the rule; Innocent holds this in c. sane, de regu.

† because regard is not to be had to the institution, but to the observance at the time of the transfer; for which that text and the texts in c. cum monasterium and c. cum causam under the same title de regu. serve exceedingly well; which is understood within limits, as noted by Io. And. in the said c. sane, de reg., reciting the opinion of the theologians, concerning which see there; and the final gloss in c. super eo, de regula. touches somewhat upon it, and something is there; and which order or which religious institute or rule is said to be stricter than another is fully set forth by Inno. and Io. And. in the said c. sane, de reg., and fully by Pan. in the cle. ut professores, de reg., and somewhat by the doctors in the said c. super eo, and somewhat by Archi. in c. presbyteros, xx. q. iij., and there by him whether a canon regular can transfer to the monastic state, concerning which by the same Archidiac. in c. mandavimus, xviij. q. iij., and by Io. An. in the said c. sane; in which places it is also contained,

† whether the said rule of canons regular is stricter or slacker than the monastic rule, as in the chapter quod Dei timorem, de statu regula., and whether it is stricter or slacker than other rules. These things having been premised, descending to the case proposed, I think it should be said that since the said canon regular departed from his monastery out of a certain levity of mind, not by divine inspiration, without having sought license from his superior, and entered another monastery of St. Dominic, and made profession there, the transfer to the said monastery of St. Dominic was in no way valid, even presupposing that it was of a stricter religious institute, since it is required of necessity for him to be able to transfer that he ask license from his superior. For the second transfer is tainted by the failure to seek it legitimately, lest the good of obedience be contemned, through the text, the gloss, and the doctors in the said cap. licet, de regula., and the concordances there; and this the gloss intended in the chapter cum singula, at the word canonicae, de praebend. in VI, and the doctors in the places cited at the beginning. And although the gloss in the said chapter licet, de reg., disputes whether, if anyone transfers to a stricter religious institute without having sought license, he is bound to return to the first religious institute, nevertheless it concludes that if he transferred for reasons of levity, as in our case, he is entirely bound to return, according to all the doctors. The same gloss and the text there in the chapter mandamus, 19. q. 4. And there the gloss, and there Ioan. And. after Butrius in the said c. intelleximus. And this is undisputed through the doctors according to the aforesaid. Although the gloss in the said c. licet, de regula. also seems to hold the opinion that if he transferred to a stricter religious institute without having sought license not out of levity, he is not bound to return to the first religious institute, and likewise Goff. there, nevertheless Ioann. And. there, and commonly all the doctors, and Butri. at length, hold that without distinction whoever transfers to a stricter religious institute without having sought license, even not out of levity of mind, is bound to return to the first, since the transfer was in no way valid; so Ioan. An. says he saw it pronounced. Likewise the gloss holds in the chapter intelleximus, de aetat. & quali., and there Inn., and the same gloss and there Archid. in the chapter mandamus, 19. quaest. 3. And if it should be asked: what effect does this have, that he return to the first, since he will be able immediately to ask for license, and return to the second? Io. An. answers in the said cap. licet that it is enough because it satisfies the law that requires that he ask for license; he cites the chapter ad petitionem, de accu., and the chapter quia regulares, de suppl. neglig. praelato.; he adduces a parallel: just as in an unordered election, an ordained person is compelled to be admitted concerning the same, and on the same title de elect. in the chapter super eo, and the chapter innotuit at the end, and the chapter examinata, de iud. Likewise, having returned to the first, he might remain there, his purpose having changed; he cites for this c. tua, de sponsa., and what is noted there on the first gloss. Paul holds the same in the clemen. ideo, de regu., lest the good of obedience be contemned, and because perhaps, returning, he will remain in his calling. And he replies there to c. sane, de regu. The same Butr. in the said c. licet, and Io. An. there also replies to the said c. sane. From all of which it is clearly concluded that since the aforesaid canon regular transferred out of a certain levity of mind to the monastery of St. Dominic without having sought his superior's license, the transfer was not valid; which also holds true even if he had not transferred out of levity of mind, through the aforesaid. I conclude, perhaps, that he may also lawfully [do so] on a second ground: because while in his first monastery they live under regular observance, and in the second monastery, to which he transferred, they do not live under regular observance, but claustral observance—holding the opinion of Inno. in c. sane, de reg., as I said above at the beginning, which however I do not affirm for now, namely that actual observance at the time of transfer is to be attended to, not the institution of the rule, as to whether it is said to be stricter or slacker, concerning which I refer to what is noted there by Io. An. and others—nevertheless, according to Inn., the aforesaid transfer was not valid, since he did not transfer to a stricter religious institute, through the aforesaid. From all of which it is inferred, as to the second question, that since the transfer was not valid, the said canon regular will lawfully be able on his own authority to return to his first monastery, and remain in his first habit and order; and this is what Io. And. and Butr. intended in the said chapter licet, de reg., when they say that they are bound to return; text also supports this in the chapter intelleximus, de aetat. & qualita., where it is said, 'you took care to return to the first house,' etc., therefore on his own authority; which return is approved there by the text, and likewise the gloss there; the same is noted in the chapter mandamus, 19. quaestio. 3., where the text says, 'we command that he return,' as likewise the gloss there; Archid. expressly intended this there. Paul clearly intended the same in cle. 1, de reg., who says that if he does not wish to return, he is to be compelled to return. Let him return, therefore, and if he does not wish to stay there, let him ask license and transfer to the second monastery. From all of which I conclude clearly in law that the transfer of the said canon regular was neither valid nor held good, and that the said canon regular can lawfully on his own authority depart and return to his first monastery, and finally remain there in his prior habit and order, as was clearly and plainly shown and approved above. Moreover, if we should say that this monk or canon regular, by transferring to another monastery of another religious institute without having sought license, is a fugitive, he must nevertheless be given back, and also restored to the first monastery, as in c. Ioan. de regu.; indeed, he even has an action against the first monastery to be received there, as noted by Io. And. on the said final gloss, and in c. fi. under the same title; and it is read and noted in the final gloss in c. cum dilecta, de rescri., and in c. cum in ecclesiis, near the end, de maio. & obed., through Host., and in chapter 1, de infan.; Cy. Lau. expounds it, unless he has fled three times from the monastery, as Ioan. And. says in the said final chapter de regu.; or whether we should say that he rashly transferred to the said second monastery without having sought license, not to mention having obtained it (for one is said then to transfer rashly, as the gloss says there, and on it Io. An. in the chapter Ioannes), the said conclusion proceeds. Nevertheless, he seems to be of better condition in transferring to the second monastery without having sought license, since, denying it, he is not called an apostate by the rule of greater apostasy, which incurs excommunication, as Io. And. says in the said c. Ioannes; he cites c. 2, ne cleri. vel monachi, in VI. Moreover, the said transfer without having sought license is void by operation of law. Therefore it provides no impediment, through what is read and noted in the rule non praestat, de reg. iur. in VI, and in c. cum accessissent, and c. cum M., and in c. pen., de consti., in c. supplemento, so much so that a cause not confirmed because of the suppressus himself is said to be vacant, and indeed can even be impetrated as vacant, as the doctors say. Nico. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A multitude cannot be governed without justice.
2. Who may properly be called licensed in a religious order.
3. The Pope alone dispenses that someone may transfer from a higher to a lesser [order].
4. Friars Preachers transferring to the black monks, if they do not observe the Rule of Saint Benedict, are true apostates.
body: In the name of Christ, amen. Since it reached the ears of the reverend and circumspect man, the Lord Pons Stéphane, precentor of the church of Auxerre and canon of Béziers, nuncio and delegate of the Apostolic See, and visitor, corrector, and reformer of the monasteries of any non-mendicant orders in the province of Tuscany and Genoa, specially deputed by the same See among other matters, while visiting the monastery of Santa Maria of Florence, of the Order of Saint Benedict of the black habit, and currently lacking an abbot, through public report conveying that in the said monastery there were several individuals conducting themselves as monks of that monastery, publicly wearing its habit, holding the places of the monks of the said monastery occupied, and unduly and unjustly receiving the goods of the monastery to its detriment, since they are not true monks of the monastery, but apostates, fleeing from other orders, or cast out from the monastery itself, intruded against God and justice through ambition and surreption, to the danger of their own souls and to the grievance and loss of the aforementioned monastery; the aforementioned Pons, considering that according to the authority of Jerome it is not good to give the bread of the sons to the dogs, that is, to delegators and intruders, 16 q. 1, c. Si cupis, warned all and singular persons carrying themselves as monks of that monastery, and by way of injunction commanded each of them within a certain and peremptory deadline, that each of them ought to establish proof of his institution or the title which he holds in the said monastery. Before whom, within the said deadline, a certain person carrying himself as a monk of the said monastery—who was first professed in the Order of Friars Preachers and was cut off and cast out from that order under the form noted below—in order to prove the title of his monastic status and institution, produced letters of the reverend father the Lord John, Cardinal Deacon of San Teodoro, Legate of the Apostolic See and administrator of the said monastery, by whose authority he was received as a monk of the said monastery, and the process conducted by the venerable father the Bishop of Fiesole, the executor deputed for this purpose by the said Legate; the tenor of which letters, process, and license of cutting off is as follows, under this form of words, etc.: In the name of Christ, amen. In the year of His Incarnation 1334, in the third indiction, on the 19th day of the month of October. Let all who shall inspect the present public instrument know that the religious man Zenobius, son of the late Richus, underwritten, having appeared in the presence of the reverend father in Christ, Lord Thedicius, by the grace of God Bishop of Fiesole, executor of the underwritten letters of the lord Cardinal Legate, in the monastic chapter of Santa Maria of Florence, in the presence of the religious men, Lords Andrea the claustral prior, and Guglielmo Bonaventura Dosso, Enrico Salvi, Francesco Bartoli, Andrea de' Pilestri, and Benedetto, monks of the said monastery, etc., assembled as the chapter of the said monastery by command of the said prior in the customary manner, presented and exhibited to the said lord Bishop certain letters of the underwritten Lord John, Cardinal Legate, fortified with his genuine and customary seal hanging from a white cord, the tenor of which is as follows: John, by divine mercy Cardinal Deacon of San Teodoro, Legate of the Apostolic See, to the venerable father in Christ, the lord Bishop of Fiesole, greeting in the Lord. The entreaties of Zenobius, son of the late Richus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, beloved in Christ, deserve that we take care to provide for the salvation of his soul, as far as we reasonably can. Since therefore, as his petition presented to us contained, he has recently been dismissed from that order, and desires, as he asserts, to serve the Lord under the rule of that order in the monastery of Santa Maria, commonly called the Abbey of Florence, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and there to live out the remainder of his life: We, inclined by his supplications, wishing to encourage him in this laudable purpose of his, commit to your paternity and command by the tenor of these presents, by the authority which we exercise, that, if this is so, you cause the same Zenobius, by our authority, to be received as a monk and brother in the aforesaid monastery, and to be treated with sincere charity in the Lord, and that the habit of the same monastery be exhibited to him, as well as a full portion of its common fruits and revenues, just as to one of the other monks; the constitutions and statutes of the aforesaid monastery concerning not receiving apostates, and any others issued to the contrary, provided they have not been confirmed by the Apostolic See, notwithstanding in any way whatsoever. Given at Siena on the Ides of October, in the 19th year of the Pontificate of the most holy father and our Lord, the Lord Pope John XXII. Likewise, he presented and exhibited to the said lord bishop certain letters of the underwritten Brother John, the prior, fortified with the genuine and customary seal of the prior provincial of the Friars Preachers of the Roman Province, impressed in red wax, the tenor of which letters is as follows: To all who shall inspect the present letters, Brother John de Pontatiis, unworthy prior provincial of the Order of Friars Preachers in the Roman Province, greeting and sincere charity in the Lord.

† Justice, without which a multitude cannot be governed, applies punishment according to the gravity of the faults and their severity, rendering to each his right and punishing crimes, visiting affliction more in accordance with the requirement of the transgressions. Therefore, Brother Zenobius de' Albizi of Florence, who committed the gravest fault by apostatizing on Good Friday, ought to have been punished with the most severe penalty and chastised with bitter sorrows—which punishment, imposed and to be imposed as penance, he perhaps contumaciously refused. I therefore, having considered the rule of the blessed Augustine and our father, which commands the guilty party to undergo corrective punishment, and if he will not bear it, orders him to be cast out from our order and our society; having also seen and most diligently inspected the tenor of our constitutions, which calls the incorrigibility of him who neither fears to commit faults nor consents to bear punishments the gravest fault, and says he must be cut off from our order; with the counsel and assent of the diffinitors, I command that Brother Zenobius himself, who has already cast off profession from his heart, be stripped of the habit of our profession, and I cut him off from the body of our order as a useless member—not out of cruelty, but mercifully, lest he infect others with a pestilential contagion. Wanting, however, in accordance with the example of the Samaritan pouring wine and oil into the wounds of the injured man, to show compassionate mercy toward this severity, I have absolved him from the sentence of excommunication which he incurred on account of apostasy. In testimony of which sentence of expulsion and absolution, I have thought fit to append our seal of the provincialate to these presents. Given at Orvieto, in our provincial chapter, in the year of the Lord 1331, on the 22nd day of the month of September. And he humbly supplicated the same lord bishop that he deign to proceed to the execution of those things which are contained in the said letters of the lord legate. And the lord bishop, having received, read, and considered the above-written letters with due reverence, and wishing reverently to execute the contents of the said lord legate's letters in accordance with the commission made to him, having first inquired of the prior and the above-mentioned monks whether the constitutions of the said monastery against receiving apostates were confirmed by the Apostolic See, and they responding and asserting that they had not been confirmed by the See itself, by the authority of the commission and mandate made to him through the above-written letters, warned the said Andrea the prior, Guglielmo, Bonaventura, Dosso, Enrico Salvi, Francesco, Bartolo, Andrea, and Benedetto, that in accordance with the tenor of the said letters they should receive the same Zenobius into the said monastery as a monk and brother, and should treat him with sincere charity in the Lord, and minister to him the habit of the said monastery and a full portion of its common fruits and revenues, just as to one of the other monks. The lord Andrea the prior, and all the other above-mentioned monks, wishing reverently to execute the aforesaid warning, received the same Zenobius into the said monastery as a monk and brother with the kiss of peace, conferring upon him the habit of the said monastery. The lord Zenobius, accepting all the aforesaid matters humbly and devoutly, on bended knees and with joined hands, gave and promised to the said bishop, the vicar of the said lord Cardinal who received him, the customary obedience and reverence to the said lord Cardinal as his lord and prelate; and the said lord Bishop commanded me, Soldus, notary and scribe, to draw up a public instrument concerning the aforesaid matters. Done at Florence in the chapter of the said monastery, in the presence of the priest Melior, chaplain of the said lord bishop, Ser Sancio and Ser Cante, notaries, and Francesco son of the lord Sananensis of Florence, witnesses called for this purpose. I, the said Soldus Palesii of Pistoia, notary by Imperial authority and ordinary judge, and now scribe of the lord bishop, was present at all the aforesaid matters, and by order of the said father and at the request of the said lord Zenobius, I wrote and faithfully published them. It is asked whether the said Zenobius is to be considered a true monk of the aforesaid Abbey. And because a matter becomes clearer through distinctions (cf. de rescriptis, c. Super literis), and also because through distinct and particular questions the nature of the whole is more apparent, I therefore use a distinction in the present question. And first, I ask whether this Zenobius, having been thus cast out, is understood to have license to transfer to another religious order. Secondly, whether the legate’s letter granted to him concerning the said monastic status is valid. Thirdly, whether the process held by the Bishop of Fiesole is valid. Fourthly, whether the reception by the monks holds, since they treated him as a monk, or not. And I say that he is not considered licensed, but rather cast out with ignominy.

† For he is properly called licensed who transfers to another order with the license of his superior, as in Extra, de regularibus, c. Licet, with similar texts. And that such a cast-out person is considered cast out with ignominy, cf. de statu monachorum, c. Ea quae. For it is one thing to be cast out, and another to be a fugitive or apostate, as in de regularibus, c. ult., and in the Extravagant of Benedict, Pastor bonus, because there they are posited as distinct. Nor is mention made there of the licensed; and why? Because the licensed transferred with license and in due manner, so that thus they are not to be recalled; cf. excellently de renunciatione, c. Quidam, where, once license to renounce is obtained, one is compelled to renounce. And likewise, once license to transfer is obtained, one is compelled to transfer. But others, such as fugitives and the cast out, are to be recalled, as in the laws cited above; therefore they are not licensed, since superiors are compelled to recall them annually; cf. excellently, and it seems to be the case of the law in Dig. de his qui notantur infamia, l. Quod ait praetor, § Ignominiae causa, where it is evident that one dismissed simply is not understood to be dismissed for reason of ignominy. But when one is dismissed for reason of ignominy, this is always expressed. Yet here, in our case, it is expressed that he is cast out for reason of ignominy; therefore he is not simply licensed, since he was dismissed or cast out for reason of ignominy. Likewise, from another reason it is evident that he was dismissed or cast out for reason of ignominy. For he was stripped of his military insignia, that is, of the insignia of religion, as is evident in the said § Ignominiae; therefore, both by reason of the expression made in the dismissal or casting out, and by reason of the degradation, he is considered dismissed or cast out for reason of ignominy; therefore, such a one cannot be called licensed, since these are very different things, as was said above; certainly, I do not see how he could be. Likewise, as is evident in the letter of expulsion, no license is given to him to transfer to any order or monastery; on the contrary, the doctors say that an abbot ought never to give his monk license to transfer to another order unless he first has a monastery prepared; otherwise he is an apostate if he departs otherwise, as noted by Innoc. and Host. in de renunciatione, c. ultimo; therefore it is evident that even if it had been said in the letter of expulsion that he might transfer to some religious order, without expressing a certain monastery, it could not be called a license, because it would have been given contrary to law; therefore, much less when the master in the letter of expulsion says nothing about this there; indeed, if the letter of expulsion is well considered (which is very remarkable), it is evidently concluded that that cannot be called a license which does not exist. Likewise, as to the second question, I say that the legate's letters are void ipso jure. For they were impetrated by concealing the truth and expressing falsehood, and thus such letters are invalid, as is evident in de rescriptis, c. Super literis; indeed, it is provided by law that in such letters nothing should be concealed that ought to move the grantor’s mind toward denying or granting, as in the said c. Super literis, in the gloss on the word 'Ex hoc', and Io. And. in de rescriptis, in c. Gratia, in the Sext, in the gloss 'quia et hoc', and in de rescriptis, c. Postulasti, and Archi. in de praebendis, c. Non potest, in the Sext, and 1 q. 7, c. Hi qui, with similar texts. But what foolish person would say that the legate would have granted it, had he known that he was cast out on account of his own so disgraceful demerits, and that he had apostatized on Good Friday? Certainly no one doubts that he would not have given him such a letter; indeed, he stated that he was licensed, as is evident in the Legate's letter, which was false, as is evident above and through the form of his expulsion. And thus the Legate ought to have understood a due license granted from a probable cause, and not an ignominious one; cf. Cod. de his qui veniam aetatis impetrant, l. fin.; therefore, as was said, the letters through which the reception of him was made are null, as in de rescriptis, c. Ad audientiam I and II. Likewise, this also supports the point: because when something is predicated of a primary and a secondary sense, stated simply it is understood to be given in the primary sense, as noted in Dig. si ager vectigalis petatur vel emphyteuticarius sit, l. 1, where under the name of ownership direct ownership is understood, not beneficial; therefore the same holds concerning license. Likewise, if you consider well, in the Legate’s letter it is said, 'if it is so'; and yet it was not so, nor did the bishop conduct an investigation regarding this, as appears in the process of the Bishop of Fiesole, and thus he exceeded the form of the mandate, and thus what was done by the bishop is invalid, even if the Legate’s letters were valid; cf. de rescriptis, c. Cum dilecta; for such mandates must be observed diligently, as in de praebendis, c. Cui de non sacerdotali, in the Sext, and Dig. mandati, l. Diligenter, with similar texts. Since therefore these letters are void and the process is void for the above-stated reasons, it is evident that the reception and the monastic status are void, because he was received by virtue of those letters and process. Likewise, as to the third question, I say that such a process is null, and this through the laws cited above. It is no objection if it is said that if it is commanded to someone to provide for a person with such a benefice, the provision holds even if provision is made to an unsuitable person, as noted by Innoc. in de praesumptionibus, c. ult., and touched upon by Io. And. in de officio delegati, c. Quia judices, in the Clementines, if the condition of him who impetrated the letters is well considered: it sounds in a condition and not in an admonition, as through what is noted there by the said doctors. And what is done while a condition is pending is null; it is otherwise when it is commanded to someone, 'provide for such a one, if he is suitable', for then, since at first sight anyone is presumed suitable, as in the said c. ult., unless the contrary appears, no proof or examination is necessary so that he must prove himself suitable. But when it is said, 'if he had a license', or the like, he certainly is not presumed to have a license unless he shows it, just as we say he is presumed suitable unless the contrary is proved. But this license does not show him to have been cast out on account of his demerits. And thus, since he did not have a license, and the mandate was given under the condition 'if he had a license', it is expressly evident that what was done by the Bishop of Fiesole is null, as in the laws cited above. Likewise, as to the fourth question, I say that the reception by the monks, and the fact that they treated him as a monk, does not make him a monk; for it is clear that these monks always relied on the consent and letters of the said Legate and on the process of the bishop. For this is evident, because they were commanded to receive him according to the tenor of the said letters of the lord Legate; and thus they received him, and thus they always intended and treated him according to the tenor of the said letters. But the tenor of the letter and the process were null, and thus the reception was null. For they are presumed to remain in that will in which they were at the time of the reception, unless it is proved to have changed, as in de baptismo, c. Majores, and de eo quod metus causa, c. Perlatum, and Dig. de probationibus, l. Eum qui, and Dig. de legatis II, l. Lucius, with similar texts. Indeed, even if they had consented expressly and had received him notwithstanding the letters, the process of the Legate and of the bishop would not be valid. The reason is that the reception of monks belongs to the Abbot and the monks of the said monastery both by law and by custom, as in de electione, c. Cum ecclesia Vulterrana, in the second gloss; therefore their reception would not make anyone a monk; rather, the consent of the Legate was necessary, because at that time the power of the abbot was in that monastery by virtue of the fact that he was the commendatory of that monastery, and the legate does not command him to be received as abbot, but rather as legate, as is clear from the form of the legate’s letter. Indeed, even the Legate as commendatory, and they themselves, could not receive him, because if it is well considered, he was cast out from the Order of Preachers, where there is the greatest regular observance, and in the aforesaid monastery there is not so great an observance as in the aforesaid order, as is notorious; cf. de regularibus, c. Sane. Indeed, perhaps he could not even have transferred with the true and express license of the lord Legate, even though the truth had been expressed to him. Highly relevant to the aforesaid is the decretal Sa-

† -ne. For that anyone should transfer from a stricter to a milder order, the pope alone dispenses; noted by Io. An. and Io. Monachus in de praebendis, c. Cum singula, in the Sext. And thus, since this man did not transfer legitimately, he is in the case of revocation according to the form of the aforesaid decretal Pastor bonus; it is evident that neither the right of monastic status nor the transfer would hold. It is no objection if it is said: 'Friend, granted that they did not make him a monk by the fact that they treated him as a monk while the legate was alive—because the creation of monks belongs to the legate as commendatory and to the convent—nevertheless, after the Legate died, they treated him as a monk, and then they themselves can make monks when the monastery lacks an abbot, as in de regularibus, c. Si ad solum, in the Sext.' Certainly, as has been sufficiently stated, they did not consent anew, but are understood to continue in that initial consent; or else they could not even make or receive him expressly, let alone tacitly, as was proved above. Likewise, because by special Apostolic privilege it is granted to the Order of Preachers that the professed of the said order cannot be received or transfer to the monastic status of the black habit. And note, for if you consider well, you will not find that this Lord Zenobius made the customary obedience to the bishop receiving it in the stead and name of the Legate, because such a promise of obedience does not induce regular profession. For clerics make such a promise, as in de majoritate et obedientia, c. His qui. But when someone transfers from one religious order to another, although he made profession in the first, nevertheless in the second he ought to make a promise, especially where the rules are different, as is the rule of St. Augustine, which the Preachers hold, and the rule of St. Benedict, which the monks of the aforementioned Florentine abbey hold. And thus it is evident through the texts cited above that this Lord Zenobius, who is not, nor ever was, a monk in the said monastery of the abbey, is thus to be expelled from there as an intruder. And for greater stability, I, Francesco, archpriest and canon of Florence and doctor of decrees, have caused the present consilium to be fortified by the appending of my own seal. I, Francesco di Pietro de' Magistri, archpriest and canon of Florence, doctor of decrees, find and advise just as is above written and alleged, and for greater firmness of strength I have subscribed to this present consilium with my own hand and caused it to be fortified by the appending of my seal. I, Recupero di Guglielmo of San Miniato, doctor of decrees, agree to all the above-stated things, and thus advise as is contained above; in testimony of which matter I have subscribed to the aforesaid consilium with my own hand and ordered my seal to be appended. I, Simone, son of the late Bernardo, judge of Bagno, together with the aforesaid lords Francesco and Recupero, and by their authority, have advised that it be done as is written above, having been consulted by the said Lord Pons; and therefore I have affixed my seal, etc. I, Io. An., having weighed all that has been written and having diligently deliberated upon the motives of the lords Francesco, Recupero, and Simone, counseling and subscribing as is evident above, etc., having invoked the names and suffrages of Christ, and of His Mother, and of the blessed Jerome, advise the same: namely, that Brother Zenobius, concerning whom inquiry is made, is not, nor has been through the things described above, a monk of that monastery which is called the Abbey. And adding to the motives of the said lords, it is to be noted that in the letter of the lord legate that man said that he was recently licensed; but before the executor he proved that he had been cast out more than three years prior. By which expulsion, even if he could be called licensed (which is denied), it had nonetheless been given not recently, but more than three years before. It is not, therefore, that which the executor ought to have seen. For, as the doctors say, 'recently' (nuper) is an adverb composed of novum (new) and tempus (time), as it were novum for noviter; since, moreover, beyond six months is called 'for a long time' (diu), de concessione praebendae, c. 2 (concerning this I wrote in de fide instrumentorum, c. fin.), therefore beyond three years is not 'recently', especially in this matter, because not even for a single day ought a monk to be without a monastery, 16 q. 1, c. Placuit, and l. 2; moreover, if this had been expressed, it would deservedly have moved the legate to deny it, as above, since lapse of time aggravates fault; the laws are well known. Secondly, it must be noted, unless there was a falsity in the calculation, or in the instrument drawn up concerning the execution: for to one observing that the first year of the Pontificate of Pope John began in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1316, on the 5th day of September, which was then the year of the Incarnation 1317, it can easily be established that on the 19th day of October in the current year 1334, it precedes the Ides—that is, the 13th day of October—of the year of the Lord of the Pontificate of Pope John perhaps by an entire year, namely by 6 days less. And thus it is concluded that the execution of the letter was performed almost a year before the date of the letter. Thirdly, I assert that I tenaciously hold that even if the new constitution of our Lord [Pope] had not issued, nor had the privilege of the aforesaid then been in force, concerning which I spoke above,

† Friars Preachers who transfer to the black monks and do not observe the rule of Benedict are true apostates, as I wrote fully on the aforesaid decretal Sane, de regularibus; and in testimony of the aforesaid assertion, I have caused a certain seal to be appended to this writing with my own hand, etc. Nicolaus, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A sentence can be confirmed in a cause of appeal as to the merits of the cause.
2. One alleging one cause in his appeal may withdraw from it and prove another.
3. A person accused after a denunciation cannot initiate an accusation against another; nevertheless, before condemnation he can pursue and complete it, but not after condemnation.
4. A cause of nullity lodged before the pronouncement of three sentences ought not to be hindered on account of supervening sentences.
body: Having invoked the protection of our Savior Jesus Christ, I shall address in order the four doubts that are drawn from the facts. The first is whether the last auditor, who delivered the said threefold sentence, was able, after the said sentence, to decree the aforesaid remission, since by that sentence he had discharged his office with respect to the case of nullity. And setting aside the arguments that could be made for the contrary side, I consider that the said remission could be made, notwithstanding the sentence delivered upon the instance of appeal. I am moved to this opinion principally because the cause of nullity and of appeal can be pleaded together and in the same libel or proceeding, according to the opinion of all the doctors, which the common style of the courts commonly approves, although some ancient doctors leaned toward the contrary view. The first opinion, however, is preferable and more common, as noted by Bar. and others in l. si expressim, ff. de appel. and l. j. C. quæ sent. sine app. refcin., and noted by the Canonists in c. dilecto, de appella. These two causes, of nullity and of appeal, can also be pleaded separately, even at different times, as in cle. j. de re iudi., joined with the gloss on the word donec. And what is more, one can proceed concerning nullity even after an appeal has been deserted, as in c. licet, de sen. excom. lib. 6. and noted in c. sæpe, under the same title in the ancient acts, and after three sentences delivered upon the same point, as in the said cle. j., joined with the previously cited gloss. Since, therefore, these two causes of nullity and of appeal are distinct and of distinct effect, by the sentence that the judge pronounces upon the instance of appeal, it cannot be said that he has discharged his office regarding the cause of nullity; for wherever several causes are committed to a judge, unless it was expressly stated in the commission that he decide them simultaneously, by a sentence rendered in one cause he is not said to have discharged his office with respect to the remaining ones not yet definitively settled; whence he may proceed to the decision of the other causes, as is proved in l. quid tamen, ff. de arbi. This applies even if they are such causes as naturally have some connection between themselves, like the petitory and the possessory over the same property, which on account of identity must be handled before the same judge, as in c. 1. de cau. poss. & prop. and in l. nulli, C. de iudi. and in c. fi. under the same title. And yet the judge who delivered the sentence in the possessory is not said to have discharged his office with respect to the petitory, although both causes were committed to the same judge together, as in c. ad ultimum, de cau. poss. & proprie. and c. significauerunt, de testi. and c. cum ad sedem, de rest. spo. and cle. unica, de cau. pos. & propie. is relevant. Whence, in our case, the causes of nullity and of appeal were committed to the last auditor; although that judge rendered a sentence upon the instance of appeal, he cannot thereby be said to have discharged his office regarding the cause of nullity; and consequently, since he remained judge in the cause of nullity, he could decree regarding that remission to the parties, since by that sentence delivered upon the instance of appeal the question of nullity was not laid to rest, because, as I said above, these causes are distinct.

† For a sentence can be confirmed in a cause of appeal with respect to the merits of the case, and yet the first sentence could be a nullity from a defect of judicial order, because it was delivered on a court holiday or on another ground. Hence it is that the laws provided that, even after an appeal on the case has been deserted, one can proceed on nullity, as in the previously cited cle. 1. This is also clearly proved by parallel in the said cle. 1, in §. similiter, joined with the gloss on the verse impediri, where it is evident that if, before an appeal from the third sentence confirming the two preceding sentences, the prosecution of a prior appeal from a grievance is not impeded, it must be stated all the more strongly in our case, since the cause of nullity is more necessary than the cause of an appeal from a grievance; therefore its cognizance ought not to be impeded by the pronouncement of the third sentence. And especially since this was not in the mind of the judge pronouncing the third sentence, who immediately after that third sentence granted the remission to the parties to prove the articles given in the cause of nullity itself. For from the things that followed immediately, the mind of the judge is sufficiently gathered: that he confirmed the prior sentences with respect to the merits of the case, but not with respect to the cause of nullity pending before him; otherwise he would have been contradictory to himself, which is not to be presumed, since he proceeded immediately upon the cause of nullity; arg. in l. non ad ea, ff. de condi. & demo., l. lecta, ff. si cer. pe. and in cap. officii, de elect. Moreover, if one can proceed concerning nullity after three sentences, as in the said cle. 1, joined with the previously cited gloss on the word donec, all the more should one be able to proceed upon a cause of nullity already attempted prior to the rendition of three sentences, since a lesser suspicion of malice arises in this case than in the preceding one; arg. in l. is qui reus, ff. de publ. iud. And this as to the first doubt. Now I shall address the second doubt, in which it is asked whether the decree of the said remission was superfluous, and consequently improperly and in vain granted, because other grounds of nullity, beyond that which arose from the falsity of the said instrument, appeared established from the articles given by the said Bar., although the judge had not accepted them, nor had the cause of nullity been concluded. To this doubt it seems to me entirely necessary to answer in the negative, namely that that decree of remission was not superfluous, although nullity might have been more fully established from other articles. I am moved principally because no one is prohibited from using multiple exceptions or defenses, even if any single exception or defense suffices by itself, since one should not restrict oneself to one type of exception or defense, as one could fail in it for lack of proofs and, through the non-proposing of others, unjustly succumb; as is proved in the rule nullus pluribus, de reg. iu. lib. 6. and l. nemo, ff. de reg. iur. and in what is read and noted in capitu. 2. de test. and in cap. exhibita, de iud. and in cap. cum iamdudum, de appella. and in capitu. audita, de restitu. spolia. and in capitu. conquerente, de cleri. non residen. and in cap. auditis, and in cap. cum olim, de præbend., fully by the gloss in the said rule nullus pluribus. It is clearly apparent that one can use various defenses in the same cause, even though they are not all necessary to obtain victory; but by way of precaution one may use such diversity, so that if proofs fail in one, one can prevail from the others. For the abundance of proofs must not be narrowed; l. curent, ff. de testi. And capitu. si fortè, de electio. lib. 6. and in c. ut circa, under the same title and book, support the aforesaid excellently, and this must especially be said in our case, in which the person alleging the nullity of the sentence grounded himself principally upon the defect of citation. For such a defect undoubtedly renders the sentence null, since citation is the foundation of the trial, as in institu. de pœna teme. liti. near the end, 3. quæst. 9. cap. caueant, and cap. 2. irruerunt, and in l. de unoquoque, ff. de re iudi. and in cap. ecclesia S. Mariæ, de constit.
