Whence this exception of nullity ought not to be excluded as principal and indubitable on account of other exceptions of nullity, concerning which there might perhaps be doubt in law or in fact, and perhaps the proofs will be more readily available to prove the defect of citation than with respect to the other defenses of nullity. From which it is concluded on the second doubt that the decree of the said remission was not frustratory, nor was it unjust, although other grounds of nullity had been alleged. And to the aforesaid the text in l. scio quæsitum, §. in fi. ff. de app. supports well, where it appears

† that one alleging a single cause in his appeal can withdraw from it and prove another, because he can justify his appeal in any ways whatsoever, as the text says there at the end. To which what Bar. notes in the said l. si expressim, in the verse quæro si prosecutus est, ff. de app. supports excellently, where he further says that if someone expressed only one cause of nullity in the libel and was defeated, he can subsequently prosecute another cause of nullity, just as we say in a real action, as in l. si mater, §. 1. and in l. & an eandem, §. actione, ff. de execu. rei iud. and in c. abbate sanè, de sen. & re iu. li. 6. All the more, therefore, from the beginning can he prosecute multiple causes of nullity, as in the laws cited immediately above. To the third doubt, namely whether before the execution of the said three sentences the cause of nullity introduced prior to the said third sentence can be heard and pronounced upon; and it seems at first that it cannot, through the text in the said cle. 1. de re iu. in the 1st response, where it is said that he who has received three sentences against himself ought not to be admitted to act or to except concerning their nullity, or that of any of them, until sentences of this kind have been fully committed to execution. Since, therefore, the person inquired about has received three sentences against himself, he ought not to be admitted to act or except concerning nullity before the execution of the said sentences. Nor does the said text distinguish whether the cause of nullity was attempted beforehand or is attempted afterward, but simply excludes him from the power of acting or excepting prior to the execution of those sentences; therefore, although the person inquired about was admitted before the pronouncement of the three sentences in the cause of nullity, nevertheless after the pronouncement of those three sentences he ought no longer to be admitted, since from the pronouncement of those sentences presumed malice immediately arises against the actor. But, these things notwithstanding, I consider the contrary opinion more true in law, namely that even before the execution of the three sentences, prosecution in the said cause of nullity can take place, provided that no impediment regarding the execution of the three sentences is posed by the party who succumbed in the principal matter. And first, the text in the said cle. j. strongly persuades to this opinion, and first by reasoning in this manner: for the disposition of that cle. j., which forbids that anyone can act or except concerning nullity before the execution of three sentences, introduces new law, as appears from the opening words there: ut calumnijs litigantium obuietur, etc.; deservedly it ought to have application only within its own terms, since it operates to the prejudice of the person acting or excepting concerning nullity; argu. in the rule odia restringi, de regu. iur. lib. 6. and in l. ij. §. si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in loc. pub. But the text there speaks of when three sentences have been rendered, so that in that case one is not admitted to act or except concerning nullity before their execution. In our case, however, action or exception concerning nullity was not taken after the pronouncement of three sentences, but before; deservedly that text does not claim a place for itself in our case. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that by prosecuting the cause of nullity after the third sentence one is said to act concerning nullity; because I say that it is not properly said to act now, but rather to prosecute an action previously brought before the pronouncement of the third sentence. For it is one thing to act concerning nullity after the pronouncement of three sentences, and another to prosecute an action attempted before their pronouncement; because the text in the said Clementine presumes malice in the person acting or excepting concerning nullity after the third sentence has been promulgated, both on account of the presumption that arises from three sentences rendered on the same matter, and because, from the fact that it is not lawful to appeal a third time, he is presumed maliciously to act or except concerning nullity in order to be able to impede the execution of the sentences; which reasons cease in our case. For since this party acted concerning nullity before the pronouncement of the three sentences, since immediately after the first sentence he raised nullity, and thus at that time when the ability to appeal was open to him, the said presumptions of malice and of impeding the execution of the sentence cease; deservedly he ought to be admitted to the prosecution of the nullity, as in the present matter. And the text in the said l. is qui reus, ff. de publi. iudi. supports this excellently by parallel, where it is clear

† that an accused person after a denunciation cannot initiate an accusation against another, yet before condemnation he can prosecute and complete it; after condemnation, not so, as is more fully contained in the said l. is qui reus; so it seems must be said in the present matter. And for this interpretation the text in the said clemen. j. in the 2nd response, joined with the gloss on the verse impediri, seems to stand, where it is held that if he against whom three sentences have been rendered appealed from a grievance before their pronouncement, he is not impeded after their pronouncement from prosecuting the appeal previously lodged from the interlocutory decree. That alone is provided there: that under pretext of the appeal the execution of those three sentences is not impeded. Whence it must be noted that the text there in the second response does not speak as in the first part of that Clementine; for in the first part it is expressly stated that after the pronouncement of three sentences one is not admitted to act or except concerning nullity before the execution of those sentences. But in the second response it is only said that under pretext of an appeal previously interposed, execution ought not to be impeded; whence it does not forbid the prosecution of an appeal previously interposed from a grievance; and this the gloss most clearly intended on verse 1 on the word impediri, at the end. And it must be noted that he who says that he previously appealed from a grievance is in effect said to prosecute the nullity of the subsequent definitive sentence, because, if the appeal is pronounced legitimate, the subsequent definitive sentence is null, as delivered by one whose jurisdiction was suspended by a legitimate appeal, as in c. non solum and in c. si a iudice, de appel. lib. 6. and in c. super quæstionem, at the end, de offi. deleg. And nevertheless the appellant is not impeded from prosecuting it after the promulgation of the third sentence, provided that the execution of those sentences is not impeded. Just so must it be said punctually in our case,

† that a cause of nullity interposed before the pronouncement of three sentences ought not to be impeded on account of supervening sentences. For it is enough that by its virtue it does not impede the execution of the sentence; and equity strongly supports this opinion, for since the cause of nullity was attempted at a legitimate time, it ought not to be impeded on account of a supervening event, arg. in the rule factum legitimè, with what is noted there in the gloss, de reg. iu. lib. 6., and so that the judicial instance does not vanish in vain, contrary to l. properandum, C. de iud. Moreover and lastly, this is nowhere expressly prohibited; therefore the prosecution ought not to be impeded, because what is not expressly sanctioned is not to be presumed through superstitious contrivances, as in c. consuluisti, 2. q. 5. And this regarding the third doubt. To the fourth and last doubt, in which it is asked whether, assuming the nullity of the first sentence, the remaining two sentences confirming the first, which was null, ought to be deemed and judged null and invalid by that very fact, because they confirm a null sentence, of whose nullity at the time of the other two sentences there had not been full cognizance nor discussion. To this doubt it is easily answered through the text in the said cle. 1, joined with the 1st gloss on the verse donec and on the verse impediri. For I say that a sentence in the cause of nullity renders the other sentences ineffective; and if execution was made, it ought to be retracted. For a null sentence does not deserve to be called a sentence, as l. 4. §. condemnatum, ff. de re iud., and the other following sentences are rendered ineffective as relying upon the first sentence, which was null, arg. in c. inter dilectos, §. cæterum, de fid. instr. Moreover, the second sentence, or its effect, was suspended by the subsequent appeal. The third sentence, however, did not simply confirm the preceding, but only with respect to the merits of the case. Whence, regarding nullity, the judge immediately gave remission to the parties. Whence, just as the pronouncement of three sentences previously rendered does not prevent one from being able to proceed anew concerning nullity to the effect of retracting the execution of those sentences, as in the said cle. 1, joined with the gloss on the word donec and on the word impediri; so and all the more three sentences ought not to impede the effect of a cause of nullity attempted prior to the pronouncement of the three sentences. And let these statements suffice regarding the fourth and last doubt, etc. And thus, as concluded by me above, I, Nicolaus, Abbot of Munich, referendary of our Lord the Pope, consider it to be the law.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A privilege granted while a suit is pending, without mention being made of the pendency of the suit, is not valid.
2. An innovation occurs if a privilege is impetrated with the pendency of the suit kept silent.
3. In doubt, a superior is not presumed to prejudice the right of others.
4. A privilege, insofar as it tends to the prejudice of others, must be strictly interpreted.
5. A second rescript is not invalidated by the fact that it makes no mention of the first, if the first was null.
6. Two impuberes, if they intend to contract marriage de praesenti, and express words suitable for contracting marriage, contract betrothal de futuro.
casus: ...dary [?], and auditor of his chamber; and in witness whereof I have subscribed with my own hand, and caused my usual seal to be affixed, always saving a sounder judgment, etc.
body: With the protection of Jesus Christ our Savior invoked from the heart: In the case and question that is presently pending between the canons of the church in Celeracolsi, plaintiffs on the one side, and the lord Johannes Messer, plebanus and canon of the aforesaid collegiate church, on the other side, concerning the revenues and proceeds of the prebend and canonry of the said church belonging to the said Johannes, it is asked in law whether an indulgence or favor granted to the said lord Johannes by our most holy lord Pope Eugenius for receiving the fruits and revenues of the said canonry in absence for five years subsists in law; so that, without contradiction by the said canons, he may freely receive the revenues and fruits of the said canonry. And first, to elucidate the matter, it seems that the said favor is of no moment, especially to the prejudice of the pendency of the suit; which is proved as follows.

† A privilege granted during the pendency of a suit, without mention being made of the lis pendens, does not subsist in law, as in capitu. fin. ut lit. pen. and clemen. 2. eo. titu., joined with the gloss on the word innouaui, and capitu. causam, il 1. de test. But the aforesaid privilege was issued while a suit was pending, nor did it make mention thereof; therefore, the said privilege is null. And that it was issued while a suit was pending seems to be most clearly proved by the text of the said clemen. 2. ut lit. penden., where it is held that a suit is said to be pending, so far as concerns that nothing be innovated, after a citation has been issued by a competent judge and has reached the party, provided that in that citation those matters are expressed through which the party can be fully informed about what he is being sued for in court. And more clearly to this purpose, the gloss intimates this there on the word innouatum,

† which said that an innovation occurs if a privilege is impetrated with the pendency of the suit kept silent. In our case, however, such a citation preceded; or, what is truer, although the citation was general, nevertheless, when the said lord Johannes appeared, on the part of the said canons it was petitioned in court that the said lord Johannes ought to be compelled by the judge to leave to the aforesaid canons the fruits, revenues, and proceeds of the canonry and prebend which he held in the said collegiate church, on account of his non-residence in the aforesaid church. And if he was informed in court that he was being sued regarding the fruits and revenues of the said canonry, therefore he could not impetrate a privilege regarding them without mention being made of the pendency of the suit. For if the pendency of a suit is induced by a bare citation with the expression of those things concerning which he is to be sued (said clemen. 2), it ought all the more strongly to be induced by a general citation, where an expression was later made in court by way of a petition, since a judicial expression ought to effect more than an extrajudicial one; to this makes what is read and noted in capitu. uenerabilibus. §. similiter, de senten. excom. libr. 6. Furthermore and secondly, from another ground, the said privilege collapses, namely from a defect in the intention of the grantor. For the apostolic lord granted that favor with a certain limitation: he willed, namely, that it should not be valid if another favor had otherwise been granted to the same lord Johannes by apostolic or ordinary authority in perpetuity or for a certain time regarding the receiving of the same fruits in absence. But favors were committed to the said lord Johannes in perpetuity by the lord abbot, to whom the said church belongs with full right; therefore the apostolic favor was of no moment. For here the favor was granted by the lord abbot in perpetuity through capitu. licet canon, in fin. de elect. lib. 6, where it is clear that an ordinary short of the pope cannot dispense in perpetuity—that is, for the life of the beneficiary—regarding non-residence in a cathedral church. Thirdly, the said favor is attacked because the condition upon which our lord granted it has not been fulfilled, namely, if the lord abbot and the parishioners of the said church should consent, who nevertheless did not consent. Nor does the lord abbot even wish to consent, although he says he does not wish to infringe what was done by his predecessor, if it subsists in law. But that favor made in perpetuity was not valid, especially as to the canonry, regarding whose fruits to be received in absence no mention was made in the favor of the lord abbot; deservingly, as something odious, it ought not to be extended to the prerogative rights of the said canons, argument in capitu. 2. de filiis presbyt. lib. 6 and the rule odia restrinxi, de regu. iur. lib. 6.

† Nor is a superior presumed in doubt to wish to prejudice the right of others, as in capitu. super eo, de offic. delega. and in l. 2. §. si quis a principe, ne quid in loco public. And Innoc. said in cap. cum dilecti, de don. and Joan. Andr. in cap. olim, de uer. sign. and Barto. in l. fin. ff. de consti. princi.,

† that in so far as a privilege tends to the prejudice of others, it ought to be strictly interpreted; therefore the said lord Johannes cannot base himself upon that favor of the lord abbot, so that by virtue thereof he could be said to have had the consent of the lord abbot. But these notwithstanding, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer in law: namely, that the said indulgence is valid in law, the aforesaid notwithstanding, since the pope can grant a favor notwithstanding any statutes whatsoever of the church; because in such statutes the authority of the pope is understood to be excepted, even if they were confirmed by oath, as is read and noted in cap. constitutus, de rescr. And not only expressly, but also tacitly can the pope grant an indulgence concerning non-residence, just as if he grants two cure churches to someone, he is seen tacitly to dispense concerning non-residence in the other because of the impossibility, and the gloss notes this in cap. non potest, de præben. lib. 6; and a privilege granted by a prince ought to be enduring, as in reg. decet, de reg. iur. lib. 6. The apostolic lord, moreover, granted the said favor notwithstanding any statutes whatsoever of the said church; therefore he willed to remove the said statutes with respect to that favor, for so general a mention suffices, as in clem. dudum, prope fi. de sepul. Moreover, no defect can be imputed to the said favor, at least that is apparent. The motifs made above do not stand in the way. And first, to that which is objected concerning the pendency of the suit, it can be answered in multiple ways:

† First, that at the time of the impetration the suit was not yet pending; for the favor preceded that citation by many months. For the favor was made in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1421, as is contained at the end of the apostolic letters. But that citation was issued in [14]32, as appears in the acts of the same case. And thus that objection ceases entirely. Secondly, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the suit had preceded the favor, nevertheless it did not have to impede the validity of the favor itself, because if the citation or petition is well weighed, the favor did not come to the prejudice of the suit, for litigation was being carried on concerning one thing, and the favor was obtained concerning another. For the suit was concerning past, or then present, fruits and revenues, as appears in the first and second petitions made in the name of the canons; regarding those to be received in the future, no question had been initiated, nor could it be initiated, since no right belonged to the canons to future revenues, whether the fruits were owed to the canons on account of non-residence with the canons; therefore, before contumacy in not residing, it did not

† belong to them; and contumacy regarding non-residence could not exist except with respect to past time, or then present, since in the future the said lord Johannes could have resided and taken the fruits; moreover, the tract of future time does not pertain to the judge, as in c. Romana, §. caueant, and what the gloss notes there, de senten. excommu. lib. 6, and l. 1. §. 1. ff. de usur., whence it is said in the text: although a debtor under interest is in default in the present, and thus present interest is owed according to civil law, nevertheless on account of a default in the present, interest cannot be demanded for future time, since the debtor cannot be said to be in default, and thus every petition ceases, as is said in the noted text. So punctually must it be said in the matter at hand. For the said lord Johannes did not impetrate a favor regarding the receiving of past or present fruits, but regarding future ones, as appears in the grant of the favor. For the apostolic lord granted that from the date of that favor for five years in the future he might receive the fruits of the canonry and church, although he did not reside there, but in the church of Saint Stephen; and thus the favor in no way prejudices the suit that had been moved, nor is it impeded by that pendency of the suit, since an inference is not made from different things, as in cap. 2. de transla. præla. and l. neque natales, C. de probat. Furthermore, the force of a privilege is annulled on account of the pendency of a suit lest anything be innovated to the prejudice of the suit itself, as the text clearly states, especially around the gloss in the said clemen. 2. But the said favor causes no prejudice to the suit, as was proved above, since it does not refer to other fruits concerning which there was contention, nor to the impediment caused by the said Johannes concerning which in truth there was contention, as is clearly gathered in the second petition of the said canons, since the favor was only made for five years from the day of the date, regarding which no impediments could have been presented; therefore in no way does the favor touch that suit, and consequently its validity cannot be impeded by that pendency of the suit, and this is the indubitable truth itself. The second motif does not stand in the way, namely that that favor was conditional—if another regarding the same fruits had not preceded—and here the favor of the lord abbot had preceded. It is answered that our lord the pope had regard to a favor that would have had validity in itself; because words are to be understood with effect, nor ought those words to be referred to a favor which did not hold in law, since it could not be called a favor; to this effect l. 3. ff. quod quisque iur., and by Innoc. in c. cum omnes, de const., makes l. 4. §. condemnatum. ff. de re iud. and c. relatum, de cler. non residenti. For our lord the pope placed that clause—and it is of the style of the Curia—lest anyone should obtain two favors concerning non-residence to the prejudice of the churches; which rationale ceases if the preceding one could not obtain effect in law, and the rule of law non præstat, de reg. iu. lib. 6 succeeds; to this makes what is similarly noted in c. ex tenore, de rescript. and in cap. relatum, de iure pat., where it is noted

† that a second rescript is not invalidated from the fact that it does not make mention of the first, if the first was null; whence the laws invalidating a second on this ground do not have place, because they ought to be understood of a first rescript that was valid, as is noted in the laws recently alleged. To the third and last motif it is answered that in the facts it is presupposed to me that the parishioners consented. Likewise, the lord abbot had already consented at the time of the favor, as appears from the grant of his favor or dispensation. For although the dispensation was not valid with respect to the fruits to be received on account of the things said above, nevertheless from it is gathered the will and consent of the lord abbot. For he wished, as far as was in his power, to grant a favor to the said lord Johannes so that he might not reside in that church; whence succeeds that rule of law: 'if what I do is not valid as I do it, let it be valid as it can be valid,' in capitul. unico, de desponsalib. impuber. libr. 6, joined with the gloss on the word matrimonium, and in capitul. à nobis, eod. titul. in the old [decretals]. Hence the text of the civil law says that often an obligation arises outside of that which is done, as in l. si is qui. §. ultimo, ff. commoda.

† And especially makes the said capitul. unicum, where it is held that if two minors below the age of puberty intend to contract marriage de præsenti, and express words suitable for contracting marriage: because they cannot contract marriage on account of age being an impediment, by interpretation of law they contract espousals de futuro; because they are seen to have wished to consent to each other in every way they could. So must it be said in the matter at hand, that although the lord abbot could not give that favor in perpetuity, he nevertheless consents tacitly that the said lord Johannes should not reside there; and the lord pope requires nothing else for the purification of his favor except to have, among other things, the consent of the lord abbot; and when this intervenes together with the consent of the parishioners, he grants the privilege concerning receiving the fruits in absence, any statutes whatsoever of the church to the contrary notwithstanding. I conclude, therefore, from all the aforesaid, that the said favor of the lord pope made for five years is valid in law, the statutes and customs of the church and the contradiction of the canons in no way standing in the way. And so, as concluded above by me, I say and advise that it is in accordance with law. I, Nicolaus de Cecilia, abbot of Munich and general auditor of the Apostolic Camera, have subscribed with my own hand in testimony of the aforesaid, and have caused my accustomed seal to be impressed. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. What is required in order for something to be called public.
2. One who maliciously conceals himself, or prevents a citation from being able to reach him, is held as cited.
3. Publicity is caused by the character of the place and the multitude of bystanders.
4. A notary ought not, without the authority of the judge, to add anything after the instrument has been delivered to the party, and especially after it has been exhibited in judgment.
5. If an instrument is found to be false in any respect, everything contained in that instrument lacks the firmness of binding force.
body: Having implored the aid of the Savior Jesus Christ, this question of law is presently asked: whether, having considered three instruments produced in judgment—namely, first, the instrument of acceptance, provision, and induction into bodily possession; likewise another instrument produced in the third instance, of the petition for induction into possession, and of publication and acceptance; likewise whether, by the relief granted by our lord the Pope, satisfaction is said to have been made to the rule of the same lord Pope Eugenius, in which he willed in effect that one accepting a benefice by virtue of an expectative grace is bound within a month from the time of acceptance to cause provision to be made to him, and within the other three months immediately following is bound to publish the acceptance and provision so made in the place of the benefice: otherwise, as to this, the grace, acceptance, and provision are null. And first, it seems that the said rule was satisfied in three ways. First, by the instrument produced in the first instance. For therein it is contained in effect that the proctor having the expectative grace accepted the parish church concerning which there is dispute, and by virtue of the acceptance obtained provision, and was also inducted into possession by the ring affixed to the door of the church, in which for a certain time he stood, remained, and slept as possessor; and thereafter committed the church to a certain chaplain in the name of his principal; all of which things were accepted in the cemetery of the same church, and concerning all and singular a public instrument was drawn up by a notary in the presence of four witnesses. For by these things it is sufficiently clear that satisfaction was made to that rule of the lord Eugenius. For not only within the month or three mentioned in the said rule, but immediately and in the same continuous context, he accepted the church, obtained provision, and published the acceptance and provision in the place of the benefice. For although in the instrument nothing is said of this publication, it was sufficient to do that from which it resulted as published, by the argument of those things which are read and noted in c. cum Ioannes, de fide instru. and in c. licet ex quadam, de testi., that publication intervened from the acts contained in the said instrument, appears first: because the acceptance was made and the provision followed in a public place where all were able to understand; to this point, c. 1. de postu. præl. where it is said that

† to this end, that something be said to be public, it is not required that knowledge of it be impressed upon the ears of every single person, but it is enough that it was done publicly. Moreover, he was openly inducted into possession by the circle or ring affixed to the door of the same church, and finally introduced into the house of the endowment of the church; there, as possessor, he stood, remained, and slept, and also finally committed the same church to a certain chaplain; which deeds surely cannot fail to be notorious, as in c. quanto, and what is noted there, de transl. præla., where there is a good text. Likewise, concerning all these things a public instrument was drawn up in the presence of four witnesses called for this purpose. Therefore, he sufficiently published the acceptance and provision, both in respect of the place and of the public person, as well as of those things which were done publicly and almost notoriously, especially since that is sometimes wont to be called public or manifest which can be proved by witnesses, as is noted by the gloss in c. vestra, de coha. cle. & mu. and noted by Inn. in c. tua, eod. tit., and especially must this be said in our case, since in the said rule it is not said that the acceptance and provision must be solemnly published, but it is simply said that it be published in the place of the benefice. For it is one thing that something be ordered to be published, and another that something be ordered to be solemnly published, as there is a notable text regarding both in Clem. causam, de elect. It is no objection if it be said that the publication was not made in the church, but outside the church: because I say that it is sufficient to be in the church since it is before the church, as is the text in the said Clem. causam, joined with the notable gloss on the word *in domo*. Moreover, the aforesaid rule does not say that it must be done in the church, but in the place of the benefice; now the cemetery and the house of the church's endowment are called places of the church, such that possession can be grasped through the circle or ring of their door; and no one will be able to deny that that is the place of the benefice. To the aforesaid, the text in c. sicut antiquitas, 10, q. 4, makes well, and the text in c. si quis contumax, of the same causa and quaestio, joined with the first gloss, makes better, along with what Bar. notes in l. meminisse, ff. de off. procons. From all of which it is clear that the said rule would be satisfied through the instrument produced in the first instance, and this by the things which I have stated above in respect of the first instrument. Likewise, and even more strongly: because in the second instrument it is openly stated that the proctor having the expectative grace requested the said expectation and provision to be published, and that in the act of this petition they went to the accepted church during the solemnities of the Mass; yet they found it closed by the parishioners shut up inside, and though the subexecutor knocked loudly and asked for the door to be opened, none of those who had shut themselves in wished to open it, maliciously, lest induction into possession and publication of the provision be made in the same church; concerning which impediment a public protestation was made then and there. And the subexecutor, as much as in him lay, published the due acceptance and provision in the same place, and said publicly that they had been made. It is therefore not to be imputed to the party if the provision or publication was not otherwise made in the church. For it can sufficiently be said to have been made, since those parishioners, among whom it ought to have been done, impeded it and closed the church in which they wished to make publication; an excellent argument on a similar point is found in the chapter quoniam frequenter, in § porro, ut lite non contesta, where he is held

† as cited who maliciously hides himself or prevents a citation from reaching him; to the same effect is the rule *imputari non debet, per quem non stat*, de regulis iu. in 6. And these things I have said as to the second instrument. Thirdly, that also in respect of the relief granted by our lord the Pope, the previously alleged rule does not stand in the way of the said provided party; for the lord Pope commanded that, once the premises contained in the said instruments were established, proceedings should be taken in the said case just as if full and sufficient satisfaction had been and were made to the said rule concerning publication; and the lord Pope can supply every defect of solemnity, 3, q. 6, c. hæc quippe, in c. 1, de transac., and he can treat an enacted constitution as unmade so far as legal effect is concerned, as is the text in c. 1, joined with the notable gloss on the word *pro infectis*, de immuni. ecc. But these things notwithstanding, I deem the contrary opinion to be truer in law. And first, for the foundation of the decision of this question, one must see how the said rule is to be understood, insofar as it commanded the acceptance and provision to be published. In which matter I think it must be said that publication can be taken properly and principally in two ways: First, that is said to be published which is brought into notoriety. Second, when through publication it passes into the public report of the place, as is the notable text in cap. tua, de coha. cle.; whence that is asserted to be public which is notorious by evidence or by report, as there; and in favor of the first is the notable gloss in 2, quæstio 1, c. de manifesta, which says that public is what is open to all, citing a good text in Instit. de suspec. tuto. in § consequens; yet I do not understand that it must be manifest to everyone in the city, but it is enough that it pass into the knowledge of the neighborhood or of the greater part in which the act is performed, just as we say of the notorious, as is a good text in c. cum dilectus, de purga. cano. and noted by the doctors in cap. vestra, de coha. cle. & mulie. and in capitul. de manife. 2, quæstio 1. Therefore, in order that something may be called public, or be published, it must be done so publicly and openly that it passes immediately or successively into the knowledge of the people of the neighborhood, or the greater part thereof, just as we say of the manifest, as noted in the pre-alleged capitul. vestra. And to the aforesaid, the notable gloss makes exceedingly well. And on our subject, there is a singular gloss in Clem. 1, de sepu. on the word *publice*, where the text provides concerning one publicly excommunicated; and the gloss there, entering into the matter of who is said to be publicly excommunicated, says that

† publicity is caused by the size of the place and the multitude of bystanders. Hence it does not suffice, according to that notable gloss, for someone to be said to be publicly excommunicated, that the judge on the bench excommunicated him in the presence of two or three witnesses, as if wishing to say that when the law requires the publicity of some act, to the effect that knowledge of that act be presumed among others, it must be understood of publicity or notoriety which consists in fact, and not of that which is caused by the law. In our case, however, it cannot be said that publication of the acceptance and provision intervened, taking publicity as it ought by law to be taken, as appears from the aforesaid, and will appear more clearly from the answers to be added to the arguments to the contrary. And first, according to the order, I shall touch upon those things which result from the contents of the first instrument. For although the proctor of that John who holds the expectative grace requested in the presence of four witnesses that provision be made to him of the church previously accepted by him, and that he be inducted into possession of it, and the subexecutor made provision to him and inducted him into possession by the circle or ring of the church door, it cannot nevertheless on this account be said that publication of the acceptance and provision intervened, because all these things could happen in that way in the presence of four witnesses, and yet pass not at all into the knowledge of others; nor is it said in the instrument that any others besides those witnesses were present. For publicity does not result from the fact that an act is done in the cemetery, or in the church, or even in the square, in the presence of four witnesses only; but it is necessary, as I said above, that the act be done before such a multitude that the act passes into the knowledge of at least the greater part of the neighborhood. Nor does it avail that he remained in the house of the church's endowment, slept there, and finally commended that church to another chaplain: because all these things can happen without publicity. For all these things could happen in the presence of those four witnesses alone; and that an act occurred does not prove that it was public, when its publicity could happen to be absent from it, as in c. 2, de transla. præla. and in l. neque natales, C. de proba. And that the aforesaid things are true is strengthened by this reason: for the aforesaid rule of the lord Pope requires, among other things, two requirements: first, that provision be made within a month of receipt; second, that publication of the acceptance and provision follow within the other three months. For it is certain that proof must be made of the provision, that it intervened within the month, as in c. unico, ut eccle. benefic. Therefore, what follows in the said rule concerning the publication to be made must be understood of another solemnity than the presence of three or four witnesses. For if publicity were brought about by the presence of three or four witnesses, it would have been enough to require proof concerning the provision; and yet the said rule, beyond proof of the acceptance and provision, required that the acceptance and provision must be published in the place of the benefice. It must therefore necessarily be understood that publication be made otherwise than through the presence of three or four witnesses. Nor does c. quanto, de transla. præla. stand in the way, because it speaks when a bishop passes from one bishopric to another, which cannot fail to be notorious, since he publicly acted as bishop in both places. To Clem. causam, de ele. the answer is that although the text there makes mention of publication simply, and of that which is made solemnly, yet the text does not say there that publication is said to be made in a place frequented by the people, as in prejudications and the like. But simple publication must be made at least before a multitude, so that knowledge thus passes into at least the greater part of the neighborhood. And by this the answer is also clear to those things which are contained in the second instrument as to this: that the aforesaid proctor requested, namely, his said provision to be published in the place of the benefice, and that by the act of the parishioners closing the church publication could not follow in the church. For if he could not have the presence of those who were in the church, he ought to have published his provision otherwise, for example by bringing in other parishioners of both sexes who were not in the church, or in the cathedral church, or in another public place, as in the said Clem. causam, where there is a good text, especially joined with the gloss on the word *publicari*. Nor does it stand in the way that the said subexecutor said that he published his acceptance and provision: because publication did not depend on the bare will of the subexecutor himself, but it was necessary that publication be made in deed, as was prescribed by the rule of Eugenius, our lord Pope; and where deed is needed, words do not suffice, as in c. 1, with the notes there, de eo, qui mit. in pos., to which makes l. alimenta, C. de neg. gest. It can also be answered to the said second instrument in another way, namely, that it does not make proof, since it is said to have been drawn up at the same time as the first, and yet many things are contained in the second itself which could not, at least plausibly, coincide with the contents in the first. For each instrument is said to have been drawn up in the year of the Lord 1432, on the first day of the month of June, at the hour of terce, or thereabouts. And yet in the first instrument it is said that the aforesaid proctor accepted the said church, and requested provision of it to be made to him, and that he be invested with the same, and inducted into the bodily and actual possession and of the rights and pertinences of the same church. And it is added afterward that the said subexecutor made provision of the said church to him, and invested him, and inducted him into bodily and actual possession and of all its rights and pertinences by the touching of the ring affixed to the door of the same church. And then the same subexecutor led the aforesaid proctor to the endowment house of the same church, and through the handing over of the seat, book, and missal inducted him into bodily and real possession; because, as is stated in the said first instrument, for a certain time the same proctor as possessor in the proctorial name stood, remained, and slept, and thereafter committing the same church to a certain chaplain to be governed, departed to his own affairs. In the second instrument, however, drawn up at the same hour, as is said, it is stated that the said proctor, who a little before had accepted the said church, and had obtained provision of it to be made to him, requested and required the said subexecutor to induct him into real and actual possession in the proctorial name, and to publish the acceptance and provision made of that church. And finally it is added in the said instrument that the said subexecutor, at the request of the said proctor, went to the said church at the time when Masses were being sung there, and finding it closed by the parishioners, taking the ring of the door, knocked forcefully before the said church and asked for it to be opened, and with those parishioners shut in there refusing to open, a public protestation was made, and he delivered the said ring into the hands of the said proctor, thereby, as he asserted, inducting him into possession of the same church as much as he could, and said that the said acceptance and provision had been published, etc. Then, a little after, going to the endowment of the said church and being present in it, nonetheless through entering the said endowment house and the assigning of the seat and book, he also inducted him into possession of the said church. All of which things, if well weighed and considered, are truly impossible or implausible. For either the notary drew up the second instrument by supplying many things that were not in the first, such as concerning the publication, the closing of the church, and the like; and this he could not do, both because these newly added things were drawn up under the guise of a new instrument,

† and because it is not lawful for a notary, without the authority of a judge, to add anything after an instrument has been delivered to a party and especially exhibited in court, as in our case, fully through Io. An. following Spe. on the date of the Sext, and through Bar. in l. si librarius, ff. de reg. iur.; or else he drew up two instruments as if upon duplicate acts, and this cannot be on account of the contradiction which results from their tenor, or the implausibility. For, since he had been inducted into possession by virtue of the first instrument, in vain did he seek to be inducted again, as is stated in the second. Likewise because in each instrument it is stated that he was inducted at the same hour into the endowment house of the church, and thus it is not plausible that the act was duplicated at the same time. Furthermore, in the first instrument it is stated that, having been introduced into possession of the house of the church, he stood, remained, and slept there for some time; in the other instrument, drawn up at the same hour, it is stated that after the acceptance and provision the proctor requested his subexecutor to induct him into possession and publish the acceptance and provision, so that many contradictions and implausibilities arise from the tenor of both instruments, as will be plain to one who looks upon them. Therefore, credit is not to be given to the second instrument on account of contradiction and implausibility, as in c. imputari, de fi. instru., and in l. scripturæ, ff. eod. ti., and in c. quia verosimile, de præsump., and through Inno. in c. fraternitatis, de hær., where among other things he says

† that if an instrument is found false in any part, everything contained in that instrument lacks the firmness of strength; and on account of the falsity of this instrument, less credit is to be given to the first, as on a similar point is noted by Inn. in c. prætereà, de test. cog. And by this the answer is clear to those things which are contained in the first and second instruments. With respect, however, to the relief granted by our lord the Pope, it can be said that it does not hold, as having been obtained by subreption, since it was suggested to the lord Pope that all things were true which are contained in the said instruments; nor can full proof be made of them, as appears from the aforesaid; to this effect c. super literis, and c. postulasti, de rescript. Nay rather, the lord Pope expressly makes the relief with the condition, 'if the premises are established,' etc., which clause is implied even if it had not been expressed, as in capitul. 2, and what is noted there, de censib. I conclude therefore from all the aforesaid that satisfaction was not made to the said rule of our lord Pope Eugenius by the contents of the said instruments and the aforesaid relief. And so, as was concluded above by me, I deem it to be the law. I, Nicolaus de Tudeschis, abbot of Maniacio, referendary of our lord the Pope and general auditor of his camera, have subscribed in testimony with my own hand and have caused my accustomed seal to be impressed, always saving a better judgment. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One succeeding into the place of another ought to use that right which he in whose place he succeeds has.
3. A conservator cannot proceed except upon what is notorious.
4. An appeal may well be made from the sentence of a judge declaring someone to have incurred the penalty of the law.
5. Although a despoiled person has obtained possession in judgment, he can nevertheless sue separately for the penalty of l. si quis in tantam.
body: Having invoked from the heart the protection of our Savior Jesus Christ, for a clear and lucid writing and decision of the case, several doubtful points must be drawn out, and I shall examine them briefly. First, whether natural and civil possession was acquired by the said count through that invasion of the castle and expulsion of the officials. From this I shall infer the second doubtful point: whether similar possession of that castle—namely, both natural and civil—was acquired by the said bishop through the donation of the community. Third, whether it was lawful for the aforesaid knight, especially on his own authority after the lapse of six months, to invade that castle, possessed not by his ejector, but by the bishop, the donee. Fourth, whether the said count acted justly in occupying that castle at the request of the conservator of the said bishop after the exceptions and appeals lodged by the said knight. Fifth and last, whether against the said count the said knight could lawfully bring the condictio of l. si quis in tantam, C. unde vi, seeking namely that he be deprived of every right, if any belonged to him in the aforesaid castle, and that it be adjudicated to the same knight; and if no right belonged to the same count, that he be condemned to pay the valuation of the aforesaid castle to the same knight. Concerning the first, I say very briefly that civil and natural possession was acquired by the said count through the first occupation made by him, and the said knight was despoiled even of civil possession; because since the knight had officials in the said castle, and thus possessed through them, by their ejection he totally lost his possession, as is the text in l. fin. C. de acquiren. posses., and the doctors there commonly affirm this, especially Barto.; to the same effect is a good text in cap. ex parte, supra, de rescrip., and through the gloss and the doctors in capit. olim, tit. 1, de restitu. spolia. And from this an inference is drawn to the second doubtful point, whether that possession passed through the donation made to the aforesaid bishop. And certainly, since delivery of possession intervened, there passed to him that which was with the said count, and no more, as in l. traditio, ff. de acquiren. rerum domi., and in capitu. nuper, de dote post di. resti.; l. 1, §. si vero uxori, ff. de acquiren. posses. supports this, where it is evident

† that possession passes even from an invalid contract. Therefore, the possession that was with the count passed to the lord bishop, the donee, but not the ownership, since it in no way resided in him. To the third doubtful point, namely whether it was lawful for the aforesaid knight to recover possession de facto and on his own authority, especially after the lapse of six months, taking into account that not the invader, namely the count, but the bishop was then possessing—who had not despoiled, nor ordered him to be despoiled, nor ratified the spoliation, since the spoliation had not been made in his name, and consequently he could not ratify it, as in c. cum quis, de sen. excom. in VI, and in the rule cum quis, de reg. iur. in VI. And it seems first that it was not lawful: because since the interdict unde vi did not lie against the bishop, as he neither despoiled, nor ordered him to be despoiled, nor ratified the spoliation, as is proved in c. cum ad sedem, de resti. spo., all the more does the extrajudicial remedy of fact not lie, so that he could cast him out on his own authority. For if the legal remedy fails, the remedy of fact, which is more odious, ought to fail, by the argument in auth. multo magis, C. de epis. & cleri., and in c. cum in cunctis, in prin., de ele., especially since the laws granting the power of immediately recovering possession speak and provide against the invader, and are grounded on violence—namely, that it is lawful to repel force with force, as in the said c. olim, tit. 1, de resti. spo., and noted in c. significasti, de homi., and l. 3, §. cum igitur, ff. de vi & vi ar., and what is there noted, especially by Bar. Moreover, the laws require that the recovery of possession on one's own authority must be done immediately, as in the laws cited above. Hence Bar. says in l. 1, C. unde vi, that it must be done within three days. But here that knight waited for six months; therefore it was rather a spoliation than a fictitious continuation of possession or a repelling of violence. But notwithstanding these points, I consider the contrary opinion to be truer. I am moved first by cap. saepe, de restitu. spol., where it is evident that one who knowingly receives a thing from a despoiler is equated with a violent person; wherefore against such a person a possessory remedy lies, just as against a violent person, as there, and noted in c. cum ad sedem, eod. tit.; and what is read and noted in c. quia vero, de iud., supports this. Deservedly, such a defective and quasi-violent possession could not, nor ought to, impede the former possessor from immediately recovering his possession, since such a receiver is said to succeed to the defect (said capitu. saepe and capitu. quia vero). But the said bishop received the castle from the count knowing it had been invaded by the said count, since that invasion was notorious in the locality, whence he is not presumed to have been ignorant of it, 41. distin., c. quod dictis, and de praesump., capitu. quanto,

† and he who succeeds into the place of another must enjoy the same right as he into whose place he succeeds, as in capitu. ecclesia, ut lit. pen., and capitu. recolentes, de sta. regu., supports this. Nor does what was said above stand in the way, namely that such recovery must be made immediately, because it must be said that something is said to be done immediately when it can be done conveniently, without turning aside to unrelated acts, as in l. 2, §. confestim, ff. ad Tertul.; whence in our case Barto. spoke most clearly in the said l. 3, §. cum igitur, ff. de vi & vi arma., that the circumstances could be such that even after six months from the time of the ejection they would say it was done immediately, and he poses almost an example on our very terms. And the same appears to be the mind of the gloss and the doctors in capitu. significasti, de homici. For this knight was absent and infirm, and he had to deal against a powerful man, so that with these things taken into account, he can well enough be said to have recovered immediately. By which it is concluded that it was lawful, even against this bishop and within the predetermined or premised time, to recover possession of the said castle on his own authority, as he did. It can also be said that he repelled force with force, as in the laws cited above. I come to the fourth, whether the said count acted rightly in occupying possession of the castle at the requisition of that conservator. And proceeding conclusively, I firmly believe that he did not, on multiple grounds. And first,

† because a conservator cannot proceed except upon what is notorious, as in cap. 1, as noted there, de offic. deleg. in VI. But in our case, although the act of expulsion had been notorious, the wrongdoing was not notorious; rather, it was alleged on the part of the knight that that expulsion and recovery of possession could be done justly and without any offense, which is clear from the points broadly alleged; and so it was done, and they conceded the offense and the notoriety of the offense; yet the conservator could not proceed further as upon something notorious, as the gloss clearly affirms almost in our very terms in the said cap. 1 next alleged. And although it may be replied on the contrary that, the offense being denied and the deed confessed—as, for instance, because he says he acted in his own defense or with the intention of recovering his possession—it was lawful for the conservator for his own instruction to inquire through witnesses, even in the absence of the party, into the notoriety of the wrongdoing, as is noted there by Joan. And. in the said capitu. 1, which this conservator seems to have done; yet to this it can be answered that the offense here could not be notorious, since no offense underlay it, whence there is no quality without a subject, 32. quaestio. 2, capitulo quod vero non formatum, and capitu. ad dissolvendum, de despon. impub. And thus, since he proceeded to further steps without pronouncing the deed and the offense to be notorious, his sentence was not valid, nor was his process, since in truth he was not a judge, as the quality upon which jurisdiction is founded was lacking, as is fully noted by Innocen. in capitulo praeterea, de dilat., and in capitu. tua, de cohabi. cler.; l. in delictis, §. de tractatu, ff. de noxa. supports this, and it is fully noted by the doctors in capitu. si clericus laicum and capitu. cum sit generale, de foro compe. And even if he had pronounced the deed to be notorious, the validity of the process would nevertheless not be induced, by virtue of the subsequent appeal, which has the effect of extinguishing or suspending what has been adjudicated, l. 1, ff. ad Turpil., and l. 1, ff. de poenis, and capitu. venientes, de iureiuran. And although an appeal cannot be made in the case of a true notorious fact, as in capitu. cum sit Romana, de appella., yet an appeal must be possible from the sentence of a judge declaring a fact to be notorious, since the judge might have declared it unjustly; just as in a similar case the gloss notably says in capitu. cupientes, §. quod si per viginti, de elect. in VI, that although one does not appeal from a sentence of the law, as in c. quia vero, de ap.,

† yet an appeal may well be made from the sentence of a judge declaring someone to have fallen into the penalty of the law. Whence, since in our case an appeal was lodged to the conservator at least on the fact, for such a person it was not lawful for the count to obey a judge whose sentence or jurisdiction was suspended on account of the lodging of an appeal, since an executor ought not to obey an evidently inequitable mandate, as noted in c. pastoralis, §. quia vero, de off. deleg.; for the secular judge ought to lend his arm at the petition of the ecclesiastical judge when it is implored according to God, but not unjustly and to the detriment of another, as the text says in c. 1, de off. ord. at the end, and the doctors there. And that the bishop proceeded unjustly is evident, beyond the aforesaid, from the sentences pronounced in this manner of cause, as is said above in the description of the case. Supporting the aforesaid is a notable statement of Barto. in l. iuste possidet, ff. de acqui. poss., where he says that one is not excused from an offense by the precept of a judge or a decree if the judge did not proceed duly. Therefore, the count is not excused by the precept of the conservator, especially since he had seen that the city wished to impede the force of the appeal through its arm. Indeed, he is presumed from past conduct to have acted with malicious intent, arg. in c. scribam, and what is there noted, de praesump. From the aforesaid an inference is drawn to the decision of the last principal doubtful point, whether against the said count the knight could bring the condictio of l. si quis in tantam, C. unde vi, in the manner aforesaid. And setting aside arguments, I think it must be said that he could, on two grounds. First, on account of the first invasion made violently. For even though someone thinks the thing is his own and that it is lawful for him to take the thing on his own authority, he nonetheless incurs the penalty of that law, as in the said l. si quis in tantam, and Inst. vi bono. rapto., §. 1. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that, since the said knight had administered justice to himself on his own authority by taking back the aforesaid possession, he ought no longer to have the capacity to bring the condictio of that law, since the vice of violence seems purged, argument in l. 2, C. quod met. cau. For to this it is answered that the disposition of that l. si quis in tantam provides regarding two things. First, that the invader be compelled to restore to the possessor the possession which he took away; and in this respect that law is not penal. Second, that he lose the ownership of that thing if he was the owner, but if he is not, that he be compelled to pay the valuation of those things; and in this respect that law is penal. Whence, although the intention of that law has been satisfied through the recovery of possession, since he cannot nor ought any longer to be compelled to restore possession, inasmuch as it has been recovered, nonetheless the disposition of that law remains regarding the second, penal part, so that as a penalty for the violence he loses the ownership thereof if he was the owner; otherwise the offense of violence would remain unpunished. For the count was not punished in any way by the recovery of possession made by the knight, since the knight only recovered his own property which he was lawfully entitled to recover, as proved above; and for this is cited the Magna Glossa in the said l. si quis in tantam, a little before its end in the version quod si egi, which concludes that if the despoiled party first sued only for the thing, nevertheless an action remains for the penalty, since the penalty of that law is owed by action, not by the office of the judge. And thus it most clearly intends

† that although the despoiled party has obtained possession even in court, he can nevertheless afterwards sue separately for the penalty of l. si quis in tantam. This is to be said all the more strongly in our case, in which he did not first sue in court merely to recover possession, but recovered his possession out of court by using the permission of the law. And this I think proceeds according to law without any doubt; for he does not sin who acts by the authority of the law, as in l. Gracchus, C. de adulte., and 24. quaestio. 3, capitu. qui peccat. And on a second ground an action can be brought against the lord count by reason of the violence alleged the second time; because, as I have said above, the conservator did not proceed duly nor rightly in invoking the aid of the secular arm, especially after the appeal had been interposed, as proved above, and as was also clear from the sentences delivered afterwards; therefore the count incurred the penalty of that l. si quis in tantam, even if he acted with the intention of obeying, because such a precept does not excuse from an offense, even if he had acted out of ignorance, as I have noted that Bar. said in the said l. iuste possidet, as touched upon above; and the said §. 1, Inst. vi bo. rap. supports this. For even the judge himself, by proceeding not rightly, is then held for violence if he inflicted it or ordered it to be inflicted, as in cap. conquerente, de restit. spol., and in cap. cum causa, de offic. deleg.; and what I touched upon above also militates against the said count. And thus, as has been concluded by me above, I deem it to be the law, I, Nicolaus de Tudeschis, Abbot of Manoppello, auditor of the Apostolic Camera and referendary of our lord the pope, always saving a better judgment. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The Pope by his privilege does not intend to prejudice the institution of a benefice, unless he expressly states this.
2. A privilege does not prejudice a settlement previously made, if special mention of it is not made.
3. If the prince granted a privilege to someone with some reservation of another's right, it is valid.
4. All prejudicial privileges are to be strictly interpreted.
5. A prescription of forty years suffices against a church, short of the Roman Church; and at no. 9.
6. Prescription does not run against a son in adventitious property during paternal power.
7. Prescription is of strict law, and only as much is prescribed as is possessed, and it is not prescribed in time of war; and at no. 8.
10. A privilege of the emperor is valid as to his subjects.
11. A privilege receives the broadest interpretation against the grantor of the privilege.
body: IN the question which is turned or is expected to turn between the monastery of Santa Croce of Monte Analense, of the diocese of Gubbio, on the one part, and the brothers of the Cistercian order on the other, concerning the subjection or status of the monastery of San Bartolomeo di Camporegio of the same diocese, I judge that three points must be examined for the clarity of the decision. First, whether by the privileges of exemption and union granted to the said monastery of San Bartolomeo, prejudice has been caused to the right of the monastery of Santa Croce. Second, presupposing that the privilege did not inflict harm before the period of forty years, whether prescription ought to exclude the right and action competent to the said monastery of Santa Croce. Third, if such prescription causes prejudice, whether the said monastery of Santa Croce can protect itself by a centenary prescription by virtue of the imperial privilege which the Pope subsequently sanctioned to remain ratified. Addressing the first in order, it seems at first that by the privilege of Alexander, subsequently corroborated by Gregory, prejudice was done to the right of the said monastery of Santa Croce. For the said Alexander sanctioned that the said monastery of San Bartolomeo should answer concerning its subjection neither to bishop, nor to abbot, nor finally to any of the clerics or seculars, but only to himself and to his successors the Roman Pontiffs. And he added a little later that if anyone, whether bishop, or abbot, or any person whatsoever, against the edict of this our constitution, through any machination and craftiness of subtlety, should arrogate the aforesaid to himself, or subject it to a monastery, both he who gave and he who wrongly received, until he comes to his senses and restores what was wrongly presumed, by the authority of Almighty God and of blessed Peter the prince of the apostles, shall be bound with the bond of perpetual damnation and anathema, &c. Since therefore the Pope, who has the plenitude of power, as in c. cuncta per mundum, and c. per principalem, 9, q. 3, exempted the said monastery from the subjection of the bishop, and of the abbot, and of any other person whatsoever—which that he could do is by no means to be called into doubt, as in c. si papa, de priu., lib. 6; c. dudum and c. quamuis, de præben., eod. lib. make for this—therefore the monastery of Santa Croce cannot pretend any subjection in the said monastery. For if prejudice is done to the bishop, whose power over the monastery is ordinary, 18, q. 2, c. monasteria, and c. abbates, and c. si quis abbas, de relig. domi., cap. cum dilectus, and cap. venerabilis, with similar texts, it ought all the more strongly to cause prejudice to the abbot of Santa Croce pretending a certain superiority merely from the foundation of the said monastery; for the said abbot could only pretend four things, namely the confirmation of the abbot, likewise reverence, and obedience, and a certain annual census. For only these four did the patron reserve at the time of foundation to the abbot of the monastery of Santa Croce. Therefore these things, which are of special law and against common law, ought to be removed more easily than the power of the bishop, which is ordinary and favorable, and is founded upon full subjection. But it is doubtful to no one that prejudice is done to the bishop, d. c. si papa, and c. 1, de priuile., lib. 6, and 16, q. 1, c. frater; much more ought it to cause prejudice to the abbot, arg. in c. dilectus, de offi. leg. Nor can surreption be alleged, since special mention of the abbot was made in the privilege, which could not be verified except in special law, since by common law one monastery is not under another, d. c. monasteria, and noted in c. in præsentia, de proba. Secondly, the union newly made by the present lord Pope Martin supports this, in that he united that monastery to the Cistercian brothers by withdrawing the abbatial dignity, which he could undoubtedly do, as in c. sicut vnire, de exce. præla., and in c. & temporis qualitas, 16, q. 1, especially since the union was made after the said privilege, and after the rights were prescribed against the monastery of Santa Croce; for prescription precludes every action, as the text says in c. ad aures, de præscr. It was not therefore necessary to make mention of the monastery of Santa Croce, since its right had already been taken away by the privilege of Alexander and by the forty-year prescription. But these things notwithstanding, I think the contrary opinion prevails, namely that by the privilege of Alexander, or of the union made by the lord Martin, no prejudice was inflicted upon the right of the monastery of Santa Croce. I am moved first: because it is the prince's intention never to prejudice the right of a third party, unless he makes special mention of it, as in c. super eo, de offi. dele., and l. 2, §. si quis a principe, ff. ne qd in loco publi., especially when derogation is made from the foundation of a benefice and from lay disposition, lest laymen be thereby drawn away from the foundation of churches. To this effect is what the gl. notes in cle. per literas, de pb., and what is noted by the doct. in c. cum dilectus, de iure patrona. But in our case, special mention was not made of the rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce; therefore such privileges do not obtain firmness to the prejudice of that monastery. Nor does it hinder that in the privilege of Alexander or Gregory it was said that it should be subject to no abbot, &c., because that is not sufficient mention to cause prejudice to the right of the monastery, since mention ought to be special, and not so general, as in c. 2, de do. & contum., and what is noted there by the doct., in c. cum dilecta, de rescrip., and the good text in cap. bonæ, de confir. vti. vel inuti.; especially in our case special mention had to be made, in which those rights were owed to the monastery of Santa Croce from the original foundation of the monastery and the disposition of the lay patron.

† For the Pope by his privilege does not intend to prejudice the foundation of a benefice unless he expresses this openly, as in cap. cum dilectus, de iure patrona.; the excellent capitul. monasteria, 16, quæstio 7, and capitul. Eleutherius, 18, quæs. 2, make for this. For the Pope in his privilege could understand the abbot who in certain religious orders is called Father Abbot, to whom little prejudice is inflicted; whence we ought not to presume, for the aforesaid reasons, that the Pope through general words understood the special disposition of the patron. To the same point is the good text in c. ex multiplici, de deci., where it is evident

† that a privilege does not prejudice a composition previously made when special mention has not been made of it; and in capitul. cum olim, de præscript., where a privilege does not prejudice an arbitral award rendered upon a submission to arbitration, all the more strongly it ought not to prejudice the foundation of a benefice or monastery without special mention of it having been made. Secondly, capitul. veniens, de præscript., makes for this, where the text notably implies

† that if a prince granted a privilege to someone with some reservation of another's right, a privilege granted afterwards concerning those rights without some reservation having previously been made is not valid, no mention of it having been had: because if the Pope had known of that reservation, he perhaps would not have granted it without it, as is notably decided there. Therefore the same and more strongly must be said in our case, that if the Pope had known that those four rights had been reserved by the patron of the monastery of Santa Croce, he would never have granted that full exemption without the reservation of those rights, or at least he would have made mention of them, especially since the exemption could have been granted with the reservation of those rights; because those rights do not induce full subjection, as is clearly implied in capitul. his quæ, de maio. & obedien., and cap. cum inter, de re iudica., where many rights entailing the penalty of subjection are enumerated, and among them obedience and reverence are enumerated as species. Thirdly is adduced capitul. 1, de constitu., lib. 6, where it is said that the Pope by his constitution is not deemed to wish to take away statutes and customs, since they consist in fact, unless he has made mention of them. Therefore all the more strongly must the same be said of a privilege, which does not emanate with so much deliberation as common law, as noted there. Therefore a statute and ordinance made in the foundation of a monastery ought not to be taken away by a papal privilege, since special mention was not made of it. Fourthly it makes for this because Gregory or Alexander wished simply to derogate from the right of the monastery of Santa Croce, since he said that this privilege of exemption ought not to depart from the charity of Santa Croce, just as he had said in another privilege; whence it is to be believed that through those words he wished to reserve all rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce. He would not, therefore, reserve charity to it if he wished to withdraw from it the census imposed from ancient times, or other rights reserved to it, as in the said capitul. Eleutherius; capit. quanto, de censib., makes for this. For charity is a right will thoroughly turned away from all earthly things, &c., as in capitul. charitas, de pœni., distinctio 2; and in these matters a broad interpretation is to be made, so that prejudice is not done to another's right without cause, according to what is noted by Barto. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iure, and l. non dubium, ff. de legib.; ca. cum dilectus, de consue., and l. 2, C. de noxa make for this; and this same thing and more clearly on our subject Innocent wished in c. dudum, de priui., where he says

† that all prejudicial privileges are to be interpreted strictly, and as far as possible, brought back into harmony with the law, ff. de vulg. & pupil., l. ex facto, and de deci., c. suggestum, and he says the same regarding a privilege of exemption. Wherefore there, after many points, he concludes that a privilege of exemption is not valid without mention having been made of the possession of another held in good faith, even if in truth he does not have ownership; and the gloss affirmed the same in c. 2, de deci., lib. 6. All the more strongly therefore must it be said in our case that the privilege is not valid without mention having been made of the possession or ownership of the monastery of Santa Croce. And the very same is to be said in every respect regarding the union newly made by the lord Martin. For since he did not make special mention of the aforesaid, it did not hold, since through it prejudice would be done to the monastery of Santa Croce with respect to the confirmation of the abbot; since through that union the abbatial dignity was exempted and suppressed. It does not hinder what was said above regarding prescription, because it will be answered immediately in the second and third doubt. These things as to the first doubt, which I think are most true and undoubted, and the response to the contrary points framed above is sufficiently clear. To the second doubt, whether at least the prescription of forty years prejudices the said monastery of Santa Croce: because, since within that time it made no confirmation of the election made of the abbot, nor received the census, nor had reverence, nor obedience. And it seems first that it does.

† For regularly against a church other than the Roman Church, a prescription of forty years with good faith suffices, as in cap. de quarta, and cap. illud, de præscrip., where the common law or a presumption is not against the one prescribing, as in cap. 1, eo. titu., lib. 6; and a prescription of forty years excludes every action altogether, as the text said in d. cap. ad aures, de præscrip. But these things notwithstanding, I think it must be said thus in our case: that with respect to the right of confirming the abbot in the monastery of San Bartolomeo, prescription does not run against the monastery of Santa Croce. The reason is unassailable: because on account of the reservation made concerning collegiate churches, especially concerning cathedrals and monasteries, by many Roman Pontiffs successively, the abbot of Santa Croce for the time being could not exercise the right competent to him in this matter. Whence, since he was impeded by an impediment of law, no prescription runs against him, as in l. 1, C. de anna. excep., and in l. in rebus, C. de iure dotium, where it is clear

† that while paternal power lasts, prescription does not run against a son regarding adventitious property: because he was not able to sue at that time, since the full administration of those things belongs to the father, as in d. l. 1; nor while marriage endures does prescription run in dowry rights against a wife: because she cannot sue then, since full administration belongs to the husband, d. l. in rebus, and l. doce ancillam, C. de rei uendi. To the same point cap. 1 and cap. 4, de præscrip., and cap. ex transmissa, eo. titu., and cap. quia diuersitatem, de conces. præben., in which laws it is clear that against a church that is vacant, or has a prelate incapable of acting, prescription does not run. But in our case the abbot of Santa Croce for the time being was impeded as to the act of confirmation, therefore prescription does not run against him. This right therefore remained habitual in him, although the exercise was prohibited at the good pleasure of the Pope through the act of reservation. Nor by exercising this right of confirmation is the Pope said to prescribe, even if he should do this for a thousand years, since he does this from the plenitude of power; and in this case the statement of Specu. in titu. de præscript., versi. illud, can be understood, where he says that the Pope does not prescribe against inferior churches, since he himself is already the universal lord without prescription. Furthermore, in prescription good faith is required, namely that he believe that that right belongs to him, so that he exercises it believing that he is using his own right, as in c. si uirgo, 34, q. 2; l. si, ff. quemadmodum serui. amit. makes for this; noted by Inn. in cap. bonæ, il 2, de postu. præla. But the lord Pope exercised and exercises the act of confirmation not by ordinary power, but by absolute power through the act of reservation, and he knows that by common law and ordinary power this right belongs to the inferior, although he can concur in the act of confirmation with the ordinary, as in c. 2 and c. si a sede, de præben., lib. 6. Therefore prescription cannot be alleged in this from the person of the Pope, nor against the abbot of Santa Croce, who is not caught in negligence, since he had his hands tied by the reservations of the Supreme Pontiffs, as in the laws alleged above. For prescription was introduced principally in hatred of the negligent, as in l. 1, ff. de usuca., and 16, q. 3, c. dilecto, §. potest, and in our case no negligence is found on the part of the abbot of Santa Croce. Nor does it hinder if it is said that he was negligent in other things, because through this prescription ought not to be extended to rights in which negligence was not committed:

† because prescription is of strict law, and one prescribes only as much as is possessed, as is proved in c. auditis, and c. cum olim, de præscr., and c. cum contingat, de decimis; noted by Bar. in l. 1, §. si quis, ff. de iti. actuque pri., and Inno. in c. dilectus, de capel. mona.
