Therefore it is necessarily concluded that the union made by our lord Martin, by suppressing the dignity of the abbot of Santa Croce, was as if surreptitious and null by operation of law: because, if he had been informed that such union redounded to the prejudice of the monastery of Santa Croce, he would in no way have made the union, or at least not so easily; therefore such suppression had to induce surreption, as in capit. postulasti, and what Hostien. notes there, de rescrip., which I say proceeds even if the Pope had made the union motu proprio, because although a motu proprio excludes surreption, it nevertheless does not confirm a grant against the intention of the one writing, who in doubt is not deemed to wish to prejudice a third party, as noted by Ioan. And. in cap. si motu proprio, de præbend., lib. sexto, and Calde. in capitul. cum dilectus, de iure patro., and the lord of the Rota decisio 105; l. secunda, §. si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in loco publico, makes for this, and what Innocent notes in cap. dudum, de priuileg., and the gloss in cap. secundo, de deci., lib. sexto. Rather, it could be maintained that even with respect to obedience no prescription has run, because although the abbot of Santa Croce could have commanded certain honest things, especially in reforming the morals of the abbey of San Bartolomeo, it is not however concluded by this that if he did not command, prescription ran against him, since this is an act of mere faculty and not of necessity. For it was not said in the foundation that the abbot of Santa Croce should exercise jurisdiction against the abbot of San Bartolomeo, but that the abbot of San Bartolomeo should be bound to obedience and reverence toward the abbot of Santa Croce. If therefore the latter did not obey because the former did not command, it is not by this prescribed against him, because from non-use custom or prescription is not induced, since it does not have a tacit act contrary to the disposition of law, as noted by Io. An. in c. Ioannes, de cle. coniu., and by Cy. in l. 2, C. quæ sit lon. consue.; it is proved in l. hæc autem iura, ff. de seru. urb. prædi., just as I shall not prescribe the freedom of building higher on my ground up to the heavens if I have not built higher, since nothing was done to the contrary, because this is an act of mere faculty, and in acts of faculty prescription does not run through non-use, as noted in the laws previously alleged and in cap. ex parte Astensis, de concess. præbend.; and perhaps a case did not occur in which he had need to command, arg. of those things which Bart. notes in l. cum scimus, C. de agrico. & censi., lib. 11. With respect, however, to reverence, it would have to be considered whether the abbot of San Bartolomeo withdrew reverence from the abbot of Santa Croce, which would be difficult to prove. For that consists in the act of salutation, or by another manner through which reverence is made according to the custom of the country, according to what is noted in c. his quæ, de maio. & obe. The whole difficulty stands around the unpaid census, as to which whether the prescription of forty years is complete, many things must be considered, and not the mere passage of years alone; for many things impede the course of prescription, such as the vacancy of the monastery of Santa Croce. For the time of vacancy must be deducted from the middle, as in c. 1, and c. de quarta, and ca. auditis, de præscr., which laws have place even in inferior churches, as Inn. notes in c. olim, il j, de ref. spo. Likewise in time of

† war prescription does not run, when there is so much hostility in a place that one is not rendered safe, as in c. ex transmissa, de præsc., and what Inn. notes there; the same in time of mortality, because that is the hostility of God, as Bar. notes in l. naturaliter, ff. de usuc. Likewise in time of schism, as noted in c. cum nobis, de præsc. I understand if there were diverse obediences, and justice was not rendered to one against the other, according to what is noted in d. c. ex transmissa. For all times must be deducted from the time of prescription, and if with these deducted the time of forty years does not remain, the monastery of Santa Croce has its intention founded, as in c. auditis, de præscrip. If however the prescription should remain complete, one must consider whether the monastery of San Bartolomeo was in good faith in not paying the census. For bad faith is proved if there was fame in the place that it ought to give the census to the monastery of Santa Croce, or it appeared by some existing writing, or they heard this from some person whom they reasonably ought to have believed. For by these and similar things bad faith is proved, as Bartolus notes in l. celsus, ff. de usucapion.; and if it can be established concerning these things, prescription is impeded, by cap. fina., de præscrip., and by reg. possessor malæ fidei, de regul. iur., lib. 6. If however it cannot be proved, so that the prescription of 40 years remains unshaken, then recourse must be had to the fact as to the last doubt: Whether the monastery of Santa Croce can protect itself by a centenary prescription by virtue of the privileges of the Emperors Frederick and Henry, afterwards approved by Pope Honorius IV. And it seems first that it cannot: since Emperors could not grant privileges to monasteries to the prejudice of the ecclesiastical forum, as Innocent notes in c. Imperatores, de testi.

† Since therefore by law a church uses a prescription of 40 years against another church, as in c. de quarta, and c. ad aures, de præscript., therefore the privilege of the Emperors ought not to profit; c. dudum, de deci., and c. ecclesia sanctæ Mariæ, de constitu., and dist. 96, c. bene quidem make for this. Nor does the approval of Pope Honorius stand in the way, for a manifold reason. First, because a confirmation made in common form profits little: whence it does not validate a void act, read and noted in c. quia diuersitatem, de conces. præben., and c. fina., de confir. uti.; for it is said to be made in common form, and not from certain knowledge, when the entire tenor of the confirmed matter is not inserted, or when the clause from certain knowledge of the confirmed matter is not appended, as noted in c. 1, and c. antepenu. and penul., de confir. uti.; but in our case the tenor is not appended in the confirmation of those privileges, nor the clause from certain knowledge; therefore, &c.

† Furthermore, the Emperor's privilege is valid as to his subjects, as l. cunctos populos, C. de summa trinit.; what is read and noted in l. fina., ff. de iurisdict. omn. iud., and in c. a nobis, de senten. excommu. makes for this; therefore the confirmation is valid as to subjects. But these things notwithstanding, I judge that the contrary proceeds by law. I am moved principally because the lord Pope in his privilege did not use the word 'confirmamus' [we confirm], and thus it cannot be said that it was a confirmation in common form; but he used the word 'sancimus' [we sanction], by which word not a confirmation, but rather the enactment of a new law is induced, argu. in c. generali, de elect., lib. 6; hence a sanction is the name of a canonical constitution, as the gloss notes in clemen. 1, de conces. præben., in versicu. sancimus; whence the words of the Emperor and the words of the Pope must be weighed. For the Emperor simply decreed that no prescription less than centenary should run against the monastery of Santa Croce. Nor did he restrict himself to secular or ecclesiastical persons. Honorius, however, supervening, spoke thus: 'Furthermore, holding ratified and pleasing all liberties and immunities of good memory granted by the Emperors Frederick and Henry to you and your order, we sanction that they remain inviolate in future times, &c.' Which words demonstrate clearer than light that Honorius did not wish to confirm simply and in common form; on the contrary, he disposed principally by enacting a private law. For what pleased the prince has the force of law, insti. de iur. natu. gen. & ciui., §. sed quod principi; and we make all things our own to which we impart our authority, as in l. 1, C. de uete. iu. enucl., and the good text in a similar case in c. si apostolica, de præben., lib. 6. Whence the law of the Pope is now more powerful than that of the Emperor. Furthermore, we see that if a civil law is canonized by the Pope, it has the force of a canon, as capitul. in primis, and the good gloss there, 2, q. 1; noted by the doctors in c. 2, de rescrip.; all the more strongly therefore ought the said privilege to have the force of a canon, since the Pope expressly sanctioned that those things remain inviolate, and although he did not express what those immunities are, nevertheless they are sufficiently held as expressed, since the Pope referred to those privileges, as in c. auditis, de præscri., where there is a good text in a similar case, and in l. penul., C. de senten. quæ sine cer. quanti., in c. cum Bertoldus, de re iudica.; this same thing is proved by an excellent simile. For in the beginning it was the Emperor who gave a privilege to churches regarding the matter of prescription, as l. fin. with auth. quas actione, C. de sacrosan. eccle. Afterwards canon law arrived, and approved those laws in general, as in c. cum nouis, with similar texts, de præscri., and through this approval they had force, even as to the ecclesiastical forum and between churches; and by this is removed one motive which is alleged against the monastery of Santa Croce, namely that the approval of the Pope ought not to have place against the Pope himself prescribing. For first it can be directly denied that here the Pope prescribed; for the withdrawn census is prescribed by the monastery of San Bartolomeo and not by the Pope. Whence, presupposing that the church of San Bartolomeo had been exempted by the Pope, nevertheless in its rights, especially when dealing with an annual prescription, it does not enjoy the privilege of the Roman Church, as the gloss notes in c. dilectus, de capel. monach., and in c. ad audientiam, de præscri., by the doct. in c. cum nobis, eod. titu., and 6, q. 4, c. uolumus. Likewise, presupposing and not granting that here the Pope prescribed, the privilege granted by him ought to have place without distinction, since he granted it generally.

† For a privilege receives the broadest interpretation against the one granting the privilege, as noted by Barto. in l. beneficium, ff. de constit. princip., and Innocen. in c. cum dilecti, de dona., and in c. olim, de uerbo. signi., by Ioan. And.; c. cum dilectus, de consue. makes for this; for this is that saying of the wise man: suffer the law which you yourself have made; and whatever law anyone establishes against another, he himself ought to use it, as in c. cum omnes, de consti.; the lord Ioan. And. clearly held this in c. cum nobis, de præscrip., where he maintained that the Pope can prescribe against an inferior church, but with a space of 40 years; and nevertheless that period of forty years the church has from a privilege and special law, approved or introduced by the Pope. Therefore the same must be said in this privilege of one hundred years; and this must be held especially having regard to the fact that prescription is odious and to be restricted, as in c. cum contingat, de decim., with similar texts. And let these things suffice. Nor is it necessary to respond otherwise to the contrary points, because they remain sufficiently resolved and clear through the aforesaid; and thus, as concluded by me above, I, Nicolaus of Sicily, Abbot of Monaco and doctor, state and advise that it is of law; and in testimony I have subscribed with my own hand and caused my seal to be impressed. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The payment of a census is said to be a kind of servitude.
2. Common fame alone suffices for title to complete prescription.
3. A confirmation made in common form is of little avail.
4. A privilege of emperors is valid with respect to their subjects.
5. Sanction is the name of a canonical constitution.
6. If a civil law is canonized by the Pope, it has the force of a canon.
body: The aid of Almighty God having been implored, in the case that is pending between the monastery of Santa Croce of Monte Savelana on the one side, and the friars of the Cistercian order on the other, concerning the subjection or validity of the union made to a certain monastery of the said friars of Monte San Bartolomeo di Camporegio, and also concerning the rights belonging to the said monastery of Santa Croce in the aforesaid monastery of San Bartolomeo, certain matters must be examined point by point for the decision of the said question. And first, what rights the monastery of Santa Croce can claim regarding the monastery of San Bartolomeo. Second, presupposing that certain rights belong to it by some special law, whether they have been derogated from by the privilege of Alexander, subsequently corroborated by Pope Gregory. Third, if the said privilege does not stand in the way, whether at least the privilege of union made by the lord Martin, the present supreme and undoubted Pontiff, must stand in the way. Fourth and last, whether, the aforesaid notwithstanding, it can at least be alleged against the said monastery of Santa Croce that it can claim the census contained in certain of its instruments as owed to it by the said monastery of San Bartolomeo. For the said census was paid to the said monastery of Santa Croce for so long a time that memory of its beginning does not exist. For although numerous payments of the said census are proved by certain instruments produced by the monastery of Santa Croce, nevertheless the beginning of the payment does not appear. For the face of those instruments made no mention of the beginning of the payment, but all appear to be continued upon an ancient and owed payment. Moreover, prescription of so great a time suffices for prescribing a census, even with no cause appearing, because from payment over so great a time a cause is presumed, as is noted by gl. 1. q. 1. c. nullus, and Hostiensis and Io. An. in c. peruenit. de censi., and Bar. in l. cum de in rem uerso. ff. de usu.; or at least it cannot be denied that the receipt of the census is proved by the monastery of Santa Croce for at least seventy-two continuous years, as is clearly gathered from the instruments produced by the monasteries, and from the depositions of certain witnesses produced on behalf of the monastery of Santa Croce. For since the beginning and the end and other intervening times are proved, the legal presumption arises that in all the intervening years the monastery of Santa Croce was in possession of receiving the said census, as is noted by Bar. in l. celsus. ff. de usuc., and the gloss in cap. uolumus. 17. quæst. 4; l. quicunque, C. de apochis. lib. 10 supports this. Furthermore, prescription runs against the church not merely for seventy-two years, but for forty years, as in c. de quarta, and in c. illud, and c. auditis, with similar texts, de præscri. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that good faith and title are required in prescription, since the prescription of this census is contrary to the ius commune, because under the ius commune one monastery is not bound to pay a census to another monastery; for this purpose, capit. primo. de præscrip. lib. sexto, and what is noted there.

† Likewise, the payment of a census is as it were a kind of servitude; therefore, good faith ought not to be presumed, since every thing is presumed free, on which see the gloss and Bar. in l. prima. §. secundo. de itinere actuque priua., Cynus and others in l. prima. C. de seruitu., and the canonists in cap. si diligenti. de foro compe. For this can be answered, and first regarding the point of good faith: for I say that it is to be presumed from the course of the longest time, even though the possession is contrary to law, as Innocent notably maintained in c. 2. de in integrum restitu.; what Bartolus notes in l. quæritur. C. unde ui supports this, and it seems to be proved in capit. cum ecclesia Sutrina. de causa possess. & proprietatis. And in our case there not only concurs possession of the longest time, but there are also present many other arguments which in themselves would suffice for the presumption of good faith, according to what is noted by Bartolus in the said l. prima. C. de serui.; for the aforesaid doctors say that it suffices that something be proved in order to exclude the presumption of bad faith, such as because the possessor heard it said by certain trustworthy neighbors that that belonged to him as a servitude, or if there was common report about this in this place, or there were certain servitudes. In our case, however, many similar arguments concur. For there was common report in the place that the monastery of San Bartolomeo was subject and tributary to the monastery of Santa Croce, as is evident from the depositions of certain witnesses. Likewise, what is stronger, a certain privilege of Innocent II is presently produced, where he relates that the said monastery of San Bartolomeo belongs and pertains to the monastery of Santa Croce; for this furnishes a presumption of good faith. Likewise also because, once a successor in a benefice finds the church in possession of receiving the census, he ought reasonably to presume that the church possesses from a just cause, according to what is noted by the gloss and doctors in capitu. de quarta. de præscriptio., and by Dynus in the rule possessor. de regulis iuris. lib. sexto. And many other things could be alleged toward the presumption of good faith, especially as noted by the doctors in capa. si diligenti., and c. sanctorum, and cap. fina. de præscript. But the aforesaid things abundantly suffice. As to the point of title, I say that on the part of the monastery of Santa Croce the abbots who were there at the time could sufficiently presume the census to be owed by virtue of subjection. For a census is customary to be paid as a mark of subjection, as in c. omnis anima, de censi., and in l. competit, C. de præscript. 30. uel 40. annorum.

† Likewise, the mere common report of a title suffices for a title to complete a prescription, as Bartolus notably maintained in the pre-alleged l. Celsus, ff. de usucap. And he says the same there when there are some probable conjectures concerning the title; as, for instance, because ancient and trustworthy men asserted the title, whence even a probable error concerning the title is held as a title, as is the notable text in l. Quod uulgo, ff. pro emptore. But in our case there was antiquity, and the common report still flourishes that that monastery of San Bartolomeo was immediately subject and tributary to the monastery of Santa Croce. To the aforesaid contributes what is noted by Hostiensis, Abbas, and Goffredus in cap. dudum, de decis., where they say that a privilege of confirmation in common form furnishes a just title for prescribing; and Baldus holds the same concerning narrative words contained in an instrument, in l. fina. C. si a non compe. iudi. To the aforesaid can be alleged the singular dictum of Baldus in l. solent, ff. de offic. procon., where after many points he concludes that if for the longest time one church should pay a census to another, it is presumed to be subject to it; which dictum at least proceeds when the census is paid as a sign of subjection, either openly, because this will be estimated, or tacitly, because certain conjectures of subjection concur in the payment. For an indeterminate payment of census is argued and certified from the circumstances; for this, see the notable gloss in l. cum quid, ff. si certum petat; what is read and noted in cap. illud, de præscript. supports this, and in c. fina. de despon. impube., in which it is noted what is similarly noted in c. 1. de iudi. In our case, however, conjectures of subjection concur. For since by that very ancient privilege granted at that time when the monastery of Santa Croce was in its greatest flourish, it was said that the monastery of San Bartolomeo belonged to the monastery of Santa Croce, and it is expressly named among other churches subject to the same monastery; and also the instruments of confirmation of many abbots of the monastery of San Bartolomeo made by the abbots or prelates of Santa Croce are proved, there cannot be in the payment of the census any other presumption than that of subjection, especially when the local common report held that the said monastery of San Bartolomeo was subject and tributary to the monastery of Santa Croce. And the text according to the common reading of the doctors in cap. fina. de causa possess. & proprieta. seems to support the aforesaid, where it is clear that through proof of the receipt of a census the possession of subjection is proved; which I understand in the aforesaid manner, when certain conjectures concur that the payment of the census is possession of subjection, as happened in our case, as is evident from the aforesaid. The dictum of Bartolus in l. cum de in rem uerso, at the end, ff. de usuca. also supports this, where he says that if in contemplation of any thing one did certain things that are customary to be done by a vassal, he is presumed a vassal. But in our case the monastery of San Bartolomeo paid a census to the monastery of Santa Croce for that monastery of San Bartolomeo. Likewise, it sought confirmations of abbots from that monastery of Santa Croce. Therefore the payment is presumed made by reason of subjection. And through the aforesaid it can newly be inferred that the monastery of San Bartolomeo is subject to the monastery of Santa Croce. For by prescribing a census by reason of subjection, the subjection itself seems prescribed, as is read and noted in the said c. fi. de cau. posses. & proprie.; and what I said above following Baldus supports this. To the same purpose what is read and noted in c. 1. de reli. domi. serves excellently, where it is clear that by the exercise of one episcopal right the debt of other rights is presumed, when no other is in possession of them. But in our case it is not proved that anyone was in possession of the subjection in the said times other than the abbot of Santa Croce. Therefore, by the payment of the census, and by the presenting of the confirmation, joined with the pre-alleged privilege of Innocent II, it is sufficiently proved that the monastery of San Bartolomeo is subject to the monastery of Santa Croce. From these things I also infer as to the right and power of confirming the abbot-elect in the monastery of San Bartolomeo. For I say that such a right belongs to the monastery of Santa Croce, or to the abbot of that monastery for the time being. First, it is proved from the fact that the monastery of San Bartolomeo is immediately subject to the monastery of Santa Croce, as is evident from the aforesaid; therefore, confirmation of the abbot ought to belong to the abbot of Santa Croce as to the immediate superior. Furthermore, the possession of the right of confirming is specifically proved through tacit times that suffice to complete prescription. For possession of sixty-seven years is proved, as is evident from the instruments produced on behalf of the monastery of Santa Croce. And although it might be said that the instrument drawn up in the year of the Lord 1240 does not fully prove possession of the right of confirming, because that instrument was drawn up only for seeking confirmation from the abbot of Santa Croce, who confirmed that election, and consequently that from then he was in possession of the right of confirming—for to this it can be answered that that objection would proceed unless other presumptions concurred. But in our case other proofs concerning the subjection concur, concerning which above. Likewise, it is not likely that the chapter of San Bartolomeo would have appointed a proctor to seek confirmation of their election from the abbot of Santa Croce unless the said abbot had been in possession of the right of confirming, since no one is presumed to cast away his right, as in l. cum de indebito. ff. de proba. and in c. super hoc. de re nun. Likewise, this is not customary to happen, that one should seek confirmation from him who is not in possession of confirming, and an argument from things commonly happening is valid, as is read and noted in c. 1. de cle. non resid. And from the aforesaid I conclude regarding the first point that the monastery of Santa Croce can by law claim that full subjection belongs to it in the monastery of San Bartolomeo, and specifically the right of confirming the elections of the abbot of the said monastery, from the payment of the said census. I come now to the second, namely, whether by the privilege of Alexander the rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce were derogated from. And first it seems that they were. For the said Alexander provided that the monastery of San Bartolomeo should answer concerning its subjection neither to an abbot, nor indeed to any of the clerics or seculars, but only to him and to his successors the Roman Pontiffs. And a little later he added: if anyone, whether bishop, or abbot, or any great or small person, against the edict of this our constitution, by any machination or cunning of subtlety, should have derogated it to himself as private, or subjected it to a monastery, and he who has wrongfully received it, until he comes to his senses, does not restore what was wrongfully presumed, let him by the authority of Almighty God and blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles, be bound with the chain of anathema of perpetual damnation, etc. Since therefore the Pope, who has fullness of power, as in cap. ad honorem. de auto. & usu pal. and cap. cuncta per mundum. and cap. per principalem. 9. quæstio. tertia, exempted the said monastery from the jurisdiction of bishop, abbot, and any other person whatsoever—which that he was able to do is by no means to be called into doubt, as in cap. si papa. de priuileg. lib. sexto; cap. secundo, and c. dubium, and ca. quamuis, in the same book support this—therefore the monastery of Santa Croce cannot claim any subjection in the said monastery. For if prejudice is done to a bishop, whose power is ordinary, even over a monastery, 18. quæst. 2. cap. monasteria, and c. abbates, and cap. si quis abbas, and c. cum dilectus, and cap. cum uenerabilis. de reli. dom., by stronger reason it ought to prejudice the abbot of Santa Croce claiming superiority in the said monastery by special law, by the argument of cap. dilectus. de offic. delega., and in authen. multo magis. C. de episco. & cleri. Secondly, approaching likewise a certain doubt, the union recently made by the lord Martin, the present Pope, lends support, because he united that monastery to the Cistercian friars, removing the abbatial dignity, which he undoubtedly could do, as in capitu. sicut unire. de excess. præla., and in capitu. & temporis qualitas. decimasexta quæstione prima. But these things notwithstanding, I think the contrary opinion prevails, that by the privilege of Alexander, or by the union made by the lord Martin, no prejudice was inflicted upon the right of the monastery of Santa Croce. I am moved first because it is the intention of the prince never to prejudice the right of a third party unless he makes special mention of it, as in cap. super eo. de offic. deleg., and in l. secunda. §. si quis a principe. ff. ne quid in loco publico. But in our case special mention was not made of the rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce; therefore such privileges do not obtain validity to the prejudice of that monastery. It does not stand in the way that in the privilege of Alexander or Gregory it was said that it should be subject to no abbot, etc., because that is not sufficient mention to prejudice the right of the monastery, since mention must be special, as in cap. secundo. de dolo & contumacia, and what is noted there by the doctors in cap. cum dilecta. de rescrip., and a good text in capitu. bonæ. de confirma. uti. For the pope in his privilege could understand this of the abbot who in certain united religious orders is called Father Abbot, to whom little prejudice was generated by that exemption; but it must be said otherwise with respect to the aforesaid rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce, since if that exemption were valid, great prejudice would be generated to the said monastery of Santa Croce. Secondly, cap. primo. de constitu. libr. sexto is adduced, where it is said that the pope by his constitution is not deemed to wish to abolish statutes and customs, since they consist in fact, unless he has made mention of them; therefore by stronger reason the same is to be said in a privilege, which by no means emanates with as much counsel as the ius commune, as is noted there. Thirdly, it is relevant because Alexander did not wish simply to derogate from the right of the monastery of Santa Croce. But he said that by this privilege of exemption it ought not to depart from the charity of Santa Croce, just as he had said in another privilege; whence it is to be believed that by those words he wished to reserve all special rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce. For he would not reserve charity to it, nay rather he would depart from charity, if he wished to withdraw from it its competent rights; c. quanto. de censi. and c. charitas. de pœn. dist. 2 support this. And in this a broad interpretation must be made, lest prejudice be done to the right of another without cause, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. omnes populi. ff. de iusti. & iure, l. non dubium. C. de legi., ca. cum dilectus. de consue., and l. secunda. C. de noxa; what Innocent notes in cap. dudum. de priuileg. supports this, where he says that all prejudicial privileges are to be interpreted strictly and, as much as can be done, reduced to harmony; ff. de uulga. & pupil. l. ex facto, and de deci. c. suggestum. And he says the same there concerning a privilege of exemption. And the very same conclusion is to be made in every respect regarding the third doubt, namely as to the union recently made by the lord Martin. For since he does not make special mention of the aforesaid rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce, it did not hold, as being surreptitious, since by that union prejudice would be done to the monastery of Santa Croce both with respect to subjection and with respect to confirmation of the abbot, since by that union the abbatial dignity was taken away and suspended; and especially without any doubt the said union falls, because it cannot be denied that the monastery of Santa Croce at least has possession of the right of confirming the abbot, although the exercise was forbidden to it and to other prelates through the reservations of the supreme pontiffs. Since therefore the abbot of Santa Croce was in possession at the time of those reservations, therefore he is also now in possession, since it was not through him that he failed to continue his possession. For prescription does not run against one unable to act, as in cap. quia diuersitatem, de concess. præben. and in l. 1. C. de anna. excep. And consequently it is clearly gathered that the privilege of union was not valid, because it did not make mention of the possession of Santa Croce held in good faith, as Innocent expressly maintained in cap. dudum, de priuileg., and the gloss in the said c. 2. de decim. lib. 6. Regarding indeed the last doubt, whether at least by prescription the rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce have been derogated from, since forty years and more have now elapsed that it exercised no right of subjection in the monastery of San Bartolomeo: and certainly with respect to the right of confirming, it must be said that the monastery of Santa Croce cannot be charged with any negligence because of the force of the reservations, as I said above. But concerning the other rights it can be doubted. And whether the monastery of Santa Croce can protect itself by a centenary prescription by virtue of the privileges of the Emperors Frederick and Henry, afterwards approved by Pope Honorius III; and it seems at first that it cannot: because the Emperors could not grant a privilege to a monastery to the prejudice of the ecclesiastical forum, as Innocent notes in c. nuper, de testibus. Since by canon law it is provided that one church can protect itself by a prescription of forty years against another church, as in c. de quarta, and c. ad aures de præscript., therefore the privilege of the Emperors ought not to benefit; c. dudum, de decim., and c. ecclesia S. Mariæ, de consti., and 96. distin. c. bene quidem support this. Nor does the approval of Pope Honorius stand in the way, for a manifold reason.

† First, because a confirmation made in common form is of little benefit; whence it does not validate a void act, as is read and noted in c. quia diuersitatem, de conces. præben., and c. fin. de confir. uti. Moreover, it is said to be made in common form, and not from certain knowledge, when the entire tenor of the thing confirmed is not inserted, or when the clause 'from certain knowledge' is not added, or it does not otherwise appear concerning certain knowledge of the thing confirmed, according to what is noted in cap. 1 and cap. antepen. de confirm. uti. But in our case the tenor is not appended in the confirmation of those privileges, nor the clause 'from certain knowledge'; therefore, etc.

† Furthermore, a privilege of the Emperors is valid as to their own subjects, as in l. cunctos populos. C. de summa trinit., and what is read and noted in l. fina. de iurisdic. omn. iudi. and in c. a nobis, de senten. excom. supports this; therefore the confirmation is valid only as to subjects. But these things notwithstanding, I judge that the contrary proceeds in law. I am moved principally because the lord Pope in his privilege did not use the word 'we confirm'—and thus it cannot be said that the confirmation was in common form—but he used the word 'we enact' (sancimus), through which word a confirmation is not introduced, but rather the enactment of a new law, by the argument in c. generali, de elect. lib. 6.

† Hence 'sanctio' is the name of a canonical constitution, as the gloss notes in 1. distinct. in summa. Thus we say regarding the word 'censemus' ('we deem'), which introduces new law, as the gloss notes in clemen. 1. de conces. præben. on the word 'censemus.' Whence the words of the Emperors are to be weighed. And the Emperor himself decreed simply that no prescription less than centenary should run against the monastery of Santa Croce, nor did he restrict himself to secular or ecclesiastical persons. Honorius, however, supervening, said: 'Furthermore, all liberties and immunities granted to you and your order by the Emperors Frederick and Henry of divine memory, we hold ratified and pleasing, and we have enacted that they remain unimpaired in future times, etc.' Which words demonstrate more clearly than light that Honorius did not wish to confirm simply and in common form; nay, rather, he principally disposed by enacting a private law. For what pleased the prince had the force of law, institu. de iure natu. gen. & ciui. §. sed quod principi; and we make all things our own to which we impart our authority, as in l. 1. C. de uete. iu. enucl., and a good text to the same effect in cap. ad apostolicæ. de præbend. lib. sexto. Whence the law of the pope is now more powerful than that of the emperor.

† Furthermore, we see that if a civil law is canonized by the pope, it has the force of a canon, as in cap. in primis, and the good gloss there, 2. quæst. prima; the doctors note this in cap. secundo. de rescrip. By stronger reason, therefore, the said privilege of the emperors ought to have the force of a canon, since the pope expressly enacted that those privileges remain unimpaired. And although he did not express what those immunities are, they are sufficiently held as expressed, since the pope referred himself to those privileges, as in capitu. auditis. de præscriptio., where there is a good text to the same effect, and l. penulti. C. de sentent. quæ sine certa quantita., and in capitu. cum Bertoldus. de re iudica. This same thing is proved by an excellent parallel. For in the beginning it was the emperor who gave a privilege to churches regarding the matter of prescription, as in l. fina. with authenti. quas actiones. C. de sacrosan. eccle. Afterwards canon law supervened, and approved those laws in general, as in capit. cum nobis. de præscript.; and this approval had force even as to the ecclesiastical forum and between churches. And by this is gathered one ground that is alleged against the monastery of Santa Croce, namely that the approval of the pope ought not to have place against the pope himself prescribing. For first it can be directly denied that the pope prescribed here. For the withholding of the census is prescribed by the monastery of San Bartolomeo, and not by the pope; whence, presupposing that the church of San Bartolomeo was exempt, nevertheless in its rights, especially when it is a question of an annual prescription, it does not enjoy the privilege of the Roman Church, as the gloss notes in cap. dilectus. de capel. monacho., and in cap. ad audientiam. de præscri., and the doctors in ca. cum nobis. under the same title, 16. quæst. 4. cap. uolumus. Likewise, presupposing and not granting that the pope had prescribed here, nevertheless a privilege granted by him ought to have place indistinctly, since he granted generally. For a privilege receives the broadest interpretation against the one granting the privilege, as Bartolus notes in l. beneficium. ff. de constitu. princ., and Innocent in ca. cum dilecti de dona., and cap. cum olim. de uerbo. sign., as by Io. Andr.; cap. cum dilectus. de consuetu. supports this. Through this applies that saying of the wise man: 'Suffer the law which you yourself have enacted,' and whatever law anyone establishes against another, he himself ought to use it, as in capit. cum omnes. de constitu. Dominus Antonius clearly holds this in c. cum nobis. de præscrip., where he maintained that the pope can prescribe against an inferior church, but only by the space of forty years; and yet that time of forty years the church has from a privilege and special law approved or introduced by the pope. Therefore the same must be said regarding this privilege of one hundred years, and this must be held especially having regard to the fact that prescription is odious and to be restricted, as in capitu. cum contingat. de decim., with similar texts. And let these things suffice, nor is it necessary otherwise to stoop to the contrary arguments, since they remain sufficiently resolved and clear through the aforesaid; and thus, as concluded above by me, I say and advise to be the law. I, Nicolaus of Sicily, abbot of Monreale and doctor of decrees, and in witness whereof I have subscribed with my own hand and caused my seal to be affixed, always saving a better judgment.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a statute of a city having imperium, providing with respect to its subjects that rebels against their homeland may be harmed with impunity, is valid.
2. One who offends in one diocese can be deprived of all benefices, even those he holds in another.
3. A city possessing the rights of a prince can, by reason of a delict, confiscate the goods of the offender wherever situated.
body: The second conclusion of the distinguished doctor dominus Benedictus pleases me; and in support of it, beyond what was alleged by him, I adduce the authority of Bartolus in l. infamem, at the end, ff. de publ. iud., where he says that any city not recognizing a superior over itself has a free people and merum imperium within itself, and has as much power over its own people as the Emperor has in the world at large. To this pertains what is read and noted in l. hostes, ff. de capt.; what Baldus notes in l. decernimus, C. de sacrosan. eccle.; and most excellently what is read and noted in c. per venerabilem, at the verse insuper, qui filii sint legi., and by Innocentius in c. cum P. Tab., de fide instru., and c. cum te, de re iudi. Therefore, just as a rebel against the Empire loses all civil rights as regards the entire world, as Bartolus maintained in said l. amissione, ff. de capi. di., so a rebel against his own homeland possessing the rights of a prince ought to lose all civil rights completely, as in l. an pars, ff. pro dere. To this pertains what the same Baldus notes in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. trini., and Bartolus in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iure, and what is noted in said c. per venerabilem, qui filii sint legi., and in said c. cum P. Secondly, to this pertains what Johannes Andreae notes in the additions to the Speculum, in the title de const., in the 3rd column, where

† he says that a statute of a city having imperium, providing with respect to its own subjects that rebels against their homeland may be harmed and killed with impunity, is valid; and Bartolus seems to intend this as well in the repetition of l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iure. If, therefore, such a city can take away life—and thus not only that which belongs to someone by civil law, but by nature, and this on account of disobedience—then a fortiori it can take away those things that belong to him by positive law, such as paternal power (patria potestas), which is of the law of the Romans, as in Inst. de patria potestate, in the beginning. For within its own people a city has full power to dispose alongside and against positive law, to such an extent that it can even exercise things reserved to the prince as a mark of universal dominion, such as restoring reputation, legitimating an illegitimate child, creating a notary, and the like, as noted by the same Bartolus in said l. infamem and in l. 1, de aqua plu. arcen., and by Innocentius in the previously alleged c. cum P. and c. cum te, and said c. per venerabilem is relevant. For if it exposes him to death and deprives him of all his goods, it is not likely that it wished to leave his sons subject to him in his power: an argument from l. nec in ea regem, ff. de adulte., where it is said that he who can kill an adulterer can much more and with greater force inflict an insult upon him, which is less. Thirdly, for the same point I adduce l. minime, and what Bartolus notes there, ff. de reli. & sump. fune., where it is clear that he who can be harmed and killed with impunity according to the form of a statute can even be killed by his son. If, therefore, a son could thus kill a rebel father, it is not to be presumed that he remained in paternal power, since according to the law of paternal power he could not merely not kill him, but could not even summon him to court, as in l. finalis, C. de in ius vocan., and the gloss noted in Inst. de pat. potesta., which enumerates all the rights of paternal power. Fourthly, I prove it through what is read and noted in c. postulasti, de foro compe.,

† where it is evident that a delinquent in one diocese can be deprived of all benefices that he holds even in another diocese from another superior. The reason is that the title of the benefice inheres in his person; whence, since by reason of the delict the person is made subject with respect to the penalty, or acquires the forum of that place where he transgressed, he can through that person be punished and deprived of all things that inhere in his person, wherever they may be, even if execution is carried out by another. Thus I say with respect to the present matter: since the father of this person concerning whom the question arises was fully subject to his city, the city was able to dispose both against his person and in all the rights that inhere in his person. The right of paternal power, moreover, inheres in his person, since it is a certain privilege granted to fathers by the law; hence it is that not all peoples have this right of paternal power, as is read and noted in Inst. de patria potesta. together with the gloss on the verse Romanorum. Nor should it move anyone to the contrary opinion that parents have this from the Emperor, and therefore it cannot be wrested from them without his authority—to which pertains what is noted in a similar case concerning the right of patronage by the noted gloss in c. filiis, 16, q. 5, which says that a layman cannot be deprived of that right by the Emperor, since he holds it by the authority of a canon; and to the same effect what the gloss notes in Clem. Pastoralis, de re iudic., on the word subiectae. For I say that this does not stand in the way: because by reason of delict, and of domicile or citizenship, he was fully subject to his city. Likewise, because this city, as regards its own subjects, can exercise the rights of the Empire, as I have stated above. Likewise, here the incapacity from the judge ceases; hence the noted gloss says in c. 1, de confir. uti., that by reason of delict someone can be deprived by a bishop of a benefice that he held from the Pope. Fifthly and lastly, I adduce this consideration:

† a city having the rights of a prince can, by reason of delict, confiscate the goods of the offender wherever situated, as noted in l. 1, C. de bon. vac., book 10, and by Bartolus in l. cunctos populos, at the end, C. de sum. trini., and in l. 2, ff. de iure fisci, and l. 1, de dam. infec. Thus, by equal reasoning, the same must be said concerning paternal power and other things that inhere in the person of the delinquent by civil law; nor does the opinion of Bartolus resist this conclusion in the case of a city possessing merum imperium. And let these things suffice. And so I say and advise to be the law, the judgment of someone having better discernment always reserved. I, Nicolaus of Sicily, Abbot of Monreale and doctor, and in testimony thereof I have subscribed with my own hand and caused my seal to be affixed, etc.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A monk must wear monastic garments.
2. A monk has neither a will nor a refusal.
3. Whether a monk can be naturally obligated.
4. Monks are dead to the world.
5. A deported person can acquire and contract after a sentence of deportation.
casus: A counsel against the friars of la Scala concerning their contracts, and of what kind they are said to be, etc. But note that this is not the counsel of the Lord Abbot, but was inserted, and I, Ludouicus Bologninus, found it thus in another book, who did not wish to remove what was already written or detract from the labors of others, and most especially since in my judgment, though small, this is an elegant counsel on its subject matter.
body: FOR the elucidation of the proposed question, three doubts must be discussed, from whose determination the decision of the proposed question will appear. First, of what kind the friars of the said hospital are and are said to be, namely, whether they are monks, or regular canons, or seculars, or clerics, or ecclesiastical persons, free or serfs, and of what manner of life. Second, presupposing in fact that the collegium of the friars of the said hospital was and is legitimately approved, whether any obligation can be contracted between one of the said friars on the one part, and the hospital, or its rector in the name of that hospital and collegium, on the other part, and what that obligation might be. Third, whether through the rector together with the said collegium, etc., the hospital itself can be obligated in any way; and if it can, what and of what kind that contracted obligation may be. And taking up the first, I say that the friars of the said hospital are not monks, nor regular canons. For monks must observe continence, regarding which even the Supreme Pontiff could not grant a dispensation, as in c. ad monasterium, in fine, de statu mona.; indeed, all clerics are bound to chastity, as in c. ut clericorum, de uita & honest. cleri. and de senten. excom. c. si concubinae; nor ought they to wander vagrant through the world, nor through villages and other places and the city, as in c. quanto, de offic. ordi., because just as a fish cannot live without water, neither can a monk without a cloister, 16. q. 1. c. placuit; indeed, he ought always to lead a solitary life, for he is called a monk from monos, which is ‘alone’, and acos, which is ‘sorrowful’, because alone and sorrowful he must remain in the cloister, note the gloss on the auth. de monachis § hinc autem a nobis in the word affectionem singulorum, and in l. decernimus, C. de episco. & cle.

† Likewise, a monk ought to wear monastic garments, namely a cowl and a scapular, noted on the said § hinc autem in the gloss on the word testem; and the text is today in clem. prima, de statu monach.; nor ought they in any way to eat meat in the refectory, even on the Nativity of the Lord, as in cap. fin. de obser. ieiunii.
† Likewise, a monk does not have a will or a refusal of his own, as in c. nolo and c. non dicatis, 12. q. 1. and c. si, de testam. lib. 6. and c. fin. de sepul. in the same book.

† And monks so completely lack a will that some were of the opinion that a monk is not even naturally obligated; so Hostiensis maintained in summa de fideiusso. § pro quo possit and the verse & quis. I do not believe this statement to be true, since I think a monk is at least naturally obligated, just as we say of a slave, l. naturaliter and l. si id quod, and there by Bartolus, ff. de cond. indeb., to which slave a monk is equated; so says Innocent in cap. cum olim, de priuile., which equation Bartolus cites and affirms in l. 1 and l. si seruus and l. liber homo and l. quod seruus, ff. de stipu. seruo., saying that this subject matter and title de stipu. seruo. is today of no or at least of little utility, except insofar as the provisions made concerning slaves have place in monks, as I said above. And similarly they are not regular canons, by the laws and reasons previously alleged. For regulars regularly agree with monks, especially in such essentials. Therefore Pope Nicholas said: 'I did not think that an Abbot was set apart from the company of the holy monks,' as in de statu monac. c. quod Dei timorem; and Hostiensis notes this in summa de regula & ad quid teneantur. And that the aforesaid things concerning monks and regulars in no way have place, nor are they found in the said friars of the hospital, we clearly see by pondering each point. They indeed must observe continence, as I said, but these men may keep their wives with them while merely serving the hospital; this is presupposed in fact concerning Friar Structius, who held and retained his wife even after entering the hospital throughout the entire time of his life, cohabiting with her together in a certain house, which is contrary to one of the essentials of the monastic and regular rule, as I proved above. Likewise, the former do not wander hither and thither, even through the city, while these go about even through the city according to the pleasure of their will, as we see in the facts. Likewise, the former wear the garments mentioned above, while these dress in a habit and clothes far different from theirs, as appears in the facts.

† Likewise, the former are dead to the world, note the gloss in the said § hinc autem, and in auth. de monachis § 1, col. 1, and in the said c. non dicatis, and they are also slaves, as in distinctio 64, cap. multos, and note in the said cap. non dicatis, and as I proved above; but these men are not so, as can clearly appear in the fact. Likewise, the said friars of the hospital are not clerics, for they have no clerical order. Indeed, one is called a cleric because he is of God's lot [sors], and one who ought to live from the altar. For in Greek cleros is termed sors in Latin, and clerics, by the institution of the Roman Church, ought to have a tonsure as a sign of the kingdom which is expected in Christ. All these things are proved in two chapters joined together, namely in cap. clericus and in cap. duo genera, twelfth distinction, second question. If we look closely, these things do not concur in the friars of the hospital. For they do not live from the altar, but from the revenues of the hospital, nor do they serve the altar as clerics do; the chapter cum secundum apostolum, de praebend. is relevant. Nor do they have a tonsure or shaving of the head, as appears to anyone looking upon them. And although they may have given their goods to the hospital, nevertheless they can retain many things in their possession in the houses of the hospital, even according to the form of the ordinances of the hospital itself. I say, however, that these friars are secular persons, not religious, but can be said to be persons devoted to God and ecclesiastical; just as we say of an unprofessed conversus, who is not bound to observe continence and is a person devoted to God, not a religious. So also we say of the Templars, who are able to bear arms and practice with them, which is inconsistent with clerics; this is found in the said cap. duo sunt genera, 12. q. 1, in the first gloss. And they are devoted persons and can be called ecclesiastical, not religious, as in the same chapter. So also we say of the brothers and sisters of the Third Order of St. Francis; for although they promise obedience, and have a rule and a certain way of living approved by the Roman Church, they are nevertheless not monks or nuns, but persons devoted to God and secular, not ecclesiastical. Whence such persons can contract marriage, and their children born thereafter can seek their legitimate portion, as is fully found in c. ut lex continentiae, 27. q. 1, where see especially the gloss. And Bartolus reports the same in l. semper, ff. de iure immunitatis, and Johannes Andreae in clem. 1, de religiosis domibus, where there is a good gloss. And that the rector of the said hospital and the other friars are secular is shown by an unanswerable reason: because it is established that a religious cannot be the rector of any hospital unless that hospital has the cure of souls, as in clemen. quia contingit, de relig. domi., and Johannes Andreae expressly affirms this there in the gloss on the word secularibus. Whence it is clear that the rector and the friars of the said hospital are seculars, since the hospital itself does not have a flock and the cure of souls, nor are the friars, or at least the rector, constituted in clerical orders. And I also hear this to be very true in fact, nor is there anything to the contrary in the proposed fact. Likewise, I say that they are free persons, having a will and a refusal, and a certain good and honest way of living together in the same house, whom we can call devoted to God. And their collegium is in a certain manner ecclesiastical, if we affirm that it has been expressly or tacitly approved by the Roman Pontiff, which approval is necessary; otherwise it would be disapproved. The case is in c. 1, de relig. domi. lib. 6, and is fully noted by Bartolus in l. sodales, ff. de colle. illicitis. Nor is it an obstacle to the aforesaid that the said friars, and especially Friar Structius, dedicated themselves and their property by promising obedience, etc., as appears in the presupposed theme. Because I say that since the said rector and friars are not religious, but seculars, as I have said, the said Friar Structius or another, by professing into the hands of the said rector or of another of the friars of the hospital, could not contract a solemn vow of religion; so affirms Innocent in cap. porrectum, de reg., and Bartolus and Baldus in auth. ingressi, C. de sacrosan. eccle., speaking specifically also of the Hospitallers. Indeed, the Speculator says even more in the title de statu monac., verse 19, that even if profession is made into the hands of a monk or of another other than the abbot, where the one receiving does not receive in the name of the abbot, then there is a dedication of property only, not of the person; and the case in the said c. porrectum seems to support this. I say, however, that although not the person, nevertheless the property of such a friar so dedicating himself and his goods is transferred to the hospital with respect to ownership, even though no delivery of them followed, l. finalis, C. de sacrosan. eccle., and Bartolus affirms this in the said authentica ingressi. Likewise, certain ordinances of the said hospital are not an obstacle: and first, that statute by which it is provided and the friars of the hospital are prohibited from seeking gain for themselves, but must offer it to the rector, etc.; likewise another by which it is provided that no one ought to be received as a friar of the said hospital unless he offers himself and his property to the hospital, and if it is done otherwise, he must be expelled, etc. Because, presupposing, as I said, the approval of the said collegium—concerning which I have doubt, and it does not appear to me from the statement of facts or the produced documents—I say that such statutes are invalid. For an approved collegium enacts statutes only concerning things belonging to their jurisdiction and to the management of the affairs and property of that collegium, not to the prejudice of a third party or of the jurisdiction of a superior, as is the case in l. 1, C. de mono., and noted by Bartolus in l. sodales, de colle. illici. and in his repetition of l. omnes populi. But to enact statutes concerning the prohibition of a contract, or the subjugation of someone's person so that he is called a slave, is not within the jurisdiction of the said collegium; on the contrary, it belongs either to the prince, or to the people, or to another having the power of so enacting by law or from the prince, l. 1, C. non lice. habi. metro. lib. 11, by the argument of the said authentica ingressi and what is noted there. For to enact such things as are noted in the said ordinances is nothing other than to take away those things that are from the hand of the prince, such as contracts, and to introduce servitude and take away liberty, which is of natural law, as in l. ex hoc iure, ff. de iusti. & iu. For such a collegium, and any other, when they convene together, ought to convene collegially to treat of those things that pertain to the collegium, not other matters, ff. de iure immu. l. semper § quibusdam; otherwise such a collegium is punished, l. sub praetextu, ff. de extraordina. crim. Who then will say that these things can be done by a collegium? Surely no one. Furthermore, I find that servitude is introduced in one of four ways: either by birth, as when one is born from a slave person; or by capture by enemies; or because someone sold himself to share in the price; or through a solemn vow of religion: these are found in sufficiently common texts of law, and this case is not one of those ways. Why say more? I find that a deported person can contract and acquire even after the sentence of deportation, after which by the sentence all his goods have been confiscated, ff. de testa. mil. l. neque and l. deportati, and note in l. 2, C. de bo. prosc. Likewise, since this could not be done by a pact and the profession of any of the said friars into the hands even of the rector, whom, as I have said, I regard as a secular, although devout and ecclesiastical, therefore it is not proved by a statute either; and note in rub. C. de decr. decu. lib. 11. I descend to the second doubt, and presupposing the approval of the said collegium, as I have said, I say that the rector and any of the aforesaid friars is a free person, and thus can contract, as I said and proved above, so that between the said collegium and hospital on the one part, and any of the friars of the said hospital on the other, any obligation, both natural and civil, can be contracted, if a contract otherwise permitted by law is made between them. For from a contract an obligation arises, and from an obligation an action, l. licet § ea obligatio, ff. de procu. I come to the third and last, to which I respond: since the rectors and governors of a hospital are equated to tutors and curators, as is proved in l. orphanotrophos, C. de epi. & cle., and there by Baldus, and in the said clem. quia contingit, then just as through tutors and curators contracting in the name of pupils or minors the pupils and minors themselves are obligated, in l. creditor, C. si tutor, uel curator inter., so through these rectors the hospital is obligated; just as we say in the case of a church, which is obligated by the contract of a prelate if this is done with the consent of the chapter, as in cap. quod quibusdam, de fideicom., and in c. 1, de depo., and what is noted there. From all of which, in my judgment, I can conclude and do conclude, as law and equity urge, submitting myself nevertheless to the correction of anyone with better judgment, I say that the said hospital was during the lifetime of Friar Structius himself obligated to the same Friar Structius for the said things and sums of money promised to him through the syndic of the said hospital having a legitimate mandate for this purpose; and that by the said Friar Structius all rights competent to him against the said hospital could be assigned by law to the said Johannes de Mariscottis of Siena, of whom mention is made in the statement of facts; which assigned rights Johannes himself could also thereafter use against the aforesaid hospital. And let these things suffice. Thanks be to God. I, Ugolino de' Marescalchi, the least among the doctors of civil law of Bologna. CONCERNING a bequest to pious causes, how it is proved, and concerning the competence of the judge, and concerning a legacy of cloths. But note that this is not a consilium of the lord Abbot, but was inserted, and so I found it in another book. I, Ludovicus Bologninus, who did not wish to remove things already written down or detract from the labors of others, and especially so since in my judgment, however slight, this is an elegant consilium in its subject matter.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A son is presumed from the quasi-possession of filiation.
2. The reason gives being to testimony in a witness.
3. What is contained under the appellation of cloths.
body: IN the name of Christ. From the process and proceedings before the lord Bishop of Cortona several doubts arise. First, regarding the competence of the judge: whether a competent judge was approached or not. Second, whether the legacy is proven, having regard to the number of witnesses, and upon examining the form and cause of the legacy, and the standing of the persons of the testator and of the legatee. Third, whether through the bequest thus made to the daughter of Paulus, filiation or quasi-possession of filiation is proven. Fourth, whether, presupposing a valid legacy of cloths, which cloths pass to the legatee and fall within the legacy; and considering the words of the legacy, sufficient proof has been made as to the cloths claimed, and let this be one doubt. Regarding the first, the form of the legacy is the cause for which jurisdiction is to be granted to an ecclesiastical judge, because he says 'for the love of God', and thus for pious causes, and for his soul, as in ff. de legat. 2. and l. si quis Titio; it is supported by extra, de appel. cogen. §. si unum de prædictis, de sepul. cap. 2. in gloss., C. de sacrosanct. eccle. l. illud. In this case, however, the cause claimed in the libel operates to establish that the matter may belong to ecclesiastical jurisdiction and be heard by an ecclesiastical judge, as noted by Inn. de fo. compe. in c. cum sit, and from the manner of suing and proceeding, because it proceeds according to the form of c. nouit. de iudic. In other causes an ecclesiastical judge would not be a competent judge, since certain matters pertain to the ecclesiastical forum, as in cap. nos inter alios, de purga. cano. And in our question, this is nevertheless rashly disputed, since he pronounced himself a competent judge and no appeal was taken, and thus, although it is an interlocutory decree, as in auth. habita. C. ne filius pro pa., de off. delega. c. significantibus, it nevertheless passes into res judicata, so that the party cannot contradict it. Regarding the second, although the rule of civil law required solemnity by reason of suspicion and to avoid fraud, as in l. hac consultissima. C. qui testamenta fac. possunt., so that in every last will, testament excepted, it required five witnesses to be employed, as in C. de condi. indebi. l. fin., nevertheless the censure of canon law, imitating as it were the ius gentium, provides otherwise, as in c. relatum. and cap. cum omnes. de testam. and there fully noted. Likewise one should not dwell upon the number, and whether those decretals have application indiscriminately, or only in the lands of the Church, or indeed when the testator is situated in extremis, whose judgment regarding solemnity is not so restricted, as noted by Bar. and others in C. de sa. san. ec. l. j. For on this account I do not deem the legacy invalid, and the bequest is said to have been made for the soul, or for pious causes, unless it were an artificial pretext, as I said, which lies within the discretion of the judge; and probable conjectures have been adduced from the statements of the witnesses that this legatee is poor, from the nature of his trade, and especially from the statement of one witness, when he said he had seen him dwelling in a hospital, residing in which is the utmost poverty, as noted in C. de mendi. uali. l. j., and similarly his daughter, upon inspecting the cause, especially as for a dowry, ff. de con. indebi. l. cum is. §. si mulier. there: 'pietatis causa', etc. As to the third, although proof of filiation is quite difficult, as says gl. in ff. de cond. & dem. l. Lucius, it is nevertheless proven by presumption, and it is sufficient proof, ff. de his, qui sunt sui uel alien. iur. l. filium, C. de nup. l. si uicinis, de filiis presby. ca. Michael, because

† from the quasi-possession of filiation a person is presumed to be a child, l. non nudis and l. non epistolis, C. de probatio., unless proof to the contrary were made; and so says Barto. in l. j. ff. de quæstionibus, as the gloss holds in said c. Michael, and as is noted in capit. per tuas, de probatio.; supported by what is noted by Iac. But. in l. j. ff. de proba. The testimony of Christophorus is indeed clear and proves it. Likewise there is the statement of Hieronymus, which at first sight does not seem to prove it, since he affirms and deposes using the word 'he believes'. But certainly it does indeed prove it, in view of his conscience, which carries more weight than the mere statement. Whence that illustrious doctor the lord Bald. said in l. conuenticula, C. de episco. & cler., that where a witness in his statement proves less, but in his reasoning proves more effectively, the reasoning is always to be considered.

† Because in a witness, the reason is that which gives existence to the matter, that is, to the testimony, as noted in de testi. c. solum; supported by what is noted in ff. de acquir. poss. l. si is, because of the intention; and thus the quasi-possession of filiation is proven. And other witnesses prove supporting circumstances and the intention of the plaintiff, which must give the greatest aid. So says the letter of the law in a similar case, de successione ab intestato, c. fin. But it remains to be seen—and this is the fourth doubt—which cloths fall under the legacy; for he says that he bequeathed his cloths of linen and wool. Nor is it to be discussed regarding the revocation of an error, because it sufficiently appears that an error was proven. And likewise one must not insist on whether he was of sound mind at the time of the said bequest, pursuant to what is noted in l. furiosum, C. qui testamenta facere possunt., 12. q. 3. c. in dictis hominum, de success. ab intest. c. fi., ff. de condi. inst. l. quidam in suo, along with similar texts. Let us therefore answer the fourth doubt. And on this Barto. says in l. diuus, ff. de bo. dam.

† that under the appellation of cloths are contained those things with which one is clothed, but cloths not suitable for human use and which are for sale do not fall under it; whence as a practical matter he answered that when someone had bequeathed to another all his cloths of wool and linen, and had there some pieces of linen cloth not suitable for human use, they do not fall within the legacy; or a distinction must be drawn, according to him: either he had those pieces of linen cloth for the purpose of making linen cloths for use, and they fall within the legacy; or they are handled as goods for sale, and they do not fall under it, as in l. pediculis. §. item cum quæreretur, de au. & argen. leg. In case of doubt it must be examined how much was beneficial to him for the use of that year, and that passes to the legacy; the rest is deemed to be for sale, as in l. cum quæritur. §. lana, de leg. 3. Barto. is therefore speaking of when those pieces of cloth were not suitable for human use, nor did the testator possess those cloths for the purpose of selling, but for use. I ask regarding the fourth, whether the proof is sufficient regarding the cloths claimed; and the 27 articles and the depositions of the witnesses upon them are to be examined, who were four, namely Silvester, Bart., ser Antonius Andrusii, and ser Anto. Angeli. And this last one proves nothing; the other witness, moreover, refers himself to the oath drawn up by the hand of that same witness; the other two prove as to certain items, but not as to all, as can clearly appear from their depositions. And from the above, I conclude first that the legacy of 25 pounds made to the daughter of Paulus, when the event of marriage has occurred, or likewise also the legacy of the cloths, [is valid]. And that it is proven that, in supplement of proof, the judge can tender an oath when it has been requested. But which cloths are proven, a diligent investigator will be able to ascertain from the deposition of the witnesses upon the 27th article; and thus, as is written above, I, Dionysius of the lord Nicolaus of Barigiano, the least of doctors of both laws, do state and advise, and for the faith thereof I have subscribed and caused my seal to be affixed, a better opinion being always preserved, in accordance with l. Claudius Fœlix, ff. qui po. in pign. habe. AGAINST fraud upon the excise tax, and concerning the granted license, etc. Nor is this the consilium of the lord Abbot; but because I, Ludovicus Bologninus, found it thus uncertain, I resolved not to alter what was already written and not to detract from the honor of those fathers, and all the more so since 'that which is not changed, why should it be forbidden to stand?' l. sancimus, C. de testa. along with similar texts.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If a thief committed theft, and the owner of the stolen property says that the thing was taken with his consent, and thus that theft was not committed, the thief is nonetheless liable to the penalty. §. recte.
2. One who readily gives an opinion against the fisc in doubtful questions does not commit an offense.
body: Having invoked the name of Christ, and having seen a certain inquest drawn up by Ser Bar., notary of unlawful damages of the territory of Lucignano, against Giovanni Bondi and Cicregiola, and the answers made by the same to the said inquest, and the whole process, certain allegations and exceptions in favor of the said persons under inquest, and the statutes and reformations of the territory of Lucignano speaking on the matter, and especially a certain statute which begins, *Bestie minute paga de passagio* etc., and a certain other chapter which begins, *In qualunche cap. si facesse mentione*, at the verse *& doue se trahe o passa sempre in ogni tempo si intende anderà con la poliza del Cauagliere, e se trahesse o passasse senza la detta poliza, sia condennato per gabella fraudata*; and also the last chapter, which begins, *Chi frauda la gabella, paga per ogni denaro* etc., and other statutes produced before me, especially the statute placed under the rubric *de elect. & officio officialis damnorum datorum*; and particularly having seen the response and confession made by the aforesaid defendants, I say that by law and the rigor of the law the said defendants are to be condemned. For toward those who have confessed and been convicted, the judge has no other role than in condemning, as in l. 1, de confess. For since they confess that they extracted without a permit (*apodissa*), even though they deny having done so with the intention of defrauding, and they confess that they did so without a permit, yet allege the license of one of the purchasers of the gabella, they thus fall under the said statute, because they went without a permit. For there it is clearly stated that in any case, whether of transit or contention, they must always go with a permit, otherwise let them be condemned for defrauded gabella, as clearly appears in the said chapter beginning *qualunque c.*, at the verse *e doue si trahe o passa*. And thus, where the case is defined, there is no room for doubt, as in l. ancillae, C. de furt., and the law, though harsh, must nevertheless be observed, as in l. prospexit, ff. qui & à quibus. Nor does it stand in the way that they deny having an intention to defraud, because the law presumes fraud, as clearly appears in the said verse where it is said, *Et unde si trahe*; which presumption is perhaps of law and by law (*iuris et de iure*) by virtue of the said chapter, and thus contrary proof is not admitted. But even assuming that it were only of law (*iuris tantum*) and not *de iure*, and thus contrary proof would be admitted, I say that their innocence was not proven, and from the quality of the act a presumption arises against them, and so the burden of proof falls upon them, as is the text in l. si non convitii, C. de iniur., and l. j, C. ad l. Corn. de sicar., which was by no means fulfilled on their part, as appears from the law. Nor does the confession or testimony of Bramante stand in the way, because the voice of one is the voice of none, as in l. iusiur., C. de testib., and especially in criminal matters, in which proofs ought to be clearer than the midday light, as in l. sciant, C. de probat. Likewise, because his confession can prejudice Bramante, but not the community of Lucignano or its official; to this effect makes very well the noted statement of Bartolus in l. inter omnes, §. recte, ff. de furtis, where he says that

† if someone committed a theft, and the owner of the stolen property appears and says that the thing was taken from him with his consent, and thus that a theft had not been committed, because theft is the handling of another's property against the will of the owner etc., but it is asserted to have been done with the owner's consent, therefore etc.; nevertheless his confession does not free the thief from punishment, as he determines in the said §. recte. And thus also in the present case the confession of that man does not free them from punishment. To this effect also makes l. licitatio, §. quod illicitae, ff. de public., where the utility of private persons and the vigor of public discipline are considered; and this I think was the mind of that chapter which requires a permit, lest thefts be committed through confession and the like, etc. Nor does it stand in the way, which is alleged by the opposing party, that the statute requires actual malice (*verus dolus*), but actual malice is denied, therefore etc., and they cite the chapter of the statute which begins, *Et qualunche persona* etc.; because the truth is to the contrary, as clearly appears in the said verse *& doue si trahe o passa*, where from the quality of the act it presumes fraud, and thus the verse speaks not only of actual malice, but also of presumed malice; and similarly also the said statute is alleged by the opposing party which begins, *Et qualunche persona*, which speaks through several words set disjunctively, not copulatively. Likewise, it does not stand in the way, which is alleged, that they were not there for the purpose of selling, but for the purpose of pasturing; because in both cases provision was made, as appears in the statute which begins, *Bestie minute paga de passagio* etc. Whereof that worthy and subtle doctor who drafted the allegations for the opposing party must not have seen the second chapter. Likewise, it does not stand in the way, which is alleged by the opposing party, that the said defendants were ignorant of such a statute and that such a permit was necessary, which ignorance of municipal law seems to excuse them, especially lest they suffer an undue loss, as is subtly alleged by the opposing party; because this is true unless such ignorance is gross and supine, as noted in the Gloss and there by Bartolus in l. si de decret. ab ordin. faciend., and Dinus in cap. ignorantia, de regul. iur. in 6., at the word which begins *ultimo distingui potest*, and in the preceding word, and it is today settled, as in c. ut animarum, Extra, de constitut. in 6.; and regarding our case the text seems there to state expressly that although someone says he was ignorant, the deified Hadrian nonetheless ordained that he falls into the penalty of the toll. And by the aforesaid, an adequate response seems to have been given to the laws and arguments adduced and subtly alleged by the opposing party, except for the last, not caring about the first, namely whether an inquest could be conducted or not; because however that may be, by municipal law an inquest could be held, as clearly appears in the said statute under the rubric *de electio. & officio officialis damnorum datorum*, and I hear that it has always been so by custom. To the last argument, however, in which contrary custom is alleged, I say that, having seen the acts and proceedings in the said case, the said contrary custom was not proven, since they did not prove their innocence; for the presumption is against them, as I said above. I say that they are to be condemned by the rigor of the law; nevertheless let the good judge consider the condition of the persons, the quality of the deed, and the custom of the land, and let him diligently investigate the truth, notwithstanding that the said defendants did not know how to defend themselves, as the most sacred Emperor clearly teaches us in l. j, in fine, ff. de quaestion., and let him be readier to acquit than to condemn. In a case of doubt,

† because I do not think that he transgresses who readily answers against the fiscus in doubtful questions, as in l. non puto, ff. de iure fisci. Nevertheless, if other things are shown, he can by law condemn the aforesaid defendants who have confessed, as was shown most clearly above. May the Lord direct him into the way of truth and justice. I, Giovanni de' Blandini of Siena, doctor of laws. ON TESTAMENTARY EXPENSES.

An heir who gathers the testament wishes that the legatees contribute to the gathering of the testament. If indeed the inheritance were solvent, the heir himself ought to pay the whole, just as an existing debt.
