But if the inheritance were not solvent, then the legacies will be reduced on account of that expense, just as on account of another debt; so notes Bartolus in l. scimus, § in computatione, C. de iu. delib., and the Speculator touches upon it as he reports there, and c. Impediat; yet he is not said to harm himself, nor to inflict an injury, ff. qui in fraudem credi. l. qui autem, § simili modo. Likewise, there is the same reason in the case of a grandson, since the inheritance of ascendants is equally due to all descendants, without regard to difference of sex, nor disparity of degrees, because a grandson or a great-grandson, who are in a more remote degree, succeed equally with a son; the text is in l. 1, C. de legi. hære., and auth. in successione, under the same title; so a statute, in so far as it gives a new form of action, as Bartolus in l. 1, ff. ad l. Fal., is nevertheless called ius commune with regard to other matters. Thus the gloss of Johannes Andreae in c. 1, de const., in Sexto, is to be understood; and thus it ought to be interpreted according to how the ius commune is interpreted, C. de noxalibus, l. si serui, where there is a notable case, and the gloss in l. si, § donec, at the end, C. de iur. delib., etc. Abbot Nicolaus. A certain subscription, whether the son of an outlawed person can make a will, etc., and it belongs to the lord Abbot, as appears below. Consilium of the Lord Ludovicus Bologninus. THE CASE is as follows: When the brothers J. and A. and their other brothers were merchants in the city of M. and had good credit, and while they were absent from the said city, on the 10th day of the month of September 1472, a certain proceeding was commenced against the said brothers J. and A. and their other brothers according to the form of the municipal law of the said city, and this at the instance of certain of their asserted creditors. These asserted creditors in the said proceeding asserted that the said J. and A. and their brothers had stopped payments or defaulted in fraud of the said creditors. While the said proceeding was pending, subsequently, on the eleventh day of the said month of September and of the aforesaid year, a new proceeding, and distinct from the first, was commenced against the said J. alone, and this on account of an affair of state. While these proceedings were thus pending, it was pronounced by the ordinary judge according to the form of the statutes of the said city upon the first proceeding of bankruptcy on the 2nd day of the month of October of the said year, namely that the said brothers J. and A. and their other brothers had been and were defaulting, and that proceedings had to be taken against them and their property as against defaulting, bankrupt, and non-paying debtors to their creditors. While this proceeding of bankruptcy was thus pending, on the first day of October of the said year, another proceeding was formed against the brothers of the said J. and A. for the said affair of state, and afterwards on the 20th day of October they were banished as rebels, with confiscation of goods. Finally, on the same 20th day of October of the said year, the said J. was also banished from the said city on account of state and as a rebel, with confiscation of his goods. These things having been thus conducted, on the 20th day of April of the year 1474 the said J. and A. and the brothers were declared debtors of the said creditors by virtue of the said proceeding of bankruptcy according to the form of the said statutes, wherefore the said J. and A. and the brothers were treated by the form of the said statutes just as if they had been condemned in the said amounts on the said day. At length, in 1474, the said city changed its constitution to such an extent that there J. and A. and their brothers obtained to be cancelled from the said bans, and the restitution of goods under the mode, form, and tenor written below, namely: 'P. C., legate, etc., to our beloved J. and A. and their brothers, greeting, etc. While we diligently consider the agreeable services rendered to us by you and each of you, and which we hope will be rendered in future times, we are moved, not undeservedly, to render ourselves liberal in favors to you, and to pursue you with favors and graces. Hence it is that, moved by reason of the premises, by the tenor of the presents and by the authority granted to us, we command you the remaining notaries and officials of the chamber of records, as well as of the treasury and of the office of the banished, and each of you, that you cancel and abolish all and singular the underwritten, whose names are specifically described below, and their names and surnames, from all and singular books or quires existing in the said places or elsewhere, and all and singular and whatever bans of condemnation, inquest, and proceedings entered, registered, copied, or made in the books themselves at any time prior to our arrival at the city of M., which was in the year of the Lord 1473 on the third day of September; decreeing also from now by the tenor of the presents and by the aforesaid authority as null, void, and of no effect the bans themselves, and the offenses committed before the said time, and the condemnations, inquests, and proceedings, so that they may freely and with impunity dwell and reside in the city of M. and its county and district without any grievance or molestation being inflicted on the aforesaid underwritten persons or on account of any of the aforesaid, namely of the bans or condemnations, or of any of them, also restoring them and each of them to reputation, honors, and to other things, as they were before. In witness whereof we have ordered the presents to be made and fortified with the impression of our seal. Whose names are these, namely J. and A. and their brothers, etc.' Successively in the said city of M., other political changes having supervened, and the regime having changed in 1475, by certain citizens, M. and A., holding power from the people of the said city, it was among other things enacted and ordained that all and singular who were condemned, confined, banished, and in any way driven into flight on account of state should be restored to their former property, goods, and rights, honors, dignities, and privileges, which they held before the said citations, and should be held as restored by operation of law. These things so standing, a certain Antonius, one of the creditors of the said J. and A. and the brothers, petitions for the execution of the aforesaid sentence rendered against the said J. and A. and the brothers upon the aforesaid bankruptcy, as well as of the other sentence of declaration, made as above, concerning the amounts in which the said brothers were alleged and declared debtors in the said proceeding of bankruptcy, which sentences were rendered at the times, in the manner, and in the form aforesaid. Against this requested execution it is opposed by the said J. and A., who allege that the said sentences cannot and ought not to be executed, because they were restored against the said sentence and the entire proceeding by virtue of the mandate issued, as above, by the said legate, as set forth above; as well as, successively, by the restitution made by the citizens of M. and the provisions and ordinances mentioned above. On the part of the said Antonius, however, it is replied that the said provisions and petitions do not stand in the way, because he asserts that they apply in a criminal case, but not in a civil one. Likewise, the said other restitutions do not extend to the said brothers J. and A., who were not banished at the time of the said provisions. It is asked what the law is. Ludovicus Bologninus.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A legatus de latere, where he does something by right of legation, is to be equalled to the prince.
2. The Pope always strives to preserve the decrees and institutions of his legates.
3. Provisions, statutes, and decrees made by presiding officers by the authority of the general council of electors, after it was granted by the authority of the prince, have the force of law and of civil law.
4. Decrees made by the people are civil law.
5. The word 'alia' [other things] includes criminal, civil, mixed, and spiritual.
6. A city can make a general law by which a right is taken away from a third party.
body: Having invoked divine aid, by whose mediation truth may shine forth (for the Lord is near unto all them that call upon him), and having seen the point expressed above, although enough and more than enough has already been said above by other learned counsel to the point of satiety, so that an answer is already apparent, as in l. fundi Trebatiani, ff. de usufru. leg., I have nonetheless deemed it necessary to elicit from the present consultation certain matters that seem to introduce doubt, and finally to resolve all of them. And first, regarding that phrase in the restitution made by the lord legate P. C.: 'Restoring them also, and each one of them, to fame and honours, and other things, as they were before ascribed to them, and to each of them.' Above, however, in the restitution, express mention was made that I. and A. and the brothers named in the point were restored against ban condemnations, inquisitions, and processes; and thus it was ordered in the recorded restitution that all things be abolished. The power of this legatus de latere is not small, but rather great and most ample, and is equalled to the power of the prince or the Pope; and first I assume this from the text joined with the elegant gloss in c. nobilissimus, dist. 97, which states:

† that where a legatus de latere does something by right of his legation, he is certainly to be equalled to the prince, having the most ample power in this regard; and so I understand Spec. in the title de lega. § superest, verse quid si de legati iurisdictione, namely that credence is given even to that legate's oraculum vivae vocis, and in the title de teste. § j. verse quid si advocatus, in l. 2 § liquet, near the end, C. de sum. tri. & fi. cath. This is affirmed by Archidiaconus in said c. nobilissimus, and Innocentius in c. cum dilectus, de accu., and Johannes Andreae in c. j. de offi. dele. in 6., de sent. exc. c. ad audientiam, de appel. c. constitutus, and the gloss on de sent. exc. c. sicut, and in c. ad apostolicae, de re iud. in 6., and c. cum olim essemus, de privil., and Lapus, allegation 12 and 33, and Bartolus in l. j. C. de superindic. lib. 10; of this opinion also is Baldus in l. exemplo, C. de proba. and in l. si qua per calumniam, C. de epis. & cle. And I weigh especially that this restitution was made concerning matters pertaining to his legation; and add the good text in c. super his, de accu., indeed Johannes Andreae says in said c. super his that it is the style of the Roman Curia that credence is given to him even outside his legation on his bare word alone, that is, by an oraculum vivae vocis. For this, an excellent reason is the text and gloss in l. j. ff. de offi. praefe. praet., where it says that the prince believed that those who, on account of their singular industry, were chosen for the magnitude of this office, would not judge otherwise than the prince himself would judge, as the text there says; whence it happens that there is the greatest presumption in favour of legates and potestas and solemnity, as Speculator explains at length in the whole title de leg., and especially in § superest. And to the aforesaid add Dominus Antonius on fide instrumentorum, c. quod super his; and specifically to our purpose, the aforesaid legate was able to grant the said restitution, because he makes statutes that are to endure in perpetuity, in c. fi. de offi. lega., in c. ex parte, de verb. sig., and c. super quibusdam; see also the notes on dist. 4 c. porro, and dist. 26 c. utinam. Indeed,

† the Pope always strives to preserve the decrees and institutions of his legates, de rescr. c. veniens. And successively, the legate can do everything that is not specially reserved to the Pope, all of which are singularly set forth by the gloss in c. quod translationem, de offi. leg., in c. sicut unire, de exces. praela., and Speculator sets it down in the title de iur. om. iud. The legate also interprets a rescript of the Lord Pope N., which is a very great matter, in c. j. de postu. prael. at the word rescriptum nostrum interpretatus; and add the notes de iudi. c. novit. What more? He has imperium over the province governed by him, as in the said § superest, by Speculator—cases which it would be more laborious than subtle to explain here. Therefore, the recorded restitution possesses the greatest power, namely that of the Pope, or similar, because of the province which the legate governs. The said restitution is also founded upon the power, imperium, arbitrium, and authority of the reformers of the state of the said city M. holding the vicariate of the said city in full form from the Supreme Pontiff; because the said lords reformers were elected by the council of the people representing the authority of the Lord Pope, and they are equated to the prince, as is noted C. quae sit lon. consue. on the rubric, and de reg. iur. l. aliud § refertur; whence Bartolus elegantly says in l. stipulationum aliae, ff. de verb. obl.,

† that provisions, statutes, and decrees, and other things enacted by presidents elected by authority of the general council, once granted by authority of the prince, shall have the force of law and of the civil law, as in the prooemium of the Institutes, in the first and second constitutions of the Code, and l. 2, C. de vete. iur. enu. To the same point I cite Bartolus in l. fi. ff. de poen.,

† where decrees enacted by the people will be civil law, and a perpetual action will arise, which is called civil, insti. de perpe. & temp. actio. in prin. And on this point there is no disagreement among the doctors, although it is debated elsewhere whether statutes enacted by a bishop, a marquis, and others are praetorian law or civil law; but in our case, the council and the people hold the place of the prince. I add Baldus in l. receptitia, C. de consti. pecu., in l. j. C. qui admit. ad bon. poss., and Baldus in l. sancimus, C. de dona., and what is noted by Johannes Andreae in the additions to Speculator in the title de instr. edit. in § porro, in the addition beginning haec subscriptio. Having laid down this foundation, I consider a certain word in the restitution made by the said lords, namely: they restored all, and willed that they be restored, to all their pristine right, even if anything belonging to the aforesaid restored persons is today, that is, at the time of the restitution, held and possessed in any manner whatsoever, with the general clause non obstante and all other suitable clauses; and this was done at one time. Afterwards another restitution was made at another time, in which all were expressly restored to criminal and civil causes, processes, prescriptions, and all things. Whence, coming in order through each restitution, I first take up that of the Lord Cardinal P., legatus de latere, in which he specifically restored the said brothers from all criminal processes, and to fame and honours, and other things, as was previously written regarding them; which restitution conforms to the ius commune, l. quod si minor, in § restitutio, de mino. And since he makes express mention of criminal matters, and subsequently says 'and to other things', this word 'other' is no longer understood to refer to criminal matters, to avoid superfluity, in § quibus, in the first constitution of the Code; but it is understood to refer to civil matters, which possess in many respects a similarity to criminal matters, although they differ in many others, as discussed at length by Bartolus in l. fi. ff. de priva. delic., in l. j. C. quando civilis actio praeiudi. criminali, and l. 1, ff. vi bo. rap., and at length by Dominus Antonius in the rubric de iudi., after Innocentius in c. qualiter & quando, de accu., and what is noted in l. quid ergo § poena gravior, de infa., in l. agraria, de termino moto. Whence, by the similarity of process, libel, contestatio litis, and sentence required in them, namely in criminal and civil matters, when it says 'and to other things', it is understood of civil matters, l. si fugitivi, C. de ser. fugi., as if the word 'such' were implicative of similar things. Moreover, such a phrase 'and to other things' must of necessity be understood of civil matters because of the word 'and', which is a conjunction and falls between diverse things, in the rubric ff. de iur. & fact. ig. where the gloss is; therefore, since he spoke above of criminal matters, this phrase 'and to other things' is understood of civil sentences, since of temporal causes and trials, with which we are dealing, some are criminal, some civil, and some mixed. Criminal causes are said to be those whose end is the benefit of the party and the public interest or public vengeance; civil causes, those whose end is the benefit of the party and private interest; mixed, those that share in the interest of the party and in private and public vengeance: an example in c. tuae, de procu. These distinctions are found in c. forus, de verb. sig., and in the above-mentioned legal texts; whence it clearly appears that it is understood of civil matters. From another perspective, that the said restitution is extended to civil processes and sentences, I argue: because if restitution is made to greater matters, it is therefore easily extended to lesser matters and to other things, as in c. sedis, and the extensive treatment in c. cum in multis, de rescrip. in 6. I add the note in Clementina non potest, de procura., and what Bartolus handsomely approves in l. sed & si quis, in § quaesitum, ff. si quis cau. Indeed, directly on point for our proposition, I cite the singular gloss in Clementina 1, at the word quamvis alia, de re iudi., where it says,

† that this word 'other' includes criminal, civil, mixed, and spiritual matters, which I magnify for my proposition, and note as principal for this decision. I also cite the singular note of Innocentius, that civil matters are included a fortiori, in c. cum olim, de offi. deleg.; and when he has expressed graver matters, the word 'other' is drawn to all things; but if lighter matters are expressed in a rescript, and afterwards someone does me some injuries, I will not be able to accuse him of homicide. But the case appears to be the opposite where graver matters were expressed, namely criminal, and we wish to make an extension through the word 'other' to lighter matters, namely civil: certainly we can, as Innocentius handsomely affirms in c. dispendia, de rescrip. in 6., and Dominus Antonius approves in the said c. sedes, de rescrip. And the aforesaid are confirmed so that the said word may have some operation and effect, de leg. 1, c. si quando, de privile., c. si Papa, in 6. Having considered all these matters, I touch upon that well-worn and common doubt, whether the said cardinal legatus de latere was able to take away a right acquired by another through a sentence by granting a restitution of this kind. Likewise, what of the restitution of the aforesaid lords reformers of the state, where the aforesaid brothers are restored to goods possessed today by others, and the said restitution is well fortified with opportune clauses, and especially the clause non obstante? For first, although it was doubted whether the prince can take away the ius gentium, namely ownership invented by the ius gentium, in l. ex hoc iure, ff. de iusti. & iure, that is, whether ownership of my property can be taken away from me, and although in doubt the gloss seems to hold that it cannot, in l. rescripta, C. de preci. impe. offe. (for which an implicit reason is provided by l. quoties, C. de preci. impe. offe., in l. fi. C. si contra ius vel uti. pub., and in l. fi. C. de errore advocatorum, by which it is provided that the right of another cannot be taken away or uprooted entirely), I say that on multiple grounds an acquired right could be taken away through a sentence from someone by the prince, and by others who are held in place of the prince. And first, for this I cite the text in l. item si verberatum § penul. de rei ven., where for cause ownership can be taken away and granted to another; Bartolus affirmed this in the prooemium of the Digest, and the same in l. 1 at the end, de constit. principi. What greater cause could there be than that the said sentences were rendered while the said brothers were rebels of the city on account of the factions or partisanship of the city, who during the time of the aforesaid rebellion were unable to defend their rights or causes? And therefore restitution issued, and by reason of prohibited defence, because access to the city was not safe, there is therefore just cause, in Clementina pastoralis, de re iudi.; Innocentius set this down in c. praeterea, de dila., in extravagans praesenti, de rescrip., and all the legists in l. 2 ff. si quis in ius voc. non ie., l. de aetate, where Bartolus comments at the end, ad Trebel. ff. Let there be added for this opinion the text in l. si quis sepulchrum, de religio., where mention is made of just cause, and one must be compelled at a fair price, etc. And let there be added the rationale of the title de bo. dam. Indeed, Angelus says more in said l. item si verberatum § pen.: without cause the prince can take away ownership from one and give it to another without prejudice to the recipient, by l. 2 and l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadri. praescrip. The same Angelus affirmed this in l. constat, communia praediorum, where not only can the prince do this, but by statute and custom the right of another individual person can be taken away, on the argument of l. si pendentes § si quid, ff. de usufru.; and Innocentius affirms this latter point in c. 1 de consue. Something similar is found in c. in nostra, de iniur. & dam. dato, and Angelus says the same in a passage in l. pactionum, ff. de pac. Nay, indeed, Bartolus says in l. Antiocheni, de pri. credi.,

† that a city can make a general law by which something is taken away from a third party, as it did in our case for the benefit of all banniti, confined persons, and rebels whatsoever. And these things are so held, the saying of Innocentius in c. quae in ecclesiarum, de consti., being explained in this way, that it is to be understood of making a particular law, l. si privatus, ff. quae & a quibus, so that it does not harm, l. quoties, ff. de pollicitationibus, just as a city can make a general statute concerning its own affairs, l. prohibere § plane, ff. quod vi aut clam, and what is noted de publi. l. Caesar, and Baldus sets it down in l. civitatis, ff. si cer. pe. In confirmation of all the aforesaid, let there be added the text in l. Lucius, ff. de evic., and what Archidiaconus noted, dist. 1 c. ius civile, and 9 q. fi. c. per principalem. Likewise on another ground: even assuming, without prejudice to truth, that the truth were such that it could not be taken away in another manner, it can always be taken away by the fullness of power. For the clause concerning the fullness of power is, among the other two principal ones, namely the clause non obstante and the clause ex certa scientia, presumed. And in truth, in all restitutions the prince, or the city, or the legate tacitly attests knowledge in the narration, but expressly in a clause non obstante, which validates a rescript or restitution by the fullness of power, if it is said 'notwithstanding anything making to the contrary'; so Bartolus affirms in l. fi. C. si contra ius vel util. publi., Baldus expressly de pace Constan. at the word livellarium, and Baldus in l. eos, C. de app.; add what is noted in l. sed & si quis § quaesitum, ff. si quis cautio., in l. iubemus, C. ad velle., in the authentica de test. imperfectis § pen., and in the authentica hoc inter liberos, C. de testa.; and Bartolus sets it down in extravagans ad reprimendum, at the word non obstantibus. Indeed, perpetual silence ought to be imposed upon one who goes against the deed of a superior, because the city granted the indult knowingly and notoriously for the good of the city, therefore ex certa scientia; therefore it cannot go against that which was done ex certa scientia, as Baldus elegantly affirmed de pace Constan. at the word si quis autem; l. idem Ulpianus, ff. de excus. tuto. is relevant. These things having been thus stated, I conclude that even if ownership acquired by another could not be taken away by a superior—which is not true—ownership acquired through a sentence can always be taken away, as I find elegantly affirmed by Baldus in l. si, C. senten. rescin. non posse. For in every sentence there is understood the clause 'saving the supreme power of the prince', l. si, C. de legi., or of him who is held in place of the prince, as I said above; which statement I note and weigh heavily for this decision, for since a right acquired through a sentence is acquired through the mediation of civil law and thus by civil law, it can therefore be taken away more easily than a right of the ius gentium, and this is undoubtedly true, since there is in it a derogatory clause. Let there be added l. humanum, C. de legi., and what is noted by Johannes Andreae in c. j. de exces. prael., c. 1 de consti., and what Cino noted in his disputation, that a derogatory provision took precedence, and elegantly in the said authentica hoc inter liberos, namely the clause non obstante § item cum sit in materia etc., certain and notorious knowledge; but even more can what belongs to the civil law be taken away, l. 2 § exactis, ff. de origi. iur., provided that it has not passed into a contract, an action, or a grant with a non-subject, as Innocentius posits, de iudi. c. novit, whom I understand in this way in c. in nostra, de iniu. & damno dato; and I add Bartolus in l. privilegia, C. de sa. san. eccl., and what Dominus Florentinus said in l. perpendimus, de senten. excom. But with a subject, even those things that have passed into a contract, many hold that he can take away by a bare word, said l. privilegia, by argument a speciali, or because the reason ceases; l. generalis; the utility of the subjects is involved in the restitution, nor had it passed into a contract; indeed they are subjects, to whom prejudice can more easily be brought by the bare word of the prince, in Clementina dudum, in § verum, de sepul. From all of which I firmly conclude in law that the said sentence, against which the restitution placed in the point was granted, does not merit execution, neither by law, nor by custom, nor by statutory law. And so I state and advise, I, Ludovicus Bologninus, the least doctor of both laws and knight, lecturing ordinarily on the civil laws in Ferrara in the morning; and in faith of the aforesaid I have subscribed my name and affixed my customary seal. OF THE CONSILIA OF PANORMITANUS.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A manifest usurer must be deprived of ecclesiastical burial until he has fittingly satisfied for extorted usury.
2. Manifest usurers ought not to be present at wills.
3. Where the law requires something under a certain form or quality, then the act being fulfilled without the form and quality does not suffice.
casus: CASE OF THE FIRST COUNSEL. A CERTAIN man named Cola, a citizen and inhabitant of Fano, a manifest usurer, as is said to be provable, wishing to spare his shame, and not to lack ecclesiastical burial, and not to be deprived of the capacity to make a will, having summoned the rector of the parish, a notary, and witnesses, gave security under the below-written form. For he asserted that it came to his notice that some whisperers and sowers of tares were attempting to defame him, alleging that he practices and has practiced usurious depravity, and he attested that this was not at all true; and wishing in every way to cut off malevolent tongues, to show to all that he was innocent of such guilt, and to draw up solemnly his will and last testament after giving the below-written security, he promised the venerable man Lord Nicolaus Bartoli, rector of the church of San Leonardo, etc., and Dominicus, notary, etc., that if at any time it shall legitimately appear, or could appear, that he had extorted anything from anyone or several persons through usurious depravity, he would restore all of that, and whatever should be legitimately shown, in full; and wishing to give fitting security in the aforesaid matters, he requested the noble man Johannes, etc., to become surety solemnly on his behalf for the aforesaid matters, etc., and so subsequently the said Johannes became surety generally. It is now asked, since he successively made two wills—in the first of which he instituted Lord Hugolinus and the adopted son of the said testator as heirs, but in the second he ordered his goods to be distributed for the work of a certain public bridge, the repair of which pertains to a certain church or hospital—whether, by virtue of the aforesaid security, any of the said wills can stand.
body: Having humbly implored the aid of Almighty God and of Mary His mother, although many things could be objected against the said security; nevertheless, because they are not clear in themselves, but situated in the opinions of the doctors, and lest I should appear to make a matter entirely beyond doubt to me seem doubtful, I therefore briefly and boldly conclude that neither of the said wills possessed any validity, but that they are entirely of no force. And for this conclusion of mine I say that there is a most clear case, which cannot be caviled at in any way, in c. 2 de usuris, in VI°, for there in the beginning it is provided,

† that a manifest usurer is to be deprived of ecclesiastical burial, until fitting satisfaction has been made for the extorted usury, so far as the means of the usurer himself allow, or fitting security has been given to those persons mentioned there concerning restitution to be made. And because in the beginning mention had been made of security in general, in the subsequent paragraph he gives a certain form to this security, saying that if the amount of the usury to be restored is manifest, we will that it always be expressed in the security; otherwise, we will that another amount be expressed, namely, one to be moderated at the discretion of the person receiving the security. Then in the paragraph nullus it is provided,

† that no one should be present at the wills of manifest usurers, unless they have made satisfaction for the usury, or give fitting security, as is aforesaid, for making satisfaction to the extent of the strength of their means. Finally, a general clause is subjoined there in these words: 'The wills also of manifest usurers otherwise made shall not be valid, but shall be void by operation of law.' For the text in the said paragraph nullus is not content with a simple and general security, but gives a form: that if the extorted amount is manifest, it must always be expressed; otherwise, another certain amount must be expressed, to be moderated at the discretion of the recipient; and this form is of necessity, as is evident from the word 'uolumus' placed there, which introduces a new mandatory law, as is the text joined with the gloss in cle. unica, de offi. uica. This is indeed clearly proved in the said paragraph nullus, where it is provided that no one ought to be present at the wills of manifest usurers unless he has made satisfaction for the usury, or has provided fitting security for making satisfaction as is aforesaid; whence that word, 'ut præmittitur' (as is aforesaid), is to be weighed, and thus it refers to the security qualified in the manner aforesaid. Thirdly, this is proved by the retractative clause placed at the end, where it is said that the wills of manifest usurers made otherwise are void by operation of law; for those words 'aliter facta' (made otherwise) are to be weighed, and thus it openly indicates that the form of security handed down there is of the substance. For a clause placed at the end refers to all the preceding things, as in c. inquisitioni, and c. secundo requiris, de app., fully by Bar. in l. talis scriptura, de leg. j. and in l. prætor, § 2, ff. ui bo. rapto, by Spec. in tit. de instru. edi. § nunc autem uidendum, at the word 'item excipere'. And that the form of that security, beyond what has been said, is plausibly substantial, is proved from its great utility, and the grave loss that follows if it is not observed. For if the general security set out above were sufficient, it would be impossible for the usury to be restored, both because the extorted amount cannot easily be proved, and because many from whom it was extorted have absented themselves, or have died, or, not being able to prove it, do not appear; therefore the dues would never be paid to the poor according to c. cum tu, de usuris, for the said Cola promised that he would restore only to those who lawfully proved that something had been extorted from them through usurious wickedness, and thus he provided no security for uncertain persons; therefore there was not sufficient security. For the laws have considered that whatever was extorted by a usurer cannot easily be proved, as in cle. unica, de usur.; therefore they willed that in the security a certain quantity be promised, to be moderated at the discretion of the recipient, so that if all those from whom money was extorted do not appear, restitution may be made to the poor: said c. cum tu, noted by the gloss in the said c. 2, under the same title in VI°, which is on the word 'satisfieri'; to which what is noted by Fed. de Sen. in consi. 102 contributes. Therefore, the said security is entirely insufficient.

† Moreover, wherever the law requires something under a certain form or quality, it does not suffice that the act be fulfilled without the required form or quality; indeed, in such a case it is the same to act against and outside the form. These things are proved in c. si cui, and c. sicut cum, de elect. in VI°, and c. si, de resti. spo., and c. cum dilecta, de rescrip., and c. prudentiam, at the word 'illa quippe', de offi. dele., and l. cum antiquitas, C. de testa., and l. hæredes palam, at the end, ff. eodem, and l. diligenter, ff. man., and that which is noted by Bart. in l. filio præterito, ff. de iniust. rup. & irri. testa., and l. 1, § sed si filius, de leg. 3. And I find that dominus Angelus de Perusio maintained this very conclusion in a certain solemn disputation of his which begins 'Astensis miles', at the word '2. dubitatur', where he asks whether the form of security handed down in c. quamquam can be changed and removed; and he says that it can neither be removed nor its form changed so that the form of giving security would be lighter, and not useful to the soul of the usurer and to those from whom the usury is presumed to have been extorted; for if we were to say the contrary, an occasion would be given to usurers of not returning to penance, nor to the contrition of making satisfaction and restoring the extorted usury, and therefore, according to him, that constitution, as disposing something shameful, is null. But if the form were heavier, and useful to the souls of the usurers and to those from whom the usury had been extorted, then the said constitution would be valid; and although a constitution introducing a heavier form may be valid, nevertheless according to him it would suffice for the validity of the wills that it was provided in the form handed down in the said c. quamquam. And this last point is according to Io. An. in the Novella, at the word 'absentibus', which is worthy of note. For a bishop or another below the Pope cannot enact a statute contrary to canon law by remitting a form introduced by it, as in c. quod super his, de maio. & obe., and c. igitur, 25, q. 2, fully by Io. An. in c. fi. de offi. archi., and c. ult. de ap. in VI°, noted by Fed., consi. 17; nay rather, constitutions even of a Cardinal Legate could not remove the solemnities of judicial proceedings, nor could he specifically mandate that a plenary case be proceeded with simply and de plano. And because an inferior cannot remove the law of a superior, as the text says in cle. ne Rom. de elec., so concludes the notable gloss in c. fi. de hær. in VI°, on the word 'figura', and it was originally said by Spec. in tit. de proba. § superest, at the word 'sed nunquid potest cognoscere'; hence the same Spec. said under the same title, § nunc ostendendum, verse 48, that a legate cannot supply a defect committed in contracts or judgments. It should also be noted from the opinion of Io. And. and Ang. that a constitution of one inferior to the Pope could not validate a will by introducing a heavier form than that contained in the said paragraph quamquam; and so in effect under other terms did Pau. Lau. and dominus Bar. de Saliceto of Bologna advise, as dominus Pet. de Anch. reports in his solemn commentary on c. canonum, de const., moved principally by the fact that the capacity to make a will, according to the common opinion, is from the ius gentium, although the solemnity is from civil law according to what is noted in l. qui testamento, § seruus, ff. de test.; nor can an inferior attempt so great a prejudice, which the prince himself did not wish to presume with so great a prejudice to a third party, nor he himself without the consent of those whose interest it is to enact, as is noted in a similar matter by Inno. in c. uestra, de loca. From these things it is clearly evident that the form of security concerning which in c. quamquam is to such an extent of substance that not only the usurer himself cannot contravene it, but neither can a constitution of one inferior to the Pope. To the aforesaid matters l. nemo potest, de leg. 1 contributes, and what is noted there by Bar., and cap. tua, de test., and ius publicum, ff. de pac., and c. fi. diligenti, de fo. compe. Arch. and Io. Abb. held the same view on the said c. quamquam in that the text there requires that some trustworthy persons from that parish be employed in that security, and they say there that this is not of substance, that they be from the parish, but for well-being; for it is enough that they be suitable, and they cite for this 4, q. 3, c. si testes, § ad fidem, and 3, q. 9, c. testes, § si debitum, and what is noted in 3, q. 5, c. canonica, in the first gloss, which indicates that the other things which are required there are of substance; to which contributes what is noted at the end by Barto. in l. 2, § prius, ff. de vul. & pup., and by the doctors in c. cum dilecta, de rescript. And both wills fall especially if it can be shown that after the security he continued the vice of a usurer, even if he had continued it not manifestly, as before; because from the continuation it appears that he was not corrected at the time of the security, but gave it in fraud of the law: de pœni. dist. 2, c. j.; which is also presumed from another ground, because this man in his security denied that he was a usurer, and pardon of sin is not given except to the contrite, as in the rule peccati uenia in VI°, and in the said cap. cum tu; and the manifest quality having previously existed suffices, because that quality is not required at every moment: ff. quod ui aut clam, l. j, § illud, with its gloss; and every relapse is worse than its root, as c. Arrianus, de hær. in VI°, to which there is a good text where the matter is in its own reasoning. And through this conclusion the will of a manifest usurer does not stand, even if he had given fitting security, since he afterwards continued the vice, although not manifestly. Fede. de Sen. holds the same and advised it in consi. 8, where he states it literally, and Io. de Lig. follows it, although he does not make mention of Fed., in cle. unica, under the same title, and Pet. de Anch. in c. quia eo; nor should it move anyone that this man would seem in effect to have made bequests for pious causes; because a manifest usurer is disqualified without distinction from making a will, so that he cannot dispose even for pious causes, even in codicils, because that text speaks without distinction, and this was openly held by Bal. and Bar. in l. j, C. de sacrosan. eccle.; to which what is noted in a similar matter by Io. And. in the said c. quamquam contributes. For since those goods pass to those succeeding upon intestacy, arguing from the auth. bona damnatorum, C. de bo. dam., such bequests ought not to be valid to their prejudice, and especially because such bequests by these sinners are seen as having to be rejected, arguing from the said c. quia in omnibus, and that which was noted by Bar. in l. j, C. de sacros. eccle. cited above, and openly Bar., which Bal. [cites] in the said l. 1, at the 6th word, according to the aforesaid conclusion, so that the form of the said c. quamquam must necessarily be observed for the validity of the will. And let these things suffice. Nic. Abbas

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Who is called a manifest usurer.
2. A manifest usurer is proved in four ways.
3. A woman is said to ply her trade openly, even if she does so at home for anyone who asks.
body: That which is inquired in fact is whether the testament of a deceased person is to be deemed void who, after death, is proved repeatedly to have practiced usurious depravity with various persons, and that during his lifetime there existed widespread public report that he was infected and entangled with this vice, assuming that he did not furnish security for the restitution of usuries, at least in the due form required by canon law. The aid of the Savior Jesus Christ and of His most devout Mother having been ever invoked, the decision of this question depends upon the understanding of c. quamquam, de usur. lib. 6; for that chapter ipso facto voids the testament of a manifest usurer if security in the form handed down there was not furnished by the testator. It must therefore be seen who is called a manifest usurer as to the disposition of that chapter, and consequently it will appear whether the testament in question is invalid. On this doubt I find various opinions of the canonists and legists. And first, Io. An. makes two glosses on this, one of which he placed on the said c. quamquam, the other on c. 1, eod. tit. and book. In the said c. 1,

† he said that a manifest usurer is he against whom a notoriety of law or of fact militates. Of law, because he was confessed or condemned; and I understand "confessed", namely, in judgment, because (as will be said below) an extrajudicial confession does not render a fact notorious. Of fact, because it had an evidence that could be concealed by no evasion, as because he keeps a table prepared [for moneylending]. These things seem to be proved in c. vestra, and c. fin. de coha. cle. & mu. and c. olim, de ver. sig.; this is supported by what is read and noted in l. ictus fustium, ff. de his qui no. infa. And in these points all agree, as is noted in c. quia, and c. cum in dioecesi, de usu., and by Fed. consi. 8, and Bar. in l. 2, ff. de fur., and Ang. in his disputation which begins Astensis miles, in the second column. Thirdly, the aforesaid gloss says that the bishop will be able to publish them if they were convicted before him, or if proof of witnesses is made against them, or there are certain arguments along with common report; it cites c. cum tu, and c. in dioecesi, de usur. And these words must be weighed, for it does not say that they are called manifest through conviction alone, or confession, or arguments with public report, but that the aforesaid suffice in order that they may be manifested and published by the bishop, and thus from the time of publication, and not before, they are called manifest usurers. For that gloss does not say that the bishop through those proofs will declare them manifest, but that he will be able to publish them, and so Fed. de Se. understands in consi. 72, near the end, and he says that the gloss openly notes this in the said cc. 1 and 2; Ang. de Peru. also affirms this in the said disputation, in the second column. And insofar as that gloss speaks of confession, I understand it as extrajudicial; for if it had been judicial, it would render him notorious, as in the said c. fin. de coha. cle. & mu. From the aforesaid we have three modes of proving a manifest usurer. The gloss on the said c. quanquam,

† adds a fourth mode, namely when before a priest and witnesses he publicly confesses that he is a usurer, and orders usuries to be restored, perhaps handing over his account books; and thus that gloss seems to hold that an extrajudicial confession made before a priest and witnesses makes the usurious crime manifest. But Fed. de Sen. in consi. 17 says that that gloss can be denied, because it does not prove what it says and cites nothing; or it may be true according to him when those things concur which are in that gloss, as because he confessed before a priest and witnesses, and returned the books or ordered the usuries to be restored; otherwise, according to him, by an extrajudicial confession made before any priest whatsoever a person is not convicted of the crime of usury such that the crime may be called manifest. Nor would a statute of a bishop on this matter be valid according to him, as being contrary to the common law. And in the same way Ang. in the said disputation seems to have understood that gloss, saying that through that gloss many things are required when a confession issues outside of court, so that it alone without publication may render him manifest. From these things he infers that since a priest and a notary, as to receiving a confession or security for usury, are of equal authority, as in the said c. quanquam, a confession made before a notary and witnesses alone, however publicly, does not render the confessor a manifest usurer except after publication. Ang. says the same if the confession had issued before an incompetent judge, for that is equated to an extrajudicial one, and it produces many effects, concerning which, however, it must be stated as is fully noted in c. at si clerici, de iudi., and c. per inquisitionem, de elect., and l. capite quinto, ff. de adul., and the said l. ictus fustium, de his qui not. infa. support this. Therefore, where public report concurs, he can according to him be said to be convicted by arguments; whence he can be published, and from then on he will be a manifest usurer, even before publication, if he ordered usuries to be restored and handed over his book of accounts to a notary, according to the laws alleged above. Bar. adds a fifth mode in the said l. 2, ff. de fur., and Ang. follows in the place alleged above, saying that a person ipso facto is made a manifest usurer when indiscriminately in his chamber he lends under usury to anyone asking, even though he has set up no counter for moneylending, and this through l. palam, ff. de ritu nup., where it is evident,

† that a woman is said to make public gain [by prostitution], even if she has not prostituted herself in public, but in her own house or another's to anyone indiscriminately asking; and according to them this proof suffices to render the testament null without any other confession and publication to be made by the bishop. Bal. posits a sixth mode in l. 1, C. de sacrosan. eccle., saying that he is to be understood as a manifest usurer concerning whom there is a common opinion that he is a manifest usurer, provided that he is proved a usurer either by two or three witnesses. If, however, the opinion or an act publicly done is not proved, he is not called manifest, even if it appears through his ledger of accounts, according to him; and he says this is singularly proved by l. scripturas, C. qui po. in pign. ha. For this last statement, when only the account books appear, I cite the notable gloss in c. sanè, 24, q. 2, on the word liberorum. A seventh mode seems notably elicited from the text joined with the gloss in cap. cum in dioecesi, de usur., namely that through public report and some arguments or adminicles he may be proved manifest; and this understanding was followed there by the lord Fran. Za. of revered memory, later Cardinal of Florence, saying that for the voiding of the testament it suffices there that after death this widespread public report be proved, I understand with some arguments or adminicles. A certain doctor held this same view in a question of fact by alleging it, as Federicus recites in consi. 62; but this does not please the same Federicus, who says that that chapter speaks with respect to imposing the penalty of the general council, of which in c. quia in omnibus, eod. tit., namely that the usurer be barred from the communion of the altar and from ecclesiastical burial, and that offerings not be received from him; because this is expedient for the souls of usurers, and it does not treat of a great prejudice; but it would be otherwise if it were treated concerning the voiding of a testament, for since a testament is a favorable matter, de re iudi. c. si, and l. in testamentis, ff. de reg. iu., a stricter proof ought to be required. Likewise, according to him, the disposition of that chapter requires a sentence to be pronounced; because public report and arguments suffice so that the usurer may be published by the judge, and then coerced by penalties; but before publication he cannot be called manifest, and thus if he died before publication, it cannot be said that the testament was made by a manifest usurer, which the said c. quamquam requires; and this understanding of that text Host. placed and held in the said c. cum in dioecesi; whence he expounds the text there, manifestos, that is, to be made manifest by the sentence of a judge; and in c. quia, on the word manifesti, he expounds it, that is, notorious; and thus Hostiensis seems to mean that the word "manifest" is placed there for notorious of law or of fact. Nevertheless (in my judgment) this understanding wrenches the letter of that c. cum in dioecesi; for the Pope would well have known how to say that they ought first to be published, arg. c. ad audientiam, de deci., but he said simply that if it should be established that they are manifest usurers through public report, so that the beginning of the chapter is understood through other arguments, then they should coerce them through the penalty enacted in the Lateran Council. Whence I weigh that word, si constiterit [if it shall be established]. Let it therefore be established to the judge concerning publication through public report and argument; this, however, is not to be made manifest by sentence, as Host. said. For no mention of a sentence is made there, and therefore I hold with the gloss and those who follow it. For the restriction which Fed. makes does not please me, namely that that proof only has place with respect to the penalties that are contained in the said c. quia; for although it must be confessed that that text speaks of those penalties, nevertheless, since c. quia speaks simply of a manifest usurer, just as c. quanquam does, and we have that word "manifest" against usurers in the said c. cum in dioecesi, so we ought to understand it also as to the disposition of c. quamquam, where it also speaks of a manifest usurer, arg. l. non possunt, ff. de legi. To this, note the theory of Bar. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iu., on the word iuxta praemissa, where he says that the proper signification of a word is taken from the authority of law, as if in any part of the law that word is found declared, as throughout the title de verb. sig. Likewise, no sufficient reason appears between the penalties of c. quanquam and c. cum in dioecesi; for in c. cum in dioecesi a spiritual penalty is dealt with, in c. quamquam a temporal one; but a spiritual penalty is more to be feared than a temporal one, arg. 12, q. 1, c. praecipimus. If therefore in spiritual penalties public report and arguments suffice, then also in temporal ones. I understand, however, that the arguments or indications must be urgent, so that at least they conclude that the deceased was a usurer, arg. of those things which are read and noted in l. indicia, C. de proba.; and this is to be admitted in hatred of usurers, who so cloak their contracts that they can scarcely be visibly convicted, as in cle. unica, de usur. For where proofs that necessarily conclude with ease are not found, lighter and more slender proofs are admitted, as in c. praeterea, de testi., and in c. cum dilecti, and what is noted there de electio., and c. veniens 2, de test. The same lord Cardinal posits an eighth mode in the said c. cum in dioecesi, saying that since that is manifest which can be proved, as the gloss notes in c. vestra, de coha. cle. & mu., if even after death it is proved that someone was a usurer, it is sufficiently proved that he was a manifest usurer, and this alone will suffice according to him for the voiding of the testament. This simply does not please me. For if the mere existence of the usurious offense were to suffice, for what reason would the laws require the quality of being manifest, as they commonly do, as the said c. quamquam, c. quia, and c. cum tu, and c. cum in dioecesi, alleged above? For the laws detest and prosecute public offenses more than secret ones, even though they can be proved, as is proved in c. vestra, and c. fin. de coha. cle. & mu., and 32, q. 5, c. Christiana religio. And Bald., Lau. de Pinu., and Bar. de Sali. advised the contrary of this statement, as Pe. de Anch. recites in the repetitio of c. canonum, de consti. But I in this doubt, as I have on other occasions advised in fact, observe that the laws in this matter do not require the necessity of fact, neither tacitly nor expressly, but demand only the quality of being manifest, as appears in the said c. quamquam. We ought therefore to take the words properly and not improperly, both because we are in an odious matter, since it treats of the voiding of a testament, and because it is treated so that provision may be made for the souls of usurers and for the public weal, as is gathered from cc. 1 and 2, eod. tit., and because in any disposition we ought not to depart from the proper signification of the words unless the intention is openly established, or at least through indications, as in l. non aliter, ff. de leg. 3, and l. fin. de verbo. signi., and l. licet imperator, ff. de leg. 1. Moreover, notorious, manifest, secret, and almost secret differ among themselves, as is noted by Ioan. And. and Cal. in the said c. vestra, alleged above, and the gloss in 2, q. 1, c. manifesta, and Bart. somewhat in l. haeredes palam, ff. de test., and Spe. in the title de notoriis crimi., § sequitur de manifesto. Now, a notorious matter of fact is defined as a deed so exhibited to the sight of men that it can be concealed by no subterfuge, as in c. evidentia, de accu., and c. cum dilecti, de pur. canonica. Secret is that which cannot be proved, as in c. unico, ut eccle. be., and c. erubescant, dist. 32, and c. si omnia, 6, q. 1. Almost secret is said to be that which can be proved by few or with difficulty, de poe. dist. 1, § haec ergo secreta. Manifest, however, properly and taken in its specific sense, is commonly defined as that which is a public or widespread intimation or proclamation, and common, arising from certain knowledge, from certain authors, and which can be proved. It is thus commonly defined by all, as is noted by the gloss in the said c. manifesta, Io. An. and Io. Cal. in the said c. vestra, and Spe. in the said § sequitur de manifesto. And in this it differs from public report, because that arises sometimes from an uncertain author and from suspicion alone. But manifest arises from certain knowledge and from certain authors, as was said above and is noted in the said c. vestra; and it is clear in what it differs from secret, almost secret, and notorious. And therefore Speculator notably said in the place alleged above that manifest is sometimes placed improperly for notorious, and thus it is taken in 2, q. 1, c. manifesta, and c. cum olim, and cap. ex parte, de verbo. sign. Properly, however, it differs from notorious, as is proved in the said l. haeredes palam, ff. de test., where the testator is said to name his heir palam, that is, manifestly, when he names him not in public, but before the witnesses who are required in a testament; to the same effect is 11, q. 3, c. eorum, and more clearly in the chapter quia suspecti, 3, q. 5, joined with what Archidiaconus notes. Or let us say what Io. Cal. notably says in the said c. vestra: that manifest is taken in two ways, namely as a genus, and it includes under itself manifest as it is a species, and notorious. Whence this is true: "Every notorious thing is manifest," and thus it is taken in the said c. manifesta, and c. de manifesta, and c. ex parte, and c. cum olim, as is proved there from the subject matter. Secondly, it is taken in its proper species as distinct from notorious, and then it is defined as I have stated above. To the point, therefore: since the proper signification of a term is taken from its definition, as in l. 1 and what is noted there, ff. de testa., and l. 1, de autho. tuto., and dist. 21, cap. cleros, and dist. 25, cap. perlectis, by Barto. in the said l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iu., and the said l. 1; and according to the distinction of manifest it differs from notorious, and from secret or almost secret, we ought in the said c. quamquam to take that word "manifest" in its proper signification, so that at least it stands in its genus, and thus includes notorious and manifest; or it stands in its proper species, and thus differs from notorious. We ought not, however, to take it for notorious alone, as some do, and badly so, because that would be an improper understanding; and from no part of the law do we have that we ought to use words improperly. Let us say, therefore, that a manifest usurer is he against whom a notoriety of law or of fact runs, or concerning whom there is a common proclamation and intimation proceeding from certain knowledge and from certain authors, and who can be proved to be a usurer; and this Bal. seems to have perceived in the said l. 1, although he did not so prove it. And this mode of proving is agreeable to law, and is proved from the proper signification of the words, nor does it rest upon the mere opinions of doctors, as do the aforesaid modes of proving handed down by others. To our purpose, therefore: since in this case it is presupposed that it can be proved that this man, concerning whose testament the question is raised, was a usurer; likewise that concerning this there was in his lifetime a common and clamorous intimation among the people, which indeed proceeded from certain knowledge and from certain authors, since it proceeded from the fact that he was lending at usury, and from the persons to whom he was lending; it can sufficiently and undoubtedly be said that he is a manifest usurer, and consequently that his testament was not valid, security in the due form not having been provided. And let these things suffice to the praise and glory of God. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One who doubts the validity of a first collation can impetrate a second.
2. We ought not to depart from common rules, except insofar as provision is found.
3. Duchies, counties, and marquisates are not divided.
4. In indivisible things, the first-born is preferred by divine law to the later-born.
5. Vassals cannot consent to another lordship without the will of the lord.
6. A judicial inquiry or delay is not necessary where human judgment has preceded in mere execution.
7. Whether the husband's heir can raise an exception of adultery against a wife reclaiming her dowry, if the husband accused the wife during his lifetime.
8. If the emperor sells another's property to someone as his own, alleging that property to be his own, he cannot bring actions against those detaining it.
9. No one can violently seize his own property.
10. Prescription is interrupted by joinder of issue (litis contestatio).
11. Although the law prohibits the division of a duchy or dignity among several persons, nevertheless a custom to the contrary is valid.
12. A peasant can purchase dignities and jurisdictions that are part of the seller's patrimony.
body: Having prayed from the heart for the aid of Almighty God and of Mary His mother, I shall strive in the present cause, on account of the multitude of doubts, to be brief, so that I may touch upon the individual doubts of each issue conclusively, as I perceive them. And first, following the order, to the first query, which was: Whether, concerning the right to the said county of Bigorre, the lord Count of Foix is able to avail himself simultaneously of two titles, namely of donation and of the testament of Lady Petronilla, formerly Countess. I observe that in the donation which the late Lady Petronilla made to the late Lord Gaston, Viscount of Béarn, and to Mathe, his wife, daughter of the same Lady Petronilla, and to all the heirs legitimately born or to be born of them, and to all their legitimate succession, no specific mention was made of the county of Bigorre, about which the present question is raised; rather, it was made in general terms concerning all the right that she had or ought to have by reason of succession in all possessions, lordships, things movable or immovable, which of right were in the goods of her father, of the same Lady Petronilla, and belonged to her, so that they should have and hold all the land of her father wherever it might be, at the will of them and their heirs, etc. Wherefore, if the said county of Bigorre did not belong to the said Lady Petronilla from the person of her father, it is clear that it was not comprehended under that donation, which was restricted to the goods of her late father, as is stated in the narration of the fact; and consequently, the said Count of Foix cannot defend himself from that donation, since those from whom he derived his cause and right in the said county could not have done so. For a donation is not extended beyond the intention of the donor, as in l. nec ignorans, C. de do., and c. cum dilectus, eo. tit.; to this pertains l. si unquam, and what is noted there, C. de reuo. dona. And in this case it must be said that the Count of Foix will be able to avail himself solely from the testament of the said Lady Petronilla and from the maternal disposition, namely of Lady Isabella: ar. in l. 3, § ex pluribus, ff. de acqui. pos., where it is said that if I am the heir to him who possessed as purchaser, I possess the same thing both as purchaser and as heir. If, however, the county of Bigorre was comprehended under that general donation—as, for instance, because it had come from the paternal succession, or traditio of the said county was made during the life of the donor herself, so that ownership of it passed to the donees—then the substitution made concerning Mathe and her legitimate succession appears useless with respect to the said county; because, since the said county had ceased to belong to the said Lady Petronilla and had begun to belong to the said Lady Mathe, she could no longer make a testament concerning that county, especially by substituting the said Lady Mathe. For a legacy is not valid when I bequeath to a legatee the property of the legatee himself, as in § sed rem, Insti. de lega. Likewise, that which is mine by one cause cannot become mine by another cause unless it ceases to be mine: as in c. inter dilectos, de fi. inst. § cæterum, and l. 3, § ex pluribus, ff. de acqui. poss., and C. de contrah. emp. l. cum res. I confess, however, that although one cannot acquire ownership of the same thing from several causes occurring at different times, as in the said laws and fully through Bart. in d. § ex pluribus, nevertheless one can defend and protect oneself by several titles, and especially when the validity of the first can be doubted, as noted by Io. An. following Io. Mo. in c. cum personæ, de priui. lib. 6, on gl. fi. in Nouella. To this strongly pertains c. post electionem, de concess. præben., and c. ex parte Astensis, e. titu.; to this pertains c. cum olim, 2, de priuile. Hence Pau. de Lea. advised

† that one who doubts the validity of a first collation or institution can, and it is useful to, impetrate a second, not that he may pursue both in bringing an action, according to c. ut quis duas, de elect. lib. 6, and d. § ex pluribus, but so that he may defend himself from them; and thus I say that in this case the said Count of Foix will be able to defend himself from both titles. For a defendant can defend himself by several and diverse exceptions and causes, as in the rule nullus pluribus, de reg. iu. lib. 6, and l. nemo, ff. de excep. If, however, traditio of the said county was not made by the said Lady Petronilla, then, since ownership does not pass from donation alone, as in l. quoties, in fin. C. de rei uen., and l. traditionibus, C. de pac., the testamentary disposition was useful and valid. For it was valid because ownership was immediately acquired without traditio; for a legacy of a thing owed to me is valid for the sake of the acquisition of ownership, as is the text in l. 3, § si rem, ff. de le. 3; and in this case several causes can concur, as Bartol. notes in d. § ex pluribus, and in doubt the said Count can defend himself in this case from the donation and from the testament of the said Lady Petronilla, from whom the authors of the said Lord Count derived their cause. And this as to the first doubt. Nevertheless, beyond what was asked, I observe that either this county is not a fief—then arises the noble question whether the firstborn always succeeds by his own right, on account of those things which I shall immediately state in the following question, or by hereditary right, as the heir of the father or mother. And Oldr., consil. 97, touches subtly upon this question and finally concludes that he takes as heir, and thus he ought to base himself on the testament, where one intervened, or as successor ab intestato, where it did not intervene. He is moved among other things because such succession of primogeniture seems to have been introduced on account of the public good contrary to the common rules, which would require one son to be admitted and the rest excluded, as in Auth. de trien. & semi. § hinc nos, and l. maximum uitium, C. de lib. pręte. Therefore, although the law and custom confers the kingdom or county, we ought to say that it confers it upon him as heir, just as the law confers the legitim upon other sons without encumbrance: l. quoniam nouella, C. de inoffic. test., and l. omnimodo, eo. titu.; and yet they cannot obtain that legitim if they wish to abstain from the legitimate inheritance, as Bart. notes in l. gerit, ff. de acqui. hære.; whence, although the law confers it, nevertheless a son can be instituted heir in it, as in capitul. Raynutius and c. Raynaldus, de testa. A good text supports the aforesaid in ca. 1, an agna. uel si. defunc. repu. hæred. po. fe. re., col. 10, where it is clear that a son cannot repudiate the inheritance and retain the fief for himself, and yet the fief is owed to the son, as in c. 1, de suc. feu., ea. col. Furthermore, we ought not to depart from

† common rules except insofar as it is found provided: l. præcipimus, in fin. C. de app.; but we do not find a departure from common rules except that the dignity is owed to the firstborn, as in capitul. licet, de uoto; therefore in other matters we ought to stand by the common rules, that it be received by hereditary right, and not by one's own right. If, however, the said county is a fief, then there is a greater doubt by what right a son instituted heir succeeds in the fief. For it does not seem to be from the testament, because the disposition of a testator can do nothing concerning a fief, as in d. capitul. 1, de suc. feu.; nor as ab intestato, because one ought not to die testate and intestate. The text in d. capitul. unico, an agna. uel filii, argues to the contrary, where it is clear that a son cannot repudiate the inheritance without benefit; therefore he takes by hereditary right. Baldus frames this question in d. capitul. 1, de suc. feu. And first he says that he takes neither from the testament nor ab intestato, but by the successory right of fiefs; nor is this surprising, since this happens to others, as in Instit. de acqui. per arrogationem, and C. de fideicom. authen. hoc amplius. And this same thing happens in a pupil, who is not properly said to die intestate, as in l. prima in princi., ff. de suis & legi., although by a benign interpretation he is held as intestate, as there. Or, secondly, it can be said according to him that he succeeds in the fief not from the testament, but because it passes into the university of goods, and on that account the fief comes into the petition of inheritance, as in ff. de petitio. hæredita. l. item uidendum, § fina., and in the edict of the divine Hadrian; and thus, along with the universality, the son can be instituted in the fief, because a thing cannot be excepted from the institution of an heir according to those things which are held and noted in l. prima, ff. de hęredi. institu.; the son can therefore say that the fief belongs to him by the successory right of fiefs, or because he was the heir of his father or mother, and the fief is in the inheritance, and from these the said Count of Foix can be instructed concerning his institution. I come to the second doubt: namely, whether, from the words of the testament of Lady Petronilla, in which she substituted Lady Mathe, her firstborn, and after her, her legitimate succession, etc., to the brothers Esquivat and Jordan, Lady Constance, the firstborn of the same now deceased Mathe, ought, after the decease of Jordan and Esquivat, to arrive at the succession of the said county of Bigorre in its entirety without her sisters. And it seems at first that she ought not, because all sons and daughters ought to succeed equally to their parents, as in l. maximum uitium, C. de lib. præte., and in Authen. in successione, C. ad Tertul., and in the body from which it is taken, even if it is a fief. In which case, if it is paternal, females do not succeed unless it was so stated in the grant of the fief, but all males succeed equally, as in capitul. primo, de succes. feu., col. 10. If, however, it is a maternal fief, males are preferred, but in default of males all females come equally, as in capitul. primo, de bene. feu., col. 10. But these things notwithstanding, I deem the contrary to be truer in our case: namely, that Lady Constance alone ought to have been preferred in the county to her other sisters. I am moved because in these dignities, since they are indivisible, as in c. imperialem, § præterea, de prohi. feu. ali. per Fede., col. 10, the firstborn ought to succeed; for they are conferred by order of birth, as is the text in capitul. licet, de uoto, to such an extent that other children cannot demand a legitim in these dignities, lest a division of the kingdom or county occur, as is the notable gloss in d. cap. licet and c. si hæredes, de testa.; Inno., Io. And., and Host., and commonly the canonists, hold this in d. c. licet. Whence Io. And. says there that by general custom these dignities—such as kingdom, county, duchy, marquisate, and the like—are conferred by order of birth, which general custom is indeed supported by canon law, as in d. cap. licet. Likewise by divine law, as is evident in Genesis 27, where the rights of primogeniture appear when the father, blessing the firstborn son, said: 'May God give thee of the dew of heaven, and of the fatness of the earth an abundance,' etc. By these words ownership of the inheritance is denoted. Then there is subjoined: 'Let peoples serve thee,' that is, rustics and plebeians; 'and let tribes adore thee,' that is, nobles. 'Be lord over thy brethren, and let them bow down before thee,' namely, by doing fealty and showing obedience. This general custom is also supported by the law of Emperor Frederick,

† according to which duchies, counties, and marquisates are not divided, in d. § præterea; to this pertains what Barto. notes in Authen. post fratres, C. de legi. hęre. And through this Ioan. And. concludes in d. c. licet that a father cannot take this right away from the firstborn so that another, namely, should succeed in the county or kingdom, since it is established by canon, divine, and customary law: ar. in l. nemo potest, ff. de leg. j., and de testa. c. requisisti, and c. tua, de foro compe., cap. si diligenti. For the legitim of the firstborn is the entire inheritance of this principality or county; therefore, without cause the firstborn cannot be deprived of it, according to him; to this belongs what is read and noted in cap. Raynaldus, de testa. And this right, that the dignity should be conferred upon the firstborn, was introduced for the sake of the public good and in favor and honor of the empire, so that the principalities that are under it may remain intact: ar. ff. de exer. l. ne in plures, and de pign. c. significante; to this pertains de præben. c. minoribus and c. dilecto. And it seemed better to the first natural philosopher that the empire be governed by one rather than by several, who speaks thus: 'Entities do not wish to be misgoverned; a plurality of principalities is not good; therefore, one prince.' Furthermore, it seemed to the Roman philosopher that the republic was more usefully governed by one: l. 2, § deinde, ff. de orig. iur. From all of which I infer for our case that, since Lady Petronilla did not have male children, but only females from her first and second marriages, the county of Bigorre or another dignity of the same ought of right to have devolved upon Lady Mathe, her firstborn daughter; nor could Lady Petronilla confer the county upon Esquivat, a grandson by a daughter, as is evident from the aforesaid; and consequently, after the death of Lady Mathe, the aforesaid county ought to have devolved upon Lady Constance, her firstborn daughter, who of right was to be preferred to the other daughters of Lady Petronilla, because a grandson is preferred to an uncle, since the dignity has taken root in the person of the predeceased firstborn. This is proved in d. c. licet, and fully by Io. And. in addi. Spe. super rub. de feu., where he maintained the same even if the dignity had never taken root in the person of the firstborn, saying that the firstborn son is preferred to the secondborn because the son represents the firstborn; and Old. maintained the same most subtly in consi. 257, where he proves this by divine, natural, and written law.

† For by divine law he says it is certain that the firstborn is preferred to the secondborn in indivisibles, such as a county and a kingdom, as was said above. It is established, moreover, that the firstborn can sell, donate, and transfer that right of primogeniture to another: 7, q. 1, cap. quam periculosum. If, therefore, that right is alienable, it is consequently transmissible to heirs, especially to a son: argu. ff. de acquir. re. domi. l. quædam. This is also proved by natural law: because the father retains his part in the son, and is represented in him, and they are regarded as one person, as in l. fin. C. de impu. & aliis sub.; whence, although his father has died, nevertheless, because his son represents his part, he seems to live through him and to be deemed as if he were wholly alive, since a part lives: ar. ff. de contrahen. emp. l. domum. It is proved by written law: because the same law applies to the whole with respect to the whole as applies to a part with respect to a part: ff. de rei uen. l. quæ de tota; but it is clear because in the succession to an inheritance several grandchildren from one deceased son are regarded as one other son, and through this they come with uncles by representation into the stirps, not per capita, in Authen. de hær. quæ ab intes. defe. § j, and in Authen. in successione; therefore, in the same way he ought to represent where the right of preference of the order of birth is at issue; to this pertains ff. de colla. l. dedit dotem auus, and eo. titu. l. si nepotes, where it is said that the grandfather, on account of the son's person, ought to give a dowry to the granddaughter. For so great is the identity of father and son that from the father to the son there seems to be a certain continuation of ownership, and even during the father's life the sons are in a certain manner deemed owners: l. in suis, ff. de libe. & posthu.; and the son will come to that right which was acquired for the father in potentiality, and thus not in act. And although Bar. held in d. Auth. post fratres that this does not have a place in feudal matters—namely, that a grandson should succeed into the place of his father—the contrary is nevertheless true, as is proved in c. 1, de succes. feu., and c. 1 & 2, de feu. mar., and c. 1, de na. suc. feu. col. 10, where a grandson succeeds with an uncle in a divisible fief, holding the place of his father, as there by Bald. And on this I have elsewhere fully advised; but because it does not pertain to our matter, I shall not insist upon it much, since Lady Mathe survived Lady Petronilla. Whence I conclude that Lady Constance ought to have been preferred to the others, and to succeed alone in the said county of Bigorre, both under the ius commune by the aforesaid reasons, and by the disposition of the said Lady Petronilla, inasmuch as she substituted Mathe and her legitimate succession. For Lady Constance is the legitimate succession, since she is the firstborn of the said Lady Mathe, as in d. c. licet. I care little about that substitution, because, as I have said, under the ius commune it was owed to Lady Mathe as the firstborn, especially because she was a daughter of the first marriage, according to what is held and noted in c. mulieri, si de feu. fue. controuer., col. 10; and after the death of Lady Mathe, it ought of right to have devolved upon Lady Constance, since she was the firstborn of Lady Mathe, and concerning the aforesaid by Old. consi. 97 & consi. 258 præall. And the said substitution made by Lady Petronilla is sufficiently valid if Lady Mathe did not object within the due time, nor Lady Constance after the death of her mother, against the institution made of Esquivat and Jordan: to this belongs what is noted by Bar. in l. filio pręterito, ff. de iniusto rup. & irri. testa., and l. 2, C. de posthu. pręte. uel exhære., and by Ioan. And. in d. c. licet, where he says that if a firstborn son is passed over in a dignity, he ought to bring an action by lodging a complaint, or for the supplement if it was otherwise arranged, as because he was instituted heir in some thing, unless he was content with the lesser part, or sells his right, as in d. c. quàm periculosum, and c. officii, de testa., and l. contra maiores, C. de inof. test. From these things an inference is drawn for the solution of the third question: namely, what is understood by those words, 'her legitimate succession,' etc. For Lady Petronilla substituted in the county of Bigorre Lady Mathe, and after her death, her legitimate succession. For I say as to our case that Lady Constance, the firstborn of Lady Mathe herself, comes, since she had no males.
