For in dignities the legitimate succession is the firstborn, as in d. c. licet, de uoto, and as I have fully stated above, and a female succeeds in dignities in default of males: 12, quæstio 2, capit. cum deuotissimam. For words ought to be understood according to the subject matter, as is read and noted in l. ex facto, § si quis rogatus, ff. ad Trebel., by Bartol. in l. Gallus, § etiam, ff. de libe. & posthu., and l. si tibi decem, § si pactus, ff. de pactis, where it is noted that in a thing transmissible to sons alone, by the designation of 'heirs' it is understood of sons; and the same is noted in cap. 1, de succes. feu. col. 10, and by Bald. in cap. 1, de natu. succes. feu., same column. For the subjects are such as the predicates allow, as in l. defensor, ff. de interroga. acti., and cap. inter dilectos, de fide instru. But in another matter, what would come under the designation of succession, as if male or female children did not survive? I believe that only those come to whom belongs the first hope of succeeding ab intestato, namely where the word 'legitimate' is added. For the word 'succession' in our matter, when I substitute the succession of someone, those seem to come to whom belongs the first hope of succeeding to him, as in l. sciant cuncti, C. de leg. hære., and what the gloss notes there, and more fully by Bar. in l. 2, ff. qui petan. tuto., and by the gloss in l. nepotibus, C. eo., in which it is read and noted that those are said to be called to the succession of someone to whom belongs the first hope of succeeding in a testament or ab intestato. But where the word 'legitimate' is added, as in our case, I believe that it ought to be restricted to those who are called ab intestato: arg. in l. j., with what is noted there, C. de suis & legi. Hence legitimate tutors are called those who are called by law ab intestato, but testamentary ones those who are appointed by testators, as is clear in the title de legitimis tuto. and the title de testamen. tute.; it would be otherwise, however, if it had been said: 'I grant these things to you and to whomsoever successors.' For then even in feudal matter not only are the three kinds of heirs included, as in Instit. de hære. quali. & diff., but also legatees, because a legatee in the thing bequeathed is in a certain manner an heir, as in l. cum in conuentionibus, ff. de uerbo. signifi. And Bald. posited this last point in ca. imperialem, first response, de prohi. feu. alie. per Feder., colla. 10. But in our case there is no need to insist upon this, because necessarily, on account of the subject matter, it had to be understood of Lady Constance, since she was the firstborn of Lady Mathe, as I said above. And through those things which I said in the second doubt, I infer the decision of the fourth question, which is: Whether the legitim owed by natural law, or the Trebellian portion, has a place in the said county of Bigorre upon the death of Count Esquivat. And I say briefly that it does not, because from these dignities no Falcidian portion is deducted, even that owed by natural law, lest a succession to the dignity occur contrary to the disposition of the law, as in d. c. imperialem, § præterea, de prohi. feu. per Feder. colum. 10; noted by the gloss, Innoc., and commonly the doctors in d. c. licet, de uoto, where the case is seen according to the common understanding, and by the gloss in c. si hæredes, de testam. Nevertheless, Io. and Host. say in d. c. licet that where the father had nothing other than the county from which the other children could live, then the firstborn who succeeds in the county is bound to assign something to the other, secondborn children from which they may live, if, having considered the nobility and the resources of the principality, he can have an honorable maintenance: argumen. C. de libe. præt. l. maximum uitium, and in c. Raynaldus, de testamen. I come to the fifth question: Whether the reception made by the general court of Bigorre of the said Constance as lady and countess conferred any right upon her beyond her own right, of which mention was made above. And in this I think a distinction must be made as follows: either Lady Constance had a right in that county, and then through the reception of the court, or of all those of the county, no right was newly acquired for Lady Constance, because since the people were not free, but subject, they did not have the power of transferring jurisdiction or conferring title; both because that is held as not given which is given by him who by law cannot give it, in cap. quod autem, de iure patrona., and cap. Daibertum, 1, quęstio septima, and no one can transfer more right than he is known to have, as in l. traditio, ff. de acquiren. rer. domi., and capit. nuper, de dona. inter uirum & uxorem; and especially if it is presupposed that that county is feudal.
† For vassals

† cannot consent to another lord without the lord's will, even by proroguing the jurisdiction of another in a certain case, as noted by the gloss and Bald. in said l. imperialem, § penul., de prohibi. feud. alie. per Fede. colum. decima; noted by the doctors in cap. cæterum, de iudi. That reception was therefore a factual execution of an already possessed right, which conferred no right anew, just as is said in the similar case of canons receiving into a canonry him to whom the Pope or another superior has justly provided a canonry; for by receiving him they do not confer a right anew; whence even excommunicates can make such a reception, as is read and noted in c. pro illorum, de præben., c. capitulum sanctæ Crucis, de rescri., and c. eam te, eod. titu. If, however, the said Lady Constance had no right: then either the court of that county of Bigorre did not have by custom or special privilege the right of electing a count, and it could transfer no right to the said Lady Constance—nay rather, the said Lady Constance would have fallen into the crime of lèse-majesté, as in l. 3, ff. ad l. Iul. maiesta.; noted by Barto. in tract. de tyranno, in versicle 6, and Bald. in l. decernimus, C. de sacrosanc. eccle. Or the court had the right and power of electing a count; and then if it had received the said Lady Constance out of ignorance, believing, namely, that she was the true countess; and then no right would have been newly transferred to her, because error even of law prevents the transfer and prorogation of jurisdiction, as in l. si quis per errorem, ff. de iurisd. om. iudi., and there by Barto., and by Innocen. in c. ad petitionem, de accus. For in every disposition power and will are required, and if either is lacking it is not valid, as in c. cum super, de offic. deleg., and l. multum interest, C. si quis alte. uel sibi. For here the will was lacking, given the error; to this pertains l. qui in aliena and l. si is ad quem, ff. de acquiren. hæredit., and c. ex parte Astensis, de conces. præben., and what is noted there, especially by Ioann. Andr. following Hostiensis, and Barto. in d. l. si is ad quem and d. l. si quis per errorem. But if they had known that no right belonged to her, and had received her as lady Countess, then the right and title of the county would have been transferred to her, as noted by Barto. in the said treatise de tyranno, and Bald. in d. l. decernimus. For even a woman can have jurisdiction when it comes accessorily to a dignity, as in c. significauit, de rescri., and d. c. cum deuotissimam, 12, q. 2, and what is noted in them. I come to the sixth question: Whether, on account of the homage and oath of fealty sworn by Esquivat and Constance to the King of England, Duke of Aquitaine, in the manner set forth in the case, the fief of the county of Bigorre was opened to the church of Le Puy, so that the same church could invade possession of the said county without judicial cognizance of the cause? And it seems at first that the fief was immediately opened to the lord, since the oath of homage was sworn to another; because, by swearing the oath to a non-lord, the vassal alienated the fief as far as in him lay, and therefore ipso facto fell from his right. Ioan. And. and Hostiensis hold this, and the doctors there commonly follow them, in c. eam te, de iureiuran. Moreover, one alienating a fief ipso facto falls from his right, and the fief is opened to the lord; nor does it benefit the vassal if he afterwards recovers it. These things are proved in c. imperialem, first response, especially joined with the gloss on the versicle reuertatur, de prohi. feu. alie. per Fed. coll. 10, in c. uno, quid iuris sit, si post alie. feu. uasal. id recu., and in c. 2, de feu.; to this pertains what in a similar matter is read and noted in c. fina. de loca. Likewise, in another respect the fief seems returned to the church of Le Puy, because a vassal succeeding newly is bound to approach the lord or heir within a year and a day, requesting investiture and promising fealty; which if he does not do, he falls from his right, as is proved in c. uno, de capi. Conra. coll. 10, and noted in capi. 2, de feu. præalleg.; but neither Esquivat nor Lady Constance did this; therefore they fell from their right, and the fief was opened to the lord. But these things notwithstanding, I say that in our case the fief, on account of the aforesaid, was by no means opened to the church of Le Puy or to another non-lord. I am moved because Esquivat, Constance, and the other successors were ignorant that the county of Bigorre belonged to the church of Le Puy, since it was not in possession of it; nay rather, it seems that the said county belonged freely to Lady Petronilla, as is presupposed in the beginning of the donation, where it is said that she was the lady and proprietress of that county of Bigorre, and that for the whole time of her life, which was sixty years and more, she was in true and peaceful possession of the said county. For she would not have been the proprietress if it had been a fief belonging to another, because the bare property of a fief belongs to the lord, whereas only the useful ownership belongs to the vassal, as in c. si diligenti, and what Innocen. notes there, de præscr., and c. uno, in fin. quibus casibus feu. amit. coll. 10; to this pertains l. 1 & 2, ff. si ager uecti. uel emphy., and what is noted in c. 1, de capi. Conra. Likewise, having presupposed without prejudice to the truth that the said county had been a fief of the church of Le Puy, nevertheless, since they were excusably ignorant of this, the possessors do not incur a penalty by swearing to another or by directly alienating it entirely; what is more, there is a singular text with the gloss in c. uno, de contro. inter dominum & emph. feu. coll. 10, where it is openly said that a fief is then opened to the lord through alienation when the benefice is sold by one who knows; it is otherwise if by one who is ignorant, and the text says the same there at the end regarding other alienations; and this last point can be adapted to an indirect alienation, when an oath of fealty is ignorantly sworn to another than the lord; and concerning that text Bald., a most subtle doctor, makes great celebration there, saying that that text is exceedingly singular in all alienations in which the alienor falls from his right, so that it is understood to apply when the alienation is made by one who knows, but otherwise if by one ignorant of the quality of the thing. A similar distinction is made in ff. de leg. 2, l. fina. § fin. Nay rather, if a vassal offends the lord while excusably ignorant that he is the lord, he does not lose the fief, as is the notable text in c. uno, quibus modis feu. amit. colla. 10, and Barto. notes this singularly there. The same must be said in that they did not seek investiture within a year and a day, nor did they offer the oath of fealty to the church of Le Puy in due time. For the penalty is incurred when the vassal knows that he is bound to these things; it is otherwise if he was excusably ignorant; and when someone has succeeded another, the ignorance is sufficiently excusable, as Bald. notably says in said c. 1, de capi. Conra. For it is not to be imputed to one who is excusably ignorant: argu. in l. nec nos, C. de capt., and l. regula, ff. de iu. & fa. igno., and in c. gratia, de rescri. lib. 6, and in the rule is qui in ius succedit alterius, de regu. iur. lib. 6; to this pertains what is similarly noted concerning an emphyteuta, that if led by excusable error, as because he succeeded another, he did not pay the canon in due time, he does not out of equity incur the penalty: as noted by gloss 2, de iure emphy., and Bartol. follows there, and Dyn. in the said rule is qui in ius, and the doctors in capit. fina. de loca. The aforesaid Esquivat and Constance also seem excused in swearing the oath to the Duke of Aquitaine, King of England, even if they had known of the right of the church of Le Puy: because they did this on account of a most just fear, fearing his power, who had begun to invade the castle of Lourdes with a large army. Therefore, through this oath of fealty sworn out of fear, no jurisdiction or power was transferred to that king or duke, because in conferring jurisdiction fear vitiates ipso facto: l. 2, ff. de iudi., and Barto. notes almost in our terms in the treatise de tyranno, in versicle 6 and following. Nay rather, even the mere power of someone, through words or threats, sometimes inflicts just fear, regard being had to the quality of the persons, as the notable gloss says in c. penul. quod metus cau.; to this pertains l. penult. with the following, C. eod., and what Barto. notes in l. ad inuidiam, and c. metum, eod. titu. And this concerning this question, in which I conclude that Esquivat and Constance incurred no penalty, and consequently it was not lawful for the church of Le Puy to invade possession of the said county, especially without judicial cognizance of the cause: argu. l. fina. C. si per uim, uel alio modo. From these and other things which I have said above in the second question, an inference is drawn for the decision of the seventh question, which was: Whether Esquivat or Lady Constance could through their act prejudice the legitimate succession of Lady Mathe, to whom by substitution the said county ought to have devolved. For, as is clear from what was said in the preceding question, the said Esquivat and Constance ought to have suffered no detriment from that oath of fealty; and consequently the innocent successors ought not to be afflicted with any penalty; and thus this question remains decided. But presupposing that they had transgressed in some respect on account of which they would have been deprived or ought to be deprived of the feudal county, whether it would have had to prejudice the other agnates or children of Lady Mathe is a great question among the doctors, and the matter is very fully treated by Dyn. in the rule non debet, de reg. iur. lib. sexto, and by Cy. in l. secunda, C. de lib. & eorum lib., by Bar. in l. eum, ff. de inter. & releg., by the gloss in c. 1, de succ. feud. coll. decima, and c. j. in fi. de pace iur. fir. ea. coll., fully by Bal. in ca. j. § aut si libellario, quibus modis feud. amitt. colla. x, and in ca. j. si uasal. feu. pri. cui debe. eadem colla. Dyn. in effect wished to distinguish whether the fief is paternal or personal, and prejudices others; or ancestral, or from a more remote lineage, and does not prejudice. Cy. distinguished otherwise: that either the children or agnates come by their own right, as because one acquired the fief for himself and his children, and there is no prejudice to the others, or they come by the right of the wrongdoer, and there is prejudice. Bartol. says this is contrary to the text in the said c. primo, si vasal. feu. priue. Therefore he distinguishes otherwise, saying that either the vassal committed an offense on account of which he is directly to be deprived of the fief, as because he offended against the person of the lord or against the agreement of the fief, and it harms the others, and thus the fief is opened to the lord, as in the said capit. primo and in cap. uno, quibus modis feu. amit.; or he committed an offense on account of which he is not directly to be deprived of the fief, but by consequence, as because he is to be deprived of all his goods, and then it does not harm the children and agnates, since he did not offend in the cause of the fief. Bald., in the said § aut si libellario, seems to have doubted much, and he considers three faults there. One fault is when the offense is against the person of the lord, truly or interpretatively, and then it reverts to the lord, so that he may at least have this vengeance for his injury, as in ca. j. § denique, quæ sit prima cau. benefi. amit. col. x; and this if the vassal did not do this intentionally to deprive the agnates; for if he had so offended fraudulently, it would be equitable to say that the lord ought not to profit from such an offense or fraud: argument. in l. fina. ff. de eo, per quem fac. erit, and in c. 2, de renun. lib. 6. The second fault is when the offense is outside the person of the lord, and then the agnates, and not the lord, succeed. The third fault is in the case of alienation. For a vassal, by alienating the fief without the lord's will, seems to contemn the lord and not to preserve fealty, and therefore he falls from the fief, as in the aforesaid title quæ sit pri. cau. bene amittend. § illud enim and § fin., and de uasal. qui contra constitu. Lot. feu. alie. cap. uno, where it seems that it reverts to the lord. But Iacob. de Belu. is reported to have said that this is true if the fief is new, or if agnates do not exist; otherwise if paternal. Which opinion is sufficiently equitable according to Baldus. And Di. also followed this, as I said above. And this opinion operates so that by the act of Esquivat and Constance no prejudice was generated to the other agnates, who by right ought to have succeeded in the county. Or, according to Baldus, the first opinion is true if not through collusion and fraud against the agnates; the second opinion, that it does not prejudice, proceeds if the vassal alienated the fief or otherwise offended in fraud of the agnates. Thirdly, he says it can be said that the fief returns to the lord, yet the sons or agnates—nay, even a daughter, in the absence of males—ought to redeem it from the lord, and the lord is compelled to invest him, as in the title qualiter potu. olim feud. ali. capit. primo, § finali; or, according to him, this distinction is to be conjoined with the preceding, and properly according to him; lastly he says, or say as in extra de feud. cap. secundo; but the doctors there commonly pass with the above-mentioned opinion, which many ancient doctors also held, as Ioan. Andr. relates in addi. Specu. in titu. de feud. § ulti. post princip., and sufficiently there through Specu. concerning this matter. But the same Bald. reports many other opinions in the said cap. primo, si uasal. feud. priue. And among others he reports that certain persons held that opinion of Din.; and ultimately he says, among other things, that the form of the investiture must be considered. For if the lord said, 'I grant the castle in fief to Titius and his heirs, reverting from one to another,' or 'I grant to all principally,' or when sons and grandsons exist, he says, 'I grant, having regard to the merits of each,' then he says that he does not think that the fault of one harms another: because each is considered by himself and not as depending on another. Hence Lord Iaco. de Ra. says in his Summa, titu. quibus modis feu. amit., that sometimes there is such a fief that it cannot be lost for any cause or ingratitude—as, for instance, because it was given because he delivered the grantor from death, or had rescued him from enemies or bandits, as in ff. de donat. l. si pater, § 1—and thus the greatness of the merits is compensated with the demerits. Bald., however, in this last point alleges an argument to the contrary, that the final demerits are weighed more than the preceding merits, because the final fault harms: ff. de actio. emp. l. si per emptorem. The first statement seems truer, because it seems to be a remuneration and the wage of distinguished and great labor rather than a benefice: arg. 12, q. 2, c. quicunque suffragio, and it is a singular statement; he says certain other things which do not pertain to the purpose. And these words of Bald. are sufficiently pleasing to me. And had the concession not been made through the aforesaid words or the like, certainly the opinion of Dyn., which very many follow, seems very equitable through l. 3, ff. de interdic. & rele., although the opinion of Barto. in subtlety and rigor seems truer through the said c. 1, si uasal. feu. pri. with its like, and seems to be the intention of Specu. in d. § fina., and Bald. seems to hold in c. imperialem, § insuper, de prohi. feu. ali. per Fede., where he says that under the ius commune the offense of the father ought not to harm the son in this, when the fief did not come from the father, but from a more remote lineage, because in this case he does not have it from the father, but his ancestors seem to have given it to him: d. l. 3, ff. de interdic. & rele. Likewise, through the offense the father seems extinguished and removed from the midst, as in ff. de contrabu. l. 1, § filium. But according to the custom of fiefs he says that it harms the son, and the motive of the custom was so that vassals might fear more, for it is natural to fear more in a son than in oneself, as in ff. quod metus cau. l. isti quidem, in fi. But in doubts we ought, especially in judging, to follow the more benign opinion, as in the rule in pœnis, lib. 6, and l. si præses, and l. penul. ff. de pœnis, with its like. From which it seems must be concluded for our purpose that, since this county of Bigorre is from a more remote lineage—presupposing that it is feudal, and that Esquivat and Constance offended—nevertheless prejudice ought not to be done to the other agnates, who at least ought to have it from a new investiture according to the aforesaid limitation of Bald.; but (as I said) it is not found that they knowingly committed anything against the lord on account of which they ought to be deprived. The text in the said c. 1, si uasal. feu. pri., must also be weighed, because it does not deprive all agnates indistinctly, but up to the third degree; but because it does not pertain much to our purpose, I do not insist otherwise. To the eighth question, which is: If the church of Le Puy could not invade de facto and without judicial cognizance of the cause, whether in such judicial cognizance of the cause Esquivat and Constance ought to have been summoned, and, having been summoned, convicted. Undoubtingly I say that wherever a defense can belong to an absent party, nothing ought to be agitated to his prejudice without him being summoned, as in cap. ecclesia sanctæ Mariæ, de consti., and in c. inter quatuor, de maior. & obed., and c. 1, de causa pos. & proprie., and 3, q. 9, c. caueant, and c. omnia, and 2, q. 1, c. nos in quemquam, and l. de unoquoque, and l. contumacia, ff. de re iudica., and l. cessante, and l. tres denunciationes, C. quomodo & quando iudex, and l. 1, § item ex eo, ff. quæ senten. sine appel. rescin. Hence it is that even in a notorious matter a citation is required, from which some defense can belong to the absent party, as noted in c. ad nostram, de iureiu., and in c. porrò, de diuor., and in c. uestra, de coha. cleri. & mulie.; and as to our case there is the gloss, and more expressly by Bal. in c. 1, ex quibus modis feu. amit. § uel cum filia, where Bal. notes after the gloss that on account of faults a fief is not lost ipso iure, except in the case of alienation, but a judgment, judicial cognizance of the cause, and a sentence are required; and the gloss notes the same in c. imperialem, § callidis, on the word reuertatur, de prohi. feu. ali. per Fede. colla. 10. And these cannot be exercised without the presence of the party, because the merits of causes are revealed by the assertion of the parties: l. fin. C. si per uim uel alio modo, and capit. tum ex literis, de in integrum restitu.; otherwise whatever is done in the absence of a party is of no validity, as in the laws alleged above, especially in cap. omnia and cap. caueant, and l. de unoquoque, to such an extent that not even an interlocutory decree prejudicial to a party can be delivered in the absence of that party, as noted in l. nec quicquam, § ubi decretum, ff. de offic. procon., although Innocen. thought otherwise in cap. querelam, de procur., and cap. auditis, eodem titu. But the first statement is commonly held. And the statement of Innoc. proceeds regarding an interlocutory decree of no or slight prejudice; Bald., however, says in d. § uel cum filia that in the case of alienation the vassal loses the fief ipso facto; he alleges Inno. in c. 2, de feu. I allege the gloss, which openly holds this in the said § callidis, previously alleged. He gives the reason for this specialty: because in this case the vassal seems to treat the fief as abandoned: argument. ff. de damn. infect. l. prætoris, with its gloss. This reason does not apply in our case, since they always possessed the county. Likewise, as he himself says, even in this case a sentence regarding the declaration of forfeiture is required; for wherever anyone incurs a penalty ipso facto, a declaratory sentence is required before apprehension or execution, as is the notable text in cap. cum secundum leges, de hæreti. lib. sexto, and l. eius, qui delatorem, and there by Barto., ff. de iure fi. And the same Bal. replicate this note in c. uno, de feudo sine cul. non amit. colum. 10,
† where

† he says that in pure execution, where a human judgment has preceded, cognizance or delay is not necessary; he alleges Innocen. in cap. ex ratione, de appel., which he says must be kept in mind. But I say that a better distinction must be made in this, as Innocen. himself in cap. cum super, de cau. poss. & proprie., near the end, on the word præiudicio; and I do not insist, because it is not our matter, and through Bar. in l. a diuo pio, ff. de re iudic. But I come to the second branch of Bald., which pertains to our matter: either it is a question of the execution of a sentence of law, and a libel is necessary, since no judgment has preceded—which is notable; the text in d. cap. uno and in cap. primo, de feu. sine cul. non amit., supports the aforesaid, where it is notably gathered that fault must first be inquired into before the vassal is ejected. It cannot, however, be inquired into except with the party present, as in cap. tum ex literis, de in integrum resti., and l. fina. C. si per uim uel alio modo; and especially does this proceed where a just cause is pretended and the offense is denied, because a lord ought not to be a judge in his own cause, as is proved in l. imperialem, § prętereà, de prohib. feud. ali. per Federic. colla. decima, and the express gloss there in § callidis, on the word reuertatur, and in cap. cæterum, de iudic., and by what is noted there this question is sufficiently resolved. For wherever there is a question between lord and vassal—as because the lord of the fief claims it has fallen into forfeiture, and the vassal denies it—the question ought to be resolved by peers of the court, that is, other vassals of the same lord; and if he does not have other vassals or peers, the ordinary judge of the matter ought to be approached, as noted by the gloss and Bal. in the said § prętereà, which is § penul., and the doctors in the gloss in the said cap. cęterum. Nay, I say more: that since in our case the church of Le Puy asserted that Lady Constance was its vassal, and she denied it, the peers of the court ought not to take cognizance, nor the church itself, but the ordinary judge of that Lady Constance, or of the other countess or count, whoever it may be, since it is denied that that is a fief. Therefore the cause ought to be brought before the natural judge of the defendant himself, because a plaintiff ought to follow the forum of the defendant. The doctors expressly hold this in d. c. cæterum, and Bal. in d. pe.; it is proved in c. j. de lege Corra. colla. x; and nay rather in broader terms, namely regarding an emphyteuta who has not paid the canon for two or three years: although the laws say that he can be expelled by the lord, as in cap. potuit, de loc., and l. 2, de iure emph., nevertheless, as Spec. notably says in ti. de loc. § nunc aliqua, uer. 48, if the emphyteuta alleges any just cause, the lord ought not to expel him by his own authority, but the cause ought to be brought before his judge; to the same effect is what Ci. notes in d. l. 2. I conclude, therefore, that Esquivat and Constance ought to have been recalled to judgment; and consequently whatever was done in their absence, they not having been legitimately cited, was not valid. And this concerning this question. In the ninth question, in which it is asked: If the said Esquivat and Constance were not impleaded in their lifetime, whether their heirs could or can be impleaded? I say that the gloss in c. 1, quibus modis feu. ami., frames the question in the converse case: namely, if the lord did not implead the vassal for faults committed during his lifetime, whether the heir can implead him; and it concludes that he cannot: argum. in l. omnimodo, C. de inoffic. testam., and de reuocan. dona. l. 1, and ff. de probat. l. procula; and the gloss intended the same in d. l. omnimodo. Bal. says that this is true if the deceased had a period for complaining and did not complain; otherwise if he did not have it, or was ignorant: alleg. in ar. l. diuus, and l. excipiuntur, § fin., which can sufficiently be admitted in this case; and this was the opinion of Ioan. Andr. in c. 2, de dona. super gl. fi., where he posits that limitation of Bal.; alleg. de elec. c. cum in ueteri, ff. de confir. tuto. l. in confirmando, and l. utilitatem. But what in our doubt, when the vassal was not impleaded during life, whether his heir can be impleaded? The gloss does not frame it there, but Bal. posits it there, and does not openly resolve it, but says that there is an argument for this question in l. rei iudicatæ, ff. so. ma.; but certainly it pertains to the preceding case, and not to this one.

† For there, according to the true understanding, the case is posed whether the husband's heir can raise the defense of adultery against the wife seeking restitution of the dowry if the husband did not accuse the wife in his lifetime, and concludes that he cannot. But in our case, l. si, C. de adult., pertains better, where it is treated whether the husband can raise the defense of adultery against the wife's heir if he opposed it during the wife's lifetime. But the gloss in d. c. fi. de do. in fi. expressly frames this question, and by the argument of that text says that he cannot; for since no question was moved against the vassal during life, his successor cannot be troubled, just as we say there in the heir of a donee, who cannot be molested if the donee himself was not molested concerning magnitude during life. The same is noted by glo. j, l. fin. C. de reuo. dona. For the injury seems remitted toward the deceased through silence, according to that gloss. But Io. And. in addi. Spec. in ti. de feu. § final. frames this question of the ancients and concludes as above, with a limitation, however; for he says that this conclusion proceeds so that the heir or successor of a vassal cannot be troubled or impleaded if the lord had knowledge of the fault of the deceased and had time for complaining and remained silent; otherwise if he was ignorant, or did not have time for complaining against the deceased: argumen. in l. confirmando and l. utilitatem, ff. de confir. tuto. Bald. intended the same in c. imperialem, § insuper, de prohi. feu. alie. per Fed., where he well touched upon this question; and Io. And. and Bal. are moved because these revocations are as it were prosecutions of injuries, which are not given to heirs, nor against heirs: l. iniuriarum, ff. de iniur. Bald. also posits another limitation, saying that if it were such a felony or fault on account of which the vassal had lost the fief ipso facto, then an action could be brought by the heir of the lord against the heir of the vassal, because an injury which drew execution with it also passes against an heir, as in l. commissa, ff. de public.; noted in l. 3, § quod ait prætor, ff. quod quisque iuris. And therefore he concludes that if a felony were committed in alienating the fief, or another which by special pact induced deprivation of the fief ipso facto, such prejudice would pass to the heir even without a complaint having been prepared, which he says is to be noted. Which is sufficiently pleasing to me through the text joined with the gloss in the said capitul. imperialem, § callidis, in fine, where it is said that through alienation the fief reverts to the lord, and the gloss says there that it does so ipso iure; in another fault, however, a sentence of deprivation is required, and that the vassal be convicted of the fault, in capitul. primo, de feud. sine culpa non amit., and the notable gloss in the said § callidis; I said something above in the preceding question. Likewise, I would limit this statement of Baldus unless the lord, knowing the vassal to have been deprived, tacitly approved him through some positive act: optimum argu. in c. ex ore, de priuileg., and c. dilecto, de præben., and l. si filius, ff. fami. erciscun., and what Barto. notes in l. quo enim, ff. rem rat. habe. I come to the tenth question: Whether the judgment of Le Puy obtained in the court of the King of France against the King of England and Duke of Aquitaine regarding the spoliation of possession or quasi-feudality or homage concerning the castle of Lourdes in any way prejudiced the said Constance, who was neither summoned nor heard, and her right? And certainly, if what is presupposed above in the narration of the fact is true—namely, that this Lady Constance was ignorant that a lawsuit was being conducted concerning these matters between the church of Le Puy and the king of England—I do not see that the said judgment could in any way have prejudiced her: because regularly no prejudice is done to one who is ignorant, even where the matter concerns that regarding which an action belonged in the first place to the ignorant party, as in l. sæpe, ff. de re iudic., and c. penul. eod. tit.; to this pertains l. nec præteriit, C. de capt.; nor should that sentence be ordered to execution to the prejudice of Lady Constance, although it was valid to the prejudice of the king of England, as in c. cum super, de re iudica. And if it is said that the said Lady Constance could claim prejudice in the execution of the sentence, at least regarding possession, since the King of England previously possessed, or when receiving the oath of fealty both from her and from Esquivat, and thus only the church of Le Puy was to be placed in the position of the said king? And according to the notable theory of Innocen. in c. ueniens, de testi., which Bald. follows in l. a diuo Pio, ff. de re iudic., a third party cannot impede the execution of a sentence for his own interest when it is sought to be done on a thing that is not vacant, but possessed by another, since that third party can afterwards bring an action for his right against this second party just as against the first: to this pertains l. is a quo, ff. de rei uen., and what Ioan. And. notes there following Innoc. in c. 1, de conces. præben. lib. 6. I reply that, on the contrary, she could claim great prejudice: because just as it is in the interest of a lord not to lose a subject, d. c. cum super, so it is in the interest of a subject not to change a lord, as Innoc. notably says in c. auditis, de rescri., and d. c. cum super; to this pertains l. principaliter, C. de lib. cau., and it seems openly proved in our case in cap. imperialem, § præterea ducatus, de prohi. feu. ali. per Fed. colla. 10, and c. 1, de lege Corra. ea. collat., where it is said that a lord cannot transfer a fief to another without the vassal's will; to the same effect is what is read and noted in c. fin. de maior. & obed., where Ioan. Andr. and Hosti. expressly maintain this; nor does the theory of Innoc. in c. ueniens, previously alleged, stand in the way, because it proceeds when the third party can claim no prejudice with respect to the execution, as for example because it is an execution regarding a thing possessed by another third party; whence it is otherwise if he could claim some prejudice, as in c. Pisanis, and what is noted there, de restitu. spolia., where there is a good text. Likewise, the said Lady Constance had another notable defense: for if she had been present, she could have denied—and so also she ought afterwards to have been able to deny—that any possession or quasi-possession of homage had been transferred to that king of England: because, as I said above in the sixth question, since they swore this oath to the King of England through fear, the act was null ipso iure, as I said fully there; and consequently it can be said that the church of Le Puy ought to be restored to his place, since of right the King of England had acquired nothing. But if the said Lady Constance had known that a suit was pending between the church of Le Puy and the king of England, and had remained silent, whether any prejudice would have been generated for her is more doubtful. And first, regarding property, no prejudice was inflicted upon her: both because property was not at issue, and a sentence rendered in the possessory does not prejudice regarding property, because property has nothing in common with possession: l. naturaliter, § nihil commune, ff. de acqui. pos., and c. pastoralis, de cau. poss. & proprie.; and because no prejudice is done regarding property to a third party, even one who knows and remains silent, as in cap. cum super, and what is noted there, de cau. poss. & proprie.; and this if we are outside the case of l. sæpe, as it was in our case, because an action concerning this right did not belong in the first place to Lady Constance; nay, no action belonged to her, since the matter concerned receiving the oath of fealty and the possession of the fief so far as pertains to the lords. But it is doubtful whether by remaining silent she will prejudice herself regarding possession? And it seems at first that she does, through the notable text in d. ca. cum super: for just as a sentence rendered against a subject prejudices a lord who knows and remains silent regarding possession, as there, so also a sentence rendered against a lord ought to prejudice a subject or vassal who knows and remains silent; and Innoc. seems to mean this in cap. auditis, de præscrip., where he says that a sentence rendered against a lord does not prejudice a subject, nor conversely does one rendered against a subject prejudice a lord, unless he knew and defended it; he alleges for this last point d. c. pe. de re iud. But in cap. cum super and cap. penul. eod. tit. he restricts that statement so that prejudice is done to one who knows with respect to possession only, which the text there seems to indicate at first sight, as if execution is made for him who obtained the sentence; and the canonists commonly seem to hold the same there. But I have elsewhere advised that even regarding possession there is no prejudice to one who possesses and remains silent, moved principally by the reasoning of Innocen. in the said c. auditis, where he says that defense, when subjection is at issue, belongs principally and equally to the lord and to the subject for the aforesaid reason; therefore a sentence against one ought not to harm the other, even one who knows and remains silent, which I prove through the said l. sæpe and cap. pen. de re iud. For then the sentence against one harms another who knows and remains silent, when he to whom the action belonged in the first place permitted the subsequent party to sue, and this because he could have repelled him from the judgment, as is said there. But if the defense belongs equally to both, the said Lady Constance could not have removed the King of England from the judgment, since he was litigating concerning a right principally his own, or which he claimed as his own; therefore it ought not to have prejudiced Lady Constance if she had remained silent and permitted them to litigate, since they were litigating for their own interest, and the sentence could have effect to the prejudice of those litigants. The text in the said cap. cum super also seems to prove this, weighing two things beyond the doctors there: first, in that it says that the sentence ought to be ordered to execution without prejudice to that bishop who claimed subjection, although he knew that the cause was being conducted; for this sentence could not be ordered to execution without prejudice to Lady Constance or her successor, since she would be compelled to obey a non-lord and swear to him, at least until the property was established; for the benefit of possession is very great, as in Instit. de interdictis, § commodum. Secondly, I weigh the reasoning of that text when it says: because a matter conducted between others ought not to prejudice others; and thus singularly does that text intend—which I do not know elsewhere—that a lord is said to be another person from the subject with respect to this, that no prejudice is done to him from a sentence rendered against the subject; therefore, by equal reasoning, the same must be said regarding the subject, because the action was conducted against the lord, by the aforesaid reasoning. And to that c. cum super, insofar as it intimates that a sentence is ordered to execution against one who knows and remains silent, it can be replied that it speaks when the knowing party was not possessing, and thus it speaks of a certain factual prejudice, because he could not impede the execution about to be made, even in a vacant thing, since he knew and remained silent; it is otherwise, however, where he himself possessed, or if prejudice were done to him in the aforesaid manner. And this understanding of that chapter was held by Lord Francesco Zabarella of revered memory, later commonly called the Florentine Cardinal, although he was not moved by the aforesaid motives. But the said l. sæpe, in § nam & si libertus, seems to stand very much in the way of the aforesaid conclusion, where it is said that if a freedman litigating concerning his status with a third party receives an adverse sentence, it prejudices the patron regarding his right of patronage. For to that text it can be replied in two ways, because that text has two interpretations. The first, when the patron intervenes in the judgment, and the text seems to sound like this when it says 'with him intervening,' etc. And Ioan. held this interpretation, and Innoc. approves it in d. c. cum super; for Ioan. said, and well according to Innoc., that if someone claims rights which I possess in some thing, with me knowing, and obtains them, it nevertheless does not prejudice me unless I defend it; and he explains the word of d. l. sæpe, namely 'with me intervening and defending,' because since I offer myself for defense, I cause prejudice to myself if I do not prove my right, as there; to this pertains l. qui se liti, ff. de peti. hæredi. The second interpretation was that of Rog., that mere knowledge suffices; and although Barto. holds this interpretation in d. l. sæpe, Innoc. nevertheless and Ioan. And. say that the Pope seems to reject that interpretation of Roge. in d. c. cum super. But if we wish to save Rog. and Barto., let us speak otherwise, and thus: that either we are speaking of a freedman litigating, and prejudice is done to a knowing patron, as in d. § nam si libertus; or we are speaking of another subject or a lord litigating, and prejudice is not done to the other, even though knowing, unless he intervened in the judgment and offered himself for defense; and so speaks d. c. cum super, and in my judgment it seems to be the intention of Barto., if it is well weighed in d. l. sæpe. The reason for the difference is: because the freedman obtained his liberty from the patron, and thus seems to have had permission to sue concerning ownership, and consequently concerning the right of patronage, by the permission of the patron himself; deservedly is prejudice done to the patron, just as by the same reasoning it is said of a creditor suing on ownership of a pledge by the hypothecary action, that prejudice is done to a knowing debtor; for he had that obligation by the act of the debtor, and thus seems to have given him permission to litigate concerning ownership, as Barto. notes in d. l. sæpe. In a non-subject, however, or the lord of a fief, this reason ceases, since he does not have the fief from the subject, although he litigates purely for his own right; therefore it ought not to prejudice a vassal, even one who knows. Likewise, on another ground silence ought not to have harmed Lady Constance: for she was certain and informed of her right that she was not a vassal, nor had any right been transferred to the said king of England, since she had sworn the oath to him through fear, as I said above. And thus it is not true to say that she permitted her lord to sue, but a complete stranger in truth, and as to her right by the aforesaid reason. And this concerning that doubt. The eleventh question: Whether the proceeding held by that knight de Longpérier, the pretended executor, was null, so that it was not necessary to appeal from it, but the exception of nullity was always preserved to the same Constance and her heirs? To which it seems to me must be said securely that whatever he did was of no effect: because he did something entirely other than what was enjoined upon and committed to him; deservedly was his act null, since he exceeded or perverted the form of the mandate, as in c. cum dilecta, de rescri., and c. uenerabili, de offic. delega., and c. Pisanus, de restitu. spoliat., and l. diligenter, ff. mandati; and expressly in our terms, namely in an execution perverting the mandate, the gloss holds in c. quod ad consultationem, de offic. delega., and the same there Ioan. And. and commonly the doctors, and Barto. in l. ab executore, ff. de appel.; and consequently it was not necessary to appeal, as noted by the gloss, Ioan. And., and Barto. in the places previously alleged; and it is proved by law: because although one can appeal from a null act for the purpose of the devolution of the matter so that in the meantime the factual grievance may be avoided, as in c. dilecto, de appel., and there by Inno., and in l. Cornelia Pia, de iure patro., it is nevertheless not necessary, because one is always heard by way of nullity, as in c. 1, and what is noted there, de re iud., and in l. 1 & 2, C. quando prouoc. non est necess., and l. si expressim, ff. de appel. That that executor, moreover, perverted the order and mandate given to him is most clearly evident from the narration of the fact. For the sentence was rendered between the church of Le Puy and the king of England regarding the possession of the quasi-homage and fealty on the occasion of the said county, and it was enjoined upon the said de Longpérier that he execute the judgment; he, however, inducted the dean in the name of the church of Le Puy into possession of the county, and commanded those of the county that they obey no one other than the church of Le Puy. Which words savor of the beneficial possession of the county, and not the possession of receiving homage or fealty. For if he had wished to execute the judgment, as by law and from the form of the mandate was incumbent upon him, he ought to have approached Lady Constance, as the pretended vassal, and commanded her that in place of the king of England or duke of Aquitaine she obey and perform homage or fealty to the church of Le Puy, until something else should be pronounced regarding the property of that right; which he did not do, but something entirely other. Whence I say that that execution was not valid, neither with respect to the possession of receiving homage, nor with respect to the county itself: because in the first the will for that execution was lacking; in the second, the power was lacking. And thus that rule had a place: 'What he willed, he could not; what he could, he would not fulfill': de offi. deleg. c. cum super abbatia, and l. multum interest, C. si quis alte. uel fi. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said executor said that they should obey no one other than the church of Le Puy insofar as the judgment and mandate of the lord king extended, etc.: because in word he said one thing, and by act he did the contrary; and thus by contrary acts he departed, as in c. cum M., de consti., and c. solicitudinem, de app.; whence there was in him a certain repugnancy; deservedly neither was valid, as in l. ubi repugnantia, ff. de regu. iur. I come to the twelfth question, neighboring this one, in which it is asked: Whether the second judgment pronounced by the king's court, not, however, legitimately ordered to execution, validated in any way the proceeding of that executor de Longpérier previously made regarding the execution of the first judgment? And I say briefly that it did not. For it is certain that his proceeding was of no effect, as was proved in the preceding question; therefore neither did it receive vigor through the second judgment: because the second judgment or decree did not intervene upon the first execution by confirming it or pronouncing that it had been well conducted, in which case it could excusably be doubted whether it was validated through the second sentence, through those things which are read and noted in l. 1, ff. quæ sen. sine ap. rescin., and in l. 1, C. quando prouo. non est neces., and by Innoc. in c. super literis, de rescri., by Bar. fully in l. si expressim, ff. de appel., in which there are various opinions, as noted in the previously alleged laws. But while Lady Constance was insisting upon her appeal against the proceeding of the said executor, it was requested in the name of the church of Le Puy that before all else the first judgment, of which mention was made above, be ordered to full execution; and through this petition it was pronounced by another judgment of the court of the King of France that the execution of the judgment made for the church of Le Puy against the king of England should be made according to the tenor of the said judgment, both in the fief of the entire county of Bigorre and in all things which the said king of England held of the said county or by reason thereof at the time of the first judgment, so that the bishop and chapter should be placed in them in that state in which the said king of England was at the time of the same judgment, etc., as is clear in the narration of the fact. Whence, if the aforesaid words are well weighed, this definitive sentence—nay, more truly interlocutory decree—pronounced pending the appeal of Lady Constance was not upon the execution already made, in any way approving it; but it was only commanded that the first judgment be ordered to execution, nor simply, but to the prejudice of the king of England alone, so that the church of Le Puy should be placed in possession of those things which the king of England possessed in the said county at the time of the judgment; and since at that time the king of England did not possess the county by full right, but had received only the oath of fealty, even the second pronouncement did not extend except to the right then possessed by the king of England; and thus it is most clearly evident that the execution unjustly and perversely made by that executor de Longpérier was in nothing validated by this second judgment, especially since the words of a sentence are to be strictly understood, as in l. una, C. si una sen. plu. fue. con., and c. dilectus, de offi. ord.; noted by Bar. in d. l. si expressim, in prin. 2. co. Nay rather, Bar. noted more in d. l. si expressim: that if an appeal had been made from a null sentence, and the judge of the appeal had pronounced the appeal unjust or that it had been badly appealed, the first null sentence would not through this be confirmed, because it does not follow: 'it was badly appealed, therefore the judgment held.' For it could have been badly appealed on account of a defect of procedure not observed, as because after a decade or something similar, and the words of a sentence, as I have said, are to be strictly understood. Coming to our purpose, the null proceeding of that executor would then have been confirmed if it had been pronounced that it was badly appealed and well proceeded by that executor, as noted by Innocen. and others in the previously alleged laws. And in this case it could be doubted whether the first execution would be confirmed through such words. And first I would hold that it would not, because that execution was notoriously null, since it was established that it was contrary to the sentence, which induces a notoriety, as in c. uestra and c. si. de coha. cle.; therefore the second sentence would be notoriously unjust if it contained that a notoriously null proceeding was valid; a sentence, however, that is notoriously unjust is null ipso iure, nor is it necessary to appeal from it: the text is notable in c. inter cæteras, de re iud.; noted by Inn. in c. fraternitatis, de fri. & mal. For a sentence passes into res judicata on account of the presumption of justice, because the presumption is in favor of the judge, as in c. in præsentia, de renun., and c. causam quæ, de iud., which presumption ceases once the notoriety of injustice is given; for when the truth is manifested, opinion yields to truth: 8, distinct. c. ueritate. And this concerning that question. The thirteenth question: Whether Lady Constance ought to be held excused, who, after she knew that the said judgments had been pronounced for the church of Le Puy, offered before the executor and the dean to perform homage to the church and the other things to which she was bound as above; and finally, languishing in illness, appointed a procurator with a special mandate to perform that homage, and the same procurator offered to perform it, but the church did not care to receive it? To this question I reply that not only is she excused, but I say that she did more than she was bound to do. For she is excused, because it suffices that a vassal, after he recognizes that he is a vassal, approach the lord and promise the oath and seek investiture and offer the other things to which he is bound by law, as is the text in c. j. de capitulis Corr. coll. x; and if it is lacking on the part of the lord, it is just as if he had done all the things to which he was bound; because it is a rule of law that if it is lacking on the part of him whose interest it is that the act be done, it is just as if the act had been performed, as in l. iu. ciui. ff. de cond. & de., and in the rule imputari, with the concordances posited there, de re. iu. li. 6. For it is enough that a man do whatever he can, and in that it consists: 22, q. 2, c. faciat homo, and c. breui, de iure iu. And the time of a year prefixed for performing the oath, etc., runs for the vassal from the time of knowledge and not before, as Bal. notes in d. c. j.; and Bal. holds this side following Iac. de Bel. in c. 2, per quos fi. inuest. col. x, where he says that if the vassal wishes to perform fealty, but the lord refuses to make investiture, it does not harm the vassal, and the lord is bound to him for his interest, as in § fi. de for. fid. ea. col. Or, according to him, he can be precisely compelled to deliver the thing and make investiture, as in c. si facta, si de feu. fue. contro. Or, thirdly, according to them, the lord shall be deprived of the bare property of the fief, just as the vassal would be deprived of his right if he refuses to perform fealty, as in de no. for. fide. § dominus, in the title qualiter dominus feu. priue. cap. unico, eadem collat. And this last is to be noted, and I said it above in the sixth question; and c. quia diuersitatem, de concess. præben., and c. licet, de supplen. negl. præla., support this. I said that Lady Constance did more than she was bound to do, because she was not bound immediately to swear, since she had not been summoned to that judgment conducted between the church of Le Puy and the King of England; whence she ought first to have been heard, wishing to speak concerning her right, because perhaps she was not a vassal, but the true proprietress, as Lady Petronilla had been, or perhaps it was in her interest not to change a lord, as I fully stated in the tenth question. The fourteenth question: Whether the lord King of France, who, according to the tenor of his judgment, was to hold the contentious property in his hand as superior during the dispute between the contending parties, by so holding it for a very long time, prescribed against the parties, so that he is bound to administer justice to the heirs of the said Constance regarding the property of the said county? To which I say by a twofold and efficacious reason that he could not prescribe, but that he is bound to administer his right to each. And first it is proved because prescription does not proceed with bad faith, as in cap. uigilanti and c. fin. de præscrip., and in the rule possessor, de reg. iu. lib. 6, by Bar. in l. priuilegia, C. de sacrosan. eccl., where he says that since this canon law concerns the salvation of the soul, it ought to be observed even in the civil forum, and the gloss notes the same in the said rule possessor; but the king of France knew that those goods belonged to others and not to himself, since he brought them into his hands through the accord of the parties; therefore he could not prescribe, as being constituted in bad faith. For he is called a possessor in bad faith who has consciousness of another's property, as the text says in c. si uirgo, 32, q. 2. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that other successor kings could have been ignorant of this: argu. of the rule is qui in ius succedit alterius, de reg. iur. lib. 6; which is not likely, nor is it to be presumed, since that king did this under pretext of a judgment; and a judgment induced a notoriety, of which one is not presumed to be ignorant: de purga. cano. c. cum dilecti. Likewise and better, presupposing that the successors had good faith, since the bad faith of the deceased harms the universal successor in prescribing, as is the notable text with the gloss in l. cum hæres, ff. de diuer. & tempo. pręscri. For the successors in the realm held the realm and other things as heirs, as I fully said above in the first question. And although Di. said in the rule possessor, previously alleged, that by canonical equity it seems that a successor in good faith can begin prescription from himself, according to what is noted in c. de quarta, de præscri., and c. cura, de iure pa., nevertheless I say that that proceeds in church lands, but not in others, where civil law ought principally to be observed, since it can be observed without detriment to the soul, as noted in the said rule possessor, and in c. 2, de arbi. lib. 6, and in d. l. priuilegia. Likewise, the canon laws speak of a successor in a prelacy, who derives his right not from the deceased, but from a superior, whence he is deemed the same person with the deceased. But the civil law speaks of an heir, who is deemed the same person with the deceased, since he obtains all his right from him, as in Authen. de iureiu. a moriente præstito. The second principal reason why Lady Constance and her successors ought not to be prejudiced is: because a suit, even one pending before the prince's consistory, ought to be without damage of delay until the prince shall have caused it to be resolved, as in Authen. sed cum lis, C. de temp. ap., and in c. ex insinuatione, de ap. And through these things the truth of this question is clearly evident. The fifteenth question: What penalty does the church of Le Puy incur by transferring the said county to the lady Queen under whatever title, Lady Constance being unheard and her appeal pending? I reply that it incurs the penalty of a litigious contract; which penalty indeed has a place even against the church when a prelate has alienated with the assent of the chapter, as is proved in capit. ecclesia sanctæ Mariæ, the first, ut lit. pend. nil innoua., and Host. and Ioan. And. expressly hold this there; 11, q. 1, cap. quia res litigio., supports this. The penalty of a litigious thing, moreover, is posited in l. fin. C. de litigio., and by the gloss in d. c. ecclesia; and with respect to the alienor himself the penalty is that, if a price intervened, he is compelled not only to restore the price, but to refund another equal amount, and it is applied to the fisc, and the contract of alienation is not valid, and he recovers the thing, so that the condition of the plaintiff may not be worse, since from the beginning the judgment began against a certain person. If, however, a price did not intervene—as, for instance, because he donated it—then he ought to be mulcted in the true and just valuation; and these things are held in d. l. fi. And that that penalty has a place here is proved thus: a thing is rendered litigious when concerning its ownership, which is disputed between plaintiff and defendant by judicial citation, or by prayers offered to the prince and notified to the judge and through him made known to the future defendant, as the text says in Authen. litigiosa, C. de litigio., and in Clemen. 2, ut lit. penden. But in our case it was a matter of the ownership of that fief or county, and the cause had been impleaded or brought into judgment. For the first appeal, since it was extrajudicial, has the nature of a provocation, as in c. cum sit Romana, de appella. Likewise and better, the cause was subsequently brought into judgment, and prayers were notified to the king, and the king commanded that justice be done, and this was often notified to the church of Le Puy; whence not only did citation and cognizance concerning the litigious thing intervene here; nay rather, many other acts intervened to induce a litigious thing, and a mere citation and prayers offered to the prince and through him notified to the judge, etc., suffice, as I said above; and both, which is more, intervened here; therefore the taint of a litigious contract had a place, and this taint remains even in the cause of appeal, as Inno. notably says in c. dilectæ, in fi. de excep. The sixteenth question: Whether the lady Queen and her heirs, who de facto in the manner narrated in the case held the said county for 130 years and more, have prescribed against the heirs of the said Constance now defending themselves? To this question I say that they could not prescribe. And concerning the lady Queen there is no doubt: because she was in bad faith, both in receiving a litigious thing, as was clear in the preceding question, and subsequently de facto and by violence occupying that county: 34, q. 2, c. si uirgo; nor could her successors prescribe, both because it is probable that in so arduous a matter they had notice of the origin of that county, and thus were in bad faith; and because the bad faith of the deceased harms the heirs in prescribing, so that just as the deceased was not able to prescribe on account of bad faith, so neither could her heir, because he is deemed the same person with the deceased, even if he had good faith, as in l. cum hæres, ff. de diuer. & tempo., and as I stated fully above in the fourteenth question, and the notable gloss in l. uitia, C. de acquir. posses. And this proceeds especially, regard being had to the fact that the taint was real: because the said lady Queen occupied the said county by force through her men; and the law says that taints of possession contracted from ancestors endure and are transmitted to the successor of the author without fault, as in said l. uitia possessionum, previously alleged, and Instit. de usuca. § furtiuæ, with the following. The seventeenth question: Whether the King of France, in the peace made at Brétigny with the King of England, as was said in the case, could give the county of Bigorre, being thus in his hands, to the said King of England? And if he could, whether after the deprivation made in the Parlement the same county returned to its prior state and cause, or was incorporated into the king's domain through confiscation? And the question is not light to me through the text and notable commentary in its own matter in l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadrien. præscri., where in sum it is said

† that if the emperor should either sell or otherwise alienate another's property as his own, one claiming that property to be his cannot prevail, but the owner or creditor cannot move an action against the possessors; rather, he can act against the fisc within a quadriennium only; afterwards indeed he has no action, even against the imperial house. But in our case the King of France, who acts in the place of the emperor in his kingdom and among his subjects, as in c. per uenerabilem, qui filij sint legi., conferred that county, which he held as his own, upon the King of England, nor was an action then brought against his fisc within the quadriennium; therefore no action remained to the said Counts of Foix, nor to their successors. Nor does the deprivation subsequently made concerning the King of England stand in the way, because an obligation or action once removed and extinguished does not return or revive, although the thing arrives at its prior state: l. qui res, § aream, ff. de sol., and in c. quæris, de conse. dist. 4. And although this motive seems to press, nevertheless, that notwithstanding, I deem the contrary to be truer in law. And to l. bene a Zenone, I reply in many ways. First, that that law speaks when the emperor donated another's property, believing it to be his own; otherwise if he knew it to be another's, because then the alienation does not prejudice the owner; concerning this there are two very notable glosses, the first in l. 2, C. de ali. re. con., the other in l. una, de alie. rerum fisca. cum priua. con. lib. 10, which thus and rightly restricted this law; and Bar. follows in d. l. una. And this is the reason: for it is a special privilege of the emperor that he can alienate another's property when he has some part in it, as in the laws immediately previously alleged; it is otherwise, however, when he has no part and knows it to be another's. For the emperor cannot regularly bestow the property of others, as noted in l. rescripta, C. de preci. impe. offe., by Cy. and Bar. in l. fin. C. si contra ius uel uti. publi., by Inn. in c. quæ in ecclesiarum, de præst.; but the King of France probably knew that that county of Bigorre belonged to them, since there had been a long dispute in the court of the Parlement concerning it between the King of England and the church of Le Puy, and between Lady Constance and the same church. Likewise, the successors of Lady Constance down to the present day have always insisted before the Kings of France existing for the time for the recovery of the said county, as is stated in the narration of the fact. And rumor ought probably to be among them that this county belongs to those lords of Foix. For by these things and by denunciations frequently made, bad faith of the possessor is presumed, as Bar. notably says in l. Celsus, ff. de usuc., especially because in a grave and notable fact such as this was, memory is presumed to survive, although much time has elapsed, as in c. cum illorum, § circa, de sent. excon., and 16, dist. c. quod dictis; to this pertains what Inn. notes in c. ex literis, de iureiur. Secondly, it can be replied that that l. bene a Zenone posits a most special privilege of the emperor and Augustus, who labor day and night by their counsels and their labors for the whole world; whence not undeservedly do they have a fortune worthy of their prerogative, as the text says there near the end. This privilege, however, the King of France does not attribute to himself; therefore it is not to be extended, as in c. sanè, de priuile., and 7, q. j, c. peritissimi. And especially because in him there is not the same reason in this as in the emperor, since he does not labor for the whole world. Third reply: it is certain that the alienation made by the church of Le Puy at the time of the litigation was not valid, as in l. fi. C. de litig., and c. ecclesia, ut lit. pen., and consequently the property of that fief remained of right with that church. The law bene a Zenone, moreover, has no place in church property, because the emperor could not privilege himself to the prejudice of the goods of the church, as in c. quæ in ecclesiarum, and c. ecclesia sanctæ Mariæ, de consti., and in l. fi. ff. de iuris. om. iudi., and c. pastoralis, de re iudi., where there is a good text for our matter. Fourthly, it could more subtly be replied that l. bene a Zenone, previously alleged, has a place while the alienated thing exists in the possession of another, and this lest he who had the thing from the emperor be troubled, nor the emperor himself be troubled in valuation; deservedly was a time prefixed for suing, as there. But in our case these reasons cease, since the thing has reverted to the king himself. Nor is it lawful for the lord king himself to be enriched with the loss of others, especially of subjects, as in c. locup. de re iu. lib. 6, and in l. nam hoc natura, ff. de condi. indebi.; and since that law is odious, it ought to be restricted as much as can be: l. si præses, and l. pe. ff. de pœn., and c. in pœnis, lib. 6. From which I conclude that either the said alienation was in no way valid, or, if it was valid, it returned to its prior state, since it has reverted to the universal successor of that lady Queen, and to a possessor in bad faith. The eighteenth question: Whether the diligent efforts made by the heirs of the said Constance, as presupposed in the narration of the fact, interrupted the prescription of the said Queen and of her heirs, if any existed? This question can first be decided through those things which I said above in the fourteenth question. For prescription could not have a place here for the reasons stated there; but presupposing that it did have a place, in order that the query may be satisfied, whether an interruption was made through those diligent efforts: in this it must be observed that Lady Constance was despoiled of the said county of Bigorre by the Queen. Whence prescription ought to be considered from that time and not before, because prescription does not proceed without possession, as in the rule sine possessione, lib. 6. From that time, however, since the lady Queen was a violent possessor, prescription could undoubtingly not be initiated: Instit. de usuca. § furtiuè, with the following. For if she had had a legitimate title, she ought not by her own authority violently to have invaded possession, as in l. fin. C. si per uim uel

† alio modo, and l. si ex stipulatione, ff. de acqui. pos. For one cannot violently invade one's own property. If one does so, one falls into the penalty of l. si quis in tantam, C. unde ui, and 16, quæstio 6, cap. placuit, so that one ought to be deprived of ownership of that thing, if it was his; but if not, he is compelled to restore the thing with its valuation, as in the said laws. Furthermore, the said lady Queen was impleaded in the king's court, and through joinder of issue (litis contestatio), or where it is not required by reason of the privilege of the cause, through the act which is customary to be done after litis contestatio, an interruption of prescription is induced civilly, as in § potest, 16, quæstio 3, and l. penul. C. ne de statu defun.; noted by the gloss in c. illud, de præscrip., and Barto. in l. naturaliter, ff. de usuc. Finally, Lord Louis, the king, her son, succeeded this Queen in the said county of Bigorre, which Lord Louis indeed could not prescribe: both because he was the universal successor of the mother, who had been a possessor in bad faith, as in l. cum hæres, ff. de diuer. & tempo. præscrip.; and because the matter had already been brought into litigation with the deceased; and because that possession of the county had been tainted, because invaded violently. Whence it harmed even the successor, as in d. l. uitia possessionum, C. de acquir. posses., and in d. § furtiuæ. Thirdly, the lord King Louis, after his coronation, transferred possession of the said county to Lord Charles, Count of La Marche, his brother. He also, although he was a singular possessor, could not prescribe: both because he was in bad faith, which is to be presumed from the rumor of the place, which held that the said county belonged to Lady Constance, according to what is noted by Bart. in l. Celsus, ff. de usuca.; and because even by civil law, at least within thirty years, it could not be prescribed by anyone, even a singular successor, on account of the real taint which accompanies every successor: d. l. uitia, with the gloss in d. § furtiuæ, with the following. Likewise, he could not transfer it to this Charles, since a lawsuit already begun with the lady Queen was pending over it, which also passed to the successor, namely Lord Louis. For a judgment is not extinguished through the death of one of the litigants, as in Authen. principales, C. de iura. cal., and noted by the gloss in cap. fin. de arbi. Others, however, subsequently succeeding in the kingdom of France and in the said county are not specially expressed in the narration of the case; nor is it specifically stated what diligence the Count of Foix, commonly called Phoebus, or other predecessors or successors of his, applied; but it is stated in general that they applied many diligent efforts; whence I could not comprehend whether they were sufficient to interrupt prescription, if any had been initiated, since not every diligence suffices to interrupt prescription, as is clear in l. ut perfectius, C. de anna. exceptio., and 16, quaestio 3, capit. placuit, § hæc de præscriptionibus, uer. is autem cuius. And therefore we cannot give a special response on this: de spon. cap. de muliere. But in general I say it must be observed that prescription is sometimes interrupted naturally, sometimes civilly, but sometimes it sleeps, so that it does not run nor is it interrupted, but that time is subtracted from the middle; and concerning these matters see fully the gloss and doctors in c. illud, de præscript., and Barto. in d. l. naturaliter, who commented on that law. And among other things pertaining to our purpose, prescription sleeps when there is such hostility or war in the locality that justice is not administered, as in capit. ex transmissa, de præscri., and there by Inno. and Bar. ubi supra. The same holds according to Bar. there when mortality or plague so rages that justice is not administered in the locality for a similar reason, because it is the hostility of God, so that these times ought to be subtracted from the prescription. And I think that these were many in the kingdom of France on account of the very great hazards of wars which flourished and flourish in that kingdom.

† Likewise, prescription is interrupted through joinder of issue (litis contestatio), as I said above. And the notable gloss says in the rule sine possessione, de reg. iur. lib. 6, that under canon law, once thus interrupted, it can no longer be prescribed, because the defendant seems to hesitate concerning his right and not to have good faith. But under civil law forty years are required anew. But in this matter of sin one must stand by canon law, as the notable gloss says in the rule possessor, lib. 6; and the notable gloss says the same in c. 1, 16, q. 3, C. de sacrosan. eccle. l. priuilegia. Likewise, during the time of pupillary age prescription does not run: l. sicut, C. de præscrip. triginta uel quadraginta annorum; to this pertains l. fi. C. in quibus cau. in integ. resti. non est neces.; and therefore if any of the successors of Lady Constance who was first despoiled was a pupil, those times of pupillary age are to be removed from the middle. Furthermore, under canon law prescription is interrupted whenever bad faith supervenes, that is, consciousness of another's property, as in capitul. uigilanti and capitul. fin. de præscriptio., and the rule possessor malefidei, lib. 6; noted by Bartol. in d. l. naturaliter, ff. de usucap. Likewise, it must be observed that if someone was unable to join issue, either on account of the adversary's absence, or the affliction of madness when he has no tutor or curator, or because he is placed in great power—and this last must be noted in our matter—for then he ought to protest before the judge of the place and bring the libel of complaint before him, and if he cannot have the magistrate, let him do this before the bishop and manifest his will, and by so doing he interrupts the prescription of the adversary; and if he cannot have the magistrate or bishop, then let him do this before a notary, and in default of a notary before three witnesses. All these things are held in l. ut perfectius, C. de anna. excep., and 16, q. 3, capitul. placuit, § hęc de præscriptionibus. From these the procurator of the lord Count of Foix will be able to be greatly instructed to enervate completely the prescription of the other party, either by alleging in its entirety bad faith, as I said above, or interruption, or by removing from the middle those times in which prescription slept, as above. And let these suffice for that question. The nineteenth question: Whether the privilege claimed by the Counts of Armagnac and Pardiac provides any impediment to the donation made to the lord Count of Foix, or gives a just cause of opposition and appeal lest it take effect; and whether such a privilege or pact entered into between the king and his subjects is legally valid and to be observed, in light of or notwithstanding many provisions opposed in the donation which seem to make mention of pacts of this kind? To this question I briefly reply that such a privilege or pact is of no effect unless some interest of the said Count of Armagnac appears. The text is clear, and the gloss and doctors there, in l. nemo paciscendo, ff. de pactis, where it expressly appears that not only a prince, but not even a private person can be bound by that pact not to alienate his own property; the same is noted by Bart. in l. filii, § diuus, ff. de leg. 1, and in l. ea lege, C. de condi. ob causam. Hence the notable text in l. quoties, ff. de seruitu., says that a servitude cannot be established if there is no interest of the recipient, as for example if I stipulate that you do not walk through your estate, or that you do not reside there; therefore, if you grant me that you do not have the right to use and enjoy your estate, nothing is accomplished, as there. If, however, the lord Count of Armagnac can claim some interest that the said county of Bigorre not be placed outside the royal hand, then I say that, although a pact or privilege not to alienate can be valid, nevertheless such a pact cannot prevent the transfer of ownership if it is alienated de facto.
