The text and gloss, and more clearly Bartol. there, in d. l. ea lege, and the same is noted in d. § diuus and d. l. nemo, and in l. fi. C. de pact. conuen. inter empt. Inno. notably says the same in cap. Raynaldus, de testa., where he pursues this matter fully, where in sum he says that a pact cannot bring it about that an alienation made does not hold, or that ownership does not pass to the recipient, but the covenanting party can sue for his interest or for the penalty; he alleges what is noted in d. l. ea lege. If therefore a pact, even clothed, does not impede the transfer of ownership, a fortiori neither does the privilege of the alienor, since a privilege binds less than a pact; to this belongs what is noted in c. suggestum and c. dilecti, de deci. For a privilege is valid if it is in the interest of the recipient, as is read and noted in l. 1, § si quis hoc concesserit, ff. de aqua quoti. & æsti., yet it cannot impede the transfer of ownership, as noted in d. l. fi. C. de pac. inter emp. This fails according to Bar. in the said laws when he who attached the pact not to alienate reserved to himself some right in that thing, and thus he understands the notable text in l. si creditor, § fi. ff. de distra. pig., where it is clear that if a creditor receiving a hypothec over some thing attaches a pact that that thing not be alienated, the transfer of ownership is impeded, as that is a singular case there. But in our case no right belongs to the Count of Armagnac in that county; therefore the pact or concession was not sufficient to impede the transfer of ownership to the lord Count of Foix. Furthermore, I say that since the King of France in the grant made to the lord Count of Foix revoked all letters and every privilege granted to anyone else containing that the said county could not be alienated, as appears in the grant made to the lord Count of Foix, the said Count of Armagnac could not nor can he allege his privilege, as having been revoked. That the revocation was valid is proved from those things which are read and noted, especially by Inn. in c. in nostra, de iniur., where the text on this is notable. From which, from the statements made by Inno. there, it is gathered that a privileging statute conferred there upon subjects can be revoked by the enactors themselves, which I understand to apply when the privilege contains a successive act, as in our case, understanding in the same way the statement of Inn. in c. nouit, de iudi., which Archi. follows in 11, q. 1, c. quicunque, and Ioan. And. in c. constitutus, de relig. do. For these say that a privilege granted to a non-subject, for instance to a church by a secular prince, can no longer be revoked: argu. in l. perfecta donatio, C. de dona. quae sub modo; it is otherwise if it was granted to a subject, because that can be revoked, as is clear in d. c. suggestum, and c. dilecti, and de conces. præben. detestanda, and c. ueniens, de pręscri., with their likes. If, however, the privilege had passed into a contract or quasi-contract, then it could no longer be revoked—as, for example, if it had been said: 'Whosoever shall go to reside in such a city shall enjoy immunity for so many years'—such a privilege or privileged statute can no longer be revoked with respect to those who went, but with respect to others it can, as Bar. notes in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iur., and l. quod semel, de decre. ab ordi. faci., and l. semper, de iure immu. I say the same when the privilege contains a momentary act that has passed into the ius gentium, as if the prince had donated or enfeoffed something to me; for that cannot be revoked without cause, as in c. 1, de feu. sine cul. non amit., and c. uno, de natu. feu., and thus I understand what Bal. notes in both places. And from the aforesaid I conclude that neither the privilege nor the appeal could impede the transfer of the said county of Bigorre: both because the privilege was not valid, and because, presupposing its validity, it was revoked, and because, presupposing that it could not have been revoked, the lord of the property could not impede the transfer of the law, as appears from the aforesaid. And concerning the appeal, that it could not impede is clear, because an extrajudicial appeal accomplishes nothing if it is unjust, as it was in our case, as appears from the aforesaid, as is proved in c. cum nobis, de ele. Likewise, however just it may be, it does not impede someone from exercising his right in the meantime, as Inno. notably says in c. cum inter canonicos, and capi. quia propter, de elect., and cap. interposita, de appell., and c. ad dissoluendum, de despon. impub. Nor does the oath of the predecessor king stand in the way, if he made any, because that is not extended to the successor: in c. ueritatis, de iureiur.; nay rather, even if it had been sworn by this donor king, it would not have impeded the transfer of ownership of that county of Bigorre; because an act done contrary to an oath holds, although the transgressor is a perjurer, as in c. sicut, de spon.; noted by Inno. in c. dilecto, de appel.; Ioan. An. holds in the rule quod semel, de reg. iur. lib. 6, in Mercu.; the third gloss feels this in 13, q. 2, cap. ultima uoluntas. Nor does it stand in the way if an objection is raised concerning c. intellecto, de iureiuran., where it is clear that an alienation made to the prejudice of the king does not hold, even with an oath. For to this I shall fully reply below on question 26, where it better falls. From these things I infer the solution to the twentieth question, which was: Whether, after the opposition and appeal of the Count of Armagnac, innovations must be retracted? For I say that they must not; because the opposition and appeal were unjust, and presupposing that they had been just, they nevertheless could not impede the transfer of ownership; and thus an action can no longer be brought against the said Count of Foix, who legitimately obtained the said county, since a pact or privilege not to alienate one's own property (even granted that there is an interest of the covenanting party) does not nevertheless affect the thing itself so that it cannot be alienated, as appears from the laws alleged above in the preceding question. Likewise the 21st question is solved: namely, whether the said Counts of Foix can, by reason of their aforesaid oppositions and appeals, demand that the said county of Bigorre be reduced before all else into the king's hand, and that afterwards cognizance be taken concerning the merits thereof? And as appears from the aforesaid in the two proximate questions, it must be said that they cannot; both because the injustice of the appeals and of those seeking that revocation is notoriously established; and because privileges which are challenged for nullity, or falsity, or another defect, ought not to waver while the cause is pending, but ought to be observed until the contrary is proved, as in cap. accepimus, de fide instru., and in c. cum personæ, de priuil. lib. 6, and l. cum in precibus, C. de proba.; nay rather, while a suit is pending one ought not to be deprived of one's possession under pretext of a privilege held, even if the privilege is contrary to law, as in c. 1, ut lite penden. The twenty-second question is: Whether the opposition and appeal of the Count of Pardiac, which he makes for his barony of Les Angles because it was transferred from a greater to a lesser lord, is efficacious, in light of the fact that the Kings of France have been accustomed every day to transfer their vassals, although unwilling, to peers or lessers, and it is so observed in France, as is presupposed? For the solution of this question I introduce the clear text in c. uno, § ex eadem, de lege Corra. colla. 10, where it expressly appears that in requiring the consent of vassals the custom of the locality is not stood upon. To the same effect is what is noted in c. imperialem, § præterea ducatus, de prohi. ali. feu. per Fede., where it says

† that although the king prohibits the division of a duchy or dignity among several heirs, nevertheless a custom to the contrary is valid, adding that there is no positive law which cannot be abolished by a contrary custom: through l. de quibus, ff. de legi. I would, however, limit this statement through c. fin. de consuetudi. I introduce furthermore the good text in l. uenditor fundi, § 1, ff. communia prædi., where it is clear that custom can prejudice an individual's own right. Secondly and principally it can be said that, although a fief cannot be alienated against the will of the vassal, at least to a lesser, as the text seems to intimate in c. 2, § ex eadem, de le. Corra., and in d. c. imperialem, § præterea ducatus, this is nevertheless true unless it is alienated with a universality, as with a city or county, as occurs in our case. For then it can even be alienated to a rustic, as Bald. notably says following the gloss in d. § ex eadem.

† And it is to be noted according to him that a rustic can purchase dignities and jurisdictions which are the proper patrimony of the seller, which he says must be kept in mind. Nay, Bald. says more there: that although under the ius commune jurisdictions cannot be sold because they are of public law and do not admit of valuation, and especially merum imperium, which is exercised over persons, of whom there is no valuation, as in ff. ad l. Aqui. l. liber homo; he says nevertheless that it has been usurped by custom; and thus daily castles and vills are seen to be sold and bought with merum and mixtum imperium and all manner of jurisdiction, which custom overcomes law according to him; to this belongs the good text in c. j. de feu. cog. col. x, where it is generally provided that feudal causes are regulated according to the custom of localities. The gloss and Bal. hold the same as to the first point, that a fief can be alienated with a universality against the vassal's will, even in the absence of custom, in d. § præterea ducatus. I conclude that on two grounds the opposition and appeal of the Count of Pardiac for his barony of Les Angles situated in the county of Bigorre is neither just nor to be admitted: first, because custom is to the contrary; secondly, because the alienation was made with the universality of the county; what is read and noted in c. 1, de capitaneo, qui cu. uendi., finally supports this. To the twenty-third question: Whether the said donation from its form savors of the nature of a donation, or of a restitution which the king was bound in justice to make to the said Count of Foix? I say that it in no way savors of the nature of a restitution, but rather of a donation, or of a concession in fief. This is first gathered in the versicle nos primò attendentes after the beginning, where the text says that he could not suitably by form of justice, without summoning the party, restore and deliver to his kinsman, namely to the said Count of Foix, the abovesaid lands, etc.; and immediately he passed to the form of grace, there, considerantes magnam legalitatem, etc., where he begins to narrate the inductive causes of that concession, all of which savor of special grace; from the causes the quality of the disposition and the intention of the disposer are gathered, as in c. intelligentia, de uerbo. signi.; nay rather, a statement is restricted by the causes, as in l. cum pater, § dulcissimis, ff. de leg. 2, and in l. ita autem, ff. de admini. tuto., and in both places by Bar. Likewise it appears from the dispositive words of the king himself, in that in the versicle ex istis causis, etc., he says: 'From these causes and others which have moved and do move us to this, we have given, delivered, ceded, relinquished, and transferred, out of special grace,' etc.; from which words it is sufficiently brilliantly gathered that the lord king did not proceed by restoring by way of justice, but by transferring by way of grace. Furthermore, if he had restored by way of justice, he would not have granted in fief, as he granted. Likewise, he could not proceed by way of justice without summoning the party, namely the church of Le Puy, as in c. 1, de causa pos. & propri., and in c. inter quatuor, de maio. & obe., and cap. ecclesia sanctæ Mariæ, de constit., and 3, q. 9, c. caueant, and c. omnis. Nay rather, a sentence is null not only when it is rendered against an absent party, but also for an absent party, since citation did not intervene, as is the notable gloss which Bar. follows there in l. ea quæ, C. quomodo & quando iudex; to this pertains l. furioso, ff. de re iudi. And the reason is because by law an acquisition cannot be made for an absent party through another: l. absenti, ff. de dona., and more fully by Bar. in d. l. ea quæ; to this pertains l. quæcunque gerimus, ff. de actio. & obliga. The twenty-fourth question depends on the preceding: presupposing that it savors of the nature of a donation, whether the lord Count of Foix, by receiving it with the conditions attached by the king, prejudiced the right of his living mother regarding the property of the said county of Bigorre? To this question I think it must be said that he in no way prejudiced the right of his mother, then living, although the grant made to the lord Count of Foix savors of grace, because it is of certain and indubitable law that no one is bound by the contract of another, nor is the right of another prejudiced, even if it is a mother, who is not in the least prejudiced by the act of a son, as is proved in l. pen. & ul. C. ne uxor pro marito. I say even more: that neither the right of the mother, nor that of the lord Count himself, or of his power, or of those deriving or about to derive cause from him, is prejudiced through this royal concession, by a twofold reason. First, because if the true owner leases, or buys, or by another title takes his own property from another as if belonging to another, he does not through this lose the ownership of that property which he previously had; the text seems clear in l. ei a quo, ff. de usuca., and in l. si rem aliquam, ff. de acquiren. pos., and in both places Bar., and especially by him in d. l. si rem aliquam, where among other things he says that he advised in a certain cause in these terms: A certain nobleman having a certain estate of his own received it from a certain monastery in emphyteusis, and it was said in the instrument that the monastery granted such estate to such nobleman in emphyteusis. Finally, that nobleman sold that estate to another without asking the monastery. The monastery wished to claim that estate as devolved to the monastery on the occasion of the alienation. Bart. advised, and other doctors followed as he himself reports, that it could not, because by receiving his own property in emphyteusis from the monastery he did not lose ownership, since he received it as the property of the monastery; for ownership is not lost by mere intention, as possession is, as in l. si quis ui, § differentia, ff. de acqui. pos., and l. qui propriam, C. locati; it is otherwise, however, if someone were to donate his own property to another and subsequently or immediately lease that property from him, or donate it and retain the usufruct for himself; for then he would transfer ownership and possession to the other, as is proved in l. quædam mulier, ff. de rei uen., and in l. quisquis, C. de dona.; for then a fictitious traditio intervenes, through which ownership is transferred: l. quod mea, ff. de acqui. pos., and l. certe, de precario; but when one takes his own property from another as if belonging to another, it is otherwise, because he does not act to transfer to another, but rather to acquire. To our purpose: when the lord Count of Foix received the county of Bigorre from the king in fief, as belonging to another and as the property of the king himself, as is clearly evident from the words of the concession, no prejudice was generated to him or his in the ownership and rights of that county. The second reason why no prejudice was inflicted upon the lord Count of Foix or his from the royal grant is gathered from the tenor of the said grant, where the lord king himself reserved all right previously belonging to the lord Count and his posterity, as appears in the versicle saluo & reseruato, etc., where it is said: 'saving and reserving to the posterity and those deriving cause from our said kinsman and his predecessors, the right of demanding and pursuing by way of action, and adding the rights which could belong to our said kinsman, to the abovesaid rights in the manner in which he could have done, or was able to do from the day of the date of the present letters,' etc. For a protestation, especially a principal one, preserves the protested right: 6, quæst. 1, c. pontifices, de pręscrip. c. nihil cum scandalo, de elect. c. Cumana, and c. ecclesia; the text with the notable gloss in l. si fideiussor, ff. qui satisda. cog., supports this; fully by Bar. concerning the matter of protestation in l. non solum, § morte, ff. de noui. oper. nun., and by Ioan. And. following Io. Mona. in the rule in generali, libr. 6, in Mercu., and by Innocen. and others in cap. cum M. de consti. And let these suffice concerning this question. Through the things proximate stated, I think the 25th question is left sufficiently decided, by which it is asked: Granted that it did not prejudice the lord Count during the mother's life, nor upon her death, how the lord Count and his heirs ought to take precautions lest he be seen in any way to approve that donation and its conditions? For, as I said before, no prejudice is done to him from such a concession, and that notwithstanding, he can pursue his right consequently by the aforesaid reasons, just as he could have done at the time of the date of that concession or donation; nay rather, the said concession benefits him greatly in another way, because if it is true that the said Count himself has a right from his predecessors in the said county, prescription is interrupted in the meantime, if any began to run from the person of the lord king, because by transferring the county to the true owner, he lost the possession which he previously had, without which prescription does not proceed, as is proved in l. si is, a quo fundum, ff. de usuca., according to the reading which Bartol. follows there. The twenty-sixth question: Whether the said donation, which was made for reasonable causes and for which the same Lord of Foix bound himself to homage and fealty, is revocable of its nature? And it seems at first that not only is it revocable de facto, but indeed by law it seems to be of no effect, because a king cannot make donations to the prejudice of his realm even with an oath not to revoke, as in capitul. intellecto, de iureiuran. For when he is crowned, he also swears to diminish nothing of the goods of the empire: d. capitul. intellecto. Furthermore, such graces to the prejudice of the community or realm are presumed surreptitious, because it is not likely that they were granted out of certain knowledge, since they are contrary to law and public utility: argu. in capitul. penul. & ulti. de capel. mo., and l. rescripta contra ius elicita, C. de preci. impe. offer.; nor ought they to be valid: l. si, C. si contra ius uel utili. publi., and l. iubemus, C. de sacrosan. eccle. And if the opposite were said, it would follow that the realm could be reduced to nothing, which must not be said, especially since one cannot abdicate merum imperium from oneself except into the hands of one's superior, as in l. legatus, ff. de offic. præsi.; many other arguments could be made which a studious person could gather from what is noted by the gloss in Auth. quomodo oporteat episco. in princ. collatio. 1, and by Bartol. in the prooemium of the Digest, and by Bald. in the prooemium on the Book of Fiefs, in that question: Whether the donation made to the church by Emperor Constantine was valid, and by Ioan. de Ligna. in Clemen. Romani, de iureiurando. Secondly, it argues principally against that grant because the king made no mention of the oath sworn to the contrary, of which it seems that mention necessarily had to be made, as in c. constitutus, de rescrip., through the gloss in l. cum non deceat, de electio. libr. 6. Furthermore, and thirdly, special mention ought to have been made of the preceding letters and privileges, and not a general one, as in capitul. 2, de dolo & contumacia, and what is noted there, to such an extent that mention must be made in revocatory letters of every notable clause placed in the prior letters, as in capitul. cum dilecta, and what is noted there, de rescri. These arguments having been premised, for the solution of the question it must be known that Bartol. in l. prohibere, § planè, ff. quod ui aut clam, frames the question whether a king can alienate anything to the prejudice of the realm? And finally he concludes that if the alienation tends to the grave detriment of royal jurisdiction, it is not valid, even if it is confirmed by an oath, as in the previously alleged capitul. intellecto; but if it does not tend to so grave a prejudice, it is valid and holds, of which he says there is a case in capitul. abbate sanè, de re iudi. lib. 6. Inno. intended the same in effect in d. capitul. intellecto, and Ioan. And. in capitul. grande, de supplen. negli. præla. libr. 6; for according to him so bitter an interpretation ought not to be made that he can donate nothing of the rights of the realm: argum. capitul. 2 & 3, and capitul. ad apostolicæ, de dona., and c. cæterum, eod. titu. Bald. in the previously alleged place framed the question: If the emperor donated or otherwise granted by cause of donation or other title an imperial castle, whether the donation or alienation will be valid? And many things having been alleged pro and contra, finally concluding and resolving he says after the ancients that either he wishes to donate with the bare property of the territory or dignity so that the donee does not recognize the emperor as superior, and this is not possible according to him, because he cannot make anyone his equal, or superior, or someone who could with impunity rebel against the empire, because the law of the realm contradicts it. And because no inferior, according to Aristotle, where distinguishing boundaries are present, participates in that which is superior; he can nevertheless grant the benefits and ownership, saving always the recognition of the empire and fealty. That an emperor should mutilate himself, that is, amputate members of the empire from himself, is to state a species of theft according to him. In feudal matter, however, he cannot diminish the honor of the realm according to Andr. de Iser., which Bald. follows there, and it is sufficiently to be noted. In our purpose, what is read and noted in capitul. 2, de feu., pertains. Coming therefore to the purpose, I say that the donation or concession made to the lord Count of Foix, the arguments made above to the contrary notwithstanding, can be sustained on multiple grounds, and consequently in the second place I shall prove that it is irrevocable. For first, the said concession stands by law, because the county of Bigorre is not of the realm of France, or a proper member of the realm itself, but belonged either to the lord Count of Foix or to the church of Le Puy, or from the concession of that church belonged to the king of France, not as to king, but by reason of his patrimony and special succession. For as appears from the narration of the fact, this county had its origin in the person of Lady Joan, Queen of France and Navarre, from a donation or exchange made with the church or by the church of Le Puy, which claimed then to have the ownership of the said county, and from her person devolved upon the present king as heir of the heir of the said Lady Joan; over his patrimony, however, the king can dispose at his pleasure, since an alienation of the realm does not occur, as in d. l. bene à Zenone, C. de quadrien. præscriptio.; and in his own property anyone, not to mention a prince, is the legitimate moderator and arbiter: l. iure mandat, C. man., and capitul. de his, de sepul.; what I said above in the 22nd question supports this. Furthermore and secondly, presupposing that it had belonged to his realm, the said alienation can nonetheless be sustained from the fact that the said king did not purely donate or alienate the said county, but granted it in fief, retaining to himself the bare property, honor, preeminence, and reversion in certain cases to him or his successors, as appears in the concession, and this is of the nature of a fief: 22, quæst. 5, capitul. de forma, and in capitul. in qui. capitul. feu. ami. col. 10; such a concession indeed does not diminish the honor of the realm, as I said above, and thus capitul. intellecto, de iureiurando, ceases to apply. Furthermore and thirdly, regard being had to the most ample realm of France and the accustomed munificence of the kings of that realm, and to the distinguished services rendered to the kings of France by the Counts of Foix, especially the present ones, as the lord king himself attests in his letters, it ought not to be said that the said concession results in grave prejudice to the realm, since a remunerative donation is not properly a donation, but rather a remuneration of merits, as the text notably says in l. Aquilius Regulus, ff. de donatio.; noted by Bartol. in the prooemium to the Digestum Vetus; hence the singular text in l. si pater, § primo, ff. de dona., says that a donation made on account of distinguished and great preceding merits is irrevocable, even on account of ingratitude, because it is the wage of distinguished labor rather than a mere donation; and especially does this proceed in our case, in which the lord king himself attests that the said county, from the rights produced by the lord Count, seemed to belong to him, and thus he restored in a certain manner that which was his, which is of necessity and not of mere liberality, but the king wished to proceed through the hands of justice on account of the absence of the party, and so that he might appear to exercise greater magnificence, as he himself seems to attest in his letters. From these things the contraries remain resolved which inferred nullity from defect of power. To the other contraries which seem to press from the cause of subjection, I say that the oath sworn by the predecessors of this king regarding not alienating the county was personal; whence by death it was removed, because an oath does not pass to a successor, as is read and noted in capitul. ueritatis, de iureiur.; for the swearer himself satisfied it, since he did not alienate; whence the successor is not bound by such an oath, as noted by Ioan. Andr. in capitul. fina. de sepul., and in capitul. cum C. laicus, de foro compe. libr. 6; and thus it was not necessary to make mention of that which did not exist. Likewise, presupposing that this lord king had sworn, nor had made mention of such an oath or privilege previously made regarding not alienating, then I say that nonetheless the grant in fief which he made afterwards ought to be valid, because he makes this grant by his own right and from his own patrimony, as I said above; whence he could not bind himself so that he would have to impede the said transfer, just as we say of a private person who bound himself not to alienate, and yet the alienation holds, although he made no mention in the alienation of the prior obligation, as in l. nemo potest, ff. de lega. primo, and read and noted in l. ea lege, C. de condictio. ob. cau., and I stated fully above in the proximate question. For in those things which a public person does as a private person, he is regarded by the law of a private person, as is read and noted in capitul. fina. de procura. Furthermore, by granting the county, he contracted with the lord Count, since an obligation arises reciprocally: d. capitul. de forma. If indeed even a prince is bound by a contract, as in capitul. primo, de proba., and as I shall immediately state more broadly, therefore the contract cannot be broken because he did not make special mention of the prior oath or antecedent grant. For a stronger bond supervened; for, as I said above, a contract holds even contrary to one's own oath, although the contracting party is a perjurer, as in capitul. sicut, de spon.; noted by Inno. in capitul. dilecto, de præben., and Ioan. And. in the rule semel, lib. 6, in Mercur. From these things I infer the answer to the second point, whether such a grant made to the lord Count of Foix by the lord king is revocable. And I say that it is not; the notable text is in capitul. uno, de natu. feu. col. 10, where it is said that if a prince has invested anyone with any fief, he cannot divest him without fault; to the same effect is a similar text in capitul. uno, de feu. sine culpa non amit. eadem col., and Bald. notes this in both places; and this is proved by a twofold reason. First, because the prince is bound by a contract just like any private person, as in capitul. primo, and what is noted there, de proba., and in the grant of a fief an obligation arises on both sides. The second reason, because the prince cannot revoke a privilege which he previously granted once it has passed into a contract or quasi-contract, or into the ius gentium, as noted in l. quod semel, ff. de decre. ab ordi. fac., and I stated fully above in the 16th question; and generally a prince cannot, in the absence of cause, deprive anyone of his ownership, as fully noted by Cyn. in l. rescripta, C. de precib. impe. offe., and Bartol. in l. fin. C. si contra ius uel utili. publi., and Inno. in capitul. quæ in ecclesiarum, de constitu. I condescend therefore to the 27th question, by which it is asked: Presupposing that on account of importunity or otherwise the lord king should wish to revoke the said grant de facto, what remedy does the said lord Count of Foix have to retain possession of that county of Bigorre, at least until a declaration has been made by sentence concerning his right which he had in it before the donation? And in this question I say it is certain that without the fault of the said lord Count he cannot revoke that grant, as was clearly evident from the points deduced in the proximate question above. If, however, he should wish to revoke de facto, Cy. seems to say in d. l. rescripta, C. de preci. impe. offe., and Bar. in l. fi. C. si contra ius, uel uti. pub., that as to observance one must stand by the disposition of the prince, because a cause is to be presumed for the prince, nor is proof to the contrary admitted, but if he does so without just cause, he sins according to them. These doctors, however, do not speak in our case, namely when the prince wishes to take away someone's own property. But in our case I say that since the prince is bound by his contract, he cannot contravene it unless the cause appears and is established, because otherwise the prince could easily destroy and break every contract made by him, which must not be said. I prove this through the clear text in c. 1, de feu. sine cul. non amit., and c. uno, de natu. feu., where it is said that unless he has been convicted of a fault, a vassal ought not to be deprived of a fief, even by the prince. I introduce furthermore this reason: since the prince is not above contracts, since they are of the ius gentium, as Bald. notes in c. proximè alleg., and Inn. in d. cap. 2, de confir. uti., therefore a cause ought not to be presumed in him, since the matter is not subject to him; what Ioan. And. similarly notes in c. 1, de offic. delega. libr. 6, supports this; to the same effect is the clear text in cap. 1, de proba., where the prince is compelled to observe his contract unless he shows a just cause to the contrary, and cap. nouit, de iudic., supports this excellently. If therefore, without an apparent legitimate and reasonable cause, the lord King should wish to contravene it, an honorable and indubitable remedy would be that the lord Count have recourse to evangelical or judicial denunciation by reason of sin, according to those things which are held and noted in capit. nouit, de iudic. The second remedy is that he appeal to the Pope, through the notable statement of Innoce. in cap. licet ex suscepto, de foro competen., where he says that recourse must be had to the Pope whether a necessity of law is imminent, because there is no other superior judge, or of fact, because lesser judges cannot help de facto; to which Hostien. notes in cap. nouit, de iudi.; and in the King of France what Innocen. notes in c. per uenerabilem, qui fi. sint legi., can excellently be introduced, where he says that he is by law subject to the Pope. The third remedy, as I think, is that he resist de facto, because where a superior proceeds de facto and unjustly, he can be resisted de facto, as the gloss notes in cap. ex literis, de offic. delega., and Innocen. in cap. si quando, eodem titu., and capi. dilecto, de excess. præla., at least in our case, in which the grievance cannot be repaired by the judge of appeal, as Cyn. maintained in l. ab executore, C. quorum appel. non reci., and in l. prima, C. unde ui. For defense is of natural law, which is conceded to anyone, even against a prince, as in cap. pastoralis, de re iudi. in Clem.; hence the notable gloss said in 1. distinct. cap. ius gentium that anyone can, in default of a superior, declare the law for himself by his own authority, and Inno. maintained the same in capi. olim, the first, de restitu. spol. Now finally, rendering immense thanks to the Most High, it remains to dispatch the last question, in order the 28th, which is: Whether the royal procurator general, in light of the mandates and non obstantibus placed in the letters of grant, as well as the clearance of the Chambre des Comptes and the reading and publication in the royal court of the Parlement, can now have a just cause to join himself to the said brothers, the Counts of Armagnac and Pardiac, in the present cause? In which consideration indeed, by a threefold reason, I deem it must be said that he cannot. And first I introduce the text in l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadrien. præscript., where the text says: 'Let no one dare to afflict with civil penalties in judgment defendants who receive property from the prince through whatever title of alienation, whether movables, or immovables, or self-moving, or incorporeal rights, or to hope that any avenue is open to him against them, but let every approach be precluded, every movement and hope of his insolence,' etc.; and I weigh that universal negative word: 'let no one dare,' etc.; for it excludes anyone wishing to sue: nineteenth distinction, capitul. si Romanorum, and capitul. solitæ, de maiorita. & obedien., and l. de pretio, ff. de publica. Secondly and principally I introduce the theory of Bartol. in l. cum quærebatur, ff. de iud., where he says that every exception by which it is concluded against the plaintiff that no right belongs to him can be opposed from the beginning before litis contestatio; because since it is certain that no one can sue without an action, l. si pupilli, § uideamus, ff. de neg. gest., anyone can be repelled from acting where it is excepted that no action belongs to him; but so it is in our case, that no action for revoking can belong to the royal procurator, nor even to the said Counts of Armagnac and Pardiac, as is clearly evident from the preceding; therefore from the beginning all, not only the royal procurator, can be repelled from acting, nor is the lord Count of Foix bound to enter into judgment with them or any one of them. Thirdly and lastly, against the royal procurator general I allege the notable text in l. honori, ff. man., where it is proved that a general procurator is not admitted against things specially provided for by the lord, unless a just cause arises anew, and probably not agitated by the lord at that time, which is not the situation in our case. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A legacy made in this manner: 'let the heir give to him for whom I shall have written that which is found written in the letter', is just as valid as if it had been expressed in the testament.
2. A legacy of quantity is not extinguished by a legacy of a specific thing.
3. Bequests left in codicils are claimed by an action arising from the testament.
4. When someone receives a fief for himself and any of his successors whatsoever, under the designation of children legatees are also included.
5. When multiple things are in an alternative obligation, if one is removed, the remaining one stands.
6. A usufructuary of all property is not bound to satisfy legatees, but concurs with them.
7. A testament receives force and consummation through the death of the testator, and not before.
8. If someone has bequeathed fifty to someone in a testament, and in a codicil written afterwards the same legacy is left, both legacies are due, unless the heir proves the contrary.
9. Legacies may be committed to the discretion of a third party, but not to his mere will.
body: Having implored the aid of Almighty God, on the question which is raised concerning the interpretation of the will of Angelo di Francesco of Gubbio with respect to the testament, codicils, and memorandum of the said Angelo, as is more fully contained in the narration of the case, I shall touch upon the principal doubts individually as briefly as I can. And first, the question arises whence the memorandum of the said Angelo makes full proof, since it was not properly recited in the presence of witnesses, but Angelo merely said in his testament that he willed that faith be given to the book or memorandum written in his own hand as to the legacies left, which should be found therein to have been made by the testator to anyone, just as faith would be given to a public instrument, or to a valid public testament written by the hand of a public notary. And concerning this doubt, in my judgment, the case falls under l. si ita scripsero, ff. de condi. & demonstra., where it is said that

† a legacy is valid if I say: 'Let the heir give to the person for whom I have written letters that which is found written in the letter,' which is just as valid as if it had been expressed in the testament; and Bartolus understands this even more clearly, saying that by that text it is valid if the testator said: 'I will that my heir give such a thing which is written in the schedule that I left with the guardian of Saint Francis,' because by reference to another writing, that which is written there is deemed expressed in the testament. To this wonderfully agrees what is read and noted in l. Theopompus, ff. de dote. præleg. and l. penul. C. de sentent. quæ sine certa quantita., capit. cum uenerabilis, in fin. de relig. do.; and this provided that it is established by comparison of handwriting, or by other manifest conjectures, that the memorandum was written by the hand of the testator himself. And this very briefly concerning the first doubt. The second principal doubt is whether the legacy of one hundred and fifty florins made to Uccia, the testator's sister, is valid, notwithstanding the legacies subsequently made to the same Uccia in the codicil and memorandum. And first it seems

† that a legacy of quantity is not extinguished by a legacy of a specific thing, even when made in the same testament, as in l. planè, ff. de legat. 1. But in the memorandum he left this sister of his as mistress and dominatrix during her life of the said testator's goods, whereas in the codicils he left to her the movable goods of the testator himself, with certain exceptions, about which below in the fourth doubt. Since therefore the legacies are distinct, their concurrence is not prohibited, especially since they were made in different writings, as in l. quinquaginta, ff. de probatio. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the testator tacitly prohibited their concurrence by the qualification he made in the said legacy of one hundred and fifty florins, in that he said that he left one hundred and fifty to Uccia, his sister, provided that she promises to claim nothing else in the goods of the said inheritance, etc.; because I say that he did not simply prohibit her from claiming anything else, but made an exception, saying that she could not claim anything else, except only and merely that which she could claim by virtue of the present testament; wherefore weight must be given to the exception, which includes the provision that, after that legacy, she may claim that which is owed to her by virtue of the testament itself. But it is certain that what is written in the codicils and the memorandum is deemed written in the testament, from which it derives vigor and confirmation, as is the text in l. 2. & 3. ff. de iure codicil., so much so that the Gloss says in the said l. 3

† that things left in codicils are claimed by an action arising from the testament; and these points seem strongly to urge the preservation of this legacy. But I say that the contrary can, in my judgment, be subtly argued: namely, that the first legacy was revoked by the bequest made in the memorandum, in which, among other things, he willed that the said sister ought to be mistress and dominatrix during her life of the said testator's goods which might happen to be found, yet in such a way that she ought to renounce all succession that might fall to her in any way from the common person of the parents or from the testator himself, etc. Whence I weigh the fact that by this bequest he intended to exclude her from everything else that she might have been able to obtain from the testator's goods, even from the person of the testator himself, and thus he seems tacitly to have revoked the first legacy. For a legatee can be called a successor of the testator, as in l. in conuentionibus, ff. de uerbo. significa., as noted by Baldus in capitu. imperialem, primo responso, de prohi. feu. ali. per Fedr., at the line quid si concessum, where he says

† that if someone receives a fief for himself and any successors whatsoever of his, by the term 'successors' legatees are also included. So in the present case, since the testator in the memorandum willed that his said sister should renounce all succession that might fall to her even from the person of the testator; and from his person she cannot hope for succession except by virtue of a testament or other last will, because a brother is not bound to leave anything to a sister, nor can a sister claim anything in the goods of a testate brother, unless when he had instituted a shameful person, as in l. fratres & sorores, C. de inoffic. testamen. Furthermore, the testator said that she should renounce 'all' succession, whence I give weight to the word 'all', which is a universal affirmative, for he who said 'all' excluded nothing, as in cap. solitæ, de maio. & obed., and dist. 29, c. si Romanorum. Nor let the aforesaid interpretation seem strange to anyone, for the revocation of legacies can occur tacitly from the presumed and conjectured mind of the testator, as in l. 3. & 4. ff. de adim. leg., and as noted by the Gloss at the end of the same title. From the aforesaid I proceed to the third doubt: namely, what the said Uccia, the testator's sister, ought to receive from the deceased's goods. And incidentally the fourth doubt will be discussed: how and when the legacies are to be satisfied, and from which goods. And these are the matters that bring great difficulty in this topic, since from the words of the testator uttered at various times there seems to arise a certain contrariety and repugnance. For in the testament he willed, ordered, and mandated that his heirs could not sell nor alienate any of the immovable goods of the said testator, except for the satisfaction of legacies, insofar as they had nothing from elsewhere whence they could satisfy the legatees; and if he did otherwise, he willed that they should forfeit the inheritance. In the second place, he drew up a memorandum in his own hand, in which he similarly and absolutely mandated that his heirs should not dare to sell or alienate any of the immovable goods; and if necessity pressed for the payment of debts or legacies, he willed that hands should first be laid on the selling off of movable goods, and if these were insufficient, recourse should be had to the fruits of the goods, from which, in the course of time, as they were collected, he willed that the legatees be satisfied pro rata, nor could the heirs otherwise be compelled to the payment of the legacies. And by all means he willed that the said Uccia, his sister, should have three hundred florins from his patrimony and inheritance, which she could distribute in whatever manner pleased her. Item, he immediately subjoined that he willed that the said Uccia his sister be 'donna and madonna'—to use the testator's words—of those goods which should happen to be found to belong to the said testator, during her life only, with this added: that she must renounce all succession that might fall to her from the common person of the parents, or from the person of the said deceased, or of any other person whatsoever of their house. In the third place, he made a codicil, in which among other things he left to the aforesaid lady Uccia all and singular the movable goods of the said testator and the claims against debtors, except only those goods and movable things which lord Angelo should be found to have left to another in his said testament, or in the present codicils, or in the memorandum of the testator himself, etc. From these there arises a certain repugnance, because in the memorandum he willed that the immovable goods should not be alienated in any way, but mandated that if the movable goods were not sufficient [recourse be had to fruits], and yet immediately in the same memorandum he seems to have left the usufruct of the goods to the said Uccia in that he willed her to be during her life the donna and mistress of his goods, and thus he seems to have removed the fruits from the satisfaction of the legacies. In the codicils he seems to have removed the movable goods and the claims against debtors, since he bequeathed them to the aforesaid Uccia; the immovable goods, on the other hand, cannot be sold according to his ultimate and latest will; and thus the legacies seem to remain ineffective, at least during the lifetime of Uccia herself, the contrary of which seems to be gathered from the words of the testator uttered in the testament, codicils, and memorandum, since his will always seems to have been that the said legacies should take effect immediately, as will be discussed more fully there. What then is to be said in such variety? To me, reflecting long upon this, it has seemed that the testator's words can bear a manifold construction. The first is that the said lady Uccia, the testator's sister, ought to have full ownership of all the movable goods and the claims against debtors, except those which were specifically bequeathed by the testator, which are many, as is clear in the testament, codicil, and in the memorandum: for he left to his wife a fabric worked with silver, a garland, rings, and other things assigned to the use of the wife herself, and a pair of baskets; item, all linens and woolens for the use and attire of the wife herself; item, to Lionello he left his bed, and so many household goods necessary to him as were worth ten florins; and he did many other similar things, and in these specifically made legacies could be preserved and verified that exception which the testator made in the codicils in that he left to his sister all movable goods, except only those things and movable goods which the said Angelo should be found to have left to another. Item, by virtue of the memorandum the said Uccia seems to be entitled to have the usufruct of the immovable goods during her life. Therefore the legatees are not to be satisfied from the fruits of the immovable goods except after the death of the said lady Uccia, because since he simply makes her mistress of the goods during her life, she is not bound in her lifetime to satisfy the legatees, since a usufructuary in the usufruct concurs with other legatees with respect to the property, so that the usufructuary has the usufruct during life, while the legatee has full right after the death of the usufructuary, as in l. Sempronio, ff. de usufru. lega., which Bartolus maintains in l. fin. of the same title; nor ought the legacies to be satisfied in any way from the movable goods, because since the testator designated the movable goods and the fruits of the immovables for their satisfaction, by later bequeathing the movable goods to the said Uccia in the codicils he seems to have removed those movable goods from the burden of satisfaction; and thus the fruits alone seem to have remained under obligation, not purely, but after the death of the said Uccia.

† For when several things are in an alternative obligation, upon one being removed the other remains, as in l. Stichum, aut Pamphilum, ff. de uerborum obligatio. But indeed, although this interpretation charms the ears, nevertheless in manifold ways it cannot stand. First, because the testator in the memorandum, before he had made this sister of his donna and madonna of his goods, had specifically obligated the fruits for the satisfaction of the legacies; whence it is not likely that he was immediately contrary to himself by leaving the usufruct to the sister to the prejudice of the legatees, as in l. non ad ea, ff. de conditio. & demonstr. Especially since the legacy made to the sister was general, because he made her mistress and donna of all the goods, whereas the designation of the fruits for the satisfaction of the legacies was special, because he designated them in supplement of the movable goods; and a special disposition made by a testator derogates from a general one, as in l. quæsitum, in fin. ff. de fund. instru. lega., and there fully by Bartolus. Furthermore, and secondly, it is not likely that he loved his sister so much that he wished through her to prejudice the legatees to such an extent, since, as appears from the testament, he left her only 150 florins. Item, and thirdly, through this interpretation there would be prejudice and derogation to many wills of the testator himself, since he made many legacies, especially for pious causes, which he willed to be executed within a year from the day of his death, which would be entirely impeded by the aforesaid interpretation, which is not to be affirmed, especially since a bequest made for pious causes, touching the soul of the deceased himself and divine religion, is more favorable than a bequest made to a sister, argument from the authentica si qua mulier, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi., noted by Bartolus in l. 1. C. eo., to which agrees chapter Iacobus, de simon. Item, and fourthly, against this interpretation: because concerning the movable goods he had previously disposed specifically, determining that from their price, as needed, the legacies should be satisfied; thereafter in the memorandum he disposed in general, bequeathing them all to his sister; but a special disposition derogates from a general one, as in the said l. quæsitum, at the end, especially since in the legacy made to his wife he expressly preserved all bequests which should be found made to others; and he seems sufficiently to have left the movable goods to others by leaving instructions that, as needed, they be sold for the satisfaction of the legacies; an excellent argument in l. quod conclaue, ff. de dam. infect., and in l. quæsitum, § 1, & § fin. de leg. 2., and l. generali, § uxor, ff. de usufruct. leg. Furthermore, after he had designated the movable goods insofar as needed, and the fruits of the immovables for the satisfaction of the legacies, immediately before he constituted her mistress and dominatrix of the goods of the testator himself, he said that he willed that in every event his said sister should have from his goods 300 florins, so that she might distribute them for the soul of the testator himself as she pleased; therefore he did not simply, to the exclusion of the legacies, intend to make her usufructuary of the goods, since it would be a most evident contradiction, since she would not have in life the means wherewith to satisfy this legacy. Another greatest repugnance would also follow from this interpretation: because his said sister, by disposition of the testator, has beyond the said 300 florins to execute other legacies, especially within a year from the day of the testator's death; for the said testator ordered 75 florins to be spent on marrying off young maidens, to be chosen and married off by his said sister, which could by no means be done according to the aforesaid interpretation. Therefore, this interpretation having been deservedly cast aside, I propose a second interpretation: namely, that the said Uccia, the testator's sister, be donna and madonna, that is, mistress and dominatrix, or mistress and housekeeper (massaria) of the testator's goods during the time of her life; item, that she have the movable goods and the claims of the testator himself, but only after the legatees have first been satisfied according to the specific disposition of the testator, and in the residue she be mistress and dominatrix, or mistress and housekeeper. For in my judgment the aforesaid words of the testator mean that she be donna, madonna, so that the word donna is explained to mean housekeeper (massaria), and the word madonna is explained to mean mistress (domina); what these words mean, I shall immediately subjoin. And this interpretation seems sufficiently proven by what was said in the refutation of the preceding interpretation, and every repugnance ceases. Nor do the points noted by Bartolus in the said l. fin. ff. de vsufruct. stand in the way, where he says

† that the usufructuary of all goods is not bound to satisfy legatees, but concurs with them, argument from l. Sempronio, in the same title; because I say that this applies when other conjectures are absent; but in our case many conjectures urge, which persuade toward the contrary interpretation. For even that which is gathered from the conjectured mind of the testator is called evident, and by these conjectures departure is made from common rules of law, as in l. licet imperator, ff. de lega. 1. And if it is asked what those words mean, that the said Uccia be donna and madonna, I think, as I said before, that they mean the same as domina and dominatrix, or mistress and housekeeper (massaria); and on the meaning of these words, see the Gloss and Bartolus in l. vna, de secun. nup., and most fully by the same in l. Titia cum testamento, § fin. ff. de lega. 2., and by the Speculator under the title qui sint fil. legit., at the line quid si quis ita dixit in testamento; combining the Speculator with Bartolus, it appears that those words mean in our case that that woman should honorably have her necessities according to the capability of the patrimony, argument from l. idemque, § idem Labeo, ff. manda.; and thus that the usufruct does not cease for her entirely, but that she ought to have a certain preeminence and her necessities honorably according to the resources of the patrimony; and this the word madonna implies; but whatever is left over ought to accrue to the increase of the inheritance; this the word donna, or housekeeper, implies; otherwise, to what purpose would he have said that she be donna, when it would have sufficed to say madonna? And this interpretation seems especially to be embraced in our case, since it is favorable to the soul of the deceased and directed toward religion, according to what is noted in l. 1, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi., and in chapter cum tibi de benignitate, de testam. And this second interpretation can be sustained quite well. A third interpretation can also be given: that the movable goods in no way accrue to the said sister, except insofar as they are specifically found bequeathed to her, but that she only be mistress and housekeeper of the goods in life, the legacies having first been satisfied. This interpretation is proved from the fact that in the memorandum, in which he made her donna, madonna of the goods, he attached the qualification that she renounce all succession that might fall to her in his goods from anywhere, even from the person of the testator himself. And thus it seems, as I first said above on the first doubt, that the testator willed that this sister of his be mistress and housekeeper, and have nothing else in his goods. Nor does it stand in the way of this interpretation if it is said that it is a renunciation of a right or succession, and therefore refers to a future competent right which was not competent at present in act or in habit, according to what is fully noted, especially in l. qui Romæ, § duo fratres, ff. de verborum obligatio., and therefore those words of the testator concerning the renunciation to be made ought not to be extended to the legacy of movable goods subsequently made to the same Uccia in the codicil. For to this I answer

† that a testament receives its force and consummation through the death of the testator, and not before, as in chapter cum Marthæ, de celebr. mis. Item, the renunciation had to be made by the said Uccia after the death of the testator, and thus after the legacy was made. If therefore she wishes to be mistress and housekeeper, it is necessary that she accept that legacy with its burden and proper qualification, according to those things which are found and noted in cap. pastoralis, de deci., and in l. Aurelius, § idem quæsiit, by Baldus, de lib. leg., and in c. 1, de conces., in the Sext, by Archidiaconus, and Johannes in cap. cum olim, de censi. From which it is inferred that since the said Uccia, the sister, willed by the very fact to be mistress and housekeeper of the testator's goods, she renounced by operation of law every benefit that could come to her from the person and deed of the testator, argument in l. illud, ff. de acq. hær., and in c. cum renunciant, 32, q. 1, and l. non tantum (otherwise beginning Paulus), ff. rem ratam habe., and 11, quæst. 3, c. æstimant, with the following chapter. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the testator, by bequeathing in the codicils, seems to have departed from his prior will expressed in the memorandum with respect to that renunciation; because I say this is not established, nor is anyone presumed to depart from his, so to speak, prior disposition, unless it specially appears that he repented, as in l. si quis, in princ. ff. de leg. 3.; to this agrees l. eum qui, ff. de probat. Furthermore, since the legacy that she be mistress and housekeeper has its qualification in the renunciation to be made, we must say either that the testator departed from it entirely when he bequeathed the movable goods in the codicil, or that he willed the qualification to remain, according to the things noted in the said l. Aurelius, § idem quæsiit, and the said chapter cum olim. A fourth interpretation can also be given: that she ought to have the movables only, deducting the legacies otherwise specifically made, because by the legacy of movable goods in the codicil he seems to have departed from the legacy made in the memorandum, by the excellent text in l. liberis, ff. de ali. & cib. leg. And in favor of this interpretation is that since he had previously obligated the movable goods and the fruits of the immovables for paying the legacies, and made the sister donna and madonna of all the goods during her life, by subsequently taking away the movable goods, which had been previously and specifically designated for the satisfaction of the legacies, it is to be presumed that he departed from the prior legacy made to the sister in the memorandum, so that satisfaction could thus be made simply without any other burden from the fruits; for it is not to be presumed that he wished to multiply so many legacies upon the person of the sister to the intolerable loss of other legacies, especially for pious causes, as I have fully said above. And indeed, any of these three interpretations lastly stated could be tolerated. And although the second in order, and the first with respect to these three, is sufficiently equitable, nevertheless this last one is not unsound, considering that in the codicils he left to the sister the movables and claims against debtors through many words removing every obstacle, and made no mention of her being mistress and housekeeper. By the aforesaid I consider that satisfaction has been made to the third and fourth doubts. I come to the fifth: whether there is owed to the said Uccia this amount of 300 florins, to be distributed by her as she pleases for the soul of the testator. The doubt arises because in the testament the testator ordered 300 florins to be delivered to her for the aforesaid cause. And he ordered the same concerning the same amount in the memorandum, nor did he make any mention of the bequest of the same amount made in the testament. And first it seems that it is not owed to her except once, so that he may be seen to have bequeathed the same amount in the memorandum with the intention of repeating the first legacy, and not with the intention of duplicating it; the text seems to be in l. planè, ff. de lega. 1. To the contrary seems the notable text in l. quinquaginta, ff. de probat., where it is said

† that if someone in a testament bequeathed 50 to someone, and in a codicil written afterwards the same legacy is bequeathed to the same person, both legacies are owed, unless the heir proves the contrary intention of the testator; and concerning that law the Gloss raises an objection in the said l. planè. And it resolves it by stating that either the same quantity is bequeathed in the same writing, and it is owed once, as in the said l. planè; or in different writings, and both are owed, unless the contrary is proved, as in the said l. quinquaginta. From this it is inferred that since in our case this quantity of 300 florins was twice bequeathed in different writings, both legacies are to be provided. But I think the contrary: namely, that it is owed only once. I am moved by the notable text in l. libertis, ff. de ali. & cib. leg., joined with the Gloss on the said l. quinquaginta, where the Gloss proposed an interpretation of the said l. libertis, saying that where in different writings the same quantity is bequeathed for a certain cause, it is not owed except once, and thus the said l. libertis applies; otherwise if simply and for different causes, because then the said l. quinquaginta applies. But in our case the legacy was doubled for the same cause: namely, so that this Uccia might spend it at her pleasure for the soul of the testator. For the word 'pleases' implies the judgment of an upright man (arbitrium boni viri), as in l. Thais, § sororem, ff. de fideicom. li., noted by Bartolus in the Extravagans Ad reprimendum, and l. alio, ff. de ali. & cib. leg.; and she ought to act as an upright man, namely to spend it on a pious cause for the soul of the testator, just as any upright man would do; to this agrees what is read and noted in cap. cum tibi, de testa., and by Baldus in l. 1, C. de sacros. eccl. Furthermore, from conjectures it is sufficiently clear that he did not bequeath in the memorandum with the intention of duplicating, but rather with the intention of repeating, which is clear from this: because he made mention of the said 300 florins in the memorandum incidentally, because in the preceding provisions he had made mention of the difficulty of paying the legacies, since he had prohibited the obligated immovables from being sold off, and permitted it from movables, and if these were lacking, from the fruits of the immovables, and if they were not sufficient, he ordered them to be paid pro rata; but so that that legacy of 300 florins might be included under the common disposition of the other legacies, he said incidentally that he willed that by all means the said Uccia should have the said 300 for the aforesaid cause; for things said incidentally do not dispose principally on account of something else, argument from those things which are read and noted in cap. si papa, de priuilegiis, in the Sext, and in chapter si, de succes. ab intest., and by Bartolus in l. ex hac scriptura, ff. de dona. And let these things suffice concerning this doubt. A sixth doubt is also formed around the aforesaid: assuming that the said Uccia is usufructuary of the goods, or mistress and housekeeper, can security and an inventory be demanded of her with impunity? And this question arises especially with respect to movable goods, concerning which it can probably be doubted whether they belong to Uccia herself, as is clear from the aforesaid. I say that with respect to immovable goods she is indistinctly bound to provide suitable security for using and enjoying the immovable property, preserving the substance of the property, at the judgment of an upright man, and for restoring them once the usufruct is ended; and this with respect to things that are not consumed by use; but with respect to goods that are consumed by use, as with movables, assuming that she has only a usufruct in them, she is bound to provide suitable security to restore their appraised value to the heirs at her death, as in chapter fin. de pignoribus, & aliis cautionibus, and l. 2, ff. de usufruct. earum rerum, quæ usu consu., and more fully in l. 1, ff. usufruct. quemad. caueat. If, however, they are goods which are not consumed by use, but wear out, the same must be said as with movable things, as in l. sed & si quid, ff. de usufru., and more fully as is gathered from the text and Gloss of the Institutes under the same title, § constituitur; and this security cannot be remitted by the testator, as in l. 1, C. de usufruct., and l. scire, C. ut in poss. leg., noted by the Gloss in the said l. 1, and the above-cited chapter fin. Item, the said Uccia can be compelled to make an inventory of the immovable goods, nor is the penalty attached by the testator incurred, since it is reasonably doubted whether they are subject to restitution, as in l. 1, § penul. and what Bartolus notes there, de uentre in poss. mit., and what he notes in l. una, C. de prohi. seque.; to this agrees l. regula, ff. de iu. & sa. igno. I come to the last question: whether the said Uccia can diminish or augment the legacies within a year, according to the disposition of the testator. Regarding which I say that a captious disposition is rejected both in inheritances and in legacies, as in l. captatoriæ, ff. de lega. 1; otherwise, however, where it is not captious; yet the common conclusion is

† that legacies can be conferred upon the arbitrament of a third party, though not upon free will, as in l. nonnunquam, ff. de condit. & demonst., and l. si sic, de leg. 1, and fully noted by Bartolus in l. 1, de lega. 2; whence, since the testator added the word 'shall please', which implies the judgment of an upright man, as in l. Thais, § sororem, ff. de fideicommis. lib., noted by Bartolus in the said l. si sic, and in the Extravagans Ad reprimendum, it can well be said that the said Uccia may do so, provided that she acts as any upright man would act; otherwise, however, the aforesaid conclusion is not valid, even if in the testament or codicil there is added the phrase 'as she shall will', provided that it is joined with the word 'shall please', or with the word 'shall have arbitrated', through those things noted by Bartolus in the said Extravagans Ad reprimendum, on the word videbitur, near the end. And let these suffice. Niccolò de' Tudeschi, the Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. An ecclesiastical judge taking cognizance of an exception raised before a secular judge inhibits the secular judge from proceeding in the meantime in the case.
2. The execution of a sentence is not to be delayed on account of an exception requiring deeper investigation.
3. The time prefixed for an instance runs also against those who are impeded.
4. A statute providing that every case is to be terminated within two months from the time of citation must be observed in its pure terms.
5. A legitimate impediment arising after a prescription has begun does not impede.
body: Having implored the help of the Savior. In the question which is pending before the respectable gentleman, the lord Captain of Siena, regarding the nullity of a sentence on the occasion of the extinction of the instance, two principal matters require examination for a clear decision of the case. The first is whether the lord podestà was legitimately impeded on account of the inhibition made to him by the officials of the Mercanzia. The second will be, presupposing the legitimacy of the impediment, whether a sentence rendered after the time limit prefixed by the statute is null by operation of law. Concerning the first, it seems that the said lord podestà was legitimately impeded, because since the statute of the city grants jurisdiction to the officials of the Mercanzia to take cognizance of the payment of a debt that is sought elsewhere on the basis of a guarentigiated instrument, it seems to suspend the process of the first judge before whom execution of the said guarentigiated instrument is sought: for he who wills the consequent is deemed also to will the antecedent, as in l. illud, ff. de acqui. hæred. and c. ex parte, de spon. and c. cum M. and what is noted there, de consti. Since therefore the statute admits before the officials of the Mercanzia the exception of debt paid, it seems necessary that the first judge of execution of the instrument supersede, since execution depends upon the decision of the exception raised; a text is seen in c. tuam, de or. cog.,

† where the ecclesiastical judge, taking cognizance of an exception raised before a secular judge, inhibits the secular judge from proceeding in the meantime in the case: because an entanglement of proceedings could arise and a contrariety of sentences follow; and through that text it seems that the officials of the Mercanzia could lawfully inhibit the lord podestà from proceeding in the meantime in the case. Nay rather, Lap. said in alle. 66, whom Ant. de But. follows in the said c. tuam, and Fed. thinks in consi. 221, that even without any inhibition of the second judge, the second judge must supersede until the peremptory exception is discussed, for that exception could be discussed before him, so that one would not proceed with it undiscussed, as in c. 1 de or. cog. and in l. 1, C. e. ti.; therefore the same must be observed when by provision of the statute the exception comes to be discussed before another judge, so that the one substituted thus partakes of the nature of him in whose place he is substituted, as in l. mortuo iudice, ff. de iud. and l. si eum, §. qui iniuriarum, ff. si quis cau. and c. ecclesia, ut li. pen. But these notwithstanding, the contrary can be maintained in my judgment. I am moved principally: because in our case execution of a guarentigiated instrument was sought, which, exceptions having been rejected, has ready execution by the form of the statute. Therefore the statute granting the officials of the Mercanzia the power of taking cognizance of the exception of debt paid, which is sought elsewhere by virtue of a privileged instrument, does not seem in doubt to wish to suspend the execution of the first judge. These two can stand together, namely that the officials of the Mercanzia take cognizance of whether the debt was paid, and that the first judge executes the privileged instrument, as is the text in authen. quæ supplicatio, C. de preci. impe. offe.; it is read and noted in capitul. suscitata, de in integ. restitu., in which laws it is clear that although a gracious supplication is admitted, the sentence is nonetheless in the meantime ordered to execution, which will nevertheless be retracted if it afterward appears that the petitioner supports justice; and this is proved in the said authen. quæ supplicatio, and in capitul. suscitata, cited above, it is proved as noted, that if against one seeking restitution in integrum by special law against a sentence there is a presumption that he seeks it maliciously for the purpose of delaying execution, restitution is granted, but the sentence is in the meantime ordered to execution, security having been furnished by the one obtaining execution that if the adversary prevails in the case, he will restore all things which he received on the occasion of the sentence. To the same point is the good text in l. fin. in fi. C. de ord. cog., where execution of a summary case is not deferred on account of a peremptory exception requiring deeper investigation than the summary case itself demands. And Bartol. generally wished this in l. 4, §. condemnatum, ff. de re iud. and Ioan. de Lig. in clem. vnica, eodem ti., where they say,

† that execution of a sentence is not to be deferred on account of an exception requiring deeper investigation; and in this case Innocen. must be understood in capitul. cum in iure, de off. deleg., where he says it is nowhere found that a suit brought impedes execution of a sentence; nay, no such exception impedes execution of a sentence, according to him; he cites the said capitul. suscitata, and C. de fal. l. 2. When therefore, as is clearly evident from the premises, the aforesaid two things can stand together, we ought not to say that, an exception having been admitted before the officials of the Mercanzia, the execution to be performed by the first judge appears suspended, since an inference ought not to be made from diverse things, as in l. neque natales, C. de proba. in capitul. 2, de transla. prælato., especially because by holding the contrary, the statute speaking of the execution of a guarentigiated instrument would be amended; and the amendment of statutes is to be avoided as much as possible, as in capit. cum expediat, de elect. lib. 6, and l. vnica, C. de inoffi. do., and the honor of the first judge would be derogated, which ought not to be done: as in cap. debitus honor, de app. and l. litigatores, in prin. ff. de arbi. Moreover, this is proved by a very good consideration: for if by this exception the statute had wished to suspend in the meantime the execution of the first judge, it would have ordered that that exception be admitted before the first judge, which was more honorable and consistent with law, because where a case is begun, there it ought to reach an end, l. vbi cœptum, ff. de iud. But because the lord podestà was not bound to admit that exception, therefore the statute afterward provided that it be admitted before the officials of the Mercanzia; what is noted in a similar matter by Bar. in l. 2, §. parvi, ff. quod vi aut clam, and what is contained in c. debitores, de iure iu., supports this. What was alleged above to the contrary does not stand in the way, for those apply when the first judge has to take cognizance of the case and utter a sentence according to the merits of the case. In which case it is most just that if cognizance of a prejudicial exception is deferred to another judge, the first should supersede in the meantime, lest the business be entangled by diverse proceedings. And this is the proper case of the said c. tuam. But in our case bare execution was to be made: because a guarentigiated instrument has execution just like a confession made before a judge, or the precept of a judge, according to what is noted by Cyn. and Bar. in l. 1, C. de confess. and by Bal. in l. cunctos populos, C. de summa tri. From this it is inferred for the decision of our doubt that, since the lord podestà ought not to have superseded execution, the instance perished after two or three months, as provided by the statute, and consequently the sentence rendered afterward was of no validity, according to what is fully noted by the gloss, and Bar. and Bal. in l. properandum, C. de iud. and by Io. An. in addi. Spe. in tit. de offi. dele. §. restat, ver. quid si statutum. And this alone would suffice for the victory of this case. But for greater clarification I will descend to the second doubt, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that that impediment had been legitimate: was a sentence rendered after the time limit null? And first it seems not: because time does not run against one unable to act, as in l. 1, in fi. C. de anna. excep. and l. in rebus, C. de iure do. and c. quia diversitatem, de conces. præb. Moreover, the statute does not provide that a sentence rendered after the time limit is null; therefore it ought to be valid, since it was within the time limit, which is the time limit of the law, d. l. properandum, C. de iud. But I judge the contrary opinion in our case to be truer: because the statute provides simply and without distinction that the instance shall not last beyond two or three months, and it excepts no case; therefore it must be understood without distinction, as noted in c. solitæ, de maio. & obe. and ca. si Romanorum, 19. dist., especially since a moderate prejudice is at stake: because when an instance is extinguished, the case does not perish, nor its records, but only the acts of the suit, Inn. in c. causam quæ, de testi. and Barto. in l. cum lite mortua, ff. iud. sol. Hence it is that on account of the slightness of the prejudice the times for presenting run against patrons even when impeded, as in c. cum propter, de iure patron. and there Pe. de Anc. openly maintained this reason,

† that the time prefixed to an instance runs even against those impeded; and this seems to be proved in l. properandum, cited above, in §. si autem, and the following, together with the gloss. Item, and secondly, the instance perishes on account of public favor, lest suits be immortal, as in d. l. properandum, and c. finem, de do. & cont.; therefore the statute putting an end to an instance is not to be restricted, but understood to speak generally, as in c. odia, de reg. iu. Item, and thirdly, this Bal. seems expressly to think in d. l. properandum, 1. responso, versi. quod ergo si statutum,

† where he says that if the statute provides that every case be terminated within two months from the time of citation, since this statute corrects the civil law because it gives a new form and a new time, it ought to be observed in its pure terms, whence a sentence rendered afterward is not valid, according to him. Fourthly, to the same point I adduce what is noted by Bar. in auth. eum qui, C. de temp. app., where he says that if an appellant is impeded from pursuing the case within two years, the time of the instance runs, but on legitimate cause restitution is given, and many follow this in c. ex ratione, de app. If therefore this proceeds in the instance of an appellate case, where a great prejudice is treated, since with the instance extinguished the case is deserted, the same must be said all the more strongly in the instance of a principal case, where only the acts of the suit perish, as I said above; what more? For a case concerning this is seen in l. sed prætorem, §. si fortè, ff. ex qui. cau. ma., where time runs for the time from which one cannot act, although restitution is given. And the statement of Bar. in l. senatus, ff. de off. præsi. elegantly supports this, where following Guil. de Cu. he maintains
