† that an impediment coming after a prescription has begun does not impede time from running, according to that text; he says it is otherwise if the impediment was from the beginning, and thus he understood d. l. 1, C. de anna. excep. and Cyn. in l. rebus, C. de iure do. alie. on the contrary sides. And whatever it may be in other cases, it is certain that to extinguish an instance, times run even against those who are impeded, because a moderate prejudice is at stake, as I have said before, d. l. properandum. Yet I would limit all these things according to those which I said in c. pe. de iudi. in a certain addition, where see altogether addition 2. Nor does it stand in the way that the statute does not provide that a sentence rendered afterward is not valid: because it is sufficient that the statute says that the instance shall last no longer. The sentence is therefore found to have been rendered without an instance, therefore null, as in l. prolatam, C. de sen. and the gloss, Bar. and Bal. in d. l. properandum, and Io. An. in Spe. in the place cited above seem to hold. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A transaction made specifically concerning certain things and rights is not extended to other unexpressed things, even similar ones.
2. The Emperor is called lord of the world.
3. Prescription of ten years in incorporeal things runs without title.
4. A judge delivering an unjust sentence can no longer change it, since he has discharged his office.
body: IN the question which is pending between the reverend father, the lord Gabriel, abbot of the monastery of San Salvatore di Monte Amiata, acting in the name of his monastery, of the one part, and the men of the castrum of the abbey of Monte Amiata, of the other, upon a full examination of the matters related in detail, five points of doubt are elicited upon which legal counsel is sought. The first is that the meat-stall pays to the persons of the said castrum a certain amount of money for the gabelle of that castrum, so that no one in the said castrum may sell meat except him; and of this money the said commune was accustomed over a long time to give a third part to the said monastery, just as it was accustomed to be given from many other obventions and revenues of the said castrum by virtue of a certain composition made concerning those certain revenues and obventions between the monastery and the commune of the said castrum. Now, however, the said commune resists and refuses to give anything from it to the monastery on the pretext of this reason: that in the composition no mention is made of the slaughterhouse, and the commune never bound itself to pay a part thereof to the monastery. On behalf of the monastery, however, it is alleged and said to be owed to it by virtue of the lordship which it holds in the said castrum, since the said castrum, together with its entire court and district, belongs by right of lordship and full ownership from the title of donations made by Roman kings and emperors to the said monastery, and in present times stands under the jurisdiction of the abbot, as is clear from the many things which the abbot exercises in that place, concerning which a full account is given in the narration of the case, and something is said below. The monastery likewise alleges custom on its behalf. And first, having implored the aid of the divine will, I shall address this point of doubt, and consequently subjoin the others in their order. For it seems at first that the community of the said castrum is justly moved to deny the payment of the part of the said gabelle:

† because a transaction made specifically concerning certain matters and rights is not extended to other unexpressed matters, even similar ones, as in l. age cum Geminiano and l. si de certa re, C. de transac., noted in c. 1, eodem titulo, and l. licet, C. de iud. But the transaction or composition concerning the third part to be paid to the monastery was restricted to certain revenues and certain goods, nor was anything expressed concerning the slaughterhouse or any other revenues whatsoever; therefore the community is not bound to pay any part of this or of other revenues not expressed in the composition, especially because a lord cannot exact from his subjects extraordinary and unaccustomed payments, 10 q. 3 c. quia cognovimus, and de pace iur. fir. l. hac edictali, § illicitas etiam exactiones, C. de pœ. and in auth. ut nulli iud. § si vero, col. 9. Secondly, the same is proved as follows: the community never bound itself to pay this part; therefore no action lies to compel payment of this part, because where there is no obligation, an action ceases to exist. For obligation is the mother of an action, l. licet, § ea obligatio, ff. de procu., and without an action no one can properly sue, l. si pupilli, § videamus, ff. de neg. gest. Thirdly, the custom alleged on behalf of the monastery does not stand in the way, because from an annual payment made gratuitously no obligation to pay in the future arises, since each agreement has already had its effect, namely a donation, as in l. si certis annis, C. de pact. and capitulo pervenit, with the notes there, de censi. Hence Bartolus said in capitulo cum in rem ver., ff. de usu., that if a peasant delivered to someone a pair of capons over a ten-year period, it does not follow from this that he is bound in the future to pay, for from those things which are done gratuitously no obligation arises for the future, 16 quæstio 1 capitulo si possessiones. Hence Innocent says in cap. cum ecclesia Sutrina, de causa possef. & proprie., that if one bishop were accommodated many times as a guest in the house of another bishop, or one knight in the house of another, a possession of a servitude would not be presumed to be acquired so that he would be bound to host him in the future. Ceasing all partiality for religion, I judge the contrary position in our case to be truer, and I believe that many remedies are available to the monastery against the said castrum, or its community, in this matter. And first, as the foundation of all the doubts, I premise that all jurisdiction and district throughout the whole world belongs by common law to the prince, 7 q. 1 cap. in apibus, and the prince is one, cap. solitæ, de ma. & obed. and cap. duo sunt, 96 distin., where it is said that there are two who rule the entire world, established by God: the pope, namely in spiritual matters, and the emperor in temporal matters; hence

† the emperor is called lord, as in l. deprecatio, ff. ad l. Rhodiam, de iac. and l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadri. præscri. with similar texts. But owners of estates have neither jurisdiction nor district, as in c. hac edictali, § ad hæc qui allodium, de pace iura. fir. col. 10. Others, however, who are inferior and exercise jurisdiction, hold it from the prince and not by their own right. For the prince himself created the dignities, as in c. 1 quis dicatur dux marchio, comes &c. And Baldus noted the same on that text, saying that all dignities flow from the prince as from the forehead, wherefore in him reside all dignities; just as is seen in the pope, who created the inferior dignities, 22 dist. c. 1 & 2. The emperor himself also confers jurisdiction upon magistrates, by creating them, or confirming them, or granting the authority to create or confirm, as in the said c. hac edictali, § iudices verò, and ff. de of. præfe. urb. l. 1 § cum urbem, and in auth. de defen. ciui. to such an extent that even the least jurisdiction cannot be conferred without the authority of the prince, mediate or immediate, according to Baldus, and rightly so, in the said § ad hæc; alleging what is noted in l. & quia, ff. de iurisdi. om. iudi. and in l. privatorum, C. eodem, and by Innocent in c. cum ab ecclesiarum, de offi. ordi. Hence Baldus gathers there that jurisdiction cannot be sold, since it belongs to the emperor. For all jurisdictions reside in Caesar as in a fountain, from which they flow and back to which they ebb, just as rivers flow from the sea; so that from him they flow by grants, commissions, and confirmations, while back to him they ebb through appeals, nullities, and complaints, concerning which, when the prince begins to take cognizance, silence is imposed upon all others, as Baldus noted in the said § ad hæc, and Baldus and Innocent in c. cum M. Ferra. de consti. From these principles I infer that jurisdiction, however minimal, does not reside with the men of the said castrum, especially considering what is noted by Innocent in c. cum ad sedem, de resti. spo., where he says that by common law a castrum has no district, jurisdiction, or appurtenances, but by special disposition a certain territory is accustomed to be assigned to a castrum which ought to answer to it in jurisdiction and taxes; and Bartolus in l. 1 ff. de dam. infec. says that in a castrum subject to a city there is no jurisdiction, but the whole belongs to the governance of the city; cap. conquestus, de foro competen. and l. qui est vico, ff. ad municipa. support this. Jurisdiction, however, belongs to the abbot, upon whom it was fully conferred by the Roman prince, as is stated in the narrative of fact, and he is also in possession or quasi-possession of many rights by which it is known that the regalia and the things pertaining to mere and mixed empire reside in him. For the goods of those dying intestate without relatives up to the third degree, which is mentioned in the composition, devolve upon him, because by common law these are so much regalia and mixed empire that they do not belong to a city or castrum, but to the prince alone, as in l. unica, C. de bo. vac. libr. 10 and capitulo uno, quæ sunt regalia, colum. 10, and as Bartolus noted in l. cunctos populos, at the end, C. de sum. trini. and l. 2 ff. de iure fisc. The same applies to goods arising on the occasion of a crime; for these are regalia, as noted in the laws immediately cited, and by common law they do not belong to a castrum or a city. Whence the castrum in question held two parts of the condemnations not by common law, but by virtue of that composition entered into between the monastery and the community. Likewise, appeals are made to the abbot both in civil and in criminal matters; nor is any magistrate or official appointed there unless the abbot has the principal role in the election; and in many other matters the abbot is in possession of jurisdiction. But whatever was brought into the composition, this much is certain: that from the grant of the prince full jurisdiction resides in the abbot, which the castrum cannot exercise even upon the death of the abbot, as Innocent noted in c. cum accessissent, de const., but the chapter/convent succeeds, according to what is noted by Innocent in c. cum dilectus, de consue.; the Clementine ne in agro, de stat. regu. supports this. From which I infer in our case that regarding those matters which are of greater or lesser jurisdiction, the community of that castrum cannot interfere, except insofar as is included in the said composition, since the abbot has an intention founded for himself in its entirety by virtue of privileges and very ancient custom, as in capitulum cum venerabilis, de relig. domi., capitulum cum dilectus, eodem titulo. Indeed, a lawful prescription would not profit except as to one article, because when someone else is in possession or quasi-possession of exercising general jurisdiction, possession in one article is not extended to the rest; rather, only so much is prescribed as has been possessed, as in c. auditis and c. cum olim, de præscript., clearly noted by Innocent in capitulum dilectus, de capel. mona., and Bartolus in l. 1, § si quis, ff. de itine. actúque priva. From these points the decision of our question clearly appears with respect to one principal remedy which may be available to the abbot. For I say that the imposition of a gabelle on meat and the prohibition against anyone else selling it belongs to jurisdiction, and can deservedly be reckoned among the regalia; and since it is an extraordinary tax, it does not belong to the castrum, but to the abbot, who holds the regalia in that place, as in the said capitulum uno, quæ sint rega.; l. 2, C. de vecti. & commis. supports this, where it is said that a city cannot exact tolls unless it holds regalia, as Bartolus noted in l. 2, ff. de iure fisci; nor can it make other exactions, for these, except to one who holds regalia, are granted to no one, as in l. una, C. de superindic. and there by Bartolus. Although a city or castrum for its own necessity, for instance for a debt, can, indeed is compelled to impose a levy on individuals so that the universitas itself may be solvent, as the Gloss noted in l. 1, ff. quod cuiusque vni. and in capitulum cum delicta, de rescript. and Bartolus fully in l. 4, § actori, ff. de re iudica. It cannot, however, impose a levy for public purposes, as in the said l. una, de superindic., where Bartolus expressly notes it. Therefore the profit of this gabelle cannot belong in any part to the castrum, but to the abbot, who holds the regalia and mere and mixed empire, except insofar as was granted to it by the said composition. For profit follows those holding jurisdiction, as in the Clementine statutum, de electione; nor can the community allege prescription in this matter, because against the Church a prescription of less than forty years does not run, as in c. de quarta and c. illud, de præscrip. Likewise good faith is required, as in c. si and c. vigilanti, de præscript. But in our case there is a presumption of bad faith, since the privileges belonging to the monastery regarding full lordship are very well known in the locality, and the report is very widespread in the said castrum and neighboring places; for bad faith is proved by these things, as Bartolus noted in l. Celsus, ff. de vsuca. The second principal remedy is that the abbot should claim the third part paid by reason of long custom. For if they have paid something annually to the church for ten years, those paying are deemed to introduce a custom by favor of a pious cause, nor can they thereafter abolish that custom, as is the text in l. penult., C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi. and there Bartolus noted this; to the same effect is a good text in c. ad apostolicam, de simo., and what is noted there. The third remedy is that the abbot should bring the remedy which is read and noted in l. cum de in rem verso, ff. de usur., where by Bartolus, and by the canonists in capitulum pervenit, de censib., where it is said that the community paid the third part for a decade by virtue of a composition, and by the lapse of a decade the composition is proved, even if it is not contained in the ancient proposal; for it could have intervened anew, which is presumed through the lapse of a decade once annual payment is proved. The fourth remedy is that he should base himself upon prescription; for in these incorporal things a prescription of ten years runs

† without title, l. si quis diuturno, ff. si ser. ven., noted by the Gloss in c. cum ecclesia Sutrina, de cau. pos. & proprie., just as in servitudes, since here the issue does not concern the greatest prejudice, as the right is not prescribed entirely, according to what is noted by Bartolus in the said l. cum de in rem verso. And let these remarks suffice as to the first doubt. From the aforesaid I infer the decision of the second doubt, which is as follows: By the form of the statute of the said castrum, the committing of homicide is prohibited under penalty of fine and person; and if it happens that a homicide is committed, it is ordered that the goods of the killer be destroyed. Subsequently, it happened that a certain man who owned a house committed homicide, whose house, under the form of the statute, was to be destroyed; which house the commune took for itself, and holds the possession/enjoyment of it. The monastery, however, claims a third part by virtue of the composition entered into between them, in which, among other things, it is provided that from the condemnations for crimes and damages inflicted which are exacted by the officials of the said castrum, a third part must be given to the monastery, while the remaining two parts must remain with the commune, which must bear all the burdens of the community. But the commune refuses to give the said third part of the house, saying that it ought to have been destroyed, and that if it had been destroyed, the monastery would have had nothing. It is asked, what is the law? I say therefore that the aforesaid commune could not relax the disposition of the statute so that the house would not be destroyed, both because, as I said before in the preceding doubt, plenary jurisdiction, except for the things excepted in the composition, belongs to the monastery; and to relax a penal statute, or to alter a penalty, is an act of jurisdiction.

† Furthermore, a judge who has rendered a judgment, even an unjust one, since he is functus officio, can no longer correct or alter it, as in l. moris, § sed damnare, verse & si fortè, ff. de pœnis, l. iudex, and there by Bartolus, ff. de re iudic., l. 1, ff. ad Turp.; nor can even an inferior judge violate without cause the disposition of a statute in imposing a penalty, as noted by Bartolus in the said l. 1, ad Turpil. and l. quod ergo, § pœna gravior, ff. de his, qui no. infa., and there is a good text in cap. licet, de pœnis; what is noted in 1 quæst. 7 cap. requiris, § nisi rigor, and by Innocent in c. 1 de consti. and c. cum ad monasterium, de sta. reg. supports this. Likewise, because in the composition it is expressly provided that without the license of the abbot, with a certain formality intervening, the statutes of the said castrum cannot be corrected or altered; hence, since the community does not have the power of correcting or altering statutes, nor does it possess imperium in the said castrum, I do not see by what right or with what boldness the community can alter a penalty, especially one already incurred, as was the case here. For to remit or impede a penalty already incurred belongs solely to him who possesses the rights of the prince, as in the said l. moris, verse & si fortè. From which I conclude that the community could not by law prevent the said house from being destroyed; but if the abbot, who holds the regalia in the place, is willing to consent, then it may be questioned whether the commune ought to have anything of the said house. For it seems that the whole of it ought to belong to the abbot, because in the composition it is only said that of all penalties which should come to the commune of the said castrum, or into the hands of the chamberlain of that commune, or to another on behalf of the said commune, the third part shall be and be understood to be the monastery's, etc. But this penalty did not come to the commune of the said castrum, since by the disposition of the statute it was to be destroyed; rather, by the alteration of the penalty made by the abbot, as the one holding the regalia in the place, it passes by operation of law into the ownership of the abbot, because the goods of offenders in the case of confiscation do not go to the community, as I said before in the preceding doubt, but to the abbot, who holds the regalia and mere and mixed empire, as in the said l. una, C. de bo. vac. lib. 10 and c. uno, quæ sint rega. coll. 10, noted by Bartolus in l. 2 de iu. fis. previously cited, and the said l. cunctos populos, at the end, C. de sum. tri. For the composition speaks of a condemnation which the official of the said castrum makes. Since therefore we are outside the terms of the composition, the whole ought to belong to the abbot as the lord and superior of the said place, de præscr. c. auditis and c. cum olim, and de reli. do. c. cum venerabilis and c. cum dilectus. I would say nevertheless that out of equity the monastery ought to leave two parts to the community, because since the statutes of the place ought not to be corrected or changed without the consent of both, namely the community and the abbot, the consent of both ought to intervene in this alteration of the penalty, and consequently it seems that the said house should be divided as a condemnation and penalty for a crime; for where there was a penalty for a crime, it was not owed entirely either to the monastery or to the community; therefore it must be divided as is provided in the great composition, because two parts are left to the community for the officials of the community and other works to which the abbot is not bound, but only the community. For when the penalty of destruction is altered into confiscation, it ought to be regarded by the right of confiscation; what Bartolus noted in a similar matter supports this in l. cum duobus, § idem respondit, ff. pro soc. and what is noted in l. si enim, § qui iniuriarum, ff. si quis cautionibus, and l. sed & si rem & pretium, ff. pet. hær. and c. ecclesia S. Mariæ, ut li. pend. I conclude therefore from all the aforesaid that the community could not remit the penalty of the destruction of the house without the consent of the abbot, and if he wishes to consent, he ought to have at least a third part. The third doubt is: It is provided by the statute of the said castrum that foreign wine may not be brought into the said castrum or its court under a certain penalty; subsequently the community of that castrum granted to certain tavern-keepers that, upon paying a certain amount of money to the community, they might bring wine into the said castrum. It is asked whether the community could grant this without the abbot's license, and whether the monastery can have anything of the said money? I think this doubt is sufficiently resolved from the preceding points. For it does not pertain to a city or a castrum to prohibit wine from being brought into the castrum, or to sell the gabelle on wine to be brought into the castrum, since these matters depend on jurisdiction, and regularly all such exactions are prohibited by law, as I said above in the first doubt. In addition to what was alleged there, l. unica, C. de mono. supports this, and better still l. 1, § cura carnis, ff. de offic. præfe. urb., where it is clear that the care of foodstuffs belongs to the office of the prefecture, so that it may decide concerning the price, and whence and how they may come, and similar matters; to the same effect are l. 1, C. de epis. aud. and in l. imperatores, ff. ad leg. Iul. de anno., where there is a good text. And if anything has been paid for the sale of these things, it ought to go to the one holding the regalia, and not to the subject city or castrum; for this see what is noted on the rubric de anno. & trib. lib. 10 and l. una, C. de superindi. eodem lib. and what is noted there. Likewise, the community, as I have said above in the other doubts, cannot by virtue of the composition change the statutes of the said castrum without the license of the abbot. Wherefore I conclude that the community could not give license to bring wine into the city without the license of the abbot, by whose authority the statutes were made (for this see what Bartolus noted in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iur.), nor could it impose that gabelle without the abbot's knowledge, nor take the profit for itself; rather, the abbot ought to be principal in all things, and I believe that whatever has been received from it up to now belongs to the abbot, who holds the regalia and mere and mixed empire in that castrum, except for the things excepted in the said composition, in which no mention was made of this case or sale; and therefore it remained in the full power of the abbot, l. age and l. si de certa, C. de transac. and the said c. cum venerabilis and c. cum dilectus, de reli. do. But for the future, I should think it quite honorable and just that nothing be done against the ancient statutes and against the composition except by the consent of the community and the abbot, and if they agree that wine may be brought in under a certain gabelle, let them also agree on the division of the profit. For it is equitable that the community have something, since it bears all the burdens of the castrum; but looking purely at strict law, the whole profit ought to belong to the abbot holding the regalia in the place, by the argument in the said c. uno, quæ sint reg. col. 10, where it is said that an extraordinary levy, such as this is, belongs to the regalia; to the same effect is the said l. una, C. de superindic. I come to the fourth doubt, which is propounded thus: The said commune of the castrum of the abbey leased certain taverns situated on the highway by which one goes to Rome; and guests are received there, and wine and other foodstuffs, if they have any, are sold to them. The monastery claims that rent which the community receives, saying that it belongs to it because the ground on which the taverns are established belongs to the ownership of the monastery. The commune contradicts this, saying that it belongs to it by virtue of the often-mentioned composition, since the monastery ought to have a third part only from the things specified therein, and not from others. It seems briefly to me that the monastery maintains justice. For by common law this is most clear, both because since the ground belongs to the ownership of the monastery, the building therefore accedes to the soil, and consequently to the monastery, especially since the community, knowing that the ground belonged to the ownership of the monastery, built taverns there, as in § cum in suo solo, insti. de rerum divi., especially at the end of the paragraph; to the same effect is what is read and noted in capitulum apostolicos, 12 quæst. 2. Nor does the composition which the community alleges on its behalf stand in the way: because it is not said there that the territory of the castrum ought to belong to the community, but the composition intervened only concerning certain revenues and goods, so that the monastery should have a third part of them; therefore, in the other matters not expressed there, the full right remained with the monastery as lord and owner of the castrum with its court and district, as appears in the privileges, as in the said l. age and l. si de certa, C. de transa., and in the said cap. cum venerabilis and in c. cum dilectus, de relig. do. I conclude therefore that the rent of the taverns ought to accrue in its entirety to the monastery, unless the community is aided by some other special right; but if it incurred expenses on the taverns in good faith, it can recover them from the monastery by an exception of dolus malus, as the text says in the said § cum in suo. I come to the fifth and last doubt. The commune of the said castrum, already many years ago, to meet the expenses of the commune, enacted and ordained that whoever works land belonging to the commune should give for land-rent to the commune certain measures of grain; for which lands, before the said statute, nothing was paid to the monastery or to the commune, but the faculty was freely given to the men of the said place of working on those lands for their own benefit, lest through poverty the men should move to another dwelling-place. The monastery now claims that such land-rent received hitherto be restored to it as the lord and owner of that territory. The community, however, says that the land rather belongs to the community, and uses this right by virtue of a certain statute of that community, by which it was provided that whoever wished to work lands of the commune should observe a certain manner, so that it disposed of them as of its own property, and the monastery knew of the will of those statutes and never made formal protest. In this doubt I think it must be said that since the monastery has a claim founded by virtue of privileges—because the entire territory of the said castrum was absolutely conferred on the monastery by right of ownership and lordship—it ought by law to have the land-rent of the said lands, since it arises from its own property; wherefore it can claim it from the community, by the argument in l. mater and what is noted there, C. de rei ven. and in l. si me & Titium, ff. si cer. pe. and what is noted there. But it must now be seen whether the community is aided by any special right. And certainly it is not aided by virtue of the composition, because no mention of this is made there; therefore it remained in the full ownership of the monastery, as was clearly evident above in the other doubts. But the doubt is whether it is aided by virtue of the aforementioned statute. And certainly it is not aided merely from the tenor of the statute, because the lands are not expressed in the statute, but it is said generally: 'Whoever wishes to work lands of the commune.' Whence this uncertainty does not place the commune in any possession of any land, as in l. 3, § incertam, ff. de acqui. pos.; the text in l. sic, ff. de leg. 1, 2. responso supports this, and by that text Bartolus says there, following Dynus, that if someone said, 'Whatever I have in such a place belonging to the monastery,' the monastery acquires nothing through this, unless it appears and is proved what pertained to the donation there; to the same effect is l. legavi, ff. de lib. leg. I say the same if in the statute certain lands were expressed and it were asserted therein that they are common; for from this naming and assertion alone no possession is acquired for the community, because for acquiring possession the intention alone does not suffice, but the body is also required, so that it enters possession corporeally, as in l. licet, C. de acquiren. poss. and l. 3, in principio, ff. eodem; hence it is said that possession consists largely of fact, as in capitulum cum nostris, de conces. præbend. Moreover, while another is in general possession of the entire district of that castrum, a bare assertion made in a statute of the commune cannot prejudice the true lord and possessor, as in l. non nudis asseverationibus and l. non epistolis, C. de proba. Hence, in a similar matter, Innocent remarkably said in c. dilectis, de capel. mo., that by a general ban made by someone as lord, prohibiting offenses under a certain penalty, possession of jurisdiction is not acquired when another possesses generally. But if the men on the pretext of that statute worked those lands as belonging to the commune, and answered to the commune, was the community then in possession of receiving the rent with the monastery knowing and not contradicting, according to those things which are read and noted in c. cum venissent, de resti. spo. and l. quamvis and l. qui universalis, ff. de acq. pos.? And I say that it acquired possession only of those lands in respect of which it received the land-rent, or exercised another act by which possession is acquired. For possession is not extended to other lands, since the monastery possessed generally, as in c. cum contingat, de deci. and by Innocent in the said c. dilectus, and by Bartolus in l. 1, § si quid, ff. de iti. actúque priva. But it must be seen what such possession effects. For I say that if they have not possessed for forty years, it is certain that prescription does not run against the monastery, as in c. de quarta and c. illud, de præsc.; and if it was in bad faith, it is bound to restore whatever it received from it, as in c. gravis, de rest. spo. and l. domum, C. de rei ven. Bad faith, moreover, is presumed if there was a public report in the place that those lands belonged to the monastery, as noted by Bartolus in l. Celsus, ff. de usucap. But if it was in good faith, then if the land-rent is still extant, it is bound to restore it to the monastery, as in l. certum, C. de rei ven. If, however, it has been consumed and the community has not been made richer thereby, it is not bound, according to all authorities, as noted in l. ex diverso, ff. de rei ven. and insti. de of. iud. § 1 and the said c. gravis. But if the community has been made richer thereby, there are differing opinions: the Glosses commonly hold that it is not bound, as noted in the laws immediately cited; but Bartolus in the said l. ex diverso and Modestinus [or the moderns] in the said c. gravis hold the contrary; and I think this is truer, and this out of equity, l. si me & Titium, ff. si cert. pet., for you ought to be held liable if you have been made richer from my property or from what is owed to me, as there. If, however, the community possesses those lands for forty years in good faith, it has prescribed them. But it must be seen whether there is a presumption of bad faith on account of the aforesaid report; for in this case it would not prescribe, as in the said c. fin., de præscr. and as noted by Bartolus in the said l. Celsus. I conclude therefore, both in the aforesaid matters and in all others, that all regalia, or those things which are of mere or mixed empire, belong to the monastery, unless by virtue of the composition or another special right they belong to the community. From the aforesaid, the answer to the counter-arguments framed above, and similar ones that could be framed, is easily apparent; and re-examining them specifically, I say that the first counter-argument does not stand in the way, because the monastery does not claim the aforesaid by virtue of the composition, which was special and restricted to certain rights and property, but by virtue of the general lordship and ownership which it has by virtue of the privileges in the said castrum and its entire court and district. In a similar manner the second counter-argument is removed; for there arises to the abbot a right of action for the aforesaid and similar things, not from an obligation acquired by an act of the men of the said castrum, but from the bounty of the Roman princes, whose prerogative it was to give to the abbot of the said monastery the regalia and mere and mixed empire in the said castrum. To the third I answer in manifold ways: and first, that the monastery founds itself, as has often been said, upon the privilege and donation of the Roman princes or emperors confirmed by ancient custom; and this in respect of the whole; while in respect of a part, it can base itself upon prescription or custom in favor of the church, as I have most fully stated above. And let these remarks suffice, in the name of God. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A church is not obligated by a loan made even to a prelate, unless the debtor [creditor?] proves that the money was converted to the utility of the church, nor even a city, no. 2.
3. The burden of proof rests on the one asserting a mandate.
4. By keeping silent and allowing [someone] to act as proctor, one is deemed to consent to a mandate.
body: The aid of Jesus Christ the Savior having been heartily implored, three points are to be examined concerning the first formulated doubt. First, whether the Lord Archbishop of Florence is, or was, a debtor in the sum of money demanded from him by the Florentine clergy as principal or capital? Second, presupposing that he was, whether he is today released by virtue of the composition made between him and the syndics, or those then acting as syndics of the said clergy? Third, presupposing that the release or composition was not valid, whether the said Archbishop is bound for interest, or the usuries, which the clergy asserts it paid to the lending creditors for the satisfaction of the entire Florentine clergy. I come to the first point: for it seems that the Lord Archbishop is bound and was and is obligated to the said clergy for the principal sought; for even if no mandate preceded on the part of the Lord Archbishop, nevertheless, since the clergy paid for a cause incumbent upon the archbishopric, it can by law recover from the church or the prelate what it expended; to this effect is the good text in c. quicunque, 12, q. 4, where it is said that if the clergy and rector of a church expends anything of his own substance on the utilities of the church, he can recover all of that from the church; and this is clearest also in civil law, through the whole title De negotiis gestis, especially in l. si quis negotia aliena, l. 1 and 2, ff. de neg. gest., and what is read and noted in l. soluendo, of the same title. Secondly, to the same effect makes c. 1, de depo., where it is proved that if money received by an individual of a church has been turned to the utility of the church, an action can be brought against the church for restitution; to the same effect is c. quod quibusdam, de fideius., where it is said that if without a mandate a cleric, even a religious, took borrowed money for the church and converted it to the church's utility, the church is bound. But in our case it cannot be denied that that money was converted to the utility of the archbishopric: because if the clergy had not paid for the portion concerning the Lord Archbishop, the Lord Archbishop would have had to pay from his own pocket, as in l. in pupillo, ff. de solut.; therefore the archbishopric is bound to satisfy the clergy for the principal sought. And that the Lord Archbishop would have had to pay from his own is proved: for the archbishop is of the clergy, and the head of the clergy, as in c. si sententia, de sent. excom., in Sexto. And it is more clearly proved by an argument a speciali in c. quia periculosum, of the same title and book; 12, q. 1, c. sunt duo genera makes to this effect. Therefore the archbishop is bound to undergo the burdens incumbent upon the clergy for the rate falling to him: because what touches all ought to be approved by all, in c. ad haec, de off. arch., and it is consonant with nature that those who embrace the advantages of things should not refuse the burdens, as the said text states in Clem. 1, in princ., de censib. And that the prelates of churches are bound together with other clerics to the procurations of legates and nuncios of the Apostolic See, and other extraordinary burdens, is the open text in Clem. 2, § sunt et nonnulli, de censib., and c. cum instantia, of the same title, joined with c. ego N., de iureiur. But notwithstanding these points, I deem the contrary opinion to be preferable in our case, namely, that the Lord Archbishop is not at all bound for the principal sought. I am moved principally,

† because a church is not bound by a loan made, even to a prelate, unless the creditor proves that the money was converted to the utility of the church, as in the Authentica Hoc ius porrectum, C. de sacrosanct. eccl., canonized in 10, q. 2, c. hoc ius; what is read and noted, especially by Innocent in c. 1, de poss., makes to this point. For even a city

† is not obligated by the giving of a loan unless it is proved that the money was turned to its utility: only he who contracted is obligated, as in l. ciuitas, and there fully by Bartolus, ff. si cert. pet., where he simply concludes that the same applies a fortiori to the church; but in our case it is not proved that that money was turned to the utility of the archbishopric directly or indirectly; therefore the Lord Archbishop cannot be sued to restore it. For if the clergy was in fact compelled to pay, let it blame itself, especially since it received no mandate from the Lord Archbishop to pay that money; for this, note the gloss which Bartolus heavily noted in l. nam et Servius, ff. de neg. gest., where he concludes that if someone was de facto compelled to pay for another, he does not on that account have recourse against him for whom he paid unduly. For one does not have an action de negotiis gestis for that which was paid unduly, as in the said l. si quis negotia; and an injury done to one ought not to harm the author also in that matter done to another, as in the final chapter, de empt. et vend., and l. si per imprudentiam, in princ., ff. de evict. Nay more, even if extraordinary burdens were incumbent, the clergy ought not to have approved them by itself without the Lord Archbishop, or distributed them among the individuals of the clergy: since the Lord Archbishop himself ought to have been principal in the approval and requisition, as is the open text in c. non minus, de immun. eccl., and in the said Clem. 2, de censib. Nay rather, concerning the state of their churches, inferior clerics are not allowed to make statutes without the bishop's consent, as Innocent notes in c. cum accessissent, de const., and c. requisisti, de testam., where he says that a cathedral church or any other can make no statute without the bishop's consent, unless perhaps they were some minimal matters; the gloss in c. 2, de verb. signif., in Sexto, makes to this effect. Therefore this business cannot be said to have been usefully begun; since perhaps if the Lord Archbishop had then been requested to pay his portion, he would not have approved those burdens, at least in whole, or he would have limited, disbursed, and distributed them otherwise; or he would have acquired the money from elsewhere; to this effect, l. sed an ultro, especially at the end, ff. de neg. gest. Furthermore, just as the corporation of a city does not freely decide arduous matters without its ruler, as in l. observare, C. de decur., lib. 10, and l. penult. and ult., de legat., in the same book, so and a fortiori the clergy ought not to have attempted these sufficiently arduous matters without the approval of the Lord Archbishop, the said c. non minus; and he ought to be ordinate in all things, as in c. perlectis, § ad episcopum, dist. 25. And this as to the first point. I conclude therefore that the Lord Archbishop was by no means obligated for the quantity of the principal sought by the clergy, unless the clergy proves that the money was turned to the utility of the church directly or indirectly in the manner aforesaid. To the second doubt, the first doubt having been presupposed, that is, without prejudice to the truth, that the Lord Archbishop was from the beginning obligated to pay the principal for the rate falling to him, whether he is today released by virtue of the composition made with the said syndics of the clergy, since it is denied by the clergy that they were mandated for this? And it seems first that not: because

† the burden of proof rests on the one asserting a mandate, as in c. 1, de procur., and l. 1, C. of the same title, so much so that if it is stated in a judgment that it was rendered against the procurator of a certain person, a mandate is not proved thereby, nor does the judgment benefit the one holding it, unless he proves the mandate, as the notable gloss says in c. cum in iure, de off. deleg.; the Authentica Si quis in aliquo documento, and what Bartolus notes there, C. de edendo, and the gloss in c. abbate, de verb. signif., make to this effect. Nor does the cancellation of the debt made in the book of the clergy have to benefit the Lord Archbishop: because it could have been cancelled by the debtor or his friend, as Bartolus notes after the doctors in l. 2, ff. de pact., rejecting the gloss which wished simply that if an instrument of debt is found cancelled in the hands of the creditor, the debt is presumed satisfied, by argument in l. si chirographum, ff. de probat.; for this is not true without distinction: because just as the debt is not proved satisfied from the fact that the instrument is found in the hands of the debtor, because he could have stolen it, as is read and noted in l. 1, § ille autem, C. de Latina libertate tollenda, so cancellation does not necessarily prove satisfaction: because just as it can be stolen and delivered to the creditor, so it can be cancelled clandestinely by one not having the power. But I judge the contrary opinion to prevail in our matter. I am moved principally on a twofold ground. First, because, as is narrated in the statement of the case, those who made the composition publicly and openly carried themselves as syndics of the clergy, and were so commonly held and reputed, and exercised the fullest office of syndic by receiving credits, paying, offsetting or compounding, and granting acquittances. Hence the clergy, seeing this and not contradicting, even if they had not had a mandate, is deemed then to have given a mandate, as Innocent notes in c. ex parte decani, de rescript., and the Lords of the Rota follow in decision 4063 and the following, although Bartolus held otherwise in l. saepe, ff. de re iud., and Cinus in l. si pecuniam, C. de negot. gest. But in truth they are not moved by good reasons. For Bartolus is moved by the fact that, since one acting as procurator was acting usefully, as the outcome declares, the silent principal is not seen to give a mandate, by argument in l. filiusfamilias, § inter, ff. de procur.; Cinus is moved by that law to this opinion: but certainly this reason is not good: because in these matters the beginning is to be looked to, as in l. sed an ultro, ff. de neg. gest. For if anyone acting in judgment for another were presumed to act uselessly, the laws would not admit a connected person without a mandate: because a connected person ought not to be admitted against the presumed will of the principal, as in l. Pomponius, at the end, ff. de procur. And in favor of the statement of Innocent I cite the open text in Inst. per quas personas nobis acquirere possumus, where it is said that a procurator is appointed neither by set words, nor in the presence of the adversary, but rather often without his knowledge. For to whomever you have permitted to manage your affair or defend it, he is understood to be your procurator. For these last words are to be noted and weighed; furthermore, it is useful to have a procurator, as in l. 1, ff. de procur.

† Thirdly, by remaining silent and permitting someone to conduct himself as a procurator, one is seen to consent and give a mandate, as in l. quae patitur, ff. mandati, and what Innocent notes in c. in genesi, de elect. Likewise, since the clergy could have hindered their office and did not do so, it is seen to have consented, as is read and noted in l. Caius, ff. de pign. act., and l. fideiussor, § pater, ff. de pign., and c. nonne, de praesumpt.; the dictum of Cinus in l. invitus, C. de procur., and l. exigendo, of the same title, makes to this effect, where he says that if a friend or a connected person acts as procurator, the silent principal is seen to consent, by argument in l. si servus communis, ff. de donat. inter vir. et uxor.; Bartolus reports and follows this in l. non solum, § qui alieno, ff. of the same title; but clerics of the same corporate body are seen to be connected and friends among themselves, by argument in c. cum R., de offi. deleg.; note the final gloss at the end in c. ult., de procur., and c. 2, de postul.; or at least we ought to hold that if he acted gratuitously as procurator with the knowledge of the principal who did not contradict, he is presumed to have had a mandate: yet so that the burden of proving the contrary rests on the demanding principal, as Antonius de Butrio holds in the said c. ex parte decani; and the text cited above, Inst. de his per quos agere possumus, at the end, makes well to this effect; and what Innocent notably states in c. veniens, de verb. signif., in Sexto, where he says among other things that if anyone seeks anything from the contract of a prelate, deceased or living, as through instruments of a notary, it suffices for the plaintiff to prove the common opinion that he was held as a prelate or notary until the contrary is proved, by argument in C. de test., l. 1, and C. de sent. et interloc. omn. iud., l. 2. Likewise, since the books of the clergy were in their hands, they are presumed to have had a mandate; to which makes what is read and noted in c. coram, de offi. deleg., and the note of the gloss in l. fin., C. de pact. dotal., by Baldus in l. si qua per calumniam, C. de episc. et cler. From the second principal head I am moved: because, since the book of the clergy is found cancelled, and the cause of the cancellation is alleged in the same place, namely, on account of the composition made with the Lord Archbishop, it is to be presumed that that composition intervened legitimately, and that it was made by one having the power and with the consent of the clergy, through that which is read and noted in l. 1, ff. de his quae in test. del.; and because the Lord Archbishop is not such a person as is presumed to have abstracted or cancelled the said book, as is noted in the said l. 1, C. de Latina libertate tollenda, and by Bartolus after Iacobus de Arena in the said l. 2, ff. de pact. Furthermore, since the cancellation of the debt was made long ago, the cause of the composition being alleged, and it was never contradicted or protested to the contrary at any time by the clergy or the officials of the clergy, it is sufficiently to be presumed that it proceeded from the will of the clergy, by an excellent argument in c. 1, de frigid. et malef., and l. fin., C. de his qui a non domino manumissi sunt. For it must be imputed to him who confirmed by silence the things done to his ruin; and the text joined with the gloss of Innocent in c. olim, de offi. deleg., makes very well to this, arguing from him who exceeded the limits of a mandate with the principal knowing and not contradicting, to him who had no mandate. Furthermore, just as the clergy adduces the book for itself—which must not be relied upon to the prejudice of the Lord Archbishop, as in l. rationes and l. exemplo, C. de probat.—so it ought to receive what is against itself, insofar as the composition made with the said Archbishop is narrated there, as is the text in l. Publia, § fin., ff. depositi, especially because a book provides proof against the master, but not for him, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. nuda, ff. de donat., and l. admonendi, ff. de iureiur., and in the Authentica Et si contractus, C. de fide instrum.; and this concerning the second doubt. I come to the third part of the first doubt, which was whether, presupposing the obligation with respect to the principal, the Lord Archbishop is bound for the usuries paid by the clergy for that portion falling to the Lord Archbishop. And it seems first that yes, because the clergy did not seek usuries, but interest; therefore it can also seek them under canon law, as is proved in c. constitutis and c. pervenit, de fideiuss., and c. dilecti, de foro compet.; note the gloss in c. conquestus, de usuris, and in l. curabit, C. de act. empt., by Innocent in c. sacro, de sentent. excom. The contrary opinion in our terms I think to be truer, namely, that the Lord Archbishop is in no way bound for the usuries which the clergy paid, through those things which Iohannes Andreae most fully sets forth on the rule Damnum, de reg. iur., in Sexto, in the Mercuriales. For either the clergy paid those usuries without the knowledge of the Lord Archbishop, and it does not recover, by the said l. si quis negotia, ff. de negot. gest., for it did not manage usefully, and therefore it does not recover, l. sed an ultro, ff. of the same title; or it paid with the Lord Archbishop knowing and suffering it, and the same applies, because it is to be imputed to the clergy, which spontaneously offered itself to this, by argument in l. 1 and l. bona fides, ff. depos., and c. bona fides, of the same title: for just as the condition of him who offered himself for a deposit is burdened, as there, so also the condition of the clergy, which spontaneously without the Lord Archbishop's mandate paid usuries; or it paid with the Lord Archbishop knowing and ordering that it obligate itself also to usuries, and it still does not recover, since no oath intervened; for it ought to have pleaded the exception that the usuries were undue; yet since it spontaneously omitted an exception competent to the Lord Archbishop—who, however much he had promised to pay, could nevertheless have raised the exception, as in c. debitores, de iureiur.—therefore it must be imputed to it, as in l. fideiussor, ff. mand., and what is read and noted in l. exceptiones quae personae, ff. de except., and l. exceptione, ff. de fideiuss. Nay rather, if the clergy had been compelled to pay usuries, it still does not recover, since it did not obligate itself at the archbishop's command, by argument of the said l. exceptione, and what is noted by Iohannes Andreae on the said rule Damnum. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said Archbishop was put in default by being demanded to pay, and a single demand suffices to constitute someone in default, as is read and noted in l. Titia Seia, § usuras, ff. de leg. 2, and l. si ex legati causa, ff. de verb. oblig., and l. mora and l. sciendum, ff. de usufructu, and an extrajudicial demand suffices, as Bartolus notes in the said l. si ex legati, and is proved in the said l. mora: because the clergy could not constitute the Lord Archbishop in default since he was not a debtor of the clergy. Likewise, the clergy ought not from the beginning to have taken money under usury without the Lord Archbishop commanding it, as was said above. What more? Under canon law, by which one must stand today in this matter according to the note by the gloss on the rule Sine possessione, in Sexto, and by Bartolus in l. privilegia, C. de sacrosanct. eccl., usuries do not arise from default, although interest arises according to the note in the said c. conquestus and the previously cited l. curabit, and by Innocent in c. sacro, de sentent. excom. But in our case no interest was proved on the part of the creditors, and since this interest arises from contract, it ought to have been proved by witnesses, the Lord Archbishop, whose interest was at stake, having been summoned, as is the text joined with the gloss in § non solum, Inst. de verb. oblig.; note the gloss in c. dilecti, de foro compet. Furthermore, positing and not conceding that usuries did arise, nevertheless, for that quantity by which the clergy is found obligated to the Lord Archbishop, usuries do not run, but a set-off of the debt is made on both sides up to the concurring amount; the text is notable in l. 3, C. de compensat.; and thus the debt of the charitable subsidy ought to be set off. Likewise the annual debt that is paid under the name of procuration, if the custom is that the clergy itself pays it collegially. And these concerning the third doubt. The first principal doubt having been dispatched, I come to the second, in which it is asked in effect whether the clergy can recover from the Lord Archbishop what it paid in money under the name of procuration, especially for that time in which the Lord Archbishop visited not by himself but through another, this being especially attended to, that whether he visited through another or not, the clerics expended the procuration in provisions beyond the money. But on the part of the Archbishop it is answered that in the city and diocese of Florence this custom prevailed for such a time that memory of its beginning does not exist. And first it seems that the Lord Archbishop is bound to restitution not only of what he received, but to the double, as is proved in c. exigit, de censib., in Sexto, and if he did not restore within a month, entry into the church was interdicted to him by operation of law, as there; and consequently if after a month he celebrated without restitution having been made, he fell into irregularity, as in c. is cui, de sent. excom., in Sexto; note the gloss in the said c. exigit. Nor does c. foelicis, of the same title and book, excuse, where it is said that a prelate can receive a procuration in money from a willing party, because by that chapter the preceding chapter is modified only in that case where he receives money from a willing party for expenses to be made moderately, so that the money succeeds into the place of provisions; similar in c. relatum, 10, q. 1. But in other respects nothing is changed from that c. exigit. But since in our case the said Archbishop received money beyond provisions, he therefore fell into the penalty of that chapter and is bound to restore the double of what he received, as there; and c. procurationes, at the end, de censib., makes to this effect; and this proceeds especially here, regard being had to the fact that the said Archbishop did not visit personally; in which case he is prohibited from seeking anything from those visited, as in c. si episcopus, de off. ordin., in Sexto; nor does a contrary custom seem to be valid, since it is unreasonable and hostile to the canons, as in c. fin., de consuetud.; that it is unreasonable is sufficiently gathered from the things contained in the said c. exigit and the previously cited c. procurationes. But although these points seem to press here, nevertheless the contrary opinion pleases more; and I judge the said Archbishop can be defended on a twofold ground and preserved in his custom. For the understanding of the first, I premise that a bishop travelling through his diocese can demand the cathedraticum, which is given in honor of the cathedra, as the text says in c. 1, 10, q. 3, and c. conquerente, de off. ordin., namely two solidi from each church, that is, gold ones, as in the said c. 1 joined with the gloss, so much so that according to the common opinion, although prescription runs in quantity, yet not entirely, as the gloss notes in c. quicunque, 16, q. 7, and fully by Iohannes Andreae in c. cum venerabilis, de censib.; and this cathedraticum is sometimes called synodaticum, as in c. olim, de censib., and this because it is frequently given in a synod, as the gloss notes in 10, q. 1, in the summary. Likewise I premise that when something has been rendered annually for so much time that memory of men of its beginning does not exist, it can be sought for the future even with no cause expressed, but it suffices to say: 'I seek a census or annual rendition imposed from a just cause from the beginning through so much time that of its beginning there is no memory.' Iohannes Andreae notably holds this in c. pervenit, de censib., and Bartolus in l. cum de in rem verso, ff. de usuris; the gloss on 18, q. 2, c. servitium senses this, and there is a notable gloss which expressly holds this even with respect to a bishop and clerics, referenced to the text of 1, q. 1, c. nullus episcopus gravamen. These things having been premised, I say that since every year at the time of visitation a certain quantity of money was handed over to the Archbishop by each rector of a church for so much time that memory of its beginning does not exist, we ought to presume that from a just cause this was imposed from the beginning, and perhaps in lieu of the cathedraticum; which to presume is most just through those things that I said above; but it is called a procuration because it is given at the time of visitation and procuration, just as it happens that it is called synodaticum because it is given in a synod, as I said above. For it cannot properly be called a procuration, since the Lord Archbishop or another visiting for him receives a procuration in provisions. For a procuration cannot be doubled; what is read and noted in l. libertis, ff. de aliment. vel cibar. legat., and what the gloss notes in l. quinquaginta, ff. de probat., makes in a similar manner. Another legitimate cause is therefore to be presumed from the course of so much time, as noted in the laws cited above; for the course of so much time has the force of a constitution and privilege, as in c. 1, de praescript., in Sexto, and l. hoc iure, § ductus aquae, ff. de aqua quotid. et aest., and l. 1 and 2, ff. de aqua pluv. arcend.; this is to be presumed especially in our case, so that an offense may be avoided, and many absurdities which would follow from the contrary, concerning which above; what is read and noted in a similar case in l. si defunctus, ff. de arbitro tutel., makes to this effect. On a second ground, the Lord Archbishop can be aided and defended in his custom by holding that the money was paid directly for other expenses which he makes in visiting the whole diocese beyond the provisions at the time of visitation; for no law expressly condemns this custom, at least when it is of so much time that there is no memory of its beginning, as in our case. For anciently he himself had sometimes half, sometimes a third part of all the revenues of inferior churches, as is read and noted in 10, q. 1, c. antiquos and c. de his; what Iohannes Andreae notes in c. requisisti, de testam., makes to this; and by reason of ancient custom he can receive services and other extraordinary things from the churches subject to him, as in the said c. servitium, 18, q. 2, and the said c. nullus episcopus gravamen, 1, q. 1. It is not surprising, therefore, if a custom—especially a most ancient one—is valid that something be given at the very time of visitation beyond the provisions; c. si episcopus, de off. ordin., in Sexto, makes to this, where it is said that when he does not visit by himself, he ought to seek nothing from those visited beyond the provisions that are furnished to the visitor; therefore, for the fact that he visits by himself, it seems otherwise. Likewise it is otherwise when there is a custom so ancient. For even public law is removed both by authority and by utility by custom, at least when the tacit consent of the Pope intervenes, as is noted in a certain Extravagante and reported by Iohannes Andreae in the final chapter, de censib., in Sexto, citing dist. 12, c. nos consuetudinem. And I think that even without the Pope's knowledge such a law can be removed by custom; because the Pope's consent is sufficiently had through what is contained in the final chapter, de consuetud.; and this the gloss notably held in dist. 4, c. in istis, § leges, and dist. 8, c. frustra; for from the course of so much time we ought to presume a most just cause, as I said above. And Baldus notably said in c. imperialem, § praeterea ducatus, de prohib. feud. alien. per Fred., coll. 10, that there is no positive law that cannot be removed by custom, by argument in l. de quibus, ff. de legibus. Which, however, I qualify, unless it be unreasonable, c. fin., de consuetud.; but by the course of so much time it is always presumed reasonable, as in the laws cited above. Nay rather, if the law reprobates a custom, it can nevertheless be introduced anew; to this I cite the text joined with the singular gloss on the word 'consuetudinem' in Clem. statutum, de elect.; and on this many things could be said, which I examined most fully in c. 2, de probat., in my lecture; but here I do not pursue it, because it does not necessarily come to be examined. For it could be that from the beginning on account of the poverty of the archbishopric this was introduced, or from another just cause. Nor ought it now, after the course of so much time, to be brought back into doubt, since it is a matter of pecuniary advantage and not of the danger of souls. Nor ought it to be reputed blameworthy if, according to the variety of times, human statutes are changed, as in c. non debet, in princ., de consang. et affin.; and let these suffice for the second principal doubt. Now I descend to the third principal doubt, in which it is asked whether the clergy can recover from the Archbishop that quantity of money which it gave him when he went to the Council of Siena. To which I say very briefly that it cannot. To which I cite expressly the notable gloss in c. 1, de statu relig., where it says that individual churches ought to contribute with the bishop when he goes to the Pope, or to the King, or to a synod, or when he makes expenses for any common business of the whole diocese; for this, 12, q. 2, c. vobis. What the gloss notes in c. quidam monachi, 16, q. 1, and what is read and noted in c. cum apostolus, de censibus, makes to this. For the Archbishop goes to a synod or council for the common utility of all, since it is held for the reform of the universal Church and its members; therefore it ought to be borne by all; what is read and noted in Clem. 2, of the same title, makes to this. Furthermore, the clerics, by paying spontaneously, even if it had been undue, are seen to have gifted it, nor can they recover it any longer, as in l. Campanus, ff. de oper. libert., and l. cuius per errorem, ff. de reg. iur. Likewise, an urgent necessity pressing, the bishop can seek a charitable subsidy, as in the said c. cum apostolus; and since the bishop sought it then and it was not denied to him, the clergy cannot recover it any longer, because a donation cannot be revoked on the ground of mere repentance alone, l. 3, C. de revoc. donat., c. fin., de donat. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the syndics of the clergy, who gave that quantity of money to the Lord Archbishop, did not have the power for this, because it is enough that the clerics, by paying spontaneously, approved this; to this effect, l. si filius, ff. ad Maced., and what Bartolus notes in l. quod enim, ff. de rem rat. hab., where he says that if something was done in my name which tends or can tend to my prejudice, and I, knowing it, perform some positive act which tends to the approval of the act, I am seen by this to approve what was done in my name; to which Clem. 1, de procurat., makes excellently, and what the same Bartolus notes in l. cum tabernam, § idem quaesiit, ff. de pign. Likewise, the syndics were accustomed openly and publicly to make similar donations by commission of their office, and thus the clergy is seen to have given this power; to this makes what is read and noted in l. quam Tuberonis, ff. de peculio, and in l. si filiusfamilias, ff. de donat., and what Innocent notes in the said c. veniens, de verb. signif., in Sexto, and what is contained in l. non tantum (otherwise beginning Paulus), ff. de rem rat. hab., and what Bartolus notes there. From a manifold way, therefore, I say that the said money cannot at all be recovered. Lastly, descending to the final doubt, which is whether the clergy can demand from the aforesaid Archbishop that he contribute and pay his part of the donations which the clergy made to the Supreme Pontiff, and pay certain duties levied by the clergy. Conclusively, for the sake of brevity, I say that it cannot, because the clergy could not, by donating even to the Supreme Pontiff, bind the Archbishop to contribute, nor otherwise impose those duties for public utility without the license and consent of the Lord Archbishop, since he is the head of the whole clergy and jurisdiction is in his hands and not in the hands of the clergy, 12, q. 3, c. sine exceptione, and c. placuit, and c. abbatibus; 10, q. 1, c. noverit, and in c. regenda, 16, q. 7, c. omnes basilicae; Clem. 2, de censib., and c. dilecta, de excess. praelat., make to this. Just as in a similar case it is said in the corporation of a city, that for public utility it cannot impose these extraordinary burdens without the prince, nay rather all are interdicted, as in l. 1, C. de superindic., lib. 10, especially with respect to churches, as in c. 1, § illicitas, de pace iuram. firm., coll. 10, and c. ad decus, § item illa communitas, de stat. contra libert. eccl., in the same collation; fully Iohannes Andreae in c. pervenit, de immun. eccles. Whence I wonder that the Lord Archbishop suffers that they impose these burdens even on inferior churches without his consent, since they can greatly damage the churches and their revenues, and diminish divine worship, and withdraw necessities from the poor; whence the bishop can demand an account from all clerics concerning the revenues of the churches, and see whether they expend the substance of Christ well, 10, q. 1, c. episcopum, and c. cum plantare, de privil., and there by Innocent; this text in c. non minus, de immun. eccles., says that the bishop and clergy ought to consider these burdens to be imposed. And it would seem strange if the clergy could compel its archbishop to donate, or to pay ordinary or extraordinary burdens, so that thus the archbishop would be subjected to the power of the clergy, since the clergy has no jurisdiction, although for its own necessities it can form a corporate body, which nevertheless will be under the bishop, according to what is noted by Innocent in c. dilecta, de excess. prael.; 11, q. 1, c. de persona, and 17, q. 4, c. in venditionibus, and c. 1 and 2, de his quae fiunt a praelat., c. cum similibus, make to this; and what the same Innocent notes in c. cum accessissent, de const., and c. requisisti, de test., where he says that clerics cannot make even simple statutes without the bishop's consent, except concerning the lightest matters, makes to this. And let these things suffice, and through the aforesaid the response to all the contrary arguments formed above is clear. Nicolaus the Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A woman can renounce the right of her hypothecs.
2. When the husband remains solvent, the renunciation of a hypothec does not contain a donation.
3. A woman is in no way obligated for her husband.
4. An oath sworn against a law enacted principally in private favour must be inviolably observed.
5. Wherever an oath is illicit and unjust on the part of the recipient, although on the part of the person swearing it can be observed without loss to the soul, absolution can nevertheless be sought from the bishop.
6. An oath, so that it be lawful in every respect, must have three companions: truth, judgment, and justice.
7. A person swearing who seeks absolution from an oath does not act contrary to the oath.
casus: Laurentia, a woman, gave and sold together with Ioannes, her husband, who consented to her and did not remain solvent, a house belonging to the same Ioannes that was mortgaged for the dowry of the said Laurentia, for the price of one hundred florins to be applied to the restitution of the dowry of Catherina, the predeceased wife of the said Ioannes, which the abovesaid Ioannes was bound to restore; and she swore not to act contrary to the contract of the aforesaid sale. It is now asked, the said Ioannes being dead, whether the said Laurentia can pursue her hypothecary rights in the said house, in the presence of a municipal law which stands in these terms: But during the subsistence of the marriage, if any woman of the city or district of Siena makes a renunciation, or donation, or remission of her dotal rights, or receives any payment from her husband or another on his behalf regarding her dowry without the consent of four of her closest relatives of good repute, of whom two are on the side of the father and the others on the side of the mother of the woman herself, it shall not hold ipso iure.
body: The aid of Almighty God having been implored, three things must be considered for the decision of this doubtful matter. First, whether, absent an oath, the aforesaid woman prejudiced herself in her hypothecary rights arising from the aforesaid sale, or from the consent given to it? Second, assuming that she did not, whether she at least prejudiced herself from the swearing of an oath? Third, granting that she prejudiced herself by the oath, whether there remains to the same woman, against such an oath, any lawful remedy? I come to the first, in which it seems first that she prejudiced herself,

† because a woman can renounce the right of her hypothecs, in l. iubemus, and l. etiam, C. ad velle. But by selling, or consenting to the sale of an asset mortgaged to her, she is seen to remit that obligation, as in l. sicut. §. si voluntate, with the following, ff. quib. mod. pig. vel hypo. sol. Therefore, this woman prejudiced herself, even without the taking of an oath. But notwithstanding this, in doubt I state that the contrary is truer, namely that from such a sale, leaving aside the oath, no prejudice was inflicted upon the woman. First, this is most clearly evident from the form of the above-written statute, which annuls ipso facto every contract entered into by a woman to the prejudice of dotal rights unless the form contained therein is observed, which in our case was not observed at all: therefore, that sale was null to the prejudice of the woman, since the husband was not at the time of that contract otherwise solvent for the restitution of the dowries. For a woman, by selling and consenting to the sale of an asset mortgaged to her for her dowry, is seen to have made a remission of dotal rights, as in the said §. si voluntate, which she could not do, the statute standing in the way. Furthermore, I say that, even apart from the statute, looking purely at the ius commune, the said sale did not prejudice the woman; for it is the common opinion of the legists, and of Barto. and others in the said l. iubemus, that that law applies to make the remission of hypothecary rights made by a woman valid when the husband remains solvent in other assets; but if he did not remain solvent, such a renunciation would not prejudice the woman. The reason is because

† when the husband remains solvent, the renunciation of the hypothec does not contain a donation, as in the said l. etiam, and l. si pignus, ff. de his quae in frau. credi. But when the husband was not otherwise solvent, it would contain a donation, which is not valid between husband and wife, as in ff. de donat. inter vir. & uxor. almost throughout. Furthermore, when the husband was not otherwise solvent, the woman by this renunciation would be obligated not to sue; for by a pact of release one is obligated not to sue, as in l. ubi pactum. C. de transactio. and l. si unus. §. pactus ne peteret, ff. de pact.

† But a woman is in no way obligated for her husband, as in the authen. si qua mulier, C. ad velle. Therefore, such a renunciation was not valid, and this was held by Iaco. de Aret. in l. Maevia. §. fin. ff. solut. matrimo., and Dy. in l. pignus, ff. de his, quae in frau. cre., and Iacob. de Belvi. in Auth. ut immobilia ante nu. do. col. 6, and Barto. in the said l. iubemus, which he said must be held perpetually in mind; but since the husband did not remain solvent here, the aforesaid renunciation of the hypothec, which tacitly resulted from the said sale or from the consent given to it, could not prejudice the woman in any respect. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the woman herself was the one who sold, and did not purely renounce; because I say that the price was not received by her, and thus fails that which is read and noted in l. si vir uxori, ff. ad velle. and what is noted by Barto. in the said l. iubemus, at the end, but the price had to be converted to the benefit of the husband, so that he would be released from the restitution of the dowries of his predeceased wife, and thus in effect the woman was obligated not to claim for the benefit of her husband, contrary to the authen. si qua mulier, C. ad velle. From all of which the premised conclusion is clearly apparent, and this as to the first point. I come to the second doubt, whether the woman prejudiced herself at least from the swearing of the oath. And briefly I think that she did, through c. cum contingat, de iureiuran. and c. quamvis, de pact. lib. 6. and authen. sacramenta puberum, C. si ad ver. ven. For the statute and the ius commune annul in this case such a remission and contract principally in favor of the woman, although secondarily in the public interest, as in l. j. ff. solut. matrim., in which case an oath taken by the person whose interest is principally at issue is valid, as in the said laws, noted fully by Barto. in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiuss. and the canonists in the said cap. cum contingat, and many legists in the said authen. sacramenta. For this oath does not tend to the prejudice or detriment of eternal salvation; therefore it must be kept, as in the said cap. cum contingat and c. si vero, under the same title. It remains therefore to examine the third question, whether any remedy is available regarding such an oath; and it seems at first that there is not, through the text in the authen. sacramenta puberum, cited above, which says,

† that an oath taken against a law enacted principally in private favor must be inviolably observed; and note the word 'inviolably', for if absolution could be sought indiscriminately, that Authentica would serve, as it were, for the wind, nor would it be inviolably observed; to the same effect is the said chapter cum contingat, which commands simply that such an oath be observed, damage to temporal goods notwithstanding, since the soul is to be preferred to all things as being more precious, xij. quaestio. j. cap. praecipimus, and c. Matthaeus, de simo. But in our case I believe the aforesaid arguments do not apply at all; whence I say that absolution from such an oath can be sought from the bishop, or it may be sought that the said buyer be compelled to release that oath. I am principally moved,

† because wherever an oath is illicit and unjust on the part of the recipient, although on the part of the one taking it it can be kept without detriment to the soul, absolution can nonetheless be sought from the bishop, or that the one receiving it unjustly be compelled to release that oath; this is proved in chapter si vero, and cap. verum, de iureiuran., in which laws the oath is released for paying usury, or when taken through fear because of the turpitude of the recipient; and it is the same by identity of reason wherever any other turpitude is involved on the part of the recipient, as Inn. thinks in cap. debitores, de iureiuran., and the doctors, especially the Moderns, in the said cap. cum contingat, and Fede. expressly holds in consil. 264, lest he who receives basely and against the law obtain an advantage from his own wrongdoing, contrary to l. itaque fullo, ff. de furt., since he ought rather to be punished on that account, as in c. & si necesse, de dona. inter virum & uxor. and ff. de nego. gest. l. sive.

† Likewise, and secondly, so that an oath may be lawful on all sides, it must have three companions: truth, judgment, and justice. If however these are lacking, it is by no means an oath, but perjury, that is, an unlawful oath; so says the text in cap. animadvertendum, 22. quaest. 2. and cap. & si Christus, de iureiuran. But the oath sworn by this Laurentia did not have judgment as a companion, because it was not discreet, or did not have within itself discretion, neither on the part of the swearer nor on the part of the recipient, since from its observance the woman would without just cause be compelled to be dowerless, since she cannot have recourse against the husband's goods because none remain, contrary to l. 1. ff. solu. matr.; for it is in the public interest to preserve dowries for women, as the text says there. Likewise, the said buyer here contracted with a woman for what was straightway for an evil use, and condemned by the law, just like a price with usury, contrary to l. si quis cum sciret, ff. pro empto, and what Bartol. notes in l. si vero non remunerandi. §. si adolescens luxuriosus, ff. manda., and in l. & mulieri, ff. de cu. fu. and other laws. For this woman sold in order to convert the price into the restitution of the dowries of that predeceased wife, and thus solely for the husband's benefit, contrary to the laws cited above; and thus that oath did not have discretion, neither on the part of the recipient nor of the swearer, especially since the said buyer had contracted with that woman contrary to common and municipal law, which prohibit the remission of the hypothecary rights of a woman, especially when the husband is not otherwise solvent, as was shown above.
