Furthermore, the aforesaid oath did not have justice as a companion, because it was not just to contract with a woman who, out of the fragility of her sex and the reverence she has for her husband, would easily promise anything, by argument of those things noted by the gloss in l. 1. §. quae onerandae, ff. quarum rerum actio non datur, and l. si pater, at the end, C. de sponsa.; and often many affectionate wives would strip themselves of their property, unless the law prohibited it, ff. de donatio. inter virum & uxorem l. 1. & 2. & 3. Likewise, the said oath was unjust by reason of fraud which intervened in the matter itself, and thus not by design, because the woman, as I said, remains dowerless without just cause; for it is the same whether fraud intervenes by design or in the matter itself, as the text says in l. si quis cum aliter, ff. de verb. obligatio.; but by reason of fraud and enormous lesion an oath is easily remitted, as in chapter cum contingat, and chapter Quintavallis, de iureiuran. And if we said the contrary, it would follow that the oath would be a bond of injustice and iniquity, contrary to chapter quanto, de iureiuran., and 22. quaestione 3 throughout. This opinion, that the oath ought to be remitted, is held even under easier terms by Federic. in the consil. cited above, where, formulating the question: when it was provided by statute that a certain grant or promise made by a son under paternal power without his father's consent is void ipso iure, even if sworn, and a certain son under paternal power, notwithstanding this, promised and swore, the said Fede. concludes that the one receiving the oath acted contrary to the prohibition of the city statute on account of the act, which he ought to have obeyed and not contravened, dist. 8 c. quae contra, and xj. q. iij. c. qui resistit, nor ought he to derive a benefit from the transgression, but rather be punished; the recipient himself can be compelled to release the oath.

† Nor in this does the swearer himself act against the oath; rather, by seeking release or absolution from the oath, he confesses that he is bound by the oath. If Feder. held that from the mere contravention of a statute someone is bound to release the oath, no other deceit having been alleged, then a fortiori in our case the said oath ought to be released, which was taken notwithstanding common and municipal law, and with the gravest damage to the woman herself, who as a result remains deceived. Likewise, Vinc. and Io. And. reciting him in the said c. cum contingat most clearly held this, where he says that a woman who swears within the terms of that c. cum contingat can insist upon being absolved from such an oath, because she consents contrary to the prohibition of the law; a fortiori in our case, the other factors mentioned above concurring. Pet. de Anchar. gave the same counsel in the case of a woman who was in fact deceived through an oath, and sets this out at length in the repetitio of c. canonum, de consti.; and do. Anto. de Butr. in the said c. cum contingat, where he says that whether the swearer was enormously lesed in the contract, or whether the one receiving the oath had contracted with someone likely to squander the property, and this was evident from the facts, because here there is a certain turpitude on the part of the contractor, who provides the material for squandering to squander his own property, and the law presumes fraud against such a person, as in the said l. si quis cum sciret, and l. ij. ff. quarum re. act. non da., such oaths ought to be remitted according to the laws cited above. I conclude therefore that the above-written oath of lady Laurentia is to be remitted in either of the premised ways, either by compelling the recipient to a release, or by obtaining absolution from the bishop; for each legal remedy is equally principal, as Ioan. Andr. finally holds in the additions to the Speculator under the title de iureiuran. over the rubric, and Anto. in cap. 1. and c. debitores, under the same title, although Inno. seems to think otherwise there. And I examine this matter most fully in a certain disputation of mine which begins Stante statuto, and it seems to be proved in c. si vero, §. verum, de iureiuran. But once the oath is removed, the said woman will be able to use her hypothecary right, by the said c. si vero, at the end, and through the doctors in the said c. cum contingat. To the contrary arguments formulated above the response is easily apparent. First, for it can be said that he who seeks absolution does not act against the oath, but rather observes it, as in cap. 1 and c. si vero. Likewise, secondly, those laws apply when, beyond the prohibition of the law, no other deceit and enormous lesion intervenes, as happens in our case. And this solution pleases more, and preserves the opinion of all. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A bishop ought not to alter the ancient customs of a church without the chapter.
2. Under the appellation of clerics, in a matter subject to restriction, canons are not included.
3. Custom is the best interpreter of laws.
casus: Case of the following consilium. In a statute issued by the Bishop of Lucca in an episcopal synod, it is provided as follows: first in the rubric thus, 'On the absence of priests from churches'; then in the black text it is subjoined thus: 'Likewise we statute and ordain, and by authority of the present constitution we warn, that henceforth, as from then, all and singular abbots, provosts, archdeacons, priors, plebani, archpriests, and rectors of parish churches are to be held as warned, requested, and cited, so that none of them may absent himself from his church for more than two months. And one having a simple benefice, over which the cure of souls does not impend, [may not absent himself] for more than four [months] without our special license or that of our vicar; otherwise, however, one acting to the contrary shall be ipso iure deprived of the benefice.' In another capitular constitution issued by authority of the same bishop, however, it is provided as follows: 'Likewise they statuted and ordained that the revenues and profits that for the time being shall be in the Chapter of Lucca are not to be divided except among those residing throughout the whole continuous year at the appointed time; but if it happens that those so residing are absent for only three months, on that account nothing at all shall be deducted from the annual prebend, but they shall be counted as residing. And if they have remained away beyond that, only a portion for that amount of time shall be assigned to them, provided that in each year they have already served at least for six continuous or interrupted months; otherwise they shall receive nothing from the prebend, etc.' It now happens that the Bishop of Lucca, by virtue of the preceding statute, has deprived, or declared deprived, two of his canons who absented themselves for more than four months, license having by no means been obtained from the bishop or the vicar. It is asked whether he could do this, having regard to the words of both constitutions. Likewise having regard to the fact that by custom of a very long time the canons of Lucca are not bound to residence except according to what is provided in the preceding statute, nor was the statute set down first ever observed in the persons of canons, although it was issued long ago.
body: The protection of Jesus Christ and His Mother having been humbly invoked. Omitting all elaborate argument because the case does not seem to me to admit of much doubt, and having briefly considered all the premises, I judge that the first statute is by no means to be extended to canonicates. I am moved first because that statute speaks of those having dignities, or personatus, or double or simple churches, as is clear from the tenor of the statute itself, combined with the rubric, where it is spoken of the absence of priests from their churches; therefore, it ought not to be extended to canons, who do not have a church, but rather a benefice in a church, for to have a church is one thing, and to have a benefice in a church is another, as is read and noted in c. fin. de praeb. and in cle. j. de conces. praeb. Secondly, and more strongly, I am moved since canons have by custom that they are not bound to residence, which custom is indeed approved by law according to what is noted in c. cum omnes, de constit. and in c. dudum, il 2. de elec.; said statute ought not to be extended to canons, both lest an ancient custom approved by law be violated, and also

† because a bishop ought not to alter the ancient customs of a church without the chapter, as is noted in c. cum consuetudinis, de consue.; and in doubt a statute ought not to be referred to a case in which an ancient custom would be violated, by the argument of c. 1. de consti. lib. 6., especially considering that that statute is penal, and therefore to be restricted, to that which Inno. noted in c. sedes, de rescrip., where he says

† that in a matter subject to restriction, canons are not included under the appellation of clerics. Furthermore and thirdly, since special provision was made concerning canons, as is contained in the second statute, the first statute, which speaks generally, ought not to be extended to a species specially provided for, as in l. sancimus, ff. de poen. Whence I consider that either the second statute preceded the first, or was transcribed first, and then the preceding argumentation holds; or the first was issued first, and then by the second, because it speaks specially of canons, the first is limited and restricted, because a species derogates from a genus, especially when it follows the genus, as in the rule generi, de regu. iur. lib. 6., and in c. 1. de rescrip., and in l. quaesitum, in fi. ff. de fide instru.; and in doubt we ought so to interpret the said statutes that they are brought into harmony, lest one be corrected by the other, as in c. cum expediat, de elect. lib. 6., through Bart. in extravag. ad reprimendum, on the word non obstantibus privilegiis, and through Io. And. in cap. 1. de constit. lib. 6., cited above. Likewise and fourthly, in the first statute the consent of the chapter or its counsel did not intervene, from which the nullity of the statute can be argued, according to what is noted by Io. And. and Archid. in c. 1., cited above.

† Fifthly and lastly, custom, the best interpreter of laws, supports this; for, as is premised, the first statute was received into the force of a canon, and thus at least on that ground, because that statute was not received by usage in respect of canons, it ought not to be extended to them, according to what is read and noted in c. in istis §. leges 4. dist. and through Bart. in extravag. ad reprimendum on the word non obstantibus privilegiis, through Ioan. And. in c. 1. de consti. lib. 6., Nico. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A successor is held for debts contracted by the deceased.
2. A guardian without the judge's authority can alienate at his own discretion old garments and similar things which cannot be preserved by keeping.
3. A prelate or rector of a church can, not only in health but also in sickness, dispose at his own discretion of some movables acquired by the church, even among those who have served.
4. If the rector of a church expends anything of his own for the benefit of the church itself, it must be restored to him in full by the church.
casus: The fact is set forth as follows. A certain cleric, newly invested with a certain parish, found in the said church certain movable goods of modest value left to the church by the immediately deceased parish priest, and many debts contracted by the same deceased in the name of the church; which successor parish priest, with the creditors pressing and since the church had no money, satisfied some of the creditors out of the said movable goods, but paid the rest out of his own money; finally, in the course of time, upon his resigning the parish, his successor in the said church, pressing him, demands back from him those movable goods left to the church by the said deceased. Now two questions are asked: First, whether this former parish priest can lawfully be constrained to the restitution of the said goods. Second, presupposing that he can, whether he can recover the money that he paid out of his own property for the satisfaction of the debts contracted by that deceased in the name of the church.
body: Having invoked the aid of Almighty God, I say briefly regarding the first point that the said late parish priest cannot in any way be constrained to the restitution of the said goods.

† I am moved [to this] because a successor is held for debts contracted by a deceased, especially when he has succeeded to his goods, as in c. 1 and what is noted there de sol. and in c. 1 de tes. Therefore, those immovable goods could be given in payment, or otherwise alienated for the satisfaction of the creditors, since the church did not then have money or another easier way to satisfy the creditors, as in the Auth. hoc ius porrectum, 10 q. 2; nor was it necessary in the alienation of those goods, since they were movable and of modest value, that the bishop's authority intervene, arg. 12 q. 2 in c. terrulas, and better in l. lex quae tutores, C. de admi. tut., where it is clear that

† a guardian without the judge's authority can alienate at his own discretion old garments and similar things which cannot be preserved by keeping; but the rector of a church has greater power than a guardian, as the gl. notes on 5 q. 3 in c. si, and Inn. in c. pe. de iur. cal.; to the same effect are c. caeterum, and c. ad haec, and c. relatum, in [title] de testa., where it is said

† that a prelate or rector of a church can, not only in health but also in sickness, dispose at his own discretion of some movables acquired by the church, even among those who have served him; therefore, he can do this all the more for the satisfaction of debts contracted in the name of the church, especially by the one who left the said goods to the church. And this as to the first [question], by the decision of which the second doubt remains sufficiently clear and not worthy of another examination. But, assuming without prejudice to the truth that the said late parish priest could be compelled to the restitution of the said goods, could he not recover the money from the present parish priest which he paid out of his own funds to the creditors of the church? And conclusively I say that he can; for the text is clear on this in c. quicunque, 12 q. 4, where it is said

† that if the rector of a church expends anything of his own for the benefit of the church itself, it must be restored to him in full by the church, since no one is compelled to confer a benefit out of his own. 10 q. 2 c. precariae; to this makes 12 q. 1 c. manifeste, and c. sicut manifeste. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The disposition of a testator must be observed like a law.
2. If it is provided by a bishop’s statute that no cleric may lease church property without his consent, if the bishop himself rents it, he is seen by renting it to consent.
3. The year does not run against an executor except from the day of the admonition to be made by the bishop.
4. An executor is one who has a bare ministry of fact in executing what has been disposed by another.
5. If someone has stipulated for Stichus or Pamphilus, whichever he himself wishes, if he once chooses the one, he can change his will until he has claimed the other in court.
6. One who has a choice by virtue of an office committed to him, if he chooses once, even an absent person, can no longer change.
casus: The fact is presented as follows: A certain master Armanus, citizen and inhabitant of the city of Fondi, while in his last moments, made his last will, in which among other bequests he disposed as follows: 'I will and order that my wife, as long as she lives, inhabit my house, which is in the parish of etc.; after her death I will that the aforesaid house be sold, and the money from the house itself be given for my soul at the provision of my executors.' The aforesaid wife, after the testator's death, stayed in the aforesaid house; finally, the said executors reached an agreement with the aforesaid woman, and sold to that woman the house thus bequeathed for a certain price. Having received the price, the aforesaid executors began to execute the will of the deceased, namely by purchasing a small house, and they assigned it for the soul of the testator himself for the purpose of marrying off a girl; after this was done, the executors themselves waited for more than a year and made no disposition regarding the remainder of the money from the aforesaid house sold. Finally, the newly appointed bishop in the city, inquiring into the execution of pious dispositions, found that the said executors had not entirely executed the will of the deceased; and upon his admonishing them to fulfill the testator's will, it proceeded by their consent and that of the bishop that two silver candlesticks be purchased for the cathedral church from the remainder of the money; and for the purpose of carrying this out, the said executors delivered the said money to the lord bishop himself. The lord bishop made efforts to obtain the said candlesticks, but could not obtain them, so that the said lord bishop retained the said money in his possession for a year and more. At length, the said woman purchaser died, while the bishop retained the money even after her death for a year and more with the intention of purchasing the above-written candlesticks. Now, however, the aforesaid executors claim back from the lord bishop the aforesaid money, saying that they wish to expend it according to their will. It is asked whether they can do so.
body: Having invoked the names of Christ the Savior and of His most pious Mother, three matters must be examined for the clear decision of the aforesaid. First, whether the said house could be sold before the death of the said legatee woman. Second, if a year had elapsed from the time the money to be distributed under the testator’s disposition was held, whether the said executors could dispose of that money, especially through the purchase of candlesticks. Third, assuming that they could, whether they have the power to change their mind and convert it to another pious use. I come to the first, in which it seems at first must be said that it could not; because from the fact that the testator provided that it be sold after the death of the legatee wife, it could not be sold beforehand, by the argument in l. si ita relictum. §. Pegasus, ff. de leg. 2., and l. in fideicommissa. §. cum pollidius, ff. de usu., and l. qui Romae. 1. responso. ff. de uerb. obl.

† For the disposition of the testator must be observed like a law, 13. q. 2. c. ultima uoluntas, and in auth. de nup. §. disponat. But notwithstanding this, the contrary opinion is more compelling: for this time was not added in favor of the deceased, but of the legatee herself, who was able in this matter to renounce her right—not only by purchasing it herself, but she could even have consented to its being sold to another during her lifetime, as in l. quoties, C. de fideic., and l. 1., and the text in l. 1. and l. cum proponas, C. de pact. serves our case excellently, where it is proved that a testator directed an heir that if he should die without children, he should restore the inheritance to Sempronius, and yet the heir could, despite this, agree with Sempronius to give him a certain portion of the inheritance during his life so that the universal fideicommissum would be discharged. Likewise, the fideicommissary can purely renounce this fideicommissum and discharge the heir, as in said l. cum proponas. For anyone may renounce the benefit of a time provision added in his favor, as in l. cum qui, ff. de uerb. obl., and l. stipulatio ista. §. inter incertam, ff. eo., and c. ad apostolicam, de regula.; and the general laws yield, which say that one can renounce that which is in his favor, said c. ad apostolicam, and l. si quis in conscribendo, C. de pac.; and this is very clear. From which I conclude that the sale of the said house was valid with the consent of the said legatee, who consented by the very fact that she bought it; to this effect l. cum pater. §. libertis, and what Barto. notes there, ff. de leg. 2., and through Bal. in l. fi. C. ad Macedo., and better in l. si filius, C. de pet. haere., and Io. An. in regula, qui tacet, de reg. iur. li. 6. in Mercu., where he says that if an episcopal statute provides that no cleric may lease a thing of the church without his consent, if the bishop rents it, he is seen by renting it to consent; so it must be said in our present case. To the second doubt, I say briefly that, notwithstanding the lapse of a year, the said executors were able to designate the money for the soul of the testator under the ius commune. This seems very clear, because

† the year does not run against an executor except from the day of the warning that must be given by the bishop, so that they execute or fulfill the deceased's will, and not before, as is clearly proved in c. nos quidem, de testi., and there commonly by the Doctors, and by Fed. consi. 124. But in our case, the bishop’s warning did not precede the lapse of the year. I say the same if in the bishopric of Fondi there is a custom, as commonly prevails in other bishoprics, which by that very fact warns and binds executors of pious bequests to execute within a year, otherwise the power devolves by that very fact to the bishop. For notwithstanding this constitution, I say that the said executors could after the year choose the cause to which that money should be devoted, through the things elegantly noted by Bar. in l. cum quidam, ff. de leg. 2., where he says that he gave counsel for that position, because under the ius commune he who has the right of choosing the poor, or another cause, if he has been in default in choosing and declaring his will, can purge that default up until the legacy is demanded in court, as is proved in said l. cum quidam; and it is said to be demanded by litis contestatio, and not before, as in l. amplius. ff. rem ra. habe. And therefore under the ius commune they are not excluded after a year, both because, as I said, the warning did not precede, and because they had to choose the persons or the pious cause, and were not simple executors. Likewise, they would not be excluded by force of such a constitution, because a constitution binds executors, but these are not strictly executors, since they have to declare into which cause the money ought to be converted.

† For an executor is one who has the bare ministry of fact in executing what has been ordered by another, as in l. executorem, C. de exec. rei iud.; hence it is that he who declares and gives judgment is called a judge, but the executor is he who executes what has been declared by the judge, said l. executorem. These men, however, about whom the question is raised, not only have to pay, but also to declare and choose; wherefore, by virtue of such a constitution, not the election, but the mere execution devolves to him; which is well to be noted, because many err in this, believing that such power is transferred indifferently to the bishop after a year, and therefore the bishop ought to be cautious in enacting statutes, so that he also encompasses those who have to choose, and declare, and execute. I conclude, therefore, that notwithstanding the lapse of a year, those called executors could declare their will, and designate that money for the purchase of candlesticks for the cathedral church. For to leave [something] for the ornaments of the church is a pious cause; indeed, such a bequest is privileged by law, so that the quarta is not paid from it, as in c. fi. de testa. I come to the third doubt, whether the said executors can, the matter still being whole, change their will and convert that money to another cause. And first it seems that they can, through l. si quis stipulatus, ff. de uerbo. obligat., where it is said,

† that if someone had stipulated for Stichus or Pamphilus, whichever one he wished, once he has chosen one of them, he can change his will until he has demanded the other in court; therefore the same should be said in the present matter. But notwithstanding this, the contrary must be held in our case through l. huiusmodi. §. Stichum, ff. de lega. 1., and l. statuliberum. §. 1. de lega. 2., and l. apud Aufidium. ff. de oper. liber., in which laws it is clearly proved that he who has an election arising from a last will, if he once chooses, or has declared his will, cannot vary any further; and this the gloss and the Doctors, especially Bartolus, commonly hold there. The contrary does not stand in the way, because it speaks of an election given through a stipulation, and not from a last will. A twofold reason for this difference is given. The first, commonly given by the gloss, is that in a last will, by the very fact that one has chosen or declared his will, ownership is immediately acquired by the one chosen, just as if the testator had chosen, as in said l. cum apud, and thus there can no longer be room for repentance. For the election made by the commissary himself is attributed to the testator himself, so that the action belongs to the chosen person to obtain that right, not from the election of the commissary, but from the aforesaid testament, as is a notable text in l. unum ex familia, in prin., and there by Bar., ff. de leg. 2.; which reason does not apply in a stipulation. But because this reason does not seem universal, since it does not hold in the case where another's property is bequeathed, since then ownership does not pass by the election, therefore Bar. and others assign another reason in the said laws, namely this: because last wills cannot, like contracts, remain in suspense, as the text in l. fi. ff. communia praedi. expressly states; therefore, the election having been made, the act is immediately exhausted, and there is no further room for variation. Since, therefore, the said executors or commissaries have declared their will, and willed that candlesticks be bought with that money for the cathedral church, and especially since for this reason they delivered the money to the lord bishop, they can no longer change their will, since they have performed their office; to this effect c. publicato, c. cum inter de elect., and c. si compromissarius, eo. ti. li. 6., and in c. in literis, de offi. deleg., and l. iudex, ff. de re iud., and regula, mutare. de reg. iur. lib. 6., and clem. cum illusio, de renun., c. si tibi absenti, de praeb. lib. 6., and what Bar. elegantly noted on a similar point in l. absenti, ff. de donat., where he says,

† that he who has an election from an office committed to him, if he chooses once, even an absent party, cannot vary any further; which the canon laws alleged immediately above sufficiently prove, demanding that the said candlesticks be bought, since a year has elapsed from the time the bishop warned them to execute, said c. nos quidem; and thus full power of execution resides in the lord bishop, said c. nos, in auth. de eccle. ti. §. si quis aedificationem. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Absolution ought not to be granted against the will of the one receiving the oath.
2. A contract entered into by a usurer is deemed to have been made in fraud of usury.
3. Everything proved in court is said to be notorious.
4. A sentence rendered without a certain amount is said to be certain, if it can be ascertained from the record.
5. One who enters into a transaction is not said to give of his own accord, but fear of litigation and vexation compels him to submit.
6. An obligation arising from an oath is acquired principally for God, not for the party receiving it dishonorably.
body: IN the name of the undivided Trinity, amen. Although a fuller counsel has been most elegantly given on the matter at hand by the distinguished and famous doctors written above—so much so that, led by their authority, I ought to be content with a mere subscription—nevertheless, for greater clarity and that the consulting party may be more easily provided for, I shall succinctly touch upon two points not openly addressed by the aforementioned doctors. For, first, it seems that the above-written transaction holds, that the penalty is incurred by virtue of the agreement, and that absolution from the oath ought to be denied; because, even though the contract was in truth a pledge-contract and usurious, drafted under the form of a purchase and sale, nevertheless, since the suit was initiated not against the party contracting fictitiously, but against his heir, who could plausibly have been ignorant of the decedent's act and is presumed to be ignorant, as in the regula cum quis in ius, de regu. iur. lib. 6., and as noted in c. cura. de iure pat. and in c. de quarta, de præscrip., in l. j. & 2. ff. depo., especially since the instrument appears drafted under the form of purchase and sale, to which one must adhere until the contrary is openly proven, in cap. cum Ioannes, de fide instrumen. and l. precibus, C. de probat.; this heir lawfully entered into the transaction, and he seems praiseworthy for having acted for the purpose of redeeming his vexation, by the argument of cap. dilectus, de simon. and l. 2. C. de transact.; c. 2. and c. dilecti, de arb. support this, as do c. cum contingat, de iureiur., and c. licet, eod. tit. lib. 6., and c. si. de foro comp. eod. lib., where it is evident that an oath is lawfully received even for another reason, namely, that through it forum may be added to forum. And by these points it is clear that, since no iniquity is found on the part of the heir receiving the oath, nor does it contain sin on the part of the swearer,

† absolution ought not to be granted against the will of the one receiving the oath, as in C. de transactio. l. si quis maior, and in c. 2. de spon.; indeed, he ought to be compelled to observance, as in c. cum contingat, and c. licet, de iureiur.; nay more, by contravention he becomes infamous, since the transaction was sworn, and he forfeits every benefit he obtained from that transaction, as in the previously cited l. si quis maior. Nor ought the transaction to be invalidated under the pretext of deception beyond half the just price of the thing sought. For even if after the transaction public instruments are found, through which it appears that the transacting party was deceived fourfold, the transaction is nevertheless not rescinded, ff. ad Treb. l. Lucius. §. ulti. And the reason in a transaction is that by this very fact, that one withdraws from litigation, there is a great advantage; whence what was not owed, paid on account of a transaction, is not recovered, C. de transact. l. ij., and ff. de condit. indebit. l. in summa; and the gloss also holds this in c. pen. de emptio. & uendit., in the previously cited l. Lucius. §. ulti. ad Treb.; what Bartolus notes in l. ij. C. de rescind. uendit. supports this. Nor do the points fully adduced above by the consulting doctors stand in the way, because their premise seems false. For they base themselves upon a remission of usury that was not freely made; but through the aforesaid points it is clear that in the aforesaid case an open remission of usury was not made; rather, through the transaction there was a withdrawal from litigation, in which the contracting parties could prevail even with a clean conscience, since the outcome of a suit is doubtful, as in c. fraternitatis, de frigi. & male., and c. si. 11. q. j. But notwithstanding these points, I deem the opposite to be true in law, because this heir knew, or ought to have known, that the contract was usurious. First, because the decedent at the time of the contract was a usurer; whence, from the fact that he leases the purchased property to the seller and allows the seller to possess it for a long time, the sale seems simulated, as in l. sicut. §. superuacuum, ff. quib. mo. pig. uel hypo. sol., and through Bartolus in l. post contractum, ff. de dona.,

† whence such a contract entered into by a usurer seems made in fraud of usury, especially because against usurers a presumption is easily made in favor of and for the salvation of their souls, in c. iuuenis, de sponsa., and in clem. exiui, de uerb. sign.; what the gloss notes in c. 1. de scruti. supports this, and dominus Petrus de Ancharano, of revered memory, holds this opinion in c. illo uos, de pig., where he reports having seen this question de facto here in Siena; and I understand this, as I said above, when such a contract is entered into by a usurer. If, however, it is entered into by someone else, solely from the fact that he remained in possession of the adjudged property, the contract is well presumed to be simulated, as in the previously cited l. sicut, §. superuacuum, and as noted by the gloss in C. de remis. pig. l. fi.; but this conjecture suffices as regards another creditor so that this contract does not prejudice him; the seller, however, or those deriving cause from him, cannot afterwards say the contract was simulated solely from that fact, because one is not permitted to go against one's own act unless there are other conjectures, which Bartolus notes in the said §. superuacuum. And that which was said above, that as regards another creditor the contract is presumed simulated, applies unless he who leased it back had paid the rent; and then the contract is not presumed simulated, as Bartolus notes in the place previously cited. Whence, since in the statement of facts it is presupposed that this decedent at the time of the contract was a usurer, it ought to be presumed that the contract was usurious, from the fact that he permitted the seller to possess for a long time, as I said above. Likewise, on another ground, this heir knew, or ought to have known, that this contract was usurious, because, as is stated in the statement of facts, it had been proved in court that the contract was simulated;

† for everything proved in court is said to be notorious, as in c. cum olim, de uerbo. signi., which the lords of the Rota say is true in deci. 403, when the proof is perfected and the case concluded, so that nothing remains except to deliver sentence, as was the case here. To the aforesaid points support is lent by what the gloss and Innocent note in c. significauerunt, de test., and c. super quibusdam, de uerb. signi. supports it, as well as what Innocent notes in c. constitutus, de fil. presby., and in c. significasti, de diuor. Indeed, Innocent said more in de app. c. ex insinuatione, and de consue. c. cum dilectus, and de testi. c. per tuas, and the gloss in c. euidentia, de accu., namely, that whatever is done in court is said to be notorious.

† Likewise, a sentence delivered without a fixed amount is said to be certain if it can be ascertained from the records, as Innocent notes in c. 2. de libel. obl., and the gloss in c. illa præpositorum, de accu., and Johannes Andreae in the additions to the Speculum, under the title de sen. prola. §. qualiter, at the word quod si iudex, and it seems to be proved in l. 3. C. de sent. quæ sine cer. quanti. Whence this heir could not be ignorant of the simulation of the contract, since the proofs were perfected and known to him; wherefore he is bound to make satisfaction for the soul of the decedent, as in c. fi. de sepul., and in c. in literis, de rap., and in c. a nobis. 2. de senten. excom., and in c. tua. de usur., for whose soul satisfaction is not made unless that which was taken away is fully restored, de usu. c. cum tu, and regula peccatum, de reg. iur. lib. 6., and 13. q. 6. c. si res. He ought not to have dragged this plaintiff, somewhat unwilling, through subterfuges and cavils and through his own power, into the act of transaction.

† For he who transacts does not donate voluntarily, but fear of litigation and vexation compels him to submit, as in l. 2. C. de transac., where there is a good text joined with the gloss; c. super eo supports this; and especially in our case, the remission and release was not free, because the plaintiff, on account of the defendant's power, was not able to obtain a sentence, and was struggling under his own penury; for this, see the good text in cap. 2. de arb. And a remission of usury, when not made voluntarily, is invalid, as was fully stated above in the other consilia; and thus it is evident that the transaction did not hold, because he ought to have looked after the soul of the decedent by full satisfaction, as in the laws cited above. Likewise, a transaction ought to be made concerning a doubtful matter and an uncertain suit, l. 1. ff. de transac., such that the transacting party believed he had a good case; otherwise, if the malice were evident, the transaction does not hold, ff. de condi. inde. l. in summa, at the first response; c. exposita, de arbit. supports this, as noted by the gloss in c. super eo, de transac. Whence, since the heir was certain here that the contract was usurious through the points adduced above, he is caught in evident malice by transacting and by not making full satisfaction for the soul of the decedent; and thus the transaction did not hold, and consequently neither did the affixing of the penalty, as noted on a similar point by the gloss in c. significantibus. de offic. deleg., and in c. 2. de preca., and in regula accessorium, de regul. iur. lib. 6., and l. pacta quæ contra, joined with the gloss, ff. de pact. And the oath ought to be relaxed, since it was basely received by the heir, as is fully gathered above; for this, see c. 1. and what is noted there de iureiur., and through the doctors in c. debitores, eod. Indeed, it seems even more that, even if this heir plausibly did not know of the simulation of the contract, nevertheless, because this plaintiff did not have the intention of freely donating and remitting that which remained to be restored, as is clear from the aforesaid, the heir ought ex officio to be compelled to make satisfaction for the soul of the decedent, as in the previously cited c. fi. de sepul., in c. literis, de rap., c. a nobis. 2. de sen. excom., and c. tua, de usur. But concerning the absolution from the oath, it must be noted that even beyond the practical methods handed down by the said consulting doctors, another method appears easier and one by which circularity is avoided: that relaxation of the oath be sought from the judge as having been unlawfully exacted, so that, notwithstanding the oath, he may demand the usury that he paid and swore not to claim back, that he be absolved from that oath; and this practice is grounded upon c. si uerò, de iureiuran. And although that chapter speaks of requesting absolution from the Pope, nevertheless an inferior can also absolve where there is some baseness on the part of the swearer, as Innocent holds in c. debitores, eod. tit.; what is noted in 15. q. 6. c. nos sanctorum, and c. iuratos supports this; and Johannes Andreae ultimately holds this practice in the additions to the Speculum, upon the rubric de iureiur. And more expressly, dominus Antonius de Butrio of revered memory in c. 1. eod. titu., where he reports having seen counsel given to the effect that one does not come to this absolution of an oath except in subsidium, because before all else relaxation ought to be sought from the party, through the previously cited c. 1., where if the party is unwilling to absolve, the bishop may absolve; and if he absolved otherwise, he would not absolve duly. But dominus Antonius did not think this was necessary, because this order is not given to anyone there, since in the chapter cited above, this swearer is absolved principally without other circularity, and thus he is also heard principally in cap. ad aures, and c. abbas, quod met. cau. And this I consider to be truer:

† because from an oath the principal obligation is acquired to God, not to the party receiving it basely; whence it suffices to seek relaxation from the judge, who in this holds the place of God, as in the previously cited c. si uerò, de iureiuran. But as to whether, in granting this absolution, the party who receives the oath ought to be summoned, I say briefly, so as to avoid prolixity, that I find two opinions on this subject. For Paulus and Johannes Calderini advised that either absolution is sought from an oath confirming a contract, and thus from this there results the rescission of the contract as confirmed by an oath; or absolution is sought simultaneously from the oath and the contract, and then the party must be summoned; it is otherwise if the oath does not confirm the contract, and absolution of the oath alone is sought, in so far as it does not confirm the contract, but is separate from the contract, so that a way may be opened to rescind the contract; for then they say the party need not be summoned, because through this no prejudice is done to the party. For this is a quasi-penitential and extrajudicial act, which can be exercised without the party having been summoned, since no prejudice is inflicted upon him. And thus, on this issue, it seems that the party is not to be cited, since this oath does not confirm the contract, nor is the contract rescinded upon its removal, but a way is given to rescind. This position—that the party is not to be summoned as far as our case is concerned, since the oath is sworn concerning the recovery of usury—is held by dominus Antonius in the said c. debitores. He is moved principally by the fact that such great baseness is present on the part of the receiver that no obligation is acquired by him, neither that he may sue nor that he may raise an exception, since from his own iniquity he ought not to obtain an action or an exception, l. itaque fullo. ff. de fur., and as noted in c. in literis. de rest. spo.; rather, the obligation is acquired solely to God, whence it suffices that God be present, and thus the judge, who in this place holds the place of God. He admits, however, that it is safer for the party to be summoned; and where he ought to be summoned, if he is not summoned, he holds that the absolution is valid, just as absolution from excommunication ought not to be given without the party having been summoned, and nevertheless if it is done, it holds, as noted in c. qua fronte. de ap. Another contrary opinion, namely, that the party is to be summoned, is held by Johannes Andreae in the additions to the Speculum, under the title de iu. iu. upon the rubric, in the last addition; and Federicus de Senis holds it in consi. 290, where he concludes that the creditor must be summoned, and before he is absolved it must be investigated whether the instrument is usurious or not, at least semi-fully and summarily; for he ought not to absolve unless it is established that the instrument is usurious, but this cannot be established unless the parties are present and cited, l. in causæ. §. causa cognita. ff. de mino., and c. cum ex literis. de in int. resti.; and afterwards in the discussion of the ordinary trial, that same matter ought to be proved fully, as the case requires, because proofs upon that preamble would not create full faith when the principal issue is pleaded, c. ueniens de test. 2.; and the lord Cardinal of Florence of happy memory follows the same view as above in the previously cited c. debitores. And this opinion I deem to be truer, because it cannot be denied that the creditor and adversary has an interest in the oath not being remitted, especially in our case, by the argument in l. si quis maior. C. de trans. and c. si de fo. comp. li. 6. Likewise, if he had no interest, why would he be compelled to relaxation in c. j. de iureiu.? Since therefore he has an interest, he ought to be summoned, as in c. inter quatuor. de ma. & obe. and c. omnia. and ca. caueant. 3. q. 8. And thus I say and advise.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Churches, and ecclesiastical persons, and their property are immune from exactions.
2. Clerics are exempt from all burdens of cities and castles, nor are they bound to burdens imposed by laymen.
4. They are bound, however, when they ought to be converted to their use.
3. 5. A city cannot impose collections for the commonwealth without the prince's authority.
6. One who evades an unjust gabelle does not sin.
casus: While the corporation of the city of Fondi was bound each year to pay certain collections to the lady Queen from the possessions and other property of those men, no longer wishing to pay the said collections in such a manner, it made and ordained in compensation for those collections certain statutes, to the effect that anyone selling wine, grain, and other goods, as well as anyone buying meat, should be bound and obliged to pay a certain amount, as is contained in their statutes. The citizens, however, and the officials of that city appointed over this matter wish to compel the clerics to pay the aforesaid gabelle from the property of the church and from the patrimonial property of the clerics themselves. The clerics, on the other hand, refuse, saying that they are not bound to the aforesaid burdens or gabelles; it is asked, what is the law?
body: The aid of Christ and His mother having been humbly invoked, lest I seem to have considered this case doubtful, all argument on the opposing side being omitted, I shall address the decision itself. For I firmly hold that clerics are not bound to gabelle-taxes of this kind. I will prove this conclusion by divine, canon, and civil law, and finally I will reinforce it with the authorities of the doctors. By divine law indeed it is proved by that which is read and noted in c. quanquam. de censi. li. 6. together with the glossa on the word, diuino; for the text there says,

† that by divine and human law churches and ecclesiastical persons and the property of those individual persons are immune from exactions. The glossa there on the word, diuino, adduces that which is found in Genesis 47 and Exodus 7 past the middle, where it appears to be proved that clerics are immune from collections, gabelle-taxes, or exactions of this kind. By canon law it is openly proved in c. fi. de ui. & ho. cle., where it is expressly proved that clerics are not subject, even as to their own property, to statutes and customs of the country enacted concerning the payment of gabelle-taxes or collections, even if they engage in business and trade like laymen, unless, having been thrice admonished by the bishop, they refuse to desist from secular business of this kind. Secondly, it is proved in c. non minus. and c. aduersus. de im. ec., where it is said,

† that clerics are exempt from all burdens of cities and fortified towns, so that they are not bound to pay anything for the common utility, unless the bishop and the clergy have perceived so great a necessity that without any compulsion they wish to relieve the necessities of those laymen in some measure, the Roman Pontiff having first been consulted, however, as in the said c. aduersus; to the same effect are the aforementioned c. quanquam. de censi. li. 6., cle. praesenti. e. ti., c. j. de im. ec. li. 6., and 16. q. 1. c. generaliter. Nor ought this to seem absurd to anyone; for the goods of churches are assigned to a special public use, 12. q. 1. c. uidentes, 16. q. 1. c. fi. de præb. The canon gives the reason for this in c. nulli liceat. 1. q. 2., that that which is consecrated to the Church, whether it be an animal or a field, is made the holy of holies to the Lord, and belongs to the right of the priests; therefore it ought not to serve worldly public use, because what is once dedicated to God ought not to be transferred further to human uses, according to the rule, semel Deo dedicatum. de re. iu. li. 6.; and public law consists in sacred things, priests, and magistrates, 1. dist. c. ius publicum. Laymen, moreover, since they are worldly and principally derive benefit from the worldly commonwealth, ought to undergo these burdens, so that temporal things may be assigned to temporal uses and spiritual things to spiritual uses; c. ecclesia S. Mariæ. de const. and c. quae in ecclesiarum. e. ti., c. fi. de re. ec. non ali., 96. di. c. bene quidem are applicable. Hence the text says in c. reprehensibile. 24. q. 8. that secular soldiers fight for the world, but heavenly soldiers fight for God. By civil law, moreover, it is proved still more clearly. For since it cannot be denied that these burdens are extraordinary, as they are not fixed and established from antiquity by the prince, according to what is read and noted in l. una. C. de superindi. lib. x. and l. omnis, C. de ang. & trib. e. li., therefore clerics are exempt from them, as is proved in l. placet. C. de sa. fan. ec. and l. 2. C. de epi. & cle. And under the newest law this is most clear, as in the authen. item nulla communitas. C. e. ti. and in the body from which it is taken, de sta. & consue. 5 lib. ec. §. item nulla. col. x., where it was generally ordained that no community or public or private person shall impose collections or exactions, angariae or perangariae, upon churches or other pious places or ecclesiastical persons, or presume to invade ecclesiastical property; and if they should do so and, when called upon, do not make amends, they are subjected to the gravest penalties, concerning which see there. And by that text the glossa in l. de his. C. de epi. & cle. maintained that clerics are immune even from ordinary duties or tributes that were formerly paid to the Emperor, although Bar. in the said l. de his holds the contrary and understands the said auth. item nulla to apply to extraordinary burdens. Bal., however, in the said l. placet. C. de sa. san. solves that glossa for the case when even ordinary burdens should be imposed by any prince other than the Emperor, because no one can do this, even though he might establish something to be paid ordinarily, by that text, which forbids this to all; and he speaks excellently. Furthermore, these burdens are imposed principally on persons on account of property; therefore they cannot be imposed on clerics, who are not subject to those enacting statutes, as in l. rescripto. §. sciendum. ff. de mun. & ho., and there Bald. maintained this. Indeed, even if the property were assessed in the tax register and came without fraud to the church or a cleric, the church or cleric would not be bound to pay for that property, as Bald. notes in the said l. placet; Bartol. holds the same in l. incola. ff. ad municip., Specul. in the title de cleric. coniuga. in the 2nd column, Ioan. de Ligna. in clem. præsenti de censi., and Archid. in cap. 1. de immu. eccle. lib. 6. Furthermore, these burdens imposed in the city of Fondi succeed into the place of those collections which the laymen alone used to pay to the lady queen; therefore they ought to be judged by the same law as those collections, because that which is subrogated ought to be judged by the law of that into whose place it has been subrogated, as in c. ecclesia, ut lit. pen. and l. si cum. §. qui iniuriarum, ff. si quis cau.; just as, therefore, laymen alone paid those, in the same way laymen alone ought to pay these gabelle-taxes. Iaco. But. very clearly held this in l. ad instructiones, C. de sacrof. eecle., where he says,

† that clerics are then bound to pay gabelle-taxes imposed by laymen when they ought to be converted to that use to which clerics were bound to contribute, as for the repair of roads in respect of possessions, l. 1. ff. de uia pub. & iti. refi.

† What more? Bald. holds this most clearly in the said l. placet, saying that clerics are not bound to gabelle-taxes imposed by laymen, because these are extraordinary duties to which clerics are not bound, as in the laws previously cited; and he reports that Bar. advised the same, and that it was so determined in a question of fact. And I especially hold this opinion, because these burdens, tolls, gabelle-taxes, or similar exactions are generally prohibited by law and cannot be imposed except by one who has regalian rights in the locality, but not by a statute of a city, as is proved in l. 2. C. de ue cti. & commis., and l. uectigalia, ff. de pub., and l. una, C. de superindi. lib. 10., and expressly there by Barto., who says,

† that a city cannot impose collections for the commonwealth without the authority of the prince, by the text of that l. unica, although for the city's own necessity, as when a debt or necessity presses, it may impose collections according to its turns; indeed, it is compelled to do this, as noted by the glo. in l. 1. ff. quod cuiusque uni. and by Barto. in l. 4. §. accusatori, ff. de re iudi. and l. 2. ff. de iure fis. But they can in no way impose them on clerics, since they are not of its jurisdiction, and are generally exempt by law, as in the laws previously cited. Hence Bart. notably said in the said l. uectigalia,

† that one who today evades a gabelle-tax does not sin, since it is not justly imposed—namely, because it is not by him who has regalian rights in the place, concerning which see c. uno, quæ sint reg. col. 10.—unless they are of those persons who imposed the gabelle-taxes by common consent, as the citizens themselves for their common necessity. I conclude therefore from all the foregoing that the clerics of the city of Fondi, or of any other, are not bound to pay the said gabelle-taxes or similar ones declared by the statutes of laymen; and this conclusion seems sufficiently according to the mind of Inn. in the previously cited c. non minus, and l. sancimus. la. 2. C. de sacrof. eccle. strongly supports it, where it is clear that goods that are transferred to churches, whether by testament or inter vivos, are exempt from the registrations of lucrative acquisitions—so that if it is provided by the statute of the locality that a certain amount be paid to the commune or to the lord of the locality from property donated or leased, such a general statute is not extended to churches, as there, and 23. q. 8. c. sancimus, noted by An. de Bu. in c. 1. de censibus. With stronger reason clerics ought to be exempt in a non-lucrative cause, as in our case, since there is a great difference between not acquiring gains and losing what has been acquired, l. si sponsus, ff. de do. inter uir. & uxo. And let these things suffice. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Prescription runs against a woman in dotal property or rights from the time at which she can bring an action.
2. If the Church succeeds a private person against whom prescription had begun, it uses the right of a private person for the past time, [and] for the future, in the property and privilege of the Church.
3. Wherever a law or statute removes prescription generally, and this cannot be verified except in the prescription of the longest time, then, so that the words may have some effect, they exclude prescription of 30 or 40 years.
4. Prescription with bad faith regularly runs against no one.
body: The aid of Almighty God having been implored, it seems firstly that the hospital of Santa Maria has no present right, and if any did belong to it, it has been lawfully prescribed. Moreover, that none belongs to it is proved by the municipal statute of Siena under the title *de praescrip. 20. vel 30. an.* in the verse *si quis autem*, where it is provided as follows: *If anyone, however, has possessed any property as his own for the space of 30 years, let him prescribe it in the said time, and let no right be granted to anyone complaining concerning it.* And thereafter it excepts from that prescription wards alone; of women and their dowries no mention is made in the said chapter. Nor does it stand in the way that at the end of the entire statute an exception is made in respect of women regarding their dowries, because women are privileged there with respect to the 10-year prescription of which mention is made in the subsequent clause. For since in the said statute as to the matter at hand two clauses are posited having diverse and separate subject matter—because in the first it is provided concerning the 20-year prescription without any required title, and from it wards alone are excepted; whereas in the second, mention is made of the 10-year prescription with title, and from it several persons are excepted, among whom a woman is reckoned in respect of her dowry—it is clearly evident that that exception ought to be referred solely to the 10-year prescription of which it had immediately beforehand made mention. For qualifications, exceptions, clauses, and qualities of this kind ought to be referred to the proximate, and not to all preceding provisions, when several separate chapters precede, and especially when preceding chapters have their own qualifications, as in our case; to this effect *c. cum dilectus, de do. leg.* and noted in *c. inquisitioni* and *c. secundo requiris, de ap.* and in Spec. in the title *de inst. edi.* § *nunc autem videndum*, at the word *item excipe*, by Bar. in *l. praetor 2, ff. vi bo. rap.* and *l. talis scriptura, ff. de leg. 2.* Since, moreover, the commune and men of the castle of Rocca Albina of the county of Siena have possessed under title as a gift the said castle of Caligrano—concerning which the hospital, under the will of the said lady Antonia, claims to have a right in respect of her dowry, as is stated in the statement of facts—not only for 30 years, which ought to suffice by the form of the statute, but even for 50 years and more, since that castle was freely given to them by the magnificent commune of Siena in the year of our Lord 1375, and the men, or their commune, have possessed it freely and quietly, uninterruptedly and continuously from the time of the donation down to the present day, it seems that the said commune has prescribed every right belonging to that woman in the said castle. That, moreover, from the time of that donation prescription ought to be computed against the said lady Antonia even in her dowry, although her husband was then surviving, is proved in *l. in rebus, C. de iu. do.*, where

† it is said that prescription runs against a woman in dotal property or rights from that time when she can initiate an action, as after the dissolution of marriage, or after the husband has begun to verged toward insolvency, even from misfortune. But from the time of the said donation the husband of the said lady Antonia began to be less solvent and to verge toward insolvency, because the commune of Siena deprived him of the said castle, by which he was sustained, and he was liable for the dowry of the said lady Antonia. Therefore, at the said time prescription began to run. And although in her lifetime the prescription was not completed—since she died in the year of our Lord 1400, and thus the commune possessed for 30 years only—nevertheless the prescription was finished against the hospital, which succeeded the said lady Antonia in her dowry. For preceding periods are computed together with subsequent ones, even though a church succeeds a private person, as is fully read and noted by Cyn., Bartol., and Bal. following the gloss in the *authen. quas actiones, C. de sacrosan. eccle.*, by Ioan. And. in *c. unico, de iure pa. lib. 6.* Nay more, according to the common opinion in the places cited above,

† if a church succeeds a private person against whom prescription had been initiated, it employs the right of the private person for the past time, but for the future time it uses the right and privilege of the church, by the argument of *l. fiscus, ff. de iure fisc.* For that reason Bald. said in the said *authentica*, and it was also the view of others, that if against a private person a period of five years had elapsed in that case where a prescription of 10 years with title suffices, and afterwards a church succeeds, half of the prescription has been completed; hence it suffices against the church to complete the other half, and thus twenty years are required, because the forty-year prescription alone runs against a church. To the purpose, therefore, whether we look at the form of the statute, which requires only 30 years, or the form of the *ius commune*, which against a church or a hospital requires a period of 40 years—as in the *authen. quas actiones*, cited above, and *l. omnia privilegia, C. eod.*, where it is clear that the goods of hospitals enjoy the same privilege as the goods of the church, which Bartol. noted remarkably there; what Ioan. Andr. notes in *c. 2, de in integ. restitu. lib. 6* supports this—prescription has been completed on the part of the commune of Rocca Albina. Furthermore, it is proved that no right ever belonged to the hospital, but rather the hypothecary action belonging to the said lady Antonia was entirely prescribed in her lifetime, in *l. 1 & 2, C. si adver. cred.*, where it is evident that if anyone has possessed a thing for the space of 10 years among present persons, or 20 among absent persons, under title of donation or other lawful title, he prescribes against the hypothecary action belonging to the creditor. Hence the noted gloss 2 in *l. cum notissimi, C. de praescri. 30. vel 40. ann.* said that the hypothecary action has four periods: Ten or twenty years, when a third party possesses with title and good faith, whether among present or absent persons, as in the said *ll. 1 & 2*; thirty, when in bad faith or without title, as the said *l. cum notissimi*; but if the debtor, or his heir, or another creditor possessed, it is prescribed in 40 years, as the said *l. cum notissimi*, where more fully on this. But the said commune of Rocca Albina possessed the said castle of Caligrano while the said lady Antonia, the creditor and the one holding the hypothecary right in the said castle, was living, for the space of 25 years with just title and in good faith; therefore it was prescribed against her; and thus the bequest made to the hospital was useless. Whether, therefore, we consider the *ius commune*, or the form of the statute, or the right belonging to the said lady Antonia, or that which could belong to the hospital, in every case the prescription seems complete, whether the said castle belonged to the commune of Siena or not. For if it did not belong to the commune of Siena, the commune of Rocca Albina could in good faith and under title of donation prescribe the ownership and the hypothecary action against creditors, *ff. per donato. l. 1* and the said *ll. 1 & 2, si adver. cre.* If, on the other hand, the said castle was occupied through a lawful libel and became the property of the commune of Siena, now by the donation and transfer of possession, ownership was immediately acquired for the said commune of Rocca Albina, *l. traditionibus, C. de pact.* and *insti. de re. divi. § per traditionem*, and thus there was no room for prescription of ownership, but only against the hypothecary action belonging to the said lady Antonia, since property passes even to the fiscus with its encumbrance, as in *l. 2, C. ad le. Iul. de vi. pub.*, supported by *l. si maritus, ff. sol. mat.* Nor does the addition made to the said statute stand in the way, where it is provided that no prescription shall run, or be able to be opposed, or be prejudicial against dotal instruments, or to dotal instruments against women, one or more, or against the heirs of a woman, whether they have remained with children or not. Because I say that, since that addition simply removes prescription, it ought to be understood of the long-term prescription, namely that which runs in the space of 10 or 20 years, but not of the longest-term prescription, such as 30 or 40 years, by the argument of *l. omnes* and *l. sicut, C. de praescr. 30. vel 40. ann.* Because it is not probable that the legislators with a single and general word wished to remove every species of prescription, as is uniquely proved in *c. 1, de cap. Conra.*, together with the gloss at col. 10; for the text there, at the verse *praeterea*, says 'that it be lawful for lords to revoke alienations of a fief that have been made, no prescription standing in the way'; and the gloss there calls into doubt concerning which prescription it ought to be understood, and finally concludes that it is of the long-term prescription, but not of the longest, since by that all action is barred, the said *l. sicut* and *l. omnes*. For these longest prescriptions were introduced against the slothful and those who disregard their rights, and there ought to be a difference between the slothful and the vigilant, *C. de anna. excep. l. ut perfectius* and *l. ult.*, and the laws aid the vigilant, but not the negligent, *l. non enim, ff. ex qui. cau. ma.* Nor, according to that gloss, is it to be believed that the prince, who protects the laws, wished by a general word of this kind to overturn the entire observance concerning the longest prescription, conceived and invented through much wakefulness, by the argument in *l. si quando, C. de inoffic. testamen.* and in *c. ecclesia, de elect.*, and Bald. follows that gloss there, as does Ioan. And. in the addition to Speculum under the title *de feu.* in the 2nd col., and records that he so advised. But although these arguments seem to press hard, nevertheless I deem the contrary opinion in our case to be truer. I am moved principally by that addition made to the said statute, where it provides that no prescription shall run against dotal instruments either for women themselves or for their heirs; which words cannot be verified, to those who understand rightly, except in long and longest prescription. For since in the statute itself mention had been made of long-term prescription and the longest, and in the addition placed at the end it is said universally that no prescription runs against dotal instruments, therefore it is necessary to understand it both in long-term and in the longest prescription. For subsequent words are understood according to the preceding ones, and receive their determination from them, *l. si servus plurium* and *l. qui filiabus, ff. de leg. 1* and *l. nummis, de leg. 3*, and noted in *c. ex literis, de spon.* Furthermore, since those words placed in the addition come by way of exception to the preceding provisions, it is necessary that they be understood in the cases preceding and described in the entire statute, because an exception must be taken from the rule, or from what is contained under the rule, as noted on the rubric *de reg. iur. lib. 6* and the gloss in *l. 1, ff. eod.*

† Furthermore and secondly, wherever a law or statute removes prescription in general, and it cannot be verified except in the longest prescription, then, in order that the words may effect something, they exclude the prescription of 30 or 40 years; this Bald. expressly maintained in the said *c. 1, de cap. Conra. col. 10*, where he says that if a statute provides that against public instruments no prescription runs, it ought to be understood of the longest prescription, because regularly against public instruments long-term prescription has no place; and therefore, that the words may effect something, the statute ought to be understood in the aforesaid manner. But in our case the words of that addition would effect nothing unless they were understood of the longest prescription, because in the statute to which the addition was made, the woman was already specifically privileged with respect to long-term prescription; therefore the addition ought to be understood of the longest prescription, especially since the words are general or universal, which by their proper meaning are verified in each species contained under the genus, as in *c. solitae, de maio. & obed.*, 19 dist. *c. si Romanorum*, and *l. de praetio, ff. de pub.* And since we are in a favorable matter, namely in a cause of dowry and of a hospital, a strict interpretation ought not to be made, by the argument in *c. fi. de re iudic.* and in *l. sunt personae, ff. de reli. & sump. fu.* And through this there is an answer to the last objection framed above. Thirdly and principally, it is supportive because without good faith prescription does not run, especially in real actions, as in our case, as is fully read and noted in *c. finale, de praescrip.* and by Ange. de Peru. in *l. sequitur. § si viam, ff. de usucap.* and proved in *authen. ut ecclesia Romana centum ann. gau. pri.* But the commune of Rocca Albina was in bad faith; therefore it cannot plead prescription. Moreover, bad faith is proved from conjectures, such as if there is common rumor in the locality that that property belongs to another, as Barto. notes in *l. Celsus, ff. de usucap.*; *c. quosdam* and *c. quanto, de praesump.* and *l. 2, C. si servus, vel lib. ad decu. aspi. li. 10* support this. But it is common rumor everywhere; nay rather, the law specifically provides this, that the goods of the husband are tacitly mortgaged for the dowry of the wife, and commonly the husband is accustomed also expressly to bind his goods to the wife and make from them a donation on account of marriage, as in *l. assiduis, C. qui po. in pig. hab.* and *c. ex literis, de pig.* and in *authen. de aequalitate dotis, col. 7.* And it was notorious that the said castle belonged to the husband of the said lady Antonia; therefore the said commune could not prescribe against the action for the dowry in good faith, especially since the husband did not have, apart from the said castle, that from which he could satisfy the said lady Antonia for her dowry. The text in *c. j. de praescr. li. 6* elegantly supports the aforesaid, where it is said that if by provision of law the presumption is against the one prescribing, it is not prescribed except through so much time that there is no memory of its beginning, unless a title of that prescription presumptively intervened. In our case, however, although a donation intervened by the community of Siena—which had to purge the bad faith with respect to ownership—nevertheless it could not defeat the rule of the hypothecary action belonging to the woman for her dowry, because it is certain law that goods, even passing in a lawful manner to the fiscus, pass with their burdens, especially dotal ones, as in *cap. ex literis* and *l. 2, C. ad legem Iul. de vi pu.* and in *l. si constante, in fine, ff. solu. ma.* and similar texts. I conclude, therefore, that on a double ground the hospital can defend itself against the alleged prescription. First, by virtue of the addition made to the said statute—and that a statute could do this, namely privilege a woman so that against her or her heir no prescription runs, Bald. noted in *authen. quas actiones, C. de sac. sanc. ecc.*, and *l. ubi lex, ff. de usuca.* and *l. si fundum, ff. de fun. do.* and similar texts support this. Second, from the lack of good faith by the aforesaid reasoning. And this last consideration concerns not only the person of the woman herself, but also of the hospital, to which the dotal rights were bequeathed,

† since against no one does prescription run regularly with bad faith. The first part of the defense, therefore, concerns the woman and her heir, as thrice in the said addition. The hospital, however, is not the heir, but had the dotal rights by right of legacy, as is clear in the statement of the case. Therefore, from this ground it remains to conclude that, even granting good faith in the one prescribing, no prescription runs in the lifetime of that lady Antonia, but after her death it begins to run against the hospital, yet from a deficiency of time it has not been completed: because, as I said above, against this hospital none runs except the forty-year prescription, but from the death of the said lady Antonia 28 years have not yet passed, since she died in 1400. And through this the response is clear to the contrary points alleged above in favor of Rocca Albina. For it can proceed when regard is had to the *ius commune* or to the first part of the statute, but otherwise with respect to the privilege which was afterwards added to the statute and brings benefit to women; let these points suffice. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A transaction ought to be revoked on the pretext of lesion, if the transacting party is found to have been deceived by fourfold.
2. A prescription of 30 years runs against a bequest made to uncertain poor persons.
3. The Pope alone can convert things destined for a certain pious use into another, not only remit them.
body: Having invoked the aid of Christ the Savior and of His most pious Mother, the glorious Virgin, there are two points that seem principally to support the son of Hieronymus. First, the settlement or transaction made with the administrator of the charitable trust for the poor (who was instituted heir on behalf of those same poor in two shares of the estate of the late Gerius, father of the late Hieronymus), and with others elected and deputed to this act of settlement by the commune of Radicondoli, which was appointed executor of the testament of the said Gerius by Gerius himself. Thus, the settlement or transaction was made with the heir, or the one having the force and name of an heir, and with the testamentary executor; therefore, it ought to be valid, since heirs and the executor have full power of suing, selling, and otherwise disposing, according to what is noted by Bart. in l. alio, ff. de alim. & ciba. lega., and Bald. in l. id quod pauperibus, C. de episco. & cler.; l. nulli, C. eod. supports this; for an administrator of property can also make a transaction, as is proved in l. iusiurandum, § tutor,
† cum seq., ff. de iureiu., and l. interdum, § qui tutelam, ff. de furt.

† Nor ought a transaction to be revoked on the pretext of lesion, even if the transacting party is found to have been deceived by fourfold, as says the notable text in l. Lucius, § fi., ff. ad Tre., because he gains enough who departs from litigation, as noted there and in c. pe., de emp. & uen. Secondly, prescription principally supports the said son of Hieronymus. For between him and his father they held the property of the said Gerius for more than 40 years, by which time prescription is completed both against the Church and against bequests left to the poor, especially when the place of the poor is expressly specified, as occurred here. This is proved in l. 1, joined with auth. quas actiones, C. de sacrosa. ec., 16, q. 4, c. neque decennii, and by Federic., consi. 101, where he seems to hold

† that against a bequest made to uncertain poor persons, a prescription of 30 years runs; nor ought bad faith to be presumed in our case, because sons are not presumed to know their father's testament, since they can possess the estate by right of sui heredes, although it is otherwise in other heirs, as noted by Bart. in l. qui Romae, § duo fratres, ff. de uerb. ob. But notwithstanding these points, which in truth do not stand in the way, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer: namely, that notwithstanding the settlement and prescription, there are owed to the poor, or to the charitable trust of the poor, two shares of the estate of the said Gerius, in which he instituted the poor and their trust, together with the fruits gathered and to be gathered from the time of the death of the said Gerius. I am moved principally because the words of the testament of the said Gerius are exceedingly clear, in which no doubt at all falls upon one who views them rightly. For he left to his sons born and to be born their legitime portion, and thus a third part, since he died leaving only three sons, as in auth. nouissima, C. de inoffic. test.; in the remaining shares he instituted the poor and the trust of those poor of the said town of Radicondoli, which he was able to do. For beyond the legitime of the sons, a father can dispose of his property as he wishes, especially for pious causes, as in l. 1, C. de sa. san. ec., and in c. in praesentia, de proba., and l. omnimodo, and l. quoniam nouella, and l. quoniam in prioribus, C. de inof. test. Since, therefore, no doubt fell upon these two shares of the estate, a transaction could not be made to the prejudice of the poor, because a transaction is made concerning a doubtful matter and an uncertain dispute, otherwise it does not hold, as in l. 1 and l. post rem iudicatam, ff. de trans., and l. eleganter, § fi. post rem iud., ff. de cond. ind.; and especially when it is done by one who is an administrator of the property, who cannot make a transaction by remitting a debt without cause, as is proved in l. praeses, C. de transa., and l. pactum curatoris, C. de pac., especially in bequests to pious causes, which must faithfully and without any diminution be converted to the use designated by the testator, as in l. nulli, C. de epi. & cle., to such an extent that only the Pope can convert things designated for a certain pious use to another, not to mention remit them, as in cl. quia contingit, de reli. do.; what is read and noted in the said l. legatum, ff. de admi. re. ad ciui. perti., and l. legatum, ff. de usufr. leg., and in both places by Bartolus, supports this. Therefore, the power of transacting and settling to their prejudice is lacking; indeed, it can be said that even the will was lacking, because it was expressly stated in the settlement, and in the power granted by the commune of Radicondoli to the elect, that no prejudice should be caused to the poor and to the trust regarding the estate owed from the testament. Nor can prescription be alleged against the poor, both because the disposition made by Gerius was very well known, and as it were notorious in the said castle of Radicondoli, from which is deduced the bad faith of the said Hieronymus and of the sons detaining the entire estate of the said Gerius, since the sons had been instituted only in the legitime; therefore they could not prescribe, since bad faith is proved from the common report of the place, as noted by Bart. in l. Celsus, C. de usuca. Moreover, the said Gerius died in the year of the Lord 1384 or thereabouts, and the said settlement, the testament having first been seen repeatedly by both parties, was made in 1408; and thus the property had been possessed up to the settlement for only 28 years or thereabouts, and thus prescription was not complete, even granting good faith; now, however, at the time of the settlement they began undeniably to be in bad faith, since it was able to be very clearly known that the said property pertained to the poor as to two shares; and supervening bad faith impedes the course of prescription, as in cap. fina., de praescrip., and the rule possessor, de regulis iuris, in the Sext. Concerning the aforesaid property, therefore, no doubt falls but that it can be claimed by the administrator of the said trust on behalf of the poor. But a doubt could fall upon the fruits, concerning which I conclude that if father and son were in bad faith, as because they knew the said property to belong to the poor, at least from the common report of the place, they are bound to restore the fruits gathered, and those which they were able to gather, as in l. 2, C. de pig. act., and noted in l. ex diuerso, ff. de rei uend., and in c. grauis, de re. spo.
