Concerning, however, the legitime left to the sons, I say that the poor, or the trust of the poor, can claim nothing henceforth, even if the said son of Hieronymus should die without children. The reason is very readily at hand: because Gerius left the legitime to the sons, and substituted them reciprocally in it pupillarly and by fideicommissum, and if all of them should die without children, he substituted the said trust pupillarly and by fideicommissum. And it is certain that a father can only substitute pupillarly to a son instituted in the legitime, but not by fideicommissum, because a fideicommissary substitution is burdensome, whereas a pupillary one is salutary to the pupillus himself, lest he die intestate; and in the legitime the father cannot impose a burden. These points are proved in l. quoniam in prioribus, joined with l. ex tribus, C. de inoffi. testa., where this is treated by the Glossa, Bald., and Bart. Wherefore I say that the shares of the dying brothers, if they died without a testament, passed to Hieronymus, the third brother then surviving: either from the pupillary substitution, if they died in pupillary age, or from the disposition of law, if they died in puberty, because brothers succeed to the whole, in the absence of descendants and ascendants, as in auth. post fratres, C. de legi. haered., and in auth. itaque mortuo, C. communia de successionibus, in the body of de haereditatibus quae ab intestato. Hieronymus, however, died after puberty, and thus the pupillary substitution expired, as in l. centurio and l. in pupillari, ff. de uulg. & pupil. But the fideicommissary substitution was never valid with respect to the legitime, as I have said above. It remains, therefore, that even if Hieronymus had died without children, since he died after puberty, the trust of the poor could have sought nothing of his legitime and that of his brothers, since upon the arrival of puberty that substitution made in favor of the poor expired through the aforesaid rules and the note of Bald. in the said l. ex tribus. The matter here was therefore exceedingly clear in law. Let this son of Hieronymus, therefore, have freely and unimpeded the third part of the said Gerius, and let him restore the remaining two parts to the poor and to the trust according to the testament of Gerius. Nor does it stand in the way that the testator said that all the property was obligated to the poor, because he ought not to have been believed to the prejudice of the sons, in accordance, however, with what is noted by Bart. in l. cum quis, § codicillis, ff. de leg. 2, and by Cyn. in l. generaliter, C. de non nume. pec. Let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A statute speaking generally ought not to be understood to correct the ius commune.
2. Wherever a time limit is fixed for proving something, if while the time limit is running an impediment arises by the act of the adversary, one is admitted to prove even after the time limit.
3. A newly commenced prejudicial case suspends an already pending case awaiting the outcome of that prejudicial case.
4. An accusation is instituted for punishment, not however for a compulsive effect.
5. The purpose of an accusation of forgery is that the witnesses be punished for forgery.
6. If an instrument was pronounced forged between other parties, it does not thereby prejudice another who uses it.
7. A sentence rendered against electors does not prejudice the person elected.
8. The peremption of the instance does not depend on the power of the parties and the judge; rather, time runs even against their will.
body: IN the present question concerning the brothers of the Camaldolese order, this alone is currently asked: whether the sentence rendered against them is null, as having been delivered after the expiration of the instance prescribed by statute. Having first invoked the protection of the deific Trinity, it seems at first glance that it must be said that the said sentence held valid, at least under the ground upon which it is challenged; which is first shown as follows. For first, although the statute shown to me fixes a time limit not only for the judge but also for the instance, it does not decree that a sentence delivered after that time limit of 60 days does not hold; therefore, since the sentence is found to have been delivered at least within the legal time limit, namely within a triennium, as in l. properandum, C. de iudi., it ought to hold,

† because a statute speaking generally ought not to be understood to correct the ius commune, arg. in l. quoties, ff. de actio. & obli., and Spec. in tit. de le. § restat, ver. quid si statuto seems to hold this. Secondly, the same is proved as follows.

† Wherever a time limit is fixed for someone to prove something, if while the time limit is running an impediment arises by the act of the adversary, one is admitted to prove even after the time limit, especially when the adversary provided the impediment judicially; for this is a good text in l. fin. C. de adul. at the end, and a most notable text in l. fi. § si cum ipse, ff. de excus. & temp. earum. Through which text Bal. said there that if a time limit of two months is fixed by statute to decide a case, and the other party requests a term to produce witnesses overseas or outside the province, such that the entire time limit fixed for the instance scarcely suffices for the delay of producing witnesses, arg. in l. 1, C. de dila. and 3, q. 3, c. induciae, § spacium, the judge will be able even after the time limit fixed for the instance to deliver sentence and bring the case to an end. And Bart. in effect intended the same there, saying that modern jurists had not recalled that law on the subject matter of l. properandum, cited above. But in our case, the monastery could not bring to an end the civil case it had commenced within the term of 60 days due to the act of the adversary, who criminally accused the witnesses of forgery, and thus it was necessary to await the end of this case, as I shall presently state in the following motive; therefore, even after the time limit it was lawful for the judge to render sentence. Thirdly, it is principally proved as follows.

† A newly commenced prejudicial case suspends an already pending case awaiting the outcome of that prejudicial case, as in c. tuam, de ord. cog. and c. lator, qui fil. sint legi. and what is noted in them, and in l. is qui reus, and there by Bar., ff. de pub. iud., and l. fi. C. de ordi. iud., and l. 1, C. qui acc. non pos. where by Cy., and 3, q. 11, c. prius; and in the meantime time ought not to run, because the suspension is made by law, as in the laws cited above; and time does not run against one unable to act, as in l. 1, C. de anna. exce. and l. in rebus, C. de iure do. But in our case the accusation of the witnesses for forgery was prejudicial to the civil case commenced by the monastery; therefore the time limit prescribed for the civil instance ought not to have run. That it was prejudicial is proved, because if the witnesses were convicted of forgery, the judge ought not to follow the statements of false witnesses, as in c. cum I. & A. de re iud., l. diuus, ff. de re iud., especially since when the falsity is proved and sentence has followed, it appears that the witnesses themselves are perjured and infamous, as in c. sicut, de testi. not., in l. Lucius, ff. de his qui not. infa., c. cum tu, and c. testimonium, de testi. Conversely, an absurdity could have followed, namely that the monastery would have prevailed in the case by virtue of the produced witnesses, and yet the witnesses would have afterward been condemned for forgery; whence it is better to intervene and provide beforehand than to seek a remedy after the case has been wounded, as in l. fi. C. in quibus cau. in integ. rest. non est necessa. To the same point cap. fin. de test. serves excellently, where it is said that while an accusation of crime is pending against someone, that accused person ought not to be admitted to testify in the meantime, as if his status were in suspense in the interim. Fourthly, this same point seems to be proved from the form of the Perugian statute under the rubric de reprobatione testium, that while their reprobation is pending the time limit does not run, where in effect it is provided that it is lawful for anyone to accuse of forgery the witnesses produced and their producer, and at the end of the statute it is generally provided that while the reprobation is pending, the periods of the civil or criminal instance do not run. It is no objection if it is said that the statute makes provision when not only the witnesses are accused, but also their producer, and therefore it ought not to be extended to our case, in which the witnesses alone were accused. For to this it can be answered that the said statute speaks through permissive words, not mandatory ones; for it says that it is lawful to accuse the witnesses and their producer, etc. But that which is permitted does not compel, l. non quicquid, ff. de iudi. and c. consuluit, de offi. dele.; otherwise an absurdity would follow, that it would not be lawful to accuse one without the other, which seems contrary to the form of the other statute placed under the rubric de poena inducentis vel induci facientis falsum testem, etc. Likewise it would be contrary to the ius commune, arg. in l. 2, ff. de fal. and the said l. Lucius, ff. de his, qui not. infa., and therefore this interpretation must be avoided, so that there may be departure from the disposition of the ius commune as little as possible, as in l. 1, C. de noxa. and c. cum dilectus, de consue. This is confirmed by the rubric of that statute, in which it is only spoken of the reprobation of witnesses and that during the pending reprobation the periods of the instance do not run; therefore the text of the statute ought to be verified even in that case where only the witnesses are accused, since the text ought to agree with the rubric, as noted by the gloss in c. tibi qui, de rescrip. in VI, and c. si super gratia, de offi. dele. in VI, and capitulum bonae, de confir. utili, vel inutili, especially because the end of the statute does not restrict itself to when both are accused equally, but speaks generally, and seems to refer more to the reprobation of the witnesses than to the accusation of the producer, in that it says that while the reprobation is pending, the periods of the civil instance do not run; but it is the witnesses who are reprobated, not the producer. But although these arguments seem to press in favor of the sentence, I judge the contrary opinion to be undoubtedly truer, if we wish subtly to investigate the intent of the law and of the statutes. And for a clearer decision of the case, I first premise that, looking strictly to the disposition of the ius commune, absent the statutory disposition, an already commenced civil case in which witnesses have given their testimony in due form ought not to be suspended because of an accusation of forgery criminally instituted afterward against the witnesses; which is proved by these reasons. An outcome that has no effect ought not to be awaited, as in c. cum contingat, de offic. dele. and l. ad probationem, C. de proba. But the outcome of a criminal case instituted against the witnesses alone can produce no effect in the civil case already instituted between the parties; therefore suspension of the civil case ought not to occur; the major premise was proved above, the consequence is manifest in itself; and the minor premise is proved thus. Every mode of proceeding has its own nature and its own effect, nor ought it to operate anything supernaturally, as in cap. 2, de ord. cog. and c. super his, and c. qualiter & quando, de accu. and c. licet Haeli, de simo.; 32. quaest. 7, capitulum adulterij malum, and cap. flagitia, and c. significauit, de ap. are relevant.

† An accusation, however, was instituted for punishment, not for a repelling effect, as in the said c. super his. Hence the text said in the said capitulum 2, de or. cog. that if one sued under the interdict unde vi or by another petitory action pleads an exception of his spoliation against the claimant and proves it, he repels the claimant from his claim; but he does not thereby obtain restitution, because suit was not brought for this. If, however, he brought forward the spoliation by way of accusation, each prosecutes his own action, nor is the plaintiff repelled from acting, even though the defendant says he has been despoiled, because the end of the action is not to repel, but to obtain. So I say to the point at issue,

† the end of an accusation of forgery instituted against witnesses is that the witnesses may be punished for forgery, not that the judge should not follow their statements, since they have already testified, as in l. 2, § poena falsi, ff. de falsis; therefore it ought not to produce another, civil effect, at least between other persons. I say this last to avoid what is read and noted in l. interdum, § qui furem, ff. de furtis; and consequently it ought not to suspend a civil case already commenced with another. Secondly, it is proved more strongly thus: a lawsuit conducted between others ought not to prejudice third parties, as in c. inter dilectos, de fi. instr. and in c. cum super, and c. pen., de re iu., and C. res inter alios acta, in the rubric and text; and in our subject matter it is proved very precisely by the converse case in the said l. Lucius, and in c. cum super, at the end, de ord. cog., where it is said that if an exception was raised against the producer that his witnesses were false, as is proved, and the judge on this account does not follow their deposition, the witnesses are not thereby affected with infamy, as they were not in the trial, nor did they undertake the opportunity of defense. And the text in the said l. Lucius gives the reason: because one ought not to be burdened by a sentence, just or unjust, rendered for another; the notable text in the said c. cum super gives the reason: because the accusation was not instituted against the witness, which comes down to the same thing. So I say in the converse case, namely when the witnesses alone are accused, it is inverted, that from this, prejudice ought not to be generated against the absent party who was not in the case, so that he would thereby lose the benefit of the depositions, lest he be punished for the act of another; for perhaps the witnesses were condemned because of their own wrongdoing and contumacy. Likewise they could be condemned through the imprudence or wrongdoing of the judge, as in l. si per imprudentiam, ff. de euict. and l. exceptione, ff. de fideiuss. And if the party had been present, he would have defended his case better and more carefully. If, therefore, the accuser wished to pursue that civil effect, he ought to have excepted concerning the forgery against the witnesses; which exception in effect is directed against the party, as in cap. licet, de probat. and the said l. diuus, noted by Innocen. in c. uerum, de foro competen. To this the text in l. 2, C. de fide instrumen. uniquely contributes, where it is said

† that if an instrument was pronounced false between others, it does not thereby prejudice another who uses it, unless the falsity is proved anew against him, and Innocen. noted this in capit. causam, qui fil. sint legit. Therefore, by equal reason, the same must be said in a trial and reprobation conducted against witnesses, so that it does not prejudice the litigant party who was not in the case; and Barto. openly held this there through that text, where he appears to approve the opinion of Ricar. Malum., who held precisely this, virtually on all fours with our case, in a certain disputation of his, as Dyn. and Bald. report and follow after many arguments in l. 1, C. qui accus. non pos., saying by this reasoning: because it does not prejudice the party, the civil case ought not to be suspended by a criminal accusation instituted against the witnesses alone. Let him therefore plead an exception of forgery civilly, according to them, if he wants it to prejudice the party, or let him also accuse the producer, as Barto. said in the said l. 2; and he himself held the same in the said l. Lucius. Ioan. Andr. also follows this in addi. Specu. in the said § restat, versicu. quid si statuto, where he reports the decision of Ricar. and follows it; and thus the common opinion seems to be in favor of this side; and those doctors speak even when a statute constrains the judge to pronounce within 60 days; and it is concluded that through an accusation criminally instituted against the witnesses alone, the judge ought not to stay proceedings in the principal business; otherwise the periods would run. And for this opinion the gloss in capitulum haec quippe, 3, q. 6, serves excellently, which after a long disputation concludes that, although there is the greatest connection between the person elected and the electors, because the person elected derives his right from the electors,

† nevertheless a sentence rendered against the electors does not prejudice the person elected who was not present, since if he had been present he could have conducted his case better. To the same point is what Innocen. noted in a similar matter in c. peruenit, de fideiuss. and in cap. per inquisitionem, de elect. where he speaks fully to the point. And it is generally provided that things done against an absent person ought not to harm the absent person, as in l. de unoquoque, ff. de re iudica. and 3, q. 9, cap. caueant, and c. omni; indeed Barto. says in l. nec quicquam, § ubi decretum, ff. de offic. procons. that not even a highly prejudicial interlocutory order prejudices an absent person. To the point, therefore: since acts done with the witnesses do not prejudice the producing party, the already commenced civil trial ought not to be suspended on account of this accusation, since from its suspension no legal effect could follow. Now we must see whether, at least from the form of the municipal statute of Perugia, a suspension of the first trial is induced, so that the periods of the instance would not have run while the accusation was pending. And I say that the running of the instance ought not to be impeded on this account, nor should a suspension of the first trial be induced. I am moved principally because that statute, deviating in many respects from the ius commune, must be restricted as far as possible, as in l. 3, § haec autem uerba, and what is noted there, ff. de nego. gest., and in cap. nostra, de iniur., to such an extent that we must not only depart from the words, but the words themselves are to be understood strictly and improperly, if possible, so that prejudice is done to the ius commune as little as possible, as is notably proved in c. cum dilectus, de consue. and in l. 2, C. de noxa. The municipal statute of Perugia deviates in many respects from the ius commune. First, in that it curtails the time of the instance prescribed by the ius commune; for whereas by the ius commune a triennium is given in a civil case, the said l. properandum, under the form of the said statute only two months are given. Secondly, by the disposition of the law the time runs from the day of the contestatio litis, the said l. properandum; but the statute wills that it run from the day of citation. Furthermore, by the ius commune, while a criminal accusation against witnesses is pending, the civil case ought not to be suspended, but by the form of the statute the case seems doubtful on account of those things that I stated above in corroborating the contrary arguments. Therefore, since by the ius commune this is clearer from the statements made above, we must say the same concerning the municipal law, so that the doubtful words of the statute may be drawn to the disposition of the ius commune as far as possible, so that the ius commune is not corrected, as in the laws cited above. And if the words of the said statutes are properly weighed, they do not oppose this interpretation. For the first and second statutes permitting an accusation for the purpose of inducing a suspension in the first case speak copulatively, when the witnesses and the one who produced them are accused; but for the truth of a copulative proposition, it is required that both connected terms concur equally principally, as noted in c. querelam, de simo. and ca. inter caetera, de rescr., on the rubric de proba. It does not suffice, therefore, for the purpose of obtaining a suspension, to accuse the witnesses alone, both because the statute for this effect demands two things—for which ca. olim, de rescrip. serves excellently—and because this is consonant with the ius commune, as I have said before. It is no objection if it is said that the statute speaks through the word 'it shall be lawful' (liceat), because I say that permission is given in accusing, but necessity is not imposed; so that if the accuser wishes to have the effect of suspending the civil instance, he must observe the statute just as it stands, since for obtaining this effect one of the two does not suffice under the ius commune; and for this is the notable text at the end of c. cum olim, de rescr.; l. saepe and what is noted there, ff. de uer. si. is relevant, for the words of a statute are to be taken strictly when it happens that one person is enriched to the loss of another, as noted by Bar. in l. omnes pop., ff. de iust. & iu. and l. non dubium, C. de leg.; l. ut gradatim, ff. de mu. & ho. and the said l. 2, C. de nox. are relevant. Nor is it an objection that in the rubric mention is made only of the reprobation of witnesses; because this occurs when it is treated principally, and the producer is accused on account of the falsity of the witnesses. Furthermore, it is nothing new that the text of a statute provides more broadly than is contained in the rubric, as is proved in C. etiam ob chirogr. pe. pi. te. po., joining the rubric and the text; to the same point are c. fi. and c. si super gratia, de off. del. in VI, for in the rubric there is contained only de off. delegati, and yet in the text provision is made concerning custom and the execution of a sentence, which in many ways differ from delegation. In the same way the other objection made above is removed, namely that at the end of the second statute it is said in general that while reprobation is pending, the periods of the instance do not run, etc.; because I say that the person accusing the producer of the witnesses acts principally toward the reprobation of the witnesses, for by their reprobation the producer is convicted, as is clear in the third statute; therefore the statute dealt simply with reprobation. Furthermore, subsequent words are determined and declared by preceding words, as in l. si seruus plurium, and l. qui filiabus, ff. de leg. 1, and l. nummis, ff. de le. 3, especially when such determination and interpretation is consonant with the law, as in our case, the said c. cum dilectus. And that this was the mind of the statute is proved thus: for the third statute provides that once the witnesses are reprobated, the one who produced them must lose the case, whether it is proved that he falsely introduced them or not; and that cannot be verified unless the producer himself has been cited and accused, l. fi. C. si per uim uel alio modo, l. de unoquoque, ff. de re iud., and 3, q. 9, c. caueant, and c. omnia, dist. 8; because the producer must lose the case in the event of the victory of that reprobation, the second statute rightly enacted that while this reprobation was pending, the periods of the instance should not run, because this case of reprobation conducted in the aforesaid manner was prejudicial to the civil case, the said l. j. C. qui accu. non poss. But where the producer is present, the effect of losing the case cannot follow, lest an absent and undefended person be condemned; rightly, the suspensive effect of the first case cannot follow, because when the foundation is removed, the building falls, 1, q. 1, c. cum Pau., l. 1, and what is noted there, ff. quod ui aut clam. It is no objection if it is said that notification was made to the monastery that the witnesses had been accused, because I say this does not suffice; for since the accusation aims principally at the punishment of the witnesses themselves, the monastery was not bound to appear, because it had no legal interest; for it knew that its right remained uninjured; it could, however, have appeared if it wished to avoid some degree of presumption, an excellent arg. in l. a snia. in prin., de ap. For mere notification or knowledge of the pendency of the accusation ought not to harm it in its right, which was already separate from the crimination of the witnesses; for this I adduce an excellent parallel text in c. cum super, de re iudi. The other motives originally alleged do not stand in the way. And first, when it is said that the sentence at least had the time prescribed for the instance by the law, the answer is twofold. First, that since the statute provides that the time limit of 60 days runs from the day of citation, it is openly apparent that the statute intended to correct the ius commune, and thus to depart from the disposition of the ius commune; therefore the sentence must be rendered within the time prescribed by the statute, otherwise it is not valid, since in this case the statute must be observed to the letter. Bal. openly held this in l. properandum, 1st response, ver. quid ergo si statutum, C. de iu. Likewise and secondly, wherever a time limit is prescribed for an instance, that time limit succeeds in the place of the legal term. To this point is what Innocen. noted in a similar matter in c. ex ratione, de ap.; therefore it must be deemed governed by the same law as that term, so that just as a sentence rendered after the statutory term is not valid—and this is the common opinion of Cy., Bar., and Bal. in the said l. properandum; Io. And. follows it in add. Spe. in tit. de le. § restat, ver. quid si statuto; at the end of c. personas, and c. cum sit Romana, de ap. serves excellently. To the second motive I say that clearly no legitimate impediment befell the adversary, because a criminal accusation is entirely separate from a civil case; therefore by its pendency the civil case ought not to have been suspended, because an inference is not drawn from separate matters, l. neque natales, C. de prob., and it was fully proved above; for each lawsuit could proceed on its own course; and by these remarks I remove the third motive. For I say that an accusation instituted against the witnesses alone is in no way prejudicial to the already commenced civil case, in which, since the witnesses had already given their testimony, and at the time of the testimony the credibility of the witnesses did not waver in the least, proceedings could move to sentence; because a condemnation of the witnesses following afterward ought not to be drawn back to an already consummated act; for it is enough, as I have said, that witnesses be tolerated at the time of their testimony, even if they are afterward reprobated, l. j. C. de testi. Likewise, since the party was not in the trial, that reprobation ought not to prejudice him; for it is enough that it have effect against the witnesses themselves, for whose punishment alone action is brought, as I have fully stated above; and if the decision of the civil case does not depend upon the outcome of that criminal case, it rightly cannot be called prejudicial. To the other arguments sufficient answer has been made above. From all these things I conclude that, by an accusation of forgery instituted against the witnesses alone, the already commenced civil case ought not to have been suspended, and consequently the sentence rendered after the time limit prescribed for the instance by the statute is not valid, since it is found to have been rendered after the instance had expired, and thus without proceedings, as in the said l. properandum and what is noted there; nor is the pronouncement of the judge made with the consent of the parties—that the times of the instance should not run in the meantime—an objection, because since that was contrary to the statute and contrary to law, as is clear from the aforesaid, it was not valid; for the expiration of the instance does not depend on the power of the parties and the judge; rather, time runs against their will, as is clear in the said l. properandum, and from the form of the first statute, where mention is openly made of the judge's pronouncement, that in the prolongation of the instance it is not to be of assistance except in certain cases specified in the statute, which are entirely outside our case. And these things suffice. Nic. Ab.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument: 1. There is room for repentance in legal penalties up to the sentence, even against the proper meanings of words.
body: Having implored the help of Almighty God, in the question concerning Ottonello I shall use few words, both on account of the remarkable haste of the petitioner, and because the present matter has been sufficiently and abundantly examined by the excellent doctor, Lord Salustio. Wherefore, as to the first doubt, I say that on multiple grounds the said Ottonello ought not to be punished with the penalty of l. si, de rei vend. First, because the text of that law expressly imposes that penalty if he is convicted by his adversary. But before this Ottonello was convicted of falsehood by his adversary, he revoked his confession; therefore that penalty has no place. To this point I cite the clear and notable text in auth. quid propriam, C. de non nu. pec., which seems to decide that question, especially in conjunction with l. eum qui, ff. de iureiu.; and auth. item possessor, C. qui po. in pig. ha., is in favor of this, because a confession can be revoked with impunity if no disadvantage accrues to the adversary, just as in our case no disadvantage underlies it, since the adversary had proved nothing to the contrary before the revocation of the confession; the text is almost on all fours with our case in l. de aetate, § si, ff. de inter. act.; c. si, de confess. supports this, and the text joined with the gloss in c. cum in positionibus, de iureiu. in 6., in the gloss at the words 'iusta causa', at the end, which notably says that just as a witness is excused from perjury, as in c. praeterea, de testi. cogen., if he corrects himself immediately, so too, by the same reasoning, is the one positing or responding. Second, it principally supports this:

† because in legal penalties there is room for repentance up to the sentence, even against the proper meanings of words, as in l. quae maior, § accusasse, and l. in servitutem, § petiisse, ff. de bo. lib., noted by Bar. in l. in criminali, C. de iud. om. iud., and Dyn. in l. amplius, ff. rem rat. hab.; the said l. si, therefore, ought to be understood as applying when the denying party has persevered in his denial, lest the humanity of just repentance be cut off, as the text says at the end in l. si quis libellos, C. de app., 2, q. 6, c. si quis. Third, Ottonello can clearly be aided from a different ground. For when in his exceptions he said that he had held and possessed the goods claimed for ten years and less, he sufficiently confessed that he had begun to possess them ten years ago and possessed them thereafter up to this point. For this is denoted by that copulative conjunction, and one that is continuative of time, as is commonly noted by the canonists in c. licet, de prob., and Bar. in l. Celsus, ff. de usucap.; whence, from those words, the said Ottonello sufficiently confessed that he presently possesses those goods claimed, especially since the said Ottonello in the subsequent words said that he ought not to be sued because Lord Pandolfo had granted those goods to him as his own, etc.; and thus he confessed that he was in possession, because otherwise, in the absence of possession, he could not have been sued by the vindication of a thing. For a vindication of a thing requires two extremes, namely ownership on the part of the plaintiff, and possession or detention on the part of the defendant, as in l. in rem actio, joined with l. finis autem and l. officium, ff. de rei ven.; therefore, since it was evident in court that this Ottonello possessed, or at least had presented himself as the possessor, he ought not to have been interrogated after the fact as to whether he possessed, because an interrogation preparatory to trial is not to be made except insofar as necessity requires; the text is in l. 1, ff. de inter. act., and there by Barto. at the beginning; whence, since the judge had ordered response to be made to the interrogatories, with the reservation of the law of irrelevant and inadmissible matters, to which if answer were not made, he pronounced that it be held as not answered; therefore, since the said interrogation for the aforesaid reason was superfluous, and thus not to be admitted for the aforesaid reason, it is to be held just as if that negative response had not been made, because acts done can be held as not done with respect to legal effect, as is noted in l. in bello, in § factae, ff. de captiv., and almost that entire title supports this. And it is no objection if it is said that an excipient does not confess, as in c. cum venerabilis, de excep., and in the rule 'exceptionem', de reg. iur. in 6., and in l. non utique, ff. de excep.; because I say that those laws proceed when the adversary wishes to base himself upon the purely factual content contained in the exception itself, as for example if against one claiming a debt I opposed an agreement not to sue, there is no doubt that I confess that the agreement intervened, but not that a debt preceded, because this latter is tacitly included and consists in law, while the former is express and consists in fact, as is noted by the gloss that intended this, to one looking rightly, in the said rule 'exceptionem', the said c. cum venerabilis, and more clearly Ant. de But. held this there. I cite the clear text in c. ex parte decani, de rescrip.; and this as to the first doubt. As to the second doubt, whether the said Pandolfo could by his statute deprive that Lady Lagia of her goods on account of her contumacy and disobedience in refusing to return to reside in the city of Fano according to the mandate of her lord made under penalty of confiscation of goods; I think it must undoubtedly be held that he could, to which in my judgment the text in l. si, ff. de decre. ab ordi. fac. seems clear, where it is evident that a statute under the most severe penalty against subjects that they reside in their municipality is valid. Add the text in l. mercatores, C. de merca. & mer., through Bart. in l. relegatorum, § interdictae, ff. de interdic. & rele.; to the same effect is what Inn. notes in c. postulasti, de foro comp., where he says that the lord of a place can make a statute regarding the confiscation of goods that are in the place, even if the owner of the goods is not subject there; whence much more strongly could Lord Pandolfo do this for just cause regarding goods situated in his territory and against persons subject to him; to this point l. incola and l. assumptio, ff. ad municip.; for Lord Pandolfo, as vicar of the Church, could exercise this jurisdiction for his own benefit, and even greater jurisdiction, according to what is noted by Barto. in l. cunctos populos, near the end, C. de sum. tri. For not only mere and mixed imperium is granted to these vicars, but also regalian rights, as is noted in the said l. cunctos populos; nor could the said woman allege ignorance, since she came to the place, was informed of the statute, and, despising the mandates of her lord, departed, as is now presupposed in fact. And this lastly answers the third doubt. As to the fourth and last doubt, indeed, I say that although at the beginning it could be called into doubt whether credit should perhaps be given to the podestà asserting that a commission regarding issuing the bans was made to him by Lord Pandolfo, through what is contained in l. unica, ff. mand. prin., and what is noted by Io. And. in c. 1, de offi. leg. in 6.; nevertheless, having regard to the fact that the podestà asserted this publicly, and that he was an honorable person, and also and more strongly because Lord Pandolfo himself wished these goods to be confiscated by virtue of the said bans; it is most clearly proved that the commission was made by the said Pandolfo; because from a subsequent act a presumption is drawn for the past, argument for all the aforesaid in c. nobis, dist. 97, and in cap. scribam, de praesump., and what the gloss notes there. It also supports this that enunciative words that are necessary to the utility of the statement fully prove, as is notably proved in l. optimam, C. de contrahen. & committen. stipu.; to the aforesaid points l. illud, ff. de acqui. haere., and c. literas, de proba., and in l. licet, C. de iudi., lend support. Niccolò Abbate.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A judgment rendered against a procurator is not valid if it is denied that he was a procurator.
2. Credence is not given to a cardinal to the prejudice of another.
3. If a procurator was appointed by me to receive borrowed money, he does not obligate me if in an instrument he confesses that he received the money, yet it does not appear that he truly received it.
4. A privilege conferred upon a corporation is lost through contrary use, even by individual members of the corporation.
5. An argument from what commonly happens is valid.
6. After a judgment has passed into res judicata, all things are presumed to have been done properly and rightly.
7. A judge who has taken cognizance of a marriage can take cognizance of the dowry accessorily as of something dependent upon it.
casus: Case of the following consilium. In the cause and dispute which is pending or expected to be pending between the community of Recanati on the one part, and the community of Osimo on the other, concerning the exemption from paying tolls or customs duties in the territory of Recanati by the men of the city of Osimo, or persons of its district, according to an award and arbitrament which is said to have been rendered once and a second time between the said parties: first by the late most reverend father Napoleone, Cardinal and at that time legate in those parts; secondly by the formerly venerable man lord Nicolaus, citizen of Osimo, then secretary of the Roman Pontiff.
body: Having invoked the protection of Jesus Christ the Savior from the heart. First, that the community of Osimo supports no justice in this regard. For from the arbitral award that is said to have been first promulgated by the said Lord Napoleone, the said community of Osimo cannot base its case; since there is no proof of an arbitration agreement made in that matter, nor of the procuracy claimed at that time by the asserting syndics, but only of the said award alone; and since it is now denied by the city of Recanati that they were syndics, nor can proof of their authority be furnished otherwise, the award or judgment is invalid, even if it had otherwise been promulgated by a competent judge. For a judgment rendered against a false syndic or procurator is null and void to the prejudice of the principal himself, as in c. ex insinuatione, and in c. in nostra, de procur., and l. licet, C. eo. tit., unless the principal ratified the act performed by the false procurator, l. licet, ff. de iudic., and l. 3, § falsus, ff. rem rat. hab., and l. si pecuniam, ff. de neg. gest. But in our case it is not proved that those asserted syndics had a mandate from the beginning, or that the community of Recanati ratified their acts; therefore, judgment must be given just as if they had never had a mandate. For to not exist or not have existed, and not to appear, are equivalent in effect, as in c. solennitates, de consecr., dist. 1, and l. in lege, ff. de contrahen. empt. For he who asserts that he was a syndic must prove it, because facts are not presumed, de offi. deleg., c. cum in iure, de procur., c. 1; for these extrinsic facts are not presumed unless expressly proved, l. quaecunque, ff. de publi. Nor does it suffice that the judge asserts in the judgment that they were syndics, because credence is not given to him, as in c. quoniam contra, de probat.; and on this point there is a notable and magisterial gloss in the said c. cum in iure, de offi. deleg., which expressly states

† that a judgment is not valid if it is denied that he against whom the judgment was rendered was a procurator, unless it is shown that he had a mandate. For this reason it advises that the instrument of procuration, having observed the due formalities, be inserted into the instrument of the judgment, or that the original itself be otherwise preserved. Inn. expressly intended the same there, and the venerable doctors commonly incline toward this opinion there. Indeed, Bartolus said in the said l. licet, C. de procur., that if a judge pronounces someone to be a procurator, that pronunciation does not harm an absent principal who was not in court and denies having given him a mandate, arg. in l. de unoquoque, ff. de re iud., and 3, q. 9, c. caveant, and c. omnia. Nor should the dignity of the cardinalate existing in the person of the said Lord Napoleone be of aid,

† because credence is not given even to a cardinal to the prejudice of another: this is a notable gloss which held this in replying to c. nobilissimus, dist. 97, in c. sicut, de sent. excomm.; it is clearly proved in c. a nobis, in c. ex quadam, and c. licet universis, de testib. Likewise, because he proceeded as an arbiter or as an arbitrator, as is clear from the tenor of the award; and credence is not given to an arbiter to the prejudice of the other party, l. ne in arbitris, C. de arbit. Likewise, neither could the judgment or award rendered by the said Lord Nicolaus assist the said community of Osimo, because the submission to arbitration was not general, but was restricted solely to the disputes that had arisen concerning the boundaries, as is clear from its tenor. Therefore, the said Lord Nicolaus exceeded his commission in many respects, insofar as he approved in all things the judgment of Lord Napoleone, which contained very many articles beyond the boundaries. Therefore, the judgment is null in those matters, since an arbiter has no power except insofar as is contained in the compromissum, as in c. cum dilectus, de arbit., and in l. non distinguemus, § finali, ff. de arbit. And above all, an amicable compositor must not extend himself to those matters which were not contemplated, as in l. cum Aquiliana, ff. de transact. And the same seems to be said even when the submission to arbitration was general; for an arbiter or arbitrator cannot thereby stretch his hands to those matters about which there was no controversy, as is the notable text in l. si cum dies, § plenum, ff. de arbitris, where it is said that although a general compromissum be made—for example, in all controversies and questions—it is nonetheless not extended to those matters about which there was no dispute between the parties. Hence Bartolus noted significantly in l. cum Aquiliana, ff. de transact., that if there was a controversy between you and me concerning a certain estate, and we submitted to an arbiter and gave him full power of arbitrating, the arbitrator cannot thereby award the estate to one and condemn that party to give the other some other thing about which there was no dispute, by the said § plenum and by l. non distinguemus, § de officio, ff. eod. But in the submission itself made to the said Lord Nicolaus, the dispute was solely concerning boundaries, nor does any discussion appear to have been made concerning other things; therefore he could not judge concerning other things, and if he did, he labored in vain. Nor does the homologation made by the syndics stand in the way: because, since the homologation and approval of a null judgment have the force of a kind of new pact or contract according to what is read and noted in l. 2, C. communia utriusque iudic., and by Bartolus in l. una, C. qui pro sua iurisdict., the act of the syndics had no validity in this matter, because they did not have the power to contract or make a pact, but only to submit to arbitration. Therefore, they exceeded their authority, and consequently the act was null, l. diligenter, ff. mandat., and c. cum olim, de offic. deleg. What Bartolus notes in l. 2, § creditum, ff. si cert. pet., and l. si debitorem meum, de novat., where he concludes, serves the purpose:

† that if I appointed a procurator to receive a loan of money, it does not prejudice me, nor does it bind me, if in the instrument he confesses that he received the money, yet it does not appear that he truly received it; for the mandate ought to have been understood of a natural loan. Thirdly and lastly, the prescription of longest time, which can be alleged by the community of Recanati, works against the community of Osimo, on the assumption that the said awards had been valid from the beginning.

† For a privilege conferred upon a corporation is lost through contrary use, even by individual members of the corporation, as in c. si de terra, and c. accedentibus, de privil., since the corporation thus allows acts to be committed against the privilege. Indeed, by a contrary act without any predefined limit of time, a privilege granted to private persons is lost; the same if it was granted to a corporation, provided it does not principally concern the favor of the Church, as in c. cum accessissent, in fine, de constit., and there fully by the gloss and doctors; and a privilege given to do something is lost through non-use over a space of 10 years, which is the notable text in l. una, ff. de nundin., and there by Bartolus. And likewise, on the assumption that a personal action belonged to the community of Osimo from the said awards, nevertheless a personal action is regularly extinguished by a space of 30 years, as in l. sicut, C. de praescript. 30 annorum. But in our case, from the time of the first or second award, almost 60 years have elapsed. Good faith, moreover, is presumed, as the gloss notes in c. sanctorum, and c. si diligenti, and c. finali, de praescript., and especially in these incorporeal things, on which fully by Bartolus in l. 1, § 1, ff. de itin. actuque privat., and l. Celsus, ff. de usucap., and by Cino in l. 1 and 2, C. de serv. et aqua. Let the truth therefore turn whither it will, because the claim of the community of Recanati is well founded. And truly, although these and many other things which could have been alleged in favor of the community of Recanati—which I have passed over for the sake of brevity—seem very pressing, nevertheless, if one examines everything correctly, and especially joins them together into one, it will clearly appear that the community of Osimo maintains justice under both heads, namely from the award of Lord Napoleone and of Lord Nicolaus; and this will be drawn forth more clearly if we direct our eyes to both at once. For first, it must be considered that the first award was promulgated by a Cardinal, at that time legate in those parts. A Cardinal, to whom even alone, outside of custom, at least in the Roman Church, full credence is given concerning acts done before him, as in c. constitutus, de appell., and there Johannes Andreae and Hostiensis follow this; noted by Speculator in the title de teste, § 1, at the word 'quid si advocatus', where he says that Pope Clement pronounced that this proceeds from general custom rather than from strict law; and that he is believed, c. quod super his, de voto, also serves very well, for there the seals of those Cardinals were unknown, and therefore they were not believed, but it would be otherwise if they had been known, as is read and noted there. To the same point c. nobilissimus, dist. 97, serves very well, where according to the common understanding credence is given to a Cardinal if he asserts that he is a legate, and thus in attributing to himself an ordinary, honorable, and desirable office; therefore, all the more should credence be given if he asserts in his judgment that syndics having the power for this from the community of Recanati submitted to him as arbiter, since this office of arbitrating is more burdensome than honorable. Nor does a great prejudice turn on this, because, as is clear from the form of the award, he attributed many things to the community of Recanati in compensation for those which he commanded to be granted or conceded to the community of Osimo. Therefore, taking into account the lightness of the prejudice, credence ought more easily to be given to the assertion of the Cardinal, especially since he was legate in those parts. For by reason of the dignity of the legation, greater credence must be given, l. liquet, in fine, C. de summ. trinit. et fid. cath., 11, q. 1, c. quicquam, and l. episcopale, C. de episc. aud., and what Innocent notes in c. nuper, de testib. Likewise and secondly, since that was an arduous matter and widely publicized on account of many scandals that arose between those two communities, as is clear from the tenor of the judgment, it is not likely that the agitation of that business before that Cardinal legate by the asserted syndics of the community of Recanati did not reach the ears of the men of Recanati, arg. in c. quorundam and c. quanto, de praesumpt. Therefore, by not revoking those syndics in so great an affair, it must be presumed that they had given a mandate, according to the notable dictum of Innocent in c. ex parte decani, de rescript.; the text of Inst. de his per quos acquir. poss. is relevant. I corroborate this most strongly: for since it cannot be denied that the syndics submitting to arbitration before the said Lord Nicolaus had a mandate, since that is clearly established, and that they homologated and approved his award, in which nothing else is contained except the form of the award of that lord cardinal, it must be presumed that they brought and presented the form of that award to the community. For this happens commonly among everyone,

† and the argument from things that commonly happen is valid, as in c. 1 and what Calderinus notes there, de cler. non resid. Therefore, by receiving the form of that award, in which mention was made of the arbitration and of the award rendered by the said cardinal with the intervention of their syndics, and by not contradicting it, they are deemed to have approved their act, by Clem. 1, de procur., and by l. si filius, ff. ad Maced., and by that which Bartolus notably sets forth in l. quo enim, ff. rem rat. hab., and l. cum tabernam, § idem quaesiit, ff. de pignor., and l. Titius Seiae, ff. de constit. pecun., in which laws he maintains that if someone receives an instrument or letter containing something to his prejudice, and does not protest to the contrary, he is deemed to consent to it; and if something was done in his name, and he receives an instrument concerning this and does not contradict it, he is deemed to approve, and this is sufficiently proved by the laws cited above. Thirdly, the notable dictum of Bartolus in l. sciendum, ff. de verb. oblig., serves, as do originally the Glossators in l. 1, C. de fid. instrum. et iure hastae fisc., lib. 10, and Innocent in c. quoniam contra, de probat., where they commonly note that credence is given to the enunciative words of an instrument when that enunciated fact could have occurred at the time the instrument was drafted. For this reason Bartolus said in the said l. sciendum that if an instrument says, 'having seen the instrument of debt, faith having been had that such is the just price, no auction of the property having been made, etc.', that instrument proves that the debt is established and that that is the just price, because these things could have occurred at the time the instrument was drawn up. So I say in the matter at hand, since the Lord Cardinal said in his pronouncement that the mandates of the syndics were established, and this faith could be given at the time of the instrument of the judgment by the provision of the instrument. Therefore, credence must be given to this instrument of judgment, especially in a very ancient matter, for it is difficult to review all the acts through very long times. For this reason Innocent says in c. bonae, de elect., and in c. cum in iure, de offi. deleg.,

† that after a judgment has passed into res judicata, things are presumed to have been transacted properly and correctly; a good text for this is in c. sicut, in fine, de re iud., noted by Hostiensis in c. cum inter, eod. tit., and Calderinus fully in c. quoniam, de probat., and especially when the judgment was rendered in the presence of the parties. For since the syndics were present and did not contradict, but rather approved, the compromissum is to be presumed, according to what is noted by Innocent in c. innotuit, de eo qui furt. ord. rec., and by Speculator in the title de sent. prolata, § iuxta, at the word 'notandum', and in the title de instrum. edit., § qualiter, toward the end, at the word 'in summa'. And just as from the lapse of time there is a presumption in favor of the judgment of a judge, so also in favor of the declaration of arbiters, as Dino held in a certain consilium of his, 13, recounted and followed by Johannes Andreae in the additions to Speculator in the title de arbit., § sequitur, at the word 'quod si actum fuit compromisso', and more clearly by Antonio de Butrio in the previously cited c. quoniam contra, col. 20. But from the judgment or award of Lord Nicolaus, the community of Osimo can undoubtedly, in my judgment, help itself on a threefold ground: first, from the form of the compromissum; second, from the new approval of the syndics; third, from the ratification of the community of Recanati, which must be presumed, as will be said below. I said first that it could help itself from the form of the compromissum, namely that disposing, because he had a mandate for this. And first, considering this very briefly—since I am a lover of brevity—the community of Recanati gave the syndics a mandate to compromise concerning boundaries and other disputes; likewise to prove, confirm, and revoke judgments and awards previously promulgated between the said parties, which words can clearly encompass the dispute that had arisen long ago regarding the non-payment of tolls, especially since an award had previously been rendered concerning them, and express mention was made in the mandate regarding the approval and revocation of the award. Nor is a mandate to be restricted, but rather broadened, as Innocent notes in c. sedes, de rescript., especially in our case, where it was given to submit to arbitration and settle for the sake of peace and quiet; for favors ought to be broadened, as in the rule 'odia', de reg. iur., in VI. The syndics indeed submitted, and although they seem to restrict it to the cause of the dispute concerning the boundaries alone, because they gave a mandate also concerning the tolls, because the dispute over boundaries was connected with the payment. For in compensation for the non-payment to be made, the boundaries had perhaps been established to the prejudice of the city of Osimo by the said Lord Cardinal; whence, a dispute having arisen concerning the boundaries, that question of the tolls was sufficiently dependent and connected, since an award had been made regarding those two together for the sake of concord; c. si postquam, de elect., in VI, serves to this point. And in a similar manner we say

† that a judge who took cognizance of a marriage can take cognizance of the dowry accessorily as something dependent, where otherwise he could not have taken cognizance principally, as in c. de prudentia, de donat. post divor.; and that an arbiter, even if it is not expressly stated in the compromissum, can take cognizance of coherent and connected matters, is stated in the gloss that cites texts for this in cap. cum dilectus, de arbit.; and where two things are connected, he who withdraws from one is deemed also to withdraw from the other, and in seeking restitution of one, it is necessary to judge also concerning the other. In addition to these points, there is what is read and noted in l. etiam, ff. de minor., and what is read and noted in l. cum actum, § 1, ff. de negot. gest., serves excellently for our case. Secondly, I said that, assuming that the award beyond the article of the boundaries had not been valid from the beginning because it was rendered by one not having authority, nevertheless, since the syndics knowingly approved and homologated that award, it has at least the force of a pact and a new contract, as in l. 2, C. communia utriusque iudic., and by Cino and Bartolus in l. una, C. qui pro sua iurisdict.; what the gloss notes in c. significasti, de foro compet., serves to this end. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the syndics did not have the authority to contract or make a pact anew, because I say that they had the authority to receive and approve whatever award was to be rendered by Lord Nicolaus, and they expressly understood that they could judge also concerning disputes other than the boundaries, as I said above. Likewise with respect to confirming and revoking judgments and awards previously given, as is stated in the procuracy. Therefore the mandate directly extends, and can extend, to all contents in the judgment of the Lord Cardinal. For what is stated generally is to be understood generally, l. de pretio, ff. de public., and c. si Romanorum, dist. 19, and c. solitae, de maior. et obed., especially because authority was given to them regarding all the aforesaid matters to do whatever that community and its men could have done personally; by which words authority is given even in those matters that require a special mandate, as Bartolus notes in l. procurator cui libera, ff. de procur., and l. creditor, § Lucius, ff. mandat. Thirdly, I said that the community of Osimo can base its case upon the ratification of the community of Recanati itself. For, as I said before, it is to be presumed from things that commonly happen that those syndics brought to the community a copy and the instrument of that award promulgated by Lord Nicolaus, in which was also contained how those syndics approved it in the name of the community. Whence, assuming that the syndics had not had a mandate for this, nevertheless, since the community knew of the approval made in its name, and received the instrument concerning this, and did not contradict it, it is deemed to have ratified it, the said l. filius, ff. famil. ercisc., and the said l. cum tabernam, § idem quaesiit, ff. de pignor., and the said c. 1, de procur., and what Bartolus notes in the said l. quo enim, ff. rem rat. hab. And this is an excellent consideration. And through this it is clear that on multiple grounds the community of Osimo can help itself against the community of Recanati regarding the non-payment of such tolls. What is said concerning prescription does not stand in the way: for, this being considered, custom properly has no place in our case, because custom is a kind of general law, but not capable of appropriation, dist. 1, c. consuetudo. Prescription, however, takes away from one and grants to another. And this is one of the substantial differences between custom and prescription, as noted by Johannes in c. finali, de consuetud.; what he himself notes in c. 3, de consuetud., in VI, and by Cino in l. 1 and 2, C. quae sit long. consuet., serves this point. Since, therefore, the issue here is the extinction of a right residing in the community of Osimo by virtue of the awards and the concession of the syndics, custom properly has no place, and thus the running of 10 years, by which custom is regularly introduced, ceases, as is read and noted in l. de quibus, ff. de legib. It is necessary, therefore, that prescription intervene, which was caused out of hatred of one neglecting his right, and consequently in favor of the one prescribing, according to what is held in 16, q. 3, c. dilecto, § potest, by Dino in the rule 'possessor', in VI, and Bartolus in l. 1, ff. de usucap. In our case, however, negligence arising from non-use of the judgment is not given. Since, therefore, the award or judgment concedes, in an act of mere faculty, immunity from paying tolls, to such an extent that if the men of Osimo had carried nothing through the territory of Recanati for a thousand years, no prescription would have been introduced, because prescription or custom is not introduced by non-use since it does not have an included act contrary to the disposition of the competent right, as Cino notes in l. 2, C. quae sit long. consuet., and Johannes Andreae in chapter Ioannes, de cleric. coniug. It is proved manifestly that they cannot be said to be negligent in this, since those are acts of mere faculty. And what is held regarding the loss of an urban servitude in l. haec autem iura, ff. de servit. urb. praed., serves this point; nor can this be called a rustic servitude, which is prescribed by the mere passage of time from non-use, as in the said l. haec autem iura, and l. sequitur, § si viam, and what is noted there, ff. de usucap., because in our case a right of passage through the territory did not belong to them, since that right is free to anyone, nor is the capacity of going or transporting granted, but a right of not paying belonged to them whenever the men might wish to bring something through the territory of Recanati. Therefore, that right is not lost except by a contrary act, namely by payments made for goods carried through the territory; nor, in my judgment, does it suffice to prove that some men of Osimo paid, because this right belonged to the community and is an incorporeal right. Whence it is not prescribed unless certain knowledge on the part of the community against which prescription runs is established, because the mere tolerance of the owner is possession in these incorporeal things, and possession cannot otherwise be had, as is proved in l. 2, C. de servit. et aqua, fully by Innocent in cap. bonae (2), de postulat. praelat., and in cap. conquerente, de offic. archid., and cap. 2, de in integ. restit., and in many other places by Bartolus in the said l. 1, ff. de itin. actuque privat., and Cino in the said l. 2, or first, C. de servit. et aqua. Unless, therefore, the majority of the people of Osimo is proved to have paid, it cannot be said that prescription was initiated against the community, or unless payment had been made so often and so openly by the majority that knowledge would likely have reached the community itself, in which that right resided, as is noted in the previously cited laws; otherwise, negligence of the community is not given, nor can possession be acquired on the part of another, as is noted especially by Innocent in the said cap. bonae. As to how much time is required in either of the aforesaid cases, I believe that a time of 30 years is required, because by such length of time a personal action, which in this case belonged to the Osimans, is regularly prescribed, as in l. sicut, C. de praescript. 30 annorum. Yet from this time there must be deducted the time of hostility, when it was so great that justice was not administered in the place, as in cap. ex transmissa, and there by Innocent, de praescript. Likewise the time of pestilence, because that is God's hostility, on which by Bartolus in l. naturaliter, ff. de usucap. Likewise the time of probable knowledge of those awards, because since prescription does not run with bad faith, it must also be considered whether bad faith can be proved from conjectures, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. Celsus, ff. de usucap. Likewise in our case, since it concerns the imposing of tolls, it must also be considered whether the community of Recanati has this right of imposing and exacting tolls through so much time that memory of its beginning does not exist; otherwise, in the absence of a prince's privilege, this right cannot belong to a city or to any other short of the prince, as is proved in l. vectigalia, ff. de public., and l. si publicanus, § in omnibus, eod. tit., and in both places by Baldus, and in l. 2, C. de vectigal. et commiss.; an excellent text in cap. super quibusdam, de verborum significat., serves this point. For in this case prescription properly runs against rights reserved to the prince as a mark of special privilege; therefore so much time is required, as in the said cap. super quibusdam. But where that right did belong to the city of Recanati, and it was a question of prescribing against a right belonging to the Osimans from those awards, I say that the time required for prescribing against the Roman Church is not required, because that privilege of one hundred years applies to rights immediately pertaining to the Roman Church, such that through the prescription prejudice is caused to the Roman Church itself. It is otherwise, however, when rights belonging to subjects of the Roman Church are prescribed, as in our case; because then the ordinary time suffices, as the gloss and the doctors after it clearly held in c. ad audientiam, de praescript., and cap. dilectus, de capell. monach., and in cap. volumus, 16, quaest. 4, and there by Archidiaconus. And this is so because the issue now does not concern prejudice to the Roman Church, but to subjects, since rights are being prescribed which were not with the Roman Church; what Innocent notes in chapter conquerente, de offic. ordin., serves this point excellently. I conclude, therefore, that in order for prescription to run against the community of Osimo, it must be proved by the community of Recanati that, with the knowledge or payment of the majority of the people of the city of Osimo, it was in quiet possession or quasi-possession of collecting tolls from the men of Osimo for 30 years, in such a way that from these 30 years there be deducted the time of wars and pestilence in the aforesaid manner, and the time of knowledge which they could likely have had of the said awards and of the right belonging to the Osimans. For an obligation is regularly introduced through a ten-year period, as noted in l. si de eo, ff. de acquirend. possess., and in l. 1, C. de serv. fugit. Likewise that it had this right of introducing tolls into their territory from a privilege of the prince, or through so much time that there is no memory of its beginning. And I have set down these statements thus generally because the case of prescription was proposed to me generally, and thus I could not give a certain response, as in cap. de muliere, de sponsal., with similar texts. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Under canon law, heirs can begin prescription from themselves if they have good faith.
2. A prescription once interrupted, even civilly by joinder of issue (litis contestatio), can no longer be commenced on account of presumed bad faith.
casus: The factual contingency is presented as follows: A certain man having two natural children by a concubine, namely a male and a female, wishing to legitimate them, took the concubine as his wife, and at length made his last will, in which he instituted his male son as universal heir, but left to his daughter, who was already married, four hundred florins by right of institution; and he made this will of his in his own house, lying sick in bed, in the presence of seven witnesses asked to attest, besides the notary who wrote the will. When the testator at last died, the male son held the entire inheritance, as was contained in the will, and lived for twenty years after his father's death, and at length died leaving several children. Nine years having elapsed from the death of their father, the children were sued before the Podestà of Siena concerning the said legacy of four hundred florins left by right of institution to the said daughter of the first testator, and a procurator appeared for them as heirs and contested suit before the Podestà; eventually the instance lapsed, and much other time having elapsed, and in the meantime thirteen years ago now, one of the said sons, the grandsons of the first testator, was sued concerning the said legacy, insofar as it touched him for his proportional share; concerning which an arbitration agreement (compromissum) was made between the parties, and suit was contested before arbitrators; now, most recently, a certain action arose between the same persons, and before the most recently chosen arbitrators, the exception of prescription of the legacy is pleaded, since fifty years and more have elapsed from the time of the said legacy. Nor ought the joinder of issue made before the Podestà to stand in the way, because he who is now sued was then a ward (pupillus), namely of the age of nine years, and according to the statutes of Siena a ward cannot be sued except before the judge of wards, and otherwise the proceeding is invalid, and thus that joinder of issue must be regarded as not having taken place. Nor does the joinder of issue made before the arbitrators thirteen years ago stand in the way, because by then the debt was prescribed [?]. It is asked what the law is.
body: Having humbly invoked the protection of Jesus the Savior and of His most pious Mother, three matters are briefly to be examined for the clear decision of this case. First, whether the son of the first testator could have prescribed from his own person. Second, what is the status of the children of the heir himself, the grandsons of the testator himself. Third, presupposing that the prescription was begun, whether it was interrupted by the joinder of issue (litis contestatio) had before a judge not his own, and what is the status of the joinder of issue afterwards had before arbitrators. As to the first, it seems that the son could have prescribed, because he is presumed to be ignorant of the paternal will, since it consists in fact according to what is fully noted by Bartolus in l. qui Romae. § duo fratres, ff. de uerbo. obli., and a possessor in good faith prescribes against legacies and an inheritance even when arranged for pious causes, as in l. fin. C. de sac. sanct. eccle. and 16. q. 4. cap. fin.; to which makes what the gloss notes in l. licet, C. de iure deli. And the same seems to be said regarding the children, the grandsons of the first testator, since they likewise and even more strongly are presumed to be ignorant of the grandfather's will, since they succeed from the person of their father; nor does the joinder of issue had before an incompetent judge stand in the way of the newly sued party, because such a joinder of issue does not interrupt prescription, as is the text joined with the gloss in l. penul. C. ne de sta. defun., noted by the gloss in c. ut debitus, de ap., and cap. ex tuarum, de pur. can., and 16. quaest. 3. c. dilectio. § potest. Nor does the joinder of issue lastly made before the arbitrators stand in the way, because at that time prescription was completed, computing the time of the son and of the grandsons; and therefore interruption has no place, as noted to this purpose by the gloss in c. uigilanti, de praescri. and Johannes Andreae in regula possessor, de regu. iu. lib. 6. in Mercurialibus; and from these the response to the second and third doubt is clear. But notwithstanding these, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer in our case, on a threefold ground. First, because the son of the testator is presumed to have had notice of the will, since as a fact it is presupposed to me that the will was found in the house of the son himself, and thus it was in the vacant inheritance, l. si quae cautiones, ff. fam. ercis., and anyone is presumed to have notice of those things that are his own, l. quisquis, C. de rescinden. uen.; to which makes c. ab excommunicato, de rescr. and c. cum illorum, de sent. excom. Furthermore, the will was executed publicly in the house of the testator himself in the presence of seven witnesses and a notary, with the son being present in the place of the testator; therefore he is presumed to have had notice of it, an excellent argument in cap. quosdam, and c. quanto. de praesum., and l. consensu. C. de repu., and what is noted by Bartolus in l. 1. ff. si cer. peta. and 16. dist. c. quod dicitis, and c. 1. de trasla. praela. Nor does Bartolus differ from these in the said l. qui Romae. § duo fratres, for there he expressly holds that from conjectures knowledge ought to be presumed even in a son. There is also another conjecture of knowledge, because since the testator had two children, namely a male and a female, and by civil law they ought to succeed equally upon intestacy, as in authen. defuncto, C. ad Tertu., and the son possessed the whole inheritance according to the disposition of the will, he is therefore presumed to have had notice of it; for otherwise we would presume in him a wrong and usurpation, which in doubt is not to be presupposed, just as we say in the case of a stranger possessing the entire inheritance, that in doubt we presume him to have had notice of the will lest an intention of usurping be presumed, as noted by Bartolus in the said § duo fratres. And there is the same reasoning concerning a part as to a part, just as concerning the whole as to the whole, as in l. an pars, ff. pro derelic.; to which makes cap. pastoralis, verse item cum totum, de offic. deleg.; and this last indeed would suffice for presuming knowledge. If, therefore, the son had knowledge of this legacy, he could not prescribe, as in c. fin. de praescrip. and what is noted by Bartolus in l. priuilegia, C. de sacrosan. eccle. And consequently, the children of this heir who succeeded to the inheritance could not prescribe either, because the bad faith of the deceased harms the heirs in prescription, so that they cannot even begin prescription on their own behalf, as is the text noted in l. cum haeres, ff. de diuer. & temp. prae. And this is undisputed in civil law, by which law the present question must be decided, since it is between laymen, according to what is noted in c. 2. de arbi. lib. 6. and regula, possessor, de re. iu. li. 6., and by Bartolus in the said l. priuilegia, C. de sac. san. eccl.

† Under canon law, however, whether heirs can begin prescription on their own account if they have good faith, is noted by Dynus in the said regula possessor; it could be said that they can, out of a certain canonical benevolence, on the argument of what is noted in c. de quarta, de praesc. and c. cura, de iure pa. But I have always held the contrary, so that in this canon law does not differ from civil law, because it is not found to be provided for by law, as in c. 1. de ope. no. nun. Nor do the points noted in the authorities alleged by Dynus stand in the way, because those do not speak of an heir who derives his right from the deceased and is deemed the same person as the deceased, as in auth. de iure iu. a mor. prae., but of a successor in a dignity, who does not derive his right from the deceased, but from a superior from whom he received institution, nor is he deemed the same person as the deceased; he deservedly prescribes if he has good faith, even if his predecessor had bad faith; and from this ground judgment must undoubtedly be given for the legatee or her heir. The second ground favorable to the legatee is that, presupposing that the son of the testator had been ignorant of the paternal will, he nonetheless could not prescribe on another ground: because he was either a possessor in bad faith, since he believed the inheritance belonged by half to his sister, as is provided by law, and nevertheless possessed the whole in its entirety and could not prescribe, and the same applies to the children heirs for the aforesaid reason; or he was mistaken in law, believing that the whole inheritance belonged to him as a male, and he also could not prescribe, because an error of law prevents prescription, as in l. nunquam, ff. de usu., nor is an error of law to be presumed, as noted in l. sine culpa, ff. de re. iu., and by Bartolus in l. sed & fi. § scire. ff. de peti. haere. and l. quod Nerua, ff. depo.; to which makes l. quemadmodum. ff. de agr. & censi. lib. 11. and regula, qui con iura mercatur, de re iud. lib. 6. Therefore, let the truth turn wherever it will, prescription cannot have a place in our case. On the third ground the legatee or her heir ought to prevail, because presupposing that the said son had lawfully begun prescription, nevertheless because after his death for nine years, and thus before the prescription of 30 years was completed, all the children, grandsons of the testator, were summoned to court, and through the legatee or her heir were certified of the grandfather's will, and the said legacy was demanded from them, the said prescription was interrupted, so that they could no longer prescribe because of the supervention of bad faith, as in c. fi. de praescr. and in regula possessor malae fidei, de re. iu. lib. 6.; to which makes what is noted by the gloss in regula sine possessione, under the same title and book, and in c. 1. 16. q. 4. where it is noted

† that prescription once interrupted, even civilly through joinder of issue, can no longer be begun on account of presumed bad faith. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that that joinder of issue was had before an incompetent judge, because I say that here it was interrupted not on account of the civil act of the joinder of issue, but on account of the supervention of bad faith, which, since it consists in fact, does not require the competence of the judge or a judicial act; this was notably held by Antonius de Butrio in c. ut debitus, de ap. on gloss 1, where he said that if from the proceedings before an incompetent judge the defendant was rendered a possessor in bad faith, the prescription is interrupted, as in a similar case is noted on the exception when through it one is constituted in bad faith, as in c. cum dilectus, de or. cog.; to which makes what is noted in c. at si cleri. de iud. But in our case such things intervened before the incompetent judge, through which he against whom the action is now brought is presumed to have fallen into bad faith, since the grandfather's will was alleged and the legacy made in it, and an extract of the will was tendered in so far as it pertained to the cause; what is more, the will was always in the house of this defendant and of his brothers, so that they could see it immediately, and it is likely that they saw it, or it is to be imputed to them if they neglected to inform themselves, argument in l. quod te, ff. si cer. pe., and elegantly by Bartolus in extraua. ad reprimen. on the word denaturationem, toward the end, where he holds that even out of court an heir can be constituted in bad faith through plausible information. Nay more, I say that even without that information these grandsons of the testator were unable to prescribe, since from the fact that they always had the will in the house they are presumed to have known of the legacy, argument in the said l. quisquis, C. de re. uen., and what is noted by Bartolus in the said § duo fratres; and consequently they could not prescribe, and this alone would suffice against them.
