For bad faith is proved from conjectures, since it consists in the mind, as noted by Bartolus in l. Celsus, ff. de usuca. and l. j. § j. ff. de iti. actuque priua.; and this alone would suffice to impede the completion of the prescription; and this is the fourth ground for obtaining victory. Nor is it of any help that this defendant was then nine years old, because he is sufficiently capable of deceit to comprehend those things that were facts, namely that a legacy was written in the will, especially since it had been alleged by the plaintiff who drew him into the suit; to this purpose excellently c. j. de deli. pue. and l. 1. ff. ad Sill. § impuberi, and what is noted by the gloss in cap. presbyter. 68. dist., through the doctors in cap. cum nobis, de praescrip.; and let these things suffice. I conclude therefore that the said legatee, or her heir, promotes a just cause, the alleged prescription notwithstanding. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A city exercising regalia has as much power in its territory as the prince has in the whole world.
2. A disposition of a prince simply made contrary to his preceding determination or interlocutory decree does not hold due to a defect of will.
3. Extraordinary burdens are odious, and they are not to be exacted without great cause and the express consent of the prince.
4. When the usufruct of houses and of those things that are in those houses, except for silver, is bequeathed, those things that were acquired for the sake of trade are not included.
casus: The case is presented in effect as follows: The city of Florence, having many places subject to it in temporal matters with full right, among which is the city of Arezzo, assigned and allocated all its ordinary revenues, with certain exceptions, for the interest of the monte, that is, of those moneys which in time of necessity it receives and exacts from its subjects, for which it answers at five, or a little more or less, per hundred. And it is the custom of that community to appoint every four years certain officials who are to make provision as to what of the revenues of the community is to be assigned for the interest of the monte and what is to be expended for other necessary purposes. Matters standing thus, it happened that, an urgent necessity arising of paying stipendiaries appointed for the service of the said community, certain elected citizens possessing power for this purpose burdened extra ordinem many persons subject to them, among whom they burdened the city of Arezzo to pay one hundred florins each month for 39 months. And all these burdens, or superindictions, imposed by the said citizens were to be paid to the chamberlain of the conduct of the stipendiaries. Meanwhile, during the said time, it was provided by the Florentines that the said superindiction of one hundred florins should be paid by the city of Arezzo for the four years following after the end of the said 39 months, from the month of December 1427; and it was ordained that the said superindiction of one hundred florins, which was paid to the chamberlain of the conduct, should be paid to the said monte for its interest. Finally, when the time of the said four years had ended, and payment had been made each month as had been disposed and ordained, certain citizens were elected who were to make provision as to what should be assigned to the monte. Having examined all things previously assigned to the monte, they reported in the council of the said city of Florence that it was useful and expedient that all revenues formerly assigned to the monte be confirmed for four years. The general council, however, without making any express mention of individual revenues, made provision by these general words that follow, namely: that all assignments made for the payment of the interest of the monte which are now in force, and which were in force in the month of December immediately preceding, are from now understood to be and are prorogated and confirmed, and remain in their former force for the period of four years, saving those which, namely, have been provided to the contrary. From this it is asked whether the said superindiction of one hundred florins is seen to be prorogated for the four years contained in the said provision.
body: Having implored the aid of Almighty God, it seems initially as follows: for power is not lacking in this prorogation;

† because a city exercising regalia has as much power in its territory as the prince has in the whole world; noted by Bar., especially regarding the cities of Tuscany, in l. infamem, in fin. ff. de publ. iudic. and in l. 1. ff. de aqua plu. arcen. and l. hostes, ff. de cap.; what is noted by Barto. in l. decernimus, C. de sac. san. eccle., and Innocen. in cap. cum P. tabellio, de fi. instru., and in cap. cum te, de re iud. supports this; the text in cap. per uenerabilem, qui fil. sint legi. and cap. super quibusdam, de uerb. signifi. strongly supports it. But it is certain that a prince can impose superindictions, or extraordinary burdens, upon subjects, as in l. una. C. de superindic. lib. 10. Indeed, he can by his own law make an extraordinary burden ordinary, as in l. 1. C. de superindic. eod. lib.; therefore a city possessing regalia can also do this, cap. 1. quæ sint regalia, colum. 10. Likewise, cause is not lacking: for the possessor of regalia, just like a prince, can confiscate even the goods of private persons for the sake of the republic, as is read and noted in l. item si uerberatum, ff. de rei uend. and l. Antiochensium, ff. de priuileg. credito., noted by Innocen. in cap. quæ in ecclesiarum, de consti. and Barto. in l. fin. C. si contra ius uel util. publi. and Cy. in l. rescripta, C. e. Nor are words lacking, since the aforesaid provision prorogated for four years the assignments made for the interest of the monte, not only those that were in force at the time of the reform, but also those that had been in force in the month of December immediately preceding, at which time that superindiction was in force; whence that law intended to feign that the prorogation had been made at the time when the superindiction of one hundred florins was still enduring, and this was intended by those words of the reform therein: 'From now they are to be understood to be, and are, prorogated and confirmed, and remain in their former force, etc.' For the word 'intelligantur' ('are to be understood') is a feigned or presumed word, and not a factual one, as in c. ex studiis, joined with the gloss, de præsump. and l. 1. §. eiectione, ff. de ui & ui arma.; and it is certain that the law can feign an act to have been performed retrospectively, as is read and noted in l. si is, qui pro emptore. ff. de usuca. and l. si maritus, ff. de adult. and cap. ad literas, de tempo. ord. and ff. de cap. & postli. re. throughout, especially in l. postliminium, eodem tit. And by this is removed what can be objected, namely that that which was not existing could not be prorogated; because to prorogate is the same as to extend, and this presupposes an existing state, as in l. sed si manente, ff. preca., and what is read and noted in cap. de causis, de offic. deleg. and l. priuatorum, C. de iurisd. om. iudic. Likewise, the will of the enactors is not lacking, because in doubt that will is gathered from the words, as in l. non aliter, ff. de lega. 3. and cap. fin. de uerbo. significa. and l. prospexit. ff. qui & a quibus. For no one is presumed to say what he did not think in his mind, l. Labeo. ff. de sup. leg. and 22. quæstio. 2. cap. is autem. Since power, cause, words, and intention concur in this prorogation, there is no reason why we should interpret to the contrary. But truly, although the aforesaid and similar arguments that could be brought forward seem to urge strongly in favor of this affirmative position, nevertheless, if we weigh the matter diligently and accurately, the contrary opinion would in my judgment prevail. And first I premise that not all things that arise can be openly decided by statute, but, in the absence of a statute, recourse must be had to analogies in the laws, as in l. non possunt, ff. de leg. and cap. cum dilecti, de confir. uti. and c. translatæ, de consti. and l. illud, ff. de consti. and l. illud, ff. ad leg. Aquil.; l. natura enim rerum, ff. de præ. uer. supports this, where, failing an analogy, recourse must be had to natural reason, as in l. scire oportet. §. sufficit, ff. de excu. tuto. and cap. secundò requiris, in fi. de ap., noted by the gloss in c. consuetudo. 1. di. But by surveying through the analogies of the laws and canons and through natural justice, this contrary side—namely that the said prorogation is not to be extended to the superindiction of one hundred florins—will be openly demonstrated. And first, on this point, there is in my judgment virtually a text in c. cum olim, de re iu., where it is openly concluded,

† that a disposition of the prince made simply, contrary to his preceding determination or interlocutory decree, does not hold on account of a defect of will, because the prince is not presumed to wish to act contrary to his preceding interlocutory decree unless otherwise expressed; and through that text Bar. says notably in l. quod iussit, ff. de re iud. in fi. that if in the same judicial proceeding regarding the same fact two contrary interlocutory sentences appear, and it does not appear that the judge rendered the second with the intention of revoking the first, the first does not seem to be revoked, because it must be clear to the judge that the first was delivered, l. hoc autem. §. 1. ff. ex quibus cau. in pos. ea. Just as we see in a similar case that someone is not deemed to renounce a right of which he is ignorant, l. mater. ff. de inoffi. testa., nor is a soldier deemed to disinherit a son whom he is unaware of having, as in C. de testa. mi. l. sicut certi.; and in an ordinary judge, on account of the multiplicity of facts, Bar. presumes ignorance, just as in the said c. cum olim ignorance is presumed in the prince. Thus and even more strongly must it be said in our case. For since a certain law and a fixed limit or lifetime had originally been given by the Florentines to that superindiction, namely that it should end at the close of four years, it is not likely that in that reform or general ordinance concerning the revenues to be assigned to the monte they wished to include that superindiction, which had already previously had a fixed lifetime and term set by the community itself, because it is not to be presumed in case of doubt that the said community wished to go against its determination previously made, and thus intolerably and constantly to vex its subjects with extraordinary burdens—subjects already vexed for a long time and afflicted by harsh wars—since it is the duty of a good prince to assist his subjects with favor, and it is in his interest to have wealthy subjects under him, as in Auth. ut iud. sine quoquo suf. §. cogitatio. And this is especially to be said in our case because the disposition and ordinance of the community can have its place and force without that superindiction, by the argument in c. 1. de iureiur. lib. 6., and because these

† extraordinary burdens are odious, and without great cause and the express consent of the prince they are not to be exacted, as in the said l. una, C. de superindi. and in Auth. item nulla communitas, C. de sac. san. eccle. and by Ioan. And. in c. 2. de immu. eccle. Secondly and principally, I introduce the case noted in c. dilecti, de dona., where it is held that if after many gifts an onerous clause is annexed at the end, although general, it is nevertheless not referred to that gift which was more unconditional and had its own special determination. And through that text Specu. said, in the title de instru. edi. §. nunc autem uidendum, under the verse item excipe, that an onerous clause placed at the end is not referred to a disposition having its own special determination; and Bartol. held the same in l. talis scriptura, ff. de leg. 1. And what he himself noted in l. prætor ait, ff. ui bo. rap. notably supports this, where he says that those things which deviate from the common law are not understood to be repeated in a law enacted generally afterwards. But in our case that superindiction was assigned to the monte with a certain determination, namely that it should last for four years only; therefore, the general provision made afterwards ought not to be extended to that superindiction having a determination and a fixed lifetime by the disposition of the community, but rather to the other assignments made to the monte which were not so privileged, nor had a determination so limited, especially because in odious matters a strict interpretation must be made. Thirdly, l. Paulo Callimacho. §. 1. de leg. 3. notably supports the same, where it is held that if many legacies were made to one person in a testament, some of which were conditional, but others unconditional, and in codicils afterwards the testator made legacies to the said legatee and added that he ought to be content with them, that general disposition made in the codicils is referred only to the legacies that were uniform and due presently, but not to those that were due in the event of the heir's death, and this out of great equity; and concerning that text Bartol. made a great celebration in l. fideicommissa. §. si quis ita, ff. eod. titu., and intended to extend it to all legacies made under a condition, which were not uniform with the others. So notably and singularly it can be said to the purpose that the reform now generally made ought to be extended to the assignments that were in force in the month of December which were uniform, but not to the said superindiction of one hundred florins, which had a fixed limit and condition or determination. Fourthly, in corroboration of the aforesaid, it supports this that the said provision newly made disposes by prorogating the assignments that were then and previously in force for the interest of the monte; but since the said superindiction had been assigned casually and for a time for the interest of the monte, it cannot be said to have been simply assigned to the monte, so as to fall under the general disposition made concerning the assignments to be prorogated. To this I notably introduce l. quæsitum, in princip. §. fina. and l. si ita legatum, ff. de lega. 2., where it is proved that those things which are present by chance are deemed to be absent. For someone there bequeathed things that were there by chance: they are not deemed bequeathed; to the same point, l. generali. §. uxori, ff. de usufructu leg., where the text notably says,

† that upon a bequest of the usufruct of houses and of the things that are in those houses, except the silver, those things that were acquired for the purpose of trade do not pass, which are feigned not to be in the house, since they had not been destined to be in the house, but had been placed there accidentally. Behold, therefore, that even an exception made from a legacy does not confirm the legacy in other things that are not of the same nature as the rest contained under the general disposition; to the same effect l. Seio. §. medico, ff. de annu. lega. So must it be said in the present matter, from the aforesaid and many other similar authorities that could be alleged, which I omit for the sake of brevity, since the aforesaid are sufficiently abundant. I conclude, always saving a better judgment, that the said provision newly made is not to be extended to the superindiction of the said one hundred florins, especially since at the time of the provision that superindiction was already extinguished, nor ought the fiction of which I spoke at the beginning to be introduced, by the laws alleged above. From the aforesaid, the answer to the laws and reasons brought forward above for the contrary party is sufficiently clear: for in our case the will of the prince is lacking, as is gathered from the aforesaid. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Legal experts are not accustomed to allege laws when opinions are sought by judges of causes.
2. If someone was captured on account of reprisals declared in hatred of you, and if I was compelled to make satisfaction, I can bring an action against you and recover.
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of our Savior and of His most pious Mother, the undefiled Virgin. In the question which is presently pending between Giacomo, formerly [son] of Tommaso, banker, plaintiff on the one side, and Matteo, formerly [son] of Simone, heir of the late lady Mattea on the other side, concerning the redemption of certain books, as is gathered from the acts of the case brought, I shall make use of a succinct and brief conclusion, since this is a decisive opinion and not one issued upon the petition of a single party, following in part dominus Johannes Andreae in the chapter sicut, de re iudi., saying

† that legal experts are not accustomed to allege laws when opinions are sought by judges of causes; otherwise if they are sought by the parties. I say therefore that in the decision of this question the duty of the lord podestà ought to consist in condemning the said Matteo, as the heir of the said lady Mattea, to the redemption of the books subjected to pledge by a certain Giovanni of Florence, an arbitrator or calculator chosen on behalf of the said lady Mattea while she was living, and in consigning the said books thus redeemed to the said Giacomo, the plaintiff. I was moved to the aforesaid opinion principally because, when a doubt arose from the beginning in the calculation of accounts, calculators of accounts were lawfully chosen by the said parties, as is proved in l. si residuum, C. de distra. pig., and l. arbitro, and there by Bartolus, ff. qui satisd. cog., and l. hac edictali, C. de sec. nup., and l. 1, ff. de uent. inspi., and c. fraternitatis, de frigi. & malefi., and chapter proposuisti, de proba. And concerning these experts in their craft, to be chosen even by the judge, fully by Bartolus in the prooemium of the Digestum Vetus at the verse item nota hic, quod illi qui periti sunt, etc., and in l. 2, in fin., C. de rescin. uendi. Moreover, to those thus chosen, something is lawfully given by way of remuneration, which is called an honorarium, as in l. prima, ff. si mensor fal. mod. dixe. And they also lawfully claim it, whether it be a salary fixed for them from the beginning, or that which they are accustomed to hire out their services for, concerning which see Bartolus in l. 1, §. ludi quoque, ff. de uar. & extraord. cog., where the text makes mention of these calculators; to the same effect, l. excepto, C. loca.; and provision must be made for them by the parties whose business they manage, just as is said regarding delegates and assessors, as in chapter statutum, §. insuper, and §. assessores, de rescrip., in the Sext. Since, therefore, this sub-pledging of the books occurred from the act of the said lady Mattea, or of her procurator having a mandate for this, and in hatred of the said lady Mattea, or of her heir not paying the agreed or customary salary to the said Giovanni, chosen as calculator on her behalf, from which pledging indeed the said Giacomo incurred damage without any fault of his own, because he lacks the use of the books, therefore he was able to bring an action against the said lady Mattea, or her heir, so that he may redeem the said books and keep him indemnified, even presupposing that the said Giovanni acted wrongfully in pledging the books. This seems clearly proved by that which is read and noted in l. nam et seruus, there by Bartolus, ff. de neg. gest., where it is proved that if I have suffered, even unjustly, any damage on account of your act, I can bring an action against you for the satisfaction of the damage; to the same effect, l. licet, in fin., ff. nau. cau. sta., and l. si non, §. cum autem, ff. de his qui deie. uel eff., and l. si merces, §. culpa, ff. locati, where there are excellent texts on our subject; and he who is the cause of the damage is deemed to have caused the damage, as in the final chapter de iniu. & dam. da., and what is noted in the chapter sicut dignum, de homi., supports this. And on these laws Bartolus notably said in the treatise on reprisals, at the tenth verse,

† that if I was captured on account of reprisals declared in hatred of you, and I was compelled to make satisfaction, I can bring an action against you and recover what I was forced to pay on account of your deed and out of hatred of you; and Bartolus affirmed the same in the said l. nam et seruus. He touches upon the same in l. 2, in fin., ff. de uerbo. obli.; to the same effect is what the same Bartolus noted in the treatise on the tyrant, and l. creditor, ff. de sol., where he says that if a debtor, through the wrongful act of the creditor, was compelled by a tyrant to pay the debt, he obtains release, at least in effect. He held the same in a similar case in l. cotem ferro, §. qui maximos, ff. de publi., where he affirms that if someone buying a toll from a city suffered very great damage on account of a war which the city waged against another, or which was waged against it, he can bring an action against the city for his interest, because he suffered damage from its act or hatred. It must be said in precisely the same way in the matter at hand, since from the act of the lady Mattea herself, in choosing that Giovanni as her calculator, the said Giacomo incurred this damage of lacking the books, that he can bring an action against the heir of the same lady Mattea for satisfaction of the damage, and thus for the redemption of the said books. And what the doctors note in c. calumniam, de poenis, supports this. It is no objection to the aforesaid conclusion if it be said that the said lady Mattea was a usufructuary, and thus the expenses of the litigation ought to belong to the heir, who was the owner of the property. For to this it can be answered in multiple ways: and first, that the said lady Mattea was bound to the said Giovanni on a contract made in her name, which is clear from the fact that she appointed a procurator even to choose the calculators of accounts, and promised under hypothec and the obligation of all her goods to hold ratified and pleasing whatever the said procurator should do in the said cause and in matters depending on it; and thus, even after the renunciation of the usufruct, the said lady Mattea remained obligated to the said Giovanni, chosen through her procurator, to provide for him for his labor. For this there is a good text with its subject-matter in l. procurator, and that which is read and noted in l. post mortem, §. tutor, ff. quando ex fac. tu. Moreover, the said lady Mattea was fighting to obtain her own right, and thus she ought to have campaigned at her own expense. Likewise because a modest expense, even when made on property on which a usufruct is established, belongs to the usufructuary and not to the owner of the property, as in l. hactenus and l. si pendentes, ff. de usufruct. Moreover, and thirdly, whether she is bound to the expenses or not is not to be cared about in our case. For it is enough that the said Giacomo incurred damage from her choice, or that of her procurator. For it must be imputed to her if she chose such a person, arguing from l. cum mandato, in fin., ff. de procur. And from the aforesaid, the answer to what is objected by the other side is clear, namely that the said lady Mattea was dead at the time when the said calculators reported. For, as I have said before, it is enough that this damage occurred from her choice, and thus from her act, for in this the beginning must be considered. For the said lady Mattea after her renunciation, or her heir after her death, ought immediately to have provided that no damage could occur to the said Giacomo from her choice, and to settle with the said calculator. For satisfaction had to be made to him for his labor, since it was not through him that the matter failed to have effect; for this see what is read and noted in l. 1, §. diuus Seuerus, ff. de uar. & extraordina. cog., and better in l. sed addes, §. cum quidam, ff. locat. It is also a matter of absolute law that an obligation incurred against the person of the deceased passes to the heir, as in l. ueteris, C. de contrahen. & commit. stipula. Lastly, it is no obstacle if it be said that the books do not belong to the said Giacomo, because this is false; for since he had contracted a partnership with Adoardo, and through him was managing the affairs of the partnership, the books of the partnership were common, wherefore a partner can bring an action against a partner by the actio pro socio for the production of the books, as in l. quaedam, in the first response, ff. de eden.; wherefore any of the partners can sue for the whole for his own convenience, especially because, since the said Giacomo carried on business through Adoardo alone, he is deemed to have appointed him his institor. Whence he was bound by the acts performed through him, according to what is fully noted by Bartolus in l. eadem, ff. de duobus reis, and had mandated him to draw up the books according to what is read and noted in the said l. quaedam, especially by Bartolus. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The hypothecary action is prescribed through a third party with a legitimate title over the space of ten years.
2. Prescription does not run against one who is legally hindered from bringing an action.
3. Prescription with good faith was introduced partly in favor of the possessor in good faith, and partly in hatred of the one who is negligent in pursuing their right.
casus: A certain Ioannes of Siena, testamentary heir of Angelus of Siena, granted, gave, and delivered to lady Nicola, daughter of the said Angelus, an estate, the Titian estate, possessed by the said Angelus and left to the same lady Nicola in the said testament, Ioannes promising to the same lady Nicola and her heirs, as the aforesaid heir and in his own name, always to defend and disencumber the said estate from every person, etc. And for the observance of the aforesaid, the said Ioannes obligated himself and his heirs, and his present and future goods, as is more broadly and clearly evident concerning the aforesaid by a public document under the hand of a public notary. After this, the said Ioannes sold certain goods of his, and among the rest he sold a certain house to a certain Titius of Siena, and eventually [?] for his transgressions he was publicly banished and declared a rebel, and all his goods were confiscated. Very recently, however, a dispute was brought against the said lady Nicola concerning the said estate left to her by the said Angelus, her father, by a certain Caius of Siena; and the said Nicola, as soon as the suit was brought against her, denounced and notified the said suit brought against her to the said Ioannes, that he should come [?] and appear by himself or through another to defend her and the said estate in the said suit brought against her by lord Caius; which Ioannes was always contumacious in the aforesaid matters. Finally, lord Caius obtained a judgment in his favor against the said lady Nicola in the said case, and the said estate was adjudicated to the said Caius, to be held by way of pledge for the debt claimed by him. Now, however, since the said estate has been evicted, the aforesaid lady Nicola, having carried out a lawful discussion against the said Ioannes and his goods, which are not found to be available, likewise brings a hypothecary action against the heir of the said Titius, the purchaser from the said Ioannes, for the release of the said house obligated to her under the hypothec by virtue of the aforesaid obligation made to her by the said Ioannes in the aforesaid manner. This heir pleads as an exception against the petition of the said lady Nicola that the said lady Nicola is not to be heard in the aforesaid matters, since he has held and possessed the said house through himself and through the said Titius, formerly his father, by the aforesaid title of purchase for a period of ten years and well beyond, and thus has prescribed the said house, and cannot be molested concerning it by virtue of a certain statute of Siena, whose tenor is known to be as follows, namely: 'And whosoever shall have possessed any thing of his debtor or of another person by a just title for ten years without contradiction or molestation by his said debtor or by the one whose thing it was, shall prescribe it, and may not be molested concerning it in perpetuity, any chapter of the constitution notwithstanding.' Now it is asked what is the law.
body: Having invoked the protection of our Savior and of His most pious mother, it seems at first that the said heir can defend himself by virtue of the said statute, since he has possessed that house by a just title without contradiction of any person for a decade and more: therefore he cannot in any way be molested by anyone, as is provided by statute, and since the words of the statute are clear, they need no other interpretation, l. ille aut ille, ff. de leg. 3. and l. non aliter, eod. titu. and de reg. iu. ca. 2. and de verbor. sig. cap. fin.; nor can there be doubt about the validity of the statute, especially in this city of Siena, which exercises princely rights, as in l. omnes populi, and which is noted especially by Bar. near the end of his repetitio, de iust. & iu., and by the same in l. infamem, ff. de publ. iudi. at the end of his apparatus. Furthermore, even if the said statute were entirely set aside, the said heir seems safe under the ius commune.

† For the hypothecary action is prescribed through a third party with a legitimate title over the space of ten years, as is proved in l. 1. & 2. C. si aduer. cre., noted in l. cum notissimi, C. de præscript. 30. annor in glo. 2. But this heir, and the deceased, had a title pro emptore, as ff. pro empt. l. 1. Moreover, good faith is presumed in this case: because one is not presumed to have knowledge of another's hypothec, since it consists in fact, as in the rule, præsumitur, de regu. iur. lib. 6. and l. error facti, ff. de iu. & fa. igno. and l. cum quis, C. eod.; and that good faith is to be presumed is noted in cap. sanctorum, and cap. fin. de præscript., noted by Bartol. in l. Celsus, ff. de vsucap. and l. 1. §. 1. de iti. actusque, pri.; for it is sufficient to allege good faith: because, since it consists in the mind, it cannot be proved, as is noted by gl. instit. de act. §. aliæ. But notwithstanding these points, which in my judgment truly do not stand in the way, I hold the contrary opinion to be truer. I am moved first by a reason that in my judgment is incontrovertible.

† Prescription does not run against one who is legally hindered from bringing an action, as l. 1. in fin. C. de anna. except. and in l. rebus, ff. de iu. do., in which it is clear that prescription runs neither against a filiusfamilias regarding adventitious property, nor against a woman regarding dotal property while the marriage stands and during the father's power, because by law they cannot sue; but prescription runs from the day on which they can bring an action; to the same effect is capit. quia diuersitatem, de conces. præben., especially when the impediment occurs before prescription had begun, according to the doctrine of Barto. in l. senatus, ff. de offi. præsi. But it is certain that in our case the said lady Nicola always, up to the present day, lacked the legal capacity to act: because before the thing is evicted, one cannot sue, although it may be said that the thing belongs to another, as in l. qui rem, and l. si post, C. de euic.; therefore, hitherto prescription has not had place against her. Furthermore,

† prescription with good faith was introduced partly in favor of the good-faith possessor and partly in hatred of the one who is negligent in pursuing their right, 16. quæst. 3. capitu. præscriptionum; to this makes what is noted by Bart. in l. 1. ff. de usucap., and Dy. in the rule possessor, de reg. iur. lib. 6., and Barto. in l. nemo potest, ff. de leg. 1. When, however, in our case the said lady Nicola cannot be marked with any negligence, since earlier, namely before the eviction, she could not legally assert her right; therefore the foundation fails upon which prescription is grounded; rightly it ought not to have run; to this makes what is read at the end and noted especially by Barto. in l. 1. ff. quod ui aut clam. For who could blame her for why she did not bring a hypothecary action, when, if she had wanted to sue, she could not have, as proved above? It is therefore very clear that the prescription of the ius commune cannot stand in her way, especially since the text in the said l. 1. C. si aduer. cred. weighs and grounds itself upon the long silence of the creditor intending to bring a hypothecary action, and thus regards him who was able to proclaim, and out of negligence was silent; which words cannot be adapted to him who could not proclaim. For he cannot be said to be silent who cannot speak; for it is properly his to be silent who can speak, just as the law says at the end that it is his to refuse who can consent, as l. eius, ff. de reg. iur. And he is said to be intestate who was able to make a testament, as l. 1. ff. de suis & leg. And that prescription does not run against a creditor holding a hypothec who is hindered by a just cause is the case according to one interpretation in l. cum postulassem, §. fi. ff. de dam. infec. and noted by the gloss in the said l. 1. C. si aduer. cre. I say the same regarding the statutory provision. For a statute must be reduced, as far as can be done, to the terms of the ius commune, as l. 2. C. de noxa. and capitu. cum dilectus, de consuetu., noted by Inno. in cap. causam, de præscrip., and Barto. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iur.; just as, therefore, prescription introduced by the ius commune does not run against one unable to act, as I said above, so it must be said regarding statutory prescription, especially because the statute simply introduced prescription, and the ius commune generally provides that prescription does not run against one unable to act. Whence it is not to be presumed that the statute-makers wished in this to correct the ius commune through a general statute, as l. si quando, and what is noted there, C. de inof. test. Likewise it is not to be presumed that they wished, without the fault and offense of another, to take away that person's right; which they would do if prescription ran against one unable to act, which must not be said: because we ought not to presume inequity and injustice in the law of a prince or a people; to this point what is noted by gl. in l. quoties, C. de preci. imp. offe. and l. 2. §. si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in lo. pub. and in c. super eo, de of. dele. For a law must be just, reasonable, and honorable, 4. dist. c. erit autem lex, and C. de legi. l. leges; to this makes what is noted by Bar. in the above-cited l. omnes populi. Likewise a statute receives a restrictive interpretation when, by understanding it otherwise, someone would incur damage without fault, as l. 2. C. de nox. and l. ut gradatim, ff. de mu. & ho., and fully by Barto. in the said l. omnes populi, and l. non dubium, C. de legi.; but in our case damage would befall the said lady Nicola if the said statute were to be understood so crudely as to run prescription against one hindered by law from acting. Furthermore, a statute speaking in legal terms receives the limitations and exceptions of the law, as c. eum dilectus, and c. ad audientiam, de cle. non residen., the said l. 2. de noxa; therefore it must be understood according as the laws give the rule to prescription. Again, if the words of the statute are weighed well, they seem to say this very thing that I have said. For it provides when anyone has possessed for the space of ten years without contradiction or disturbance by his debtor, or another, etc.; and thus in our case, he to whom the thing belonged, or who had the hypothecary action, could contradict or disturb the possessor; but in our case the said lady Nicola could not contradict for the aforesaid reason. Therefore the statute has no place against her, just as I said above regarding the provision of the ius commune. From all these things it is clearly concluded that neither statutory prescription nor that of the ius commune has place against the said lady Nicola, since from the time of the eviction of the said land, when she began to be able to act, and consequently the prescription began to run, a decade has not elapsed. That the hypothecary action regarding the said house belongs to the said lady Nicola is clearly gathered from the promise made by lord Ioannes, who also in his own name promised regarding the eviction of the said land under hypothec of all his goods, among which was the said house sold to Titius, which ought to pass with the burden of the hypothec to the buyer, even if it was sold with the creditor knowing and remaining silent, as l. sicut, §. non videtur, ff. quib. mod. pig. vel hypo. sol. and capitul. ex literis, de pig., especially since by legal provision the said Ioann. as heir was bound for eviction, especially since the legacy was made to a daughter, about which is fully read and noted in l. si domus, §. de euictione, ff. de leg. 1. Moreover, that she cannot bring a hypothecary action against the said Ioannes, since the said Ioannes is absent as a rebel, nor is he found to possess anything, is clearly evident from those things which are read and noted by gl. and Bar. in auth. hoc si debitor, C. de pignoribus. And let these things suffice. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. An interdict is given to a usufructuary, so that he cannot use and enjoy, if he was ejected.
2. One seeking restitution must prove two things, namely possession and ejection.
body: IN the case currently pending between lord Antonius, rector of the church of S. Andrea, plaintiff in the name of the said church on the one part, and the abbess and nuns of the monastery of S. Clara of Siena on the other, in and upon the fact that the said lord Antonius has sought to be restored and reinstated in the name of his church into the pristine state of receiving annually the pension of six florins and three lire both from the said abbess and convent, and from anyone else detaining the property mentioned in the libel, and that the said abbess and convent be condemned to pay the said pension withheld for certain times mentioned in the libel. Two matters are very briefly to be examined for a clear decision in this case. First, whether the said lord Antonius could bring a possessory action in this case. Second, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that he could, whether he has proved his claim; so that sentence ought to be rendered in his favor according to the form of his petition. As to the first, it seems that he has acted ineptly, because in these personal obligations a petitory action is not granted, but rather an action is brought against the person that he do what he bound himself to do, insti. de act. in prin.; therefore, neither is a possessory action granted, because a possessory action is spoken of in relation to a petitory one, and where the first does not lie, neither does the second, as noted by Cy. in l. si certis annis, C. de pact., and Bar. in l. si. ff. quorum bo. If, therefore, he has acted ineptly, sentence is to be rendered against him, as in c. examinata, de iud., and l. 1. ff. si men. fal. mo. di. But these notwithstanding, the truth stands to the contrary, and on this side I cite an express and clear case squarely on point in our circumstances in c. querelam, de elec., where for a withheld pension, which was owed on occasion of one church to another church, action was brought by a possessory remedy. Nor does the contrary formed above stand in the way, for it can proceed in purely personal obligations; but in our case the pension is owed not by reason of a personal obligation, but on occasion of the thing, namely the property mentioned in the libel; in which case a possessory remedy lies, just as it would lie for the thing itself, d. c. querelam. The same would be true if I have an obligee bound to give something annually on account of a right I have over the person, as because he is my vassal or an adscripticius, as noted by Bar. in d. l. si. And that a possessory remedy lies in our case is expressly affirmed by Io. An. in c. peruenit, de censi., and Inno. in d. c. querelam. And such is the opinion of Cy. in d. l. si certis annis; for we see at the end,

† that an interdict is given to a usufructuary if he has been ejected so that he cannot use and enjoy, l. 3. §. unde ui. §. interdictum, ff. de ui & ui ar.; and yet a usufruct is owed to a person on occasion of a thing, ff. de usufructu. l. 1. Likewise, we see this in the interdicts de itinere actuque privato and the interdict de aqua quotidiana et aestiva, as in ff. de iti. actuque; priua. l. 1. and de aqua quo ti. & æsti. l. 1., in which it is clear that for those servitudes which are owed by a thing to a person, one can proceed possessorily; what the gl. notes in c. nullus secundo. 2. q. 2. makes very well for this; and let these suffice for the first point. As to the second, whether the said lord Antonius has proved what is necessarily incumbent upon him to obtain restitution to the pristine state, etc. It seems first that he has not:

† because one seeking restitution must prove two things, namely possession and ejection; if either is lacking, the possessory remedy ceases, as in c. consultationibus, de of. dele., and c. olim. 1. and 3. de rest. spo. But the said lord Antonius did not prove possession, because in these incorporeal things quasi-possession is not acquired without the knowledge and sufferance of the owner, as in l. 2. and what is noted there by the doctors, C. de serui., noted by Inn. in c. bonæ. 2. de postu. præl., and in c. conquerente, de offi. ord., and c. 2. de in integ. rest., and in many other places by Bar. in d. l. 1. ff. de iti. actuque; priua. But in our case it was not proved that the rector of S. Andrea collected the pension on occasion of the said property with the knowledge of the abbess and nuns; therefore, he did not acquire quasi-possession of the pension. Nor does it suffice that he who held the property leased from the nuns paid it, because the tenant could not prejudice the ignorant owner by paying the pension to another, especially since he always paid the rent to the said nuns, as is read and noted in l. quamuis. §. 1. ff. de acq. pos. Likewise, he did not prove ejection, especially a violent one, which is required in this matter, as in d. l. 1. ff. de ui & ui ar. But in truth the contrary side prevails in our case. For first, the said Antonius clearly proved possession by receiving the said pension, since he proved that he received it with the knowledge, and what is more, by the express disposition of the abbess and nuns of the said monastery; who, when they appointed a syndic to lease the said property, expressly ordered the bursar to lease it with the charge of paying the said pension that is owed to the rector or church of S. Andrea. And it is proved that by him to whom the said property was so leased, the said pension was thereupon paid for very many years to the rector of S. Andrea for the time being. Nay rather, it was expressly proved that even before the said property came into the hands of the said nuns, the aforesaid pension was paid for it to the church by earlier possessors. Likewise, it is proved that it was transferred to the said nuns with the burden of paying the pension; wherefore the said Antonius proved far more than was necessarily incumbent upon him, since a single payment would have sufficed to prove that quasi-possession, because such a thing is not wont to be granted as a favor, as is read and noted in c. cum ecclesia Sutrina, de causa pos. & proprie., by Inn. in c. bonæ, de postu. præl., and by Bar. in d. l. 1. ff. de iti. actuque; priua.; c. cum de beneficio, de præben. lib. 6 makes very well for this. The aforesaid ejection is also proved, because by the very fact that the nuns refused to pay, they despoiled the said church of S. Andrea of that quasi-possession. For spoliation cannot occur otherwise; wherefore it is sufficient to prove quasi-possession in these matters, because spoliation is proved by the very fact that payment is denied, as is proved in c. suborta, de re iudica., and there Inno. notes this in the beginning; to the same effect in c. querelam, cited above, where on both questions there is an exact case deciding this issue; what is noted by Bar. in l. prius, ff. de no. oper. nun. and the doctors in cap. mandatum, de rescrip. makes for this. From all of which I conclude that the said apostolic vicar subdelegate in this matter ought to restore the said lord Antonius in the name of his church to the pristine state of receiving annually the said pension of five florins and three Sienese lire on occasion of the said property, or properties contained in the libel, and to condemn the syndic of the said monastery and the monastery itself to the said lord Antonius in the aforesaid name of the church to the payment of the pension withheld for past times in which they improperly refused to pay, as mentioned in the libel of the said lord Antonius. And let these things suffice. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Pacts entered into with the prince, or by those having the authority of the prince, have the force of laws.
2. Restitution of usuries ought not to be made by a suspect person.
body: It is asked in law whether, upon examining the first and second pacts and agreements entered into between the commune of Siena on the one side and Lorenzo Toscano of Milan on the other, the said Ranieri is entitled by himself to make restitution to those who ought to receive the usury, without depositing annually eight hundred florins, etc., with a depositary to be elected by the commune, as was contained in the first articles. Secondly, presupposing that he is entitled to make restitution by himself, whether he can agree with the creditors of the said usury for a lesser amount, so that he may thereby obtain an acquittal for the entire debt. The help of the Savior having first been implored, and turning now to the first doubt: it is argued that the said Ranieri is entitled to make restitution by himself, because the newest pacts are to be observed, and not the earlier ones, as in l. pacta novissima, C. de pact. But in the latest pacts it was simply stated that the said Ranieri should restore five thousand florins within certain times, nor was it added that a deposit of them should be made; therefore he himself will have to make restitution. A second point tends to the same: because in the new pacts it was expressly agreed that it should not be lawful for the commune to sue in any way under any sought pretext; therefore nothing extrinsic is to be implied by which the said articles might be conflicted with in any part; l. si ita stipulatus fuero, §. plane, otherwise Chrysogonus, de verbo. obligatio, is in point. But notwithstanding these things, I consider the contrary opinion to be truer. I am moved principally because, whereas in the old pacts many things were stated—first, that restitution should be made beyond five thousand florins; secondly, that the said restitution should be made first to citizens, secondly to dwellers of the contado, etc.; thirdly, it was said that the money to be restored by the said Ranieri should be deposited and paid to those who ought to have it through a citizen to be elected by the commune; fourthly, that the uncertain claims should be given to the Casa della Sapienza, etc.—yet in the newest pacts, as to our subject-matter, only one thing was expressed, with the limitation as above, namely that the said Ranieri should restore 5,000 florins unless he were reconfirmed in the business of lending; which event occurring, the said Ranieri was bound to restore the entire sum, namely 8,000 florins. But of the remaining matters contained in the first articles, which are entirely connected with the aforesaid matters contained in the second, nothing is said in the second ones; for it is not probable that they were departed from altogether, since today a novation of an obligation does not occur unless this was expressly stated, as in l. fi. C. de nova. as fully noted by Bart. in l. 1, §. 2, ff. de praeto. stip. But in the second articles it was not said that they were making them with the intention of novating. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that where a novation occurs tacitly, relief is granted by way of exception, as noted by the Gloss on the said l. fin. and by Barto. in the Gloss on l. 2, ff. eod.; because that is true where it can appear that a tacit novation was made. But in our case it cannot be understood except with respect to the quantity, because only, as I have said before, the said Ranieri bound himself to restore 5,000 florins, but the remainder if and in so far as he were reconfirmed in his business of lending; and thus a tacit novation was made with respect to the quantity, since under the earlier pacts he was bound simply to the entire quantity simply and absolutely, without waiting for a new reconfirmation. But in the other matters it cannot be said that they were tacitly departed from, since from no part of the pacts can this be gathered. For in the second pacts it is not said to whom the restitution ought to be made; therefore it ought to be understood of the depositary to be elected by the commune, as was stated in the first articles, since an extraneous person ought not to be understood in a stipulation, according to the said §. Chrysogonus. And doubtful and general words ought to be understood in accordance with the preceding ones, l. si servus plurium, ff. de lega. 1, and l. qui filiabus, eod. titu., and cap. inter dilectos, de fide instrum. And if we were to say the contrary, an absurdity would follow, because in the second articles it was not provided what should be done concerning the uncertain claims, nor concerning the prerogative of citizens over dwellers of the contado and other foreigners, as was stated in the first articles. For it is not to be presumed that the magnificent lords and other citizens who made the second pacts wished to prejudice the Casa della Sapienza and make no disposition regarding the uncertain claims, or to take away from their own citizens the privilege of preference. For all these things provide the most ample argument that they did not intend, either expressly or tacitly, to depart from the prior obligation, except in so far as was expressed in the second. This also seems to be expressly proved in l. qui usumfructum, ff. de verb. obliga., where it is clear that in doubt a novation is not presumed to have been made because more is contained in the first obligation than in the second; which Barto. expressly confirms in the said l. 1, §. 2, de praeto. stip.

† Secondly, principally, because pacts entered into with the prince, or with those having authority from the prince—as is this community of Siena—have the force of laws, as is read and noted in l. Caesar, ff. de publ., and l. pen. C. de do. inter vi. & uxo. But a later law receives limitation according to a preceding one, as in l. sed & posteriores, ff. de legib., and is notably proved in a similar case in l. sciendum, ff. qui satisd. cog., joined with auth. offeratur, C. de litis conte., understanding it as noted by the Gloss and Bartolus in the said l. sciendum. For although the newest law, namely the Authentica Offeratur, simply says that the defendant is bound to provide security to appear in court, it is nevertheless supplemented and determined by the old law, namely if he does not possess immovables, as is said in the said l. sciendum; on this also see Bar. in his extravagans Ad reprimendum, on the word non obstantibus. So it must be said in the matter at hand: since in the second pacts it is simply spoken of making a restitution of 5,000 florins, and it is not said by whom, and what is to be done about the uncertain claims, and to whom restitution is first to be made, it had to be supplemented and determined by the old articles; and truly to think the contrary smacks of the greatest unfairness, especially since the second agreement was reached solely with respect to reducing the quantity and not with respect to the manner of restoring, since the said Ranieri is entirely suspect concerning the restitution to be made; because, since he is not restoring his own usuries, it is not probable that he would integrally and faithfully restore another's, by the argument of distinctio 47, sicut, 2, §. necesse.

† And restitution of usury must not in the meantime be made through a suspect person, as in chapter cum sit nimis, de Judæ., and what Hostiensis notes there, through Ioan. And. in chapter 2, de testa. lib. 6; whence it is not probable that by the general second pacts the power of restoring by himself was given to him. For in obscure matters we look to what is more probable, as in the rule inspicimus, de reg. iu. li. 6. And in a general grant that is not included which someone would not likely have granted in a specific case, as in c. fi. de off. vic. li. 6; and in agreements the intentions of the parties rather than the words are to be looked to, as in l. in conventionibus, ff. de ver. sig. And by this the solution to the second doubt is evident: for since the restitution to be made individually to the creditors does not pertain to the said Ranieri, but to the depositary to be elected by the commune, we ask in vain whether he can agree with his creditors for a lesser amount. But presupposing, without prejudice to the truth, that the specific restitution did pertain to the said Ranieri, whether he could agree in the aforesaid manner, I firmly believe that he could not. For although one is said to satisfy someone in whatever manner one satisfies his will, even without payment, as in l. si rem, §. omnes, ff. de pig. act., the word 'to restore' (restituere), to which Ranieri bound himself, smacks of complete restitution, since restitution is a restoration to the pristine state, 2, q. 3, in fi., l. 1, C. de sen. pas., and elsewhere it is said that in the word 'restitution' every interest of the plaintiff is contained, as in l. cum praetor, ff. de ver. sig. For he would not be restoring five thousand florins if he could agree for two thousand; and these words are especially to be taken thus in our case because of the subject-matter, since this restitution succeeds in the place of the restitution ordered by the deceased Zeno, which ought to be made integrally so that his soul may be freed from sin, de usur. c. cum tu, and in the rule peccatum, de regu. iu. li. 6. Rather, because of this suspicion, so that such restitution should be made integrally on account of hidden agreements, it is said that by the foresight of the superior such restitution ought to be made integrally, said c. cum sit, de Judæis, and by Io. And. in said c. 2, de testam. lib. 6. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that creditors can remit their right, because I say that they are not presumed to do so spontaneously, since no one is presumed to throw away what is his and remit it to another usurer, especially one from whom he has received no service; rather he would give to the poor. Moreover, this non-spontaneous remission does not discharge the one who has to make restitution, just as we say of the one who originally paid the usury, as in c. debitores, and what is noted there, de iureiur. And especially does this apply when someone is bound to make restitution in the person of another. For the disposition of the testator must be observed integrally without any diminution, l. nulli, and l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de epis. & cler. The contrary framed in the preceding does not stand in the way: because that proceeds in a pact entirely contrary to the first, as noted there, which is not the case in our matter except with respect to quantity, as I have said above. I conclude therefore that the specific distribution of the usuries does not pertain to Ranieri, but to the depositary to be elected by the commune; and having presupposed, though not granted, that it did pertain to him, he is bound to restore integrally the promised quantity, as is contained in the articles. And let these things suffice. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A judgment which is confirmed by the opinion of several persons is firmer and more stable.
2. A convent, congregation, or collegium can according to civil law consist from the beginning of three persons, according to canon law of two.
3. When a scrutiny is conducted secretly, one cannot consent to oneself.
4. For an election to be valid, it is necessarily required that someone be elected by the greater part of those having the right to elect, with respect had to the entire congregation.
5. Whether a constitution confirmed by a superior can be revoked without his consent.
body: Having invoked the protection of the Savior Jesus Christ and His most pious Mother: because, regarding the underwritten doubts, in order to satisfy the consciences of good men—since they do not have to wander through the intricacies of judicial trials—I shall therefore touch upon them with a succinct and light decision, as the poverty of my intellect permits, omitting arguments on either side. And first, it is asked whether, if in any monastery or priory subjected with all its rights and members to the Abbot General of the Order of Monte Oliveto, a prior has not hitherto been deputed by the said Abbot General, perhaps for a reason, the said abbot is able, whenever it shall seem good to him, to establish a prior there, just as he freely establishes one in other monasteries and priories subject to the same monastery? Concerning this first doubt, I think one should incline to the affirmative side, that he can. Indeed, it appears at first glance that he is bound to do this by provision of law. For from the fact that it is presupposed to be a monastery or priory, it therefore ought to have monks if it can be done, as in c. inter quatuor, de relig. do. and c. relatum, ne cleri. uel mo.; and from the fact that there is a congregation of monks there, a prior ought to be instituted there who may preside over the place and the persons, as in cle. 1. de sup. neg. præla. Indeed, it is further provided that a prior should not dwell alone in a priory, but the abbot is bound to depute at least one companion of his order. And if the revenues of the priory do not suffice for two, then the priory ought to be united to another priory or to the principal monastery by one having the power, and a secular cleric ought to be deputed for the divine service, as is the text in cle. ne in agro, § ad hoc, de statu mo. Nor does it stand in the way that, after the subjection was made regarding the said priories of the Order of Monte Oliveto, a prior was not deputed there; because in these matters concerning propriety and divine worship, one ought not to look at what was done, but at what ought to have been done, as in c. cum causam, and c. cum in magistrum, de elect.; to this makes de uita & hone. clem. c. cum decorem domus Dei. Likewise, I see that even in the granges of a monastery where there are only oratories, the abbot can at will send certain monks and establish a prior there according to the note in cap. fi. de censi. For both the care of the entire monastery and of the places subject to it pertains to the abbot, as in cap. nulla, 18. q. 2. and c. cum ad monasterium, versic. tales, de sta. reg., and every superior can do that by which divine worship and the beauty of the Church are increased, according to the note in cap. cum accessissent, de consti. And this is undoubted if such a priory concerning which inquiry is made has property distinct by itself from the property of the monastery. But if its property pertains to the principal monastery—for instance, because it belongs to the mensa—I say that although the abbot cannot then be compelled to place a special rector there according to what is read and noted in clemen. frequens, de exce. præla., he nevertheless can if he wishes: because from this no prejudice is done to anyone if divine worship is increased and the goods of the place are better disposed of, by argument of those things which are noted in the said cap. cum accessissent. And from these things it is inferred regarding the second and third doubts, whether a prior who is to be established there, together with one or two monks who are to be deputed in the same priory by the abbot, ought to have a voice in the election of the Abbot General, in view of the words of the constitution of the order, by which it is provided that the prior of each monastery of the said order and one or two of the monks of the said monastery should have a voice in the election of the Abbot General. And truly it seems to me that in every case it must be said that they do. For either the goods of such a priory are not separated from the goods of the greater monastery, and then, since by common law such persons ought to have a voice in the election of the abbot according to the note by Inn. and Io. An. in c. fin. de reli. do., the said constitution of the order admitting the prior and one or two monks of the inferior monastery ought to be understood broadly, so that it also includes such a prior and his monks; because a statute ought to be drawn to the common law as far as can be done, as in c. cum dilectus, de consue. and l. 2. C. de noxa, Inn. in c. cum causa, de præsc., and Bar. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iur., especially where the words allow it, as happens in our case. For it is true to say that this man is a prior, although he is removable at the will of the abbot, as in cle. et si principalis, de rescri. and cle. 1. de sup. neg. præla. and c. cum singula, de præb. li. 6. with similar texts. Likewise, the monks designated to such a priory by the abbot can truly be called monks of that monastery, although they are removable by the abbot; the text is noted in c. 1. de priuile. lib. 6. § fin. Or, on the other hand, the goods of such a priory are entirely separated from the goods of the greater monastery, both as to administration and as to utility and use; and the same must be said: because it is in the interest of each priory to concur in the election of the Abbot General under whose rule it is governed, and upon this interest was founded the constitution admitting the prior and one or two monks of each monastery of the said order to the election of the abbot. Whence, although by common law it is doubtful whether the monks of such a priory having distinct property ought to have a voice in the election of the Abbot General according to the note in the said c. si. de reli. do., nevertheless, since the constitution in this case speaks generally and clearly about every monastery, such persons ought to be admitted, especially since these priories do not have the election of their own prior, but they are deputed in each monastery at the will of the abbot; nor ought a strict and bitter interpretation to be made in our case, since it is not an odious matter, but rather a favorable one:

† because firmer and more stable is the judgment that is confirmed by the sentence of several persons, as in c. prudentiam, in the words illa quippe, ff. de of. dele., and especially in an election, as in c. obeuntibus, 83. dist. To the fourth doubt, what if it happens that in some priory there are only two or three monks together with the prior, whether one or two of the said monks can come to the election of the Abbot General? A doubt is created because according to the words of the constitution the monks of the aforesaid priory are to be taken for the act of election by the convent of the priory itself, but in such a priory they must be taken by the convent, when there are none there except those two, or one with the prior; therefore, such persons do not seem admissible. But that consideration notwithstanding, I think the contrary must be held in law.

† And first I say that a convent or congregation or college can from the beginning consist of three, l. Neratius, ff. de regu. iur. Under canon law it seems that it can consist of two, as in c. 1. de elect., noted by the gloss in c. 1. 10. q. 1., concerning which, however, more must be said fully as noted in the said c. 1. de elect. Likewise, a college, or the virtue and power of a college or of a chapter, can consist in one alone when the others fail, as is read and noted in cap. gratum, de postula. præla., and in l. sicut, quod cuiusque uni., and 65. dist. c. fin. These things having been premised, I say that a remedy can be applied to this in multiple ways. And first, if there are three in the congregation, they can first elect one, who will be elected by two; afterwards they can elect another, who will also be able to be elected by two: because although the third was first deputed so that he might be one of the electors, he did not thereby lose his voice and the right of being present and advancing the affairs of the priory: because this is nowhere provided, since by that deputation he is not removed from the congregation, as he does not cease thereby to be a monk of the monastery, nor is that act incompatible with the first; for officials also nonetheless have a voice in the chapter of the monastery, arg. in c. edoceri, de rescri., c. fin. de præben. lib. 6. The second mode is that they openly and publicly treat of sending certain persons to the election of the Abbot General, and then the one deputed by another will be able to consent, since it does not originate from himself, but he is summoned by the deed so that he may consent for the good of the monastery; and thus the whole convent concurs in this election, and this will be able to take place even if there are only two in the congregation. Nor in this case are they bound to make this deputation by secret scrutiny, even if this is provided in the constitution; because such a form is not possible in fact, since one cannot scrutinize the vote of the other in secret. And therefore the constitution claims no place for itself in such a priory as regards the form of secret scrutiny: because the law does not bind where in fact it cannot be observed, 4. dist. cap. erit autem lex, and l. fin. ff. quæ sen. sine appel. rescin., and l. ita autem, ff. de admini. tuto. Here Io. And. notably said on the rule in toto, de regul. iur. lib. 6. in Mercuriales, that if in a collegiate church there are only two, they can proceed to an election without the form of scrutiny: nor do they lose the election on account of defect of form, capitul. quia propter, de electio., which they cannot observe on account of the smallness of the number: but rather the election is reserved to them, and that form is remitted. He also says that one will be able to elect the other openly, and that elected person will be able to consent, and he will be said to be elected by the whole convent: because although the voice of the person elected is not counted in the number when one proceeds by the form of private scrutiny, as in c. Cumana and what is noted there, de elect., which must be understood in this way, it is otherwise, however, when one proceeds by way of manifest scrutiny, as is read and noted in c. cum in iure, under the same title. The reason for the diversity is:

† because when scrutiny is done secretly, a person cannot consent to himself, because since he is then ignorant whether others have consented to him, he would be rejected as ambitious if he elected himself, since no one ought to elect himself and have the beginning arise from himself: but he ought to be called, just as Aaron, as in c. qualiter & quando, de elect.; but when the scrutiny is done openly, and he sees that he is elected and deputed by others, he can then consent to his election: because he is then called by his companions; nor can he be called ambitious, and by consenting he increases the number; and this text is noted in the said c. cum in iure, and there by Ioan. And. Thirdly, I say that if in the congregation there are two, or only one with the prior, they can all collegially arrange to go together to ordain, provided, however, that in the meantime the church does not lack the due worship of divine offices. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that they are not elected by the convent, as is said in the constitution: because I say that not only are they deputed by the convent, but rather they are the convent; and in arranging that all should go, the convent has sufficiently arranged this. For the body also can arrange concerning individuals; thus the chapter can consent that the chapels be aided by their individual prebends, as in c. exposuisti, de præb.; to this makes what Inn. notes in c. cum non ignores, under the same title, and in c. irrefragabili, § excessus, de offi. ord. Moreover, the right of electing is not given to the prior and two monks in consideration of form, but in consideration of substance and effect, so that each priory may have in the election of the abbot its prior and only one or two monks; therefore, in consideration of the effect, the intention of the constitution has been satisfied. For the constitution provided that the monks should be assumed by the convent lest any should come by their own authority, or lest they should be assumed at the pleasure of the prior, so that thus the whole congregation might be honored and concur in the election of the Abbot General. But in our case, when there are only two or one in the priory besides the prior, if they collegially arrange this beforehand in public, they do not therefore go there by their own authority, nor do they assume at the prior's pleasure; but they themselves, or he himself, does this by exercising and promoting the rights of the college, which resides with them, or with one alone in default of the others, as I said above. For the intention of the constitution and its purpose ought to be attended to, not, however, the words, as in c. intelligentia, de verb. sign. and l. cum pater, § dulcissimis, ff. de leg. 2. And so much for the fourth doubt. Concerning the fifth, I say,

† that in order for an election to be valid, it is necessary that someone be elected by the greater part of those having the right to elect, having respect to the whole congregation; whence the greater part in comparison to a smaller part would not suffice: but it must be the greater part of the entire congregation; the text is noted in c. ecclesia, 1. de ele., and the person elected cannot be counted in the number when proceeding by private scrutiny, as I said above; otherwise if it were proceeded with openly in the hearing of all, as I said before. I also say that where the form of c. quia propter, de ele. does not have to be observed of necessity, the electors could agree from the beginning that he should be elected upon whom the greater of the parts agrees in comparison to the lesser, because on account of the initial consent and agreement all seem to consent, just as the cardinals generally observe in the election of the Pope, as the doctors note in c. licet, de electio., and there is the ordinary gloss in c. socii, under the same title, lib. 6., and there is a good text with the gloss on this matter. And this could be observed in practice in choosing the electors: because in deputing them, the form of c. quia propter is undoubtedly not to be observed, since that chapter applies to the election of a prelate. To the last doubt concerning the manner, namely, to be observed in establishing a constitution, so that it may not bind those agreeing to the pact except those who hold it in contempt: I say that it is sufficient that the greater part of the congregation consent, according to what is read and noted in c. 1. de his, quæ fi. à ma. par. cap., and that such a constitution be founded upon contempt, not only in respect of fault, but in respect of punishment upon any culpable transgression; for instance, if it is said thus: 'Whoever does so shall be punished with such a punishment; and if he agreed out of contempt, he shall be ensnared and entangled in both fault and punishment.' And I think that where such a constitution was made by a college and confirmed by the Pope, the college will be able to modify it, provided it is such a matter regarding which the college itself, or the greater part, could have enacted it without the Pope, c. cum accessissent, de const., noted by Bar. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu. in that question,

† whether a constitution confirmed by a superior can be revoked without his consent. And he distinguishes that either it is such a people or congregation that was able to make a statute without the authority of a superior, and then by the same reasoning it will be able to revoke it, and in the present case all the more modify it—to this is the said c. cum accessissent, and c. cum M. de const. Or it was not able to enact it without the authority of a superior: and then either it wishes to eliminate the statute by enacting otherwise, or it wishes simply to eliminate it and return to the common law. In the first case, it cannot, unless the same solemnity intervenes in repealing as intervened in establishing. In the second case, it can without the authority of the superior, by argument in l. hac consultissima, § si quis autem, C. de testa., where a prior testament is eliminated by a second made less solemnly, when through it there is a return to the common law: because those who succeed intestate are instituted; otherwise it is different; to the same effect are the laws cited above in the first branch. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Monasteries can be visited by the bishop of the place, and procuration may be demanded by him.
2. The bishop can by Apostolic authority visit monasteries of nuns that are exempt and immediately subject to the Apostolic See.
3. Monasteries are bound to pay the fourth part of bequests made to them. And monasteries can be exempted by privilege, or by long custom.
4. 5. Prescription in the fourth part of tithes and of the dead runs against the bishop.
casus: In the question presently pending between the clergy of Cortona on the one part, and certain monasteries of nuns of the Order of Saint Benedict situated in the city or diocese of Cortona on the other, in and concerning this: that the clergy asks that the said monasteries be compelled to contribute together with the said clergy towards the payment of the procuration of the nuncios of the Apostolic See, and of the procuration owed to the bishop by reason of visitation, and towards the promised charitable subsidy, and towards other burdens daily falling upon the clergy, to all of which the said monasteries are asserted by the clergy or their syndics and officials to be bound both by provision of law and by virtue of a certain episcopal constitution. To the contrary, however, on the part of the monasteries the common law is alleged, which seems to exempt religious places from all [these burdens]; likewise a custom of such time that there is no memory of its beginning.
body: Having humbly invoked the protection of Jesus Christ the Redeemer and of his most pious mother, it appears at first that the said monasteries are bound without distinction to the aforesaid burdens. And first, concerning the procuration of the nuncios of the Apostolic See, it expressly appears that all churches are bound, unless they are fortified by an Apostolic privilege, as is proved in cap. cum instantia, de censi. and c. procurationes, eo. ti. and in c. accedentes, de præscrip., and in both places it is provided that a custom, even of the longest time, does not stand in the way, because that which threatens all ought to be borne by all, as there stated, and it is specifically provided for religious, even exempt ones, in cle. 2. §. sunt & nonnulli, de censi. Concerning the second point, regarding the procuration owed to the bishop of the place by reason of visitation, there appears the text in c. cum ex officii, de præscri. and c. uenerabili, de censi., in which it is clear,

† that monasteries can be visited by the bishop of the place, and procuration may be demanded by him, prescription notwithstanding, since it is annexed to visitation. Whence just as visitation itself is imprescriptible, as in cap. cum non liceat, de præscri., in the same way also the procuration itself annexed to the visitation; because there ought to be the same judgment concerning connected matters, as says the text in d. c. cum ex officii. Nay rather, the bishop can,

† by Apostolic authority, visit monasteries of nuns that are exempt and immediately subject to the Apostolic See, as in clem. accedentes, de sta. regu., and there is a notable gloss there on the word alia, which notably says that whether he visits those subject to him or exempt ones, the bishop can demand procuration, since it is annexed to visitation, as I said above. Concerning the third point, on the charitable subsidy, there are differing opinions as to whether by law monasteries and religious houses are bound to pay it. For Innocent seems to think in c. 1. de sta. reg. that they are exempt from these burdens, as if it belongs to the diocesan law, from which monasteries are exempt by common law; and this he seems to hold there post prin. on the word nos igitur, at the verse moderatum auxilium, &c., although at the end of his gloss he seems somewhat to waver. Archidiaconus and Io. An. hold this opinion in c. 1. de præb. li. 6.; Paulus thinks so in clem. 1. de exces. præl.; the gloss also tacitly thinks so in 10. q. 3. in summa. In favor of this opinion, the text strongly makes in d. cle. 1. de exces. præla. in §. exigendo, especially joined with the gloss on the word in exigendo, where it is implied that a charitable subsidy can even be demanded from exempt religious, provided that the bishop does not exceed due measure. For there a complaint was set forth that the bishop was exceedingly overreaching in this; it is otherwise, therefore, if he observes due moderation. And some doctors have held this; dominus Zabarella held it there, later Cardinal of Florence in c. dilectus, de of. or., and he said he had advised thus. It supports this,

† because monasteries are bound to pay the fourth part from bequests made to them, as in c. requisisti, de test.; therefore all the more so to a charitable subsidy, since religious places are more strictly bound to those things which are paid by reason of charity than others, by the argument in c. recolentes, de sta. reg. And it concerns everyone in the diocese that their bishop be sustained, and all are bound to almsgiving in time of necessity, as read and noted in c. sicut. 47. dis. It also supports this that c. cum apostolus, §. prohibemus, de censi., permits without distinction that he may demand a charitable subsidy from his subjects; therefore he can from religious persons, since they too are subjects of the bishop, 18. q. 2. c. abbates, and c. monasteria, and c. quanto, de of. or. cum fi.
