Although this case has been sufficiently argued on behalf of the latter party, to me it is nevertheless not absolute in his favor, since the laws and opinions vary. Likewise I say regarding the fourth point demanded by the clergy, in that it is sought that the aforesaid monasteries be compelled to contribute to the expenses occurring daily. For that they are bound, cle. 2. de censi. supra cited in §. sunt & nonnulli strongly argues, where the text almost appears to mean that even exempt religious are bound to extraordinary burdens incumbent upon the clergy, provided they are constrained to a fitting portion and not burdened excessively; to the same effect is the text in cle. 1. e. ti. and the rule quod omnes tangit, de reg. iu. li. 6. To the contrary, however, makes a very notable text in d. c. quam sit. 18. q. 2., where it is so provided near the end: Monasteries shall in no way be subject to ecclesiastical conditions or burdens (angariis) or to any secular services whatever, nor shall they serve any canonical laws, but with exactions and city burdens removed, they shall carry out the divine work with the highest devotion of mind. From which words it is clearly gathered that monasteries are exempt from these services to which secular churches are bound, and those words are to be weighed: 'they shall serve no canonical laws, &c.'; and thus they are not bound to burdens that have been justly and lawfully introduced by the canons, such as the cathedraticum and similar things. To this is a good text in c. inter cætera. 10. q. 3., and what the gloss notes in the same causa and question in summa; to the same effect is what Innocent notes in said chapter 1. de sta. regul. near the end, in the verse nam de lege diœcesana, &c., where he says that it belongs to the diocesan law that individual churches must contribute with the bishop when he goes to the Pope, or to the King, or to a synod, or when he incurs expenses for any common affairs of the entire diocese. From all these, monasteries are exempt according to him; and this he says the aforesaid chapters, especially c. quam sit, supra cited, mean. But afterwards he seems to withdraw from this, saying: or say that this is not of diocesan law, but of jurisdiction; yet he brings forward nothing specific for this position. From all these things it clearly appears that this case is quite doubtful, but the text in d. cle. 2. strongly supports this opinion against the monasteries, which text Innocent did not see, because it was promulgated after his time. Furthermore and lastly, on the part of the clergy there seems to support the episcopal constitution, which provides that all goods, even of monasteries, be assessed for paying the burdens incumbent upon the clergy in proportion to their means; and the constitution of a bishop has the force of a canon in his diocese, 11. q. 3. c. nemo contemnat, and what is read and noted in c. 2. de consti. libr. 6. But the aforesaid notwithstanding, I think the contrary must be said in our case, yet with the modifications written below. I am moved principally on account of custom of such a time that the memory of its beginning does not exist, which is alleged by the said monasteries in their favor; for such a custom or prescription has the force of a title, as in c. 1. de præscri. libr. 6., l. hoc iure. §. ductus aquæ, ff. de aqua quoti. & æsti., l. 1. in fi. ff. de aqua plu. arcen.

† For just as monasteries can be exempted from these burdens by privilege, as in c. accedentes, de præscrip. and c. cum instantia, de censi. with similar texts, so also through such a long custom of whose beginning no memory exists. Nor do those laws stand in the way which seem to reject the prescription of the longest time, because they do not speak of that of whose beginning there is no memory; for from the running of such time a lawful cause is presumed, as noted in the said laws. Furthermore, just as through custom of such time the rights of any church, and even a census with no cause appearing, can be prescribed without any other title, to such an extent that a census can be demanded from the fact that it was paid for so much time of whose beginning there is no memory, and a cause is to be presumed from the running of such time, as the gloss notes in c. nullus episcopus. 1. q. 1, and Io. An. in c. peruenit, de censi., and Bartolus in l. cum de in rem uerso, ff. de usu.; so all the more strongly could the said monasteries prescribe through so much time against the other churches or the remainder of the clergy, so that they may be exempt from these burdens. And for the confirmation of this opinion, I bring forward the almost explicit text in cle. 1. de censi., joined with the gloss on the word legitima, where it is proved that prescription is advantageous in avoiding these burdens—in those, however, which are prescriptible, according to the gloss there; and therefore it added that limitation, 'which are prescriptible, &c.', because in certain matters it is doubted whether prescription runs; yet the text speaks there of the prescription of such time of whose beginning there is no memory. And concerning those in which it is doubted whether prescription runs, it is noted by Io. An. in c. cum uenerabilis, de censi. Furthermore, we see

† that against a bishop prescription runs in the fourth part of tithes and mortuaries, as in c. de quarta. de præscr.; likewise one church prescribes tithes in the parish of another against common law, as in d. c. 1. de præscr. lib. 6. and c. ad apostolicæ, de deci.; all the more strongly can one church prescribe liberty against the others so that it is not bound to common burdens. And these things I think undoubtedly apply with respect to common burdens and the charitable subsidy, and this for a twofold reason. First, because prescription is valid against common burdens, as I said above. Second, because since it is doubtful in law whether monasteries are bound to a charitable subsidy and common burdens, as has been sufficiently stated above; therefore recourse must be had to, and one must stand by, custom, which is the best interpreter of laws, as in c. cum dilectus, de consue. and l. si de interpretatione, and l. minimè, ff. de legi., especially when there is such a time that the memory of its beginning does not exist: nay rather, when the law is doubtful, prescription or custom contrary to that which is the objective truth is valid, as is the notable text in d. c. cum dilectus. For custom has a derogative, interpretive, and limitative force, as noted by the gloss on Inst. de iu. na. gen. & ciui. §. ex non scripto, and especially if provisions are established in favor of religion, l. sunt personæ, ff. de reli. & sump. fune. Whence both by reason of doubt, and by reason of so much time, from the running of which some cause must be presumed, one must conclude in these two matters in favor of the monasteries. But a greater doubt remains in the other two, namely in the procuration of legates and of the bishop of the place. For, as I said before, it seems that just as visitation cannot be prescribed, so neither can procuration, since it is annexed to visitation; whence these rights seem imprescriptible, nor is there any doubt underlying here; and thus the interpretive power of custom ceases. But these things notwithstanding, I judge that a distinction should be made as follows: Either the clergy has, for such a time that the memory of its beginning does not exist, undergone the entire procuration of the legates or nuncios of the Pope and of the diocesan without the said monasteries paying anything; and then the said monasteries can help themselves by prescription, introducing it not indeed against the bishop or the legates of the Pope, but against the clergy, so that the clergy itself pays and provides that entire procuration; because in this case there is no prescription against the bishop or the legates of the Pope—in which case speak the above-alleged texts which condemn prescription in these matters—but against the clergy, which can be done, by the argument in d. cle. 1. de censi.; for in this case visitation is not impeded, nor the convenience of the legates, since the clergy is bound by virtue of prescription to pay for those monasteries, and this Ioan. de Lignano uniquely held in d. c. accedentes, de præscr., thus notably limiting that text. Or the clergy did not pay the entire procuration for so much time, and thus in effect prescription is introduced against the legates of the Pope, or the diocesan of the place; and I think the prescription is valid by the laws alleged above. I conclude therefore from all the aforesaid that the said monasteries can defend themselves by virtue of the said prescription or custom against the charitable subsidy and other extraordinary burdens incumbent upon the clergy; but in the other two, namely the procuration of the bishop and of the nuncios of the Pope, a distinction must be made as I have said immediately above. And although Io. An. following Hostiensis in c. says in c. cum venerabiles and ca. cum apostolus, de censi. that against a charitable subsidy prescription does not run, just as it does not against charity; nevertheless that is understood of secular clerics, who are bound to it by clear law, as I said above. But since in monasteries it is doubtful, as I said before, one must stand by custom. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A father cannot disinherit a son on the ground that he enters religion.
2. Entry into religion removes every cause of ingratitude, from wherever it arose.
3. Friars Minor are no more capable by their rule than the Preachers, who are so by constitution.
4. If a house is bequeathed to mendicants, they can receive it in order to sell it.
casus: The doubt upon which a legal counsel is at present sought is such: A certain father of a family died intestate, leaving surviving him legitimate and natural sons, one of whom has professed the rule of the Hermits of Saint Augustine. It is asked whether this professed religious is able, for the benefit of the monastery, to enter upon the inheritance of the father for his portion, and to succeed together with the remaining brothers who remain in the world.
body: Having prayed for the aid of Almighty God, for a clear and lucid decision on the present doubt, I say that, as far as our purpose is concerned, attention must be paid to three species of religious orders. There is a certain religious order which, although it denies to individual members the ownership of any thing, nevertheless grants it to them in common, as in the order of the Blessed Benedict, and of the Carthusian friars, and similar ones; and in these no doubt arises that individual religious may succeed their parents and agnates for the benefit of the monastery, just as others remaining in the world may do. Indeed, their parents are not permitted to exclude them from the legitimate portion, as is proved in l. Deo nobis, C. de episc. & cle., and in c. vno, 18. q. 1, and c. non liceat parentibus, 19. q. vlt., where it is granted far more remarkably in favor of religion, namely that parents are not permitted to exclude from their inheritance children who have become monks, even if, while they were in the world, they fell into a cause of ingratitude. And although Guilelmus, as Cynus reports on l. Deo nobis, aforesaid, in his additions, also reported and followed by Baldus in the same place, distinguishes that either the son fell into a cause of ingratitude solely by his own deed, as because he was a gladiator/sandsman, and then by entering religion such ingratitude is removed, because he passes over to the fruit of a better life, arg. in auth. de mona. in prin.; or he fell into a cause of ingratitude from a cause concerning the father, and then it is not removed by entry into religion, arg. in l. 2, ff. de capi. di., and the text in the said l. Deo nobis supports this,
† where the father is prohibited from disinheriting the son solely on the ground that he entered religion against his will. I, however, hold without distinction, saving a better judgment,

† that every cause of ingratitude, from wherever it arose, is removed by entry into religion, through that aforesaid text in 19. q. vlt. non liceat, where it is provided simply in favor of religion, without any distinction, that the vice of ingratitude is removed; and to the same effect is the text in the said auth. de mona. in prin., where it is said that entry into religion wipes away every human stain, although the Gloss there considers that it does not thereby remove a son's ingratitude. But the former opinion pleases me more in favor of religion, arg. l. sunt personae, ff. de relig. & sump. fu. Likewise because we see greater privileges established in favor of religion even to the prejudice of others, as in c. in praesentia, de prob., and auth. nisi rogati, C. ad Tre., and in auth. de san. epi. § sed hoc praesenti. Likewise penance, however grave, is diminished, as in capitul. admonere, 33. quaestio. 2, and in what is noted in capitul. scripturae, de voto. Likewise, in those belonging to an order of non-mendicants, another rule is clearly established by law, that the goods which those who enter possess, unless they dispose of them otherwise before entry, are acquired for the monastery: concerning which, however, the discussion is to be made as is fully read and noted in auth. si qua mulier and auth. ingressi, C. de sacr. ecc., and 19. q. 1. c. quia ingredientibus, and c. nunc aut si qua, and the said c. vno, 18. q. 1. As to our purpose, therefore, if these Hermit friars can have ownership and dominion of property in common—to know which their Rule must be examined, as well as their Constitutions—our case admits of no doubt: since the said professed son could succeed just like his other brothers remaining in the world, through the laws cited above and through Speculator in tit. de statu mo. near the end, through the middle of the column. A certain and second order is that which, by its own Rule, forbids the dominion and ownership of any thing both to the individual and to the order in common, as is the order of the Blessed Francis; and in these the common opinion is that they are not admitted to the succession of their parents, but others who succeed ab intestato come in, as if they were dead; which Bartolus holds in his Minorica, near the end, and Johannes de Lignano after him in cle. exiui de paradiso, de ver. sig., and Baldus in the said l. Deo nobis, where he says that one who dies leaving a son in the order of St. Francis is said to die without a son, argu. in l. metallum, ff. de his, quae pro non rescrip., and he holds the same more broadly in auth. si qua mulier, C. de sacrof. ecc.; Hostiensis holds this in c. in praesentia, de proba.; Johannes Andreae considers this in the additions to Speculator in tit. de statu mona. § 1. ver. 2, remitting regarding them to the said cle. exiui, although Speculator felt otherwise there, but he had not seen the said Clementine, so he is excused; but the text is clear enough there in § dubitauerunt and § cupientes, where it is plain that these friars, on account of the strictest vow of poverty, cannot be instituted heirs by anyone, because dominion cannot pass to them. Nor can they claim anything from the property of an entrant; on the contrary, they cannot take it, even if the entrant wishes to give them all his property; yet they can take certain modest things if they are given to them as to other poor persons, as is stated there. And so for the same reason I say the same concerning other religious of the Mendicant Order by Rule: because in them underlies the same ratio that is set forth in the said cle. § cupientes; which Bartolus sufficiently held in his said Minorica, near the end, and Bartolus in the said auth. si qua mulier, and Federico da Siena, consi. 75. And these Hermit friars are by no means in the number of those friars: because the Rule does not prohibit to them the holding of goods in common; and therefore, in our case, we stand outside that case. There is also a third species of religious order, which does not forbid the holding of goods in common by its Rule, but does so by a constitution of the order confirmed by the Apostolic See, as can be seen in the Friars Preachers, who by their Rule are not mendicants, since they have the Rule of St. Augustine, but are so by the constitutions which their order made afterwards, approved by the Apostolic See; and thus must the text be understood in c. nimis, tit. 2. de excef. praela. in prin., where it is said that the Friars Preachers serve Christ the Poor in the most strict poverty. And concerning these there is a doubt as to whether they can succeed their parents for the benefit of the monastery. And if they have a privilege from the Pope concerning this, as is said of the Preachers themselves, the case is clear, as Johannes de Lignano says, and rightly, in the said cle. exiui; but, failing a privilege, there is a doubt against them, that they cannot succeed; it supports this that they are called mendicants, as is plain in c. 1. de reli. do. lib. 6; but mendicants are forbidden to have revenues or possessions for their suitable support, rather precarious begging through public soliciting is accustomed to provide them with food, as the text says in the said c. 1; therefore they cannot claim the goods of those who enter their religion: because the goods could be so great that they would cease to be mendicants. Likewise, precarious begging would not provide support, as ought to be the case; therefore they cannot aspire to those goods. Likewise, it seems equivalent whether some are mendicants by Rule, or by a constitution approved by the Pope,

† whence the Friars Minor are no more capable by Rule than the Preachers who are such by constitution; the text in the said c. nimis equates them as to the strictest poverty. And the same reasoning seems to apply to both. For if they cannot have dominion in common, therefore they cannot succeed: because dominion passes to the heirs, as in l. cum haeredes, ff. de acq. haer., especially since an inheritance or succession by its nature relates both to money and to other movable property, all of which are repugnant to poverty, as the text stated in the said cle. exiui. To the contrary makes the fact that, since statutes are of strict law, as is read and noted in c. in nostra, de iniur., and in l. 3. § haec autem actio, ff. de neg. gest., they must be interpreted strictly. For if they simply prohibit the holding of possessions and revenues, they do not seem to prohibit that which is otherwise granted by law, namely the inheritance and goods of entrants, preventing them from at least taking and selling, and relieving their necessities from the price thereof. For even slaves, who cannot have property of their own, nevertheless take legacies and other goods, so that they may have whence to live, as in l. seruos ad custodiam, ff. de ali. & cib. leg., and what Bartolus notes there; l. 2, ff. de his, qui sunt sui uel alie. iu., supports this. Likewise, a legacy can be left to these friars in common and in particular for their necessities, as in clemen. dudum, and what the Gloss notes there, de sepult. And certainly on account of these and similar arguments, which could be framed for either side, there are opinions among the Doctors: Johannes Andreae reported many in the said c. in praesentia, de proba., and did not take a firm stand. Hostiensis, however, held that they cannot take even to sell; and Cynus also reported many opinions in the said l. Deo nobis. But Speculator in the said § 1. versicu. 3. de sta. mona. clearly held that they can demand such goods, not to keep them, but to sell them and convert them to necessary uses, since the poor also ask for that whence they may live, 47. distin. cap. sicut. And Johannes Andreae held this opinion there in the additions; the noted Gloss in cap. 1. de reli. do. on the word 'domum' supports this, which stated,

† that if a house is bequeathed to these mendicants, they can receive it in order to sell it, since they ought to live from alms; what is read and noted in l. filius, § si quid, ff. de lega. 1, and l. mortuo, § Labeo, ff. de lega. 2, and l. ab administratione, C. de lega., and l. apud Iulianum, at the end, with the following law, ff. de lega. 1, supports this, in which legal texts it is held that if a thing is bequeathed to someone who, without his own fault, does not have the legal capacity to deal in it, its estimated value is owed. The same should be said in the matter at hand. Antonius de Butrio clearly follows this opinion of Speculator in the said cap. in praesentia, and Gaspar de Calderinis there, at least so that they may implore the office of the judge; Cynus takes this view in the said l. Deo nobis, at the end; Baldus pursues it exquisitely in the said authen. si qua mulier; and he concludes this side, if there is a custom that these friars succeed, because constitutions can be derogated by contrary custom, since this is not of the nature of crimes. And this opinion pleases me, so that if they succeed by custom, the custom is to be observed, since this is not against the Rule, but against the constitutions, which, although they are confirmed by the Pope, nevertheless can be remitted by contrary custom, especially since there is a return to the common law; in which case it would seem that the friars themselves could return to the common law, joined with what is noted by Bartolus in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu., at the verse iuxta praedicta quaero; cap. cum accessissent, de consti., and c. pro illorum, de praeben., support this. Likewise, custom is the best interpreter of laws, as in c. cum dilectus, de consuetu., and l. si de interpretatione, ff. de legi. As to our purpose, therefore, I say that if the said Hermit friars are not mendicants, even by their constitutions, then there is no doubt that the said friar can succeed, as I have said above. If, however, their constitutions forbid them ownership even in common, one must stand by the custom, so that if by custom they succeed, the said friar is to be admitted; otherwise, to the contrary according to what has been said above. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The Pope can grant the right of collating and electing to pure laymen.
2. A patron is bound to present within four months.
body: Having implored the aid of Almighty God, in the case of the commune of the castle of Trignanda the matter seems to me entirely without doubt. For it is certain that the commune of the said castle legally acquired the right of patronage in the parish church of the said castle by indulgence of the Roman Pontiff, as is clearly gathered from the letters of our Lord Pope Martin V and the process followed thereupon toward the execution of the said letters; and it can come into doubt to no one that the Pope can grant the right of patronage to laymen, in c. quoniam, and almost throughout the whole title, de iure patron.

† Nay more, he could grant the right of collating and electing to pure laymen, just as the Roman Pontiffs themselves afterwards granted to many, as in c. in synodo, and c. adrianus, 63. di. I say further, that in our case not only the Pope, but even the bishop could have granted them the said right of patronage, since they conferred ten [measures/amounts] upon the less endowed church, even though after consecration, as noted by Io. An. in c. 1. de iure pa., and thus the gloss must be understood and distinguished in c. piae mentis. 16. q. 2. Since, therefore, the said parish church or plebs belonged to the patronage of laymen, and by special indulgence of the Roman Pontiff the presentation of the rector to be instituted belonged to the men and commune of the said castle of Trignanda, as is evident in the Apostolic grant, no one by virtue of an expectative grace could accept the said vacant plebs: because such a grace does not extend to a church subject to lay patronage, unless express mention of such patronage were made in the apostolic letters, as noted in cle. per literas, de praeb. in gl. antepen. and by Ioan. And. in c. cum dilectus, de iur. pat. Nor were the said men here negligent in presenting, since they had four months to present, as in c. unico, de iur. pat. lib. 6., and within the said time they presented a suitable cleric to the reverend father, the lord Bishop of Arezzo, and institution was legitimately carried out by him.

† Nay, I say more, that it suffices for the patron to present within four months, even if within that time institution by the bishop has not followed; because the patron did what was in his power, as in c. unico, cited above, and what is read and noted in c. fi. eo. tit. For no time is fixed by law for the one who has to institute or confirm, but one must urge the superior to fix a time for him to do this, arg. c. nullus, de iur. pat. and noted in c. ex parte Astensis, de conces. praeben., and so the Lords of the Rota determine in decis. 251. I conclude, therefore, that it must undoubtedly be held that the one presented and instituted by the patron and the bishop is preferable, and that no right in the said plebs belongs to the apostolic expectant, since the presentation was made to the bishop within four months from the time of vacancy and notice, according to what is noted in d. c. fi. de iu. patr. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. An extraordinary remedy ceases where an ordinary one is available.
2. A perversion of the order of cause to cause does not invalidate a sentence by operation of law.
3. If the principal defendant is contumacious, proceedings can be taken against a third-party possessor without any discussion having been made.
4. The fisc, after confiscation of property has taken place, is not an heir, but a successor of vengeance.
5. A pupil can be cited.
body: In the present question, namely whether restitution should be granted to the said Guido and Nicola, three matters must be examined to elucidate the case. First, whether the sentences rendered against Carolus, the father of the said Guido and Nicola, had validity and effect. Second, whether the compromise and the arbitral award resulting from it between the aforesaid minors Guido and Nicola on the one part, and the said Nicolaus on the other, inflicted grievance and injury upon the said minors such that restitution in integrum belongs to them. Third, we shall discuss the validity and effect of the first decree interposed against the said Guido. Returning therefore to the first point, it seems initially that the said sentence rendered against Carolus lacked force: since the principal debtor had not been discussed, an hypothecary action was brought against the said Carolus, possessor of the goods, contrary to the order of law, especially since the said Carolus excepted that the principal debtor ought first to be sued and discussed, as is proved in auth. hoc si debitor, C. de pig., where under the newest law an hypothecary action against a third-party possessor is prohibited until action has been taken against the principal defendant and the sureties; moreover, it is established that an act done contrary to the provision of a statute, especially one concerning the order of law, is null, l. prolatum, C. de sen., and ij. q. vj. c. sententia, and l. non dubium, C. de legi., and x. dist. c. uides, and in the rule quæ contra ius, de re. iu. lib. 6. And from these points an inference is drawn with respect to the second principal doubt. For if the said sentence rendered against the late Carolus, parent of the said minors, was null, then the compromise subsequently entered into between the said minors after the death of the said Carolus and Nicolaus regarding the execution of the said sentence, and the arbitral award resulting from it, inflicted grievance and great injury upon the aforesaid minors: because, since the arbitrators or arbiters approved the said null sentence, they were enormously injured on two grounds. First, because they approved a null sentence, and thus inflicted harm in the matter itself; second, because the compromise deprived them of recourse on eviction against and with respect to those in the said goods, as in l. si dictum, §. si compromisero, ff. de euic. And consequently they can now seek restitution in integrum, l. quod si minor, §. 1. & seq., and almost through the whole title, ff. de mino. Concerning the third point, namely against the first decree interposed against the said Guido, a contumacious minor, it can be said that by operation of law, without any other restitution, the said Guido, and especially the said Nicola, his sister under puberty, are preserved uninjured on account of a defect of solemnity; because against minors, especially those under puberty, one ought not to proceed to the first decree unless their friends are first asked whether they wish to defend the minors; and with no one defending them, recourse is had to the refuge of the first decree, as the text seems to hold in l. hæc autem, ff. ex quib. cau. in pos. ea., and l. ergo sciendum est, ff. ex quib. cau. maio.

† But where an ordinary remedy is available, an extraordinary one ceases, as in l. in causæ, ff. de mino. From all of which it seems that restitution in integrum is available against the arbitral award; but with respect to the first decree they are preserved uninjured by operation of law. Nevertheless, notwithstanding the aforesaid, I consider the contrary opinion to prevail, moved principally because the aforesaid sentence rendered against the said Carolus held by pure law on multiple grounds, even though discussion had not been made against the principal debtor, and it passed into res judicata. First,

† because an inversion of the order of cause to cause does not vitiate a sentence by operation of law, but an appeal is required, as in l. j. and what is noted there, C. de appella., and l. j. §. si, ff. quæ sent. sine appel. rescin., where there is a good text; what is noted in ij. q. j. in summa supports this. But such is the inversion in our case: because the principal debtor ought to have been discussed before a transition was made to the third-party possessor. Yet there is no vice in the substance of the action, because the hypothecary action is indeed available against a third-party possessor, as in l. persecutione and l. distractis, C. de pign., nor is it an inversion of the order within the same cause; therefore such an anticipation of order does not vitiate it, since no appeal was lodged; and that such an inversion does not vitiate it ipso facto in our case is clearly held by Bart. following Iac. But. in the said l. persecutione, in the last question. Nor is it an obstacle that an exception was raised by the said Carolus that the principal debtor ought first to be discussed; because it is the same not to except as to except and not appeal from an express or tacit rejection, as in c. ex parte M. de app., and by Bar. in l. a procedente, C. de dila.; what the gloss notes in cle. una, de dolo & contumacia, on the word manifestè supports this. For against such an inversion of the order of cause to cause it is not sufficient to except unless, upon the exception not being admitted, an appeal is lodged, as in the said l. j. C. de appe. and the said l. j. in fi. ff. quæ sen. sine appel. rescind. And this applies most especially in our case. For since for many reasons an action can be brought against a third-party possessor without discussion having been made against the principal debtor, according to what is noted by the gloss and Bar. in l. decem, ff. de uerb. obli., and by the same Bart. in l. fi. primo responso, ff. si cer. pet., and as I shall explain more broadly below, by the very fact that the judge, without an exception of discussion having been made, proceeded to further steps and delivered sentence against the said Carolus, possessor of the goods, he is deemed to have tacitly pronounced that there was no place for discussion; and thus, presupposing that there had been a place for discussion, yet since it was tacitly pronounced to the contrary, what was done to the contrary held: because it is seen as an act done against the right of the litigant rather than against the law of the constitution, as in c. cum inter, de re iudi., and l. res iudicata, ff. de re iudic., and l. ingenuum, ff. de statu homi., and c. cum dilecti, de elect., and by Bart. in the said l. a procedente; it must therefore be imputed to the one not appealing. Hence, since the sentence created law between the parties when it passed into res judicata, its validity is no longer to be discussed, as in the laws just alleged; nor can these minors seek restitution against such a grievance—supposing that the judge had truly aggrieved him—because it was rendered against their parent and passed into res judicata during his lifetime; and thus, since nothing was done with the minors themselves, they cannot seek restitution in integrum, as is read and noted in l. Aemylius, ff. de mino. Secondly, the said sentence held principally by pure law without any discussion having previously been made, because, as is set forth to me in fact, the principal debtor was at that time a rebel, and all his goods had been confiscated, and thus it was notoriously established that in the said place where the judicial proceeding was being conducted, he was not solvent; in which case there is no need to make discussion, as the gloss and Bart. note in l. decem, ff. de uerb. oblig., and it is the text according to one interpretation which Bart. follows there in the said l. fi. primò responso, ff. si cer. peta. This is proved by reason, because superfluous remedies are not to be used, l. hæc stipulatio, §. diuus, ff. ut leg. no. cau.; for to what purpose should discussion be made if it is notorious that the debtor is not solvent? Surely the law would be imposed on words rather than things, contrary to c. commissa, de elec. lib. 6, and l. 2. in fi. C. communia de leg.; what is read and noted in a similar case in l. post rem iudicatam, ff. de transact., and l. eleganter, §. si post rem iudicatam, ff. de condit. inde., and what is noted there by Bar. in the first response supports this. And Bar. in l. decem and the said l. fi. ff. si cer. peta. seems most openly to have intended this within our terms, where he expressly said

† that if the principal defendant is a rebel, one can proceed against the third-party possessor without any discussion having been made; and he speaks properly in the said l. fi. when the goods of the debtor were bound. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that action ought first to have been brought against the fiscus, which possessed the goods of the said debtor, since the fiscus itself is bound to satisfy creditors, even those having a personal action, as in l. 2. C. ad leg. Iul. de ui. pub. and l. si ut proponis, C. de bo. proscr.; for I say

† that the fiscus, after the confiscation of the goods, is not an heir, but is a successor of vengeance, and succeeds not by representation, but by the annihilation of the person, as is fully noted in l. si constante, §. fi. sol. ma. Hence, since the said auth. hoc si debitor, previously alleged, is corrective of the ancient law, and only impedes the hypothecary action against a third-party possessor with respect to the debtor and his heir, it ought not to be extended to the fiscus, because, as I have said, it is not an heir, nor does it represent the person of the deceased, but is a successor of vengeance. For the fiscus can be called a third-party possessor; and thus a private third-party possessor ought not to be more privileged than the fiscus, especially because here the prejudice of the creditor is at issue, who by law has an hypothecary action against any possessor; yet since we are outside the case of the said authentica, the said creditor ought not to be impeded from using his hypothecary action against any possessor, since corrective law must be greatly restricted, as noted especially by Bart. in auth. quas actiones, C. de sac. san. ecc.; what is noted by the gloss in c. cupientes, §. quod si per uinginti, de elec. li. 6, and in l. præcipimus, in fi. de appel., and l. sancimus, C. de testa. supports this. And this seems sufficiently to have been the view of Bar. in the said l. fi. and the said l. decem. And from this second ground it appears clearer than daylight regarding the validity of the said sentence. Third, the notable gloss in the said auth. hoc si debitor can be adduced, which Cy. and Bal. follow there, which says that the hypothecary action against a third-party possessor is then impeded when the principal debtor is present, but otherwise if he is absent, just as we say in the case of a surety, as in auth. præsente, C. de fide iu. But in our case the debtor was absent and a rebel; nor could an action be brought against him for the purpose of referral. Therefore it was not necessary to make discussion; and this last point Bart. also intended in the said auth. hoc si debitor. From all of which it is clearly gathered that the said sentence rendered against the said Carolus, the father of these minors, was valid by law. Nor is any restitution available to the said minors against it, both because there was no grievance, but proceedings were juridically conducted against him, as is clear from the aforesaid, and because, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that something had been done contrary to the right of the litigant, nevertheless restitution is not available to the minors, since nothing was done with them, but with their father, said l. Aemylius. And from these points it is clearly inferred with respect to the second question that no restitution is available against the compromise or the arbitral award, because no grievance, but rather a relief, accrued to the minors, because the arbitrators reduced that sentence to a smaller sum, and thus relieved the minors and burdened dominus Nicolaus; nor was the ability to have recourse on eviction against the author taken away, on two grounds. First, because the said sentence held, as is clear from the aforesaid; and thus by virtue of it they could sue on eviction, since their father had made denunciation, as in the final chapter de emptione & uenditione; but the compromise had been made with respect to execution alone, in favor of these minors. Secondly and principally, because the compromise was made out of necessity, because it was by order of the officials, to whom full and free power concerning these matters was granted by the public authority, as Bartolus notes in the said l. si dictum, §. si compromisero, ff. de euict.; for this compromise was necessary and not voluntary, and thus the rationale of the said §. si compromisero ceases. From which it is clearly evident that no restitution is available, especially since it is not granted except for serious injury, l. Scio, ff. de in integr. restitu., and the penultimate chapter de rebus eccle. non alie. As to the third point concerning the interposition of the first decree, I think there is not much to dispute over its validity, although it could be alleged that the rector acted rightfully, because it was interposed against the said Guido, who was an adult, and thus according to the opinion of many it was not necessary to summon friends and blood relatives, on which see Barto. in the said l. hæc autem, and Cyn. in l. cum proponas, C. de bo. autho. iud. pos., especially since the citation reached the said major, according to what is noted by the gloss in l. 2. ff. ex qui. cau. in pos. ea.; nor should the said Guido be assisted by the benefit of restitution: both because contumacy is a fault, as noted in l. omne delictum, ff. de remis., and against a fault a minor is not assisted, l. auxilium, ff. de minoribus, and l. j. C. si aduer. do. For he ought to have appeared and requested that a curator be assigned to him, as in l. qui habebat, ff. de tut., and what Bartol. notes there in §. si pupillus, where he says

† that a ward can be cited: because it is understood that he appear with a tutor. Likewise, since the first decree inflicts a moderate injury, especially in our case, since it has not yet taken effect, because dominus Guido has always remained in possession and still is today, restitution cannot be sought, which is not granted for a moderate injury, said l. Scio, ff. de in integr. resti., and previously alleged c. pe., especially since he has a most prompt ordinary remedy, namely of satisfying him on whose behalf the first decree was interposed. For although placing into possession is otherwise lifted upon giving security for appearance in court and upon paying costs, as in cap. quoniam, §. in alijs, ut lite. non contest., that however applies when placing into possession was made on account of contumacy in not appearing: because by such security satisfaction is made to the cause of the placing into possession. But in our case the placing into possession was made on account of contumacy in refusing to execute the sentence of the arbitrators; therefore, unless execution is first made, the placing into possession ought not to be revoked, as is noted in the said §. in alijs, and by Bartol. in l. si finita, §. Iulia, ff. de damno infecto. Likewise, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the said placing into possession was not valid: nevertheless, since the validity of the said sentences is most clearly established, as appears from the aforesaid, the said minors Guido and Nicola must anew be compelled to obey the sentence of the arbitrators, or placing into possession must be made by the first decree, having cited the minors themselves with their tutor and curator according to the form of l. j. ff. de administr. tuto., or according to what is read and noted in the said l. hæc autem. And if they do not obey, the judge, on account of their excessive contumacy, taking into account that they have shown greater contempt and continue to show contempt today, will be able to decree that the person placed into possession by the first decree shall gain the fruits, according to the singular text in l. Fulcinus, in fin. ff. ex qui. cau., following the common reading which Bartol. holds there, and Spe. in the title de primo & secundo decreto, §. restat, verse hoc autem notandum. And let these remarks suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. To whomsoever an emphyteutic property has come, that person can be sued to pay the canon.
2. If an owner leases his estate for a certain rent, not he himself, but the lessee is bound to pay tithes.
3. One who knows an estate belongs to another, or is encumbered, if he buys it and has provided for himself concerning eviction, can, his knowledge notwithstanding, sue for eviction.
casus: A certain most illustrious prince, having considered the innumerable virtues, faith, urgent ardor, devotion, magnificent deeds, and most renowned and perpetually memorable actions of a certain magnificent and distinguished man, a count, etc., among other benefices conferred upon the said count, gave, delivered, and granted to the same count in noble and gentle fief a certain notable castle or town with all its district and jurisdiction. And among other things, the aforementioned prince promised to the said count, present and accepting, to defend, maintain, authorize, and disencumber the said castle with its district, jurisdiction, and appurtenances, etc., from every person and persons, and commune, college, and corporation, and to hold ratified, pleasing, and firm whatever the said count shall henceforth do, establish, and ordain in the said place, provided that they are such as do not look against the honor and state of the lord prince himself and of his successors, and that follow the nature of a fief, etc. Now, however, the said grant having been thus made, the bishop of the territory of the said castle or town hinders the lord count, the feudatory, by demanding from him four hundred florins annually, submitting that they are owed to him on account of the said castle. It is now asked whether the said lord count, the feudatory of the said castle, can have recourse against the said prince, so that he may defend him against the lord bishop, disencumber, and free him from every obligation that the said lord bishop claims.
body: The aid of Jesus Christ the Savior and of His mother Mary having been humbly invoked. It seems at first that the said Lord Bishop can direct an action and competent right against the aforesaid count, the possessor of the said castle, and that the said count has no recourse in this matter against the said prince, because, since the burden of paying that canon or pension is real, it passed with its burden to the possessor, a text being seen as notable in Authen. De non alie. § scire, col. ij, where it is notably proved,

† that anyone to whom an emphyteutic property has come can be sued for paying the canon; and through that text Baldus affirmed this in Authentica Si quas ruinas, C. De sacr. sanct. eccle. We see the same in the burden of paying tithes; for it passes to any possessor whatsoever, nor does the one paying have recourse against his author, as in cap. Tua, and cap. Pastoralis, De deci.

† that if a master leases his estate for a certain pension, not he himself, but the lessee is bound to pay the tithes, because he is understood to have sold the fruits, saving the tithe; he cites the said cap. Pastoralis. But I cite the notable text in l. j, C. De anno. & trib. lib. x, where it is said that he ought to pay the annona who holds the possession and gathers the fruits; and through that text the Gloss and Bartolus said there that when a master leases an estate for a certain pension, the burden of paying tributes belongs to the lessee himself; to the same point I adduce the good text in Auth. De mandatis principum § non permitta, col. iij, and in l. Inter debitorem, ff. De pact., where it is proved that the burden of paying tribute belongs to the possessor, even if a pact had been added that not the possessor, but the transferor should be bound to pay, because such a pact is valid to the prejudice of the one having the possession that is obligated for the pension. Nay rather, I say that even for past time the new possessor can be sued, as is the notable text in l. Imperatores, ff. De publi. The same, therefore, and more forcefully, must be said in our case, in which the prince reserved no benefit to himself in enfeoffing the said castle; for it ought to be understood that he granted it saving the real burden, to which he does not seem justly to be bound, since every benefit was passing to the said count, the feudatory. But the aforesaid notwithstanding, which truly in no way stand in the way of our case, I say that although the Bishop has an action against the said count, the possessor, yet the count, the feudatory himself, has recourse against the lord prince, who granted the said castle in fief, especially a noble and gentle one; for this conclusion I cite the texts to be noted in proper terms in c. 1, De inuesti. de re. ali. fac. col. x, where it is said that when an investiture is made of another's property or of property obligated to another, a distinction must be made as to whether it was made to one who knew or to one who was ignorant. For he who knowingly received the investiture of another's property, unless he provided for himself regarding eviction by a special pact, cannot sue for eviction; but he who receives it unknowingly rightfully sues that another property of the same quantity or goodness be furnished to him; but with respect to the one investing or enfeoffing, let no distinction be made, whether he knew it to be another's or obligated to another, or was ignorant of it, as is notably stated in the said first chapter. To the point, therefore: either the said count was ignorant that that castle was obligated to the Bishop, and then he undoubtedly sues against the prince to defend him from the Bishop, just as the said prince expressly promised in the investiture, or that he grant him another fief of the same goodness and quantity; and that is a marvelous text according to Baldus, in which one species is sought for another. But it must be observed in our case, because a feudal case ought principally to be decided according to the laws and customs of fiefs, and in default of them recourse must be had to the common law, as is the notable text in the first chapter, De feud. cog. in the same collation. And I judge that it is in the choice of the said count whether in this case he sues against the prince to defend him, just as was specifically agreed, l. j, ff. De pactis, or that he give him another fief of the same goodness and quantity. For by that provision of man there was no departure from the ordinary benefit of law, as Bartolus notes in the said l. Si constante, ff. Soluto matrimonio, though otherwise from the extraordinary; and in this case the text in l. fin. C. De pactis, conuen. must be understood. Likewise, that same point can be defended from the force of the pacts, since the prince promised to disencumber the said castle from every person; he is therefore bound to disencumber it, or to give a thing of the same goodness and quantity. And Baldus says in cap. fin. De noua forma fide. that the feudatory can sue against the lord for his interest in a twofold way: either that he be paid in money, or that he give him another fief, on the argument of that text in the first chapter, De inuestit. de reb. alie. fac. And the same must be said in our case. And ignorance of the said obligation on the part of the said count is to be presumed, because in another's deed ignorance is presumed, De reg. iur. lib. 6, and l. Regula, ff. De iur. & fac. igno.; or the said count had knowledge, and then he would have specially provided for himself in case of eviction or challenge, as appears in the grant of the fief; and he can sue against the lord prince as in the preceding case, as says the text previously cited in the said c. 1; l. Si fundum sciens, C. De euict. agrees, where it is clear,

† that if one, knowing a fief to belong to another or to be obligated, bought it and provided for himself regarding eviction, he can, notwithstanding his knowledge, sue for eviction. For one can also sell another's property to one's own prejudice, as in l. Rem alienam, ff. De contrah. emp. Secondly and principally to the same point, I cite the text in c. fi. De noua forma fide. in the same collation, where it is said that once the investiture is made, the lord must by all means be compelled to put the investee into vacant possession; and if he fails, he is bound to furnish him every utility. And I weigh that word, 'vacant': he ought therefore to deliver it without any obligation and servitude, as noted by Bartolus in l. 1, ff. De actio. emptio. Thirdly, I prove it through the first chapter, Per quos fiat inuesti. in the beginning, in the same collation, and what Baldus notes there. Fourthly, it makes for this that the said castle was granted as a noble and gentle fief and the said prince reserved nothing to himself, whence he seems to have granted it without any burden of obligation, and the count is only bound to those things that are owed under the common laws and customs of fiefs, cap. 1 in fin., Quid sit inuesti., and cap. 1, De noua forma fide. col. 10; and fully on this matter through Johannes Andreae in the additions to the Speculum, in the title De præscri. on the rubric, where he continues concerning a noble and free fief. Fifthly and lastly, the causes make for this on account of which the fief was granted, namely the magnificent deeds and the most illustrious and perpetually memorable merits of the said count, etc., as appeared more fully above in the recital of the case; for they cause the grant to receive the broadest interpretation in favor of the said count, the feudatory. Hence Baldus, following Jacobus de Ravanis, singularly said in cap. 1, Si uasal. feu. priue. cui. defe. col. 10, that a fief granted on account of the magnitude of merits—suppose because he delivered the grantor from death, or rescued him from enemies or bandits, or something similar—is forfeit by no law, cause, or ingratitude, for it seems to be the reward of extraordinary labor and not a liberal grant. To this is the notable text in l. Si pater, and l. Aquil. Regulus, ff. De don. For the magnitude of merits is to be set off against demerits; that makes for this which Bartolus notes in a similar matter in l. Si stipulatus § Si tibi nupsero, and l. Si diuortio, ff. De uerb. obliga., and l. 1, C. De donatione ante nup. I conclude, therefore, from the aforesaid that the said count has recourse against [the prince] to free the said castle from every obligation, or to give him another fief of the same goodness and quantity. The contrary arguments formulated above do not stand in the way; for they proceed in quasi-natural burdens, as in a tribute owed to the emperor by reason of possession, for that always follows the possessor, and in doubt it seems to have been agreed that the possessor should pay; and we see the same in ecclesiastical matters, 16. q. 1, c. Si quis laicus, in the said c. Pastoralis; it is otherwise now in an accidental burden, the said l. 1, ff. De act. emp. And whatever the case may be in other matters, in the grant of a fief this is most clear: that if a property granted simply in fief is found to belong to another or to be obligated, an action can be brought against the grantor in the aforesaid manner. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument: 1. To an injured minor there belongs within four years the benefit of restitution against lesion.
casus: In the case and question that is pending, or was recently ventilated, between Paulus, a minor, with the authority of his guardian, on the one part, and a certain Sanctus of Arezzo, on the other, two matters are principally to be examined. First, whether a minor claiming lesion from an award that followed by virtue of a compromise made by order of the judge, as is provided by the statute of Arezzo, can be aided through the benefit of restitution, the aforesaid lesion not having otherwise been proven. Second, whether, upon enormous lesion having been shown, he can seek this restitution, or otherwise object concerning the iniquity of the award, especially since an evident lesion is alleged, which can be proven immediately from this: that a hypothecary action was brought against the ward himself, without discussion against the principal, who was solvent, having otherwise been made; because, although an exception was raised, the arbiter or arbitrators rendered a sentence on the hypothecary action against the ward himself, adjudging that certain goods possessed by that ward were to be detained in place of a pledge or hypothec until satisfaction should be made by the ward himself for the amount of one hundred florins that were being claimed, and the aforesaid things can be immediately proven.
body: Having humbly invoked the protection of Christ and of His most pious Mother. Regarding the first point, it seems that the said minor can seek restitution without having otherwise proven lesion extrinsically, because by the very fact that a minor enters into a compromise, he is deemed to be injured, as is the notable text in l. si minor uiginti quinque annis. §. minores, ff. de minori. The reason is, as the glossa and Bartolus note there, that no appeal can be taken from an arbitrator's sentence, l. 1. C. de arbit.; and if he loses the benefit of appeal through a compromise, he is deservedly granted restitution as one injured. And this seems to apply even in a compromise made as if into arbitrators (arbitratores), having regard to the statute of the city of Arezzo, which prohibits asserting nullity and iniquity against the sentence or award of arbitri and arbitratores; and thus, by virtue of the statute, the same reasoning holds in both, whereas it would be otherwise in the case of arbitratores under the common law, as Bartolus notes in the said l. si minor. But notwithstanding this, I think otherwise should be said in our case. For the contrary holds when the minor has compromised voluntarily, in which case lesion is presumed for the aforesaid reason. But in our case the compromise was made by order of the judge, to whom power was granted by the statute of the city in favor of the minor, lest he be harassed by the windings of judicial proceedings, and in favor of the republic, lest lawsuits be immortal. Furthermore, that the statute is valid is supported by what Bartolus notes in prooemio C. and the glossa in l. neque pignus. §. priuatorum, ff. de re. iu. Supporting the first assertion exceedingly well is what the same Bartolus notes in l. si dictum. §. si compromisero, ff. de aedil. edic., where he says that if someone is compelled to compromise by virtue of a statute, he nevertheless has recourse for eviction against his author, just as if he had been convicted in court. Moreover, that statute would be harmful rather than useful, and would serve only for wind, if the minor could say that he was injured solely from having compromised; but the law ought to be applied to realities, not to words, as in c. commissa, de ele. li. 6. and l. 1. in fi. C. communia, de le.; c. ab arbitris and what is noted there, de offi. dele. li. 6., also supports the aforesaid. Therefore, coming to the second doubt and concluding briefly, I say that the said minor can be aided against the said lesion on a twofold ground, notwithstanding the statute of the city.

† First, through the special benefit of restitution. For to an injured minor there belongs within four years the benefit of restitution against a non-slight lesion, as in ff. de mino. throughout, and l. si, C. de temp. in inte. rest.; for minors and the church are succored against contracts and sentences of judges, as in c. 1. and 2. de in inte. resti. li. 6. and l. in causae, with the following law, and l. quod si minor, ff. de mino.; all the more strongly must they be succored against the award of arbitri, since it is a kind of contract, or quasi-contract, as in auth. si uero contigerit, C. de iud. and in the body of the text, ut disse. iud. Indeed, far more strongly ought he to be succored in this case, since he is injured by another, namely an arbitrator, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. societatem. §. arbitratorum, ff. pro socio. And this is clearest when common law is inspected. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the minor is not much injured in this case, since he has recourse against his author, who is presupposed to be solvent, and restitution is denied for a slight lesion, l. scio, ff. de in inte. rest. and in c. pen. de re. eccl. non ali. For I say that, on the contrary, he is gravely injured, since it will behoove him to involve himself in the windings of judicial proceedings. Whence a notable text says that minors are succored not only when something of their goods is diminished, but also when it is in their interest not to be harassed by lawsuits and expenses, as in [l.] minoribus uigintiquinque annis, ff. de min. And if this matter in question were of slight prejudice, auth. hoc si debitor, C. de pig., would not have emanated with such solemnity, correcting the old law. Likewise, it is far better to rely on a pledge and on the thing itself than to sue against a person, as the text says in §. furti autem, insti. de obli. quae ex deli. nas. We must therefore see whether the censure of the municipal statute contradicts this conclusion; and indeed I think not. For, regarding the matter at hand, the statute only says that from such awards or arbitraments rendered in a cause involving minors, no appeal or objection may be made, nor can iniquity or nullity be opposed, in the same manner that is observed and provided for compromises and awards that are made and rendered in the court of the lord Captain of the said city. But the statute of the court of the lord Captain is as follows: Against awards or arbitraments one may not appeal, or claim to be aggrieved, or oppose nullity, under penalty of twenty-five pounds for anyone who acts to the contrary; whence the words of the said statutes must be weighed diligently, which only seem to exclude the complainant from the general benefit of the common law, so that iniquity cannot be asserted, etc.; and thus it excludes the minor insofar as he would proceed by the common law, but not when he sues by the law of minors, seeking restitution in integrum against lesion. For since I have said that two remedies belong to the minor in this case, when one is taken away generally by the statute, the other remains: an optimal argument from what the glossa notes in c. pe. de empt. & uen., which says that if a minor swore not to contravene a contract, he is understood to be excluded only from the benefit of age; whence if he was deceived beyond half of the just price, he can proceed by the common law, from which he does not appear excluded by those general words. And the same is held by Bartolus and others in l. ij. C. de rescin. uendi. And this interpretation is benign, especially to be adopted in our case by a twofold consideration. First, because since that statute is contrary to the common law, and odious, it must be interpreted most strictly, so that it harms the common law as little as possible, as is the notable text in c. cum dilectus, de consue. and l. ij. C. de noxa. Second, because since that statute speaking of minors emanated principally in favor of minors, it must be greatly restricted insofar as it is turned to their injury, lest what was established in their favor be turned to their detriment, as in l. quod fauore, C. de legib. and in the rule quod ob gratiam, de reg. iur. lib. 6. And the aforesaid I understand provided that a non-slight lesion is proven by the minor, as I said before. Secondly and principally, in my judgment, the said minor can proceed under the common law, seeking that the said award be reduced to the arbitrament of an upright man, just as any person of full age could, notwithstanding the said statute; because since the statute speaks generally in an odious and restrictable matter, it ought not to be extended to a case where an evident, enormous lesion is alleged that can be proven immediately. For it is not likely that the statute intended to foster evident iniquity, since in doubt a law must be presumed just and reasonable, dist. iiij. c. erit autem lex. And it must be interpreted that the legislators intended just as they would have enacted if the case of evident iniquity had been specially presented before them, as the glossa says in l. tale pactum, ff. de pact. And that the legislators did not intend it in the case of evident iniquity, especially against a minor, is clearly gathered from the words of the statute, when it says, 'lest lawsuits become immortal'; which rationale ceases when the lesion is evident and can be proven immediately. To this I allege the notable glossa in c. suscitata, de in integr. resti., at the word effectum sententiae, which expressly holds that where a legitimate exception against a sentence is removed, it must be understood unless that exception is proven immediately. To this c. literas, de restit. spo., is exceptionally pertinent, where an exception is admitted that can be proven within a brief delay, which otherwise by the common rules of law was removed; to the same effect is the notable glossa in l. j. §. siue autem, ff. de tab. exhib. and what Oldradus notes in consi. 45, which begins Cum litera executoria, where he notably said the same thing; for a provision generally removing an exception must be strictly understood, as in cap. ex parte, ij. de offic. delegat.; and Bartolus notably said in l. j. ff. quod ui aut clam that where a statute generally removes every exception, the office of the judge can be implored, by the argument in l. plene, ff. de peti. haeredi. The aforesaid is very well supported by l. iij. §. ibidem, ff. ad exhib. And by what the glossa notes in cap. 1. and c. literas, de restitu. spol., where it is clear that an exception generally denied is admitted if proof is offered immediately; and this must be said most especially in our case, in which the statute is contrary to law and harms the right of the party by taking away every remedy belonging to the injured party, by the argument in the said l. ij. C. de noxa and c. cum dilectus, de consue. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Every solemnity of civil law ceases in bequests to pious causes.
2. A soldier can substitute to a pubescent son through direct words.
3. A captatory will is valid in legacies to pious causes.
4. Hospitals and any other places in which works of charity are exercised are called pious places.
5. The Falcidian contains within itself the Trebellianic.
body: Invoking the name of Christ, with respect to the two written doubts, I will add only certain points omitted by the above-written doctors. And first, regarding the first, namely that the said substitution made in favor of the consortium or confraternity is valid as a fideicommissary substitution, I expressly cite Bar. holding this in the same or entirely similar terms, to wit, in the repetition on l. Centurio, ff. de vulg. & pupil., in the 16th col., at the words, 'quaero principaliter quarto,' where he establishes the conclusion that when a substitution is made through direct words and through common words, the direct word remains in its proper signification, and the common word is drawn to a fideicommissum, so that the addition of the common word may thus effect something; and then he says that it is in the choice of the substitute to embrace the direct words or the common, or oblique, words—namely, either to take the inheritance from the direct substitution or from the fideicommissary one. He cites l. testamento, ff. de manumi. testam., and l. recusare, §. Titius, ff. ad Treb., and provides an example: if the testator used these words, namely, 'if my son shall die without children, I substitute such a person, and I make him heir to him'; or, 'if my goods shall come to such a person, I institute him heir in them.' He says the same if the testator said, 'if my son shall die without children, I institute and substitute Titius.' For since the word 'instituto' is direct, as in l. j, in prin., de vul. & pup., but the word 'substituo' is common, the substitution will be valid under both laws; to this point l. pe., ff. de ven. insp., is pertinent. He says the same if the testator uses a common word and an oblique word, saying thus: 'if my son shall die without children, I will that my goods come to Titius by right of substitution and of fideicommissum'; for 'substitution' is a common word, while 'fideicommissum' is oblique; therefore it must be understood that both are valid, and it is in the choice of the substitute, as the text proves in the said l. recusare, §. Titius. This occurs point for point in the present case. For in the testament, among other things, it is said that the testator substituted and made the said consortium or confraternity universal heir, and bequeathed and bequeaths all his goods, etc. For the word 'heir' is direct, but the word 'substituted' is a common word, as noted in the said l. Centurio, and in c. 1, de test., lib. 6, and in c. Raynu., under the same title; therefore, the said substitution must be made oblique by reason of the common word, as is fully noted in the laws cited before. And it seems even more indubitable in our case, since the testator added those words, 'and bequeathed and bequeaths all his goods,' which most clearly denote a fideicommissum; and if one were to say the contrary, those words would effect nothing, which must not be said, because words must effect something, as in c. si Papa, de privil., lib. 6, and l. si quando, C. de inoffi. testa., especially where the disposition cannot otherwise be preserved—in which case words are even to be taken improperly, as is the text noted in c. si sententia, de sen. excommu., lib. 6; l. si stipulatus fuero per te, ff. de verbo. obliga., and in l. stipulatio ista, §. sed si servus, and §. possidere, under the same title, are relevant, as well as Bal. in cap. 1, de Capitaneo, qui curiam vendi., col. x, and per the Archdeacon, xiij. q. j. ca. 1. The same testator also intended the same thing in another place in the testament, where he said that 'in any of the aforesaid cases, etc., then his inheritance and goods should come to the aforesaid consortium'; whence I weigh the word 'goods' and the word 'should come', which are common; therefore they must be drawn to a fideicommissum so that the substitution may be valid, as in the said c. Raynutius and c. si pater, de test., lib. 6. Whence, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that a substitution made to a person above puberty through direct words is not valid, according to one interpretation given to l. verbis civilibus and to l. in pupillari, ff. de vul. & pup., that nevertheless applies when the substitution is made through direct words alone; it is otherwise where it is made through direct and common words, or through common and oblique words, as occurs in our case. For a thing ought to be interpreted rather so that it may be valid than that it should perish, in c. abbate sane, de re iud., li. 6, and in l. quoties, ff. de ver. obli., especially in testaments, in which a broad interpretation ought to be made, as in c. cum dilecti, de dona., and in l. in testamentis, ff. de re. iur., and above all in favor of a pious cause, as in our case, as in l. sunt personae, ff. de reli. & sump. fu., and in auth. de ecc. ti., in §. si quis autem unum sanctorum, and in c. cum tibi, de testa. Secondly and principally, I am moved by another, no less conclusive reason.

† For in bequests to pious causes, every solemnity of the civil law ceases, and the mere intention according to the ius gentium is regarded, as in c. relatum, de test.; Bal. holds this in l. 1, C. de sac. san. eccl. Indeed, Bartol. in the said l. 1 maintained that the same applies under the civil law by virtue of the said l. 1, and maintained that just as a soldier has free discretion in making a testament, so also does one who disposes to pious causes.

† Moreover, that a soldier can substitute to a son above puberty through direct words is certain, as in the said l. centurio; therefore, such a substitution can also be made directly to pious causes by a civilian (paganus). Supporting this is that it cannot be denied that this prohibition of direct substitution after puberty is of civil law and not of the ius gentium. For if it were of the ius gentium, it could not be remitted in the case of a soldier, because those things that are of the ius gentium are not abolished by the prince, as in clement. pastoralis, de re iud., per Inno. in cap. quae in ecclesiarum, de constitu., and Bart. in l. fin., C. si contra ius vel utili. pub.; therefore, since such a prohibition is of civil law, it has no place in bequests to pious causes. We see, furthermore, that almost all the rules of the civil law handed down in the matter of last wills cease in bequests to pious causes, as is fully read and noted in cap. cum tibi and c. relatum, de test., per Barto. and Bald. in l. 1, C. de sacros. eccle., cited above; hence it is that, according to the common opinion of the doctors,

† a captatory will is valid in these bequests to pious causes. Likewise, one can die partly testate and partly intestate, just like a soldier, nor are bequests invalidated if the inheritance is not entered upon from the testament; and the same in similar questions, as is most fully noted by the doctors of both laws in the places cited above. The substitution, however, made in favor of the said consortium or confraternity is said to be to pious causes. And although some cite for this the gloss in cap. si qui clericorum, 11. quaestio. 1, and the Archdeacon in cap. si quis, 42. distin., nevertheless the gloss and the Archdeacon do not say this, but only assert that such confraternities or consortia are not reprobated. But I cite Specu. in the title de instrum. edi., in §. nunc vero aliqua, at the word 'scias,' among bequests to pious causes, where it is concluded

† that hospitals and any other places in which works of charity are exercised are called pious places; I cite to this end a good text and what Bartol. notes there in l. omnia privilegia, C. de epi. & cle., and more expressly the same Bar. in l. 1, §. fi., ff. de colle. illi.; the text in c. requisisti, de test., is also pertinent. And from these things I infer with respect to the second doubt, whether the Trebellianic portion is to be deducted from the aforesaid inheritance; and I say that it is not, on two grounds. For if the consortium wishes to enter upon the inheritance by direct right—which it can do by special privilege, as I have said above, and because the testator also substituted directly—the Trebellianic portion ought not to be deducted, because it does not take from the hands of the heir, but immediately from the testator himself, and thus just as we say in the case of a soldier, as in the said l. centurio. If, however, it wishes to claim the said goods by fideicommissum, which it can do by the aforesaid, then by special right the Trebellianic portion ought not to be deducted, by auth. similiter, C. ad le. Fal., although the gloss holds the contrary in the said c. si pater, de test., li. 6, which sought to restrict that authentic to the Falcidian portion, which is deducted from individual legacies, but did not want to extend it to the Trebellianic portion, which is deducted from the whole body of the inheritance. Nevertheless, the common opinion of modern doctors of both laws is to the contrary, and Bar. holds it in l. Marcellus, ad Treb., and Bal. in l. id quod pauperibus, C. de epi. & cle., and Cy. in auth. sed cum testator, C. ad legem Fal., and I have seen consilia of solemn doctors on this matter. And the principal motive for this opinion is

† that the Falcidian contains within itself the Trebellianic. For the Trebellianic is in a broad sense called the Falcidian; and the text seems to support this in authen. de eccle. titu., §. cum autem, in l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de episco. & cleri., where mention is made of a particular legacy and of an inheritance to be restored, and nevertheless every Falcidian deduction is there prohibited in bequests to pious causes. Likewise, today legacies and fideicommissa have been equated, as in l. 2, C. communia de leg.; whence, just as the Falcidian ceases in legacies, so it must cease in fideicommissa. Nor does the aforesaid cap. si pater stand in the way, because it only proves by an argument a contrario sensu, but such an argument ceases where the contrary is found in law, as in c. a nobis 1. & 2., de sentent. excom. Likewise, an argument a contrario sensu would proceed there with respect to the legitim, but not with respect to the Trebellianic portion. Nor does the motive of the gloss in the said c. si pater stand in the way, namely that the heir would be heir in vain if he does not deduct the Trebellianic portion; indeed he is not so in vain, because he will have merit from God by exercising the act itself, both with respect to the deceased and with respect to the poor, to whom the restitution or distribution is to be made; what Bald. notes on a similar point in the authentic cited before is pertinent. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Clerics can submit to arbitration by laymen concerning temporal matters, especially those pertaining to their patrimony.
2. And they can approve a sentence rendered by their judge.
3. Statutes of laymen not specifically providing concerning clerics, nor against ecclesiastical liberty, provided they are otherwise honorable, must be observed among clerics, even in the ecclesiastical forum.
4. If a cleric litigates before a layman, following the forum of the defendant, he tacitly submits himself to all statutes of laymen concerning the order of trial.
5. Arbiters can be called judges, taking the word broadly.
6. Jurisdiction can be tacitly prorogated.
7. A fine imposed by a judge by reason of contumacy, if at the time of knowledge the contumacy of that person is not evident to the judge, is not valid.
8. A sentence rendered against several colleagues simply induces an obligation for a part, so that each is deemed condemned for one half.
9. An arrest made by a secular judge against a married cleric not walking in habit and tonsure is valid.
body: The aid of the Most High having been sought from the heart: Because five doubts principally come up for examination, I shall address each doubt by itself according to the order of the consultation. And first, concerning the first, by which it is asked in effect whether a submission to arbitration (compromissum) made to four lay merchants in the court of the officials of the merchant guild by two brothers on the one part—namely, Iacobus and Philippus, who conducted themselves as merchants—is valid, since one of them, namely Iacobus, now alleges that he is a cleric in minor orders, while the other, namely Philippus, is found to be a married cleric. And, on the presupposition that the submission was valid, it is asked whether the said Iacobus could, through a proctor, submit himself to the decision and order of that case, to the statutes, customs, and style of the merchant guild; and thus in effect they can be called two doubts. Addressing the matter conclusively, I say that the submission was valid, even if both had been clerics in holy orders.

† Because submission to arbitration concerning temporal matters can well be made by clerics to laymen, especially regarding matters pertaining to their patrimony, as is proved in c. exposita and c. dilecti, de arbi., and by an argument a contrario sensu in c. contingit, and noted in c. si diligenti, de foro compet., in gl. 1, near the end, which says that although a cleric cannot consent to a lay judge, as is stated there, he nevertheless validly consents to an arbiter without the bishop's consent. And the reason for the difference can well be because a judge has jurisdiction, whence by prorogation he would be subjected to the jurisdiction of a secular judge, because through prorogation jurisdiction is extended into the prorogated matter, and the judge judges by his own right and by prescriptive jurisdiction, as in l. 1 and 2, ff. de iudi., which cannot happen regarding a cleric, both because a layman cannot have jurisdiction over clerics by reason of incapacity, 96. dist., c. denique, and c. si imperator, and c. cum ad verum, and because jurisdiction cannot be prorogated to another kind of jurisdiction, because then it would not be a prorogation, but the grant of a new jurisdiction, as is noted in c. P. & G., de offi. deleg., and by Cy. in l. testamenta, C. de testa. An arbiter, however, does not have jurisdiction, but a certain cognizance (notio), and his pronouncement is abided by through fear of the penalty placed in the submission, l. ait praetor, and l. a divo Pio, in prin., ff. de iud., and in c. dilecti, and c. pervenit, de arbi., and l. diem proferre, § stari, ff. eo. And this applies especially when the submission is made to a layman as an arbiter and arbitrator.
