For such a one is an amicable compositor between the parties, as in auth. si vero contigerit, C. de iudi., and in corpore, as on the difference of judges is noted by Inn. in c. Quintavallis, de iureiur., and Bar. in l. societatem, § arbitrorum, ff. pro socio. Nor is it an obstacle that the submission was made in the court of the officials of the merchant guild, and that their authority intervened, because by this the nature of the submission is not altered, and the authority of those officials could intervene for greater caution, at least with respect to those who were not clerics; and abundant caution does no harm, l. testamenta, C. de testam. And this applies especially in our case, in which neither of them was in holy orders, but rather both conducted themselves as laymen and merchants, by the argument of c. ex parte 3, de privileg., and c. finale, de vita & honesta. clerico. With respect to the second part of the doubt, I say that the said Iacobus could, through his proctor or by himself, subject himself before those merchants to the statutes, customs, and style of the court of the officials of the merchant guild, provided that they are such as concern the ordering and decision of the case, and do not violate the privilege of immunity of person or forum; because those [privileges] were granted to the entire clerical body, not to individual persons, and therefore renunciation is not valid in them, as in the said c. si diligenti, and in c. contingit, de sentent. excommu. But that a case be ordered or decided in a certain manner and order does not violate the clerical privilege, since the parties agree that a certain judgment be rendered by a judge, and the judge ought in this to follow the agreement of the parties, l. si convenerit, ff. de re iu., for this tends to nothing else than to recall the parties to concord, l. 1, § inde quaeritur, ff. de no. ope. nun.; to the same effect is the gloss noted in c. significasti, de fo. comp.,

† which says that clerics can approve a sentence rendered by a judge not their own, and such a sentence will have the force of a pact; in favor of this is the good text in l. 2, C. communia utriusque iu., and what is noted there. For just as they can submit themselves to a sentence rendered by an alien judge so that it has the force of a pact, so they can submit themselves to lay statutes as to the decision of the case by force of a pact, though not by force of the statutes. And this would especially hold true following the opinion of Barto. in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. tri., where he held

† that statutes of laymen not specifically providing concerning clerics nor against ecclesiastical liberty, provided they are otherwise honorable, ought to be observed among clerics even in an ecclesiastical forum, by the argument of c. constitutus, de in integ. resti., and in c. 3, de eo qui mit. in poss., and c. cum causa, de re iu., although I do not believe that dictum to be simply true by c. ecclesia S. Mariae, joined with the statement of the case which the gloss made in c. ecclesia, ut lit. pend.; but nevertheless that dictum serves extremely well for the argument of our decision, that at least by force of a pact such statutes ought to be observed in cases of clerics. Furthermore, I see

† that by the very fact that a cleric litigates before a layman, following the forum of the defendant, he tacitly submits himself to all lay statutes concerning the ordering of the trial, as noted by the gloss in c. quod clericis, de foro compet., and Io. Cald. in a certain disputation of his which begins 'statutis &c.', and Bart. in the said l. cunctos populos; indeed, Hostiensis in the said c. quod clericis maintained that if an inheritance question of a cleric is litigated, or otherwise a temporal one, it ought to be decided in the secular forum according to the laws, and what he notes in the Summa, in tit. de testa., § conficiuntur, verse 'verum', supports this, and what Dom. Anto. notes in the said c. quod clericis. And however it may be concerning this question, which I examined most fully in the said c. quod clericis in my lecture, it nevertheless seems undoubted that a cleric could by pact subject himself in the ordering and decision of that case to those lay statutes and customs, since they do not diminish the clerical privilege, but only the favor of the person is considered purely in this, because they were merchants; therefore the case ought to be decided, even absent a pact, according to the laws and customs of the merchant guild, because this seems tacitly agreed, as Cald. notes in the said disputation; and l. quod si nolit, § quia assidua, ff. de aedil. edic., supports this. And these things as to the first principal doubt. I conclude, therefore, that the said submission to laymen was valid, even as to the clerics, and that they could give the arbiters or arbitrators the power of ordering and deciding the case according to the custom and statutes of the merchant guild. And concerning the married cleric there is no doubt, because in civil matters he does not enjoy clerical privilege, as in c. unico, de cleri. coniug., in Sexto. I come to the second doubt, by which it is asked whether, by virtue of the said submission made by the parties themselves to arbiters, there was attributed to them that authority and jurisdiction which is attributed by the statutes of the said court of the merchant guild to the judge of that court; so that three arbiters out of four could not proceed without the fourth, he not having been sought out and summoned, although power was given to them that all four, or three of them, might proceed. And the doubt arises because in the submission it was stated that these arbiters should succeed into the place of those officials of the court of the merchant guild as to all things contained therein, to be done, heard, seen, cognized, handled, prosecuted, examined, calculated, reviewed, finished, decided, adjudged, arbitrated, awarded, confirmed, and determined according to the form of law, of the statutes, customs, style, and use of the said court of the merchant guild, &c. And in a certain statute of the said court it is provided that in decisions of questions above a certain sum there must be present and consenting the judge and four consuls of the said court, the other two consuls of the said court having nevertheless been sought out. I arbitrate regarding the first part by saying that no jurisdiction was conferred upon the said arbiters, because the consent of private individuals does not make those men judges who preside over no jurisdiction, as in l. privatorum, C. de iurisd. om. iud., and c. significasti, de foro compet., especially because here the submission was made to them as to arbiters, of whose nature it is that jurisdiction is not transferred to them, but a certain cognizance, as I said above. And although it was said that they should succeed into the place of the consuls, this must nevertheless be understood with respect to cognizing and concluding, as is clear from the tenor of the submission. Likewise, because arbitrations have been brought into conformity with judicial proceedings, l. 1, ff. de arbitr., it could deservedly be said that they succeeded into the place of those consuls before whom that question had first been brought.

† Hence it is that, the term being taken broadly, arbiters can be called judges, as is the text joined with the gloss in 2. q. 6, c. a iudicibus. As to the second part of this doubt, whether three were bound to seek out the fourth who was absent, and wait for him for the due time: it seems at first that they were, because, since they were appointed after the likeness of those consuls, and had to proceed according to the style of that court, and it is of the style and statute of that court that although four of them can proceed, they must nevertheless first seek out the other two, as I said above; therefore the same is to be said of these arbiters, that although it was said in the submission that all or three of them could proceed and decide, it ought nevertheless to be understood as being with the fourth having first been sought out, after the likeness of the consuls, since they were appointed in their place. What is read and noted in a similar case especially by Bal. in l. omnia privilegia, C. de episc. & cle., and by Inno. in c. inter dilectos, de fide instru., supports this, for that which is subrogated must also savor of the nature of that in whose place it is subrogated, as in c. ecclesia, ut lite pendente, and in l. sed si rem & pretium, ff. de peti. haere. But notwithstanding this, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer. And first I say that by law, where power is given to several with this expressed, that all or some of them may proceed, since their own advantage is not at issue, some can proceed without the rest, even without their having been sought out; on this there is an express text and note in c. cum plures, de offi. deleg., in Sexto; noted by Bar. in l. si uni, otherwise beginning Pomponius, ff. de re iudi., and in l. haeredes mei, § peto, ad Trebel. And thus, looking at pure law, by reason of the form of the submission, three of them could proceed without the fourth having been sought out. Nor does it stand in the way that the consuls do not proceed without two having been sought out, because I say that these arbiters did not succeed into the place of the consuls in all respects, but only with respect to hearing, handling, and concluding the dispute according to the statutes and style of the court of the merchant guild, as is clearly evident from the form of the submission, where it is said that for the things below to be handled, concluded, etc., they succeeded in place of the consuls, and thus with respect to the contents of the submission, not with respect to exercising power together or separately, because this is not among the things contained in the submission. Likewise, it is gathered from another point that this subrogation into the place of the consuls does not extend to this case, because the consuls are six, and four of them can proceed; but these arbiters were four, and three of them could proceed; and thus the words cannot be adapted to this case. Whence from the diversity of fact and nature a diversity in law is inferred, by the argument in l. si idem codicilli, C. de codicillis; l. si ex plagis, § in clivo, ff. ad legem Aquil., supports this. Furthermore, on account of those general words we ought not to depart from the proper meaning of the words, by the argument in c. fin., de verbo. significa., especially because a general provision ought not to be extended to a case specially provided for, as in l. sanctio, ff. de poenis, and l. doli clausula, ff. de verbo. obligatio. Therefore, those general words, that they should proceed as the consuls to handling and concluding the case, are not to be referred to the special provision of the power of proceeding, namely that four or three of them might proceed, so as to understand that the absent third had to be sought out; which would be contrary to the nature of the words and the disposition of the law; and this I consider most true. Wherefore I conclude that three of them could proceed, the absent fourth not having been sought out. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the fourth was sometimes present at the proceedings, contrary to the said c. cum plures, where it is clear that once three begin to proceed, the fourth ought not to meddle further unless the others are impeded, etc.; because I say that although he could not intrude himself, nevertheless, since the parties did not object, he seems on those occasions to have received power from the parties. For

† jurisdiction also can be tacitly prorogated, as is proved in c. cum olim, de offic. delegat., noted by Barto. in l. 1, at the end, ff. de iudi., and Inno. in c. ad petitionem, de accu. But, having presupposed without prejudice to the truth that the said fourth arbiter ought to have been sought out, it is asked whether credence should be given to the writing of the notary alone, in which he attests that he was sought out and waited for during the due time, although in the same acts there appears no report made by a messenger, as is accustomed to be done? And first it seems that it should not, because others ought to be certain whose power is consolidated from another's will or inability, as is read and noted in c. prudentiam, in princ., de offic. delega., and by Bar. in l. si finita, § Iulianus, ff. de damn. infect., and l. multa, ff. de conditio. & demonstratio.,

† where he says that a fine imposed by a judge by reason of contumacy is not valid if at the time of the sentence the contumacy was not established to the judge, because the messenger had not yet made his report. But I think the contrary is true, because that requisition could have been made in the presence of the notary, and thus the notary could write that he had been sought out; he could also have been sought out by the other arbiters in the presence of the notary, as in the said c. prudentiam, and l. 2, C. quo. & quando iudex. Moreover, credence is given to the enunciative words of a notary when the matter enunciated could have occurred at the time the instrument was drawn up, as noted by Inn. in c. quoniam, de prob., and Bart. in auth. si quis in aliquo documento, C. de eden., and gl. 1 in l. 1, C. de fide instru. & iure hastae fisc., book 10. And this applies especially, considering what is presupposed to me in fact, that from ancient times and down to the present day, concerning the requisition of an absentee, reliance is placed solely on the writing of the notary of the acts without any citation made by a messenger appearing in the acts; for custom is the best interpreter of laws, l. si de interpretatione, ff. de leg., and c. cum dilectus, de consue.; and custom can make an instrument authentic which otherwise is not authentic, as is the notable text in c. cum dilectus, de fid. instr.; l. de quibus, ff. de legi., supports this. And this concerning the second principal doubt. To the third doubt, whether the sentence of the arbiters holds good when rendered in the absence of the parties, they having nevertheless first been warned and cited by the said arbiters to come on a certain day to hear the sentence: and truly, although looking at pure common law, since power was not given to them of pronouncing in the absence of the parties, a sentence rendered in their absence is not valid, although the penalty is incurred, as is the notable text in l. diem proferre, § si quis litigatori, ff. de arbi., and in l. 2, C. eo., and noted in both places by Bartolus; nevertheless, considering that these arbiters were to proceed according to the statutes and style of the court of the officials of the merchant guild, as was said above, and it is of the statute and style of the said court that sentence may be rendered with the parties absent, provided they have been cited; therefore the said sentence was valid. And this applies especially if the said arbiters were arbitrators and amicable compositors, through what is noted in c. Quintavallis, de iureiur., and l. si quis arbitratu, ff. de ver. obl., and especially by Bald. in l. si qui ex consensu, C. de epi. audi. I come to the fourth doubt, whether the decrees of the magnificent Lord of Lucca providing concerning submissions to arbitration, delegations, and instances of the said court are of such power that they bring it about that the said instance is not extinguished (perempta), and since the said Iacobus, a cleric, submitted himself to the said decrees by virtue of the pacts placed in the said submission, which decrees the said judge and consuls are bound to obey, and to terminate cases coming both in the said court and those which are committed by the said court both by command and by the will of the parties according to the form of the said decrees; otherwise they incur the penalty of the decree, etc. In this doubt, considering the contingency of the case, I observe that, looking at pure common law, the instance was not extinguished here, because a three-year period had not yet elapsed from the time of the joinder of issue (litis contestatio). For even by common law an instance lasts for three years before arbiters, just as before a judge, as is the common opinion, and noted by the gloss and Bar. in l. item si unus, § si multo post, ff. de arbi., and by Spe. in tit. eo., § differt, verse 'intra triennium', and by modern writers in c. presbyter, de iudi. But because the submission was made here for the term of one year, and the arbitral award was rendered after the year, it seems that it does not hold, because it was outside the period of the submission. But this does not stand in the way, because by consent of the parties the submission was prorogated, as is stated in the premise, and the sentence was rendered within the prorogated time; deservedly, the sentence ought to stand, as is proved in l. si cum dies, ff. de arb. Nor ought the decrees of the magnificent Lord of Lucca to stand in the way, because he himself consented to the prorogation; and also afterwards prorogated it. For he did so as one having the rights of a prince in the said city, because just as he could promulgate a law concerning the instance, so also he could dispense regarding it. What is noted by Bar. in l. infamem, at the end, ff. de pub. iu., and in l. hostes, ff. de cap. & postl. re., and Io. An. in the rule cui licet quod est plus, de reg. iur. in Sexto, in Mercurialibus, supports this; and without doubt the law and the dispensation were valid on account of those who were not clerics. Nor is it said to bind clerics, but it makes the act valid or invalid by reason of the others; but with respect to Iacobus, who was a cleric, it is enough that the submission and sentence held good looking to the common law, as was said above. Likewise, because he subjected that case to the decisions of the statutes of that court and to its style; what is noted by Arch. 2. q. 6, c. non ita, and Io. Cal. in the said disputation 'statutis', and by the doctors, especially modern ones, in the said c. clericis supports this, where it is concluded that if the case of a cleric is ventilated before a secular judge, it is understood to be governed also regarding the extinction of the instance according to the statutes of that court, so that in all respects it must be regulated according to the style of that forum. Nor does it have to stand in the way if it is said that concerning the prorogation first made by the magnificent Lord at the petition of the parties no writing appears, because it was lost, etc.; because I say that since in the second petition afterwards made to the said Lord with the will and subscription of the parties, it is recounted that the Lord had at another time prorogated it, and it was asked that he prorogate it again for three days, which was also done by the said Lord, the first prorogation is sufficiently proved. Because when something is enunciated by the parties which is necessarily required for the validity of that which is being transacted, the enunciative words prove the enunciation for the validity of that act, as is also noted in l. optimam, C. de contrahen. & commit. stip.; what is noted by Bar. in l. 1 & 2, C. de rela., also supports this. Likewise, regarding acts that are even substantial, reliance is placed on the confession of the parties from which a probable doubt arises; this is the notable text in c. fin., de proba. And these things concerning the fourth principal doubt. Fifthly, it is principally asked whether, on account of the exception of connectedness of the case (connexitas causae) raised by Philippus in the court of the Podestà with respect to Iacobus, a cleric constituted in minor orders, the case itself ought to be remitted to the episcopal court, or whether the court of the Podestà ought to proceed to the execution of the said award requested by the said Philippus for his share only? Likewise, it is asked whether, before the said Philippus is heard in any respect in the said court, he ought to be compelled to give the requested security according to the form of the statute, etc.? In which doubt having several parts, I say it must principally be considered whether the sentence rendered against the said brothers, one of whom is found to be a cleric in minor orders, is valid at least with respect to the other, who is not a cleric, and whether, presupposing its validity, execution thereof could be sought before a secular judge? And as far as our case is concerned, it must undoubtedly be said that the said sentence held against both, because it was rendered by arbiters to whom submission could be made, even though they were laymen, as I said above. Nay, I say more: that if the sentence had been rendered by a secular judge, the sentence would have to hold against the one who is not a cleric for his share, and this in severable matters; but in indivisible matters it must hold regarding the non-cleric in its entirety. This I prove by the text in l. una, C. si plures una sen., joined with what Bal. notes there after the beginning, in col. 1. For it is said there in the text that

† a sentence rendered against several associates simply induces an obligation pro rata, so that each seems condemned for half; and thus such a sentence has a severable effect; deservedly, what is useful is not vitiated by what is useless, reg. utile, and what is noted there, de reg. iur. in Sexto, and l. 1, § Trebatius, ff. de aqua quoti. & aesti. And the same must be said in indivisible matters. For just as from the beginning any associate or partner can be sued for the whole, as is the text in l. loci corpus, § si fundus, with the following, ff. si ser. ven., so also if several are sued, one of whom could not be sued there, the sentence is valid, and each is obligated for the whole, and the sentence ought to be valid with respect to the one who could be sued there; in support of this is what Bal. notes in the said l. una. Whence, to the point regarding execution of the sentence, I say that insofar as the sentence of the arbiters contains a severable matter, execution can be sought before the Podestà against Dom. Philippus, who is not a cleric, for his share; nor can he plead the clerical status of the other, because as to him, for his share, no impediment exists, by the argument of the said l. una, and the said l. loci, § competit, for as to this 'he has a free house,' etc., as is said there in a similar matter. Insofar, however, as the said sentence contains an indivisible matter, as in the rendering of an account, the said Philippus can be sued for the whole, because he is seen to be condemned as was said above, and he can be compelled according to the statute to give a surety, at least for his share. For the other share, however, the ecclesiastical judge can and must be approached, so that he may commit the sentence to execution against the cleric, to which he is bound, as in the said l. a divo Pio, ff. de re iudi. Nor by the aforesaid is the unity of the case (continentia causae) divided, because cognizance and execution have a severable effect with respect to different persons. Nor must one be concerned about the contrariety of sentences which a judge might execute between different persons, arg. l. a sententia, ff. de ap. Likewise, on account of different qualities of persons the rule on the unity of the case is not observed, as is proved in c. fin., de iudi. And indeed in our case no unity of the case can be alleged, since against each execution can be sought before his own judge insofar as the obligation of the sentence touches him, as is clear from the aforesaid; and what is read and noted in c. unico, de obl. ad ra., and l. 1, ff. de poenis, supports this.

† To the last [question], whether the arrest made by the secular judge against a married cleric not walking in clerical habit and tonsure, nor thrice warned, etc., is valid: I say that it is, because such a person enjoys ecclesiastical privilege in nothing. Nor is any warning required in his case; but as soon as he does not walk in habit and tonsure, he loses every privilege, as is the text in c. unico, de cleri. coniug. in Sexto, and there Io. And. openly notes this, and he himself notes the same in addi. Spe. de cleri coniug., after the beginning. Nicolaus, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One must abide by the writing of one holding a public office in matters pertaining to his office.
2. If a monastery is exempted with the chapels held, the exemption is not extended to chapels to be held.
3. An official cannot donate, nor remit the right of the clergy, of a city, or of a collegium.
4. If a notary stated in the protocol, "this was quashed by the will of the parties", and did not append witnesses, he is not believed.
5. Subreption vitiates letters of grace ipso facto without the aid of an exception.
6. Just as a grace already granted does not expire by the death of the grantor, so neither does the power given to the executors.
7. Although the Pope orders someone to be inducted into possession, any unlawful detainer having been removed, it is understood to be with the party summoned, unless the Pope expressly orders the contrary.
8. If the prince makes a commission by way of inquisition, he is understood to have made it by way of a judicial commission.
body: IN the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of His mother Mary. On the matter of the question that is presently pending between the clergy of Pisa on the one hand, and the New Hospital of the Holy Spirit of Pisa on the other, concerning certain common burdens newly distributed by the said clergy of Pisa, a proportionate share having been assigned to the said hospital: I say, in the first place, it must be noted that the said clergy has a well-grounded claim against the said hospital, to the effect that it should contribute with it for the share falling to it, both by common law and by the custom of the place, an excellent and virtually express argument in c. accedentes, de praescript., in c. requisisti, de testa., and in c. cum instantia, de censit., and de statu mo. c. recolentes. Nor is this called into doubt, especially on account of a very long custom, which in such burdens is pre-eminently to be observed, as is read and noted in xviij. q. ij. c. seruitium, by the gloss in c. quia cognouimus, x. q. ij. From which I infer that upon the hospital, which now alleges that it is not bound to undergo a share of the burdens imposed by the clergy of Pisa, lies the burden of proving exemption and release, so that if it does not prove its claim most clearly, it must succumb, as in c. praesentia, de proba., and in c. cum uenerabilis, and c. cum dilectus, de reli. do., and in c. incumbit, in l. 1, ff. de proba., and l. 1, ff. de exce., in prin. It must therefore be examined whether the hospital fully proves its claim, namely release or exemption in respect of the contribution to the said burdens. And first, we must examine the release that is alleged to have been granted by the officials of the clergy of Pisa, commonly called captains. Secondly and principally, presupposing that the said release extends to our case, whether the said hospital can protect itself by virtue of apostolic letters obtained after the fact, especially in view of the proceeding that followed thereupon by the apostolic subdelegate? Regarding the first part, I remember having written elsewhere quite fully in counsel in favor of the said clergy; and because the said consilium is still in the possession of the officials of the said clergy, I will not extend myself regarding that part, except by very briefly adding certain points for the greater corroboration of the conclusion then reached by me. For since the release that is claimed to have been made by the captains of the said clergy was reduced to writing by dominus Talanus, then syndic and chamberlain of the said clergy, as appears in the book of the clergy itself, one must abide by it,

† since it is the writing of one holding a public office, and one must also abide by it in matters concerning his office, as in l. quaedam, §. nummularios, ff. de eden., where Bart. expressly holds this; this is supported by what Inn. notes in c. 1, in fi., de fi. instr. For the said chamberlain and syndic have, by virtue of their office and long custom, the duty of recording in the books of the clergy all things concerning the said clergy, and by custom credit is also given to those books, for which c. cum dilectus, de fid. instru., serves. And this must pre-eminently be said in our case, in which the said release cannot be proved by any other more authentic writing, as will appear from what is to be said below. But the said release, written by the hand of the said Talanus, refers only to the burdens distributed at that time, and assigned and recorded for each member of the clergy, for the proportionate share falling to him, in whichever books of the said clergy, as clearly appears from an inspection of the writing drawn up thereupon; therefore, it ought not to be extended to other debts of the whole clergy that were not then distributed nor recorded in the books of the clergy. For although a release is favorable, as is read and noted in l. tale pactum, ff. de pac., and l. non solum, §. liberationis, ff. de lib. leg., and arg. in c. ex literis, de proba., nevertheless, when it is limited either to a certain time or to certain places, it does not exert its force beyond what is expressed and included, as is the notable text in l. Aurelius, §. totius, ff. de

† lib. leg.; l. talis scriptura, in fi., ff. de lega. 1, supports this. Hence it is that if a monastery is exempted together with its existing chapels, the exemption is not extended to chapels to be acquired, as is noted in c. quia circa, de priui.; this is supported by what is read and noted in a similar case, and especially by Bar., in l. si ita, ff. de au. & arg. leg. And in case of doubt, it must be interpreted against the hospital, which bases itself upon the said release, as to why it did not cause the words of the release to be written in broader and clearer terms, as is fully noted by Bar. in l. ueteribus, ff. de pac. Nay rather, it could be maintained that even if the said Talanus had expressly written down a release simply from all burdens imposed and to be imposed, the said release made solely by the captains would not have been valid, because to remit a clear and liquidated debt is to make a gift, as in l. 2, ff. de calum., read and noted in c. ueniens, il 1. de test.

† An official, however, cannot donate nor remit the right of the clergy of a city, or of a chapter, as in l. praeses prouinciae, C. de transac.; nor can anyone holding administration, no matter how plenary, make a gift, as in l. contra iuris regulas, ff. de pac., and l. filiusfa., ff. de do., in c. si., de offi. uica., li. 6. Nor do I think that in this case a custom to the contrary is valid, since the rights of other churches cannot be remitted without the due solemnities required by law, nor is a custom to the contrary valid, as Io. An. notes in c. nulli, de rebus ecc. non alie., and there is a notable text joined with the second gloss in c. cum causa, de re iud. From these things I draw an inference concerning the release that the said dominus Talanus afterwards made as chamberlain and syndic of the said clergy: for that release does not extend to burdens to be imposed afterwards, both from a lack of power, as appears from the aforesaid, and from a lack of intention, because he always referred back to the form of the release made by the captains of the clergy, in which nothing was said about burdens to be imposed and distributed. Therefore, the said release by the chamberlain himself must be restricted to the contents of the captains' release; to this effect is the notable text in the said l. Aurelius, §. testamento facto, ff. de libe. lega.; what is noted in c. uenerabilis, de exceptio., supports this. Thirdly, a certain writing that is found on this matter in the protocol of a certain ser Gaspar, then notary of the said hospital, does not stand in the way: because insofar as it mentions burdens to be imposed and not yet distributed, that writing is found to have been made in the margin of the said protocol by another's hand, without witnesses, and without date and place; wherefore, for multiple reasons, it ought not to produce belief. First, because it was made by another's hand, it is therefore suspected of forgery, as is the text in c. inter dilectos, de fid. instru.; the said c. cum uenerabilis, de relig. dot., supports this. Secondly, because even if it had been written by his own hand, it ought not to produce belief, because a notary cannot, without the judge's authority, add even in the protocol that which he omitted, when it is not among those things necessarily accompanying the contract, but among those validating and corroborating it, because there is a suspicion of forgery, as Io. And. notes after Spe. in tit. de instru. edi., §. instrumentum, at the verse sed nunquid confecto; for which the text in the authentica de haere. & Falci., §. si uerò absunt, makes excellently; Anton. de Butr. follows him in cap. ex literis, de fide instrumen.; to the same effect is the notable statement of Joan. Andr. in addi. Specu., in the title next cited, §. ostenso, at the verse illud quoque, where, following the opinion of a certain doctor, he says

† that if a notary stated in the protocol 'this was struck through by the will of the parties,' and did not append witnesses, the notary is not believed, and such cancellation is not valid, and notwithstanding it, a public instrument may be drawn from it; and this statement is followed by Anto. de Butr. in c. cum P. tabellio, de fide instru. And this must especially be said in our case, since another notable conjecture is present, namely that the said addition was not written by the said ser Gaspar: because the same ser Gaspar, in a certain other instrument drawn up concerning matters dependent on this subject, referred to the release of the captains recorded by the hand of dominus Talanus, now chamberlain, in the books of the clergy. From all of which, and from the things that I stated elsewhere in the other consilium cited above, it appears clearly enough that the said hospital fails in its claim through the words of the release made by the said captains. I come now to the second part: whether it can defend itself on the basis of the apostolic letters and the process that followed therefrom? And it seems at first that it can: because the Sovereign Pontiff can render valid an invalid contract concerning the rights of churches, even against the will of the parties, since in these matters he possesses fullness of power, and in them his authority is always understood to be excepted, as in c. uenientes, de iureiur., and in c. proposuit, de concessio. praeben., by Joan. And. in c. a nobis, de deci., through the text with the gloss in c. constitutus, de rescrip., with similar authorities; but the Pope ordered that release made by the captains of the clergy to be confirmed, supplying from the fullness of power all defects, if any should perchance have intervened in it, as appears in the apostolic letters; therefore, no defect can be alleged any longer, as in cap. 1, de trans., and iij. q. vj. c. haec quippe, and what is read and noted in cap. 1 and 2, de confir. util., and it is not permitted to dispute concerning the act of the prince, xvij. q. c. iiij. si quis suadente, §. qui autem. But notwithstanding the aforesaid, which truly do not stand in the way, I consider that the contrary opinion prevails. And in the first place, I firmly hold that the said letters, as surreptitious, are ipso facto void and of no effect. For the petitioner committed obreption principally in two respects: first, when he asserted that the captains of the clergy had acquitted and released the said hospital from all burdens imposed, and thenceforth to be imposed and enjoined, etc., although of burdens to be imposed and assessed, no mention had been made in the release of the captains; secondly, when he asserted that the aforesaid captains had sufficient power for these and for other matters to be performed from the entire clergy
† of Pisa, although he will never be able to prove on the aforesaid matters that power had been granted to them by the clergy.

† Moreover, surreption vitiates letters of grace ipso facto without the aid of an exception, as is read and noted in cap. ad audientiam 2, de rescrip., and in cap. si eo tempore, of the same title, in the Sext, and c. 1 & 2, de fil. presby., in the same book, and there is a good text in l. 1, ff. de nata. rest.; nor, according to all authorities, is the process following thereupon valid when the one possessing power by virtue of them proceeded not in the form of a trial, as occurred in our case where the party was summoned, etc., as noted by Joan. And. after Compost. in the said capit. ad audientiam. To this effect I cite the clear text in the said cap. constitutus, in fi., de rescrip. Nay, in lecturing I have further held on the said capitu. ad audientiam that even if the executor of surreptitious apostolic letters should proceed in the form of a trial, the process would nonetheless not be valid if in the same letters grace is granted and jurisdiction is conferred, because since jurisdiction is then accessory to the grace, just as the grace itself is rendered null by operation of law through surreption, so also is the jurisdiction as an accessory, as seems to be proved in the said c. constitutus, in fi., which speaks indistinctly, and c. si super gratia, de offi. dele., in the Sext, supports this, where it is proved

† that just as a grace already granted does not expire with the death of the grantor, even while the matter is intact, neither does the power given to the executors, as accessory to the grace itself; so just as the force of a letter of grace is sustained beyond its nature by reason of the accessory, so it must fall when the grace itself falls, nor is the contrary proved in any part of the law. Moreover, no one can doubt that in the aforesaid case that surreption must vitiate it, since anything stated, which if silenced would have resulted in the prince at least not granting the letters so easily, must induce surreption, as in c. postulasti, and c. super literis, de resc. But if he had disclosed to the pope that the release had been made with respect to imposed burdens, and that the captains did not have power for this, etc., he would not have obtained those letters; which is gathered especially from the fact that the pope orders the confirmation to be made 'if it is so' as was narrated, and the burden of proving that it is so lies upon him who expressed those things, as Io. And. notes in c. 1, de lit. contest., in the Sext. Furthermore, the pope granted those letters under the condition 'if it is so,' as appears in them; therefore, the condition failing, the grace fails, as in c. cum adeo, de rescrip.; nor can the confirmation made afterwards by the subdelegate of the pope stand against the clergy, both because it was made by virtue of a null grace, and because the party was not summoned, as in c. omnia, and c. caueant, 3, q. 9, c. pen., de re iud., and c. inter dilectos, de fide instru. Secondly and principally, the process followed thereupon was not valid in itself, because I firmly believe that the clergy ought to have been cited in the confirmation, since there had already been a controversy between the parties concerning this matter at another time, as the pope himself narrates in his letters, and the pope orders the confirmation to be made under that clause, 'if it is so,' he clearly seems to have committed the examination of the cause. But where an examination of the cause is required, the adverse party must always be cited; to this effect notes the gloss in cle. praesenti, de censi, on the word constiterit, and in clementi. 2, de poenis, on the word constiterit, and in clement. 1, of the same title, on the word commode, at the end, which are quite notable. To the same effect I cite the text joined with the gloss and Barto. in l. nec quicquam, §. ubi decretum, ff. de offi. procon.; I cite Innoc. in c. 1, near the end, de confir. utilit., where they expressly hold that in the confirmation of a lawful and judicial act the party must be summoned: what the same Bart. notes in the said §. ubi decretum supports this, where he holds that in any interlocutory order of a judge from which a party can be harmed, the party must be summoned; it is proved by c. caueat, and c. omnia, 3, q. 9, where it is clear that nothing prejudicial is to be attempted against an absent party. To the same effect is c. 1, de causa pos. & prop., and cap. inter quatuor, de maio. & obed., where the pope expressly says that nothing is to be done against an unheard party; nor can it be denied that the clergy would be harmed if the said confirmation were to hold, by the argument of those things noted in cap. 1 and 2, de confirm. utili., especially by supplying every defect from the fullness of power, as the pope orders to be supplied in it. Nor does it stand against this conclusion if it should perchance be said that the lord pope gave an executor rather than a judge; and an executor can proceed without observing the order of law, and thus adopt the path of a mere executor, according to what is noted in clem. unica, de offi. dele., and by Inn. in c. fin., de praescrip. And therefore I hear that in this matter a certain person has advised to that effect—at which I cannot marvel enough, in view of the authorities cited above—and there is a gloss that holds the same in c. pastoralis, §. quia uero, de offi. dele.; for it speaks of an executor given to confer a benefice. For he can proceed without the party having been summoned, because by the act of collation no prejudice is generated for an absent possessor, or for one claiming a right. Hence it is that even an inferior ordinary claiming that some benefice is vacant by law can confer it without summoning the possessor, as is the text in cap. licet episcopus, de praebend., in the Sext, and there is a good gloss which gives the aforesaid reason; but he would not exercise an act prejudicial to an absent party, whence he can induct him into possession without the possessor having been summoned, as is the text there. But where power is given to an executor concerning an act that can be prejudicial to a party, and the delegating authority did not previously apply an examination of the cause concerning the execution to be made, not only a simple execution is commanded, but also an examination; so that such commissioner is bound to summon the party, and hear its exceptions, because he succeeds to the place of the mandator, who ought to have done the same, as is the clear text according to the common reading in l. et si non cognitio, C. si contra ius uel util. publ., canonized in 25, q. 2; and expressly on our point, Bar. held this in the said law, where he says that when the execution of any act is committed with no preceding judgment, one cannot arrive at execution without a preceding examination, l. 1, C. de execu. rei iud., and by commanding execution, he is deemed to command an examination, as in the said l. et si non cognitio; and he meant the same in effect in l. a diuo pio, §. 1, ff. de re iu., where he explains this point more fully, and it is noted by the canonists in c. de caetero, de re iu. To the same effect is what Inn. notes in c. cum olim, 2, de priuilegiis, where he says

† that although the pope commands someone to be inducted into possession, removing any unlawful possessor, it is understood 'with the party summoned,' unless the pope expressly commands the contrary, or previously rendered a judgment upon it with the parties summoned, because it is not the intention of the prince to generate prejudice to an absent person, l. si, C. si per uim uel alio modo, l. meminerint, C. unde ui, c. tum ex literis, de in integr. rest., l. 2, §. si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in loco publi., and c. super eodem, de offi. deleg., with other laws cited above. To the aforesaid makes the notable theory of Vin. and other doctors in c. examinata, de iud., where they say

† that unless it evidently appears that the prince made the commission by way of inquisition, it is always understood that he made it by way of a judicial commission, an argument from that text; and because a matter easily reverts to its nature, 35. distinct. cap. ab exordio; and this must especially be said in our case, in which the pope, through that clause 'if it is so,' ordered an examination of the cause by asserting that he did not have full knowledge of that fact; and there what is narrated is for the most part an act done by the clergy and against the clergy. How then could it be established to the commissioner that it was so, without the clergy having been summoned, since the merits of cases are disclosed by the assertion of the parties, the said cap. tum ex literis, and the said l. si, C. si contra ius uel util. pub.? And truly the counsel arguing to the contrary did not attend to the aforesaid. And from all the aforesaid I conclude that the said apostolic letters were and are null from the vice of surreption, and that the process following thereupon was not and is not valid, both because it was made by virtue of null letters, and because the party was not summoned. The contrary argument made by me above does not stand in the way, because it proceeds in that case where the lord pope had confirmed simply out of certain knowledge, which he did not wish to do here. Nor can it be of assistance that he ordered every defect to be supplied from the fullness of power: both because he did not order this simply, but under the condition, 'if the things narrated were true'; and because that clause only refers to defects regarding the solemnities of law, noted by Spe. in tit. de leg., §. nunc ostendendum, ver. 18, and Archi. in c. Coenomacen., 17. distin. In our case, however, that release of the captains does not extend to our case from a defect of power and of will, as I said above. And thus the said clause operates nothing as to our case, even if it had been inserted simply. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A restitutio in integrum granted in respect of the principal is not extended to the interest following therefrom.
2. A legacy of release is extended to the accessory of interest contracted after the will.
3. A personal privilege follows the person and is extinguished with the person.
4. If the pope grants a privilege to a monastery, that no bishop may dare to excommunicate, suspend, or interdict the monks of that monastery, how and concerning whom it is understood.
casus: The fact is set forth thus: The late lord Pope John XXII established certain apostolic officials in the city of Florence, to whom he gave the power and license of levying an assessment of eighty thousand florins among all benefices situated in the dominion of the commune of Florence, both exempt and non-exempt, as is contained more fully in the grant itself, and he exempted from that contribution the benefices of the lords Cardinals; and in accordance with the power conferred, the imposition and apportionment followed among all benefices, only those benefices of the Cardinals being exempted. Then, in the course of time, when the clergy—both by virtue of the above-written imposition made and the exemption of the Cardinals in the aforesaid manner, and by virtue of certain other impositions simply made—was heavily burdened with interest and damages because it had taken those moneys on loan, it very recently obtained from Pope Martin that, for the interest and damages of the aforesaid impositions, which amount to the sum of nine thousand florins, it might levy a tax on the benefices of all, even of the exempt, for their contingent share, so that each might more easily be able to bear and endure his contingent portion. From this imposition certain abbeys, which at the time of the imposition of the said eighty thousand florins were held in commendam by Cardinals, but now have their own abbots, strive to withdraw themselves, alleging that this sum of nine thousand florins depends upon the above-written imposition from which those abbeys were exempt in respect of the Cardinals. The question is what is the law.
body: Having invoked the protection of the Savior Jesus Christ and of His Mother, I consider that on a three-fold ground the said Abbeys are bound to contribute to the said nine thousand Florins. First, because the benefices of the Cardinals were exempted from that imposition of the principal alone, and no mention was then made of the interest and damages that would subsequently follow; therefore it ought not to be extended to the interest and damages that followed afterwards; the text is notable in l. fin. § Lucius Titius, ff. de condit. indebit., where it is proved that

† a restitutio in integrum granted in respect of the principal is not extended to the interest following therefrom, even—what is more—to that existing at the time the restitution was granted. To the same effect is what is read and noted in l. iiij, C. deposi., and by the excellent gloss in l. eleganter, § non solum, ff. de dolo. Likewise, an inference is not drawn from distinct things, in c. 2, de transla. prælato., and l. neque natales, C. de proba.; but the interest and damages following therefrom are distinct from the first imposition in respect of the principal; therefore an exemption regarding the one is not extended to the other. And this must especially be said regarding this privilege, which tended to the prejudice of other benefices; for insofar as a privilege harms the right of another, it must be strictly interpreted against him, as in cap. cum dilectus, de consue., noted by Inn. in c. cum dilecti, de do., and Bar. in l. beneficium, ff. de consti. prin. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that this interest arose by occasion of that principal from which those benefices of the cardinals were exempted, and thus it must be imputed to those dilatory clerics who satisfied within the term, nor ought the delay of one to be harmful to others, and the loss that someone suffers through his own fault ought to be imputed to himself and not to another, as in c. mora, and the rule damnum, de reg. iu. lib. 6, and c. peruenit, de fideius., and cap. dilecti, de foro competen. To the same effect is the text in l. Aurelius, in § legatum est, ff. de liber. lega., where the text notably says

† that a legacy of release is extended to the accessory of interest contracted through a testament; because I answer that this holds when looking to the ius commune; but here the imposition of these Florins is made by the authority and benefit of a papal grant, because considering the wars and other perils that rendered difficult the payment of the principal, he granted that all should feel these damages following therefrom; whence it could be contended that even if the said cardinals held the said benefices now in commendam, those benefices could be coerced to this contribution, since they are not exempted from that imposition. On the second ground the said monasteries are bound, because the said exemption was granted to them not on account of the benefices, but in favor of the Cardinals who held those benefices; whence, since they have passed into their hands, the said exemption ceases,

† because a personal privilege follows the person, and is extinguished with the person; as in the rule priuilegium, de regu. iur. lib. 6; and when the cause ceases, the effect ought to cease, as in cap. cum cessante, de appe., which proceeds even in privileges, as in l. generaliter, C. de episco. & cleri., canonized in 16. quæst. 1. cap. generaliter; hence it is that when a privilege begins to be harmful, the privilege ceases, or at least is to be revoked, as in c. suggestum, and cap. dilecti, de deci., and in l. ex facto, ff. de uulg. & pupil., and 63. distinctio, quia sancta, § uerum; and it is fitting that those who lead a life with others should feel a similar discipline in the laws, de statu monacho. cap. recolentes. To the same effect is the notable text in cap. 1, de priuileg. lib. 6, where it is said

† that if the pope grants a privilege to a monastery, that no bishop may dare to excommunicate, suspend, or interdict the monks of that monastery, the privilege stands wherever the monks betake themselves, provided that they are always monks of that monastery; but if any of them are sent to any priories subject to the said monastery, and there carry on the governance of those priories, or reside there as monks, then, even though they may indeed be recalled to the first monastery, and are monks both of the first monastery and of the priory, nevertheless, by reason of that same non-exempt priory, those monks could be excommunicated, interdicted, or suspended by the bishop, a legitimate cause demanding it, because the privilege ceases, since they are not monks of the first monastery only; to the same effect is the text in c. cum capella, de priuilegiis. Therefore I say in our case, that since the said monasteries have left the hands of the cardinals—presupposing that the said cardinals had been exempt from this imposition—the abbots ought not to enjoy that benefit, for the reasons prescribed above. On the third ground, at least in respect of the whole, the said monasteries cannot claim exemption, because this imposition of 9,000 Florins does not derive entirely from that principal of 8,000 Florins from which the benefices of the cardinals were exempted, but also from other impositions from which they had not been exempted, as is clear in the letters of the pope, and thus all excuse fails in their case. From this it is evidently gathered that it was not of the mind of the lord pope to free those benefices from this imposition in that respect; for if he had wished to do so, he would have distinguished by exempting them from the interest of that imposition. Wherefore, from all the aforesaid, I conclude that the said monasteries are entirely bound, just as other benefices, to the contribution of the said 9,000 florins, the said excuse notwithstanding. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a younger brother can demand from the elder that the shop and the debts of debtors recorded in the book of the partnership be communicated.
2. Whether that which was acquired by a son in paternal power during the father's lifetime, if it does not appear whence he acquired it, ought to be presumed to have come from the paternal goods.
body: † IN the name of God, amen. Regarding the first doubt, by which it is asked,
† Whether the younger brother can demand from the elder that the shop and the book debts recorded in the partnership's account books be communicated; I say that the doubt depends upon another,

† Namely, whether acquisitions made by a son in paternal power, during the father's lifetime, if it does not appear whence he acquired them, ought to be presumed to have arisen from the father's property, or from the son's industry, or from elsewhere. For in our case it is presupposed that the son in power contracted a partnership with a stranger under his own name, and acquired many things therefrom, nor does it appear whether he had the capital from his father, or from paternal goods, or from elsewhere. For if the capital did not proceed from the paternal goods, it is surer than certainty that it and whatever derived from it is deemed adventitious, and does not come into the division of goods with the younger brother; rather, it is his own preferred share (præcipuum), as in l. fi. and l. filio licet in sacris, C. de colla., noted in l. cum oportet, C. de bonis, quæ lib. and more expressly held in Inst. per quas perso. no. acqui. in the first column, at the verse ne quod ei ex suis laboribus, uel prospera fortuna accesserit etc. If, however, the capital proceeded from the father’s goods, then that which is customarily attributed to the money is acquired for the father, and thus will enter into the division; but that which is attributed to the person is acquired for the son himself, and by no means enters into the division; and in doubt, half of the profit is attributed to the money, and half to the person, as the Glossa intended to note, and Bartolus after it, in l. pro socio, and the text in l. si non fuerit, ff. eod. tit., supports this. And Bartolus decided punctually thus in that case in the said l. cum oportet, and in the said l. j. where he says that if the son legitimately profited with the money, half is acquired for the father as profectitious, and the other half for the son as adventitious, because it stems from his labors; wherefore I say regarding our proposed matter that if it could appear that the capital proceeded from paternal money, half of the profit will be the son’s preferred share (præcipuum)—and I speak of the profit touching the son pro rata—while the other half comes into the division with the younger brother. If, however, there is doubt as to whence the capital proceeded, as is presupposed in our case, this question is formally framed by the Glossa in the said l. cum oportet, and in Inst. per quas perso. nob. acqui. on the words ne quod, on the word prospera. And some have held that it ought to be presumed that he acquired it from the paternal goods, just as it is presumed in the case of a wife, who, whatever she acquires while marriage lasts, is presumed to have acquired from the husband’s goods, as in l. etiam, C. de do. inter uir. & uxo., l. Quintus, ff. eo. tit. Others held entirely the opposite: that he is presumed to have acquired it from his own industry or good fortune, just as is presumed in a guardian, as in l. si defunctus, C. de arb. tu. But the Glossa in both places, following Johannes, distinguishes: whether the father was poor, while the son was industrious and diligent; and then the son is presumed to have acquired from his own industry; or conversely, the father was rich, while the son was negligent, and then he is presumed to have acquired from the father’s goods; and Odofredus and Bartolus approved that opinion there, saying that it is otherwise in the case of a wife. For in her case that presumption is made to avoid base suspicion and lest a delict be presumed; but in an industrious son no presumption of delict falls. And certain jurists held the same in the case of a wife, as is noted in the said l. etiam. The aforementioned Glossa posed another solution in the said l. cum oportet, saying a distinction must be drawn as to who brings the claim: whether the brother, that he may communicate it, or he who acquired it, claiming that he should have it as a preferred share. In the first case, let the brother prove that he acquired that capital from the father’s goods. In the second case, let the elder brother himself prove it, because he who asserts and claims must prove, ff. de proba. l. ei qui, and vj. q. ulti. c. actor; and it follows this second opinion there. It confirmed this more clearly in Authentica ex testamento, C. de collat.; the reason being that in doubt, facts are not presumed, l. in bello. §. facta, ff. de capti. & postl. re. and de offi. delega. c. cum in iure; therefore, let the party asserting prove. As to how it must be proved, it says that it is by conjectures in the manner aforesaid in the first solution. And this pleases me well enough, and in effect it coincides with the first solution. And what is noted in the similar case of a cleric supports this: for if he does not have the administration of the goods of the benefice, he is not presumed to have acquired from the goods of the church, but from his own industry or good fortune, even if he had nothing, as in c. 1. de pec. cle. and noted in c. cum in officijs, de testa. and xij. q. iiij. c. 1. In our case, therefore, I conclude in favor of the elder brother, who contracted the partnership with the other apothecary, and it is presupposed that he was exceedingly diligent. For on a twofold ground he ought to prevail: First, because he was and is in possession of the goods, and thus upon the younger brother, who asserts that the capital proceeded from paternal goods, rests the burden of proving, according to what is said above. Secondly, because even granted that recourse must be had to conjectures, he has many on his side. First, because from the present a presumption is drawn concerning the past, as in c. cum per bellica, xxxiiij. q. ij., noted by the Glossa in c. scribam, de pręsumpt. For just as he was most diligent in acquiring once the partnership was contracted, as is stated in the premise; so it is to be presumed that he acquired that capital by his own diligence little by little, or otherwise from good fortune; to the same effect is c. mandata, de pręsump. Secondly, the presumption of paternal poverty concurs. Thirdly, because he contracted the partnership in his own name; and thus the books were entitled in his name and that of his partner; of the father, however, no mention was made. Fourthly, in that the father never demanded an account from the son, nor any profit, and no one is presumed negligent in his own affairs, ff. de proba. l. cum de indebito, and c. super hoc, de re nun. Fifthly, because the son, during the father’s lifetime, purchased certain real properties in his own name out of the profit, without the father objecting. For from the paternal silence and the son's act, it is presumed that the profit was acquired for himself alone, by the argument in l. si filius, ff. de peti. hær. and what is noted in c. peruenit, de emp. & uen. and c. ratione, de præsum. and l. quæ dotis, ff. sol. ma. and l. cum oportet. §. sin autem res, frequently cited. Sixthly, because the father in his will made no mention of the said shop; whence he is presumed to have acquiesced to the things that were being arranged by the son while he was alive, by the argument in the said §. sin autem res. And by these considerations the other doubts framed around this matter remain superfluous, except that by which it is asked, whether the donation made to the elder brother himself by his foreign partner is valid, since it exceeds the value of 500 florins, and although it was not registered (insinuata), it was nevertheless made before the priors or lords of the city of Recanati, who approved it. In which matter I think attention must be paid to the power that those lords or priors hold. For if they have the rights of a prince, then I deem that donation to have been sufficiently valid: because the presence of the prince supplies every defect of solemnity, as in l. omnium, C. de testa., especially since registration is made for no other reason than to prevent hidden frauds and deceptions, as noted by Bartolus in l. Modestinus, ff. de do., proved in l. data, C. eo. tit., which are not presumed given the presence of the prince, by the argument in l. si. quod me. cau. and l. transactionem, C. de transac. To the same effect are l. pe. C. de do. inter uir. & uxor. and l. illud, C. de sac. san. eccle. where this matter is fully treated by Baldus. If, however, the said priors do not have the rights of a prince, but a limited power, as commonly happens in popular cities: then either the statute validates donations made before the priors, nor does it otherwise require registration; and then, that the statute may effect something, I would understand it to be valid, even though it was not registered in public records, and it suffices that it can be proved by witnesses, by the argument of the said l. omnium, and so that there may be something special given the presence of the lords. For there seems to be a departure from the ius commune, since the statute provides otherwise than the ius commune, as noted on a similar point by Baldus in l. 2. C. de iu. calum.; what Bartolus notes in l. 4. §. prætor ait, ff. de dam. inf. in that question where the statute provides that someone be summoned in person or at his house supports this. Or the special statute provides nothing on this, and then I do not think it valid insofar as it exceeds 500 gold coins, unless it has been registered, by the text in the said l. illud, C. de sacros. eccl. and in l. donatio, and l. hac, C. de dona. For in a power generally granted to priors, the power of contravening general laws and statutes is not understood to be given, as is fully noted by Bartolus in l. ambitiosa, ff. de decr. ab ord. fa. Registration, indeed, is nothing other than making the donation in writing before a judge, as noted in the said l. in donationibus, and l. donatio, and l. sancimus, C. de dona., noted by Bartolus in l. modestinus; nor is a judicial examination of the cause (causæ cognitio) or a decree required, but it suffices that it be done in the presence of any magistrate whatever, as in the said l. in hac; l. si. C. de prædi. decu. sine decreto non alie. lib. 10. supports this admirably; Bartolus holds this in l. Modestinus, and more fully Baldus in the said l. illud. And that registration is required in a remission, see fully Bartolus and Baldus in the places cited above. But whether in that case where it were proved that the capital truly or presumptively proceeded from paternal goods, the father is presumed to have donated it to the elder brother, since he permitted the whole profit to remain with the son during the entire time of his life; I say no, because that would be a profectitious risk (periculum profectitium) which comes entirely into the division, even if at the time of the father’s death it is found in the son's possession, as in the said l. filio licet in sacris, C. de colla. To the same effect I cite a good text, arguing by a locus a speciali in l. cum oportet, often cited, at the verse sin autem res, where a special provision is set down regarding adventitious goods, the usufruct of which is acquired for the father, and it is provided that if the father wished those goods to remain with the son, whose property they were, during the whole time of his life, the father’s heirs cannot claim the usufruct of those goods as due to the father, but it remains with the son as if by a longstanding donation; it is otherwise in other goods of the father himself, or profectitious goods. Furthermore, whether in this case reliance must be placed on the books of the shop in rendering the account, I say that although this doubt is superfluous, as appears from the aforesaid; nevertheless, so that satisfaction may be given to the inquirer in all respects on account of cases that may occur, I would say that although elsewhere one can approve all the books of a person insofar as they make for him and reject them insofar as they make against him in separable matters, as is the notable text in l. publia, ff. dep. (which, although it speaks of a letter, yet by the same reason is the same in any other writing, as noted by Bartolus in l. Aurelius. §. idem quæsiit, ff. de lib. leg.); nevertheless, in our case I think otherwise must be said, because the father, by giving the son money to trade with in the shop or in another way, is seen to have delivered it so that he may make books and writing therefrom according to the custom of that trade, by the argument in l. quod si nolit. §. quia assidua, ff. de ædil. edic.; what Bartolus notes in a similar case in l. nemo est qui nesciat, ff. de duob. reis, and what is noted in l. quædam, ff. de eden., supports this. Whence it suffices that in rendering the account of the capital and profit, he prove according to the custom of other partners and apothecaries. Whence in those matters concerning which formal instruments are not accustomed to be made, as in modest transactions, it suffices to prove through the book, both for and against the partner or brother. An oath may also be tendered; for which what Baldus notes in a similar case in l. id, quod pauperibus, at the end, C. de episco. & cler. and Speculator in the title de instru. edi. §. nunc uerò aliqua, at the verse sed nunquid secundum, supports this; l. si negocia, ff. de nego. gest. supports this. And especially is this to be admitted between partners; for a greater diligence is not required in common affairs than in one’s own, Inst. pro socio, at the end, and partnership has the likeness of brotherhood, l. uerum, ff. eo., and therefore one should not proceed very strictly, especially since there appears no modest profit. And the account must be rendered from the beginning of the administration until the end, presupposing that he conducted business with the paternal money; for this is general, as in l. j. C. ubi de ratio. agi oportet. For it is special in the case of a father who administered the adventitious goods of his son, on account of the usufruct due to him, that he is not held to render an account to the son, as in l. cum oportet, at the verse nec ratiocinia; it is otherwise, therefore, in other goods, if the father had administered any from the son’s goods, and vice versa, by the argument in the said l. j. C. ubi ratio. Nor do I dwell upon this further, because I do not think it necessary, as I have said before. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. When the capacity to participate in the election of a bishop belongs to a university of conventual churches, the prelates of those churches are counted by heads.
2. If a testator said, "Let Titius be heir, let Seius and Maevius be heirs," how these three are understood to be called.
3. If a bishop has to perform an act with the assent of the chapter, it suffices that the university be called.
casus: The case in effect is as follows: A certain testator provided that certain moneys should be distributed by the consuls of a certain guild in marrying needy girls, with which consuls in making the said distribution two votes of the below-written heirs ought to intervene. He wrote his heirs, however, in this manner: for in all his goods etc. he instituted, made, and willed to be his universal heirs his legitimate, natural male sons, both born and to be born, for one part, and Dominus Dynus and Petrus, brothers, sons of the late Bartholomaeus Jacobi, for another part, and Franciscus and Thomasius, brothers and sons of the late Thomasius, for another part. Now, the testator having died, it is doubted how and by whom the said distribution ought to be made: namely, whether the consuls, who are six in number, have six votes and the heirs two, and thus all constitute eight votes; or whether the consuls have one vote and the heirs two, and what if they disagree with one another.
body: The aid of the Savior having been humbly invoked, I consider that the said words can have four interpretations. To me, however, only the last is pleasing. The first is that the consuls should have votes by head, so that since they are six, they will have six votes; in favor of which there seems to be a case, according to one interpretation, in c. scriptum, de elect., at the word de studijs, where it is clear that

† if the power of participating in the election of a bishop belongs to a university of conventual churches, the prelates of those churches are counted by head, so that they have votes according to the number of prelates. Secondly, it is supported by the fact that we see the same thing in judges; for if power is given to multiple judges, one stands by the majority part of them according to the number of persons, in l. duo ex tribus, ff. de re iudi. and distin. 65, c. 1. The same in arbitrators, as in l. si in tres, with l. seq., ff. de arbi. and c. 1, de arbi., lib. 6, and what is noted there. Thirdly, because in a doubtful disposition recourse must be had to preceding and following words, as in l. si seruus plurium, ff. de leg. 1, and l. nummus, de leg. 3, and l. qui filiabus, de leg. 1, with similar laws; but the testator, with respect to the heirs, spoke through votes: because he willed that their two votes should intervene; therefore he seems to have intended the same concerning the consuls. But this interpretation does not please me—namely, that all should be joined together simultaneously and constitute eight votes, and thus stand by the greater part in number—for multiple reasons. First, because since the consuls are called under an appellative name, and simultaneously to expedite the act with a third party, they all seem to be called as one body, nor ought they to be joined with a third party in like manner by heads, by the excellent argument in l. fin., C. de impu. & ali. sub., and in l. si quis Titio, ff. de usufru. accre., and what the gloss notes there; and it makes very well to the point in l. interdum, ff. de hære. insti.; and it is supported by the argument of l. Titius fundi, and l. liber, § Titius, under the same title. And I will speak more broadly below in the fourth interpretation. Moreover, by holding this interpretation, an absurdity would follow, because the distribution could be made without the consuls, and without the votes of the heirs. For suppose that three consuls take one side, and the other three another, with whom the two votes of the heirs agree: certainly, according to the aforesaid interpretation, these latter will prevail, since they are five, and the others three; as in said l. duo ex tribus, and said c. 1, 65 dist.; nevertheless it is not true to say that the consuls are present here; because since they are appointed as a certain body, they do not represent that body except through the greater part of the individuals of that body, as in l. mortuo, ff. de fideius., joined with l. quod maior, ff. ad munic., and l. aliud, § refertur, ff. de reg. iu., and cap. 1, de his quæ fi. a ma. par. cap., and c. fi., de rescrip., lib. 6, and noted by the gloss in c. 1, ne sede uac., lib. 6, and by Io. And. in c. a collatione, de appel., lib. 6, and by Fede., consil. 1; for the consuls are not said to do what three of them do; and yet the testator willed that the distribution should be made by the consuls. Likewise, suppose another absurdity: imagine that all the consuls agree together into one view, and the two votes of the heirs incline to the other side; according to that interpretation, the disposition of the consuls, who are six votes, will prevail, and the distribution would be made by the consuls alone, which is openly contrary to the intention and the words of the testator. For the testator willed that, in making the distribution, two votes of the heirs should intervene with the consuls; therefore without their consent the consuls cannot make the distribution, just as when a chapter has to do something with the consent of the prelate, or a prelate with the consent of the chapter; for it is necessarily required that there intervene at least the greater part of the chapter and the consent of the bishop, as is the noted gloss joined to the text in said c. uno, ne sede uacan., lib. 6, and as Ioan. And. confirms in said c. a collatione, and fully Fede. in consi. 1, and what is noted in c. postulasti, de conces. præbend. The second principal interpretation is that the consuls should have one vote, since they are called by appellative names, as one fictitious and represented body, while the heirs should have another vote; and that the words of the testator should be explained to mean that the heirs have two votes, that is, two parts of the heirs, which are four, have one vote; and so certain persons seem to have thought in their allegations. But truly that interpretation does not please me, because it distorts and destroys the words of the testator, who willed that two votes of the heirs should intervene in the distribution to be made. Nor must one depart from the words where a contrary intention is not clearly established, as in l. non aliter, ff. de leg. 3, and c. si., de uer. sign. Likewise because from the words of the testator it clearly appears that he willed the consuls to be the authors and principals in making this distribution, but the heirs to be secondary. For they are called accessorily to the consuls, as appears from those words 'with the consuls'; to this effect is l. si cui, ff. de fun. instru., and what is read and noted in c. uno, ne sede uacan., and in c. cum Marthæ, § quæsiuisti, de cele. mis. The third principal interpretation is through l. si quis Titio, ff. de usufru. accre., and l. Titiæ textores, § nihil, ff. de lega. 1, so that the meaning is that this distribution belongs equally to the consuls and to the heirs—yet so that the heirs have two votes, but the consuls one, if the act to be expedited pertained to three equally principally; because the testator called the consuls by themselves, as one body, whereas he called the heirs for two shares, just as is gathered through the contrary case in l. liber homo, § Titius, ff. de hære. instit., where the case is posed

† that if a testator said, 'Let Titius be heir, let Seius and Maevius be heirs,' two halves are made, that is, two shares of the entire inheritance, of which one is given to Titius, who was called alone, the other is given to Seius and Maevius, who were called together. So in the matter at hand, since the heirs were expressly called to have two votes, whereas the consuls were called simply under an appellative name as one body, they ought to have only one vote. But this interpretation does not please because of the absurdity that would follow: because, discord having arisen between them, it could happen that the heirs alone without the consuls would distribute, since they have two votes, according to the things fully noted by Io. An. in c. scriptum, de ele.; which is expressly contrary to the mind of the testator, who willed that the consuls should be principals in making this distribution, as I have fully said above. Moreover, when an act belongs to two simply, and power is not given in solidum, what is done by one of them is not valid, as in c. si duo, de procu., lib. 6, and c. causam matrimonii, and c. uno delegatorum, de offi. dele. But in our case, the consuls and the heirs are called as two bodies, because the testator did not want to trust the one without the other; therefore, what is disposed by one body alone is not valid; to which what is read and noted in c. pastoralis, in the first response, de rescrip., applies excellently. Fourthly, I deliver the fourth interpretation, which seems agreeable to equity, reason, and the mind of the testator, and no absurdity follows from it: namely, that we should say that the consuls are called as one body among themselves, yet the computation will be made by heads so that it may thus appear where the body itself stands, as in said l. interdum, and l. si quis Titio, along with the others alleged above; just as when something belongs to the canons with the consent of the bishop: for the canons are called as one body, and that body is represented by the greater part of the individuals, as is noted in said c. uno, ne sede uacante, joined with the gloss on the word assensu; to the same effect is c. abbas, 18, q. 2, joined with c. ecclesia, de elect.; and this was expressly held by Fede. in said consil. 1, in the resolution of the question, and by Io. And. in said c. a collatione, and in said c. postulasti; to the same effect is the gloss in said c. pastoralis, where it says that multiple judges appointed for a certain act are in the place of one; and what is noted by Ioa.
