An. following Hostiensis in said c. scriptum, whose statements apply excellently to this question. And I consider that that distribution belongs principally to the consuls themselves through the points which I stated above, and because the testator expressly in the beginning called only the consuls themselves, but the said consuls cannot dispose anything without the consent of the two votes of the heirs, so that it is necessary that the two votes of the heirs agree with the judgment of the consuls; just as when something belongs to a chapter with the assent of its bishop: for the chapter cannot dispose anything in that act unless the bishop consents, nor does it suffice that half of the chapter concur with the judgment of the bishop, because there would not be the chapter, but it is necessary that at least the greater part of the chapter concur in the disposition of the act, and have the consent of the bishop. And so, on the other hand, when

† a bishop has to perform an act with the assent of the chapter: for they are not all called by heads, but the university is called by itself, and with respect to itself the computation is made by heads, but not with respect to the bishop, because his assent is required equally principally, as the gloss previously alleged notes in said c. pastoralis, and Fed. in said cons. near the end; to the same effect is c. si pro te, de rescri., lib. 6, joined with the gloss. For the testator expressly willed that the consuls should distribute, but with them he willed that two votes of his heirs should concur; therefore the act will not be valid unless the consuls dispose it, or at least the greater part of the consuls (said l. duo ex tribus, ff. de re iud., and said c. si., de rescrip., lib. 6, with similar passages alleged above), with the assent of two votes of the heirs themselves; for the testator did not wish to give power to any of them in solidum. As to how the two votes of the heirs ought to be obtained, I think that, since the heirs were called distributively, all those called for a fourth share have one vote, the others for another fourth have another, and so on for the rest; an excellent argument in cle. plures, de iure pa., and in the previously alleged l. interdum, and in c. quoniam, de iure pa.; whence it is sufficient that the consuls have in making the distribution two of the aforesaid heirs taken in the aforesaid manner; and it will be safe that all be requested, since the testator did not specify which heirs' votes should be had; and it will suffice to have two of them, by argument of what Bar. notes in l. Pomponius (otherwise it begins si uni), ff. de re iud., and l. hæredes mei, ff. ad Treb. But I do not think it necessary that all the heirs should give two votes, because no good effect would result, since, as I said, the act belongs principally to the consuls, and here the consent of two heirs suffices; for the testator did not wish that all must necessarily consent, lest he render the matter exceedingly difficult on account of the facility of men in disagreeing, as in c. nec nouum, 8, q. 1. To c. scriptum, § alleged in the first interpretation, an answer can be given as is gathered from what was noted by Feder. in the place previously alleged. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Subreption in letters of grace vitiates the grace.
2. One possessing two benefices with cure of souls at the same time, if a lawful title does not appear, is to be presumed to have possessed unlawfully.
body: On the question that is currently pending between dompnus Nicolaus, son of the late Brandinus de Brandinis of Urbino, on the one side, and dompnus Iacobus Thomasii, on the other, concerning a canonry and prebend of the church of Urbino, I shall reach the decision of this question conclusively, since this consilium is decisive, and not persuasive implored at the request of a party. And first I shall discuss the rights of the said dompnus Nicolaus; secondly, those of the aforesaid dompnus Iacobus. From the examination and decision of these, the third matter will be made clear, namely, what the duty of the judge is in the determination of this case. And first, omitting the allegations that could be made in favor of the said dompnus Nicolaus—both because of the cause mentioned above and because they are sufficiently evident in the acts produced by that dompnus Nicolaus himself—adhering firmly to the acts of the case exhibited to me, I judge that the said dompnus Nicolaus sustains no right in the said canonry, nor to obtaining it by virtue of the apostolic letters impetrated by him and exhibited to me, being moved to this opinion by several causes and reasons. First, because the said letters were subreptitious, since in them he asserted that he was the rector of the church of Santa Barbara, and that that church did not have the exercise of the cure of souls, the contrary of which is openly proved by the witnesses produced by the said dompnus Iacobus and by the response of that dompnus Nicolaus himself to the position of the opposing party. And it is certain that every expressed falsehood, or concealed truth, which, if suppressed or expressed, the prince would not have granted his letters, at least not so easily, must induce subreption, as is notably proved in c. postulasti, and there by Host. de rescript., and c. super literis, eod. titu.; l. et si non cognitio and l. si legibus consentaneum, C. si contra ius uel uti. publi. make to this point. Moreover, that this was of such a nature is evident: because the Pope more easily grants a canonry when the cure of souls is neglected, since a canon must reside in the canonry, as in c. extirpandae, § qui vero, de praeben.

† Furthermore, subreption in letters of grace vitiates the grace ipso facto, as well as whatever has followed by virtue of such letters, as is noted in c. ad audientiam ij and c. constitutus, de rescr., and c. 1 and 2, de fil. presb. lib. 6, and in cle. j, de praeb., and in l. j, ff. de nata. resti., and what is noted in l. praescriptione and l. si legibus, C. si contra ius uel util. publi. Nor does it stand in the way that the said dompnus Nicolaus now says that he was not the rector of that church at the time of the impetration; for since he himself asserted this in those letters, his first assertion must be stood by; for this a good text is in l. cum precum, C. de lib. cau., and Io. And. openly maintained this in c. cum in positionibus, de iureiur. lib. 6, where he confirms that the narratives in a rescript made by the impetrator provide faith against him, even if the rescript appears subreptitious; what Inno. notes in c. cum venerabilis, de excep., and c. olim, de censi., makes to this point. Besides, it is sufficiently proved by the witnesses that it was held and possessed in his name, and that he was commonly reputed to be the rector of that church. Nor did dompnus Nicolaus himself prove another legitimate title; whence he was either possessing as rector, or as an intruder; and, to his disadvantage, it is the same as if he had legitimately possessed, lest an intruder be of better condition than a legitimate rector; this is proved in c. eum qui, de praeben. lib. 6, and 'what each one has protested with a clear voice etc.', c. per tuas, de proba., and l. generaliter, C. de non nu. pe., especially when fraud is detected, in c. inter dilectos, de do., and c. cum super, de conces. praeb., and l. si creditorib., C. de fer. pig. da. ma. Secondly and principally, the provision made for the said dompnus Nicolaus is attacked because, as is clearly proved by his confession and the witnesses produced by the opposing party, he retained, and still holds, two churches with cure of souls, namely the pieve of Sant'Andrea and the church of Santa Maria in Castiglione. Nor was a dispensation by one having authority alleged or proved by him, nor a union legitimately made, although it was alleged by him; but the assertion of the party is not to be stood by, since a union consists in fact. And thus one must not presume against the law; for every church with cure of souls is presumed to stand by itself and ought to have its own rector, as in the chapter cum non ignores, de praeben.; nor is prescription sufficient so that they are held as united, unless it is of such long time that no memory of its beginning exists, as is fully noted by Io. Andr. on the rule qui contra iura, de regu. iur. libr. 6 in Merc.; chapter 1, de praescript., and 7, quaestio 1, capitulu. sicut, de offic. ordi. capitulu. ordinarii, lib. 6, make to this point. Since, therefore, it is established that the same dompnus Nicolaus possessed at the same time

† two benefices with cure, and no legitimate title appears, it must be presumed that he possessed unjustly, because he possessed contrary to the prohibition of law, as in l. quemadmodum, C. de agri. & censi. lib. 11, and in the said rule qui contra iura mercatur; and consequently he fell under the penalty of the Extravagant Execrabilis of John XXII, where it is provided that such a person is deprived of both benefices and rendered disqualified for any other benefices whatsoever; therefore it is concluded that the said dompnus Nicolaus was disqualified from obtaining the said canonry, and consequently the collation of the canonry made to him by the executor was not valid; for this, what Innocen. notes in capitulu. inter dilectos, de exces. praela., where he says that the collation of a benefice made by an executor upon one notoriously unworthy is null; and what he himself notes in capitulu. fin. de praesumptio. makes to this point. In our case, however, there is more: because he was not only unworthy, but indeed disqualified by law from any benefice, as I have said above; and what the same Inn. notes in capit. cum nostris, de conces. praeben. makes to this point. Thirdly and principally, clementi. gratiae, de rescriptis, works against the said dompnus Nicolaus, where it is provided that if someone, after a grace made for obtaining a benefice, receives a benefice which he cannot retain simultaneously with the benefice owed to him by virtue of the grace, he is deemed to renounce the said grace. But in our case the said dompnus Nicolaus, after the grace made to him, obtained two benefices with cure, which he can by no means obtain together with the canonry and another benefice, since he has been rendered disqualified from obtaining any benefice whatsoever; therefore he is deemed to have renounced the said grace, and consequently could not seek the said canonry by virtue thereof: because a right once extinguished does not revive, as in clemen. gratiae; 7, q. 1, cap. quam periculosum, and cap. ex transmissa, de renun., and de consec. dist. 4, capitulu. quaeris, and l. qui res, § aream, ff. de solu. Nor does it stand in the way here that the text in the said clem. gratiae speaks of one who impetrated a grace for a benefice with cure or for a dignity: because the said dompnus Nicolaus impetrated also for a benefice with cure or without cure. Likewise, the same reason exists in our case in both, as is evident from the aforesaid; therefore the provision ought to be the same, as the glos. on the said clem. gratiae in the word beneficium curatum est, and in the preceding gloss, clearly feels. Fourthly, it could be urged that, even if all the aforesaid were absent, the said canonry was not included under the letters impetrated by him: because no mention was made that the canonry pertained to the election of the canons, but it is only commanded to provide from that pertaining to the collation, presentation, provision, or disposition of the bishop or chapter, etc. But it is certain that under the designation of the aforesaid modes election is not included, as is proved in cap. cum in illis, de praeben. lib. 6, § illis vero, and in clem. 1, de praebend. § 1. And although those laws speak when it is commanded to provide concerning prelacies, dignities, or personatus, nevertheless the same reason holds in inferior benefices. For since letters for obtaining benefices are ambitious, they must be understood strictly, as in capitul. quamvis, de praeben. libr. 6; therefore, when one mode is expressed, another is not included, as in the previously cited cap. cum in illis, and ca. susceptum, de rescrip. eo. lib. And the ordinary gloss holds this in the said clemen. on the word de dignitate; likewise Paul. there. From all of which it is evidently clear that the said dompnus Nicolaus is destitute of all right in the retention or acquisition of the said canonry. I come now to the rights of the said dompnus Iacobus; and, allegations that could exquisitely be made against him being omitted on an equal basis, I judge that he is supported by good right. For it has been sufficiently proved by the confession of the opposing party and by the witnesses produced by him that possession of the right of electing canons is presently in the hands of the canons residing in the city of Urbino, so that those existing outside the city do not necessarily have to be called, and such custom is stood by even in elections of canons; this is proved in c. cum in ecclesiis, in fi., de praebend. lib. 11. Moreover, it has been sufficiently proved that in the said church, at the time of the election made, there were only eight canons, of whom one was dead; and thus seven remained: three are proved to have been absent outside the city at the time of the election made. The power of electing, therefore, remained entirely in the hands of the four residing in the city; which can be so, since the right of the collegiate body can reside in one person even in the election of a prelate, as is read and noted in c. gratum, de postu. praelato., and 65. distinct., c. si, and l. sicut, ff. quod cuiusque univers.; 10, q. 2, cap. hoc ius porrectum, after the beginning, at the words maiori parte ibidem servientium consentiente etc., makes to this point. Truly, those four canons, in whose hands the entire power of electing remained, could compromise upon one of themselves, as in c. cum in iure, and cap. causam, and c. quia propter, de elect. lib. 6, with similar texts. Therefore the election made by their arbiter concerning the said dompnus Iacobus was valid and held, since the chapter, a vacancy of a canonry having occurred, may assemble and elect at their pleasure, since time runs for it from the day of the vacancy and notice, as in c. quia diversitatem, de conces. praeben., and c. licet, de sup. neg. praela., with similar texts. And as to how the chapter ought to be convoked, custom must be stood by, as in c. in causis, de elect., noted by Bar. in l. observare, C. de decur. lib. 10. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the custom that absentees are not called is not fully proved: because, since that is against the law, a span of forty years is required, as in c. fin. de consuetu., noted by the gloss in c. si, eo. tit. lib. 6; for it is at least proved that those present in the city are in long-standing possession of electing canons, those existing outside the city not being called at all; and this quasi-possession suffices for the validity of an election already made, as in c. querelam, de elect., and c. cum olim, de cau. poss. & propriet., and cap. consultationibus, de iure patron., and what is noted in them; what Inn. notes in c. 2, de integ. rest. makes to this point. And from all these things the third matter is concluded: that since nothing has been canonically proved against the election of the said dompnus Iacobus or his person, and his rights are clearly evident, the duty of the judge in this case will be to confirm the election made of him, and to impose silence upon the said dompnus Nicolaus and upon that canon who said he was disregarded in that election, since it has been proved by the witnesses produced by the said dompnus Nicolaus that he came to the city after the election was legitimately made of the said dompnus Iacobus. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Interest on a dowry [?] can also be claimed today, notwithstanding the prohibition of canon law.
2. The formality in usury is the loan itself.
3. Statutes, if they order that maintenance be furnished, or a certain amount per pound, are not valid.
4. A husband does not maintain his wife principally because of the dowry received, but because the wife serves the burdens of marriage.
5. If a woman does not have the means to maintain herself, she cannot on that account claim maintenance within the year.
6. A wife cannot claim interest by reason of a delayed dowry.
casus: The question in law is in effect whether a statute of a city, in which it is provided that maintenance is owed to a surviving wife by the heirs of the deceased husband from the time the marriage was dissolved until the dowry has been paid to her, can be observed without sin, especially taking into account that, after the husband died, the woman was received by her wealthy father and maintained by him in his house until she was married to another, to whom she was married with the rights belonging to her against the heirs of the first husband? Hence it is that both the father, who maintained his daughter in widowhood, and the second husband, who maintains her and sustains the burdens of marriage, daily claim maintenance from the time of the death of the first husband; but on the part of the husband's heirs it is alleged that the said statute contains usurious depravity. Likewise, that on another ground maintenance was not to be furnished to the woman, because by another statute of the city it is provided that a wife is bound to restore everything delivered and gifted to her by her husband, which however the said woman by no means did, since she still keeps certain precious garments for herself. It is asked what the law is, both with respect to the woman and with respect to the father and the second husband, who maintained the said woman, the dowry not having been paid up to the present day.
body: The help of Christ the Savior and of His most pious Mother having been invoked. It seems at first that the said statute is valid and free from all scruple of sin; for just as civil law was able from the beginning to establish that a dowry consisting of immovable property is subject to restitution after a year, so that, if restitution is not made thereafter, the heir is bound to restore the dowry itself with interest, as is express in l. unica, § exactio, C. de rei vxo. actio., and Bartolus says in l. cunctos populos, C. de summa trinita., that

† such interest can also be claimed today, notwithstanding the prohibition of canon law, because it does not arise from an agreement of the contracting parties, but from the disposition of the law on account of default. For just as the law can condemn in double or triple as a penalty, Institu. de actio. § tripli (what is read and noted in capitul. unico, de plus pe. supports this), so could the law condemn the husband’s heir on account of default and contumacy in restoring the dowry according to the provision of the law. So by equal reason, a statute of a city, especially one holding the rights of a prince, could introduce that a dowry consisting of any property whatsoever is immediately subject to restitution, and as a penalty upon the person in default introduce that maintenance be provided to the woman until the dowry has been paid; argument in l. omnes populi, ff. de iustit. & iure, and what Bartolus notes in l. infamem, in fine, de publi. iudic. And this seems especially admissible for the sake of maintenance, since it is the opinion of many that even within the year maintenance is owed to a woman who has no other means of living, even if all statutory provision ceases, as the Gloss notes in the said § exactio, which many follow, and the Speculator affirms in the title qui fil. sint legi.; and since the husband, in order to support the burdens of marriage, gains the fruits of the property pledged to him on account of the dowry, as in capitul. salubriter, de vsuris, all the more, therefore, may he claim, without any sin, maintenance of this kind from the heirs of the first husband on account of his interest. For even under canon law interest can be claimed as damages (interresse), as the Gloss notes in c. conquestus, de vsuris, and in l. si traditio, C. de act. emp., and it appears express in c. salubriter and c. 1 de feu. Second, it principally supports this

† because the formality in usury is the loan itself; hence usury does not exist except in a contract of loan, an agreement intervening either tacitly or expressly, 14, quaestio 2, through the whole, and in capitul. consuluit, de vsur., fully by Ioannes Andreae on the rule peccatum, de regu. iur. in 6., in Mercurialibus. But in our case no loan intervened, nor any agreement, express or tacit, but everything derives from statutory provision; therefore, usurious depravity ceases. But notwithstanding these points, which in truth do not stand in the way of our case, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer. And first I allege the authority of Ioannes de Lignano on the single Clementine, de usuris, where he frames this question in its specific terms and says that such statutes are invalid and that those enacting them incur the penalty of that Clementine; and he says further,

† that such statutes are not valid even if they order maintenance to be provided or a fixed amount per pound after the year; in support of which he alleges the statement of Innocent in cap. salubriter, where he affirms that a surviving wife does not gain the fruits of property pledged to her for the dowry because she does not serve the marriage; for just as a husband does not gain the fruits of dotal property, nor of pledges given to him for the dowry, if he does not sustain the burdens of the marriage, as is read and noted in cap. per vestras, de do. post divor. rest., and l. si ante, ff. solu. matri., and in the said cap. salubriter, so neither ought the wife to have anything for the interest of the dowry, since she does not sustain nor serve marital burdens,

† for the husband does not appear to maintain the wife principally on account of the dowry received, but because the wife serves the burdens of marriage. Hence we see that if a husband married a wife without a dowry, he is nonetheless bound to maintain his wife according to his dignity, and as a sister, as Innocent notes in the said c. per vestras, and it is read and noted in l. si cum dotem, § fin autem, ff. sol. mat. And especially maintenance cannot be demanded within the year, since before that there is no default; nor even after default, because although the heirs do wrong by not paying the dowry as provided by law, nevertheless on account of the running of time nothing quantifiable can be claimed, because whatever accrues to the principal is usury, 14, q. 3, throughout. But a law or statute cannot bring it about that usury is lawfully paid, since in a matter of sin one must stand with canon law, as in c. fi. de praescr., noted by Bartolus in priuilegia, C. de sacrosan. ecc., on the rule possessor, de reg. iur. lib. 6. Furthermore, and secondly it is subtly proven, for the reason why usury was most especially prohibited is that the creditor attains two remunerations. First, he attains his money intact. Second, he attains some gain beyond the debt, which is contrary to the nature of things, since of itself it does not generate other money, nor is the use of money separated from the ownership of the money itself, as is noted fully and subtly by Ioannes Andreae on the said rule peccatum. In our case, however, this happens directly. For the woman would have two remunerations from her money. First, she attains her money in its entirety. Second, she attains the gain of maintenance, which is not to be conceded, nor do the statutes of the city excuse it, as in the said single Clementine, de usur. Nor does it stand in the way that she claims by reason of her interest; for the interest of the woman is not proven from this. First, she cannot by law claim within the year, especially since she was not in need, having been maintained by her wealthy father. Indeed, many hold, as Cynnus reports in the said § exactio, that

† even if the woman does not have the means to maintain herself, she cannot on this account claim maintenance within the year, since this is provided for. Nor does her poverty stand in the way, since she can provide for herself by selling the right currently belonging to her. And indeed that opinion is truer and more subtle, although the other is more equitable, as Ioannes Andreae thinks in the additions to the Speculum, in the title qui filii sint legi., § 1. This conclusion is also strengthened by the reasons immediately to be made to the contrary points. And supporting this conclusion is what Bartolus notes in l. insulam, § usuras, ff. sol. matr., where he says that

† the wife cannot claim interest on account of the delayed dowry, so that according to him it has no place in canon law, l. unica, § exactio, previously alleged; and Azo thinks the same in the Summa de usur., and Ioannes Andreae and Innocent in c. salubriter, de usuris, where they say that if the husband's heir mortgaged an estate to the wife for the restitution of the dowry, he is bound to account for the fruits; which is to be noted. Nor does the first contrary argument formed above stand in the way. For I say that although the law can inflict a certain penalty on one who is in default and contumacious, as in the contrary argument, it cannot, however, bring about gain for a party on account of the running of time, as it does in the said l. unica, § exactio, and the statute in our case. And so Butrigarius reports on the said l. cunctos populos that a certain theologian answered him. Indeed, the statute in our case is not founded upon any default, because it does not bind the heir to pay the dowry immediately, but to provide maintenance until the dowry has been paid; and thus it induces an occasion for sinning, because the wife will not care to claim the dowry, in order that in the meantime she may obtain that gain from the mere running of time. Nor secondly does what is said regarding interest stand in the way, because there is no interest within the year, since there is no default there, said § exactio; nor is interest proven by operation of law even after the year, but it is necessary that it appear that the woman or the husband was accustomed lawfully to make a profit from money, and then he will have a claim by proving the interest; but he will not be heard claiming maintenance by virtue of the statute; what Innocent notes in capitul. sacro, de senten. excom., and Bartolus in l. una, C. de senten. quae pro eo, quod interest, and what is noted in capitul. conquestus, de usu., supports this; for the second husband claims the dowry from these heirs of the first husband like any other private debt. Third, it does not stand in the way that it is said that no loan intervened; because I say that it is not an express loan, but the law feigns that a loan intervenes, as if the heir had paid the dowry, and afterwards the woman compensated him, nor may she receive from it the gain of maintenance, just as the law provides in the case of one who sells a thing for more than it is worth because he defers payment of the price, as is fully read and noted in capitul. in civitate, de usur.; for since she has an action for the dowry after the year, or before, if the statute introduces this tacitly or expressly, and she does not pursue it, she is seen to agree tacitly with the debtor; this is deservedly to be condemned. And let these things suffice, and especially this is to be said in our case, in which the woman did not obey the statute, as far as was in her power, in restoring the clothes; and he who offends against the law invokes the aid of the law in vain, as in c. quia frustra, de usuris. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A donor, when he obligates himself through words of obligation, is bound.
2. One who is prohibited from alienating inter vivos is not deemed prohibited in a last will.
3. A donation mortis causa, when it is not made in a testament nor in codicils, approaches more the nature of a contract than of a last will.
4. A guardian is not said to consent to a minor's contract unless he expressly approves.
5. Wherever a statute demands someone's consent in the act of another, it is deemed to require it as a formality.
6. One who is prohibited from donating without someone's consent cannot make a donation unless donating has been specially permitted to him.
7. One who remains silent is not held to consent where an onerous and undesirable matter is concerned.
body: The fact is in effect stated thus: A statute of Siena provides that no married woman may make any contract or obligation concerning her dowry or to its prejudice with her father, brother, grandfather, or any person whatsoever without the consent or ratification of her husband, and if it should be made, it shall not be valid ipso iure, etc. But another statute provides that in any last will three witnesses suffice, etc. These being the provisions, a certain lady Checcha, married to Giovanni de' Bandinelli, having had an only daughter from the marriage, when coming to her death in the presence of her said husband the Count, with the consent of her father, donated mortis causa to her said father—who was present and receiving on behalf of the natural brothers of the said lady Checcha and the sons of the said Count—a fourth part of her dowry in every way she could. It is asked whether the said donation stands in law. For its decision four matters must be examined. First, whether by donating mortis causa the woman is deemed to contract, or to make an obligation to the prejudice of her dowry? Second, presupposing that she is deemed to have made a contract or obligation, so that the husband's consent ought to intervene as required by the first statute, whether the husband's presence in the act of donation together with his silence is held as consent, so that the statute is thereby satisfied? Third, presupposing that silence ought to be held as consent, whether the said donation can be invalidated on the ground that five witnesses did not intervene? Fourth, presupposing that it cannot be invalidated on the said grounds, whether it can at least be impugned on the ground that the father consented to, or provided authority for, a donation made to his own sons established under his paternal power? Regarding the first, it seems initially that it should be said that by donating causa mortis the said lady Checcha does not seem to have made any contract or obligation. That she did not contract seems very clear: because for the existence of a contract it is required that an obligation arise reciprocally, as in l. Labeo. 2. ff. de verbor. significa., which does not occur in a donation causa mortis. For, since delivery of the donated property did not intervene, no obligation arises on the part of the donee; for he is not obligated to the donor in anything. It is otherwise if delivery intervened: because then he is obligated to restore it if the donor recovers, or if the donee dies first, as in l. non omnis, ff. si certum petat. Nor does the donor himself seem to be obligated: both because before the death of the donor the donation is not deemed perfected, as in l. non videtur, ff. de donat. causa mortis, and because, moved by repentance, he can revoke that donation at will, as in l. mortis causa donatio, and l. qui mortis causa, ff. eodem titul.; therefore the donor is not obligated, since an obligation is a legal bond by which we are bound by necessity to pay something, etc., as the text says in institu. de oblig. in princip. And this Dyn. seems to have expressly held, saying,

† that when the donor binds himself through obligatory words, as because he says, 'I promise to donate to you', then he is obligated, although he can revoke; or not through obligatory words, as because he said, 'I donate', and then he is not obligated, but the heir, once the aditio of the inheritance has taken place, is held by an actio utilis ex testamento; he cites l. 1. C. eod. Therefore, as is evident from what has been said, since the said lady Checcha did not, by donating causa mortis, make any contract or obligation, but simply donated causa mortis, the husband's consent was therefore not required. She was therefore able to donate with the sole consent of her father, as in l. tam is. §. 1. ff. de donatio. causa mortis. To this lends support what we say in a similar matter, that

† one who is prohibited from alienating inter vivos is not deemed prohibited in a last will, an argument from l. pater. §. fundum, ff. de lega. 3., fully through Bartol. in l. si ita quis promiserit. §. ea. l. ff. de verbor. obligatio. But a donation causa mortis is assimilated to a last will, as in institu. de donatio. in princip. and in l. fina. C. de donatio. causa mortis. Therefore, a married woman prohibited from making a contract or obligation regarding her dowry without her husband's consent is not deemed prohibited from disposing in a last will, and consequently not in a donation causa mortis either. But the statute prohibits a married woman from making an obligation to the prejudice of her dowry without her husband's consent. Yet no one doubts that by donating causa mortis she creates an obligation to the prejudice of her dowry: because, revocation not having been made, the dowry or a part of it is owed to the donee by virtue of the donation, as in ff. de donat. causa mortis throughout; and that an obligation arises from such a donation is plainly evident: because of old it is certain that a stipulation had to intervene, as in l. mortis causa donatio, and l. senatus. §. final. ff. eo., noted by Cyn. in l. 1. and l. fin. C. eo.; today, however (according to the common opinion), a nude pact suffices, just as in a donation inter vivos, as the gloss notes in l. cum pater. §. Maevio, ff. de lega. 2. and institu. de donat. in prin.; Cyn. holds this in the said l. 1. and fi. and Bar. in the said §. Maevio, and in l. 1. ff. de dona. cau. mor. cited above; and thus an obligation arises, which is induced by the consent of the parties, as in l. cum amplius. §. is natura debet, de reg. iu. and l. stichum. §. naturalis, ff. de so. Nay, I say that not only is an obligation to the prejudice of her dowry induced from such a donation, but even the donee herself is obligated by her stipulation or pact, though not irrevocably according to what was said above, since she did not make it in a testament, as Bartol. clearly maintained in impugning the opinion of Dyn. in the said l. 1. ff. de dona. causa mortis; the gloss holds this originally there, and more clearly in l. legatum est quaedam donatio, ff. de lega. 2. and institu. de dona. §. 1. in the word 'satis', and the said l. 1. and fin. C. eod. mean this. Therefore, there is room for the statute by which it is provided that she can make no obligation to the prejudice of her dowry without her husband's consent. For the statute had regard to the fragility of the sex, an argument from l. si mulier, C. de velleia.; whence just as a woman is induced to donate causa mortis, so she can be induced not to revoke, an argument from the said l. si mulier, and what Barto. notes in l. generaliter, C. eod.; whence it cannot be denied, especially in a woman, that she is said to have made an obligation to the prejudice of her dowry: because, since she did not revoke, just as she did not revoke, prejudice is caused to her daughter and her heirs, and she remains always obligated, even though she could absolve herself against the donee's will; but before she did so, she was obligated. From these points the response to the contrary arguments is evident. For I say that she did not properly contract, but she made an obligation to the prejudice of her dowry. Likewise, when

† a donation causa mortis is made neither in a testament nor in codicils, it approaches more to the nature of a contract than of a last will, as is proved in l. tam is. §. 1. cited above, and there Barto. holds this, and the same is noted in the said l. 1. and fin. C. de dona. cau. mor.; it would be otherwise, however, if it were made in a testament or codicils, and we would be outside the words of the statute; and in this case the contrary arguments proceed. From all of which it is concluded that the solemnity of the statute was necessary for the validity of the said donation. Therefore it is now necessary to discuss the second doubt, whether the husband, by remaining silent, is deemed to have consented. And for the affirmative side, the regula 'qui tacet', de reg. iu. lib. 6. can be alleged, along with many legal texts there alleged as concordances, in which it is clear that he who is silent seems to consent. I say that almost infinite laws can be alleged pro and contra, which are fully discussed by the gloss and Dyn. in the said reg. 'qui tacet', and regu. 'is qui tacet', and by Cyn. in l. invitus, C. de procu. and Bart. in l. quae dotis, ff. sol. mat., and by the canonists in cap. nonne de praesum. But in our proposed case I firmly judge that that presence and silence of the husband ought not to be held as consent. For this I cite the notable text together with the gloss in l. 3. ff. de autho. tuto. where it is evident

† that a tutor is not said to consent to the contract of a minor unless he expressly approves, whence silence alone is not held as consent. And expressed through that text and gloss, Bar. intended this in the said l. quae dotis, where to the point, through what is there noted, he delivers the theoretical principle, saying that when it concerns the prejudice of a third party whose goods concern someone as to care and solicitude, one who is silent is not presumed to consent; but the wife's dowry regards the husband as to care and solicitude, especially taking heed of the statute that prohibits a woman from making an obligation without the husband's consent; therefore the husband by being silent does not seem to consent. Secondly, I prove it

† thus: wherever a statute requires the consent of someone in the act of another, it is deemed to require it for solemnity; because otherwise it could not require it, since the transaction does not pertain to him, nor is he the superior of the contracting party; thus Anton. de Butri. notably held in capitul. cum consuetudinis, de consue. Where, however, consent is required for the solemnity of the act, it is necessary that it intervene expressly and clearly, nor does silence suffice; for this is what is read and noted in c. quia propter, de elect. joined with the notes in c. quod sicut, and c. ecclesia, eo. titu.; what the gloss notes in a similar matter in c. ut circa, de elect. lib. 6. lends support. Thirdly, there seems to be a text on this in a similar matter in l. filiusfamilias. §. pari autem rone, ff. de dona. where it is evident

† that he who is prohibited from donating without someone's consent cannot make a donation unless to donate was specially permitted to him. And I weigh the word 'specially', by which it is proved that express consent is required. And through that text Bartol. openly holds this in the said l. tam is. §. 1. at the word 'quaero an requiratur expressa, & specialis', etc. Thirdly, the theory of Innocen. in capitulu. in genesi, de elect., which the gloss follows in the regula 'qui tacet' cited above, supports this; for he says that

† where it concerns an onerous and undesirable matter, one who is silent is not held as consenting, as in l. filiusfa. §. invitus, ff. de proc. But in our case, by that donation prejudice was caused to the daughter of the husband himself, to whom the entire dowry would go, and consequently to the husband himself, who during the daughter's lifetime had the usufruct, as in l. non solum, C. de bo. quae libe.; therefore by remaining silent he is not deemed to have consented. From the aforesaid it is clear that the said donation was not valid, and consequently it is pointless to examine the third question, whether it falls because five witnesses did not intervene; and it could be alleged that it also falls on this ground through l. si. C. de dona. cau. mor. where it is ordained that for the validity of such a donation five witnesses must intervene. Nor does the aforementioned statute stand in the way, because it speaks of a last will; but when a donation is made by itself, and not in a testament or codicils, but in a third distinct species, it approaches more to the nature of a contract than of a last will, as I have fully stated above. Therefore the statute permitting the number of witnesses in a last will ought not to be extended to this case, especially since it is to be restricted as deviating from the disposition of the common law, as in c. cum dilectus, de consue. and in the regula 'quae a iure communi exorbitant', de reg. iur. with its likes; what Bal. notes in l. si. C. de testa. fits excellently, where he says that if a statute prohibits one under twenty years of age from testating, it ought not to be extended to a donation causa mortis for the aforesaid reason, although Barto. said otherwise in l. 2. ff. de leg. 1. To the contrary, however, l. Marcellus, ff. de dona. causa mor. singularly supports, where it is evident that a solemnity remitted in a last will seems tacitly remitted in a donation causa mortis; to the same effect is the text in insti. de dona. in princ. and in l. fin. C. de dona. causa mor. Assuredly the point is quite doubtful, but for the present I shall not examine it further, because from the aforesaid the decision of this question is sufficiently clear. And for the same reason I do not care to examine the fourth doubt, which could arise here, whether the father could provide his consent in a donation made by a child to his brothers, sons established in the power of the same common father, concerning which see gl. and Bar. in l. 1. ff. de autho. tuto. and better through Bart. in l. impuberum. §. 1. ff. de sal. where he seems to feel that he could not, although he felt otherwise in the said l. 1. The first seems truer because of the usufruct, which is acquired for the father himself, who could not authorize in his own affair. Nicolaus Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A grant made contrary to a preceding interlocutory decree of the prince, of which no mention was made in the grant, is judged surreptitious and void.
2. A first will is revoked by a second simply made.
3. Not every perjurer is infamous with civil infamy, but only he who acts contrary to a sworn provision.
4. A donation is presumed to be made inter vivos when no mention of death appears, even if it is made by an infirm person.
5. A contract inter vivos made under a condition impossible by law, or under an immoral condition, is ipso iure null.
body: In the question that is pending or is expected to be pending between Antonius Ioannis on the one side, and Nicolaus Nicolai on the other, concerning the prevailing validity of two wills made by the same lady at different times, and also concerning the validity of a certain donation inter vivos made by the same lady in the event that she should change the first will, two principal matters fall to be examined. First, whether, taking into account the words of both wills, it can be said that the first was revoked by the second? Second, presupposing the revocation of the first, whether at least the donation made in that same will is valid? Concerning the first, it is argued for the negative side, that the first is not revoked by the second. For wherever in a first will a derogatory clause regarding a subsequent intention is placed, the second will is not valid unless mention is made of that clause, as in l. si quis in princip. ff. de legat. 3; to this makes capitul. nonnulli, de rescript. and capitul. penult. and ultim. de capel. mona. But in our case such a clause was added in the first will, nor was any mention made of it in the second; therefore, etc. The minor premise is proved from the words of the first will, in which, among other things, it is provided as follows: "And this my present will I wish and command to prevail over all others, and to have perpetual legal effect, and to be unchangeable and firm, and from now on I spontaneously swear, having bodily touched the letters upon the holy Gospels of God, not to establish or make anew a present will and my present last will, etc."; wherefore, among other things, those words are to be weighed: "And to have perpetual legal effect, and to be unchangeable and firm, etc." From which it is clearly evident that she wished that will to be valid. Secondly, to the same effect makes capitul. cum olim, de re iudicat., where

† a grant made contrary to a preceding interlocutory decree of the prince, of which no mention was made in the grant, is judged surreptitious and void; and by that text the notable Bald. says in l. quod iussit, ff. eod., that if two contrary interlocutory sentences should appear concerning the same matter, and it should not appear that the judge delivered the sentence with the intention of revoking the first, the first does not seem to be revoked. So it must be said in the present case, and so much the more securely as in the first will she firmly said that she wished that to be her firm and unchangeable will. And this seems most especially to be held from the fact that in the first will she added an oath not to revoke it. Lest, therefore, she be called a perjurer, we ought to interpret that she did not have the intention of making another will, but rather of complying with her son's wishes, especially since an oath has the force of a derogatory clause, namely: "if what I do is not valid as I do it, let it be valid as it best can be valid," as is read and noted especially by Bartol. in l. cum pater. §. filius matrem, ff. de leg. 2. and in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiusso. and in capitul. ad nostram 3. and cap. quanto, de iureiurand. Thirdly, to the same effect makes: one who goes against an oath is infamous, as in l. si quis maior, C. de transact. and 6. quæst. 1. cap. infames; note the Gloss in cap. querelam, de iureiurand. and cap. peruenit, de fideiusso.; but an infamous person cannot make a will, as in l. is cui bonis. §. fin. ff. de testam.; therefore the second will ought not to be valid, since it is found to have been made by a perjurer. But notwithstanding these points, I think the contrary opinion prevails. I am moved principally by l. sancimus, C. de testam., where it is clear that

† by a second will simply made, the first is extinguished. For a last will is ambulatory until death. Indeed, a will is confirmed by death alone, as in capi. cum Marthæ, de celeb. miss. and 13. quæst. 2. cap. vltima voluntas. Nor can anyone impose a law upon himself from which he may not depart, as in l. si quis, in princip. ff. de leg. 3. Nor is it required that a special revocation of the prior will be made; but a tacit revocation, which is elicited from the contrary intention, suffices; a good text to this effect is in l. fin. §. 1. de leg. 2., by which text Cyn. held there, and the doctors commonly follow, and especially Bar. in d. l. si qs, in prin. in fi. primę colum., that even if in the first will there is a derogatory clause tacitly understood from the contrary sense, it is nevertheless not necessary that it be expressly extinguished: but a tacit one suffices. For just as it is tacitly introduced, so it is tacitly extinguished. And by the aforesaid our question seems to be decided. For if the words of the first will are well weighed, there is no clause there expressly derogatory of a subsequent intention, but only tacitly. Nay rather, she did not simply and absolutely say that she did not wish a contrary will to be valid; rather, she expressly wished it to be valid, when she added these words, namely: "And insofar as it should happen that I depart from this last will, or establish another will or another last will, from now as from then, and from then as from now, I give inter vivos, etc." From which words it is clearly gathered that for the validity of the second will she did not wish any solemnity to be applied, or any derogation to have to be made, or that mention of the first will ought to be made, but only that upon the change of the prior intention she wished the donation inter vivos to be valid; to this makes what is noted especially by Bald. in l. non dubium, C. de legi. in that question whether an act done against a penal law is valid. And truly from this consideration alone the second will can be sustained. And to the contrary arguments framed above I reply: and first to the first, the reply is clear from what was said above. For no clause derogatory of the will was expressly added, but rather those words savor of a clause derogatory of power in that she said she wished that last will to be firm and unchangeable, which subsists by no bond, because no one can render themselves unable to change a will, as in dict. l. si quis, in princip., and there fully by Barto.; makes l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, and what is noted there, ff. de uerborum obligat. To capitu. cum olim, and the dictum of Barto., I say that they apply in those matters in which probable ignorance of a prior act is conceded on account of a multitude of deeds. For forgetfulness often deceives even the prince, 23. distinct. capitu. præterea; but we are speaking of a prior will, in which ignorance is not presumed, both because it is one's own act, as in capitu. ab excommunicato, de rescript., and because it is an act so notable and so rarely customary to be done that oblivion ought not to be presumed, as in capitu. cum illorum, prope fin. de senten. excommu.; and in a will this is clearly proved in d. l. sancimus, C. de testamen., where it is clearly proved that a second will made a long time after the first is valid, although the first was not expressly revoked by the second. Wherefore it must be said that the second will is valid and holds. And in our case, although those customary words, "annulling and voiding every other will, etc.," are not inserted, she annuls it sufficiently by the fact that she made another will, since she cannot die with two wills: dict. l. sancimus. Nor does it stand in the way that an oath was added in the first: because that does not impede the revocation of the will; to this effect is the notable Gloss in capitu. ultima uoluntas, 13. quæstio. 2. and fully by Ioan. Andr. in regu. quod semel placuit, de reg. iur. lib. 6. in Mercu., where he finally concludes that the will is valid notwithstanding an oath sworn not to revoke it; he admits, however, that the testator is a perjurer. And to this makes what Innocen. notes in capitu. dilecto, de præben., where he says that the validity of an act is not impeded against an oath; whence if someone has sworn not to sell a book, and afterwards sells it, the sale holds, although he himself is a perjurer. Nay rather, Barto. held further in l. cum duobus. §. idem respondit, ff. pro socio, and in l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, ff. de uerbo. obligatio., that such an oath, being contrary to good morals, is not binding, as in regula non est obligatorium, de reg. iur. lib. 6.; and thus the one changing the will is not a perjurer. From these points the reply to the last argument is clear, to which one can reply in multiple ways: first, by denying that by changing the will she fell into perjury, because it was not binding, but rash; which does not bind the transgressor to perjury, as in capitu. quanto, de iureiuran. and 22. quæstio. 4. throughout.

† Moreover, not every perjurer is infamous with civil infamy, but only he who goes against a sworn promise to the injury of his neighbor, as in l. si quis maior, and what is noted there, C. de transa. and in l. fin. joined with l. 2. ff. de crimi. stellio.; note Archid. in capitu. autem, 15. quæstio. 6.; note in capitu. testimonium, de testib., where a case on this point is seen. Moreover and fourthly, not every infamous person is disqualified from the capacity to make a will; on the contrary, regularly every infamous person has the capacity to make a will, as in l. 2. C. de secund. nup. and l. fin. ff. de lega. 1.; Barto. holds this in l. is, cui bonis, de uerbo. obliga., and to the case of that law he responds that it speaks in its own particular case; and concerning this see there. I come now to the second principal doubt, whether at least the donation inter vivos made in the said prior will is valid? And it seems first that it is: because it was made by way of contract, for it was made to those present and accepting, etc.; and it is clear that one can contract in a last will, nor is a contract revoked upon the revocation of a will, according to that which is read and noted in l. hæredes palam, ff. de test.; and a donation inter vivos is irrevocable, except for ingratitude, as in l. fin. C. de reuoc. don. and capitu. fin. de dona.

† and a donation is presumed to be made inter vivos from the fact that no mention of death was made, even if it is made by a sick person, as is the notable text in l. Seia. §. fina. ff. de dona. cau. mortis. Nor did that lady donate all her goods, present and future (in which case it could be called void as indirectly taking away the freedom of testation, according to the opinion of Barto. in l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, ff. de uerbo. obliga. and l. fin. C. de pact.); but she donated a fourth part of all goods; in which case the donation ought to be valid, since it is valid even if all present goods are given, since a will can be made with respect to goods to be acquired, according to what is noted by the same Barto. in dict. l. fina. But notwithstanding the aforesaid, I think the contrary must be said in our case. I am moved principally because what cannot be done directly and by way of disposition ought not to be admitted indirectly and by way of condition, as in l. Seius & Augerius, ff. ad l. Falc.; but directly no one can render themselves unable to change a will, as in dict. l. si quis, in princip. ff. de lega. 3.; therefore neither indirectly by way of condition, by providing that if she changes it, she donates those goods. For in our case that lady did not make the donation inter vivos in the will purely, but by way of a condition, namely, if she should change the will. And it must be noted that by virtue of the statute, a woman having children cannot dispose, even in a will, to the prejudice of the children, except of a fourth part. And this lady in her will donated that fourth part to non-children, instituting them heirs in that fourth part; and in the event that she should change the will, she donated that fourth part to them inter vivos, and thus in effect she was taking away from herself the free capacity of testation in a two-fold way. First, through fear of the donation inter vivos. For if she changed the will, she was thereupon deprived of a fourth part of all goods, because the donation inter vivos would have taken effect from that moment; and thus that donation was made in fraud, in place of a penalty. Whence there was a direct transgression against that l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, cited above, where it is clear that the addition of a penalty in the event of changing a will is not valid, because it is contrary to good morals; but there is nothing that is more owed to men than that the style of a last will should be free, l. 1. C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi.; and elsewhere the notable text said that the freedom of a last judgment cannot be constrained even indirectly, as in l. cum duobus. §. idem respondit, ff. pro socio. Secondly, it took away the free power of testation, because she was donating the entire fourth part, of which alone she was able freely to dispose. And this opinion, that this donation made under the condition "if she should change the will" is not valid, I find that Barto. expressly held in three places, and he says that he so advised in l. cum duobus. §. idem respondit, cited above, and in l. si quis, in prin. de leg. 3. in 6. col. ver. quæro, an si remedium, and in l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, cited above, in prin. He is moved principally,

† because a contract inter vivos made under a condition that is impossible in law, or under a base condition, is void by operation of law, as in l. impossibilis, and l. generaliter, ff. de verb. oblig. But this donation is made under a base condition contrary to good morals, namely, "if it should happen that I change the will": because it takes away the free capacity of testation; therefore it is not valid, d. l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta. And he relates that he found Din. to have advised thus, although he wrote the contrary upon the rule quod semel, lib. 6. And the words and reasons of Barto. must be weighed. For it is inferred that a donation under such a condition is not valid, even if it had not been made concerning all goods present and future, but concerning a certain part of the goods. For when it is made concerning present and future goods, then he held that the donation is not valid even if it had been made purely, as he himself notes in d. l. stipulatio, and d. l. fin. C. de pact. And thus he most clearly perceives that in our case the donation was not valid, especially considering that the said lady could not freely dispose except of that fourth part; and by these points the reply to the things alleged above for the contrary opinion is clear. Wherefore from all the aforesaid I conclude that the first will was revoked by the second. Likewise, that the donation made in the first will under the condition "if she should change the will" is not valid. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One can renounce the benefit of the cession of goods with an oath.
2. If it is provided by statute that someone be cited personally or at his house, it is not understood according to the ius commune.
body: ON the question of Domenico Placidi of Siena, whether his debtors, in respect of a dowry instrument, can be personally seized and detained in prison until they have satisfied the said creditor Domenico, notwithstanding that the said debtors offer their property for the satisfaction of the debt. It seems at first that they cannot; for if for a monetary debt hands are not first laid upon immovables, nor upon debts owed to the debtors, if movables can be found, as in l. a diuo Pio, §. in venditione, ff. de re iudica., and thus the judge harms as little as he can in the execution of a matter judged, therefore by stronger reason equity ought to be observed with respect to personal capture, so that it may never occur so long as sufficient goods of the debtor are found; and this view the gloss and Barto. in l. 3, §. tutores, ff. de suspec. tuto. openly appear to support. But these things notwithstanding, I judge that the contrary view prevails. And I judge that on two grounds the said debtors can in our case be seized. First, by virtue of the agreement entered into between the parties; for they promised that they could be sued really and personally for that sum. And this agreement is indeed valid in law: because, just as it is provided by law in many cases that a defendant may be detained in prison until he has satisfied the debt, l. 1, C. qui bo. ce. pos., l. cum eo, and what is noted there by Bar., ff. ad l. Iuli. penult., with similar texts, therefore this can also be done by pact. And that this side is valid is expressly held by Angel. de Perusio in l. nemo carcerem, C. de actio. tribu., l. 10; Bartol. took this view in l. si decessero, ff. qui satisdatio. cogan.; and Specu. in titul. de renunc. & conclu. §. 1, versicul. item est beneficium, at the end; and Fede. de Senis, consil. 58, where he went further and held that

† with an oath one can renounce the benefit of the cession of goods, on the argument of authent. sacramenta puberum, C. si aduersus vend., and c. cum contingat, de iureiurand., and c. 2, de pact., lib. 6, and c. significante, de pig.; and cap. ex rescripto, de iureiuran., makes very strongly for this. In our case, moreover, an oath intervened. Indeed, many have held that even without an oath that benefit of cession can be renounced, although Bartol. held the contrary in l. alia, §. eleganter, ff. soluto matrimo. In our case, however, no doubt seems to exist, both because he did not renounce the benefit of cession—and thus the pact cannot be called contrary to good morals, since he can avoid prison by ceding his goods—and because an oath intervened. This conclusion proceeds above all because nowhere is it expressly proved that without a cession one may avoid prison; on the contrary, l. 1 and almost throughout, C. de cessio. bo., and what the gloss notes in capitul. 2, de pigno., make for this. Let the debtors themselves therefore sell, if they wish, and satisfy the creditor; nay rather, the creditor is not bound to sell the pledge, as in the said l. a diuo Pio, §. si qua res, and much less is he bound to take it in payment, lest he be compelled to receive a specific thing instead of a sum of money. On the second ground he can be seized, namely by force of the statute of Siena, in which it is provided that by reason of an instrument one may be seized and detained until satisfaction has been made to the creditor, as is clear in the statute contained under the rubric that debtors cannot be seized personally, etc. And I weigh that this statute in its beginning speaks concerning the matter of the law providing that as a general rule one cannot be seized personally, and then excepts the case of the obligation of a dowry instrument and certain others. In order therefore that the exception be of the rule, it must be understood that in those cases capture is to be made, even in cases not expressed by law; otherwise that exception would accomplish nothing, against l. si quando, C. de inofficio. testamen., and capitul. si pater, de priuileg., lib. 6. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that it removes the common law with respect to the order, because I say that the first part of the statute, laying down the rule, makes no mention of the order, but concerns the substance of the capture; and afterwards it excepts our case. And an exception must be of the rule, as is noted on the rubric de re. iur., lib. 6. The notable statement of Bartol. in l. 4, §. praetor ait, ff. de damn. infect., makes for this understanding, where he says

† that if it is provided by a statute that one be cited personally or at his house, it is not understood according to the common law as an alternative of order—namely, that he be cited first personally and in default thereof at his house—but it stands properly such that it is sufficient to cite him at his house, because in adopting the first understanding the statute would introduce nothing beyond the common law; which is to be noted. Furthermore, since the statute does not speak in its exceptions in the terms of the law, it therefore intended to correct the common law and introduce this anew, as Bald. notably says on a similar point in l. properandum, C. de iudic., at the verse quid ergo si statutum dicit. And these things seem to be of the mind of Bartol. in the said l. 3, §. tutores, ff. de suspec. tuto., at the end, where he says that although under the common law debtors ought not to be seized seeing that they have sufficient goods, as the gloss notes there, nevertheless the statutes and customs of Tuscany are otherwise. The words of our statute are clear enough; therefore there is no need to persist further in caviling, as in l. ille aut ille, ff. de legat. 3, especially since custom supports justice, as Bartol. himself attests. I conclude therefore that, as well in respect of the agreement, especially being sworn, as of the statute of the city, the said debtors can be personally seized and detained until they have satisfied, notwithstanding that they offer their goods, especially since an oath must be fulfilled in specific form, as in capitul. ad nostram, ii 1, de iureiurand., to such a degree that by virtue of an oath one can be compelled precisely to the deed, as in the said c. ex rescripto, de iureiurand., as Anto. de Butr. affirms in c. veniens, eod. ti.; what the gloss notes in l. si pecuniam, ff. de cond. ob causam, makes for this; and let these things suffice. To the contrary argument framed above in the beginning the response is easily evident: for it can apply where no agreement intervened and statutory provision is absent, so that looking purely to the common law he would not be imprisoned, seeing that he has sufficient goods and is not in contumacy, according to that opinion of the noted gloss in §. tutores, previously cited, which Bart. follows there and Ang. in the repetition of the said l. nemo carcerem, which is quite pleasing on account of its great equity, for which l. ob foenus, ff. de admini. tuto., and the said §. tutores make, although it is not proved by clear law, as I said above. Nicolaus Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether the first decree interposed at the petition of a mother demanding her dowry in her own time holds valid in the goods of the ward.
2. Putting into possession under the first decree, since it entails slight prejudice, can be made against an absent person on account of the state, if he is defended by no one.
3. One ought to be cited personally when he can be found.
body: Having invoked the protection of Jesus Christ the Savior from the heart, out of all the matters narrated by the party four questions can be elicited for a clear decision. First, whether the interposition of the first decree was valid. Second, what about the second decree. Third, presupposing the nullity of those decrees, whether the mother put into possession made the fruits her own in the meantime. Fourth, whether the goods of the husband are tacitly encumbered for maintenance due to the wife, having regard to the ius commune and municipal law. I return to the first, in
† which it seems it must be said that the first decree stood firm in the goods of the ward, interposed at the petition of the mother demanding her dowry in her own time.

† For putting into possession under the first decree, since it entails slight prejudice, is also made against an absent person on account of the state, if he is defended by no one, in l. ignorare, C. de rest. mi., and against the church, as in capit. 2. and 3. de eo qui mit. in posses. Therefore, the same seems to be said against an undefended ward who was cited; text in l. apud Iulianum, ff. ex quib. cau., and more openly on our precise terms Barto. holds in l. 1. ff. de administ. tuto., where he says that if the cited ward does not appear through a lawful person, putting into possession under the first decree can be made against him; but in our case it is presupposed that the ward was cited at the house of his late father, and no one appeared for him; therefore, etc. For from a citation made at the domicile, one can proceed to the first decree, according to what is noted by Innocen. in capitu. fin. de eo qui mit. in posses., as seems to be proved in l. 4. §. praetor ait, ff. de dam. infect. But notwithstanding these points, I think that in our case the first decree does not subsist in force. I am moved first, because against a ward one cannot proceed to the interposition of the first decree unless the tutor was first cited, who in our case was not cited at all; if, moreover, the ward does not have a tutor, his blood relations or affines must be sought out, and anyone else who might be, whom it is probable will not omit the defense of the ward, whether on account of kinship, or charity, or other reason; which was likewise not done at all in our case. These points are expressly proved in l. haec autem, §. non defendi, with the following, ff. ex quib. cau. in posses. ea. Secondly, I am moved by a defect of citation considered otherwise: for when someone can be found, he ought to be cited to his face, and thus

† personally, and not at his house, since the person to be cited never appeared in court, as is the text joined with the gloss in capitu. causam, de dolo & contu., even to the effect of proceeding to the first decree, as noted there, and especially by Hostien., who held that one can be said to be found if he is in the province. But presupposing as truer the opinion of Barto., who held in the said §. praetor ait that if he is not found in the city, he is said not to be able to be found, so that a citation at the house can be made—which opinion many follow in the said capitu. causam, and he alleges for this case what is contained in the authen. de exhib. & intro. reis, §. si vero quidam—the word 'city' must nevertheless be taken broadly, since we are not in an odious matter, but indeed a favorable one, so that it also includes the surrounding district (comitatus); an excellent argument in l. 1. §. cum urbem, ff. de of. procon. But the ward lived in the comitatus; therefore he ought to have been cited to his face there, and not at the house of his former paternal habitation. And presupposing that in our case the word 'city' ought not to be taken so broadly, the citation can nevertheless be overturned on another ground: because, as is presupposed to me in fact, after the death of the father, or at least long before the citation, the ward never lived in the paternal house, but with his tutor, who notoriously lived in the comitatus, and it was also notoriously established that the ward lived in the same place; therefore the first citation ought to have been made to his person, or at the house of his habitation, as in the said l. praetor ait, and l. scire oportet, ff. de excu. tuto., and the said capitu. causam, with its gloss, de dolo & contu. Thirdly, it can be overturned principally because it was done through the fraud of the present party against the absent party, since she knew that a defense was available to the ward, at least as to the greater part of the dowry, since payment had previously been made for the greater part, as Innocen. meant to note in capitu. 2. de dila., where he says that if admission against an absent person was made through the fraud of the present person, as because she knew a defense was available to the absent person, he who was absent will be able to seek that the possession granted in his absence be revoked; and if the person put into possession excepts, 'You were contumaciously absent,' the person who suffered the possession will be able to replicate, 'And you fraudulently except regarding my fraud or contumacy, since you acted fraudulently around the same matter, knowing that I was protected by a defense.' And for this opinion of Innocen., l. si praetor, §. Marcellus, ff. de iud. is applicable; for the placing in possession ought to have been made according to the measure of the debt declared; l. cum proponas, joined with the authen. ei qui iurat, C. de bo. auth. iud. pos., and capitu. quoniam, §. in aliis, ut lit. non contesta. This mother, however, fraudulently sought placing in possession in respect of the entire dowry, although she had nevertheless been satisfied for the greater part. Wherefore, from all these aforesaid points, I conclude that the first decree was not valid at all. The contrary laws alleged at the beginning do not stand in the way: because they ought to be limited according to the aforesaid. I come to the second doubt, namely, whether the second decree was valid. And indeed that decree can, in my judgment, be overturned on multiple grounds. First, because since the first was not valid, the second ought not to be valid; because the second decree is a second aggravation of the judge in hatred of the contumacious party, as noted in l. si finita, §. Iulianus, ff. de dam. infect., and capitu. 1. de eo qui mit. in posses. But in our case the first aggravation was not valid, nor could the ward be said to be contumacious, as is clear from the aforesaid; therefore the second aggravation ought not to have been made, since the second decree is founded upon the first; an argument from those things which are read and noted in capitu. quoniam, at the end, ut lit. non contesta.; and if the principal is not valid, neither is the accessory; de fide instrumen. capitu. inter dilectos, §. caeterum. Secondly, it was not valid for the most powerful reason, because it was not interposed against someone in hiding (latitans). For in this context, he is said to be in hiding who does not obey the order of the judge for the sake of defrauding a creditor, as l. Fulcinius, in the beginning, §. quid autem sit latitare, ff. ex quib. cau. in posses. ea., and noted by Innocen. in c. dilecto, de verbo. signi. But the ward was not in hiding from multiple points of view. First, because he was never cited in the interposition of the second decree; nor does it suffice for him to be cited unless the tutor is also cited, since he had one, as I stated above; for if the first cannot be interposed (as I said in the preceding doubt), a fortiori neither can the second, according to Innocen. in the said capitu. dilecto. Nor does it stand in the way that the judge appointed for him a curator ad litem, which he seems to have been able to do since he was not being defended, as in the said l. Fulcinius, §. plane, with the following; because I say that this applies when the ward did not have a tutor, or had one who was less suitable. But in our case the ward had a suitable tutor, who was never cited to that suit; therefore a curator ad litem could not be given to him, as is proved in §. interdum, insti. de cura. The second decree was therefore interposed with a person not having the power; it is therefore null, just as a trial conducted with a false procurator; l. licet, C. de proc., and in c. in nostra, and c. ex insinuatione, e. ti.; nor from the ignorance of the judge who was ignorant that the ward had a tutor ought the condition of the undefended ward himself to be deteriorated; ar. l. clarum, C. de auth. prae., and l. quaesivit, ff. de re iudic. Thirdly, it falls principally because the judge interposed it without having first fully examined the principal business, as is clear from the recitation of the fact, against l. cum proponas, C. de bo. authen. iud. poss.; and if it was interposed by someone insufficiently informed, it rightly ought not to be valid, since even a definitive sentence would collapse from such a fact, as in capitul. tum ex literis, and what is noted there, de in integ. restituti., and noted by Bartol. in l. prolatam, C. de senten. & interlo. Fourthly, it was not valid because it was interposed through the fraud of the present party, on the occasion of the entire dowry, which had nevertheless been satisfied for the greater part, as I said above in the preceding doubt. Fifthly and lastly, the notable statement of Innocen. in the said capitul. dilecto, de verbo. significa. supports this, where he says that since the interposition of the second decree is an interlocutory sentence—which is clear from this, because it is made before litis contestatio, as in the said l. cum proponas—the judge will be able to revoke that decree for a just cause, such as if he now learns that there was no debt, or another legitimate cause underlies it, as was true in our case, because the legitimate defender of the ward did not intervene. For an interlocutory order does not pass into res judicata as far as the judge is concerned; therefore the judge can revoke it whenever he finds that there was an error in it, or a grievance unjustly inflicted upon the other party, as in l. iudex, ff. de re iud., and c. cessante, de app., noted by Inn. in c. querelam, de elect., and through Bar. in the said §. Iulian.; and this reason is indubitable and incontrovertible. I come to the third: whether this woman, put into possession, made the fruits her own in the meantime; and I say that she did not, because she did not possess with the law standing by her, since proceedings were not conducted against the ward as the law provides, as is clear from the aforesaid; therefore good faith does not excuse her, which is also not presumed, as Bar. notes in l. sed scire, ff. de pet. haere. Likewise, what he notes in l. iuste possidet, ff. de acqui. poss. supports this. Furthermore, a minor could seek restitution against injury, as ff. de mi. l. quod si minor, and in l. causae, almost throughout. As to the last point, whether the goods of the husband are tacitly hypothecated for the maintenance of the wife: Spe. established this question in titu. de do. inter vi. & uxo. §. formatis, at the word 'sed nunquid', and there he recites contrary opinions, nor does he plant his feet firmly; but Bar. in l. Lucius, ff. de ali. & cib. leg. pursues it more fully, and finally seems to determine that they are not, because this is provided for by no law; and goods are not tacitly encumbered except in cases expressed by the law, as in ff. and C. throughout, in which cases pig. taci. contrahi licet. For although a hypothec is found for the dowry, as in l. una, C. de rei uxo. actio., and l. assiduis, C. qui po. in pig. hab., nothing however is provided for maintenance; and this side also pleases me, especially in our case, where it is asked whether they are encumbered for maintenance due after the dissolution of marriage; for it is provided by no law that maintenance be furnished upon dissolution of marriage, as Cyn. notes in l. unica, §. exactio, C. de rei uxo. actio. And presupposing that it were provided, it still does not prescribe that the goods are encumbered. And so I answer to the municipal law: for in it only an obligation of maintenance is introduced, but the goods are not encumbered. The aforesaid fail, according to Bar. in the place previously alleged, unless the dotal land had been given unappraised; for since it is then principally allocated for the burdens of marriage, it can sufficiently be admitted that it is encumbered for maintenance; but it does not apply to our case, since unappraised goods were not given. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If goods have been left to a certain monk, with the proviso that the abbot cause him no molestation concerning them, how they are understood to have been left.
2. The full disposition and administration of a monastery belongs to the abbot, and not to the monks.
3. If anything is left to a monk under this condition, that it not be acquired for the monastery, whether such a bequest is valid?
4. An abbot can give a monk licence fully to administer certain goods.
5. Silence is held for consent where it is a question of slight prejudice.
casus: A certain Lady Catherina, drawing up her last will, among other things bequeathed four hundred florins from her goods to Bartholomæus Ioannis, her grandson.
