Moreover, in all her other goods, movable and immovable, present and future, she instituted as her universal heir the aforesaid Bartholomæus, her grandson, and this in the event that he should reach full age; and in the event that he should die in pupillary age, she then willed that disposition should be made of her said goods as it should seem fit and pleasing to Dom Bartholomæus Hugolini, her legitimate and natural son, whom she left as usufructuary of all her goods for his lifetime, always saving, however, the aforesaid 400 florins which she had left to the said Bartholomæus, her grandson. And in the event that the aforesaid goods could not be distributed and arranged by the said Bartholomæus, her son, as was said above, then in that case she substituted her fideicommissaries, so that they might distribute her goods to the poor of Jesus Christ, and to pious places, or to her blood relatives, as it should seem fit and pleasing to them, discharging their conscience, however, in this matter. Afterwards, when the testatrix died, the said Dom Bartholomæus, her son, brought the said goods into his own hands, and wishing to execute the maternal testament with respect to the legacy of the said 400 florins made to the said Bartholomæus, gave in payment and satisfaction to a certain woman, the paternal aunt of the said Bartholomæus, who received it on behalf of the said Bartholomæus, a certain house, reserving to himself the usufruct, under this condition, however, that in the event that the said Dom Bartholomæus gave and paid to her the said 400 florins, the instrument of the said transfer in payment should become void, and the said house should remain unencumbered in the hands of the said Bartholomæus. Subsequently, after some time had elapsed and certain disputes had arisen over the said house, and after the said Bartholomæus, the grandson left in pupillary age, had died in the absence of his father, his said paternal aunt, in the name of the absent father and with the due guarantees, on the one part, and Dom Bartholomæus on the other part, compromised upon certain mutual friends concerning the said house, giving them full power, sureties also having been furnished for the observance of the award. The arbitrators, having heard the parties, arbitrated in this manner, namely: that the said Dom Bartholomæus is bound and ought to give, pay, and count out 400 florins in cash from now until the middle of the month of August, for which money the said Dom Bartholomæus had given in payment the said house to the said woman on behalf of that grandson; and that the said house should remain free and unencumbered in the hands of the said Dom Bartholomæus; and in the event that the said payment was not made, recourse was reserved against the sureties, as is fully contained in the award itself. Finally, the said house was transferred to a certain third party, both by the obligation of the said Dom Bartholomæus and by the act of the court interposing the first and second decree. From which third-party possessor the father of the said predeceased grandson, arriving on the scene, strives to revoke that house, saying that it belongs to him as heir, since it had been given to his son in payment and satisfaction for the said 400 florins bequeathed to him. Nor ought the compromise and the award that followed from it stand in the way, because, since the said Dom Bartholomæus was a religious, he could not enter into a compromise, nor obligate himself to anything without the licence of his prelate. And it should be noted, for the understanding of the matter, that the said Dom Bartholomæus was promoted to abbot, and, being in the end without any abbey, he was administering the aforesaid goods outside the monastery, with his superior knowing and not contradicting. Now it is asked whether the aforesaid father, or another to whom he had ceded his right, is able to invalidate the said compromise for the aforesaid reason, and under such pretext to recover the house from the third-party possessor?
body: † Having invoked the protection of Christ and of His most glorious Mother, two matters are principally to be examined for the decision of this question. First, whether the bequest made to the said Brother Bartholomaeus was valid in the manner in which it was made. Second, presupposing its validity, whether the said compromise thereafter made by him was valid in law. Regarding the first, I note that two things were bequeathed. For first, the said Lady Catherina, the testatrix, made the said Dom Bartholomaeus usufructuary of all her goods. Second, she willed that if the said Bartholomaeus, whom she instituted heir under a condition, should die in pupillary age, then it should be disposed concerning her said goods as it should seem fit and pleasing to the said Brother Bartholomaeus. And she added that, in the event that the aforesaid goods could not be distributed and arranged by the said Brother Bartholomaeus, her son, then the goods should devolve to the fideicommissaries, etc., as was said above. Whence it seems first, having inspected the said words of the testament, that the bequest was valid, but that that annexed burden—namely that the goods devolve to the fideicommissaries if those goods could not be arranged and distributed as it should seem fit and pleasing to the said Brother Bartholomaeus—was not valid as being against the laws, since she wished to make a monk capable of ownership and to attribute to him the power of disposing of goods contrary to the substantial elements of monasticism. To this makes what Barto. notably posited after the gloss in l. Lucius, §. tres haeredes, ff. ad Trebel., where he establishes this question:

† A certain man bequeathed certain goods to a certain monk, with the proviso that the abbot should cause him no molestation concerning them; but if he should do so, he willed that those goods should devolve upon another. It is asked whether, in the case of molestation, there is room for the fideicommissum? The gloss there holds that there is; it reports, however, that certain persons hold the contrary; and the same is said by Archi. in cap. quia ingredientibus, 19. quaest. ult. But Bar. there said that those who held the contrary spoke more truly, because that condition—that the abbot not cause him molestation—is base, since it is against the rule of monks, by which it is provided that monks may have nothing, as in cap. cum ad monasterium, in fin., de statu regu.; therefore, according to him, such an imposed encumbrance was not valid. But if it were such a bequest as would be valid in a monk—as if it were bequeathed for maintenance, because things can be bequeathed even to a slave, as in l. seruos, ff. de ali. & cib. leg.—then perhaps the statement of that gloss would proceed. So it seems should be said in our case: that that encumbrance—namely, that the goods devolve upon the fideicommissaries if those goods could not be arranged and distributed by the said Brother Bartholomaeus—is held as not added; and consequently it must be said that those goods were acquired for the monastery. From which it is inferred negatively to the second doubt: namely, that the compromise made by the said Brother Bartholomaeus concerning the said house was not valid, since a monk cannot compromise concerning goods acquired for the monastery, as in capit. quod quibusdam, de fideius., and what is read and noted in cap. contingit, de transac.

† For plenary disposition and administration of the monastery and of its goods belongs to the abbot, and not to the monks, especially individually, as in capitul. nullam, 28. quaest. 2, and in capitu. edoceri, and what is noted there, de rescr. Nor does it stand in the way if it be said that these goods were bequeathed to the said Brother Bartholomaeus, because I say that the bequest cannot abide in the person of the monk, but through him the acquisition is immediately made for the monastery, as is fully noted by Innoc. and others in capitu. in praesentia, de proba. But these things notwithstanding, I deem that the contrary must be said in our case. And first, I weigh that the goods were not simply bequeathed to the said Brother Bartholomaeus as owner, but to be arranged and distributed by him as it shall seem fit and pleasing to him; in which case a bequest made to a monk is valid, since he is deemed a kind of administrator and distributor of the goods, as in capitu. religiosus, de testamen. lib. 6. And that this can be done, I adduce the notable statement of the same Barto. in authen. excipitur, C. de bo. quae lib., where it is asked concerning this question: suppose

† that something is bequeathed to a monk under this condition, that it not be acquired for the monastery: whether such a bequest is valid. And it seems first that it is not, because it contains an impossibility and a certain repugnance; for a monk cannot have anything, but all belongs to the monastery, 12. quaest. 1, capitu. nolo, and capitu. non dicatis, and in auth. ingressi, C. de sacros. ecc.; whence to say that it belongs to the monk and is not acquired for the monastery is a certain contradiction in itself and a kind of perplexity which tends to vitiate a legacy and a disposition, as in l. si Titius, ff. de condi. insti., and l. ubi repugnantia, ff. de regu. iuris. Bartol. concludes there to the contrary, saying that the aforesaid words ought to be understood thus: 'I bequeath to the monk under this condition, that nothing be acquired for the monastery,' that is, that the monastery suffer him to have it in the manner in which he can, namely with closed eyes; just as we say in the case of a slave, that he can have something with the closed eyes of his master, as in l. 3, ff. de manu.; and thus nothing is acquired for the monastery, namely by act; and to this he adduces the text with what is noted there in the said l. Lucius, §. tres haeredes. Thus, therefore, an improper use of words is made so that the bequest may be valid, and free administration without ownership may be acquired for the monk. In favor of this I adduce the notable text together with the gloss and Innocen. in capitu. insinuante, ne cler. uel mona. Therefore, all the more strongly ought the bequest to be valid in our case, in which the words of bequest do not savor of ownership in the monk, but rather of lawful administration and dispensation. Whence those words are to be weighed: 'as it shall seem fit and pleasing to the said Brother Bartholomaeus,' which sound in the judgment of an upright man, as is proved in l. Thais, §. sororem, ff. de fideicom. lib., and in l. fideicomissa, §. quamquam, ff. de leg. 3, noted in capitu. 2, de corpo. uitia., and fully by Barto. in extravaganti, ad reprimendum, and in l. alio, ff. de ali. & cib. leg.

† For the abbot can give license to a monk fully to administer certain goods, as in the said capitu. religiosus, and in capitu. cum ad monasterium, and capitu. 2, de sta. regu., and what is noted in both places; it is proved more specifically and singularly in the said capitu. insinuante, together with the gloss; and in this grant the express consent of the superior is not required, but tacit consent suffices, and because the superior sees him having that administration in this way and remains silent, as is proved in the case of a slave in l. quam Tuberonis, ff. de pecul., and in the said l. 1, de manu. Barto. sufficiently held this in the said auth. excipitur, where he said that it suffices that the monastery suffer him with closed eyes to have it in the best manner in which he can. To the same effect is what the same Barto. noted in l. quae dotis, ff. solu. matr., where by that l. quam Tuberonis he gave the general rule,

† that where a slight prejudice is concerned, silence is held for consent. In our case, however, not even a slight prejudice to the monastery was concerned; rather, it was a pious work to offer assent to a maternal disposition, argum. in l. 1, C. de sacrosan. eccle., and 13. quaest. 2, cap. ultima uoluntas; therefore the silence of the superior ought to have been held for consent. Furthermore and secondly, wherever a monk has the administration of a peculium, the abbot is bound by the contracts of the monk to the extent that the peculium allows, as noted by Inno. in cap. cum olim, de priui.; to which makes what Barto. noted in l. communis Seruus, ff. de stipu. ser., just as is said in contracts entered into by a slave, and as is noted there; therefore the said contract of compromise ought to be valid to the extent that the administration of the said goods allows; otherwise, however, where a monk contracts without any administration, in which case the abbot is bound in nothing; and in this case the laws cited to the contrary speak. Likewise and thirdly, most clearly, whichever way the matter turns, it is proved that the third possessor can defend himself against the father of the said Bartholomaeus, or another to whom he assigned his rights. For either the said compromise was valid, and then the case is most clear: for it was arranged through the arbitral award that the house should remain entirely free in the possession of the said Bartholomaeus, and failing payment of the 400 florins, recourse was reserved against the sureties, but the house did not remain obligated, and thus the house cannot be vindicated by reason of the first giving in payment; or else the said compromise was not valid due to a defect of power, as is alleged—which is nevertheless denied—and then by an even stronger reason that giving of the house in payment that was made would suffer from the same defect. For just as a monk cannot compromise without the authority of his superior, so, and all the more, he cannot give in payment, since through that giving an alienation occurs, which undoubtedly a monk cannot perform, indeed not even the abbot alone, 17. quest. 4, cap. in venditionibus, and 12. q. 2, cap. Abbatibus. Through the compromise, however, he bettered the condition of the said goods. Nor ought the father to be admitted alleging a defect of power in the monk with respect to the compromise, since he himself also bases his intention upon that giving in payment made by the monk alone; for one alleging contrary things is not to be heard, as in cap. solicitudinem, de appel., l. vbi repugnantia, ff. de reg. iur.; especially since he had more ample power at the time of the compromise than at the time of the giving in payment, since in the first case the said Bartholomaeus had died in pupillary age, and thus there had been room for the substitution made concerning the said Brother Bartholomaeus; but in the second case the said Bartholomaeus, the heir instituted under condition, was still living, and consequently he had no power at all to alienate the said house, since he was then a mere usufructuary. And the same must be said in every respect if those goods had been acquired for the monastery in any event, for there would be the same defect of power in both cases. And from the right of a third party one can defend oneself, provided that it is exclusive of the right of the plaintiff, which would happen in the present case, as read and noted in l. cum seruum, C. de ser. fug., and there by Cy. most fully, and by Bart. in l. 2, ff. de exce. rei iud. From all the aforesaid I conclude that the said house cannot be revoked from the said third possessor by reason of a defect in the compromise, and by reason of that giving in payment. And the response to the contrary arguments is sufficiently clear through the aforesaid. And let these things suffice. Nicol. Abb. Case of the following consilium.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A legacy of another's property made to a joined person is valid.
2. Notification can be made at any time, provided it is not made near the condemnation itself.
3. That which can be accomplished only by the act of one person is considered impossible.
4. Property of the church can be alienated for the redemption of captives, unless it was given in such a manner that it cannot be alienated.
casus: The case in effect is as follows. A certain Franciscus, late son of Petrus of Villa Casalis in the district of Prato, diocese of Pistoia, in his last will instituted among other things as universal heir Nannes, his grandson, son of the late Johannes, son of the said testator. But after the death of his said heir dying without children, by title of legacy, for the remedy of his soul, he left that a chapel be built in the parish church of Santo Stefano of Prato, which chapel he willed and ordered to have, for its dowry [?] and for maintaining the priest to be instituted there from successor to successor in perpetuity, a piece of land of about 52 stadia situated in the community of Prato; and he provided in the said will that the said piece of land, given as dowry, could not in any manner, right, or cause be alienated, pledged, sold, donated, or exchanged, or its ownership transferred in any way directly or subjected indirectly. And if the contrary should occur, he willed that the contract then be void by operation of law. Thereafter, the testator having died, the said Nannes, the instituted heir, entered upon the inheritance, and finally dying without children, having made a will, he left by title of legacy the said piece of land with its appurtenances to the said Lady Thomasia, his mother, who after the death of her son had possession of the said piece of land. Having obtained it, she was sued and summoned into court by virtue of the will of the said Franciscus, who had bequeathed the said piece of land for the dowry of the chapel in the aforesaid manner, and she received the libel in court, and issue was joined regarding the said land bequeathed to her, and many days after the day of joinder of issue made by her, she notified the heir of the said Nannes of the action brought against her concerning the land. And finally proceeding in the case, she incurred an adverse judgment; from which she appealed, and again succumbed. Now, however, the said Lady Thomasia, the legatee, urges against the heir of the said Nannes—who is a cleric, and a minor, having a curator, though his curator was not at all present in court—and reciting both legacies and the eviction that occurred, requests that the heir be compelled to give [?] and deliver the said land. It is asked what the law is; and many other things are related in fact, but the aforesaid seem to suffice in effect.
body: Having humbly invoked the help of Christ and of his mother, it seems at first that the said legatee ought to be heard in her claim:

† because a legacy of another's property made to a joined person is valid, even if made in ignorance, and the heir is bound to redeem the property, if he can, and deliver it to the legatee. But if he cannot, because the owner does not wish to sell, he is bound at least to its estimation at a competent price; in support of this is what is read and noted in l. cum alienam, C. de leg. and insti. eodem § non solum, ff. de leg. 3. l. non dubium. And it seems that from the beginning the thing bequeathed itself can be claimed specifically, as the text intimates in the said l. cum alienam, and Bart. notes this there in the beginning, although the second gloss there seems to give another theory regarding claiming; but the text there supports the former, as does l. Iulianus, ff. de confes. and what Bar. notes in l. si seruum, near the end, ff. de uerbo. obli. Nor is it an obstacle that the said land was once delivered to her; since, when it has been lawfully evicted from her, she can then sue on the eviction, as in l. qui concubinam § si hæres, ff. de lega. 3. and l. si domus § de euictione, ff. de leg. 1., and there the case appears that the evicted bequeathed thing itself can be claimed under the testament. Nor should it stand in the way if it is said that the notification was made to the heir after joinder of issue (litis contestatio),

† because notification can be made at any time, provided it is not made near the very condemnation, as is the noted text in l. si rem quam § quolibet tempore, ff. de euic. and what the gloss notes there at the end supports this. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the legatee was contumaciously absent at the time of the judgment, and thus, since she seems condemned through her contumacy, she ought not to have recourse for eviction, as in l. si ideo, ff. de euic. and l. emptor fundi, C. eodem and c. si. de emp. & uen.; because I say that this applies when someone permitted the case to be clarified in his absence; for then he seems rather to be condemned from his contumacy than from the injustice of the cause; therefore he has no recourse for eviction. But when all things were previously clarified while the party was present, even though he was absent at the time of condemnation, he nonetheless has recourse for eviction, because he was then condemned not from contumacy, but because of the injustice of the cause. So said Bar. singularly and well in l. si superatus, ff. de euic. Bal. gave another solemn limitation to those laws in l. res inter alios, C. quibus res iudi. non no., saying that if from an inspection of the acts it can appear that the contumaciously absent party lawfully succumbed, the absence of the condemned party ought not to harm. In our case, moreover, it can sufficiently appear that the said Lady Thomasia lawfully succumbed, because it clearly appears that that piece of land had been bequeathed for the endowments of the chapel upon that Nanne, the heir, dying without children. Nor lastly does it stand in the way if it is said, as is assumed in the facts, that the said Lady Thomasia ought to have appealed not to the Archbishop of Florence, but to the Bishop of Pistoia, because one must appeal from a rural vicar to the bishop himself who appointed him, since an outlying official is said to have delegated, not ordinary, jurisdiction, nor does he make one and the same consistory with the bishop as does a vicar general, as noted by the gloss in cle. et si principalis, de præsc. and Inn. in c. Romana, de of. or. li. 6.; because the reply is that although an appeal must be made step by step, nevertheless if an appeal is made with an intermediate step omitted and no exception is taken, the appeal is valid, because this pertains to the circumstances, not to the essentials of an appeal, as noted by the gloss and commonly by the doctors in c. dilecti filii, j. de appel.; what the gloss notes in c. 2 de consue. li. 6. at the word officiali supports this. But notwithstanding these points, which in my judgment do not stand in the way of our case, I deem the contrary to prevail, namely, that the said heir must be absolved from the petition of the said Lady Thomasia. I am moved first by an unassailable consideration: for wherever a thing is bequeathed that can be alienated solely by the decision of the prince, the legacy is not valid, nor is its estimation owed, even if it was made knowingly; the text is well-known and notable in l. apud Iulianum, ff. de leg. 1, where it is held

† that that which can be accomplished solely by the act of one person is deemed impossible; noted by the gloss in l. continuus § cum quis, ff. de verbo. obl., Dyn. in regula semel Deo, de reg. iu. lib. 6, and Bart. in the said l. apud Iulianum. But this piece of land bequeathed to the said Lady Thomasia was of this kind; therefore, the estimation is not owed. The major premise is most clearly proven in clement. quia contingit, de relig. dom. after the beginning, where it is said that things assigned to a certain use by the bounty of the faithful cannot be assigned to another use, saving always the authority of the Apostolic See. And that text applies especially in our case, in which the testator not only assigned that land for the sustenance of the chaplain to be instituted in the said chapel, but also for the endowments of the chapel itself; for dowries ought to be unencumbered and in no way alienated, in support of which is what is read and noted in cap. 1 de censibus. Indeed, in our case the testator most strictly prohibited alienation and pledging, as appears from the aforesaid; and this prohibition is valid and operates powerfully, as is the noted text in Auth. de ali. & emph. § sanctissimas, where it is said

† that the property of the church can be alienated for the redemption of captives, unless it was given in such a manner that it cannot be alienated; and thus the testator's prohibition renders the alienation of those goods more difficult than is provided by the ius commune. And on that text the gloss in cap. verum, de cond. ap. notably says that a thing left to the church generally, not only for a dowry nor for a certain use, cannot be alienated for the necessity or utility of the church if the testator prohibited it from being alienated; and although some there insist on holding the contrary, nevertheless in our case there seems to be no doubt, because the said piece of land was left for the endowments of the chapel for a certain use in perpetuity, and thus, except by the authority of the Pope, it ought not to be transferred to another use, nor does any utility or necessity of the chapel press for its alienation—rather the complete opposite, since it would remain unendowed. Therefore its alienation could not take place except by the authority of the Pope; therefore it must be deemed impossible, and consequently the legacy made of it is not valid, even such that its estimation would be owed, as in the said l. apud Iulianum, and in the said § cum quis, and as Bar. notes in both places. Indeed, in broader terms, the gloss in c. si episcopus, 12 q. 5, and Innoc. in cap. filius, de testa., took this same view, holding that if church property is bequeathed, the legacy is not valid, nor is its estimation owed, and this on account of the difficulty that attends its alienation, as throughout the entire title de re. ecc. non alie. And although some have been unwilling there to follow the opinion of Inno. and Io., Bar. nevertheless follows it in the said l. apud Iulianum, and in the said l. continuus § cum quis. Likewise in our case, having considered the reasons of those holding the contrary, no one seems to disagree. For the argument raised is that church property can be alienated in many cases, concerning which see the gloss on 23 q. 2 in summa, and thus the alienation is not deemed impossible. But in our case this consideration ceases, because the said piece of land was bequeathed for the endowments of the chapel for a certain use and was most strictly prohibited by the testator from being alienated, and thus that difficulty of alienating is present which is discussed in the said l. apud Iulianum § si, as I said above. From this ground, therefore, it is most clearly evident that the said legacy was not valid, nor is its estimation owed. Furthermore, on another ground I say that the heir is not bound for eviction, and thus ought to be absolved from the claim of the said Lady Thomasia: because before undertaking the lawsuit she ought to have given notice of the action brought against her; but she undertook the lawsuit by contesting the suit (litis contestatio), and made the notification many days later; therefore, even assuming that the legacy were otherwise valid, yet because she did not give notice at the beginning before undertaking the lawsuit, she has no recourse for eviction against the heir; the text is singular, without quibbling over the letter, in the said l. qui concubinam § si hæres. Bar. and Cy. follow this interpretation of that text (which Dy. favored there) in l. emptor, C. de euic., and the gloss in the said l. si rem § si, ff. eodem, in the second solution, and it is a special rule in a legacy that notification be made before joinder of issue and not afterward, because the legatee sues from a lucrative cause. But where one sues from an onerous cause, relief is more readily granted to him against his predecessor in title; in which case the said l. si rem § fin. cited above for the contrary applies. For it is not the same rationale to fail to acquire gain as to lose what has been acquired or suffer losses, as in l. si sponsus § si maritus, ff. de do. inter vir. & vxor. And through these points the solution to the contrary arguments formulated above at the beginning is easily apparent. Wherefore, from all the aforesaid, I conclude that the said heir must be absolved on a twofold ground from the claim of the said Thomasia. A third point could be added, which however does not concern the merits of the case, namely, from a defect of instance: because the trial was conducted without a curator for the minor heir, from which a condemnation of the minor cannot follow, but rather absolution, as in l. non eo minus, C. de proc. and in l. 2 at the end, C. qui leg. perso. stan. in iud. non ha. And although the said heir is a cleric, since a temporal matter is at stake, he could not stand in judgment without a curator, as is proved by an argument from the special case in c. si annum, de iud. li. 6. Likewise, just as clerical status does not liberate from paternal power, as In. notes and the doctors commonly follow in the said c. indecorum, de æta. & qua. l. 3 (although the gloss less correctly took a different view there), so it does not liberate from the appointment of a curator, especially because the appointment of a curator does not operate to the prejudice of the cleric, but rather in his favor, lest he be deceived in judgment: the said l. non est minus, and l. clarum, C. de auth. præ. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If a cause is committed to be handled with all solemnity of law omitted, the party must nonetheless be cited for the reception of witnesses.
2. Prescription does not run in time of war, when it is so great in the place, and justice is not administered.
body: In the question currently pending between the commune of the land of Serziano on the one side, and the commune of the castle of Castiglioncello on the other, concerning certain boundaries, I shall briefly address two points. First, in the cause of appeal, whether the sentence rendered against the said land of Serziano is valid, or at least whether it is unjust, and consequently to be retracted. Second, which claim of those communities prevails regarding the right and ownership of those boundaries. Concerning the first, I will omit the arguments customarily made on behalf of the parties, lest I seem to have called this into doubt. For it seems to me undoubtedly to be held, if the narrated facts rely on the truth, that the said sentence has no force in itself on multiple grounds: first, because it was rendered in a church, and consequently is undoubtedly null by operation of law, as is proved in c. decet, de immu. ecc. in VI, near the end. Second, because it was rendered upon proofs that are entirely null. For the depositions upon which the commissioners based themselves do not legally subsist, since the witnesses were received without the adverse party having been cited, who ought by all means to have been cited, as in c. 2 de test. and in the Authentica de testi. § hoc autem, coll. 6, even if the cause is summary: because this concerns the defense of the party, as noted by Bartolus in the Extravagante Ad reprimendum, on the word "figura". Nay, even more remarkably the same Bartolus stated in l. filius, ff. de do.,

† that if a cause is committed to be handled with all solemnity of law omitted, the party must nonetheless be cited for the reception of witnesses: because such citation savors of defense, lest unworthy witnesses be admitted; and indeed this defense is of natural law, as in Clem. pastoralis, de re iudi., and consequently cannot be taken away even by the prince, as is found there. Therefore, the sentence is found to have been rendered without the necessary means, and is therefore null, as read and noted in c. ecclesia, de constit., and in l. prolatam, C. de sen., and 2, q. 1, c. nos in quemquam; to which supports what is read and noted in c. cum I. & A. de re iud. Third, the said sentence collapses because it was rendered without any petition, at least without one having been entered into the record, as read and noted in Clem. saepe, de ver. sig., in the gloss on the word "necessario", and by the doctors in c. 1 de lib. obl., by Baldus in the Authentica offeratur, near the end, C. de li. cont., and in the Extravagante Ad reprimendum, on the word "figura". Fourth, it collapses as having been rendered by commissioners insufficiently instructed on the merits of the cause, since they refused to receive the witnesses offered by the community of Serziano, denying the due adjournment. For even if a cause is summary, nevertheless delays must not be so shortened that the truth is concealed; but the two-day delay given by the said commissioners was not sufficient for the production of witnesses, as is presupposed to me in the fact. Whence, since they only saw the proofs of the one party and not of the other, they could not be fully instructed in the cause, as in c. dudum, II, de elec.; to which l. ult. C. si per vim vel alio modo contributes, and consequently such a sentence is null, as in c. tum ex literis and what Innocent notes there, de in integ. rest., and by Bartolus in the said l. prolatam. And even presupposing, without prejudice to the truth, that the said sentence holds: nevertheless it cannot at least be denied that it is unjust and inequitable for the aforesaid reasons, and on this account entirely to be retracted, as in c. cum ad sedem, de rest. spo., and l. per hanc, C. de temp. appel., although I firmly believe the said sentence to be supported by no strength of law. And so much for the first point. Coming to the second, I will dispatch it very briefly, since I have not seen the proofs to be made by the adverse party. For the depositions of the said witnesses furnish faith in no respect on account of the aforesaid reason, wherefore they are to be produced anew and after the party has been cited. But since the claim of the community of Serziano over the said boundaries is sufficiently founded on instruments, it is necessary that the adverse party found its claim either upon better instruments or upon witnesses basing themselves upon prescription. And a prescription of thirty years is required, as in l. ult. C. finium regun. It should be noted, however,

† that in time of war prescription does not run, when it is so great in the place that justice is not administered, as in c. ex transmissa and what is noted there, de praescript., and as noted by Bartolus in l. generaliter, ff. de usuca. The same must be said in a time of plague, since that is God's hostility, as the same Baldus notes in the said l. naturaliter. For these times ought to be deducted from the middle. For prescription sleeps during these times, as in the laws cited above. Furthermore, good faith is required even by civil law: because in a matter concerning sin one must abide by the canon and not by the civil law, as in the matter of prescription, noted by Bartolus in l. privilegia, C. de sacrosan. eccl. and by the gloss in regula possessor, de reg. iur. in VI, and is proved in c. ult. de praescri. Bad faith, moreover, is proved from conjectures in many ways, concerning which see Bartolus in l. Celsus, ff. de usuca. And especially that manner is to be observed, namely, that the common report of the neighborhood concerning the true state of the boundaries be proved. For from this the adversaries, as neighbors, are presumed to have knowledge, as noted there by Niccolò de' Tudeschi.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. How an ecclesiastical benefice is recognized, and what a benefice is. 3.
2. The nature of a thing is rather to be attended to than a simple designation. 4 Custom, or the common understanding of a place, is preferred to the proper meaning of a word.
body: Invoking the name of Christ, the legal question is asked: Whether in letters graciously granted by the Supreme Pontiff for a benefice with or without cure of souls, there is included a prestimony, which is indeed reputed locally to be an ecclesiastical benefice, yet possesses certain qualities separate from the nature of other benefices with cure. For, as is presupposed to me in the fact, such a prestimony does not require residence, nor is it subject to public burdens or other exactions, even with respect to episcopal rights, and in the place of the impetration it is reputed by common custom to be a prestimony as a species distinct from other benefices with or without cure; so that by common usage of speech, a prestimony does not come under the designation of benefices with or without cure unless it is specially named. And it seems at first that a prestimony is included in such letters, because it cannot be denied that it is an ecclesiastical benefice.

† For an ecclesiastical benefice is recognized from the part of the person providing, from the quality of the one for whom provision is made, from the quality of the benefice itself, and from the manner to be observed in the provision. The first is observed because provision cannot be made by common law except by a bishop or an ecclesiastical prelate, although presentation sometimes pertains to a layman, as in capitulum 3 de iure pat., Innocentius in capitulo quod sicut de elect. Likewise, that he who has to provide cannot retain it for himself, as in capitulum finale de insti.; what is noted in capitulo relatum de præbend. is applicable. The second is observed because provision of it cannot be made except to a cleric, as in capitulum cum adeò de rescrip., in capitulo ex literis de trans., and in capitulo 2 de institu. The third is considered because it has something of spirituality annexed to it, or to which it is annexed; whence an ecclesiastical benefice is given on account of divine service, as in capitulum finale de rescrip. libro 6, 86 distinctione, capitulo si quis sacerdotum. Likewise because it is perpetual as far as concerns him upon whom it is conferred, for this is proper to ecclesiastical benefices: 70 distinctione, capitulo sanctorum, de cleri. ægro. capitulo penultimo, noted in capitulo si gratiosè de rescrip. libro 6. The fourth is considered because one must provide to an ecclesiastical benefice purely, and without pact and condition, and not for other temporal gain, otherwise simony would be committed: 1 quæstione 2 capitulo quàm pio, and in capitulo finale de pact., de simo. capitulo consulere, along with many other chapters of the same title; nor ought there to be force in the name, since it has all the aforesaid qualities, whether it be called a benefice, an office, a possession, a prestimony, or a pension: argument from 16 quæstione 1 capitulo possessiones, and in capitulo conquerente de cle. non resi., and in capitulo saluator 1 quæstione 3, and in the said capitulo consulere. For the substance of a thing is not diversified by a diversity of names.

† For the nature of the thing must be looked to rather than the mere appellation, as in capitulo ea quæ de simo., and in lege si uno ff. loca. Therefore, since a prestimony has all the aforesaid qualities or conditions—since provision of it is made only by an ecclesiastical prelate, to an ecclesiastical person, and in perpetuity, not for a time, nor under a pact or condition, nor is it conferred for temporal gain, but on account of spirituality annexed to it, or to which it is annexed—it must therefore be deemed an ecclesiastical benefice, and consequently it must be included in a favor granted for a benefice with or without cure: regula beneficium de regu. iur. libro 6 is applicable. Hence also the general definition of a benefice fits.

† For it is a benevolent act granting joy to the recipient, in capitulo 1 ex qui. cau. feu. amit. collatione 10. In favor of the aforesaid is what is noted by Ioannes Calderinus in capitulo in nostra de rescrip., where he tacitly seems to share the aforesaid conclusion. But these notwithstanding, I think the contrary proceeds in law, taking into account the custom of the place, concerning which above. For custom,

† or the common understanding of a place, is preferred to the proper meaning of a word, as in lege cum delanionis § asinam ff. de fund. instr., and lege liberorum § quod tamen Cassius de legatis 3, and in lege Labeo de supellectile legata; what is read and noted in capitulo ex literis de sponsa. is applicable, noted by Innocentius in capitulo olim de uerborum significat., and the Glossa in capitulo nonnulli de rescrip., and Bartolus in lege omnes populi ff. de iustitia et iure. But it is of the custom of the place that under the designation of a benefice with or without cure a prestimony does not come unless it is specially named; therefore it ought not to be included in gracious letters, especially since in them a strict interpretation is to be made to suppress ambition, as in capitulo quamuis de præbendis libro 6, and capitulo si eo tempore de rescriptis eodem libro. The diversity of the name aids this conclusion, for if a prestimony were entirely the same as another benefice with or without cure, it would not have had a diverse name, as in a similar matter the text says, as noted, in lege si idem codicilli C. de condictione; the condition of the prestimony itself, quite diverse and separate from the nature of other benefices, also supports this, for if they were the same, they would not have a diverse nature: 2 quæstione 1 capitulo duo sunt genera, and in the said lege si idem; to the same purpose is what is read and noted in a similar matter in capitulo sedes de rescriptis, and especially by Innocentius in capitulo statutum de electione libro 6, where there is an excellent text in which it is said that under the designation of a parochial church, a collegiate parochial church does not come in a matter subject to restriction on account of the quality of a chapter which it has beyond the parish, which nonetheless would otherwise come where the matter was not odious, as Ioannes Andreæ notes there in the Novella. Thus, it can be notably inferred for our purpose: for since a prestimony has a diversity from other benefices (concerning which above), and also differs, and especially since the custom of the place agrees, and we are in a matter subject to restriction, it ought not to be included under the designation of a benefice with or without cure. How, moreover, the common usage of speech or of understanding is proved, is fully treated by Bartolus in the said lege Labeo de supellectile legata. And through these points an easy answer to the contraries is clear; for they proceed by looking to mere common law, and where a diversity of things would cease, so that there would be only a diversity in the name, which does not happen in our case, as is clear from the aforesaid. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a donation of all present and future goods made to a private person is valid; he holds that it is not.
2. What is not valid directly ought not to be admitted indirectly.
3. The word "pleases" does not import free will, but the arbitrament of an upright man.
4. An act performed against an oath is valid as a rule, even though the one who contravenes it is a perjurer.
casus: Augustinus and domina Chatarina, husband and wife, through a solemn stipulation fortified by an oath, as is contained in the public instrument executed concerning it, through the formal words that follow, mutually and reciprocally mortgaged to each other, and one party solemnly obligated to the other and the other to the one, all the goods of each of them, present and future, movable and immovable, rights and actions, and claims against debtors, which mortgaging and obligation should take effect and obtain force and effect between them after the death of either one of them, namely if Augustinus should survive the said domina Catherina, and not otherwise or in another manner, and thus the said goods should pass to him; and in like manner if the said domina Catherina should survive dominus Augustinus, the aforesaid goods should pass entirely to her, provision being made for funerals in contingent cases. And if legitimate and natural children should exist born of the said Augustinus and domina Catharina, male or female, one or more, the present contract should immediately vanish, and the goods should pass as the laws and statutes of Siena provide; and with the condition and pact that the said domina Chatherina, upon the occurrence of the death of the said Augustinus, should live honestly and in widowhood; and if she should act to the contrary and not maintain a widowed life, she should forfeit every right that could accrue to her by virtue of the present settlement and contract; and also with the pact and condition that the survivor should be bound to give alms for the soul of the predeceasing party discreetly, as it shall please him or her. Likewise with the pact and condition that whatever should remain after the death of the said domina Catherina as the survivor, she nevertheless observing the aforesaid, ought to pass to and belong to Angelus, the natural brother of the said Augustinus, then present and accepting for himself etc. At length it happened that the said domina Catharina and Augustinus remitted to each other this aforesaid obligation, mutually releasing each other; and the said Augustinus, when facing death, made a will and instituted the said domina Catharina, his wife, simply as heir; and upon his death, the said domina Catharina entered into another marriage. It is asked whether, because of this, the goods of the said Augustinus ought to be transferred to the said Angelus by virtue of the aforesaid settlement?
body: The protection of Christ and His mother having been humbly invoked, it seems at first that it is so. For although someone cannot bind himself through a last will so as to have a specific heir, as in l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, ff. de verbo. oblig., he can nevertheless through a stipulation irrevocably donate his goods to another: because it then passes into a contract, which is irrevocable, as the glo. notes at the end of C. de pact. Dyn. seems to have intended this same thing in reg. quod semel placuit, near the end, de reg. iu. lib. 6; Ange. de Peru. intended this same thing more clearly in his disputation which begins, in refulgenti palatio.

† where he openly holds that a donation of all present and future goods made to a private person is valid, moved principally because anyone is the lawful moderator and arbiter of his own property, l. in re mandata, C. mand. and in c. de his, de sepul. Also because that donation of all goods is prohibited by no law: for through it he is not deprived of the free capacity to make a will, since he can nonetheless donate and institute an heir, since an inheritance is a legal term [nomen iuris]; what Bar. notes in authen. ingressi, C. de sacrosanct. eccle. supports this. Likewise, through that donation made to a private person ownership is not transferred ipso facto, but delivery is required, as in l. traditionibus, C. de pact. Therefore ownership remains with that donor; and thus goods are not lacking so as to prevent him from making a will, although the heir could be compelled under penalty to make delivery. But in the present case it cannot be said that the said spouses deprived themselves of the free capacity to make a will, since no mention was made of the inheritance, but solely through a solemn stipulation they bound themselves so that the goods of the predeceasing party should pass to the survivor, and thus in effect there was a certain donation of present and future goods, which was to take effect only after death; therefore it could not be revoked to the prejudice of dom. Angelus, to whom a right had already been acquired through his presence and stipulation. Furthermore, and secondly, this was not a pure donation, since the survivor was obligated to give alms for the soul of the first to die; moreover, it seems that anyone can donate all his present and future goods to a pious cause, according to the note by Bartol. in l. fin. C. de pact. pre-alleged. Furthermore, and thirdly, there intervened here the oath of each party, which could be observed without the loss of eternal salvation; therefore at least by virtue of the oath, that donation or stipulation ought to be irrevocable. But notwithstanding these points, I think that one must by no means depart from the contrary opinion, at least in advising and judging, since the common and celebrated opinion is that such a donation is not valid: because although testamenti factio is not impeded with respect to the act of making a will, it is impeded with respect to the effect of having an heir: because no one would be found who would be willing to accept the inheritance, since all goods would have to be transferred to the donatary; to this Instit. ad leg. Fal. in

† And that which is not valid by a direct route ought not to be admitted by an oblique route. Whence, just as an ultimate judgment cannot be impeded directly through a solemn stipulation, as in said l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, so neither indirectly through a stipulation of all present and future goods, as in reg. cum quid una via, de regu. iur. lib. 6 and in c. tuae, de procu. and in l. non dubium, C. de leg.; l. Seius & Augerius, ff. ad leg. Fal. supports this. And Cyn. advised this side, that such a donation is not valid, and Bartol. follows it in said l. fin. C. de pact. and in said pre-alleged l. stipulatio and in l. si quis in princip. de leg. 3; and he relates that Dyn. advised for this side, although he wrote otherwise upon the said regu. quod semel. Bald. also followed this side in the said l. fin. and said that this opinion is common. And whatever name we assign to this contract of settlement, it could not bind irrevocably, because, as Bar. said in the pre-alleged places, there is no way of binding anyone irrevocably so that his present and future goods pass to someone during life or after death, for the aforesaid reason: because it would be against good morals. Furthermore, from other reasons as well the said Angelus cannot claim anything from the said domina Catharina by virtue of that settlement or mutual donation: because either that was a mutual donation causa mortis, and it could be revoked, l. 1, ff. de dona. cau. mor., on account of death, especially since there intervened the mutual consent of both spouses whose interest was principally at stake, as in l. nihil tam naturale, ff. de reg. iu. and in c. 1, extra eo. ti.; or it was inter vivos, and it was not valid: because between spouses donation is prohibited lest through mutual love they despoil themselves, as in ff. de don. inter virum & ux. throughout. But in our case this was occurring: because the predeceasing spouse did not have the power of disposing irrevocably of the smallest single thing, since all present and future goods were to pass to the survivor; and they certainly did this out of the mutual love by which they were held. Likewise thirdly, on another ground dom. Angelus does not have the capacity to demand anything from the said goods: because he was not called principally to that stipulation, but accessorily, and rather in favor of the said contracting parties than his own; which is clear from this, that mention of him was only made with respect to the goods which would remain after the death of the said domina Catharina by virtue of that settlement, that they should pass to Angelus himself; nor was it even said that they should pass unconditionally, but with the burden that from them he should make alms as it should please him. Wherefore, since nothing has passed to the said domina Catherine by virtue of that settlement, because she possesses by virtue of the last will and not by virtue of the settlement, or stipulation, or mutual donation, since they had departed from it of their own accord; therefore he cannot claim anything: because when the principal ceases, the accessory ceases, de regu. iur. lib. 6, capitulo accessorium. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that they could not depart from it to the prejudice of dom. Angelus: because, as I have said, Angelus was called accessorily to the validity of the said settlement or donation: because when the mutual consent ceases, the disposition conceived in his favor ceases, by the argument of those things which are read and noted in l. si cum Cornelius and l. vero procuratori, ff. de solu. And what I said above supports this excellently: because dom. Angelus was to make alms from those goods for the souls of those spouses, and thus he was adjoined principally in their favor. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that he was bound to make alms as it pleased him. For to this I respond,

† that the word "pleases" [placet] does not imply free will, but the arbitrament of a good man, as is the text noted in l. Thais § sororem, ff. de fideicom. lib., noted by Barto. in extravaganti, ad reprimen. And through these points I conclude that the said settlement, or mutual donation, or stipulation was not valid from the beginning; and, granted without prejudice to the truth that it had been valid, it could be revoked by the mutual consent of the spouses, notwithstanding the absence of dom. Angelus, and consequently the said Angelus or his heir cannot now claim anything by virtue of that settlement. The contrary points formulated above for the other side do not stand in the way: because the argument from things that commonly happen is valid, as in capitulo 1, de cler. non resi. and l. neque natales, C. de proba.; but it commonly happens that, once a donation of all present and future goods is made to another, no one would wish in vain to be an heir. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that everyone is the lawful moderator and arbiter of his own property: because this is true unless he disposes contrary to good morals, because it is in the public interest that no one use his property badly, as in § sed hoc ipse, Instit. de his, qui sunt sui vel alie. iur. and in § cogitatio, in Auth. ut iud. sine quoquo suffra. The second point does not stand in the way, for a double reason. First, because not all goods were disposed for pious causes, but principally they donated all goods mutually to one another, with the burden, however, that the survivor should distribute and make alms as should please him, and thus the principal effect of the donation was directed toward a private person. But it can be answered that even to pious causes a donation of all present and future goods is not valid, since a person remains sui iuris without the ownership of any goods, as Angelus maintained in the said disputation, at least in our case, in which the goods were not conferred upon a church, but there was only imposed the burden of making alms at pleasure; and thus the reasons of Bar. in the said auth. ingressi cease. To that which is objected concerning the oath, it can be answered in a twofold manner. First,

† that an act performed against an oath is regularly valid, although the one contravening it is a perjurer, as in c. sicut, de spons., noted by Inn. in c. dilectos, de praeben.; and Io. An. in reg. quod semel placuit, de reg. iu. li. 6, in Mercurialibus expressly said that if someone swears not to change a will, he can change it notwithstanding the oath, although he incurs perjury. Secondly, it can be answered that since that oath is against good morals, it could not bind the swearers, as in reg. non est obligatorium, de reg. iu. li. 6; moreover, it is against good morals that someone should lose, at least indirectly, the free capacity to make a will, or the supreme judgment, as in said l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta. And this last point was held by Bar. in said l. stipulatio and said l. si quis in prin., ff. de leg. 3, and in l. Seius & Augerius, ff. ad legem fal. And let these things suffice. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A judgment rendered against a debtor who has knowledge prejudices a creditor who knows and remains silent, although nothing was notified to him.
2. One who is bound to the defense of another is not bound to offer himself to the suit, even though he knows that it has been initiated, but notice must be given to him.
3. One who promises to assist or defend another is not bound to fulfill the promise, however much he knows that the other needs help, unless he has been requested.
body: Invoking the aid of the Savior. In the question which is turned, or is expected soon to be turned, between Antonio del Vigna and his former partners on the one part, and certain Florentine citizens claiming to be their creditors on the other, it seems at first that the said creditors have justice on their side against the said Antonio and his partners: because the said Antonio and partners promised two things to the said creditors, namely to pay them ten shillings per pound of the entire debt; likewise that, as to the said ten shillings to be paid to them, they were bound to protect them against every other creditor of whatever partnership who at any time might demand anything or in any way molest the said creditors. However, although Antonio and his partners observed the first obligation, because they satisfied them regarding the said ten shillings, they nevertheless did not observe the second, since they did not keep them indemnified regarding the said ten shillings, when they were compelled by a judgment to restore half to those merchants who, by virtue of reprisals granted in the City [Rome], were compelled to pay the creditors of the said Antonio and his partners living in the City; to this point is what is read and noted in l. nam et Servius, ff. de neg. gest., and l. licet, ff. nau. cau. stab., and l. qui sic solvit, ff. de solu. Nor does it stand in the way if it be said that no notice [denunciatio] was given to the said Antonio and his partners to defend them against those merchants, because from the moment they knew that a suit had been commenced, there was no need for another notice; for he who is certain does not need to be further certified: l. 1, ff. de act. emp., and in reg. qui certus, de reg. iu. lib. 6; relevant is what is read and noted on a similar point in l. si superatus, ff. de pig., and in l. saepe, ff. de re iud.,

† where it is read and noted that a judgment rendered against a debtor who has knowledge prejudices a creditor who knows and remains silent, even though nothing was formally notified to him; and so conversely in the case of a judgment rendered against a debtor, so that it prejudices a debtor who has knowledge. For without any notification he ought of his own accord to appear and defend the case; so it should be said in the present matter. Furthermore, and secondly, the said Florentine merchants were detained and subjected to exactment on account of the reprisals granted in the City to the prejudice of Antonio and his partners; therefore, returning to Florence, they could lawfully have recourse against them: an argument from l. si merces, § culpae, ff. loca., which Bart. openly seems to hold, although he does not strongly confirm it, in l. 2, in fi., ff. de verbo. obli. In vain, therefore, is it alleged that the suit was not notified to the said Antonio and his partners, since in any event they were liable and would have been condemned. For presence is required for the sake of the defense that might have been available, but in our case no defense was available; therefore, the lack of notification ought not to relieve them; to this effect is what is noted by Bald. in l. res iudicata, C. quibus res iudi. non nocet. Thirdly, I cite l. fi., C. de bonis autho. iudi. possiden., and l. cum unus, eod. titu., in which laws it is clear that when one of the creditors is put into possession by the praetor, all are deemed to have been put into possession; so that others may use the benefit of the putting into possession. Since, therefore, by the benefit of the syndics the Florentine creditors obtained the goods of the said Antonio and his partners, the creditors of the City, or the merchants in their name, were able to act directly against those creditors by demanding their share; nor was there need to notify the said Antonio and his partners, because goods already transferred to the said creditors were being sought, and the action being brought was not a personal action, nor another which at least secondarily was directed against Antonio himself and his partners. It cannot, therefore, be said that those Florentine creditors who made the settlement had their full ten, since, as I have said, by the disposition of law and the judge, the other creditors of the City concurred in their share. Fourthly, it makes against the said Antonio and his partners that Doffo, one of the partners, intervened in the settlement made at Rome with the creditors residing at Rome and approved it; therefore, the others were bound to its observance; to this effect is what is read and noted in l. 1, ff. de exerci., and l. eadem, ff. de duo. reis, and by Bald. in tracta. de constitu. But notwithstanding these points, I deem the contrary opinion to prevail in our case. Several reasons move me toward this opinion. And first, it cannot be denied that the said Antonio and his partners fulfilled the first part of the promise: since they satisfied the said creditors at ten per pound according to the settlement; nor is this called into doubt. It remains therefore to be seen whether they fulfilled the second part of the promise, namely in so far as they promised to protect those creditors in those ten shillings per pound against any other creditor; in the elucidation of which it is necessary to investigate what those words signify, namely that they will protect them, etc. And indeed those words can at first glance have three meanings, just as on a similar question is noted by Barto. in l. stipulatio ista, in principio, ff. de verbo. obligat., on the question of one who promised to defend a buyer against every person de jure and de facto. For those words can be understood in three ways. First, as meaning if a dispute is brought in court and eviction occurs de jure or de facto. In the second way it is understood de facto: namely that in court he do those things which are of fact, such as appearing before the judge's tribunal, producing witnesses, paying expenses, and the like. In the third way they can be understood de jure and de facto, that is, resisting with an armed hand and recovering. This last way, however, because it does not arise from the nature of the contract, does not please Barto., so that these words should be reduced to this sense—to this is the good text in l. fin., C. de act. emptio. et vendi.—but rather to the preceding ways. So we can say in our case, where he promised less, namely that those words are not to be understood as protecting them de facto in those ten shillings, but rather by defending them in court, or assisting them. And it is certain that

† he who is bound to the defense of another is not bound to present himself for the litigation, even though he knows that it has been commenced, but it is necessary that it be notified to him, as we say in the case of a seller who is bound to defend a buyer; nor is it imputed to him if he knew that the suit was commenced and did not defend him, if it was not notified to him; for in this case notification is required, not for the purpose of inducing simple knowledge, but for the act of deploying the defense, as noted by Specu. in tit. de empt. et vend. in fin., and this is followed there by Joan. And. in addi., and by Barto. in l. denunciasse, ff. de adulteriis, and in l. emptor, C. de evict., and the Moderns commonly follow this in cap. fi. de empt. et vend. For the buyer, perhaps confident in his own right and the skill of his person, does not care to notify the seller, and consequently the seller is not bound to go, since the buyer does not request him. So to the present matter, the creditors here could trust in their right and the skill of their persons; therefore they did not care to call upon Antonio and his partners, who promised to protect them against any creditor. Therefore, the latter were not bound to go spontaneously either. Thus they did not act contrary to their promise. For they were bound to protect and defend them, namely if they had been requested; it must therefore be imputed to those creditors who did not make the due request and notification. In addition to others, I cite for this a good text in c. 1, de nova fidei forma, col. fi., where it seems to be proved
† that one who promises

† to help or defend another is not bound to fulfill the promise, however much he knows that the other needs help, unless he has been requested; and Bald. says there that that text is to be kept in mind for this purpose. To the same point makes what is read and noted in cap. brevi, de iureiu. Secondly and principally, I am moved by this: wherever someone has been unjustly subjected to exactment on account of another, he has no recourse against him to whose prejudice he was subjected to exactment, if the latter's act was not ordained for that purpose; to this is the notable gloss which Barto. follows and notes in l. nam et Servius, 1. responso, ff. de nego. gest.; the gloss on l. si quis dolo, § 1, ff. de re iud., serves very well. But in our case those Florentine merchants were unjustly subjected to exactment and detained, because the reprisals were not justly granted. For perhaps the Pope granted them upon the false suggestion of another. For, as is assumed for me in fact, the Florentine officials, when requested concerning the satisfaction to be made to the merchants of the City, replied that they were ready to render justice, and without it being demanded otherwise, the reprisals were granted; which by law cannot be done. For reprisals are odious and are to be granted only in defect of justice, as is read and noted in capit. uno, de iniu. lib. 6, and 23, quaest. 2, cap. dominus; by Innoc. in cap. dilectus, de app.; Joan. And. on the reg. non est sine culpa, de reg. iur. lib. 6, in Merc.; and more broadly by Barto. in the treatise on reprisals, where among other things he requires for their justice that first the ordinary judge must be requested to render justice, and if he refuses, the superior, and finally in defect of the superior, a foreign judge and lord can grant reprisals. But in our case it is not established that justice was denied; rather, the contrary is established by the reply of the officials. Likewise by the reply of the Florentine Signoria, insofar as it was provided that if foreigners were unwilling to abide by the settlement made with the Florentine creditors, justice would be done to them according to the imperial laws; therefore, the said merchants had no recourse against the said Antonio and his partners, or against the Florentine merchants. Therefore the said creditors were unjustly condemned; therefore it must be imputed to them, both because they did not notify Antonio and his partners, and because they were condemned through an injustice; to this effect in l. si per imprudentiam, ff. de evic., and the said l. emptor, C. eod. titu., and capitulo fi. de empt. et vend. Thirdly and principally it is relevant that on another ground the said merchants who had been subjected to exactment in the City had no action against the Florentine creditors. For they had received those ten per pound either under color of a judgment by the hands of the syndics, or by virtue of the settlement made with the debtors; in which cases, since ownership had passed directly to them, they could not be disturbed by other creditors who did not possess a prior hypothec, but only a personal action or a subsequent hypothec, as is fully noted by Bart. in the said l. cum unus, ff. de bo. auth. iud. poss., and in l. a divo Pio, ff. de re iud.; whence in those cases the laws cited above do not apply, namely l. fi., C. de bo. auct. iud. poss., and the said l. cum unus, because they speak only of a praetorian pledge, but not of a payment made by the creditors themselves, or of things given under color of a judgment, as Barto. held, and rightly so, in the places pre-alleged. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that by virtue of the provision of the Florentine Signoria the foreigners ought to concur in the execution of that settlement: because I answer that the provision was made toward foreigners subject to two concurrent conditions: first, that they consented to this settlement; second, if they were willing to contribute the goods existing in the Roman partnership. But if the creditors themselves, when requested, were unwilling to consent, nor to contribute the goods, they therefore remained under the other peril of the reform and provision, namely that right should be done to them according to the Imperial laws. For once one way has been chosen, one cannot return to another: l. si cui, ff. de servi.; relevant are l. quod in haeredem, § eligere, ff. de tribu., and cap. ut quis duas, de elect. libr. 6. And by this what is objected by the said creditors can be removed, namely, that the officials or syndics did not observe the form of the statute in distributing. For this is beside the point. For the settlement was made with the creditors so that they should have ten per pound; and the Florentine Signoria ordained that if the foreign creditors were unwilling to acquiesce in the settlement or to contribute goods, right should be done to them according to the Imperial laws. Whence, they being unwilling, the Florentines alone could lawfully be satisfied by virtue of the settlement. Likewise the statute speaks of a settlement not intervening between the payer and the creditors. But in our case a settlement did intervene, and by virtue of the settlement the payment of ten shillings per pound was made; whence that payment drew its force rather from the act of the parties approved and confirmed by the Florentine Signoria than from the form of any statute. Nor could the said foreign creditors avail themselves of the form of the settlement since they challenged it from the beginning: in the regu. ex eodem, de regu. iu. lib. 6. Wherefore, from all the aforesaid, I conclude that the said creditors do not have recourse against Antonio and his partners by virtue of the settlement not being kept: because, as appears from the aforesaid, they kept it so far as in them lay. The arguments formed above do not stand in the way. And first, it was sufficiently answered to what is said regarding knowledge: because knowledge is not sufficient in this case, but notification is required, and especially because it must be imputed to those creditors who did not appeal from that unjust judgment. Nor does l. saepe stand in the way, with similar laws, because that proceeds when an action or defense belonged to me in the first place, and I suffered the next person to act, or when the matter concerned my property principally. But in our case the action or defense pertained in the first place to the creditors themselves, since the ownership of the money paid had passed to them completely and simply; and thus it concerned their own property, and the defense belonged in the first place and principally to them. But Antonio and his partners were only bound to protect and defend them in those things, just as similarly when an action is brought against a buyer. For a real action is directed against the possessor, but the seller only has to assist the buyer and defend him, as in l. 1, C. ubi in rem act. The second does not stand in the way. For I say that it proceeds when reprisals were justly granted. Indeed, even if it were justly doubted whether the person subjected to exactment could act against the principal debtor, since reprisals are granted on account of the act of the lord unwilling to do justice, and not on account of the act of the debtor not answering. And therefore Bar. in tra. represaliarum near the end, where he better examined this matter, said that this person subjected to exactment ought to demand that actions be assigned to him against the debtor, and thus afterwards act by virtue of them; and to that treatise Bart. refers himself in the said l. nam et Servius. But in our case this was omitted: both because no assignment of actions is apparent, and because no action was brought against the debtors, namely Antonio and his partners, but against the creditors, against whom no action was available, nor were the reprisals granted on account of prejudice to them. Nor is it true that in any event they would have succumbed: for I deny this. For that payment made to the creditors would not have been revoked, but they might have agreed with them otherwise. To the third argument, it was sufficiently answered above. To the fourth and last, it is answered that Doffo had ceased to be a partner at the time of that approval, since all had departed from the market [cessissent foro]; and thus he could not prejudice the others by his act, as in l. 1, C. de transact., and C. res inter alios acta, throughout. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Brothers and sisters are excluded from the succession to incestuous siblings.
2. Under civil law a father cannot give anything to spurious and incestuous children.
3. Just as a brother is bound to maintain an indigent sister, so he is bound to endow her.
4. Where the subject matter is not proportionate except to children, under the designation of heirs only children are included.
body: Having besought the aid of Almighty God, it seems firstly that the said Ser Ioannes ought to succeed to the said Domina Constantia, his wife, because, in the absence of legitimate or natural succession, a husband succeeds to his wife ab intestato, as in l. unica, C. unde uir & uxo. But in our case legitimate or natural succession was lacking, because the said Constantia was born of an incestuous and damnable union, and consequently could not be called natural; whence parents do not succeed to her, nor she to her parents. For such persons are unworthy of every legal benefit, as in authen. qui. mo. natu. effi. leg. §. fin., where this appears to be proved. What Barto. noted in authen. si qua illustris, C. ad Orficia., and l. si gener, ff. de his quibus ut indi., supports this. Nor can it be said that the said sister, Domina Gratiosa, must of necessity succeed to her on the same ground; because, as I said before, since these women were born of an incestuous intercourse, they cannot be called agnates or cognates among themselves, since they do not deserve to be called children, as is held in the said authen., 35. quæstio. 7. in cap. unico; and that such persons do not succeed among themselves was the opinion of Din. in his tractate de succes. ab inte., and I have seen the opinion of a solemn doctor on this, which supports it.

† For if the father and mother are excluded from the succession of such children because such persons ought not to be named children, with greater reason brothers and sisters ought to be excluded, since they are not called connected, or agnates, or cognates except by reason of the persons of the parents; to this effect is what the singular gloss wished in l. 2. ff. unde cogna. in a similar case. Thirdly, the said Ser Ioannes, the husband, ought to have succeeded, since in this case all legitimate or natural succession ceases. But notwithstanding these points, I consider that the said Ser Laurentius, the father of the said Constantia, lawfully brought back into his hands the said property given in dowry to the said Constantia, because to him as father, and not to Ser Ioannes as husband, that property was to devolve. I am moved principally,

† because under civil law a father cannot donate anything to spurious and incestuous children. For they are unworthy of any paternal estate, as in authen. ex complexu, C. de incest. nup. Under canon law, however, it was introduced out of natural equity that they ought to be maintained, as in c. cum haberet, de eo, qui duxit in matrimonium. And by that text Bar. said notably in the said authen. ex complexu, and l. si gener, that by reason of alimony a father can leave something to such incestuous children. Likewise, he can endow daughters, because since the cause of dowry is no less favorable than the cause of alimony, a father can endow just as he may provide alimony; what Cy. similarly noted in l. non ex omni, C. de admini. tut. supports this,

† where he says that just as a brother is bound to maintain a destitute sister, as in l. cum in plures, ff. de admini. tuto., so he is bound to endow her. Therefore the said Ser Laurentius was able legally to endow the said Constantia, his incestuous daughter, but upon her death without children, the dowry ought to return to him, because the dowry in this case takes the place of the alimony to which the father was bound. Therefore, she being dead, the cause of alimony ceased, and accordingly that property ought to return to the father. For the said Ser Laurentius could not, even if he had expressly wished, have donated the said property to the incestuous daughter according to the aforesaid laws: but he was only able to donate it during the life of Constantia herself by reason of alimony; he could, however, have donated it to her during her life, and after her death to her children, if any were to be. For a grandfather can indeed donate to the children of an incestuous daughter, as in l. fi. C. de nat. lib. And this was noted by Bal. in the said l. si gener, where he adopts the aforesaid view quite plainly. And therefore in our case the said Ser Laurentius could rightly stipulate that, upon the dissolution of the marriage, the dowry should be restored to Constantia or her heirs. For those words ought to be understood as meaning that it should be restored to Constantia during her life on account of alimony. Under the designation of 'heirs', however, only the children of Constantia herself are understood in this case:

† because where the subject-matter is not adaptable except to children, only children come under the designation of heirs, as noted in l. Gallus, ff. de lib. & posthu. Therefore, no children of the said Constantia being in existence, that property ought to be returned to the said Ser Laurentius, from whom it had originated. The contrary arguments formulated above do not stand in the way. For they would proceed if those dotal goods had not originated from the father, but had been acquired by the said Constantia from elsewhere; for then I would quite believe the husband was to be preferred. But in our case they ought to return to the father, not by right of succession, but by right of reversion and because the cause has ceased: because, as I said, upon her death the cause of alimony ceased. Moreover, the mother or sister can claim nothing: both because they are not to be called agnates or cognates for the aforesaid reason, and because the said Constantia could not have that property except during her life. And from the aforesaid it is inferred that the said Ser Laurentius could alienate the said property to another; and he to whom the alienation was made could donate it to a hospital, because everyone is the lawful governor and arbiter of his own property, especially in donating to churches and hospitals, as in l. j.
