C. de sacr. san. eccle. and l. in re mandata, C. manda. and in c. de his, de sepul. And let these things suffice to the praise and glory of Almighty God. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The whole world is the territory of the emperor.
2. When confiscation of goods is made simply, it is understood of present goods, not of those to be acquired in the future.
3. In doubt, interpretation must always be made against him who founds his claim on an agreement.
4. Jurisdiction prorogated through fear collapses by operation of law.
5. Departure from the common law is odious.
body: Having implored the aid of the Savior, for the clarification of that dispute—whether a townsman of the land of Scarlino could lawfully be arrested in the said land of Scarlino by an official of the salt customs of the land of Piombino, to the effect that he be punished and judged in the said land of Piombino by the officials deputed over salt by the magnificent Lord Gherardo, lord of Piombino—it must principally be investigated what power the said lord of Piombino has in the land or commune of Scarlino. For if that land was merely commended to the said lord, and mere and mixed imperium was not otherwise transferred to him, then the question does not present so much doubt; because although one castle or city is commended to another, the people of such a land does not thereby cease to be free as before, even if it pays a mantle or something similar in sign of superiority to him to whom it commended itself, as, for instance, if it chooses a podestà from its own land, as happened there in our case, as noted by Bart. in l. non dubium, ff. de capti. For by such commendation he is seen to receive them under his protection, namely, that he protect and defend them, by which act jurisdiction is not granted, nor is anything subtracted from the right of anyone, as noted fully by Bar. in l. j. C. de excu. mu. li. x., where he held further that even if it is committed to protection and governance, mere or mixed imperium is not thereby transferred, on the argument of that law, although this last point is more doubtful on account of that word 'governance' (which I do not care to investigate further, since this last point does not pertain to our proposition, but rather the first, concerning which see also Bar. in proœ. fforum, in versi. item dicitur; to the same effect is what is read and noted in c. recepimus, and c. ex parte tua, de priuile.). And this being presupposed, the doubt of the present question arises from the tenor of that agreement entered into after the said commendation between the said lord and the commune of Scarlino, in that, among other things relevant to the matter at hand, it was solemnly agreed and established between them that the said commune and men of Scarlino cannot or ought not henceforth in the future at any time or in any manner have, receive, or buy other salt from any other person, commune, place, or corporation in any other land or place, except from the magnificent lord himself and the salt of the magnificent lord himself, under and upon the penalty contained in the statutes and ordinances of the said magnificent lord disposing in any way concerning the said matter or topic of salt, etc. It is certain, however, that since the land of Scarlino was free, recognizing no one as its lord, it could in this and in other matters subject itself to the jurisdiction and statutes of the said lord, according to what is noted by Bal. in l. decernimus, C. de sac. san. eccle., and by Bar. in tract. de tyranno. But in the statutes of the said lord speaking of this matter, it is disposed, among other things, that the present and future officials of the salt customs may punish, condemn, or fine pecuniarily or materially, according to their discretion, as it shall seem discreet to them, etc., all and singular persons selling or buying salt in any way to the detriment of the salt customs of the magnificent lord himself, and any others culpable in any way regarding the matter of salt; therefore, the said townsman of the land of Scarlino could be arrested in the land of Scarlino to be punished by the said officials. Which penalty is to be imposed according to the discretion of the said officials, for otherwise the statute of the said lord disposing in this matter would not be observed, since that statute does not precisely impose a certain penalty, but disposes that it be imposed at their discretion; the whole must therefore be observed, since it is a single qualified fact, on the argument in l. in delictis, § si detracta, ff. de noxa, and in c. fin. de restitu. spolia., and what is noted in a similar matter by Barto. in l. Aurelius, § idem quæsijt, ff. de libe. lega., and in l. si quidem, C. de except., and by Ioan. And. in c. 1. de confes. lib. 6. And the words of that agreement strongly urge this interpretation, when it says, 'disposing in any way,' etc. In whatever manner, therefore, the statute disposes concerning the penalty, it must be observed, l. j. ff. de pact. If, on the other hand, all manner of jurisdiction regarding the said land of Scarlino was transferred to the said lord of Piombino, then the case seems clearer in favor of the intention of the officials, because although the territories are distinct in respect of the officials of each land, nevertheless, in respect of the lord of both territories, it can be called one territory.

† A similar point is evident in the Emperor, who, although he divided territories by provinces and diverse governments and prohibited one from violating the territory of another, C. ubi de crimi. agi opor. throughout, joined with auth. qua in prouincia, under the same title, and authen. de defen. ciui., and in auth. ut nul. iudi., and ff. de offic. præsi. throughout, especially in l. ij. with many similar texts; whence the Emperor himself can bind anyone throughout the entire world, because the whole world is to him one territory; hence he is called lord of the world, l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadri. præscriptio., and l. deprecatio, ff. ad leg. Rhod. de iac., and more clearly to the point it is proved in clemen. pastoralis, de re iudi.; whence in him that saying has place: 'where I find you, there I will judge you,' as noted in c. fin. de foro competen. and in l. ij. C. ubi de crimi. agi opor. Similarly in the Pope with respect to spiritual matters, as in c. cuncta per mundum, and c. per principalem, ix. quæstio. iij. And in a bishop with respect to his diocese, such that he can sit on the tribunal in any part of it and judge concerning the business of the whole diocese, as in c. cum episcopus, de offi. ordi. lib. 6. And in a legate having several provinces under him, for he can judge in one province concerning an act of another, because he does not exceed the limits of his jurisdiction, as in cap. nouit, de offi. leg. Let us say the same in our case: for although by pact the land of Scarlino has a podestà, and thus mere and mixed imperium, it is not thereby prevented that the lord himself may, through himself or his officials, take cognizance of certain cases in the land of Piombino, even concerning acts done in the land of Scarlino, since with respect to him it must be deemed a single territory. Similarly we see in the Pope, who in matters of faith deputes inquisitors throughout the whole of Christendom so that they may exercise jurisdiction against heretics, although bishops are not permitted to do so outside their dioceses; and the said inquisitors can order those suspected in a matter of faith to be arrested and brought to the said places to be punished by them, as in c. inquisitionis, de hære. li. 6. And this seems especially to be said in our case, in which a special pact, concerning which see above, concurs together with universal jurisdiction. But these things notwithstanding, I deem the contrary opinion in our case to be truer. And first, if we hold, as is presupposed to me in fact, that the said land of Scarlino is merely commended to the said lord, the case seems clear enough to me, because jurisdiction ceases in the said land and over its inhabitants, as I said above in the beginning. Whence it only remains to remove the obstacle of the said convention or pact. To which I reply in multiple ways: first, that in the pact the said land did not subject itself to his statutes enacted and to be enacted, but simply bound itself to the penalty contained in the statutes of the said lord. But where someone binds himself indefinitely to statutes, and it is a matter of grave prejudice, it is not understood of statutes to be enacted in the future, but only of those enacted and existing at the time of the obligation; this is the noted doctrine of Bar. in l. si stipulatus, § cum stipulamur, ff. de uer. ob., for which the text in c. pe. de iu. makes excellently, and Hos. openly holds there, and the text makes similarly in l. si mandauero, § is cuius, ff. man., where it says,

† that upon a confiscation of goods simply made, it is understood of present goods, not however of those to be acquired in the future, with which the text in capitu. fœlicis, § uerum, de pœ. lib. 6. agrees; it is otherwise where a matter of slight prejudice is concerned. For then, under the appellation of goods, both present and future goods are included, as in l. si, C. quæ res pig. obl. pos.; which laws are commonly reconciled through the distinction just made. The same is to be said in our case; for since this is a matter of the gravest prejudice—if the men of the land of Scarlino could be seized from the said land and led away to be punished by foreign officials in the land of Piombino, and thus that their territory be violated—that pact ought not to be understood of statutes to be enacted, but of those already enacted. Since, therefore, that reform of the lord of Piombino—that those officials take cognizance and punish, etc.—supervened after that pact, it does not claim a place for itself against the men of Scarlino. And we are in a matter in which strict interpretation must be made, as in reg. odia, and in reg. in pœnis, de re. iu. li. 6., and in l. interpretatione, and l. si præses, ff. de pœnis; and l. quicquid astringendæ, ff. de uer. obl. makes excellently, and still better makes l. ueteribus, with its subject matter, ff. de pac., where among other things Bar. notes

† that in doubt, interpretation must always be made against him who founds his claim upon a pact, because he must clearly prove the pact, since he founds himself upon it, as in l. non nudis, and l. non epistolis, and l. neque natales, and l. matrem, C. de prob. But in our case the lord, or the officials of the salt customs, found their claim upon that pact; therefore in doubt interpretation must be made against them, and a doubtful proof does not relieve the one bearing the burden of proof, as in c. in praesentia, de prob. Furthermore, presupposing without prejudice to truth, and not conceding, that that pact were extended to statutes to be enacted thereafter, nonetheless it does not follow that a townsman of Scarlino committing fraud regarding the salt customs could be seized from the said land and led to the land of Piombino, because the pact was made solely with respect to the penalty, but not with respect to a foreign judge. For they bound themselves to the penalty contained in the statutes, and therefore it is enough that he be punished with the penalty contained in the statutes of the said lord, but it ought not to be interpreted so harshly that through this the territory of the said land of Scarlino could also be violated. For pacts must be understood strictly, especially when they deviate from the disposition of the common law, d. l. quicquid astringendæ, ff. de uer. obliga., and d. l. ueteribus, and l. si unus, § ante omnia, ff. de pact. makes excellently, where it is said that a pact made in one matter does not harm in another; especially in our case this must be observed, where it is a matter of proroguing the jurisdiction of another judge with the violation of another territory, for a clear and free consent is required.

† Hence it is that where acts performed through fear are regularly valid, jurisdiction prorogued through fear nevertheless collapses ipso iure: because, as I said, in such consent a free and clear consent is required, as in l. 2. ff. de iud.; and interpretation must be made against the lord, because he ought to have stated the law and the pact more openly, as in the said laws; for an interpretation ought not to be made through which many laws would be derogated from, as is read and noted in l. si quando, C. de inoffi. testam.

† for every departure from the common law is odious and strictly to be interpreted, as in capitu. 1. & 2. de filiis præsb. lib. 6. Hence it is that statutes are to be understood strictly, so that the common law is harmed as little as possible through them, as in capitu. cum dilectus, de consuetu., and l. 2. C. de noxa, through Innocent in capitu. causam, de resc., and Bar. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iure. And most especially in our case a strict interpretation ought to be made, lest the general pact previously made—that the land of Scarlino have its own podestà and mere and mixed imperium of itself—be harmed, by the argument in l. non ad ea, ff. de condict. & demonstra.; capit. ueniens, de præscrip. is to the point. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the contrary interpretation conforms to the common law, since by reason of a delict a remission must be made to the place of the delict, as in Auth. ut nul. iudi. § si quis uerò comprehensorum, and in clem. pastoralis, de re iudica. For to this I respond in two ways: first, that this delict was not committed in the territory of Piombino, although on account of the pact entered into with the land of Scarlino he defrauded the tax or customs of the salt of the land of Piombino, and therefore there is no place for remission. For although someone offends against the property of some place, from the fact that he offends outside the territory of that place, he cannot be sued by reason of the delict in that place, as noted by the doctors in c. postulasti, de foro competen., and Barto. in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. trini. Furthermore, presupposing that the delict had been committed in the territory of Piombino, nevertheless remission today has been abolished by contrary custom, which is valid, since the delict can be punished in the place of domicile, as noted by Ioan. Andr. in capitu. primo. de rapt. If, however, it be presupposed that the lords of Piombino have jurisdiction in the land of Scarlino, then although the case is more doubtful, I would nonetheless think that the same conclusion I stated just above must be reached: namely, that the said capture could not be made, nor do the officials of the customs have jurisdiction against him. I am moved principally because the said land of Scarlino willed by pact to have mere and mixed imperium in the said land, and its own official who was to exercise jurisdiction, which pact must by all means be observed. Nor can it be violated by the lord of Piombino, even if he has jurisdiction there, because even the prince is bound by a contract, even one entered into with a subject, as in capitu. primo. de pact.; and especially in our case, in which at the time of the pact the said land of Scarlino was entirely in its own liberty; to this effect is what is read and noted, especially by Bartol. in l. pen. ff. de decre. ab ordi. facien.; and a pact entered into with a lord has the force of law with respect to subjects, as in l. cæsar, ff. de publ., and l. pen. C. de do. inter ui. & ux. For if in the matter of salt he could draw subjects from there and transfer jurisdiction to other officials of the land of Piombino, he could by the same token do so in another case; and thus he could take away mere and mixed imperium from the said land of Scarlino, which is not to be said according to the above. For Inno. makes this argument in a similar question in c. cum uenerabilis, de censi. For by virtue of the pact, cognizance must be taken there concerning all things that are committed there, or by its own citizens elsewhere; otherwise, however, the said pact could be annihilated; and by this is rebutted what I said concerning the Emperor and the Pope, for they distinguished territories by their own laws, by which they are not bound, l. princeps, ff. de legib., and cap. proposuit, de concessio. præben., and only with respect to their officials, not however with respect to their power; therefore in their case there is no distinction of territory, as I said above, but it is otherwise in our case. For the lord of Piombino is not the natural lord of the land of Scarlino, and by pact the said land has the right to elect for itself a podestà who takes cognizance in civil and criminal matters; he cannot, therefore, violate the territory of that land for the aforesaid reasons. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a municipal statute providing that all instruments from a certain sum upward must be registered in the archive of the commune, and if it be done otherwise, such instrument is of no validity and efficacy, nor can anything be claimed under it, etc., extends to foreigners contracting in the place of the statute and causing an instrument to be drawn up there, etc.; this doubt extends up to number 6.
2. The statutes of a city cannot qualify or disqualify foreigners.
3. Wills ought to be registered according to the laws and customs of the places in which they are registered.
4. A statute by which it is provided that a will executed before three witnesses is valid extends its force with respect to foreigners staying there.
5. A statute disposing upon the registration of wills or instruments extends to churches and ecclesiastical persons.
6. Whether a statute of a city extends to the whole county of the city.
7. When citizens are condemned, inhabitants of the county are deemed condemned, unless something else appears from the disposition of the words.
body: In the question of Raynerius de Tuscanis, after invoking the aid of the divine name, three points will remain to be examined. First:

† Whether a municipal statute providing that all legal instruments from a certain sum upward must be registered in the communal archive, and that if it be done otherwise, such an instrument is of no validity and efficacy, nor can anything be claimed under it, extends to foreigners contracting in the place of the statute and causing an instrument to be drawn up there, to the extent that the instrument drawn up between them there is ipso facto void if it has not been registered as contained in the statute. Second, presupposing that such a statute extends to foreigners in the aforesaid manner, whether the said statute concerns all places and castles of the county of the city in which the said statute is in force, such that if an instrument executed in the county is not registered in the aforesaid manner, it is void. Third, whether, upon inspection of the acts and allegations in the said case, it is sufficiently proved that the castle in which the said instrument is said to have been executed belongs to the county of that city in which the statute is in force. I come to the first. And it seems at first that such a statute does not extend to foreigners, because such a statute is called the proper law of the legislators themselves, as in c. ius civile, 1 distinctio; nor can it concern non-subjects due to a defect of power, as in l. omnes populi, ff. de iustitia et iure, and what is read and noted in l. cunctos populos, C. de summa trini., and l. si non speciali, C. de testa., and c. ecclesia Sanctae Mariae, de consti., and what is read and noted in c. a nobis, bis, 1: de sen. excom., with similar texts. Hence Bar. and Bald. explicitly said in the said l. cunctos populos,

† that the statutes of a city cannot qualify or disqualify foreigners, even in the land of the legislators; whence they conclude that if a statute provides that a filiusfamilias may make a will, or that he cannot bind himself, or that one cannot leave anything to one's wife, such statutes do not extend to foreigners, even if they wish to make a will, or bind themselves, or leave something to a wife there. But these notwithstanding, I consider the contrary to proceed in law in our case. For if the words of the said statute are properly weighed, they do not dispose regarding persons by qualifying or disqualifying them—in which case the aforesaid remarks apply—but rather provide a solemnity for an act to be executed in their territory. For the statute provides that the instrument must be registered in the communal archive, and otherwise is of no efficacy; and thus it gives form to instruments to be drawn up in the territory of the city; and this is done lest fraud be committed, which to avoid pertains to the office of him in whose territory the instruments are drawn up: argu. in l. congruit, ff. de offic. praesi. And that such a solemnity ought to be observed among foreigners having an instrument executed there, is seen from the text in l. ij. C. quemadmo. test. ape., where it is explicitly said,

† that testaments ought to be registered according to the laws and customs of the places in which they are registered; and thus it is clearly evident that such registration concerns the solemnity of the act. And it is certain that in respect of the solemnity of the act, the statute and custom of that place in which the act is performed must be observed: l. j, C. de eman. lib., l. iij, ff. de testib., and l. si non speciali, C. de testamen.; the doctors commonly hold this in l. cunctos populos, C. de summa trinita., in cap. quod clericis, de foro competen.; to which c. illa and c. istud, xij. distin., and what is noted in them, contribute. Bartolus explicitly shares this view virtually on our identical terms in l. cunctos populos, in versic. circa secundum, where

† he concludes that a statute providing that a will executed before three witnesses is valid extends its force to foreigners making a will there, because according to him such a statute concerns the solemnity of the act, but does not qualify or disqualify the persons making the will. Baldus holds the same and even more clearly in the said l. cunctos populos, where he says that an act is sometimes brought into being, and sometimes, having been brought into being, it is brought into court. In the first case, the statute of the place disposing how the act is brought about must be observed, because it concerns the solemnity of the act. In the second case, the place of the court is looked to. To the point, therefore, since the said statute disposes how an instrument is brought into being, requiring in this that it be registered, and disposes that what is done otherwise is of no efficacy, it must without doubt be extended to foreigners causing an instrument to be executed in that place. For foreigners ought not to violate the statutes and customs of a city, viij. distinctio, c. quae contra, especially when they aim at preventing the vice of falsification from being committed in the place of the legislators. For the lord of a place must strive as much as he can lest forgery be committed in his place: l. j, C. de fal. mone., and what is read and noted by Bartolus in l. ne quid, ff. de inced. rui. naufrag.; indeed, Bartolus went further in the said l. cunctos populos, namely

† that a statute disposing over the registration of testaments or instruments extends to churches and ecclesiastical persons, since it does not dispose over persons or churches, but generally over the solemnity of the act; although in respect of churches and ecclesiastical persons I doubt his statement, in light of what was noted by Bartolus in the said l. cunctos populos, and by c. ecclesia Sanctae Mariae, and what I said fully there, de constitu. And let these remarks suffice as to the first point. I conclude, therefore, that the said statute extends to foreigners causing an instrument to be executed

† in the territory of the legislators. As to the second, namely whether a statute of a city disposing simply in the aforesaid manner extends to the entire county of the city, briefly concluding, I believe that it does. I am moved first because, where the governance of a city and thus of the people is concerned, the county is said to be of the city; whence all buildings that are in the adjoining parts of the city are seen to be in the city: the text is explicit in l. aedificia, ff. de verbo. significa. Hence elsewhere the text says that those born in the suburbs of the city are understood to be born in Rome, as in l. qui in continentibus, ff. eodem titulo; and elsewhere a notable text says that he who originates from a village is understood to have that patria to whose republic that village belongs, as in l. qui ex vico, ff. ad municip.; to the same effect is capitulum 1, de usuris, in Sexto, joined with the gloss in versic. alienigenas. To the same effect is the notable text in l. 1, § cum urbem, ff. de offi. praefec. urb., where it is clear that when the governance of the city is committed, there comes not only what is contained within the circuit of the walls, but also the entire county of the city; and thus it is clearly evident there that the county is governed by the laws of the city, since city and county are deemed one city. And therefore all inhabitants of the county are called citizens of the city in whose county they are, as in l. qui ex vico, and the said l. qui in continentibus, noted by Bartolus in l. 1, ad municipa., and more clearly in l. non dubito, ff. de captiv.; through that text he says it is to be noted that castles that belong to the county of any city can properly be called an unfree people, and the men of that castle are called citizens of that city, citing the said l. qui ex vico. Finally, I bring to this opinion what is noted by Bartolus in l. 2, ff. de verbo. significa., where, from many points deduced by him there, it is inferred

† that when citizens are condemned, the inhabitants of the county appear condemned, unless something else appears from the disposition of the words: citing l. civitatibus, ff. de lega. primo, and l. civitas, ff. si certum pet., with similar texts; he also says that when 'city' is used for the people, then the inhabitants of the county are included. I conclude, therefore, that unless the contrary is proved, the claim of the party relying on the statute is sufficiently proved, because once it is proved that the castle belongs to the county of the city, it must be regulated according to the statutes of the city principally disposing, since by common law castles have no jurisdiction, but are subject to the city in whose territory they stand, according to what is noted by Innocent in cap. cum ad sedem, de restitutio. spolia., and by Bartolus in l. 1, ff. de damn. infect. And in our case it is most clearly evident that the said castle does not have jurisdiction, since in matters arising the men go to the magistrate of the city, as appears in the depositions, and as I shall say more broadly in the following doubt. I descend to the third point, whether it has been sufficiently proved that the said castle belongs to the county of that city where the statute is in force. I believe sufficiently that it is. For which I introduce an almost explicit text joined with the second gloss in capitulum cum olim, de censib., where the gloss clearly deduces from that text that when it is contained in any public writing concerning the boundaries of any bishopric, it must be adhered to until the contrary is proved, even though that writing was principally made for another purpose; it cites many laws in argument as concordances, but among others capitulum cum causam, de probatio., is especially relevant, where it is clear that in proving the boundaries of a bishopric, the strictest proofs are not required, since these ancient facts cannot easily be proved: l. si arbiter, ff. de proba., and capitulum quid per novale, de verbo. signi.; whence proof by reputation, and ancient books, and other adminicular aids suffices, and many things are joined together to complete the proof according to that saying, 'And what do not assist singly, many help,' as noted there. And Innocent held the same as that gloss in the said c. illud, de praesum., through the doctors in c. fi., de suc. ab inte. Whence, since in our case it is stated in many public instruments—especially those produced on behalf of the adverse party—albeit incidentally, that the said castle belongs to the county of that city, they must be adhered to until the contrary is proved, especially since the statements of witnesses concur with the assertion of the instruments, which statements, even if they do not provide full proof by themselves, nevertheless cannot be denied strongly to support them; which, together with the assertion or testimony of the instruments, undoubtedly ought to provide full proof through what is read and noted in the said c. cum causam, especially since in our case the ownership of the castle is not at issue, but a modest prejudice, namely to the effect of whether in our case it ought to be regulated according to the statutes of the city. Whence it cannot be denied that at least such a strong presumption arises that the burden of proving the contrary is shifted to the adverse party, as is read and noted in c. ut nostrum, ut eccle. benefi. And especially, as I have said, since the instruments were produced by the adverse party. For he who produces them is seen to admit the contents of the instrument, not only as to those matters which principally dispose therein, but also as to matters incidentally said and reported; wherefore upon the words enumerated therein the said Raynerius can base his claim; the text is explicit and notable in the said c. cum olim. Furthermore and lastly, the witnesses say that they saw the men of that castle come to the said city for matters pertaining to jurisdiction; therefore, nothing else having been proved, it must be presumed that they belong either to the district or to the county, and in either case the claim of Raynerius is grounded through the aforesaid points. And that this argumentation is valid is seen from the very sayings of the doctors in the said c. olim. For, as is noted there, these are convertible: a church is in the diocese, therefore it must pay episcopal dues; and a church is bound to episcopal dues, therefore it is presumed to be in the diocese; cap. 1, de relig. domi., and what is noted there, is relevant. So to the point, this argumentation is valid: the castle is in the county, therefore, nothing else having been proved, it is subject to the city and to its laws through the aforesaid. Likewise, the castle answers to the city in jurisdictional matters, therefore it is presumed to be of the county or district of the city. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that the witnesses only testify concerning fourteen months; because I say, since it is not proved that in prior time it answered to another city, it is presumed that it always was and is of the county of this city, through the notable text and what is noted there by Innocent in the said c. 1, de reli. domi., where it is proved that if it is doubted in whose diocese a church is, it is presumed to be in the diocese of him who is proved to have exercised some episcopal rights there, since it is not proved that another is in possession of other rights. And let these suffice. Nicolaus, Abbot of Sicily, Panormitanus. On the same matter.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The practice of women does not introduce a custom.
2. A single witness is not believed, even if he shines with synodal dignity.
3. Neither the word nor the writing of a judge is to be believed.
4. Credit is not given to the writing of any prelate concerning matters not pertaining to his office.
casus: In the aforesaid case of the said Raynerius Toscanus two new doubts have arisen. The first: since in the instrument produced against him the name of the emperor is missing; and to prove custom regarding the validity of the instrument almost eight instruments are produced, drawn up in the same territory in which the testament concerning which is the present question was executed, in which the name of the emperor was not affixed. Likewise testimonial letters of the podestà of that castle where the said instrument was drawn up are produced; which podestà attests that both in the city of Modena and in its district, county, and diocese many notaries were accustomed to publish their instruments without inserting the name of the emperor. It is asked whether from the aforesaid things the custom of the place is proven, so that for the validity of a public instrument it is not necessary to affix the name of the emperor. The second principal doubt is whether l. fina. C. si cer. peta. applies to public instruments, even according to modern times, so that it is not said to have been corrected by the law of the Authenticae, especially since the instrument in question was drawn up outside the walls of the same castle.
body: Having invoked the protection of Christ and of his mother, touching upon the said doubts conclusively on account of the shortness of time, I believe that custom has not been proven by the aforesaid things, since to prove a custom it is necessary that the tacit consent of the people, who have the power to establish a law anew, be proven, as in l. de quibus, and what is noted there by Bartol. and others, ff. de leg. and by Ioan. Andr. in c. fina. de consuetu.; Barto. stated this notably in l. 1. de legi.

† and that the practice of women does not introduce a custom, since they cannot issue laws, seeing that a law and a custom are equivalent, as in the said l. de quibus. But since in our case there are produced almost eight instruments drawn up without the name of the emperor, nor does it otherwise appear concerning the consent of the people, or of the greater part thereof, tacitly or expressly, that they wished to take away the disposition of the Authentica, ut nomen imperatoris præponatur &c., therefore it cannot be said that a contrary custom has been introduced. For it is certain that instruments are not made in the presence of the whole people, or the greater part, and it may be that the people, or the greater part, never saw those instruments, whence it cannot be said that from them a custom contrary to law was introduced, for that which happens to be absent from a thing does not prove it to be, l. neque natales. C. de proba. and in c. 2. de transla. præla. For since it is possible that no one besides those who had those instruments published saw those instruments, therefore it cannot be said that a custom of the people was introduced, since to introduce a custom of the people it is necessary, as I have said, that the act was practiced so many times and so publicly that it plausibly came to the notice of the people, as I said in the said l. de quibus, and there by Bartol. in l. 1. and 2. C. quæ sit lon. consuetu. and there by Cyn.; nor indeed is it proved in our case that credit was given to those instruments in court or outside so openly and publicly that it came to the notice of the people. And to this end that which is read and noted in l. cum de consuetudine. ff. de leg. serves excellently, where to prove a custom it is observed whether it was obtained in a contradictory judgment, because by this public and notorious act the consent of the people is presumed, and by this I remove the opinion of certain doctors who said that where there is doubt about the validity of one instrument, other instruments must be examined to see if they are of the same substance. For their saying ought to be understood soundly, namely when such instruments are produced to which it is proved that credit was given as public documents, otherwise before all things they would collapse from the same defect, because a full proof ought not to be drawn from an invalid proof. Hence the text says in c. 1. de fi. instr., if we do not see the authentic writing, we can do nothing with copies. Nor is it new or unusual that in the same city eight and ten instruments are found to lack the due solemnities, yet we ought not, on account of the ignorance of those notaries, to say that the laws have been derogated from, but rather that those instruments are void by authority of law, arg. in l. fi. in fi. C. de fideius. Nor can it be said that that custom was introduced among notaries, both because it is not proved truly or presumptively that those instruments came to the notice of the notaries of the greater part of that city, and because in order that a custom be introduced that credit be given to a non-authentic writing, it is necessary to prove that credit was given to such a writing, as is the clear text in c. cum dilectus, de consue., which was in no way proved here. Likewise, notaries alone cannot introduce a custom concerning the whole people, of which sort this custom is, since it is a matter of full credit being given in judgments and outside them to such instruments lacking in the due solemnity, just as I said above concerning the customs of women. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that by virtue of such instruments a proceeding was formerly conducted, as is said to be apparent from the production of the acts. For to this there is a multiple reply: first, that those acts were not transacted before a judge, but before arbitrators and good men, who are not accustomed to proceed according to the rigor of law, but according to equity, and often for the sake of concord take away from the right of one and give to the other, as in capit. nisi. de præbend. and noted in l. si de meis. §. recepisse, ff. de arbitr. and l. societatem. §. arbitrorum, ff. pro socio, and what is read and noted in l. si dictum. §. si compromisero, ff. de euic. Furthermore, those acts were not conducted entirely in the district of Modena, whose custom is in question. Likewise and all the more, it does not appear that a sentence was rendered therefrom, and if any was rendered, it was not rendered in the said district, and so on; and thus it cannot be said that the people of Modena tacitly consented that such instruments without the name of the emperor should make faith, nor was it even called into question whether such instruments were valid. Likewise, only a single act is proved, but a single act does not suffice to introduce a custom, because custom requires a frequency of acts, as in l. 1. and 2. C. quæ sit lon. consuetu., Bartol. holds following Guil. in the said l. de quibus. Nor does the letter of testimony of the podestà of that castle attesting to the custom stand in the way, because in the decisions of cases reliance is not placed on the word of a judge, even with an oath, as in capitu. licet ex quadam, de testi. where the text says that one witness is not believed, even if he shines with synodal dignity,

† and credit is not given to the sole statement even of the governors of a province, as is there, and all the more credit ought not to be given to the podestà of a single castle. To the same point is the good text in cap. cum a nobis, de testi. joined with the gloss, where it is clearly evident that in the decisions of cases reliance is not placed on the word of any judge, unless there are several who depose in the form of testimony before another judge, as noted by the gloss, especially the doctors, and Innocen. holds there, who expressly says,

† that credit must not be given to either the word or the writing of a judge, since he does not have the office of attesting, but of judging. Nay rather, the common opinion of the doctors in c. post cessionem, de prob. is that credit is not given even to the testimonial letters of a bishop, unless the slightness of the prejudice induces otherwise. In our case, however, the matter concerns a very heavy prejudice, because if the custom is not proved, the defendant must be absolved from the demand of 12 thousand florins, whence the podestà of a single castle could easily be corrupted to testify to a custom. And Innoc. said in cap. 1. and 2. de fide instru.

† that credit is not given to the writing of any prelate concerning matters not pertaining to his office, since this power has been given to notaries and not to judges; and attesting that a custom exists in a place does not pertain to the office of a podestà. Furthermore, the laws require that a custom be proved, since it consists in fact, as in l. 1. and 2. C. quæ sit lon. consue. and Cy. says in the said l. 2. that a custom ought to be proved through witnesses formally deposing, two at least. And it is most difficult to prove a custom, as is proved there, in c. si. de consue., whence many believe there is a custom, and for the most part they are mistaken. Whence among other things witnesses ought to prove three things, according to Cy. in the place previously alleged: namely, the use of the people, the frequency of use, and the long duration of time, which in our case has by no means been proved; nay rather, having presupposed and not conceded that credit ought to be given to the letters of the podestà in this matter, nevertheless the letters produced in this case do not prove a custom, since the podestà only said that many were accustomed to publish their instruments without the name of the emperor, in that he says 'many' and does not say 'all' or 'the greater part', nor does he say that faith was given to those instruments in judgments or outside, which is necessarily required to introduce a custom, as is proved in the said c. cum dilectus. Likewise he simply says that they were accustomed to publish &c., for he does not say that they were accustomed for such a duration of time through which a custom would be introduced, and thus he does not depose concerning the long duration of time, which is necessary to prove a custom. For the word 'were accustomed' does not always denote a perfect custom, according to what is read and noted in c. cum ecclesia Sutrina, de causa pos. & propriet., but this can well be verified in a twofold or threefold act, as in l. 3. C. de epi. audi. 25. q. 2. in c. ita nos. Proof, however, ought to conclude necessarily, as in c. in præsentia, de proba. From these things I clearly conclude as to the second point that a custom has not been proved by the aforesaid things that in the city and district of Modena it is not necessary to append the name of the emperor; consequently the said instrument produces no faith, as in Auth. ut præpo. no. imp. Nor can it be said that this is a slight solemnity, the defect of which ought not to vitiate the act, as in l. j. ff. de uen. inspic., because I say that this is not a slight solemnity, since the said Authentica emanated to introduce it with such great solemnity, and as is gathered there from the text and the gloss, otherwise the instrument is of no validity by operation of law. Therefore a special solemnity is inherent, especially since the word 'every' is placed there, which serves to exclude every dispensation and disposition of an inferior, according to the noted gloss in cle. ut hi qui, de æta. & qualita. Upon this last point it could perhaps be argued that a custom introduced without the consent of the prince in the contrary was not valid, especially since the emperor introduced that solemnity not only so that falsity might be more easily detected, but also for their honor and the remembrance of the empire; subjects, however, cannot enact statutes, and consequently cannot introduce a custom contrary to things introduced in favor of the prince. Unless perhaps it were such a custom of whose beginning there is no memory, as in c. super quibusdam, de uerbo. significa.; what is noted by Bar. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iustitia, & iure supports this. And c. cum dilectus, de fide instru. could be understood with moderation; concerning this last matter, however, I make no determination at present. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Prescription does not run against a wife in respect of dotal property, while the marriage subsists.
2. A prescription of forty years runs in bequests made to uncertain poor people.
casus: The fact upon which legal counsel is sought is in effect contained in the terms written below. A certain man, approaching death, instituted the hospital of Saint Mary as heir, and among other things burdened the said hospital to distribute every year at certain times specified in the testament one peck of grain to the poor coming to the said hospital to ask for alms. Finally, after the death of the testator, forty years and far more elapsed, within which times the said legacy was never carried into execution. Then the diocesan of the place insists upon the execution of the said legacy. The hospital replies that, since for forty years and more it has had no memory of the said legacy, prescription has run in its favor; wherefore, just as it can dispose of other goods freely and absolutely for pious causes, so also of those goods left by the testator. It is asked whether the said hospital can defend itself by prescription.
body: Having invoked the protection of Christ and His mother, it seems first must be said that it does not run: because prescription does not run against someone unable to bring an action, as in l. j. C. de anna. exceptio., where it is said that while paternal power lasts, prescription does not run against a son in regard to adventitious goods: because, while it lasts, the son does not have the administration of those goods, but all administration belongs to the father.

† The same is proven in the case of a wife during the subsistence of marriage. For prescription does not run against her with respect to dotal property: because while the marriage subsists she cannot bring an action, l. in rebus. C. de iur. do. To the same effect c. quia diuersitatem, de concessio. præben. & c. ex transmissa, de præscrip. But in our case the bequest was made to uncertain poor people, who by reason of their uncertainty cannot bring an action. Therefore prescription ought not to run against them. And this opinion was held by An. de Butr. in capitu. nihil, de præscrip., and in this case he so understood that text. Secondly, in the main, it is argued against prescription in another way, and thus: prescription, when good faith is lacking, does not assist the one prescribing, as in capitu. uigilanti, & capitu. fina. de præscrip. & in the rule possessor malęfidei, de regu. iur. lib. 6. But in our case good faith ought not to be presumed, but bad faith, since, the hospital being an extraneous heir, it is presumed to have knowledge of the testament, as noted by Bartol. in l. qui Romæ. §. duo fratres, ff. de uerbor. obligatio. Bad faith, moreover, can be proved from conjectures, as the same Bartol. notes in l. Celsus, ff. de usu ca., and l. dolum, C. de dolo, and capitu. secundo, de renunciat. lib. 6. support this. Therefore, since the hospital is presumed to have knowledge of the testament in which the said bequest was contained, it cannot allege prescription, because it is presumed to be in bad faith. Thirdly, l. fina. C. de sacrosanct. eccle. supports this, where it is clear that for a bequest made for the redemption of captives, only the centenary prescription runs. Whence at least in this case a prescription of one hundred years ought to intervene. It is proven otherwise, and thus: all goods of the hospital are principally assigned to the alms of the poor, as in clementi. quia contingit, de religio. domi.; therefore it does not seem that the hospital can allege prescription so as not to distribute the said peck of grain among the poor. For such a prescription is contrary to law, or requires the course of so much time that there is no memory of its beginning, as in the said capitu. primo. de præscript. lib. 6. But these things notwithstanding, I judge the contrary opinion to be truer in our case. And first, that in our case prescription has a place, against the opinion of Dominus Antonius I am accustomed to cite the express text, to which it is impossible to reply, in l. ut inter diuinum, C. de sacrosanct. eccle., where it is proved that against a bequest made for the redemption of captives, prescription runs, and yet the captives could not bring an action on a twofold legal ground: first, because they are captives; secondly, because they are uncertain; but these things notwithstanding, prescription runs, because to the bishop, as administrator of the poor, an action is given against the church in its property; although the body of the church itself, as an inanimate entity, cannot bring an action, nonetheless from negligence of administration prescription runs, as in the title de præscriptio. throughout. We see the same in the property of a minor, who, although he cannot be in court without the authority of a curator, institu. de cura. and in l. clarum, C. de auth. præstan., nonetheless from the negligence of the administrator prescription runs, as in l. sicut, C. de præscrip. triginta annorum. And this very thing in our case the gloss intended in the said l. ut inter diuinum, which says that the same is to be said of a bequest made to the poor as of a bequest made for the redemption of captives. And the gloss ought to be understood as applying to a bequest made to uncertain poor, just as the text speaks of captives. Likewise because the text there makes express mention of bequests made to a hospital. To the same effect I introduce another most beautiful text in authen. de ecclesi. titulo. in §. pro temporalibus, where the text says generally that in bequests and inheritances for pious causes a prescription of forty years is nowadays observed. Whence the words of that text are weighty, in that they indistinctly admit forty-year prescription in bequests for pious causes,

† but it cannot be denied that a bequest made to uncertain poor is for pious causes, since every bequest made for the soul is said to be for pious causes, as noted in l. si quis Titio ff. de leg. 2. and in l. relatum, de test. And this opinion I maintained long ago in my reading on the said c. nihil; this I say so that any presumed bias in the present case may cease, and I find that Fede. de Sen., an egregious doctor, expressly held the same view in consil. 101, where he went further, holding not only that prescription would run in this case, but even that thirty years would suffice, moved by the fact that in this case an action belongs to the bishop, not as bishop, but as administrator of the poor. For according to him the condictio from l. nulli and l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de episcop. & cler. belongs to the bishop for these bequests made to the poor, which condictio indeed is barred by the space of thirty years, as in l. sicut, C. de præscriptio. xxx. anno.; and thus Feder. wished to make a distinction between bequests made to the poor and those made to churches, because in respect of churches he requires forty years, but in respect of the poor he says that thirty years suffices. This last point, however, I am not accustomed to approve; on the contrary, against him is the case in the said §. pro temporalibus, where it is generally said that in bequests for pious causes a prescription of less than forty years does not run. To the same effect l. j. C. de sacr. san. eccle. serves excellently, where a bequest made to churches and one for the redemption of captives, or to the poor, are placed on an equal footing as regards the introducing of prescription. For in both cases a period of one hundred years was established at that time, from which it is evidently gathered that this action is not regulated according to ordinary actions, but is privileged in favor of the poor, just like that which belongs to churches; for the laws favor the poor no less as to the introducing of prescription than churches, as in the said l. fin. and 16. q. j.; for on account of nourishing the poor, goods were reserved to the church in the early Church, xij. q. j. cap. videntes. From all these things it is clearly concluded that in bequests made to uncertain poor forty-year prescription runs. If therefore prescription runs so that an heir is not compelled to pay, but gains it for himself, as in the said l. fi. and the said §. pro temporalibus, then a fortiori prescription must be admitted in our case, which operates not to profane, that is, to convert to profane uses, but to commute to another pious cause. For the hospital wishes to deploy the hereditary goods for a pious cause, just as it did with the other goods of the hospital. We see the like in a church whose goods by disposition of the testator or founder are assigned to a certain use, as for instance for the maintenance of the ministers of that church and for other necessities of the church itself, as in c. pastoralis, de his, quæ fiunt a præla., and nevertheless prescription runs against it by another church in those goods, as if they are assigned to the use of that church which prescribes, as in cap. ad aures, and cap. sanctorum, and cap. 1. de præscrip. and c. quarta, and c. illud under the same title, and xvj. q. iij. c. licet, and cap. inter memoratos, with similar texts; nay, even a layman prescribes against such goods of churches assigned to a certain pious use, as in c. 1. de præscript. lib. 6. and in c. causam, under the same title, by an argument a speciali; a fortiori, therefore, prescription ought to prevail in our case, where a slight prejudice is involved, since such goods are entirely to be expended on a pious cause. I conclude therefore that in our case the hospital can defend itself against the diocesan of the place by a prescription of forty years. Good faith, moreover, is regularly presumed in the person prescribing, as noted in c. si diligenti, and c. fin. de præscript., and by Bar. in the said l. Celsus. The contrary points alleged above do not stand in the way. And first, reply is made to l. j. and l. in rebus: for those laws proceed in the case of a wife and a filiusfamilias, who are in no way able to bring an action during paternal power and marriage; but in our case the bishop can bring an action as administrator of the poor, as in the said l. nulli and l. si quis; whence through his negligence prescription runs, just as it runs in the goods of a church, which are no less privileged than bequests made to the poor. And in the same way reply is made to c. quia diuersitatem and c. ex transmissa, for they proceed in the case of one unable to bring an action; the opinion of Dominus Antonius, moreover, is not proved by law, for he grounded himself on the said l. j., to which sufficient answer has been made, and through the text of the said c. nihil, which the doctors commonly understand in another way than he understands it. To the second contrary point concerning the presumption of bad faith on account of the testament, reply that it would proceed if the testament had been found in the hospital, but in our case it was found elsewhere. Likewise it would proceed if the rector of that place, to which the inheritance was left, had been perpetual; but the administrators of that place are removed daily at the pleasure of the rector of the main hospital. Whence, granted that knowledge is presumed in him who was administrator at the time of taking possession of the goods—in which case the pre-alleged statement of Barto. proceeds—nonetheless in a successor that knowledge is not presumed, for since he found the hospital possessing those goods, he could presume that they are possessed from some legitimate title, and thus he could begin prescription from himself, as is the text together with the gloss in c. quarta, de præscript.; Dyn. holds this in cap. possessor, de regu. iur. lib. 6.; what Barto. notes in l. cum hæres, de diuer. & tempo. præscript. supports this. To the third concerning l. fin., reply that it proceeded according to those times, but today and for these bequests for pious causes a prescription of forty years suffices, and centenary prescription is reserved only to the Roman Church, as in authen. quas actiones, C. de sacr. san. eccle. and there by the doctors, and as noted in the said §. pro temporalibus and xvj. q. iiij. cap. fi. To the fourth and last argument, I say that it would proceed if the rector of the hospital wished to convert the goods of the hospital to profane uses, in which case prescription would be contrary to law; but in our case he wishes to dispose these goods toward a pious cause, just as the rest of the goods of the hospital itself, and thus it is not contrary to law, but rather conforms to law, as in the said cle. quia contingit; and thus good faith together with the course of forty years suffices. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A cause of nullity devolves the entire matter to the superior.
2. A statute removing the pleading of nullity must be understood [with this limitation], unless the nullity is patent.
3. Prescription does not proceed without possession.
body: In the case that is currently pending between the commune of Sarteano on the one part, and the community of Castiglione on the other, concerning certain boundaries, since a full written argument was previously made by others and by myself in favor of the community of Sarteano, I shall at present use few words by way of conclusion, proceeding with the induction of arguments omitted, and I shall pursue four principal heads. First, concerning the validity of the appeal interposed by the commune of the said Sarteano from the sentence rendered against them on the said possessory matter. Second, having presupposed without prejudice to the truth that an appeal could not be made, whether they ought at least to be heard by way of nullity of the sentence. Third,

† whether in the cause of appeal, or of nullity, the said commune ought to prevail in the possessory matter. Fourth, whether the same is to be said in the petitory matter, namely, that sentence is to be rendered for the said community. Regarding the first, although l. unica, C. si de momen. pos. fue. appel. may seem to stand in the way of this appeal interposed on behalf of the commune of Sarteano, nevertheless Barto. examined the understanding of that law better than elsewhere in l. ij, ff. de appel. reci., where, among the other notable limitations that he posits for the resolution of that law, he says that that law does not apply when one's possession is unjustly taken away from him: because then such a sentence rendered on the possessory matter entails great prejudice, since it is most grave to lose possession without cause, as in l. fi., C. si per uim uel alio modo, and l. ulti., C. de rei uendi., and in § commodum, insti. de interdi., at least for one who can only bring the possessory remedy, and from the difficulty of proving ownership, ownership is often lost when possession is lost, as in effect in cap. sæpe, de restitutione spolia., where the text notes. Therefore, Barto. understands the said l. unica to apply when by the sentence the possessor is restored to his pristine state, because then it causes modest prejudice; since just as he had the right to claim previously, in the same manner could he claim the thing now after the sentence. He proves this by reason, for that single law is founded on the removal of an appeal upon the modesty of the prejudice, as is noted there, and by the gloss on the said l. 2. But it cannot be denied that prejudice occurs when possession is taken away by sentence without cause from one who legitimately holds it. Therefore, an appeal can then be made; and especially must this be held, because under canon law an appeal can be made indifferently from such a sentence, as is read and noted in capitu. cum ad sedem, de restitutio. spoliato., and in clementi. unica, de sequestra. possef. in fin. Therefore, the civil law, deviating from this most equitable disposition, ought to be restricted as much as possible. The same Bartol. posited another solemn limitation with respect to our purpose in the said l. 2, saying that the said l. unica does not simply prohibit an appeal in a possessory matter, but only provides that, notwithstanding the appeal, the sentence shall take its effect; as if to say that although an appeal from a definitive sentence otherwise suspends the execution of the sentence, as in l. 1, ff. ad Turpil., and l. 2, ff. de pœnis, and l. unica, § inter, ff. nil noua appellat. penden., and capitu. uenientes, de iureiuran., and the like, nevertheless in this case, on account of the modesty of the prejudice, execution is made; but nonetheless the proceeding upon the appeal continues, and once it is justified, the execution is retracted. Nor is this novel: for we see the same in an appeal interposed from an executor; for through such an appeal, execution is not wholly suspended, but proceeds, as is held in l. ab executione, C. quo. appellat. non reci. Likewise, we see a similar thing in an appeal from an interlocutory sentence, which does not impede the process of the judge, nor does it induce the retraction of attempted acts, unless it is first justified, as in capitu. non solum, de appellati., lib. 6. And these are the views of Bartol. in the said l. 2, which statements I consider most true and to be noted. Whence, for our purpose, since by the sentence rendered by the commissioners of the lords the legitimate possession of the community of Sarteano is unjustly taken away from them, the community could appeal from such a sentence. Likewise, for the other reason just stated, the said appeal can be justified; and this as to the first head. As to the second, having presupposed without prejudice to the truth that an appeal could not be made, whether the said community of Sarteano ought at least to have been heard by way of nullity: in doubt, I think that they should, by the notable text in capitu. licet, de senten. excommunica., lib. 6, where it is proved that the way of nullity is not excluded by the desertion of an appeal. It is likewise proved by the argument from a special case in clementi. unica, de re iudic. What is read and noted in l. 1, C. quando procura. non est necess., and in l. si expressim, ff. de appellatio., and in capitu. sæpe and capitu. dilecto, de appellationibus, supports this. Indeed, Bartol. stated notably in the said l. si expressim,

† that a cause of nullity devolves the entire matter to the superior; so that the superior can correct in part and in whole, and supply, and do everything that the first judge ought to have done, just as occurs in the remedy of appeal, citing the words of Inn. in capitu. cum contingat, de offic. delega. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the statute of this city of Siena opposes the claim of nullity; for one can reply to this in multiple ways: for as is presupposed to me in the fact, the statute only says that if an appeal is rendered deserted by the lapse of two months within which the appeal ought to have been expedited, the abandoning party ought no longer to be heard in that cause by way of nullity. For this statute, first, does not stand in the way, because it is denied by the party that the appeal was deserted, and at least it was not deserted under this head of the statute, because it was not through the lapse of two months. Whence, since that statute operates contrary to common law, it must be understood most strictly, so that it ought not to exceed its own proper case in which it speaks, as is read and noted in capitu. cum dilectus, de consuetudi., and in l. 2, C. de noxa., in capitu. in nostra, de iniur., and l. 3, § hæc autem uerba, ff. de nego. gest., and what Bartol. notes in l. omnes populi, ff. de iustit. & iu., and Ioann. Andr. on the rule pro possessore, in Mercuria. Likewise, because a correction of the law ought not to be introduced by identity of reason, at least one that is not expressed, as Bartol. notes in authen. quas actiones, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi., and what Barto. notes in l. liberorum, ff. de verbo. significatio. supports this.

† Furthermore, a statute removing the claim of nullity must be understood to apply unless the nullity is patent, or can be proved immediately; for this, capitu. cum Bartoldus, in fin., de re iudic., and the notable gloss in l. 1, § siue autem, ff. de tab. exhi., by Bald. in l. data opera, C. qui accu. non poss., in the larger commentary, by Old. in his consi. 45, which begins 'cum litera executoria', and he cites for the case l. penult., C. quando prouo. non est ne., and de rest. spol., capitu. literas, in the penultimate response, where it says, 'and proofs are offered immediately.' And I adduce the notable gloss in cap. suscitata, de in integ. rest., on the word 'effectum sententiæ', which clearly concludes that a provision removing the claim of nullity ought not to be understood of that which can be proved immediately. And what Pau. notes in clem. vnica, de renunc. supports this. It is proved by reason: for in doubt it is not to be presumed that the makers of a statute wish to openly foster injustice, and take away the right of one and give it to another; nay rather, such a statute nourishing open iniquity would be null, dist. 4, capitu. erit autem lex, and in cap. final., de præscr., noted by Barto. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu., and in l. fi., C. si contra ius uel uti. pub. If the nullity of the sentence were notorious, such that it can be proved immediately, it would be inequitable for such an exception to be excluded; for it would be taking away defense, which is of natural law, as in clem. pastoralis, de re iud. Therefore, the interpretation of that statute is not to be applied to our case, in which the nullity of the sentence is evident, especially in that it was rendered in a church, as in c. de cet, in fi., de immu. eccle., lib. 6. And I have fully touched upon this and other grounds for the nullity of this sentence in another consilium which I wrote on this matter of nullity. Furthermore, it is proved by another consideration: wherever a statute or law disposes without expressing the cause, we must consider the natural reason that could have moved the legislator; and if it is sole and undoubted, because no other reason can naturally be conjectured, we ought to extend and restrict the law to the limits of that conjectured reason, as Cyn. notably said after others in l. non dubium, C. de legi., and Bal. in l. maximum vitium, C. de lib. præte.; the text in l. scire oportet, in the verse 'sufficit', ff. de excu. tuto., and the notable gloss in l. tale pactum, ff. de pac. support this. But in the said statute, no other reason can naturally be considered in its removing the claim of nullity of an appeal induced by the lapse of two months, except that the statute presumed that because the party did not expedite the appeal within two months, it is presumed that he opposes nullity maliciously for the sake of delaying the execution of the sentence; a similar thing is found in the said clemen. vnica, de re iud. But where there is an evident and clear nullity, the presumption of malice ceases; therefore the disposition ought to cease; for this there is a good text in the said capit. literis. Furthermore and lastly, since the party of Sarteano was de facto admitted to prove the iniquity or nullity of the sentence, and proved it, sentence is to be rendered in its favor; for this, see the notable statement of Innocen. in cap. constitutus, de fil. presby., where he says that a defendant in the possessory remedy for recovering possession ought not to be heard before restitution on the property; nevertheless, if he was de facto admitted and proved it, the judge ought to render sentence in his favor. Hence, Innocen. also notably said in capitu. dilecta, de rescript., and in capit. cum Bertoldus, de re iudica., that although, after a sentence has passed into res judicata, the adverse party ought not to be heard on the nullity of the sentence, nevertheless, if he was de facto admitted and proved the iniquity, the sentence is to be retracted, notwithstanding the passage into res judicata, because the judge must pronounce on the matter of which he has taken cognizance, as in cap. cum super, de causa poss. proprieta., and in l. de qua re, ff. de iud. And let these suffice as to the second head. In the third head I shall proceed more briefly: because in fact it is presupposed to me that the community of the castle of Sarteano proved possession of the said boundaries more ancient than the adverse party; likewise by more and better witnesses, and adduced a title or titles, whereas the adverse party seemed only to prove possession. Wherefore, upon a threefold ground, any one of which is sufficient in itself for victory, I say that the said community of Sarteano ought to prevail in the possessory remedy for retaining possession; because wherever both parties prove possession through witnesses, and base themselves on the same species of possession, since it is impossible that two persons possess or have possessed the same thing in whole and in the same manner, as in cap. licet, de probatio., and l. 3, § ex contraria, ff. de acquiren. posse., sentence is to be rendered for that party which proved by more or better witnesses; and where there is equality of witnesses on both sides, sentence is to be rendered for the one proving longer and more ancient possession; and if the witnesses of both parties depose regarding the same time, sentence is rendered for the one who, beyond possession, proved title. For in these cases, he who proved better is presumed to have truly possessed; but the other party is presumed to have rashly occupied rather than to have possessed. These things are notably proved by the text and gloss and doctors in the previously cited c. licet; Bar. held this most clearly in l. si duo, ff. vti poss. The same is held by Iacob. de Are., But., and Cy. in l. 1, C. eo. But in our case, the community of Sarteano not only prevails in one of the aforesaid, but in all three: it proved not only by more and better witnesses, and likewise more ancient possession, but also title. Therefore, the community ought to prevail in the interdict uti possidetis; and the other party, who must be presumed to have occasionally entered into unjust possession and received some benefit, ought to be enjoined henceforth from daring to molest the community of Sarteano; and the form of rendering sentence is clearly gathered from the said c. licet. And by this I infer as to the fourth principal head. For I say that sentence is to be rendered for the said community of Sarteano also with respect to ownership. For beyond proven title, they prove prescription of the longest time; but the community of Castiglione cannot claim prescription:

† because prescription does not proceed without possession, as in the rule sine possessione, de reg. iu., lib. 6; but the men of the said castle themselves are not presumed to have possessed, but rather to have entered into possession unjustly, as I said above; therefore they do not prove prescription. For, as I said before, it is certain that the community of Sarteano, which is truly presumed to have possessed, prescribed by reason of possession, and good faith is presumed, especially when title intervenes, as in l. penultim., C. de euict., by Bar. in l. Celsus, de usucap., and the gloss holds this in cap. si diligenti, and cap. fin., de præscr. Therefore, the adverse party did not prescribe during the same time, because just as it is impossible for two to possess the same thing in whole and at the same time, so it is impossible for two to prescribe the same thing at the same time; and what Dyn. notes on the rule sine possessione, de regul. iur., libr. 6, supports this. And let these suffice. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Regard must be had to the ancient money in the provision of the law.
2. Whether someone is to be punished according to the law existing at the time of the delict, or according to that which is found at the time of the sentence.
body: That payment ought to be made according to the valuation of the old money that existed at the time when our lord the Pope made provision regarding the purchase of immovable property, or regarding the annual payment to be made to the monastery of Montmajour, is shown by the text joined with the gloss on the word "duos solidos" in cap. conquerente, de offic. ord. For by the provision of canon law it was introduced that everyone should pay annually two shillings for the cathedraticum or synodaticum to the diocesan bishop, 5 q. 1 cap. 1 and in the said c. conquerente; and yet the gloss notably says that these shillings are to be paid according to the valuation of that money which was customarily paid from antiquity and from the beginning, unless there has been prescription regarding the payment of the lesser money that is now in use, whether it be a greater money or a lesser, and for this it alleges cap. olim, de censi.; and that gloss is rejected there by no one. Secondly, the text in the said c. olim, de censi. seems to support the same; for that text cannot be understood of a payment to be made by contract, but by provision of law, since it speaks of a payment to be made in the name of the cathedraticum, which is owed by provision of law, as I said above; and yet the text there commands that payment ought to be made according to the valuation of the old money. To this same point makes clearly what Hostiensis noted in his Summa under the title de censi., §. ex quibus cau., at the verse quid si moneta; for although in the beginning he felt that the cathedraticum ought to be paid in current money if money frequently changes, nevertheless he affirms in the said §. quid si, pre-alleged, that if for sixty years payment was made in a certain money, it ought in the future to be paid according to the valuation of that money, if that old money is changed, through the said cap. olim. But in our case payment was made for more than sixty years according to the old money, or at least according to its valuation; therefore payment ought to be made according to it, through the said cap. olim. Thirdly, the case seems to appear in l. quoties, C. de suscep. & archa. lib. 10, where the law generally provides that wherever a certain sum of shillings is to be paid, it is not understood of the usual shillings and those current for the time, but of those ancient ones whereof seventy-two make one pound of gold; and thus, although the law commands the payment of certain shillings to be made, it is nonetheless not understood of the usual and current shillings, but of the ancient ones existing at that time of the law. The gloss felt this very same thing more clearly in l. si, ff. de ius vocan., where the text in a certain case commands that someone be condemned in fifty gold pieces; and the gloss says the text is to be understood of those gold pieces whereof seventy-two make one pound of gold; and thus it did not have regard to the usual money. And the gloss intended the same in l. quicunque, C. de fer. fugi., and Inst. de poena teme. li. §. fina. at the end; and Johannes Andreae after Vincentius in c. deinde, upon the final gloss, 26 dist.; and in the Additiones to Speculum under the title de instr. edi. §. porro, at the end, where he clearly felt

† that even in a provision of law regard must be had to the old money, and not to the current. And through this and other things immediately to be said below, Speculator seems thoroughly to speak repeatedly in the title de sol. §. nunc aliqua, verse pone, where he says that in a payment to be made by provision of law, the money current at the time of payment must be considered, and he alleges the text joined with the gloss in c. 2 de maledi. and in c. olim, de iniur.; and it is relevant that the law always speaks, l. Arria, C. de haere.; and Baldus seems to follow the statement of Speculator with respect to the payment to be made in l. illud, C. de sacrosanct. ecc. For first, his statement seems contrary to the aforesaid, and is nowhere proved; for the legal authorities he alleges rather make for the contrary; for they are understood of usual coins because they expressly so provide. For if it had not specifically provided this, it ought to have been understood of gold shillings, whereof seventy-two make one pound, through the said l. quoties and the others alleged above. Therefore, in my judgment, the glosses there wrongly felt, saying that even if it had not been said of usual coins, it ought nonetheless to have been understood of them; which is false through the said l. quoties. Moreover, against the statement of Speculator I advance this reason: the penalty ought to be commensurate with the delict, l. respiciendum, ff. de poenis, and cap. non afferamus, 24 quaestio 1. But the law, when appointing a certain pecuniary penalty with respect to a delict, had regard to the value of the money existing at the time of the provision, since it did not express otherwise; therefore it ought not to be understood of other money, which might be diminished to such an extent that the penalty would be so meager as to offer material and audacity for offending, against cap. pauper, 11 q. 3. Likewise, it might be increased to such an extent that it would exceed due vengeance; and in odious matters the law is not seen always to speak, but must be restricted, if it can be done, to the time of the provision; what is read and noted in l. certa forma, C. de iure fis. lib. 10 makes for this. Furthermore, presupposing that the statement of Speculator were true in itself, nevertheless in our case it can in no way proceed. For he speaks when no obligation has been acquired by anyone from the provision of the law; whence, since the effect of the law is pending, it can well be maintained that regard is had to the money current at the time when someone incurs the law, by the argument in the said capitu. 2 de maiorit. & obedien. and the said capitul. olim. But in our case the obligation was acquired for the monastery of Montmajour at the time of the papal provision; therefore it must be understood of the money then current, lest the obligation be varied in these matters; for Bartolus felt this sufficiently in a similar question in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu., when he asks

† whether someone is to be punished according to the law existing at the time of the delict, or according to that which is found at the time of the sentence; and he concludes that if an ordinary penalty is imposed by the law existing at the time of the delict, judgment must be given according to it, because regard must be had to the time when the obligation arose, for which he alleged the said capitul. olim; and immediately by the delict someone is seen to be obligated to the penalty then existing, l. 1, ff. de poenis, and capitul. pueris, de senten. excommu., with similar texts. So undoubtedly it must be said in our proposition; for on account of an obligation having arisen at the time of the contract, we say that regard is had to the money then current, according to what is read and noted in l. cum quid and l. vinum, ff. si cer. pe. The same therefore in a provision of the law, since from the time it emanates, an obligation is born from it and acquired by another. What more?
