I bring forward an unanswerable consideration: our lord the Pope disposed and ordained for a payment to be made to the monastery of Montmajour in compensation for those things that had been withdrawn from it by him in favor of the monastery of Saint-Antoine; therefore it necessarily had to be understood of the money then current, because compensation for damages inflicted cannot be made unless a valuation is made by certain and invariable money, by the argument in l. 1, ff. de contrah. emp. For money has a certain weight, form, and material, as in the said l. 1; whence in ordaining payment in compensation of damages it could not be understood except of that money then current, because by virtue of uncertain and variable money, a correct valuation and compensation of those damages could not be made, by the argument in the said l. vinum, and l. cum quid, and what is noted in them, and in l. Paulus, otherwise beginning creditor, ff. de solu. We see a similar thing when action is brought for the rescission of a contract on account of deception and damage caused beyond half of the just price; for in considering deception we look to the value of the thing at the time of the contract, because otherwise one cannot be said to be deceived in a contract, according to what is read and noted in c. cum dilecti, and c. pe. de emp. & ven., and l. 2, C. de rescin. ven. So to the proposition, our lord the Pope could not have made compensation for damages through a payment to be made annually, unless he had had regard to the money then current at the time the compensation was made. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The prince's intention is not to prejudice a third party, unless he makes special mention of him.
2. The pope is not deemed to wish to abolish statutes [and] customs by his constitution, since they consist in fact.
3. Prejudicial privileges are to be strictly interpreted.
4. Prescription requires good faith.
5. Prescription was principally introduced in hatred of negligence.
6. A privilege is valid with respect to his subjects for the impetrator [?].
7. A civil law, if it is canonized by the pope, has the force of a canon.
casus: See above in the first part, consilium 101, which is repeated here.
body: IN the question that is pending, or expected to be pending, between the monastery of Santa Croce of Monte Avellano, of the diocese of Gubbio, on the one part, and the friars of the Cistercian Order on the other part, concerning the subjection of the monastery of San Bartolomeo di Camporegio of the same diocese: I judge that three points must be examined for the clarity of the decision. First, whether by the privileges of exemption and union granted to the said monastery of San Bartolomeo, prejudice has been done to the right of the monastery of Santa Croce. Second, presupposing that the privilege brought no harm, whether a forty years' prescription must exclude the right and action competent to the said monastery of Santa Croce. Third, if such prescription causes prejudice, whether the said monastery of Santa Croce can protect itself by a centenary prescription by virtue of the imperial privilege which the pope subsequently deemed to remain ratified. Approaching the first point in order, it seems at first that by the privilege of Alexander, subsequently corroborated by Gregory, prejudice was done to the right of the said monastery of Santa Croce. For the said Alexander deemed that the said monastery of San Bartolomeo should answer concerning its subjection neither to bishop, nor to abbot, nor in fine to any cleric or secular person, but only to himself and his successors, the Roman Pontiffs; and he added a little later that if anyone, whether bishop, or abbot, or any great or small person, contrary to the edict of this our constitution, through any machination or cunning of subtlety, shall have arrogated to himself or subjected the aforesaid monastery, both he who shall have given it and he who shall have wrongfully received it, until he repents and restores what was wrongfully presumed, shall be bound by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul by the bond of perpetual damnation and anathema, etc. Since, therefore, the pope, who has fullness of power—as in the chapter ad honorem, de autho. & usu. pal., and the chapter cuncta per mundum, and the chapter per principalem, 9, quæst. 3—exempted the said monastery from the subjection of bishop, abbot, and any other person whatsoever, which, since he had the power to do it, is by no means to be called into doubt, as in cap. si papa, de priuileg., lib. 6, and like cap. 2, and cap. dudum, and c. quamuis, de præb., eodem libro: therefore the monastery of Santa Croce cannot claim any subjection in the said monastery. For if prejudice is done to the bishop, whose power over monasteries is ordinary and plenary (18, q. 2, c. monasteria, and c. abbates, and c. si quis abbas, and de relig. domi., c. cum dilectus, and c. venerabilis, with similar texts), a fortiori prejudice ought to be done to the abbot of Santa Croce, who claims some sort of superiority solely from the institution of the said monastery. For the said abbot could only claim four things, namely the confirmation of the abbot, likewise reverence and obedience, and a certain annual census. For only these four things did the patron reserve, at the time of the foundation, to the abbot of the monastery of Santa Croce. Therefore, these things, which are slenderer and arise from special law contrary to common law, ought more easily to be taken away than the power of the bishop, which is ordinary, and favorable, and founded upon full subjection; but it is doubtful to no one that since prejudice is done to the bishop (dictum c. si papa, and c. 1, de priu., lib. 6, and 16, q. 1, c. quia frater), much more ought prejudice to be done to the abbot: argument in c. dilectus, de off. leg. Nor can subreption be alleged, since no special mention was made of the abbot in the privilege—which could not be verified except in special law, since by common law one monastery is not under another, as in the said c. monasteria, and as noted in c. præsentia, de prob. Secondly, there helps the union recently made by the present lord Pope Martin, in that he united that monastery to the Cistercian friars, taking away the abbatial dignity, which he could undoubtedly do, as in c. sicut, de conces. præb., and in c. temporis qualitas, 16, q. 1, especially since it was done after the said privilege and after the rights were prescribed against the monastery of Santa Croce; for prescription excludes every action, as the text says in the chapter ad aures, de præscript. It was therefore not necessary to make mention of the monastery of Santa Croce, since its right had already been removed by the privilege of Alexander and by the forty years' prescription. But these things notwithstanding, I think the contrary opinion prevails: namely, that by the privilege of Alexander and by the forty years' prescription of Alexander, or of the union made by the lord Martin, no prejudice was inflicted upon the right of the monastery of Santa Croce. I am moved first,

† because it is of the prince's intention never to prejudice a third party, unless he makes special mention of him: as in the chapter super eo, de off. deleg., and l. 2, § si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in loco publico; especially when there is derogation from the institution of a benefice and from a lay disposition, lest laymen be thereby deterred from the foundation of churches: to this effect is the notable gloss in clem. per literas, de præb., and what the doctors note in the chapter cum dilectus, de iurepatro. But in our case, no special mention was made of the rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce; therefore such privileges do not obtain validity to the prejudice of that monastery. Nor is it an obstacle that in the privilege of Alexander or Gregory it was said that it should be subject to no abbot, etc., because that is not a sufficient mention to prejudice the right of the monastery, since the mention must be special and not so general, as in ca. 2, de dolo & contu., and what is there noted by the doctors, in c. cum dilecta, de resc., and the good text in the chapter bonæ, de confir. vti. Especially in our case special mention had to be made, wherein those rights that were owed to the monastery of Santa Croce had to be expressed in the institution of the monastery by the disposition of the lay patron. For the pope by his privilege does not intend to prejudice the institution of a benefice unless he expresses this openly, as in c. cum dilectus, de consue.; to which makes c. constitutus, de rescri., especially against the disposition of a lay patron, as noted in the said cle. per literas, and c. cum dilectus, de iurepa.; c. monasterium, 16, q. 2, and c. eleutherius, 18, q. 2, serve excellently. For the pope in his privilege could understand abbots who, in certain united religious orders, are called Father Abbot, to whom slight prejudice is inflicted; wherefore we ought not to presume, for the aforesaid reasons, that the pope understood, by those general words, the special disposition of the patron. To the same effect is the good text in c. ex multiplici, de decimis, where it is clear that a privilege does not prejudice a composition previously made unless special mention is made of it; and in c. cum olim, de præscri., where a privilege does not prejudice an arbitral award rendered upon a compromise; a fortiori it ought not to prejudice the institution of a benefice or monastery if special mention is not had of it. Secondly, there makes c. veniens, de præscr., where a notable text indicates that if the prince granted a privilege to someone with some reservation of the right of another, a privilege granted in the same manner concerning those rights is not valid without some sort of reservation of the right of the other previously made, if no mention is made of it; because if the pope had known of that reservation, he would not perhaps have granted it without it, as is noted there. The same, and a fortiori, is therefore decided and to be said in our case: that if the pope had known that those four rights had been reserved by the patron to the monastery of Santa Croce, he would never have granted that full exemption without the reservation of those rights, or at least would have made mention of them; especially since the exemption could have been granted with the reservation of those rights, because those rights do not denote full subjection, as is clearly indicated in c. his quæ, de maio. & obedien., and ca. cum inter, de re iud., where many rights entailing full subjection are enumerated, and among them are listed obedience and reverence as species. Thirdly, there is adduced c. 1, de const., li. 6, where it is said,

† that the pope by his constitution is not deemed to wish to take away statutes and customs, since they consist in fact, unless he makes mention of them; therefore a fortiori the same must be said in a privilege, which does not emanate with so much moderation as does the common law, as noted there: therefore his statute and ordinance made in the institution of the monastery ought not to be taken away by the privilege of the Pope, seeing that no special mention was made of it. Fourthly, it makes for this because Gregory, or Alexander, did not wish to derogate simply from the right of the monastery of Santa Croce, but said that through this privilege of exemption it ought not to depart from the charity of Santa Croce, just as he had said in another privilege; whence it is to be believed that through those words he wished to reserve all the rights belonging to the monastery of Santa Croce. For it would not observe charity toward it if it wished to withdraw from it the census imposed of old, or other rights reserved to it, as in the said chapter eleutherius; to which makes the chapter quanto, de censi. For charity is a right will entirely adverse to all earthly things, etc., as in the chapter charitas, de pœn., distinctio. 2; and in these matters a broad interpretation is to be made, so that prejudice is not done to the right of another without cause, according to the note by Bartolus in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iu., and l. non dubium, C. de legi.; to which makes the chapter cum dilectus, de consuetu., and l. 2, C. de noxa. This same thing and more clearly in our proposed case Innocent wished in the chapter dudum, de priuilegiis, where he says,

† that all prejudicial privileges are to be interpreted strictly and, as far as possible, reduced to the order of law: ff. de uulga. & pupil., l. ex facto, and de deci., chapter suggestum. And he says the same regarding a privilege of exemption; wherefore after many points he there concludes that a privilege of exemption is not valid if no mention is made of another's possession held in good faith, even if in truth he does not have the ownership; and the gloss affirmed the same in cap. 2, de deci., lib. 6. A fortiori, therefore, it must be said in our case that the privilege is not valid if no mention is made of the possession or ownership of the monastery of Santa Croce. And the same is to be said in all respects regarding the union recently made by the lord Martin. For since he made no special mention of the aforesaid things, it did not hold, since by it prejudice would be done to the monastery of Santa Croce in respect of the confirmation of the Abbot, seeing that by that union the abbatial dignity was taken away and suppressed. What was said above concerning prescription does not stand in the way, because it is immediately answered in the second and third doubts. And these things as to the first doubt, which I deem most true and indubitable; and the response to the contrary arguments formed above is sufficiently plain. As to the second doubt, whether at least the forty years' prescription prejudices the said monastery of Santa Croce, since within that time it made no confirmation of an election made of an abbot, nor received the census, nor had obedience or reverence: and it seems that it does. For regularly against a church other than the Roman Church, a prescription of forty years with good faith suffices, as in the chapter de quarta, and the chapter illud, de præscriptio.; nor is title required, since the common law is not against the one prescribing, as noted in chapter 1, eodem titulo, lib. 6; and a forty years' prescription completely excludes every action, as the text says in the said chapter ad aures, de præscript. But these things notwithstanding, I think it must be said thus in our case: that in respect of the right of confirming the abbot in the monastery of San Bartolomeo, no prescription has run against the monastery of Santa Croce. The unanswerable reason is that, on account of the reservation made concerning collegiate churches, especially concerning cathedrals and monasteries, by many Roman Pontiffs successively, the Abbot of Santa Croce for the time being could not exercise the right belonging to him in this matter; whence, since he was impeded by an impediment of law, no prescription runs against it: l. prima, C. de an. 1. exceptio., and l. in rebus, C. de iure dot., where it is clear that during paternal power prescription does not run against a son in adventitious property, because he could not sue at that time, since the full administration of those things belongs to the father, as in the said l. prima. Nor during the subsistence of marriage does prescription run against a wife in dotal property, because she cannot sue, since the full administration belongs to the husband, as the said l. in rebus, and l. doce ancillam, C. de rei vend.; to the same effect are chapter 1 and the chapter de quarta, de præscriptio., and the chapter ex transmissa, eodem titu., and capit. quia diuersitatem, de concess. præbend. In which legal texts it is clear that prescription does not run against a church that is vacant or having a prelate unable to sue; but in our case the Abbot of Santa Croce for the time being was impeded as to the act of confirmation: therefore prescription does not run against him. This right therefore remained with him in habitu, even though its exercise was forbidden at the pleasure of the pope through the act of reservation. Nor, by exercising this right of confirmation, is the pope said to prescribe, even if he were to do this for a thousand years, since he does this out of the fullness of power; and in this case can be understood what the Speculator says in titu. de præscriptio., versicu. illud, when he says that the pope does not prescribe against inferior churches, since he is already the universal lord without prescription.

† Furthermore, in prescription good faith is required, so that he thus believes that that right belongs to him, in such a way that he exercises it believing that he is using his own right: as in capitul. si virgo, 34, quæstione. 2; to which makes l. final., ff. quemadmodum seruit. amit., and the note of Innocent in the chapter bonæ, the 2nd, de postulatio. prælato. But the lord pope exercised and exercises the act of confirmation not by ordinary power, but by absolute power, through the act of reservation; and thus, by common law and ordinary power, this right belongs to the inferior, although he himself can concur in the act of confirmation with the ordinary: as in capitul. si a sede, de præbend., lib. 6. Therefore prescription cannot be alleged here from the person of the pope against the abbot of Santa Croce, who is not caught in negligence, since he had his hands tied by the reservations of the Supreme Pontiffs, as in the laws cited above.

† For prescription was introduced principally in hatred of the negligent, as in l. 1, ff. de usucap., and 16, quæstione. 3, capitul. placuit, § potest. And in our case no negligence is found on the part of the abbot of Santa Croce. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that he was negligent in other things; because by this, prescription ought not to be extended to rights in which no negligence was committed, since prescription is of strict law, and one prescribes only as much as is possessed, as is proved in the chapter auditis and the chapter cum olim, de præscriptio., and the chapter cum contingat, de decim., and as noted by Bartolus in l. 1, § si quis, ff. de itin. actuque priua., and Innocent in the chapter dilectus, de capel. mona. Therefore it is necessarily concluded that the union made by our Lord Martin, suppressing the dignity of the abbacy with no mention made of the right of confirming belonging to the abbot of Santa Croce, was, as subreptitious, null ipso iure; because if he had been informed that such union redounded to the prejudice of the monastery of Santa Croce, he would by no means have made the union, or at least not so easily; therefore such suppression had to induce subreption, as in the chapter postulasti, and what Hostiensis notes there, de rescript. Which I say holds even if the pope had made the union of his own motion (motu proprio); because motu proprio, although it excludes subreption, nevertheless does not confirm a grace contrary to the intention of the writer, who in doubt is not deemed to wish to prejudice a third party, as noted by Johannes Andreae in c. si quis motu proprio, de præben., lib. 6, and Calderinus in cap. cum dilectus, de iure patro., and the lord of the Rota, decisio 102; to which makes l. 2, § si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in loco publico, and what Innocent notes in cap. dudum, de priuileg., and the gloss in c. 2, de deci., lib. 6. Indeed, it could be maintained that even in respect of obedience no prescription would run, because although the abbot of Santa Croce could have commanded some honest things, especially by reforming the conduct of the abbot of San Bartolomeo, it is not thereby concluded that if he did not command, prescription ran against him: since this is an act of mere faculty, and not of necessity; for it was not said in the institution that the abbot of Santa Croce should exercise jurisdiction against the abbot of San Bartolomeo, but that the abbot of San Bartolomeo should be bound to obedience and reverence toward the abbot of Santa Croce. If, therefore, the latter did not obey because the former did not command, prescription has not thereby run against him; because custom or prescription is not induced from non-use, seeing that it has no tacit act contrary to the disposition of law: as noted by Johannes Andreae in the chapter Ioannes, de cler. coniug., and by Cynus in l. 2, C. quæ sit long. consue.; and it is proved in l. hæc autem iura, ff. de seruitu. urba. prædio., and in l. altius, C. de serui. & aqua. For if I have the faculty of building higher on my own ground up to the sky, there is no prescription against the right if I have not built higher, seeing that nothing was done to the contrary: because this is an act of mere faculty; and in acts of mere faculty prescription does not run through non-use, as is noted in the laws previously cited, and in capit. ex parte astensis, de conces. præbend.; and perhaps a case did not occur in which he had need to command: an argument from what Bartolus notes in l. cum scimus, C. de agri. & censi., book 11. In respect of reverence, however, it must be considered whether the abbot of San Bartolomeo withdrew reverence from the abbot of Santa Croce, which would be difficult to prove, for that consists in an act of payment, or through some other manner by which reverence is rendered according to the custom of the country, according to what is noted in the chapter his quæ, de maiori. & obedien. The whole difficulty stands around the unpaid census: as to whether the forty years' prescription is complete, many things must be considered, and not the mere lapse of years alone. For many things impede the course of prescription, such as the vacancy of the monastery of Santa Croce; for the time of vacancy must be deducted from the middle, as in capit. 1, and in the chapter de quarta, and the chapter auditis, de præscript., which laws have place even in inferior churches, as Innocent notes in the chapter olim, first, de restitu. spoliato. Likewise, in time of war prescription does not run, when hostility in the place is so great that justice is not administered: as in the chapter ex transmissa, de præscript., and what Innocent notes there. Likewise in time of mortality, because that is hostility of God: as Bartolus notes in l. naturaliter, ff. de usucap. Likewise in time of schism: as in the chapter cum nobis, de præscript.; I understand this if there were different obediences, and justice was not rendered to one against the other, according to what is noted in the said chapter transmissa. For all these times ought to be deducted from the time of prescription; and if, with these deducted, a time of forty years does not remain, the monastery of Santa Croce has its case well-founded: as in the chapter auditis, de præscript. But if the prescription should remain complete, it must be observed whether the monastery of San Bartolomeo was in good faith in not paying the census. For bad faith is proved if there was a rumor in the place that it ought to pay the census to the monastery of Santa Croce, or if it appeared through some writing existing in their monastery, or that they heard it from some person whom they reasonably ought to have believed; for by this and similar means bad faith is proved, as Bartolus notes in l. celsus, ff. de usucap.; and if certainty can be had regarding these things, prescription is impeded by cap. fin., de præscript., and the rule possessor malæ fidei, de reg. iur., lib. 6. If, however, it cannot be proved, so that the forty years' prescription remains unshaken, then recourse must be had to the third and last doubt: whether the monastery of Santa Croce can protect itself by a centenary prescription, by virtue of the privileges of the Emperors Frederick and Henry, afterward approved by Pope Honorius IV. And it seems first that it cannot, because emperors could not grant a privilege to a monastery to the prejudice of the ecclesiastical forum, as Innocent notes in c. nuper, de testi.; since therefore it is provided by canon law that one church can protect itself by a forty years' prescription against another church (as in c. de quarta, and c. ad aures, de præscri.), the privilege of the emperors ought not to be of benefit: to this make c. dudum, de deci., and c. ecclesia Sanctæ Mariæ, de const., and 96. dist., c. bene quidem. Nor does the approval of Pope Honorius stand in the way, for a manifold reason: first, because a confirmation made in common form is of little benefit, whence it does not validate a void act, as you read and as is noted in cap. quia diuersitatem, de conces. præben., and cap. fin., de confir. uti. Now it is said to be made in common form, and not from certain knowledge, when the entire tenor of the confirmed thing is not inserted, or when the clause ex certa scientia is not appended, or it does not otherwise appear concerning certain knowledge of the confirmed thing, according to what is noted in cap. 1, and antepenult, and penultimate, de confirm. utili. But in our case, the tenor is not inserted in the confirmation of those privileges, nor the clause ex certa scientia: therefore, etc.

† Furthermore, a privilege of the emperors is valid as to their subjects, as in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. trin.; to which makes what you read and is noted in l. fi., ff. de iur. om. iudi., and cap. a nobis, de sent. excom.; therefore the confirmation is valid only as to subjects. But these things notwithstanding, I judge that the contrary proceeds according to law. I am moved principally because the lord pope in his privilege did not use the word 'we confirm' (confirmamus), and thus it cannot be said that it was a confirmation in common form, but he used the word 'we sanction' (sancimus), by which word a confirmation is not induced, but rather the enactment of a new law: argument in the chapter generali, de electio., libro 6; for 'sanction' is the name of a canonical constitution, as noted by the gloss in distinction 4, in sum.; so we say concerning the word 'we deem' (censemus), which is inductive of new law, as noted by the gloss in clementi. 1, de conces. præben., and on the word censemus. Wherefore these words of the emperors and of the pope are to be weighed. For the Emperor simply decrees that no prescription less than a centenary one should run against the monastery of Santa Croce, nor did he restrict himself to secular or ecclesiastical persons. But Honorius, intervening, speaks thus: 'Furthermore, all liberties and immunities granted to you and to your order by the Emperor Frederick of good memory, we hold ratified and pleasing, and we sanction that they remain inviolate in future times,' etc.; which words demonstrate more clearly than light that Honorius did not simply wish to confirm in common form, but rather principally disposed by enacting a private law. For 'what pleases the prince has the force of law': insti. de iu. na. gen. & ciui., § sed quod principi; and 'we make all things ours to which we impart our authority,' as in l. 1, C. de vete. iur. enu.; and there is a good text in a similar matter in the chapter si apostolicæ, de præben., lib. 6; whence the pope's law is now more powerful than the emperor's. Furthermore, we see

† that if a civil law is canonized by the pope, it has the force of a canon: as in cap. in primis, and there the good gloss, 2, q. 1, and as the doctors note in cap. 2, de præscr.; a fortiori, therefore, the said privilege of the emperor ought to have the force of a canon, since the pope expressly intended that those things remain inviolate. And although he did not express what those immunities were, nevertheless they are sufficiently held as expressed, since the pope referred to those privileges: in cap. auditis, de præscrip., where there is a good text in a similar matter, and in l. penult., C. de sente. quæ sine cert. quantita., and in cap. cum Bertoldus, de re iudi. This same point is proved by an excellent parallel: for in the beginning it was the emperor who gave a privilege to churches regarding the matter of prescription, as in l. fin. with the authentica quas actiones, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi.; afterward canon law intervened and approved those laws in general, as in the chapter cum nobis, de præscriptio.; and through this approval they had force even with respect to the ecclesiastical forum and between churches. And by this is removed one argument that is alleged against the monastery of Santa Croce, namely that the papal approval ought not to have place against the pope himself prescribing. For first, it can be directly denied that here the pope has prescribed; for the withdrawal of the census is prescribed by the monastery of San Bartolomeo, and not by the pope. Whence, presupposing that the church of San Bartolomeo were exempt, nevertheless in its rights, especially when dealing with the prescription of spiritualities, it does not enjoy the privilege of the Roman Church, as noted by the gloss in c. dilectus, de ap., and as noted in c. ad audientiam, de præsc., and by the doctors in c. cum nobis, eodem titulo, and 16, q. 4, c. volumus. Likewise, presupposing and not conceding that here the pope had prescribed, nevertheless the privilege granted by him ought to have place without distinction, seeing that he granted it generally; for a privilege receives the broadest interpretation against the one granting the privilege, as noted by Bartolus in l. beneficium, ff. de constitu. princip., and Innocent in the chapter cum dilectus, de donatio., and in the chapter olim, de verbo. sign., by Johannes Andreae; to this makes the chapter cum dilectus, de consue.; in favor of this is that word of the wise man: 'Suffer the law which you yourself have made.' And what law each establishes against another, he himself ought to use, as in c. cum omnes, de constitu. Lord Antonius openly deemed this in c. cum nobis, de præscrip., where he maintained that the pope can prescribe against an inferior church by the space of forty years; and yet that forty-year period the church possesses by a privilege under special law approved or introduced by the pope: therefore the same must be said in this privilege of 100 years. This must be held, taking especially into consideration that prescription is odious and to be restricted, as in c. cum contingat, de deci., with similar texts. And let these things suffice, nor is it necessary to respond otherwise to the contrary arguments, because they remain sufficiently resolved and clear through the aforesaid. Nicolaus, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A fideicommissum left by an heir if he should die without children is not owed if he died leaving a grandson whom he had begotten from a daughter.
2. In a direct substitution made by a collective term when two sons under the age of puberty have been instituted, namely "if both should die in pupillary age, let such a person be heir", upon one dying in pupillary age, the other is substituted.
3. The intention of the disposer, whether express, or implied, or conjectured, must be attended to in last wills, of whatever nature it may be, whether it is a direct substitution, or fideicommissary, or a condition, or a testament, or a codicil.
body: A certain Nicolaus made his testament, in which he instituted his five sons as his heirs in equal portions and substituted them reciprocally to one another; and if all should die without legitimate and natural children, then, upon that event taking place, he willed that his house, together with its household furnishings, should devolve upon and belong to his legitimate nephews by his brother, and he instituted and created the said nephews his heirs under the aforesaid condition in the said house and furnishings. Subsequently, after the testator died, three of the said sons instituted as heirs by the said testator passed away, leaving behind no legitimate and natural children surviving them; a fourth son in fact died after the death of those three, having left an only son named Ioannes. Afterward, the said Ioannes died, leaving surviving him only Nicola, a son of the said testator. Lastly, the said Nicola died without legitimate and natural children, having made a testament in which he instituted strangers as his heirs. Now it is asked whether the said nephews by the brother of the first testator are admitted to the legacy or to the substitution of the said house, at least for the shares of those sons who died without legitimate and natural children. And first, having implored the aid of the most high Creator of all, it seems that the said nephews ought in no way to be admitted, because since they were called under the condition "if all should die without children," and one of them died having left a legitimate and natural son, therefore, the condition having failed, they ought not to be admitted, as in l. 2, C. de cond. inser., where it is clear

† that a fideicommissum left by an heir "if he should die without children" is not owed if he died leaving a grandson whom he had begotten from a daughter. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that in certain of the sons the condition was fulfilled, whence for their share the fideicommissum is owed, or the substitution ought to be admitted, as in l. Lucius, § Caio, ff. ad Trebel., because that would proceed when a substitution had been made or a fideicommissum left to each of those sons separately; but in our case it was made to all under a collective term, namely "if all should die without children." Therefore, since one of them had a son and died leaving him surviving, the condition fails, because it was not true to say that all died without children; in support of this is l. si fuerit and l. is qui ducenta, ff. de reb. dub. For a condition must be fulfilled in specific form, as in l. cui fundus and l. qui hæredi, ff. de condi. & demonst., and c. ad nostram, in 1, de iureiu. Secondly and principally for this side, the text in l. pen., C. de impub. & aliis substi., seems to stand, where it is said that a certain man, having instituted as heirs two sons under the age of puberty, added: "if both should die under the age of puberty, let that person be heir to them." Subsequently only one of them died in pupillary age, and it was asked whether the substitute ought to be admitted to the share of that one; and it is decided there that he is not, because since the substitution was made under a collective term, namely "if both should die in pupillary age," the condition was not fulfilled when only one died in pupillary age. And many things could be alleged for this side, but one must not insist on them much, since the words seem clearest for this side; therefore recourse to interpretation is in vain, as in l. ille aut ille and l. non aliter, ff. de leg. 3. But notwithstanding these points, which I judge truly not to stand in the way of our case at all, I think that these nephews by the brother ought to be admitted to the whole right that pertained to that deceased son over the said house and furnishings. I do not say, however, that they ought to be admitted to the shares of those who died in the first place without children: because these nephews were not simply substituted to the sons dying without children; rather, the sons were reciprocally substituted among themselves in such a way that one ought to succeed the other down to the last one; and thus in the inheritance of those three who first died without children, the two surviving sons equally succeeded by the disposition of the testator. Nor are the nephews, who were substituted in the third place, admitted, as in the said l. pen. and c. si pater, de test., li. 6; while to the fourth son, who died leaving a male son, those nephews could in no way succeed, neither in the share falling to them from his own person nor in the other portions falling to them from the persons of the deceased brothers: because not only are they themselves excluded, since in his person the condition under which they had been called failed, as in l. hæredes mei, § cum ita, but I even say that the last brother also is excluded from their succession: because although they were reciprocally substituted simply, yet it is tacitly understood, "if any should die without children," as is the notable and singular text between conjoined persons in l. cum auus, ff. de cond. & dem., where it is said that a certain man instituted a son and a grandson by another son, and added that if the grandsons died within twenty years, they ought to restore the inheritance to their paternal uncle; subsequently the grandson died below that age, leaving children; it seemed that, since in the substitution no mention had been made of children, he was bound to restore the inheritance to his paternal uncle according to the words of the testator; yet the contrary is decided there. For it is said that in the event of children the condition fails out of a conjecture of affection, as if less had been written than was said; and that text is, as I have said, singular in that the restitution was to be made not to a stranger, but to the testator's son; and yet it is understood, since a grandson by a son was instituted, "unless he should die leaving a son"; and by that text the notable points in l. cum acutissimi, C. de fideic., and l. generaliter, § cum autem, C. de inst. & subst., are greatly amplified, for those laws are usually understood when the restitution was to be made to a stranger, so that tacit mention of the instituted person's son is then understood to have been made; but it is the same where the instituted and the substituted are conjoined persons and each had his own portion. Thus it must be said in the matter at hand that although the sons were substituted to one another with no mention made of their children, nevertheless it had to be understood "unless one should die with children"; the said l. cum auus. Wherefore I would conclude that the fourth son, who for his half had succeeded the three brothers who died before him without children according to the testator's substitution, transmitted the entire right pertaining to him to his son, and as to his person the condition completely failed, both with respect to the sons and with respect to the nephews, as is evident from the aforesaid. But the whole doubt remains with respect to the share pertaining to the last son, both from his own person and from the person of those three brothers who died before him without children, to whom he succeeded for a half according to the disposition of the testator: whether that share ought to come to these nephews? And indeed, if that son of the brother were living or had lived at the time of the death of this last Nicola, the matter would be more doubtful through the notable remarks in l. quidam testamento proculum, ff. de uul. & pup., and l. hæredes mei, § cum ita, ad Treb., and l. pen., C. de impu. But it is not necessary to dispute this, since he was already deceased, and there survived only this Nicola, who died without his own children and without children of the deceased brothers. In which case I think, as I said above, that these nephews ought to come to the entire right that pertained to the said Nicola over that house and furnishings from his own person and from that of the others to whom he succeeded: I am moved principally by the text of the said l. hæredes mei, § cum ita, where this seems expressed. For there a father instituted his two sons and added that "if both shall have departed this life without children, I will that the whole inheritance pass to my granddaughter Claudia." Subsequently one of the sons died with children; the other, however, died afterward without children. It is decided there that the substituted granddaughter Claudia is admitted to the share of him who died without children, and thus into the share of him in whom the condition was fulfilled, although the substitution had been made through a collective term, as "if both should die without children," etc. The text gives the reason there: that this is admitted not on account of the words, because they entirely resist it—since it was true that both did not die without children—but on account of the deceased's intention, which ought to be looked to, she had to be admitted. Thus punctually it happens in our case: for although it had been said "if all should die without children," etc., nevertheless, since in the person of the last one the condition was fulfilled, and what is more, no one had remained from the earlier brothers, these nephews ought to be admitted not from the meaning of the words, but on account of the presumed intention of the testator. Secondly, this seems openly proved from the reasoning of l. pen., C. de impu. & aliis subst., by adducing it otherwise than I adduced it above.

† For where, after two sons under the age of puberty were instituted, a direct substitution was made through a collective term, namely, "if both shall have died in pupillary age, let such a person be heir"; and subsequently only one dying in pupillary age, it is decided there that the substitute ought not to be admitted to that one's portion on account of the presumed intention of the testator: because it is to be presumed that the father thought that to the one dying first his brother ought to succeed, and thus that on account of filial love he substituted them to one another. Therefore, from the reasoning of the text, which ought to be attended to in amplifying or restricting the said l. cum pater, § dulcissimis, ff. de leg. 2, it is openly concluded that if that presumed intention of the testator, which is caused by the love of the children, had not existed (arg. in the said l. cum accutissimi), the substitute would have come into the portion of him in whom the condition was fulfilled, even though it was not fulfilled in the person of both, no matter how much it had been said "if both," etc. And in this respect that text, thus adduced, is quite remarkable for our case; and by that text the objection that could be made against the said l. hæredes mei is removed, namely that that law speaks of a fideicommissary restitution. For it is the same in a direct one, where a substitution was made through a collective term in the aforesaid manner, as is proved in the said l. pen., and Bartolus expressly maintained in both places; and what he himself noted in l. quidam testamento proculum, ff. de uul. & pu., supports this. Furthermore, in our case there is no room for a direct substitution, since this last brother had died after pupillary age, and the substitution was made through common and direct words, according to what is noted in l. Centurio, ff. de uul. pup., and c. si pater, de testa., lib. 6. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that in our case the substitution was not made through a collective term, as in the said § cum autem and in the said l. pen., because the contrary is true, since the word "all" is more collective than the word "both," and in our subject matter Bartolus equated them in the said l. pen. and in the said § cum ita. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that in § cum ita the testator first spoke singularly and distributively: "If any of my sons shall have departed this life first without children, let him restore his share to the surviving brother," etc., because this has nothing to do with the point. For that distributive and reciprocal substitution is not referred to those substituted there in the second place under a collective term, but to the brothers themselves originally instituted. And thus it happens punctually in our fact: for here the testator first instituted the sons; then he substituted them singularly to one another, and secondly, or in their place, he substituted these nephews under a collective term; so that I do not see that the case has any doubt on this point, and most clearly
† Bartolus confirms this in the said passages. Thirdly and principally, it is proved thus:

† in last wills, of whatever quality they may be, whether it is a direct substitution, or a fideicommissary one, or a condition, or a testament, or a codicil, the express, tacit, or conjectured intention of the disposer ought to be attended to in the first place, as in l. in conditionibus, ff. de condit. & demon., and l. non aliter, de lega. 3, and l. cum acutissimi, C. de fideicommis., and l. generaliter, C. de institu. & substi., and the said l. penul., de impu. & aliis substi., and the said l. hæres mei, with countless similar ones; to such a degree that that which is evident from conjectures is called obvious, as in l. licet imperator, ff. de lega. 1. And from natural reason we can conjecture the intention of the deceased, as in the laws previously alleged, and l. scire oportet, § sufficit, ff. de excu. tuto., supports this, as does what Cynus notes in l. non dubium, C. de legi., and Baldus in l. maximum vitium, C. de lib. pręt. But, for God's sake, let us see: in our case, what was the testator's primary intention? For he undoubtedly wished to favor his own sons and grandsons by sons above all; but, they failing, he did not wish to give his sons the free capacity of disposing of that house, but wished to prefer the nephews by his brother; and perhaps he also did this for the sake of his own memory, lest his own house pass to men of another kinship. But since in our case, at the time of the last one dying, none of the sons or grandsons by them existed, what then can stand in the way of these nephews being admitted, at least for the right pertaining to this last one, in whom the condition was purified? Truly nothing, except an empty and bare sound of words, about which the jurisconsult did not care in the said l. hæredes mei, nor in the said l. Lucius, § Caio, nor in the said l. pen., and deservedly so, lest words prevail over intention, since the intention ought not to serve the words, but the words ought to serve the intention, as the text says in cap. secundo requiris, de app. Furthermore and fourthly, where there is the same reason in part as to the part as there is in the whole as to the whole, the argument from the whole to the part is valid: l. quæ de tota, ff. de pet. hære., and in l. an pars, ff. pro derelict., and c. pastoralis, § item cum totum, de off. deleg. But if all the sons of the testator had died without children, these nephews by the brother are called in solidum to that substitution; therefore, in the share of this one, who in part died without the other brothers substituted in the first place and without children from the brothers, these nephews ought to be called, since in the share of this one no reason appears why these nephews ought not to be admitted. For in his person the favor toward the children of the brothers who died before him does not concur, since none was surviving at the time of the death of this Nicola. The primary intention of the testator is therefore qualified in this: that he wished to prefer the nephews by his brother to the bare judgment of his sons. And through the aforesaid things, the response to the contrary arguments is plainly evident. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One who has the right of presenting can present whomsoever he wishes.
2. The right of patronage in a church is acquired on only three grounds.
3. One is made a patron by constructing a new church.
casus: A certain Lord Iacobus of Recanati disposed in his last will and testament, among other things, as follows: 'Item, upon the occurrence of the aforesaid condition, he substituted the high altar of the church of Santa Maria de Platea of Recanati in a certain parcel of vineyard land, etc., which property he willed to be held and cultivated for the said altar for perpetual divine worship, and that one priest must be elected for the aforesaid perpetual divine worship, who is bound and must celebrate the divine office at the said altar, as the sanction of law demands and requires, for the soul of the said testator and of his parents; which priest to celebrate in the aforesaid manner must be elected by the said Lord Ser Claudius, if he is then alive, but after the death of Ser Claudius by his sons; and thus subsequently in perpetuity from sons to sons successively. And if all the aforesaid should not be living, he willed that the said priest be elected by the priors of the confraternity of Santa Lucia who are in office for the time being.' It is to be noted, however, that the aforesaid church of Santa Maria, whose altar was substituted, is a monastery of the Order of Blessed Sylvester or of Monte Sano, which monastery is governed by priors and monks assigned conventually and monastically by the General of the said order, which is properly the Order of Saint Benedict, and it is a monastery suitably endowed with possessions and goods. Now inquiry is made concerning three matters. First, whether the said Ser Claudius can obtain the right of patronage by virtue of the aforesaid bequest. Second, whether a secular priest, or a monk of the said monastery, can or must be elected, presented, and instituted. Third, what the person to be presented and instituted ought to receive from the said property.
body: Having implored the aid of the Savior Jesus Christ, I shall address in order the first doubt, upon whose decision the other doubts depend. And it seems at first that the said Ser Claudius and successively the others mentioned above acquired the right of patronage of the said altar: because this right of patronage is acquired by gift, 26. quæstio. 7. c. filiis, noted by the gloss in capitul. piæ mentis, in the same causa, and noted by Ioan. And. in capitu. 1. de iure patro. and glo. 73. distin. in summa. But the said lord Iacobus endowed the said high altar; therefore he acquired the right of patronage. Nor does it stand in the way that he did not construct it, because the said c. filiis speaks alternatively, namely constructed or endowed, and thus it suffices to exercise either of those acts of liberality, as in the rule, in alternatiuis, de regu. iu. lib. 6. and in c. inter cætera, de rescript.; and this acquisition of the right of patronage proceeds not only with respect to a church constructed or endowed, but also with respect to a chapel, as in c. nobis, de iu. patro. Nor does it matter whether that right is acquired in a secular church or in a monastery, since the law makes no distinction, but generally conferred the privilege upon the one endowing, or founding, or constructing, so that from the aforesaid acts, or either of them, he acquires this right, as in the said cap. filiis, de iure patro. throughout; and through these considerations that objection seems to be removed, namely that the aforesaid church of Santa Maria is a monastery of monks. For this does not impede the birth of such a right, since even the very body of a monastery can be under the power of a patron, 16. q. 7. c. monasterium, and in the said ca. nobis, in prin. and in cap. cum dilectus, de consue. with similar texts. From these points it is inferred as to the second doubt,

† that a secular priest can be elected, because he who holds the right of presenting can present whomsoever he wishes. For in this the laws intended to indulge the patron himself, provided he is otherwise suitable, as in capitu. 1. 16. quæst. 5. and in the same causa, quæst. 7. decernimus, and in c. pastoralis, de iure patro. and ca. cum dilectus, eo. tit. Indeed, it seems that he must elect a secular and not a monk, because a monk cannot be promoted to a benefice without cure of souls, as in cap. super eo, and what is noted there, de regula. noted fully in ca. quod Dei timorem, de stat. regul. But notwithstanding the aforesaid, which truly do not stand in the way in our case, I deem the contrary opinion to be entirely truer in the case set forth: namely, that neither the said Ser Claudius, nor the sons of the said lord Iacobus, nor any others whomsoever have obtained, or are able to obtain, the right of patronage in the said church of Santa Maria or its high altar from the aforesaid institution; and I have been moved to hold this opinion and conclusion on multiple grounds. And first,

† because the right of patronage in a church is acquired on three grounds alone: namely, by the construction of the church, 16. quæst. 7. c. monasterium; by the donation of the church, in the same causa and quæstio, c. filiis uel nepotibus; and by the provision of the ground for founding the church, 18. quæstio. 2. cap. abbatem, and in capitu. ad audientiam. 2. de eccle. ædifi. and capit. 3. de iure pa. and noted by Ioan. And. capitu. 1. eod. titu. and the gloss in capitu. piæ mentis. 16. quæst. 7. Hence it is that from diverse acts three patrons of the same church can be created: as, for instance, because one endowed it, another gave the land where the church was built, and another built or fabricated it by himself or at his own expense, as noted by Ioan. And. in capitu. nobis, de iure patro.; to which makes what is noted by the gloss 63. distinct. in summa. But no other mode of acquiring the right of patronage has been handed down by law; whence, if someone has left or given anything to a church beyond the aforesaid causes, he is not made a patron, but is called a benefactor, as noted by Ioan. And. in the said capitu. nobis; to which makes capitu. requisisti, de testa. and what is noted by the gloss in capit. 3. de iure pa. But since in our case the said lord Iacobus the testator neither built, founded, nor endowed the church of Santa Maria itself nor its altar; therefore he could not acquire the right of patronage for himself or his successors. The consequence and the major premise are manifest; the minor premise is proved. For it is clear that he did not construct, nor did he found it, since it had been founded long ago; nor did he even endow it, since it had also already been endowed at the time of its foundation; nor is it required that the high altar of a church must be endowed, since it is a part of the church, but it suffices that the church itself be endowed, as is sufficiently implied in capitu. nemo, de consecr. distinct. 1. and in cap. cum sicut, de consecr. eccle. uel alta. Indeed, if the words of the testator are truly weighed, he did not leave the said piece of land as an endowment, but simply instituted the altar itself for perpetual divine worship; and thus he is rather called a benefactor than a patron, which Ioan. Andr. more expressly maintained in our case in the said capitu. 1., where he says that even if someone were to give something, even something great, before the foundation of a church, he does not thereby acquire patronage, because he did not give it by reason of endowment. But in our case he not only did not give it for an endowment, but he also gave it after the foundation, endowment, and construction of the church; therefore he by no means acquired the right of patronage. And this consideration truly admits of no doubt to the contrary. Secondly, I am principally moved because the said church of Santa Maria was already constructed and consecrated together with its high altar; whence, even assuming that the said lord Iacobus had left the said piece of land for an endowment, he would not nevertheless thereby acquire the right of patronage in a place already consecrated.

† For one is made patron by constructing a church anew; because just as a father brings a son from non-being into being, as noted in the said capitu. 1. and the said capitu. nobis, and the said capitu. piæ mentis, so one is made patron before the consecration of the thing. But in a place already consecrated beforehand, one cannot be made patron by donating something to it in place of an endowment or by repairing it; because since the right of patronage is a kind of servitude in a religious church, and sacred places do not admit of a servitude, as in l. seruitutes, §. fin. ff. de seruitu. and elsewhere the text says that what ceases to be of human right does not admit of a servitude, as in l. caueri, ff. communia prædio. And this opinion in our terms is affirmed by the gloss in the said capitu. piæ mentis. 16. quæst. 7. and the doctors commonly follow it, and especially Inn. upon the rubrica de iure patro. and Ioan. And. in c. 1. eo. tit. Yet Inn. excepts one case, namely when a church already consecrated is without an endowment, and someone wishes to endow it. For then the right of patronage is acquired: because spiritual things cannot exist without temporal things, 1. q. 3. c. si quis obiecerit. Which nevertheless Io. An. limited in the said c., provided he does this with the consent of the diocesan: which the gloss in c. 3. eodem titu. affirmed with respect to repair; for then, by favor to the church, it is feigned that this act preceded the consecration, arg. c. tanta, qui fil. sint legi. He also limits this to proceed when a master cannot be had from the one causing it to be consecrated, or even from the consecrator himself, on the argument of the things noted in the said c. cum sicut, de consecrat. eccl. uel alta., as if in subsidium and not otherwise is this admitted; but since in our case neither of these occurred, because the church was endowed. Likewise, assuming that it had not been endowed, nevertheless the endowment was not given with the authority of the diocesan so that the right of patronage might be acquired anew; therefore the acquisition of the right of patronage ceases entirely. For I think it absurd that a layman, by leaving an estate at the discretion of his own free will to a church already consecrated or to its high altar, should from this entirely be made patron of the church or of the high altar. Whence, since the right of patronage is acquired by laymen out of the mere grace and tolerance of the church, since by common law they are not capable of this right, as it is annexed to the spiritual according to those things that are read and noted in c. quoniam, de iure patrona. and by Inno. in cap. quod sicut, de electio., the ability for this acquisition must not be relaxed, but restricted, as in the rule, odia restringi, de reg. iu. lib. 6. and in l. quod uero contra rationem, ff. de legib. And this second consideration also admits of no contrary. Thirdly, I principally consider that on another ground also this man could not acquire the right of patronage in the said church of Santa Maria, since neither from construction nor from donation does anyone acquire the right of patronage unless he does this with the consent of the diocesan, that is, of the bishop, or of one holding episcopal right in the place, as in our case is the General of these friars of Santa Maria; this is expressly proved in the said cap. nobis, de iurepatrona. For it would be quite absurd that anyone at his own pleasure could construct a church anew or erect an altar anew, since laymen cannot handle these spiritual matters on their own authority, as in cap. 2. de iud. and 16. quæstio. 7. c. omnes basilicæ. Ioan. And. noted in the said cap. nobis, through that text, that it does not suffice to ask the advice of the diocesan, but rather it is necessary to have his consent; if, however, he were unwilling to consent without just cause, he could be compelled by a superior, on the argument of cap. 1. de iure patronatus. In our case, however, this lord Iacobus did not have the authority or consent of the diocesan; therefore from his own act he could not acquire the right of patronage, especially in the high altar. For if he had said this to the General of the Order, perhaps he would in no way have consented, nor even could he have consented, since this is contrary to the aforesaid laws; and this consideration is also conclusive. On a fourth ground the right of patronage can be excluded, because even if the aforesaid concurred in our case—which in truth do not concur—nevertheless, taking into account that a secular cleric cannot be beneficed in a church of regular clergy, as is proved without caviling the letter in c. fin. §. prohibemus, de statu regu., where it is said that even with the abbot and monks consenting, a secular cleric cannot be beneficed so as to have a title in a monastery; therefore, a fortiori the acquisition does not proceed in our case, where the monks not only did not consent, but even utterly object. And although Hostiensis there, in truth destroying the letter, says that this applies when a secular cleric wishes to be of the body of the regulars by giving a vote in chapter and doing similar things as one of the college—whence he says it is otherwise if the cleric were willing to be content with his benefice and to officiate the church without being of the college of the monks—nevertheless this statement is not true and utterly conflicts with that letter. For there it is simply prohibited that anyone be received to a prebend in a regular church, and with respect to those already received it is provided that they do not mingle with the assemblies of the monks. For if this were permitted, as Hostiensis said, the text would not have restricted itself there to those already received, tolerating them, but would have provided this both with respect to those received and those to be received. Whence the sense of the letter was this, if well weighed: that henceforth no one should be received to a prebend in a regular church, but the Pope wished there to tolerate those already received, lest they be deprived of a right already acquired, with this limitation, that they do not mingle with the assemblies and congregation of the monks; similar in c. 1. de reli. do. li. 6. And this opinion against Hostiensis is followed by the said Antonius in the said c. fi., and in my lecturing I have always held against Hostiensis, at least as to our case where the monks resist; and for this, beyond others, I cite c. dudum. 18. q. 2., where it is said that secular clerics must not in any way go to celebrate in a regular church unless they are invited by the monks; and even a bishop cannot publicly celebrate in a monastery, even one subject to him, if the monks are unwilling, lest through the concourse of the people the monks, who ought to lead a solitary life, be scandalized, as is proved in c. luminoso, and c. 2. and 3. 18. q. 2.; to the same makes 16. q. 1. c. placuit, and c. si cupis. Nor do I believe that Hostiensis would have contradicted this case. For he speaks of when the abbot and monks wish to receive someone to be beneficed in their church; and we are speaking of when, against their will, these persons wish to acquire the right of patronage in their church, especially in the high altar, which I judge can in no way be done, lest by the approach of seculars they suffer any scandal, and lest their church suffer this servitude. I conclude therefore that from the aforesaid institution the right of patronage was not acquired by anyone; and from this it is inferred for the decision of the other doubts. For I say that no one is to be elected or presented: because if the right of patronage ceases, every effect that is caused by it ceases, as in c. cum cessante, de appel. For that piece of land is acquired by the church of Santa Maria for perpetual divine worship, that is, for the necessary uses of the church and of its persons, by the argument in c. pastoralis, de his, quæ fiunt a præla., since the institution was made purely, and the other conditions added and adjoined by the testator are held as not adjoined, since by law they cannot be made, as is proved in a similar matter in c. significatum, de præben. Nay more, if the testator had left that piece of land under the condition of having the patronage, nevertheless, since that condition is contrary to law, as is clear from the aforesaid, it must be held as not adjoined, and the bequest remains, as in l. conditiones, and l. si filius, and l. quidam in suo, ff. de condi. insti. with similar texts. The friars of the said place, however, must pray to God for the soul of the testator, just as they do for their other benefactors. And let these things suffice; for it is not expedient to respond to the opposing arguments, because the response is abundantly clear from the aforesaid. Nicolaus Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Wherever a sentence involves danger to souls, the exception of res judicata does not bar, whether it was adjudicated in the civil forum or in the ecclesiastical forum.
2. Any sentence from which an appeal was not taken regularly passes into res judicata.
3. A sentence makes law between the parties, no matter how much it was rendered against the right of the litigant.
4. Evangelical denunciation does not proceed, unless it is clearly proved that the denouncer acts against conscience.
5. When a judge narrates certain matters in a sentence or in court, with the party present and not contradicting, such narrative words prove to the prejudice of the non-contradicting party.
6. A party succumbing in a claim for an estate is not admitted when wishing to claim the fruits on the occasion of the estate.
body: IN the cause and dispute pending between Giovanni on the one part, and Antonio his son and heir of Pietro on the other, the aid of the Savior Jesus Christ having been invoked, it seems first that the said Giovanni ought to be heard on his petition, notwithstanding the exception of res judicata raised by master Antonio. And first, it is proved thus.

† Wherever a sentence involves danger to souls, the exception of res judicata does not bar, whether it was adjudicated in the civil forum or in the ecclesiastical forum. The first point is remarkably proved in c. 2, de exce., li. 6. The second in c. lator, together with the gloss, and in c. consanguinei, and in c. tenor, de re iudi. But the sentence at issue in our case involves danger to souls; therefore, from it the exception of res judicata does not lie. The minor premise is proved: for since it is presupposed that the said contract of loan was usurious, and by virtue of it a great amount of money was paid in usury to the said Pietro, and the opposite was adjudicated, the usurer is sustained by that sentence in his sin, since sin is not forgiven unless the usury is restored, seeing that it can be restored, as in c. cum tu, de usur., and in regula peccatum, de reg. iur., lib. 6. Likewise, the said Antonio, son and heir of the said Pietro, sins in not giving satisfaction for the soul of the deceased, as he is bound to do, as in c. a nobis, de sen. excom., and in c. literis, de rapt., and in c. fi., de sepul. Nor does it bar if it is said that an appeal was not taken from such a sentence: because through this the defect of the sentence is not purged with respect to the soul of the one obtaining an unjust sentence, as noted by Innocent in c. quia plerique, de immu. eccle.; to the same effect is what is read and noted in l. Iulianus, ff. de condi. indeb., where it is held that a natural obligation is not removed by an unjust sentence, nor is a natural obligation induced by it, as noted by Bartolus in l. ab eo, C. quomodo & qndo iudex. Secondly and principally, it is adduced in favor of the said Giovanni: because the exception of res judicata bars when the action is brought for the same thing; it is otherwise if an action is now brought for something other than at first, as in l. quæritur, with the two following laws, ff. de excep. rei iudi., and c. abbate sane, de re iudi., lib. 6. But in our case an action is now brought for something else; therefore, the exception of res judicata ought not to impede, even presupposing that that sentence had passed into res judicata. The minor is proved: first, it was not only litigated whether the loan was usurious or gratuitous, and it was adjudicated that it was gratuitous; whence, presupposing that from the beginning it had been gratuitous, nevertheless usury could subsequently have been paid so that it would not be reclaimed, argument in c. consuluit, de usur. For these things are compatible, nor does the fact that something happens to be absent prove that it is absent, as in c. 2, de transla. præla., and l. neque natales, C. de proba. Now, however, it is found that it was paid unduly and through usurious depravity so that it would not be reclaimed, and thus an action is now brought for something entirely different than at first; for in the first judgment usury was not reclaimed, but it was only opposed that that contract had been simulated and illicit and made in fraud of usury. Thirdly, the said Giovanni seems to be admissible on another ground, even if the aforesaid did not avail. For since the said Pietro at the end of his life mandated the restitution of whatever had come to him on the occasion of illicit traffic or contracts, he seems tacitly to have remitted the oath and every obstacle by which the said Giovanni had previously been unable to make a demand, as seems to be proved in c. ad nostram ij, de iureiur., according to one interpretation. And although the aforesaid appear to urge in favor of the said Giovanni, I deem that one must incline toward the contrary opinion, to hold which I am moved on three grounds. First and principally:

† that regularly any sentence from which an appeal is not taken passes into res judicata, so that by either law an exception based upon it can be raised against one suing anew, as in c. cum inter, de re iudi., and c. abbate sane, under the same title, lib. 6, and in l. cum quæritur, with the two following laws, ff. de excep. rei iudi. And this exception was introduced to uphold the rigor of the law so that there would be an end to litigation, as the gloss notes in cap. pastoralis, § quia verò, de offic. delegat., in l. qui exceptione, ff. de conditio. indebit. This rule is not found to be impaired except in certain cases expressed by the law, as in a matrimonial cause, and in certain others according to what is read and noted in the said cap. lator, among which cases our case is not found, namely when an action is brought for the reclaiming of usury. And although it is generally said that wherever danger to the soul is involved a sentence does not pass into res judicata, as noted by the gloss and Innocent in c. inter monasterium, de re iudi., according to the gloss in c. lator, under the same title, and more clearly by Hostiensis there and in c. consanguinei, yet this is understood of a sin that is not remissible by the parties, as the gloss holds in the said cap. lator, and in c. iuravit, de proba., and more clearly Antonio de Butrio in the said c. lator, as for example when a sentence is pronounced unjustly against the matrimonial bond, or in favor of a marriage when consanguinity or affinity in degrees prohibited by divine or human laws stands in the way; but it is otherwise where it is pronounced unjustly in favor of a marriage when no impediment stands in the way. For then it passes into res judicata, because the defect of the sentence is remissible by the parties. For since it prejudices only the party, it passes into res judicata because the defect of the sentence is remissible by the parties, as is proved in capitulo quod ad consultationem, de re iudic., and l. ab eo, C. quomodo & quando iudex, where it is said that he who does not appeal from a sentence is seen to grant his consent, and elsewhere the text said that by not appealing he is seen to confirm the sentence, in l. fi., C. de senten. quæ sine certa quantita. In those matters, however, in which the defect of the sentence is not remissible by the parties, this construed consent ceases, since the parties could not expressly approve an unjust sentence, as in capitulo si diligenti, de foro competen. But in our case, even presupposing that the sentence was unjust by which it was pronounced that the contract of loan had been gratuitous and licit and neither fictitious nor simulated, yet the defect of the sentence was remissible by the parties, because the debtor can remit usury to the creditor, as noted by the gloss and the Doctors in regula peccatum, de regulis iuris, libro 6, and Federico, consilio 18, and Giovanni d'Andrea in the additiones to the Speculum in the title de usu., in the 3rd column; therefore such a sentence passed into res judicata, and especially beyond doubt in our case, in which the said Giovanni, the debtor, expressly acquiesced in the sentence, and presented himself as ready for the execution of the sentence as it was contained therein, and afterwards willingly receiving a postponement for payment took an oath to pay, and thus renounced every right to speak of the injustice of the sentence, as in l. ad solutionem, C. de re iudica. Hence the laws say

† that a sentence makes law between the parties, no matter how much it was rendered against the right of the litigant, as in the said capitulo cum inter, and l. ingenuum, ff. de statu. homi., and it is accepted as the truth, as in l. res iudicata, ff. de re iudica.; therefore doubts concerning the injustice of the sentence can no longer be revived. Nor does it bar if it is said that he who knowingly obtains an unjust sentence sins, as noted by Innocent in the said c. quia plerique, and Bartolus in the Extravagante ad reprimendum, on the word 'denunciationem'—which is evident from the fact that by an unjust sentence a natural obligation is neither removed nor induced, as noted by Bartolus in the said l. ab eo, and in l. Iulianus, ff. de cond. indebi.—for by reason of sin the one who obtains an unjust sentence, though he did not appeal, ought to be heard when defeated. For to this a twofold answer is made. First, that the injustice of the sentence is not established, and in case of doubt the passing into res judicata stands in the way, because it is presumed to have been rendered justly, and this is a presumption of law and by law (iuris et de iure), against which proof to the contrary is not admitted, except through the confession of the prevailing party, as noted by Innocent in the said cap. quia plerique; to this what is read and noted in l. is qui fidem, de sponsa., is relevant. Furthermore, this same reasoning applies in every unjust sentence; for he who knowingly obtains an unjust sentence always sins, as noted by Innocent in the said c. quia plerique, and Bartolus in the places cited above, yet on account of this sin the adverse party is not heard, since he did not appeal, and he was able to acquiesce in the sentence to his own prejudice; indeed, even to the prejudice of the Church this passing into res judicata stands in the way, as in the said cap. cum inter, and cap. cum semper, under the same title, by reason of the presumption of justice, so that there may be an end to litigation. Furthermore and with greater force, in our case there intervened the express consent of this Giovanni, as is stated in the fact-pattern; for he expressly consented to the sentence, and thus even as to the one obtaining it, every defect, if there was any in the sentence, was removed, and a natural obligation was induced, which arises from consent, as noted by Bartolus in the said l. ab eo; relevant is l. stichum, § naturalis, ff. de solu., and l. cum amplius, § is natura debet, ff. de re. iu. And by this the first contrary argument made above is removed. For it ought to be understood as applying when the defect of the sentence is not remissible on the part of the party; likewise when the express consent of the party did not intervene. Indeed, I think further that even by way of evangelical denunciation this Giovanni ought not to be heard, both because the sin was remitted through the express consent of this Giovanni, and because the justice of the sentence ought no longer to be disputed, and this Bartolus expressly affirmed in the said Extravagante ad reprimendum, on the word
† 'denunciationem'. I allege another, better and incontrovertible reason in our case.

† Evangelical denunciation does not proceed unless it is clearly proved that the denounced party acts against his conscience, as I have read and noted, and especially by Innocent in cap. novit, de iud. But since here the action is against Antonio, the heir of the said Pietro, who is by no means presumed to have knowledge of the character of the said contract of loan, but entirely had a good conscience, since he has a sentence in his favor, which he must presume to be just, as in the laws cited above; therefore, even evangelical denunciation cannot have a place; with greater reason the said Giovanni ought not to be heard when seeking directly, especially since he comes against his own oath. And let these suffice as to obtaining victory on the first ground. The second ground for prevailing in the cause, by which I was also moved, is the confession of the said Giovanni; for since he confessed in court that the said loan was gratuitous, and acknowledged the debt as true and just, as appears from the tenor of the sentence, he ought not now to be admitted to prove the contrary, since a confession voluntarily made cannot be revoked even by proving the contrary, except up to the definitive sentence, as in c. fi., de confe., and l. error facti, C. de iur. & fac. igno.; to the same effect is c. per tuas, de probatio., and l. generaliter, C. de non nu. pec. Nor does it bar if it is said that the confession is established only through narrative words of the sentence, which do not provide proof, as in c. si papa, de priuil., li. 6.

† For I say that when a judge narrates something in a sentence or in court in the presence of the party and without his contradiction, such narrative words provide proof to the prejudice of the non-contradicting party, as is proved in l. 1, C. de rela., and there Bartolus expressly affirms this and says it is well to be noted, just as in our case the said Giovanni was not only present and silent, but expressly consented to the sentence. On the third ground the said Antonio can prevail, because one ought not to be admitted to prove that which, even if proved, is not relevant, as in c. cum contingat, ff. de offi. dele., and in l. ad probationem, C. de prob. But even presupposing that the said Giovanni proved that he paid certain sums of money to the said Pietro over and above the payment, he would not by this prevail; therefore he ought not to be admitted to prove this. The minor premise is proved: whatever is paid or given by a debtor in the absence of a pact, gratuitously and out of affection, can be licitly received by the creditor, for the other element which is formal in usury is lacking, as Giovanni d'Andrea fully notes in regula peccatum, de re. iu., li. 6, in the Mercuriales; relevant is c. tua, de simo., and a good text in capit. sicut episcopum, 1, q. 2. But in our case the loan was gratuitous, as Giovanni himself confessed; therefore what was paid gratuitously cannot be reclaimed; indeed, even if it had not been gratuitous from the beginning, since it was pronounced that it was gratuitous, and he himself expressly consented to the sentence, everything and the whole of that which he could have reclaimed seems to have been remitted; for he who consented to the antecedent consented to the consequent, as in c. 3, de consti., and in l. oratio, ff. de sponsa. Nor does it bar if it is said that although it was gratuitous from the beginning, nevertheless ex post facto usury was paid. For this can in no way stand, because the plaintiff is deemed to bring into the suit all his right that he has at the time the judgment is begun, as in l. solemus, ff. de iudi., and c. cum ecclesia Sutrina, de cau. pos. & prop., and c. abbate sanè, de re iud., lib. 6.
