Whence, since in the judgment he did not contend whether from the beginning the contract was illicit and usurious, but rather there was dispute over his rights existing at the time of the sentence—which is clearly evident, because against the petition Giovanni did not except that the contract was usurious, and thus clearly referred himself to the time of the sentence; and even if he had not said so, it is sufficiently tacitly understood, since in the judgment the contest was over the right existing at the time of the sentence—therefore, since the said Giovanni lost and confessed that that contract was licit, he is seen by consequence to have wished to remit every right belonging to him, presupposing that it had been illicit. For this usurious question, or the reclaiming of usuries, depends on that question: whether the contract was usurious. For if it was not usurious, nothing can be reclaimed, since it is presumed to have been given as a gift. From which an inference is drawn for the solution of the other contrary argument: for I say that an action is not now brought for something other than at first. For this is folded into the subject matter of the first question.

† For he who was defeated in claiming an estate is not admitted when wishing to claim the fruits by reason of the estate, l. fundi, and l. fundum, ff. de except., and l. si quis eum, ff. de except. rei iudi.; so it happens point for point here. What is finally objected concerning the security or instruction of the said Pietro, that every illicit extortion should be restored, does not bar: for I say that it does not extend to this case, since here it is denied that the contract was illicit, nor ought he to be admitted to prove the contrary, standing the presumption of law and by law (iuris et de iure) which arose from the sentence, as I said above. Likewise, from the remission already presumed, as I said before, a right was acquired for the said Pietro. Likewise, a right has now been acquired for him from the sentence, not only from the pact; and therefore that security ought not to be extended to this quasi-contract, by the argument of those things which Bartolus notes in l. more, ff. de acquiren. hæredit., and in l. apud Iulianum, ff. ex quib. cau. in pos. ea. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Privileges ought to be perpetual.
2. A city, although it is under lordship, can nonetheless by contract make a citizen someone who is otherwise not a citizen.
3. A lessor, if he has promised under a certain penalty not to expel the lessee during the term of the lease, is understood [to have done so] if the lessee has paid the agreed rent.
4. A father, if he has promised not to disinherit his son, is understood [to have done so] unless the son has given cause for disinheritance.
5. A city that is not free cannot impose a tax on its citizens, even for public utility, without the consent of the prince.
6. A city cannot cause someone to be regarded as a non-citizen, except in matters pertaining to the city itself.
7. One who directly acts contrary to a privilege granted to him loses the privilege by a single contravention.
8. If a privilege is granted to do something, and it is not done within a decade [?], the privilege is lost.
casus: The fact upon which counsel is sought is submitted in these terms: At the time when the Perugian citizens were living under a popular government, so that de facto they recognized no superior or lord, they solemnly granted to all Sienese citizens full right of citizenship both in the payment of gabelles and in any other matters whatsoever, both in bringing actions and in defending, so that they ought to be held and regarded as native citizens of the city of Perugia. And this if and insofar as the Sienese citizens themselves granted equal immunity and citizenship to the Perugians; and by virtue of this conditional and reciprocal grant, an equal immunity was issued by the Sienese citizens toward the Perugian citizens. And in the course of time, the city of Perugia repeatedly lost its liberty; for it was subjugated by King Ladislaus, and successively by Braccio da Montone, and finally came under the lordship of the Roman Church, under whose shadow it currently rests at present. It also happened that for many, many years, both during the time of King Ladislaus and of Braccio and of the lordship of the Roman Church, the said privileges issued reciprocally were not observed, but Sienese citizens both in the payment of gabelles and in other matters were held and treated in Perugia as foreigners; and the same happened to the Perugians themselves in the city of Siena. Now, however, a certain Perugian citizen strives that the aforesaid citizenship be observed for him in the city of Siena, so that in all things he may be held and treated as a native Sienese citizen, as is contained in the grant of citizenship, while the Sienese citizens resist on account of the aforesaid causes. It is asked what the law is.
body: The assistance of Jesus Christ the Savior having been sought from the heart, it seems at first that the said Perugian can legally use the said citizenship in the city of Siena:

† both because privileges ought to be perpetual, 25 q. 2 c. 1 & 2 and in the rule decet, de reg. iur. in 6; and because they were granted to non-subjects, and consequently are irrevocable according to what is noted by Inn. in c. novit, de iudic.; and because they passed into a quasi-contract, since the Perugians granted citizenship and immunity to the Sienese on account of the grant to be made by them. Therefore such a grant is irrevocable according to what is read and noted, especially by Bart. in l. pen. and l. ambitiosam, ff. de decre. ab ordi. fac. Nor should the subsequent subjugation of the city of Perugia stand in the way:

† because although a city may be under a lord, it can nevertheless by contract make a citizen someone who is otherwise not a citizen, as is proved in l. 1 in prin. ff. ad munici.; and this Barto. openly confirms upon the same text according to the reading which has 'cives electio', in l. sal. C. de incol. lib. 10; the text together with the glossa in l. aedificia, ff. de verbo. signifi. supports this. Nor does non-observance in the case of certain citizens stand in the way: both because they did not allege this privilege; and because although some paid voluntarily and did not use that privilege, the privilege and liberty is not thereby renounced in other acts, as the notable text in l. voluntariae, C. de excu. tuto. seems to show; and because, since that privilege was granted to the whole people of the city, individual persons not constituting at least the greater part of the people could not tacitly renounce that privilege through their contravention, by the argument of the things noted by Inno. in c. accedentibus, de privi. For one can renounce a right and favor only insofar as it touches his own person, but not insofar as it touches the person of another; for this see what is read and noted in c. dilecti and c. si diligenti, de fo. compe. and in l. si quis in conscribendo, C. de pactis, and c. ad apostolicam, de reg. iu., with similar authorities. But since these have very little force in our case, I consider that the said Perugian cannot, against the will of the Sienese citizens, use that immunity and citizenship, since it was extinguished and taken away for the causes to be alleged below. I am moved to this opinion because the grants of the said immunity and citizenship were granted respectively and reciprocally. For no grant was in itself unconditional, but each was made with respect to the other that had been obtained, or was to be obtained. Whence the Perugians would not have granted that immunity to the Sienese except for the sake of obtaining a similar grant from the Sienese; and so conversely the Sienese would not have granted it except on account of the grant made to them by the Perugians, as this is sufficiently gathered from the tenor of both privileges. Therefore, once the grant made by the Perugians ceased, the grant made to them by the Sienese immediately ceased and was extinguished: because when the cause of a privilege ceases, the privilege ceases, in l. generaliter, C. de epis. & cle. and 16 q. 1 c. generaliter, with its glossa. The text in l. ex facto, and what is noted there, ff. de vul. & pup., and c. suggestum, de decimis, support this; and in argument the whole title ff. and C. de conditio. ob causam supports it, and most excellently supports it l. quaero, § inter locatorem, ff. loca., where it is held that

† if a lessor promised under a certain penalty not to expel the lessee during the time of the lease, that tacit condition with respect to which he leased is understood, namely, if the lessee pays the agreed rent; otherwise, however, if he ceases from payment, he can be expelled without fear of the penalty. And through that text Bartol. says there

† that if a father promised not to disinherit his son, it is understood unless the son gives cause for disinheritance, as in l. quidam cum filium, ff. de verbo. obligatio. Likewise, if I promised not to harm you, it is understood unless you commit a cause of offense, as l. qui servum, ff. de verbo. obliga. For that which is tacitly present is held as expressed, l. cum quis, ff. si certum peta. And generally Bartol. said that that § must be noted for all contracts in which something is promised mutually on both sides, so that one is not bound to fulfill effectively if everything has not been observed by the opposing party; l. Iulianus, § offerri, ff. de actio. emptio., and l. aediles, § fin. with the following law, ff. de aedi. edict., and the rule frustra fidem quis postulat, de reg. iu. lib. 6, and what is noted there by Io. And. and by Cyn. in l. cum proponas, C. de pact., support this; and the text in l. cum precibus, C. de praescrip. ver., and what is read and noted in cap. pervenit, de iureiur., and cap. constitutus, de poenis, and 33 quaest. 2 cap. quod Deo patri, also support this. That, moreover, once liberty was lost, the immunity granted by the Perugian citizens vanished, at least for the greater part, is easily proved. To impose taxes, to exact tolls, to institute and lay upon others gabelle and ordinary and extraordinary levies pertains to the prince, and not to a non-free city, as is proved in l. vectigalia, ff. de pub., and in l. unica, quae sint regalia, col. 10, and in cap. super quibusdam, de verbo. significa.; it is more expressly proved in l. 2, C. nova vectiga.; nay, Barto. said more in l. unica, C. de superindi. lib. 10, namely,

† that a non-free city cannot impose a collection on its citizens, even for the public utility, without the prince's consent, although it may impose it for an imminent necessity of the city itself to pay debts; and thus must be understood what is read and noted in l. 4, § actori, ff. de re iudica., and l. 1, ff. quod cuiusque univers. no. But just as a non-free city cannot impose these burdens, so, and even more strongly, it cannot grant an exemption to anyone, because it cannot issue a statute, ordinance, or privilege to the prejudice of the rights of the prince, as Barto. notes in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu., and it is clearly proved in l. omnes, C. de ann. & tribu., where it is evident that no one short of the prince can grant immunity from rights owed to the prince, and there by Bartol. To the same effect serves what is read and noted in l. fin. § si quis professus, ff. de public., and excellently capitul. venientes, de iureiurand.; and specifically in our case Bartol. wished this in l. si maritus, ff. de adulte., where he says

† that a city cannot cause someone to be held as a non-citizen except in things pertaining to the city itself; but it is otherwise as to things pertaining to the Prince. Since, therefore, the city of Perugia granted immunity and citizenship to the Sienese citizens with respect to not paying gabelle and tolls, all of which pertain to the prince, therefore once liberty was lost that privilege was annihilated, especially against the Roman Church, which is truly the mistress of that city. Whence, the lord of the Church having been expelled, the citizens could not grant or decree anything regarding things pertaining to the Roman Church, as in the said capitul. venientes, de iureiuran., and what is read and noted in capit. quanto, 63 distinct., and Bartol. clearly held in the said l. omnes populi, ff. de iu.; and consequently the privilege granted ought to cease, as I said above. To the same effect serves what in a similar matter is read and noted in l. si vero, § item cum quidam, ff. loca., where it is clear that even if by fortuitous accident a lessee cannot perform the services of the lease, he is nonetheless bound to restore the rent received to the lessor himself, especially since this occurs due to hatred of the Perugians, by the argument in l. si merces, § culpae, ff. eod. titu. And these things would suffice to exclude the said privilege. But for greater caution I will introduce other causes of the loss of this privilege.

† Wherever anyone directly contravenes a privilege granted to him, the privilege is lost by a single contravention, as in cap. cum accessisset, in fine, de consti., and there by the doctors in c. pro illorum, de praebend., and in l. fin. C. de iu. do. impe., unless the favor of the Church works otherwise, and so speaks c. accedentibus, de privileg.; 32 q. 2 c. quando renunciatur serves to the same effect. But in our case the Perugians contravened the privilege of citizenship granted to them many and many a time by paying gabelle in the city of Siena as foreigners, and the Sienese citizens did the same in the city of Perugia; therefore the mutual privilege was tacitly renounced. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that individual citizens could not do this to the prejudice of all citizens; because that is true unless the contravention had been made so many times that it would likely have come to the knowledge of the citizens, for then the citizens are seen to approve, by the argument of that which Innocent notes in capitul. bonae, II 1, de postulatio. praelato. And especially in our case, in which the said privileges were not observed for ten years and more, and thus at least a custom to the contrary was introduced, as on our exact terms Cyn. notes in the said l. voluntariae, C. de excusatio. tuto. Furthermore,

† and lastly, if a privilege is given to do something and it is not done within ten years, the privilege is lost, as is notably proved in l. una, ff. de nundi.; and this Barto. confirms there, saying on that text that if a city having a privilege concerning a studium generale does not use it within ten years, it loses it; therefore, a fortiori in our case it is lost at least by the lapse of ten years, in which they not only did not use it, but expressly contravened it by paying as foreigners. For a privilege is more strongly lost by contravening than by not using, as is noted in the said capit. cum accessissent, and especially in our case, in which Sienese citizens were many and many a time forced to pay in the city of Perugia as foreigners. Whence the Perugians themselves ought to have observed their privilege toward the Sienese if they wanted that granted by the Sienese to be observed toward them, because in vain does one demand faith to be kept with him by one with whom he refuses to keep the faith promised by himself, as in the rule frustra, de reg. iur. lib. 6, with similar authorities cited above. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the privilege was not alleged in the city of Perugia, because indeed it was tacitly alleged when they alleged to avoid payment that they were Sienese, as is clear in the acts. Likewise because it is sufficient that by non-use a custom to the contrary was introduced, in l. de quibus and l. diuturna, ff. de legi., 4 dis. c. in istis, § leges. Furthermore, they would in vain have alleged a privilege that was already void and annihilated upon the coming of the prince, as I said above; l. decernimus, with its subject matter, C. de sacros. eccl. supports this. And let these things suffice. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Possession is proved by an oath of fealty.
2. If a submission to arbitration was made concerning a certain thing, the arbiter cannot adjudicate that thing to one party and condemn the other party to give a thing not brought into the submission.
3. Although the capacity to allege nullity against a sentence may be removed by some law, nullity arising from a defect of jurisdiction can nevertheless be alleged.
4. An exception denying jurisdiction removes the quality of a sentence upon which a law or statute is founded.
5. Although an arbiter cannot render judgment concerning matters entirely foreign to those expressed, he can nevertheless decide and render judgment concerning matters coherent with those expressed, without which the expressed matters cannot suitably be determined.
6. Although a conservator appointed by the Pope in favor of a church cannot by law take cognizance except of notorious injuries, nevertheless, if it is denied by the adverse party that the injury is notorious, he can take cognizance summarily and pronounce upon this.
7. A mandate is not extended beyond the things contained in the mandate.
8. One is said to repel force immediately (incontinenti) who does so as quickly as he comfortably can, without turning aside to other business.
9. Witnesses and ancient writings, especially produced from a public archive, prove appurtenances.
10. A student, even if he remains for a thousand years at university, does not acquire a domicile there if he has the intention of returning to his own region.
11. If a city enacts a statute for the sake of making an alienation to a tyrant, such an alienation and everything that was done can be revoked.
12. The boundaries of places are proved by ancient books or writings.
13. A castle of itself, viewed under the common law, does not have jurisdiction.
14. A possessor is bound to restore the thing that he possesses unless he fully proves ownership.
15. If a city is enlarged and enclosed with new walls, ditches, or plantings, the entire enlargement is included under the designation of "city."
16. A second office excludes the first when they are incompatible.
17. The privilege of clerical status is not lost except through an act entirely contrary to clerical status.
18. If a cleric in minor orders contracts marriage by words of present consent, he forfeits an ecclesiastical benefice ipso facto.
body: In the controversy arisen between the Duke of Burgundy on the one side and the Duke of Austria on the other side, arising out of certain chapters of the peace made between them, having prayed from the heart for the aid of Jesus Christ the Savior, I shall address the doubts in order according to the consultation submitted to me. And in that order, this question occurs first: Whether those fourteen places expressed in the consultation, which the Duke of Burgundy asserts to be fortifications and to belong to him by virtue of the chapters of the peace entered into, are to be adjudicated to him, or whether they belong to the Duke of Austria and are to be left to him, to whom they undoubtedly belonged before the war was begun. It seems at first sight that they are to be adjudicated to the Duke of Burgundy, notwithstanding the arbitral award rendered by the Bishop of Trent; because in one chapter of the said peace it was expressly agreed that all castles and places acquired and to be acquired by the Duke of Burgundy up to the conclusion of that peace are and shall remain, with their jurisdictions and appurtenances, to the same Duke of Burgundy; with this clarification, however: that the villages and any places whatsoever of the Trentine territory, if any there be, which were not of the districts, jurisdictions, or appurtenances acquired as written above, and had only bell-towers, or bell-towers with churches alone, or even a fortified church without bell-towers, or were without churches and bell-towers and without fortifications, and if it should fall into doubt whose they were, because each of the parties asserted that they were its own, concerning them one must abide by the arbitration and judgment of the Lord Bishop of Trent, etc. Since, however, these fourteen places now claimed by the Duke of Burgundy are of those acquired during the war, they are therefore to be adjudicated to him; for nothing is so fitting to human good faith as to observe those things that have pleased the parties, as the text stated in l. 1, ff. de pact., at the beginning; and elsewhere the text says that one must diligently strive so that the things that are promised may be fulfilled in deed, as in cap. 3, de pact.; moreover, so that peace may be preserved, the Church interposes itself imperatively, even among laymen, so that pacts entered into may obtain their firmness, as in c. 1 and what is noted there under the same title. Furthermore, that these places were among those acquired, the Duke of Burgundy proves by the oaths of fealty sworn to him by the inhabitants of those places at the time of the acquisition.

† For by an oath of fealty possession is proved, as in capitu. longinquitate, 12. quæst. 2., and in cap. si diligenti, de præscrip., and Ioan. And. holds this more expressly there. Nor does the arbitral award rendered by the Bishop of Trent juridically conflict with this view or intention of the Duke of Burgundy, because those places, as fortifications, did not fall within the submission to arbitration; for the submission was concerning villages or places without fortifications, etc., as was said above, of which kind these are not. Therefore, the arbitral award in this respect was null by operation of law, since an arbiter has no power concerning things not comprehended in the submission, as in cap. cum dilectus, de arbi., and in l. non distinguemus, §. de off., and in l. si cum dies, §. plenum, ff. de arb.; hence Bar. notably held in l. Aquil., ff. de transac.,

† that if there was a submission concerning one thing, the arbiter cannot adjudicate that thing to one party and condemn the other party to give some other thing not brought into the submission; although he may award that he give a certain quantity of money for that thing, as in institu. de offic. iudic., §. officium, and more fully on this by him in the said l. If, therefore, an arbiter cannot extend his hand to an extrinsic thing in compensation for the thing submitted to arbitration, all the more was the Bishop of Trent as arbitrator not permitted in this case to extend his power to these places, which had no community with the matters brought into the submission. But moving to the opposite view, with the aforesaid by no means standing in the way, I am influenced by several reasons, and most especially by one with respect to which I see no subterfuge, which is this: Since the arbitral award was rendered by the Bishop of Trent over all places of the Trentine territory in favor of the Duke of Austria, with certain ones specifically named being excepted and adjudicated to the Duke of Burgundy, and such an arbitral award is said to have been homologated and approved by both parties, a defect of power or of justice cannot now be alleged; since not only an arbitral award, but any judgment whatsoever that is void from a defect of power, can be approved by the parties after the fact, so that it has not the force of a judgment, but of a kind of pact and contract, so that such a judgment cannot henceforth be impugned; the text is clear in l. 2, C. communia utriusque iudi., and Barto. held this more clearly after the gloss in l. 1, C. qui pro sua iurisd., as noted by the gloss and the moderns after it in capitu. significasti, de foro competen. All the more, therefore, could an arbitral award, however null, be approved, arg. in l. cum antea, and what is noted there by the doctors, C. de arb.; nor is this surprising, since it does not derive its strength from the power of the arbitrator or the one delivering judgment, but by virtue of a contract or pact tacitly entered into from the subsequent approval or homologation, as noted in the said legal authorities. And by these considerations the objection is resolved which could be formulated from the remarks of the glo. on clemen. 1, de sequestr. pos. & fru., where it is concluded in effect

† that although by some law the ability to allege nullity against a judgment is removed, a nullity arising from a defect of jurisdiction can nevertheless still be alleged; so it seems one should say in the present matter, that although it was said in the chapter of the peace that nothing could be opposed against the definition of the Bishop of Trent as arbitrator, a defect of power can nevertheless be raised. For I say that that gloss posits a case quite different from ours; for we are speaking of where the parties approved the arbitral award after the fact, by virtue of which approval they are seen anew to contract and bargain concerning the matters expressed in the arbitral award, as in the legal authorities cited above; but the gloss cited to the contrary proceeds where the consent of the parties did not intervene, but the law or a statute removes the ability to speak against the judgment on the grounds of nullity; in which case it is permissible to allege a nullity arising from a defect of jurisdiction, and the reason is because the statute or law, in removing the exception, founds itself upon a judgment.
† But an exception de-

† nying jurisdiction removes the quality of a judgment, upon which the law or statute founds itself; because if it was rendered by one who was not the party's judge, it does not merit the name of a judgment, as in l. 4, §. condemnatum, ff. de re iudi., and in capitu. at si clerici, de iudi., and C. si a non compe. iud. throughout; to this effect is the notable doctrine of Barto. in l. 1, ff. quod ui aut clam, where through that text and the gloss he held that whenever any provision taking away an exception founds itself upon a quality, every exception is admitted notwithstanding by which that quality is taken away, because then one does not go against the provision; whence if a statute provides that no exception shall be admitted against a public instrument, it can nevertheless be objected that that instrument was not drawn up by a notary, because through this the quality of a public instrument is not removed; and the same in similar cases, as noted there by Bar. These matters, however, in no way stand in the way in our case, as is clearer than light from the aforesaid. Furthermore and secondly, it seems that even in the absence of the aforesaid homologation, judgment must be given for the said Duke of Austria. For since it had been agreed in the chapters of the peace that if any dispute should arise between the said parties concerning the villages and any places whatsoever of the Trentine territory which had only bell-towers, etc., as was said above, so that they were without fortifications, that concerning them one must abide by the arbitration and judgment of the Bishop of Trent; and it was doubted, or could deservedly have been doubted, between the parties: if certain places were said to be without fortifications, whether the said Bishop, once a general submission had been made over all places, etc., could lawfully and with a good conscience declare which are those places that are said to be with fortifications or without, to the effect of decreeing concerning them whose they were, so that thus all discord or kindling of discord might be removed, even though it had not been expressly said in the submission that he should decree which places are said to be without fortifications, but that he should decree concerning those places whose they were. I say

† that although an arbiter cannot render judgment concerning things entirely foreign to what is expressed—in which case the laws cited by me above must be understood—he can nevertheless decree and render judgment concerning things coherent with the expressed matters, without which the expressed matters cannot conveniently be terminated. For this I cite the notable glo. in the said capitu. cum dilectus, de arbi., and Innocen. held the same there, as does the gloss of civil law in the said l. non distinguemus, §. de officio. But this question, to whom the said places belonged, could not conveniently have been decided unless the preliminary question were first determined, whether those places are said to be without fortifications so that they would thus be comprehended in the submission; for otherwise each party could have said that those places were with fortifications or without, and thus the peace would easily have been broken, for the preservation of which the parties so freely placed themselves in the hands of the Bishop of Trent; in support of this is cap. in causis, de elect., together with the glo. on the word "quia verò" at the end, where it is gathered that, the power of electing having been given through a submission, the power of postulating seems tacitly given, because all things that are proximate and connected to a mandate come tacitly, as there. To the same effect is that which is held in a similar case regarding an ordinary or delegated judge, to whom, power having been given over the principal right, it is understood to be accessarily given in taking cognizance whether that cause pertains to his power, as in l. si quis ex aliena, ff. de iudic., and l. 2, si quis in ius uocan. non ierit, as per Bartol. there, and capitu. super literis, de rescrip., as per Innocent. and other doctors; hence the notable glo. said in capitu. primo, de officio, lib. 6.,

† that although a conservator appointed by the Pope in favor of any church cannot by law take cognizance except of notorious injuries, nevertheless, if it is denied by a party that the injury is notorious, he can summarily take cognizance of this and pronounce upon it, even though he was appointed simply over what is notorious. To the same effect is the text together with the gloss in capitu. cum personæ, de priuile., lib. 6., and in capitu. primo, de pœnis, in the same book, where also see the gloss. Furthermore, we see

† that a mandate is not extended beyond the things comprehended in the mandate; indeed, it speaks through taxative words, saying that an agent is understood to be appointed only for those things that are found expressed in the letters of commission, as noted in capitu. cum olim, tit. 2, de offi. delega.; and yet the agent can perform those things that are preparatory to the mandate, even though they are not expressed in the mandate, as noted in l. ad rem mobilem and in l. ad legatum, ff. de procura. Likewise, he can perform that which is close to the mandate, as in c. in causis, de elect., and de renun., c. post translationem, and ff. iudi. sol., l. iam tamen, §. ult. Likewise, he can extend the mandate to its accessories or consequences, as in ff. de instito., l. cuicunque, §. si ei, apud quem; and this the gloss notably confirmed in the said cap. cum olim. The same must therefore be said in our case, and all the more strongly as the parties seem tacitly to have intended that the said Bishop of Trent should be the general decider of questions that might arise from the chapters of peace concerning things acquired or handed over, so that the peace might be preserved within its bounds. Thirdly, it is principally relevant that in doubt an interpretation ought to be made so that the disposition may hold, as in l. quoties, ff. de uerborum obligatio., and capitu. abbate, de uerbor. significatio. Hence it is that words are even used improperly and extended beyond their proper force so that the disposition may be saved, as is notably proved in capitu. sententia, de senté. excommu., lib. 6.; relevant is l. si ita stipulatus fuero per te, ff. de uerbo. obliga.; relevant is what Bald. noted in capitu. 1, de cap. qui cu. uen., col. 10, and Archid. 13. quæst. 1, capit. 1. Especially since the Duke of Austria is contending here to avoid a loss, and the Duke of Burgundy to capture a gain, according to what is read and noted in l. apud Celsum, §. Marcellus, ff. de doli excep., and in capitu. dilecti, de exceptio., and by Bart. in l. cum mulier, ff. solu. matr. To the same effect is the theory of Bar. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iur., and l. non dubium, C. de legi., by which it is provided that in statutes and other provisions a strict or broad interpretation ought to be made so that no one without legitimate cause suffers a loss, while another enjoys a gain; to which l. ut gradatim, ff. de mune. & hono., and l. 2, C. de noxa, and capitu. cum dilectus, de consuetu., are exceedingly relevant. The remaining points will appear from the replies to the opposing arguments. And first, when it is said that those fourteen places were acquired during the war, and thus in no way came into the submission, it is answered in two ways: First, by denying that the factual allegation is true; for the peasants and inhabitants of the places could not transfer them to the Duke of Burgundy, since they themselves possessed neither in their own name nor in the name of the Duke of Austria, but they were possessed by the Duke of Austria, as Innocen. held in capitu. olim, part 1, and capit. olim, part 3, de restitu. spolia. For the jurisdiction that the Duke of Austria had in the person of the men he could not lose, just as he could not lose ownership by a mere act of fact; because since jurisdiction is an incorporeal thing, it is retained by intention alone, nor can it be lost without the knowledge and sufferance of the possessor, as in l. 2, C. de ser. & aqua, and there by the doctors, and noted in l. 1, ff. de itine. actúque priua., fully by Innocen. in capitu. bonæ, part 2, de postu. præla., and in capitu. conquerente, de offic. ord., and capitu. dilectus, de capel. mona., and in capitu. olim 2, de restitu. spoli., and in many other places. Here, however, in the loss, there was no sufferance on the part of the Duke of Austria, who possessed that jurisdiction, as I shall immediately state with respect to the places; for since the Duke of Austria possessed those places for himself, he did not lose civil possession through the entry of the Duke of Burgundy, but only natural possession, as in l. clam possidere, §. qui ad nundinas, and l. peregrè, ff. de acquiren. possessio., and in capitu. olim, part 1, de restitu. spolia., where see the glo. and the doctors. For in two cases civil possession is lost in such a circumstance: The first, when the possessor arrived by force and was not admitted; the second, when he did not go to his possession because he suspected he could be repelled, as noted in the laws cited above. But in our case neither of these happened; because the Duke of Austria was striving to gather such forces as he could to recover those and other lost places, nor did he turn away to extraneous business; and although Bar. in l. 1, C. unde ui, said that the former possessor ought to recover within three days, he nevertheless handles the matter better in l. 3, §. cum igitur, ff. de ui & ui arma.; for there he said that the quality of the fact, of the persons, etc., must be considered; whence one would be said to act immediately if he came to recover within six months, as where it was necessary to gather a great army, etc. And this opinion is commonly held, and seems to be the view of the glo. in capitu. significasti, de homic.,

† which says that one is said to repel force immediately if he does so as soon as he conveniently can without turning aside to other business. It is certain that before the Duke of Burgundy acquired civil possession, he does not seem to have acquired those places, as is proved from the things read and noted in the said laws, and especially in the said capit. olim, part 1. Furthermore and secondly, it can more easily be answered that, presupposing that he had completely acquired those places, nevertheless, because he approved the arbitral award concerning them, he can no longer contravene it, by reason of those things which were fully stated above; the other points were resolved above in the strengthening of the opposing position. And let these things suffice as to the first doubt. Secondly, there is principally turned into doubt between the said parties whether certain villages and lands of the Trentine territory, claimed under the name of appurtenances and jurisdictions by the Duke of Burgundy, ought to correspond to the castles adjudicated to the same Duke of Burgundy by virtue of the said peace, or rather to the city of Trent, and consequently ought to be subject to the Duke of Austria, who is the lord of Trent. And first it seems that they ought to correspond to the said castles, and consequently those places ought to be subject to the Duke of Burgundy with all their rights, jurisdictions, and appurtenances; but these villages and lands, which are said to be one hundred twenty-two in number, are of the appurtenances of those castles; therefore they ought to be adjudicated to the said Duke. The major premise is clear from the tenor of the chapters of peace; the minor is proved thus: A castle by the common law has neither appurtenances nor jurisdiction, as noted by Inno. in c. cum ad sedem, de resti. spo., and to this is relevant what Bar. noted in l. 1, ff. de dam. infect.; but by statutes and provisions of superiors, castles today have a certain territory, and so Inno. must be understood in cap. ex literis, de iure patr. When, however, any property is claimed or adjudicated with its appurtenances, under the name of appurtenances come those things which belonged to the property claimed or adjudicated by common law, statute, and local custom, as noted by Inno. in cap. ex literis, de iure patronatus, and in c. cum ad sedem, cited above; but it is the custom of the place that the villages and lands claimed contributed together with the said castles to the burdens incumbent upon that castle; likewise they were subject in jurisdiction and obedience to the officials of the said castles; therefore they are among the appurtenances of those castles. The major premise is proved by law; the minor is presupposed in fact; the consequence is proved, arg. l. 1, ff. ad municipales, where it is evident that by the very fact that someone is received into a city to bear burdens along with the others, he acquires the rights of the city; to the same effect is l. quod conclaue, ff. de dam. infec., where it is evident that if a certain structure is assigned for the use of any house, it seems to be among the appurtenances of that house. But I judge the contrary view to be truer. I am principally moved because in fact it is presupposed to me that the said places claimed by the Duke of Burgundy as appertaining to the said castles are within the territory of Trent, and that according to the statutes of that city they are among the appurtenances, rights, and jurisdictions of that city. And also in past times, especially before the war, they in truth answered to the city with respect to jurisdiction, and this is said to be established from witnesses and writings taken from the public archive of the city, whereas they did not answer to those castles except perhaps during the time of certain disturbances. For if the aforesaid things are true in fact, I prove most clearly that the said places are not to be adjudicated by reason of appurtenances to the Duke of Burgundy; for as I said when arguing for the contrary part, under the appellation of appurtenances come those things that pertain to a thing by common law, or by particular statute, or by custom; but if the aforesaid things are diligently weighed, the said places claimed are among the appurtenances of the city not only by common law, but also by custom and the statute of the place. By common law it is clear, because they are within the territory of the city, as is proved in l. ædificia and l. qui in continentibus, ff. de uerb. sign., and l. qui ex uico, ad muni., and l. 1, §. cum urbem, de offic. præfec. urb.; exceedingly relevant is what Bar. noted in l. 2, ff. de uer. sign., which is read and noted in c. si ciuitas, de sen. excom., lib. 6., and by the glo. in cap. 1, de usur., in the same book; that it was among the appurtenances by disposition is clear from the statute of the city, and a statute can concur with the common law, as is read and noted in c. 1, de consti., li. 6., and c. sopitæ, de censib. By custom, moreover, it is proved by witnesses and by writings produced from the public archive that in past times they answered in all things to the city in the aforesaid manner; and witnesses and ancient writings, especially produced from a public archive, well prove appurtenances, as in c. cum causam, de proba., and in auth. ad hæc, C. de fide instr., and c. ad audientiam, de præscri.; therefore it is concluded that the aforesaid places cannot be claimed as appurtenant to the said castles, but must be left under the obedience and rule of the Duke of Austria, to whom the city of Trent is subject. Nor should it stand in the way of the aforesaid that at some times in the past, especially during that war, they corresponded to those castles; because an assignment made casually according to the exigency of the times cannot alter the nature of the thing, as is elegantly proved in l. quæsitum, in the beginning, and l. fi., ff. de leg. 3, where it is proved that he who is absent for the sake of studies does not seem to be absent, and through that text Bar. confirms there at the beginning

† that if a student were to remain in a place of study for a thousand years, he does not acquire a domicile there, since he has the intention of returning to his home regions; and at the end there it is proved that he who is casually absent does not seem to be absent, nor does he who is casually present seem to be present; to the same effect is the good text in l. generali, §. uxori, ff. de usufru., where it is proved that, upon a legacy of the usufruct of houses and of all things that are in the houses, things that were in the house for the purpose of merchandise do not pass, even though—what is more—the testator had excepted something from the legacy, as because he said "except the silver"; whence, although an exception confirms the rule in non-excepted cases, it does not nevertheless expand it to comprehend those things which by their nature it does not comprehend, as is elegantly proved there, and Bar. confirms there, who by that text said that if a testator bequeathed to his wife all things that were in the house, things that the testator had in the house for the purpose of selling do not pass, because since they are there casually and for a time, they do not seem to be in the house. So I say to the purpose, that although those lands or villages were casually, on account of prosecuting wars, assigned to correspond to those castles, they do not by this seem to be of the appurtenances of the castles, unless that assignment had been made in perpetuity; which in doubt is not to be presumed, lest there occur an alienation of the goods and rights of the city, which is not easily to be presumed, but rather is to be executed with no small solemnity, as is read and noted in l. fi., C. de uendi. rer. ad ciui. perti., li. 11, and by Bar. in l. prohibere, ff. quod ui aut clam; indeed, it is notably proved in the said l. prohibere, §. illud, that in a general mandate of a commonwealth the alienation of its property is not included, and Bar. there heavily notes that text; Bart. also says there

† that if any city should make any statute for the purpose of an alienation to be made to any tyrant, such an alienation and all things that were done could be revoked, as having been made under just fear, arg. of those things that are read and noted in l. 1, §. quæ onerandæ, ff. quarum rerum actio non datur, in l. ad inuidiam, C. quod met. cau. And through this the response to the contrary arguments is clear. Concerning the third doubt, whether the places Ponte, Scantu, Gearifalegii, Valino, and Palagagi are of the Valley of San Martino, and the Valle Martina, and Upper Lemen and Lower Lemen are of the appurtenances of the said Valley of San Martino, which was adjudicated to the Duke of Austria, and thus by consequence the said places also seem adjudicated to him; or whether they are different and separate valleys, and thus belong to the Duke of Burgundy, to whom was adjudicated the city of Agrigento, in whose territory the said valleys seem to consist. And first it seems that the said valleys regard and belong to the Duke of Burgundy, because the said city of Agrigento was adjudicated to the same with its entire territory, castles, places, waters and passes, and valleys, and mountains, and any places whatsoever that are comprehended under it by law, or custom, or even possession, or quasi-possession, in the appurtenances of the said city of Agrigento, at least by reason of possession or quasi-possession; therefore they belong to the Duke of Burgundy. The minor premise is proved in many ways: First, because the said valleys rendered obedience to the officials of Agrigento for great lengths of time; for this, l. 1, §. cum urbem, ff. de offic. præfect. urb., and in cap. licet, de probatio. Likewise, because in the statutes and books of descriptions and taxes of the Agrigentines they are called and named separate and diverse valleys; for from a diversity of names a diversity of things is gathered, as in l. fi. idem codicilli, C. de codicil.; therefore, since these adjudicated valleys are diverse from the Valley of San Martino, other diverse valleys ought not to come to the Duke of Austria himself, but ought to remain with the Duke of Burgundy, to whom the city was generally adjudicated with its entire territory and appurtenances; for from separate things an inference ought not to be made, as in c. 2, de transla. præla., and l. neque natales, C. de proba., especially because a judgment is of strict law, as in l. unica, C. si una sententia plu. sue. condem., and in c. dilectus, de offic. ordi., noted by Bartol. in l. si expressim, ff. de appellatio. Thirdly, it supports the side of the said Duke of Burgundy that in the said valleys the officials of the city of Agrigento issued precepts, and they live by the statutes of that city, and they abide by the books of the public archive where they are found recorded as subject places, all of which sufficiently intimate that those places are among the appurtenances of the said city by the said l. 1, ff. ad munici., and in the said l. 1, §. cum urbem, ff. de offi. præfec. urb., with similar texts. And it is especially influential that a ditch divides those territories; therefore it cannot be said that they come under the name of the Valley of San Martino. On the contrary side, to the effect that the said places come accessarily to the Valley of San Martino, several things also lend support. First, very many public instruments drawn up of old in the said places, in which those places are named the valleys of San Martino. And thus they all come under the appellation of the Valley of San Martino. For in ancient facts such enunciative words concerning boundaries or the unity or situation of places afford no small proof, as is the notable glo. in c. cum olim, de censi., and Inno. holds the same there, and the glo. in c. series, de testi., and c. illud, de præsum.; although Barto. in l. penult., C. de iure delibe., said that such words create full faith when uttered between parties, arg. of those things that are read and noted in l. optimam, C. de contrahen. & committen. stipula. But it can be said that they then make full faith, as in the said l. optimam, but between strangers they create no small presumption, according to the note in the said c. fi., de succes. ab intesta.; relevant is what is noted in l. nuda, ff. de don. Furthermore, in our case those words were uttered between men of those places, so that they ought to create greater faith, especially because they were presumed to know the condition of their own places, arg. in c. uidetur, qui ma. accu. pos., and in l. si chorus, ff. de le. 3, and what is read and noted in c. cum causa, de probat., in cap. ad audientiam, de præscriptio.,

† where it appears that the boundaries of places are proved by ancient books or writings, ff. de lega. 3, l. prædiis, §. Titio. Secondly, there supports the Duke of Austria a certain privilege granted of old by the said Duke, in which those places are comprehended under the single term of the Valley of San Martino, and by the same privilege they are subjected to the podestà of another city in criminal and major civil matters, as is contained therein; whence, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that those places had been of the appurtenances of the city of Agrigento, they nevertheless could, by disposition of the prince, be assigned so that they would be of the appurtenances of another city. For a province is changed and divided by disposition of the prince, 10. distinctio, cap. 1, and in Auth. ut iud. sine quoquo suffr., §. hoc autem, with similar authorities; to the same effect in a similar matter is what is read and noted in c. sicut, de exces. præla., and 17. q. 1, cap. temporis, with similar authorities. I, in the presence of these mutually conflicting proofs, consider that it should be said: that if it can be proved that at the beginning of that war, or in its progress, concerning the peace of which it is now treated, those places were possessed by the said city of Agrigento as being of its territory or of its appurtenances, judgment would have to be given for the said Duke of Burgundy by virtue of the chapters of the said peace; for there was adjudicated or given to him the city of Agrigento with its entire territory and appurtenances which belonged to the said city by law, custom, or possession, or quasi-possession, etc., even if they belonged by law to another bishopric or had a special concession, provided, however, they were possessed by the Duke of Austria at the time the war began or from that time forward, etc., as is more fully gathered from the chapters of peace. If, however, this cannot be proved, then I think those places are to be adjudicated to the Duke of Austria by the aforesaid reasons; and especially because, since those places were transferred by the Duke himself or his predecessor before the war was begun, as to criminal and major civil matters, to another city from that of Agrigento, and in minor matters had their own magistracy, they ceased to be of the territory and appurtenances of the city of Agrigento, and were of the territory and appurtenances of that city to which they were dedicated; because territory (territorium) is so called from terrorizing (terrendo), as noted in l. pupillus, §. territorium, ff. de uerbo. signific.; whence through that text Bartol. says there that if any city has any army in another place, and someone commits an offense there, the podestà of the city can punish him by reason of territory, because it sufficiently seems to be of the city's territory, since its army strikes terror and rules there. To the same effect is what Barto. notes in l. 1, ff. de dam. infect., where he says that if a castle has a magistracy of its own and is not subject to the city in which it is, it is deemed in its rights as a city. To the same effect is what Bald. notes in cap. 1, §. ad hæc, de pace iu. fir., coll. 10, where he says

† that a castle of itself, looking to the common law, does not have jurisdiction unless the prince has given it to it or it has prescribed it. Relevant is what the same Bal. notes in l. fi., C. si à non compe. iud., and Ioan. And. in cap. cum æterni, de re iudic., libr. 6., where they hold that if a castle has jurisdiction of its own, it does not in any way follow the city; and Barto. seems to mean the same in the said l. 1, de dam. infect. Since, therefore, by the disposition of the Duke of Austria made before the war, those places were not subject to the city of Agrigento, therefore, the Agrigentine city having been granted with its territory and appurtenances, those places do not pass, since they are not of the territory or appurtenances. And since the Duke of Austria granted that city not out of pure liberality, a broad interpretation ought not to be made, but the strictest; because in odious matters a strict interpretation must be made, as in the rule odia restringi, de regu. iur., lib. 6.; and it must be imputed to the Duke of Burgundy that he did not frame the words more broadly and clearly, according to the note in l. veteribus, ff. de pact. For it is to be presumed that the Duke of Burgundy understood those words strictly, since one is not presumed to throw away his own: l. cum de indebito, ff. de probatio.; relevant is the notable gloss in l. cum quis, ff. si certum peta., and the text in capitul. super hoc, de renunciatio. The contrary arguments cited above in favor of the Duke of Burgundy do not stand in the way. To the other argument, in truth, I reply at the same time and say that although those places contributed and underwent taxes and any other burdens whatsoever with the city of Agrigento, nevertheless, since these things could have occurred before the assignment and transfer made by the lord of Austria, they do not prove that they are at present of the territory of that city. And presupposing that they at some time contributed casually for a time, they do not by this cease to have a distinct nature, by l. generali, §. uxori, ff. de usufruct. lega., and l. quæsitum, in the beginning and at the end, ff. de legat. 3. For it is necessary to prove that after that concession or transfer the city of Agrigento possessed those goods for such a time as appertaining to it that they were legitimately prescribed, arg. in capitul. ad audientiam, de præscript., and in l. fin., C. finium regundo. As to that, however, which is said concerning the designation, it can be answered in two ways: First, that presupposing that those places are diverse from the Valley of San Martino, nevertheless it is enough for the Duke of Austria that they are not of the territory and appurtenances of the city of Agrigento, as is clear from the aforesaid. Furthermore, the designation does not fully prove it, since it was not made between the contending parties, as noted by Bart. in the said l. penu., C. de iure delib.; relevant is what Bart. notes in l. fin., C. si à non compe. iud. Finally and better, it can be said that since witnesses and instruments ought to be reconciled to harmony if it can be done, as in c. cum tu, de testi., noted fully in c. in nostra, under the same title; relevant is c. periculosè, de pœn., dist. 1; we ought to interpret that those places have special designations, but were generally comprehended under the designation of the Valley of San Martino. Nor is this anything new; relevant is what is read and noted in c. inter dilectos, de dona., by Innocen. in capitu. petitio, de procur., and 99. distinct., capitu. 1, where there is a good text, and in capitu. periculosè. I come to the fourth doubt, concerning which it is asked whether the towers situated at the head of the bridge of the castle of Trezzo belong to the Duke of Austria, to whom the said castle belongs, or rather to the Duke of Burgundy, to whom was adjudicated the city of Agrigento, in whose territory the said towers seem to stand. It seems first that they regard the Duke of Burgundy, because a building yields to the soil, as in §. cum in suo, with the following section, institu. de rerum diui., and in l. adeò, §. ex diuerso, ff. de acquiren. re. do.; but the said towers are built in the territory of the said city; therefore they yield to the city itself, and consequently to the Duke of Burgundy, to whom that city was adjudicated. The major premise is proved by clear law; the minor, moreover, is established from this, that Agrigentine citizens are proved to have inhabited the said towers at certain times, and in them taxes were sought and exacted by Agrigentine tax-gatherers. They ought therefore to be presumed to be in the territory, since the citizens in the name of the city exercised such things there, at least in this case, where it is not established that they are of another's territory; to this is a good text in capitu. 1, de relig. domi., together with what is noted there by Innocen., where it is proved that if it is not established in whose diocese a certain church is, it is presumed to be in the diocese of him who exercised some jurisdictional acts there. Secondly, presupposing that originally those towers had been built next to the bridge for the use of the castle, nevertheless, since the bridge has now for a long time been broken down and removed, the towers remained separated from the said castle, and consequently they remained in their liberty; therefore they immediately accrued to the city in whose territory they were, since when the cause ceases, the effect ceases, as in capitu. cum cessante, de appella., and a thing easily returns to its nature, 35. distinct., capitu. ab exordio, and l. si unus, ff. de pact.; at least taking into account that the lord did not care to rebuild the bridge for a long time, although he could have; and thus he seems no longer to have wished to use them for the service of the said castle. To this effect is what is noted in a similar case by Ioan. And. in capitu. querelam, de elect., on the word "de nouo", and by Barto. in l. si de eo, §. si forte, ff. de acquiren. posses.; nor could he, once the city with its entire territory was transferred to the Duke of Burgundy, rebuild the bridge anew, because it would be to impose a new servitude, since from the prior servitude that territory was liberated, which is not permitted without the consent of the new lord: l. 1, quemadmodum, ff. ad l. Aquil., at the beginning, and in l. quoties, ff. de seru. But notwithstanding these things, which by no means stand in the way of our case, I judge that judgment must be given for the Duke of Austria. I am principally moved by a twofold ground: First, because since it is not clearly established that the soil on which the said towers were built was or is of the territory of the city of Agrigento, as is presupposed to me in fact, it is to be presumed that they were and are of the territory of the said castle, both because of the use for which those towers were built, and because of the connection or contiguity that they had with the bridge and other buildings of the said castle, and because the castle used them as its appurtenances; for this, the said cap. 1, de relig. do., and what is noted there by Innocen.; for as is clearly gathered there, if it is unknown in whose diocese a church is built, it is presumed to be in the diocese of him who exercised some episcopal acts there; so that by reason of the exercise of certain rights, ownership of the whole is presumed. So to the purpose: since the castle used those towers as its appurtenances, and from the beginning they were built for the use of the said castle, it is to be presumed that they were built on the soil of the said castle; to the same effect is l. si, C. de rei uen., where it is evident

† that a possessor is not bound to restore the thing he possesses except to one who fully proves ownership; for a possessor is presumed owner, as noted in c. cum ad sedem, de rest. spo., and once an owner is always presumed owner, as in l. siue possidetis, C. de prob. Likewise, as I said above, although a castle by common law does not have appurtenances and territory, nevertheless today by statutes, customs, and privileges they commonly do, as noted in the laws cited above in other doubts; nevertheless, to prove an appurtenance of a castle it is sufficient to prove custom; here, however, it is not only proved that these towers are of the appurtenances of the castle by custom, but indeed it is proved that originally they were built for this purpose, that they should serve the castle itself for its custody. Furthermore, it is not to be presumed that fortifications would have been built in the territory of the city for the custody of a castle of another territory distinct from the city, since even on one's own soil it is not permitted to make fortifications that could redound to the emulation of another city, as noted in l. opus nouum, ff. de oper. pub., and noted by Innocen. in capitu. fin., de restitut. spoliato.; therefore they are presumed to build on the proper territory of the castle itself. On the second ground I am moved: because presupposing without prejudice to the truth that they were built on the proper territory of the city of Agrigento itself, nevertheless, because the lord of both places built them and designated them for the use of the castle, he seems to have granted that building with its soil to that castle, or to the territory of the castle, by l. quod conclaue, ff. de dam. infect., so that the soil yielded to the building, just as in a similar case we say, when a cleric built on his own soil with money of the Church, that in favor of the Church the soil yields to the building, as the gloss notes in capitu. apostolicos, 12. quæst. 2.; for the prince seems to have wished to enlarge the territory of the said castle. For a King or Duke can grant some things from the heights of his dignity, provided they harm no one, as noted by Ioan. And. in capitu. grandi, de sup. negli. præla., lib. 6., and Barto. in l. prohibere, ff. quod ui aut clam, and especially in this case, in which an alienation outside of his dignity was not being made, as is held in a similar case in l. uoluntas, C. de fideicom., and in capitu. cum apostolica, de his quæ fi. a præla. To the same effect is what is read and noted very well in l. 1, ff. de fer. leg. Thirdly, I principally adduce the statement of Barto. in l. 2, ff. de uerbo. signifi., and Iacob. de Are. in l. si finita, ff. de dam. infect.; for he maintained that if the prince grants me a dignity, he seems to grant it with its whole jurisdiction and territory. To the same effect is what Barto. himself notes in the same law near the end,

† where he maintains that if a city is enlarged and enclosed with new walls, or ditches, or plantations, the entire enlargement is comprehended under the appellation of the city; so, by the prince enlarging the buildings of the castle by making new towers, the whole ought to be comprehended under the appurtenances of the castle. Now it remains to answer the contrary arguments adduced for the other party. And first, to the first, the answer is sufficiently clear from the aforesaid. For I admit that a building made purely on another's soil yields to the soil; but in our case this does not happen, because the builder of the towers was the lord of both territories; whence, by building in one territory and assigning that building to the use of the other territory, he seems to have transferred that building with all jurisdiction to the use of the castle, as I said above, especially by l. quod conclaue and by what was noted by Barto. in the said l. 2, ff. de uerbo. significa.; nor does the text at the end of the said l. quod conclaue stand in the way, with the note there, where it is intimated that ownership yields to the soil, but the other place ought to have the use by right of servitude; to the same effect is l. 1, de serui. leg.; because I say that that proceeds when the owner of both buildings bequeathed or disposed of those buildings to different persons, for then one obtains the legacy with the right of servitude. But in our case another thing occurs; for I say that the soil where the towers were built yields to the building, and the towers with the building have been made of the appurtenances and territory of the castle, just as happens with a portico and a private room. For the contrary would proceed when the owner of both territories had specifically granted that soil to another, because then the building would yield to the soil with the right of servitude. But this does not occur in our case, nor is it likely that the lord intended this, because that soil would remain uselessly with the lord of the whole territory, arg. in l. antiquitas, C. de usufruct. Furthermore, it is denied in fact that the towers were built on another's territory; and in doubt it is to be presumed that they were built on his own, by the things stated above. That which is said about taxes having been exacted there by Agrigentine citizens does not stand in the way: because it is presupposed in fact that this happened casually in time of war, when the Duke was the lord of both territories; whence, although the lord uses things for another use for some time, he does not seem to have intended entirely to alter the nature of the things, since at least through urgent conjectures this does not appear, an excellent argument in l. quæsitum, in the beginning and at the end, ff. de legat. 3; especially since this collection of taxes does not have to exclude them from also remaining assigned to the use of the castle; for these things are compatible with one another; therefore a second use does not have to alter the nature of the thing; otherwise when they are not compatible with each other; so speaks l. quod conclaue, cited above; to this effect as an argument is l. nemo, and what is noted there, C. de assess.,

† where it is evident that a second office excludes the first when they are incompatible with each other, otherwise not; relevant are l. neque natales, C. de probatio., and capitul. officii, de testamen., and l. si consul, ff. de adoptio., and capitul. ex literis, de probatio., and what is noted there, and a natural and original cause overcomes an accidental one: l. qui habet, ff. de tutel. The second principal argument, which is made concerning the destruction of the bridge and the negligence of the lord in not repairing the bridge, through what was noted by Ioann. And. in the said capitu. querelam and by Bartol. in the said l. si de eo, does not stand in the way, because since the castle has a well-founded claim from the first construction and foundation of the towers, the destruction of the bridge can harm it in nothing, since it does not appear to have been done seriously by the lord so as to separate the towers from the appurtenances of the castle, especially since the lord destroyed the bridge for a temporary cause, namely so that the castellans, then rebels, might not be able to have assistance; whence that which is done casually does not alter the nature of the thing, as in the said l. generali, §. uxori, ff. de usufruct. leg., and in l. quæsitum, in the beginning and at the end, cited above. Furthermore, since the bridge and towers were for the use of the castle, although the bridge is removed, the things nevertheless ought not to be withdrawn, just as when one of two servitudes is removed, another remains, as in l. si dominus, ff. de seruitu. vrbano. præd., and in capitul. ex tuarum, de aucto. & vsu pal.; nor can the alleged negligence in the rebuilding of the bridge cause harm: First, because negligence is denied in fact; for since the Duke of Austria was involved in many and great storms, he ought not to be called negligent if he did not rebuild the bridge within eight years, especially because, since he was the lord of both territories, he was not constrained by any law in its rebuilding, and thus he cannot be called negligent; indeed we see that Jews, who cannot erect a synagogue anew, can nevertheless repair it if the ancient one collapses, as in capitul. consuluit, de Iudæis, even without the fixing of any time limit, as there; nor can anyone be called negligent when he cannot conveniently do so: l. Nepos Proculo, ff. de verbo. signifi., especially when he was not constrained to this in our case; nor can the notes of Ioan. Andr. and Bartol. in the places cited above assist the Duke of Burgundy in any way; for they speak of when through negligence civil possession is lost while another occupies natural possession; for certainly, if someone entered upon my land, and I, who possess civilly, neglect to go and recover possession, I lose civil possession through negligence, because I am seen to suspect that I could be repelled, according to what is noted in the said l. clam possidere, §. qui ad nundinas, ff. de acquirend. possess., and in the said capitul. olim, part 1, de restitu. spolia. But we are in a completely separate case, since no one occupied those towers once the bridge was broken down; indeed, the Duke of Austria was able to possess them to the harm of the castle; for in possession the same is also established: for if in my absence from my possession no one has entered upon it, I do not on this account lose civil possession if I neglect to go to my possession, unless I have remained away for so much time that oblivion would be induced, say for a decade, as noted in the said l. si de eo, and by Dyn. in the rule sine possessione, de reg. iu., lib. 6.; indeed, if another had entered upon my land and I, being ignorant, neglect to go to the same land, I do not on this account lose civil possession unless I have remained away for a decade, because then from presumed oblivion possession is lost; this the remarkable gloss, of which Barto. there makes a great celebration, clearly held in l. 1, C. de seruis fugiti., and Dyn. agrees in the rule cited above; and the conclusion reached above especially proceeds in our case, since a decade has not elapsed from the time of the destruction of the bridge, nor is there evidence of any act by which the lord seems entirely to have intended to separate the said towers from the use of the castle. To the aforesaid, what Innocen. notes in a similar case in capitu. 2, de apost., is exceedingly relevant,

† where he concludes that the privilege of clergy is not lost except by an act entirely contrary to clergy and which is incompatible with clergy; otherwise not. To the same effect is what the doctors note in capitu. 1, de cleri. coniug., where they say

† that if a cleric in minor orders contracts marriage by words of the present, he loses by that very fact his ecclesiastical benefice; otherwise if he contracts betrothal for the future, because betrothal for the future can be dissolved in many ways, and thus is not entirely repugnant to the retention of the benefice; otherwise in a contract of marriage by words of the present; so it is entirely to be said in our case. And let these things suffice as to the fourth doubt. The fifth doubt, to whom the ferry near Trezzo ought to belong: whether to the Duke of Burgundy by reason of the city of Agrigento, which was adjudicated to him with its entire territory and all appurtenances; or to the Duke of Austria, to whom belongs the place or land of Trezzo? It is alleged for the Duke of Burgundy that it ought to be adjudicated to him at least as to a half part: because the territory of the city of Agrigento extends to the middle of the Adda; hence it is that the citizens of Agrigento have in the said waters of the Adda many mills and certain fisheries, and at times held ships at a certain higher ferry; and therefore, since that ferry of Trezzo is on the said waters of the Adda, the said Duke of Burgundy ought to have that ferry as to a half part, just as the territory of that city extends to the middle of the Adda. To the contrary, on the part of the Duke of Austria, it is alleged that the said ferry is always accustomed to be auctioned at Trezzo and collected in its entirety, and because the ownership of the said ferry belongs to certain citizens of another city; likewise because licenses and passes have always belonged to Trezzo and to the lords of Trezzo for so much time that there is no memory of its beginning; for this were cited capitu. super quibusdam, de uerborum significatio., and in l. cum de in rem uerso, ff. de usuris, with similar authorities; that right of passage, therefore, ought in no way to be divided, since it always pertained to Trezzo even at the time when the city of Agrigento belonged to another lord than to the Duke of Austria. To me, however, it seems that the Duke of Austria prevails in justice over this ferry on multiple grounds: First, because since it is not clearly established in whose territory it is, it ought to be presumed to be in the territory of Trezzo, since the lords of Trezzo exercised the right of issuing passes and auctioning, and doing other things mentioned above, as is proved in capitu. 1, de religio. do., together with the statement of Innocen. and other doctors there. Furthermore and secondly, presupposing that that territory had from the beginning been common, or even entirely of the city of Agrigento, nevertheless, because for so much time that there is no memory of its beginning that city, or whoever previously held that city, did not exercise the right of territory there, but only the lords of Trezzo, that place was therefore prescribed; since the rights of a place can undoubtedly be prescribed, even as to jurisdiction, and not only against an inferior, but even against the Pope and the Emperor, as in l. comperit, C. de præscript. 30. uel 40. ann., and in capitu. ad audientiam, and capitu. si diligenti, de præscrip., noted by Inno. in c. bonæ 2, de postu. præla.; relevant is l. si, C. finium regun.; indeed, those rights that are reserved to the prince as a mark of prerogative and special privilege can be prescribed by so much time that memory of its beginning does not exist, as in cap. super quibusdam, de verbo. sig., such as the right of exacting taxes, legitimating, and similar things, as there, in l. si publicanus, §. in vectigalibus, and there by Bartol., ff. de publi.; and he concludes there that if these rights belong in a place to another than to the prince, it can be prescribed in a lesser time; and on this by the same in l. 1, ff. de aqua plu. arcen. Other rights of the prince, however, which are not reserved as a mark of special privilege, are prescribed in a lesser time, as in the said l. comperit, and fully by Barto. in l. intra quatuor, ff. de diuer. & tempo. præscr., unless they are reserved as a mark of supreme dominion, because those are imprescriptible while subjection stands; an example is in tribute; so speaks the said l. comperit at the end; whence in our case, where there is no prescription against the prince, prescription by common law proceeds in doubt. All the more strongly, therefore, does prescription proceed in our case, which is of so much time that there is no memory of its beginning, which has the force of a title, as in l. hoc iure, §. ductus aquæ, ff. de aqua plu. arcend., and in l. 1, §. final., ff. de iti. actúque pri.; because when someone exercises certain rights with the intention of acquiring universal jurisdiction, he acquires it while no other possesses it, and the intention of acquiring universal jurisdiction is presumed from the fact that he exercises certain general rights, or those that are signs of universal jurisdiction, such as entering the praetorium through the place, or the right of issuing passes and licenses, and auctioning the ferry, and similar things. And these seem clearly to be of the mind of Innocen. in capitul. dilectus, de capel. mona.; relevant is what the glo. and the doctors note in capitul. quod clericis, de foro compe.; so it happens indirectly in our case, as is clear from the aforesaid. We ought therefore to conclude that the lords of Trezzo prescribed total jurisdiction over the said ferry. And from the same reasons the same seems to be said concerning the ferry situated near Soncino, since it is said that for many and many times the said ferry was auctioned and awarded by the men of Soncino, established by them, and brought to their bank, and was always named from Soncino; and because the men of Soncino claim and prove that their territory extends beyond the Oglio, and beyond the Oglio they execute justice and are accustomed to have a place of justice; whence it is to be presumed that the said ferry is in their territory, or that it was legitimately prescribed by them through the aforesaid. The things alleged on the part of the Duke of Burgundy do not stand in the way. And first in that which is alleged, that by an imperial privilege the territory of the city adjudicated to him comprehends the entire Oglio or the waters of the Oglio: To this, indeed, it can be answered that, presupposing that it had been so, nevertheless against the privilege there was legitimate prescription to the contrary by the men of Soncino; for against privileges of the prince prescription runs to the contrary, as in capitul. ad hoc, and capitul. accedentibus, de priuileg., and capitul. ad audientiam, de præscript. Furthermore, to the contrary is shown another privilege, to which the second does not seem to have derogated, since special mention is not made of it, as is required for the derogation of a privilege, as in capitul. veniens, de rescript., noted by the gloss in the rule generi, de regul. iur., libr. 6., 25. quæstio. 2, in summa. And if there is doubt concerning the revocation, or concerning the authority of the time, judgment must be given for the Duke of Austria, who is the possessor, as in the rule cum iura partium sint obscura, de regul. iuris, libr. 6., and in capitul. ex literis, de probatio. It does not stand in the way, secondly, that when the peace was made, this ferry was included; for this rather makes against the Duke of Burgundy than for him: by virtue of that peace nothing can be claimed, since it did not take effect, as in c. ad peruenit, de iureiu., and cap. constitutis, de pœnis, and in the rule frustra fidem, de regu. iu., libr. 6., and in l. quæro, §. inter locatorem, and what Bartol. notes there, ff. loc. Furthermore, if it was then specifically included, and now both in the renewed peace was omitted, it is therefore clearly concluded that it was tacitly excluded, arg. in l. pacta nouissima, C. de pac., and in l. pacta, ff. de contrahen. emp., since those things that seemed worthy of special note, if they are not now expressed, are seen to be neglected, and thus not included in the disposition, as in cap. quamuis, de præb., lib. 6. Furthermore, since that adjudication of places was sufficiently odious on the part of the Duke of Austria, that which was not now expressed is held as omitted, arg. in l. commodissime, ff. de lib. & posthu., in c. susceptum, de rescrip., lib. 6., with similar authorities. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A bequest made to an incapable person is held as not written.
2. Friars Minor, and others who belong to the mendicant order, are called mendicants.
3. A bequest made to individual friars for the purpose of buying books, and for life, or for their necessities, is valid.
4. An annual bequest made for matters concerning divine worship is valid.
5. Every cathedral church is bound to maintain a master at its own expense.
6. A slave is capable in a matter of maintenance.
7. If something is left to a monk with the condition that it is not acquired for the monastery, the bequest is valid.
8. Today, a stipulation is not required for the validity of a gift.
