casus: A certain lady B. made an inter vivos gift to the venerable man Master Lucas of the Order of Friars Minor of sixteen gold florins to be paid each year for the entire lifetime of the said Master Lucas for the purpose of buying books and supporting other necessities for the study of theology; for the payment of which she mortgaged the rent of a certain shop belonging to the right and property of the donor herself. Afterward, the said lady B. made a will and left the said shop to a certain Nicolaus, her kinsman, with the charge of paying to the said Master Lucas sixteen gold florins each year from the rent of the said shop in accordance with the tenor of the above-written gift; with this added, however, and specified by the said testatrix, that if it should happen at any time or in any event that the said Master Lucas should not be capable of receiving the said gift—since the Friars Minor cannot have or obtain any property, and especially in particular—then, upon the occurrence of the said event that he is not capable of the said sixteen florins, she bequeathed the said shop freely to the said Nicolaus, etc. Afterward it happened in fact that the said Master Lucas obtained from the Apostolic See, mention having been made of the said gift and last will, the faculty of receiving the said moneys each year for buying books and supporting other necessities for the study of theology, at the pleasure of the Apostolic See and with the license of his superior, etc., as is more fully contained in the said apostolic letters. Now, however, the testatrix having died and the said sixteen florins having already been paid for several years to the said Master Lucas, the said Nicolaus, or his heir, refuses to pay, saying that he is not capable of the said moneys by law and according to his Rule; and consequently that the said shop ought to remain freely to him without any charge according to the intention of the said testatrix. It is asked what the law is.
body: Humbly invoking first from the heart the protection of Jesus Christ the Redeemer, so that the truth of this question may shine forth more clearly, I will first argue the negative side, namely, that the said Master Lucas is not capable of this gift or bequest, and consequently that the said shop ought to remain with the said Nicolaus or his heir without the above-written charge. And first thus: the Friars Minor cannot appropriate anything to themselves, either in particular or in common, since they have expropriated themselves from all temporal goods, as the text says in cle. exiui de paradiso, de ver. sig., in § cupientes; therefore the said Master Lucas could not receive the said gift, either by himself or in the name of the convent. The text in capitul. nimis. 2. de excessio. prælato., at the beginning, seems to confirm this, where it is said that the Friars Preachers and Minors serve Christ the poor man, etc. Since, therefore, they ought to exist and serve Christ in the strictest poverty, they are therefore not capable of an annual income. Furthermore, why should one engage in these ambiguities, since the text on this matter seems round and clear in the aforementioned clementi. exiui, in § cùmque, where it is said that, since annual incomes are reckoned by law among immovables, and retaining such incomes is contrary to poverty and mendicancy, there is no doubt that the said friars, considering their condition, are not permitted to receive or hold any incomes whatsoever and possessions, or even their use, since it is not found to be granted to them, because perfect men must especially avoid not only what is recognized to be evil, but also everything that has the appearance of evil. These are formally the words of that text, which seem to press heavily against the said Master Lucas, especially in that it forbids receiving any incomes whatsoever, even in respect of use; since it said "whatsoever", excepting nothing, it seems to have included annual income of whatever quality and condition; argument in capitul. solitæ, de maiori. & obedien., and distinct. 19, capitul. si Romanorum, and l. de pretio, ff. de pub., with similar laws. The general reason that follows also supports this, where it says that they ought to avoid everything that has the appearance of evil; for this legacy seems to be of such a kind, because it seems to have been made fraudulently under the pretext of books, since it extended to the entire lifetime of the said Master Lucas, who has already long since been made a master in the Sacred Page. Whence, a fortiori, it ought not to have any effect, especially in our case, as in the said clemen. exiui, § cupientes, and as Baldus notes regarding these friars in authen. ingressi, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi. Likewise, and second principally, the said donor had regard not to the church of the friars or other convents, but solely to the person of the said Master Lucas. For she made the gift to the said Master Lucas to have, hold, possess, and distribute as shall seem good and pleasing to him for buying books, for the study of theology, and for his other necessities, as more fully appears in the drawn-up instrument of gift. Which words are in many respects repugnant to the law and to the Rule of the Friars Minor. First, insofar as she gave to Master Lucas to hold, possess, and expend, etc.; and yet it is certain that every handling of money is forbidden to the said friars, so that they cannot touch it, as in the said clementi. exiui, in § porrò cum dictus, etc. Second, because she intended to give to the person of Master Lucas, and thus to make him capable in particular, which is not permitted, not only to a Friar Minor, but to no religious person, as in capitul. non dicatis and capitul. nolo, 12, quæst. 1, and in the said clemen. exiui, § cupientes, previously cited. Third, in that she gave it for his necessities; for by this it cannot be denied that the mendicancy incumbent upon the Friars Minor is relieved contrary to the disposition of the law, since uncertain mendicancy through begging ought to provide sustenance to mendicant friars, as the text says in capitul. 1, de religio. domi., in the Sext; and the words of the testatrix uttered in the will support this, where she said that if the said Master Lucas is not capable, since the Friars Minor cannot have anything, especially in particular, etc.; and thus she clearly understood that she had made the gift to the person of the friar, and not to the church or the convent. Since, however, these things are contrary to their Rule and to the law, therefore the said gift was not valid, because an act done contrary to the law is void, as in l. non dubium, C. de legi., and dist. 10, c. vides. This is clearly proved in a similar case in l. si in metallum, ff. de his quæ pro non scrip., where it is clear

† that a bequest made to an incapable person is held as not written, and consequently it is just as if it had not been made, as there; and what is read and noted in l. quod meo and l. si me in uacuam, ff. de acquir. posses., supports this. In our exact terms, Bartolus seems to have held this opinion in his Minorica on the clemen. exiui de paradiso, where he said that a legacy can be made to the Friars Minor for books. In another part, however, he said that an annual legacy for a not inconsiderable time cannot be made to the friars, according to the said clemen. exiui, § cumque; and thus he feels that even for books an annual legacy for a not inconsiderable time cannot be made to the friars; and so, as I hear, some have understood, grasping his words, as I judge, according to the bark rather than the true meaning. But I consider a different opinion to be consistent with the law, namely that the said gift made to the said Master Lucas was valid. I am moved first,

† because the Friars Minor and others who belong to the class of mendicants are called mendicants because uncertain mendicancy must furnish them with sustenance, as the text says in c. 1, de reli. do., in the Sext; and thus they are called mendicants only in matters pertaining to sustenance, and Federicus de Senis, the distinguished doctor, expressly held this in his Consilia, consi. 12. But under the term 'sustenance' come only those things that are necessary for eating, drinking, and clothing the body, such as garments and the like, as the text stated in l. uerbo uictus, ff. de uerb. sig. The text held the same with respect to maintenance (alimenta) in l. legatis, ff. de ali. & cib. leg., where it is said that when maintenance is bequeathed, those things are owed without which the body cannot be nourished, such as food, clothing, and lodging; but other things that pertain to instruction are not contained in the legacy; and these words, especially the last, are to be noted, by which it is clearly proved that those things that tend to study and the acquisition of instruction are not comprehended under the designation of maintenance or sustenance. Through which law Bartolus said there that when maintenance is bequeathed to someone, the heirs are not bound to provide the legatee with expenses for study. Therefore, the Friars Minor and other mendicants ought not to be called mendicants with respect to those things that concern the learning of instruction; the reason being that through these, mendicancy is not relieved with respect to virtue. And consequently it is inferred that the said friars are not incapable of an annual income that is left not for sustenance or maintenance, but for study and the purchase of books. And Federicus de Senis held this opinion most clearly in the said consi. 12. The gloss held this in clemen. dudum, de sepul., on the word 'indirectè', where it says

† that a bequest made to individual friars for the purpose of buying books is valid. And although he frames the question there concerning the Friars Preachers, because that was how it happened then in fact, nevertheless his arguments are conclusive also for the Friars Minor, and he makes express mention of them in the consilium, and specifically answers that clemen. exiui, which speaks of the Minors, stating that that Clementine is not extended to this chapter. Baldus seems to have confirmed the consilium of Federicus regarding the Friars Minor in auth. ingressi, C. de sacrosanct. eccle., as I shall state more expressly in the following argument. Secondly, it is principally proved thus:

† an annual bequest made to the friars for matters concerning divine worship is valid according to everyone, because the bequest does not principally concern the conveniences of the friars, but divine worship itself; Baldus held this most clearly, following the consilium of Federicus, in the said auth. ingressi, C. de sacrosanct. eccl. And more clearly, Johannes de Lignano, following Bartolus, in clemen. exiui de para., in the last question of the treatise, where he said that an annual bequest for divine worship made to the Friars Minor is valid, for example if grain is left annually for the hosts, or wine for the sacrifice, or money for the lights, and the like. And Federicus held the same in the said consi. 12, and a certain other solemn doctor after him, as appears there in the following consilium. It is proved by reason, because, as I have said before, through this bequest the mendicancy of the friars is not relieved; Bartolus also held this in the Minorica in another question, when he affirmed that although the friars themselves cannot be instituted as heirs, as in the said cle. exiui, § cupientes, their church can nevertheless be instituted as heir, as in the said clemen. exiui, § cupientes; and thus he clearly held that in those things that are acquired for the church and not for the friars themselves, every bequest is valid, because the laws generally provide that every church can be instituted as heir, as in l. 1, C. de sacro. san. ecclesi. The church of the Friars Minor is not found anywhere to be excepted, but only the friars themselves, because they must seek their sustenance by begging. But by a bequest made to the church for repairs and the like, the mendicancy of the friars is not removed. But an annual bequest or gift made for the study of theology and the purchasing of books concerns divine worship; therefore, the bequest or gift made to the friars is valid. The minor premise is clearly proved by the authority of Federicus in the previously cited consilium, where he reckons study among bequests made for divine worship. It is proved by reason: the universal Church needs learning above all for its governance; therefore it has granted that the bishop may dispense with those who wish to study, so that one who has obtained a parish church is not bound to be promoted to the priesthood within seven years, nor is he bound to serve the church, but may absent himself for the sake of study, as is proved in capitul. cum ex eo, de elect., in the Sext; and this happens especially in the study of sacred theology, as is the notable text in cap. fin., de magistri.

† Hence every cathedral church ought to maintain a master at its own expense, etc., as in capitul. quia and almost throughout the whole title de magistra.; all of which things were established for the increase of divine worship, for, as the text notably says in authen. habita, C. ne filius pro pat., through knowledge the world is illuminated to obey God, and the life of subjects is formed by its ministers, etc. And God says through the prophet: 'Because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me', as is held in capitul. nisi cum pridem, de renun. Moreover, study belongs properly to religious, and especially to the friars, through whose learning and preachings the world is illuminated, and the faith is increased and defended, as in the previously cited clement. exiui, and in clemen. dudum, de sepul.; Johannes Andreæ fully discusses this in capitul. sanè, de regu. Hence he said in capitul. quia, de magist., that by favor of study a religious can be appointed to the office of learning, just as by favor of souls he can be promoted to a bishopric or to another church with cure of souls, as in capitu. quod dei timorem, de stat. reg., and in clemen. 1, de electio. For who will deny that the Church of God shines more brightly through learned men, especially in theology, than through tapers or lamps that are figuratively lit in the church? For if a bequest made for them is said to be made for divine worship, as in capitu. fin., de testamen., and what is noted there, a fortiori the same must be said of a bequest made for the study of theology; for as the text says in the said cap. fin., de magist., doctors in theology shine in the Church of God like the brightness of the firmament. Hence the notable text in cap. super specula, ne cle. vel mona., says: 'Because indeed we desire the study of theology to be enlarged, so that extending the place of its tent it may make its cords longer, so that the faith may be surrounded with an impregnable wall of warriors, by whom it may be able to resist those who mount up against it', etc. From all of which it is demonstrated clearer than light that a bequest made for the study of theology and buying books must be said to be for divine worship; therefore, the said gift of an annual income made for the life of Master Lucas was valid. This is also confirmed by another reason: the said lady donor made that gift to the said master for the salvation of her soul and the remission of her sins, as is expressly stated in the instrument of gift; therefore, it was a bequest for pious causes. For everything given or left for the soul is said to be for pious causes, as Bartolus and the gloss note on l. si quis Titio, ff. de legat. 2, and the Speculator in the title de instrumen. ædi., § nunc verò aliqua, verse & scias, quòd inter legata ad pias causas; what is read and noted in c. requisiti and c. relatum, de testa., supports this. From all of which it is clearly concluded that the said gift held good: both because it was made for pious causes, and because it was for divine worship, and because the mendicancy of the friars, which concerns sustenance and maintenance, is not relieved, as I said above. Indeed, Federicus intended more in the said consi. 12:

† that an annual bequest made to a friar or convent for the life of one friar, or for a certain time simply, or for their necessities, without adding the cause of study or another concerning divine worship, is valid. He is moved principally because just as a lump sum can be bequeathed to a friar or convent for their maintenance, as is proved in the said clement. exiui, § cupientes, and in clemen. dudum, de sepul., joined with the gloss on the word 'indirectè', so it must be possible for a sum to be bequeathed payable each year, as happens in an annual income for the life of a friar, or for another time, not in perpetuity; and it was an excellent consideration. And in this sense the second allegation or conclusion of Federicus ought to be understood. For the first part was when it is left for pious causes, as for study and the like; the second was when it is left simply to a convent or to one friar for their conveniences; this is clearly gathered from the premise framed by him. For the premise is framed simply in an annual bequest made simply, but afterwards in what follows he does not touch upon the first case as being beyond doubt, namely when it is made for pious causes; afterwards he passes to the case generally proposed. Nor does the said clemen. exiui, in § cumque annui reditus, stand in the way, because according to him that text can be understood as meaning that the annual income is perpetual, or for an extremely long time, so that the mendicancy of the friars would be relieved; but in our case, when it is left for the life of one friar, although with respect to the friar it may be called perpetual according to what is noted by the gloss in 10, quæst. 2, capitul. hoc ius porrectum, verse perpetua, nevertheless with respect to the convent, to which the acquisition is made, it cannot be called perpetual or for an extremely long time, since the convent never dies, as in l. proponebatur, ff. de iudic. For in a bequest made to a friar or another religious person, the condition of him for whom it is acquired must be looked at, just as in the capacity of a slave the capacity of the master, for whom the bequest is acquired, is considered, as the notable text says in l. non minus, ff. de acquiren. hæred., and in l. si in metallum, ff. de his quæ pro non scrip. hab. Moreover, an individual bequest to a friar, even a mendicant, is acquired for the convent, as the previously cited gloss notes in the said clemen. dudum, and l. Deo nobis and what is noted there, C. de episco. & cle., supports this, and what is read and noted in capitul. in præsentia, de proba., and in authen. ingressi, C. de sacrosanct. eccl., and Bartolus held this in the said treatise of the Minorica. And truly these are excellent considerations. But I follow this opinion of Federicus in this last case, when it is made simply to a friar or a convent, with two qualifications. First, that it is not made in a large amount, because then their mendicancy could be relieved, and it could be done in fraud; a good text for this is in the said clemen. exiui, § cupientes. The second limitation is that it is not made for an extremely long time, as Federicus himself maintained; and it pleases me that it is not said to be for an extremely long time when it is made for the life of one friar, especially an aged one, as Master Lucas was; because nothing is more uncertain than the hour of death, and nothing more certain than death, as in l. 2, ff. de condi. & dem.; whence, since that bequest or gift could be extinguished daily, it cannot be said to be an extremely long time; nevertheless, by reason of uncertainty it could be tolerated, by argument of those things that are read and noted in l. si ea pactione, C. de vsur., and in cap. fin. and in cap. in ciuitate, of the same title; for although someone can live up to a hundred years, as in l. fin., C. de sacros. eccl., the reality is nevertheless denied in most cases. Whence Innocent says that today, according to inferior causes, death may well be feared for anyone after his fiftieth year; so he notes in c. quoniam frequenter, de rest. spol. And this opinion, thus qualified, is more pleasing than the opinion of Bartolus, who seems in this last matter to have held the contrary, namely that an annual legacy cannot be made to the convent or to the friar himself for the life of one friar; yet he did not strongly affirm this, but hesitated when in deciding he said that it is safer to abstain; he did not, however, precisely deny that it could be done. But Federicus held precisely that it could, and so gave counsel, and was moved by better reasons. Nor ought such an annual income then to be counted among immovables, since it is not to last perpetually, nor for an extremely long time, but rather among movables, since it belongs to movables and for a not extremely long time; just as in a similar case we say of an action, that if it is granted for movables, it is counted among movables, as the gloss and Bartolus note in l. potest pupillus, ff. de autho. tuto., and the gloss in Auth. de non alienan., § 1, colla. 2, and by Bartolus in l. mouentium, ff. de uerbo. signifi. In our case, however, when the legacy or gift is made for study or another pious cause, Bartolus does not object; because he speaks simply of an annual bequest made to friars; indeed, as I said above, he rather feels the opposite in this, since he said their church is capable, and books are acquired for the church rather than for the convent, since the convent cannot eat books, and just as the friars have the use of the church, so they ought to have the use of the books. Likewise, Johannes de Lignano, following Bartolus at the end of the treatise, expressly held what I have previously said regarding an annual legacy concerning divine worship. It remains therefore to conclude clearly that our case is without any scruple of doubt in favor of the gift, since no one is found who expressly holds the contrary, but the common opinion is for this side, and the apostolic letters granted to the said Friar Lucas provide much support. For the Pope seems tacitly to approve the conclusion made above, that a gift or annual bequest for buying books and for supporting other necessities for study is valid. For if the said gift had not been valid, the Pope would not have granted to the said Master Lucas, who feared being molested by someone concerning the receipt of those moneys, as is stated in the letters, the power freely and lawfully to receive and have the said money annually. For he could not have given the power lawfully and freely to receive and have it, as he does, if the said gift had not been valid. For since he recounted in the letters that the said testatrix and donor had died, the Pope knew that if the said Friar Lucas had been incapable, that gift would have been void, and the said rent would have remained with the donor or with the heir after the death of the testatrix, as in l. si pluribus, ff. de lega. 1, and in the said l. si metallum, ff. de his quæ pro non scrip., or with the said Nicolaus by the special disposition of the testatrix herself, or even perhaps by common law according to the very notable text in l. fin., de auro & argen. lega.; and thus he could not have received what was not owed without sin, nor would the ignorance of the payer have excused him from sin, as throughout the entire title de cond. indeb., ff. and C. In case of doubt, moreover, one must stand by the interpretation of the Pope, because it belongs to him to interpret the canons, just as their promulgation does, as in capitul. inter, de senten. excommu. And if it is said that the said Master Lucas does not need books, it is answered first that this cannot be denied, for it is not to be thought that he is stuffed with all the books necessary for the study of theology. Secondly, presupposing without prejudice to truth that this were true, the effect of the said gift will not cease on this account, because it was made for a twofold cause, namely for buying books, and for supporting other necessities in study; whence, although the first cause ceases, the second does not cease; therefore the disposition does not cease, Inst. de nup., § affinitatis. Furthermore, a legacy or gift made for the soul does not collapse if it cannot be converted to the destined use, but it ought to be destined for another pious use, in l. legatum, ff. de usufruct. lega., and in l. legato, ff. de admi. re. ad ci. pertinen., as is read and noted in capitul. 2, de test., and fully by Bartolus in l. pater, § Tusculanus, ff. de leg. 3, and in the said l. legatum, and by Johannes de Lignano following Baldus in the said cle. exiui. Now it remains to respond to the contrary arguments framed above. And first, to the first concerning incapacity, it is answered that ownership is not acquired for the said Master Lucas, nor for the convent, but he will have the bare use, just as the friars have from those things that are given to them daily, either for divine worship or for sustenance, as in the said cle. exiui and the said cle. dudum. In whom, however, the ownership resides, is fully noted in the said treatise of the Minorica and in a certain Extravagant; I do not care to pursue this, because it is not our matter, for it is enough that the use is not forbidden to him. And although otherwise the Friars Minor cannot by themselves receive money, even when bequeathed, but the syndic appointed for this purpose can do this, as is fully noted by Bartolus in the said treatise; nevertheless, in our case the said Master Lucas will be able to receive it by authority of the apostolic bull and with the license of his superior, as is stated in it. For the Pope granted this favor notwithstanding any constitutions whatsoever, as appears in it. To the second argument from the said clement. exiui, § cùmque, sufficient response has been made above. To the third, I say that although she had regard to the person of Master Lucas, nevertheless a bequest can be made to him for the benefit of the friar, but the acquisition takes place according to the disposition of the law; a good gloss on this is the previously cited one in the said clemen. dudum, de sepul., on the word 'indirectè'. We see the same in a slave; for although someone instituted him as heir, the master can neither enter upon the inheritance nor precisely compel the slave if he does not wish to enter, as in l. cum proponas, C. de hæred. institu.; nevertheless, through the slave it is acquired for the master upon his entering the inheritance, so that it does not reside even for a moment in the person of the slave, as in l. placet, ff. de acquiren. hæred. Furthermore, she could well have regard to the person of one friar in matters concerning divine worship and a pious work, so that he may exercise that pious work in the person of one friar, as specifically for buying books and study was held by the gloss, Federicus, Bartolus, and others in the previously cited places; hence Bartolus clearly held this in l. seruos ad custodiam, ff. de ali. & cib. leg., where he affirmed that a bequest for maintenance can be made not only to a convent of the Friars Minor, but also to individual friars, just as a bequest made to a slave for such a cause is valid, as there; and thus the friar cannot be said to be incapable, since he is not incapable of the bare use, which alone belongs to the friars.

† Similarly we see in a slave, who is not capable of ownership in his own right, and yet is capable in a matter of maintenance, as in the said law, and compulsion takes place by the office of the judge, as is said there. And the aforesaid points apply especially having regard to the fact that in the present case nothing was said in the gift about capacity or incapacity, but it was simply made for the salvation of the testatrix's soul and for the redemption of her sins; whence, since it was inter vivos, she could not afterwards attach any condition of capacity or incapacity, as is the text in l. perfecta donatio, C. de don. quæ sub modo. Nay, even if she could have, those words would have had no effect to prejudice it, because the express mention of those things that are tacitly inherent operates nothing, as is read and noted in capitul. significasti, de elect., and is more clearly proved in l. 2, ff. de leg. 1. For in every bequest or gift it is tacitly understood, 'if he is capable', as in the said l. si in metallum and the said l. quod meo. Furthermore, that condition is verified by law, because he is capable for the study of theology and supporting other necessities for the study itself, as was said above, or for maintenance, as I touched upon above, understanding it as above. The argument made last does not stand in the way, namely that many things were expressed contrary to the disposition of the law and of the Rule, because she gave 'to have, possess', etc.; because I say that although she expressed many modes, some of which were not lawful in themselves, nevertheless the expression of them does not vitiate the other lawful modes not disapproved by law, such as for study, etc.; but those unlawful ones are held as not expressed; a good text with the notes there is in cap. significatum, de præben., and l. filius, and l. conditiones, ff. de cond. insti., and l. sancimus, C. de dona., and 12, q. 2, c. ecclesiarum seruos, and c. 2, 10, q. 1, where there is a good text together with the gloss; to the same effect is the notable statement of Bartolus in l. Lucius, § tres hæredes, ff. ad Treb., where he says that if something was left to a monk with the proviso that if the abbot raised an action against him, it should devolve to another, the bequest is valid, but that grievance, as contrary to law, is held as not written. Furthermore, in confirmation of the aforesaid, I add another notable statement of Bartolus in auth. excipitur, C. de bo. quæ libe., where he says

† that if something is left to a monk with the proviso that nothing be acquired for the monastery, the bequest is valid, and it is understood in the best way it can be, namely that nothing in fact is acquired for the monastery, but that it suffers the monk to have it in the best way he can; what Archidiaconus notes in cap. quia ingredientibus, 19, quæstio vlt., supports this. So to the purpose, that which was said about capacity or incapacity, and likewise about 'having and possessing', etc., either is held as not added, as in the first statement of Bartolus, or must be understood in the broadest and best way possible, so that no absurdity, or contravention of the common law or of the Rule, follows from it. And since by several persons who strive to defeat the said gift, three things, as I hear, are objected beyond the aforesaid: first, that since the Friars Minor ought to induce no one to leave anything to them, as in the said clemen. exiui, § dubitaverunt, and § cum etiam, and since the said gift was made at the persuasion of the said Master Lucas, no natural or civil obligation ought to have arisen from it, as being made against the prohibition of the law, for which see what is read and noted in l. cum lex, ff. de fideiusso. Second, because it was not lawful for the said Master Lucas to stipulate for his own advantage. Third, because the gift was made to the said Master Lucas before he obtained the honor of the mastership; and thus it tacitly seems to have been made until he should be a master, as if the cause of the gift then ceases, and so the said gift ought deservedly to cease; argument in l. à filia, ff. ad Trebel. But truly, if the aforesaid points are considered diligently, they conclude nothing necessarily against the conclusions made above. For to the first it can be answered in many ways: first, by denying that any underhanded dealing by the said Master Lucas occurred here; for the contrary is clearly gathered from the tenor of the gift, especially in its beginning, which must be greatly considered in conjecturing the mind of the disposer, as in l. final., ff. de hæred. institu., noted by Bartolus in l. ambitiosa, ff. de decret. ab ord. fac. Secondly, it is answered that inducement to bestow alms for divine worship, such as for the study of theology, is not forbidden. For it is only forbidden to the friars to induce those newly entering to leave anything to them, lest they seem to have induced them to enter on account of temporal goods; or when they have recourse to special friends for relieving their mendicancy, and thus with respect to those things that consist in food; and thus the laws speak; but in our case these cease. Furthermore, if it is lawful to have recourse to special friends for the necessities of the sick and for clothing the friars, as in the said clement. exiui, § cum etiam, a fortiori it is lawful for the study of theology, in which not the benefit of the friars, but that of the universal Church is principally involved, as I said above. Nor does the text stand in the way, although it speaks there in restrictive words, and thus seems to exclude other cases not expressed there; because that text speaks of those things by which their mendicancy is relieved, which does not happen in our case. Likewise, as Bartolus elegantly says following the gloss in l. Seruius, ff. de vsucap., although a law excludes some case with a restrictive word, it does not thereby exclude cases expressed elsewhere, or similar ones, if we are in a favorable subject matter; and our case seems not only similar, but even greater than those expressed there, and we are acting for the amplifying and defending of the faith, as in the said capitul. super specula. Furthermore, and thirdly, presupposing without prejudice to truth that a prohibited persuasion had intervened here, it is not therefore inferred that the gift is void; because the matter is not opposed to the gift, but to the persuasion; for this I bring in the very clear text in cap. constituit, 20, q. 3, where it is said that religious ought not to induce anyone to enter religion in order to obtain his temporal goods, but if they do so, the entry nevertheless holds good; because that is an honest craft, nor can one who has entered religion be said to be deceived, as in capitul. penultim., quod met. causa. So in the present case, since the gift was made out of pure divine love and without any fraud, it ought not to be avoided on account of an inducement to good. We see the same in a contract entered into by an excommunicated person; for communion is forbidden to him, and he sins in intruding himself into communion, c. illud, de cle. exc., and yet the contract entered into by him holds good, as Innocent notes in c. veritatis, de do. & contu., and is proved in c. fælicis, § verum, de pœnis. What is objected secondly concerning the

† stipulation does not stand in the way: because today a stipulation is not required for the validity of a gift, as in l. si quis argentum, C. de don., especially for a pious cause; what the gloss notes in c. quoties cordis, 1, q. 7, supports this. Likewise, that lady gave unconditionally to Master Lucas being present and receiving, as is stated at the beginning of the gift. Likewise, a slave stipulates in favor of his master, although he conceives the words in his own person, as in ff. de stipu. ser. throughout; so also a religious in favor of the convent, especially in matters concerning divine worship; what Innocent notes in c. dudum, de conver. coniu., supports this, where he says through that text that just as any priest seems to be an official of the universal Church so as to receive an obligation in favor of the universal Church, so for the favor of the study of theology the said Master Lucas could receive an obligation. Furthermore, the said testatrix left that same thing freely in her will, provided that the said Master Lucas is capable of this; but he is indubitably capable for buying books and supporting the burdens of study, as was said above. Furthermore, since that lady did this spontaneously in order to provide for her soul, as appears at the beginning of the instrument of gift, it ought to be valid at least by way of a kind of dedication to a pious cause, according to what is noted by Bartolus following the gloss in l. illud, C. de sacros. ecc., in the question of the man who, being alone in his chamber, gave certain goods to the poor; and thus that objection is removed on multiple grounds. To the third, the answer is very easily apparent. And first, since she left it for the entire lifetime of the said Master Lucas, it is said in vain that it ought to last until he was made a master; for it is impossible that he should be made a master after death, nor is it likely that she thought he ought to spend his time on scholastic study for his entire life; whence, since the words are clear, captious interpretation ceases, l. ille aut ille, ff. de leg. 3, in c. fi., de verb. sig. Furthermore, the study of sacred theology is more profitable to Christianity after the mastership than before, as in c. de magistris and c. super specula, ne cle. vel mo., and he needs more books than during his time as a student. Likewise, presupposing that he does not now need books, the gift for pious causes does not cease on this account, through what I said above. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus de Tudeschis, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. When a certain time is prefixed by the law or by a statute for doing something, it must be understood if it can be done within that time.
2. In pecuniary cases, a judge cannot grant more than one delay.
3. The oath of calumny does not exclude the condemnation to expenses in case the suit is lost.
4. The custom of the court is a legitimate cause for restricting terms and delays.
casus: The case in effect is this. By a certain statute of Siena it is provided that every appeal case must be decided within 40 days, and the instance may not endure beyond 40 days. But by another statute it is provided that during the time when someone is to produce witnesses outside the province, the time for determining the case does not run ipso iure. It happened that in the case of a certain appeal, the appellant had a delay to produce witnesses; afterwards, however, asserting that he wished to produce witnesses outside the province, he requested and obtained that the said delay be prorogued; but at the end of the said delay, claiming that an impediment had befallen him within it, he obtained again a prorogation of the said delay, without proof of the impediment having been made to the judge; then, at the end of the said prorogued delay, he requested for a third time that the said delay be prorogued for him, swearing that he was not requesting this with malicious intent, and the judge, having received only the oath of calumny, prorogued the said delay for a third time. Now it is asked whether the instance of the case is extinguished, since much time has elapsed beyond 40 days?
body: Having invoked the help of the Almighty, it seems firstly that the said instance was by no means extinguished, although 40 days and more have elapsed. For the statute seems expressly to prove this position in that it expressly decrees that time does not run ipso iure during a delay granted for producing witnesses residing outside the province; therefore, the delay granted, although repeatedly prorogued for producing those witnesses, ought not to be computed in the term of 40 days; toward this is what is read and noted on similar matters in cap. auditis. de in integ. resti. and cap. auditis, de præscr. and c. 1. and c. de quarta, eo. titu. Secondly, the same seems to be said on the basis of mere law, even setting aside that statute.

† For wherever a certain time is prefixed by the law or by a statute for doing something, it must be understood if it can be done within that time; otherwise, the act can be performed even after that term; toward this are l. fin. C. de adult. and cap. ex ratione, de appel. and l. ut gradatim, ff. de mune. & hono. and l. 2. de noxa. For a law ought not to be imposed upon an impossibility, 4. distin. cap. erit autem lex; the text in l. si cum ipse, joined with l. præce. ff. de excu. tuto. serves excellently, and there Bald. holds this in our precise terms, and Ioan. An. plainly agrees in addi. Specu. in tit. de leg. §. restat, uersi. quid si statuto. But it is certain that where witnesses are to be produced from outside the province, the case cannot be decided within 40 days, since a delay of six months is granted solely for producing those witnesses, as in l. 1. C. de dila. and 3. q. 3. c. spatium; therefore, after that time a judgment can be rendered, since the instance was by no means extinguished. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the second delay was given without judicial inquiry into the cause. For to this one can answer in multiple ways. First, that here a second or third delay was not given, but only a single one, which was repeatedly prorogued before its expiration. For it is one thing to give a new delay, and another to prorogue one already given before its end, according to what is read and noted in l. quod si manente, ff. de preca. and l. 4. ff. de dam. inf. where see Bar. Likewise, when the first delay was not complete, it can not only be prorogued, but even a second can easily be granted, as noted by Inno. in c. ultra tertiam, de testi. But in our case the first was not complete, because it never had the term of six months or three; therefore, a second could easily be granted without another inquiry, or it could even be prorogued, since such a prorogation seems justified by the law itself. Likewise and thirdly makes what Bar. noted in l. 1. C. de dila. in fi. where he says that proof made within a delay granted without judicial inquiry into the cause is valid when the first delay was not complete. But although these arguments seem to press hard, I nonetheless think one must lean toward the opposite view. I am moved first by the text in l. fi. ff. de dila.

† where it is said that in pecuniary causes the judge cannot grant more than one delay; and that text is to be weighed in that the negation precedes the verb "potest" (can), whereby the power of assigning another delay is taken away from the judge, since then the verb "potest" induces a necessity, as noted by the gl. in regula prima, de reg. iu. li. 6. and noted by Bar. in our terms in d. l. fi. And because the text in l. oratione, ff. eo. seems to intimate the contrary, various solutions are given; but that one is commonly held, that every evidentiary delay is peremptory, so that without judicial inquiry into the cause another cannot be assigned; and so must d. l. fi. be understood, namely that with judicial inquiry into the cause a second can be assigned, and thus speaks d. l. oratione. But this judicial inquiry into the cause consists in making proof to the judge concerning an impediment arising within the assigned delay; without this inquiry into the cause, however, the granting of a second delay is not valid, as the text of d. l. fin. clearly intended, and Bar. plainly holds there; what is read and noted in c. in causis, and by the gl. in c. 2. de dila. supports this. What sort of proof of the impediment there ought to be, however, is not found well decided in that section. Fed. de Senis consi. 109 seems to maintain that the oath of the one alleging the impediment suffices, which the gl. in c. unico. 4. q. 5 seems to have held. But the opinion of Io. Mo., Arc., and Io. An. in capitu. 1. de dolo & contuma. lib. 6 pleases me more, who conclude after many points that this is discretionary, having considered the impediment of the person and the quality of the case; whence the judge will be content with an oath when he requires semi-full proof, not when he requires full proof; and for this I cite the notable text in cap. ex literis, de in integr. restitut. where it is proved that an oath does not indistinctly prove an impediment. Since therefore in our case, in the second delay or prorogation, no judicial inquiry into the cause intervened regarding the impediment, it was therefore invalid; and the same can be said of the third, both because only the oath of calumny was exacted, which does not seem to suffice especially in granting or proroguing a third, since a third ought to be granted only after an exacting judicial inquiry into the cause, as noted in the said laws, and especially in d. l. fin. ff. de fer.; and also because the oath ought not to have been de calumnia, but de veritate, because it is possible that in the first or second delay there was negligence and not malice (calumnia), and by negligence one is excluded from a second or third delay, as noted in the previously cited laws; and cap. licet, de probatio. supports this; just as in similar cases we say,

† that the oath of calumny does not exclude condemnation in expenses in the case of losing the lawsuit, because one could have litigated temerariously, not calumniously, as noted in cap. finem, de dolo & contuma. and in cap. calumniam, de pœnis, and in l. ex diuerso, ff. de rei uendi. and l. sancimus, C. de iudi.; and this does not prove that that exists which happens to be absent from it, l. non hoc, C. unde cogn. and cap. 2. de transla. præl. For proof must necessarily conclude, cap. in præsentia, de probatio. and cap. auditis, de in inte. resti. and l. ad probationem, C. loc. From the aforesaid it is clearly inferred that the said instance was extinguished by the lapse of so much time, since those prorogations or grants of delays could not be made in the aforesaid manner; therefore, the statute ceases to apply which willed that during the term prefixed for bringing witnesses from outside the province, the time of the instance does not run, because that statute must be understood as concerning a term lawfully granted, argum. l. 3. §. condemnatum, ff. de re iudi. and c. non potest, de præben. li. 6. Excellent is what Bart. noted in l. iustè possidet, ff. de acqui. poss. where he says that one put into possession by authority of the judge without observing the proper order is not excused by reason of the judicial authority from the penalty of the statute punishing those entering and disturbing the possessions of another, c. sæpe, de uerb. signi. and as noted in c. conquerente, de resti. spo. Also in favor of this is that statute under the rubric "within what time a cause should be defined," where it is provided that not even the parties by mutual consent can prorogue the prefixed term of the instance; therefore, the sentence pronounced remains valid, nor ought the party to be heard any further against it, just as he would not be heard after the legal term, as in cap. personas, and c. cum sit, de appe.; for that statutory term takes the place of the legal term, as noted by Inn. in cap. ex ratione, eo. titu. and the Doctors in c. pen. de iudi. and Bar. and Bal. in l. properandum, C. eo.; and through these points the response to the first contrary argument cited above is evident, and also to the second. For I admit that if from the magnitude of the cause or the long distance of the men the cause could not have been concluded in the time prefixed by the statute, then the cause can be concluded after that time; but in our case this did not happen. For as is presupposed in the narrative given to me, the first delay was competently extended according to the distance of the places, so that the party could have produced the witnesses had no other extraneous factor arisen. Therefore, a second or third delay could not be given without the cause of the impediment being lawfully proven, as I said above. Nor does it stand in the way when it is said that here a second or third delay was not given, but only a single one repeatedly prorogued. For I say that the laws prohibit giving a second or third delay without inquiry into the cause, looking to the effect and not merely to the mode. For they introduced this lest a cause be delayed beyond what is proper without a just and manifest cause, and thus lawsuits would become immortal, ar. l. properandum, C. de iud. and c. finem litibus, de do. & cont.; therefore, what is prohibited by one path ought not to be admitted by another, as in the rule "cum quod una via," de reg. iur. lib. 6. and c. tuæ, de procu. and what is noted in them. And from the contrary opinion room would be given for deceits and frauds contrary to c. quanto, de divor. For the judge could, through this path of prorogation, if it were lawful, circumvent the disposition of that l. fina. ff. de fer., which must not be said. Moreover, even the first delay ought not to be prorogued without an inquiry into the cause, although a slight one suffices, as noted in l. a procedente, C. de dila. and d. l. fi. and c. 2. eo. tit.; therefore, a fortiori it ought not to be prorogued without an inquiry into the cause, especially so many times as happened in our case; and this Bal. plainly seems to intend in l. j. C. quomodo & quando iudex, in fi., where he says that just as an inquiry into the cause is required in granting a delay, so also in altering it; although, as I hear, Ange. de Peru. thought otherwise and less correctly in d. l. fina. ff. de ferijs. Finally, to the statement of Innoc. and Barto. cited above, I reply in multiple ways. First, through what Barto. himself intended in d. l. fina., where he rejected that statement of Inno., saying that although the judge prefixed a term shorter than the legal term, he cannot on that account give a second delay without an inquiry into the cause; because the term concerning which mention is made in d. l. j. C. de dila. was prefixed not so that the judge must prefix the entire, complete period, but so that he cannot extend it, though he may shorten it; whence the judge may evaluate within that term of delay as seems fit to him, as the text there clearly intimates; therefore it is not true to say that he shortened the legal term; rather, he established a competent term according to his discretion. He cannot therefore give a second delay under that pretext. Secondly, it can be answered that today, by the common custom of the courts, legal terms are shortened;

† whence it is the custom of the forum to restrict terms and delays for a legitimate cause, as Barto. noted in authen. qui semel, C. quomodo & quando iudex. Therefore, the party will not be able to complain about the shortening of the term, and consequently there was no legitimate cause for proroguing that grant. Thirdly, I respond, having considered the form of the statute, or new reformation, where it is simply provided that the judge of appeal is bound to finish the cause within 40 days, etc., and that that instance shall last no longer; for by shortening the time of the year prefixed by law, as in cle. sicut, de appella. and in authen. ei qui appellat, C. de tempo. appella., it seems tacitly to provide that judicial terms ought to be shortened, because otherwise the cause could not be decided within so short a time, as Inno. held in c. super eo, §. de appel.; and the judge ought so to restrict delays that he can decide the cause within the term prefixed for him, since it is possible; but in our case the judge did not observe this, because without an inquiry into the cause, at least a lawful one, he prorogued the delay several times or granted new delays; therefore, that instance is extinguished. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether parents can marry off their children, and induce daughters to consent.
2. Girls who do not choose betrothed husbands for themselves ought to be commended.
3. Where multiple things are mandated, and the mandate cannot be fulfilled in all respects, it ought to be fulfilled in that manner in which it can.
4. Women often strive against their own interests.
casus: A certain Raynerius de Tholemeis of Siena made his will, in which he instituted as his universal heirs his four granddaughters from a predeceased son, and made and appointed as his fideicommissaries and executors of the will five persons in number, and gave them full power, and ordered, mandated, and ordained that two of his said granddaughters should be married in the house of the Tholomei of his lineage to those persons who shall seem fit to the said fideicommissaries, while the other two should be married to whomsoever it shall also seem fit and pleasing to the said fideicommissaries, etc. It happens that after the testator's death all those girls died, with only one surviving, concerning whose marriage a dispute arises among the said fideicommissaries, as to whether by the testator's disposition she ought to be married within the house of the Tholomei, or outside it. Also, whether three out of the five fideicommissaries can marry her outside the testator's kinship, or whether the two who wish to marry her within the kinship ought to be preferred, and whether these two can do so without the others if the others, upon being requested, refuse to consent. Also, whether they can contract betrothals, since nothing was said of them in the will, but of marriage only. Lastly, it is also asked whether the said fideicommissaries can marry her or make betrothals without the consent of three nearest blood relations or kinsmen, notwithstanding the form of the Sienese statute providing in the form that follows, namely: 'No person shall dare or presume to celebrate nuptials, marriage, or betrothals with any citizen of Siena without the consent of the father or paternal grandfather, if she has one, and if she does not have a paternal grandfather or father, without the consent of three nearest blood relations.'
body: Having humbly invoked the help of Christ Jesus and His mother, several matters must be examined for the decision of the aforesaid questions. And first, whether the disposition of the paternal grandfather regarding the marrying off of the granddaughters was valid in any case. Secondly, presupposing validity in some respect, whether this surviving granddaughter is to be married off by the fideicommissaries into the house of the Tolomei, or outside it. Thirdly, presupposing that it is in the house of the testator's kin, whether two, who agree on this, can marry her off notwithstanding the other three fideicommissaries, since they refuse to consent, or what remedy there will be in order that the testator's will may take effect. Fourthly, whether the said fideicommissaries can contract betrothals (sponsalia) on behalf of the said girl, since she is not presently fit for marriage due to the impediment of age, taking into account that nothing was said in the will concerning betrothals. Fifthly, whether, the said statute notwithstanding, the said fideicommissaries can contract marriage or betrothals on behalf of the said girl without the consent of the other close relatives. Returning to the first: it seems that the testator's disposition regarding the contracting of marriage or betrothals was not valid, because regarding spiritual matters, and especially marriage, paternal power is not considered, since a father has no right to intermeddle in these things, as in c. si annum, de iud. lib. 6; to the same effect c. unicum, de despon. impu., where it is said that children are in no way bound by a marriage or betrothals contracted by parents unless they have consented tacitly or expressly, as is there more fully noted; this is supported by capitulum unicum, xxx. q. ij., and xxvij. q. ij. capit. sufficiat, where it is clear that for contracting marriage the sole consent of those whose union is at issue suffices, even if the parents were unwilling to consent. Whence under canon law, which must be followed in these matters, as in c. pe. and ulti. de secund. nup., with what is noted there by Bart. in l. priuilegia, C. de sacro.san.eccle., if a daughter contracts without her father's consent, she cannot be disinherited on this account, and indeed she can seek a dowry from the father, as noted by the gloss in xxxij. q. ij. c. si, and c. de raptoribus, xxxv. q. j., at least when she could not be married unless she promised a dowry, according to what is noted by Barto. in l. obligamur, ff. de actio. & obli. Furthermore and finally, the will of the grandfather testator extends to a time when the granddaughters were not in his power; therefore it is not valid. For paternal power is dissolved by death, and he disposes after death; to this effect the gloss noted in l. illa institutio, ff. de hære. insti.; and it is equivalent to dispose at an incapacitated time or at a capacitated time if the effect refers to an incapacitated time, as in l. quod sponsę, C. de donatio. ante nup., and l. eum qui, ff. de iurisdi. omn. iudi. But these things notwithstanding, I judge that according to law it must be said as follows: that either it is asked whether parents can bind an unwilling daughter or granddaughter to marriage or betrothals, and it must be said that they cannot; for the daughter is bound to consent only out of decency (ex honestate), but not of necessity, as noted in capitulum 1, de spons. impu. lib. 6. And so l. sed ea quæ patris, ff. de spon., which says that a daughter cannot depart from the paternal will unless when the father chooses for her one who is unworthy in morals or base, has no place in canon law, as in the laws cited above and the noted gloss in the said cap. 1.

† Or it is asked whether parents can marry off their children and induce their daughters to consent. And I say that they can: under civil law there is an explicit text in l. si patre, ff. de rit. nupt., where the singular text says that even if the daughter consented under her father's compulsion to one to whom she would not have consented if she had been of her own independent discretion, the marriage nevertheless holds; under canon law, however, it does not: text in capitulum honorantur, 32. quæst. 2, where there is the text of Saint Ambrose, and among other things he commends girls who do not choose betrotheds for themselves, but consent to the disposition of their parents;

† whence, in the person of the woman, he says: "My father undertook the care of my betrothals; for this is not mine"; and at the beginning, in the person of Rebecca, it is said: "The parents are honored, gifts having been left; the girl is consulted, not about the betrothal. For she awaits the judgment of her parents; for it is not of virginal modesty to choose a husband for herself, but having already been betrothed to the man, she is consulted about the day of departure," etc., as there. And the text in the said capitulum 1, de despon. impu., says that if a father contracted a marriage for his daughter, the daughter ought to consent, namely out of decency, as noted there in the gloss. So also we see in the end that parents can offer their children to a monastery, and they ought to consent out of decency, as in cap. 1, 20. quæst. 2, noted by Innocen. in cap. 2, de re.; this is supported by c. cum uirum, under the same title, with similar texts. It must therefore be concluded that parents can contract marriage and betrothals on behalf of their children, and they ought to consent out of a duty of decency. Moreover, the paternal grandfather, who had the granddaughters in his power, was able to entrust this choice and induction of the children to his fideicommissaries, for he himself is seen to do what they did, as in l. unum ex familia, ff. de leg. 2. Nor is this surprising, for he gives to his children a tutor who has the pupillus in his power, as in ff. de test. tut. throughout; all the more can he entrust this bare choice and persuasion, argument in the authentic multo magis, C. de episco. & cler.; and especially since among them is the maternal grandmother, who is the tutrix of the said girl, and a tutor can do this, argument of capitulum 1, 20. quæst. 2, and of the things which Innocen. noted in the said capitulum 2, de regu.; and thus the making of a testament and the appointment of a tutor are generously granted, according to what is noted by the famous gloss in the said l. illa, and so too the power of this choice and persuasion; and this as to the first point. I conclude therefore that the paternal grandfather was able to give this power to his fideicommissaries, according to what he himself had, and in doubt he is seen to have given it according to the disposition of law, because general words must be restricted according to the subject matter, l. si uno, in princ., ff. loca., and c. cum dilectus, de cons., and l. 2, C. de nox., with similar texts. I come to the second doubt: whether the said girl ought to be married off by the fideicommissaries into the house of the Tolomei, and the girl induced to consent in the manner aforesaid. And conclusively it seems to me that she must. For wherever several things are commanded, and the mandate cannot

† be fulfilled in all respects, it ought to be fulfilled in that manner in which it can be, as in c. cum dilecti, de do. & cont., and l. Celsus, ff. de arbit., and cap. Pisanis, de resti. spol., noted by the gloss in c. constitutus, de rescri.; for the wish of the testator cannot have its effect in all respects on account of the death of the others; therefore it ought to be carried into execution in the person of the survivor so far as can be done, as in the laws cited above and l. Stichum aut Pamphilum, ff. de uerb. obl.; she is therefore to be married off according as it seems good and shall please the fideicommissaries. But whether in the kin of the testator or outside it, I judge that according to law it must be said: that it is in the house and family and kin of the testator, though within a degree not prohibited. I am moved because where something is arranged by a testator or another to be done in the persons of several, and the mandate cannot be verified except in the person of one, then one must stand by the order of the writing, so that the act is performed with the person first named, as in cap. mandato, de præben. lib. 6, and l. quoties, ff. de usur., especially where an ordered affection is present, as is the excellent text in l. hæredes mei, § si, ff. ad Treb., and noted by Barto. in l. Gallus, § quidam, ff. de li. & post. In our case, moreover, he disposed first concerning those to be married in the house of the Tolomei, and afterwards concerning those to be married outside the family; therefore he seems to have had greater affection toward those of the family, and this must especially be said in our case, for anyone is presumed to desire the honor, preservation, and increase of his own kin, as in l. 1, ff. de uen. inspi., and what is noted there, and by Cy. in l. publi., C. de adult., with similar texts; but through this marriage wealth is preserved in the house and kinship; therefore he seems to have had an affection principally toward those of the house rather than toward outsiders; this is also supported at the end by what is noted in l. duo sunt Titii, ff. de testa. tu. As to the third doubt, namely whether two of the fideicommissaries can marry her into the house of the Tolomei when the other three refuse to consent, or what remedy is to be applied: I judge it must be said that either a suitable person is not found in the house of the Tolomei, and then she ought to be married outside the house, because that mandate ought to be understood if and insofar as a suitable person is found in the house, as in c. causam, de electio., and c. abbate, de uerb. signi., and l. ut gradum, ff. de mu. & hono.; this is supported by l. sed ea quæ patris, C. de spon. If, however, a suitable person is found in the house and agnation of the testator, then it could be said that with the others unwilling to execute the will of the testator, two will be able to execute it; and it can be maintained that even one alone could, an excellent and almost express argument in c. 2, § sanè, de test. lib. 6, where it is said that if one of the executors of a testament has died, or is removed, or does not wish to execute it, the other alone will be able to fulfill the testator's will, lest the testator's will be impeded; and the same by Bar. in l. 1, § si plures, ff. de exerci., and Bald. in l. nulli, C. de epi. & cler. And although Fede. de Senis, consi. 65, said that the minority part cannot execute without the majority part, responding to § sanè that it applies when two had been appointed, because then either one can, since there is no majority part, nevertheless he reports that certain others held the first view indistinctly, so that even a minority part can execute when the majority part is unwilling, and I think this is truer through the rationale of that text; for it bases itself on lest it happen that the will of the testator be impeded; whence, the unwillingness of the others, or their death or prolonged absence being given, that power seems to belong in solidum, just as is observed in the case of multiple procurators appointed simply in a spiritual case according to the things contained in cap. si duo, de procura. lib. 6; this seems to have been tacitly of the mind of Barto., Bal., and Iac. de Are. in the places cited above. In response to § sanè, insofar as it makes mention of two, it can be said that it recounts the contingent fact, for the rationale of the letter proceeds in the laws if a minority part does not wish to execute, and the rationale of the law is to be considered, even against the words, as in l. cum pater, § dulcissimis, de leg. 2, l. non dubium, C. de legi., and the rule certum, de regu. iur. lib. 6. Similarly, for greater caution another remedy can also be observed, namely that the magistrate (potestas) be approached and his office implored so that he may compel the others to consent according to the will of the deceased, argument in c. nullus, de iure patro.; for wherever someone must grant consent in the act of another, he can be compelled to consent if he objects without cause, as there; and this is supported by what is noted on similar terms by Bald. in l. si cum dotem, § eo autem tempore, ff. solu. mat., and in l. fi., ff. de ape. reci., and in l. cum non solum, § necessitatem, C. de bo. quæ lib., and by Barto. in l. coniunctione, C. de nup., and Bart. in l. 1, § si plures, ff. de exerc., who commonly conclude that if a statute provides that a woman cannot contract or make a will without the consent of two close relatives, and if those closer relatives refuse to consent, the woman can approach the judge so that he may compel them to consent if they do not have a just cause for objecting, or, if they resist, pronounce that she can contract or make a will without their consent; thus punctually it must be said in the present matter that if the fideicommissaries wish to avoid doubt, they should approach the judge, who may compel the other fideicommissaries to consent, or pronounce, if they resist, that these men can act without them; and this as to the third doubt. Concerning the fourth doubt, whether the said fideicommissaries can contract betrothals when in the will mention was made simply of marriage: and I believe that they can, through l. tutor, § fina., and l. oratio, ff. de spon., where it is generally said that that which is disposed concerning marriage also has place in betrothals; nor is this surprising, since through betrothals one arrives at marriage, whence if marriage is prohibited, betrothals are prohibited, and if it is permitted, betrothals are permitted, as there; to the same effect l. non sine, and what is noted there, C. de bonis quæ libe., and c. in causis, de elect., where it is proved that when the power of electing is given, the power of postulating seems to be given, since postulation is conjoined to election, and through it one arrives at the effect of election; and this seems to me indubitable. I come to the fifth and last: whether the consent of these fideicommissaries suffices, the above-written statute notwithstanding. And I believe undoubtedly that it does, because the statute punishes one who contracts with a girl without the consent of the father or grandfather; but in our case the consent of the grandfather concurs, because by virtue of the power granted to the fideicommissaries the grandfather testator himself is seen to do what they have done, as is proved in l. unum ex familia, § 1, de leg. 2. And this is supported by that question to which Dy. and Bart. after him introduce that text, for they ask: what if a testator left one hundred to be distributed for pious uses as the executor of the testament shall have chosen, and the executor chose the fabric of a church: it was asked whether the bishop ought to have the fourth from that legacy, for from a legacy made to the fabric a fourth is not owed, as in c. fin. de testa., but from a legacy made to a church simply it is owed, as in c. requisisti, e. ti.; it is doubted now in our case, because not the testator, but the executor chose the fabric, and it is commonly concluded through that text that it is not owed, because the testator is seen to have chosen since he gave the executor the power of choosing; to the same effect what is noted in l. Theopompus, ff. de dot. prælega., and the rule qui per alium facit, de reg. iur. lib. 6. Furthermore, the rationale of the statute was none other than that girls should not be deceived by those contracting without the consent of parents and close relatives,

† since women often strive against their own advantages, as in l. iiij. in fin., C. de sponsa., which rationale ceases in our case, since the grandfather, who is presumed to love his granddaughters more than others, argu. l. fina., C. de cura. fur., chose these fideicommissaries or executors of his testament, in whom he seems to have had the greatest confidence, and they are presumed to be very close friends, and also some of them are of the deceased's kin, whence deception is not to be presumed when they intervene, argu. l. transactione, C. de transact. Hence we see in the end that tutors appointed by parents in a testament are preferred to legitimate and dative tutors, as in l. si sub conditione, ff. de testa. tuto., and thus even outsiders appointed in a testament are preferred to blood relations, because the testator is presumed to have chosen those more affectionate toward him. And especially must these things be held having regard to the form of the said statute, which is against the ius commune; indeed it could be said that it is null, since it impedes the free capacity to contract marriages, and this was openly held by Ioan. And. in c. statutum, de homi. lib. 6. But concerning this I do not extend myself further, since even presupposing the validity of the statute, the aforesaid conclusion undoubtedly proceeds. And through this the answer to all the doubts is clear. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Just as a father is bound concerning the peculium arising from a son's contract, so also from a condemnation rendered in court.
2. A fictitious payment [?] does not suffice to give an action against the principal.
3. A division made by a father among sons during paternal power is not valid.
body: With the name of Christ auspiciously invoked. Although many arguments could be alleged in favor of the said Antonio, father of the aforementioned Pilio, I, for the sake of brevity, will touch upon only two, which without any doubt are sufficient even distributively for dominus Antonio to obtain victory in the suit, not only in this judgment, but also in another. And first, in this: that dominus P. at the time of the condemnation rendered against him on account of his contumacy was in paternal power, in which he also subsequently died. Moreover, a condemnation rendered against a son on account of his contumacy—in such manner that he was never in court, at least for the purpose of joinder of issue (litis contestatio)—ought not to harm the father, even with respect to the peculium profectitium, nor the adventitium, as noted by the final gloss in insti. de noxa and Bar. in l. si finita, in § si de uectigalibus, ff. de dam. infect., to the same effect as what he himself notes in l. cum filius, ff. de uerbo. obli. For although a son's delict harms the father with respect to the peculium profectitium when the son was present in court,

† because just as the father would be bound concerning the peculium arising from the son's contract, so also from a condemnation rendered in court—because in court we quasi-contract, l. iij. previously cited—and the same must be said in this case regarding the peculium adventitium, because the father left it with the son without retaining the usufruct for himself, which he can do, as in l. cum oportet. § fin autem, C. de bo. quę libe. For there is then the same rationale in this peculium adventitium as in the profectitium when the son is condemned, especially for a delict on account of his contumacy; and such a judgment ought not to prejudice the father, neither with respect to the peculium profectitium nor the adventitium. The reason is that a contumacious person is held, by virtue of the statute, as confessed; and since this confession is a legal fiction and not real, it ought not to harm another, as in l. eius qui delatorem, ff. de iure fis. and what is noted there. Likewise, we see that wherever a judgment rendered against one prejudices another, that rule fails when the judgment is rendered against a contumacious person, as in l. qui repudiantis in fi. and l. Papinianus. § meminisse, ff. de inoff. test., to the same effect l. duobus. § 1. de iureiur.,

† where a fictitious payment does not suffice to give an action against the principal, and this position Barto. expressly affirmed in the said l. cum filius, and the said § si de uectigalibus, and Cy. in a similar question in l. si quando, C. unde ui. But in our case dominus Pi. was in paternal power, and was condemned on account of his contumacy by virtue of the statutes; therefore, such a sentence ought not to be ordered into execution against the father, whether we say that those goods possessed by dominus P. during his lifetime had proceeded from the father, or had come to him from the favor of fortune or the industry of his person. For in the case of profectitious goods there is no doubt, since they belong to the father by full right; while in adventitious goods the same must be said by reason of the usufruct which is owed to the father during his life, as in l. non solum, C. de bo. quæ lib. and l. j. C. de bo. mater. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that at least with respect to the bare ownership (proprietas) of those goods that sentence ought to be executed against the father, since the ownership pertained to the son, as in the laws immediately cited above; because I say that during paternal power the son cannot in any way dispose even of the bare ownership—whence he cannot even make a will, as in said l. non solum. § illis autem, and l. pe. C. qui testa. fa. non pos.—and therefore, just as the son cannot during the father's life alienate adventitious goods directly, so he cannot indirectly by committing a delict, as the same Bar. affirmed in said § si de uectigalibus. And through this that dispute is avoided, whether the goods possessed by the son ought to be presumed adventitious or profectitious, concerning which see the gloss and Doctors in l. cum oportet, C. de bo. quæ lib. For whether we say they were profectitious or adventitious, the aforesaid conclusion always claims its place, as is clear from the premises. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that, by virtue of an arbitral award (laudum) rendered between dominus An. and the son, a division of the goods was made and full capacity to dispose of the divided goods was granted to the sons; because I say

† that such a division made by a father among his sons, during paternal power, is invalid, and has only the force of a last will, as noted in l. si ancillam, § si pater, ff. pro suo, and l. si filia, § si pater, ff. fa. erc. and the notable gloss joined to the text in l. quoties, C. eo. For between a father and a son during paternal power no civil obligation arises, as noted in l. frater à fratre, ff. de cond. ind. Hence it is that, as a rule, a donation made to a son existing in power is not valid, on which see fully the notes in auth. ex testamento, C. de colla. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that the division was made under the pretext of an arbitration (arbitramentum), because that which the parties cannot do expressly, they cannot do by virtue of an arbitration, since arbitration is a kind of compromise (transactio), as in Auth. ut differentes iudices § si uerò contigerit, to the same effect l. cum hi. § sed cum lis, ff. de transa. Furthermore, the arbitration must be understood to mean that the father permits the sons to have the disposition of those goods with eyes closed (conniving), just as a master permits a slave, as in l. 4. ff. de manu., or even that he leaves the usufruct with the sons by allowing them to use it, not, however, that that division has the force of a contract between father and son during paternal power. For Bar. expressly affirmed in said § si uectigalibus that even if the father permitted adventitious goods to remain with the sons, the sentence rendered on account of contumacy against the son ought not on that account to be ordered into execution against those adventitious goods to the prejudice of the father. Lastly, it does not stand in the way if it is said that dominus P. was not condemned solely on account of contumacy, but also because of the confession of Micha.; but because the confession of one person, especially of one confessing his own crime, does not prejudice another, c. 1. de confes. and l. si. C. de accu.; nor do the judicial proceedings held against one of the co-defendants create proof against the other who is said likewise to have committed the delict, l. denunciasse. § fi. ff. de adul., and on our specific terms Bar. affirms this in said l. cum filius; and so much as to the first consideration. Secondly and more briefly, the said Ant. can defend himself on the grounds of the nullity of the sentence, because the judge pronounced the sentence of condemnation after the lapse of eight years from the time the delict was committed, whereas by virtue of the statute the podestà (potestas) cannot inquire or judge except concerning delicts committed during the time of his office, and during the six months prior to the beginning of his office; therefore the said sentence was null. For since the podestà receives his authority by virtue of the statutes, and that limitation is set down in the statutes, therefore whatever he does contrary to such a statute is null by operation of law; for this the notable gloss in cle. 1. de iu. pat.; c. at si clerici, de iudi. and C. si a non compe. iudi. throughout support this. However, one need not care much about this, since the first consideration is sufficiently and abundantly enough for the victory of the case, namely that the said Ant. be acquitted, and the adverse party condemned in expenses. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. An emphyteuta can vindicate the emphyteutic property, even from the lord, provided that he has paid the rent.
2. A lord can by his own authority expel an emphyteuta on account of negligence or contumacy in paying the due portion.
3. The will of a man cannot be proved except by conjectures, in the absence of an express will.
