4. A successor in a fief ought to seek that the investiture be renewed.
body: IN the case which is pending, or is expected to be pending, between the noble man Guido Paulus on the one part, and the daughter of the late Philippus, full brother of the said Gui. P., on the other part, regarding certain emphyteutic property originally granted to a certain Matthaeus, father of the said G. P. and Philippus, and to his male descendants down to the third generation, in such manner that the share of the predeceasing party should devolve upon the survivors, and upon the failure of males should devolve upon the daughters. Two questions must necessarily be examined, one principally, the other accessorily. First, therefore, the duty of examining arises, whether the emphyteusis granted to the said M. was resolved ipso facto by the cessation of the payment of the ground rent, since for four years on the part of the said M. or his heirs the due ground rent was not paid to the monastery of Saint Thomas from the years of the Lord 1412 up to the year 1417. Secondly, it will be examined decisively whether the grant or renewal made during that same time solely to P. and to his children, even females, before the said property had devolved to the monastery according to the pacts placed in the first grant, was valid. Concerning the first, there have been various opinions, since the law on this point does not appear clear. And if we hold the opinion of certain authorities, which Innocentius reports and does not reject in c. potuit, de loca., that the authority of a judge is required in the resolution thereof, and that it is not resolved ipso iure by non-payment, the decision of this question would be quite clear; because since the said contract was never resolved by the authority of a judge, it would have to be concluded manifestly that the grant or renewal made to the said P. was not valid, since the emphyteutic property had not yet reverted to the church, and the grant made to M. and his descendants would remain in its status, both by common law and by virtue of the grant made, all emphyteutic property ought to abide in the person of the said G. P., since he alone has remained male from the issue of the lord M., especially since in the name of the said M. and his heirs payment was afterwards made in 1417 and 19 and 20, even for the past years. But if the contrary opinion is held, namely, that in the resolution of an emphyteusis the authority of a judge is not required, but that it occurs ipso iure on account of the ground rent not being paid at the due time (which opinion seems truer and more common, as is the view of the gloss in the said cap. potuit, and in l. secunda, C. de iure emphyteu., Barto. holds there, and l. ij, ff. si ager uectig., and in the authentica qui rem, C. de sacro. san. eccle., and Specu. clearly holds in the title de loca. in §. nunc aliqua, verse lxxxvj, and it seems to me clearly proved through the text of l. j, joined with l. ij, ff. si ager uectig., where it is clearly said

† that the emphyteuta can vindicate the emphyteutic property, even from the lord, provided that he has paid the ground rent; therefore, a contrario sensu, when he does not pay the ground rent, the emphyteusis is resolved with respect to the lord himself, for otherwise he could vindicate the property before it were resolved by the authority of a judge, according to the note at the end by Innocen. in c. inter dilectos, de exces. praela., and this the gloss and Barto. clearly understood; the same seems to be proved in the said l. ij, C. de iure emphyteu., at the end, for there the emphyteuta is advised that, if the lord refuses to receive the money, he should consign it, lest it be alleged afterward that he has forfeited his right on account of non-payment; to the same effect is the text in the said c. potuit, where it is said that on account of non-payment the emphyteuta can be expelled, and the word 'expelled' must be weighed, for it sounds in fact, not in law, and thus intimates that a sentence of deprivation is not necessary, but that an expulsion in fact suffices; and therefore the glossators of both laws have commonly said

† that by his own authority the lord can expel the emphyteuta on account of negligence or contumacy in paying the due ground rent, as is noted in the said c. potuit and in the said l. ij)—then this question becomes doubtful. For since the text in the said l. ij prescribes a period of two years, after the lapse of which it gives the lord the authority to expel the emphyteuta, which the text in the said c. potuit tempers, unless the emphyteuta provides for himself by speedy satisfaction. (Nor in our case can speedy satisfaction be alleged, since it stood for two years and beyond two years, for those words refer to a brief period, as is noted in the said c. potuit; nor can it be said that it is required that the emphyteuta have been sued in judgment or out of court, since this would be plainly contrary to the text in the said c. potuit, where it is said that an admonition is not required so that he may pay on time, since it is prescribed by law; to this certain authors who held that opinion do not pay attention.) Therefore, the grant or renewal made to the lord P. and to his children alone held good, which grant indeed was made to him in the year 1416, and thus four years after the payment of the ground rent ceased. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the abbot of Saint Thomas, in the renewal made to P., did not say that he made it on account of the unpaid canon, for it is enough that he made it generally, and in doubt we ought to presume that one performs an act in the best manner that he can, as in l. 3, ff. de milita. testa., and in doubt a matter must be interpreted so that it may rather be valid than perish, as in capitulum abbate, de uerbo. signi., and l. quoties, ff. de uerbo. obliga. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the payment of the ground rent was afterwards made in the name of Mat. or his heirs, when default could not be purged to the prejudice of the lord P., to whom a right had been acquired through the grant made to him before default was purged, by the argument in capitulum quamuis, and what is noted there, de rescrip., in the Sext. Nor also should it stand in the way if it is said that at least a declaratory sentence ought to have preceded before the grant was made to the lord Pet., through cap. cum secundum leges, de haere., in the Sext, and what is noted in l. eius, qui delatorem, ff. de iure fisc., because those laws proceed with respect to the seizure of property to be made by reason of a forfeiture induced by law, but with respect to the grant of a devolved right to be made, a declaratory sentence is not required, as is the notable text in capitulum licet episcopus, de praeben., in the Sext, and what is noted there by the fourth gloss. But these things notwithstanding, I think that the grant made to the lord Pet. was by law null, and that today the grant previously made to Matthaeus and his male descendants down to the third generation persists in its validity, and consequently that today the said property ought to abide with the lord G. P., and not with the daughter of the lord P. I am moved principally because, even presupposing that opinion that an emphyteusis is resolved ipso iure through the failure to pay the ground rent at the due time, nevertheless in the resolution it is necessarily required that the will of the lord intervene, otherwise it is not resolved. This the text proves in two places, C. de iur. emph., in the said l. 2, where the text says twice, 'if the lord will have wished,' and by that text Barto. affirmed this there, and likewise Bal. in the said auth. qui rem, C. de sacrosanct. eccle.; the gloss in the said l. 2, ff. si ager uecti., expressly perceived this, and more expressly Bart. there; for it is concluded in the aforesaid places that against an emphyteuta vindicating the property it cannot be objected by a stranger that he did not pay the ground rent, but only by the lord, and this because ownership is not transferred ipso iure by non-payment, but only if the lord wills it, which Bar. there said was to be noted and kept in mind; to the same effect is the text in the said c. potuit, at the end, where it is said that an emphyteuta who does not pay can be expelled. Wherefore the word 'can' must be weighed: for it gives the lord the power of expelling, but it does not expel ipso facto; and concerning this word 'can', see the note by the gloss in the first rule, de re. iu., in the Sext, and Bar. in l. si., ff. de dilatio. But in our case it does not appear that the abbot of Saint Thomas wished M. or his heirs to be deprived on account of the non-payment within that four-year period; nay rather, if all the deeds are rightly weighed, he never seems to have contemplated this situation. For he never said expressly before the purging of the default that he wished M. or his heirs to be deprived, nor can it even be tacitly gathered that he wished this, but rather the contrary; which is clearly gathered from the receiving of the ground rent which was afterwards paid to him for the past and future years. For, as appears in the census book of the same monastery, to which faith is to be given, especially to the prejudice of the monastery, or as to declaring the will of those of the church, according to those things which are held and noted in c. ad audientiam, de praescriptio., and c. cum causam, de prob., and l. Nesennius makes to this point, and what is noted there, ff. de nego. gest., and by Bal. in l. admonendi, ff. de iureiurand., and l. nuda, ff. de dona., the ground rent was paid to the monastery in the name of M. or his heirs in the 17th, 19th, and 20th years, as well for the past as for the future years. From which it evidently appears concerning the will of the lord that he did not wish him on this account to be deprived, according to the notes by the gloss and doctors in the said c. potuit and l. 2, C. de iure emph., where Bartol. after others expressly affirms this; and if it is said that credit ought not to be given to the census book to the prejudice of the lord P., by the argument of l. solennibus, C. de rei uendi., and what is noted there by Bald. in the beginning, I say that this proceeds when the entry was made or tended directly to the prejudice of another, but in our case it is adduced solely to infer the will of the abbot, for it cannot be denied that it does make a presumption concerning the will of the abbot, that he did [not] wish the first grant to be resolved on account of non-payment, by the argument in l. instrumenta domestica, and what is noted there, C. de probatio., especially because

† the will of a person cannot be proved except by conjectures in the absence of an express will, as in capitulum si uero, de senten. excommuni., and l. dolum, C. de dolo, makes to this point, and capitulum 2, de renuncia., in the Sext. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that he had already declared his will by granting that property to the lord P., and in doubt the interpretation ought to be made that the grant may be valid, through the things said above; because I say that if the words of the said grant are rightly weighed, they cannot be referred to this case, since the lord Pet. did not express this case of deprivation, but only asked that the said emphyteusis be renewed to him; but a renewal requested by a son does not taste of a case of paternal deprivation, but rather presupposes the existence and validity of the first grant; but lest on account of the death of the father or the length of time the memory of the origin of the property perish, a renewal is customarily requested, as the text proves in 12, quaestio 2, capitulum longinquitate, and capitulum 1, de preca.; hence it is that

† a successor in a fief ought to ask that the investiture be renewed, and also the heir of the lord ought to be recognized through a renewal to be made, as in capitulum 1, quae sit prima causa benefic. amit., collatio 10, and noted in the said capitulum longinquitate; for when an emphyteutic property has completely reverted to the lord, especially on account of an unpaid canon, there is not a renewal, even as to the son, but a new grant, since the right of the first is totally extinguished; to this point is capitulum 2, de feu., and what is noted in the single capitulum, de uas. decrepi. aeta., coll. 10. Moreover, the abbot of Saint Thomas granted or renewed to the lord P. under the condition, 'if he should rightly ask to be renewed'; therefore, he does not seem to have contemplated this case of deprivation, for then he would not have made it under a condition, especially the aforesaid, but would have said assertively that the emphyteusis was resolved on account of the unpaid canon, nor would he have said that he was renewing, but rather granting anew. For since the deprivation of the beneficial ownership, which results in our case, is something penal, since it diminishes the estate of another, according to the note by Ioan. Andr. in capitulum finale, de electio., in the Sext, and Bald. in the said l. 2, C. de iure emphy., expressly affirms in our case, we ought to make a strict interpretation, wherefore it is necessary that the lord's will be clearly established, by the argument in l. si praeses and l. interpretatione, ff. de poenis, and in the rule odia, de re. iu., in the Sext. For through those words inserted in the second grant, the Abbot seems to have doubted concerning the validity of the prior renewal; but one who is ignorant is not deemed to will, especially in penal matters, as in l. nec ignorans, C. de dona., and C. de condi. inde., l. si, where there are good texts; and through this the motive is removed which can be framed to the contrary, if it is said that the default could not be purged after the grant made to the said P., because it must be said that since that grant was not valid, the default could be purged at any time, for at the time of the payment of the ground rent made for past and future years in the name of M. or his heirs, it was not established that the abbot had willed that the emphyteuta be deprived on account of non-payment, as I have said before, nay rather the contrary is presumed, as is clear from the aforesaid. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the Abbot declared after the fact that he had made that grant on account of the canon or ground rent not having been paid, because since such declaration was not made [until] after the default was purged by the said M. or in his name or by his heirs, it could not be made to the prejudice of the first grant. For there had been a cessation in payment from the years of the Lord 1412 up to 17, and payment was afterwards made in 17 for the past years, likewise in 19, and thus for the future years after the default was purged, but the declaration was made by the abbot in the year 1422; wherefore he could not now declare this, especially since a contradiction would result. For from the receipt of the ground rent for past and future years he seems to have willed [not] to have deprivation; therefore he could not afterwards declare by word the contrary, since a declaration is contrary to a deed, just as in a similar case we say regarding a protestation: because one contrary to a deed is not valid, as is noted in c. cum M., de consti., and l. non solum, §. morte, ff. de no. oper. nun., and c. solicitudinem, at the end, de appel., where it is said that he is to be repelled who is found contrary in word and in deed; to this point makes ff. de reg. iur., l. ubi repugnantia. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that he who declares introduces nothing anew, and thus it seems that if he desires, he can declare, as is noted in l. haeredes palam, ff. de testa.; because I say that that proceeds where it is established that the act which is declared had preceded, and so c. pastoralis, §. 1, de appe., properly speaks. But where it is not established that the act preceded, a declaration cannot be made, but it is necessary that it first be proved in the presence of the party that the act preceded, as is proved in c. peruenit ad nos, de app., and cle. praesenti, joined with the gloss, de censi., and c. cum secundum leges, de haere., in the Sext; but in our case it was not established that the abbot wished the first grant to be extinguished on account of the unpaid canon, therefore he could not declare this, especially without the party having been summoned. Nor, lastly, does it stand in the way if it is said that for other years up to the present day the payment of the ground rent was not made by the said G. P., but by the said P., wherefore from 1420 the payment was made by P. or in his name, and not by Gui. P., and thus it seems that at least under this head the said G. P. is deprived of his right, since he did not pay for so long a time. To this I reply through the notable and singular statement of Gui. de Cu., which Bal. reports and follows in l. solennibus, C. de rei uendi., where he poses that question to the letter. For he says that if an estate granted in emphyteusis is not de facto in the hands of the emphyteuta, but possession has passed to a third party who possesses and pays the canon for eight or ten years, the true emphyteuta does not by not paying forfeit his right, because the church, which is the lord, cannot object to me non-payment; for it is enough for it that payment was made to it by the third possessor. For this ground rent is equated to a tribute: but it suffices that a tribute be paid by anyone to the effect that the property does not fall into forfeiture; he alleges for this case l. forma, §. si cum ego, ff. de censi. He also alleges a similar case in another matter: for upon the death of the father the vassal ought within a year to approach the lord and request investiture, otherwise he loses the fief, the said c. 1, quae sit prima causa benefi. amit. Suppose that upon my father's death, a third party began to possess the fief, and was unwilling to restore it to me; because I was not in possession of the fief, I did not seek investiture within a year, nor did I perform the oath of fealty: whether, however, I am on this account deprived, Gui. and Bald. after him hold that I am not, through the said §. si cum ego. For, inasmuch as I do not have the enjoyment, I am not bound to undergo the burdens of the fief. Likewise, inasmuch as I am not in possession, I am not said to be in bad faith in not seeking investiture; therefore I ought not to incur the penalty, as in c. finale, de prohibi. feu. alie. per Lo., col. x. Nor can the third-party possessor who pays exclude me, nor can he allege prescription, since he does not have a lawful title, and especially if he is in bad faith, as in our case. I conclude therefore from all the aforesaid that the said emphyteutic property ought to abide with G. P. by virtue of the first grant, since he alone has remained of the male issue of the said M. Nicolaus the Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Wherever an ordinance requires an oath upon the touching of the writing, the ordinance is not satisfied if the oath is tendered without the touching.
2. The writing of a non-notary does not make faith unless it is approved by statute or custom.
3. A notary who has been requested must complete the entire instrument by himself and not through another, unless he does this by the authority of a judge.
4. Wherever a judge declares someone to be ineligible for an office or to have incurred the penalty of a statute, he must first cite the party and hear his defenses.
body: IN the name of Christ. Although regarding the vacation granted to Ser Bartolomeo, a Sienese notary, by the officials appointed for this purpose, many things are alleged in favor of its justice, nevertheless two matters chiefly arise for me, if they rest upon truth in the facts, one of which entails the injustice of that vacation, while the other entails its nullity. For, first, it is presupposed for me that it was provided by the Sienese statutory law that debtors of the commune must be inscribed by the chamberlain appointed for these matters in his own hand, and those thus inscribed in that book, commonly called the *Specchio*, must be canceled if they are drawn or elected to any office of the commune; but the said Ser Bartolomeo is found to have been written not by the own hand of the chamberlain, but by that of another. Therefore, such writing ought not to produce sufficient faith; which I show in multiple ways. For first I introduce the notable gloss that is commonly approved in c. ut circa, de elect. lib. 6, which says

† that wherever an ordinance requires an oath upon the touching of the writing, the ordinance is not satisfied if the oath is tendered without the touching, since the ordinance requires the touching for the solemnity of the act and for greater terror; to this pertains what is noted by the gloss in clemen. 1. de hære. Much more strongly, therefore, in our case has the statute not been satisfied, if it requires that the chamberlain inscribe debtors in his own hand, and the master Ser Bartolomeo is found inscribed by the hand of another. Second, it is supported

† because, regularly, the writing of a non-notary does not make faith unless it is approved by statute or custom, as in capitulum dilectus, de fide instrum.; to this pertains what is noted by Bald. in l. 1. C. de su. trini. Therefore, the Sienese statute, by granting the chamberlain the power to inscribe debtors and by according faith to his writing, seems to have chosen the good faith and diligence of the person of the chamberlain, especially in our case, wherein the statute expressly requires that the inscription be made in the chamberlain’s own hand; therefore, the writing of another’s hand found there ought not to make faith, especially since the chamberlain does not attest there in another writing that another person wrote it by his mandate. To this excellently pertains what is similarly noted in capitulum finale, de offi. deleg. §. is autem, where it is said that he who is enjoined to execute a matter personally cannot commit it to another, so that the faith and diligence of the person appear to have been chosen; concurring is c. is cui, eodem titulo, in 6., where the text proves even more: that he to whom there is simply committed not merely a ministry, in which faith and diligence are involved, even though it is not said that he execute it personally, nevertheless in doubt the diligence and faith of the person seem to have been chosen, so that he cannot commit it to another; therefore, it ought not to make faith in our case, in which it does not appear that a commission was made to another by the chamberlain. To the same effect is what is noted by Bartolus in l. 1. C. de præposi. agen. in reb. lib. 12, where by that text he says that one placed in any office cannot regularly serve through another, unless he has labored much for the commonwealth in other matters, and even then, if he wishes, he must serve through a man of equal condition, and not through just anyone; all of which cease to apply in our case. Moreover, it is supported by what is noted concerning a notary by the gloss in authen. de tabel. §. nos autem, col. 4, and c. cum P. de fide instru.; for those glosses say, on the basis of the text and the aforementioned §. nos autem,

† that a notary who has been requested must complete the entire instrument by himself and not through another, unless he does this by the authority of a judge; and this statement is followed by Hostiensis in c. inter dilectos, de fi. instr., and Johannes Andreae in the additions to the Speculum in the title de instru. edi. §. instrumentum, at the verse item op. And that statement seems at least indubitably true when in an instrument, or in the book of a notary, writing in the hand of another is found, concerning which he does not attest there in another writing; for there is a presumption that it was falsely inserted by another, as in the said cap. inter dilectos and cap. cum venerabilis, de religio. domi. Much more strongly must this be said in our case, where the duty of writing and the credit of faith are given to a notary, so that a writing made by another does not produce faith, as is noted in c. quoniam contra, de proba., where Hostiensis expressly held that those appointed to record judicial acts cannot write through another without the authority of a judge, since their diligence and faith were chosen; although Innocent held the opposite there, nevertheless it is required that he to whom the office was committed declared by subscription or seal that it was done by his authority, which by no means intervened in our case. From all of which it is evidently concluded that the writing made in the said book by a hand other than the chamberlain’s does not make faith, so that the said Ser Bartolomeo ought to have incurred a vacation, and consequently the vacation given to him by the officials was unjust; and especially in our case is there a presumption against the said inscription, because in the brief summary which the chamberlain had made of those inscribed in the book, the said Ser Bartolomeo was not inscribed; hence it is that he was drawn, the office was accepted, and he was not canceled, as is customary with others; for all these things lend circumstantial support against the said writing, by the argument of cap. cum causa, and what is noted there, de probatio., and l. 3. ff. de testi. On the second head, the vacation given to the same Ser Bartolomeo seems null from a lack of citation. For it is said that the said officials gave him the vacation without him first having been called or heard, from which it can certainly well be said that their declaration was null,

† Because wherever a judge declares someone to be disqualified from an office, or to have incurred the penalty of a statute, he must first cite the party and hear his defenses: the text is notable in cap. cum secundùm leges, in fi. de hære. lib. 6; noted by Bartolus in l. eius qui delatorem, ff. de iure fisci. Hence the notable gloss in c. cupientes. §. cæterum, de electio. lib. 6 stated that although one cannot appeal from a sentence or penalty of the law or statute, as in l. si qua pœna, ff. de uerb. signifi. and cap. quia nos and c. consuluit, de app., nevertheless one can appeal from the sentence of a judge declaring that someone has fallen under the penalty of the law or statute, because the judge could have declared or sentenced wrongly. Moreover, regularly whatever is done by a judge in the absence of a party to his prejudice, without prior citation, is invalid, at least with respect to those things that involve grave prejudice, as in c. omnia and c. caueant. ix. q. ij; noted by Bartolus in l. nec quicquam. §. ubi decretum, ff. de offic. pro con. The text and gloss in c. ecclesia sanctæ Mariæ, de consti., and the good gloss in cle. præsenti, de censi. and clemen. 2. de pœnis, on the word "constitit", are on point, where it is clear that a judge ought not to declare that someone has incurred excommunication without his having been summoned; for the merits of causes are unfolded by the assertion of the parties: l. i. C. si per uim uel alio modo; c. tum ex literis, de in integ. resti. Indeed, Innocent went further in c. tua, de cohabi. cleri. & mune. near the end, holding that even in notorious matters a sentence is invalid unless the defendant is first cited, the fact is set forth to him, and his defenses are heard, since many things are called notorious which are not: c. consuluit, de app.; this is supported by c. fin. de offi. deleg. lib. 6, joined with c. j. eodem titulo et libro. And although what is noted by him in c. quanto, de translatio. præla., and the text in c. cum olim, de re iud., and c. bonæ, de elect. might seem to point to the contrary, the truth is nevertheless that wherever a defense can belong to an absentee, a citation is always required, however much the fact may be called notorious; it is otherwise where it is certain that no defense belongs to the absentee, in which case the contrary authorities proceed. To this pertains l. 2. §. quòd si de frumentaria, ff. de admit. re. ad ciui. perti., and there by the gloss, where by that text he notably said that auditors of the accounts of a debtor to the commune can pronounce against absentees because they submit their books, in which all things, namely receipts and expenditures, are inscribed, wherefore no other defense could belong to them; but in our case this does not apply, since that book was not written by the said Ser Bartolomeo, and therefore he could have raised many objections against it, especially since the writing was made by the hand of another. Likewise, he could have proved that he was not a debtor of the commune, because although the statute at first glance gives faith to the writing of that book, it does not thereby preclude the proving of the contrary, especially in our case, where the proof is not full: to this pertains cap. continebatur, de despon. impuber., joined with capitulum proposuisti, de proba. From all of which it is inferred that that pronouncement of the officials was null for lack of citation, and because the defenses of the said Ser Bartolomeo were not heard; he must therefore be heard and cited, and an inquiry must be made into the aforesaid matters, which, if they are true, he ought not to have a vacation. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A contract made in the form of a sale is presumed fictitious, simulated, and truly a contract of pledge wherever the low level of the price and an agreement of reselling concur.
2. If a buyer paid part of the price, although he cannot bring the action on purchase before he pays the entire price, yet after he has paid the entire price, he will be able to seek the fruits or revenues in proportion to that part of the price which he paid.
casus: The case is proposed in these terms: A certain lord Antonio di Matteo sold a certain house of his to a certain Maritano, retaining the ownership of the said house in his possession until lord M. should pay the entire agreed price. When, however, lord M. defaulted in the payment of the greater part of the price, lord Antonio, the seller, obtained as a precaution from the judge the power to sell the said house for the remainder of the price, it being nevertheless expressed in the aforesaid license that he should sell it to the highest bidder after public auctions had been conducted. When the said auctions were at length conducted by the court messenger, since no one had appeared who offered more than 150 florins, lord Antonio and M. by common accord sold the aforesaid house in its entirety to a certain Angelo for the price of 150 florins. Lord Antonio then asserted that he was selling by virtue of the ownership and property reserved to himself at the time of the sale made to lord M., and by virtue of the aforesaid license granted to him by the court. Lastly, about three days thereafter, lord Antonio, voluntarily and out of pure liberality, solemnly promised the said M. to sell the said house for the said price of 150 florins once five years had first elapsed, and not before, and to draw up an instrument of sale. Now, however, lord Antonio having died, lord M. says that the said contract of sale made to the said Angelo was fictitious, simulated, and a pledge, and conceived in the form of a sale, and insists that the rents collected from the said house in the intervening time, or which could have been collected, ought to be credited toward the said price, or principal of the said 150 florins, with lord Antonio contradicting and saying that the said contract was a true sale. It is asked what the law is.
body: The aid of Jesus Christ and of His Mother having been first invoked: It seems at first that the said rents ought to diminish the principal, or the price of the said 150 florins; which is proved thus:

† Wherever two things concur, namely, the low level of the price—which is here alleged in fact by the said M.—and an agreement to resell, the presumption of law is that a contract made in the form of a sale is fictitious and simulated, and truly a contract of pledge; whence the fruits gathered, and those that could have been gathered, ought to be credited toward the principal, as appears to be established in c. ad nostram, de emptio. & uend., to which makes c. illo uos, de pig., the gloss noted in c. conquestus, de usu, and Archidiaconus in c. quia plerique, 14. quæst. 3. And fraud must especially be presumed in our case, in which the agreement to resell was not free and absolute, if he promised to resell after five years from the time of the sale, and so he wished, on account of usury, to have the use and enjoyment of the house for those five years; and regarding this the text in the said c. ad nostram seems at first glance to support this, for a presumption of fraud arises from the aforesaid circumstances in multiple ways. First, from the low level of the price, which is alleged here; for the character of a contract is presumed from the amount of the price, l. per diuersas, C. manda., and the gloss noted in l. 1, ff. de superfi., and Bartolus in l. cotem, § qui maximos, ff. de pu. Secondly, a presumption of fraud arises because he was unwilling to bind himself to resell at any time whatsoever, but only after a five-year period, so that he would thus be certain to receive the use and enjoyment or the rents of the house for five years, as the doctors note in the said c. ad nostram. But these considerations notwithstanding, I judge that in our case a contract of pledge ought not to be presumed; and even presupposing that it were, the said M. ought not to be heard when seeking the set-off of the rents in the same manner as he seeks it. That it ought not to be presumed simulated, and consequently not a pledge, but rather a true contract of purchase and sale, I prove first by those things that preceded the sale itself. For the judge was approached by lord Antonio so that power to sell for the remainder of the price might be granted to him, and after many preliminaries, power was granted by the judge with the provision that public auctions should take place, and that it should be given to the higher bidder; which was followed, as I have said, in our case, nor was anyone found who offered more than the said price of 150 florins. Therefore, fraud ought not to be presumed: argument from l. non est uerosimile, ff. quod met. cau., l. transactione, C. de transactio., and l. 1, C. de præd. decu. sine decr. non ali. lib. 10, and what Bartolus says there, and by Speculator in tit. de emptio. & uendi., § nunc dicendum, verse breuiter scias, and Baldus in l. quicunque, C. de bo. quæ libe., and in the first constitution in lib. feud.; for in these laws it is read and noted that, when judicial authority intervenes, no fraud is to be presumed. Secondly, it serves principally to exclude fraud that the sale to the said Angelo was made principally by lord Antonio, in whom resided the ownership of the said house, although in the instrument, for greater caution, it had been stated that the said M. also sold, and each of them in solidum; but it is certain that from the person of lord Antonio no fraud or simulation is to be presumed, since he was very wealthy, nor was he selling out of necessity, as is known to all in this city of Siena, but for the remainder of the price that he was entitled to receive, nor was any agreement to resell made with him, nor indeed did any cheapness of price intervene on his part; for in his person all conjectures inducing a presumption of fraud cease. Therefore every presumption ought to cease: argument from c. cum cessante, de appella., with similar laws. Thirdly, I am moved by the interval of time between the sale made to lord Angelo and the agreement to resell made with the said M.; for the sale was made on the 20th day of February, and the agreement was made on the 1st day of March of the same year. Hence the sale was made unconditionally, and not under an agreement to resell; but the agreement to sell was made afterwards out of the pure liberality of lord Angelo, as is stated in the instrument, and thus a conjecture of simulation cannot be drawn from this. What is noted in similar fashion regarding the lex commissoria strongly supports this, which is disapproved in pledges if it intervenes at the time the pledge is constituted, but otherwise if after an interval, since he is not then constrained by necessity, as Cino notes in l. fi., C. de pac. pig., and canonists in c. significante, de pig.; so it must be said in the matter at hand, especially—what is of greater weight—because the said lord Antonio, with whom the ownership of the same house had remained, principally sold, with whom neither before nor afterwards did any agreement intervene. Fourthly and principally, because even presupposing that the said Angelo had bought the said house for less than the fair price, the power of recovering the rents or of computing them into the price of 150 florins would not on that account belong to the aforesaid M., for multiple reasons. First, because if it was a true sale, it held good, although an action might have been brought by the condictio of l. 2, C. de rescin. uen. and c. cum dilecti, de empt. & uen., so that the fair price might be made up or the property returned, and this if deception beyond half the fair price had intervened, which is here denied to have intervened. Nor in this case could this M. have sued, or be able to sue, because, although he sold in words together with the said lord Antonio in solidum, he did not nevertheless effectively deliver the property, since the ownership of the house was not with him, but with the said lord Antonio, who reserved the ownership of the house to himself until the entire price was paid in full; which nevertheless would have remained with him even presupposing that that agreement had not been added, because in law a sold thing does not become the buyer's unless it is delivered and the price paid in full, unless credit had been given for the price, as in Inst. de rer. diui., § uenditæ, and l. traditionibus, C. de pac. Therefore, this M. can bring no action against the said Angelo, since the sale made by him had no effect; for, as I said before, each of them sold in solidum, but lord Antonio alone, with whom it was, transferred the ownership. Thirdly, his sale alone took effect. Likewise, presupposing and in no way conceding that the said sale was simulated, nevertheless I do not see by what law this M. could recover all the rents, as he seems to wish to recover; because, since he never acquired ownership of that house, as is clear from the aforesaid, he therefore cannot claim the rents arising therefrom, which belong to the owner and not to the buyer; nay rather, the said M. could not have brought the action on purchase to deliver the thing, inasmuch as he had not paid the whole price, as is the text in l. Iulianus, § offerri, ff. de act. emp. Nevertheless, Bartolus noted to the point in the said § offerri:

† that if the buyer paid part of the price, although he cannot bring an action on purchase before he pays the whole price, yet after he has paid the price in full, he will be able to claim the fruits or returns in proportion to that part of the price that he paid; he cites for this case l. si, ff. de fun. do., and confirms the same there; so that even presupposing that it had not been a true surrender but a simulated one, the said M., wishing now to pay the remainder of the price, could not nevertheless claim the rents except in proportion to that part of the price which he paid; but in our case he can claim nothing, because the sale ought not to be presumed simulated, for the reasons stated above. The answer to the contrary arguments formulated above is clear from the aforesaid:

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The Prince never intends to prejudice a third party, unless he makes mention of him.
2. Surreption in letters of grace vitiates the grace ipso facto.
body: IN the name of Christ. The legal question is raised whether, in view of a certain apostolic indult granted to the city of Montefiascone, the castle of Castellonchio is seen to be granted to the said city; and in fact it is presupposed that the said castle was not, nor is, of the territory, county, or district of the city of Viterbo, or of the castle of Bolsena, or of those of that castle of Bolsena. And truly, if that which is presupposed above in fact rests upon the truth, the matter seems to me utterly beyond doubt for many reasons. And principally because Pope Gregory made that grant under an extrinsic condition, namely if and insofar as that castle, and certain others granted in the same place, are, or ever have been, of the territory, county, and district of the city of Viterbo or of any persons from the city of Viterbo and the castle of Bolsena, etc., as is clearly evident from the tenor of the privilege. Therefore, the condition being false, the grant is annihilated, as is evident throughout the whole title C. de condit. appos. and especially in c. super eo, and c. per tuas, eod. tit., and throughout the whole title C. de condit. insert., and as noted by the gl. on similar terms in clem. unica, de off. deleg., and Innoc. in c. finali, de praesumpt. Nay, I say more in our case: that since the condition was of the present and of the past, as is evident through those words, "are, or ever were, etc.," the grant was of no validity from the beginning as to that castle; because a condition concerning the past or present does not suspend the act: but if the disposition is false, it is void; if true, it holds immediately, as in l. cum ad praesens, ff. si cert. pet., and l. conditio in praeteritum, ff. de verb. obl., and Instit. eod. § conditiones, with the like; and this consideration alone would suffice for the victory of the cause. But for greater clarity I shall subjoin other motives, and thus the second in order.

† The Prince never intends to prejudice a third party unless he makes mention of him, l. 2, § si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in loco pub. Hence it is that if he commits a cause between two parties, removing the right of appeal, he is not seen to have removed the appeal with respect to the prejudice of a third party; whence a third party feeling himself aggrieved in the same cause can, the removal of appeal notwithstanding, appeal, as in c. super eo, de off. deleg.; the gl. said this notably in c. 2, de decim., lib. 6, and Innoc. in c. dudum, de priv., that a privilege is not valid if it does not make mention of the possession acquired in good faith by that person, even though it makes mention of the ownership of another; but in our case the Pope did not make mention of the ownership and possession of those to whom the said castle of Castellonchio truly belonged; therefore, the said grant is void. Thirdly, it is proved by another reason: the Pope intended in this matter not only to confer a benefit upon those of Montefiascone, but also to punish those of Viterbo and Bolsena, as is expressly gathered from the aforesaid indult in the words "We therefore, considering..."; but in our case he would not punish them, since the said castle did not belong to them, but to others; therefore, the said grant ceases. For wherever the Prince is moved by two causes considered together, when one of them fails, the disposition ceases, as is proved in c. quoniam frequenter, § porro, joined with § si autem, ut lite non contest.

† Moreover, and fourthly, subreption in letters of grace vitiates the grace in fact, as in l. fin., ff. de natal. rest., and c. 1 and 2, de filiis presbyt., lib. 6, and in c. ad audientiam, and what is noted there, de rescript.; but in our case subreption intervened in many ways, as is gathered from the aforesaid matters and from the tenor of the privilege; therefore the said grant is void as to castle C., although it could be valid as to the other things granted in the same privilege in which no subreption was committed, as is the text in c. super eo, de rescript., lib. 6. But here arises another question, necessarily to be examined here and omitted by the other counsel, namely upon whom lies the burden of proving whether the said castle of Castellonchio belonged or did not belong to those of Viterbo or Bolsena: whether upon those of Montefiascone to prove that it was theirs, or does the burden of proof lie upon the taxpayers to prove that it pertained to them—which is to ask, if subreption is raised against letters of the Prince, upon whom lies the burden of proof, the impetrant or the exceptor? Jo. And. fully examines this question in c. 1, de lit. contest., lib. 6, where after many points he distinguishes what is expressed from what is tacit, so that the impetrant must prove the expression of the truth. For the exceptor in this case denies, while the impetrant asserts; therefore, he must prove that his assertion is true, arg. ff. de probat. l. ei incumbit; to the same effect I cite c. 2, de rescript., where it is said that the clause "if the prayers rest upon the truth" is understood in a rescript; therefore, for the purification of the grace, it is necessary that the impetrant prove the matters narrated by him to be true; but let the exceptor prove what was kept silent, since he asserts that something was kept silent which, had it been expressed, the Pope would not have granted the letters; but in our case subreption is objected, not suppression; let the impetrants themselves therefore prove that which they narrated in the petition. Secondly, another difficulty arises here: whether it suffices for those of Montefiascone to prove that the said castle of Castellonchio at some time belonged to those of Viterbo or of the castle of Bolsena, even though at the time of the grant it belonged to another. And it seems at first that it does, because the Pope expressly willed this in his privilege, as is evident there, "are or ever were, etc."; therefore it is enough that they belonged to them, even though at the time of the grant it was under the Pope alone; and then it suffices to prove that it at some time belonged to them, although at the time of the grant it was not theirs, and in this case those words uttered in the past tense are verified. For the Pope seems to have wished to prejudice his own right, arg. c. cum dilectus, and what is noted there, de consuet.; for a privilege ought to be broadly interpreted to the prejudice of the grantor, as noted by Innoc. in c. olim, de verb. signif., and Bar. in l. beneficium, ff. de constit. princ. Or, if that castle belonged to those of Viterbo or of Bolsena, and at the time of the grant belonged to others with respect to ownership or lawful possession, then the privilege is not valid, as not making mention of the right of a third party, as noted by Inn. in d. c. dudum, and gl. in c. 2, de decim., lib. 6. For a privilege ought to be strictly understood insofar as it prejudices the right of a third party, as noted by Inn. in c. caeterum, de donat., and Bar. in d. l. fin., and gl. in c. canonice, de off. ordin., lib. 6. Let the privilege therefore be understood in the case written above. And it is enough that it can have some operation according to what is read and noted in l. si quando, C. de inoffic. testam.; for by general words the Prince is not presumed to wish to prejudice the right of another without mention having been made of it, especially to the prejudice of those who were formerly lords, since no one ought to be aggrieved by another's malice, as in regula nemo, de reg. jur., lib. 6, and dist. 56, cap. satis perversum. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One who exercises certain episcopal rights prescribes those alone.
2. What is called a novale with respect to the payment of tithes.
3. One who exercises one jurisdictional act with the intention of acquiring universal jurisdiction in a place is deemed to acquire jurisdiction in its entirety, provided that another is not in general possession.
casus: The case is as follows. A certain cleric in the name of his church collected tithes not due to him by common law [?] from a certain field, cultivated in part, for so long a time as suffices for prescription. Now, however, another part of the field, of which there is no memory that it was ever cultivated, is brought under cultivation, so that fruits are gathered from it from which a tithe must be paid to the church. It is doubted to whom this tithe is owed: whether to the church that prescribed the tithes of the cultivated part, or rather to the one to whom the tithes of that territory are owed by common law or by custom.
body: Humbly invoking the aid of Almighty God, it seems at first glance that it should be said that this tithe is owed to him to whom the tithes of that place are owed universally by common law or by custom, as clearly seems to be proved in c. cum contingat, de deci., where it is said that to one who has prescribed tithes in a certain parish, the tithes of novalia arising in that same parish are not owed, but rather to him to whom the collection of tithes belongs in that parish by common law; and the reason for that decision according to the doctors there is that one prescribes only as much as one possesses, since prescription does not proceed without possession, c. si diligenti, de præscript. and in the rule sine possessione, de reg. iu. in VI°. Therefore the part not possessed, and consequently not prescribed, remains with the proprietor, by the argument of l. siue possidetis, C. de proba. and l. 1. §. si quis hoc interdicto, and what Bartolus notes there, ff. de itine. actuque pri., and by Innocent in capitul. Cumana, de electio. Therefore the very same must be said in our case. For since this man about whom the question is raised did not possess, with respect to the right of tithing, anything except the cultivated part of the field, and indeed gathered nothing from the remaining part, it must therefore be concluded that he did not prescribe it, and consequently that that part remained unimpaired with the proprietor, whether he is the proprietor by common law or by custom, so that in this regard no distinction seems to need to be made: because thereby the uncultivated part was not acquired by the one prescribing on account of a defect of possession, nor does it seem taken away from any proprietor whatsoever. For, as the text stated in l. nec utilem, ff. ex quib. cau. ma., it is most unjust to take away an ownership which usage has not taken away, nor is that understood to be lost which was not taken away by another; to the same point is capitul. auditis, de præscript. and capitul. cum olim, eodem titulo, where it is proved

† that one exercising certain episcopal rights prescribes them, nor is possession extended to other rights, even similar ones; and Bartolus meant the same in effect in the said §. si quis hoc interdicto. Furthermore, prescription is odious, as absorbing the right of another, 16. quæst. 3. §. potest; therefore it ought to be restricted as much as possible. To the aforesaid also pertains capit. tua 1. de deci., where it is provided that the tithe of novalia does not pass under a grant of tithes of a certain parish made in fief to laymen, the text rendering the reason there: because license is not to be extended to such persons, but rather relaxed; and this reasoning must be weighed, which is quite relevant to this point of prescription, although it is otherwise in a grant made to an ecclesiastical person, as in capitul. ex parte, eodem titulo, because there favor is involved, and not odium. But these things notwithstanding, I judge that the contrary opinion prevails in law, namely that this tithe concerning which the question is raised is owed to the one prescribing. I am moved first by the text in capitul. 1. and capitul. quid per nouale, de uerbo. signifi., where it is said

† that, as regards the payment of tithes, a novale is said to be a field newly brought under cultivation, concerning which there is no memory that it was ever cultivated; but this field, concerning which the inquiry is made, cannot be said to have been newly brought under cultivation, since it was in part cultivated from antiquity; therefore it cannot be called a novale, and consequently we are outside the case of the said capitul. cum contingat. For a field cultivated in part cannot be said to be newly cleared, even if the part not cleared before is now cleared; to this effect is what is read and noted on a similar point in clemen. in plerisque, de elect., especially since the laws require that there be no memory that that field was ever cultivated, as in the laws just cited, which cannot be said of this field, which was cultivated in part. By this consideration Ioannes Andreae after Vincentius held this view in the said capitul. 1. de uerbo. signi.; Vincentius also recites the same in c. fin. de priui., and Speculator follows him in the title de proba. §. 1. vers. quid si una pars. And at least this position is truest where that field was cultivated for the greater part. For then the lesser part is drawn to the greater part, arg. c. quod in dubiis, de consecr. eccl. uel alta. and c. unico, eodem titulo, in VI°. The text and what Bartolus notes there in l. cum de lanionis. §. Sabinus, ff. de fun. instr., serve exceedingly well; this perhaps is what Ioannes Andreae meant in his addition to Speculator in the said verse quid si una, where he said this question must be decided according to the variety of the newly cultivated part. For it rarely happens that a field is entirely cultivated; it is harsh to hold that that small uncultivated part is deemed of another nature than the greater cultivated part is, since one and the same thing ought not to be judged under different law, as in c. cognouimus. 12. q. 2. and c. cum in tua, de deci. Secondly and principally, I bring forward as an argument the excellent text in the said c. tua, de deci. according to one reading which accords well with that letter, and is commonly approved there by the doctors, where it is proved that if one prescribing the tithe in a certain land collected the tithe from all the fruits proceeding therefrom, except from certain fruits gathered there annually concerning which the tithe was paid to no one, the tithe of those fruits is owed not to the parish church, to which the tithe of that land pertains by common law, but to the church which prescribed the tithe in that field, the text rendering the reason there: because that land is tithable to it, and one and the same thing ought not to be judged under different law; as if to say that by collecting the tithe of some fruits in one field, with no one collecting the tithe of the other fruits, the right of tithing seems acquired entirely for the one prescribing. For he does not seem to have had the regard and intent to acquire a part, but the whole, on account of the unity of the subject. If, therefore, one taking the tithes of some fruits seems to have prescribed the right of tithing with respect to the whole field, although he had not collected the tithe of all fruits that were gathered there; therefore it must be said a fortiori in our case that this man, who collected the tithes of all fruits that were harvested there, seems to have prescribed with respect to the right of tithing that field, even for the uncultivated part, so that he thus possesses there the right of tithing habitually, lest one and the same thing be judged under different law. Nor in this latter case can it be imputed to him why he did not collect tithes from the uncultivated part, since nothing was produced from it; nay rather, if something had been produced from it, since the tithe was paid to no one, the tithe is now owed to him who prescribed, and not to the former proprietor, as in the said capitul. cum in tua, where this seems to be proved, and the doctors hold it commonly on that text. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that this prescriber did not possess the whole field as to the right of tithing: because I say that he sufficiently possessed the whole, since it is a single field, and he alone collected the tithes there. For he seems to have had the intent of possessing and prescribing the whole, an excellent argument in l. possideri, in principio, ff. de acqui. posse., where it is said that he who wishes to possess an estate does not need to walk around every clod of earth, but it suffices to enter upon any part of that estate, provided he has this mind and thought, that he wishes to possess the whole estate up to its boundary. Thirdly, to the same effect is what Innocent notes in capitul. dilectus, de relig. dom.,

† where he says that one who exercises a single jurisdictional act with the intent of acquiring universal jurisdiction in a place seems to acquire jurisdiction over the whole, provided that another is not in general possession. For then he acquires only with respect to the chapters or acts which he exercised; and in this case the statement of Bartolus in the said §. si quis hoc interdicto can proceed, as well as capitul. auditis, and capitul. cum olim, de præscri., with similar passages. But this cleric, who in the name of the church collected tithes from an estate cultivated in part, seems to have had the intention of acquiring it in its entirety as to the right of tithing, and not in part; moreover, the intention is inferred from the unity of the subject. For since it was a single estate, it would not be likely that he wished to acquire it for a part only, an excellent argument in the said capit. cum in tua, nor was another in possession of collecting the tithe from the uncultivated part. Whence, with one alone collecting the tithe from the same field, the same field ought not to be tithable to several persons, either in act or in potency, lest one and the same matter, etc., as the doctors commonly hold in the said cap. cum in tua. And through this the response to the contrary authorities alleged above is sufficiently clear. For cap. cum contingat, where the case at first sight seems to favor the contrary opinion, speaks of one prescribing tithes in a parish in which there are diverse fields, some of which are completely uncultivated. For if these are newly brought under cultivation, novalia arise there, all of which are of diverse right and separate from the cultivated fields, since it is true to say that those fields are now cleared for the first time. But in our case we are speaking of the same field, which was cultivated in part, nor can it be said that it is newly brought under cultivation. Likewise, by reason of the part, the whole seems to be possessed; it is not so where there is a plurality of fields. And by these things I think that when someone prescribes tithes in a village in which there are diverse fields having diverse boundaries, if some fields of that same village that are completely uncultivated are newly brought under cultivation, the tithe proceeding therefrom is owed not to the one prescribing, but as if from novalia it is owed to him to whom the tithe of that village belongs by common law or ancient custom; because it could not seem to be denied that such fields are now cleared for the first time. Therefore they are novalia, and consequently the said capitul. cum contingat, and cap. 1. and c. quid per nouale, de uerb. sig. ought to have place. Furthermore, just as novalia do not fall under the prescription of the tithes of one parish, said c. cum contingat, so neither do they fall under the prescription of the tithes of any village. Furthermore, one who possesses the tithes of cultivated fields in a village does not thereby seem to possess the uncultivated fields, since an inference is not made from separate things, as in c. 2. de transla. præl. and l. neque natales, C. de proba., nor ought possession to be extended from place to place, especially against common law, according to what is noted by Innocent in c. in literis, de resti. spo.; and the text and what Bartolus notes there in the said l. 1. §. si quis hoc interdicto, ff. de iti. actuque priua. serves exceedingly well; but it does not happen so in the same estate, where unity of boundaries exists. And this conclusion proceeds especially if the uncultivated fields were brought together by a temporal lord after the prescription of the cultivated fields, so that together with the other cultivated properties they newly constitute one village: because a prescription already completed with respect to the cultivated fields ought not to be drawn to the uncultivated fields, which were never possessed. For it would be against the rule sine possessione, de reg. iur. in VI°. Likewise against the case in c. 1. 10. dist., where it is said that although one province is divided into two by a secular prince, the province ought not on that account to be divided as to spiritual matters so that two archbishops are established. For, as the text says there, the Church of God and spiritual rights ought not to be changed at the mutability of worldly necessities. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus de Tudeschis, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Anyone may renounce exceptions and the benefits of the laws competent to him, both in legal proceedings and in contracts.
2. Notorious matters are not to be brought into court.
3. An action against the principal defendant is not extinguished by a mere judgment rendered against a third party in a hypothecary action.
body: The aid of the Savior Jesus Christ having been implored, it seems, first, that an exception stands in many ways against the said Guido. First, indeed, there seems to stand an exception that excludes the claim, since no action appears to be available to master Guido against the heirs of Bonaventura; which seems to be proved from this: that the small fortress or estate, which is presently possessed by master Guido, was among the property of the said Lady Christophora, from whose person the action is principally brought. And this fortress she gave and assigned in dowry to the said Angelus, her second husband, although appraised; the ownership of which, looking to natural law, remained in the property of the said Lady Christophora, although by the disposition of civil law it passed to the husband. But, looking to that natural law, in favor of women the law introduced that upon the dissolution of the marriage the woman has an action for the recovery of the thing in those goods, as if they had remained perpetually in her own goods, and she is preferred in them to all other creditors of the husband, even those having an earlier and stronger claim in the husband's goods, as is singularly proved in l. in rebus, C. de iure do., where it is said among other things that the woman has an action for recovery in those goods brought into dowry by appraisal, since the same things both were the wife's from the beginning and naturally remained in her ownership and subjection; for it is not by the subtlety of the laws that their transfer into the husband's estate appears to be made, and therefore the truth of the thing has not been deleted or confused. Since, therefore, master Guido has in his possession the said fortress, which is worth far more than the amount he is seeking from the heirs of the said Bonaventura, no action can be available to him, namely because there is no obligation, since there exist dotal goods sufficient for the satisfaction of the dowry. For upon the dissolution of the marriage the dowry reverts to the woman, and the gift on account of marriage to the husband, as in c. 1 and c. nuper, de do. post di. rest. It can therefore be said to the said Guido: 'What you seek, you have within.' Second, principally, an exception of order seems to be available against the said Guido. For since there were two co-debtors of the dotal goods of the said Lady Christophora, namely Bonaventura and Angelus his brother, as appears from the dotal instrument, with ratification followed by the said Angelus—which may be done in dotal matters is of undoubted law, as is proved in l. si, C. de dote cauta non nume.—and the dotal goods reached only one of them, namely Angelus the husband of the said often-mentioned Christophora, the said Angelus, to whom the benefit of the said goods came, ought to be proceeded against first, before a transfer is made to master Bonaventura the co-debtor, who in no way had any benefit from those goods, according to the doctrine of Bartolus in l. in duobus, ff. de duo reis, through l. vnde quęritur, ff. commo. Third, it stands against master Guido because, since he acts from the person of Angelus, son of the said Lady Christophora, by virtue of an assignment of action made to him—to which Angelus indeed no action was available at the time of the assignment, since he had already obtained a judgment that had passed into res judicata upon a hypothecary action against the late Carolus, father of master Guido—he cannot claim any action, since he could not assign what had already ceased to be available to him, since from the judgment he had a right against the said Carolus and his heir, l. res iudicata, ff. de re iudic. and cap. cum inter, de re iud. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that, by a compromise made afterwards, master Guido's action ceased; because since a compromise is voluntary, it could not generate prejudice to the heirs of master Bonaventura, to whom release occurred through the judgment rendered upon the goods of master Angelus the co-debtor, which were more properly bound and before all things for the restitution of the dowry, especially since a judgment had been rendered upon the said fortress, which had belonged to the said Lady Christophora, and by the same had been consigned in dowry to master Angelus, her second husband; to this point l. si dictum § si compromisero, ff. de euict., which law indeed seems to make against master Guido even on another ground: because since he satisfied the said master Angelus principally by virtue of an arbitral judgment, and by virtue of the aforesaid payment received the assignment, it does not seem that he can have recourse against the said Bonaventura the co-debtor; for it must be imputed to him that he entered into a compromise and did not await a judicial judgment. But, these things notwithstanding, I judge the contrary opinion to prevail: namely, that no exception that can at least be gathered from the things narrated in the statement of facts ought to stand against the said Guido. I am moved principally because the said Bonaventura, against whose heirs the action is now brought, bound himself and all his property for the restitution of the dowry in case of restitution, renouncing the exception of fraud, the benefit of the law regarding sureties, the letter of the divine Hadrian, of the new constitutions, and generally all other help and favor of the laws, along with other appropriate clauses customary in such matters, especially with an oath receiving an order to this effect from a notary in the form of a guarentigia. Therefore he cannot now raise any exception by which the obligation may be totally extinguished, or deferred under the pretext of a discussion to be made first against the person of the said Angelus, the second husband of the said Lady Christophora; to this point l. iurisgentium § item si quis pactus, ff. de pact. and l. 1 § si conueniatur, ff. de posthu. and l. sed & si § quæsitum, ff. si quis cau. and cap. unico, de commo., with the notes there, in which laws it is read and noted

† that both in judicial proceedings and in contracts, anyone can from the beginning renounce exceptions and legal benefits available to him; and in general l. si quis in conscribendo, C. de pact., makes for this, where it is generally stated that one can renounce a favor introduced on one's own behalf; to the same effect cap. ad apostolicam, de regula.; and more specifically to our matter is the Gloss in Auth. de fideius. after the beginning, at the word 'acceden.', and in Auth. de duo. reis, at the word 'cedere'; for in both places it is noted that one can renounce the benefit of order, so that the surety himself may be sued before the principal. The same applies in two co-debtors, so that each is liable for the whole without a division being made; and the same is noted in Auth. præsente, C. de fideius., and the Gloss in c. 2, under the same title. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that this exception—that the said Angelus be first proceeded against—was not specifically renounced in our case, which seems to be necessary for the renunciation to be valid, and at first glance the text in the said § quæsitum seems to intend this. For to this a response is given in many ways. First, indeed, that law speaks of judicial proceedings, but it is otherwise in contracts, as is noted there by the Gloss and the Doctors; and whatever may be the case in judicial proceedings, I do not pursue it, because it is not our matter. In contracts, however, of which we are speaking, it is commonly held that it is at least sufficient to express certain cases followed by a general clause under which all equal or lesser cases are included, by the argument in capit. sedes, de rescript., and it seems expressed in capit. qui ad agendum, de procur. in 6., and in clemen. non potest, under the same title; so hold the Gloss and Bartolus in the said § quæsitum, and the Doctors note in the said cap. unico, de commo., on which see Speculator and Johannes Andreae in the additions under the title de loca. § nunc dicendum, at the word 'ad euidentiam'. Thus it happens in our case: for the said Bonaventura specially renounced certain exceptions, some of which concern the benefit of order, and afterwards subjoined a general clause renouncing every exception and the help and favor of the laws, by which clause indeed all exceptions concerning the benefit of prior discussion of the other, or of order, are included, since they are equal to those expressed. Second, it principally supports this opinion that the said Bonaventura himself alone received an order to pay in the case of restitution to be made, in the form of a guarentigia according to the disposition of the Sienese statutes; in which case he cannot, according to the disposition of the aforesaid statutes, allege any exception, at least not the aforesaid one concerning a prior discussion to be made against the person of the said Angelus, as appears in the statute placed under the rubric de except. contra guarentigiam. For there, as a rule, every exception is denied except certain ones specially permitted there, among which the aforesaid is not found to be granted; therefore it is seen to be denied, because the exception of certain things confirms the rule to the contrary, as in capit. dominus, 32. quæst. 7, and capit. 2, de coniu. lepro.; to this point makes l. de pretio, ff. de pub., and capit. solitæ, de maio. & obed., dist. 19 capit. si Romanorum, with similar texts; and most especially he ought not to be heard in our case, since the said Bonaventura confessed that he himself had received the dowry, and received the order for restitution; he cannot therefore now say the contrary, the said statute standing in the way. Third, it also makes for this that the said Bonaventura and Angelus his brother were in joint ownership, so that all their property was undivided and unseparated, and all of it was bound for the restitution of the said dowries; whence it cannot be said that the property of one was more bound than that of the other, by the argument of those things that are noted similarly in l. Marcellus, ff. ad Treb.; whence by the division that afterwards occurred between them, the right of the said Lady Christophora and her heirs ought not, at least as to hypothec, to be prejudiced, an argument good in l. si nupta filia § si filius, ff. fami. ercis.; and this especially holds if they had tacitly contracted a partnership of all property, as undivided brothers by blood are accustomed to do, as is commonly the case in this city of Siena, according to the matter treated by Bartolus in his treatise De duobus fratribus, and in l. si patruus, C. com. utri. iud., with similar texts; for then, as to the personal obligation, it cannot be alleged that Angelus received the said goods, since each of them is seen to have had them, from the fact that they were partners of all property. Fourth, it is principally adduced that the exception that Angelus be first proceeded against is not to be admitted, because it is notoriously clear that the said Angelus is not within Sienese territory, since he is a rebel with all his property confiscated, and thus neither he nor anyone in his name possesses anything; therefore the prior discussion of him would be superfluous, and therefore not to be made, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. decem, ff. de uerbo. obliga., and in l. fin., ff. si cer. pet., and noted in the Authentica hoc si debitor, C. de pig.

† For notorious facts do not need to be proved in court, as in capit. quoniam, de fil. presby., and in c. vestra, de coha. cler. & mulie.; to this point makes l. ictus fustium, ff. de his qui not. infa. To the contrary arguments formulated above for the opposing party, an answer can easily be given. And first, to l. in rebus, it can be answered in two ways: that law does not say that the wife or the heir is bound to vindicate those goods given in dowry, omitting the hypothecary action with respect to other goods, or omitting the personal action, but in favor of the woman it gives a beneficial action for recovery and a hypothecary action; whence it is not precluded that the woman or her heir can use the personal or the hypothecary action against others, as in l. persecutione, C. de pign., and better in l. unica § accedit, C. de rei uxo. actio. Furthermore, and secondly, that law speaks of a third party possessing those dotal goods; for it must be understood of the husband, or of the heir possessing them, so that it may be reduced to the terms of the Authentica hoc si debitor, C. de pign. But in our case a third party, namely the said Guido, possesses the said fortress; moreover, he acts not from his own person, but as the assignee of the said master Angelus, heir of Lady Christophora. But by the Sienese statute it is provided that the same right is preserved for the assignee as ought to be preserved for the assignor; and the same would seem to be said in our case by the common law, since he acts as another, by the argument in l. si consul, ff. de adopt., and what is noted in capit. cum inter canonicos, de elect. To the second contrary argument concerning l. unde quæritur and the statement of Bartolus in the said l. in duobus, the response is twofold. First, that it has no place in our case, in which the said Bonaventura confessed that he alone had received the said dowries, and bound himself then principally to make restitution in the event that the dowry must be restored, although he also bound his brother and promised that the latter would hold it ratified; nor can he now say the contrary, the said statute speaking of a guaranteed instrument standing in the way; whereas the contrary holds in two co-debtors equally principal, of whom the other, who is sued, did not have any benefit. Furthermore, and secondly, in our case the said Bonaventura promised to restore the dowries renouncing all help of the laws, just as I have fully stated above; whence, at least by virtue of the renunciation, he cannot raise the objection that the said Angelus be first proceeded against. To the third argument I also respond twofold. First, that by a judgment alone rendered against a third party in a hypothecary action, the action against the principal debtor is not extinguished, but it is necessary that payment or other satisfaction precede, by the argument in l. fi., C. de fide., and the said l. in duobus, and what Bartolus notes there. But in our case only a judgment preceded. Furthermore, and secondly, the said master Angelus the assignor entered into a compromise not voluntarily, but by virtue of the statute; whence the same is to be said of the judgment of such an arbitrator as of the judgment of a judge, by the argument of that which is read and noted in capit. ab arbitris, de offi. dele. in 6., and l. apertissimi and l. cum specialis, C. de iud. And the same can be said when it is objected against Guido that he entered into a compromise, for he proceeded to the act of compromise by virtue of the statute. Furthermore, and better, he does not now act by virtue of the arbitral award, but by virtue of the assignment made to him by the said Angelus, who could assign even if no compromise had been made, l. pe., C. mand., and thus the contrary argument fails. For it speaks of when someone has recourse against a third party because he brought back an adverse arbitral award, which he cannot do, because there is something to be imputed to him as to why he compromised; but in our case the said Guido bases himself solely upon the assignment. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus de Tudeschis, Sicilian Abbot of Palermo.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a husband, if he confesses in a dotal instrument that the dowry was given to him, can oppose the exception of uncounted money.
2. A person positing or responding, or confessing, can immediately revoke his confession without any prejudice.
3. One is not deemed to wish to use superfluous remedies.
4. Bartolus is rarely deemed to have strayed from the path of truth and equity.
5. When there is doubt in the laws, favor must be shown to the dotal cause, even if the plaintiff stands for the dowry.
6. If a statute does not admit an exception against a public instrument except in a case of forgery, the exception of simulation cannot be opposed.
7. What conditions an inventory ought to have in order to be valid.
8. If a guardian has not included all assets in an inventory, he is deemed to have acted with fraud.
9. If an heir has stolen a single item, he loses the benefit of inventory entirely.
10. If an heir does not draw up an inventory, whether he is bound beyond the hereditary assets in the court of conscience.
11. If the heir of a church does not draw up an inventory, whether he is bound beyond the hereditary assets.
12. A judicial act is not required to establish a custom.
13. A bishop, if without just cause he did not admit the first person presented by a patron, but instituted a second, is bound to provide the first with an equivalent benefice.
casus: In the question that is currently pending between Lady Florida, on the one part, and the heir of Paulus Iordanus, on the other part, concerning the restitution of the dowry of the same Florida and the payment of the legacies made to the same Florida by the said Paulus, her predeceased husband, I will, for the decision of this question, very briefly touch upon three points on account of the constraints of space and time.
