First, whether the exception of uncounted dowry stands in the way of the same Florida claiming the dowry by virtue of a confessionate and guarentigiated instrument, especially since immediately on the same day and in the same place in which the instrument was made, the brother of the said Florida, who had received the confession in favor of the said Florida, promised that he would pay the dowry to the said Paulus, notwithstanding the confession of dowry received previously made by the said Paulus. Second, presupposing that the said instrument warrants execution notwithstanding the aforesaid exception, whether the said heir can use the benefit of inventory in the payment of the dowry, so that he is not bound to pay except insofar as the assets of the inheritance permit, and to give property from the hereditary assets in payment, since it is replied by the said Florida that the said inventory at no time affords assistance to the said heir, since it is deficient in the requisite formalities, especially because the hereditary assets were not integrally described therein; and the same question revolves around the payment of the said legacies, namely whether, notwithstanding the said inventory, the heir is bound to the entire legacies, without taking into account the insufficiency of the said inheritance. Third, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the said heir is aided by the benefit of inventory, whether the heir ought to pay the said dowry and legacies according to the hereditary assets with a deduction of a third part of the valuation or value if he wishes to give any hereditary assets in payment, and this in light of the custom of Città di Castello, or whether he can give them in payment with no deduction made, in light of the provision of the ius commune and the statute of the said city of Castello, in which the deduction of a third part is permitted only against a debtor contumacious in not appearing.
body: The protection of Jesus Christ and of His most pious mother, the glorious Virgin, having been asked from the heart, regarding the first doubt framed above, it seems that the said exception of uncounted dowry stands in the way of and opposes the said Florida. And first, I cite almost the entire title C. de do. cau. non nu., where it is clear that there is a special rule in the confession of a dowry received, so that it does not stand in the way, however unconditionally made, within the times prescribed there; and this appears most strongly in the text in l. fin. of the same title, where it is said,

† that however much the husband confesses in the dowry instrument that the dowry was given to him, yet because it is not established that a donation intervened, but a promise followed, the exception of uncounted money can nevertheless be opposed not only by the husband himself, but also by his heir. This seems precisely to have happened in our case. For first the said husband Paulus confessed that he had received the dowry from the brother of the said Florida, and then the said brother of the said Florida, notwithstanding the confession previously made, promised to pay. The aforesaid seems to be confirmed by the gloss in capitul. si cautio, de fide instrumen., on the word confessioni, which, among the special cases in which one's own confession does not prejudice the confessant, enumerates this case of confession of a received dowry; just as a debtor is similarly induced to confess a debt received in the hope of future counting, as in the whole title C. de non nume. pecu. Secondly, primarily against the said confession operates that rule well known in law, that things done immediately seem to be inherent, as in l. 2, ff. si cer. pet., and in cap. officii, de elect. But in our case, immediately and in the same place, the brother of the said woman confessed the contrary by promising to pay the said dowry, notwithstanding the husband's confession previously received by him; therefore, the said confession of the husband is to be held just as if it had not been made. For this makes very well cap. nam & ego, de verbo. signifi., where it is clear that that which did not endure does not seem to have been done; and in agreement are ff. de in rem ver., l. si pro parte, § versus, de pœn., distinct. 1, cap. diuortium. Thirdly, the statement of a witness immediately revoked by the same person does not make faith, but one stands by the second statement, as is the notable text in cap. prætereà, de testib. cogen., through which text the notable gloss in cap. cum in positionibus, de iureiur., lib. 6, said that

† the person positing, or responding, or confessing can immediately revoke his confession without any prejudice; to the same effect is the gloss in cap. apud, 32, q. 1. Therefore, it is enough for the heir if he cedes to the said Florida the action against her brother, who promised to pay the said dowry, as in l. si socer, § Lucius, ff. sol. mat., nor ought it to be imputed to the heir why the deceased did not exact it from the brother. For this objection would have place if the woman's brother were solvent now; but since the name of the promisor is solvent, it seems sufficient to cede the action; to this effect is l. si extraneus, ff. de iure dot. But the aforesaid notwithstanding, I think the contrary opinion should be preferred in our case. For which reason, note that a husband can confess to have had a dowry for a threefold reason. First, in hope of future counting because of the desire to obtain the wife; and this confession is that of which the whole title C. de dote cau. non numera. speaks, which indeed in effect does not harm the confessing husband, nor his heir, the exception of uncounted money standing in the way, provided it is raised within the times cautioned, as in the Authentica sua, C. de non nume. pecu. In our case, however, it cannot be said that the said confession emanated for this reason, namely of money to be counted, since the husband was certain from those things which immediately followed that money was not owed to him immediately, since the brother of the said woman, by an agreement previously had between them, promised to pay immediately on certain terms to be declared afterward by a certain friend. For by those things which follow immediately, prior things are presumed and declared, as in l. si seruus plurium, and l. qui filiabus, ff. de lega. 1, and what is read and noted in capitul. ex literis, de sponsalib.

† Furthermore, one is not presumed to wish to use superfluous remedies, in l. hæc stipulatio, § diuus, ff. vt leg. nom. cauea., and in capitul. 2, de probatio., especially if such remedies turn against one's own advantage, argument in l. cum de indebito, ff. de probatio., and in capitul. super hoc, de renunc. For to what end would this husband, in hope of future counting, have confessed that he had received the dowry, when he knew immediately that he was to receive a promise concerning the dowry to be paid at a certain term and in certain manners? And therefore it is not acceptable that that confession emanated solely for this reason of the dowry to be counted. Secondly, the husband can confess that he received the dowry with the intention of donating the confessed dowry itself to the woman; which donation indeed is valid if it is remunerative, and consequently the said confession prejudices, as for instance if a plebeian contracted with a noble woman, or with one from whom he had received many services, as noted by Barto. in l. si diuortio, ff. de verbo. oblig., and the same noted after the gloss in l. si voluntate, C. de dotis promis., and in l. 1, C. de do. ante nupt. Thirdly, he can confess because in truth he previously received the dowry. A fourth reason for confessing, more pertinent to our matter, can also be added: namely, when he confesses in hope of a future promise to be made to him by someone who wishes to endow the woman, as if the husband wishes that claim against the promisor to be assigned to him for the confessed dowry, so that the risk of the claim belongs to him, but he himself is held to the woman for the restitution of the confessed dowry. For just as the woman can give the claim against a debtor as a dowry in payment, so could the husband confess that he received the dowry in hope of obtaining a future claim. Whence it is necessary that in our case we conjecture that that confession of the husband emanated either because he received the dowry, or because he wished the claim against the woman's brother to be ceded to him for the dowry; and on each of the said cases, it seems that the said Florida can base herself. For, since the husband confessed that he had received the dowry for Florida, his future wife, and promised to restore that confessed dowry to Florida in the event of the dowry having to be restored, and made that promise to the notary public stipulating for the said Florida, and renounced in the said instrument the exception of uncounted money, he ought not to be heard alleging that the dowry was not paid, as in our case is the notable gloss which Barto. follows there in l. 1, C. de non nume. pecu. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the brother of the said Florida immediately confessed the contrary by promising to pay the dowry in the future; because the confession of the brother, however much made immediately, ought not to harm Florida, for whom a right was already acquired through the stipulation of the notary public, who was able to stipulate for the said absent Florida; and the gloss in § si quis alij, Instit. de uerborum obliga., which enumerates the notary among the persons able to stipulate for another. Dyn. follows in l. 2, ff. rem pupil. sal. fore, and the same Barto. there, where he pursues this matter more fully, although Innocen. in capitu. dudum, de conuer. coniuga. seems to have thought otherwise and not well. For it could well enough happen that the wife paid the dowry to the brother to be assigned on her behalf to the future husband; the brother, however, provided for the woman through the confession received from the husband, an agreement having been had beforehand that he himself should remain obligated to him for the dowry, the woman's right being preserved intact. Secondly, she can base herself on the ground that he received the claim against the brother for the dowry in payment, since the said confession could not reasonably have emanated for another reason, given that the brother's obligation was hoped for immediately; otherwise, the said confession would be entirely superfluous, and such a confession would be said to have been made by mistake, into which this custom of confessing a dowry received and immediately receiving a promise grew up, which is not to be presumed according to what is noted by the gloss in said l. 1, C. de non numerata pecu. And this opinion, that the said confession seems to have been made so that the subsequent claim might be ceded in payment, that most excellent doctor, who is judged rarely to have strayed from the path of truth and equity, openly affirmed: Barto. after Iacob. de Are., an eminent doctor, in l. penul., § penul., ff. solu. matri., although Bal. thought otherwise there and in l. legem, C. de pact., making a distinction as to whether the promise followed immediately or after an interval, so that in the first case the opinion of Iaco. de Are. does not proceed, but in the second it does. But I, always saving a better judgment, would rather say the opposite; for when the promise is made immediately, it is not apparent why the preceding confession emanated, unless on account of the future promise. But when it emanated after an interval, the promise could follow, not so that the claim might be in payment to him, but so that the times fixed against the exception of uncounted dowry might run; the said l. fin. makes for this; whence I follow in this the opinion of Iaco. de Are. and Bar. Furthermore, two things strongly move me toward this view in our case. First, because at least it cannot be denied, whichever way the truth turns, that this case is doubtful;

† but given a doubt in the laws, favor must be shown to the dotal cause, even if the plaintiff stands for the dowry, as is the text in c. fi., de re iud., and a better text joined with the penultimate gloss in c. ex literis, de proba.; what Host. said in a similar case in c. super eo, de cogn. spi., makes for this, where he concludes that judgment is to be rendered for marriage as for a favorable matter if an opinion of one doctor is found in its favor, although many doctors hold the contrary. So it is to be said, and more strongly, in our case, in which the opinion of Iac. de Are. and Barto. concurs for the favor of the dowry, although Bald. alone thought otherwise, whom nevertheless in certain other places Bar. simply followed. Furthermore, and secondly, the municipal statute of the city of Castello makes most urgently, in which it is provided that against a guaranteed instrument (instrumentum guarentigiatum) no exception can be opposed except that of payment and satisfaction, or of forgery; for any other exception that is not permitted under some head of a statute, although it descends from some part of the common law, seems to have been removed by the said statute, as Barto. expressly affirms in l. 1, ff. quod vi aut clàm. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the exception of simulation can be called an exception of forgery, since forgery is nothing other than an alteration of truth, as read and noted in Auth. de tabellioni.; because it is not true to say that the instrument is false, since it was executed with the consent of the parties. For the notary only attests to the confession of the husband, which in truth he made and could legitimately make from any of the aforesaid causes; whence, however much the husband had not received the dowry, not through this can the instrument be called false, because it is true to say that the husband confessed; and thus the notary did not alter the truth; and this opinion Bartol. expressly affirmed in l. 1, ff. quod ui aut clàm., where

† it is said that if a statute does not admit an exception against a public instrument except in a case of forgery, the exception of simulation cannot be opposed, because simulation does not make the instrument false, although it causes the contract to cease. Nor would Bald. in this case have said the opposite; on the contrary, he thought the same on the rubric C. de priuil. do., where he said that although a merely confessed dowry does not have the other privileges of a dowry according to the gloss in l. assiduis, C. qui po. in pig. ha., nevertheless, with the concurrence of the said statute of guarentigia, it will have all the privileges of a dowry just as if truly counted; and the same is concluded there if the confession of the dowry is supported by any presumptions. But in our case there concurs not only the promise of the dowry immediately following, but also the said statute of guarentigia, and also the legacy made by the husband in that he bequeathed many things to the woman beyond her dowries; and thus it appears that he had confessed himself to be the debtor of the woman for the confessed dowry, argument in l. 1, C. de fal. cau. adiect. leg., and what is noted by Bartol. in l. si vltra, C. de fideiuss. Through all these things I conclude, always saving a better judgment, that the said guaranteed instrument must be ordered for execution, the exception of uncounted money notwithstanding. To the contrary arguments alleged above, the response is sufficiently clear from what has been said: for the husband did not deny or revoke at any time the confession previously made, although he immediately received the promise of the brother. And these two things can stand together; for they could have emanated for diverse effects, as is clear from what has been said. For the sake of brevity, therefore, not touching upon the contrary arguments in more detail, I descend to the second doubt, in which I conclude that if the things that are narrated to me in the fact are true, I think the inventory is void, and that the heir ought to obtain no advantage or benefit from it. For first,

† in order for an inventory to be valid, it is necessary that before all things the sign of the venerable cross be made by the hand of the heir, and that the creditors and legatees be cited to come on a certain day and to a certain place to see the confection of the inventory be made, as in l. final., C. de iure deliberan., and in the Authentica sed cum testator, C. ad legem falci. Likewise, the citation ought to be made by name, if they are known; otherwise it suffices to send a proclamation through the city, as noted by Barto. after Rich. Mal. in the said l. fin. Likewise, in place of absent creditors and legatees, beyond the witnesses described in the inventory, three other wealthy witnesses of good reputation ought to be employed, in whose presence the inventory ought to be drawn up, as in Auth. de hæred. & Fal. in § sancimus, at the word si absunt. The inventory must also be drawn up within thirty days after the heir knows that the inheritance has been devolved to him, and within the sixty following days he must complete it, and he must write down all goods found in the inheritance. For these and other similar things ought to be observed in drawing up an inventory, as is fully read and noted in the said l. fin. and the said § sancimus, and by Specu. in the title de instrum. edi., § dicto, verse nunc dicamus, where among other things he says at the beginning of that verse that if he fails in any one of these requisites, the whole inventory will fall into ruin; which seems to be proved in the said l. fin., in the word & si præfatam, on the word solidauerint, joined with the gloss placed on the same word, and in the said § sabinus, and by Specu. in the title de instrum. edi., the said verse nunc dicamus, and in the said Auth. de hæred. & Falc., in § si uerò non fecerit inuentarium secundum hanc figuram, etc. But in our case many things are alleged against the aforesaid solemnity, which, if they are true in fact, I do not doubt will render the inventory of no profit to the heir. For first it is said that all creditors and legatees were not cited, nor were three witnesses employed in place of the absent, but only one notary. And although it is proposed on the part of the heir that for thirty years and less only this solemnity was observed in the confection of an inventory in the city of Castello, nevertheless this custom contrary to law is not fully proved; because although many inventories drawn up under the same form are adduced, it is nevertheless not proved that faith was given to them in judgment as legitimately drawn up, or that it was so openly done that they came to the knowledge of the people. For since custom is introduced by the tacit consent of the people, l. de quibus, ff. de legi., first distinction, cap. consuetudo, it is necessary that acts be proved through which the tacit consent of the people to introduce a custom may be elicited; what is noted by Barto. in the said l. de quibus and Ioan. And. in capitu. si., de consue., makes for this. Likewise, the judge in our case did not cite those creditors and legatees to appear on a certain day and at a certain place, as ought to be done by law, according to what Barto. thought in the said l. fi. and Ange. in his treatise on the inventory; but a citation went out that they should appear within three days. For such a citation was not a citation to appear on a certain day, but one can appear at any time within those days, as noted by Barto. in l. qui ante calendas, de uerbo. oblig., although through what is noted there by him the said citation could to some extent be tolerated if a certain place had been assigned. Furthermore, the things found in the inheritance were not fully described; especially in the description of the grain, fraud seems to have been committed in the inventory, in which the heir is found in a lie, whence he is presumed in fraud, as in the Authentica item possessor, C. qui po. in pign. hab.; for in doubt the heir ought to be presumed to have known all the goods of the testator, unless he proves ignorance otherwise, because although regularly the heir is presumed to be ignorant of the rights of the deceased, as in the rule is qui in ius succedit, de regu. iur., lib. 6, nevertheless, where one is bound to investigate the act of another by reason of his own act, he is presumed to know it, as is the notable text joined with the gloss in capitu. innotuit, de electio. But in our case the heir is bound in the confection of the inventory to investigate the goods of the deceased; therefore he is presumed in doubt to have known all the goods of the testator; and knowledge is especially to be presumed since in the quantity of grain he was found variable and mendacious; what Barto. noted in l. tutor, qui repertorium, ff. de administ. turo., in the verse quæro, quid si tutor, where he says makes very well,

† that if a guardian did not put all things into the inventory, he seems to have acted fraudulently, since all things ought to be put. These things are true according to him, unless some just cause was present on account of which those things were plausibly hidden from him; which in our case by no means happened, since many things that were or ought to have been known to him were not described in the inventory, and especially three pieces of land which were not described, although they now assert that those come accessorily in the description of certain estates, since they are cultivated by the same laborers. Which excuse is quite frivolous in my judgment, since those three pieces of land are in a place sufficiently separated from the other estates, and immovable goods ought to be described and designated at least by the two nearest boundaries, as in l. forma, ff. de censib., noted by the gloss in c. 2, de lib. obl. Furthermore, the inventory was neither begun nor completed within the time established by law, which undoubtedly induces the nullity of the inventory, as in the said l. fi.; indeed, Ioan. And. maintained more in the addition to Spe. in the previously cited § dicto, verse in huius autem: that although the inventory was completed within the due time, yet because it was begun at an illegitimate time, concerning which above, the inventory is void, nor ought he to use its benefit in anything, since the form of the law was not observed; and this he reports that Mar. Syll. and most other doctors held, although he reports that some held the contrary, as Cyn. in the said l. fin., and Bar. seems to follow there, provided that the inventory was completed at the legitimate time. But in our case it was neither begun nor finished at the legitimate time. And therefore there is no doubt that the inventory is not valid; and many other things could be alleged which are contained in the allegations made on the part of the woman, but the aforesaid seem to suffice; one thing nevertheless is not to be omitted, which the notable gloss touched upon in the said Authentica de hæred. & Fal., in § sancimus, at the word lucrari, which says

† that if an heir has purloined one thing, he loses the benefit of inventory entirely. Barto. said more in l. Paulus and l. in ratione, § quod uulgo, ff. ad leg. Falc., that if the heir did not put certain things into the inventory, he loses the benefit of inventory in all things, because he is seen to have embezzled them; which is to be understood unless a just cause of ignorance excuses him, as he himself noted in the said l. tutor, qui repertorium; and the same in effect Bald. wished in the said l. fin., C. de iure delibe., § cum igitur; and since he has offended in the confection of the inventory, he ought to lose the benefit entirely; capitu. priuilegium meretur amittere, 11, q. 3, makes for this. But in our case a just cause does not occur, especially since he had the grain and wine in his hands, and wrote them down in a smaller quantity than they were. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that in the lands of the Church, such as the city of Castello is, the penalty of one not making an inventory ought not to have place. For to this I answer twofold. First, that with respect to creditors the making of an inventory confers a benefit and a privilege. For before the Emperor introduced the benefit of inventory, the heir was obligated to creditors in solidum, as appears in the said l. fin. in the beginning; and this because the heir, by entering upon the inheritance, seemed as it were to contract with the creditors, as in l. apud Iulianum, in fi., ff. quibus ex cau. in poss. ea. Therefore, he who omits the making of an inventory incurs no penalty with respect to creditors, but only fails to obtain the privilege of the prince; and thus no one can allege in the lands of the Church, even if he were a cleric or a church, that he is not held to creditors in solidum: it is to be imputed to him if he did not wish to use the benefit of the law, just as doctors similarly note on the exception of uncounted money in capitu. si cautio, de fide instrumen., that even a cleric is not heard wishing to propose the exception of uncounted money beyond two years, because beyond two years he is not said to be punished by the law, but rather the benefit of the law does not extend further, as in l. in contractibus, C. de non nume. pecu. But with respect to legatees, it can be said that the omission of an inventory today has added a penalty: because formerly the heir was not held simply to pay the legacies in full from the failure to make an inventory; today, however, the common opinion is that he is held to pay the legacies intact, even if they exceed the assets of the patrimony of the inheritance itself, through the text in the said Authentica de hæred. & Falci. in § si uerò non fecerit. Barto. holds this in the said l. in ratione, § quod uulgo, ff. ad l. falc., and Ioan. And. in the said § and in the said verse nunc dicamus, in the addition to Specu.; whence today from the non-making of an inventory the heir not only loses the benefit of the Falcidian law, but is also held to all out of his own assets beyond the inheritance's means through the said § si uerò non fecerit; and in this case the contrariety framed above seems to stand in the way somewhat. But if the canon laws are well weighed, because statutory constitutions generally disposing, although they have added a penalty, nevertheless have place in the canonical forum, even against clerics and churches, since the contrary is not found disposed in canon law, as seems to be proved in cap. ecclesia, tit. 1, vt lit. pend., and there Hostien. and Ioan. And. affirmed this; to the same effect is capit. 1, and what is noted there, de no. ope. nunc.; and this proceeds especially when a penal law can relate to the church for both advantage and disadvantage, as happens in our case. For a legatee church will be able to obtain the whole legacy beyond the inheritance's assets if the heir did not draw up an inventory. And that the laws speaking of the inventory have place in canon law, the text in cap. Raynaldus, in fi., de test., seems to show, and there it is commonly held by the doctors; indeed, it is only doubted

† whether in the forum of conscience the heir is held beyond the inheritance's assets if he did not make an inventory. It is commonly concluded, however, that he is not held in the forum of conscience, as noted by Ioan. And. in c. quamquam, de vsu., lib. 6; otherwise in the contentious forum. The reason for the diversity is that the law introducing the penalty from the failure to make an inventory bases itself upon a presumed offense. For the heir is presumed to have embezzled the hereditary goods if he did not make an inventory, as the text implies in the said § sancimus, and Bartol. notes in the said § quod vulgo. Which presumption indeed ceases in the forum of conscience, in which one who confesses concerning everything is believed, since there it is treated only regarding his own prejudice, as in cap. significasti, de homi., noted by the gloss in Clem. si quis suadente, de pœnis; whence the presumption of law gives way to the truth there, 8. dist., cap. veritate manifesta. Indeed, the gloss, with which Ioan. And. passes there, maintained

† that even against a church the heir is held beyond the inheritance's assets if he did not make an inventory, although I believe the contrary out of favor for the church; but the former proceeds regularly in all other cases. And this opinion, that it is special in the church, was held by Bar. in l. 1, C. de sacrosanct. eccl., and Bald. in l. fin., C. de iure deliberan.; what Cyn. noted in l. tutoris, C. ad legem Iul. de vi publ., makes for this; and this because an inheritance is understood to be devolved to a church insofar as it is not burdensome, lest its goods be indirectly alienated, argument in auth. sicut, C. de sacros. eccl. And from these things I conclude regarding the second doubt, that since the heir of Paulus did not legitimately draw up an inventory, he is held from his own property to satisfy the said Florida completely, as well in respect of the dowry as of the legacies, nor does it suffice to satisfy from the hereditary things. And by these things the third doubt is left superfluous, namely whether, presupposing the validity of the inventory, the heir is held to satisfy, after deducting a third part of the true value of the things, if he chose to satisfy from the hereditary goods, and this in view of the custom of the city of Castello; nevertheless, so that by way of greater caution satisfaction may briefly be given to that doubt, I think the custom is to be observed. For although the statute of the place providing for the deduction of the third part speaks only against a contumacious person in not coming, nevertheless, since the custom of the city has it that the deduction of the third part is made without distinction, even against the will to satisfy from the goods, the custom of the place is to be observed, although it was not obtained in a contested proceeding. For it is enough that for ten years and less it was thus observed many times in judgment. For since the people saw it observed so often against the law and did not resist, they seem to have wished tacitly to introduce a custom; Bartol. expressly affirmed this in the said l. de quibus, in the penultimate column, in the verse quæro nunquid, and in the verse quæro, quid si iudex, where he affirms that if a judge judged against the law, and a decade passed, a custom seems to be introduced so that it may be so judged in the future; not that a custom is introduced from a sentence, especially since it was delivered as it were against the law, but a custom is introduced from the act of the sentence, from which the tacit consent of the people is gathered. Ioan. And. also seems to have affirmed this in capitul. fin., de consuetu., on the last gloss, on the word contradictorio. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that it was never contradicted so as not to be pronounced thus; first, because it seems to have been sufficiently contradicted, since judgment is rendered against an unwilling person, as in l. inter stipulantem, § sacram, ff. de uerb. obl.; indeed, I say more,

† that to introduce a custom a judicial act is not required, although through judicial acts a custom could be introduced; and thus must be understood l. cum de consue., ff. de legi., where it appears that when there is a question concerning the custom of a city, it must be investigated whether the custom was ever affirmed in a contested proceeding. For the jurist advised that because it is one way of easily proving a custom; it does not follow, however, that custom cannot be proved in other ways, even extrajudicial, as is expressly proved in c. cum dilectus, de consuetu., and Instit. de iure natura. gen. & ci., in § ex non scripto, where it is said that long-standing usage confirmed by the consent of those using it introduces a custom; and this Io. And. and Barto. hold in the places previously cited. It is proved by reason: custom is not caused by the act of the judge, but by the tacit consent of the people; whence it suffices however the consent of the people is tacitly elicited, whether they be judicial acts or extrajudicial. And by these things let satisfaction be briefly made to the third doubt. After the aforesaid were written and completed, it was newly asked of me, presupposing the validity of the inventory, whether the heir of the said Paulus is held to satisfy the said Florida in full concerning the legacy of 50 florins made to her, although the inheritance is now insolvent, since the said Florida demanded the said legacy at that time when the said inheritance was solvent, and the heir without just cause ceased to pay, and afterward satisfied certain later-coming legatees, through whose satisfaction the inheritance was rendered insolvent; and I think briefly that he is. For since by law the heir is held to satisfy the first-coming legatees, as in the said l. fi., § & si præfatam, the said Florida, a legatee, was harmed by the act of the heir; therefore, he ought from his own substance to render this Florida harmless, an excellent argument in c. pastoralis, de iure pat., where it is held

† that if a bishop without just cause did not admit the person first presented by a patron, but instituted the person presented second, he is bound to provide for the first presented person with an equivalent benefice, since he was unjustly harmed by the act of the bishop. Nor does the said l. fi. stand in the way, where it is said that the heir has to suffer no loss since he made an inventory; because that proceeds if the heir observed the disposition of that law, as is sufficiently implied there, but in our case he came against that law, since he did not satisfy the said Florida, a legatee coming first, but satisfied those coming later; whence in vain does he invoke the aid of the law, since he offended against the law, as in c. quia frustra, de usuris. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. What the word 'to consign' denotes.
2. An institor is said to be placed in charge of a general profit-making enterprise.
3. When a flock is bequeathed, if animals died while the testator was alive and others were substituted, they constitute the same flock.
body: The name of Christ having been invoked, this question of law is asked: whether, having examined the pacts and agreements entered into between the magnificent commune of Siena on the one part, and Ranieri Toscano of Milan on the other part, and the suretyship that followed through the honorable citizens Goro di Francesco and Francesco di Tuzio, and then upon the intervening death of the said Ranieri, the citizens deputed over the restitution of usuries according to the tenor of the testament of the late Geno of Lombardy, or the community of Siena itself, can lay hands on the loan-bank (præstum) over which the said Ranieri presided, and deduct therefrom the amount due for the restitution of usuries, and afterwards demand from the said sureties the capital of the said loan-bank in the amount of 3,000 pounds; or whether instead the said sureties can tender and consign to the said commune the said loan-bank in the aforesaid amount before any deduction is to be made, and, by so consigning the said loan-bank, entirely free themselves from the said suretyship. And first, so that the following decision may appear more clearly, it seems that the deduction of the amount for the usuries to be restored can be made before all else, notwithstanding the objection of the said sureties. For the whole of the said loan-bank, or the capital of the said loan-bank, was bound to the restitution of usuries by the disposition of the testament of the aforesaid Geno, as even the said community and the aforesaid Ranieri acknowledged in contracting, as is sufficiently clear from the testament of the said Geno and the legal opinions (consilia) taken therefrom; therefore the said loan-bank, being thus subject to restitution, was consigned to Ranieri with the said encumbrance, because an encumbered thing passes to anyone whomsoever with its encumbrance and obligation, even if this is not expressly stated, as in l. sicut, in § non uidetur and § debitor, ff. quib. mod. pig. uel hypo. sol., and in c. ex literis, de pig.; therefore the said citizens appointed and deputed by the community over the said restitution ought to be able to lay hands on the said loan-bank, notwithstanding the objection of the said sureties, pursuant to what is read and noted in c. cum tu and cap. tua, de usur., and in l. ij, C. si unus ex plu. hæredi., and in l. j, C. qui po. in pig. habe., to which l. fin., C. si antiquior credi. pign. uendi. is relevant; and, with the said deduction having been thus legitimately made, the said sureties will be bound to consign the loan-bank in the aforesaid amount. Second, principally and more strongly it makes for this: because Ranieri, in the second pacts entered into with the commune, obligated himself in the said amount of 3,200 pounds for the capital of the said loan-bank, and also promised to restore 5,000 florins on account of the said restitution to be made; and for the fulfillment of all the aforesaid matters he bound all his present and future goods; and consequently he seems to have bound all the goods of the said loan-bank, the ownership of which seems to have passed to him, having regard especially to the second chapters, since he received the said loan-bank; and he obligated himself to restore not the very same goods that were then in circulation (in trafico), but he obligated himself in a quantity, or to restore other equivalent goods in kind; in which case ownership seems to have passed to the recipient, as is read and noted especially by Bar. in l. incendium, C. si cert. peta. cum si. If therefore the goods of that loan-bank, as future goods of Ranieri himself, were bound, even for the said 5,000 florins on account of the restitution to be made, the community, and consequently the citizens deputed by it, can lay hands on the goods of the said loan-bank, calling them away and revoking them from the said sureties, since they were bound to the said community prior to the sureties, by the argument in l. si fundum, in fi., and l. generaliter, C. qui po. in pig. ha., and in d. l. j. The sureties, moreover, will be bound to satisfy the commune for the remainder, since they can pay out of the principal debtor's estate, as in l. si procuratorem, in § si ignorantes, ff. manda., and if anything is lacking for making the said payment, they are bound to pay out of their own, as in l. non rectè and the authentica præsente, C. de fideiuss. Furthermore, presupposing that the ownership of the said loan-bank had not passed from the beginning to the said Ranieri—because, since the community was not the owner of the said loan-bank, it could not by contracting transfer ownership, since a transfer cannot transfer more right than exists in the transferor himself, as in l. traditio, ff. de acqui. rer. do., and in c. nuper, de dote post diuor. restit., and j. q. vij. c. Daibertum—nevertheless, from the new contracts that the said Ranieri made by receiving moneys anew from debtors, he seems to have acquired the ownership of those moneys, and the right, or obligation, in the pledges; just as we say in the case of one who sold a stolen thing, that the coins received therefrom become his, nor are they stolen, as were those things sold, as in l. qui uas, § fin., ff. de usur. Third, the said view is principally confirmed, considering the ancient chapters in that part in which no novation was made, tacitly or expressly, by the new chapters afterwards entered into with the said Ranieri. For in the first chapters it is contained among other things that the said Ranieri ought, at the end of the agreed term, to consign the entire capital that was consigned to him by the commune, as is found at the end of the first chapter. But in the seventh chapter it is said that the said Ranieri ought to restore the usuries that Geno ordered to be restored out of the goods of the said Geno; and insofar as those should not suffice, he ought to restore them out of the goods of the said loan-bank. Finally, in the new agreement a certain amount of usuries to be restored was expressed, nor was it added whence the moneys should be deducted; therefore it ought to be understood according to the ancient chapters, so that the deduction should be made from the goods of the late Geno, and, these being deficient, from the goods of the loan-bank, or of the trade. For since express mention was not made, in accordance with the subject matter of l. fina., C. de nouat., it cannot be said that it was made even tacitly, since these things are compatible, according to what is noted by Barto. in l. j, ff. ui bono. rapto., and l. pen., de prætor. stipula., and better in the extravagans Ad reprimendum, on the word legibus non obstantibus. Therefore, before all else, in default of Geno's goods, the said 5,000 florins ought to be deducted from the loan-bank, and the sureties remain obligated to consign the loan-bank in the said amount of 3,200 pounds according to their obligation. But although the aforesaid things seem at first sight to press strongly for this side, nevertheless, if all things are weighed diligently, the truth holds to the contrary: namely, that the said sureties are released by consigning the said loan-bank in the aforesaid amount, nor ought any deduction to be made before consignation for usuries to be restored. I am moved principally by denying that ownership of the said loan-bank ever passed to the said Ranieri, but that it always remained among the goods of him in whose goods it was at the time when the said loan-bank was consigned to the said Ranieri; and I say that the said Ranieri was deputed and appointed by the commune of Siena not as owner, but as a business manager (institor) in his own affair—that is, for his own benefit—with a certain encumbrance, namely of restoring the said usuries within a certain time, and afterwards consigning the capital itself; and consequently, since he was never the owner, but a simple institor and administrator, he neither bound, nor could bind, the said loan-bank for the restitution of usuries, because no one can encumber another's property, as in l. si rem alienam, ff. de pignor. action., and C. si res alien. pignor. dat. sit, almost throughout. Therefore the said Ranieri bound his own goods only, as is apparent in the chapters executed on this matter, and consequently the goods of the said loan-bank did not fall, nor could fall, into the said obligation, but he was only bound to consign the said loan-bank in a certain quantity as an alien specific entity (speciem alienam), just as these institores—namely, general administrators who are placed in charge of some moneymaking enterprise—are accustomed to do and to obligate themselves. Moreover, that the said Ranieri was not the owner of the said loan-bank, but a kind of institor, is proved from this: because since the community of Siena was not the owner of this said loan-bank, it could not transfer an ownership that it did not have, as in the said l. traditio; nor is it even probable that the community intended this, for since the government of this community is peaceful, benign, and just, free from all tyranny, it is not probable that it wished to transfer an ownership that was not in its hands, especially since the said loan-bank was subject to a pious cause, namely the restitution of usuries; and in guessing the intention of a contracting party, his condition is much considered, as in c. illo uos, at the end, de pig., and in l. qui semisses, ff. de usur. Furthermore, this is evidently gathered from the words of the ancient and new chapters executed with the said Ranieri. And first it is gathered from the words of the first ancient chapter at the beginning, there: 'Taking good and singular confidence in the person of Ranieri Toscano, and wishing through his hands to continue the loan-bank in the city of Siena, etc.' Which words clearly intimate that they wished to make him the institor of the said loan-bank, and its administrator. For it was not said that they transferred to him the said loan-bank, but that they wished that it be continued through him out of singular confidence in his person. For if ownership had been transferred, it was not necessary to add these words. Furthermore, this is more clearly proved at the end of the said first chapter, where it is said that if at the end of the agreed term the said Ranieri wished to withdraw, he should be bound and obligated to surrender (relaxare) into the hands of the commune the entire capital consigned to him; and I carefully weigh that word, 'surrender' (relaxare), which openly denotes that ownership never passed to the said Ranieri, but remained in its prior state. To the same point makes what is contained in the said chapter 1, in that the community by agreement wished to place a certain man for the custody of the said loan-bank, lest it be dissipated by the said Ranieri. Likewise makes what is contained in the seventh chapter at the end, in that it was said that, if the goods of the late Geno were deficient, the restitution of usuries ought to be made out of the said trade, because it was bound to the restitution of usuries; therefore, since each party expressly confessed the said trade to be subject to the restitution of usuries, and that it had been Geno's loan-bank, it is not probable that the community wished, or was able, to transfer ownership to Ranieri; this seems to be confirmed in the new chapters in that it is said there that the said Ranieri ought to obligate himself to consign the said loan-bank in the said amount at the requisition and will of the magnificent lords, etc., whence I weigh the said words 'to consign the said loan-bank.'

† For this word 'to consign' openly denotes that not ownership, but bare administration was transferred to Ranieri. For that is a word denoting a certain act of fact, nor does it denote a transfer of right or ownership to be made by Ranieri to the commune. For there are many other similar words both in the new and in the ancient chapters which, diligently weighed, confirm the aforesaid conclusion: namely, that the said Ranieri, by virtue of the said agreements, was appointed the institor and general administrator of the loan-bank, and not its owner, and that he was bound to consign the loan-bank as a certain specific thing in the manner in which he received it, or in the aforesaid quantity. And that he who is set over moneylending is called an institor is openly proved in l. institor, in § labeo, otherwise beginning l. quicunque, § Labeo, ff. de instit.; and every

† institor is said to be set over some general moneymaking enterprise, as in the said l. institor, and there by Bar. The said Ranieri was therefore set over a moneymaking enterprise; moreover, he was appointed there in his own affair (in rem suam), as I have said before, because it was for his own benefit, since he was to have the profit of that gain under that burden of making the restitution of usuries, just as in a similar matter Bart. notes in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. trin., in the last column, concerning a city that has by privilege or ancient custom the right of confiscating goods; for according to Bar. they can be called procurators of the fiscus in their own affair in that city, because for their own benefit they exercise the fiscal right by tacit or express concession of the prince. These things having been laid down as most true by way of foundation, it is most clearly inferred for the decision of that which I said before: namely, that the said sureties are not bound except to consign the loan-bank in the aforesaid quantity, nor are they bound first to suffer any deduction. For they consign the loan-bank in the promised quantity, and thus they consign that to which they obligated themselves, which they can do; for they seem to have had a tacit mandate from Ranieri, as in the said l. si procuratorem, § si ignorantes, ff. man., and what is noted there. Nor can the deduction of usuries be made first according to the chapters, because Ranieri for these bound all his own goods; because, as I have said before, the aforesaid loan-bank was never among the goods of Ranieri; nor is it an objection, as I said before, that from the new dealing or contracts subsequently entered into by Ranieri the money proceeding therefrom was acquired for Ranieri through the said l. qui uas and through the note in l. qui urbana, ff. de condictio. indeb., because these hold in particular things, in which a thing does not succeed into the place of a thing; but it is otherwise in universalities of things. For in these the money or thing proceeding succeeds into the place of the other thing, and the transaction is deemed rather to have been carried on as an act of universal enterprise than as his own act, as is the text in l. si & rem & pretium, and there by Barto., ff. de petitio. hær. To the same point is the good text in l. imperator, at the end, ff. de lega. 2, where it is said that if anyone was requested to restore whatever remained of the inheritance after his death, and bought other things with the price of the things sold, he who sold is not deemed to have diminished the inheritance, as if those newly purchased things succeeded from the price into the place of the pious things, so much so that they are not deemed newly acquired things; so it must be said in the present case. For the money and other obligations of pledges subsequently proceeding by reason of that business and trade would succeed into the place of the primary moneys and obligations of the said trade, even if they are renewed. To the same point is what is held similarly in l. grege, ff. de lega. 1, where it is said,
† that if, a flock having been bequeathed, the sheep had died while the testator was alive,

† and others had been substituted in their place, it is seen as the same flock. l. proponebatur, ff. de iudi., also makes for this, where it is said that a people is the same, although many die and others are subrogated. The other contrary arguments framed above do not stand in the way. And first, to the first, I admit that the said loan-bank is subject to the restitution of usuries, not however by Ranieri's obligation, but by the original disposition of Geno of the said loan-bank. Restitution of usuries therefore can and ought to be made therefrom, but not to the prejudice of the said sureties; for just as Ranieri received the loan-bank with the said obligation, so it ought to suffice that consignation be made with the said obligation; for the sureties did not obligate themselves except to restore the said loan-bank, and thus with its encumbrance; to this point is chapter pastoralis, de deci. To the second motive sufficient answer was made above, by denying that ownership of the loan-bank passed here to Ranieri. To the third and last it is answered that the sureties obligated themselves only to restore the said loan-bank in the said quantity, which obligation they satisfy by restoring the loan-bank in that quantity; for by payment of that which is owed, every obligation is extinguished, as in insti. qui. mo. tol. ob. in prin.; they did not, however, obligate themselves that a deduction should first be made from the said trade for the usuries to be restored, but Ranieri obligated himself to this without a surety, by obligating his own goods; let recourse therefore be had against the goods of Ranieri, if he did not do that to which he obligated himself without a surety. Furthermore and more strongly, since the said capital already bound to the restitution of usuries before the contract made with Ranieri remains, and restitution can be made therefrom as is according to law, it seems an absurd thing to demand beyond that capital other usurious money for the restitution of usuries; on the contrary, it could be maintained that the entire contract entered into with the said Ranieri was null, since it was on a base matter (super re turpi), from which no obligation arises, as in l. generaliter, ff. de uerbo. obliga., and in l. si remunerandi, § rei turpis, ff. mand., and in the final chapter, de pac. Nor is it an objection if it is said that it is not base to restore usuries; I grant that, if he had obligated himself simply to this; but the obligation was made so that restitution should be made out of moneylending funds, as is clearly gathered from the merits of the said chapters, whence from such a contract no natural obligation arose, and consequently even the surety is completely released, as is expressed in l. cum lex, ff. de fideius. And from this second head alone the said sureties could defend themselves, although they are also legitimately defended from the preceding head, even presupposing the validity of the contract. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas Siculus Panormitanus.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. An exception confirms the rule in all other things not excepted that are comprehended under the genus.
2. If a clause is placed among the words of one chapter, it refers only to that chapter.
3. An obscure or ambiguous agreement ought to harm him who uttered the words.
4. An obscure obligation receives an interpretation against him who bases his claim upon it.
5. When an enumeration of certain species follows after a genus for the sake of limitation, the signification of the genus is diminished and restricted to the enumerated species.
body: Having invoked from the heart the help of Jesus Christ the Savior, the legal question asked is the following. Having examined a certain instrument in which is contained a certain petition or provision made by the magnificent lords of Siena, the Captain of the People, the magnificent Standard-bearers, and three citizens elected concerning the matter regarding the late Raynerius Toscanus of Milan, lender or usurer; and also a promise made by Gorus, son of the late Franciscus, merchant of Siena, in his own private name as well as in the name of Franciscus Tutii, money-changer of Siena; to what things the said Gorus and Franciscus, the aforesaid sureties, are bound to do and perform by virtue of the said suretyship. And first, it seems that they are principally bound to three things, just as by virtue of the promise made by the said lords, etc., and the subsequent promise made by the said late Raynerius, the same Raynerius was bound. For, as is gathered from the said instrument, Raynerius was first bound to obligate himself in thirty-two thousand pounds of pennies for the principal of the loan to be made, computing however one thousand pounds; then for the household goods or furnishings that belonged to the late Geno of Milan, and for all that amount by which the said furnishings were worth more than one thousand pounds and the said quantity of twenty-two thousand pounds, the said Raynerius was bound to consign at every requisition of the magnificent lords, etc. Secondly, the said Raynerius is bound to continue the loan or usurious lending begun by the said Geno up to the Kalends of June of the year 1430. Thirdly, he is bound principally to the restitution of usuries on the occasion of the testament made by the said Geno, namely to the sum of five thousand florins, and this within the times contained in the said instrument. And that the said sureties are obligated to all the aforesaid is most clearly proved at first sight from the words contained in the said suretyship. First, in that the said Gorus in his own name and in the name of the aforesaid Franciscus promised and agreed with the said magnificent lords, etc., stipulating in the stead and name of the Commune of Siena, that he would cause and see to it, all exception removed, that the said Raynerius would observe and fulfill all and singular the things contained in the said petition or provision, and all and singular the above-written things to which the said Raynerius is obligated in the petition to provide a surety, and so he stood surety. But in the said petition are principally contained those three things written above; therefore the said sureties are bound to all these three things with their determinations and qualities. For sureties are bound by a solemn stipulation, which intervened here, as in l. blanditus, C. de fideiuss., and where the words are clear, there is no need for interpretation, as in l. ille aut ille, ff. de leg. 3, and in c. si. de uerb. sig. Furthermore and secondly, the said Gorus in the aforesaid names obligated himself that, in the event the said Raynerius did not observe the aforesaid, Gorus himself in the said names would observe and execute them; whence that word "the aforesaid" placed in the said suretyship must be weighed. For it refers to all and singular things contained in the said petition or promise, which is gathered from the fact that the said Gorus obligated himself at the beginning of the suretyship to cause and see to it that the said Raynerius will observe all and singular things in the said petition; for that word "the aforesaid" must be referred to preceding matters, as in l. si ita stipulatus, § Chrysogonus, ff. de uerb. obli. Thirdly, it is proved by another consideration, namely from the fact that the said Gorus, in the aforesaid suretyship that he made, wished to be bound to that amount by which the said furnishings of Geno were found to be worth more than one thousand pounds; and thus he wished to stand surety for that surplus, giving as the reason in the said instrument that it had been deliberated in the councils that Raynerius alone would be obligated for them without any suretyship to be provided. For since the said Gorus excepted from the said suretyship only one case, or one particular item of the obligation, he seems to have wished to obligate himself to all other things contained in the said petition or provision.

† For an exception affirms the rule in all other things not excepted that are comprehended under the genus or under the rule, as in c. dominus, 32 q. 7, and in c. 2 in fine, de coniugi. lepro. Fourthly and lastly, it works against the said sureties that in the said petition or provision mention is made twice—namely, in the beginning and at the end—of the suretyship to be provided by the said Raynerius; and a quality or clause added in one chapter of any transaction ought to be referred to all chapters of the same transaction, as in c. 2. requiris, ff. de appel., the noted gloss in c. inquisitioni, eod. tit., to which agrees 22 q. 7 c. apostolus, and l. Titia, ff. de uerb. obli., where it is said that those things conceived in prefaces are understood to be repeated in stipulations. Furthermore, no reason appears why the said sureties ought to be bound to one chapter more than to the rest; therefore the said clause concerning the suretyship to be provided ought to be referred to all; to this makes l. generaliter, ff. de fideiusso., and what Bartolus notes in l. talis scriptura, ff. de lega. 1. From all these things it seems concluding that, since the said Raynerius has departed this present life, his said sureties are bound at the will of the lords of Siena, etc., to consign twenty-two thousand pounds for the principal, and to continue the aforesaid loan up to the Kalends of January, and to restore five thousand florins, just as the said Raynerius was bound to all these things. But notwithstanding these points, which in our case I judge by no means prevail, I think the said sureties were obligated from the said suretyship to two things only: first, to consigning thirty-two thousand pounds for the principal of the said loan, computing however the one thousand pounds to which the said Raynerius obligated himself for the value of the furnishings of the said Geno; likewise to restoring one thousand six hundred florins, which ought to have been restored at the first term from the sum of the said five thousand florins; which quantity of the said one thousand six hundred florins was nevertheless entirely restored by the said Raynerius, as was orally reported to me; which, if it rests on truth, in my judgment the said sureties are obligated only to consign thirty-two thousand pounds for the principal of the said loan; but they are not bound to continue the said loan or usury, nor to restore up to the amount of five thousand florins. And that these things are true is proved most clearly from the words of the suretyship made by the said Gorus, in that it is there expressly said that he stood surety only for those things to which the aforesaid Raynerius was obligated to provide a surety, and not otherwise nor in any other manner; which words are to be weighed most diligently in this business, from which it is most clear that Gorus in the aforesaid names did not wish to stand surety simply for all things that the said Raynerius was obligated to do and fulfill, but only for those for which the said Raynerius was obligated to give a surety. Moreover, a surety is not obligated beyond his own consent, but only to those things which he promised by solemn stipulation, as in l. qui ultra, and in the said l. blanditus, C. de fideiuss., to which makes l. consensu, ff. de actio. & obligatio.; whence the aforesaid words contained in the suretyship must be weighed, namely that he did not wish to stand surety otherwise or in any other manner, except only and precisely for those things to which the aforesaid Raynerius was obligated to provide a surety. But the said Raynerius, although he had obligated himself to several things, was nevertheless not bound to provide a surety except in two chapters alone contained in the petition or provision of the lords, which is gathered from the fact that, although many things had been expressed in the said provision concerning the obligation of the said Raynerius, mention of suretyship was made only with respect to the said chapters; therefore in the others the said suretyship is seen to be passed over and neglected; for this is an excellent text in l. 3, ff. de libe. & posthu., to which makes c. nonne, de præsumptio., and c. qualis, dist. 25. Secondly, this seems expressly proved by the theory of Bartolus in the said l. talis scriptura, ff. de lega. 1, where, discussing a clause contained in a disposition, to what things it is to be referred when there are many chapters in such a disposition, he says among other things

† that if a clause is placed within one chapter, or among the words of that chapter, then it refers only to that chapter, and not to other preceding or subsequent ones; he cites the said l. tertia, § filius, ff. de libe. & posthu., which law well supports this; and this reason can be adduced: for when a clause is placed among the words of the same chapter, it seems to be part of the chapter, and therefore it ought to be restricted to that chapter itself, and not concern preceding or following ones. For if the author of the disposition had intended by the clause to qualify all things contained in the disposition, he would not have added the clause among the words of one chapter, but would have added it generally at the beginning or at the end of the chapter without restricting himself to a specific chapter, in which case the said c. secundo requiris, cited to the contrary, speaks. For from the words of the disposition we understand the mind of the disposer, as in c. ad audientiam, de decimis, and c. porro, de priuileg., and c. si., de uerbo. signifi., and in l. non aliter, and l. si quis in principio, ff. de leg. 3. So it happened punctually in our case. For in that petition or provision of the lords in which is contained and treated the suretyship to be provided by the said Raynerius, it is said in effect at the beginning that the said Raynerius ought to obligate himself in the quantity of thirty-two thousand pounds, and in that surplus by which the said furnishings of Geno were worth more than one thousand pounds. And it is added in the same place: *Giving of this good and sufficient sureties to consign the said loan in the said quantity at the request and will of the magnificent lords, etc. Which sureties, where Raynerius should fail to perform the aforesaid things, shall obligate themselves to observe them if Raynerius should fail, etc.* Which words, diligently weighed, indicate that the suretyship is to be provided with respect to this chapter only, and not with respect to the following ones, in which nothing is said about suretyship. Next, those words must be noted: *Giving of this good and sufficient sureties to consign the said loan, etc.* And those other words: *Which sureties, where Raynerius should fail in the aforesaid things, shall obligate themselves, etc.* For those words, *Giving of this*, and those, *The aforesaid things*, restrict the obligation of the suretyship to be provided to that chapter alone, since they are placed among the words of the same chapter and openly refer to that chapter. Likewise it happened punctually in the last chapter of the said provision, where mention is made of the five thousand florins to be restored by the said Raynerius. For mention was made of suretyship only with respect to the payment to be made in the first term, which amounted to the quantity of one thousand six hundred florins; whence with respect to the whole sum of five thousand florins no mention of suretyship was made, nor with respect to the other sum to be restricted in the other term, as is clearly gathered from the words of the said provision, there: *In which time he must render and restore five thousand gold florins in this time, namely from the day this present provision shall be obtained, within one coming month one thousand six hundred florins; of which one thousand six hundred florins and of usuries to be restored in the first payments he must in like manner give good and sufficient sureties, etc.* Which words, if diligently weighed, restrict the obligation through the suretyship to be provided by the said Raynerius to this sum alone of one thousand six hundred florins to be paid in the first term. For these are placed among the words of that chapter, and thus concern only that chapter, as is most clearly gathered from those words, *Of which one thousand six hundred florins he must in like manner give good and sufficient sureties*; but it was not said: *Of which five thousand florins, etc.* And thus those words about providing a suretyship only determine the restitution of the said sum of one thousand six hundred florins, by the aforesaid reasoning. Furthermore, in the continuing of the loan to which the aforesaid Raynerius was obligated, there was absolutely no mention made of a suretyship to be provided by the said Raynerius; and thus the obligation of providing a suretyship remains only in the aforesaid two cases, because whatever is not expressed in clear words is held as omitted where it is a question of contracting or augmenting an obligation, as is the express text, and there through Bartolus, in l. quicquid astringendæ, ff. de uerbo. obligatio. Nor is it sufficient to say that the other party had this in mind, because it is to be imputed to him from the fact that he did not express it, as in l. si repetendi, C. de condict. ob causam. Hence Bartolus says in the said chapter [or law] quicquid astringendæ that if things that are not of the nature of the contract are omitted in a contract, they are not held as expressed, even if they had been tacitly understood by one of the parties alone. In doubt, however, only those things that come from the nature of the contract are deemed understood by both parties, as in l. cum quid, ff. si cer. peta. Furthermore, the text in l. ueteribus, ff. de pactis, makes excellently for this opinion, where it is seen
† that an obscure or ambiguous agreement ought to harm the one who uttered the words, because it was in his power to write the words more clearly. Hence Bartolus said in the said l. ueteribus

† that an obscure obligation receives an interpretation against him who bases himself upon the obligation, because he cannot sue upon an obscure and doubtful obligation, as in c. in præsentia, de probatio., and in the said l. quicquid astringendæ. Likewise an interpretation is made against him who uttered the words of the obligation, as in the said l. ueteribus, and in the said c. contra eum sit interpretatio, de reg. iur. in 6. In our case, however, the words of the obligation regarding providing a suretyship were not uttered by Raynerius. Likewise the sureties do not base themselves upon an obligation, since they are defendants in this case; rightfully the interpretation must be made for them and not against them; rightfully the said Gorus, knowing on account of the aforesaid that the said Raynerius was not bound to give a surety for all things to which he himself was obligated, spoke in the said suretyship the aforesaid words, namely that he stood surety only for those things to which the said Raynerius was obligated to provide a surety in the said petition, and not otherwise or in any other manner; and especially that the said sureties would not be obligated to continue the loan, by certain reasons beyond the aforesaid. First, through the theory of Bartolus in l. prætor, § 2, ff. ui bono. rapto., where he says among other things that where things stated in preceding parts are contrary to the common law, or exorbitant from the common law, they are not understood to be repeated in subsequent parts, which the gloss notes in the said l. talis scriptura; to this makes c. 1 with the following, de filiis presbyte. in 6. But in our case it is exorbitant from the common law—indeed, it is contrary to divine and human law—that a Christian should practice usury in his own name or in another's, as in c. sicut non suo, dist. 46, and in c. super eo, and c. cum tu, and c. quia in omnibus, de usuris. Therefore those words concerning providing a suretyship, that the sureties should be bound to do what should be omitted by Raynerius, are not to be referred to continuing the loan and practicing usury. Secondly, another theory makes for this, which Bartolus posited there in the said l. talis scriptura, where he says that even where a clause is placed at the beginning or at the end of a chapter, it is not to be referred to other chapters when a reason can be given why it ought to be referred more to one chapter than to the rest. But in our case a most evident reason underlies: for no base act is committed in sureties obligating themselves to restore the principal, or for the restitution of usuries, but baseness and a most grave sin and horror among Christians would indeed be committed if a Christian, especially a leading citizen, openly practiced usury in his own name or in another's; rightfully that obligation of continuing the loan is not to be referred to the sureties. Nay, I say more: that even if the sureties had expressly obligated themselves to continue it, such an obligation would not have been valid, because a stipulation of a base thing is not valid, as in l. generaliter, ff. de uerb. obli., and in c. fi. de pac.; nor can a surety be added where no obligation arises from the primary obligation, as in l. fideiussor, § fideiussor, ff. de fideius. But in practicing usury no civil or natural obligation can arise, since divine and canon law resist, as in the said c. fin. de pac.; to this makes l. cum lex, ff. de fideiuss., where it is expressly proved that a surety cannot attach to that contract which the law resists. From all the aforesaid I conclude that the said sureties are not obligated to continue the loan of the said Raynerius, nor to restore the whole sum of the said thousands of florins, but only to consign thirty-two thousand pounds for the principal, and to the restitution of one thousand six hundred florins on the occasion of the testament of Geno, and this insofar as the said quantity has not been restored by Raynerius. Now it remains to answer the contrary arguments formulated above, to which the answer is easily apparent. To the first, in fact, I reply that those general words "to all and singular, etc." are restricted by the special words immediately following, in that the said Gorus subjoined in the suretyship that he stood surety only for those things to which the aforesaid Raynerius was obligated to provide a surety, and not otherwise or in any other manner; and thus those preceding words, that he obligated himself to all and singular things contained in the promise, ought to be understood of all and singular those things for which the said Raynerius was obligated to provide a surety. For preceding words are declared by subsequent ones, as in l. si seruus plurium, in fi., and in l. qui filiabus, ff. de lega. 1; for also those things that are subjoined immediately are seen to be inherent, as in l. lecta, ff. si certum peta., and in c. officij, de elect.; Bartolus openly held this in l. quæsitum, in § fin., ff. de fun. instru., where he says

† that where an enumeration of certain species follows a genus for the sake of limitation, then the meaning of the genus is diminished and restricted to the enumerated species, in l. legata, in the second response, ff. de suppe. leg. In our case, however, it is clear that through those general words, special words were added for the purpose of restricting the preceding generality, as is openly gathered from the words recited above, especially from the word "only and precisely" [*tantum & duntaxat*] and from those others, that he wished to be obligated neither otherwise nor in any other manner. To the same point I cite the notable and clearer text in Clem. exiui de paradiso, in § exigitur in primis, de uerbo. significat., where it is clearly gathered that a preceding genus with an enumeration of certain species is restricted to the enumerated species; otherwise, as the text says there, those species would have been added superfluously and nugatorily. So in the present matter, if Gorus had wished to be obligated simply to all and singular things contained in the said promise, he would have immediately subjoined superfluously and nugatorily that he stood surety only and precisely for those things to which the said Raynerius was obligated to provide a surety, and not otherwise or in any other manner. And by this the second contrary argument is also removed, in that which is objected, that the said Gorus obligated himself to all the aforesaid things. For that word "the aforesaid" concerns the genus with the subsequent restriction, so that it is understood as to all the aforesaid things, namely to which the said Raynerius was obligated to provide a surety. For relative words refer to antecedents with their restrictions and determinations, according to what is noted in l. cunctos populos, C. de summa trinita. & fide catho., and in c. 1, de cleri. non residen. To the third contrary argument the answer is that Gorus for this reason excepted that he did not wish to be obligated in that surplus by which the furnishings were worth more than one thousand pounds: because in the aforesaid provision it was clearly contained that a surety ought to be provided also for that; whence it was necessary to except that case, otherwise he would have been obligated. For an exception affirms the rule only in those things which are otherwise comprehended under the rule, and not in others, as is the notable text in l. generali, in § uxori, with the commentary of Bartolus there, ff. de usu & usufruct. lega. To the fourth and last contrary argument, that the clause ought to be referred to all subsequent things, the answer is sufficiently clear from the premises. For the contrary would proceed when the clause was simply placed at the beginning or at the end of the chapter, so that it could equally and properly comprehend all things. But in our case that clause concerning providing a suretyship was restricted to certain chapters, and thus was part of those chapters, as I have fully stated above. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that there is no reason to restrict that clause more to one chapter than to the rest; because I say that, on the contrary, a most urgent reason for restricting underlies: first, lest a Christian and good citizen seem obligated to practice usury; secondly, lest anyone be obligated in a greater quantity than he wishes to be obligated; likewise because the said Raynerius would have more easily found a surety for part of the obligation than for the whole; likewise because that clause expressly refers to preceding things; and thus, since the intention of the one stating the clause is clear, the clause ought not to be referred beyond that intention of the one stating it, as Speculator notes in the title de instru. edi., in § nunc autem, in the verse *item excipe*, and citing the text in l. si quis in princi., ff. de leg. 3, and 32 q. 7 c. apostolus. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus, Abbot of Sicily, Panormitanus.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. When presentation belongs to several as individuals, it is not necessary that all assemble in the act of presentation, but they can present separately.
2. Patrons, although they are absent, can present a cleric who is present by their letters.
3. The ordinary can confer a benefice on an absent person.
body: Having invoked the help of Christ, several points must be examined for the decision of this question. First, whether the right of presenting their own rector can belong to the parishioners by ancient custom. Second, whether the greater part of the neighbors can present when the lesser part has not been called. Third, presupposing that the greater part can present, whether a presentation made concerning a cleric who was absent at the time of the presentation was valid, especially when a proctor specially appointed to present for this act intervened. Fourth, presupposing that it was valid, whether such a presentation is voided on the ground that the person presented in absence did not ratify the presentation within the time established by law for laymen to present, but after the lapse of that time, yet immediately upon returning home and being informed of the presentation made in his absence, he ratified it. Fifth, it remains to conclude, presupposing that he was able to ratify at the said time, who is now to be instituted: whether the one presented by the greater part of the parishioners in the aforesaid manner, whose presentation was admitted by general words by the one to whom it belonged; or rather the one presented personally by the lesser part of the parishioners, though within the time established by law. Regarding the first point, the common opinion inclines in favor of the parishioners. For although by the common law the power of presenting does not belong to them if it is established that the church does not have patrons, or if it does not appear who the patron is—in which case it is presumed to be free, as noted by Innocen. in c. cum uenerabilis, at the end, de except., to which what is noted by glo. in c. quanquam, de electio. lib. 6 and the text in c. Osius, de electio. are pertinent—nevertheless, when by ancient custom the presentation belongs to the parishioners, the custom must be observed, regarding which the text in cap. querelam, de electio. seems relevant, as Ioan. And. and the doctors commonly establish there; and the same Ioan.
