Andr. confirmed it while disputing, as appears from the things fully discussed by him on the rule quod alicui gratiosè, de regu. iur. in Mercur. And although the Archdeacon seems to resist this opinion in capitu. hortamur, dist. 71, where he pursues it at length, saying that from prescription or custom alone this right of presenting cannot belong to a non-patron; nevertheless, whatever might be alleged for the sake of disputation, the preceding opinion as the common one would be observed in judging, and at least in our case no debate should be made, since they are in possession of presenting by ancient custom, nor does it appear who founded or endowed that church. Whence at least in doubt we ought to presume that it was founded and endowed by the parishioners, since a church does not grow naturally, and in obscure matters we look to what is more probable and what is usually done, as in the rule inspicimus in obscuris, de regu. iur. libr. 6; whence we ought in doubt, for the aforesaid reason and on account of the long custom, to presume that the parishioners are the patrons. Likewise because a presentation made by one who is in good-faith possession of presenting is valid, as in capitu. consultationis, de iure patrona. and in the said cap. querelam, by Innocen. in cap. 2, de in integr. restitu. and capitu. in literis, de restitut. spoliato., with similar texts. I conclude, therefore, regarding the first point, that the aforesaid presentation cannot be invalidated on the ground that it was made by the people of the parish, who are in possession of presenting by ancient custom. To the second doubt, whether the greater part could present when the lesser part had not been called: and indeed the common opinion is that they could, as noted by Ioan. Andr. in capitu. 3, de iure patr., and other doctors writing after him commonly follow this, and Federic. de Senis held this very recently in advising, as appears in the work of his consilia, consi. 17; for these doctors commonly conclude,

† that where the presentation belongs to several persons as individuals, then it is not necessary that all convene in the act of presentation, but they can present separately; for this, l. per fundum, ff. de serui. rusti. prædio. They say it is otherwise if it belongs to several as a corporate body; then the laws apply which state that the contempt of one is more prejudicial than the contradiction of many, as in capitu. bonæ 2 and capitu. quòd sicut, de elect., with similar texts. In our case, however, it is certain that the presentation belongs to the parishioners as individuals, but not as to a corporate body, since such a corporate body is not found to be approved by law, in l. 1, with the notes there, ff. de colle. illici.; what Bartol. notes in l. fina. ff. eod. titu., and Innoc. in cap. dilecta, de exces. præla., and c. cum ab ecclesiarum, de offic. ordin. are pertinent. And this opinion would be observed as the common one in practice, although in my judgment it could be somewhat caviled at through the theory of Bart. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iur., based on the argument in l. & suum hæredem, ff. de pact.; nevertheless, in our case all controversy ceases, since as a matter of fact it is presupposed that there is a custom in the place that the greater part of the parishioners presents, with the lesser part being absent, as though it were concluded that the said presentation cannot be challenged on account of the absence of the lesser part. On the third doubt, whether the said presentation falls at least on the ground that it was made concerning an absent cleric.

† Conclusively I say that, although absent patrons can present a present cleric by their letters—for which I allege the clear text in cap. ea noscitur, de his, quæ fiunt a præla., and so have advised, as the Lord Cardinal reports in cap. sanè, de iure patro., Ioan. An., Abbas, and Lapus de Castil.—nevertheless I think that, if the ordinary or the one to whom the institution belongs resists, the patrons cannot make a presentation of an absent person. The reason is that the time for presenting a rector is granted to patrons by law; whence they do not satisfy the law solely by electing that rector and not presenting him, as in capitu. fina., and Ioan. An. and the doctors commonly note this there; capitu. unicum, de iure patrona. lib. 6 is also pertinent. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the presentation here did not occur in absence, especially with the intervention of a proctor, since through a proctor one can be instituted in absence, which is a greater matter, as in capitu. accedens, de pręben., because by this, as I judge, the law is not satisfied. For that which is done concerning an absent person cannot be called a presentation. For to present is the same as to exhibit personally and bodily, as is the text joined with the gloss on the word pręsentari in clementi. dudum, de sepultu.; l. 1, ff. de uerbo. obligat., and l. coram, ff. de uerbo. signi., and l. diem proferre, § coram, ff. de arbitr., with similar texts, are extremely pertinent. Moreover, if we said the contrary, grave prejudice could be inflicted upon the church by the delay of provision. For if it were enough for the patron to elect and to present in absence, the one thus presented could delay his arrival for a year and years, nor could the bishop provide for the church in the meantime. For he could not provide concerning this presented person, because he cannot examine him in his absence, argument in capitu. si fortè, de elect. lib. 6; nor could he provide concerning the person of another as not having been presented by the patron, as in capitu. decernimus, 16, quæstio. 7. And on this account I would think that a custom to the contrary is not valid, argument in capitu. 1, de consuetu. And that a presentation cannot regularly be made concerning an absent person, I have already held absolutely in the reading of cap. ea noscitur, pre-alleged. But in our case, I judge that the presentation was valid, because in fact it is presupposed for me that the ordinary, when the presentation was made, accepted that presentation. For he admitted and received it, with reservation of another's right, as is recounted in the case. Therefore, by pure law it held, especially since in fact it is also presupposed that the presented person himself was suitable and known to the ordaining prelate himself. And this opinion or limitation to the aforesaid I held long ago while lecturing on the said cap. ea noscitur, which I prove by this reason: For personal presentation is not required for any other end than that the superior who has to institute may examine him for the purpose of approving or rejecting him, argument in capitu. uenerabilem, de electio., and capitu. cupientes, de electio. lib. 6; but if the person to be presented is known, at least to the ordinary himself, another examination is not required for the purpose of the institution to be made; the text is in capitu. constitutus 2, de app., and in ca. nullus, dist. 24. Therefore, the ordinary could, without injury to anyone and without violation of the laws, admit that presentation. I confirm the aforesaid by another reason:

† the ordinary can confer a benefice on an absent person, as in capitu. si tibi absenti, de præbendis, lib. 6, and in cap. gratia, de rescr. eod. lib. He can also invest an absent person through a proctor, or invest the proctor himself for the absent person, as read and noted in the said capitu. accedens. Therefore, a presentation made concerning an absent person ought all the more to be able to be admitted, since presentation is a certain beginning toward obtaining institution, as in capitu. quod autem, de iure patrona., and the entire spiritual right is transferred through the institution of the ordinary himself, argument in the said capitu. quòd autem, noted by Innocen. in c. quia sicut, de electio.; the text and what is noted there in capitu. dilectus, de offic. lega. are pertinent. For the right of presentation is included under the free collation that the ordinary makes; for collation has the force of election and confirmation, as Innoc. notes in c. cum olim, de causa poss. & proprie. If, therefore, collation can be made to an absent person, as in the pre-alleged laws, therefore so can presentation and institution, by an argument from parity of reason, de consti., as in c. cum dilecta and c. translatio, de constit., with similar texts. And I presume that the ordinary had knowledge of the absent person from the fact that he accepted the presentation, just as he is presumed to have of one upon whom he confers a benefice in absence. For he who wills the consequent is seen to approve the antecedent, as noted in c. cum M., de consti., and in c. ex parte, de sponsal. And this part I consider most true, nor do I believe that any of the writers would have disagreed with it if he had considered this limitation, nor is anyone found who holds the contrary. From these points I infer with respect to the fourth doubt: for I say that the said cleric had no need to accept or ratify the said presentation, since he sufficiently ratified it within the lawful time through a specially appointed proctor, who could very well intervene in this act, since the person to be presented was known, as in the said c. accedens; which I understand thus: For if a proctor can intervene for an absent known person for the act of collation, through which the full spiritual right is transferred, much more can he intervene in the act of presentation, through which little right is transferred; rather, it is called a certain beginning toward obtaining institution, as in the said c. quòd autem. For the argument a maiori is valid, as in c. cum in cunctis, at the beginning, de elect., and in the authentic multo magis, C. de episcop. & cleri., with similar texts. From the aforesaid things gathered together, the inference is drawn for the decision of the fifth doubt and of the entire question, namely, who is to be instituted by the ordinary. For I say that the one presented by the greater part of the parishioners, since he was lawfully presented and accepted and is suitable, as is proved in c. quoniam, de iure patr., and institutions made of another are not valid, argument in c. cum Bertoldus, de re iudi., and in c. decernimus, pre-alleged; cle. ij., de iure patr., with similar texts, is pertinent. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether the ten-day period granted by law for appealing runs against the dilatory minor himself who had a tutor.
2. Whether an arbitral award rendered by two in the absence of the third is valid.
3. Whether an arbiter in making an award ought to follow the common law or the statutes of the place.
4. Whether an appeal can be brought from an arbitral award.
body: IN the name of the undivided Trinity, amen. In the question which is presently pending between Giacomo Thitrameli and associates of the one part, and Mariano Falchi of the other part, a legal opinion is requested concerning several doubtful points, which I shall touch upon individually according to the petitioner's order, conclusively, and as briefly as possible. The first doubtful point is,

† whether the ten-day period granted by law for appealing runs against the dilatory minor himself who had a tutor and did not appeal within the ten days. Secondly, whether the course of the said time is suspended on account of a submission to arbitration (compromissum) made, and positing that it is not suspended, whether he can be granted restitution with respect to this time, and by whom. Thirdly, whether
† an arbitral award (laudum) rendered by two in the absence of the third is valid under both civil and canon law. Fourthly,

† whether an arbiter in making an award is bound to follow the local statutes or the common law (ius commune). Fifthly, whether, if the submission was sworn under oath, a petition for reduction can be sought without first obtaining absolution from the oath. Sixthly,

† whether an appeal can be brought from the award, or reduction sought; and what if a statute permits an appeal, whether an appeal, reduction, and restitution can be accumulated in the libel, and to whom the appeal is then directed. Regarding the first point, it could be argued that the ten-day period does not run against a minor: because today temporal prescriptions do not run ipso iure against a minor, as in l. fin. C. in quibus cau. in integ. rest. non est neces.; but this is a temporal and brief prescription, since it is of ten days; therefore, it ought not to run against a minor, no matter how much he may have a curator. But indeed, the truth is to the contrary, in support of which I allege the clear text in the newest law in auth. de appel. & intra quæ temp. §. i.; Bar. explicitly holds this in l. fi. C. in quib. cau. in integ. rest. non est necess. and Bald. agrees there; this is supported by the fact that this time runs even against the Church, as in c. beneficio, de in integ. rest., c. cum inter, de re iu. and c. cum super, eo. tit., along with many similar authorities. The previously cited l. fi. does not stand in the way, for it does not apply to prejudicial prescriptions; for those run without distinction in favor of judgments, lest lawsuits become immortal: for this see l. properandum, in fi. C. de iudi., noted by Io. And. in c. beneficio and c. constitutus, de in integ. resti. Therefore, it must undoubtedly be concluded that this ten-day period runs against a minor having a tutor. As to the second, whether on account of a submission to arbitration made with the adverse party within the time for appealing, the running of the said time is hindered: It seems initially that it is, by cle. quandiu, de appel. and in auth. si tamen, C. de tempo. appel., where it is evident that the time fixed for prosecuting and concluding an appeal is impeded by a submission made with the consent of the parties; but the ten-day period that is granted for appealing is computed within the one-year period that is fixed for prosecuting and concluding an appeal, for the year runs from the day the appeal was lodged, as in cle. sicut appellationem, de ap.; therefore, etc. I consider the contrary to be more true, especially in our case, on a two-fold ground. First, because here there was no submission in the criminal cause upon which sentence was passed, nor could there even have been a submission, especially since it could have redounded to the prejudice of the fisc, as in c. pe. 2. responso, de in integ. restit. and l. non distinguemus. §. Iulianus, ff. de arbitr.; therefore, a submission made concerning a civil question ought not to have impeded the running of the ten-day period for lodging an appeal in a criminal cause: because an inference cannot be drawn from separate matters, as in cap. secundo, de translatio. pręlato. and l. neque natales, C. de probatio.; and in this case the rationale of the legal authorities alleged to the contrary ceases; and this is beyond doubt. Furthermore, the running of the said time is not impeded on another ground: for the time fixed for appealing is not impeded by a submission, but only the time fixed for prosecuting the appeal itself; thus the text speaks clearly in cle. quamdiu, and the text intimates the same in the said authenti. si tamen; for it speaks of when the submission was made after the cause had already devolved through an appeal to the judge ad quem; and this opinion was expressly held by Paul. de Leazar. and Ioan. de Lig. after him in the said clement. quandiu, and Bal. in l. Centurio, ff de vulgarib. & pupillarib. The reason for the difference is that the time for prosecuting is granted to both parties; therefore, it is no wonder if it is impeded by a submission made with the consent of both parties. But the ten-day period is granted only to the aggrieved party for the relief of the grievance; therefore, it ought not to be impeded by a submission, because the other party ought to have no power in this, since that deadline was not appointed for him. Whence, if we were to say that that deadline is impeded by a submission, it would necessarily follow that even without a submission it would be impeded by the sole will of the one obligated to appeal, which is nevertheless false. The second reason for the distinction is that the time for prosecuting is granted for litigating to both parties, as l. fina. C. de temporis appella. and authenti. ei qui appellat, C. de tempo. appella.; but the parties sufficiently litigate before the arbiters; therefore, the running of time is not unjustly impeded; but the ten-day period is granted for devolving the cause to a superior, and lest one be seen to acquiesce in what has been judged, as in c. quod ad consultationem, de re iudica. and l. ideo, C. quomodo & quando iudi. Furthermore and thirdly, it is enough that this is not provided for in the law; for regularly all time is continuous, as noted in ff. de diuer. & tempo. pręscrip. lib. 1. and in c. super eo, de appel. But positing that the said ten-day period ran against the minor himself, notwithstanding even the submission, can the Governor of the city of Fermo, presiding on behalf of our lord the Pope, by his rescript restore the said ten-day period, and thus in effect restore the said Mariano to the right of appeal? It seems at first that he cannot, because a right has been acquired by the other party, at least with respect to what was declared in the said criminal sentence, namely that the said Mariano inflicted violence in the said possessions, etc., argument in the said capitu. quod ad consultationem. For a sentence establishes the law between the parties after it has passed into rem iudicatam, and it is accepted as truth by presumption or fiction of law, as in l. ingenuum, ff. de statu homi. and in l. res iudicata, ff. de regu. iur. and in capitu. cum inter, de re iudic. with similar texts. But a governor or legate cannot take away a right acquired by another, as in cap. fin. de confirm. utili.; this is supported by what the gloss notes in c. fina. de hær. lib. 6. and better by the gloss noted in cap. pro illorum, de præben. on the word authoritatem, which says that a legate cannot contravene that which has been granted to another by special privilege; therefore, a fortiori, he cannot take away what has been granted to another by common law, as in our case through a sentence that has passed into rem iudicatam. For it belongs to the prince alone to take away the right of another, according to what is noted by the gloss in capitu. constitutus, de religio. domi.; nay rather, it seems that even a rescript of the prince would not be valid in this case, since the decided cause was not suspended by an appeal, as seems to be proved in l. fin. C. senten. rescin. non poss. But these things notwithstanding, I think the distinction must be made as follows: either the governor wishes to grant restitution for an appeal when no legitimate cause exists, and I believe that he cannot, because not even a legate could do so in this case, since it would be to contravene the disposition of the law, which is not permitted to anyone below the prince, even in the orderings of a trial, which is more; whence the gloss notable in c. fina. de hære. lib. 6 said that a legate cannot commit a cause that is by its nature plenary to be examined simply and de plano, without the noise and formality of a trial, and Specu. held the same in titu. de lega. §. superest, at the word sed nunquid possit instituere; supported by clementi. ne Romani, de electio., and the gloss in the pre-alleged cap. pro illorum, and the text in capitu. dilectus, primo joined with the gloss, de præbend. The prince, however, could do so, provided it was established that he did this out of certain knowledge, because since this right from the sentence belongs to the party by disposition of law, the prince, who is above the law, can grant restitution against it, argument in capitu. proposuit, de conces. præbend. and capitu. innotuit, de electio., l. princeps, ff. de legi. and l. digna uox, C. eod.; which is excellently supported by what Innoc. notes in capitu. quæ in ecclesiarum, de constitu., where he says that the prince can extinguish an action, since he himself instituted actions, l. 2. ff. de orig. iur.; and specifically in our case, Bald. confirms this in d. l. fin. C. senten. rescin. non pos., where he markedly says that either a right is acquired by a party by the ius gentium or natural law, and against that the prince cannot dispose without cause, as I read and is noted in l. 2. C. de preci. impe. offe., fully by Bartol. in l. fin. C. si contra ius uel util. publi. and by Cyn. in l. præscriptione, C. de preci. impe. offe.; or the right is acquired by a party from positive law, such as by prescription or a sentence or something similar, and then the prince can dispose against such a right, especially by restoring him to a hearing of the cause, supported by auth. quæ supplicatio, C. de prec. impe. offe. and l. unica, C. de senten. præ. præto. Or there underlies a legitimate cause for restitution; and then I say that, whether it belongs by right of an adult or by right of a minor—as occurs in our case, for whether the said Mariano is called an adult without cause—the governor can grant restitution against the running of the ten-day period, and thus restore the party to appeal against his own sentence as well as those of other magistrates; and not only can the governor do this, who has broad power, but even another inferior ordinary, as in l. præfecti prætorio, ff. de minor. and l. ab hostibus, and what is noted there by Bartol., ff. ex quib. cau. maio. and in capitu. cum Bertoldus, de re iudica. by Innocen. in capitu. querelam, de procur.; for even against a sentence someone can be restored in such a case, not only to appeal merely, as in l. 1. C. si aduer. rem iudi. and in capitu. 1. & 2. de in integr. restit. lib. 6. and cap. beneficio, eod. titu., with infinite similar passages; for the praetor says, 'If any just cause shall appear to me, I will grant in integrum restitution,' as in l. 1. ff. ex quib. cau. maio., whether the said Mariano was a minor and was harmed by the omission of the appeal; therefore, he could be restored by the governor to appeal. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that he ought first to have sued the tutor, if he is solvent, for the interest, and in default seek restitution, as in l. properandum, in fi. C. de iud. and l. cum mandato, ff. de mino.; for I say the contrary in our case: nay rather, it is the rule that wherever a minor is harmed with the intervention of a tutor or curator, it is in his choice to seek restitution or to sue the tutor or curator, as is proved in d. l. etiam, C. si tu. uel cur. inter.; Barto. and Bald. hold this there, and the gloss of canon law in cap. 2. de in integ. rest. on the word restituimus, and Host. in c. suscitata, eodem titu. Nor does d. l. properandum stand in the way, because it speaks of when the instance has perished, for then, because the action does not perish and a modest prejudice is at issue, the law willed that the minor first sue the tutor or curator, as in d. l. etiam, noted by the gloss, Bar., and Bald.; it is otherwise where the action would perish and wound the right of the minor, as in our case; for it is in the interest of minors not to be harassed by the costs of litigation, as l. minoribus, ff. de mino. To the said l. cum mandato it is answered that it speaks of a procurator, who is a voluntary administrator; it is otherwise with a tutor and curator, who are necessary, as noted in d. l. cum mandato. Careful attention must be paid to this, however: whether the governor could restore him to appeal without harm having first been proved by the minor otherwise. Barto. in l. fin. C. in quibus cau. in integ. rest. non est neces. held that he could, because by the very fact that the minor did not appeal from the sentence, he was harmed, and thus it is not necessary to prove harm otherwise; and this is proved by l. minor. 25. annis. §. 1. joined with the gloss, ff. de minori, where it is evident that a minor seeks to be restored against a submission to arbitration, because, as the gloss says there, by the very fact that he submitted to arbitration he was harmed, since he lost the power of appealing. But Bal. in d. l. fin. relates that others hold the contrary, whom he himself follows, saying that it is necessary that the minor first prove that he was harmed by the sentence; otherwise he ought not to be restored to appeal, because the sentence could have been just, and thus he was in no way harmed in not appealing; nay, he could be aggrieved if he were restored to appeal without the injustice of the sentence first being established, since, given the justice of the sentence, he would succumb. The said l. minor, upon which Bartol. founds himself, does not stand in the way, because there the harm was evident from the beginning, since in submitting to arbitration he promised to abide by a just or unjust sentence, as in l. diem proferre. §. stari, ff. de arbitr.; therefore, he could immediately seek restitution; but in our case it was otherwise, for in litigating before the captain he was not harmed, since he could appeal; that he did not appeal, however, he could have done from just cause, because perhaps he saw the sentence was just. Whence it is not inferred that he was aggrieved in not appealing; and this position is most true. For the one seeking restitution must first show the harm in reality or by proof, as noted by Innocen. in capitu. auditis, de integ. resti.; and I cite the same Bartol. in another place where he holds what I have said, namely in l. si vnica. §. si procurator, ff. si quis ius dic., where he holds that the act of a procurator in not appealing prejudices the principal, because he could have refrained from appealing for a just cause, argument in l. 1. in fin. ff. quando appella.; therefore the same and even more strongly must be presumed in a tutor, that he did not appeal because he saw the injustice would favor the minor. From all of which I conclude that the governor could not have granted restitution to appeal unless the harm to the minor arising from the injustice of the sentence had first been proved before him, and I speak of a sentence rendered in a criminal cause. I come to the third principal doubtful point, whether an arbitramentary award rendered by two arbiters is subject to retractation, since the said arbitrators, following the path of arbitrators, in their sentence acquitted the said Giacomo and associates from the claim made on behalf of the said Mariano, since it was evident to them that the said defendants had held and possessed the claimed property without contradiction for the space of 20 years, according as the local statute, confirmed by the Pope, requires. And this doubtful point can be subdivided into a doubt referring it to the narrative, since it is presupposed that two arbiters pronounced in the absence of the third, who was lawfully requested and unwilling to be present. First, therefore, let us see whether it is subject to retractation or is null on the ground that it was rendered by two in the absence of the third, although requested. Secondly, we shall see whether it is subject to retractation because they followed the local statute, which seems contrary to law in that it says that a prescription of 20 years without title suffices regarding immovable property, whereas by law a time of 30 years is required, as in l. si quis emptionis, C. de præscript. 30. anno. Likewise, the law clearly requires good faith, as in c. si. and c. uigilanti, de præscr. The statute, however, makes no mention of good or bad faith, but is satisfied with the sole running of 30 [sc. 20] years without lawsuit and controversy. To the first point, I say that under civil law such an award would not be valid, because power given to several arbiters belongs not to each individually, but to all joined together, as l. Pedius, ff. de arbi., noted by Barto. in l. 1. §. plures, ff. de exerc.; hence it is that a sentence rendered by two in the absence of the third is invalid, as in l. si in tres, ff. de arbi.; nay, Barto. says more in l. si duo ex tribus, ff. de re iudi., that if the third was present at the discussion of the merits of the cause and stated his opinion and departed, two still cannot make an award in the absence of the third, from defect of power, although Inn. held the contrary in this last case, as he notes in cap. Raynaldus, de testa.; but the statement of Bartol. is more true under civil law by the legal authorities alleged above and their reasons. But under canon law such an arbitration is valid by c. si. de arbi. in 6., and one must abide by this canon law in the ecclesiastical court and in the lands of the Church, as noted in d. c. 2. and by Bart. in d. l. si duo. Since therefore we are now in the lands of the Church, it must firmly be said that on this ground the said award is not subject to retractation. Whether, however, it is subject on the second aforesaid ground, I firmly believe the same, namely that it is not; nay, it would be subject to retractation if the arbiters had not had regard to the local statutes. I am moved first because the said statute is just and valid, nor does it in any part nurture sin. For the people by themselves can enact statutes contrary to the civil law to the prejudice of themselves alone, since they do not touch rights reserved to the prince, nor do they otherwise enact against natural good morals, as in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iu., and Barto. confirms this there in repetitio, and there is a notable gloss in l. neque pignus. §. priuatorum, ff. de regu. iuris. For this statute only reduces the time fixed by law; for where the law requires 30 years since title is lacking, said l. si quis emptionis, the statute is satisfied with twenty; nay, it could have required a shorter time, for instance ten years, accompanied by good faith; for this, see what is noted by Bart. in said l. omnes populi, and Ioan. An. in c. 2. de excep. lib. 6. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the statute does not require good faith and thus is not valid, since it is nutritive of sin, as noted by the same Bar. in said l. omnes populi and Io. An. in d. capit. 2; I say that that statute speaks generally; whence in doubt it ought to be understood to speak of good faith accompanying it, because a general statute must be restricted so as to harm the common law as little as it can, argument in l. si quando, and what is noted there, C. de inoff. testa., by Inno. in c. causam, de rescrip.; and especially in this case it ought to receive a restrictive interpretation, lest anyone gain unduly and with sin, and another unjustly lose his right, argument in l. ut gradatim, ff. de mune. & hono. and in cap. cum dilectus, de consuetu.; and this Barto. clearly intended in l. omnes populi and in l. non dubium, C. de legi. In our case, moreover, the bad faith of Giacomo and his predecessors is not established. First, good faith was alleged by him, as appears in the acts, nor is there need that they prove it otherwise, since it cannot be proved, but is presumed when the prescription of immovable things is concerned, as noted by the gloss in c. si diligenti, and c. sanctorum, and c. si. de præscr., and Bald. in l. Celsus, ff. de usucap., and the gloss in §. aliæ, Insti. de act.; especially the statute is valid since it was confirmed by the Pope; whence it can be called the law of the Pope, because we make all those things our own to which we impart our authority, l. 1. C. de ue. iure enucle. and capitu. si apostolicæ, de præben. lib. 6. From all of which it is inferred that the arbitrators or arbiters did well in following the local statute, because in the decision of causes deference must be paid to the common law, as in l. si fundus, ff. de eui. and l. an in totum, C. de ædif. priua., l. 1. C. de eman. libe., and l. 2. C. quemadmo. testa. ape., 12. distinct. cap. illud, and cap. illa, and 8. dist. cap. quæ contra mores, and l. quod si nolit. §. quia assidua, ff. de ædil. edict. and l. 3. ff. de sti. ser., by Cyn. in l. 2. C. de consti. pecu. and in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. trin.; and this is indubitable to me. From these points the decision of the fourth principal doubtful point is inferred, namely whether the said arbitrators are said to have acted in fraud (dolus) by following the said statute, etc.; for they can be found in no fraud; nay rather, they could instead have lacked fraud if they had not followed the said statute. For fraud is a certain cunning employed to circumvent and deceive another, as l. 1. ff. de dolo, which in our case can least of all be noted; nay rather, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the statute were invalid in some intrinsic circumstance, the arbitrators could not be said to be in fraud by following a statute confirmed by a superior, since a probable error resulting from a statute excuses from calumny and fraud, l. 2. ff. de iu. & fact. igno., capitu. 1. de electio. lib. 6. in fin.; supported by what the gloss notes in capitu. unico, de postu. præla. lib. 6. and capitu. cum uenerabilis, de consuetu. I come to the fifth doubtful point, whether the said reduction of the arbitration could be sought without first having obtained absolution from the oath sworn in the submission; and without lingering much, I say that if fraud and enormous deceit are alleged, such as a good man would not have committed, reduction can be sought without seeking absolution from the oath. The text in cap. Quintauallis and cap. ueniens, de iureiur. proves this; supported by l. si libertus, ff. de ope. liber. Nor is the penalty affixed in the submission incurred, because the oath and penalty not to contravene must be understood if it was pronounced according to the judgment of a good man, as is proved in the pre-alleged laws, noted by Innocen. and Hostien. in the said cap. Quintauallis, and Spec. in titu. de arbit. §. 1. uersi. sed pone. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that in the submission it was stated that the arbiters could dispose and award altè & bassè, taking away from the right of one and giving to the other; because I say that those words are restricted by the subsequent words, when it was stated, 'as it shall seem and please them'; which words indeed sound in the judgment of a good man, and not free will, as in the law Thais. §. sororem, ff. de fideicom. libe. and l. fideicomissa. §. quamquam, ff. de lega. 3., noted by Barto. in l. alio, ff. de ali. & ciba. lega. and in the extravagante Ad reprimendum, where he treated it more fully than elsewhere; supported by the gloss in cap. 2. de corpo. uiti. with similar passages. I say, however, that if the said Mariano does not prove the injustice and iniquity of the arbitration, he falls into perjury and the penalty affixed in the submission, because then it appears that he clamored unjustly and contrary to his oath; which is to be understood if the judge of the complaint has declared the arbitration to be equitable. Likewise if no probable cause excuses the said Mariano, concerning which see fully by Bartol. in l. societatem. §. arbitrorum, ff. pro socio, more fully in l. qui Romæ. §. duo fratres, ff. de uerbo. obl. and l. Iulianus, ff. de condi. indeb.; it was regularly stated by Di. in a certain consilium of his, which Ioan. Andr. relates in addi. Specu. in ti. de arbit §. excipitur, versiculo quod si compromissum. To prove the iniquity of the arbitration, moreover, it does not suffice to prove that the arbitrator harmed in some respect the right of a party, because he has from law the power to harm a party to some degree for the sake of peace, namely by taking away from one and giving to the other, as noted by the gloss in l. si de meis. §. recepisse, ff. de arbit. and noted by Inno. in cap. Quintauallis, de iureiu. and Bartol. in d. §. arbitrorum, even if those words altè & bassè etc., which were affixed here, had never been included; therefore, much more strongly does it not suffice to prove this in our case, where beyond the power handed down by law those words were included, which ought to operate something beyond the law, argument in capitu. si papa, de priuileg. lib. 6. It must therefore be proved that he harmed so enormously that no good man would have done so, argument in d. §. arbitrorum, with the following paragraph. Barto., however, in d. §. arbitrorum, said that harm in a sixth part of the whole must be proved, and he pursues this more fully in d. §. arbitrorum; which does not please me, as I said fully in the lecture on the said capitu. Quintauallis, where I finally concluded that when enormous harm is spoken of, a certain fixed doctrine cannot be given, but from various circumstances, a good man, that is, the judge, will decide. For an arbitrator ought more easily to be induced to give from the right of one to the other when otherwise peace cannot follow; otherwise if this reason ceases. Likewise, otherwise when the right of the parties is obscure and involved than when it is clear and indubitable. Likewise, otherwise when one is rich and the other poor, and so of other circumstances, which having been considered, the judge will have to determine whether the arbitration was equitable or inequitable. The last doubtful point concerns the force of the appeal lodged from the sentence of the arbitration to the said governor, in which several things can be questioned. First, whether an appeal could be brought from such an arbitration. Secondly, whether to the said governor. Thirdly, whether those three remedies could be accumulated, in that the aforesaid Mariano appealed, and sought to be reduced to good equity, and sought that restitution be granted to him. Regarding the first, I say that whether under common law an appeal can be brought from the sentence of arbitrators (arbitratores)—I do not say arbiters (arbitri)—is doubtful. For Barto. in l. fin. ff. de appe. reci. held that it can, through the reasons which he pursues there; but he himself thought the contrary in l. 1. C. de arb., and Bal. thinks the same there; and this latter is the common opinion. For reduction can be sought, but a true appeal cannot be interposed. For this, the text in d. §. arbitrorum, joined with the following law; it seems better proved in l. non distinguemus. §. cum quidam, ff. de arbi., where it is proved that that petition for reduction is a certain species of appeal; it is therefore not a true appeal. The gloss agrees in capitu. causam, de electio. and 2. quæst. 6. capitu. a iudicibus, and it is proved by the reason which the text posits in l. 1. C. de arbi., which applies as much to arbiters as to arbitrators; whence I say that an appeal could not be brought unless an appeal is granted by municipal statute. But leaving aside the statutory provision, it is doubtful whether an appeal could be brought to the governor, since by the statute the appeal ought to have been to the captain of the place. I think that under civil law an appeal could not be brought to the governor, because an appeal ought not to be made, bypassing the intermediate judge, to the prince or to him who holds the place of the prince: l. imperatores, ff. de appel. But under canon law the contrary appears, as in capitu. si duobus, de appel., where it is evident that even in the lands of the Church an appeal can be made to the prince, bypassing the intermediate judge; therefore to his lieutenant; argument 93. distinct. capitu. fin.; therefore the statute must be understood unless the appeal were made to the prince or to the lieutenant. Hence the gloss said elsewhere that an appeal can be made to the legate of the Pope, bypassing the intermediate judge, as noted by the gloss in capitu. 1. de offic. leg. and Barto. Brixi. 2. quæst. 6. capit. 3., although Io. held the contrary there; Guil., however, in Spec. de le. §. superest, at the word illud autem, said that by custom it is observed that an appeal may be made to him bypassing the intermediate judge; the gloss says this fully in c. 2. de consue. lib. 6. And this latter pleases me, because he concurs with any jurisdiction in the province decreed to him, as I read and is noted in cap. 1. de offi. leg. Regarding the last point concerning accumulation, there is not much need to linger: because, presupposing that an appeal could be made to him, the libel of appeal could be so interpreted that it contains no contradiction. For it ought to be interpreted most broadly so as to conclude the intention of the libellant, as in l. si quis intentione ambigua, ff. de iud., as I read and is noted in c. constitutus, de reli. do. For the appeal can be excused by pretext of the statute, if there is one. The petition for reduction, however, can be accessory to the appeal, so as to reduce to equity the force of the appeal; restitution could not be sought on pretext of the criminal sentence, etc. Little care need be taken concerning this, however, since from the aforesaid the said Giacomo and associates have been sufficiently advised. And let these things suffice. Nic. Abbas Sicu. Panor.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The will of the testator holds the first place in conditions.
2. That is called the evident will of the testator which is gathered from conjectures.
casus: The point of the question is proposed in these terms. A certain Benedictus Chaterini made his testament, and among other things left Stephana, his mother, and Antonia, his wife, as mistresses, managers, and usufructuaries of all his goods, so long as they should live honorably and chastely and observe a widowed life in his houses together with his heirs written below. In all his goods, moreover, movable and immovable, etc., he instituted as his universal heir or heirs one or more posthumous child or children to be born of the body of the aforesaid Antonia, his wife, if they or he should come to light. With this condition added, that if any of the said posthumous children should die in pupillary age, or thereafter at any time without legitimate children, etc., that one should die to the other, and the other to the other, and if all should thus die without legitimate children, he substituted to them Bellavita, his daughter then surviving, and the posthumous female child or children to be born, etc.; and if the said posthumous children should not come to light, he instituted and made the said Bellavita and the said posthumous female child or children universal heirs in equal portion, so that one should die to the other, etc. And if the said posthumous child or children should come to light, as is said above, he left to the said Bellavita and to the said posthumous female child or children 800 pounds of pennies and the customary gear for each of them, and in the aforesaid he instituted them heirs, etc. He added these words: 'Likewise, upon the occurrence of the aforesaid condition, he left to the church of St. Augustine for his soul, etc., one hundred', and he made certain other bequests, always adding those words, 'upon the occurrence of the aforesaid condition.' And lastly he said: 'Likewise the said testator left, willed, and commanded, upon the occurrence of the aforesaid condition, that the residue of his goods, after first deducting all the aforesaid bequests, be given and distributed for the love of God, and for his soul and those of his dead, etc.' When this testament had been made, the testator died, the said Bellavita, his daughter, surviving him; thereafter a posthumous female child was born, namely Diavina, daughter of the said testator; at last they ended their days, having left no children. Regarding the aforesaid, three doubts arise. First, whether the said legacies are due. Second, whether the usufruct of the said goods of the said testator remains with the said women, Stephana and Antonia. Third, if the said Lady Antonia, wife of the said testator, should pass to second vows, whether the said Stephana ought to have the full usufruct of all the goods of the said testator.
body: Concerning the first point, having invoked the aid of the Savior, omitting for the sake of brevity arguments that could quite easily be formulated on behalf of the legatees, I firmly judge that the said legacies are not due because of the failure of the inserted condition. For the failure of a condition causes a legacy to fail, no matter how favored it may be, as in ff. de condict. & demon. almost throughout, C. de condi. inser. throughout, and extra de condict. apposi. in chapter uerum, and chapter per tuas, with similar texts. As to whether the condition attached to the legacies failed, which depends upon the understanding of those frequently repeated words, namely, 'upon the occurrence of the aforesaid condition'—for although the testator had set down several conditions, yet in the legacies he did not express under which condition he willed them to be provided, but spoke generally, 'upon the occurrence of the said condition'—it is incumbent to investigate which condition the testator understood; to investigate which, we must first conjecture the mind and will of the testator,
† because in conditions the will of the testator holds the first place, as in l. conditionibus, ff. de cond. & demonstra., which indeed can be gathered from conjectures.

† For that is called the evident will of the testator which is gathered from conjectures, as in l. licet imperator, ff. de leg. 1; l. non ad ea, ff. de cond. & demon. is relevant. Likewise, an interpretation must be made, as far as can be done, to avoid absurdity and an understanding contrary to law, as in c. cum dilectus, de consuetud. and l. 2 and what is noted there, C. de condi. inser. In this testament, however, the testator had premised three principal conditions. The first and principal was that if any of the said posthumous children, namely males, should die in pupillary age, or thereafter at any time without legitimate children etc., that one should die to the other [i.e., that one should succeed the other], and if all should die, he substituted Bellavita, the surviving daughter, and the posthumous female child or children to be born, etc. The second condition was that if the said posthumous male child or children first instituted should not come to light [i.e., be born alive], he instituted as universal heirs the said Bellavita and the posthumous female children or child to be born, so that one should die to the other. The third condition was that if the said posthumous male child or children should come to light, he left to Bellavita and to the posthumous female child the dowries written above, in which he instituted them heirs, etc. For if we wish to refer those words subsequently added in the legacies, 'upon the occurrence of the said condition' etc., to this last condition, namely if the posthumous male child or children should come to light etc.—which seems ought to be done, because a condition in doubt is referred to the nearest antecedent, as the gloss notes in l. 1, ff. de leg. præstan.; l. quod traditum, ff. de cond. & demon. is relevant—it is certain that the legacy is not due: because that condition fails, since no posthumous male child thus came to light, but only a posthumous female child, although on this ground the legatees would be excluded. Yet it does not please me that those words ought to be referred to that condition, because an absurdity would follow, and it would be an understanding contrary to the tacit will of the testator. For if this understanding were retained, it would follow that the father wished to burden the male children more than the females, because he was leaving legacies in the event of males, but otherwise in the event of females, which sounds absurd on account of the preservation of the family and agnation, l. 1, ff. ven. inspi. and what Cynus notes in l. fin. C. de adult. Likewise, it would be entirely contrary to the intention of the testator, because he loved the males more, by instituting them in the first place, than the females, whom he instituted in default of males. Moreover, the absurdity would follow that he would have willed to leave nothing in effect to the male children, since in the event of the said condition he had ordered the residue of the goods beyond the legacies to be distributed to the poor, which is not likely, 17. quæstio. 4. chapter final. and in authent. si qua mulier, and what is noted there, C. de sacrosanct. eccles. Moreover, there would arise from this understanding a certain condition contrary to l. non ad ea, ff. de condit. & demonst. Therefore, this understanding is to be rejected. If, however, we wish to refer those words, 'upon the condition occurring' etc., to the other condition, which is in the middle, namely that if posthumous children or a posthumous child should not be born, he instituted the female daughters etc., an absurdity also follows: because in that case he instituted the female daughters unconditionally, without pre-legacying anything to them. Whence, if the legacies took place in this case, it would follow that nothing would remain for the daughters, since in the event of the condition he directs all things to be distributed for his soul, which certainly is not likely, arg. in said c. fi. 17. quæst. 3, where the text says: 'He who, having disinherited his children, institutes the church as heir, let him seek another than Augustine to accept it; indeed, God willing, he will find no one,' etc. Moreover, this seems contrary to the mind of the testator, who after the male children favored the female daughters, as is evident there in the substitution and the second institution; therefore, it is not likely that he wished to exclude them in effect on account of legatees, especially since it is not likely that anyone wished to prefer others to his own offspring; rather, words are given an improper meaning so that one's own offspring may be preferred, as in l. cum acutissimis, C. de fideico. and in l. generaliter, C. de insti. & subst. Furthermore, if the testator had had this understanding, he would have left to the daughters at least their dowries, as he did in the case where he wished the goods to come to the male children. It remains therefore to conclude necessarily that those words, 'upon the occurrence of the said condition' etc., are to be referred to the first condition, namely to the case where a posthumous male child or children were born and died without children, in which case he substituted the daughters. And that this understanding must be adopted, I prove in multiple ways. First, from the proper meaning of the words: for since the testator in no part of the testament said that he was leaving under a condition, except in that first part, as is evident from the tenor of the testament; therefore those words, 'upon the occurrence of the said condition' etc., must be referred to that first part. For the words expressly indicate this, and no contrary intention appears; therefore one must not depart from the words, as in l. non aliter, ff. de legat. 3; especially must this be said in the disposition of unlearned persons, who do not grasp what a condition is unless it is specially expressed. And words must sometimes be understood in a rough manner according to the status of the speaker, as is read and noted in l. si ita stipulatus. §. his quoque, ff. de verbo. obliga.; l. Labeo, de supel. leg. and chapter ex literis, de sponsa., with similar texts, are relevant. Furthermore, and secondly, from this understanding no absurdity follows, since in this case the daughters are found to have been provided for regarding their dowries; whence it is not incongruous that the testator wished, upon the death of the male children, that the goods be distributed in legacies to pious causes, argument in said authen. si qua mulier, but for the sake of honor he wished the daughters to be substituted; and according to this understanding the testator provided for the male children, so that upon coming to light they would have all the goods, he provided for the daughters regarding their dowries, and for his soul after the death of the male children. Thirdly, this understanding must be adopted and preferred to the others, so that all absurdity and contravention of law may be avoided, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iur. and in l. quod Labeo, ff. ad Carbo.; and in order to avoid an incongruous understanding, reference must be made to remote provisions, as noted in clemen. ne in agro. §. cæterum, de statu reg.; l. non ad ea, ff. de cond. & demonst. is relevant, and what Bartolus notes in l. talis scriptura, ff. de leg. 1. and in l. prætor, ff. vi bo. rap., with similar texts. Since, therefore, that condition was lacking here, because male children were not born, or a male child was not born, therefore those legacies fail. And if you should say, why are the legacies not due in this case, when the daughters are found to be instituted, just as they are due in the other, when they are substituted for the deceased males, since in any event the goods come to the daughters themselves, and it is the same whether sons are not born or whether they die in pupillary age; I say that the reason for the difference is: because, if male children had been born, the testator had provided for the daughters regarding their dowries, therefore it is no wonder if he wished the goods to be distributed in legacies to pious causes; but with them not being born, the daughters were not provided for with anything, and therefore he willed the goods to be distributed to the poor and in legacies. Furthermore, one loves females more when one has never had males than after the birth of males; whence, when male children were not born, he instituted the females simply; but when they were born, otherwise. I conclude therefore that in the above-written case the said legacies are not due because of the failure of the condition. To the second doubt, whether to the said two women Stephana and Antonia the usufruct of the goods of the said testator is due, it seems first that it is: because although by those words, 'I leave such a woman mistress, manager, and usufructuary of all my goods,' according to common custom and interpretation only maintenance is due, when the children are instituted heirs, as the gloss and the doctors note in l. unica, C. si secundò nup., nevertheless, when a legacy is made in the aforesaid manner under a condition, say if they live chastely and honorably etc., and the inheritance comes to outsiders, the entire and full usufruct is due to the legatees, as Bartolus fully explains in l. Titia cum testamento. §. fi. ff. de leg. 2; since therefore in our case, the children being dead, the inheritance has come to persons not the children of the testator, therefore the entire usufruct of the goods would be due to them. To the contrary, that nothing is due, the reason is that the aforesaid applies when the legacy was made purely in the aforesaid words, but in our case there was added, 'if she remains with his children in the houses of the testator'; whence since this last condition fails on account of the death of the said pupillary children, therefore nothing is due to them. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that it does not fail through these legatees, because as to the invalidity of the bequest it is the same whether the condition fails on the part of the legatee or by a fortuitous case, as is proved in C. de condi. inser. l. si a conditione, joined with the following law, as noted there by Bartolus. To the same effect is what is read in l. Mævia, ff. de annu. lega. and in l. Caio, ff. de ali. & ciba. lega. And certainly this side would be truer if it had been a pure legacy of usufruct; nevertheless, because in our case it was a legacy by common custom and interpretation of maintenance only, since it was left while they lived chastely and honorably with the children of the testator, according to what is noted in said l. unica, C. si secundò nupt. and said l. Titia cum testamento. §. fina., there is a special rule in favor of maintenance, that it is not extinguished even by a fortuitous case or by the death of those with whom they were to dwell. For it is enough that it does not fail through the legatees, as is the express text in l. illis liberis, ff. de alimen. & ciba. lega., and Bartolus confirms this in both places. From which I conclude that even after the death of the daughters maintenance is due to the said ladies, which must be provided according to the resources of the deceased and the affection that the testator had toward the legatees, according to that which is read more fully and noted in l. penul. ff. de ali. & cib. lega. And through this the third doubt is decided, whether, if the lady Antonia, wife of the testator, passes to a second marriage, her share accrues to the lady Stephana, mother of the testator; and I certainly say that it does not, but only maintenance is due as before, because in maintenance the right of accrual has no place, even if the usufruct of some estate had been left for maintenance, but the share of the one failing accrues to the heir or owner, as is the text very well noted in l. dominus, ff. de usufr.; what is noted in l. illis liberis, ff. de alimen. & ciba. leg. is relevant. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. These words, 'husband' and 'wife', are sometimes taken strictly, sometimes broadly, sometimes most broadly.
2. A betrothed woman is so called as if promised.
3. The meaning must cease when the rationale of the strictest meaning ceases.
casus: Under a statute providing that a husband gains a third part of the dowry if the wife dies beforehand without children, if he has led the wife to his house and lived with her, or has gone to live with her, etc.: It is asked whether one who married a woman by words of present consent, and brought her to the house of his customary dwelling, and lived familiarly with her, enjoys the benefit of the statute when the aforesaid spouse or betrothed woman dies in the house of the husband himself before the marriage was consummated by carnal intercourse.
body: Having invoked the names of Christ and His mother, it seems at first that it does not apply, because the statute makes mention of a wife and a husband, but by the designation of wife and husband are sometimes understood only those who have consummated the marriage through carnal intercourse, as is proven in cap. ex publico, in fi. de conuer. coniug.; for then the marriage is complete as to its essence and signification, as in c. debitum, and c. nup, de biga.; to which makes what the gloss notes in c. quapropter. 27. q. 2. Sometimes, however, are understood those who contracted by words of present consent only, short of carnal intercourse, as is proven in l. cui fuerit, fuerit, ff. de cond. & demonstra. and l. 3. ff. de donatio. inter uirum & uxo. joined with the gloss on the word concubina, and instit. de nupt. §. nuptias, and there the good gloss; it is also proven by many canon laws, by which it is provided that consent of the present alone makes marriage as to its essence, and they can be called husband and wife, as in cap. fin. de sponsa. duo. and 27. quæst. 2. cap. sufficiat, and cap. cum initiatur, with many chapters following there; this is also proven by the definition of marriage which is found and declared by the gloss in the same causa and quaestio, in principio, and institu. de nup. in principio, where there is a good text with the gloss; cap. unicum, de uoto, li. 6 also supports this. Sometimes, however, those words 'husband and wife' are verified of betrothed persons by words of future consent only, out of a certain benign interpretation, as is the notable text in l. non sine, C. de bonis, quæ lib.

† From which it can be inferred that these words, 'husband' and 'wife', are sometimes taken strictly, and signify those who have consummated the marriage; sometimes broadly, and denote those who have contracted marriage by words of present consent alone; sometimes most broadly, and encompass a betrothed man and woman by words of future consent. Therefore, since in our case we are in a penal matter—since the statute diminishes the woman's patrimony, l. 3. ff. de dam. infect., noted by Ioan. And. in c. fin. de elect. lib. 6—and it is likewise odious insofar as it deviates from the disposition of the law, according to which the husband gains nothing upon the death of his wife, as in c. 1. and cap. nuper, de donatio. inter uirum & uxor. and de dote post di. resti. C. de rei uxo. act. l. una, the words must be interpreted most strictly, so that there is as little departure as possible from the common law, and the other party is not harmed, as in cap. 1. and 2. de fil. presb. lib. 6. and l. si præses, and l. interpretatione, ff. de pœnis, and l. 3. §. hæc autem uerba, and what is noted there, ff. de nego. gesto. and cap. cum dilectus, de consuet. the rule odia, and the rule in pœnis, de regu. iu. lib. 6. with many similar texts. Let it therefore be understood in our matter in its stricter meaning, and thus be understood of those who have consummated the marriage. But notwithstanding these points, I deem that the contrary prevails in law in our case: namely, that the said husband, who contracted by words of present consent, and brought her into his home, and lived familiarly with her, enjoyed the benefit of the aforementioned statute. I am moved first because the words of the statute do not resist making this interpretation; rather, they thoroughly persuade it. For the words of the said statute require three things: first, that she be a wife; second, that she be brought to the husband's house; third, that he lived with her or went to live with her; which things were entirely verified in our case. For first, she is a wife from the moment he contracted marriage with her by words of present consent, even though he did not carnally know her, as in the laws cited above; and that man can be called the husband of that woman, as is also proven in the Gospel: 'begot Joseph, the husband of Mary'; elsewhere the angel: 'Do not fear, Joseph, to take Mary your wife', etc., which words are taken up in capitulum Joseph, and capitulum priusquam. 27. quæst. 2. where it is clearly decided that from the moment present consent intervened, especially when followed by common cohabitation, they can be called husband and wife, or man and spouse, as in the marriage that truly existed between the Blessed Mary and Joseph, although carnal intercourse never intervened, as there, and in capitulum omne itaque, in the same causa and quaestio; this was most clearly the intention of this statute, in which she is called a wife before she is brought, and thus before carnal intercourse has followed, by the argument in cap. institutum, in the same causa and quaestio; for she cannot be called a sponsa from the moment present consent has intervened:

† Because a sponsa is called as it were 'promised' (promissa), for sponsalia are derived from spondeo, spondens, which is the same as 'I promise, you promise', as is read and noted in capit. nostrates. 35. quæstione. 5. and on the rubrica de sponsa; but from the moment marriage has been contracted, she cannot be called promised, but married and a wife, said l. non sine, C. de bonis quæ liberis, and said capit. sufficit, with the other laws cited above. Second, this woman was brought to the home. Third, she lived with her husband, even though she was not carnally known; for the meaning of this word, 'cohabited', does not require carnal intercourse, but the companionship of a shared dwelling, as is expressly proven in our matter in the said capitulum priusquam. 27. quæstio. 2. Therefore, since the words bear this interpretation, and a contrary intention of the legislators is not established, one must not depart from the words, l. non aliter, ff. de lega. 3. and it is sufficient that it was so written, l. prospexit, ff. qui & a qui. and capit. scriptum est. vi. quæstio. 3.; indeed, if we wish to conjecture the reason and mind of the legislators, it will not deviate from the above-written interpretation, but will rather corroborate it. For although no reason is expressed in the said statute, it is nevertheless permissible to conjecture the natural reason that could have moved the legislators, and according to that conjecture we can and ought to extend or restrict the statute, as noted by Bald. in l. maximum vitium, C. de libe. præte. and in l. scire oportet, ff. de executio. tutorum. and Cyn. in l. non dubium, C. de legib.; what Dyn. notes in regula fin. de regu. iur. lib. 6. supports this, and for this is the text in said l. scire. §. sufficit, where natural justice is invoked to conjecture the mind of the disposer, and that ought to be presumed as the reason of the law by which the disposer was plausibly moved, as the gloss notes in l. tale pactum, ff. de pact. But the reason for the statute granting the gain, upon dissolution of the marriage, to the husband and not to the wife cannot be said to be on account of carnal intercourse, because this reason is found equally in both; and with respect to the carnal debt they are judged on equal terms, as in capitulum quanto, and capitulum gaudemus, de diuor.; indeed, the gain would rather be owed to the wife, who loses her virginity, which is a second dowry, and renders many services to the husband, especially concerning offspring, as in l. assiduis, C. qui pot. in pigno. hab. nor can virginity be restored any further, 32. quæstione. 5. capitulo. Palus; nor can it be conjectured that it was on account of conjugal affection, or the remnants of the dissolved marriage, because this reason also militates in the wife; hence it is that the law does not want an agreement for obtaining a gain to be valid unless it is common to both spouses, as in capitul. final. de donation. post di. restitu.; what is contained in authentic. de æquali. do. §. hoc igitur, and in authent. sed iam necess. C. de donatio. ante nupt. supports this. Therefore, no other good reason can be assigned except that the husband, in sustaining the burdens of marriage, incurs many losses; and although he has the dowry to bear these, as in capitul. salubriter, de usuris, and l. si constante, ff. soluto matrimonio, nevertheless, for the most part, the dowry is not sufficient for these burdens; indeed, such great expenditures are made on clothing and ornaments that the dowry is consumed by them. Baldus set forth this reason in the aforementioned l. non sine, and Bartolus in his treatise De duobus fratribus, where through this reason he stated a notable point: that if the father sustained the burdens of his marriage, that gain which is acquired by the husband by virtue of the statute falls to the father, because it is seen to arise on account of the paternal property, from which he sustained the burdens of that marriage; and thus you see that regard is not had to intercourse—otherwise the father would gain nothing—which factor is indeed found in our case. For, as you presuppose in the case, the husband brought the woman to his home and made all the expenditures, just as a husband is accustomed to make for a wife cohabiting with him; he prepared, as I hear, many clothes, and had made many preparations so that he might afterwards consummate the marriage with her with the customary solemnity of wedlock; he ought therefore to enjoy the benefit of the statute, since the words and the natural intention of the statute persuade this; to the same effect is the text, and there Baldus held expressly in l. deo nobis, C. de episc. & cle. For the statute does not require a bringing with solemnity, but is satisfied merely that she was brought and that he lived with her, because through cohabitation the burdens of marriage are sustained; indeed, the statute says more, namely that it suffices that the husband went to cohabit with her, which words are to be weighed heavily; for they indicate that although he did not cohabit for long, nevertheless, from the moment he went with the intention of living with her, he enjoys the benefit of the statute, and thus it does not require that he made great expenditures in bringing her or in dwelling together. For if the husband went to live with her, there is no need for a solemn bringing, and nevertheless the statute confers the gain upon the husband. Therefore, the preceding part, which speaks of when the woman is brought to the husband's home to live with him, must be understood even without a solemn bringing. For the statute is satisfied with the effect and does not care about the manner. This last consideration is truly excellent in favor of the husband; for the reason of the statute must be uniform, in capit. maiores, de baptismo, with similar texts. The motive framed above to the contrary does not stand in the way. For it proceeds when marriage is inquired into on account of its perfect signification; in which case it must be understood of consummated marriage, because then it has its perfect signification, as in the laws cited there; it is otherwise when mention is made of marriage, or of husband and wife, for another purpose, as happens in our case. For then the words are taken in their proper sense, because there is no underlying reason to take that most strict signification.

† For when the reason for that most strict signification ceases, that signification ought to cease, capitulum cum cessante, de appellatio. with similar texts; but in our case mention is made of husband and wife not on account of the perfected signification of marriage, but on account of the burdens of marriage, as I said before. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Neither a sale nor a lease stands if the price or rent was placed in the discretion of a third party.
2. If a testator said, "I institute such a one as heir under the below-written conditions," and afterwards expressed no condition, the institution of the heir is valid just as if it had been made unconditionally.
3. If an arbitrament is attached to the substance of a matter, when the arbitrament fails, that which is principally being done does not expire.
4. The judgment of the heir is not the judgment of the deceased.
5. How the rule is to be understood that every agreement, whether it consists in giving, or in doing, or is mixed, passes to the heir, lest the judgment of the deceased collapse through various rivalries.
casus: The case actually arising, upon which it is asked what the law requires, is as follows: The late Angeletus the Jew agreed with the magnificent commune of Florence, in return for a certain sum of money to be paid annually to the said commune of Florence, that he himself, his sons, and his heirs, servants, agents, and partners might freely have a loan-bank and operate it in the town of Colle for a term of five years. Likewise, that the said Angeletus should be permitted to nominate his partners within a certain time contained in the chapters. Finally, before he nominated partners, the said Angeletus departed this life. It is asked whether it is lawful for the heirs of the said Angeletus to nominate partners, since they are within the time in which it would have been lawful for the said Angeletus to nominate them, if he were alive?
body: Having invoked the help of Almighty God, for the decision of the present matter two points must principally be examined. First, whether by the death of the said Angeletus before the nomination of partners was made, the said contract utterly collapsed, so that no obligation remained on either side? Second, presupposing that the principal contract entered into with the said Angeletus remained and passed to the heirs of the same Angeletus, whether it is lawful for those same heirs to nominate partners according to the agreements and agreed terms, and this within the time in which it would have been lawful for the said Angeletus to nominate them? Proceeding in order, I come to the first, and it seems that by the death of the said Angeletus the said contract is utterly annulled by l. fina. C. de contrah. emp. and l. si merces, in princ. ff. locati, in which laws it is clear,

† that neither a sale nor a lease stands if the price or rent was placed in the discretion of a third party, and that party is unwilling or unable to declare his judgment and arbitrament, just as if the lease or sale had been made without rent or price, without which such a contract cannot subsist, Inst. de empt. & ven. §. pretium. But in our case, the said Angeletus has died, who was supposed to nominate the partners, without whom the contract does not seem to subsist; therefore, the said contract utterly collapsed. But these things notwithstanding, I firmly judge the contrary to prevail in law. I am moved principally because in our case the contract was firmly settled in the person of dominus Angeletus, who was the principal in that agreement, as is clearly gathered from the tenor of the said chapters; for he bound himself firmly, for himself and his heirs, to make payment annually to the said commune of Florence, and he willed that those chapters entered into with his factor should be observed for himself and his heirs. Likewise, it is gathered more clearly from another chapter, wherein it is provided that the said Angeletus is not permitted to nominate partners except up to a certain time, and thus if he did not nominate them, the contract remained valid for him alone and his heirs. Since therefore the contract had its substantials in the person of the said Angeletus, even though certain surrounding accidentals were to be expressed by the said Angeletus within a certain time, the contract ought not to be invalidated if those accidentals do not intervene, that is, if he did not nominate partners; this seems to be excellently proved in a similar case in l. penultim. C. de instit. & substitu., where it is clear

† that if a testator said, 'I institute such a one as heir under the below-written conditions,' but afterwards expressed no condition, the institution of the heir is just as valid as if it had been made unconditionally. This was also generally the opinion of Baldus following that text in l. fina. C. communia de leg., where he held

† that if the determination is applied to a substantiated—that is, already perfected—thing, for instance in accessorial matters, upon the failure of the determination that which is principally done does not expire, which is also supported by l. officio, ff. de contrahen. emptio; it is otherwise if it is applied to a thing to be substantiated, that is, to a contract yet to be made, in which case the contrary formulated above holds. Nor can there be said to be a sale or a lease without a price, as in the laws cited above; rightly, by the death of the one who was to arbitrate the substantials of a contract, the contract expires, because in this case one does not depart from the person arbitrating, l. si quis arbitratu, ff. de verbor. obliga.; but in our case it is otherwise, because the partners were not of the substance of that contract, since the said Angeletus had bound himself principally, and the nomination of the partners was placed at his option; whence, during his lifetime, he could have nominated no one, the contract remaining in its full force, as is clearly gathered from the said chapters. I conclude therefore as to the first point that that contract remained valid and passed to the heirs of Angeletus, since he had agreed for himself and his heirs. It would also have been the same even if he had not expressly made mention of his heirs, because regularly every contract passes to the heir actively and passively, even though no provision was made concerning him, as in l. veteris, C. de contrahend. & commit. stipu. and l. si pactus, ff. de probatio., and similar texts. Regarding the second, it is more doubtful whether the power of nominating partners passed to the heirs of dominus Angeletus, given that the principal contract passes to them. It seems at first that it does not: because since that nomination depended on the judgment and will of the said Angeletus, it cannot pass to the heir, because an heir cannot interpret the will and judgment of the deceased, as noted by the gloss in l. idem Pomponius scribit, §. si frumentum, ff. de rei vindica. and l. inter stipulantem, §. 1, ff. de verborum obligatio. It is proved by reason:

† for the judgment of the heir is not that of the deceased, since there is a great difference between them, l. si non sortem, §. libertus, ff. de condit. indeb. and l. inter artifices, ff. de solu. Hence it is that the Doctors commonly say that wherever something adheres to the mere person of the contracting party, it does not pass to the heir, as noted by Bartolus in l. ea, ff. de verbor. obligat. and in l. si decesserit, ff. qui satis. cog., which is proved in l. una, §. ne autem, de cadu. tollend. But I judge the contrary opinion to be truer in law in our case. I am moved principally by l. veteris, C. de contrahen. & commit. stipu., where the rule is given

† that every agreement, whether it consists in giving or is mixed, passes to the heir, lest the judgment of the deceased collapse through various enmities; and it is within the intention of that text that everything which can conveniently be fulfilled by the heir just as by the deceased passes to the heir. Just as, from the fact that the contract and the faculty of exercising the loan pass to the heir, as was said above, presupposing the validity of the contract, so therefore does the power of contracting a partnership, and consequently of nominating partners; for it does not appear why this should belong more to the said deceased Angeletus than to his heir. Bartolus's theory in l. si quis arbitratu, ff. de verbo. obliga. supports this, in that question whether a submission to arbitration made to someone as an arbitrator passes to the heir, whereas otherwise one made to someone as an umpire would not pass, as in cap. fin. de arbit. and in l. diem proferre, §. 1, ff. eod. And he concludes that either an arbitrator is taken for celebrating a contract, and it does not pass, just as is said of an arbitrament; or he is taken for a contract already celebrated, for example regarding accessorial matters, and then just as the contract itself passes to the heir, so also does the submission to arbitration itself by reason of the accessory, by the argument in l. fundi venditor, ff. de contrahen. emp. and in cap. si super gratia, de off. deleg. lib. 6. The same is to be said in a similar case: that since the nomination of partners comes accessorily to the principal contract, which passes to the heir, the nomination itself ought to pass; which seems to be expressly the intention of Baldus, following Butrigarius, in the said l. fin. C. communia de leg., where they hold that, because a contract does not collapse upon the failure of an arbitrament when the arbitrament concerns accidentals, that which is lacking in the contract itself can be supplied.
