Furthermore, to this opinion I bring forward the theory of Bartolus in l. si quis a filio, §. fin. ff. de leg. 1, where he openly limits that well-known rule that an heir cannot interpret the will and judgment of the deceased to hold where, from that interpretation, the defendant is to be condemned or might suffer loss, such that a defense would be taken away from another—in which cases the contrary authorities are said to proceed; but it is otherwise where from that declaration no one is to be condemned or injured, even though perhaps the gain might be restricted through the interpretation, as is excellently proved in the said l. si quis a filio, where it is clearly gathered that if the deceased bequeathed the slave Stichus to someone, and it does not appear which Stichus he meant, since he had several slaves of the same name, the declaration belongs to the heir, who by declaring can restrict the gain of the legatee; for perhaps the testator meant the better one, and the heir will be able to choose an average or cheaper one. If therefore the heir declares the will of the deceased where another can claim some interest, namely regarding a greater gain, then all the more so in our case ought the heir of the said Angeletus to be able to declare his partners, since the community of Florence can claim no interest between the will of the deceased and that of the heir. To the same point l. fi. C. communia de lega. cited above serves excellently, where if a testator bequeathed one slave to someone and gave the choice to a third party, if that third party does not wish to or cannot choose because he has died, the power of choosing devolves upon the legatee himself, whose benefit is principally at stake. So let us say in our case that, since the deceased Angeletus is unable to nominate partners, the power of contracting a partnership and nominating partners ought to pass to the heir, to whom passes the said principal contract and its benefit; nor ought anyone to be admitted to object to that which does not benefit himself and is intended to harm another, l. 1, §. denique, ff. de aqua plu. arcen.; and the heirs and the deceased are deemed the same person, in Auth. de iureiu. quod præsta. ab his, especially when a son is the heir, l. fin. C. de impub. & aliis substi. and 35, quæst. 3, §. Hæc authoritate. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that at least a good man—that is, a judge—ought to be approached to declare the partners, and that the heir ought not to declare them, as in the said l. officio, ff. de contrahen. emp. and l. domum, eod. tit., because I say that this applies when someone would arbitrate for his own advantage and to the prejudice of another, which ceases in our case: both because it is not a matter of prejudice to the community of Florence, and because in our case not a third party, but Angeletus himself was to make the nomination; whence, just as the deceased was able to nominate, so too the heir himself ought to be able to do so. For it would be absurd that a judge should nominate the partners, since partners are chosen of their own spontaneous will, to such an extent that no one can impose upon his heirs that they have certain partners, l. nemo potest, and l. adeò, and l. cum duobus, §. Idem respondit, ff. pro socio. And let these things suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Reputation together with other supporting evidence suffices to prove someone a manifest usurer.
2. In order that long-standing possession be proven, it is not an obstacle if one witness speaks of one time, another of another.
3. A woman is said to ply her trade openly, even though she has not prostituted herself in public, but in her own house or another's to anyone indiscriminately demanding.
4. A bishop can enforce the penalties of the Lateran Council against usurers.
5. A legate and cardinal cannot dispense against a council.
casus: From the statement of the case related to me, three doubts in effect must be examined for a clear decision on the fact. First, whether the said Ser Stephanus ought to or could have been buried in a sacred place, since he was called a usurer by public reputation, and the usury can also be proven through the witnesses to whom loans at interest were made. Second, presupposing that he ought not to have been buried in a sacred place, whether he ought now to be exhumed and cast far away from the sacred place, if it can be proven that he was a usurer in life in the aforesaid manner. The third doubt: at whose instance, or accusation, or proceeding this exhumation can be carried out.
body: The protection of Jesus Christ the Savior having first been devoutly invoked, it seems that the said Ser Stephanus could lawfully be buried in sacred ground: because the laws exclude from ecclesiastical burial only manifest usurers, as in c. quia in omnibus, de usur. and cle. eos, de sepul. It is not proven that Ser Stephanus was a manifest usurer, whether we take "manifest" for notorious, or in its own proper species, insofar as it differs from notorious. For he cannot be proven a usurer except through reputation (fama), which does not establish notoriety or manifestness, as is fully noted in c. vestra, de coha. cle. & mu. and in ca. cum diœcesi, de usur., where it is expressly evident that reputation alone does not suffice for one to be called a manifest usurer; to the same point is what Barto. notes in l. de minore, § tormenta, ff. de quæstio. Nor do the witnesses, to whom it is said usury was lent, prove that he was a manifest usurer: both because they testify concerning their own act, therefore credit ought not to be given to them—because although someone may testify against himself, he may by no means do so on his own behalf, 14 q. 4 in princip. and in l. nullus, ff. de testi. and 3 q. 3 ca. nullus; and because they are singular in their statements, since each one deposes that usury was lent to himself; but singular witnesses do not make proof, as in c. cum dilecti, de ele. and in c. tam literis, de testi. with similar texts; and especially they do not prove the quality of "manifest," since the usury was practiced with them taken individually. For "manifest" results from acts performed openly and publicly, as in c. 1 de postu. prælato. and noted in the said c. vestra. But these things notwithstanding, I say that the contrary opinion prevails according to pure law. And first, regarding this, I judge there to be an express case in the said cap. cum in diœcesi, de usur., where it is clearly evident,

† that reputation together with other supporting evidence (adminicula) suffices to prove someone a manifest usurer, so that he may be excluded from ecclesiastical burial, and the glossa holds the same there; and Joan. Andr. is of this opinion in his glossa on capitul. 1 de usuris, lib. 6, on the word manifestos, at the end; Ange. de Perusio follows this in a certain disputation of his, which begins Astensis miles, as does Fede. de Senis, consil. 62, where he says that reputation alone with certain supporting evidence suffices when the issue is that a usurer be barred from ecclesiastical burial, and that he be removed from communion of the altar, and that offerings not be accepted from him, and thus with respect to the penalties contained in the General Council, concerning which in capitul. quia in omnibus, de usu., for in the said capitul. cum in diœcesi reference is made to that council. But in our case there concurs, first, public reputation, as is presupposed in fact. Likewise, the testimony of many witnesses to whom usury was lent, which cannot be denied to constitute supporting evidence in our case, since their own advantage is not at issue, but only a spiritual penalty. Whence legatees depose in this manner for the validity of a testament, since their own advantage is not principally at issue, although secondarily it may redound to their advantage, as in Instit. de testam. § legatarii; to this purpose is l. dictantibus, C. eo., and what is noted in capit. 1 de testib. and the doctors in capitul. insuper, eod. titu. Thus, all the more could these persons depose to prove that man a usurer; especially since the matter then concerns solely a spiritual penalty, nor is their own advantage at issue principally or secondarily; indeed, lord Ange. de Perusio maintained in the said disputation that where the matter is solely to prove someone a manifest usurer, the witnesses to whom usury was lent provide full proof, because their own advantage is not principally at issue, and thus they do not depose regarding their own act. Nor does it stand in the way that they are singular: because they cannot be called singular when the issue is to prove a certain universal containing within itself several particulars, if the witnesses depose singularly concerning particular acts; just as in a similar case the singular glossa says in l. ob carmen, ff. de testib., which says,

† that when long-continued possession is to be proven, it is no obstacle if one witness speaks of one time and another of another: because from their statements the whole matter that is in inquiry results. And what Innocen. notes in a similar manner in capitul. qualiter & quando, 2, de accusa. is to this purpose. And whatever may be the case regarding the statement of Angelus as to whether the witnesses there provide full proof—since I do not intend to debate that now—that which is entirely true and absolute is that they at least provide a great deal of supporting evidence; therefore, since public reputation fully proves that Ser Stephanus to have been a manifest usurer, at least with respect to the aforesaid special penalties, since it concerns a slight prejudice, and it is expedient for the souls of those usurers and of others that they be more readily barred. Furthermore, that the said Ser Stephanus was a manifest usurer is expressly proven through the authority of Barto. in l. 2 ff. de fur. and Angel. in the said disputation Astensis miles. For Bartol. says, whom Ange. follows, that someone becomes a manifest usurer by the very fact that he lends indiscriminately under usury in his chamber to all who ask, even though he has set up no counter for moneylending; and for this is l. palam, ff. de ritu nuptia., where it is clear,

† that a woman is said to engage in profit-seeking openly, even though she has not prostituted herself in public, but in her own house or another's to anyone indiscriminately asking; and what is more, according to them this proof suffices to render a testament void without any other confession and publication to be made by the bishop. That he lent indiscriminately to all coming and asking will be able to be proven through those to whom usury was lent, according to Angelus. Furthermore and thirdly, to the point that the said Ser Stephanus was a public usurer, the authority of Bald. in l. 1 C. de sacrosanct. eccle. contributes, stating that he is to be understood as a manifest usurer concerning whom there is a common opinion that he is a manifest usurer, provided that it is proven by two or three witnesses that he was a usurer; and he speaks correctly. For from these things there results properly a "manifest" in its own species, which the laws against usurers require. For the laws do not require a notorious fact, but a manifest one. Nor does any ground exist for taking that word improperly or restricting it, since this would be in favor of usurers, which is not to be said. For words are to be understood in their proper signification, since a contrary intention is not established, as in capitul. fina. de verbo. signific. and in l. non aliter, ff. de leg. 3. From all of which he clearly concludes that through the said proofs the said Ser Stephanus ought to have been called a manifest usurer, and consequently ought not to have been buried in ecclesiastical burial, as in the laws previously cited. From these points it is inferred regarding the second doubt, whether he ought now to be exhumed from there, the aforesaid proofs having been made. It seems, first, that he ought not: because after death someone cannot regularly be accused, unless at least the crime of the deceased was evident, such that no other proof is required, as the glossa notes, and more clearly after it the Archid. in 88 distinc. capitul. fin.; to this purpose is what is noted in 14 q. 3 capitul. usura. For crimes are extinguished by death, and the deceased are left to the judgment of God, distin. 13 capitul. quorumdam and 32 distin. c. erubescant, with similar texts. Furthermore, the body of this Ser Stephanus was sequestered on account of this matter of usury by the bishop of the place, and subsequently a release was made by the same; therefore this ought not to be examined any further: both because an inquiry is not to be made repeatedly concerning the act of one man, as in l. licet, ff. nau. cau. sta. and noted in capitul. de his, de accusa., namely that the bishop, by releasing the interdict, seems to have ruled interlocutorily that he had not been a usurer, and thus it passed through the lapse of ten days into res judicata, as in clemen. sicut, de appel.; to this purpose is capitul. cum dilecti, de elect. with similar texts. But although the stated things seem to stand in the way, nevertheless the truth stands to the contrary. And first, the text is seen in the said capitul. cum in diœcesi, de usur., where it is held,

† that the bishop can enforce the penalties of the Lateran Council against usurers concerning whom it is established through reputation and other arguments. And among the other penalties of the Lateran Council is that they are not admitted to ecclesiastical burial, as in the said cap. quia in omnibus; but against the said Ser Stephanus there was public reputation. Likewise, very many other arguments, as is clear through the statements of those to whom usury had been lent, or otherwise; therefore he ought not to have been buried in ecclesiastical burial. Furthermore, that is evident which is established through conjectures, as in l. licet imperator, ff. de leg. 1; to this purpose is cap. ad nostram, de emptio. & vend.; but against the said Ser Stephanus were the aforesaid urgent conjectures; therefore his sin was sufficiently evident. Proofs can therefore be received concerning the aforesaid matters, not for the purpose of publishing the sin now, but to establish faith that the sin was then manifest, and consequently that he ought not to have been buried in the cemetery. Furthermore, one who dies in mortal sin ought not to have ecclesiastical burial, in capitul. fin. joined with the glossa, 88 dist.; the glossa notes the same in capitul. ex parte, de sepul. and in cap. 2 and capit. cum ad monasterium, de statu regu., and in cap. quia in omnibus, de usur. But this Ser Stephanus died in mortal sin, since he did not order usuries to be restored; therefore he ought not to have been buried in an ecclesiastical cemetery: and if he was buried de facto, he ought to be exhumed from there, if his bones can be distinguished from the bones of the faithful, as in capitul. sacris, de sepult.; and that a usurer buried de facto ought to be exhumed is held by the glossa in clemen. eos, de sepult. on the word eis a quibus, and there likewise Pau. and Joan. de Lig. The contraries do not stand in the way, because they proceed in the case of a hidden sin, but this cannot be called hidden, but manifest, since public reputation together with other arguments pointed against him; to this purpose is c. tua, and what is noted there, de coha. cler. & mu. The second point does not stand in the way, because the bishop made that release without examination of the case (cognitio causæ), and at the prayers of the friends of the son of the said Ser Stephanus. Likewise, an extrajudicial act does not pass into res judicata, as in c. concertationi, de ap. lib. 6, especially when it is done without examination of the case, as noted by the glossa and Inn. in c. ex parte prima, de verb. fig.; and that which was badly done, that same person who did it can correct, since he could not dispense in that matter according to the theory of Hostiensis in capitul. diversis fallatiis, de cler. conjugat.; to this purpose is capitul. qualiter & quando, primo, de accusa. and capitul. nosti, de electio., especially when he does this by public authority, as did the bishop in our case, according to what is noted in cap. si quis presbyterorum, de reb. ecc. non alie. For the bishop could not dispense against a council, concerning which in the said c. quia in omnibus, arg. cle. ne Romani, de elect., through the text joined with the glossa in c. dilectus, 1, de præben. and cap. dilecto, eod. titu., in which it is evident,

† that as a rule not even a cardinal legate can dispense against a council. And this regarding the second point. As to the third and last, I say briefly that the bishop can ex officio, faith having been made to him concerning the reputation and other arguments, cause the body to be exhumed, through the express text in the said c. cum in diœcesi. Likewise, I think that any good Christian will be able to denounce this to the bishop and petition that he ought to be exhumed, since it is in the interest of every good Christian that holy things be treated most devoutly, and that others, struck with terror, desist from this most nefarious crime, argum. in capitul. fi. qui ma. causa pos. and in capitul. præterea, 2, and cap. cum in diœcesi, de spon. and 2 quæst. 1 cap. si peccaverit. Furthermore, public law consists in sacred matters, 1 dist. cap. ius publicum. Lastly, I also say that although the said Ser Stephanus did not order usuries to be restored, nevertheless his heirs can be compelled to restore the usuries extorted by the deceased; for just as he himself is obligated to restitution, throughout the title de usuris, so also the heir, who succeeds into the place of the deceased, whether he be a son or a stranger, as is the clear text in capitul. tua, de usuris; this proceeds especially if one holds that usuries are reclaimed through the condictio indebiti, which the glossa holds in c. si episcopum, 17 q. 6 and in c. Michael, de usur. And let these things suffice. Nicol. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A creditor is not liable for levissima culpa, or for fortuitous casualty.
2. What is called levissima culpa, what levis, what lata.
body: Having implored the aid of Almighty God, the legal question is asked whether the heir of the late Angeleto, the Hebrew moneylender, is bound to make compensation for damage if anything should happen to the things pledged with him; and this both after examining the chapters and pacts entered into between the said Angeleto and the Commune of Siena, and under the scrutiny of the ius commune. And certainly from the aforesaid chapters and pacts no decision on this matter can be derived, since they provide nothing at all on this article. Recourse must therefore be had to the provision of the ius commune, to which Jews also are subject, as in l. Iudaei and l. si qua, C. de Iudaeis.

† Under the ius commune, however, it is settled law that a creditor is not liable, whether the pledge is lost or deteriorated, except for dolus, lata culpa, and levis culpa; but for levissima culpa or fortuitous casualty, the creditor is not liable, as is proved in l. 2, l. quae fortuitis, l. si creditor, l. si nullam, and l. creditor, C. de pig. act., and in l. si servus, ff. eod., and Inst. quibus modis re contrahitur obligatio, § finalis, and in l. contractus, ff. de regulis iuris, along with many other similar laws. Therefore, if the pledge is lost or deteriorated through the dolus, lata culpa, or levis culpa of the creditor himself, that creditor is liable to the debtor for damages (ad interesse), as is read and noted in the said texts of law; it is otherwise if the pledge has perished or deteriorated by fortuitous casualty or levissima culpa. Nor is the creditor liable for levissima culpa, because this contract is made for the benefit of both parties, namely creditor and debtor, as is read and noted in the said § finalis, Inst. quibus modis re contrahitur obligatio, and in the said l. contractus. But regarding the aforesaid matters, doubt can principally be raised about two points: first, upon whom does the burden of proof lie as to whether the pledge perished or was deteriorated with fault or without; second, because it was said above that the creditor is not liable for levissima culpa, but only for levis or lata,

† it must be seen what is meant by levissima culpa, what by levis, and what by lata culpa. Regarding the first, namely upon whom the burden of proof rests, there are various opinions, as is fully noted by the gloss and doctors in l. si creditor, C. de pignoratitia actione, and in l. si quis ex argentariis, § penultimo, ff. de edendo. And, not dwelling on the contrary opinions, the common and true view is that the loss or destruction must always be proved by the creditor himself who alleges the casualty; but as to whether he lost it without his own fault, this distinction must be made: Certain casualties are such that they do not easily happen without fault, such as theft or fire; and in these, the creditor must prove that he lost it without his own fault. Certain casualties are plausibly detached from fault, such as an incursion of enemies, and then it is sufficient to prove the casualty, since through it fault is plausibly excluded; thus Bartolus stated, harmonizing the contrary opinions, and rightly so, in the said l. si creditor. As to how the casualty is proved, it must be said that certain casualties are very manifest, such as collapse of a building, fire, enemy force, and the like, and these are proved manifestly. Certain fortuitous casualties are clandestine and secret, such as theft, and then proof is made through conjectures, such as because the door is found broken and the servant has fled, and the like, by argument in l. non omnes, § a barbaris, ff. de re militari; so concludes Bartolus, and rightly so, in the said l. si quis ex argentariis, and this was the mind of the doctors in the said l. si creditor. And I think the same distinction must be made when damage occurs to pledged goods: for the creditor must prove, either openly or presumptively, that the deterioration occurred without his fault, at least without levis culpa. To the aforesaid I add one notable mode of proving deterioration, which is elicited from the text and what is noted there by Bartolus in l. 3, C. de murilegulis, lib. 11: namely, that it suffices to prove that in such a length of time so many of those furnishings or of those goods were bound to be corruptible, by argument in l. finali, ff. de alimentis publicis praestandis; for there are many things that are accustomed to deteriorate merely by the passage of time, however diligently they may be kept, such as furs and the like. Regarding the second point, namely what lata, levis, and levissima culpa are: although much is written on this, as noted in l. quod Nerva, ff. depositi, nevertheless, following Bartolus there, whose statements are commonly approved, it must be said that lata culpa is an incircumspect deviation from that diligence which men of the same condition and profession commonly possess; levis culpa, however, is a circumspect deviation from that diligence which diligent men, and those who are of the same condition and profession, employ; but levissima culpa is an incircumspect deviation from that diligence which diligent and most diligent men of the same condition and profession possess. All of these matters are to be expounded as is fully noted in l. quod Nerva; nevertheless, for the present purpose, it must be said briefly that it is enough for the creditor-moneylender to have exercised over the pledged items that diligence which diligent men of the same condition and profession are accustomed to employ; but he is not liable if he did not employ that diligence which the most diligent men of the same condition and profession are accustomed to employ. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. What is common is called mine not properly, but by fiction.
2. The word "his" (suum) is ambiguous.
3. No one short of the prince can impose taxes by common law.
casus: The statute of the town of Colle providing that whoever passes through the territory of the said town with animals or other goods upon which a gabelle ought to be paid is bound to pay a certain amount there by way of gabelle or toll, and that whoever defrauds the gabelle incurs a certain penalty contained in the same statute: it happened in recent days that a certain foreigner with certain pigs passed along the road and common territory of the said town of Colle and of San Gimignano, and finally turned aside into the territory of San Gimignano and paid the gabelle there. It is alleged by the men of the town of Colle that the said foreigner defrauded their gabelle, because he passed along that public road which was of the territory of the said town of San Gimignano [?], and paid no gabelle there. It is replied by the said foreigner that he was not bound to pay the gabelle there, since he did not turn aside into their own and exclusive territory, but only passed along that public road which belongs to the territory of both towns, namely of Colle and San Gimignano. The question is what the law is.
body: Having implored the help of the Savior Jesus Christ, it seems at first that the aforesaid foreigner was bound to pay the toll or gabelle in the said town of Colle, because the now ancient statute of the said town provides that one passing through the territory of the said town is bound to pay the gabelle on imported goods; but common territory can be called one's own, as in l. serui electione. §. 1. ff. de le. 1., to which l. si domus. §. fi. ff. eo. ti. contributes; therefore, one passing through common territory was bound to pay. But these considerations notwithstanding, I deem the opposite opinion to be the truer one. I am moved to this opinion on a two-fold ground. First, from a lack of intention; for a lack of intention is gathered from the words of the statute, through which, nothing else appearing, the intention of the disposers is gathered, as in l. non aliter, ff. de le. 3. and l. Labeo, de supel. leg. and c. fin. de uerbo. fig. with similar texts. For since the words of the statute dispose concerning one passing through or entering the territory of the town of Colle, and say nothing of a territory common with another town, it is evidently gathered that they intended to dispose of a gabelle to be paid in their own territory, and not in a common one. The consequence is clearly proven from this: because that which is common cannot be called mine properly taking the word; for those words of the statute, 'territory of the town of Colle', encompass the proper territory of the said town of Colle: because that genitive, 'of the town of Colle', denotes ownership, just as this pronoun 'mine' and 'thine', as noted in c. 1. de postu. præl. and in l. Quintus, ff. de auro & ar. leg.

† That, however, which is common is called mine not properly, as I have said, but by fiction, as noted by the gl. in l. id quod nostrum, ff. de reg. iu. and Bar. in l. serui electione, in fi. previously cited; see the text in l. illud, ff. de ritu nup. and 12. q. 1. c. si ergo, although the gl. thought otherwise and less well: because it ought to be understood according to the aforesaid, and as noted by Bar. in said l. serui electione; and a good text makes for this in l. pupillus, in fin. ff. de uer. fig. where it is said,

† that the word 'his' (suum) is ambiguous, that is, doubtful, because it can be referred to the whole and to a part. And therefore the jurist there advised that he who swears a thing is not 'his' should add to the oath, 'nor is it common to him', as if the common thing would not be included in that oath, since in an oath a strict interpretation must be made, lest someone fall into perjury, as noted in c. pe. de iur. Therefore, the same and more strongly must be said in our case, which is odious as being against common law and prejudicial to another, as in regu. odia, and reg. in pœnis, de reg. iur. li. 6. and l. si præses. and l. interpretatione, ff. de pœ. And according to the aforesaid must also be understood the gl. in c. præsenti, de præb. lib. 6. But in statutes exorbitantly departing from the common law, as are these concerning the payment of tolls, according to what is read and noted in l. uectigalia, ff. uectig. and c. super quibusdam, de uer. fig., an improper and fictitious sense has no place, but words ought to be understood properly and strictly, as in l. si quando, C. de inof. test. and l. 3. §. hęc autem uerba, ff. de neg. gest. and in c. nostra, de iniur. by Bart. in l. omnes populi. ff. de iust. & iu., Io. An. in reg. pro possessore, de re. iu. li. 6. in Merc. Therefore the said statute ought not to be extended to territory that is common to the town of Colle and San Gimignano or any other whatsoever, and consequently the intention of the enactors was lacking in this case; therefore the statute must cease to apply, de sentent. excommunica. capitu. a nobis. Secondly, the aforesaid conclusion is proven from a lack of power; for since the territory is common, the town of Colle, even if it wished, could not impose the burden of paying a toll without the consent of the town of San Gimignano, because where one of the co-owners wishes to dispose of the whole for a use to which it was not destined, he cannot; wherefore whatever he does is invalid until the other owner provides consent, as is proved in l. per fundum ff de ser. rusti. prædio., noted in l. Sabinus, ff. communi, di. and in regula in re communi, de re. iu. lib. 6., noted by Barto. in said l. serui electione. For it is special in the fiscus that by reason of a share it can dispose of the whole, as is read and noted in l. 1. C. de alie. rerum fi. cum priua. and in l. 2. C. de communi rerum alie.; but a public way is not destined for the levying of a toll,

† indeed under the common law no one below the prince can impose tolls, even in his own territory, as in said capitu. super quibusdam, and l. uectigalia, previously cited; therefore the town of Colle, or its commune, could not have, nor could it even today, impose tolls, even in its own territory, as in said capitu. super quibusdam, and l. uectigalia, previously cited; therefore the town of Colle, or its commune, could not have, nor could it today, impose any burden of a gabelle in the common territory without the consent of the town of San Gimignano. To the contrary objection formed at the beginning, it must be said that it holds good in legacies, in which interpretation is broader, as in l. in testamentis, ff. de regu. iur., and in capitu. cum dilecti, de dona. And because the aforesaid matters are sufficiently clear in law, I insist no further. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The first decree ought not to be interposed except against a contumacious person.
2. When the party denies it, proof must be made that lawful citations preceded.
3. The second decree cannot be interposed except against one who is in hiding.
4. A proceeding begun against a condemned person expires once confiscation has taken place.
casus: The case upon which legal counsel is sought is in effect proposed as follows. At the petition of a certain Mino de Tholomeis, procurator of his mother, the judge of Siena, in a personal action brought or proposed against dominus Guido of Siena, on account of the alleged contumacy of Guido himself, inducted the said Mino in his procuratorial capacity into possession under the first decree of certain goods of the said dominus Guido. Finally, after the interposition of the first decree and before the interposition of the second, the said dominus Guido was condemned in the city of Siena for the crime of lese-majesty, all his goods being confiscated. After his condemnation and confiscation, at the petition of the said Mino, the second decree was interposed over the said goods, citations having previously been made at the house usually inhabited by the said dominus Guido, while the Commune of Siena, to which the goods of the said dominus Guido had been confiscated, was not at all cited or summoned. Now, however, the said Commune, or the officials deputed over this, say that the said goods belong to the said Commune and not to the mother of the said Mino. It is asked what the law is.
body: Having humbly invoked the aid of Jesus Christ the Savior, I am of the opinion that without doubt the said goods are and belong to the Commune of Siena, and not to the mother of the said Mino, those decrees standing in the way in no manner. I am moved because not only was the second decree, by which those goods were adjudicated, not lawfully interposed, but indeed not even the first stands by law, if the acts of the case are carefully weighed. And I shall begin first from the nullity of the first decree, and consequently descend to the second. For the first decree falls on multiple grounds. First, because a threefold citation against the said dominus Guido did not precede, nor a single peremptory one, but only a two-fold citation, which does not suffice for the validity of the first decree, as noted by the glo. & Barto. l. si finita. §. Iulianus, ff. de dam. infect. The same is noted in capitu. quoniam. §. in aliis, ut lit. non contesta. It is proved by reason.

† The first decree ought not to be interposed except against a contumacious person; moreover, he is said to be contumacious for the purpose of commencing proceedings against him who, having been summoned by three citations or by a single peremptory one, disdains to come, as in l. contumacia, ff. de re iud. Secondly, it falls more strongly because those citations made twice were insufficiently lawful: because by law one ought to be cited personally; and finally, if he is not found, an inquiry having first been made throughout the city, he can be cited at his house, whence a citation ought not to be made at the house except in subsidium, as in l. 4. §. praetor ait, ff. de dam. infect. & l. 1. ff. de libe. agno.; Barto. confirms this in dict. §. praetor, & the glo. in capitu. causam, de dolo & contu., which the doctors there commonly follow. And it seems to be proved there in text. & by Ioan. And. in regula, pro possessore, de regu. iur. lib. 6. But in our case, although the judge gave a commission to cite personally or at the house, and thus his precept ought to have been reduced to the terms of law, namely so that he would first be cited personally if he could be found; secondly, in default thereof, at the house, when the messenger in his report ought to have said that he first diligently sought the person, and since he could not have him, he cited him at the house; nor does it suffice to state it in general, as Barto. notes expressly in dict. §. praetor ait. But in this case, the messenger simply reported that he had cited him at his house, nor did he say that he first diligently sought him. Nor does it stand in the way that the messenger afterwards added that he had said or done all things to which he is bound by law and according to the form of the statutes, because those general words do not suffice, for there is no presumption in favor of a messenger, since he is a base person, as there is in favor of a judge, by the argument of those things which are noted in l. 1. C. de usuris, and Barto. expressly confirms this in our subject matter in dict. §. praetor. Finally, it falls on a third ground, because the judge interposed the decree itself when no report had been made by the messenger concerning the second citation, and thus without his contumacy being established; whence, even presupposing without prejudice to the truth that he had been truly contumacious, yet because it was not established to the judge, he could not proceed upon contumacy, because he was ignorant of that which was the foundation of his pronouncement, by the argument in l. hoc autem, ff. ex quibus cau. in po. ea.; Barto. notes this expressly, and says that he so advised and caused a certain process to be retracted, in dict. l. si finita. §. Iulianus, and in l. multum, ff. de cond. & demon. Moreover, this, namely that no report was made, is expressly gathered from the acts of the case, and the burden of proving that the due citations preceded lies upon the party standing for the decree itself; for they are not presumed to have preceded when the decree was interposed in the absence of the party, nor ought the words of the judge to be believed, as in capitu. quoniam contra, de proba. And this opinion,

† that, when the party denies it, proof must be made that lawful citations preceded, was confirmed by Fed. de Senis when counseling, as appears in consil. 165; capitu. sacro, de senten. excom., serves very well. From these points it is most clearly evident that the first decree itself was interposed insufficiently lawfully; and this would suffice for the nullity of the second, because one ought not to arrive at the second without the first having been lawfully interposed, as in capitu. quoniam. §. fi. ut lit. contest. & l. cum proponas, & auth. ei qui iurat, C. de bo. autho. iudi. poss.; this is according to the mind of Bar. in l. cum unus. §. fin. ff. eo. tit. But nonetheless, for abundant caution, I will prove by multiple reasons that the second decree falls no less, indeed even more strongly, than the first. And first, its nullity is caused,

† because the second decree cannot be interposed except against one who is in hiding with the intent of defrauding creditors, so that it does not suffice that he is basely in hiding otherwise, unless he is in hiding, that is, basely conceals himself, with the intent of defrauding the creditors themselves, as is the clear text in l. Iulianus. §. sed & his qui, ff. ex quibus cau. in pos. ea.; the rule joined with the gloss in capitu. consultationibus, de offi. deleg., and through Inno. in capitu. dilecto, de uerbo. significa., supports this. But in our case the said dominus Guido, since he was at the time of the second decree condemned and banished for the crime of lèse-majesté, was not in hiding on account of defrauding the creditors themselves, but out of fear of death had absented himself from the entire territory of Siena. Therefore, that second decree could not be interposed as if against a contumacious person in that manner in which it was interposed. Furthermore and secondly, since his goods were vacant both through his absence and because of the condemnation made concerning him, at least a curator ought to have been appointed for the goods; it ought not, however, to have proceeded solely through a citation made at his house, since he was not dwelling there, nor could have dwelled there, as noted by Barto. in dict. §. Iulianus; l. ab hostibus, ff. ex quibus cau. ma. §. 1, serves here. Furthermore and thirdly, the nullity of the said second decree is proved more strongly and most clearly. For the second decree ought to be interposed around his goods, as in d. l. cum proponas, & auth. ei qui iurat, & ff. de bonis. autho. iud. pos. throughout; but in our case all the goods of the said Guido were confiscated at the time of the second decree; therefore, the second decree could not be interposed in the goods formerly his; d. l. cum unius, in fi. cum l. seq. ff. de bon. autho. iudi. pos., supports this. Nor could the first decree impede the confiscation of those goods: both because it was not valid, as was said above, and because, assuming its validity, it could not impede the transfer of ownership; because since it had been interposed upon a personal action, neither ownership nor true possession was transferred, but custody only, as in l. is cui, ff. ut in poss. leg. & l. si finita. §. si quis autem, ff. de dam. infect. Therefore, mere custody given to him could not impede the confiscation of the ownership; nay more, not even true possession could have impeded it, since ownership has nothing in common with possession, l. naturaliter. §. nihil commune, ff. de acquiren. pos.; l. si conuenerit, ff. de pigno. act., serves very well. Therefore, once the confiscation of the goods was made, the said Mino, the procurator, ought to have brought his personal action against the fisc, which is bound to answer the creditors of a condemned person, as is read and noted in l. 2. C. ad l. Iul. de ui publica, uel priua.; nay more, regularly,

† a legal proceeding begun against a condemned person expires once the confiscation has taken place. For an action ought not to be brought against the fisc, which has its own separate judges, as is remarkably proved according to the common understanding of l. si constante. §. fi. ff. solut. matro. With respect, however, to the fruits gathered from the said goods, I say that those received after the first decree, and before the interposition of the second, undoubtedly must be restored: because he who is put into possession from a personal action does not make them his own, unless the judge, on account of the excessive contumacy of the defendant, had decreed that in the sentence of placement; which here was by no means done, as is the text noted in l. Fulcinius, ff. ex quib. cau. in pos. ea., noted in d. §. Iulianus, & in c. quoniam in aliis, ut lit. non conte. Concerning those gathered after the interposition of the second decree, it can be reasonably doubted: because the mother of the said Mino was in good faith, although she erred in law; and an error of law, although it impedes usucaption, l. nunquam, ff. de usucap., noted in c. apostolicae, de dona., nevertheless does not impede a bona fide possessor from making the fruits his own, as in l. sed & si. §. scire, ff. de peti. haere., noted by the glo. in l. si fur, ff. de usuca., noted by Dy. in regula, possessor, de reg. iur. lib. 6., & Bar. in l. ex diuerso, ff. de rei uen. & do. in d. c. grauis; and this seems true. But it is doubtful whether she is bound to restore them through the office of the judge, since, although they have been consumed, she nevertheless was made richer, since she converted them to her own use; the gl. in d. l. ex diuer. says that she is not, from the fact that they do not survive; the same glo. insti. de offi. iud. post prin. & in §. si quis a non domino, insti. de re di.; but Bar. in dict. l. ex diuerso, holds the contrary: because, from the fact that she was made richer out of those things that were owed, it is equitable that she be bound to restore through the condictio sine causa by the disposition of l. si me & Titium, ff. si cer. pet.; and dominus Ant. in d. c. grauis seems to follow the same, and it also pleased me, as I wrote fully there. I conclude therefore that she is bound to restore all the gathered fruits, or their value if they do not survive. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If a promised dowry is not paid to a husband, it is lawful for him to repel his wife from himself and refuse her maintenance.
2. If a testator in a will confessed that he was the debtor of Titius from a certain cause, with the party present and accepting, the debt is proved through that confession made in the will.
3. By natural reason one is bound to expend what is necessary on a slave or a loaned horse.
4. In default of dowry and patrimony, a husband is bound to satisfy [?] his wife with the conjugal debt.
5. A wife cannot be sued for the payment of a promised dowry beyond what she is able to do.
casus: The contingency of fact is in effect set forth thus: A certain Dominicus of Cortona, the future husband of a certain Lady Albissima of Cortona, solemnly confessed before a notary and witnesses that he had had and received as the dowry of the said woman 340 florins, namely two hundred and fifty from the said Lady Albissima and ninety from the carnal brother of the said woman, and he solemnly promised to restore the said amount of the dowry in every event of dowries to be restored, etc. Finally, on the same day and hour before the same witnesses, the aforesaid persons, namely Lady Albissima and her carnal brother, promised the said Dominicus to pay the said amount of 340 florins at his request on the occasion of the said dowry, notwithstanding the confession of receipt previously made by the said Dominicus. Afterward the marriage between the aforesaid took place, nor can it appear that the aforesaid dowry was paid; yet a certain transaction appears, made between the said spouses after 20 years had elapsed from the time the marriage was contracted, in which it is said among other things that, since the said Dominicus had had from the dowry promised by the said Lady Albissima, his wife, only 180 florins, and in order to have them it was necessary for him to litigate against the heirs of the first husband of the said Lady Albissima, so much so that he expended from his own monies 19 florins; and moreover, since he maintained his said wife for 10 years without the whole dowry having been paid, and thus the said Lady Albissima was obligated to the said Dominicus in the said 19 florins and in the remainder of the dowry promised by her, and for the maintenance had and to be had, therefore, since the said Lady Albissima did not have the means to pay, they arrived at that transaction, that the said lady discharged him from the said amount of dowries received, so that in the event of the dowry to be restored the said Ser Dominicus or his heir would not be bound to restore anything, and the said Dominicus discharged his said wife from every obligation made and contracted on the occasion of the promised dowry and of the maintenance had and to be had. Most recently the said Dominicus died, the said Lady Albissima having died previously. The heirs of that lady reclaim the entire dowry from the heirs of the said Dominicus, against whom it is excepted that the receipt of the dowry is not established. Moreover, the transaction recited above stands in the way. It is now asked what the law is.
body: Having implored the aid of Almighty God, it seems firstly that the heirs of the said Lady Albissima are not to be heard for multiple reasons: because a woman or her heir cannot reclaim a dowry unless she proves that it was paid, as in l. 1, C. de dote cau. non numera. and in l. antepe. & ulti. C. so. ma.; to this makes l. unica, C. de rei uxo. act. But in our case it is not proved that the said dowry was paid; therefore it cannot be reclaimed; nor does the confession previously made regarding the dowry stand in the way, both because a confession does not of itself furnish proof in our case, since it could have been made in the hope of future payment, as in C. de dote cau. non nu. throughout; and because the confession was immediately followed by a contrary statement by the said Albissima and her brother, and things done on the spot (incontinenti) are deemed to be inherent, l. lecta, ff. si cer. pet. and in c. officii, de elect. Nor do the words placed in the said transaction stand in the way, because those words were uttered not principally for their own sake, but for the sake of making the transaction, and thus were words enunciatively uttered on account of another thing, namely, to the end of making the transaction; wherefore they seem to furnish proof regarding the one hundred and eighty florins only for the purpose of the transaction, but not if the principal action concerns their receipt for the purpose of reclaiming them, as is being pursued in our case; regarding this, see the text joined with the gloss in l. optimam, C. de contrahen. & commit. sti. pu., to the same effect the text joined with the gloss on the word 'donationem', in cap. illud, de præsumpt. Moreover, even assuming that proof of those one hundred and eighty florins was established by that transaction, nevertheless, by virtue of the transaction, every claim was extinguished, as is clear therein. That the transaction was valid, moreover, is proved:

† For whenever the dowry promised to a husband is not paid to him, it is lawful for the husband to repel his wife from himself and refuse her maintenance (alimenta), as appears to be proved in capitu. per tuas, de don. inter uirum & uxo.; Baldus confirms this in l. quod in uxorem, C. de nego. gest., citing the gloss in Auth. de non eligen. secundo nu. § penul. col. 1. Therefore he could lawfully transact with her concerning the maintenance to be provided to her, by diminishing or satisfying himself out of the part of the dowry paid to him; for during the subsistence of the marriage the dowry is rightly paid to the wife by the husband so that she may maintain her destitute parents or brothers, as is notably proved in l. quamuis, ff. solu. matri.; therefore with greater force can it be paid to her so that she may maintain herself. And although the aforesaid arguments in favor of the husband seem pressing at first sight, nevertheless I deem the contrary side to be truer in law: namely, that by those things which were done in the said transaction, it is fully proved that the said Dominicus received in the name of the wife by title of dowry 180 florins, and that that transaction was not valid to the prejudice of the woman or her heir. And that payment of the said amount is proved through the words used in the said transaction appears expressly in the instrument of transaction, in which not only is the said payment declared for the purpose of the transaction, but principally the said Dominicus in the presence of the woman first confessed that he had received the said amount, and added that, in order to recover the said amount from the heirs of the first husband, it was necessary for him to expend 19 florins, in which he said his wife was obligated to him; the wife herself also, in the presence of the husband, recognized that those 180 florins had been paid out of her goods, etc., as is more fully contained in that instrument; and finally they came to that transaction. Since, therefore, the said Dominicus confessed this before the wife, who accepted that confession for herself, full proof arises from the said confession, as in capitu. fina. de confessis, and l. generaliter, C. de non nume. pec., and l. certum, § si quis absente, ff. de confess., and what is there noted. Moreover, on this point the text seems decisive, especially joined with the remarks noted there by Bartolus, in l. cum quis decedens, ff. de lega. 3, where it is clear

† that if anyone while making a will confessed that he was the debtor of Titius from a certain cause, the party being present and accepting, the debt is proved through that confession made in the will; so that it could be demanded as a debt by acting principally, and it is not necessary that it be demanded as a legacy; to the same effect is the text and what is noted there in l. hæredes palam, ff. de testamen., where it is clear that a contract can even be entered into in a last will; therefore, it is not to be doubted that payment of the said amount is proved by those words used in the said transaction. And what is found in l. publica, ff. deposi. makes toward the same conclusion. Nor does the said l. optimam stand in the way of the aforesaid, because it speaks of a case where someone, when stipulating for an absent third party, said that he was that person's slave; for he is not thereby proved to be a slave if an action were brought principally concerning slavery; but in our case this Dominicus confessed in the presence of his wife, and stated by himself first in the preamble that he had received that amount for his wife's dowry; and statements made in the preamble furnish proof: argument in l. fi. ff. de hære. insti. and by Bartolus in l. liberorum, ff. de uerbo. significa.; and this as to the first point. That the transaction does not prejudice the woman, moreover, is proved by an excellent and manifold reason. And first, although it may be admitted that a husband is not bound to maintain his wife if the promised dowry is not paid, as I said before, nevertheless, since the husband took the wife and maintained her without reservation, as occurs in our case, he cannot subsequently by law reclaim maintenance from the father of the wife or from the wife herself: because, since he did not abstain from the conjugal society of his wife, but rather kept her continually in his service, he is bound to maintain her, as Bartolus expressly confirms in the aforementioned l. quod in uxorem, C. de nego. gesto; it is proved in a similar case by l. in rebus, § possunt, ff. commo., where it is clear

† that by natural reason one is bound to provide necessaries for a loaned slave or horse, since one has him in one's service, and is even bound to provide medicines of modest cost; therefore with greater force is he bound to maintain a wife, however undowered, since he has her in his service. Likewise, on account of conjugal affection, he is deemed to have donated that maintenance to her, even in the case where he could have reclaimed it, since he did not make a contrary protestation, as the text in the said l. quod in uxorem shows; to the same effect is l. si paterno affectu, C. eodem titu., where a stepfather in a certain case is bound to maintain his stepson gratuitously, since he did not make a protestation to the contrary; therefore this is to be said with greater force in the case of a wife, especially where both appear to have confessed that the wife had not the means to maintain herself.

† For in default of dowry and patrimony, the husband is bound out of conjugal duty to maintain his wife, as noted by the gloss and Bartolus in l. si cum dotem, § sinautem in in sæuissimo, ff. solu. mat., and noted by Innocent in the said cap. per uestras, de dona. inter uirum & uxo.; the text in l. quod si nulla, ff. de reli. & sump. fune. serves excellently. Nor

† can a wife be sued for payment of the promised dowry beyond what she is able to do, as the text notably says in l. cum post mortem, ff. de admi. tuto. But in our case it does not appear that the said Dominicus made any protestation, but simply maintained his wife for 20 years up to the time of the transaction, continuously using the services of the wife; therefore he could not afterwards reclaim maintenance, both because, as I said, he was bound to this, and because, even granting that he had not been obligated, by not protesting he is deemed to have liberally donated it. Moreover, and with greater force, a husband cannot claim anything on the occasion of a delayed dowry, except insofar as he proves his interest (damage), as noted especially by Antonius de Butrio in c. salubriter, de usu. But in our case the interest of that Dominicus is not proved. For although a debtor does not pay a debt to a creditor, it is not thereby inferred that he suffered a loss to the extent that he can bring an action against the debtor; otherwise it would be usury received by reason of delayed payment; it is necessary, therefore, that interest be proved, as for instance that he was accustomed to trade and commonly make a certain profit in a year, or was accustomed to deposit money with a merchant and receive a share of honest profit: for then he can claim interest, but otherwise not, as is fully noted in l. conquestus, de usuc. and l. curabit, C. de act. emp. and by Bartolus in l. 2, C. de usu. and Innocent in c. sacro, de senten. excommu. Nor can the husband say that he claims interest by reason of the maintenance provided, because this is false, since he did not expend maintenance entirely in vain, seeing that he had the benefit of the service and society of the wife. And although the husband could, by abstaining from her society, likewise refuse maintenance, as I said above, nevertheless, since he kept the wife with him, he cannot claim anything except the interest of the delayed payment of the promised dowry; and in our case the transaction was not made upon interest, but upon maintenance, which could in no way be reclaimed. Moreover, and with greater force, I say that not even any interest could be claimed in our case, because it does not appear that the husband ever put the wife in default (mora). For in the promise of the dowry no certain day was set for its payment, so that we might say that the day demanded on behalf of man according to what is held in l. magnam, C. de contrahen. & commit. stip. and c. potuit, de loc.; rather, it was promised upon the request of Dominicus himself, and thus an express demand was required to put the wife in default, as is fully noted in l. mora, ff. de usuris and l. si ex legati causa, ff. de. uer. ob. But in our case no demand appears; therefore there was no default, and consequently no interest could be claimed; therefore the transaction was calumnious, as is clearly gathered from the premised reasons. For a transaction ought to be made concerning a doubtful matter and an uncertain lawsuit; for if it is made concerning that which is notoriously not owed, it is invalid as calumnious, as in l. in summa and l. eleganter, ff. de cond. indeb. and l. 1, ff. de transa. and c. super eo and c. 1, de transa. and l. sub prætextu, C. e. ti. But maintenance in our case notoriously could not be reclaimed, yet the woman was ignorantly deceived, as appears clearly from what was deduced above; therefore the said transaction was not valid. And the aforesaid holds especially in view of the fact that it seems to have been tacitly agreed that the dowry ought not to be paid immediately. For if it was owed, was it paid immediately, to which that Dominicus would first have confessed that he had received the dowry, and notwithstanding this, he accepted the confession and promise of payment from the woman and her brother? Whence he seems to have wished to have the debt-claim (nomen) of the woman and her brother for the dowry, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. pen. ff. sol. mat.; let it therefore be imputed to him if he did not pursue the claim against the wife and her brother. I conclude, therefore, that the heirs of the said Dominicus are held and obligated to restore the said amount of 180 florins, and also the other amount if proof of its payment is had, reserving to them, however, the profit owed by virtue of the municipal statute, since he maintained the wife; and it must be noted that where maintenance had been refused, the husband ought to gain nothing from the dowry, even though the statute speaks simply: an excellent argument in l. si ab hostibus, § ubi, and Bartolus notably confirms this there, ff. solu. mat. And the aforesaid applies most especially in our case, in which the payment of the entire dowry was not delayed, but only of a certain part; whence I say this on account of what is noted in a similar matter by Bartolus in l. Iulianus, § offerri, ff. de acti. emp. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If there are multiple partners, after the death of one the partnership is dissolved entirely.
2. Although one cannot directly stipulate for another, one can nonetheless stipulate in another's name, and the stipulation is valid if he ratifies it.
3. Every obligation regularly passes actively and passively to the heirs.
4. If it is provided by a statute that a debtor may be seized for a debt, such a statute is extended to the heir.
5. A contract cannot be made directly in the name of a partnership.
body: Having examined the articles entered into between the magnificent commune of Siena on the one part, and the late Angeleto the Hebrew in his own name and that of his partners on the other, three doubts happen to arise. First, whether by the death of the said Angeleto the contract entered into between the said commune and Angeleto was extinguished. Second, presupposing the contract remains alive, whether by the death of the said Angeleto the partnership contracted between him and certain of his partners was dissolved. Third, whether, the said partnership being dissolved or not, it is lawful for the remaining partners to keep several locations for lending. And first, regarding the first doubt, it seems that the said contract was extinguished by the death of Angeleto: because the said Angeleto contracted in his own private name and that of his partners, from whom he did not hold a mandate, nor could he stipulate for them, especially since they were not partners at that time, as in l. stipulatio ista. §. alteri, ff. de uer. oblig.; the contract therefore remained valid only for Angeleto's share, as in l. si mihi, & Titio, ff. eo. ti.; therefore the said obligation was extinguished by the death of the said Angeleto, at least with respect to those whom he subsequently named as partners. Furthermore, that obligation was contracted with the commune in his own name and that of his partners, and thus in consideration of the partnership, since he expressed them under a collective appellation, based on the argument in l. si seruus communis, ff. de stip. ser. and c. quoniam abbas, de offic. deleg. Secondly, because by the death of the said Angeleto the said partnership was dissolved, nor could it pass to the heirs, however much mention had been made of them in the contract of partnership, as is proved in l. nemo, and l. adeò. and l. cum duobus. §. idem respondit, ff. pro socio, and Insti. eod. §. soluitur, where it is clear,

† that even if there were very many partners, nevertheless after the death of one the partnership is dissolved entirely; therefore the said obligation or contract entered into with the commune could not pass to the partners of the said Angeleto, since they can no longer be called partners; to this makes what is held in l. item Mela, ff. de alimen. & ciba. lega. Thirdly and more strongly, what is contained in the 20th article makes against the former partners of Angeleto and the heirs of the said Angeleto: where it is provided that those articles must be observed only with respect to the partners of the said Angeleto and during that partnership; but it is certain that by the death of the said Angeleto they ceased to be partners of the said Angeleto, nor does the said partnership any longer endure, as was shown above; therefore the commune did not remain bound to the observance of the said articles. But notwithstanding these points, the contrary opinion is truer in law, namely that the said obligation contracted with the commune was not extinguished by the death of Angeleto, and even more so not by the death of certain others from the aforesaid partnership. It is proved first from the fact that the said Angeleto contracted in his own private name, and in the place and name of the partners to be declared by him, and of their heirs, as is clear at the beginning of the said articles, which partners he indeed subsequently declared, who, pursuant to the settlement made between the commune and Angeleto, came and approved before a notary the contract entered into by the said Angeleto in their name; therefore the said contract held with respect to them through subsequent ratification. For in contracts ratification relates back and is compared to a mandate, as in l. si. C. ad Maced., to which makes l. licet, and what is noted there, ff. de iudi. and l. si absentis, C. si cer. pe., l. mater, C. de rei uend. and the rule, rati. de regu. iur. lib. 6, in which it is held that

† although one cannot stipulate directly for another, one can nonetheless stipulate in the name of another, and the stipulation will be valid upon that person ratifying, as in l. actione, ff. de neg. gest., noted by Bartolus in the said §. alteri. Therefore, from the aforesaid it is clearly concluded that the said contract was valid, even in the person of the partners. Secondly, it must be seen whether the contract was extinguished by the death of the said Angeleto; and I certainly say that it was not: because that obligation was contracted, as I said above, not only in the name of Angeleto and the partners, but also for their children and heirs, as is clear at the beginning of the articles and in chapter 20; therefore it must pass to the heirs, since the matter is transmissible to heirs; for this purpose, l. ueteris, C. de contrahen. & commit. stip. and l. si pactum, ff. de proba., where it is clear

† that as a rule every obligation passes actively and passively to the heirs, even if mention of them was not made in the contract, provided that the matter, as I have said, is transmissible to the heir, as noted by Bartolus in l. 3 ff. de uerbo. obligatio.; and what he himself notes in l. stipulante, ff. ad Treb., makes very well to this point, where he says

† that if it is provided by statute that a debtor can be seized for debt, such a statute is extended to the heir, although against this in this last point one could allege what he himself notes in l. si decesserit, ff. qui satisd. cogan.; but properly considered, those statements are not contrary, nor do I dwell further on this, because they are not very pressing in our matter. A fortiori, therefore, in our case the said obligation had to pass to the heirs of these contracting parties, since express mention was made of them. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the contract was entered into in the name of the partnership, which is now extinguished by the death of Angeleto. For I say the contrary is true, since in the said contract mention was made of their heirs; therefore they did not contract in the name of the partnership, since it was certain that a partnership does not pass to heirs. Moreover, as Innocentius notably says in c. dilecta, de exces. præl.,

† a contract cannot be made directly in the name of a partnership: because a partnership is not a corpus, or a collegium; otherwise it would follow that upon all others having died, the right of the partnership would reside in one, as in l. sicut, ff. quod cuiusque uni. and c. gratum, de postu. præla., which is false, as is clear from what was said above, because on the contrary it is dissolved by the death of one. Therefore, even if it had been expressly said, 'in the name of the partnership', it must nevertheless be understood according to him in such a way that the contract may be valid, that is, in the name of the partners. For words are used impropriously so that a contract or disposition does not collapse in odious matters and those that are of strict law, as is notably proved in c. si sententia, de sen. exc. li. 6 and l. si stipulatus fuero per te, ff. de uer. oblig. Nor does it stand in the way that the stipulation was made under an appellative name, namely 'of the partners' etc., because I say that from this it does not follow that that contract follows the partnership, on account of what I have said above regarding their heirs. Likewise, it is enough that they were then partners, and thus that that quality was present at the time of the contract: because a quality placed in any statement must be understood according to the tense of the verb to which it refers, as in the said l. item Mela, as Bartolus notes in l. ex facto, ff. de uul. & pup., namely in the 1st response. Furthermore, it was agreed that the said partners should be named within a certain time, and that they ought to come and ratify the said contract; and so within the agreed time they were named, and came and in their own private names, for themselves and their heirs, ratified the said contract entered into in their name, as is clear in the instrument of ratification; therefore it cannot be said that they did this in the name of the partnership, or as partners. This same point is proved more expressly in the 20th chapter, where among other things it is said that the said articles must be observed for the period of 10 years for themselves and their children and heirs; therefore they do not expire by the death of certain individuals, or upon the dissolution of the partnership. It does not stand in the way that it is said at the end of the said 20th chapter, 'during the aforesaid partnership' etc.; for I say that the words must be understood impropriously according to the nature of the contract, as is proved in l. si uno, ff. loca.; what Bartolus notes in a similar context in l. cotem ferro. §. qui maximos, ff. de pub. supports this, as does what the Gloss notes in l. 1, ff. de superfi.; and the character of pacts is to be gathered no less from the words than from the intention of those establishing them, as the text—which is quite good to the point—notably says in l. iurisgentium. §. pactorum, with the following, ff. de pac., adding that although the first person is inserted, a pact is not thereby always personal, because very often a person is expressed in order to designate with whom the pact was made; so must it be said in the present case, since, as is clear from the aforesaid, the subject-matter of the obligation was transmissible to the heirs, as if it had been expressly agreed that it should pass to the heirs, and through the supervening of heirs the partnership is dissolved; therefore it is not likely that the said words stand strictly: because a certain contradiction would arise, which is not to be presumed without warrant, as in l. non ad ea, ff. de condi. & dem. Let those words therefore be understood, 'during the aforesaid partnership', that is, while those of that partnership survive, just as I said above in a similar case following Innocentius, as if to say that the said articles cannot be extended to others than to their children and heirs, and what is contained in the said 20th chapter and in chapter 17 supports this. And with these remarks I conclude that the said contract was not extinguished by the death of Angeleto and of certain other partners; on the contrary, it remained in the persons of the others, and passed to the heirs of those dying, all of whom are bound of debt to be observed for the said term of 10 years to the community of Siena, having promised for themselves and their heirs. From the aforesaid, the second doubt also remains resolved, namely whether by the death of the said Angeleto the said partnership was dissolved, and it must undoubtedly be said that it was, in accordance with the aforesaid. I proceed therefore to the third, namely whether it is lawful for the said Hebrews to have multiple counters or multiple places for lending; and I certainly believe without doubt that it is, whether they wish to conduct business in partnership, or separately and in their private names. This is proved most openly from chapters 1, 17, and 25, if they are carefully weighed. For in chapter 1 it is said, 'it shall be lawful for them to exchange in one or more places', and in chapter 17 it is said that they cannot create competition in that gainful business in any place, unless those lenders who were expressed in the said contract were in that place; they themselves therefore can create competition, and thus keep multiple lending-banks in the same place. In chapter 21 it is said even more expressly that it was lawful for the said Angeleto, and for any one of those who should be named by him, to lend in one or more places throughout the whole county and district of Siena etc.; and those words, 'and for any one of them', must be weighed carefully; for they support what I have said above, that even upon the division of the partnership, any one of them can lend in one or more places throughout the whole Sienese district, for they are expressed individually and power is given to them also severally; and thus it is not necessarily required that it be done in partnership, though they can nevertheless (as I said above) also do it in partnership, if they should wish to do so in partnership; on the contrary, it was the intention that they might conduct business as they wished, as is clear from the aforesaid. And let these remarks suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A partnership can be contracted tacitly through acts that tacitly imply a partnership.
2. The heirs of all partners, if they have entered into a partnership by a new consent, are bound as partners from subsequent transactions.
3. When the term of a lease has ended, if anyone has remained on the leased property, he is deemed to have hired it anew.
body: Certain persons made and contracted among themselves a certain partnership for a certain time; thereafter it happened that some members of the partnership died, their heirs surviving them. These heirs, knowing of the aforesaid partnership after the death of their parents, did not abstain from conducting new transactions; on the contrary, they contracted multiple times and frequently with the common money, just as their parents had done, placing the profit into common funds. The question is asked whether they appear to have contracted anew, or confirmed, the partnership, so that from the supervening deed the former partnership may be said to be reviewed and renewed. And briefly, I deem that they have. For it is certain

† that a partnership can be contracted tacitly through acts that tacitly imply a partnership, even if no partnership preceded beforehand; to this effect is l. coiri, ff. pro socio, and better in l. denique, ff. eod., where it is proved that a partnership can be tacitly dissolved, therefore also contracted, by the argument in regula omnis res, de re iud. and in l. nihil tam naturale, ff. de reg. iu., which Barto. and Bald. and others expressly affirm in l. si patruus, C. communia utriusque iu. and in the treatise De duobus fratribus. Furthermore, I cite an express text directly on point with our case in l. plane, ff. pro socio, where it is said

† that if the heirs of all the partners entered into partnerships, they are bound as partners by a new consent arising from subsequent transactions; and that text, in my judgment, must be understood directly on point with our case, when they tacitly consented by continuing prior transactions, which the text implies in those words: "they entered into the intention of a partnership, etc." For intention would be weighed in vain if they had expressly contracted the partnership, by the argument of l. Labeo, ff. de sup. leg.; for no one is presumed to say what he did not conceive in his mind; and also the text in said l. plane, there: "what they subsequently conducted," and thus the transactions conducted by the supervening parties are weighed. Likewise, a law ought to be understood in a doubtful case, as in l. quod Labeo, ff. ad Carb. and l. 1 in fi. ad muni. and c. cum in iure, de off. deleg.; but to whom was it doubtful that heirs could contract a partnership anew through express consent? Therefore it must be understood as applying when they contracted tacitly in the aforesaid manner. To the same point l. item quæritur, § qui impleto, ff. loca. serves exceedingly well, where it is clear

† that if, when the term of a lease has ended, someone remains on the leased property, he is seen to have leased it anew; therefore let us say the same in the matter at hand: that if, upon the partnership being ended by death, an heir remains in the same partnership just as the deceased had, the partnership appears to be contracted anew, since in both cases consent suffices without any other performance, as in l. consensu, ff. de act. & oblig. And these things appear to be the opinion of Bar. and Bal. in the said treatise De duobus fratribus and the said l. si patruus. For they maintain that after the death of the father, of whom one was a partner, he remained in the common property, contracting in respect of it in the name of the partnership, and is thus seen to contract tacitly anew according to the purpose of the deceased, even if he is a ward, provided that the guardian tacitly consents. So and even more strongly must it be said in the matter at hand, since in our case the deceased's son is eighteen years of age, who can bind himself, and he himself contracted anew in his own right in the name of the partnership after his father's death. And let these things suffice. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. When an estate is bequeathed with its equipment, only those things pass which pertain to the cultivation of the said estate.
2. In the vernacular, massaritiae mean the same as household goods.
3. Vessels fit for cooking pass under the designation of the equipment of an estate, if they were there for cooking for the use of the said estate.
body: IN the name of Christ. The case is stated in fact as follows: The late dominus Antonius Matthaei in his testament made, among other things, a legacy of the following tenor, namely: "Item, he left and bequeathed to Guinocio Thomæ, his grandson, his estate situated &c., with all its jurisdiction and appurtenances, and with all and singular household goods/farm equipment (massaritiis) pertaining to the said estate; also, if the sharecroppers (mediarii) of the said estate should have any debt with the said testator, let it remain and belong to the said Guinocio, &c." And after some provisions he added: "Item, he left and bequeathed to the said Guinocio two hundred gold florins, which the said testator willed should be understood to be for the remainder of all administration that the same testator had conducted up to this point for the said domina Christofora and Guinocio. With this condition, that the said domina Christofora, mother of the said Guinocio, and Guinocio himself, must remain silent and content with the aforesaid legacies, namely that they may not further seek, nor be able to seek, anything in his goods; otherwise they shall not be valid &c." Now, having seen and weighed the words of the said testator, doubts principally arise concerning two matters. The first doubt is whether the beds or mattresses existing in the houses of the said bequeathed estate, which the testator kept there for a long time for his own use and that of his family who went to that estate, pass under the said legacy. The second doubt is whether the said Guinocio, without any opposition from the will of the said testator, can vindicate and claim certain items of furniture, such as couches, chests, and similar things pertaining to his ownership, which at present are in the house of the said testator, and which were there during the lifetime of the said testator, as well as many items of furniture among those that had been brought there. Concerning the first doubt, it seems at first glance that one must say that the said beds or mattresses do not pass under the said legacy, by l. Item pictoris, with l. seq. ff. de fund. instru., where it is clear

† that when an estate is bequeathed with its equipment (cum instrumento suo), only those things pass which pertain to the cultivation of the said estate, whence a mill-donkey existing there is not included; the same seems true when the equipment of some trade is bequeathed, so that only things pertaining to that trade or craft pass. But beds do not pertain to the cultivation of the field; therefore they are not included in the said legacy; let there pass, then, mattocks or hoes, and vats, and similar things which properly concern the estate itself. But notwithstanding this, I judge that the contrary proceeds in law. I am moved principally because in the aforesaid legacy it was not simply spoken of the equipment of the estate; on the contrary, the testator bequeathed the estate with all and singular the massaritia pertaining to the said estate; and it is certain that under the designation of massaritiæ falls whatever falls under the designation of furniture (suppellectilia).
