† For massaritiæ in the vernacular mean the same thing as suppellectilia, as Barto. notes in l. 1 ff. de supel. leg. But it is certain that under the designation of suppellectilia, even in legacies, beds and mattresses pass, as is the notable text in l. suppellectili legata, in princip. ff. eod., and Barto. notes there; therefore, in our case it must most certainly be maintained that under the designation of massaritiæ beds and mattresses pass; and the same must be said regarding similar furniture, such as chests, benches, and the like. It must be noted, however, that the testator did not simply bequeath the massaritiæ existing there, but the massaritiæ pertaining to that estate; therefore there pass the massaritiæ, or furniture, which the testator had destined to remain on the said estate for his use and that of his family when they went to the said estate; to this effect is the good text in argument in l. quod conclaue, ff. de dam. infect. Whence I say further that if the testator was accustomed to keep a great deal of furniture there with respect to that estate, even if out of some temporary necessity he had carried some of it away, since he did not do so with the intention of removing it permanently, I think it is included in the said legacy, although it was not there at the time of the testator's death or when the testament was made; for this I cite the good text in l. quæsitum, ff. de lega. 3. and l. generali, §. uxori, ff. de usufruct. leg. Indeed, it can be said that even if the testator had said, "I bequeath the estate with its equipment," nevertheless the said beds and other furniture would pass which the testator kept there solely for the sake of the estate, by the text in l. cum de lanionis, §. deputatoribus, and in §. asinam, at the word item cacabos, de fun. instru., where it is clear

† that vessels fit for cooking pass under the designation of the equipment of an estate, if they were there for cooking for the use of the said estate; therefore the same applies to beds and other massaritiæ existing there for the use of the said estate. I conclude, therefore, as to the first doubt, that under the said legacy pass all the massaritiæ, or furniture, which the testator kept there on the occasion of the said estate, whether they be beds or other massaritiæ. Concerning the second doubt, whether the said Guinocio can vindicate and claim the furniture or things existing in the house of the said late dominus Antonius without any opposition from the will of the said testator, I briefly think that he can. For in law it is indubitable law that he is able to do so: l. incivile, C. de fur., Inst. de act. post princip., and l. sive possidetis, C. de proba., and l. mater, C. de rei vend., with many similar texts. It remains therefore to be seen whether the testator's intention resists. Truly I judge that it does not, because the testator stated that he had bequeathed those two hundred florins for the remainder of all the administration that the testator himself had conducted concerning the goods of the said Guinocio, and thus in compensation for the revenues and fruits which he had collected by administering the goods of the said Guinocio, or if he were in any way bound on account of maladministration; but the said furniture does not fall under the name of administration, and he is not said to have administered it, since it was simply brought into the house of the said Antonius as into the house of a relative; therefore the legacy does not appear to have been made in compensation for that furniture, since the administration of goods and furniture brought into a house for its safekeeping are entirely different things, argument in l. 3 de supel. leg. Therefore a provision made regarding one species ought not to be extended to another which was never under administration, argument in l. licet, C. de iudi., and l. 1 C. si adver. rem iud. And especially must this be said in a testamentary disposition, which ought to be broadly understood in favor of the legatee: l. in testamento, ff. de regu. iur., and capit. cum dilecti, de dona. And that this was the intention of the testator—which must principally be attended to, l. in conditionibus, ff. de condi. & demon.—is clearly shown by the words of the said testator; for when he had premised that the said Guinocio should be content with the aforesaid legacy, he added by way of declaration of the aforesaid words, namely, "so that he can seek nothing in the goods of the said dominus Antonius"; but it is certain that by vindicating his own goods he is not said to seek anything in the goods of the said dominus Antonius, for that furniture of Guinocio is not among the goods of the said dominus Antonius, as in l. Quintus, ff. de auro & argen. leg., and l. bonorum, ff. de verborum signifi. Likewise, the said Guinocio, by vindicating his furniture, does not say that dominus Antonius or his heir is or was obligated to him, for this real action lies concerning the thing and not concerning the person, as in Inst. de act. post princi., especially joined with the gloss on the word nullo iure; and the aforesaid points especially hold true given that the said testator never raised any dispute concerning that furniture, nor ever denied that it belonged to the said Guinocio. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A church, chapel, or oratory cannot be erected or constructed without the authority of the diocesan.
2. One who constructs a church, chapel, or altar is ipso facto bound to provide an endowment, no. 8.
3. A bishop ought not to ordain anyone as a cleric unless he first assigns a benefice from which he can live.
4. When a church is vacant, if the chapter has alienated any of the goods of the church without the authority of a superior, it is left to the choice of the future bishop whether he wishes to ratify the said alienation.
5. A sentence rendered against a minor without a curator is null; it is otherwise, however, if it was rendered in his favor.
6. A priest having people is bound to have a cleric.
7. One having a benefice that requires the solemnity of masses is bound to have a cleric.
9. If a debtor donates his goods to the prejudice and fraud of creditors, such a donation is not valid.
body: Invoking the protection of Jesus Christ the Savior, many doubtful questions could be drawn from the proposed theme; but because very many of them remain resolved through the discussion of some, I shall therefore take up only a few. And first, it must be seen whether the said Lady Vanucia could lawfully cause the said altar to be constructed solely with the license of the prior of the church of San Salvatore of Rieti. The second doubt, presupposing whether she could or could not, is whether the said Lady Vanutia is bound, through herself and her heirs, to cause the said chapel to be endowed. Third, presupposing that she is bound to the endowment of the said chapel, whether the endowment must be sufficient for an instituted priest in the said chapel only, or also for a cleric who ought to assist in celebrating divine services. The fourth doubt is whether, presupposing the obligation of the said Lady Vanutia arising from the foundation alone, the said obligation is rendered ineffective by the donation of her goods made to a certain altar of San Domenico of Fermo before she was sued concerning the aforesaid donation. Regarding the first, it seems it should be said that the said Lady Vanutia could not erect, or cause to be erected, the said altar solely by the license and consent of the said lord prior:

† because a church, or chapel, or oratory cannot be erected and constructed without the license of the diocesan in a non-exempt place. If, however, the place is exempt, the license of the Apostolic See is required, as is proved in capitu. authoritate, de priuileg. lib. 6. and in Auth. ut nul. fac. ora. do. post princip. colum. 5. and in Auth. de eccle. tit. §. sinautem; to the same effect de cons. distin. 1. capitu. nemo. The said prior is not the diocesan in that place, since the church is subject to the Abbey of San Salvatore; therefore, by the consent of that abbot, who is called the diocesan in the place by reason of plenary subjection, the said altar ought to have been constructed; to this effect is what the gl. notes in cle. 1. de reb. ec. non alie. and Inno. in c. statuimus, de transac. Since, therefore, the said altar was not lawfully constructed, it ought to be destroyed, arg. in cap. 1. de nou. ope. nun. The text in the said authen. ut nullus sa. ora. do. post princ. supports this; and what is done contrary to law ought not to have any effect, l. non dubium, C. de leg. and 10. distin. cap. uides fili, and the rule quæ contra ius fiunt, de reg. iur. lib. 6. But notwithstanding these points, I deem that according to law it should be stated that either the said abbot, to whom that church is subject pleno iure, does not wish to have the construction of the said altar ratified; and then what was said above applies, namely, that the said altar can be destroyed, or retained within the jurisdiction of the church, without the said Lady Vanucia or her heir being able to claim a right of patronage or any other right therein for herself, argumen. 12. q. 2. capitu. apostolico, and in d. Auth. de eccle. titu. §. si quis autem in sua domo. If, however, the said abbot ratified, or wished to ratify, the construction of the said altar, by that very fact I consider the said Lady Vanucia to have been obligated to endow the said altar. I am moved principally,

† because one who constructs a church, or chapel, or altar is obligated ipso facto to endow it, just as a natural father is obligated to endow his daughter. 16. q. 7. capitu. piæ mentis. So notes the glo. in cap. nemo, de consec. distin. 1. and the same glo. in cap. cum sicut, de consec. eccle. uel alta. Insofar, however, as that gl. says that an action should first be given against the consecrator, who consecrated the church without an endowment, and effectively it ought to be given against the founder and his heir, nevertheless that glo. on that point is not commonly held by the Doctors commenting there, who say that indeed it lies first against the founder by that text; and the glo. held the same in d. capitu. nemo. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said chapel was not constructed with the consent of the diocesan: because I say that although the consent of the diocesan ought to have been employed, yet that was introduced in favor of the church, lest it happen that the work be begun and not finished, or not sufficiently endowed thereafter, as because perhaps the resources of the builder's patrimony are by no means sufficient; hence that which was established in favor of the church ought not to be turned back to its injury, as in l. quod fauore, C. de leg. and capitu. quod ob gratiam, de reg. iu. li. 6. And that this was established in favor of the church is clearly proved in d. Auth. ut nullus sa. ora. do. post princ. and d. capi. nemo. And many similar points can be adduced in confirmation. First, it is evident in the ordination of clerics.

† For a bishop ought not to ordain anyone as a cleric unless he first assigns a benefice from which he may live, as in cap. 1. & 2. 70. distin. Nevertheless, if he has ordained him, the bishop is bound to provide from his own funds until he provides him with a benefice, as in capitu. cum secundum apostolum, and capitu. episcopus, de præben. To the same effect is a good text in capitu. si qua de rebus. 12. quæst. 2. where it is said,

† that if, while the church is vacant, the chapter has alienated some of the church's property without superior authority, it is left to the option of the future bishop whether he wishes to ratify the said alienation: because perhaps it is more advantageous for the church to have the price than the thing; and thus an alienation that is null as having been made without solemnity—concerning which 12. quæst. 2. cap. sine exceptione—can be held ratified by lapse of time: because the nullity arises in favor of the church; therefore it ought not to be turned back to its injury, if the future prelate sees that it is advantageous to the church; and the glo. expressly confirmed this in c. 1. ne se de vacan. To the same effect is a good text in l. non eo minus, C. de procu. where it is evident,

† that although a judgment rendered against a minor without a curator is null, it is otherwise, however, if it was rendered in favor of the minor; which point in a similar case is noted by the gl. and Bar. in l. si tutor, C. in qui. cau. in integ. rest. non est neces. and l. si mater. §. hoc iure, ff. de excep. rei. iud. and what the Doct. note in c. causam, de iud. Moreover, that which was established in hatred and punishment of those building churches or chapels without the authority of the diocesan, as in Auth. de eccl. tit. §. si quis autem, cum seq. ought not to turn to their favor, as in c. si necesse, de dona. inter ui. & uxo. and c. 2. de transl. præla. and l. Papinianus exuli, ff. de mino. And through these points the second doubt also remains decided. From all of which it is concluded that the said Lady Vannucia was obligated by the construction of the chapel or altar to endow it sufficiently, provided the aforesaid abbot ratifies the construction of the said altar. I come now to the third doubt, whether for the sufficiency of the endowment it is required that a cleric also be able to live from it in addition
† to the priest. And it seems first that it is not, through c. ut quisque presbyter, de ui. & hone. cle. where it is implied,

† that a priest having a congregation is bound to have a cleric: therefore it is otherwise in one having an altar. I held the contrary elsewhere in the lecture on the said capitu. ut quisque, and now I also confirm it: because it is certain that the solemnities of the Mass ought not to be celebrated without the assistance of a cleric, as in capitu. proposuit, de filiis presby. Therefore

† anyone holding a benefice that requires the celebration of Masses is bound to have a cleric, even if it is not otherwise a cure of souls; which seems to have been the opinion of the glo. in dict. capitu. ut quisque; and the text joined with the glos. in clemen. ne in agro. §. ad hæc, de statu regu. strongly supports this. Therefore, in building a sacerdotal altar, she is seen to have obligated herself to give an endowment for the necessary things concurrent with the solemnities of the Mass. For he who wills one thing is seen to have willed all things through which one arrives at it, as in l. oratio, ff. de spon. and l. ad rem mobilem, and l. ad legatum, ff. de procur. and capitu. prudentiam, and capitu. præterea, de offic. delega.; l. illud, ff. de acquiren. hæred. supports this. I conclude, therefore, on this third doubt, that the endowment of the said altar must be sufficient for a priest to be instituted there, and for a cleric who has to provide assistance at the solemnities of the Mass; the said capitu. nemo supports this, and in the said Auth. ut nullus fa. ora. do. post princip. To the fourth and last doubt, whether the said obligation is rendered ineffective by the donation of all her goods subsequently made to another. And it seems first that it is: because through the construction of the altar it does not appear that the goods of the builder are tacitly encumbered; on the contrary, only a personal obligation seems to have arisen, just as is evident in one who vows a certain thing. For the thing is not encumbered before it is delivered, but only the person, as in l. 2. ff. de polli. But the person has nothing, at least sufficiently, on account of the donation made to the other; therefore the obligation remains ineffective. For an action that the poverty of the debtor excludes is idle, as in l. nam is, ff. de dolo, and capitu. olim, li. 1. de restitu. spolia. But I deem that the contrary proceeds according to law. I am moved first,

† because one constructing a church or a chapel is bound to endow it, just as a father is bound to endow his daughter, as the glos. considered in dict. capitu. cum sicut, de conse. ecclesi. uel alta. and in dict. capitu. nemo, de consec. distin. 1. But if a father makes an immense donation to one of his children that tends to the prejudice of the other child as to the portion owed to him, the said donation is revoked as inofficious, as in l. 2. C. de inoffi. dona. and what is noted there; therefore the same must be said in our case. For these altars are seen to have been in the place of daughters with regard to the soul of Lady Vanucia herself, argumen. in capitu in præsentia, de probat. and of what Barto. notes in auth. si qua, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi. and the text there in a similar matter supports this, and what is read and noted in 19. q. ultima. capitu. si qua mulier. Moreover, and by another unanswerable reason, wherever

† a debtor donates his goods to the prejudice and fraud of creditors, such a donation ought to be revoked, even if it was made to someone ignorant of the fraud, as is proved in l. 1. joined with l. qui autem. §. simili quoque modo, ff. de his, quæ in frau. cre. Therefore the said donation ought to be revoked insofar as it comes to the prejudice of the altar to which the said Vanucia was a debtor with respect to the endowment. And a third consideration could be added, if it is posited that the said Vanucia donated to the second altar all her present and future goods. For such a donation does not hold, upholding the very equitable opinion of Angelus de Perusio, which he set forth in his disputation that begins 'in refulgenti', rejecting Bartolus on l. 1. C. de pact., who held that a donation of all present and future goods is likewise valid, but Angelus was against him; however, I do not intend at present to discuss which opinion is truer, since the other prior party has been sufficiently provided for by the premises, nor in our case is it said that she donated present and future goods. Therefore, the said donation does not render the first obligation ineffective, both because she could not free herself from an obligation previously contracted, and because it is seen to have been made in fraud of a creditor. From all the aforesaid I conclude that, upon the said abbot ratifying the said construction of the altar, the said altar must first be sufficiently endowed for a priest and for a cleric, and the residue, if any there shall be, will be applied to the second altar to which the donation, or final disposition, was made in the second place. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Not managing and managing without due solemnity are equivalent.
2. A mother is not excused from being deprived of the succession of the pupil if she did not assume the tutorship with due solemnity.
3. One who manages the affairs of a pupil when the tutorship has not been decreed to him by a judge, and without an inventory having first been drawn up, ought to be punished most severely as suspect.
4. A testamentary or datory tutor, by not excusing himself within fifty days after he knew he was designated tutor, is deemed to bind himself and accept the tutorship.
5. A substitute, although he refuses the tutorship, is not thereby excluded from the succession.
casus: A certain Antonius, having Franciscus, his legitimate and natural infant son established in his power, made a solemn testament, in which he instituted the said Franciscus as universal heir, and made such an institution, namely, that if the said Franciscus should die in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time without children, he substituted Paulus Petri, maternal uncle of the testator himself, vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum, and gave the said Paulus as tutor to his said son. At length, upon the death of the said testator, the said Franciscus, surviving for three and a half months, died an infant, the said Paulus the substitute and the mother of the infant himself surviving. Now the mother of the late infant has raised a dispute against the said Paulus the substitute, who possesses by virtue of the said substitution the inheritance formerly of the said Antonius, and successively of Franciscus, asserting that the succession of the said deceased infant Franciscus, her son, belongs to her; and she says that the said Paulus the substitute is excluded because he did not assume the tutorship of the said Franciscus in court, nor did he immediately request that another tutor be given, nor did he excuse himself within fifty days from the death of the testator. On behalf of the said substitute Paulus, however, it is said that the said succession and inheritance belong to him by virtue of the said substitution, adding that he, appointed tutor in the testament of the said Antonius, although he did not draw up an inventory for the said infant, nevertheless caused the said infant to be nursed, and administered his tutorship both in paying levies and debts, and also in paying the salary to the said nurse, and in administering, governing, and having cultivated the goods of the said inheritance of the said Antonius, when he knew that he was given as tutor in the said testament. And even positing, without prejudice to the truth, that he had not administered, nor conducted the tutorship, nor requested that another be given, nor excused himself, he ought not on that account to be deprived of the said succession, and that no default or negligence is to be imputed to him because the said Franciscus survived the father for only three and a half months, and the laws seem to grant a year to a substitute to request a tutor; whence, since death overtook the said Franciscus in so short a time, it cannot be said that he was negligent so as to be deprived of the succession. What is the law, it is asked.
body: Having besought the aid of Almighty God, two matters truly fall to be examined for the decision of this question. The first is whether the said substitute is excused on the ground that, being designated tutor in the testament, he managed the affairs of the pupil, even though the tutorship was not assumed with the due solemnity. The second, presupposing that he is not excused on that first ground, is whether he ought to be deprived of the pupil's succession because he did not immediately seek a tutor, since he was able to do so during the lifetime of the pupil, a year not having yet elapsed. Regarding the first, it seems that the said substitute is not to be excused,

† because not compelling and acting without due solemnity are considered equivalent; l. fin. C. arb. tuto. and l. 2. C. de tuto. & curato. and l. 3. §. tutores, ff. de suspect. tuto.; and l. si unus, C. de testamē. and c. 2. de trans. præla. are to the point. Secondly, the notable gloss on this point appears in l. 2. §. si mater, ad Tert. which says

† that a mother is not excused from being deprived of the succession of the pupil if she did not assume the tutorship with due solemnity, nor sought that a tutor be given to the son, even though she or others managed and administered the goods of the pupil without due solemnity; and Bartolus and Baldus follow that gloss there in l. matres. C. ad Tert. But the aforesaid substitute, although he managed the affairs of the pupil, nevertheless did not do this lawfully, because the tutorship was not decreed to him by a judge after an inventory was first drawn up, as ought to have been done, as noted by the gloss and Bartolus in l. fin. C. arbi. tute. and in l. legitimos, ff. de legi. tut., nor did he do the other things that are noted in the said l. legitimos; therefore, he ought not to be excused on the basis of that management; rather, he ought all the more to be blamed,

† because one managing the affairs of a pupil when the tutorship has not been decreed to him by a judge and an inventory has not first been drawn up ought to be punished most severely as suspect, as is held in the said l. fin. C. arbit. tut. in fin. and in the said l. 3. §. tutores, de suspect. tut. But notwithstanding these points, the contrary can be maintained. I am moved to this opinion principally

† because a testamentary or datory tutor, by not excusing himself within fifty days after he knew he was designated tutor, is deemed to bind himself and accept the tutorship, so that he is no longer able to excuse himself, and the tutorship begins to stand at his risk, as is proved in l. si pater. §. oportet, and l. quinquaginta, ff. de excusa. tut.; and l. 1. in prin. ff. de admist. tuto. is to the point. Therefore, the said substitute given as tutor in the testament, by not excusing himself within fifty days after he knew he was designated tutor, is deemed to have accepted the tutorship, nor could he any longer excuse himself; consequently, he could neither seek that another tutor be given, and consequently he cannot be punished on the ground that he did not seek a tutor to be given to the pupil. In favor of this is what Baldus notes in l. tutor, qui repertorium, ff. de administra. tuto., where he says that although the tutor did not draw up an inventory, he is nonetheless tutor; he can, however, be barred from bringing actions, as in l. tutor qui repertorium, and be utterly deprived of the office of tutorship, as the text says in the said l. fin. C. arb. tute. It remains, therefore, to conclude that this tutor was at fault only on the ground that he administered the property when the tutorship had not first been decreed to him by a judge, nor an inventory drawn up; but on this ground it is not found provided by law that he ought to be deprived of the succession; rather, he may be punished with other penalties, concerning which see l. final. joined with the previously cited gloss, C. arbit. tute. For since this penalty of deprivation of the succession is not expressly provided by law in this case, it ought not to be imposed, as the gloss notes in capitulo fin. de iure patrona.; de pœni. distinct. 1. cap. pœnæ, and l. interpretatione, and l. si pręses, ff. de pœnis are to the point; and it serves as an argument in l. amicissimos, ff. de excusa. tuto., where it is clear

† that although a substitute refuses the tutorship, he is not thereby excluded from the succession. Thirdly, a new consideration works in favor of this substitute so that he is not deprived: he who has not sought a tutor to be given to his son is deprived of the pupil's succession, but the pupil in our case had nothing, because he did not enter upon the inheritance, nor did the existence of a *suus heres* have operation in our case, because the pupil himself, although he was in power at the time of death, nevertheless had a vulgar substitute, by the appointment of whom *suitas* is removed according to the common opinion, through l. si filius, ff. de libe. & posth.; Bartolus holds this in l. si filius, qui patri, ff. de uul. & pup. and Baldus in the said l. fratris, C. de iure delibe.; the gloss notes this in l. Papinianus, ff. de inoff. testamen. Therefore, this substitute succeeds to the father, and not to the son; for it is the inheritance of the father, not of the son, as in the said l. si filius, de libe. & posthu. Furthermore, it does not seem imputable to him if he did not seek that the tutorship be decreed to him by a judge, nor drew up an inventory, because he could not do this by law. For since he was a testamentary tutor, he could not do anything unless the inheritance was first entered upon by the pupil, because tutorship is confirmed by the adition of the inheritance, as in l. si nemo, ff. de testa. tut.; nor in this case does the existence of a *suus heres* have the effect of confirming the tutorship, because he had an instituted vulgar substitute, as Bartolus notes in the said l. si nemo. And if it is said that it is therefore to be imputed to him if he did not seek in the meantime, until the inheritance should be entered upon, that a tutor be given to the son through l. si quis sub conditione, ff. de testam. tute. and Inst. de att. tute. post princip., to this indeed it can be answered in a two-fold way. First, because although on this ground he could be deprived of the pupil's succession, yet in our case that succession never belonged to the pupil, since he did not enter upon the inheritance and had a vulgar substitute; for it is the father's inheritance and not the son's; nor can the mother seek the legitimate portion, because the son cannot repudiate the father's inheritance and seek the legitimate portion; for he must either acknowledge the whole or repudiate the whole, as Bartolus notes in l. gerit, ff. de acquirend. hæred. Secondly, it can principally be answered, entering into the second doubt formulated above, that presupposing that the son had had some goods, nevertheless, because a year had not elapsed before the death of the son, the substitute, or another who was to succeed on intestacy—at least short of the mother—ought not to be deprived of the pupil's succession. For concerning this the text seems express in l. sciant cuncti, C. de legi. hære., and the text in Inst. ad Tertul. in fin. is exceedingly relevant; Baldus and also Angelus held this in the aforesaid l. sciant, and in l. matres, and Bartolus in his solemn repetition on l. 2. ff. qui pe. tut.; although Bartolus himself in l. 2. §. confestim, ff. ad Tertul. and in the said l. sciant, following Ricardus Malumbra, held the contrary, saying that if he did not seek a tutor within fifty days, he is deemed to be in negligence, because he ought to have sought, just like the mother, as quickly as he could, as seems to be proved regarding the mother in the said l. 2. §. si mater and §. confestim; and that the same applied to the substitute and to another who could succeed on intestacy, he deduced from the said l. sciant, there where it is said "according to our constitution," etc., as if to say that only a year was given according to the earlier constitution, concerning which in the said l. 2. §. confestim, so that it should be expected immediately (*confestim*), that is, as quickly as could be done, yet in such a way that a year would not be exceeded. Nevertheless, Bartolus himself, as I have said above, in his solemn repetition, examining this point more diligently, held the contrary, namely that the substitute, or another who was to succeed to the pupil on intestacy, has an entire year through the said l. sciant and l. 2. These points especially support this: formerly, before the law of the Code, it was not provided that any substitute or other blood relative was bound of necessity to seek a tutor for a pupil, although he might have been able to do so voluntarily, except in the case of a mother and freedmen, as in l. 2. ff. qui pe. tu. and in the said l. 2. ad Tertul. Therefore, the intervening law of the Code imposing the necessity of seeking must be understood strictly, namely so that a year is granted entirely and absolutely to others who previously were not under this necessity; for since that law is odious, especially in that it deprives of succession on intestacy and under a testament, it ought to be strictly interpreted, as is notably proved in capitulo Statutum, de electio. lib. 6; capitulum Cum in cunctis, de electio., and the rule *odia*, and the rule *in pœnis*, joined with capitulo Si compromissarius, under the same title, in lib. 6, and l. si præses, ff. de pœn. are to the point. Nor does the text in the said l. sciant stand in the way of the aforesaid, in so far as it says "according to our constitution," etc., because, as Bartolus says—and rightly so—in the said l. 2, those words ought not to be referred to the Senatusconsultum Tertullianum, but to other laws which provide what kind of tutors ought to be appointed, so that the sense is that a tutor ought also to be sought by these persons within a year according to legal disposition. Furthermore, a mother is bound to seek a tutor for her son on a two-fold ground: first, on account of maternal affection, as in l. matris pietas, C. qui pe. tu.; secondly, on account of the hope of future succession, in the said §. confestim. In other persons who are to succeed under a testament or on intestacy, however, there is only one cause underlying, namely the hope of succession; therefore, one should have proceeded more leniently with them than with the mother; argument in l. re coniuncti, ff. de lega. 3. and in the Authentica Cessante, C. de legi. hære. Indeed, it could be maintained that even the mother is not deprived within the year, through the text which openly intimates this in Inst. ad Tertul. in fin.; and to that text could be reduced the text in the said §. confestim, so that thus, by interpretation of law, she may be said to act immediately by seeking within a year; or let us say that she ought to seek a tutor immediately, that is, as quickly as she can, yet she is not punished unless she is negligent for a year, as the text previously cited intended. And since we are in an odious matter, it is better and more equitable to say that the said l. 2 is understood according to the text in Inst. ad Tertul. in fin. rather than the reverse; argument in l. placuit, C. de iudi.; Bartolus agrees in the said l. sciant and l. matres. From all these things I conclude that the said substitute ought not in our case to be deprived of the succession, whether it be the inheritance of the father or of the pupil. And these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A usufructuary, who does not transmit his right to an heir, can nevertheless sell the usufruct to another.
2. If a statute, or a testator, or an agreement of contracting parties has prohibited alienation, not only the transfer of ownership but also of usufruct is deemed prohibited.
3. One who is prohibited from selling cannot even lease for a long time.
4. A usufructuary is not prohibited from alienating the right that he has.
casus: A certain Sempronius, condemned for the crime of lèse-majesté, his goods having been expressly confiscated, before he committed the aforesaid offense and incurred the sentence, donated certain goods to certain brothers of the blood for their lifetime only, yet in such a way that one should succeed the other, and upon the death of all, the said goods should return directly to the same donor; and it was added at the beginning of the donation that they might do with the aforesaid donated goods during their lifetime whatever pleased them without anyone's contradiction. At the end of the instrument, however, it is said that the aforesaid donor made the abovesaid donation under these condition, tenor, law, and pact, namely that the present donation be valid and take effect only until the lifetime of the said donees, and of each of them, and not beyond, and that the donees themselves, or any of them, cannot and should not sell, donate, or alienate, exchange, obligate, nor otherwise barter, nor transfer the donated goods themselves in whole or in part at any time to any person or corporate body, since otherwise the aforesaid donor would not have made nor been about to make it, nor does he wish the present donation to be regarded as made, but he wishes the present donation, whenever it should happen otherwise, not to be valid, nor hold, nor ought to take effect, and by operation of law the right and ownership of the donated goods themselves should devolve in full to the aforesaid donor. These are the formal words set down at the end of the said instrument. It happened that after the sentence of the aforesaid condemnation and the confiscation of the goods was made, the said donees, or some of them who survived, sold the said goods, donated under the aforesaid condition, to a certain citizen of Siena for a certain sum of money for their lifetime only. Now it is asked whether the Commune of Siena, to which the goods of the said donor were confiscated, can vindicate those donated goods by virtue of the confiscation and of the said pact attached to the donation.
body: The aid of the Savior having been invoked, it seems at first that it is not so, through the earlier words set down in the instrument, namely that it was stated that they might do with the aforesaid donated goods during their lifetime whatever pleased them; therefore they can dispose of them during their lifetime, even by selling. For we see

† that although a usufructuary does not transmit his right to his heir, he can nevertheless sell the usufruct to another; nor is this surprising, because, as the jurisconsult says, he who enjoys the price is deemed to enjoy the thing itself, as is held in l. non utetur, with l. sequen. ff. de usufructu. So it must be said in the present case: for these persons sufficiently use the donated goods during their lifetime, from the moment they use the price. Furthermore, to alienate is a contract through which ownership is transferred, as in l. 1. C. de fun. dota.; but the aforesaid donees sold only for their lifetime, therefore that cannot be called an alienation, especially so as to incur the penalty of forfeiture. But I judge the contrary opinion to be truer in law. And first I will prove that the said donees fell from their right. Secondly, that the said goods devolved to the Commune of Siena. It is proven by the clear text which cannot be caviled at, in l. fina. C. de rebus alien. non alien., where it is said

† that whether a statute, or a testator, or a pact of contracting parties has prohibited alienation, not only the transfer of ownership is deemed prohibited, but also of usufruct and of pledge; but it cannot be denied that the said donees alienated at least the usufruct of the said things; therefore they acted contrary to the pact inserted in the donation. Secondly, this is expressly proven from the tenor of the said donation, in that it was expressly prohibited that they should encumber, or barter, or transfer the said goods; but it cannot be denied that through that sale they transferred or encumbered the said goods; therefore the said goods fell under forfeiture. Nay, I say more:

† that one who is prohibited from selling cannot even lease for a long time, because through such a lease a right in the thing is established, and thus a certain alienation of the thing is made, as noted by Bartol. and Dyn. in l. codicillis. §. a substituto, ff. de legat. 2., although the gloss there asserts otherwise, which nevertheless is commonly condemned there on this point, and the former view is held by the gloss in clemen. 1. de rebus ecclesiae non alienan., and the text there strongly supports it. Furthermore and thirdly, the donor simply prohibited those goods from being sold; but it cannot be denied that the donees sold them and transferred ownership to the buyer, as is clear from the instrument of sale drawn up thereon. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that they sold only for their lifetime: because by this it cannot be denied that a sale was made, albeit for a time. For even the prohibition of sale could not be understood except concerning a temporary sale; because concerning a perpetual one there was no doubt, since the donation had been made only for their lifetime; hence, even absent that prohibition, they could not have sold beyond their lifetime, because no one can transfer to another more right than he himself has, capitu. nuper, de donationib. inter uirum & uxorem, and l. traditio, ff. de acquiren. rerum domi. Words must therefore be understood in that sense in which they can effect something, as in capitu. si papa, de priuileg. libro 6., and l. si quando, C. de inoffic. testam., and l. quod Labeo. ad Carbon. Moreover, that by the said pact the transfer of ownership is impeded and a devolution to the donor takes place is proven in capitu. caeterum. de donatio., and in l. ea lege, C. de conditione ob cau., and more expressly Barto. maintains it in l. filius, §. diui, ff. de lega. 1. Furthermore, that these goods were acquired for the Commune is proven because by the said sentence all goods were confiscated, and therefore also all rights belonging to the condemned person, as in l. 3. C. ad legem Iuliam maiesta. joined with l. bonorum, ff. de uerborum significa.; therefore the right reserved to the said donor passed to the said Commune through the said confiscation. Indeed, it can be said that not only were the goods confiscated, but also the person was condemned to death; in which case even goods acquired afterward fall under confiscation, as in l. 2. C. de bon. praescri., noted in l. certa forma, C. de iur. fisc. libro 10. Conclude therefore from all the aforesaid that the said donees, by selling, even if only for their lifetime, fell from their right; and the donated goods reverted to the Commune of Siena, which can vindicate them as its own. To the contrary arguments framed above it can easily be answered: for the prior words must be understood according to the subsequent ones, l. si seruus plurium, ff. de lega. 1., and thus they might do with those goods whatever pleased them, yet not by alienating or transferring; because specific terms derogate from general words, capitu. 1. de rescrip., and l. quaesitum, at the end, ff. de fun. instru., and regula, generi, de regulis iuris li. 6. To the second argument it is answered

† that a usufructuary is not prohibited from alienating the right that he has, but in our case this was expressly forbidden to them; for the donor willed that they retain them in their own possession, d. l. finali, C. de rebus alien. non alien. To the third argument it is answered in two ways: First, that it proceeds when alienation is taken strictly. But in a prohibition made by a pact of contracting parties it ought to be taken broadly, as in d. l. finali, and Bald. notes there. Furthermore and secondly, a transfer of this ownership was sufficiently made, albeit for a time, as is clear in the said sale; therefore, etc. And let these things suffice. Nico. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A legacy made to a daughter for a dowry is unconditional, and not conditional.
2. A statute cannot entirely remove the legitime.
3. A woman can be entirely deprived of the legitime in order to preserve the family of the house.
4. If it is provided by a statute that as long as a male exists, a female does not succeed, a daughter is excluded only while the male is living; but, when he is dead, she ought to be admitted.
body: † IN the name of Christ, amen. It is an unquestioned rule of law that, looking solely to the common law,

† a legacy made to a daughter for her dowry is unconditional and not conditional, when it does not exceed her legitime. Whence it can be demanded by the daughter herself immediately after the death of the father. Nor is it necessary to await the time of marriage, especially in our case, in which the daughter was instituted by the father in that very dowry; whence, just as the legitime itself admits of no delay or other burden, l. quoniam in prioribus, C. de inoffic. testamen., and in Auth. ut cum de appellat. §. aliud quoque capitulum, so neither does the dowry itself, which succeeds in place of the legitime, since a surrogate savors of the nature of that in whose place it is surrogated, as in capitulo ecclesia, ut lite penden., and l. quia qui pretio, ff. de usufruct., with similar texts. And this opinion—that it can be demanded immediately—is commonly confirmed by the doctors, especially Bartolus in l. Titio, §. Titio genero, ff. de conditio. & demonstra., following Richardus Malumbra and others in l. generaliter, C. de episcop. & cleric.; and to the text of the said §. Titio genero, which seems to mean that a legacy of a dowry is conditional and that its collection ought to be postponed until the time of the contracted marriage, reply is made in many ways, as noted there and in said l. generaliter. But a doubt arises in our case on account of the statute of Trent, in which it is provided, among other things, that when males are living, a female daughter does not succeed; in which case Bartolus said in said §. Titio genero that a legacy of a dowry made to a daughter is conditional, just as if it were made to a stranger; so that it cannot be claimed except at the time of marriage: because there is no dowry without marriage, l. 2. ff. de iure dot. Therefore such a legacy contains in itself a tacit condition; and thus, if she dies before she marries, she does not transmit the legacy to her heirs, said §. Titio genero; which also Cynus seems to maintain in l. sancimus, C. de nup. And although Richardus Malumbra held the contrary, as Bartolus himself reports in said §. Titio, being moved

† by the reason that a statute cannot entirely remove the legitime, although it may diminish it—which Dynus also seems to think in regula, indultum, de regulis iur. libr. 6—therefore, since in this case the dowry succeeds in place of the legitime, it does not admit a burden or a delay, any more than does the legitime itself, in the laws alleged above. Bartolus, however, following Cynus, maintained the first view; he is moved because, even presupposing Richardus’s opinion that a statute can diminish although not remove, nevertheless, just as it can diminish, so it seems that it can postpone it to a certain time, namely the time of marriage, since this is a kind of diminution, by the argument in l. minus, ff. de regu. iur. But Baldus in said l. sancimus follows the opinion of Richardus, rejecting the opinion of Cynus and Bartolus; he is moved because, if the statute could postpone it to the time of marriage, it could follow that that daughter might die before marriage, as happened in our case, and thus she would transmit nothing to her heirs, and consequently would be entirely deprived of her legitime; which is contrary to the presupposition made by Bartolus in agreeing with the opinion of the said Richardus, that it cannot be taken away entirely. And certainly, in my judgment, this consideration of Baldus was excellent, if that opinion were simply true that the legitime cannot be taken away entirely; but since Baldus himself thinks the contrary in l. cum lege Leonina, C. de episcop. & cleric., where he affirmed

† that for the sake of preserving the family of the house a woman can be utterly deprived of her legitime, since it is of positive law. He says, however, that the right to claim alimony is reserved to her, as if those rights were of natural law, 1. distinctio. capitulo ius naturale; therefore his foundation does not hold, since the statute seems to preserve alimony for the woman until she marries; therefore it was able simply to exclude her from all succession, especially while reserving a dowry in the event of marriage; therefore the legacy of the dowry ought to be understood as unconditional. But these things notwithstanding, I think that in our case the heir of the aforesaid daughter is provided for in three ways. First, indeed, she is clearly provided for by holding that opinion that the legitime can be entirely taken away even for a time, which the compiler of the decisions of the Rota seems to have held in deci. 19, who, having related various opinions, held that the statute is valid provided it does not take it away entirely or absorb a great part of it. And Antonius de Butrio seems to intend the same in capitulo Raynaldus, de testa. But in our case it would absorb it entirely if it first diminished it, reducing it to the dowry alone, and afterward postponed it to the time of contracted marriage to such an extent that it could happen that she was entirely deprived, as happened in our case, since that daughter died before marriage was contracted. And truly this opinion pleases me in our case, in which the statute does not expressly take it away entirely, but rather gives a dowry, as it were, for the woman’s marriage, l. 3. ff. de mino. Therefore the dowry itself savors of the nature of the legitime, lest the daughter die completely without an heir and without any property; what is noted on a similar point in cap. ex insinuatione, de app., supports this, where it says that if a term is fixed for an appellant by man, such a term succeeds into the place of the legal term, because a surrogate must savor of the nature of that in whose place it is surrogated, as I said above; and this interpretation, as the more benign, is to be accepted in doubtful matters, as in regula, odia, and regula, in pœnis, lib. 6., and l. interpretatione, and l. si præses, ff. de pœ. The second way is that by virtue of the statute of Trent there accrued simply the right to claim immediately the dowry bequeathed, with the joined intention of the testator at least. For the statute provided that if the father made provision concerning the son in his testament, the daughter ought to be content with the paternal disposition; so that if he left her a dowry, she should be content with it, and beyond that quantity she can claim nothing. Therefore the statute seems to intend that if a dowry is left to a daughter in a testament, she can immediately claim the quantity left to her by the contrary sense, which is quite valid, l. cum inter socerum, ff. de pac. do., and by Baldus in l. conuenticulam, C. de episco. & cleri.; that word “quantity” etc. supports this, for it did not refer simply to the dowry, but to the quantity left for the dowry. Furthermore, the statute, in the case where the father left a dowry to the daughter in a testament, did not provide for alimony until she should be married, but only provided for it in the case where the father died intestate; therefore, by simply providing that the daughter be content with the dowry left to her and that she can claim nothing beyond it, it seems to have intended that the dowry itself be the daughter's patrimony, and thus ought to succeed to her in place of the legitime, and consequently ought to accrue immediately upon the father's death, especially since the father said nothing about alimony to be furnished to the daughter in the meantime; and the statute says that the daughter must be content with the paternal disposition. Whence, if we were to say the contrary, it would follow that the statute could deprive the daughter of alimony and of all succession; which is contrary to the common opinion and contrary to l. cum ratio, ff. de bo. dam. And this interpretation is most particularly to be adopted in our case, in which the father not only left a dowry to the daughter, but indeed instituted her heir in that quantity; therefore he intended utterly to exclude her from succession. The third way of counseling the heirs of the said daughter can, in my judgment, be subtly opposed by the words of the modern statute, from which at the beginning it is evidently shown that the daughter is not simply excluded from the succession of the parent when a male exists, but only for a time, namely while the male survives. For the statute did not simply say that when males exist a female does not succeed; but it says that a female does not succeed, nor is she to be heard in acting or excepting, while a male survives; whence those words, 'superstite masculo,' since they are in the ablative case, create a condition, as in l. a testatore, and there by Bartolus, ff. de cond. & demonst., and qualify the following words, 'non audiatur' etc. The meaning is therefore that a woman ought not to be heard regarding the succession of the father while a male survives; therefore after his death she ought to be heard. For qualified words must be understood according to the time of the word to which they refer, as Bartolus notes in l. ex facto, ff. de uulg. & pupil., and l. præcipimus, C. de appell., and Baldus in l. generaliter, C. de episco. & cler., and the glossa on c. statutum, on the word 'canonicis', at the end, de rescrip. lib. 6. What Bartolus notes in l. fin. ff. ad Tertul. applies excellently to the aforesaid, where he says,

† that if it is provided by a statute that as long as a male exists a female does not succeed, the daughter is excluded only while the male is living, but when he is dead she ought to be admitted: because by that adverb, 'quandiu' [as long as], the statute seems to have intended to make the male heir for a time; and it is more fully held there by him. Let us therefore say the same in the matter at hand, since the statute says she is not to be heard in acting and excepting while a male survives; therefore, when he is dead, she ought to be heard, in acting or excepting; for the contrary sense is valid in a statute, especially when it agrees with the common law, as it does in our case, as Bartolus notes in l. omnes populi, ff. de insti. & iure, and more fully Baldus in said l. conuenticula. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the statute also uses the word 'succedat' [succeeds], in which case Bartolus held in l. fin. that a female is not admitted upon the death of the male, since it is now treated as concerning the inheritance of the son and not of the father, because that adverb 'quandiu' or the like was not added—which also Ioannes Andreae seems to hold in his additions to the Speculum in the title de succe. ab intest., on the rubric, in the 3rd column—because I say that that applies if the statute had simply said: 'if any male exists, a female does not succeed.' For then the female is simply excluded, and the inheritance is deferred to the male; deservedly, after the death of the male, the daughter cannot claim the inheritance of the father, because it has already ceased to be the father’s and is now the son’s, although in this case certain ancient authorities maintained the contrary, as Ioannes Andreae notes in the aforesaid addition; but the first is truer. But in our case that qualification was added: 'she does not succeed nor is she heard while a male survives.' For preceding words are qualified by succeeding words, as in l. si. §. cui dulcia, ff. de uino, trit. & oleo leg., and clemen. exiui, de uerbo. signi., and l. si seruus plurium, de leg. 1., and l. nummis, de lega. 3. And other words of the statute greatly assist this understanding, insofar as they provide for the woman so that, upon dissolving the marriage to be contracted by her, she can return to the house of the male heir and receive alimony there; and thus it seems to exclude the female while the male exists: but when he is dead, that refuge ceases, especially in our case, in which the goods of the father are to be distributed to the poor. From all of which it is concluded that there accrued immediately to the said daughter the right to claim the legacy made to her by the father as unconditional, which passed to her legitimate heirs, l. unica, C. de cadu. tol. Likewise, that with the males dead, there accrued immediately the right to claim the legitime; so that it is in the option of her heirs whether to claim the legacy or the legitime, insofar as there is more in the legitime than in the legacy, according to what is read and noted in l. scimus, C. de inoff. test., in §. repletionem. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A case ought not to be delegated or subdelegated by authority of the Apostolic See, except to one holding a dignity, personatus, or canonry in a cathedral church.
2. If something is bequeathed to a bishop by a close relative or kinsman, with only the name of the dignity expressed, the bequest is deemed made in contemplation of the person on account of the quality of the one bequeathing.
3. If a soldier said that he wished to make a testament under the ius commune, and could not complete the testament, the testament is valid under military law.
4. When a proper and an appellative name are expressed in a disposition, the distribution ought to be attributed to the quality expressed first.
body: First having invoked from the heart the help of Christ the Savior, on the question which is presently pending between the Chapter of Tortona on the one side and the Bishop of Chur on the other, concerning the execution of a certain sentence rendered by a certain treasurer and canon of the Church of Seckau by virtue of a subdelegation made to him by a certain provost of Vrätz, conservator and delegate in the causes of the Chapter deputed by the Apostolic See, in and concerning this: that it is denied on the part of the said Bishop that the said treasurer had jurisdiction, since the commission was made with an express proper name and the appellative name of that treasureship, but absolutely no mention of the quality of the canonry was made in the subdelegation; and it is denied that the treasureship is a dignity or personatus in that place. It being presupposed therefore, without prejudice to the truth, that in those parts the treasureship is not deemed a dignity or a personatus, [the question is] whether the said sentence can be sustained on the ground that the said treasurer was also a canon of the cathedral church, and this was very well known in the locality, and indeed in fact a statute is presupposed to be in force in the church, that no one can obtain a dignity, personatus, or office there unless he is a canon of the same church. And first it seems that the said sentence was by no means valid due to a defect of jurisdiction:

† because a case ought not to be delegated or subdelegated by authority of the Apostolic See except to one holding a dignity, personatus, or canonry in a cathedral church, as in c. statutum, in princ. and in § nullo, de praesc. in Sexto, and whatever has been attempted is null and void ipso iure, as is proved at the end of the said c. statutum, through which the Gloss said on the word committatur that a proceeding conducted through certain persons is null, even though exception was not taken to the condelegate or subdelegate. But in our case the cause was subdelegated to the treasurer, and thus to the office of the treasureship, but not to the canon, since no mention was made of the quality of the canonry; therefore the sentence ought not to stand. For there is a difference between a dignity, a personatus, and an office, as in c. 1 de consue. in Sexto, and there by Archidiaconus, and noted in c. de multa, de praeb.; and concerning the treasureship the greater part of the Lords of the Rota held that unless the local reputation holds otherwise, by the ius commune it is deemed a simple office, as fully noted by them in decis. 166. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said treasurer was likewise a canon, because although these two qualities concurred in his person, the commission nonetheless seems made to the expressed quality, not however to the tacit one, as in c. quoniam abbas, de off. delega.; for those things which are passed over in silence do not seem to have been considered, but rather neglected, especially since they are worthy of special note, as in our case through c. quisquis, de praeb. in Sexto, and l. si repetendis, C. de cond. ob causam, l. Labeo, ff. de supel. leg.; and that which is done externally represents the interior disposition and habit of the mind, as in Clem. exivi, de ver. sig., and l. non aliter, ff. de leg. 3 and c. fin. de ver. sign. makes to this point. But these notwithstanding, I judge that in our case the contrary opinion prevails, to holding which many things impel me. And first, the theory of Johannes Andreae in the rule privilegium, de regu. iur. in Sexto, in the Mercuriales, which seems also of the mind of Bartolus in l. quia, ff. de iurisd. om. iudi., and l. si servus communis, ff. de stipu. servo, and is expressly proved through the laws to be alleged below: namely, that to conjecture the quality of a disposition or commission, we ought not simply and principally to consider whether a proper or an appellative name is expressed in it; rather, that consideration is to be applied as a last refuge, but first we must recur to the subject matter. If indeed the matter is proportioned to the person and not to the dignity, or rather to the person than to the dignity, we ought to judge the disposition personal rather than real, and so conversely, even though the dignity and proper name be expressed, or conversely; these things are proved in c. requisisti, de test., and c. pontifices, 12, q. 3, in which it is clear,

† that if something is left to a bishop, expressed only by the name of the dignity, by a relative or kinsman, the bequest seems made in contemplation of the person on account of the quality of the testator; but if it is by a stranger, it seems made in contemplation of the church, even though the proper name is expressed, as there and in l. annua, § a Titia, ff. de ann. lega. Hence the Gloss noted in c. 2 de testa. in Sexto said that if any prelate was appointed testamentary executor with the name of the dignity alone expressed, upon his death the office will not thereby pass to his successor if the prelate was a relative of the testator, for that office is usually conferred by reason of friendship and kinship. The same is to be said in the matter at hand. For although in our cause the quality of the treasureship was expressed, nevertheless, because the proper name was also expressed and the quality of the canonry concurred in the person, we ought to interpret that the commission was made to the person on account of the concurring quality of the canonry, and not to the office of the treasureship, since the subject matter, that is, the subdelegation itself, was not proportioned to the office of the treasureship itself; whence that quality seems expressed more for the sake of designating the person to whom the commission was made; just as on a similar point the text said in l. iurisgentium, § pactorum, ff. de pac., that in considering whether a pact is personal or real, we ought not simply to consider whether the person is expressed or not. For frequently a person is inserted into a pact not that the pact be made in rem or in personam, but that it be designated with whom the pact was made; which is to be estimated no less from the words than from the mind of the contracting parties, because the office of the treasureship is usually valued more than a simple canonry; therefore a canon-treasurer is usually named from the office of the treasureship, even in a matter pertaining to and concerning the canonry itself, just as I said above regarding a bishop, that in a disposition concerning the person he is usually named by the title of his dignity, for the sake of honor and on account of custom, for greater designation: d. l. relatum and the other laws alleged above. To the same point makes c. dilecti, de fo. comp., where a rescript obtained with the proper name of the prelate himself expressed, yet in a cause concerning the church itself, passes to the successor in the dignity, so that by reason of the matter concerning the church alone, the rescript is deemed real and not personal, even though the quality of the dignity had been expressed. For words ought to serve the things and the intention, and not conversely, because the law is imposed upon things and not upon words, as in c. 2 requisisti, de appe., and c. commissa, de ele. in Sexto, and l. 2, C. communia de leg. Lo, therefore, a quality entirely suppressed is held as expressed on account of the subject matter; so let us say in the matter at hand. And to the aforesaid I add the text with the Gloss in c. adversus, de immu. eccl., and in c. 1 de offi. vic. in Sexto, in which laws it is read and noted that an excommunication pronounced against any official, with only the name of the office expressed, does not pass to the successor in office, because on account of the subject matter the sentence is deemed personal and not real, since excommunication is not proportioned to the office, but to the person, as it is pronounced on account of contumacy, which follows the person. So in the matter at hand, the subdelegation cannot belong to the office of the treasureship, since it is not a dignity or personatus; therefore it is deemed made to the person, especially since the proper name was expressed, on account of the quality of the canonry concurring in the person. Nor does it stand in the way that the quality of the canonry was not expressed, because by no law is it provided that in a delegation the quality on account of which the person is rendered eligible must be expressed. For it is enough that he be eligible, because the laws require only that the quality of dignity, personatus, or canonry concur at the time of the commission, as is proved in the said capitulum statutum, in the beginning. Hence the Gloss noted there upon the word canonicis intended that it suffices that at the time of the giving or commission one be a canon, although at the time of presentation or prosecution he ceases to be a canon, because that decretal requires the existence of the quality only at the time of the commission. It is otherwise therefore if it had then been absent, which Baldus expressly held in l. generaliter, C. de episco. & cler., because, according to him, and rightly, that quality is required on account of the presumption of learning by reason of the canonry, which does not cease to exist although he ceases to be a canon; the theory of Bartolus makes to this in l. ex facto, ff. de vulga. & pupil., and l. praecipimus, C. de appella. Furthermore, the text is seen in the said capitulum requisisti and capitulum dilecti, previously alleged, where it is not required that the quality be expressed in order for the disposition to be real or personal. For it is enough that this can be perceived from the subject matter; and this proceeds especially in our case, in which the quality of the canonry was notorious. For the commission is not made to the canonry, but to the person of the canon, as is clear from the aforesaid; therefore it suffices that the commission be made to the person having the quality that qualifies the person himself. I am moved secondly and principally because by virtue of the statute of that church no one can hold a dignity, personatus, or office unless he is a canon; therefore by committing the cause to the treasurer of that church, it sufficiently seems committed to a canon. For since one cannot be without the other, by expressing one tacitly, one seems to express the other, as in capitulum si quis obiecerit, 1, q. 3; and cap. translato, with what is noted there in the Gloss, de constitu., makes to this. Thirdly, l. 3, ff. de mili. testa., makes very well to the argument, where it is said,

† that if a soldier said that he wished to make a testament according to the ius commune, and was not able to complete it, the testament is valid by military law, because he does not seem by this to renounce the military benefit, the text there giving the best reason: because in doubt no one is deemed to have chosen a way through which his judgment could be impugned. Hence Bartolus said there that in things depending on mere will, one seems to have done the act in the best manner in which he can, as is proved through that text. So let us say in the matter at hand, that the subdelegate seems in doubt to have wished to make the delegation in the best manner in which he could, nor by expressing the quality of the treasureship is he to be believed to have chosen the way through which his will could be invalidated. For in doubt we ought to make the interpretation that the thing may rather be valid, as in capitulum abbate, de verbo. signific., and ff. de verb. sign. l. quoties. Fourthly and principally makes l. qui habebat, with what is noted there, ff. de reb. dub., where it is said that if someone having two slaves, of whom one was a fuller named Flaccus, the other a baker named Stichus, erred in making a bequest, say, because he bequeathed Stichus the fuller, when he was a baker and not a fuller: if he had the names of the slaves known, he seems to have bequeathed having regard to the proper name and not to the appellative; and therefore Stichus the baker is owed to the legatee; and so through that text it is clear that an expressed quality does not have to vitiate the disposition, even though it be falsely expressed. Therefore the same, and all the more strongly, is to be said in our case, in which there was no error in the quality, but such a quality was expressed as was not required for the validity of the commission, nor was it capable of the commission itself, whereas the person to whom the commission was made was known to the subdelegator himself, and it was notoriously established that he was capable by reason of the canonry. To the aforesaid make very well the things noted by Innocent in c. significante, de rescrip., where he says that if a rescript was granted against V. of the diocese of Reims, and it can be established through other means that he meant V. of the diocese of Liège, the commission ought not to be vitiated. For it is enough that for another the commission can be sustained and certified. The Lords of the Rota say the same in decis. 126, if there was an error in the given name or family name, and Hostiensis holds this in Summa, de rescr., § possunt obiici, at the verse idem si in nomine; which proceeds even in letters of grace, as the same Lords of the Rota maintained in decis. 259 in the ancient decisions. Therefore the same and more strongly is to be said in our case, where no error was committed, so that the subdelegation made to the person is sustained, since he is capable by reason of the quality inherent in him, even though it was not expressed. Fifthly make the things noted by Bartolus in l. si servus communis, ff. de stip. ser., where he confirms that if in a disposition two qualities were expressed, and according to one the disposition would be ineffective, the disposition ought to be governed and regulated according to the other disposition so that the matter may rather be valid, while the other quality is held as not expressed. So let us say in the matter at hand, that where according to the expressed quality of the treasureship the disposition would be rendered useless, the subdelegation seems made to the person. For it can be made to the person, since he is otherwise capable of subdelegation; indeed, as I said above, since the commission is to the canon, it follows the person and not the canonry; hence it is that he can judge, although he has ceased to be a canon, as I said above. And this is an excellent consideration. Sixthly and finally make the things noted by the Gloss in l. cum ita, § 1, ff. de condi. & demon., and Petrus and Bartolus in l. & quia, ff. de iur. om. iud., where they say,

† that when in a disposition a proper name is expressed together with an appellative name, the disposition ought to be attributed to the quality expressed first. Whence, if the proper name precedes, it is deemed made to the person, and not to the dignity, which is subsequently added, as seems to be proved in l. si communis servus, ff. de stipu. ser.; and this statement ought to be limited to when the disposer knew the person; otherwise the appellative name ought to be considered through l. qui habebat, previously alleged. Thus Bartolus notably limited it in the note on the said l. si communis servus. And it must be observed, because they speak when the disposition could be preserved whether it were real or personal; all the more strongly therefore ought it to proceed in our case, in which the proper name was expressed first, nor can the subdelegation be preserved if the office of the treasureship were understood to have been contemplated. From all the premises I conclude that since it was known to the delegator himself that the subdelegate was a canon, it must be judged that the commission was valid, even though he expressed the quality of the treasureship along with the proper name, and kept silent about the quality of the canonry. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If a cleric builds on his own ground with money of the church, by exceptional law the ground accedes to the building.
2. The Pope, just like anyone else, can prescribe by using the right of a private person.
3. If a legate says that he has something by a special commission beyond what is included in the general legation, he is not to be believed.
4. One who impetrates a privilege contrary to prescription is deemed to renounce prescription.
5. If a lord does not give the promised fief, the vassal is not bound to keep the oath of fealty.
body: Invoking the name of Christ, in the question of the heirs of the late lord Petrus de Clavavalle, very many things come to be examined for their clear decision. First, to whom the direct ownership of that palace with the adjoining possessions pertained or pertains: namely, whether to this city of Todi, or rather to the Roman Church, to which that city of Todi is immediately subject in temporal and spiritual matters. Second, whether the grants of that palace made to the said lord Petrus, and successively to his sons after his death, or any of them, were valid. Third, whether the grant made by the Roman Pontiff to a certain third party, with no mention made of the right belonging to the said sons, was valid. Fourth, presupposing that it does not subsist by law, whether at least by reason of prescription the third-party possessor can defend himself against the sons of the said lord Petrus. Fifth, whether the sons of the said lord Petrus can vindicate the said goods from the possessors. Concerning the first: because it is not established to me from whose money that city of Todi bought the said palace—namely, whether from the goods of that universitas itself, or rather from regalian revenues, since at the time of the purchase the said city had withdrawn itself from the devotion and fealty of the Church, and was governing itself popularly and freely, as if that city possessed the rights of its own imperium—I would make this distinction: that either the said city had bought the said palace from the revenues of that universitas, and then the said palace will pertain to that universitas of Todi, and not to the Roman Church. For just as private persons can have ownership of things, concerning which the prince cannot dispose at the whim of his own will, since ownerships are of the ius gentium (dist. 1, c. ius gentium, and l. ex hoc iure, ff. de iust. & iu., and Inst. de iu. natu. gen. & civi. § sed naturalia, and Inst. de leg. agna. suc. in fi., and dist. 50 in prin.; noted by Inn. in c. quae in ecclesiarum, de const.; Cy. in l. praescriptione, C. de preci. impe. offe.; and Bar. in l. fi., C. si contra ius, vel uti. pub., and in prooem. ff. vete., something in l. Antiochensium, ff. de privi. credi., and l. 1, § per hanc, ff. de rei ven.), so also the universitas, which holds the place of a person (l. mortuo, ff. de fideiussor.), can have certain particular goods entirely distinct from the fiscal chamber, concerning which that city can dispose and which it can alienate as seems expedient to it, as in l. in tantum, § universitatis, ff. de rerum divi., and l. fi., C. de ven. re. civili. lib. 11. If, however, the said palace had been purchased from regalian revenues seized by the said city at the time of the rebellion, then I would say that the said goods pertained to the Roman Church. First, from the common theory of the glossators of both laws: namely, that if any property is bought with the Church’s money, the beneficial ownership of that property ipso iure belongs to the Church by special right, just as we say in the case of a ward and soldiers, as noted by the gloss in l. si ut proponis, C. de rei ven., and in c. inquirendum, de pecu. cle., and in c. apostolicos, 12, q. 2. And although Bar. on the said l. si ut proponis, limiting this, stated that this proceeds in the case of a ward and the Church when the thing was bought through the administration of the ward or the Church, but if through a third party, then he says that it becomes the Church's only in subsidium through l. filiae, ff. de sol. (which statement did not please Bal. there, who says that if a specific thing is bought with the ward's money by someone other than his administrator, it does not become the ward's even in subsidium, but rather that thing is obligated to the ward for his money, alleging a good text in l. 3 in prin., ff. de reb. eo.; and he perhaps under doubt said the same should be held in the case of the Church, which enjoys the right of a minor, as in c. 1, de in inte. rest.), nevertheless, in the case of the Church, the statement of the gloss pleases me more simply, so that indifferently the beneficial ownership is acquired for the Church, whatever the case may be in a ward. For if a soldier of the world has that privilege indistinctly (said l. si ut proponis)—which without doubt is to be extended also to clerics with respect to their patrimonies, since they are soldiers, through the noted gloss which Bar. and commonly the other doctors follow there in l. miles, ff. de re iu., and l. stipendia, C. de execu. rei iud., and Bar. in l. miles ita, § mulier, ff. de mili. test., and l. affectionis, ff. de dona.—with greater force the same must be said in the churches themselves, since the Church ought not thus to enjoy a lesser prerogative in its own property than the soldiers of the world, or of God, in their property, but indeed a greater one, according to what is noted in c. fi., de vita & hone. cleri., and through the gloss in c. unico, de in integ. resti., and c. quamquam, de censi. lib. 6, and 16, q. 4, c. possessiones. To the same effect is the singular gloss on the said c. apostolicos, which says

† that if a cleric builds on his own property with the money of the Church, the building yields to the soil by singular right, by argument in that text. Secondly and primarily, and more strongly, I say that the said palace with the adjoining possessions belonged and pertained to the Roman Church, and today also pertains to it with respect to the direct ownership, by another and clearer consideration: namely, because the city of Todi bought it as its own fiscal chamber. Whence those goods were made fiscal and imperial, since at the time of the purchase the said city possessed all regalia in the said city, and did everything as possessing the imperium of itself, by the argument of those things which are read and noted in l. unica, C. de bo. vac., and especially by Bar. there; by the same in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. tri., and in l. hostes, ff. de cap. & postli. re., and l. infamem in fi., ff. de publ. iud. Therefore, by subsequently transferring or recognizing the supreme right of imperium pertaining in the said city to the Roman Church, and by recognizing the Pope as lord also in temporal matters, they seem to have passed over and to have recognized this also with respect to fiscal goods, which are accessories to that supreme lordship, by argument in c. translato, de consti., and dist. 8, c. quo iure, and c. unico, quae sunt rega. col. 10, and in the said l. unica, de bo. vaca., and in l. deprecatio, ad legem Rho. de iactu, and l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadri. praescr. with the notes there. And the people of Todi, by tolerating that the said palace with the possessions be granted and disposed of by the Roman Pontiff as fiscal goods, seems tacitly to have confessed that they pertain to the Roman Church for the aforesaid reason, by argument in l. si filius, C. de peti. haere. For in doubtful matters one must have recourse to conjectures, in c. in ambiguis, de regu. iu., and that which is more probable and which is accustomed to happen for the most part must be held, as in the rule inspicimus in obscuris, de re. iu. li. 6, with similar texts.
