And by these reasons I conclude that, nothing else appearing, it is to be presumed that the said palace pertains to the Roman Church; and this today seems to be held indistinctly, at least by reason of prescription, since the Roman Church by itself or through another has possessed it for so long a time with good faith and with a just title plausibly presumed, that it has prescribed it; for this, see what is noted in c. cum nobis, de praescrip., and l. Celsus, ff. de usucap., and by Inn. in c. bonae, tit. de posthu. prael., where he affirms,

† that the Pope, using private law, can prescribe just as anyone else, provided he does not do this from the plenitude of power; and the same says Archid. in 16, q. 4, c. volumus, and Anto. de But. in c. cum nobis; it is otherwise where he uses the plenitude of power, and in this case Spec. can be understood, who seems to feel the contrary in Spec. in tit. de praescrip., verse illud autem; and I think that he could prescribe through a decennium with that presumed title, through those things noted by Ioa. Andr. in the rule qui ad agendum, de regu. iuris, libr. 6 in Meru., and through the gloss and Barto. in auth. quas actiones, C. de sacrosan. eccl. I come to the second point: namely, whether the grants made to the late lord Petrus and his sons were valid, or at least whether any of them has force. And first it seems that the first grant made by a certain lord Cardinal P., then vicar-general and legate in the patrimony, and specially in the said city of Todi, was valid in law through that which is noted by Bald. in l. exemplo, C. de probat., where he says that if a Cardinal legate has said in any grant beyond the things included in the general legation that he has a special grant for this from the Roman Pontiff, credence is to be given to him, provided he acts publicly and has been accustomed to do that; he alleges what is noted in c. cum ex literis, de in integr. restitu.; to the same effect is what is noted by Specu. in titu. de lega., § superest, and the verse quid si delegati iurisdictione, where he says that rarely and almost never is his power doubted, and that a Cardinal legate is not accustomed to provide proof of his power. Yet Io. An. after Hos. in c. 1, de of. leg. lib. 6, holds the contrary, affirming

† that if a legate says that he has something by special commission beyond the things included in the general legation, credence is not to be given to him; and I think this is truer, especially in our case, where it concerns the alienation of beneficial ownership to the prejudice of the Roman Church. For a special mandate is required for this, by argument in l. prohibere, § plane, ff. quod vi aut clam, and Bartol. affirms this there, and Specul. in the title de leg., § nunc dicendum, penultimate verse. Nor ought a mandate to be presumed, at least with respect to an alienation to be made, by argument in l. contra iuris regulas, ff. de pact., l. filiusfam., ff. de donat.; and I allege the notable gloss in c. sicut, de sen. excommu., which clearly agrees, alleging c. nobilissimus, distinct. 98, that the honesty and dignity of a person is never sufficient for credence to be given to him alone to the prejudice of another; c. cum a nobis, de testi., is to the same effect, and excellently l. unica, C. de supraindi. libr. 10, through which text Bart. said there that credence is never to be given to anyone, no matter how placed in dignity, who says that he has the power to do things depending on the prince's power; and especially must this be said in our case, in which it does not appear that that vicar was accustomed to make similar alienations of property belonging to the Roman Church, although he asserted that he had special power for this; and thus we are also outside the opinion of Bald. To the statement of Spec. it must be said that he referred himself not to the law, but to the fact. Yet on this point I do not think one should dwell much: because Pope Gregory, subsequently newly elected, gave to the aforesaid vicar a special mandate to make that grant; whence by force of the special mandate the said vicar confirmed the aforesaid grant anew, and granted to him anew the renewed fief. Moreover, that the Pope can grant certain temporal goods of the Church to laymen in fee is not to be doubted, through c. ad audientiam, and c. si diligenti, de praescr., and those things noted by Host. in c. a nobis, de deci. Nor also in this grant, although it was valid in law, is one to dwell much: because it was departed from by common tacit consent, in that upon the death of the said lord Petrus, his aforesaid sons, when they had been de facto despoiled of the possession of the said palace and possessions in time of wars, petitioned from the same Pope, when he was at Todi, that those goods be granted to them in emphyteusis up to the second generation for an annual rent, and an executor was given by the same Pope for the execution of possession, although it has not yet taken effect on account of the dangers of wars. Since, however, this contract cannot concur with the preceding one, there seems to be a departure from the former, by the excellent argument in l. si quis antea, ff. de acquir. poss., and l. quod in haeredem, § eligere, C. de tribu., and c. ut quis duas, de elect. lib. 6; and the text in c. veniens in fin., de praescript., serves excellently, where it appears

† that one who petitions for a privilege contrary to prescription seems to renounce prescription. Therefore, this grant in emphyteusis, as the last, and made by one having power, held by pure law. Nor do I care about the grant made by the commune of Todi which preceded this grant made in emphyteusis, because that can be impugned in many ways, since it was made by one lacking power, by a city which had violently usurped for itself the lordship belonging to the Roman Church; for acts done by a tyrant are not valid, especially to the prejudice of the Church, as in l. decernimus, C. de sacrosan. ecclesi.; what is noted by Barto. in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iu., and in said l. prohibere, § plane, quod vi aut clam, supports this; and that which is given by him who cannot by law donate is held as not given, as in c. quod autem, de iure patro., and 1, quaest. 7, c. didici; l. traditio, ff. de acqui. re. domi., and c. nuper, de dona. inter vi. & uxo., also support this. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the Pope in course of time approved all statutes, constitutions, and ordinances made by the people of Todi: because I say that in those general words the confirmation of an alienation made of goods belonging to the Roman Church is not included; for a special confirmation is required there, just as a special grant is required from the beginning; so that under words, however general, the power of alienating is not included, said l. contra iuris regulas, ff. de pact., and said l. si filiusfami., ff. de dona. But if we suppose that the said goods pertained to the commune of Todi in the aforesaid manner, and had not yet been prescribed by the Pope, the said grant would have been valid, provided the legal solemnities intervened in that grant, at least according to the custom of the place, l. 1 with the notes there, C. de eman. libe., l. 2, C. quemad. test. ape., with similar laws. And then, by receiving the grant in emphyteusis from the Pope, one does not lose the right that he previously had from the true owner, through the text in l. neque pignus, ff. de regu. iu., and l. ei a quo in fin., ff. de usucap., and l. qui rem propriam, C. loca. From all these things the answer to the second point is clear. For I say that the sons of the said lord Petrus have a right in the said palace and possessions either from the grant made to them in emphyteusis by Pope Gregory, or from the grant of the city of Todi, if we suppose in the aforesaid manner that those goods by right pertain to the said city. As to the third point, whether their right was prejudiced by the grant made to another by the Roman Pontiff, no mention of their right having been made: I say without doubt that it was not, both from lack of power and from lack of presumed will. The first is proved, because even the prince is bound by a contract entered into with a subject, nor can he breach that contract without a most just cause, as in c. 1, de proba., through Ioan. And. in c. significasti, de foro compe., through Barto. in l. quod semel, ff. de decr. ab ord. fa.; it is also proved in c. 1, de feu. sine culpa non amit., and c. uno, de feu. col. 10. And just as an emphyteuta cannot renounce the emphyteutic property against the will of the lord, as noted by the gloss in c. 1, de vasa. qui contra consti. Lot. feu. alie. in fin., collatio 10 (what Barto. notes in l. is a quo, ff. de aqua. plu. arcen., supports this), so the lord ought not to be able to deprive the emphyteuta of his right and transfer it to another. For contracts are voluntary at the beginning and of necessity after the fact, l. sicut, C. de act. & obliga. The second is proved, because every grant made by the prince with no mention made of the right of a third party is not valid, as in l. 1, ff. de nata. resti., and l. 2, § si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in loco publ., and c. super eo, de offi. deleg., and c. cum nostris, de conces. praeb., with similar texts. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said sons had been deprived of all goods by the very fact that they, along with others, rose up against the state of the Church, through l. quisquis, C. ad leg. Iul. maie.: because I say that they were most fully restored by Pope Martin; and restitution relates to all goods not alienated to others at the time of the restitution, l. 1, C. de sen. pas., and through Bar. in the last law, same title. Indeed, the said grant made to the third party did not precede the said restitution, but followed it; and thus it was made at that time when they had already been restored to their rights through restitution; which, since it is a reinstatement to the pristine state (said l. 2, and 2, q. 3, c. Euphemium, § notandum), must be understood of emphyteutic goods, and all goods whatsoever; because he who says all excludes nothing, dist. 19, c. si Romanorum, and c. solitae, de maio. & obe., and l. de pretio, ff. de publ. Secondly, it does not stand in the way if it is said that those sons had already fallen from their right, since they never paid the rent (c. potuit, de loca., and l. 2, de iur. emph.), and thus it was not necessary to make mention of their right (what Bal. notes on said l. 2 supports this); because I say the contrary applies when they had possession by force of that emphyteutic grant, but since the lord Pope, by himself or through another, never delivered possession to them, they were not bound to pay the rent (by argument in l. Iulianus, § offerri, ff. de act. emp.; Bal. openly agrees in l. solennibus, C. de rei ven. in fi.). For he is excused as long as a third party raises a dispute against him, and he cannot obtain possession, by argument in l. quamdiu, C. qui admit. ad bon. pos.; l. 1, ff. de ac. emp. & ven., serves excellently, and the gloss holds this in c. fi., de nova forma fid. col. 10, which says

† that if the lord does not give the promised fief, the vassal is not bound to keep the oath of fealty; to the same effect is l. quaero, § inter locatorem, and what Bar. notes there, ff. loc.; and this especially applies when another was holding of the Pope, through the singular text in l. forma, § si cum ipse, ff. de censi., and through Bald. in the said l. solennibus. And through this it is clear what must be said to the third point. I come now to the fourth doubt, whether prescription at least stands in the way of the sons of the said lord Petrus, since almost fifty years or more have elapsed during which they did not possess the said palace with the possessions: I believe it does not, first from the defect of good faith. For today no prescription with bad faith is valid, especially in the lands of the Church, as in c. vigilanti, and c. fi., de praesc.; Inn. in c. si duobus in fi., de appe. The same, however, is true in the civil forum among laymen, even in the lands of the Empire, because where sin would be imminent, one must stand by canon law and not civil law, and especially in the matter of prescription, as noted by Bart. in l. privilegia, C. de sacrosan. ecc., and the gloss in the rule possess., de re. iu. li. 6, and what is noted in c. 2, de no. ope. nun., and the said c. fi., de praescri. Moreover, bad faith is proved in our case by the common report, which was most widespread in that place, that the said goods were granted to the said lord Petrus and his sons; whence these possessors, who were in the place, are presumed to have known it, as in c. quosdam, and c. quanto, de praesum.; what is noted by Bar. in l. 1, ff. si cer. pet., supports this; and that bad faith sufficient to impede prescription is proved in this way was openly held by Bart. in l. Celsus, ff. de usuc., and what is noted in c. si diligenti, de praescr. The same is true if any other conjectures underlie, showing that the possessors knew that those goods pertained to the said sons of lord Petrus: for instance, because they happened to state this, or it was denounced to them from the beginning, l. si fundum, C. de rei vend., and the notes in the laws recently alleged, and especially by Bart. on the said l. Celsus. Secondly and primarily, it bars prescription because the said goods were invaded at the time of the sedition that occurred in the said city, through which the said sons of lord Petrus together with many other citizens were expelled from the said city of Todi; therefore those goods, as affected by a defect, could not be prescribed either by the occupiers, or by those to whom they transferred them, according to that which is read and noted in l. vitia, C. de acqui. poss., and Inst. de usuca., § furtivae. Thirdly and primarily, it bars the said prescription because no one possessed those goods for so long a time as to suffice for prescription; for those goods passed through many hands, nor is it a case in which one could use the accession of another's time, according to those things found in l. de accessionibus with the following laws, ff. de diver. & tem. praescrip. Fourthly, because when there is such great hostility or mortality in a place that justice is not administered in the place, prescription does not run, as in c. ex transmissa, de praescri., noted by Barto. in l. naturaliter, ff. de usuc.; but to the sons of lord Petrus, as expelled persons, justice was not administered in the said city of Todi; or, if we were to hold that prescription ran, restitution would nonetheless be given under the general clause 'if any just cause shall appear to me,' etc., ff. ex quib. cau. maior. l. 1, and l. sed & si per praetorem, same title, noted by Barto. in said l. naturaliter. That also is certain: that he who cannot prescribe by himself due to lack of good faith, neither can his heir prescribe, as in l. cum haeres, ff. de diver. & tempo. praescri. From these things, therefore, the said prescription can be broken by many and various considerations. Now, however, the aforesaid having been discussed, it remains to ask whether to the sons of the said lord Petrus having a valid grant any ownership was acquired, to the extent that they can vindicate the said goods from the possessors? And at first it seems not, because ownership is acquired by delivery and not merely by the intervention of title, as in l. traditionibus, C. de pact. For before delivery only a personal action against the grantor is available, to assign vacant possession, l. 1, ff. de act. emp. Since, in fact, the possessors did not contract with them, they cannot be sued by them by a personal action, nor even by a real action, since that is not available because ownership was not transferred, l. in rem actio, ff. de rei vendi., and without an action no one sues, l. si pupilli, ff. de neg. gest. Nor does it stand in the way that the contract was entered into with the prince, because in doubt the prince seems to wish to contract according to the ius commune, by argument in l. digna vox, C. de legi.; and Bald. openly affirmed this in the second chapter, de nova for. fide, collat. 10 in the second column, where he says that from a contract entered into with the prince, nothing else externally accompanying, ownership is not transferred without delivery; he interprets l. omnes and l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadr. praescri., as meaning that delivery had intervened there. But notwithstanding these things, I think the contrary must be said in our case on a twofold ground: first, because the sons of the said lord Petrus had possession and also beneficial ownership from the earlier grant made to them in fee by the Pope's vicar having a special mandate for this. For by the investiture of a fief alone, ownership, or at least a right to the thing, is transferred, as noted by Bar. in the said c. 2, de nova for. fide. Furthermore, they undoubtedly acquired a right in the thing and beneficial ownership through the delivery of possession made to them under the aforesaid title, as in c. unico, in quibus casibus feu. amit., col. 10 in fi., through the gloss and Bal. in c. uno, de cap. Contra., same column; the final gloss in c. cum Bertoldus, de re iud., and Inno. in c. si diligenti, de praescrip., and c. ad apostolicae, de re iud. l. 6, hold this; which beneficial ownership indeed they did not lose, although they fell from possession, because ownership is retained by intention alone, l. si quis vi, § differentia, de acquir. poss., for property has nothing in common with possession, l. naturaliter, § nihil commune, ff. eod. Whence, by reason of the remaining ownership, he who fell from possession can bring an actio utilis rei vindicatio against the possessor, as in l. 1 & 2, ff. si age. vect. Nor by acquiring a new title—namely, the emphyteutic title—did they lose the first ownership they had from the feudal title; because since each contract tends toward this, that beneficial ownership be had (said l. 1 & 2, si age. vectig.), through the intervention of the second, the ownership or possession had from the first is not lost; whence the ownership had from the first contract can be retained by force of the second without any delivery needing to be made from the second, as is clearly proved in Inst. de rerum di., § interdum, and in l. si quis antea, ff. de acq. pos., and what Bar. notes there at the end, and better through him in l. si proprietarius, ff. dam. inf. Whence if a pledgee later sues by a personal action and causes himself to be put into possession by the first decree through the judge, he does not thereby lose the possession which he had before, but expressly pursues the praetorian pledge directly without any delivery, because that already made from the prior agreement suffices, although otherwise a praetorian pledge does not suffice for the transfer of possession, as in l. non est in fi., de pig. act. And Bar. holds this last point in the said l. si quis antea. We say the same when a usufructuary is sent into possession of the bare property by the first decree: for no delivery is required, since the thing is detained by the usufructuary, as in the said l. si proprietarius. So in the present matter, since beneficial ownership was had through the first contract or grant of the fief, there was no need that delivery should intervene from the second emphyteutic contract; but it can now be held and exercised by force of the second contract; and this is most true. On the second ground, the sons of the said Petrus are said to have beneficial ownership even if they had never had the prior feudal grant, because they had the said goods in emphyteusis from the Pope by way of supplication and of a certain privilege and grace, as appears from the tenor of the grant, in which case by such a grant beneficial ownership is transferred without delivery, by argument in c. si tibi absenti, de praeben. lib. 6; and Bald. affirms this in chapter 2, de nova for. fide, in the tenth column. The same must be said if the grant was not made by way of supplication, but the Pope in the grant itself used words apt for the transfer of ownership, as because he said 'we give, assign, and transfer,' or something similar. For just as the law can transfer ownership without delivery (l. commissa, ff. de pub., noted in l. traditionibus, C. de pact.), so can the prince, since he is the animate law on earth (in Auth. de constitu. in fin., 9, q. 3, c. ipsi sunt; what Innoc. notes in c. fin., de accu., and in c. Raynaldus, de test., supports this; and Bald. expressly confirmed this theory in the said c. fin., de nova for. fide; and the notes through Host. and Ioan. And. in c. continebatur, de his quae fi. a praela., serve excellently for the aforesaid). From the aforesaid I conclude that the said sons of lord Petrus can vindicate the aforesaid palace with the adjoining possessions granted to them from any possessors unjustly detaining them, by an actio utilis rei vindicatio. And let these things suffice. Nic. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A gift exceeding five hundred gold coins, not registered, is confirmed by an oath.
2. A patron cannot present himself.
3. A prelate having the right of collation can confer an ecclesiastical benefice on blood relatives, provided that they are honorable.
body: In the name of Jesus Christ, the case is stated thus: A certain married lady B. executed her solemn testament, and among other things bequeathed to her husband under this form, namely: "Item, she left and bequeathed to Francis, her husband, who was present and accepting, and to me, the notary, as a public person receiving and stipulating on behalf of master Francis, one hundred florins; which bequest the said lady B. willed to have and hold the force of a gift inter vivos, so that it cannot be revoked on any ground of ingratitude or offense; and under the said title of a gift inter vivos she gave, etc." And the said testatrix swore upon the holy Gospels of God, corporally touching the scriptures, never to revoke the said gift and legacy. The question is asked: Can the lady B. revoke the said legacy or gift inter vivos? This question falls within that common and difficult inquiry which is still under debate today,

† whether a gift made between spouses is confirmed by an oath, or at least binds the swearer so that they cannot contravene it. For it is certain that the said legacy passed into a gift inter vivos, both on account of the express words (and it is certain that a contract can be entered into within a last will, as noted in l. haeredes palam, ff. de testa.; to which belongs what is noted, and especially by Bart., in l. cum quis, §. codicil., ff. de leg. 3, and what is held in Auth. de iureiuran. a maiori prae., after the beginning), and because a legacy is a species of gift, as in l. legatum, ff. de leg. 2; and although it may be revoked, ff. de adi. leg. throughout, it seems, by reason of those added words, that it cannot be revoked; for it passed into another species of donation, which is called inter vivos, just as a donation mortis causa passes into a gift inter vivos by reason of similar words, l. ubi ita donatur, ff. de dona. causa mort.; for there are three species of gift, as noted in the said l. legatum. It must therefore be examined whether a gift made to a husband is confirmed, or whether at least the oath binds against contravention. And it seems at first that such an oath is invalid. For it seems contrary to the goods of marriage, concerning which see cap. omne itaque, 27, q. 2. For it is contrary to the good of offspring: because through such a gift the care of educating children is neglected, since through poverty caused by the gift the donor does not have the means to nourish the children, l. 2, ff. de dona. inter virum & uxo. Secondly, it is contrary to the sacrament, because such a gift is often the cause of discord and divorce, since through it an emotional turmoil arises. Thirdly, it is contrary to the fidelity of marriage, by which not only adultery must be avoided, but all chastity and purity ought to be in marriage; but through such a gift marriages become venal, and often lust is the cause of the gift, and they strip themselves contrary to good morals, as the text intimates in l. 1, 2, and 3, ff. de do. inter vir. & uxo. Therefore such an oath ought not to hold, as in the rule, non est obligatorium, de reg. iu., in 6., especially since a wife makes a gift to her husband, when she is to be presumed to give induced by the persuasions and deceptions of her husband; and an oath taken through fraud contrary to law is invalid, c. cum contingat, de iureiu. But, notwithstanding these points, I consider the contrary opinion to be truer in law. I am moved first by that common rule that an oath is always to be observed whenever it can be observed without the loss of eternal salvation, even though it entails the detriment of temporal goods, ca. si vero, and c. cum contingat, de iureiurand. But this oath is of such a kind, for the said woman incurs no sin by observing the said oath; therefore she is bound to its observance. For the obligation of an oath, at least primarily, is directed to God, with whom no turpitude is found, and in the swearing woman there is no sin; therefore it must be observed, even if some unworthiness were found on the part of the husband who exacted the oath, as is proved in the case of one who promised by oath to pay usury to his creditor. For he is bound to pay by reason of the aforesaid, as in capitul. debitores, with what is noted there, de iureiurand. Furthermore and secondly, I see that an oath binds in an act invalid in law and reason in a hateful matter, as appears in the lex commissoria clause, which is condemned in pledges on account of the greed of the creditor, l. 1 and 2, C. de pact. pig., and capitul. significasti, de pigno.; and yet I see that an oath binds, at least so that one cannot contravene it by virtue of the oath, according to the said cap. significante, as noted by Barto., l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiusso. For it is no more detestable that someone unjustly and contrary to the duty of charity should lose their property through that pact, and acquire it for a creditor through cupidity, than that a spouse should give something to a spouse, with whom they are one flesh, especially since in the former case that pact arose out of excessive anxiety to obtain and find borrowed money. In our case, however, the gift proceeds from mere liberality, as the text clearly intimates in l. si maritus, ff. de donatio. inter virum & vxo.; and the cause of giving seems most honorable, namely, on account of chastity, whence it seems a reward for chastity, l. res uxoris, C. eo., where see Bald. Furthermore, an oath is valid concerning the alienation of dotal property, or of property given in a donation propter nuptias, through which alienation the wife can indeed remain completely undowered; which can run contrary to the public good, concerning which see l. 1, ff. solu. mat., and the children can be deprived of maintenance and succession; and nevertheless it is valid, because the soul must be consulted more than the body, since it is more precious than all things, 12, q. 1, c. praecipimus. A fortiori it ought to be valid in our case, in which she gave a part to her own husband, such that there is no fear of poverty, since she will obtain maintenance from her husband even if she had nothing in her dowry, l. quod si nulla, ff. de re li. & sump. fune., noted in l. si cum dotem, §. sinautem in squifsimo, with the following, ff. solu. matr., and c. per vestras, de dona. inter vir. & uxo., and there by Inno.; nor is anything lost to the children, since whatever the father has belongs in effect to the children, so that they lack only administration, as the text says in §. sui, Insti. de haere. qua. & dif., and noted in l. in suis, ff. de libe. & posthumis; and the husband ought to share in all the woman's casual losses, the said l. si cum dotem, §. si maritus, at the word quid enim.

† Item, an oath is valid to the prejudice of a future succession contrary to civil law, l. pactum, C. de col., joined with c. 2, de pact., in 6., through which oath one is deceived in many ways and could remain without any property; a fortiori it ought to be valid in our case, where the one is bound to maintain the other in case of need, as well as their common children, d. c. per vestras, and d. l. si cum, and l. 1, and l. si quis a libe., ff. de libe. agno. It is also valid to the prejudice of a minor alienating his own property without the required solemnities contrary to the disposition of the law, which was issued to provide for the indemnity of minors and to meet the deceptions and frauds of others, authen. sacramenta puberum, C. si adver. vendi. It is no wonder, therefore, if in our less doubtful case it is valid and imposes a bond, especially since nearly all doctors of both laws agree on this opinion: Guil. de Cu. in l. sed & si possessori, §. item si iuravero, ff. de iuraiurand., and Barto. in l. Seius, and Angerius, ff. ad l. Falci., and he disputes it more fully and follows it in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiussor., although in l. 1, ff. de dona. inter virum & uxo., he seems to have held the opposite, but there he did not discuss the matter, but passed over it with a slow foot, remitting himself to the matter of d. l. si quis pro eo, where after a long inquiry he held the first opinion. Cyn. also seems to hold this according to the ius commune in l. 1, in fin., C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi., and Bald. in l. cum multae, C. de dona. ante nupt., in that he finally refers himself to Barto. in d. l. si quis, and intimates that the oath confirms such a donation, although he previously seemed to hold the contrary opinion through certain arguments, to which I shall presently reply thus. Anto. de But. follows this in c. cum contingat, de iureiuran., and Joan. And. and Joan. de Lig. in cle. Romani, under the same title, and Fed. de Sen. advised for this position, as appears in consi. 135. It remains now to respond to the contrary arguments. And first, when it is said that through such a gift the care of children happens to be neglected, I say that that consideration was very remote, and such remote and secondary causes ought not to impede the force of an oath, joined with the glo. in fi. in c. 2, de pac., in 6.; to which belongs what is noted by the glo. in c. de caetero, de homici., which says that remote causes are not to be regarded, 23, q. 1, c. de occidendis. Item, because this does not happen when the property reaches the father, who loves his children above all things, so that he would be more alarmed in the person of his children than in himself, as in l. isti quidem, ff. quod met. cau., and paternal affection conquers all affection, l. fi., de cura. furio. And if it were said that this gift removes the care of children, namely those perhaps to be procreated from another marriage—because if the woman remained undowered, or without a competent dowry, she would not find a husband, l. 1, ff. sol. matr.—I reply that these causes do not impede the force of an oath, by d. c. cum contingat, and c. licet, de iureiuran., in 6., in which it is clear that an oath taken regarding the alienation of dotal property, or property given on account of marriage, is valid; for more (as I said before) must the soul be consulted than the body, and this is especially to be said in our case. The second objection does not stand in the way, namely that this gift provides a cause for divorce: both because today a marriage cannot be dissolved as in former times, 32, q. 7, c. 1 and 2, and c. gaudemus, de divor., c. ex publico, de conver. coniu., and c. tua, de iureiuran.; nor is this cause always true and perpetual; it is enough that the oath does not tend toward the destruction of eternal salvation, d. c. si vero, because the cause is quite remote; on the contrary, it could be said that greater love is induced between them on account of the liberality and munificence which one exercised toward the other, for the recipient is naturally bound to antidora, that is, to making a return, l. sed & si, §. consuluit, ff. de peti. haere., c. cum in officiis, de test., with similar authorities. To the third argument, that there ought to be all purity in marriage and there should not be venality in marriage, the answer is that through these things purity is no less present; for liberality is exercised and a reward for chastity is sometimes given, as the text says in d. l. si maritus, and l. res uxoris, C. de dona. inter vi. & uxo. Item, the oath is sworn to God, with whom no injustice is found, nor is there any sin on the part of the swearer; therefore the oath must be kept, d. c. debitores, and c. significante, de pigno. And if it is said that this oath is contrary to good morals, arguing from d. l. 1, ff. de donat. inter vi. & uxo., and therefore is not obligatory, as in regu. non est obligatorium, de reg. iur., in 6., I reply that the said law is to be understood of the good morals of any individual, as the gloss expounds there, in which an oath binds, since the law principally fosters private good, as is clear in many cases cited above in which an oath binds contrary to civil law, and thus contrary to civil good morals. For every law is founded upon civil good morals and upon reason, 4. distin., c. erit autem, and 1. dist., c. consuetudo. But the bond of an oath is impeded when it is contrary to natural good morals: because it is taken concerning something containing within itself some turpitude and natural instinct; for natural things are immutable, 5. dist. in prin., and Inst. de iure nat. gen. & civi., §. sed naturalia. Therefore an oath to the contrary is invalid: because it is taken concerning what is immutable, and thus concerning what does not depend on the power of the swearer; rightly it is not valid, just as when an oath is sworn contrary to a law enacted for public benefit, or having a perpetual cause of prohibition; in which cases an oath is not valid, because the swearer cannot bind himself concerning what does not depend on his own power; which also holds under canon law, capitul. si diligenti, de fo. comp., and c. quanto, de iniur., and 22, q. 4, almost throughout. And it is concerning these cases that l. non dubium, C. de legi., must be understood; it is otherwise when the law is founded principally on private benefit, even though secondarily it redounds to public benefit. For then an oath to the contrary is valid, capitul. cum contingat, with many citations to the contrary, and authen. sacramenta, C. si adver. vendi.; and this occurs in our case. For by natural law all goods are common, 12, q. 1, cap. dilectissimus, 8. dist. in princ.; therefore it cannot be said that this oath is contrary to natural good morals. Nor does presumed fraud in the husband stand in the way: both because no law expressly presumes fraud, but rather liberality and munificence, d. l. si maritus, and a reward for chastity, dict. l. res uxoris. Furthermore, if fraud were presumed, it would not be confirmed by death; rather, it would always be void, d. capitul. cum contingat, where it is clear that even an oath taken through fraud and deceit is invalid, as in d. authen. sacramenta; and nevertheless it is confirmed by death if delivery has taken place, l. Papinianus, ff. de dona. inter virum & uxo., and d. l. res uxoris, and capitul. finale, under the same title, with similar texts. Furthermore, unless the law firmly presumed fraud so that it was a presumption of law and of right, the oath would not seem to be impeded: because on a slight presumption, especially of civil law, the obligation of an oath ought not to be impeded, by the argument in cap. literas, de praesump., and what Joan. And. notes in addi. Specu. de instru. edi., §. porro, at the line & no., where he says,

† that a gift exceeding 500 aurei not officially registered is confirmed by an oath, and yet civil law superficially presumes fraud in such a gift, l. data, C. de dona., although Bald. in this last point holds the contrary in l. id quod pauperibus, C. de epis. & cler. But the first view is truer through those things that were cited above, and let them suffice, especially because, doubt having been raised, the oath must be observed: because in doubtful matters the safer path, and that which is less dangerous to the soul, is to be kept, as in c. iuvenis, de sponsa., noted in c. 1, de scruti., and c. venerabilem, de elect., with similar authorities. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a donation made between spouses is confirmed by an oath.
2. An oath to the prejudice of a future succession is valid against civil law.
body: May Jesus Christ be present. For a clear decision of the narrated theme, three matters must be examined in order. First, whether the said lord Paulus, the patron, was able to present lord Assensus, his son, to be instituted in the benefice of his patronage. Second, presupposing that the presentation cannot be challenged on the ground of filiation, whether it can at least be voided because the said lord Assensus is a canon in the said church, in which the said benefice without cure is known to have been instituted. Third, posited that the accumulation of the said benefices does not stand in the way, whether the said lord Assensus can be compelled and constrained by the bishop and chapter of that church, by virtue of the said altar or benefice without cure, to say Mass at other altars of the same church, and to perform the weekly duty in the said church, having regard to the fact that the foundation of the said altar or benefice constrains the priest instituted therein to celebrate only at the said altar, although varying instruments are found regarding the celebration to be made; for the same notary, in one instrument exhibited to the bishop and chapter, wrote that the priest is bound to celebrate at the said altar five times in each week, but in another instrument, which he delivered to the heirs, he wrote that the said priest is bound to say Mass always and continuously upon the said altar. Regarding the first doubt, it seems at first that the said lord Paulus could not present his son to the said benefice, by c. consuluit and c. quia clerici, de iure patro., and Innocent holds this in the said c. quia clerici through that text. Furthermore,

† a patron cannot present himself, as in c. per vestras, under the same title; therefore neither can he present his son, since by nature father and son are understood to be the same person, as the text says in l. fi. C. de impu. & aliis substi., and elsewhere the text says that father and son are one flesh, 35. q. 3. §. hoc autem. But, the aforesaid notwithstanding, the contrary opinion is the more common, which the glossa follows in the said capitu. quia clerici and cap. consoluit, and Innocent held the same in the said cap. consuluit, although he felt the contrary in capit. quia clerici; but Host., Philip., and commonly other doctors, even the More Modern ones, follow the first opinion of the glossa. For since this is nowhere found to be prohibited by law, it seems permitted, since this matter is not prohibitive, but rather permissive, according to what is noted in cap. 2. de transla. præla., especially since in these spiritual matters paternal power is not regarded, cap. si annum, de iud. lib. 6., and a father's vote in a corporate body can benefit his son, ff. quod cuiusque uniuer. nomi. in l. illud. Furthermore,

† a prelate having the right of collation can confer an ecclesiastical benefice upon his relatives, provided they are otherwise upright, cap. dilecto, de præben., through Arch. in cap. episcopum. 10. q. 1.; the text makes for this, joined with the glossa, c. decenter. 89. dist., and Fed. consi. 203. All the more, therefore, can a presentation be made of a son or other relatives, since through it there is merely a kind of inception toward obtaining institution, de iure patronatus c. quod autem; nor do I linger further on this doubt, since the common opinion holds this. c. quia clerici, alleged to the contrary, does not stand in the way, for it speaks of when patronage is acquired unjustly so that the son may be presented; it is otherwise, therefore, if justly. To c. consuluit it is answered that it speaks of when the son intrudes himself on his own, or through a paternal grant without institution by the bishop, which cannot be done even in the case of a stranger, since the patron has merely the right of presenting, but not of conferring or granting the church to another, c. illud, and c. fi., and c. quoniam, de iure pa., fully noted in 16. q. 7. c. piæ mentis. To the last argument concerning the identity of persons, I say that this proceeds by a fiction, and not in truth, especially in these spiritual matters, as was said above. I conclude therefore that the said presentation cannot be challenged on that ground: because he presented his son. To the second doubt, it seems at first that it can, by c. literas, de concess. præben., clem. fi. eo. titulo, where it is clear that by the acquisition of a second prebend in the same church the first is vacated ipso iure; let us say, therefore, that since these benefices are in the same church, either the presentation to the second ought to be impeded, or by the acquisition of the second the first will be vacated ipso facto. Furthermore, since the bishop sees that this presented person cannot serve in the second benefice, since he is bound to the first, he ought not to institute him in the second, argument from cap. quia nonnulli and cap. relatum, de cle. non resi. Furthermore, one cannot by law hold multiple benefices, especially in the same church, 70. dist. c. sanctorum, and c. quia in tantum, de præben., and c. conquerente, de cler. non resi.; for one can scarcely fulfill one office, and one ought not to claim for oneself the stipends of several, c. ad hæc and c. cum non ignores, de præben., with similar texts. I judge the contrary opinion to be truer, since in fact it is presupposed to me that the canonry of the said church does not require residence, just as today is the common custom throughout all Italy, which custom is approved by law; there is the text and glossa in c. cum omnes, de const., the doctors follow it there, and the glossa in c. dudum. 2. de ele. in fi., through Inn. in c. cum iam dudum, de præb., and the glossa in cle. gratiæ, de rescrip., and c. gratia eod. tit. lib. 6. Moreover, under the ius commune one can hold multiple benefices without cure, provided both do not require residence, said cap. gratia and said cle. gratiæ, through Inno. in said capitu. cum iam, especially in our case, in which one benefice by itself does not suffice to comfortably sustain the canon; therefore he can, with a safe conscience, receive a second, noted by the glossa in said cap. cum iam dudum, in fi., In. said c. cum iam. And today general custom holds that even in the same church one can hold not only two simple benefices, but a dignity and a canonry, which custom is indeed valid; text and glossa in versicle nisi unicum, de consuetu. lib. 6.; cap. eam te, de rescript. makes for this. Nothing therefore prevents the said lord Assensus from obtaining the said altar. It does not stand in the way that he is a canon, since by reason of the canonry he is not bound to reside and to serve at the said altar, because then, although those are benefices without cure, nevertheless he could not hold them together, since they require residence, noted in c. fi. de cleri. non resi., glossa of said cle. gratiæ; yet in this case the bishop could dispense, as noted by Fede. consi. 115 through said cap. de consue. lib. 1; but in our case a dispensation is not required, both by general custom and because the canonry does not require residence. The contrary arguments are easily answered, and first, to c. literas and cle. fi., I say that they speak of two prebends of the same church, which one cannot hold even by dispensation of the bishop, nor is a custom to the contrary valid, said c. literas, through Ioan. An. where he pursues the reason of this statement; it is otherwise in other cases, as noted there, especially when the benefices are of different kinds, as in our case. To the other legal authorities it is answered that they speak of benefices requiring residence, as is clear in them. To the third doubt, I say that the said lord Assensus is to be instituted by the bishop, as is clear from the aforesaid, and cannot be compelled to celebrate at other altars, or to perform the weekly duty, like the other chaplains, since the foundation of the benefice does not contain this. For one is not bound to serve beyond the burden annexed in the foundation of the benefice, c. cum in cunctis. §. inferiora, de elect., and c. cui de non sacerdotali, joined with the glossa, de præben. lib. 6.; c. significatum makes for this, with what is noted there eo. titu. in antiquis, and c. extirpandæ. §. quia uero, de præben., through the great glossa in c. licet canon, de elect. lib. 6., with many similar texts which can be alleged for this. Nor does it stand in the way that certain beneficiaries at the said altar served in the said church, because by service unjustly rendered, and as it were through extortion by the prelate and chapter, a custom to the contrary was not introduced, as in c. quia cognouimus. 10. quæst. 3., where there is a good text joined with the glossa; what the glossa and Barto. note in l. 1. §. quæ onerandæ, ff. qua. re. act. non da., makes for this, especially since it is not of so much time as would suffice to introduce prescription or custom, since a period of 40 years is required by what is read and noted in c. fin. de consue. and cap. de quarta, de præscript.; for the foundation of a benefice ought not easily to be removed, indeed the bishop can dispense against it, as noted by Cald. in c. cum accessissent, de constit.; 16. q. 3. cap. monasterium makes for this. And through this it is clear that there is no force, nor a matter of difficulty, in how the instrument speaks concerning the manner of celebrating at the said altar; for it is sufficient that the foundation of the benefice only binds him to celebrate at the said altar, and not elsewhere. Nevertheless, to choose the truth, I say that the original ought to be inspected, by which the exemplifications made therefrom are declared, as in c. quoniam contra, de proba.; and in the event that the original says that the priest to be instituted there is bound to say Mass always and continuously at the said altar, it ought not to be understood so bitterly that he should omit no day without celebrating, but that whenever he can more frequently, he ought to celebrate at the said altar, always preserving his uprightness and the due devotion of the Masses, as is the notable text in c. significatum, de præben.; for he ought not, nor can he be compelled to celebrate, unless he can do so honorably and devoutly; for one is not always devout and fit to celebrate. For as the canon says, 'He is happy enough who can worthily celebrate daily', de conse. di. 1. c. sufficit, and Augustine says, 'To receive the Eucharist daily, I neither praise nor blame', de consecra. di. 2. c. quotidie. And let these things suffice. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Where the words are clear, no place is left for interpretation.
2. A pact made not to claim further ought to be referred to the amount not paid.
3. When a debt is liquidated, a settlement does not apply to it.
4. Words uttered indefinitely ought to be understood generally, wherever the same rationale underlies.
body: IN the name of Christ, amen. Having examined the instrument of release and acquittance made for one thousand five hundred florins by the lady Minochia as guardian of the wards contained in the said instrument, the question is raised in doubt whether that clause contained at the end of the said instrument, namely: a pact made not to make any further claim, ought to be referred to the said sum of one thousand five hundred florins only, or rather to the entire dowry in respect of which the payment of the said amount was made. And first it seems that the said clause ought to be referred to the entire sum of the dowries owed; because words contained in any disposition ought to have some operation, as in l. si quando, C. de inoff. testamen. and in c. si papa, de priui. lib. 6. But if the said clause is referred to the amount paid only, the words of the clause effect nothing: because an obligation is extinguished by the payment of that which is owed without any other pact of not claiming, as in Inst. quib. mod. tolli. obli. in princ.; nay rather, by a payment made by a third party in the name of the debtor, the obligation is extinguished ipso iure, as in l. soluere, with the following, ff. de solu. and in l. soluendo, ff. de nego. gesto. Therefore, in order that the said clause may have some effect, it ought to be referred to the said amount of the dowries then owed. For a pact not to claim a debt is accustomed to be made so that an exception of a pact may stand against an action belonging to a plaintiff, as in Inst. de except. §. præterea. Likewise, general words indefinitely uttered ought to be understood generally, in l. de pretio, ff. de publicia. and noted in cap. ut circa, de elect. lib. 6. and 31. q. 1. c. quod si dormierit; but the said guardian made the pact indefinitely not to make any further claim; therefore it ought to be understood generally. Moreover, the guardian could do this by way of a certain transaction, especially with the authority of the judge, which intervened in this act, as in l. interdum. §. tutelam, and l. pignore. §. fina. ff. de fur. And although the aforesaid points may flatter the ears, I deem the opposite opinion to prevail in law, namely that the said pact not to make any further claim refers only to the amount then paid, and not to the whole amount then owed; which is shown by several reasons. And first,

† because where the words are clear, no place is left for interpretation, as in l. ille aut ille, ff. de lega. 3. and in cap. ex toto; de regul. iur. and in cap. fin. de uerbo. significa. But the words of release of the said instrument refer only to the amount of 1,500 florins then paid, as is clear in the beginning of the said instrument, while it is stated therein that she acquitted, released, and discharged of 1,500 gold florins out of the sum of the dowries of the lady Christophora, etc. For it was not said that for that sum she released the debtor from the whole amount of the dowries; but that she released of one thousand five hundred florins from the sum of the dowries clearly indicates that a discharge was not being made for the whole sum of the dowries, argument in l. decem, ff. de uerbo. oblig. Therefore that clause, not to make any further claim, ought to be referred only to the release upon the payment made: because it is not probable that the said guardian would immediately have contradicted herself, argument in l. non ad ea, ff. de cond. & demon. For if she had wished to release the debtor from the whole debt of the dowries, she would not have restricted herself in the words of release and acquittance to the amount of one thousand five hundred florins; for she would have known how to say, as is customary, that for the said amount paid she released and acquitted the debtor from everything that could be claimed on the occasion of the dowries of the lady Christophora, argument in cap. ad audientiam, and cap. dilecti, de deci., especially because in stipulations and contracts we must first inspect what was done; and if it does not appear, we must have recourse to common observance; concerning which, if it does not appear, that which is least must be followed, and it must be imputed to the stipulator, as in l. semper in stipulationibus, ff. de regul. iur. and in the rule in obscuris, and in the rule in dubiis, de regu. iur. lib. 6. Secondly, and more strongly, this is shown by another consideration: a clause placed at the end ought to be referred to the preceding matters, and not to extraneous matters, in capitu. inquisitioni, de apppella. joined with capitul. super eo, de offic. delega., as is fully proved in l. talis scriptura, ff. de lega. 1. and in l. prætor, line 2, ff. ui bono. rapto. But in the said instrument only an acquittance and release of one thousand and five hundred florins preceded; therefore

† the pact made at the end not to make any further claim ought to be referred only to that amount paid, and not to the remainder of the debt, since no mention was made of that; for just as an extraneous person is not understood to be added in a stipulation, as in l. si ita stipulatus fuero. §. Chrysogonus, at the end, ff. de uerbo. obliga., so too extraneous and unexpressed matters ought not to be understood in stipulations and contracts. Thirdly it is supportive because in the said instrument it is not said that by reason of a transaction she released the debtor from the whole debt; and thus no cause appears why the said pact of not claiming ought to be referred to the whole debt. For since the debt is liquidated and clear, as is evident in the instrument of dowries, of which mention is made in the said instrument of release, the guardian could not tacitly release the debtor of the wards from the remainder of the amount, with no cause appearing, as in l. preses, C. de transact. and Bartolus expressly affirms there. Nor does the authority of the judge stand in the way: because since it was interposed without cause, and especially without knowledge of the cause, it operates nothing, as is proved in l. magis puto. §. illud, ff. de reb. eo. Therefore it is to be presumed that the said pact was added from the intention of the contracting parties and of the judge so that it would concern the whole debt, since it is not to be presumed that anyone wishes to do that which he cannot by law fulfill, 22. q. 2. c. faciat, and noted in l. 3. ff. de inoffi. testam. Under this head the said clause ought to be restricted both from defect of a pact and of presumed will; nor, as I have said, ought a transaction to be presumed:

† both because where a debt is liquidated, a transaction does not lie there, as in l. eleganter. §. post rem iudicatam, ff. de conditio. inde., especially to the prejudice of wards, as Bartolus notes in the said l. pręses; and because in the said instrument nothing is said concerning a transaction; nor is it probable on another ground that a transaction was made concerning the entire debt: because a contract ought not to limp, as in l. si dum dies, §. si arbiter, ff. de arbitr.; but in the said instrument the debtor makes a pact that if the said wards ought not by law to have that amount of 1,500 florins, that which was paid beyond what was owed ought to be paid back to the debtor himself; therefore it is not probable that the guardian wished to pay the said amount purely. For it is absurd that something should stand on one side which does not stand on the other, as in the said §. si arbiter; for that pact is repugnant to the nature of a transaction, argument in l. Lucius, ff. ad Treb. and in l. sub prætextu, C. de transac.; therefore a transaction is not to be presumed, in c. ad nostram, de emp. & uend. and in c. illo uos, de pigno. and in l. ubi ita donatur, ff. de dona. causa mor., and this proceeds especially in the case of wards. Fourthly and lastly, this opinion is most clearly proved in my judgment in l. ueteribus, joined with that which Bartolus notes there, ff. de pac., where the law notes that in doubtful matters a pact must always be interpreted against him in whose favor it was added. The reason is because, since he grounds himself upon that pact, he must clearly prove his intention; otherwise he must fail, because a doubtful proof does not relieve the party proving, as in cap. in præsentia, de probat. and in l. non nudis, and l. neque epistolis, C. eod. But the debtor in our case grounds himself upon the said pact, which is indeed at least doubtful, as is clear from what has been said; therefore the interpretation is to be made against him; that which is read and noted in l. quicquid astringendæ, ff. de uerb. obl. supports this. Nor do the contrary points adduced above stand in the way. And first I respond to the first; I say that it is not absurd for someone to provide himself with a multiple remedy in the same instrument, argument in l. quoties, ff. de act. & obli., supported by what Bartolus notes in l. 2. ff. ad l. fal., and especially because the custom of notaries has this; for they duplicate many remedies as a precaution in the act of discharge, argument in l. fi. C. de fideius., which is clearly evident from the contents in the beginning of that instrument; for the said guardian released the debtor and acquitted him from the aforesaid amount paid to her; which release and acquittance was nevertheless not necessary, because from the payment alone a release occurred ipso iure as to the amount paid, as is read and noted in l. quidam æstimauerunt, ff. si cert. peta. and in capitu. constitutus, de pœnis; and from this it can be conjectured what the parties intended in that pact not to make any further claim; for all doubtful words contained in any disposition are explained by preceding and following words, as in l. qui filiabus, and l. si seruus plurium, de lega. 1. and l. nummis, de lega. 3.; but it would be absurd for the said clause to refer to the entire debt through those things that have been said above. The second motive does not stand in the way,

† for words indefinitely uttered ought to be understood generally wherever the same reason underlies, but otherwise if a different reason can be assigned, as noted in the said c. ut circa, and by Bartolus in the said l. talis scriptura; nay rather, general words ought to be restricted lest an absurd understanding arise, and lest anyone be enriched without cause to the loss of another, as in l. ut gradatim, ff. de mune. & hono., l. 2. C. de noxa., and in capitu. cum dilectus, de consuetu., and in capit. abbate, de uerbo. significa.; fully by Bartolus in l. non dubium, C. de legi. and l. omnes populi, ff. de iustit. & iure; for an absurd and contrary understanding would follow, as is evident from the aforesaid, if the said pact of not claiming were referred to the entire debt. From all the aforesaid, I conclude that both from the defect of power of the said guardian, and from the defect of presumed will, the said pact not to make any further claim ought not to be referred except to the said amount of 1,500 florins. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a writing in the hand of the testator is valid among children.
2. Although a testament that is less solemn by reason of solemnity establishes proof among children, it must nevertheless be proved that it was made by the father or by his authority.
body: IN the name of the Savior Jesus Christ, amen. On the question pending between certain sons of Ser Antonio concerning the validity of a certain writing, in which it is said that the last will of the said Ser Antonio is contained without solemnity.

† First, it seems that the said writing, written in the hand of the said Ser Antonio making a will among his children, is valid; because, since the said Ser Antonio was a notary, he could therefore draw up his own testament, since there is no question here of prejudice to another, as noted by Bartol. in l. si servus communis, ff. de stipu. servo. Moreover, since the said Ser Antonio made a will among his children, the testament, although less solemn with respect to solemnity—for all solemnity of the civil law is remitted by law among children, and the sole solemnity of the ius gentium suffices, as in l. hac consultissima, §. ex imperfecto, C. de testamen., and in auth. quod sine, under the same title, where it is proved that the sole writing of the father himself suffices, even though he is not otherwise a notary, provided it is established that that writing belonged to the father, at least by two witnesses, as noted there by Bartol. and Bald., and as the gloss holds in l. fina. C. fami. erc. But in our case it seems to be proved by two witnesses, or by the examined arbitrators, that that was the writing and the last will of their father; therefore it ought to establish full proof between them. And this Bartol. seems expressly to hold in l. si is, qui testamento, ff. de testam., where he says that if someone wrote his last will on a schedule, even if he did not publish it before a notary, it is nonetheless valid among children by the laws cited above. But these notwithstanding, which truly do not stand in the way of our case, although in themselves they appear to be true, I think the contrary is true, namely, that the said schedule or writing does not establish proof, even if it is found to have been written in the hand of the testator, notwithstanding the disposition of those two witnesses. And I prove this on multiple grounds. First, because it does not have a certain day, nor the consul, or the name of the prince; therefore the testament is void, even among children, as is openly proved in the said auth. quòd sine, C. de test., where it is required that a certain time must be affixed to such a writing; and Bald. openly holds this there, saying that this is a special case in which the day must necessarily be affixed in a private writing, although the contrary is generally true through l. cum tabernam, §. idem quęsiit, ff. de pigno. And the reason for this exception is that a testament is often wont to be changed; therefore the day pertains to its substance, l. 3, §. diem, ff. quemadmo. testa. aper. But in the said writing there is neither month, nor certain day, nor the name of a consul or prince; therefore, undoubtedly on this ground alone, the said writing does not establish proof, even if it were established that it had been made by the said Ser Antonio.

† Furthermore and secondly, although a testament that is less solemn by reason of solemnity establishes proof among children, it is nevertheless necessary that it be proved that it was made by the father or by his authority; and proof of this must be made at least by two suitable witnesses, as noted by the glo. and Barto. in the said l. fina. C. fami. ercis., and Bald. in auth. quòd sine, and Barto. in the said §. ex imperfecto. This is proved by reason, because the solemnity of the ius gentium is not understood to be remitted, although the solemnity of the civil law is remitted, as noted in l. filiusfamilias, ff. de donatio.; but it belongs to the ius gentium and divine law that every word should stand at least in the mouth of two or three, as in cap. licet universis, de testi., and cap. cum esses, and cap. relatum, de testa.; therefore, etc. In our case, however, although there appear to be two witnesses, they are nevertheless not suitable witnesses, even under divine law, because they are singular in their testimony. For they were not present at the same time at which the said Ser Antonio is said to have stated that his last will was contained in that schedule. Diversity in time, therefore, causes them not to be regarded as two witnesses, as in cap. nihilominus, 3, quæstio 9, cap. cum dilecti, de electio., and cap. tam literis, de test., and l. ob carmen, ff. de testi., and similar texts. Moreover, the said witnesses do not depose as to what was contained in the said schedule, and what is more, they do not firmly recognize the said schedule, or whether it was properly that which was then shown to them; indeed, one of the witnesses states that he does not know his letters; therefore he cannot perfectly know whether this is that writing which was then shown to him. For the said Ser Antonio could have shown them another writing at that time, rather than this one which is now produced. Proof, however, must conclude necessarily, as in cap. in præsentia, de probatio. Likewise, the said Ser Antonio said, as the witnesses themselves depose, that he wished to have that writing authenticated by a notary. Therefore, he did not hold it as perfected, through l. contractus, C. de fide instrumen.; for in the meantime he could have changed his will, arguing from l. si is, qui testamentum, cited above, and what Bartol. notes there. From all these things I conclude that the said writing does not establish proof, even among children. And to the contrary arguments formed above, the response is that they proceed when it is proved at least by two suitable witnesses that that writing was issued by the aforesaid Ser Antonio; likewise, when the writing has a certain day. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. One wishing to hear Mass must hear the Mass of that day.
2. Provisions that are contrary to good morals are considered in last wills as not written.
3. The prayers and sacrifices of priests greatly benefit the souls of the deceased.
4. A priest may say a private Mass on a solemn day, provided that the people are not thereby drawn away from hearing the solemn Mass of the day.
5. A bequest made to a church not otherwise specified or declared is understood to be made to the church whose parishioner the testator himself is.
6. A Mass benefits an individual more when it is celebrated for him specially, or in view of him alone, than when celebrated for souls, or for several persons together.
casus: A certain man made a testament directing that after his death he should be buried in the cathedral church, and that every day after his death, for the soul of the testator himself in perpetuity, thirty Masses of the dead should be celebrated by thirty priests, to each of whom twelve pence should be paid by his testamentary trustees from the fruits or revenues of the testator's bequeathed property. The said testator having paid his final debt to nature was buried in the cathedral church, and the aforesaid Masses were commenced in the said church by beneficed clergy, as the majority, of the said church, and by other unbeneficed clergy. From the aforesaid theme, three doubts arise: First, whether the said priests are bound according to the testator's will to say every day, even when there is a proper Mass of a Sunday feast or of Lent, a Mass of the dead; or whether it suffices to say the current Mass of the day with a commemoration of the soul of the deceased. Second, whether the said Masses are to be celebrated in the said church where the body of the said testator is, if they can be celebrated there, and not in another place, since in the testament it was not specified by him in which place they ought to be celebrated. Third, whether these Masses may be said by priests beneficed in the said church, who are obligated by reason of their said benefices to say two, three, or more Masses in the week in the said church, and thus on days on which they are obligated to celebrate Masses for their benefices, such that the said Masses may be counted in the number of those thirty priests, lawfully receiving twelve pence each; or whether they must be celebrated by mendicant friars, or others who are unbeneficed, or not obligated to celebrate for someone else.
body: With the assistance of Jesus Christ the Savior and of His mother first invoked from the heart, it seems first, regarding the first doubt, that those thirty priests are by no means bound, nor could or can they be bound, to celebrate daily the Mass of the dead, by c. quidam laicorum, de celebra. missa, where it seems to be proved that neither priests celebrating nor those hearing divine services ought to omit the Mass corresponding to the quality of the day on account of private Masses, that is, those for which one has a special devotion; to the same effect is a good text in c. & hoc attendendum, de consecra. distinctio. prima, where almost the same thing seems proved at first sight. And this seems especially to apply to Masses of the dead, since in the Masses of the day, or of the living, however solemn, prayer must also be offered for the dead, as is the text in c. penulti. eadem distinct. And this is what the text in the said c. quidam laicorum, at the end, intended to say when it says,

† that one wishing to hear Mass ought to hear the Mass of that day for the salvation of the living and also of the deceased, as though in celebrating for the living it is celebrated also for the deceased; to the aforesaid let the authority of the Archdeacon be added on the previously cited c. penul., where he says that Masses of the dead are private Masses. Secondly and principally, there appears in favor of the aforesaid conclusion a text better than all others that can be cited on this subject, in c. significatum, de præben., where it is gathered that not only if a testator, but even if the chapter of a cathedral church institutes a benefice with this burden attached, that a Mass of Saint Mary must be celebrated daily by the priest to be instituted there, such an institution does not bind the priest to celebrate such a Mass daily; rather, it suffices that he celebrate the solemnity of the Mass. For this is proved there from the fact that, although the chapter added that burden in the institution among other burdens, and afterwards asked that the institution be confirmed by the Pope, the Pope nevertheless did not approve that burden, but confirmed it with certain changes; and among other things, where in the institution it was said that he ought to celebrate a Mass of Saint Mary every day, the Pope confirmed it in these terms: that as often as he could, without prejudice to devotion and due propriety, he ought to celebrate the solemnities of Masses. For because it was not proper that on account of a private Mass the Mass of the day should be omitted, the Pope was unwilling to confirm it, as the text there clearly indicates and the doctors there hold. Nor in this matter would I require any commutation to be made by a superior; rather, I would say that where such an institution of a benefice is made even by a bishop, such an institution in that part would receive interpretation according to the form of that chapter; because an improper condition or mode attached to an institution must be regarded as not added, as the Gloss noteably states in the said c. significatum, and this seems proved in 10. quæstio. 1. c. 2. together with the Gloss; c. fin. with the notes there, de condit. apposi., supports this, as does the text in l. conditiones and l. filius, ff. de cond. inst., where it is stated that those things which offend our piety, reputation, and sense of decency, and generally

† those things which are done contrary to good morals, are regarded in last wills as unwritten. Therefore, in order that the said testator's will may conform to the common law and to propriety, it ought to be understood or reduced to the bounds of the common law, so that on account of the Mass of the dead the Mass of the day is not omitted, especially on a Sunday, above all since there is an opinion that on a Sunday one should not pray for the deceased, since it is to be presumed that out of reverence for God they rest on that day, as the Archdeacon reports on the said c. pen., although he himself does not affirm it. But notwithstanding these points, which do not conflict with our case, I consider the contrary opinion to be truer: namely, that thirty Masses of the dead ought to be said every day for the soul of the said testator, however much a Sunday or other solemn day may occur. I am moved first because it cannot be denied that this was the intention of the testator, as is clearly gathered from the words of the testament: there, 'for his soul', and there, 'Masses of the dead.' For it is certain that a Mass of the living is one thing and a Mass of the dead is another, as is proved in c. sufficit, de conse. di. 1. and c. quicunque. 26. q. 5., noted by the Archdeacon on the said c. pe.; to the same effect is the text in c. cum creatura, de cel. miss. Therefore, from the words of the testator, if the law does not expressly resist, one must not depart, l. non aliter, ff. de leg. 3.; nay rather, the canon says that the last will of a testator is to be observed in all ways, as in c. ubicunque. 13. q. 2.; and elsewhere it is also said that those things which have been assigned to a certain use by the bounty of the faithful ought not to be converted to another use, except by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff, as in cle. quia contingit, de relig. dom.; and the civil law says that the last will is to be observed as law, as in Auth. de nup. §. disponat; and this is especially to be observed when the will of the deceased concerns pious causes,

† for the prayers and sacrifices of priests greatly benefit the souls of the deceased, as in c. animæ defunctorum. 12. q. 2., and the canon urges that sins be redeemed by alms, as in c. medicinam, de pœni. di. 1. It must therefore be examined whether the disposition of the law obstructs this will of the above-written testator, or whether it is contrary to good morals. But where it is not assailed by the laws, it is to be observed in all ways. That it conflicts neither with the law nor with propriety, but is rather harmonious with the law, I clearly prove by the said c. cum creatura, de celeb. miss., where the text commands that in collegiate churches two Masses ought to be celebrated daily conventually: one for the deceased, but the other for the feast or ferial day according to their occurrence. Therefore, even on feast days it is lawful to celebrate a Mass for the dead, even conventually, which is more. And the doctors say there, especially Johannes Andreae following Hostiensis, in explaining that text, that if an anniversary of the deceased falls on a feast day, it is to be performed at least privately, and the solemn Mass of the feast in the convent; and if it is not a feast, the anniversary Mass can be said solemnly and the ferial Mass privately. And they say this can take place even in chapels, as if this were a just cause for celebrating twice, as in the said c. consuluisti; and they especially say that those to whom something is bequeathed on this account are bound to this almost by debt. Nor is this simoniacal, citing de pręben. cap. significatum, previously cited, and c. 3, ne præla. uices suas. Behold, therefore, it is clearly proved that even on solemn days, especially where something is bequeathed for the office of the dead, the Mass of the dead is not to be omitted. For 'anniversary' in the said c. cum creatura is taken for the Mass of the dead, as the Gloss notes there. Therefore, the will of the said testator is not to be altered, since it does not conflict with the law; indeed, it is rather conforming to it. The said c. quidam laicorum, cited to the contrary, seems to prove this very thing if it is well weighed. For it does not simply prohibit hearing private Masses; rather, it permits it, provided it is done out of good devotion and not out of superstition, as certain people were doing, believing that on account of them they would have better crops; and this when there are several priests in the church, so that one can celebrate the Mass of the day and another the private Mass. If, however, there were only one priest in the church, then the Mass of the day ought not to be omitted on account of a private Mass; in which case the text of the chapter speaks there at the end. And this Johannes Andreae expressly holds, saying that if there were several priests in the church, one could out of good devotion hear one private Mass in secret and hear the other Mass of the day, by c. & hoc attendendum, de conse. dist. 1.

† And thus a priest can say a private Mass on a solemn day, provided that the people are not thereby drawn away from hearing the solemn Mass of the day. Therefore it ought to be said privately, and this the text intended and proves, if it is well weighed, in the said c. & hoc attendendum. Hence it does not prohibit a solemn Mass from being said then, but rather permits it, provided that it does not pose an impediment to the solemn Mass. And that even on a Sunday a Mass of the dead could be said in the aforesaid manner is affirmed by the Archdeacon in the said c. & hoc attendendum, and was sufficiently indicated in the decision of that chapter, as he himself relates there, and he indicates the same in the said c. pen. From these points the answer to the contrary arguments cited above is clear. For they proceed when there is only one priest in the church, or when the same priest is bound to say daily one private Mass, which does not appear proper, and is proved in the said c. significatum. But in our case the testator did not bind, nor did he order the said thirty Masses of the dead to be celebrated every day by the same priests, nor in the same church, but simply arranged that they should be said by thirty priests. I say that this ought to be understood so that, without prejudice to the Mass that is to be said in the church according to the requirement of the day, thirty Masses of the dead ought to be celebrated there by other priests, who may be changed and chosen with the knowledge of the executors of the testament. And from this no absurdity arises, nor is the testator's will obstructed; nay, in no way do I think it equitable that the Mass of the day should be said with a commemoration of the dead; because since more suffrages are offered for the dead in a Mass of the dead than where there is a mere commemoration, such suffrages ought not to be withdrawn from the deceased, especially since for saying them an alms of twelve pence is bestowed. For we ought to succor the deceased as richly as possible, by the argument in the said c. cum creatura. Furthermore, if a commemoration were to benefit as much as the whole Mass of the dead, to what end would the Church have instituted a special Mass for the dead, as in the laws cited above, especially since in every Mass prayer is also to be offered for the dead, as in the said c. pen.? I conclude therefore, as above, that if priests can be found, thirty Masses of the dead ought to be said every day for the soul of that testator, yet in such a way that the one Mass of the day, which is customarily said at the high altar, is not withdrawn from the church; nor must they always be said by the same priests, at least throughout the whole year, by the argument of the said c. significatum. And this concerning the first doubt. Concerning the second doubt, namely in what place or church the said Masses ought to be celebrated, since the testator did not expressly designate a certain church, I think it should briefly be said that it must be in the church in which the testator himself is buried, especially since it is a cathedral church, by the text in Auth. de eccle. tit. §. si quis autem in nomine Dei, where it is said that if anyone leaves an inheritance or a legacy in the name of the great God and of the Savior Jesus Christ, without specifically designating to whom it ought to be assigned, in that case the inheritance or legacy thus left ought to come to the church of that place in which the testator had his domicile in that city where he is buried.
