Therefore it ought to be given to the cathedral church; but in our case the testator had his domicile in that place, especially since he is buried there, since he in a certain manner chose his domicile there after death, according to that word of the Psalmist: 'and their sepulchres are their houses for ever.' What is read and noted in c. cum grauia, 13. quæst. 2., and 12. quæst. 2. cap. aurum supports this, where it is held that the bodies of the dead are said to rest in cemeteries or churches; therefore, by every consideration, the said Masses ought to be said in the cathedral church. Furthermore, in our case the matter is clearer, since the testator had a church in mind, because he ordered Masses to be celebrated, and Masses cannot be said except in churches and consecrated places, de consecra. distinct. 1. cap. nullus presbyter, and cap. unicuique, and following; therefore he tacitly understood a church, by the argument in l. interdum, ff. de uer. ob. A bequest,

† however, made to a church not otherwise specified or declared is understood to be made to the church whose parishioner the testator himself is, by the argument in l. quæ conditio. §. cum in testamento, ff. de condict. & demonstra., where Bartolus affirms this, and that text supports it quite well; for it is said there that if a testator ordered something to be done in the forum, and it was not specified in which forum, it is understood of the forum of that municipality in which the testator had his domicile. But these Masses are to be said after the death of the testator, and for the soul of the testator himself; therefore it is to be presumed that the testator had in mind that church in which the testator chose burial, since he is said in the future to be its parishioner with respect to the divine services to be celebrated there. For in doubtful matters we ought to consider what is more likely, and that which is generally accustomed to be done, as in regu. inspicimus in obscuris, de regu. iur. lib. sexto; and that which can be gathered from conjectures is called the evident will of the testator, l. licet imperator, ff. de lega. primo. But it is more likely that the testator had in mind the church of burial. For it is more fitting that Masses should be celebrated for his soul there than elsewhere, since they are aided by the patronage of those saints in whose honor that church was built and consecrated, as in c. non existimentur, at the end, 13. quæst. 2.; and there bodies are more easily defended from unclean spirits, as the Gloss notes in c. cum grauia, eadem causa & quæstione; therefore it is more fitting that prayers be poured forth for him there. From all these things it is presumed that the testator had a greater affection toward that church; therefore he is to be presumed to have had it in mind, by the argument in l. nulli, C. de sacros. ecc.; what Cinus notes in l. 1, C. de sacros. ecc. and Speculator in tit. de instru. edi. §. nunc, under the word 'sed quid si testator' supports this. And the text in l. cum acutissimi, C. de fideic., and in l. generaliter. §. cum autem, C. de insti. & subst., with similar texts, supports exceedingly well the consideration of affection. Likewise, where most people are concerned, they are accustomed to offer suffrages for deceased family members sooner in the churches in which their bodies are buried than elsewhere; which seems harmonious with the law, by the argument in the said c. cum graui, with what is noted there in the Gloss; therefore the testator seems to have had that church in mind, by the argument in the said rule inspicimus, and in l. semper, ff. de uerb. sign. But if they cannot conveniently be celebrated there for the soul of the deceased himself, they ought also to be celebrated in other churches, by an excellent argument in c. nos quidem, de testa., and l. legatum, ff. de usufr. leg., and in Auth. de eccle. tit. §. si quis autem unum sanctorum, col. 9, since God is everywhere, 12. quæst. 2. c. ubicunque, with similar passages. And this concerning the second point. I conclude therefore that in the church where the body of the said testator is buried, the said Masses are to be celebrated, and if they cannot be suitably celebrated there, according to the things which I have said above on the preceding doubt and those which I will say on the following, they shall celebrate them in other churches. Now, approaching the third doubt, it seems first to suffice that the said Masses may lawfully be celebrated by priests otherwise beneficed and bound to celebrate in the said church, with the testator's will by no means resisting; so that they may be counted in their number by c. non mediocriter, de consecra. distin. 5, where Saint Jerome says that when a psalm or Mass is said for all souls, nothing less is received than if it were said for each one of them; which seems special in the sacraments according to some, as the Gloss notes there, on account of the Holy Spirit, who is not given by measure, as in c. quemquam, de consec. distin. 4. For since the value of prayer and other suffrages is considered chiefly from the perspective of charity, by the argument of 1. q. 1. cap. ipsi sacerdotes, and charity is not diminished if its affection is distributed among many, but is rather increased (for charity is not envious, nor does it seek its own, de pœ. di. 2. c. charitas, and de pœ. di. 6. c. 1. on the line credendum); therefore it is worth as much if it is celebrated for many as if for one alone; and consequently one must conclude that it does not matter whether the said Masses are celebrated by other beneficed clergy who are obligated to celebrate in the said church, or by others obligated to no one. Secondly, a common consideration could be adduced: for if on one day two or three causes for fasting concur, as happens in this year in the month of February (for there occur on the same day the Lenten fast, the Ember fast, and the vigil of Saint Matthew), all can be satisfied by a single fast; to this effect is c. 2, de obser. ieiu., noted by Johannes Andreae in c. cum in cunctis, de celebr. miss., and what he himself notes on the merging of penalties concurring at the same time, and through the Gloss in c. 2, de magi. Thirdly, the presumed will of the testator supports this, namely that the aforesaid Masses be said in the church of burial, as I said on the preceding doubt; which could not easily occur unless they were said by those beneficed there. Nor does it seem proper to say that clerics beneficed there should be excluded from that alms, since the testator is presumed to have had an affection toward them, by submitting his body to that church and consequently to their prayer, by the argument in the said c. non æstimemus, and c. cum grauia, previously cited. But truly, I think the contrary opinion must be sustained entirely: namely, that by those who are on that day otherwise obligated to celebrate, the said Masses ought by no means to be celebrated, but rather by those who are free; so that they offer the sacrifice specially and in consideration of the testator alone. I prove this first through the words of the said testator, in that he ordered that the said Masses should be celebrated for his soul. But if they were celebrated by priests otherwise obligated to celebrate, they would not be celebrated for the soul of the testator himself, but rather principally for the soul of those who instituted the said benefices, since that obligation came first, by the argument in l. qui prior, ff. de iud. and l. cum ex pluribus, ff. de sol., and excellently through Innocent in c. cum iamdudum, de pręben., with similar texts. Or if we were to posit that it were celebrated equally for both, it would nevertheless not be true to say that it was celebrated for the soul of the testator; to this effect is a good text in similar matters in c. cum in illis, de præbend. lib. 6, at the end, where it is said that if a mandate is given to provide a benefice belonging to the collation of one person, the mandate cannot be fulfilled in a benefice whose collation belongs to him together with another; to the same effect is the text in l. si fuerit, ff. de rebus dub., where it is said that a legacy made to one of the relatives who first ascends the Capitol is impeded if two are said to have arrived together, or if it was made to him who built a monument and several are said to have built it; and what Bartolus fully notes in l. hoc art., ff. de hære. inst., supports this. Furthermore and more strongly, in case of doubt one is presumed to have chosen the way through which more abundant provision is made, by the argument in l. 3, ff. de mili. testa.; c. super hoc, de renunc., and l. cum de indebito, ff. de prob., with similar passages, support this. But it is certain that in so far as suffrages are considered from the perspective of satisfaction, they benefit more when they are performed for one person than for several, because in so far as a suffrage is satisfactory, it has a finite efficacy; therefore it benefits less when it is distributed among several, by the argument in c. cum M., de constitutio. and c. 1, de institu., with similar texts. And this position was held by Saint Thomas on the 4th book of the Sentences, dist. 45, quæst. 4, art. 1 and 2; Johannes Andreae affirms it, and Calderinus after him, and commonly other doctors following there in c. fraternitatem, de sepu.; and it seems to be the mind of the Archdeacon in the said c. non mediocriter, where he affirms

† that a Mass benefits an individual more when it is celebrated for him specially, or in view of him alone, than when it is celebrated for all or for several together. Therefore the said testator seems to have willed that the said Masses should be said specially for him, and not together for others, especially since his words indicate this clearly enough, since he willed that they should be celebrated for his soul; therefore for his soul and in view of him alone; to this effect is the good text in c. cum Apostolica, together with the penultimate Gloss, de concess. præben. And this consideration seems to conclude this position completely. For where the words and the matter are clear, there is no need for interpretation, l. ille aut ille, ff. de lega. 3, and c. fin., de uerbo. sig., and the said l. non aliter, de lega. 3. Likewise and thirdly, beneficed clergy are bound to say the Mass of the day according to the calendar; but the testator willed that Masses of the dead should be celebrated for his soul. Therefore the will of the testator cannot be satisfied by them, as is gathered from what I have said fully on the first doubt. Fourthly, the text in l. reipublicæ causa, ff. ex quib. cau. ma., supports this, where it is said that those alone are said to be absent on state business who are not absent for their own advantage, but are absent under compulsion; to the same effect is l. si cui, under the same title; but since the said beneficed clergy are otherwise bound to celebrate by reason of their benefices out of the advantage that they receive, they would not be said to celebrate for the soul of the testator, since they celebrate under compulsion out of the advantage of the benefices that they hold. Nay rather, and lastly, many laws support this which indicate that someone is not seen to do something from a certain cause when he was bound to do it from another cause, as is proved in l. sed & si. §. 1, ff. ad exhib., and ff. de peti. hære. l. sed & si. §. quod ait, and ff. de rei uend. l. si res; and what the Gloss notes in c. cum ab omni, de uita & hone. cler., and in c. statutum. §. insuper, de rescrip. lib. 6, supports this. Therefore these beneficed clergy cannot say that they celebrate for the soul of the deceased, since they were otherwise bound to do this by reason of their benefices. To the contrary arguments framed above, an answer can easily be given. And first, to c. non mediocriter, I say that that chapter is understood in multiple ways, as noted there in the Gloss by the Archdeacon; and that solution pleases me: that those words are referred to the priests themselves, so that it is worth as much to them to celebrate for one as for a hundred; or it is understood when a priest says Mass for each individual with sadness and anxiety, for one Mass said with joy and good devotion for a hundred is worth no less than if it were said for each with anxiety. And these solutions accord well with the mind of that chapter and the words preceding there. Or thirdly, and beyond the Gloss, it can be understood in so far as a suffrage is considered with respect to charity; but it is otherwise when it is satisfactory, as Saint Thomas held in the place cited above and our doctors commonly in the said c. fraternitatem. To the second motive, that by a single fast several causes for fasting can be satisfied, I respond that this applies when each of those causes concerns a certain day; therefore it is necessary that it be satisfied on that day in the best manner possible. But in our case this reason ceases, since through several priests the will of the testator can be satisfied on the same day. To the third and last, I say that although the testator is presumed to love the clerics of that church of burial, he is nevertheless presumed to love his own soul more, by the argument in c. licet, at the end, de reg., and de pœn. dist. 4, in the chapter hæc quæ de charitate. For a man ought to make no exchange for his soul, as in c. Matthæus, de spon.; therefore it is to be presumed that he had in mind that manner through which his soul could be more richly and more quickly assisted. And in the same way I speak with respect to the church: for, other things being equal, I concede that he seems to have had that church in mind. But in the said church, because of a lack of suitable priests, he cannot be so well assisted. He seems to have willed that they should be said wherever, because places do not sanctify, but merits do, 60. dist. c. non loca, and c. multi; and for this reason perhaps the testator by no means restricted himself to a certain church, but spoke generally. And all churches are members of one universal church, whose bridegroom is Christ Jesus, as in c. firmiter. §. una, de sum. tri., and c. Nouatianus episcopus, 7. q. 1., and c. loquitur, and c. pudenda, 24. q. 1. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus de Tudeschis, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument: 1. Collectae cannot be imposed on foreigners dwelling in a place where they have not yet established [domicile].
casus: It is called into question whether the distinguished doctor of arts and medicine, Master Ioannes de Salmoneta, could be assessed for tax or placed on the tax-roll (estimo) in the city of Siena, in which he owns certain property, has married a wife, and has resided for more than ten years, especially with respect to his personal practice, or what he earns by reason of teaching, or in view and by the industry of his person.
body: Having invoked the protection of the Savior Jesus Christ, it seems at first that one must say yes; for although he is not a citizen of this distinguished city of Siena, according to what is read and noted in l. ciues, C. de incolis, lib. 10, he is nonetheless an incola of this city. For domicile makes an incola, d. l. ciues. Moreover, that he established domicile in the said city is evidently proven by the fact that he dwelt there for ten years and more; for from so long a delay even students are deemed to acquire a domicile, as is proven in l. 2 in prin. C. eod. And Bartol. affirmed that this is to be held in a doubtful case in l. lex Cornelia, § si domum, ff. de iniu., and Ioann. Andr. following Aegid. in prooemio Greg. and c. quod clericis, de foro compe. Furthermore, to incolae may be enjoined munera, or collectae, which are imposed on persons on account of property, just as to citizens, as is proven in l. incola, ff. ad municipi., and l. rescripto, in fin. ff. de mu. & ho. Indeed, the gl. no. in d. l. incola stated that after the imposition of a collecta an incola cannot change his status as incola by departing thence to the prejudice of the enjoined burden, since he has already been preempted, an argument in l. si quis postea, ff. de iudi., and l. penultim. ff. de iurisd. omnium iudic., and cap. proposuisti, de foro compe. And, above all, the acquisition of immovable property and the bringing of a wife into the said city seem to prove the intention of establishing domicile in the said city, said cit. l. ciues, § 1. But notwithstanding these points, I deem that the contrary proceeds in law in our case. For first, it is certain,

† that upon foreigners dwelling in a place, who have not yet established domicile there, personal burdens cannot be imposed, nor collectae which are imposed on persons on account of property even existing there. For these cannot be imposed except on subjects; the text is clear in d. l. rescripto, ff. de mu. & ho., and there Bartol. confirms this more clearly, saying that for that reason, because clerics are not subject to laymen, such collectae cannot be imposed upon them. And the same was affirmed by l. placet, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi., and l. unica, C. de mulie. & in quo loc. mu. lib. 10, Bald. in d. l. placet, and this is supported by what he noted in auth. item nulla communitas, C. de episc. & cler., and Car. in cap. fin. de ui. & hone. cle., and clem. praesenti, de censi., and in c. 1 de immu. eccle. lib. 6. It only remains therefore to examine whether the said Master Giovanni established domicile in the place by reason of the aforesaid, so that he may thus be called an incola. And first I say that, although in case of doubt one is said to establish domicile in the place of habitation by a stay of ten years, as in said l. 2, that nevertheless proceeds unless other conjectures militate to the contrary, which declare that he dwelt there for the whole time for another cause; when these concur, even if he dwelt in the place for a hundred years, he is not said on this account to establish domicile there, as is read and noted in l. quaesitum, in prin. de legato. 2. For domicile is established by intent, as in l. si quis instructus, ff. ad municipa., as for instance where he established his hearth there with the intention of not departing thence, as in d. l. ciues; but intent is proven from conjectures, as in l. licet imperator, ff. de lega. 1, and in clem. exiui, de uerbo. sig., and cap. 2 de renun. lib. 6, and l. dolum, C. de dolo, and similar texts. In our case, however, very many conjectures and also most evident proofs occur, showing that the said Master Giovanni did not have the intention of establishing domicile in Siena. First, because he came to this city of Siena as a foreigner, hired to lecture in medicine, just like other foreigners, and when the first contract had expired he was re-hired again, and frequently in succession as a foreigner, continually treated as a foreigner with respect to the amount of salary, and in his re-hiring he always had occasion to say that unless he were re-hired with a competent salary, he intended to depart thence, as other foreigners do. For from these things the intention of this Master Giovanni is sufficiently declared, that he did not intend by that stay to establish domicile here, an excellent argument in l. Nesennius, ff. de neg. gest. Indeed, said Ant. de But. in poe. Gre. pal. maintained that in the case of a student the sole conjecture of study suffices to declare the intention that he did not stay for so long a time for the purpose of establishing domicile there. Concerning which statement, however, doubt could be raised by d. l. 2, C. de incolis, which speaks of a student; but in our case, in which the aforesaid conjectures and proofs of intent concur, I think there is no room to hesitate in any way. Furthermore, during the time of his habitation he never bore any burdens as a citizen or incola, which provides the greatest support to this conclusion of ours, ar. i. l. 1, ed muni. Moreover, the acquisition or purchase of immovable property made by the said Master Giovanni in the said city of Siena is not sufficient to make him bound to personal burdens, as is the clear text in l. libertus, § sola domus, ff. ad munic., and there Bart. affirms that even collectae cannot be imposed upon foreign possessors, on account of those things which I have said above. Nor does it stand in the way that he married a wife in this city; for bringing a wife does not induce citizenship in a place, nor the status of incola, as in d. l. ciues; rather, I say that the wife herself becomes an incola or citizen of the place of origin of the husband, and there, and not in the place of her second origin, they must undergo the burdens of the fatherland, as is the text in l. fi. § idem rescripserunt, ff. ad muni., and there by Bar. and by the gl. in l. ciues, and l. origine, C. de mune. & ho. li. x. Moreover, the wife changes her forum, at least with respect to burdens, and not the husband, because the wife is bound to follow the husband, and not vice versa, as in c. unaquaeque mulier, 13, q. 2, read and noted in c. 1 de coniu. lepro., and similar texts. And let these suffice. Nicol. Abb.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If anyone has been ordained a bishop and is not received by the church to which he was ordained, he ought not to be cast out from his prior dignity.
2. If the Pope translated any bishop to an archiepiscopal see, he having first been absolved from the bond of the prior church, the bishopric does not become vacant immediately by that absolution and translation, but begins to be vacant after the translated bishop has given his consent.
3. The benefices of one elected and confirmed as bishop do not become vacant except after full translation, which is effected by consecration and corporeal possession.
4. Spiritual acts do not admit of a condition.
5. A prince, by knowingly performing an act contrary to the law, is seen to dispense with regard to it.
6. The Pope can, out of certain knowledge and with inquiry into the cause, confer two bishoprics on one person.
7. A bishop cannot acquire another bishopric by common law.
casus: The fact upon which counsel is sought is set forth in the terms written below, namely: the bishop of Speyer, at his own postulation and instance, was translated by Pope Martin V to the archiepiscopal see of Trier, he having first, as is customary and lawful, been absolved from the bond of the church of Speyer to which he was bound, and provision of the church as vacant through the aforesaid translation was made by the same Martin to the illustrious man Lord Adolph of Germany, now licentiate in decrees. Finally, after the said provisions, the said translatee, at his postulation, obtained through the same Roman Pontiff to be decorated with the pallium of the archbishop. Lastly, it happened that the said translatee could not obtain corporeal possession of the said archbishopric on account of the resistance of someone who de facto intruded himself into the archbishopric. For which reason he strives to hold the said church of Speyer as before, while the same Lord Adolph contradicts this and says that the said church of Speyer must by law be surrendered to him as having been lawfully provided with it. It is asked, what is the law?
body: Having humbly invoked from the heart the protection of the Savior Jesus Christ and of his most glorious Mother, it seems in the first place that by law the said translatee is by no means to be compelled to surrender the church of Speyer, unless he first obtains peaceful corporeal possession of the church of Trier, or unless it is through his own fault that he does not obtain that possession. For the first church becomes vacant by translation to the second, as in c. 2 de transla. præla., and c. bonæ 2 de postu. præl., and 21 q. 2 c. si quis translatus. But one is not properly said to be translated unless he has first had possession of the second church, as the notable gloss says in the said c. si quis iam translatus; to this makes excellently c. cum in cunctis, § cum uerò, de ele. Therefore, this man ought not, by the word 'translated', to be constrained to relinquish the former church, unless he first obtains corporeal possession of the second. In the second place, this seems principally proven by the notable text, especially joined with the gloss, in c. si quis, dist. 92, where it is said,

† that if anyone was ordained a bishop and is not received by the church to which he was ordinary, he ought not to be cast out from his former dignity, even if in the meantime it was conferred upon another, according to the notable gloss there, which adds this last point to that text, by the argument of the said c. cum in cunctis, and 7 q. 1 c. eos, and C. de repu. hære. l. ult. And it is to be weighed that the text there speaks even if the first benefice were a dignity; therefore the same must be said in our case. The case there, joined with the gloss, therefore seems to be directly on our question. In the third place, an excellent argument is furnished by c. si beneficia, de præben. lib. 6, where it is held that if anyone resigned his benefice on account of another conferred upon him, which is afterwards found to be due to another, it can be reclaimed, provided he relinquishes the second without difficulty to the one to whom it is due; behold, therefore, that a benefice lawfully conferred on another can be reclaimed, since the second cannot be lawfully retained. Let us therefore say the same in our case, so that, notwithstanding the provision made to Lord Adolph, the translatee can retain the former church, namely Speyer, since he cannot take possession of the second church. For he seems to have been translated and absolved from the bond of the former church under a certain tacit condition, namely if he could obtain possession of the second church, by the argument of the said chapter si beneficia. For since this translation was made in favor of the said translatee, it ought not to redound to his injury and to the diminution of his honor, by the argument in the rule quod ob gratiam, de regu. iur. lib. 6, and l. quod fauore, C. de legi. To this makes what Io. Mona. noted in a similar case in the chapter generali, de elect. lib. 6, whose statement Ioan. And. reported and did not reject in the said rule quod ob gratiam, in Mercurialibus; for he said

† that if the Pope translated a bishop to an archiepiscopal see, having first absolved him from the bond of the former church, the bishopric does not become vacant immediately through that absolution and translation, but begins to be vacant after the translated bishop has given his consent: because he seems to be absolved under a tacit condition, namely if he should give his consent; and he gives the reason: because since this translation is made in his favor, it ought not to redound to his injury. The lord Fr. Zab., Card. Flor., and many other doctors advised the same in the case of the Bishop of Florence, whom the Pope, having absolved him from the bond of his bishopric, promoted in his absence to Cardinal; for they concluded that the bishopric was not vacant except from the time when the said bishop gave his consent, and on this account that bishop, before giving consent, administered the bishopric for almost a year. The same must be said in our case, so that the said translation and absolution seem made under a tacit condition, namely if he could obtain possession of the second church, since only then is he properly said to be translated, as is noted in the said c. si quis iam transslatus; otherwise the translation would turn to his injury, which must not be said. In the fourth place, many laws support this side which induce the vacancy of the first incompatible benefice through the acquisition of the second, not from the time of the provision of the second, but after the obtaining of peaceful and corporeal possession of it, as in c. licet episcopus, de præb. li. 6, and clem. si plures, eod. tit., and c. commissa, de ele. li. 6, and the said c. si quis iam transslatus, joined with the gloss cum similibus; and a virtually express text on our case appears in c. cum in cunctis, previously cited, in § cum uerò, where it is clear

† that the benefices of one elected and confirmed as bishop do not become vacant except after full translation to the bishopric, which is caused by consecration and corporeal possession, as is there stated. Behold, therefore, that benefices incompatible with a bishopric do not become vacant by the mere provision of the bishopric, but it is necessary that corporeal possession of the bishopric itself be had first. Therefore the same must be said in our case; for although two bishoprics in the same person are incompatible by common law, 21 q. 2 c. sit in unaquaque, and 7 q. 1 c. sicut, nevertheless the vacancy of the first ought not in effect to be induced except after possession of the second has been obtained. And that that text applies to two bishoprics, the gloss in c. relatio, 21 q. 1, seems tacitly to intend, which in the case of two bishoprics cites that text. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that from this it would happen that this translatee would have two bishoprics at the same time: because it does not seem absurd that he should have the first habitually and actually, and the second in respect of title, since he cannot have corporeal possession of it, as is proved in c. pastoralis, 7 q. 1, where there is a notable text to this effect. But notwithstanding the aforesaid, which by no means obstruct our case, I judge that the contrary proceeds in law. For I think that that church of Speyer became purely and simply vacant through the absolution and translation previously made, and that it was lawfully provided to the said Lord Adolph, and consequently that the said translatee is to be compelled by legal remedies freely to surrender the church of Speyer to be governed and disposed of by Lord Adolph as by the true pastor of that church. I am moved to this opinion in the first place principally by that rule of law, whoever wills the consequent is deemed to will the antecedent, as in c. cum M. de consti., and l. illud, ff. de acq. hær., c. ex parte, de sponsa., c. prudentia, c. præterea, de of. del., and l. ad legatum, and l. ad rem mobilem, ff. de procu. But the former Bishop of Speyer pressed with the lord Pope that provision be made to him of the archbishopric of Trier. Therefore he seems to have willed and consented that, before all things, he should be absolved from the bond by which he was held to the church of Speyer. For he could not by law be transferred even verbally to another see unless he was first absolved from the former; and so it is also according to the custom of the Roman Curia observed of old, as is proved in the said chapter 2 de transla. præla., and chapter bonæ 2 de postu. præla., Ioan. Mona. in the said chapter generali, and Ioan. And. in the said rule quod ob gratiam, in princ. quæst. Since, therefore, by his own consent he was absolved from that former church, and thus consequently it became vacant, 7 q. 1 c. sicut, in 1, and in § ecce, he cannot, by a circumstance supervening de facto, retain that former church, especially after provision was made to another: because to those who renounce their rights expressly or tacitly, re-entry to them is not granted, nor is there locus poenitentiae, as in c. quàm periculosum, 7 q. 1, and c. ex transmissa, de renun., and c. ex ore, de priui., and an action once extinguished does not revive, de conse. dist. 4 c. quæris, and l. qui res, § aream, ff. de sol. Nor can the said translatee allege that he consented to this act under a tacit condition of obtaining the second church: both

† because these spiritual acts do not admit of a condition, as in c. 2 de ele. li. 6, and in the rule actus legitimi, de reg. iu. li. 6, and he who renounces a benefice must renounce purely and entirely, as in c. ex parte 2, joined with the gloss, de of. dele.; and because he expressed no condition when, through himself or through another, he pressed with Pope Martin that provision be made to him of the archbishopric. Therefore, no condition ought to be understood, as in c. unico, at the end, 32 q. 8. Especially in our subject matter, which by its nature ought to be pure and simple; nor does a condition retained in the mind provide relief, as in l. si repetendi causam, C. de condi. ob cau. Furthermore, the said translatee can find no legal refuge in this, since he obtained the archiepiscopal pallium, which is not customary for the Roman Church to grant except to one who strongly and frequently requests it, as in c. Prisca, 100 dist., noted in c. significasti, de ele. Therefore he consented to the absolution previously made concerning him with respect to the church of Speyer, especially since he requested the pallium after the provision of the church of Speyer was made to Lord Adolph. Whence, by this act proper to an archbishop, he seems most clearly to have consented not only to the absolution previously made, but also to the provision of Lord Adolph, by the excellent argument in the said c. ex ore, de his quæ fi. a maio. par. capi., and c. solicitudinem, de appel., and l. ubi repugnantia, ff. de reg. iur., and c. cum M. de consti. Therefore the said church of Speyer became vacant through that translation made in the aforesaid manner purely and absolutely. And Ioan. Mona. clearly held this opinion, if it is well weighed, in the said c. generali, and Ioan. And. after him in the said rule quod ob gratiam, when they say that if the Pope translates an absent person, even in favor of the person, the first bishopric does not become vacant except from the time of consent given by the translatee: but in our case the said translatee consented repeatedly, as is evident from the aforesaid. Egid. Cremon. seems to have held the same in his disputation, as Ioan. And. reports in the said rule quod ob gratiam, who said more, namely that the first bishopric became vacant immediately after the translation was made by the Pope, without awaiting the consent of the translatee: because his consent depends on the will of the Pope; this is supported by 7 q. 1 c. scias, and Io. An. seems there openly to approve vacancy at least in that case in which the bishop was postulated by the chapter as archbishop, and he, although he did not consent, nevertheless did not contradict, but submitted himself to the will of the lord Pope. For the translation having followed by the Pope concerning an absent person, Io. And. affirms that the bishopric immediately became vacant, since it was not made entirely without his consent; therefore, much more so ought the bishopric of Speyer immediately to become vacant in our case through that translation verbally made, since the said Bishop of Speyer openly consented to it from the beginning, both by asking for the pallium and by strongly pressing for his provision. Therefore, by the aforesaid, this case seems most clearly decided in favor of Lord Adolph, the providee. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the said translatee remains without a bishopric; because it must be imputed to himself, as if he sought this. For he could have thought from the beginning that this impediment might occur, a good argument in l. si quis domum, ff. loca., especially since it was said openly at Rome by the father of the intruder that no one besides that intruder was able to have possession of the archbishopric; and also because he is not said to be entirely without an archbishopric, because he who has an action to recover a thing seems to have the thing itself, l. qui actionem, de regul. iuris. Let him proceed, therefore, by legal remedies to obtain possession, and let him surrender the bishopric which he possesses without any title, as is clearly evident from the aforesaid. Likewise, since the said Pope of certain knowledge provided the said Lord Adolph to the bishopric of Speyer as being vacant, there was no room for the disposition of c. cum in cunctis, § cum uerò, previously cited, presupposing without prejudice to truth that that chapter had application to multiple bishoprics. For the Pope, by not awaiting that possession of the second bishopric should first be had, seems to have wished to dispense by a contrary act against the disposition of that law, as in l. idem Vlpianus, ff. de execu. tut., and what Bar. notes in l. quidam consulebant, ff. de re iud., and Inn. in c. ueniens, de filiis presby., and Hostiensis in c. diuersis fallaciis, de cle. coniu., and Bal. in the repetition of l. Barbarius, ff. de of. præsi., in which laws it is commonly read and noted that

† a prince, by consciously doing an act contrary to law, is deemed to dispense concerning it. Now, in our case, it was clear from the certain knowledge of the Pope that he himself had previously absolved the Bishop of Speyer from the bond of that church, and provided Lord Adolph to that church made vacant by his act; whence in one's own act, especially in a prince, it cannot be presumed except from certain knowledge, as in cle. unica, de proba., with what is noted there; to which makes what the gloss notes in cle. 1 de iudi., and in cle. pastoralis, § præterea, de of. dele., and by Inn. in c. statutum, which formerly began præsertim, de rescr. li. 6. Moreover, the Pope could, through that act of absolution, declare a pure vacancy of the church, by what the singular gloss notes in c. per principalem, 9 q. 3. And he seems to have so willed, since after that act he proceeded to provide the said Lord Adolph to it as vacant, arg. in l. Labeo, ff. de suppel. lega., and c. dilecti, de app., and 9 q. 3 c. æstimat. For the Pope knew that provision ought not to be made to another of a church that is not purely vacant, especially a bishopric, since spiritual adultery would threaten there, 7 q. 1 c. sicut, 21 q. 2 c. sicut in una; and Ioan. And. clearly assists this conclusion in c. ex ore, de his, quæ fi. a maio. par. cap., upon the verse confirmatus, in the last solution, when he says that there the provostship of one elected and confirmed as bishop was conferred before consecration out of the certain knowledge of the Pope; therefore the collation was valid, notwithstanding that the time fixed for consecrating bishops had not elapsed, because he seems to have dispensed over that law, arg. c. proposuit, de conces. præb., which is notable. The same must be said in a similar case, presupposing without prejudice to truth that the first bishopric had not purely become vacant before obtaining possession of the second; nevertheless, since the Pope knowingly previously provided another to the first bishopric, the provision holds, nor ought its effect to be impeded by a supervening fact, since the marriage has already been initiated and confirmed between the church of Speyer and the said Adolph, de transla. præla. c. 2, at the end, and c. cum inter, de elect., with similar authorities. Finally, all the rules of law make in favor of Lord Adolph; for it is certain that from the moment the Pope knowingly absolved the Bishop of Speyer from the bond by which he was bound to that church, the church of Speyer itself was entirely released from the law of that bishop, wherefore she was deservedly able freely to marry whomever she wished, 7 q. 1 cap. in apibus, § ecce, and cap. sicut, and de secun. nup. cap. penult. and ult. Therefore, he now holds the said church of Speyer occupied entirely without title. And if we were to say the contrary, an absurdity would follow, that the same man would be archbishop and bishop of different churches, and thus the spiritual marriage which is contracted between bishop and church would be violated, in token of which he wears a ring, as is noted in chapter clerici, de uita & hone. cler., and 7 quest. 1 chapter sicut, and chapter 2 de transla. præla. Nor does chapter pastoralis, in the same cause and question, cited to the contrary, stand in the way: for there the Pope of certain knowledge conferred upon one expelled from his own see a bishopric due to no one else.

† For the Pope of certain knowledge and with knowledge of the cause can confer two bishoprics upon one person, as is the notable text in cap. relatio, cited above, 21 q. 1. But in our case the Pope did not confer the church of Speyer anew upon this translatee; on the contrary, he previously absolved him from the right of that church; furthermore, the church of Speyer was conferred upon another, namely Lord Adolph. Whence, since she is betrothed to another, she ought not to be detained by this translatee as a harlot without any title, contrary to the said cap. sicut. For spiritual adultery is committed when the church of another is unjustly detained, just as carnal adultery is committed with the spouse of another, said cap. sicut in una, 21 q. 1 and 2, with similar authorities. Therefore, from the premises, the intention of Lord Adolph, the bishop-elect of Speyer, is most evidently founded. It remains now that we respond to those things that I adduced above on the opposing side, to which, if the premises are diligently weighed, the response will be very easy. And first, when it is said that one is not said to be fully translated before he obtains corporeal possession, by the said cap. si quis iam translatus, I reply that properly one is not said to be fully translated, since the vacancy of the church of Speyer was induced by the absolution previously made by the Pope, the Bishop of Speyer himself consenting, as I said above; especially since, after the provision was made to Lord Adolph, he urgently requested the archiepiscopal pallium, in which the fullness of the pontifical office is conferred with the appellation of the archiepiscopal name, as in cap. nisi, de autho. & usu pal., and c. quod sicut, de ele.; and thus he most clearly approved the translation made concerning him, and the preceding absolution, and the provision of Lord Adolph that followed from it. The second motive concerning cap. si quis, dist. 92, does not stand in the way: for it speaks not of a translated bishop, but of one newly ordained, who ought not to be cast out from his former dignity if he cannot obtain possession of the bishopric. For this is law, as is proved in c. cum in cunctis, § cum uerò, de elect., although in the meantime his first dignity was conferred on another, as the gloss says there; which I understand when it was conferred on another without his consent before he had possession of the bishopric, which was contrary to c. cum in cunctis, previously cited. For I think it otherwise if it had been conferred on another with his consent: because then, on account of supervening resistance, the first collation lawfully made ought not to be revoked, by what is held in c. post electionem, de conces. præben., joined with the first gloss, and the said c. ex ore; this is supported by the rule factum legitimè, and the rule scienti & consentienti, de regu. iur. lib. 6. And the reason for the difference between the minor benefices that were previously held and a bishopric previously held is that minor benefices do not become vacant through the provision made of a bishopric unless the providee or elect first obtains full right, namely that he has been consecrated, or the time for consecrating bishops has passed, and he has obtained corporeal possession of the bishopric, as is proved in the said § cum uerò; deservedly, if he cannot have possession of the bishopric, he ought not to be cast down from his former dignity, as in the said cap. si quis, whose title he still holds. But in our case, before the translation, the vacancy of the church of Speyer was induced through the absolution made by the Pope, and provision was made by the Pope himself to another, namely Lord Adolph. Which vacancy indeed does not cease to be on account of resistance de facto occurring around the see of Trier; nor ought the collation or provision made to the other to be delayed or quashed, since this is provided by no law. Furthermore, in the case of minor benefices previously held, it is not necessary that absolution previously intervene, because a spiritual marriage is not strictly contracted with them, as is noted in chapter clerici, de ui. & ho. cler., and chapter finale, de postu. præla. Whence it is not incongruous that one holding minor benefices should be promoted, during the continuance of their title, to a bishopric, since even after obtaining a bishopric a bishop can for cause acquire minor benefices anew, according to what is read and noted in c. cum nostris, de conces. præben., and in c. postulasti, eod. tit., and c. cum in ecclesia, de præb. li. 6.

† But a bishop cannot acquire another bishopric by common law unless he is first absolved from the former: because, since he is an ecclesiastical person matrimonially bound, he cannot, during the continuance of the former bond, consent to another spiritual marriage; otherwise spiritual adultery would occur, as in the said c. sicut, de transla. præl., throughout. Deservedly, by law and by the custom of the Roman Church, he is to be translated to another see, having first been absolved from the former bond, said c. 2 de transla. præla., and c. bonæ 2 de postul. præla., noted by Io. Mo. and Io. An. in the places cited above. And by this, answer is also made to c. cum in cunctis, and to the other laws which induce the vacancy of prior benefices through the corporeal acquisition of the second, and not before. For they speak of inferior benefices short of a bishopric, from which it is not necessary to effect an absolution for the aforesaid reason; it is otherwise if absolution, and consequently vacancy, intervenes beforehand; for the acquisition of corporeal possession is awaited in vain, when the absolution was made beforehand, prior even to the verbal translation; and this seems in itself most clear and agreeable to all reason. And so that this may become clearer, let us see a parallel in carnal marriage. For suppose that a spouse de praesenti, the marriage not having been consummated, makes profession into the hands of some abbot, and thus the marriage was dissolved through c. ex publico, de conuer. coniu. Afterwards, the monastery de facto resists his reception; wherefore the monastery does not wish to receive him. Shall we say that this man, who has already professed as a monk, can, through this de facto resistance, reclaim his former spouse, especially if she was married to another after his profession? Certainly no one would be so foolish as to say this. For that spouse was released from the law by his profession; deservedly, the first marriage ought not to be reinstated without new consent, especially with the profession standing as an impediment; so must it be said in this spiritual marriage, arg. c. 2 de transla. præl. And by this, answer is also made to the gloss in c. relatio; which, however, understood as it stands, supports the conclusion previously reached. For it intended that by the very fact that one flies to a second bishopric, the first becomes vacant; which, however, proceeds understanding it as I have said above. To c. si beneficia, it can be answered that it speaks when someone, led by just ignorance, accepted a benefice due to another, in contemplation of which he gave up his own; whence, lest he be entirely without a benefice, and lest a just and probable ignorance harm him, it emanated from the greatest equity against strict rigor, as is noted there, that the disposition of that chapter should apply, and that he may return to the first, having relinquished the second without difficulty. But in our case it is otherwise: because the church of Trier is not due to another, but belongs to this translatee, although de facto he cannot have corporeal possession. Let him press, therefore, that he may have it, whence he does not remain without his title; on the contrary, he is deemed to have that church, since he has an action to obtain it, said l. qui actionem habet, ff. de reg. iu. And because, as I have said, he could reasonably have thought that this could happen, he therefore ought not to have pressed, nor to have approved the provision made to the other by urgently requesting the pallium, as has been fully stated above; and by this, the response to all contrary points is clear. I conclude, therefore, from all the aforesaid, that the church of Speyer is by law to be surrendered freely and absolutely to the said Lord Adolph, who was provided to it, and by no means to be retained by the former translated Bishop of Speyer, although on account of de facto resistance he can by no means obtain possession of the church of Trier.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Several modes of offering are set forth.
2. A donation of all present and future goods made to a church is valid.
3. If someone becomes a conversus of a church after the imposition of taxes, he is presumed to do this in fraud.
4. Under the designation of goods, when treating of the transfer of goods, and thus of great prejudice, future goods are not included.
5. All privileges granted to churches are, as a rule, to be extended to hospitals.
6. The fisc seizing someone's goods on account of an offense is liable to the creditors in proportion to the goods that have reached it.
body: IN the name of the Trinity, amen. Concerning the oblations of persons and goods which are frequently and repeatedly made to the most excellent and renowned Hospital of Santa Maria della Scala of the illustrious city of Siena, doubt primarily arises regarding three matters.

† For sometimes someone offers his goods to the hospital without himself; sometimes he offers himself without his goods; sometimes he offers both himself and his goods. And in these, especially, the doubt is examined whether, and when, and to what extent the hospital is obligated for debts contracted before the oblation, or contracted thereafter by those very offerors or oblates. And first, according to this order, I will touch upon the first branch—namely, when someone offers his goods without himself. And this branch can be subdivided: for sometimes someone offers all his goods, present and future; sometimes his present goods only; sometimes his goods simply; sometimes a certain part of his goods. In the first case, since it is a donation of all present and future goods, it can reasonably be doubted whether such a donation holds. For Bartolus, in l. si, C. de pact., held

† that such a donation made to a church or pious place is valid; but he holds otherwise when it is made to a private person. He is moved principally because one can donate oneself and one's goods to a church or pious place, as in capitulo praesentia, de proba., and in authen. ingressi, and auth. si qua mulier, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi., and 19. quaest. ult. ca. si qua, and c. quia ingredientibus; therefore, a fortiori, one can donate one's goods without oneself. But when it is made to a private person, the donation does not hold, because at least indirectly the free power of testation is impeded, since without goods one cannot make a will, at least with effect, as no one would wish to be an heir under such a testament; therefore such a donation is invalid, just as a stipulation would not be valid, l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, ff. de verbo. oblig. And this latter point the same Bartolus also affirmed in the aforesaid l. stipulatio hoc modo, and in l. si quis, in princip. ff. de lega. 3.; and what he himself noted in l. Seius & Augerius, ff. ad leg. Falc., supports this. This latter point was also confirmed by Iacobus de Arena, Petrus, and Cynus in the said l. fin. C. de pact. Baldus also seems to follow this there, stating that this is the common opinion. However, these jurists, apart from Bartolus, do not expressly touch upon the case when such a donation is made to a church or pious place; nevertheless, I once advised on this point regarding when such a donation is made to a private person, as appears in the book of my consilia, consilio 143. But regarding a donation made to a church or pious place, I find that dominus Franciscus Zabarella, Cardinal of Florence, formerly indeed an excellent doctor and my preceptor in the canons, held most authoritatively with Bartolus that such a donation is valid. But Angelus de Perusio, in a certain disputation of his which begins In refulgenti palatio, held the complete opposite of what Bartolus held, saying that such a donation made to a private person holds, but it is otherwise if it is made to a church or pious place. He is moved, among other things, by the fact that when it is made to a private person, ownership of the donated property—especially future property—does not transfer to the private person by title of donation alone, but delivery is required, as in l. traditionibus, C. de pact.; hence the donor retains ownership of the things concerning which he may make a will, although his heir after his death can be compelled to deliver the goods in execution of the donation already made by the deceased. Also because anyone is the lawful moderator and arbiter of his own property, l. in re mandata, C. mand., and such a donation is not found to be prohibited anywhere. But when it is made to a church or pious place, it does not have validity according to him, because ownership of any thing would never remain with the donor, since by title alone ownership is acquired by the church without delivery, as in l. si, C. de sacros. ec., and as noted in c. 2. de consue.; and thus he would not have the capacity to make a will, since he would have nothing in his goods, which seems contrary to good morals, l. stipulatio hoc modo, cited above. Nor, according to him, does Bartolus's reasoning stand in the way: because it is one thing to give oneself and one's goods to a monastery or pious place, and another to give one's goods only. For the first is approved by the church, because he passes from the active life into the contemplative; but remaining in the world, to be left completely without goods, even present and future, seems something indecent; and this last consideration of his seems quite subtle. To me, however, regarding a private person, the opinion of Bartolus has been pleasing, because although one is not strictly impeded from making a will—especially since inheritance is a legal term and can exist without property and without any utility, as in l. haeredis appellatio, ff. de verbo. sign., and l. haereditas, de peti. haere.—nevertheless the lack of goods directly impedes the faculty of having an heir, since, knowing that the goods belong to another, an heir will readily repudiate such an inheritance, Inst. ad leg. Falc. in prin. Nor should we regard the argument that this donor does not lose ownership of the donated goods without delivery: both because it is enough that the heir knows he is bound to deliver them in order for him to repudiate the inheritance, and because during his life the donor could immediately be compelled—even regarding acquired goods—to deliver them, if the donation held, since he donates inter vivos; hence such a donation is found to be indirectly prohibited by what is read and noted in the said l. stipulatio hoc modo. But with respect to a donation made to a church or pious place, I doubt more. And for the affirmative opinion equity and the favor of the church argue; for many things have been admitted in favor of religion contrary to the rules of law, as in l. sunt personae, ff. de reli. & sump. fu. To the contrary stands the text of Augustine, 17. q. 4. c. fi., where it is said: he who, having disinherited his son, wishes to make the church his heir, let him seek another than Augustine; indeed, God willing, he will find no one. If, therefore, the church ought not to receive all the goods of someone when a son is disinherited, then a fortiori when someone wishes to divest himself in the present and in the future, his status otherwise not being changed. Nevertheless, out of favor to the church, I would follow Bartolus, which is supported by what Baldus noted in auth. ingressi, C. de sacros. eccl.; and the same Baldus most openly maintained that such a donation holds in auth. si qua mulier, under the same title, in the last column, where he says this is beyond doubt in the church, alleging l. iubemus nulli, post prin. C. eod., where the text supports this excellently. Also, voluntary poverty for God's sake, even without changing one's secular status, is not disapproved by the law; rather, it was commended and advised by Christ our Savior and master Himself, when He said in the Gospel, 'If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and follow me,' and elsewhere, 'Unless one renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple.' Hence, in the primitive church in the time of the Apostles, all who converted to the Christian faith, even though laymen, sold all things and placed the price before the feet of the Apostles, as noted in 12. q. 1. in sum. and in c. dilectissimis, in the same causa and quaestio; for whatever is donated to the church is said to be consecrated to God and dedicated to divine uses, 12. q. 2. c. nulli liceat, and in c. mancipia, with the following, de re. permu., with similar texts. Therefore such a donation ought not to be disapproved, since all things belong to God, de deci. c. tua; and thus such donated goods return to their nature; it is otherwise when the donation is to a private person, since then the tenacity of the one receiving the donation can be noted. From these points I conclude that such a donation can be sustained when it is to a hospital, by the argument of l. omnia privilegia, C. de episc. & cle. Rarely, however, does this question arise for a hospital, because for the most part when someone gives all his goods, present and future, to a hospital, he always retains for himself the usufruct of those goods, or bargains for an annual payment to be delivered to him by the hospital; in which case, according to all, such a donation is valid, since he has the free capacity to make a will in the reserved goods, as is commonly noted by the legists in the said l. si, C. de pac. In this case, therefore, when it is asked whether the hospital is bound to the creditors of this donor, I conclude thus: either the question is about debts contracted after such a donation, and it must indubitably be said that the hospital is not bound, since the goods were transferred to the hospital beforehand, and this donor could not prejudice the hospital by his agreement entered into afterward, since regularly no one can be sued on the contract of another, as in l. fin. C. ne uxo. pro mari.; I say, however, that since the donation was made so extensively, the hospital is bound to support that indigent donor, as fully noted by Cynus in l. fin. C. de revo. do. and by the canonists in c. si, de dona.; nor is the hospital equated in this case to an heir on account of the universality of the goods, since the transfer was made by contract, the donor's status not having been changed, according to what was noted by Baldus in the aforementioned auth. ingressi, by argument of l. si mulier, §. ex asse, ff. de iu. dot. Or the question is about debts contracted before the donation; and then several cases must be considered. For either those goods were previously obligated for the contracted debts, expressly or tacitly; and those goods pass with the burden of the obligation, as in c. ex literis, de pig. and c. pastoralis, de deci. and l. sicut, §. non videtur, ff. quib. mo. pig. vel hypo. sol. For a preceding hypothec, even tacitly contracted, is preferred not only to donees, but also to other creditors having a personal action or a tacit or express hypothec, as noted by Dinus in reg. qui prior est tempore, de reg. iu. li. 6.; and it seems to be proved that one having a prior tacit hypothec is even preferred to the fiscus, as in l. 1. in the second responsa, C. rem alie. geren., although the gloss doubts against the fiscus, ff. qui pot. in pig. ha. l. Titius, in prin. §. negotiari, though according to some there is a special rule for a woman having a hypothec for her dowry, about which it is to be stated as in l. assiduis, C. qui po. in pig. ha., but this does not pertain to our proposition. Or those creditors had only a personal obligation; and then the hospital is not bound on the ground that it would be deemed an heir on account of the universal transfer of goods, as I said above. But as to whether it is liable to the revocatory action, so that the goods can be revoked as having been alienated in fraud of creditors, a distinction must be made: either the hospital received those goods for a non-lucrative cause, for instance because it gave something in compensation, or promised that it would give it, and revocation of the goods ought not to take place if the hospital was not aware of the fraud, as in l. qui autem, §. hoc edictum, in fi. de his quae in frau., nor in doubt ought fraud to be presumed, l. quoties, §. qui dolo, ff. de proba. Or the hospital held those goods by a purely lucrative cause; and then the hospital is bound to the extent that the goods suffice. For revocation ought to take place, because the donation is presumed made in fraud of creditors since the donor does not have sufficient goods from which he can satisfy his creditors; nor in this case does it matter whether the hospital acted with deceit, since it only contends to capture a gain. For it is sufficient that the donor acted in fraud, and he is presumed in fraud since, as I said, he does not have enough goods to satisfy his creditors, and thus knew that he was not solvent, as in l. si quis cum haberet, ff. de his quae in frau., and there Bartolus expressly notes this; and what he notes in l. incola, ff. ad munic., where he says,

† that if someone, after the imposition of taxes, becomes a conversus of a church, he is presumed to do this in fraud, supports this. And this concerns the first principal branch, namely when someone has donated all his goods, present and future, to the hospital, his status otherwise not being changed. However, concerning this branch it could be doubted: What if he simply donated his goods, or a certain part of his goods? I say that with respect to creditors it must be stated as concluded above: because no reason for a difference can be assigned if this donor is not solvent; but where he were solvent, he himself ought to be sued before the hospital, even if the creditors had a hypothec, even an express one, as in auth. hoc si debitor, C. de pigno. But it could be doubted whether, when goods are simply donated to a hospital, only present goods pass, and which ones, or future goods as well? And I say that since this donor remains in his status, present goods simply pass, of whatever kind they are,
† but not future goods, by the argument in l. bonorum, ff. de verb. sig., joined with l. si mandavero, §. is cuius, ff. mandati, and c. foelicis, §. verum, de poenis, lib. 6., where it is clear

† that where the transfer of goods is concerned, and thus a great prejudice, future goods are never included under the designation of 'goods'; it is otherwise where a slight prejudice is concerned, such as an obligation of pledges, in which case future goods are included; so speaks l. fin. ff. quae res pig. obl. poss. And the aforesaid holds even when the donation is to a church, as the gloss holds and more clearly Archidiaconus, 27. q. 1. c. ut lex continentiae, and Baldus and Bartolus in auth. ingressi, C. de sacros. eccle.; it is also supported by the argument in 17. q. 4. c. si. But if he said, 'I donate my movable and immovable goods,' whether rights and actions are included must be answered as fully noted by Bartolus in l. moventium, ff. de ver. sig., and better in l. pen. de autho. tut. I come now to the second principal branch, namely when someone offers himself to the hospital without his goods; which can occur, since the hospital does not have among its brothers religion strictly understood. For its brothers may use marriage, at least previously contracted, and possess their own property; therefore they are not religious, nor are they properly said to have a rule, since they do not profess those three essentials of any religious order, concerning which in c. cum ad monasterium, in fi. de statu. mona., but rather they are said to have a certain manner of living, as the gloss notes in cle. 1. de rel. do. and in cle. pen. de sen. excom. Therefore, these persons can offer themselves to the hospital and promise obedience, just as secular clerics, and nonetheless retain their goods, like a conversus of a secular church according to what is noted by the gloss and doctors in the said c. ut lex continentiae, and by Bartolus and Baldus in the aforementioned authen. ingressi, and in those goods they will be able to make a will; in which case l. generali, C. de sacros. ecc. and the note in the said c. ut lex continentiae can be understood. And if it is asked whether in this case the hospital is bound for the debts contracted by these brothers or oblates, I say that for debts contracted before the oblation it is undoubtedly not bound: both because the goods did not come to the hospital, and because the church ought not to be held liable for the contracts of others, especially those who contracted before the oblation. But the obligors themselves are bound to satisfy them, and they can be effectively sued, since they retain the goods, according to what is noted by Johannes Andreae and Innocent in c. unico, de obl. ad ratio., and by the doctors in auth. causa, quae sit cum monacho, C. de epi. & cle.; for even a monastery in this case would not be bound for debts previously contracted by a monk, since it does not have his goods, as noted in the laws cited above; a fortiori neither is the hospital, since the obligors or brothers themselves cannot strictly be called religious, as I said above. But whether the hospital is liable for debts contracted after the oblation, I say yes, if he had a mandate from the hospital for contracting them; otherwise not, except to the extent that they were converted to the benefit of the hospital, as is read and noted in c. quod quibusdam, de fideius. And the matter should be seen through Innocent in c. cum olim, 2. de privil. in the second column; and what Bartolus notes in l. si communis servus, ff. de stip. ser. supports this. If, however, the hospital should obtain the goods of the oblate by his testament, then it would be bound as heir: I say, however, that it will not be bound to creditors beyond the assets of the inheritance, even if it had not made an inventory. The church also would not be bound beyond the hereditary assets, just as the fiscus is not, as noted by Baldus in l. fin. C. de iu. delib. and Bartolus in l. 2. C. de sacros. ecc., although the gloss tacitly holds the contrary in c. 1. de testa. But the former is more common and truer. For goods are understood to be devolved upon the church insofar as they are not burdensome, lest church goods be indirectly alienated, as in auth. sicut, C. de sacros. eccl. And the same must be said of a hospital:

† because regularly all privileges granted to churches are extended to hospitals, as in the said l. omnia privilegia, as noted there by Bartolus, C. de episco. & cle. And what Johannes Andreae notes in capitulo 2. de in integ. rest. libr. 6. supports this. If, however, during his life this oblate should give his goods to the hospital after the oblation, or part of his goods, it must be stated as I said above in the first branch. And this briefly concerning that second branch. Now I will touch upon the third and final branch, namely when someone offered himself and his goods to the hospital; and in this two matters can be considered: first, concerning the efficacy of the transfer of goods; second, concerning the burdens of creditors. In the first case it must be stated as I said in the first branch: for since the hospital is not a religious order, when someone offers himself and his goods simply, future goods do not pass, but present goods only, as noted in the said c. ut lex continentiae, and by Bartolus and by Baldus in the said auth. ingressi, unless the custom of the hospital provides otherwise, as Huguccio and Archidiaconus note in the said c. ut lex; for a contract in doubt is seen to be made according to the custom of the place, as in l. quod si nolit, §. quia assidua, ff. de aedi. edic.; what Bartolus notes in l. nemo est qui nesciat, ff. de duo. re. supports this. Concerning the second, whether the hospital is bound in this case to the burdens of debts, I distinguish: either the question is about debts contracted before the oblation, or about subsequent ones. In the first case I think the hospital is bound to the extent that the goods suffice, or let it surrender those goods received, because since the universality of the goods passed to the hospital, the person's status having been changed in a certain manner, it ought to be held liable as a universal successor, just as in a monastery with respect to an entrant, as noted by Hostiensis in c. unico, de obli. ad ratio. and the gloss and Baldus in authen. ingressi, C. de sacrosan. eccl.; and what is noted in capitulo in praesentia, de prob. supports this; l. 2. C. ad l. Iul. de vi pub. supports this, where it is clear

† that the fiscus, seizing someone's goods on account of a crime, is bound to creditors pro rata for the goods that come to it. But if he gave only a part of his goods, then it must be said as I stated above in the first branch. Or the question is about debts contracted after the oblation, and a distinction must be made as I said above in the second principal branch. For the same is to be said as when he had dedicated himself without his goods, because he could not contract to the prejudice of the hospital without a mandate, by the said c. quod quibusdam, de fideiuss., with similar texts. And through this it appears most clearly what must be said regarding all the premises and cases that can occur in practice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If a fief was granted to two brothers, upon the death of one, whether his share accrues to the other brother; and at no. 3.
2. If a testator said, "if such persons die, I will that all my property devolve upon such a person," the substitute does not seem called unless both instituted heirs have died.
casus: The case that occurred consists in these terms. The syndic of the convent and chapter of the monastery of Santa Maria of the Order of Servites, the due formalities having preceded, granted by title of lease a certain possession of the same monastery to Meus and Bartoccius, natural brothers, with certain pacts and conditions, about which is set forth in the instrument of the said lease. And among other things it was expressly agreed and stated that after the life of both of the aforesaid, namely of Meus and Bartoccius, the said possession ought by full right to return to the aforesaid convent, as it was previously, free and unencumbered, as is contained in certain other writings; and the notary seems to have wished to refer to the form of the power conferred upon him shortly before by the convent of the said monastery, in which grant indeed it was stated that the said syndic could, in the name of the convent, lease the said possession to the aforesaid Meus and Bartoccius for the life of the said Meus and Bartoccius, and not beyond; and they subjoin there these words, namely with the pact that the lease to be made shall in no way pass to the heirs of the said Meus and Bartoccius, but solely for their life and the life of each of them, and not otherwise, or in another manner, for an annual rent, etc. It happened in the course of time after the said lease was made and completed that the said Meus, one of the contracting parties, departed this life. It is now called into doubt whether the said possession, or at least the half that pertained to the said Meus, ought to return to the said monastery, or whether indeed the death of the said Bartoccius must also be awaited.
body: Having implored the aid of the Savior, it seems at first that, for the half falling to the said Meus, the said possession ought to return to the monastery, because in contracts the right of accrual (ius accrescendi) has no place; therefore the failing portion ought to return to the owner of the possession, as read and noted especially by Bar. in l. si mihi & Titio. ff. de uerbo. oblig. and by Bald. in l. una. C. quando non peten. partes. and Specul. in the title de loca. §. nunc aliqua, verse 69; and the text seems to support this in the said l. si mihi & Titio, and in l. per seruum. §. quod unus, and the case seems specifically in point regarding the grant of a fief in chapter one, de fratribus de no. bene. inue. column 10, where it is said,

† that if a fief was granted to two brothers, upon the death of one, his share does not accrue to the other brother, but returns to the lord; and the reason is because in contracts the right of accrual has no place; as fully noted by Bartol. in the said l. unica. But these notwithstanding, the contrary seems to proceed from the law in our case, namely that the said monastery can claim nothing of the said possession while the said Bartoccius lives, beyond the agreed rent. I am moved principally by the words set down in the instrument of the grant. For the lease was not made simply to Meus and Bartoccius—in which case the authorities alleged above on the opposing side would proceed—but it was specifically added that after the life of both, namely of Meus and Bartoccius, the said possession ought to return to the convent of the said monastery. Whence those words must be weighed, 'after the life of both', etc., which clearly indicate that while either is living, the monastery can claim nothing; in support of this is l. final. ff. in ius uocand. ut erant, where it is said that if someone promised to produce two men in court, presents one, and does not present the other, the promise does not seem to be satisfied; to the same effect is l. penultim. C. de impu. & aliis substitu. where it is held that if someone, having instituted two prepubescent sons, added that if both died under the age of puberty, such a one should be heir, the said substitute is not called except after the death of both; and many similar cases can be adduced to the same effect, especially what is read and noted in l. si fuerit, and l. si quis ducenta. §. utrum, ff. de rebus dub. and chapter olim, de rescript. Furthermore, one must not depart from the words of the contracting parties unless their intention is established, l. semper in stipulationibus, ff. de regu. ius.; l. Labeo, ff. de supel. leg. and c. si. de uer. sig. and c. ciuitate, de usur. with similar texts. But in the said contract it was expressly stated that after the death of both the said possession should return to the monastery; therefore the death of one does not suffice, as in the legal authorities alleged above. And Specu. in the place previously alleged states this question almost in point for this side, and says that many doctors who were consulted responded thus. Bar. also seems to maintain this position in l. quidam testamento, ff. de uulg. & pupil. where, arguing from that law, he says,

† that if a testator speaks thus: 'if such persons die, I wish all goods to pass to such a one', the substitute does not seem to be called unless both instituted heirs have died, for the meaning of the words conveys this, although sometimes something else is observed based on the presumed intention of the testator; in which case l. hæredes mei. §. cum ita, ff. ad Trebel. proceeds, as is noted there. In our case, however, the contrary intention of the contracting parties is not established; therefore one must stand strictly by the meaning of the words, l. non aliter, ff. de lega. 3. Furthermore, that this was also the intention of the contracting parties—that while either of them was alive, the convent could claim nothing of the said possession—is expressly proved by those words of the procuration (syndicatus), in that they gave the power of leasing to them such that the lease should not pass to their heirs, but solely for the life of them, 'and of whichever of them'. For these last words, 'and of whichever of them', must be weighed carefully, because they openly show that the said lease endures not only for the life of both, but of whichever of them; and since the words are clear, there is no need for interpretation, as in l. ille aut ille, ff. de lega. 3., nor can any cavil be made against these words unless it is manifestly frivolous. And to this effect, in a similar case, Bald. notes in the said l. unica, C. quando non pe. part. where he says that if a thing was granted in emphyteusis to two brothers in solidum, these words seem to imply that after the death of one the possession, or a part of it, ought not to return to the owner of the property, but the death of both must be awaited, so that in this case the right of non-diminution (ius non decrescendi) has place rather than accrual, as is more fully noted by him there. I conclude therefore from all the aforesaid that, while the said Bartoccius is living, the convent of the said monastery cannot claim the said possession or any part of it, but must be content with the receipt of the established rent. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. By virtue of an arbitrary discretion generally granted to certain officials, the power of disposing contrary to already enacted statutes and ordinances of a city is not deemed to have been given.
2. A lord having jurisdiction can not only grant to one who is already a notary that he may exercise the notarial craft in his territory, but can even create a notary anew there.
3. The corporation of a certain land can statute something contrary to public law to the prejudice of that land itself.
4. A privilege generally granted by a prince must be interpreted most broadly against the grantor himself.
casus: The fact in effect is proposed in these terms: The commune of Monte Santa Maria came under the obedience [?] of the city of Recanati under certain pacts, in which among other things it is contained that the said land of Monte Santa Maria, and its curia, fortress, and district shall be in perpetuity, and be understood to be, of the district, county, and jurisdiction of Recanati with certain modifications and pacts. And among other things it was agreed that the said commune and men of Monte Santa Maria should have in the said land, curia, and district mere and mixed imperium, and full jurisdiction in all and singular matters that are not to the prejudice of the aforesaid commune of Recanati, or contrary to the form of the chapters entered into between the said lands, and that they may make laws and statutes in those manners and dispositions that shall please them, provided that they are not contrary to the honor and standing of the said commune of Recanati, or contrary to chapters of this kind, etc. Finally, it happened that the said commune of the land of Santa Maria granted to a certain notary the power of exercising the notarial craft in the said land.
