It is said that it could not transfer this power to him, on account of certain reforms of the city of Recanati in which it is contained that no notary should dare to exercise the notarial craft in the county and district of Recanati unless such notary has first been approved and matriculated in the guild of notaries of the said city of Recanati, as will more fully appear from what is said below.
body: The aid of Christ the Savior and of His most pious Mother having first been invoked, it seems at first that it is not permitted to the said notary to exercise the notarial craft in the said castle of Santa Maria by virtue of the said power. For since it had been specially prohibited by a statute of the said city of Recanati that no notary might exercise the notarial craft in its county and district unless he were first approved and matriculated in the guild of notaries of the said city of Recanati, it was not permitted to the said commune of Santa Maria, by virtue of the power generally granted to it, to dispose or decree anything contrary to the special statutes of the said city of Recanati, on the argument of l. bonorum, ff. de iure fisci, and the remarks noted by Bartol. in l. ambitiosam, ff. de decre. ab ord. fa., and in proœ. C., where he said

† that by virtue of an arbitrary discretion generally granted to certain officials, the power of disposing contrary to already enacted statutes and ordinances of the city is not deemed to have been given; for this reason, because it is not likely that someone has granted in general that which he would not likely have granted in particular, as in regula in generali, de regulis iuris, in the Sext. Moreover, and secondly, it is not permitted to an inferior to dispose contrary to the law of a superior, as in cle. ne Romani, de ele., and C. de usur. l. eos. §. ne liceat. But the men of the said castle are subject to those of the county of the city of Recanati; therefore it was not permitted to them to transfer that power, or to decree concerning this contrary to those reforms of their superior. Thirdly, the exceptions made in the grant of that power persuade this. For to the men of that land was given mere and mixed imperium, and the power of making law, provided that they did not exercise that power to the prejudice of, or contrary to the honor and standing of the said city of Recanati; but the grant of that power to exercise the notarial craft in the said land comes contrary to the honor and to the prejudice of the said city; therefore it was not permitted to transfer the said power. That it is, moreover, to the prejudice and contrary to the honor of the said city of Recanati is evident from this: because those reforms were not made for any other reason than that notaries not approved and matriculated by the guild of the city often made false, fictitious, and simulated instruments, and sometimes, on account of the ignorance of the notaries themselves, instruments collapsed contrary to the will of the contracting parties; all of which undoubtedly seem to tend to the prejudice and contrary to the honor of the said city, since such illicit acts are committed in its territory and county, ar. in l. congruit, ff. de of. præsi., and 43. dist. c. si inimicus. But notwithstanding these points, I firmly think the contrary opinion to be truer in law. I am moved principally because a land, or

† a lord having jurisdiction, can not only grant power to an existing notary to exercise the notarial craft in his territory, but can even create a notary anew in that same place. For just as custom of the place can do this, as in c. cum dilectus, de fide instru., so much the more can a statute of the place, argu. l. de quibus, ff. de legi. And Hostiensis held this side, and the Doctors commonly follow it in c. cum P. tabellio, de fi. inst., whatever Innocent may have said to the contrary there. Bartolus also held this opinion in l. 1, ff. de of. procons.; in l. hæc autem, de adop., Bartolus holds the same in l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. tri., where Baldus expressly confirmed this same point; and Speculator in the title de instr. edi. §. restat, at the verse 'sed quis potest'. But the aforesaid land of Monte Santa Maria had the power of enacting statutes, likewise mere and mixed imperium and jurisdiction, which can not only give power in the said land to an existing notary, but can even create notaries there anew. By law, therefore, by virtue of the said power reserved or granted to it, it was able to grant that power to the said notary, and consequently all instruments drawn up and to be drawn up by the said notary ought to be valid. It only remains, however, to see whether the reforms made by the city of Recanati, or the reservations or exceptions made in the transfer of the said power, might present an obstacle. And truly I believe most firmly that they do not. For first, the reforms do not stand in the way; because from the fact that a prince gives to the people of a certain land the power of enacting statutes, he is deemed to give the power of enacting in that land even contrary to the general law of the superior, unless they should wish to enact contrary to natural good morals, or contrary to those things specially reserved to the prince as a mark of supreme power, as Baldus concludes in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iur., and in l. repetitione, at the word 'tertiò iuxta prædicta quæritur etc.', and it seems to be proved in the said l. omnes populi; nay rather, the Gloss noted notably in l. neque pignus, §. priuatorum, ff. de reg. iur.,

† that the corporation of any land can enact something contrary to public law to the prejudice of the land itself or of the inhabitants there, although it cannot do so to public prejudice generally; but in our case, the permission to exercise the notarial craft in the said land is not contrary to natural good morals; on the contrary, it conforms to good morals, since they have otherwise legitimately attained the notarial office. So it happens in our case; for the laws also devised the use and exercise of notaries, as in de fide instrumen. throughout, and in the Authenticum de tabel. de fide instrument.; nor is it required by law that he must be approved by the guild of notaries or otherwise matriculated, as I said above. Nor is this among the things reserved to the city of Recanati as a mark of supreme power; for although it prohibited the exercise in its county and district without approval and matriculation, it nevertheless did not reserve to itself the power solely of doing the contrary; for it is deemed to have prohibited with respect to its subjects generally, because otherwise they could not enact, nor did they enact; but it is not extended to places in which there are statutes legitimately enacted to the contrary, as appears in a general law of the prince: because, notwithstanding it, a land having jurisdiction from the prince or by prescription can enact the contrary, as in the said l. omnes populi, and what is there noted, and in the said l. cunctos populos, C. de sum. trin. And this proceeds especially in our case, since the exercise of the office of this notary does not tend against an unwilling person, but only toward a willing one, and concerns only the men of that land, or those voluntarily contracting there; this is supported by what Cardinalis notes on a similar point in l. 3, ff. ad l. Iul. repe. Moreover, the power generally transferred to the said land would be of little use if it could not enact contrary to what was specially provided by the city of Recanati, since the statutes of the said city provide for all cases commonly occurring, whence that power would be illusory; which is not to be said, argument from l. 1, in fine, ff. ad muni., and in l. quod Labeo, ad Carb., and l. si quando, C. de inoff. testam., together with the Gloss, and in c. 1, de priu., in the Sext, with similar texts. Likewise, the power was transferred to the said men generally, so that they might enact and make laws concerning everything that pleased them; therefore the said case, or one similar, is not understood to be excepted: because he who says everything excludes nothing: l. de pretio, ff. de pub., and in cap. si Romanorum, 19. distin., and c. solitæ, de maio. & obe.,

† and a privilege granted generally by a prince must be interpreted most broadly against the grantor himself, as in ca. olim, de uerbo. sign., where by Innocent, and in l. fi. ff. de const. prin., where by Bartolus; and interpretation ought to be made against him who could have spoken the law more clearly, as in regula contra eum, de regu. iu., in the Sext. Lastly, this is expressly proved by the exceptions made in the transfer of that power, which truly seem to establish the intention of the community of the said land, although at first glance they seem to favor the city of Recanati. For, since it generally granted to that people mere and mixed imperium, and jurisdiction, and the specific power of enacting laws and statutes, and only two cases were excepted, it is deemed to have confirmed and transferred the power generally in all things not excepted, as in cap. dominus, 32. q. 7, and c. 2, de coniu. leg., and l. si uerò, §. de uiro, ff. solut. matr. Let us see therefore now whether this case is comprehended under those excepted cases, and I certainly say that it is not. For the first excepted case was when they might wish to exercise power to the prejudice of the said city of Recanati; but the permission of the exercise of that office in their land alone does not come to the prejudice of the city of Recanati; indeed no prejudice can it claim from this, since by law, as I said before, they can create notaries anew in their jurisdiction and land. Nor do notaries exercise their office against any unwilling persons; on the contrary, it is necessary that they be requested by them, as Innocent notes in capitul. 1, de fide instrumento; and prejudice smacks of a diminution of patrimony, which in no way occurs in our case: otherwise it would follow that no one short of the prince could create a notary in his jurisdiction, since subjects may not enact to the prejudice of the prince, as in cap. venientes, de iureiuran., the contrary of which is true, as proved above. The second excepted case was when they might wish to make a statute contrary to the honor and standing of the said city of Recanati; but who of sound mind will say that that permission to exercise the notarial office there tends contrary to the honor and standing of the prince? Especially since by law no other license is necessary, and the city of Recanati made those reforms principally for the convenience of the subjects only; if those of the land of Monte Santa Maria, having the power to make law, wish to provide otherwise to their own prejudice, their wish must be complied with, since they can, as I said before, even enact to their own prejudice, to the prejudice of public law, which is more, as noted in the said §. priuatorum; l. circa, ff. de proba. supports this. Moreover, if this tended contrary to the honor and standing of the prince, it would not be permitted to an inferior to create notaries in his jurisdiction, the contrary of which is true, as I said before. The contrary arguments formulated above for the opposing opinion do not stand in the way. For from the aforesaid, the answer to all of them is clear except for the first; to which I say that it proceeds when an arbitrary discretion is given in the same land with respect to a certain faculty; for then it is not permitted to enact contrary to what was specially provided there; but we are speaking of when power and jurisdiction are given generally in one land, and statutes are made there to the prejudice of that land alone, but not contrary to laws enacted in the other lands of the grantor. From all the aforesaid, I conclude that from the preservation or grant of the aforesaid power it was permitted to the commune of the said land to give that power to the notary to exercise the notarial craft in that land, and consequently all instruments issued and to be drawn up by that notary are valid; nay rather (as I said before), I think that the said community can create notaries anew as to the exercise of the notarial office in the said land, without such notary being otherwise approved or matriculated in the guild of notaries of the said city of Recanati. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The will of a deceased from an imperfect testament is not valid, except among children.
2. A legacy of freedom is owed from an imperfect testament.
3. If a testator began and expressed that he was instituting the poor of Christ, and before the testament was completed frenzy or death intervened, such an institution is not valid, even in favor of children.
casus: The case in fact is proposed thus: A certain man named Migliore de Pauluzo, having a lawful wife, two surviving daughters, and two grandchildren by a predeceased daughter, being afflicted by bodily illness and asserting that he did not wish to die intestate, began to make his testament; and before he instituted any heir, he began to make certain legacies both to the said grandchildren and to the daughters, as well as to certain others. While he was in the midst of disposing of the legacies, even before he completed them, a great weakness overcame the said testator, so that he was forced by it to desist from the making and completion of the said testament, and thus he died with it left imperfect. Afterwards, one of the daughters died, who left all her goods to her mother. Now it is asked whether the said legacies hold in law, especially those made to the grandchildren, and in what manner the said inheritance ought to be divided.
body: Having prayed for the aid of Almighty God, it seems firstly that the said legacies, at least those made among the daughters and the grandchildren by the predeceased daughter, are valid, because an informal expression of will among children is valid and holds among them; concerning which see the text in l. hac consultissima, § ex imperfecto, C. de testamen., where it is said,

† that from an imperfect will, the intention of the deceased is not valid except among children alone. If, however, some outside person is mixed with the children in an expression of will of this kind, the expression of will is not valid as to that person, but their portion accrues to the children; therefore it must be said that the legacies made to others accrue to the said daughters and grandchildren, and that among them the said imperfect testament should be deemed valid. For under the name of 'children' come not only sons, but also grandchildren and great-grandchildren and other descendants, as in l. liberorum, ff. de uer. sign. Therefore these daughters and grandchildren will have the goods pre-legated ab intestato, and the remaining goods concerning which no disposition was made they will divide among themselves; for the useful is not vitiated by the useless, as in regula utile per inutile, de regu. iuris, libr. 6. And the remarkable text in the matter in l. testamento, ff. de fideicommiss. lib., seems to support the aforesaid exceptionally well, and that which Barto. notes there, where it seems to be proved,

† that a legacy of liberty is owed from an imperfect testament; and Barto. seems to hold the same opinion there regarding a legacy for pious causes; and what he notes in l. fideicommissa, § quoties, ff. de lega. 3, also supports this, where he opines, though in doubt, that such an imperfect testament is valid among children. But notwithstanding these points, I deem the contrary opinion to be truer in law, namely that such an imperfect expression of will is not valid even among children. And first I prove this by reasons and by the laws; secondly, by the authorities of the most accomplished men, who have commonly inclined toward the just opinion. And first an express text seems to be, especially when joined with the gloss, in l. is qui, ff. de testamen., where it is said that if someone began to make a testament and did not finish it, such an expression of will is treated as nothing. To the same effect is the good text in the said l. fideicommissa, § quoties, previously cited; and this must especially be held in our case, in which the institution of heirs had not yet been made; therefore it cannot be called a testament, even though he had the intention of testating, as appears from the facts of the case; to this effect is Instit. de lega., § ante hæredis institutionem, and better in § primis, Institut. de fideicommiss. hære., where it is said that a testament is useless in which no one is instituted heir. Nor does the said § ex imperfecto cited to the contrary stand in the way: because it ought to be understood of an imperfection with respect to solemnity, but not with respect to will; because also by natural reason something cannot stand from which an absolute and resolved intention of disposition does not appear—an excellent argument in l. contractus, C. de fide instrument.; and elsewhere the text says that nothing seems to have been done when something remains to be done, as in l. penultim., C. ad Sylla.; and chapter 1, de successio. ab intesta., in the word perfecerint, supports this. For the testator could have limited, qualified, or revoked those legacies in the course of making the testament. Furthermore, we see that if the inheritance is not accepted under the testament, the legacies are not owed: because the testator did not intend to burden those coming ab intestato, but the written heir, as in l. 2, C. si omis. causa test., where it is remarkably proved that even bequeathed liberties are not owed in this case; all the more strongly, therefore, must it be said when the testator, overtaken by death, did not complete the testament, especially when he had not arrived at the institution of an heir, as happened in our case. And this position—that the legacies are not valid, even among children—was maintained most openly on our exact terms by Bald. following Guil. de Cu. at the end of C. famil. erciscund. And he affirmed the same in the said l. hac consultissima, § ex imperfecto, C. de test., being moved principally because he who did not complete it, having been overtaken by death, is not said to have testated, but to have wished to testate; and those laws that seem to suggest the contrary he understands (as I said above) regarding imperfection with respect to solemnity, because he had not testated before seven witnesses, for then the testament holds among children who were going to succeed ab intestato, since the intention of the deceased is apparent through two witnesses. Bartol. affirmed this same opinion in the said l. fin. and in the said § ex imperfecto, although he seems to have vacillated and doubted in § quoties and the said l. in testamento. Dominus Petr. de Ancha. expressly followed this opinion in cap. 2, de testament., where he said further

† that if a testator began to make a testament and expressed that he was instituting Christ's poor, and, the testament not being completed, madness or death supervened, such an institution and the other things he expressed are not valid, even in favor of children, through those things that are noted in the legal texts cited above. Likewise, dominus Anto. de But. seems to hold the contrary in c. 1, de succes. ab intest. The said l. in testamento does not stand in the way; for to it Bal. responds in l. cum quis, C. de iur. fac. igno., in the third column, at the verse tu distingue, at the end, where he says that a certain unwritten equity is posited there, or the jurist persuades rather than disposes there; or otherwise, as that same Bald. responds in l. si iure, C. de testa. manu., where he says that the case of that law proceeds on account of the great affection the testator had toward that foster child, as is gathered from its words; hence it is not to be drawn into a precedent according to him; in favor of this is the said l. si iure, where it says that if a testament does not subsist by law, not even liberties are owed from it. I conclude therefore from the aforesaid that the said legacies are by no means owed among children, but that there must be succession ab intestato to the goods of the said testator. As to the second point, how the said inheritance is devolved ab intestato, I say that, looking at pure common law, the daughters of the said testator succeed together with the grandchildren by the predeceased daughter, who succeed into the place of their mother and take only a third portion, just as their mother would have taken. The other two portions, however, go to the daughters, as is proved in the Authentica cessante, C. de legi. hæredita., and Instit. de successione, quæ ab intesta. deferun., § cum filio. But the portion of that daughter who died having instituted the mother reaches the mother herself, for she could institute her, having passed over the sister and the children of the predeceased sister, as in l. fratris uel sororis, C. de inofficioso testamento. Moreover, upon the death of the mother, that portion must accrue to the heirs themselves, with the legitim due to the surviving daughter and to the grandchildren by the daughter nevertheless preserved, as in chapter Raynutius, de testamen.; and if she died intestate, the goods of the mother accrue to the daughter for one portion, and to the grandchildren by the daughter for the other, as is clear from the legal texts cited above. And let these remarks suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The right of patronage, or the right of presenting, can belong to the people by ancient custom.
2. One who builds a church is made patron.
3. The institution of benefices belongs to the bishop alone under the common law.
4. The union or division of churches cannot be made without the consent of the chapter.
casus: The case upon which counsel in law is requested is stated in the terms written below, namely: the church of Santa Maria of Marmonia, in the diocese of Siena, was built and consecrated, now two hundred years ago and more, together with three altars, namely one in the middle, the principal one, and two on the sides for the ornament of the said church, so that the solemnities of Masses could more easily be celebrated for the peoples gathering for divine worship, as can sufficiently be gathered from the writing of the church and of the said altars [?], and from an ancient writing issued concerning the consecration of the said altars performed at the same time; nor was any dowry specifically assigned to the said altars at the time of establishment; on the contrary, before forty years ago the said altars possessed no property under the title of dowry or by any other title, nor were they considered chapels distinct from the body of the church. But the plebanus of the said church for the time being, celebrating at the said altars sometimes by himself, sometimes through others, satisfied the people flocking to the said church. Finally, within the past sixty or fifty years, certain properties were bequeathed or donated to the said altars situated at the sides by certain parishioners of the said church, and under pretext of these things the said parishioners, considering themselves to be patrons, placed and established certain clerics at the said chapels with the consent of the plebanus of the said church, and such establishment lasted for almost thirty years; after which elapsed, the said parishioners, considering, as above, that they were patrons, began to present chaplains for the said altars to the lord bishop of Siena, from whom those thus presented obtained institution for almost thirty years. Very recently, however, a newly canonically instituted plebanus in the said church says that the said chapels, together with the property bequeathed and donated to them, belong to him, just as other property does, denying that any right of patronage belongs by law to the said parishioners. The said parishioners, however, assert the contrary, and to establish their claim regarding the said right of patronage they allege the donation of the said property made by their ancestors, and one specifically made so that the people of the said church might obtain the presentation of the chaplains to the said altars. It is now asked what the law is? And consequently it is doubted concerning a certain parish chapel situated within the limits of the said pieve, which formerly belonged to the mensa of the plebanus of the said church, but was ultimately divided from the said pieve by a certain bishop of Siena without the consent of his chapter [?], reserving an annual census of five pounds of wax to be paid to the said church, and the said bishop also granted the right of patronage of the said chapel to certain laymen; yet no property was granted to that chapel by the said laymen. Now the said plebanus claims that the division is null, saying that its right of patronage could by no means be granted to the laymen themselves, and in the name of his church he claims the said chapel as united to his mensa, or as a member of his said church of Santa Maria.
body: Invoking the protection of Christ and of his Mother, I shall address the first point first according to order, and thereafter the second. And concerning the first, the said plebanus seems to be moved by an unjust petition: since the right of patronage is acquired not only by construction and foundation, but also by donation: 15. quæst. 7. c. filiis ac nepotibus, noted by the gloss in c. piæ mentis in the same causa and questio; 63. dist. in summa by Inno. in rub. de iure patronatus; by Ioan. And. in c. 1. eod. titu. But a dowry was conferred upon the said chapels by the said parishioners; therefore they acquired the right of patronage. Moreover, presupposing that the title of acquisition of that right of patronage had not been entirely legitimate from the beginning, it nevertheless gave the said parishioners a cause for prescribing.

† For the right of patronage, or the right of presenting, can belong to the people by ancient custom, and thus be prescribed by the people, as appears at first sight from the text in capitu. querelam, de elect., noted there by Ioan. And., and more fully upon the rule quod alicui gratiosè, de regu. iu. lib. 6. in Mercu. But the said parishioners were in quasi-possession of presenting for almost sixty years; therefore they prescribed the said right, since prescription of forty years also suffices against the church, as in capi. de quarta, de præscrip., and in c. 1. in 6., with similar authorities. Likewise, thirdly, since it is not established that any persons were patrons of the said chapels, and the people exercised the act of presentation for so long a time, we ought to presume that the parishioners were the builders of the said chapels, since it is certain that a church is not born, but is built by human intervention; therefore these parishioners, who exercised the act of presentation, ought to be presumed patrons, since others are not in possession of the other rights belonging to patrons. To this purpose is c. 1. de reli. domi., and what Inno. notes there; and what Ioan. And. notes upon the said rule quod alicui, at the end of the question, supports this. Moreover, and fourthly, what Ioan. And. notes in c. nobis de iure pa. supports this, where he concludes that

† he who builds a church is made patron, and consequently has the presentation not only of the principal rector of that church, but also of the chaplains to be instituted in the chapels. But notwithstanding these points, which, when diligently weighed, do not stand in the way, I think that the contrary is to be held in law: namely, that the said parishioners can by no means claim the right of patronage or the right of presenting from the aforesaid, and that the said altars, with the property donated to them, freely belong to the disposition of the plebanus of the said church. I am moved by a manifold consideration. And first, because, since the said altars were not constructed by the said parishioners, they cannot claim a right of patronage in them. For they cannot do so by reason of construction or foundation, nor by reason of dowry. For one obtains the right of patronage from the assignment of a dowry when he exercised this act at the time of consecration. But once chapels are founded and consecrated, a right of patronage cannot be newly acquired unless several things concur. For first, it is required that the property was conferred upon it not under a simple title of donation, for from a simple title one is called a benefactor rather than a patron, as noted by Ioan. And. in cap. 1. de iure patro.; it is necessary, therefore, that the property be conferred as a dowry. Likewise, that the chapels be without a dowry, and that the acquisition of the right of patronage be made with the consent of the bishop; because, since the chapel is consecrated, this servitude cannot be imposed on a sacred place without the bishop's consent, as by Ioan. And. in cap. 1., and Innocent upon the rubric of the same title; nay rather, the gloss in the said cap. piæ mentis. 16. q. 7. in no way wished to admit that from the assignment of a dowry after a church is consecrated a right of patronage could be acquired. That gloss, however, is limited according to the aforesaid. But in our case that property was not conferred as a dowry. Likewise, the bishop's consent did not intervene in the acquisition of that right of patronage; therefore, from such a donation of property, even if it had been made under the title of a dowry, the right of patronage could not have been acquired. Nor ought the bishop's consent to be presumed, since it is an extrinsic solemnity which is not presumed, just as, by analogy, the authority of a guardian is not presumed to have intervened in a contract of a ward: l. quæcunque, ff. de publiciana; noted by the gloss and Barto. in l. sciendum, ff. de uerbo. oblig.; noted by Innocen. in cap. innotuit, de eo, qui fur. or. re.; c. 1. de re. ecclesiæ non alie. lib. 6. strongly supports this, where in an alienation by a bishop the consent of the chapter is not presumed; all the more in this case the consent of the bishop himself ought not to be presumed. Moreover, and secondly, I say that even if those altars had been constructed by the parishioners of the said church, since they were not endowed by them, the right of patronage was not acquired. To this purpose is the singular gloss in c. quicunque, ii. 2. 16. q. 7., which states that one who gives a modest dowry is not made patron; all the more neither is he who conferred none. For that which is said, that one is made patron from construction and foundation, must be understood when others concur with him in endowing; for three can be made patrons of the same benefice, as if one constructs, another funds, and a third endows, as in the gloss on 63. dist. in summa, and the said c. piæ mentis; it is otherwise where one alone constructs without the assignment of a dowry. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that they endowed it afterward: because, since so much time elapsed from the time of construction, and they never presented, they do not appear to have constructed with the intention of acquiring patronage, but so that the said altars might be free and for the adornment of the said church. And furthermore, since the said chapels stood for one hundred and fifty years without any institution of chaplains, their founders lost all the right that they had, and the church prescribed their freedom; c. significauit and what is noted there de testi. supports this. For a servitude is lost by non-use, as in l. si sit constituta, ff. quemadm. serui. ami.; c. de quarta and what is noted there by Inn. de pręscri. supports this; therefore the new acquisition of patronage through the collation of that property was merely presumed. Second, it principally militates against the said parishioners that they prove neither a legitimate title nor a canonical prescription; for first, a legitimate title is not proved, as is clear from the aforesaid. For they are not proved to have constructed, nor to have endowed at a competent time and with legitimate solemnity; nor do they even prove a caused prescription; nay rather, holding the opinion of Archid., which seems truest in c. hortamur. 71. distin., prescription has no place in this case. For after long investigation he held that the right of patronage cannot be prescribed by a layman, although Ioan. Andr. attempts to refute him in the said rule quod alicui gratiosè. But the opinion of Arch. pleases me more, as I fully touched upon in a certain disputation which begins Augerio, responding most clearly to c. querelam, de cle., upon which the contrary opinion of Io. An. is founded. But I presuppose, without prejudice to the truth, that the opinion of Ioan. And. is truer: nevertheless, I say that the said parishioners ought to succumb, because they can by no means prove a caused prescription. First, because since this prescription is contrary to law, there is required either a legitimate title, or prescription of so long a time that memory of its beginning does not exist, as in cap. si diligenti, de præsc., and more clearly under the same title in lib. 6. c. 1. But in our case prescription of so long a time does not run, since there was memory of its contrary, nor a legitimate title sufficient for prescribing. For the title of the donation alleged above is contrary, because, as above, the collation of property or dowry alone does not suffice without the bishop's consent; whence the said parishioners err in law, but an error of law impedes prescription, so that such a title is not sufficient for prescribing, as in cap. dudum, joined with the gloss, de decimis; l. nunquam, de usuca.; noted by the gloss in cap. apostolicæ, de dona. Moreover, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the aforesaid prescription had been valid, yet it was not of so much time as suffices to complete a caused prescription. For quasi-possession of the right of presenting is not acquired unless the institution of the superior follows; to this purpose is what is noted by Inno. and Io. An. in c. 2. de integ. rest., and by the same Io. An. upon the said gloss of the rule quod alicui at the end of the question. But in our case the institution of the bishop followed only for the last thirty years; therefore the prescription of forty years—which alone runs against the church—was not completed, as in the said c. de quarta, and auth. quas actiones, C. de sacrosan. eccle. Nor does the institution or consent of the plebanus furnished in the prior thirty years stand in the way, because institution did not belong to the plebanus. Hence it is that recourse was afterward had to the bishop of the place; what is noted by the gloss in c. quamquam, de ele. li. 6., and what is noted by Io. An. in the said rule quod alicui, supports this, where it is clear

† that institution to benefices belongs by common law to the bishop alone, as is the text in c. cum ex iniuncto, at the end, de hære. Moreover and lastly, prescription cannot be alleged even if it had been continued for sufficient time, because the church was vacant for a period of 55 years. For the plebanus who was present at the time of the running prescription did not have a legitimate title, and thus was an intruder, since he had been deprived of his ecclesiastical title for a legitimate cause; whence he was more truly called a thief and a robber, in c. dudum. 2. de elect. But during the time of the vacancy of a church, prescription does not run, as noted by Inn. in cap. olim, de resti. spo., where he uniquely says that prescription does not run even for a vacant lower church, because there is no legitimate and immediate defender who can protect and reclaim the rights of the church. For those intruders, fearing to be cast out, do not dare to reclaim property that has been encroached upon, nor do they have affection for the church, but only strive to seize; whence having no rector and having an intruder are equivalent, as in c. 2. de transla. pręla.; what is noted by the gloss in c. 1. de integ. resti. lib. 6. and the text with the gloss in c. sacerdotes. 16. q. 3. support this. And from all the aforesaid I conclude that the said parishioners can by no means claim for themselves the right of patronage, or of presenting to the said chapels; and that the said chapels belong to the disposition of the plebanus together with the property conferred, nor could the parishioners reclaim the property donated by their ancestors, because a donation once perfected cannot be revoked, as in l. si, C. de reuo. do., even if the property had been conferred under pretext of an insufficiently legitimate cause, because an insufficiently legitimate cause is held as not added, and the donation remains pure, as is proved in 10. q. 1. c. 2., where the text is noted with the gloss; what is read and noted in c. significatum, de pręb., supports this. I say, however, that if the people of the parish were in possession of presenting in good faith, the one instituted upon the presentation of the people ought not to be removed, as in c. querelam, cited above, and c. consulta, de iure patro.; but the people were in bad faith, as noted by Inn. in c. 1. de in inte. resti., c. ex literis, de resti tu. spo., and c. cum ecclesia Sutrina, de causa pos. & propr., and the said c. consultationibus. And through the aforesaid, the response to the contrary arguments is clear. And through this the response to the first question is clear. Now entering upon the second doubt, namely, whether the said division made by the bishop stands in law, it seems first that it does. For the bishop can unite lesser churches, as in capitu. sicut unire, de exces. pręla. and c. uacante, de pręb.; therefore he can also divide them, as in c. sicut duo. 15. q. 1., and noted in the said c. sicut unire; the first rule de re. iu. supports this. For every thing, by whatever causes it is born, is dissolved by the same, as there. But these notwithstanding, I think that the contrary proceeds in law as to our case. For the division itself collapses by operation of law from a manifold cause. First, because it was made from a notoriously unjust cause. For the bishop asserted in the said division that he was making it on account of the slender nature of the revenues of that church of S. Maria. For this cause does not induce the power of dividing a church annexed to it, but rather of newly uniting to it, as in capitu. exposuisti, and cap. uacan. de præben., and noted in the said cap. sicut unire, and 10. q. 3. c. unio. Moreover, just as without a legitimate cause the rights of a church cannot be alienated, as in cap. sine exceptione. 11. q. 2. and in cap. 1. de reb. eccle. non alie. lib. 6., so too the division of the said annexation ought not to have been made without a legitimate cause, since to no one is it doubtful that the said division pertains to the alienation of the rights of the said church of S. Maria; what is read and noted in cap. constitutis, de elec. supports this. Moreover, the said division collapses from the defect of omitted solemnity. For it was not made with the consent of the chapter, nor with preceding deliberation: since, just as a union

† cannot be made without the consent of the chapter, nor does a custom to the contrary avail, as is the text joined with the gloss in clem. si una, de reb. eccl. non alie., so all the more ought a division not to be made without the said solemnity, by the argument in the said first rule. And because, as I have said, through this division the rights of that church of Santa Maria are alienated, deliberation also ought to have preceded, as in cap. tua, de his quæ fiunt a prælat., and in cap. 1. de reb. eccle. non alie. lib. 6. Moreover, in the said division the right of patronage was granted to certain laymen who neither constructed, nor founded, nor endowed the said chapel; therefore such a right could not be granted to them by the bishop, especially since the said chapel was already constructed and endowed at the time of the grant of the said right of patronage; for neither can the bishop impose this servitude upon a sacred thing without legitimate cause, as noted by the gloss in the said c. piæ mentis. 16. q. 7., and Io. An. in c. 1. de iur. iur., and Inno. upon the rubric of the same title; what is read and noted in c. cum dilectus, de consue. and c. 2. de iudi. supports this. From all of which it is evidently concluded in this second doubt that the said division by no means stands in law, nor was the grant of the said right of patronage valid, but that the said chapel can be claimed by the plebanus of the said church of S. Maria as from of old united and annexed to his church as a member pertaining to the mensa of the said plebanus. And although instruments concerning the said union or incorporation do not exist on account of the antiquity of the time, it nevertheless suffices that the said chapel was held by the said plebanus in the name of his church as united and incorporated into the church or mensa for so long a time that memory of its beginning does not exist; to this purpose is the text joined with the gloss in cle. 1. de exces. præl., and arguing Io. An. concludes this in reg. qui contra iura li. 6. in Merc. It can also be maintained that without any prescription or union the said chapel belongs to the plebanus, because it was built within the limits of his parish, and is adjacent to the said pieve; whence it ought to be presumed constructed and endowed from the goods of the said pieve, since it was possessed by this right by the said pieve for so long a time that there is no memory to the contrary: for this is the singular gloss in c. eam te. de æt. & qua., and what Io. An. notes upon it; and it supports the presumption that it was endowed and constructed from the goods of the said pieve, because it does not appear that another was founder or patron, and all rights of that chapel were always possessed by the plebanus of the said church; to this purpose is what Io. An. notes in reg. quod alicui, de reg. iu. li. 6. in Merc. at the end of the question, and what is noted in c. 1. de reli. do. supports this. And let these words suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. For several gifts to the same person to be valid, it is required that they be made at different times.
2. The solemnity of registration was not introduced in favor of the gift, but in hatred of those receiving clandestine gifts.
3. Wherever an oath is shamefully received, it ought to be released.
4. Absolution ought to be granted wherever someone swears contrary to the provision of the common law or of a statute.
5. If a daughter renounces a succession with an oath on account of fear and paternal reverence, she can seek absolution from the oath.
6. An oath sworn upon a contract solemnly entered into removes the praetor's benefice in obtaining restitutio in integrum.
7. Fraud is presumed in the most enormous lesion.
8. When a sworn contract can be challenged for fraud, a minor can first seek absolution, and afterward seek restitutio in integrum.
body: The protection of Jesus Christ the Redeemer having been devoutly invoked from the heart, four matters are to be investigated for the full clarification of the cause of the lady Baptista, daughter of the late Andrea Giovanni, and now wife of Francesco di Messer Cino. First, whether the gift made by her to her brother-german collapses from the lack of registration (*insinuatio*), insofar as it exceeds the sum of five hundred gold coins, notwithstanding that in the instrument of the said gift that clause was inserted, that there are as many gifts as there are items, and thus it should be permitted to the notary requested concerning it to draw up an instrument of gift for each single item so that it does not exceed, nor could exceed, the sum of five hundred gold coins, etc.; likewise notwithstanding the oath sworn by the said lady Baptista to the validity of the said gift. Second, it being presupposed that at least the oath obligates her not to contravene, whether absolution from that oath can be sought by her. Third, whether, absolution having been granted, she can vindicate as her own the said goods given by her, without first having sought *restitutio in integrum*. Fourth, it being presupposed that registration was not necessary under some head, say of custom or another occasion, whether at least by reason of *laesio* she can contravene by seeking absolution from the oath, and afterward *restitutio in integrum* against the gift, since at the time of the gift she was a minor, and now stands within the time for seeking *restitutio in integrum*. A fifth doubt can also be added, which ought to be first in order, namely, whether the said lady Baptista can be excluded from the maternal succession (the gift of whose goods is at issue) by virtue of a certain statute of Siena placed under the rubric: That a married woman does not succeed when males are extant; in which it is provided thus, insofar as it pertains to our purpose, namely: A married woman dowered by her father, brother, or paternal uncle shall not succeed to her mother intestate so long as there are male sons from her, etc. But the mother of lady Baptista died with a male also surviving, to whom the said lady Baptista made a gift of those maternal goods in any way accruing to her. I come to the first, and it seems that the said gift was valid without registration on a twofold ground. First, on account of that clause, that there be understood to be as many gifts as there are items, and that it be permitted to the notary to make an instrument of gift for each one by itself. For these words imply that there are several gifts, none of which exceeds the sum of five hundred florins, by argument in l. scire debemus, ff. de uerbo. obliga., and this Speculator seems to feel in tit. de instrum. edi. §. porro, ver. donatio, especially when the things given are enumerated; and in this case the same Speculator affirmed that the gift is valid in the said place, and more clearly in tit. de dona. §. 1. versic. quod si aliquis. But in our case they can be called enumerated, since the power was given to the notary of drawing up an instrument concerning each single item, so that no gift would exceed the sum of five hundred gold coins; therefore, the said gift cannot be broken from the defect of registration. But these notwithstanding, the truth stands to the contrary through the open text in l. sancimus. §. quis autem per diuersa, C. de dona., where it is expressly implied

† that, in order for several gifts made to the same person to be valid, it is required that they be made at diverse times, but otherwise if at the same time, just as happened in our case. For then that clause seems inserted in fraud of the law; and therefore it ought to accomplish nothing. For when several gifts are made at the same time to the same person, the person of the donor can be no less deceived than if it were a single gift; whence the law would be imposed on words, and not on things, against cap. commissa, de elect. lib. 6. and l. 2. C. communia de leg.; and through that §. quis autem, cited above, Bartolus disapproved the dictum of Speculator in l. Modestinus, ff. de donatio. and in §. si quis autem, and Johannes Andreae in the additions to Speculator on the said verse donatio, and Baldus holds in l. illud, C. de sacrosanct. eccle. I conclude therefore that the defect of registration is not supplied under the head of that clause. But a greater doubt is concerning the oath, namely, whether it supplies the defect of registration. Baldus in said l. illud affirmed that it does not, saying that from such a gift, even with an oath interposed, no obligation arises, not even a natural one; he is moved because, among other things, in order that an oath bind, it is required that the matter about which it is sworn not be prohibited by law, as in l. si quis inquilinos. §. fin. de lega. 1; but such a gift without registration is prohibited, as in l. donatio siue, C. de dona.; they also add that a law introducing a solemnity cannot be renounced, ff. de lega. 1. l. nemo potest.

† Likewise because the solemnity of registration was not introduced in favor of the gift, but in hatred of those receiving clandestine gifts, and lest anyone use his property prodigally. He also adduces to the aforesaid that which Cino notes in l. 1. C. de sacrosanct. eccle. and Bartolus in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiuss. But Johannes Andreae understands this point more broadly, both with respect to the renunciation of this solemnity and with respect to the oath, in the additions noting Speculator in tit. de instrum. edi. §. porro, cited above, at the word item notat; he seems, although he does not speak clearly, to incline toward the side that a simple renunciation is not valid—although Guilelmus de Cuneo held the contrary in the said l. illud, and Johannes Andreae recites him in the place cited above—but an oath is indeed valid, if it was sworn without force, fraud, or fear; to this they adduce the laws that approve an oath sworn in many cases prohibited by law, as in cap. cum contingat, de iureiuran., and cap. licet, under the same title in Liber 6, and cap. quamuis, de pact., in the same book, and the authentica Sacramenta puberum, C. si aduer. uen., with similar texts; and in my judgment Bartolus seems to have held the same in said l. Modestinus, at the end, joining what was noted by him in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiusso., to which law he refers in the said l. Modestinus. And I approve this opinion as safer; nevertheless because in a doubtful case we ought always to stand for the oath, lest from contravention anyone incur perjury, by argument in cap. iuuenis, de spon., and what the Gloss notes there in cap. uno, de scruti., and in matters concerning peril of the soul the safer side is to be held, as noted in the laws cited above; and there is an open text in Clem. exiui, de uerb. signifi. Moreover, it is certain that this registration does not primarily concern public utility, but the private utility of the donors themselves, although as a consequence it concerns the public, for it is of interest to the commonwealth that no one use his property badly, Inst. de his, qui sunt sui, uel alie. iur. §. sed hoc tempore, and in the Authentica Ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio; an oath to the contrary is valid, whether it is prohibited primarily in favor of the donor through cap. cum contingat, cited above, or whether such a gift is prohibited in hatred of those receiving clandestine gifts through the text in cap. significante, de pig., by which text, in my judgment, the opinion of Baldus is confounded. For the pact of the *lex commissoria* is rejected primarily in hatred of creditors, and yet the oath binds the swearer, as is read and noted in the said cap. significante; and through that text Cardinalis in said l. si quis pro eo, at the third word prohibetur, wished to give a rule that where a contract is prohibited in hatred of the creditor, an oath sworn in the contract must be observed, although it does not confirm the contract, according to him. So it must be said in our case; but the statement of Baldus and l. si quis inquilinos cited by him proceed when something is prohibited primarily in public favor, or because it would be against good morals, in which cases even under canon law an oath does not hold, as in cap. si diligenti, de foro competen. and in the rule Non est obligatorium, de regu. iur. lib. 6; and in this case l. non dubium, C. de legi. can be understood; otherwise when in private favor or hatred, as in the authentica Sacramenta puberum and in l. 1. C. si aduer. uen. For since that oath can be observed without peril of the swearer's soul, it must be observed, as in cap. si uero and cap. debitores, de iureiuran. Whence I conclude that the oath obligated the said lady Baptista, at least personally, not to contravene. It remains now to examine the second doubt: ought she to be heard seeking absolution from the oath? I believe undoubtedly that she should;

† because wherever an oath is basely received, it ought to be relaxed, as is read and noted in cap. 1 and in cap. debitores, de iureiuran. But this oath was basely received on multiple grounds. First, against the law providing that without registration a gift exceeding the sum of five hundred gold coins may not be made, l. si quis pro redemptione and l. donatio, C. de dona. Likewise there intervened great *laesio*, and thus fraud, at least *re ipsa*, l. si quis cum aliter, ff. de uerbo. oblig. Likewise fraud seems to have intervened even by design from the fact that three kinsmen called in to give consent according to the form of the Sienese statute swore in the presence of the lady Baptista herself that they believed that gift would turn to the benefit of the lady Baptista the donor herself, when this is utterly false: because to give is nothing other than to lose, l. filiusfam., ff. de dona.; and thus the *laesio* was manifest to the contrary, as Johannes Andreae says in the additions to Speculator in the place cited above; whence she seems to have been fraudulently induced into that gift. For this could have occurred since she was of minor age and saw her kinsmen swearing this in the presence of her father. And that in this case, even where so many factors did not concur, absolution from the oath ought to be granted seems to be the common conclusion of the doctors. For first, Federico da Siena held this in advising, consil. 264, where he concluded

† that absolution ought to be granted wherever anyone swore against the disposition of the common law or of a statute; because the contracting party seems to have basely received the oath by contracting against the disposition of the law; whence he ought rather to be punished than to carry off any advantage, dist. 8, cap. quae contra, and in cap. si necesse, de dote post di. resti. Vincentius seems to hold the same, Johannes Andreae reciting him in cap. cum contingat, de iureiur., where he said that the woman in the case of that chapter can insist on being absolved from the oath; therefore, all the more strongly in our case ought such absolution to be granted. Antonius de Butrio followed this same opinion in cap. cum contingat, when enormous *laesio* concurs: because then fraud is presumed, argument in cap. omnes. §. Lucius, ff. de his, quae in fraudem credi. Here, however, an extremely enormous *laesio* occurred: because she gave all the maternal goods accruing to her person, which amounted to the value of two thousand florins. The lord Pietro d'Ancarano of good memory seems to have advised almost on our terms in this city of Siena, as he himself reports in the repetition of cap. canonum, de constitu., especially with regard had because along with the enormous *laesio* there concur legal prohibition, minority of age, and fragility of sex, as that conclusion is very fully examined in the said places. But I do not care to proceed more extensively here, because the common opinion of the doctors concurs in this legal conclusion. For an oath ought not to be a bond of iniquity, as in cap. quanto, de iureiuran., and in cap. 1, under the same title in Liber 6. But it would be a bond of iniquity if it held indissolubly a young woman extremely enormously injured and deceived and induced by fraud, at least bound *re ipsa*; for frauds are to be confronted and not indulged, as in cap. sedes and cap. super literis, de rescrip. After a long investigation I decided this point thus in my lecture on the said cap. cum contingat, where the motives and reasons of this step appear very fully to the same effect, which Baldus notes in l. pactum, C. de colla., where he says

† that if a daughter, out of fear and paternal reverence, renounced the succession under oath, she can seek absolution from the oath, by argument from what is noted in l. 1. §. quae onerandae, ff. quarum re. ac. non datur; but the same occurs in our case, since the father was the author of this gift, so that the whole maternal inheritance would remain to the male son, whence it seems that she did this on account of paternal reverence, especially with that preceding oath of the kinsmen present, of which I spoke above. And these things concerning the second principal doubt. To the third doubt, whether, having obtained absolution from that oath, the said lady Baptista can vindicate those goods as her own, with no absolution having first been sought against the contract. This point also I examined fully in the said cap. cum contingat, in my lecture, and as the lord Antonius da Perugia said there in a certain consilium of his which begins Domina Catherina, on this point he held this distinction: that either the oath validates the contract, and then it is not permitted, once absolution is obtained, to come against the contract, because it was already validated from the interposition of the oath (absolution, however, avails according to him in this case so that the one contravening does not fall into perjury); or it does not validate the contract, but only obligates the swearer not to contravene, and then, absolution having been made, it immediately remains in its prior state; and thus he holds that in our case it is not necessary to seek *restitutio in integrum*, but immediately upon obtaining absolution from the oath she will be able to vindicate her goods. For in our case the oath does not serve to confirm the contract, since a gift beyond the sum of five hundred gold coins is prohibited in hatred of those receiving clandestine gifts, as I said above in the preceding article following Baldus in said l. illud, C. de sacrosanct. eccle.; therefore it is not confirmed by the oath through the theory of Bartolus in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideius., at the word quarto prohibetur contractus, etc. And the lord Antonius holds the same in cap. cum contingat, cited above, where he affirmed the same in his lecture; and this seems to be proved in cap. significante, de pig., where the pact of the *lex commissoria* in pledges is not validated by the oath, but the Pope only bases himself upon the personal oath, which being satisfied, no further care is had for the pact; rather, Johannes Calderinus and Paulus in a certain consilium held that indifferently, once the oath is removed, the contract is rescinded; and that opinion was followed in the said cap. cum contingat, when the contract was null without the oath: because, once the nourishment of the oath is removed, the contract remains ineffective without any prop, just as, the foundation being removed, the building is taken down, 1, q. 1, cap. cum Paulus. From these it is concluded that, especially in our case, the oath having been removed through lawful absolution, it is not necessary to seek restitution against the said gift insofar as it exceeds the sum of five hundred gold florins, since such a gift is null without an oath, as in said l. sancimus and l. si quis pro redemptione, even though it was made to a brother-german, as in l. datam, C. eod. titu.; and concerning that registration, how it is to be made, it is fully noted by Johannes Andreae in the additions to Speculator in said §. porro, and by Baldus in said l. illud, and Bartolus in l. Modestinus, ff. de sol. To the fourth doubt, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the said registration was not necessary on some ground, whether at least by reason of *laesio* the said lady Baptista can contravene by seeking first absolution from the oath, and afterward restitution against the contract. It seems first that she cannot, through the text in l. 1. C. si aduer. uen., through which text the doctors there commonly say, and especially Bartolus and Baldus,

† that an oath sworn upon a contract solemnly entered into takes away the benefit of the praetor in obtaining *restitutio in integrum*. But truly, in my judgment, that text does not decide our question. For it speaks while the oath is standing. For, during the bond of the oath, *restitutio in integrum* cannot be sought, whether the contract was entered into with solemnity or not; and to this effect the Authentica Sacramenta puberum works today, which seems today to approve the opinion of Martinus concerning which it is discussed there, as noted in the said l. 1 and in the Authentica Sacramenta, and it seems to be proved in cap. cum contingat, de iureiurand.; and this the text in said l. 1 most openly implies when the Emperor says, 'you ought not to have hoped that I would be the author of either faithlessness or perjury,' etc. But once the oath is removed through lawful absolution, perjury cannot be noted in granting or seeking *restitutio in integrum*; nay, the oath is observed if absolution is sought beforehand, as in cap. uenerabilem, de elect., cap. uerum, de iureiuran., with similar texts. And therefore Innocent notedly said in cap. 2, de iureiuran., with similar texts, that to no one against his own oath is *restitutio in integrum* given, but absolution only; but against an oath sworn by another, *restitutio in integrum* is indeed given; say, if a minor was harmed by deferring the oath to another in court, as in l. nam postea. §. 2. de iureiuran. Whence it must be seen whether in this case absolution from the oath can be sought; and I think that it can: because, given an extremely enormous *laesio* along with minority of age and fragility of sex, there appears a lawful and just cause for seeking absolution. Because an oath ought not to be a bond of iniquity, cap. quanto, de iureiuran. But who doubts that it is most iniquitous that an oath should bind a young woman without the remedy of absolution to tolerate an extremely enormous *laesio*? Argument in cap. uerum, de iureiuran.

† Furthermore, and more strongly, in an extremely enormous *laesio* fraud is presumed, in l. Lucius. §. omnes, ff. de his, quae in frau. cre., and l. creditor. §. Lucius, ff. mandati; nay rather, in our case open fraud intervened, because the kinsmen swore that they believed this gift would turn to the benefit of lady Baptista herself, whom she reasonably had to believe, argument in l. transactione, C. de transact.; therefore this oath is to be remitted through cap. cum contingat, in fine, and what is noted in the previously cited cap. 2, de pact. lib. 6. And the lord Antonius and Pietro d'Ancarano seem sufficiently to hold this side, as I said, in said cap. cum contingat; moreover, the oath being removed, I do not see what prevents the said lady Baptista from seeking *restitutio in integrum* against the *laesio*, since she is still within the times for seeking *restitutio in integrum*, as in l. fi. C. de tempo. in integ. rest.; and Baldus held this opinion openly in said l. 1, in fine, C. si aduer. ven., where he says

† that when a sworn contract can be accused of fraud, a minor can first seek absolution, and afterward seek *restitutio in integrum*; which is most equitable, and harmonious with the law; l. si ex falsis, C. de transact. serves excellently, where, notwithstanding an oath, one who has suffered fraud is aided against the contract. All the more strongly therefore does this proceed when fraud was employed against a minor. Nor let it move anyone that the gift was made to a brother-german: because that is not a sufficient cause for giving from the goods of a minor, argument in l. cum plures, and what is noted there, ff. de admi. tut.; and from the oath previously sworn by the kinsmen it is clear that the said lady Baptista did not have the will of simply giving, especially so great a quantity. It remains now to descend to the fifth and last matter, which was to be examined first. For if she is excluded on the pretext of the statute from the maternal succession, it is discussed in vain whether the gift can be impugned; and truly, without other argumentation, for the sake of brevity to the parties, I think firmly that the said lady Baptista was by no means excluded by the aforesaid statute: because the statute speaks of a woman married and dowered by her father, etc. But the said lady Baptista at the time of the death of her mother, when the succession was opened, was neither dowered nor married; therefore the said statute had no place in her case. For since a statute is odious as excluding females from maternal succession contrary to l. maximum uitium, C. de li. prete., it ought to be strictly understood; therefore it ought not to be extended to a cause in which the quality required by the statute is not found, as in cap. statutum, de elect. lib. 6; nor ought we to depart from the common law except insofar as it is found in the statute, as in l. praecipimus, in fine, C. de appel.; nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the said lady Baptista was then dowered and married by her father: because I say that the statute excludes a female when at the time of the succession she is found married and dowered by her father, etc.; but it does not suffice that after the inheritance was opened she was married and dowered. For a quality attached in any proposition is understood according to the tense of the verb to which it refers, according to the theory of Bartolus in l. ex facto, ff. de uul. & pup., in said l. praecipimus, C. de app., and through the Gloss in cap. statutum, in principio, on the word canonicis, at the end, de rescr. lib. 6. But those words of the statute, 'a woman married and dowered, etc.,' refer to the verb 'shall succeed.' She must therefore be dowered at the time of the succession, but not afterward; whence the statute wished to exclude from succession her who had been provided for with a husband and dowry, but not her who had not yet been provided for; nor did it wish to deprive of an inheritance already acquired, but to repel from one to be acquired; and great is the difference between not taking a gain and losing what is acquired, as in l. si sponsus. §. maritus, de do. inter ui. & uxo.; nay rather, in this case, in which the statute is odious, under the appellation of 'married woman' a daughter betrothed only through words of the future is not included, as the doctors note in l. non solum, C. de bo. quae lib., through which notable law the lord Pietro d'Ancarano advised, as he himself reports in the repetition of the said cap. canonum: if it is provided by statute that a married daughter shall not succeed the father together with the brothers, a betrothed daughter ought not to be excluded by virtue of the statute. For the words of a statute must be greatly restricted insofar as it brings odium, as noted in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iur.; it is proved in cap. cum dilectus, de consue. and in l. 2. C. de noua. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. There is no difference between a pubes and a ward capable of deceit with respect to an oath-bound obligation.
2. A ward capable of deceit is effectively bound if he swore that he would perform services.
3. A judicial decree is not required under common law in a peace to be made by a ward.
body: That which is effectively sought in law is whether a peace made by a ward [pupillus], who is nonetheless capable of deceit [doli capax], confirmed by oath with the tutor's authority, and without a judicial decree, was valid, notwithstanding a statute which provides that a minor cannot contract without a judicial decree. And first, having invoked the aid of Christ the Savior, it seems it should be said that it was not: because since the ward is bound to observe the peace, especially in our case, in which a penalty was affixed to both sides, it cannot be denied that he is said to have contracted, as in l. omnem obligationem, ff. de iud. where it is said that every obligation is to be held as a contract, so that wherever anyone is bound, he is seen to contract, etc.; therefore, from the lack of a decree, said peace was not valid; and this especially proceeds if we hold the opinion of those who said that, even in the absence of a statute, a tutor cannot authorize a peace to be made by a ward, as noted in l. 1. C. de in inte. rest. mino. where by Cy. and Bal. in l. pactum curatoris, C. de pac. where by Bal. and Iac. de Are. and by Spe. in ti. de homi. ver. illud, as if the tutor were seen to remit a liquidated and clear right of the ward without cause, contrary to l. præses, C. de transa. and l. pactum curatoris, cited above. But notwithstanding these points, I think the contrary must be said in our case on two grounds. First, by reason of the oath sworn by the ward, which oath indeed renders him of full age, and supplies every defect of a decree, or of any other formality, as is read and noted in auth. sacramenta pub. C. si aduer. ven. and more clearly in c. cum contingat, de iureiu. and by Fed. cons. 260. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that auth. sacramenta speaks of a pubes [one arrived at puberty], but we speak of a ward, whom an oath does not bind, as the gloss thinks in the said auth. sacramenta, and more clearly there Bald. and Cy.

† Because I say that with respect to an oath-bound obligation there is no difference between a pubes and a ward capable of deceit; for just as each is bound by perjury, as in cap. 1. de deli. pue., so each is bound by the oath. For these are correlatives. And that a capable ward is bound by an oath, I cite the notable and full gloss in cap. paruuli, 22. q. 5. and the gloss in c. 1. de delic. pue. There is also a notable text of civil law in l. fi. §. in eum, ff. de libe. cau. where it is held,

† that a ward capable of deceit is effectively bound if he swore that he would perform services, so much so that even when he becomes a pubes he can be sued upon that oath, as is remarkably proved there; and that text was expressly cited to this point by the gloss in said cap. paruuli; and through that text in l. fin. the gloss said there, wishing to save its opinion on auth. sacramenta, that in a contract the oath of a ward is not obligatory, namely through the said auth. sacramenta, but in other matters it is so, through the said l. fin.; but this distinction is not approved. For no reason of diversity appears, as regards the one to whom the primary obligation of the oath is acquired, between one contract and another, especially because in a broad sense, wherever anyone is bound, he is seen to contract, as in said l. omnem obligationem. That, however, an oath also binds a ward capable of deceit in a contract, I cite the clear text together with the second gloss in cap. ex literis. 2. de spon. where an oath binds a ward in a contract of espousals where it is a matter of keeping the peace, which is to be sought, and persuaded, and meritorious, as throughout distinction 90, especially in c. placuit. Furthermore, Host., Ioan. An., and commonly the Canonists hold in said cap. cum contingat that the said authentica applies also to an impubes capable of deceit, and likewise Bartolus there, saying that this is commonly held; whence by the aforesaid the text of that authentica ought to be supplemented, so that the same holds in an impubes capable of deceit. Since it is not novel that one law be supplemented by another, as in c. cum expediat, de elect. lib. 6. and l. unica, C. de in offic. do. Above, moreover, I adduced canonical and civil laws which maintain that the oath of such persons must be preserved by all means. The said peace can be sustained on a second ground, even without consideration of the oath: because since the aforementioned statute deviates from the rules of the ius commune insofar as it requires that in every contract of a minor a judicial decree must intervene, contrary to l. interdum. §. qui tutelam, ff. de fur. with similar texts, it must be interpreted strictly, as in c. cum dilectus, de consue. and l. 2. C. de noxa. It ought therefore to be understood of a contract strictly taken. A contract properly taken, however, is when an obligation arises reciprocally [ultro citroque], as in l. Labeo, ff. de uer. sig.; but in a peace to be made, or made, an obligation does not properly arise from both sides, but rather it is a kind of reconciliation, as noted by Bal. in said l. pactum curatoris, or a kind of remission of an injury, as in c. si illo, and c. si is, qui prælatus, 23. q. 4. and what is noted in both places to the same effect as what the gloss notes in c. Adrianus, dist. 63; hence we see that an injury is erased by intention without any other obligation, as in the Institutes, de iniurijs, at the end, and C. de iniur. l. si non conuitii; hence it is that the podestà can compel the parties to peace, according to the points fully noted by Bartolus in l. congruit, ff. de offi. præsid.; there is also the text joined with the gloss in cap. placuit, distinction 90. Therefore it was not the intent of the statute to require a judicial decree for that to which one could be compelled; rather, the statute only intended that the ward, by obligating himself, should not diminish his estate. I admit, however, that in this case the stipulation of a penalty is not valid; nevertheless, the peace remains binding, because in severable matters the useful is not vitiated by the useless, as in the rule utile, de regu. iur. lib. 6. with its gloss, and capitulum dilectus, first, de præbend. where the case is found. And under this consideration it must unquestionably be said that the oath sworn by the ward capable of deceit was valid, through said l. fina. ff. de libe. cau. and said capitulum ex literis. And this opinion seems more common,

† so that under the ius commune a judicial decree is not required in a peace to be made by a ward, since it is not detrimental to the ward, as noted in the passages cited above, and Io. And. thinks in addi. Specu. in §. 1. in tit. de homi. at the end, and Iac. de Are. and Bald. in l. 1. C. de in integ. resti. mino. and said l. pactum curatoris, and to me this is undoubted, by argument in l. pater, ff. de lega. 3. with similar texts. I conclude therefore from all the premises that the said peace is valid and holds, and by no means falls on account of the lack of a decree. And let these things suffice. Nicol. Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A thing can be vindicated from him who was put into possession for the sake of custody.
2. Whether he who was put into possession by the first decree can be sued by a rei vindicatio.
3. Fraud cannot truly be proved, since it resides in the mind.
4. I deposited a sealed pouch with you, and you do not restore it, or you restore it opened; because of your presumed fraud in not restoring or in opening it, my oath will be stood by regarding the things that were said to be inside.
body: IN the name of Christ, amen. Concerning the fact narrated and advised upon above, three rather good novel arguments are made against the party of Guglielmo. First, that since Petrus, who was sued, was not a possessor, but solely a custodian or detainer, having been put into possession by the first decree in a personal action—in which case he does not possess, as in l. is cui, ff. ut in possessionem lega., and l. si finita, § si quis autem possessionem, ff. de dam. infect., as noted by Specu. under the title de primo et secundo decreto, § iam de effectu, verse sed utrum missus and the following verse, and noted in cap. contingit, de dolo et contuma.—therefore the rei vindicatio did not lie against him, as noted by Inno. in c. quoniam contra, de proba. The second argument is that, by the authority of the judge interposing the second decree in the vindication of those goods, this Petrus is excused from fraud (dolus), even though he sold after a suit was initiated against him concerning the ownership of the goods into whose possession he had been put by the authority of another judge; therefore the oath in litem could not be deferred to the adversary, according to the note in l. 1, in § in actionibus, ff. de in litem iuran., and similar laws. The third argument is that the oath in litem must be deferred after the judgment and not before, according to the note by Barto. in said l. in actionibus, ff. de in litem iur. In the present case, however, the oath was deferred before the judgment; therefore, now in this cause of appeal, it must be pronounced that it was well appealed and badly judged. And although these arguments seem refined, nonetheless, if all things done in this matter are weighed, together with the laws speaking to this subject, they least of all stand in the way of our case. And first, as to the first argument, I say that the text in l. officium, at the end, ff. de rei ven., clearly proves the contrary. For it says, limiting or correcting the preceding statement of Pegasus, that from all who detain and have the ability to restore, the property can be vindicated; and Bartolus himself, the illuminator of the civil law, most clearly willed this even in our case, so understanding that law, which is evident from his summary, for he summarizes it in these words: that this—namely, the rei vindicatio—is given against him who possesses, or is in possession for the sake of custody, or otherwise detains. These are formally the words of Bartolus. Hostiensis clearly willed this same thing in c. contingit, de dolo et contum., at the end, and Io. And. agrees with him, reciting it and saying

† that from him who has been put into possession for the sake of custody, the property can be vindicated. I confess, however, that Inno. seems to have thought otherwise in our case in the said c. quoniam contra. But truly, if it is well weighed, he did not think otherwise. For within our terms, Inno. touched upon this question in § quod si super, on the word 'possessionem', where he tacitly asks

† whether he who was put into possession by the first decree can be sued by rei vindicatio; and he reports contrary opinions. For some have held that he can, because he has the faculty of restoring, by l. officium, ff. de rei vendi., cited above; but he himself feels the contrary, moved by this reason: because he does not have the faculty of restoring, since he merely guards, and as a custodian is sometimes a detainer; and Specu. also goes along with this, reciting Innocent under the title de primo et secundo decreto, § iam in effectu, verse sed nunquid missus, at the end. But the reasoning of Innocent must be carefully weighed: for he was moved because, regularly, the person who suffers putting into possession in a personal action is not expelled from possession, even natural possession, but remains in possession, and the person put into possession only has custody lest the former squander, and so that, affected by weariness, he may obey the judge, as in the said l. is cui, and more clearly noted by Specu. in the said § sed nunquid missus and following. Yet in our case this reason ceases, because that Petrus, having been put into possession, had free detention, because the judge so decreed on account of the absence of the contumacious defendant; deservedly does the statement of Innocent cease to apply, as in l. cum pater, § dulcissimis, ff. de lega. 2.
