And therefore, in resolving and reconciling these opinions, it can be said that either he who is put into possession does not have free detention, but only custody—and then the statement of Innocent and Specu. proceeds, for then the rationale of l. officium, at the end, ceases, as he does not have the faculty of restoring the thing, and therefore the thing cannot be vindicated from him; or he has free detention, as this Petrus had in our case—and then he can be sued by rei vindicatio, because he can restore that which he himself has; and the same must be said of other detainers, as of depositaries and the like. And thus reconciling them, the Lord Antonius de Butrio, that solemn doctor, held in c. examinata, de iud., and he opines in the said c. quoniam contra, § quod si super, as in li. non conte. It must be admitted, however, that he who detains in the name of another will be able, if he wishes, to avoid the trial by naming the owner in court, according to the benefit of l. 2, C. ubi in rem actio, and the said § quod si super rebus. From these points it is most clearly inferred for the decision of the second argument: for since the said Petrus can be sued, it follows that he ought not to have alienated those goods while the suit was pending; and since he did so, he is presumed to have acted in fraud, and this presumption of fraud is proved by law, because from the fact that he traded contrary to the law, he is presumed in fraud, as in l. quemadmodum, C. de agri. et censi. lib. 11, and in the rule qui contra iura, de regu. iur. in 6., as noted by Barto. in l. sed et si, § scire, ff. de peti. haere.; nor does the authority of the judge excuse him, because he circumvented the judge through surreption by maliciously keeping silent that a suit was pending over those goods; deservedly is he presumed in fraud, on the argument in capitulo cum dilecta and what is noted there, and capitulo super literis, de rescr., and l. si quis obrepserit, ff. de falsis, and what Barto. notes there in l. iuste possidet, ff. de acq. poss.

† Fraud, moreover, cannot be truly proved, since it resides in the mind, but it is proved from conjectures, as in l. dolum, C. de dolo, and in cap. 2, de renun. in 6. The conjectures here, however, are sufficient and approved by law, both because he sold contrary to the law, and because he practiced surreption on the judge, and because at the beginning of the suit he denied that he detained those goods, and yet later, having circumvented the authority of the judge, he sold them; to this effect is l. pen., ff. de rei vendi., and in auth. item possessor, C. qui potio. in pig. hab. To the third and last point I reply that the oath in litem is sometimes deferred on account of contumacy in not obeying the judge, and then it is deferred after the judgment, according to l. qui restituere, ff. de rei ven. Sometimes it is deferred in place of proof, because on account of the adversary's fraud, proof is rendered difficult; and then, since the oath succeeds in the place of proof, it is deferred before the judgment, and afterward the condemnation follows, as is proved in c. si., quod met. cau., where the text is open; and therefore Innocent said there, and Bartolus follows in the said l. in actionibus,

† that if I deposited a sealed bag with you, and you do not restore it, or restore it open, because of your presumed fraud in not restoring or in opening it, my oath will be relied upon regarding the things that were said to be there. So in the case at hand, on account of this man's fraudulent alienation, proof of the ownership of those goods was rendered difficult for Guido; deservedly could the oath in litem be deferred to him, as in l. 3, ff. ad exhibend., and afterward the condemnation follows, as in the said c. si., quod me. cau. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The words "it seems" and "it shall please" savor of the arbitrament of a good man.
2. If a testator has said, "I commit my last will to your disposal," he is deemed to die testate for pious causes.
3. A bishop does not receive the fourth from exempt places.
4. That which is disposed by an executor or fideicommissary is deemed disposed by the testator.
body: In the case of the hospital of Santa Caterina of Todi regarding the validity of the donation made to it by Iacopo di Abramuzio out of the estate of the late Iacopo Massanuzio, four questions must be examined, having invoked the name of Christ. First, whether the said Iacopo di Abramuzio could retain the property of that testator Iacopo Massanuzio as devolved upon himself, or whether he is bound to distribute it for the soul of the testator. Second, presupposing that he was obligated to distribute it, whether he alone could dispose of that property, since three persons were designated in the will, two of whom passed away before the distribution of that property. Third, assuming that he could do so alone, whether it was valid to give that property to the said hospital after a year from the time when the said distribution ought to have been made. Fourth, if it is held that the lapse of the year was no impediment, whether the validity of the said donation is impeded at least on account of the dispute, or process, of the lord Bishop of Todi. Regarding the first, I say briefly that that property was not devolved purely upon the said Iacopo and the other colleagues mentioned in the will, but they were chosen and designated by the testator as universal fideicommissaries to distribute that property to pious causes. The words of the testator clearly prove this, which were as follows: 'The residue, however, of my inheritance and property, upon the occurrence of the said condition, I have remitted and left to the conscience of Lady Lucretia, and Lady Perina, and Iacopo di Abramuzio, who may dispose of the said residue and do whatever shall seem good to them and please them; making them in the aforesaid matters his universal fideicommissaries, etc.' For first, those words must be weighed: 'He left to the conscience, etc.' For he did not leave the property to them simply, but to their conscience, as if burdening their conscience; according to what is noted in c. statutum, § assessorem, together with the Gloss, de rescri. in Sext., and what is noted by the Gloss in Clem. 1, de iure patro., at the word oneramus. Second, those words contribute: 'They may dispose and do as it shall seem good to them and please them.' For those

† words 'shall seem good' and 'shall please' savor of the arbitrament of a good man, as in l. fideicommissa, § quamquam, ff. de lega. 3, and in l. Thais, § sororem, ff. de fideicommiss. lib., noted by the Gloss in cap. 2, de corpo. vit., at the word visum, noted by Bartolus in extravagantibus ad reprimendum, and l. alio, ff. de ali. & cib. lega. Furthermore, what need is there for another interpretation, when afterwards at the end of the words the testator expressly said that he made them his universal fideicommissaries? He therefore committed to their faith that they distribute that property according to the arbitrament of a good man; and in case of doubt, it must be understood, namely, to pious causes, because a good man ought so to decide, unless he should show the contrary through legitimate reasons. And in favor of this understanding, the text according to the common reading in cap. cum tibi, de testa., is apparent, where it is decided

† that if anyone says, 'I commit my last will to your disposal,' he is deemed to die having made a bequest to pious causes; all the more, therefore, is this to be said in our case, where the testator used clearer words. Bartolus and Baldus also held this in l. 1, C. de sacrosanct. eccle., where Bartolus said further, namely, that if anything is left to the arbitrament of another simply, and it is not stated for what purpose, in doubt it is understood to be for pious causes through the said c. cum tibi; but it is otherwise, according to him, if he said 'to the will of such a one,' and did not express 'for pious causes,' because then through that word 'to the will' he is deemed to leave it to his free will, as in the said § quamquam. And this must be held without doubt. Wherefore, regarding the first point, I conclude that the said Iacopo was in effect designated as a minister and dispenser of that property to pious causes. To the second doubt, whether he alone could distribute that property, or give it to the hospital; and I believe that he could: because, since they were, as I have said, in effect the executors and ministers of the said will, the other colleagues being dead and thus unable to fulfill the deceased's will, he alone could carry it out through capitulum 2, § 1, de testamen. in Sext.; it seems to be of the opinion of Bartolus in l. 1, § si plures, ff. de exercito., at the words ut igitur liqueat materia, at the end; what Federicus de Senis posits in his consilia, consil. 65, contributes to this, for that special provision is introduced lest the will of the deceased be frustrated, as is stated there. And this concerning the second doubt. Regarding the third: whether the said Iacopo could give the said property to the hospital after a year from the time the condition placed in the will occurred. It seems at first that he could not: because, although by law a year is granted to execute the will of the deceased from the time a warning is to be made by the superior, as in capitulum nos quidem, de testamen., and in Authen. hoc amplius, C. de fideic. lib., yet because a constitution of the diocesan bishop warns and establishes a year from the day on which the distribution is to be made, it is certain that the bishop was able to do this, because he can assist the canon by imposing a penalty and aggravating the act, as noted by the Gloss in Clem. ne Romani, de elect., by Ioannes Andreae in cap. fin., de off. archi.; the text in cap. 2, de consti. in Sext., seems to support this, and on our exact point Federicus de Senis agrees in his consilia, consil. 124. But, these things notwithstanding, I think that according to law the contrary must be said in our case. I am principally moved because, as I said before, under the ius commune the said Iacopo is not deprived of the power of fulfilling the will of the deceased through the lapse of a year, unless the lapse occurred after a warning made to him, as I stated above; which did not happen here. Nor does the synodal constitution stand in the way: for that proceeds with respect to bare testamentary executors; but the said Iacopo was not a bare executor, but a bare minister—indeed, he had the power of choosing the poor or pious places. For this was left to his conscience, so that he might do as it seemed good to him and pleased him. But it is certain that when someone has the power of choice, the year does not immediately run; rather, it is necessary that he first be placed in default through a formal demand, as is the text noted in l. cum quidam, ff. de lega. 2; and through that text Bartolus expressly confirmed this there in our case, saying through that text that he had answered on the facts that, although in an episcopal constitution it is provided that the executors of last wills must carry them out within a year, otherwise the execution is transferred to the bishop, nevertheless, if the testator left a thousand to those poor whom such a one should choose, even though he did not make the choice within a year, the power was not thereby devolved upon the bishop; because it is certain that under the ius commune the power does not devolve ipso facto upon the bishop through the lapse of a year, as is clear from the aforesaid, nor from the form of the constitution: because the constitution says that executors must execute within a year. But this man, concerning whom the question is raised, is not an executor, which is clear from the fact that there is a difference between him who declares and him who has execution. For a judge is called he who declares and passes sentence; but an executor is called he who has bare ministry, as in l. executorem, C. de execu. rei iud. But he who has the choice ought not to be called an executor, because he did not have bare ministry in paying (which passes to the bishop from his constitution), but the right of choosing the pious cause; and in this he cannot be called an executor, but a chooser. Bartolus meant this in effect most beautifully in the said l. cum quidam, and Petrus de Ancharano follows him in the said cap. nos quidem, de testament.; all the more, therefore, is this to be said in our case, in which the said Iacopo had greater power than the one in Bartolus's example, because that man had to choose the poor, whereas this one could choose any pious cause whatever; for this, see what Bartolus noted in the said l. cum quidam, and what is noted in the said cap. cum tibi. For that property was left to his conscience, so that he might dispose and do whatever seemed good to him and pleased him, etc. He ought, therefore, first to have been requested and formally demanded by the bishop to dispose of it, and only upon his refusal or delaying could the bishop have disposed of it; which was not done here at all. Therefore the power remained with the said Iacopo, the lapse of the year notwithstanding. And this concerning the third. It remains to examine the fourth doubt: whether on account of pending litigation the said donation ought to be impeded; and it seems that it should: because that property had been made litigious on account of the bishop's suit; but litigious property cannot be alienated, even to a church, as in capitulum ecclesia, ut lit. penden., and in Authen. litigiosa, C. de litig. But the truth is to the contrary: because between the bishop and this Iacopo there was no dispute concerning the ownership of that property. For the bishop was not saying that the ownership of that property belonged to him, but the dispute was over another, extrinsic right, namely over the power of distributing that property; in which case no one will say that the property is rendered litigious, as is read and noted in the said Authen. litigiosa, and by Bartolus in l. lite, C. eod., and by Innocent in capitulum cum M., de constitu., especially since here no joinder of issue had intervened, nor indeed even a citation regarding the bringing of a suit, because the bishop only deprived the said Iacopo of the said power of distribution without any hearing of the case, or declared him deprived, and commanded him henceforth not to meddle with it, which command the said Iacopo was not bound to obey as notoriously unjust and contrary to law, as in the rule ea quae sunt a iudice, de regu. iur. in Sext., and by Innocent in cap. ad aures, de tempo. ordi., and in cap. inquisitioni, de senten. excommu., and by the Gloss, 11, quaest. 3, in the opening summary, and similar authorities. And a fifth doubt could be added here: whether from the said property the bishop ought to have a fourth; and I say that he should not: because the hospital is said to be exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop,

† and from exempt places the bishop does not receive the fourth, as is commonly held by the doctors in c. officii, de testam.; Federicus de Senis so states in his consilia, consil. 96, and Baldus in l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de episc. & cler.; what is read and noted in Clem. dudum, de sepul., together with the Gloss at the word quarta, also supports this. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that not the testator, but the aforesaid Iacopo chose the said hospital. For this is no impediment:

† because what is disposed of by an executor, or fideicommissary, is deemed to be disposed of by the testator as the efficient cause, and by the fideicommissary as the instrument; and so in our very terms Bartolus confirms in l. unum ex familia, ff. de lega. 2, through that text, which serves excellently, and Baldus in l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de episco. & cle.; the text in Clem. dudum, de sepul., § verum, together with the Gloss at the word indirecte, also supports this. And let these remarks suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A nun is said to be married not properly, but fictitiously.
2. One who has carnal knowledge of a nun can be accused of adultery.
3. Whatever a father offers to a monastery at the time of his daughter's entry must be calculated after the manner of a dowry into the legitima of that daughter.
4. A correction of the laws ought not to be introduced by similitude of reason.
5. When the prince intends that, with respect to a decision, a constitution is extended to pending matters, he always makes mention of them.
6. Possibility with respect to a dowry is considered from three things.
body: Having humbly invoked the protection of the Savior Jesus Christ and of His most pious Mother. In the case of Caterina, a nun, or of the monastery claiming on the one part, three matters must be examined. First, whether the said Caterina is excluded from the paternal succession by virtue of the municipal statute providing that a married and dowered woman shall not succeed when males are surviving, etc. Second, if she is not excluded under that head, whether she can be excluded by virtue of the other statute which was enacted while the suit concerning this succession was pending, in which it is among other things provided that a woman who has entered a monastery cannot claim anything in the paternal inheritance, etc., when male sons are surviving, always with the reservation that it shall be lawful for her parents to leave to her as to them shall seem good and pleasing; to which statute there was added the clause, “and let this apply to present, past, and future cases.” Third, if the said statute does not stand in the way of the said Caterina, it is asked what portion in the said inheritance is owed to her. Concerning the first, it seems that the said Caterina is excluded as married and dowered;

† for from the time she was made a nun, she is said to be wedded to God, as in cap. quæ Christo specialiter nubunt, 27. quæst. 1; hence the glossa notably stated in cap. virginibus, in the same causa and quæstio,

† that one who has carnal knowledge of a nun can be accused of adultery, because he has known the spouse of another. Likewise, she is said to be dowered, because at her entry the father gave one hundred florins to the monastery, and in common parlance this is said to be given for the dowry of the one entering; hence Bartolus stated in the said l. 1, §. si parens, ff. si quis a pa. tue. manumiss., and Baldus follows him in l. quoniam novella, C. de inoffic. testamen., saying

† that whatever a father offers to a monastery at the time of his daughter’s entry must be calculated after the manner of a dowry into the legitima of that daughter, because it succeeds into the place of a dowry. But these things notwithstanding, I say that the contrary proceeds in law: because a nun is not properly said to be married, but fictitiously and by way of similitude, argument from cap. 1, 27. quæst. 1; nay rather, she is feigned to be dead, 16. quæst. 1, capit. placuit; and it is certain that a provision made for a true case has no place in a fictitious case, especially in a statute, as is the text in l. 3, §. hæc autem verba, ff. de nego. gesto., and what is read and noted in capitulo in nostra, de iniu.; Bartolus confirms this in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iure, in the repetition; and this must be said above all in our case, wherein the statute amends the civil law in that it excludes a married and dowered female from the paternal succession when males are surviving, contrary to l. maximum vitium, C. de libe. præte., and the authentica in successione, C. de suis & legi.; therefore it must be restricted and understood in its proper terms; nay rather, it must be taken improperly, if it can be done in a correct manner, so that it amends the common law as little as possible, as in capitulo cum dilectus, de consuetu., and in l. 2, C. de noxa., with similar authorities; and what the same Bartolus notes in the authentica quas actiones, C. de sacro. sanct. ecclesi., supports this, where he maintained

† that an amendment of the laws must not be introduced through a similitude of reason; and the glossa maintained the same in cap. indemnitatibus, de elect. lib. 6, on the word confirmetur. Nor is the reason entirely the same in both cases; and this I say in order to satisfy the arguments of Baldus in the said authentica quas actiones. I conclude here briefly that the said Caterina is not to be excluded from the paternal succession under the head of that statute, since she is not properly wedded and married; but the statute speaks through these two qualities to the end that females be excluded by a male; when they are lacking, the statute ceases to apply, argument from cap. fin. de resti. spol., and l. præcipimus, and what is noted there, C. de appell.; and so much for the first doubt. I come now to the second, whether she is excluded under pretext of the other statute; and truly in our case the statute is of no effect, because it could not prejudice women who had already entered the monastery at the time of the statute, as was this Caterina, who had not only entered but had also adited the paternal inheritance, as Bartolus maintained in l. fin. C. de pact., and Baldus in l. deo nobis, C. de episco. & cler.; nay rather, in respect of those who entered afterwards, it can be doubted whether the statute was valid, as noted in the laws alleged above; I said this in capitulo quod clericis, de foro compe., in the addition; and what Johannes Andreæ notes in regula sine culpa, de regu. iur. lib. 6, in the Mercuriales, supports the aforesaid, where he holds generally that a statute does not extend to ecclesiastical persons if the bond attaches after entry into the clergy or religious life, as in capitul. cum M. Ferrarien., and capitul. ecclesia, de constitu., and in capitulo bene quidem, 96. distinct., with similar texts. In vain, therefore, is it asked whether she is excluded by the said statute. But presupposing without prejudice to the truth the validity of the statute, does it stand in the way of the said Caterina, or prevent the judge from rendering justice out of fear of the penalty fixed therein? And first it seems that it does, through that clause added to the statute, namely: “And let this apply to present, past, and future cases,” etc. For pending matters are included under one of those three: present, past, or future; and a statute is extended to past matters when express provision is made concerning them, as in l. leges & constitutiones, C. de legi., and in capitulo fin. de consti. Moreover, the statute says that she cannot claim anything; but by standing in court, she is always claiming, and persists in her claim, as in capitulo si diligenti, de foro competen.; therefore, etc. But I think the contrary is true, at least in our case. First, because matters already pending in court have a nature separate from past matters, and from present matters not yet brought into court: because the Emperor expressly willed that pending matters ought not to be decided according to subsequent laws, but according to prior laws, as is the text in the Authentica in medio litis, [C.] sac. ius. non fier.; although it seems otherwise with respect to the ordinary proceedings of a trial regarding future acts according to what is noted by the glossa in cap. licet canon, de elect. lib. 6, and in the Clementina dispendiosam, de iudic.; hence it is

† that where the prince intends that with respect to the decision a constitution be extended to pending matters, he always makes mention of them, as is evident in the said Clementina dispendiosam, at the end, de iudic., and in Clementina 1, at the end, de sequestra. poss. & fruc., and de re iudica., Clementina 1, de senten. excommu. cap. 1, with similar texts. Bartolus expressly confirmed this opinion in l. omnes populi, ff. de iusti. & iure, in the repetition, at the verse secundò quæritur, vtrum postquam statutum; where he affirms that although that clause is inserted in a statute and is extended to past matters, etc., it is never extended to pending matters—that is, matters brought into court—by the text of the said Authentica ut cum de appell. cog., and he also cites the glossa placed there, and says this proceeds especially in the statutes and reformations of cities, which the dogs of the courts and devourers of all commonalities cause to be made according to the pleasure of their will. And dominus Antonius de Butrio also follows this opinion in capitulo fin. de constitu., at the end; nay rather, Bartolus most beautifully willed more in l. sancimus, C. de sacro. sanct. eccle., at the end, for he says that a city statute is in no way extended to pending matters, even if provision is made concerning them in the statute, because the Emperor expressly forbids it in the said authentica, although it is otherwise in a statute of the Emperor when he expressly so disposes. Furthermore, this opinion is altogether to be embraced, at least in our case, since that statute is exceedingly odious and contrary to religion and all the laws of the world; therefore it must be restricted as far as possible so that it prejudices the common law as little as possible, as in the said cap. cum dilectus, and in the said l. 2, de noxa.; and thus it ought not to concern pending matters, since it makes no express mention of them, as in regula odia restringi, de regu. iur. libr. 6. Likewise, on another ground the said statute ought not to be extended to this matter: because in the statute it is said that a woman who has entered a monastery cannot claim anything in the paternal succession, etc.; but the said Caterina had already claimed at the time the statute was enacted, since she had laid her complaint; and what is more, joinder of issue had occurred, as in l. si decem cum petiero, ff. de verbo. oblig., and in l. non amplius, ff. rem ra. habe., and what Bartolus notes there; therefore, since that statute speaks by words of the present tense, namely that she cannot claim, and is contrary to law and prejudicial to the right of another, it ought not to be extended to those things which she had already claimed at that time, argument in l. cum lex, and what is noted there, ff. de legib., and in l. leges & constitutiones, C. eodem titulo. Likewise, and on another and third ground, the statute ought not to be extended to the said Caterina: because that statute speaks of when parents give to their daughters at the time of entry that which is also possible for them, as appears in the preamble of that statute. For in the understanding of a statute, the reason that is set forth in its preamble must be considered, as in l. final. ff. de hære. insti., noted by Bartolus in l. liberorum, ff. de verbo. signifi.

† Possibility, however, in respect of a dowry is considered from three things, namely from the dignity or condition of the persons, from the wealth, and from the number of children, as is the text in l. si filiæ, ff. de lega. 2; l. cum post, §. si gener, ff. de iure do., supports this; but since the father of the said Caterina was very wealthy in estate and had only four children, of whom three were females, he does not seem to have given to the said Caterina what was possible for him by giving only 100 florins; deservedly the said statute ought not to be extended, even on this ground, to the said Caterina, since the reason of the statute ceased in her case. And the aforesaid proceed especially when regard is had to the fact that the said Caterina had already adited the inheritance, at least with the intention of claiming in court the portion owed to her at the time when the said statute emanated; whence it is not plausible that the statute intended to deprive the said Caterina, or the monastery, of a right already acquired and incorporated into the monastery, since through the adition of an inheritance ownership is already acquired by an heir, especially a sui heir, as in l. cum hæredes, ff. de acqui. posse., and in l. in suis, ff. de libe. & posthum., with similar texts, since the prince cannot do this, as noted by Innocentius in c. quæ in ecclesiarum, de consti., and Bartolus in l. fin. C. si contra ius vel vti. pub., and Cynus in l. præscriptione, C. de preci. impe. offe.; moreover, a statute in doubt must always be restricted so that it is not extended to an impossible case, as in c. a nobis, de sen. excommu., and in c. 2, de consti. lib. 6; what Johannes Andreæ notes in c. fi. de immu. eccl. lib. 6, and Bartolus in l. filiusfa. §. divi, ff. de leg. 1, supports this, where he concludes that a statute in which it is provided that one may not dare to sell or donate an immovable thing to someone not subject to the jurisdiction does not extend to churches, because it would be contrary to ecclesiastical liberty, since by privilege of the prince one can freely donate and sell to churches, and ownership is acquired by these without delivery, as the text in illud, and l. fi. C. de sacros. eccl.; and thus a statute ought not to be extended through general words to an illicit case; c. 1, de iureiu. lib. 6, serves excellently; so we say in the present case that, since in the said statute no mention is made of those who had already at the time of the statute adited the inheritance, it ought not to be extended to them even de facto. Nor does that clause stand in the way, “that they have place in past cases,” etc., because it can be understood of those who had already entered, yet the parents had not died, and thus they had no right in the property at the present time, as in l. 2, §. si impuberem, ff. de colla. bono., noted by Bartolus in the authentica ingressi, C. de sacrosan. eccl., with similar texts. For it is restricted as much as can be done, as in the said cap. cum dilectus, with similar texts. And this is an excellent consideration. From all these things I conclude regarding the second question that the words of the said statute do not encompass the said Caterina; and consequently the rectores and other judges of the city of Siena may with impunity in this case exercise jurisdiction and render justice to the said Caterina, or to the monastery claiming in her person, which must be admitted to make the claim even if the said Caterina has died, since all rights had passed to the monastery according to the note by Innocentius and others in cap. in præsentia, de proba., and Bartolus in l. 1, ff. de vulg. & pupil., and the glossa on 19. quæst. ult. cap. si qua mulier. I come now to the third and last point, namely what portion is owed to the monastery in the person of the said Caterina. And briefly, without dwelling upon it, I say that the father did not make a testament; and she ought to have as much as any one of the male or female children. For her right is not diminished in anything through her entry into the monastery, as in l. Deo nobis, C. de episcop. & cler., and in the authentica ingressi, and what is noted there, C. de sacrosanct. eccle., and in the said c. in præsentia, with the note there; nor by the common law is there today any difference between male and female, but all succeed equally, as in the authentica de hære. quæ ab intest. defe. §. 1. Nor by virtue of the statutes can she be excluded, by reason of those things which I stated above in the first and second questions; and thus she ought to have a third of the whole inheritance, since there were four children at the time of the father’s death, and thus the other married females are excluded by the statute when males are surviving, and their portion does not accrue to the nun, but to the male, in contemplation of whom they are excluded, by reason of those things which Bartolus notes in l. 2, §. & si fortè, ff. ad Tertul., and Johannes Andreæ in the additions to Speculum in the title de succes. ab inte. upon the rubric, in the second column. If, however, the father made a testament valid in law, for the validity of which it is required among other things that the said Caterina, as a daughter, was instituted heir at least in something, as in the authentica ut cum de appella. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum, noted by Bartolus in the authentica novissima, C. de inoffi. testam., and in l. 1, §. si parens, ff. si quis a paren. fue. manumis., then she sues for the supplement of the legitima, even if she was instituted in a small amount, as in l. omnimodo, and in l. scimus, C. de inof. testamen. But the legitima in respect of those four children is a third part of the whole inheritance, as in the said authentica novissima, and consequently it is owed to the said Caterina, or to the monastery, for that fourth part of the third part of the inheritance. For concerning the remainder the testator could dispose at will, as in the said authentica ut cum de appel. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum, and in the said authentica novissima; and by these things the clear decision of all doubts is evident, to the praise of the Holy Trinity. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Whether a sentence otherwise solemnly delivered can be challenged on the ground that the messenger, who cited the party at the judge's mandate for the purpose of its delivery, made the report of the citation not at the judge's bench, nor in the presence of the judge, but solely to the notary being outside the place where justice is administered; the notary nevertheless having entered the citation into the acts before the sentence was delivered. 3. And whether it can be challenged on the ground that the judge delivered it ex officio, and not at the petition of the party. 4.
2. The act of citing is the execution of the judge's interlocutory order concerning citation.
body: In the name of God, amen. The question of law is,

† whether a sentence otherwise solemnly delivered can be challenged on the ground that the messenger, who cited the party at the judge's mandate for the purpose of its delivery, made the report of the citation not at the judge's bench, nor in the presence of the judge, but solely to the notary being outside the place where justice is administered, the notary nevertheless having entered the citation into the acts before the sentence was delivered. Briefly I say that it cannot be challenged on this sole ground, because since that act is not judicial, it does not require the warmth of the court; whence the report can be made to the notary alone, even outside the place of judgment; in support of this I allege the text with the notable gloss in l. uoluit, ff. de interro. act., where it is clear that in those matters which do not require cognition of the cause, the place of judgment is not of substance, but they can be published while the judge is traveling or in his own house, as is fully noted by Cyn. in l. 1, C. de confes. in the third question; to the same effect is that which is read and noted in l. 2 procedente, C. de dila. and in c. 2, de dila. The report of the messenger, however, does not require summary cognition, nor is it a judicial act. For citation has three parts, namely the interlocutory order of the judge to cite, the act of the citing messenger, and the messenger's own report. The first act is judicial and jurisdictional; therefore it cannot be performed outside the territory, as in clem. pastoralis, de re iudi. and what is noted there. But the second and third are not jurisdictional, therefore they can be performed outside the territory, as in l. omnis §. uerum si apparitor, C. de episc. & cler. and noted in cap. fi. de fo. compe. and Io. Mo. in c. Romana §. contrahentes, de fo. comp.; it is also proved from the fact that the messenger does not have jurisdiction, but simply executes the act of the judge.

† Whence the act of citing is the execution of the interlocutory order of the judge concerning citation. The report, truly, is the notification of the execution already performed; deservedly, since these acts do not require cognition, they do not require the place of judgment, as in the said l. uoluit. Nor does it even require the presence of the judge: because the report is made so that the fact of the citation may become apparent. It is therefore enough that it be made to the notary of the cause, and by him written into the acts; in support of this is c. quoniam contra, de proba., where it is clear that it pertains to the office of the notary to write citations; and this position Bartolus expressly confirms in l. si finita §. Iulianus, ff. de dam. infect. at the word iuxta prædicta quæro, where he concludes it is sufficient

† that the report of the messenger be made to the notary, nor is it necessarily required that it be made to the judge, provided that it subsequently becomes known to the judge; nor is it necessary, second, that it be made while the judge is sitting on the bench. To this he adduces a good text in l. eos §. super his, C. de app., where it is proved, especially joining the gloss, that the instruments of the cause can be produced to the notary; nor is it required there that the production take place in court. Whence through that l. eos §. super his, joined with l. voluit, alleged above, the decision of this question is proved. For it is sufficient that the notary, having been informed of the citation, entered it into the acts before the sentence. And this opinion I have elsewhere confirmed in the said c. quoniam contra, in the lecture.

† There is also another doubt: whether the sentence can be challenged on another ground, namely that the judge delivered it ex officio and not at the petition of a party. It seems at first that it is so: because regularly a judge ought never to proceed ex officio to private benefit, as noted by Inno. in c. ad nostram. 2. de iureiu., and it seems from the text and there through Bar. in l. 4 §. hoc autem iudicium, ff. de dam. infect. and more clearly by the same author in l. ad peremptorium, in prin. ff. de iud., and there it seems to be proved that a citation is not valid unless made at the petition of a party. These things notwithstanding, I hold the contrary in our case, for since the time of peremption of the instance was imminent here, the judge could and ought to intervene and cite ex officio to hear the sentence, by the argument in l. properandum, C. de iud., and Bartolus expressly confirmed this dictum in l. Seius & Augerius, ff. ad l. Falci.; for the judge can always supply, lest the judicial instance vanish in vain; to this effect is c. causam, quæ iudici, and what the gloss notes in c. 1, de elect. lib. 6; Bald. in l. 1, C. ut quæ desunt ad uo. Furthermore, as the same Baldus elegantly says in the said l. 1, a sentence in favor of the plaintiff is valid even if it is not found specifically to have been delivered at the petition of the parties: because the plaintiff from the beginning seeks that the defendant be condemned; whence it cannot be said that it was delivered without the petition of a party. In our case, moreover, the sentence was delivered in favor of the plaintiff; deservedly, on this twofold ground, the said sentence is undoubtedly sustained, especially since the judge, by the form of the statute, incurs a penalty unless he renders judgment within the time of the instance. To the contrary arguments framed above, the response is that they proceed regularly: but it is otherwise in our case by the aforesaid reason, and in other special cases concerning which see fully Bartolus in the said §. hoc autem iudicium, and Baldus in the said law, and the canonists in c. bonæ, ti. 1, de postu. pręl. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus de Tudeschis, Abbot.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. The crime of usury is most grave, and akin to robbery.
2. A debtor claiming back a possession pledged to another does not obtain a condemnation regarding the fruits, unless he proves the amount collected by the creditor.
3. Judgments have equal force with instruments.
4. A remission of usury is not valid, unless the creditor offers the money to the debtor, or at least has it ready for restitution. A spontaneous remission ought not to be presumed, when the debtor is poor and the creditor rich, and especially when the money is not trifling.
5. A transaction, wherever it is fraudulent on the part of the plaintiff, does not hold by operation of law, and an action for recovery is available.
body: Having invoked the aid of Jesus Christ, three principal matters are to be examined for the plenary decision of the cause brought by Tommaso and Antonio, sons of the late lord Count Filippo de' Scorti, against the heirs of Nanne, son of the lord Angelo de' Scorti. First, whether the contracts entered into between the said Filippo and Nanne, while they were among the living, ought to be presumed usurious, by such a presumption as would lead to a judgment being rendered against the heirs of Nanne himself. Second, assuming that they are to be deemed usurious, whether the said Tommaso and Antonio, the plaintiffs, ought to be barred by virtue of a compromise and the arbitral award that followed therefrom, both in respect of those contracts and in respect of the other assets granted by virtue of the said wrongdoing by the first and second decree to the said Nanne, which are also now in dispute. Third, assuming that they are not to be barred, what the duty of the judge of the cause ought to be in pronouncing judgment upon the said cause. Having previously reviewed the acts and proceedings in the said cause, regarding the first question according to the order proposed, it seems that the said contracts—two of which are drawn in the form of a loan, and the third in the form of a grave purchase and sale—are by no means to be deemed usurious. For if the witnesses, or rather their depositions, are diligently weighed, nothing of fraud is found to be proved against those contracts; indeed, they depose nothing at all concerning fraud, or simulation, or the usury of the said contracts; therefore, silence must be imposed upon the plaintiffs as having by no means established their claim with proofs, as in capitul. in præsentia, de proba. and l. 1 and l. actor, qui asseuerat, C. eodem; indeed, where the proofs are obscure, judgment ought to be given against the plaintiffs, as in capitul. ex literis, de probatio. and in regula, cum sunt partium iura, de regu. iur. libr. 6; and this seems especially to be said in the crime of usury.

† For since it is a most grave crime, and akin to robbery, 14. quæstio. 4. capitu. qui vsuram, the interpretation in case of doubt ought to be made so that a crime is avoided, as in c. estote misericordes, de regu. iur. libr. 6. and excellently by Barto. in l. non solum. §. sed & probari, ff. de nou. oper. nunc. And by this, the argument of certain persons can be dispatched, if it be said that judgment should indeed be given against those contracts, since it has been proved that the said Nanne was accustomed, at the time of those contracts, and before and after, to make similar usurious contracts. For it is not concluded from this that those contracts were usurious, because an inference ought not to be drawn from different matters, capitu. 2. de transla. prælato. and in l. neque natales, C. de proba. and in l. Papin. exuli, ff. de mino. Also because in doubt (as I have said before) the sentence is to be given in favor of the defendant, and a wrong is not to be presumed; nor ought anyone on a slight presumption to be condemned of so grave a crime, as in capitu. literas, de præsumpt.; and what Innocen. notes in cap. quia verosimile, de præsump. supports this. Furthermore, the witnesses are singular, who regularly do not prove, as in cap. dilecti, de elect. and in cap. tam literis, de testib. with similar texts; especially in our case, since each deposes concerning a usurious contract conducted with himself, and thus appears suspect, argum. in cap. personis, de test. and what is read and noted in l. de iure, ff. ad municip. And Cyn. after others seems openly to hold this view in l. 1. C. de proba., where he seems to conclude that for one seeking restitution of usury, it is not enough to prove that the defendant was accustomed at the time of the contract, and before and after, to lend at usury—say, at the rate of four pence per pound—and that he was accustomed to execute an instrument for double the true principal, and that the plaintiff himself received a loan from him and satisfied him as to the principal: because, according to him, since he proves nothing concerning the usury paid by him, a condemnation cannot follow therefrom; for this see cap. ad nostram, de iureiuran., where it is clear,

† that a debtor seeking the recovery of his possession pledged to another does not obtain a condemnation regarding the fruits unless he proves the amount received by the creditor. So in the present matter, it does not suffice to prove the loan received and the satisfaction of the principal, unless the amount of the usury paid is proved. Archid. in c. 2. de vsur. lib. 6. and Bald. in d. l. 1. C. de probatio. seem to hold the same, and more clearly, moved by the reason that upon that which is variable a condemnation cannot follow; where, although it is proved that the creditor was accustomed to lend at four per pound, nevertheless it could have been that to this person, who now sues, he lent at one per pound; and thus no certain condemnation can follow; and this seems especially to be said in our case, in which consanguinity occurs between Nanne and Filippo, the former contracting parties. For consanguinity excludes the presumption of fraud, argumen. in l. in transactione, C. de transact. and in capitu. literas, de præsump.; whence it is to be presumed that to the said Filippo, as a kinsman, he lent gratuitously, and without any fraud bought from him the quantity of grain contained in the acts. And Ange. de Peru. seems to have held this last view in a certain disputation of his, which begins, Astensis miles. But, these things notwithstanding, I consider the contrary opinion to be truer in law in our case: that wherever circumstantial evidence is very pressing, it constitutes full proof, even in a criminal case, as is proved in l. sciant cuncti, C. de probat., canonized in 2. quæstio. 8. capitu. sciant. To the same effect is l. iudicia, C. de rei vendica., where it is said,

† that indications have equal force with written instruments, as the gloss notes in capitu. tertio loco, de probat. and there fully by the doctors; and this is most of all to be admitted in our case, in which action is brought against usurers. For usurers are accustomed to enter into and feign their contracts very cautiously and secretly, lest they could in any way be convicted of usurious depravity, as the text says in clementi. vnica, de vsur., near the end. And therefore they are convicted on lighter presumptions than others, as in capitu. cum in diœcesi, de vsur. and capitu. ad nostram, de emptio. & venditio., and capitu. illos vos, de pig. Likewise, the laws generally provide that one proceeds from lighter proofs in acts in which outsiders are not accustomed to be employed; whence proofs that are regularly not conclusive are admitted; to this effect l. consensu, C. de repudiis, and cap. veniens, 2. de testib., and cap. fin. de testib. cogend., and what the gloss notes in cap. cum dilecti, de electio.; the text in cap. præterea, de testib., with similar texts, supports this. In our case, however, many indications concur against the said Nanne. First, because he himself at the point of death confessed that he had extorted diverse sums of money through usurious depravity, and gave solemn security regarding their restitution. Likewise, it has been proved that he was accustomed to practice usury indifferently with all, and to lend his money under usury, especially feigning contracts under the form of a purchase of grain, although he never afterwards received the grain, but only the money; whence judgment is to be presumed concerning secret matters according to his custom, for in doubtful matters the custom of the head of the household is looked to, as in l. qui semisses, ff. de vsur. and in cap. illos vos, de pig. and in regula semel malus, de regu. iur. libr. 6. and in regula, inspicimus in obscuris, eodem titu. & lib. and in l. semper in stipulationibus, ff. eodem titu., at least in the same species of fraud. For the said Nanne was accustomed to lend under usury, and also to feign contracts under the form of a purchase of grain; therefore, the said contracts of loan and of the purchase of grain entered into with the said Nanne are to be presumed usurious in the said two species in which the said Nanne was engaged at the time of the said contracts. Nor is this surprising. For even in brute animals their custom is looked to, institutio. de rerum diui. §. in his autem, and by one act a person is presumed habituated to that evil, so that he appears to have reduced it to a custom, as in l. 3. C. de episco. audiend. and cap. ita nos 25. q. 2. and there by Arch. Furthermore, the said Nanne was not a grain merchant, as is proved in the acts, nor was the said Filippo accustomed to sell grain, nor did he collect so much from his possessions that he could have sold 20 modii of grain, as the instrument seems to state; therefore, that contract ought to be presumed fictitious, and feigned, and conceived in fraud of usury. Furthermore, the said Nanne was deceitful, and exceedingly crafty in his contracts, as is proved by witnesses and by the common report of the place; therefore it is more easily to be presumed against him, by the argument of what Bar. notes in l. fi. ff. de quæstio.; c. illos vos, in fi. de pig. and 16. q. 1. c. visis support this. Likewise, it is expedient for the soul of Nanne himself so to presume, especially since he ordered the usuries to be restored, and in doubt an interpretation ought to be made such that it is more expedient for the salvation of the soul, as is noted in capitu. unico, de scruti. and in cap. iuuenis, de sponsa. and in cleme. exiui de paradiso, de uerbo. signifi. And if we were to require full and conclusive proof against usurers, they would rarely or never be convicted of the usurious sin, against the laws cited above. And toward this opinion Ioan. Andr. most clearly inclined on easier terms in capitu. ex literis, de iureiuran. and in the said capitu. quamquam, de usur. lib. 6., where he says that it suffices for one seeking restitution of usury to prove that someone was accustomed to lend at usury at a certain rate, and that he received a loan from him, and to prove that he satisfied him as to the principal; for it is proved from this presumptively that the contract of loan entered into with him was usurious, and that he paid him usury. And Ioan. Andr. said that it had often been so judged in the bishopric of Bologna; and to the statement of Archid. to the contrary cited above, he says that it is not accepted in the schools, and is rejected in judgments; to the statement of Cyn. he responds that the quantity of the receipt of fruits does not pass thus presumptively, as does the quantity by reason of custom, and in detestation of usurers themselves who carry out their deeds secretly. Anton. de Butr. follows this same opinion in the said capit. ex literis, and the other canonist writers commonly concurred with him there. Angel. de Peru. also followed that opinion in his solemn disputation which begins, Astensis miles, at least in the case where there occur some other conjectures that have the power to induce the judge's mind to belief, and to suffice when coupled with the plaintiff's oath; and in our case, beyond the proved custom of the said Nanne, many other conjectures concur, which are mentioned above, and especially that of the feigned purchase of grain, made with many; and an argument from what commonly happens is valid even for a sentence when dealing with a crime civilly, as in the said capitu. primo. de cler. non resid. and there by Ioan. Cald. Furthermore, against the heirs of the said Nanne there militates another sufficiently urgent presumption, because they never willed to produce the books of the said Nanne, contrary to the provision of the law, of which in the said clemen. unica, although it was proved by witnesses that the said Nanne had those books; nor are the heirs to be believed when asserting that they had lost those books, since they assert this for their own advantage, and to the detriment of others, as noted by Ioan. de Lig. in the said clementi. unica, de usur. Likewise, the heirs of the said Filippo, the plaintiffs in the said cause, are ready to produce the books of the said Filippo, in which among his other accounts he made mention of how the said contracts entered into with the said Nanne were usurious, and that he paid 25 per cent. Moreover, to these books, although written in his own matter, even if not full faith, yet no slight faith is to be given, especially after the death of the said Filippo. For it is not likely that he would have said this contrary to the truth, especially against a kinsman from whom he had received a benefit; for this the text in capitu. literas, de præsump. and better in l. rationes, C. de probatio., where this seems to be proved, especially according to one reading which Bald. follows there. Likewise, the sons of the said Filippo are ready to swear that they believe their father wrote the truth, and that from many conjectures they believe the said contracts were usurious; for an oath of credulity provides support where, from the subject matter, true knowledge cannot be had, as happens now in these sons and heirs of Filippo, who are not fully informed concerning the acts performed by their father; to this effect what is read and noted in capitu. quoties, and cap. licet ex quadam, de testi., with similar texts. Therefore, there concur here very many indications to constitute proof in full, especially against usurers, such as the books of this debtor, the sons' oath of credulity, the wicked custom of the said Nanne in these two usurious species, the common report against the said contracts, and the contumacy of the heirs of the said Nanne in producing the deceased's books, contrary to the said clemen., which indications no one of sound mind will say do not suffice to make full proof against a usurer. The arguments alleged above to the contrary do not stand in the way. And first, as to the earlier points, the response is clear from what has been said above. For they proceed when there is no proof by the plaintiff, or at least not sufficient proof according to the subject matter; but in our case they are quite sufficient, as is gathered from the aforesaid, and the case seems to fall under the said capitul. cum in diœcesi, de usur., and capitu. ad nostram, de empt. & uendit., and capitu. illos vos, de pig., with similar texts cited above, and the authority of Ioan. And., Anto. de But., and other writers in d. capitu. ex literis, and Ange. in the said disputation, support this. What is objected concerning the consanguinity between Nanne and Filippo does not stand in the way; for this presumption is removed by a contrary, more vehement presumption, argumen. capitu. literas, and what is noted there, de præsumptio. First, because there is no presumption of a gratuitous loan on account of the feigned sale of grain, since neither of them was a grain merchant; rather, the said Nanne was accustomed so to feign contracts with others. Furthermore, a gratuitous loan is not presumed in a usurer in a large amount, as this was; for if he was devouring his own soul, it is more strongly to be presumed that he did not spare his kinsman; whence Angel. in the said disputation speaks of a small sum of money, when no other presumption is present except that the creditor was accustomed to practice usury; but in our case there are other presumptions to the contrary, as is clear from the aforesaid. What is said concerning the singularity of the witnesses does not stand in the way: because, since they are introduced to prove that he was accustomed so to practice usury, singularity does not stand in the way, because they agree in that which they were introduced to prove. For they are not introduced to prove a specific act or contract—in which case, if they were singular, they would not prove, as in the laws previously cited—but they are introduced to prove that he was accustomed to practice usury, and to draw up simulated contracts under the veil of the purchase and sale of grain; in which case it ought not to be prejudicial that the witnesses depose regarding the singularity of the acts from which the whole of that which was to be proved results; just as in a similar case the singular gloss says in l. ob carmen, ff. de test. when possession of a certain time is to be proved, so that the witnesses may conclude the proof if one deposes concerning five years and the rest concerning another five; and what Innocen. notes on a similar point regarding the proof of the celebration of mass in capitu. qualiter & quando. 2. de accusat. supports this; and Angel. affirms the aforesaid in the said disputation, Astensis. Or we can say, and better, that since the dispute here is not about a great prejudice, since Nanne himself, in the security that he gave, confessed that through illicit and fraudulent contracts he had extorted much, with usurious depravity intervening, and now it is only a question of proving the species of fraud of those contracts, and of proving now in specific terms what Nanne himself confessed in general terms, slight proof ought to suffice, according to what is noted in capitu. nuper, de test.; in our case, however, proof is made through public fame, which in this case ought to prove, according to what is noted by Bartol. in l. de minore. §. tormenta, ff. de quæstio., especially and undoubtedly if it is joined with one witness; in our case, however, many witnesses concur, wherefore full proof ought to result. And even if they were singular, since one witness and fame regularly prove when the proceeding is civil, as noted by the glo. in capitu. veniens, 1. de testibus, and 4. quæst. 3. §. item sæpe, and in l. 3. ff. de testibus, and by Bartol. in the said §. tormenta. Nor does it stand in the way if it be said that these witnesses depose in their own matter: because they will have no advantage from this; whence they ought to be admitted, just as legatees are admitted in the case of a will, inst. de test. ordi. §. legatariis, and Ange. maintained this in the said disputation in terms identical to ours; and especially they are excused from all suspicion because they only depose specifically that Nanne himself confessed in general, and thus so strict a proof is not required. And by these reasons I conclude regarding the first point that the said contracts entered into between the said Nanne and Filippo are to be presumed and judged usurious. I come now to the second question, namely, whether Tommaso and Antonio, the plaintiffs, are to be barred at least on the grounds of the compromise and the arbitral award that followed therefrom between the said Nanne and Filippo. And it seems first that they are. For a compromise can be made concerning past usuries, as Bald. in capitu. similiter, de controuersia inuesti. colla. 10. Furthermore, a compromise is a kind of transaction or composition, in authen. ut differen. iudi. §. 1. and in authen. si verò contigerit, C. de iudi., noted by Innoc. in capitu. Quintavallis, de iureiurand. and Bartol. in l. societatem. §. arbitrorum, ff. pro socio. For just as a remission can intervene in past usuries according to what is noted by the gloss and doctors in regula, peccatum, de regu. iuris libr. 6., so too can a transaction or composition; but against one acting contrary to his own transaction or composition, an exception stands, C. de transact. l. sub prætextu, and l. 2. with similar texts. But these things notwithstanding, I say the contrary in our case, which is shown more clearly. And first, if we hold the opinion of certain theologians, which Dyn. follows in regula, peccatum,

† that a remission of usury is not valid unless the creditor offers the money to the debtor, or at least has it ready for restitution: because the sin is not forgiven unless that which was taken away is restored, as in the said regula, peccatum, and in capitu. cum tu, de usur. Moreover, restitution means that a restoration to the pristine state is made, as in l. cum prætor, ff. de regulis iur. and l. restituere, eod. titu.; therefore the money cannot be said to have been restored either truly or fictitiously if the creditor was not ready to restore, just as he was not in our case; therefore even an express remission would not have been valid, and consequently neither an indirect one, which seems to arise from the compromise and the award that followed therefrom. If, however, we wish to hold the opinion that a remission made by the debtor is valid as to avoiding the burden of restitution, though not as to the sin, even though the money is not offered to the debtor nor ready for restitution—which Ioann. Andr. seems to hold on the said regula, peccatum, in the Novella, and Feder. de Senis affirms in consi. 18—I still say that that compromise does not present an impediment to restitution: because a remission is valid only when it is entirely free and voluntary, and not in any way coerced or extorted, or induced through fraud and fear; for God looks upon the heart and not upon the mouth, as in capitu. si quid inuenisti. 14. quæst. 5.; whence neither truly nor fictitiously can money be said to have been restored in this case. And that the remission must be liberal and voluntary, the gloss and Ioan. Andr. and Dyn. affirm on the said regula, peccatum; more clearly Fede. in the said consi. 14., and Ioan. Andr. in addit. Specu. super rub. de usuris, in the 3rd column; and it has been so advised multiple times. But it cannot be called voluntary in our case, since the compromise was made, and the award followed therefrom, at a time when the obligation between the said Nanne and Filippo still endured, and especially since it was made because the said Nanne, by the first and second decree, had received almost all the property of the said Filippo, and had already caused an order to be issued to him that he clear out or vacate the house of his own dwelling and also hand it over to Nanne himself; and thus, driven by fear of the aforesaid, he was led to the compromise and to accepting the award that followed therefrom; and consequently it ought not to prejudice the recovery of the usury, especially since the said Nanne expressly ordered the usuries to be restored to all from whom he had extorted them through illicit, feigned, and fraudulent contracts; and Ioann. Andr. expressly affirmed this in the said addition, where he reports that he had advised in a question of fact with his adoptive son Ioan. Cald. Furthermore, as he says,

† a voluntary remission ought not to be presumed when the debtor is poor and the creditor is rich, and especially when the money is not slight, as happens precisely in our case. For, as has been sufficiently proved, the said Nanne was very wealthy, and Filippo the debtor was so poor that he could barely support his family. Likewise, before the said compromise and award there was a great dispute over the said debt between them, so much so that it arrived at the first and second decree against the said Filippo; therefore, a voluntary consent ought not to be presumed, since a transaction is commonly made on account of fear of litigation, and especially when one is poor and does not have proofs readily at hand, as happens in our case, as is proved in l. 2. C. de transactio.; the text in l. item si res, ff. de ali. iudi. mu. cau. fac. supports this excellently. Furthermore, and more strongly,

† wherever a transaction is malicious on the part of the plaintiff, it does not hold by operation of law, and an action for recovery is available, as is the text in l. in summa, in princip. ff. de condictio. indeb. and the gloss notes in l. sub prætextu, C. de transact.; or according to Bartol. in d. l. sub prætextu, at least the transaction is void when the plaintiff litigates maliciously. And thus according to him the text in dict. l. in summa can be understood. But in our case the said Nanne litigated maliciously against the said Filippo, because he knew the debt was usurious, and he never willed to produce his books; rather, he denied that that debt was such; therefore he acted in calumny and deceit, according to what is noted by Innocent. in capitul. 2. de dilat.; and consequently the transaction was also void by operation of law on this second ground. From these considerations I conclude that the said Tommaso and Antonio are by no means to be barred by the said transaction, or compromise, and the award that followed therefrom. And to the contrary argument formulated above, it can be said that a compromise regarding past usury is valid when the fact is doubtful, but not when it is not voluntary or is extorted in the manner aforesaid. From the aforesaid it is inferred as to the third question, namely, what the duties of the judge ought to be in pronouncing judgment in this case. For, as is gathered from the aforesaid, he ought to pronounce that the said contracts entered into between the aforesaid Nanne and Filippo, which are mentioned in the libel, were and are usurious, feigned, and drawn up in fraud of usury, and to condemn the defendants to restore and release the property claimed in the libel, together with the fruits and revenues received and that could have been received; in such a way, however, that the true debt, and whatever the said Filippo subsequently had from the said Nanne by virtue of the said award, be set off against the fruits, and if anything remains of the fruits, he should order them to be restored. Moreover, that it is to be pronounced that those contracts are usurious is sufficiently proved from what was deduced in the first question. That the property is to be restored together with the fruits is clearly proved from what Ioann. Andr. notes after Blessed Thomas in capitu. 2. de usur. libr. 6., where he concludes that if anyone, by virtue of usury, held an immovable thing, he is bound to restore not only that thing, but also the fruits received therefrom; and besides those, I make this unanswerable argument in our case: it is certain that that transaction, as being calumnious, did not hold, as I have said above; therefore the ownership of the said property remains with the said Filippo, and the said Nanne was a possessor in bad faith, and consequently he is bound to restore the property and whatever was received or could have been received from it, as in l. ex diuerso, ff. de rei uend. and better in l. domum, C. eodem titul. and what is read and noted in capitu. grauis, de restitutio. spolia. and in capitu. cum contra, de pigno. and in capitu. de usuris, with similar texts. And in addition to the aforesaid, it must be subtly considered that the said Nanne, in his solemn security which he gave at the end of his life concerning the restitution of usuries, confessed that through those contracts he had acquired much money and goods, both movable and immovable, etc. Whence those words, 'both movable and immovable,' are to be weighed. He therefore expressly confessed that he had obtained immovable goods; but no one appeared against him who complained concerning immovable goods; therefore it is to be presumed that he meant these immovable goods, argu. in l. 2. C. de alime. pu. præstan. and what is noted there, in l. cum seruus, ff. de uerbo. oblig. and what Bar. notes there in a similar question, and by Innoc. in cap. qualiter & quando. 2. de accus.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Usury is not committed except in a contract of loan (mutuum).
2. The type of contract is recognized not from the words, but from its nature.
3. A genus generally approved is as valid as an enumeration of the species contained under the genus.
4. General words ought to be restricted to the preceding species, whenever this can be done while preserving the sense of proper speech.
5. A general renunciation of fortuitous cases is not valid in judgments, but it is necessary that they be specially expressed.
6. Marriage has a subject-matter distinct from other obligations, and requires spontaneous and free consent.
casus: In the question to be raised between Antonius on the one side and Marianus, son of the late Iacobus, on the other, formerly partners in the trade of the wool craft, three matters are to be examined. First, whether that agreement entered into between the said Antonius and Iacobus, while he was living, was usurious in that, after a partnership was formed and a certain quantity of money was deposited on both sides, it was agreed between them that if either of them contributed any moneys beyond the quantity he was bound to bring into the said partnership, he ought to be provided for by the said partnership according to the rate and custom of trade; and by virtue of this agreement the said Iacobus, who contributed five hundred florins beyond his share, received as profit on them five or six percent during the said partnership for several years. Second, presupposing that such agreement was usurious, it must be examined whether the said Antonius can be barred from the recovery (repetitio) of the usuries received, by virtue of the confession and acquittance made afterwards by the same Antonius. For upon the death of the said Iacobus, and with the said Marianus his son succeeding him, who made a certain settlement with the said Antonius having received a certain quantity of money for his share which he had in the said partnership, they released each other under this tenor of words, namely: Antonius, son of Petrus, on the one part, and Marianus, son of Iacobus, on the other, of their free and spontaneous will, from certain knowledge and not through error, confessed and acknowledged to each other, between themselves and reciprocally, that they had been and were completely paid and fully satisfied concerning all and singular the matters which they had had to deal with together from today backwards and up to the present day, and which up to the present day one party could claim from the other and ought to have by reason and on the occasion of any partnership, and traffic, and accounting made between them, and of the said wool craft for whatever reason, cause, or title, by virtue and on the occasion of any writing, both public and private; quashing, invalidating, and annulling all and any writing, both public and private, etc.; wherefore the said parties reciprocally between themselves, both themselves and their heirs and goods, generally released and quitclaimed each other from all and singular the aforesaid; and made a general release, acquittance, liberation, and discharge, and an agreement of not claiming anything further reciprocally concerning the aforesaid, etc. Third, it is principally to be examined, if the aforesaid mutual confession and release has to exclude the said Antonius from the aforesaid recovery of usury, whether he could at least be excluded by virtue of another acquittance that followed afterwards between them. For afterwards, after several years, when for several reasons the said Antonius and Marianus had a certain dispute between themselves, without any mention being made of the said allowances (provisiones), they generally quitclaimed each other anew from every and whatever cause for which one could claim from the other, yet without any mention made of the said allowances or usuries. And it is presupposed in fact that not only did the said Iacobus, father of the said Marianus, receive certain allowances from the said five hundred florins while he was living, but also Marianus himself, son and heir of the said Iacobus, received some after the death of the said Iacobus his father, as is clearly apparent in the book of the said partnership.
body: Having implored the aid of Jesus Christ the Savior, and addressing the first point in order, it seems at first that the said arrangement was not usurious:

† because usury is not committed except in a contract of loan (mutuum), as is clear from its definition. For it is profit from a loan, etc., as is fully noted by Ioan. Andr. in regula, peccatum, de regulis iur. libr. 6. in Mercu., and the same is noted in capitu. conquestus, de usur.; 13. quæstio. 3. capitu. 1 is relevant. But between the said Antonius and Iacobus no loan intervened, because Iacobus placed those five hundred florins into the partnership, and it was arranged that the one putting in the money should be provided for according to the use and custom of trade; therefore, it was not usury. For it is certain that it is lawful to deposit money with a merchant so that he answers to the owner of the money with a share of honest profit, as is the notable text in capitu. per uestras, de dona. inter uirum & uxorem, & de do. post di. resti. But notwithstanding these points, I consider the contrary to be true in law. For since this Iacobus did not expose himself to the risk and loss that could occur to those funds, but only willed that he be answered according to the custom of trade, and (as is now said) the custom is that a fixed amount is given annually for profit, whether profit accrued from that money or not—indeed the capital must always be safe—it must undoubtedly be held that whatever he received therefrom was usury, as is proved in capitu. 1. 2. & 3. in fin. 14. quæstio. 3. And that it is not lawful so to give money even to a merchant is the text in dict. capitu. 3., and more clearly the gloss in capitu. plerique, the same causa and quæstio, touches on this question, asking whether it is lawful to deliver money to a merchant so that he buys merchandise therewith and gives him a share of the profit; and it concludes that it is not, if the risk pertains only to the recipient, and thus a contract of loan is formed between them. Rather, for this to be lawful, it is required according to that gloss that they contract a partnership between themselves, so that the risk pertains to both, and thus one partner contributes money and the other labor, as in l. 5. ff. pro socio. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the money here was not lent to the said Antonius, because I say that it was in effect lent to the partnership. But a partnership is not a body, rather it consists of the partners; whence what is done with the partnership is said to be done with the individual persons constituting the partnership, as noted by Innocen. in capitu. dilecta, de exces. præla. Nor does it stand in the way that the word “mutuo” (I lend) was not expressed:

† because the type of contract is recognized not from the words, but from its nature, as in l. si uno, ff. loc., noted by the gloss in l. 1. ff. de superfi., and more fully by Barto. in l. cotem ferro. §. qui maximos, ff. de publica.; capitu. ad nostram, de empt. & uend. is relevant, and capitu. illo uos, de pigno., and better 15. quæst. 3. in capitu. plerique, cited above. Whence in effect this was a contract of loan entered into with those of the partnership, for he willed to deliver money for the use of the partnership and each year to obtain profit, which is undoubtedly usury, as in dict. capitu. plerique. I conclude therefore that the said arrangement was usurious, and whatever the said Iacobus and Marianus received under the name of profit from the said money thus lent was usury, and is subject to recovery (repetitio), as is read in the laws cited above and noted throughout the whole title de usuris. It remains now therefore to examine the second doubt, which seems more difficult: namely, whether the said Antonius can be excluded from recovering the above-written usurious profits by virtue of the first confession or acquittance written above. And it seems first that he can, for it is enough that satisfaction be made to the creditor concerning usury, as in capitu. 2. de usu. libr. 6., as Archid. says there. To satisfy is in any way whatever to satisfy the will of the creditor, and this is proved in l. si rem. §. omnis, ff. de pig. actio. But the aforesaid Antonius recognized and confessed that he had been fully satisfied and paid concerning all and singular the matters which he could have demanded up to that day from the said Marianus. Therefore he can no longer demand anything from him. For a confession or release made generally concerns all singular debts, even if they were not specially expressed, as is proved in l. pluribus, ff. de accep., noted by Bartol. in l. aurelio. §. Caius, ff. de lib. leg., where it is treated fully by him; and thus it does not stand in the way if it is said that no mention was made of the usurious profits and provisions.

† For a genus generally proven avails as much as an enumeration of the species contained under that genus. For he who says “all” excludes nothing: 19. distinct. capitu. si Romanorum, and in capitu. solitæ, de maior. & obedien. But notwithstanding these points, in my judgment the truth is to the contrary, namely that the said confession or acquittance does not extend to a usurious debt. I am moved to this opinion on multiple grounds. First, because the said confession or acquittance was not purely general, nor simply releasing and gratuitous, but was principally special, namely with respect to the debt contracted on the occasion of either partnership, as is gathered from those words: “by reason and on the occasion of whatever partnership and traffic, etc.” But this usurious debt was not contracted on the occasion of the partnership; rather it was contrary to the law of partnership. For since a partnership is a kind of fraternity, as in l. uerum, ff. pro soc., it abhors usurious wickedness, since it is against the nature of partnership. For it is of the nature of partnership that losses and profits be shared among the partners, as in l. cum duobus. §. si coeunda, ff. pro socio. The whirlpool of usury, however, devours souls and exhausts fortunes, as in capitu. 1. de usur. libr. 6.; and thus that debt cannot be said to have been contracted by reason of the partnership, since it is entirely separate from the law of partnership. This is also supported by the fact that they, namely Antonius and Marianus, mutually and reciprocally acknowledged that they had been satisfied and paid concerning whatever debts were contracted on the occasion of the partnership; and thus they had regard to the transactions conducted on the occasion and in the name of the partnership, from which an obligation is usually born mutually on both sides. This usurious debt, however, was contracted solely on the part of the one recipient of the profit. It does not stand in the way if it is said that although mention was made of the partnership, nevertheless general words immediately followed thereafter, as appears there: “by whatever reason, cause, or title”; for I say that general words following a species in an act of release are restricted to the preceding species, so that the meaning is: by whatever reason, cause, or title the one were obligated to the other, namely on the occasion of the partnership of which he had spoken before. For since the prejudice of the said Antonius is at stake, a strict interpretation must be made, as no one is presumed to throw away his own: l. cum de indebito, ff. de probat., and capitu. super hoc, de renuncia.
