And in case of doubt, the interpretation must be made against the said Marianus, who grounds himself upon that confession and acquittance, as in l. ueteribus, and what Bartol. elegantly notes there, ff. de pact. And in favor of the aforesaid interpretation,

† that general words must be restricted to the preceding species whenever this can be done while preserving the meaning of proper speech, the text seems to be in l. si ex pluribus, ff. de solu. and there by Bartol., and more fully by him in l. sub prætextu, C. de transact.; on this more fully in dict. l. Aurelio, §. Caius, ff. de lib. lega.; and that the words permit this restriction is proved by the words placed at the word “wherefore” (quapropter), there: “they generally released and acquitted from all and singular the aforesaid.” And those last words, “from all and singular the aforesaid,” are to be weighed, which clearly restrict the preceding general words; to the same effect are the words following there: “And a general end, acquittance, release, and discharge, and an agreement further not to demand anything mutually concerning the aforesaid, etc.” For those words are to be weighed: “anything concerning the aforesaid, etc.” And thus they did not intend to make a general end and acquittance concerning any debts whatsoever; otherwise they would not have added those words: “anything concerning the aforesaid, etc.” Furthermore, wherever words are obscure, as in our case, because generality produces obscurity, l. ita fidei, ff. de iur. fisc., regard must be had to that which is more probable and which has generally been accustomed to be done, as in l. in obscuris, and in l. semper in stipulationibus, ff. de regu. iur., and in regula inspicimus in obscuris, de regu. iur. lib. 6. But since the said Marianus had exacted a part of those usurious profits and provisions for himself, it is not probable that upon the dissolution of the partnership he would have restored the usury. For (as I have said) that first acquittance was not a gratuitous release; rather, the said Antonius confessed that he had been paid, etc. For men today—especially merchants, who believe their contracts to be lawful—are not accustomed spontaneously to restore usury and illicit gains, when they can scarcely be induced to make restitution after death, as in capitu. 2. de usuris. libro. 6. and clementi. una, eodem titu.; nor is it probable that he reformed himself so immediately without any demand, argument in regula semel malus, de regu. iur. libro. 6. and l. non ad ea, ff. de condic. & demonstra., with similar laws. Likewise, upon the dissolution of a partnership, the partners are always accustomed mutually and reciprocally to make said confessions, acknowledgments, releases, and acquittances; therefore, the said confession and release must be understood in this manner, and it ought not to be extended to that which was probably not contemplated, since an ignorant person is not presumed to donate, as in l. nec ignorans, C. de donatio.; l. tres fratres, ff. de pact. is relevant; indeed the said Antonius was in doubt whether the said contract or composition was usurious, since it had been stated under a veil that payment should be made according to the use and custom of trade, and thus in a general acquittance it is not probable that he had thought of that debt which he did not believe would be a debt, as appears in the laws cited above. Furthermore, since the sin of the said Iacobus and Marianus is established, it is necessary that satisfaction be clearly shown, because a sin is not forgiven unless what was taken away is restored, as in capitu. cum tu, de usur. and in regula, peccatum, de regu. iur. lib. 6. The said acquittance, however, does not clearly show satisfaction; therefore he must be compelled to satisfy, since a doubtful proof does not relieve the party having the burden of proof, as in capitu. in præsentia, de probat., especially where the salvation of souls is treated. For then the interpretation must be made in the milder direction, by which the danger to the soul is avoided, even if it is harsher [to the party], as in clementi. exiui de paradiso, de uerbo. significat. and in capitu. iuuenis, de spons., and there is a good gloss in capitu. unico, de scruti. in ord. fac. And this is a good consideration in our matter. From these points it is inferred for the decision of the third doubt, whether at least by virtue of the second acquittance the said Antonius is to be excluded from recovering the said usury; and truly I believe it must be said that he is not, based on the arguments multifacetedly made in the preceding doubt: both because a dispute had preceded only concerning certain disagreements, and no dispute had taken place concerning the said provisions and usurious profits, wherefore the subsequent general words must be restricted to the special dispute, argument in l. licet, C. de iudic. and what is noted in dict. l. sub prætextu, and by the gloss in capitu. primo. de transactio.; and because obscure words must be restricted to that which is more probable and generally accustomed to be done; and because each believed that that agreement did not contain sin, as I said before, and thus the said release cannot extend to matters unthought of, because an ignorant person does not donate, dict. l. nec ignorans and dict. l. tres fratres, with similar laws. Likewise, because danger to the soul is treated, the interpretation must therefore be made in the milder direction, even if it is harsher, as I said above; and through these considerations that which Bartol. notes in dict. l. Aurelius. §. Caius, cited above, is set aside, for it proceeds generally wherever there is a general release with no preceding species and the aforesaid considerations do not concur, but otherwise it is different, as I said in the preceding doubt. Furthermore and finally, the said acquittance and release is most clearly set aside if we hold the opinion of certain theologians, or of Dinus in reg. peccatum, de reg. iu. lib. 6. For they held that a remission and release of usury does not hold unless the money extorted through usurious wickedness is offered to the debtor himself, and to the same creditor, or at least according to Dyn. the money is made ready for restitution; for then it is deemed restored and returned by the short hand (brevi manu), and thus satisfaction is given to those words: “a sin is not forgiven unless what was taken away is restored.” For restitution is found, and thus there must be a replacement of the money into its former state, at least fictively, as in l. cum prætor and l. restituere, ff. de uerborum signific. But in our case the money already extorted was not offered to Antonius himself, nor at least made ready for restitution; indeed it was not even disputed; therefore that acquittance and release was not valid as to the release of the usury that must be restored, and this is beyond doubt holding either of those opinions. If, however, we hold the opinion of Ioann. Andr., which he set forth in his gloss on the said regula, peccatum, and Feder. de Senis, consil. 18, that the tender of the money or that it be made ready for restitution is not required, but that a liberal and spontaneous remission suffices, while one extorted by fear or deceit or by any contrivance does not suffice, as is noted in the said places by them; still the same seems to be said in our case. For from that general acquittance which preceded by virtue of certain differences, with no mention made of these usurious provisions, it can be said that the remission of the usury was not made liberally, since no special mention was made of it, nor did any discussion precede concerning the remission to be made. And I believe that in this matter it can be maintained that under a general remission or release, a release or remission of usury never falls unless it is specially expressed: because since this remission has a special nature, as is clear from the aforesaid and more broadly noted in the places cited above, this remission ought not to be included under generality, since one could be deceived under the entanglement of words, and thus danger to souls would be imminent. For it is enough to hold that a remission of usury benefits without the money being offered or being made ready for restitution; and against those opinions cited above, this capacity ought not to be extended so that it is also comprehended under a generality of words; to the aforesaid I cite an excellent parallel, l. sed & si quis. §. quæsitum, ff. si quis cauti.,

† where it is held that a general renunciation of accidental events (casus fortuiti) is not valid in judicial proceedings, but they must be specially expressed; whence genus there does not avail as much as species, and Bartol. says there that this is common: because a praetorian and judicial stipulation is judged according to the mind and equity of the praetor, who does not allow anyone to be deceived under the entanglement of words. Let us say the same in our proposed case: since danger to souls is treated here, and there are opinions as to what kind of remission of usury it must be, we ought at least not to say that it comes under generality, lest anyone be deceived and incur danger to his soul under an entanglement of words. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that a special case is contained in dict. §. quæsitum: because I say that even a special case is extended on account of identity of reason, as noted by the gloss in l. 1. C. de condi. indeb. and the text seems to be in capitu. cum dilecta, de confir. uti.; and especially where the favor of souls is treated, an extension must be made, even of penal law, as noted by the gloss in capitu. sciant cuncti, de elect. lib. 6. and in c. fi. eodem titu. & lib. Furthermore, we see in a similar matter:

† because marriage has a special subject matter distinct from other obligations, and requires spontaneous and free consent, as in c. cum locum, de sponsa., it is provided in law that a mandate to contract marriage does not fall under a general power of attorney, but it must be specially expressed, as is proved in l. generali, ff. de ritu. nup., noted by the gloss in c. fi. de procu. lib. 6. Likewise we see that notable cases and those worthy of note do not fall under a generality of words unless they are specially expressed, as noted by the gloss in cle. non potest, de procur. and c. qui ad agendum, eodem titu. libr. 6.; and those things that are worthy of special note, unless specially expressed, are deemed to have been neglected, as in c. quamuis, de præben. lib. 6. with similar laws. And let these things suffice. Nicolaus Abbas.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. A legitimate dowry is according to the condition of the woman.
2. A father can leave to a spurious child for maintenance up to a sufficient amount.
3. If a woman is given in marriage by her father, and the dowry proceeds from that same father, when the woman dies leaving children of that marriage, by the ius commune the dowry returns to the father.
4. If a father wants what was left, or given causa mortis, to pass to the children of a spurious son or daughter, how he ought to express it.
casus: The point of the question is as follows. A certain Nanni di Pietro Cursi of Siena died, no will having previously been drawn up by him, the ladies surviving him being Evangelista, his full sister, and Catharina, the spurious daughter of the said deceased Nanni. When the inheritance was finally assumed by the said lady Evangelista as the next-of-kin through the legitimate line, the same lady Evangelista, or another on her behalf, gave the said Catharina in marriage to a certain Matteo, and assigned to her for her dowry four hundred florins; and in the said instrument of dowry it is stated among other things that the said lady Evangelista, daughter of the late Pietro Cursi, and heir of the said Nanni, gave, etc. And finally it is subjoined in the said instrument that the said Matteo promised to return and restore the said dowry together with the antifactum to the said lady Catharina, and to a certain Francesco, present and receiving on behalf of the said lady Evangelista, or to whomsoever by law they ought to be returned and restored in every case and event of dowries to be restored, etc. Finally the said Catharina predeceased, leaving a son of that marriage; subsequently the said lady Evangelista died, having instituted her sons as heirs in equal shares; she had, however, previously disposed of a fourth part of all her goods in favor of certain of her daughters, as was permitted to her under the form of the Sienese statutes. Now it is asserted by the other sons and heirs that the said lady Evangelista could not donate that fourth to those two daughters, because she had already disposed of it beforehand by giving a dowry to the said Catharina, whom she was not bound to endow, since she was a spurious daughter of the said Nanni, and thus she is seen to have donated from her own property, especially since it is not stated in the instrument that she did this as heir, although she is named heir. On the part of the daughters the contrary is asserted. It is asked what the law is, and whether that dowry ought to remain with the said Matteo, since the common son has now deceased.
body: The aid of Jesus Christ and of His most pious Mother having been humbly invoked, it seems, first, in touching upon the first doubt, that the said lady Evangelista could not dispose of her fourth share unto those persons as is permitted to her under the Sienese statute, by reason of that assignment of dowry which she had previously made to the said Catharina; for in assigning a dowry to her whom she did not have under her paternal power, she is deemed by interpretation of law to have donated that dowry to the said Catharina, as in l. unica, § accedit, C. de rei uxo. actio.; therefore she could not afterward dispose of the entire fourth share, since she had already freely disposed beforehand of four hundred. Nor is it an obstacle that in the said instrument the said lady Evangelista is named heir, because from this it is not inferred that she acted as heir, since those are purely enunciative words, which do not effect a disposition, as in capit. si Papa, de priuile. libro 6., and in clementi. si summus pontifex, de senten. excommun. Furthermore, even granted that she might appear to have acted as heir, nevertheless, because the heir was not bound to do that, she is deemed to have donated, by the argument in l. Campanus, ff. de operis lib., and in l. cuius per errorem, ff. de regu. iu., to which accords l. cum de indebi., ff. de prob. That, moreover, she was not bound to provide a dowry as heir is clear, because neither was the deceased himself bound, nor could he do so even if he had wished, since she was a spurious daughter, born namely from an illicit union, under civil law, as in authenti. ex complexu, C. de incestis nuptiis. But, these things notwithstanding, I judge that in this case it must be stated in law as follows: that the said lady Evangelista was bound as heir of the said Nanni to maintain the said Catharina; for although under civil law not even the deceased was bound, as in the said authentica ex complexu, it is otherwise nonetheless under canon law, which is adhered to in this matter as being founded upon natural equity, as is held in capitu. cum haberet, de eo, qui duxit in matrimo., as the Legists also commonly hold, especially Bartolus and Baldus in the said authentica ex complexu; whence just as the deceased was bound, so also is the heir bound who succeeds into the place of the deceased; to this purpose there is a good text in authenti. licet, C. de naturalis liberis, and what is noted there, especially by Baldus. If, however, she was bound to provide maintenance, as was proved above, then she was also bound to give a dowry, since the cause of a dowry is not less favorable than the cause of maintenance, indeed it is more so, as Cynus notes in l. non omni, C. de administra. tuto., and the gloss and Bartolus in l. cum plures, ff. eod. titu., and in our case Bartolus affirmed this in l. si gener, ff. de his quib. ut indig., and in the said authen. ex complexu, and Baldus says the same there. However, I say that in giving the dowry she ought not to exceed the measure of maintenance, or the amount of dowry that was appropriate for a spurious daughter.

† For a dowry is called legitimate according to the condition of the woman and the means of the patrimony, as in l. filiae, ff. de legat. 3., and l. cum post, § gener, ff. de iure dotium. If, therefore, she exceeded that amount which was plausibly owed to her, regard being had to the fact that she was spurious and that the father was not a very wealthy man nor of great lineage, she is deemed to have given that amount out of her own property to the extent, I say, that it exceeded the due measure—an excellent argument in l. sancimus, C. de donat., and 12. quaestio. 2., in capitu. si quos de servis; and this seems to have been the view of Bartolus in the previously cited l. gener, and in the said authen. ex complexu, and in l. fina., § si a genero, de his, quae in fraud. credi. And that amount in which she exceeded must be computed within the fourth share of lady Evangelista herself; but if she exceeded in nothing, she is deemed to have done this as heir, and thus to have donated nothing of her own, and consequently she was able afterward to dispose of the entire fourth share of her property. That she appears to have done this as heir, moreover, and not spontaneously from her own property, I prove first from the fact that she is named heir therein. For if she had not acted as heir, that word would have been inserted there in vain; which is not to be said, by the argument in capitu. si papa, de privilegiis, libro 6., l. si quando, C. de inoffic. testamen., since words ought to have some effect, as there. Furthermore, wherever mention is made of any quality in any disposition which has the effect of altering that disposition, that act is deemed to have been made by virtue of that quality; to this purpose is the excellent text, with what is noted there, especially by Bartolus, in l. penult., C. de iure deliberan., where it is clear that if something is left to a son and mention is made of paternal power, it is deemed to have been left to him in contemplation of the father, because by reason of paternal power the son acquires for the father himself. So to the present matter: since she was bound to provide a dowry as heir, as I said above, if in the act of donation she stated that she was heir, she is deemed to have done this as heir by virtue of a lawful obligation. To the same point serves excellently what is read and noted in l. cum post mortem, ff. de administra. tuto., where if a tutor or curator promised a dowry for a girl, he is deemed in case of doubt to have promised it from the goods of the girl herself, but not from his own, because he was administering those goods; to the same effect is l. fina., C. de dotis promi., where the same is proved in the case of any administrator and manager of affairs, so that in case of doubt he is deemed to have paid the dowry from the property of the woman, and not from his own; this is supported by the fact that in case of doubt no one is presumed to wish to donate their own property, since donating is nothing other than losing, as in l. filiusfamil., ff. de donatio.; to which accords l. cum de indebi., ff. de probatio.; and this must be said especially in our case, in which an interpretation can be made such that the dowry was nonetheless owed and the said lady Evangelista is preserved in her rights: an excellent argument from those things which the gloss notes in l. cum quid, ff. si cert. pet., and capitu. cum inter P., and capitu. super hoc, de renuncia., with similar authorities. And these things as to the first doubt. As to the second, however—namely, with whom the said dowry ought now to remain after the death of the said Catharina—it seems at first that it ought to remain with the said Matthaeus, the husband of the said Catharina, not by person of Catharina, but of their common son: because after the death of Catharina the common son born of that marriage succeeded to the dowry. For the dowry is deemed the patrimony of the woman, l. 3, ff. de mino., to which accords l. Pomponius Philadelphus, ff. famil. erciscun. Moreover, the son succeeds ab intestato to the maternal property, as in authentic. in successione, C. de suis & legiti., and in the main body [of the Novel] from which it is taken, de haered. quae ab intesta. defe., § 1, and C. ad Orficia. throughout. To the son, however, the father Matthaeus himself succeeds, as in authenti. defuncto, C. ad Tertul., and in the body from which it is taken, as in Authent. de haered. quae ab intest. defer., § consequens, and § in hoc quidem. But in truth I think another view must be stated in our case, for the aforesaid points proceed in the case of a dowry that purely belongs to the mother, but the said dowry was not purely Catharina's own. For, as I said before, since she was spurious, under civil law she could obtain nothing from the father or from his heir, as in the said authen. ex complexu; but only by the disposition of canon law could she have the necessaries of life, and to this parents can be compelled, as in the said capitu. cum haberet, and consequently their heir, by the argument in the said authenti. licet, C. de natu. lib.; as I said before, just as maintenance is owed, so is a dowry, since it is not less favorable, but indeed more so, as I said above. The dowry was therefore given in our case in lieu of maintenance, since it was given by the heir of the deceased for the reasons stated above; therefore, the said Catharina having died, the dowry must return to the said lady Evangelista or her heirs, just as other goods simply given for maintenance ought to have returned. For maintenance is owed only during life, and the cause of maintenance ends with death, as in l. Mela, ff. de alimen. & cib. lega., and l. cum hi, § constat, ff. de transact., and l. haereditatem, ff. ad l. Falcid.; and the text in the said capit. cum haberet, at the end, from which that obligation originates, serves this excellently, for it commands only that necessaries be supplied; but necessity ceases with death; and this in truth seems to have been the opinion of Bartolus in the passages cited above, and first in the said authenti. ex complexu, C. de incest. nupt., where he says that he advised, on the basis of the said capitu. cum haberet,

† that up to an amount sufficient for maintenance, a father can leave property to a spurious son, and in the same way to a spurious daughter for her dowry, because without some dowry she cannot be maintained nor marry. Likewise he opined more expressly in the said l. fina., § si a socero, where he says that if a spurious daughter was married off by her father, the dowry cannot be recovered from that husband by the heirs of the father, because he holds it by an onerous title; but after it has returned to the woman, it can be revoked, because she holds it by title of donation, whereas a donation cannot be made to a spurious daughter, l. 1, C. de natu. li.; and he says this is true except to the extent that under canon law the son or daughter ought to have it for maintenance, as in the said capitu. cum haberet. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that according to this the son will have nothing from the maternal goods, because this is not absurd if the mother has nothing. For imagine that the mother had been married without a dowry: certainly he succeeds to nothing; therefore the wife must then be maintained from the husband's goods, as Innocent notes in capitu. per vestras, de dona. inter vi. & uxo., to which accords the text and what is noted there in l. si cum dotem, § sin autem in saevissimo, ff. solu. mat.

† Furthermore, see another closer parallel: if a woman is married off by her father, and the dowry proceeds from the father himself, upon the death of the woman, children having been left from that marriage, the dowry under the ius commune returns to the father, but not to the children of the deceased woman, even though custom holds otherwise, as is the text according to the common understanding in l. dos a patre profecta, C. sol. mat., and Bartolus examines this fully, and thus concluded finally in l. post dotem, ff. sol. mat. A fortiori, therefore, in our case the said dowry ought not to have passed to the son, since it is permitted by law solely in lieu of maintenance; but the cause of maintenance expires upon death, as I said above. And that this was the opinion of Bartolus, I allege what is noted in l. fin., ff. de his, quibus ut indig., at the word quaero, utrum sit alius modus, in the second column, where he says that something can be left to a spurious son or daughter for maintenance, and likewise for a dowry, provided that the proper measure is not exceeded in the leaving, because then fraud would be presumed under l. 1, C. de natu. libe.; and he holds

† that if the father wishes that what is left or given by reason of dowry pass to the children of the spurious son or daughter, the father ought to speak thus: 'I leave such-and-such an estate to Titius, my son, for maintenance during his life; afterward it remains to the children of that spurious son'; for, as he says, a father can leave property to the children of that spurious son; concerning which one must state as is more fully read and noted in l. fin., C. de na. li. And thus he clearly and correctly wills that by person of a spurious father the children, even if legitimate, cannot aspire to what was left to that spurious person for maintenance, because, as I said before, the cause of maintenance ends with death; but it is necessary that they take by disposition of the person leaving or providing the dowry, which can be done, d. l. fi. But in our case this was not said by the said lady Evangelista—and if it had been said, she would be deemed to have donated from her own property to the children of that spurious daughter; indeed, she said the opposite. For she willed, and so caused it to be stipulated in her own name, that the said Matthaeus should restore the dowry to Catharina herself and to that Franciscus receiving it on behalf of the said lady Evangelista, or to whomsoever it ought by law to be restored and returned, etc.; for these are the formal words of that instrument. But by law it ought to be restored to lady Evangelista herself or to her heirs, because the cause of maintenance ceases, as noted in the legal authorities cited above. Wherefore, from all the aforesaid, I conclude that the said dowry ought not to remain with the said Matthaeus, but to return to the heirs of the said lady Evangelista to the extent that she did this out of necessity as heir, as I said above: because then it purely succeeds into the place of maintenance.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. If a father institutes a son in any property for less than the legitim, the son can claim a supplement.
2. A pact not to succeed a father or a son is valid when one receives as much as is owed to him on the occasion of the succession.
3. One cannot submit to the adverse party as an arbitrator.
body: Having invoked the aid of Almighty God, the legal question is raised: whether, in view of the submission made by Antonio di Colombino to Nardo, the father of the said Antonio, and to Nerotio di Mariano Nicaletis, and the award subsequently rendered by the said Nerotio with the consent of the said Nardo—the said Antonio not objecting thereto—and the donation subsequently made by the said Nardo to the person of the said Antonio, his aforementioned son, the said Antonio is able, especially after the death of the said Nardo his father, to claim anything in or from the property of his said father on account of his legitim? And first, it seems that he can claim his legitim, at least after the death of the said Nardo his father, because a son cannot be excluded and deprived of his paternal inheritance without legitimate cause; otherwise, the father's testament would be void, as in Authen. ut cum de appel. cog. § aliud quoque capitulum, and as is read and noted in l. filio praeterito, ff. de iniust. rup. & irri. testa.

† And if the father had instituted the said Antonio in any property worth less than the legitim, he would be able to claim a supplement, as in l. omnimodo, and l. quoniam novella, and l. scimus, C. de inof. test.; nevertheless, what the father donated to him must be brought into collation, even though he stated so in the preface of the emancipation: because that is a simple donation, and not one made for the sake of legitim, since the father ought rather to be rewarded by the son when he emancipates him, than vice versa, as is proven in l. cum oportet. § cum autem, C. de bon. quae lib. And that such a donation made by the father as a reward for emancipation must be brought into collation for the other sons is confirmed by Bartolus in said l. cum oportet, and l. ut liberis, C. de col., and seems virtually proved there at the end of the text. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the said Antonio seems to have renounced the paternal inheritance in that he submitted himself to the judgment of the father and of the said Nerotio, promising that he would be content with that portion which should be assigned to him by them, and that he would never further claim anything in the property of the said Nardo: because a pact not to succeed a father is void, as in l. pactum, C. de pactis, and l. pactum, C. de col. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that here an oath intervened, which has the power to validate such a pact, as is proven today in capitulo quamvis pactum, de pact. li. 6, and as the doctors of civil law note in said l. pactum, and in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiusso., and in l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta, ff. de verbo. obliga., and l. fin. C. de pact. For to this a twofold answer can be given. First, that the oath does not extend to our case, because the said Antonio compromised into the father and Nerotio, and swore to observe whatever they should arrange regarding this. In the end, not both, but Nerotio alone rendered the award, to the effect that he should be content with certain property to be given to him by his father; and thus the oath, being of strict law, ought not to be extended to this case, as in capitulo penul. de iureiuran., even though the said Nerotio said that he did this alone upon the commission of the said Nardo: because it seems that Nardo could not remit this to the person of that one alone, since there must be no departure from the person of an arbitrator or arbiter, as the uprightness and trust of the person appear to have been chosen, as in l. si quis arbitratu, and what is noted there, ff. de verbo. oblig., and l. si merces, ff. locati, with similar texts. Furthermore, and secondly, the said Nardo transferred those goods to the said Antonio, his son, not as the portion falling to him, nor to satisfy the award previously rendered, but purely and voluntarily as a reward for emancipation; and thus he donated for another cause than that which was expressed in the award, as appears in the instrument drawn up thereupon. Therefore, neither the award nor the oath placed in the compromise can exclude the said Antonio from the paternal succession; and at least in doubt, the interpretation must be made in favor of the said Antonio, because it is odious for a son to be excluded from the paternal succession, as in said § aliud quoque capitulum, and in l. maximum vitium, C. de lib. praete., especially today, when the distinction of sex and paternal power has been abolished, as in auth. defuncto, C. ad Tertul., and in the body from which it is taken, in Auth. de heredit. quae ab intesta. defe. § consequens, and § hoc quidem. Also because words are to be interpreted against the said Nardo, who could have expressed his intention more clearly in the said donation, as in l. veteribus, ff. de pact., and in regula contra eum, de regulis iur. libr. 6. But notwithstanding these points, which I judge truly do not prejudice our case in the least, I consider the contrary opinion to be truer in law, namely, that the said Antonio can claim nothing further on account of his legitim in the property of the said Nardo his father by reason of the paternal intention. And I am moved to hold this principally from a twofold head, either of which would seem sufficient in itself for his conclusion. And first, by reason of the bare pact.

† For a pact not to succeed a father or a son is valid when one receives as much as is owed to him by reason of succession, as is singularly proved according to one understanding in l. 1. § si parens, ff. si quis a paren. fu. ma., and Bartolus confirmed this in two places: namely, in the said § si parens, and more clearly in l. fina. C. de pactis. Nor have I found that statement to be rejected by anyone; on the contrary, that it is valid is supported by the fact that the reason why the pact is annulled ceases to apply. For the reason appears to be lest someone should renounce a paternal succession for a trifling sum, whence the law wished to obviate deceits, as Bartolus notes in said l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiusso. Which reason indeed ceases in our case, since in the fact it was presupposed for me that the said Antonio received as much as was then due to him by reason of his legitim, and it can be said that he had more by reason of time, because he had those goods during the father's life, whereas they were not due to him except after the father's death, as in l. 1. § si impuberi arrogato, ff. de colla. bo., and as Bartolus notes in the same law, § nec castrense, and in authen. ingressi, C. de sacrosanct. ecclesi. The said Antonio is excluded from a second, clearer head, namely, by reason of the annexed oath. For he swore that he would be content with that part of the property which would be given and assigned to him by the said Nardo and Nerotio, and he promised not to seek further in the property of the said Nardo; yet an oath undoubtedly validates this pact, as in said capitulo 2. de pactis, libr. 6, and as the Legists hold in the passages cited above. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the oath does not extend to this case: for I say that it certainly does extend, if the words of the said submission and of the donation subsequent to the award are weighed properly. For the said Antonio, having solemnly appeared before the officials of the Mercanzia in the presence of his father, and with his consent and authority, asserted that he was no longer willing to live with Nardo his father, and, wishing to place himself into the hands of the said Nardo and Nerotio, so that they might give and make over to him that portion of the property of the said Nardo which should please the said Nardo and Nerotio, in every way, right, and form, etc., freely and purely and simply submitted himself to the said Nardo his father and Nerotio, granting and conceding to the said Nardo and Nerotio full license and authority to grant and give to the said Antonio out of the property of the said Nardo all and whatever should seem fit and pleasing to the said Nardo and Nerotio, and the said Antonio promised and agreed to the said Nardo stipulating, etc., not to claim further from the property of the said Nardo his father, but to remain quiet and content with the portion that should be made over to him by the said Nerotio and Nardo, and he swore corporally, touching the scriptures, not to contravene the aforesaid, etc. Whence, carefully weighing all the words recited above, which are formally the words of the instrument drawn up concerning the said submission, the said Nardo and Nerotio were not to judge anything judicially or in the form of a trial, but this was submitted to them purely as a factual matter; this is supported by what is read and noted in capitulo Quintavallis, and capitulo veniens, de iureiurand., and in l. societatem. § arbitrorum, with the following law, ff. pro socio. Whence the said Nerotio was assumed as a good man and friend, as in l. 3. ff. de arbit. Nardo, however, was a party; whence he could take action by virtue of the submission made to him, because one can submit oneself to an opposing party as to an arbitrator and good man, as in the said capitulo Quintavallis, and capitulo veniens, and l. si libertus, ff. de operis liberto. Therefore, for the validity of the act, it is enough that the will and pleasure, or judgment of their minds, appear in whatever manner, since, as I have said, they did not have to judge judicially, nor could there be a judicial proceeding before them, as Innocent notes in said capitulo Quintavallis; otherwise he could not have compromised into the said Nardo:

† because one cannot compromise into an opposing party as into an arbiter, as in l. penult. ff. de arbit. But someone's will is expressed not only by words, but by deeds; indeed, deeds are powerful in declaring the will, just as words are, which are often uttered contrary to the intention of the speaker, as in capitulo dilecti, de appella., and capitulo aestimant. 11. q. 3, with many legal texts cited there in the gloss. Nerotio, however, sufficiently declared his intention in words, by expressly making an award and specifying the goods that ought to be assigned to the said Antonio for his share according to the tenor of the submission. Nardo, moreover, approved that award not only by approving it, but also by deeds: because he punctually assigned to the said Antonio all the things awarded by the said Nerotio. Therefore, it sufficiently appeared concerning the will and pleasure of the said Nardo and Nerotio, into whom the submission was made, that the said Antonio should be content with the said goods for his portion. And for this, what Bartolus notes in a similar matter serves very well in l. cum pater. § libertis, in fi. de lega. 2, and Bartolus in l. filius, C. de pe. haered., and Giovanni d'Andrea in regula qui tacet, de regu. iur. lib. 6, in Mercurialibus. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the father donated as a reward for emancipation, and not by virtue of the submission made to him or of the preceding award, as appears from the words of the donation; for I say that those words were inserted through ignorance, from the common style of those who emancipate sons today, believing that it ought to be said and done thus, as Bartolus considers in said l. cum oportet, and in l. ut liberis, previously cited. But the principal cause was that those goods should be assigned to the said Antonio for his portion, under title of donation nevertheless, by virtue of that submission and the award following thereupon, which I prove by multiple considerations. First, since the son was in discord with the father and was no longer willing to live with him, as the son himself confessed in the presence of the officials, and from this followed that submission, or compromise, and it was expressly agreed that a certain amount of the goods of the said Nardo should be assigned to him by them for his portion, it is not likely that the father afterwards wished simply to emancipate and simply to donate those goods to him, since it is not likely that he immediately changed his intention, especially because before the said Nerotio each of them, namely father and son, alleged and proposed his own side and his rights; to this effect is l. non ad ea, ff. de condi. & demonstr.; for one is presumed to persist in his prior will, as in cap. maiores, near the end, de bapti., and in l. eum qui, ff. de probatio. Likewise, doubtful deeds and words receive interpretation according to the preceding facts, as in l. servus plurium, in fin. ff. de leg. 1. Furthermore, this is gathered from another fact, because the father punctually assigned to the son the goods that by virtue of the submission were expressed in the award by the said Nerotio; therefore, he wished to approve and execute the contents of the said award, and not to make a completely new, unconsidered donation, by the argument in l. plane, ff. de lega. 1. Nor is it an obstacle that he used the word 'donation'; because this does not contradict, but confirms the aforesaid. For the said Nerotio in his award said near the end that that division or donation should be made with the reasons and causes, so that it might be valid in law, etc.; whence that word, 'or donation', is to be carefully weighed, for he intended that it should be made by way of division, or donation, so that it would be valid. Whence the father, wishing to approve and execute this, knowing that a donation made to a son under paternal power is regularly not valid, as in l. antepe. C. de dona. inter vi. & uxo., and a paren. in li. fa., chose the more valid way. For he first emancipated him; but he said 'as a reward for emancipation' through ignorance, since from the emancipation he himself ought rather to have been rewarded by the son, as I have said above. But attention must be paid to the manner of ordinary speakers, and they must be understood roughly, just as they are in common usage, and not taken strictly, as is read and noted in l. stipulatio ista. § hic quoque, and § plane, ff. de verborum obli. But that this Nardo the father wished principally to donate by assigning him his portion according to the form of the award, principally as a reward for emancipation, is proven most clearly, beyond the aforesaid, by certain words inserted in the said donation, where among other things it is said thus: 'Item, he gave into the other hand one hundred and twenty-five gold Florins in those terms, manners, and form which are declared and specified in those places by a certain award rendered by Nerotio di Mariano in the court of the officials of the Mercanzia, etc.' Whence those words, 'in those terms, manners, and form, etc.', are to be diligently weighed, through which it is expressly gathered that the said Nardo did not intend to donate purely, but under those manners and form which are contained in the award. Now, the manner and form contained in the award were that this Antonio should have those goods for his portion, and could not further claim anything in the goods of the said Nardo; whence, since he made that donation referring to the said award, and under mention of it, it appears most clearly that he did not intend to depart from it, but rather to execute and observe it, by the argument in capitulo cum venerabilis, de excep., and in said l. non ad ea, with what is noted there. In my judgment, this motive closes the matter against interpreting the said donation otherwise, nor ought we to care that he used those words, 'he donated as a reward for emancipation'; because a contract and disposition is judged rather according to its nature and the subject matter than according to the words expressed in it, as is the notable text, and there by the gloss and Bartolus, in l. si uno, ff. locati, and noted by the gloss in l. 1. ff. de superficie., and by Bartolus in l. cotem. § qui maximos, ff. de publi. And for the understanding of a stipulation we must always first consider what was agreed upon, as in l. semper in stipulationibus, ff. de regu. iur., and if it does not appear, that which is more probable must be considered, as in capitulo inspicimus in obscuris, de regulis iuris lib. 6, and in l. in obscuris, ff. eod. In our case, however, it was first agreed that to this Antonio his portion should be given, and that he could not further claim anything, as appears from the aforesaid. Likewise, it is more probable, because of the discord between father and son, especially since he was born of a predeceased wife, that he wished to donate for the aforesaid cause rather than purely and simply. Furthermore, the disposition of the award by the said Nerotio escapes this interpretation, which commanded that those goods later donated ought to be donated on the occasion of his portion; therefore, the subsequent donation is seen to have been made for the sake of fulfilling that award, through the notable text and what is noted there by Bartolus in l. fin. C. de ali. pup. praest., and by the same author in l. cum servus, ff. de verborum obliga.; and by donating those goods he is seen equally to have donated and to have approved the disposition of the award, l. 3. § filius, ff. & C. eod. ad Mace. Wherefore, from all the aforesaid, I conclude that the said Antonio cannot further claim anything in the paternal goods of the said Nardo his father on account of the legitim owed to him by natural law, but that he ought to be content with the goods formerly donated to him by his father. And to the contrary arguments formulated above, the response is sufficiently clear through the aforesaid.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. By the ius commune, a woman is permitted freely to dispose of her property beyond the legitime owed to children.
2. A woman having children from a first marriage, if she passes to second vows, cannot in a testament, or inter vivos, or by a betrothal gift confer and donate more to the second husband than she gives to any of her children. 3.
body: In the name of the Holy Trinity, amen. It seems, first, that the husband ought to gain nothing from the dowry of his predeceased wife. Moreover, this is certain in the first place: that by the ius commune he gains nothing, but the dowry must return entirely to the heirs of the woman, as in l. unica, C. de rei uxo. act. and in l. assiduis, C. qui poti. in pigno. hab. and in capitu. 1. & 2. and in capitu. nuper, de do. post diuor. restit. Nor even under municipal law: because the statute of Siena, not only in our case, in which children of the deceased woman survive, does not grant the husband any part of the dowry; on the contrary, it expressly provided in an addition correcting the ancient statute that he gain nothing, as is clear from the statute placed under the rubric, what portion falls as a gain to the husband when marriage is dissolved by the death of the wife. For the words of the addition made to that statute are these, namely: that if a woman marries a second husband and has one or more sons, the said husband gains nothing from the dowries, but the sons of that woman born of both husbands from that woman succeed per capita. So it occurred precisely in our case. For that lady died, leaving sons from each marriage; therefore, by virtue of the statute, the husband ought to gain nothing from her dowry. And consequently it seems it must be said that neither by virtue of the pact entered into between the said spouses at the time of contracting the marriage—for although it was expressly agreed between them that whichever of them survived ought to gain a certain amount from the dowry, or from the donation on account of marriage under the name of antifactum—nevertheless, such a pact seems not to have been valid, as being made against what is prohibited by statute; for this, see what is noted by the gl. in l. 1, C. ne fideius. do. dentur and the gl. super rub. de decurio. lib. 6; and thus it seems that by no law ought this husband to gain anything from the dowry of the deceased wife. Furthermore and secondly, it seems that, presupposing the husband ought to gain something by virtue of the pact, nevertheless this gain ought not to be deducted from the fourth part, but from the remaining three parts which by virtue of the statute are assigned to the sons, because the statute gives the woman the power to dispose at her discretion of a fourth of her property, notwithstanding the disposition that she had first made. For that statute, since it is against the ius commune, restricting the woman's power, must be interpreted broadly insofar as the favor of the woman is concerned, and strictly insofar as her power is restricted, because any departure from the ius commune is odious and therefore to be restricted, as in c. is qui, de fil. presb. li. 6 and in c. quod dilectio, de consang. & af. and in c. cum dilectus, de consue. and l. 2, C. de noxa.

† For by the ius commune, a woman is permitted freely to dispose of her property beyond the legitime owed to children, which in our case would be the third part of all property, since she did not have more than four sons, as in auth. novissima, C. de inoff. testa. and in Auth. ut cum de appe. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum. Therefore, the said statute ought to be strictly interpreted insofar as it takes away from the woman the power of disposing of three parts, and reserves power only in respect of a fourth. It ought therefore to be understood that, with all burdens deducted, the woman can dispose of the fourth part, so that the ius commune may be prejudiced as little as possible, as in the laws cited above. And this interpretation is especially to be embraced because the words of the statute permitting the woman disposition of the fourth part are stated generally and without any distinction. Therefore, they ought to be understood generally and without distinction, as in c. si Romanorum, 19. di. and in c. solitae, de mai. & ob. and in c. quod si dormierit, 31. q. 1 and l. de pretio, ff. de pub. To this also contribute those words of the statute placed at the end: Notwithstanding the disposition that they had first made, etc., which imply that although the woman had earlier disposed of something, nevertheless, this notwithstanding, she has the power to dispose at her discretion of the fourth part of all her property. But although the aforesaid arguments may appear superficially compelling, I nevertheless consider the contrary opinion to be truer in law, namely, that the said husband ought to gain that which was agreed between them under the name of antifactum, and that such gain must be deducted from the fourth of which the woman can dispose, but not from the remaining three parts, which are left to the sons. Now, that this husband ought to gain what was agreed between them, I prove by the text in l. hac edictali, C. de secun. nup., where it is proved,

† that if a woman having children from a first marriage passes to a second marriage, she cannot in a will, or inter vivos, or by spousal largesse confer and donate more to the second husband than she gives to any one of her sons. Therefore, by not exceeding that measure, she can add a pact that the husband gain a certain portion, or a certain amount, per hundred from her dowry, or as the Doctors there more clearly hold. Supporting this is that before the lex of the Code, a woman was able to confer whatever she wished upon a second husband, provided she did not deprive the children of their legitime, as in the said §. aliud quoque capitulum, and in auth. novissima. But her power in respect of a second husband was restricted by the lex of the Code, as in the said l. hac edictali, read and noted; therefore, short of the prohibition, a woman can dispose in favor of her husband as she pleases, since everyone is the legitimate manager and arbiter of his own property, as in l. re mandata, C. man. and c. de his, de sepul. But in our case, the gain accruing to the husband does not exceed the portion left to each of the sons; therefore, under the ius commune, such a pact was valid. Nor is it an obstacle if it is said that the parts owed to the sons exist by disposition of the statute, and against the will of the woman, while from that part of which the woman can dispose, nothing was conferred on any of the sons, and therefore she could transfer nothing to the husband through the said l. hac edictali: because to this I answer twofold. First, indeed, the said lady instituted all the sons equally, once that fourth part was deducted. Nor is the woman prohibited by the statute from disposing of the three parts, but rather she cannot dispose of them so that the sons are deprived; and so speaks the statute. But if she wishes to dispose in favor of the sons, she is not prohibited; indeed, it is granted by an argument a contrario sensu from the statute, which contrary sense is to be embraced, both since it accords with the disposition of the ius commune, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. omnes populi, ff. de iust. & iur. and Baldus in l. conventicula, C. de epis. & cle.; supporting this are c. cum apostolica, de his, quae fiunt a praela. and what is noted by Io. An. also in c. publicato, de ele. Secondly, it can be answered that the aforesaid objection proceeds having regard to the ius commune, according to which a woman can, as I said above, freely dispose of her property, except for the legitime owed to the sons, which was modest; whence it seemed dishonorable for a woman to prefer a second husband in her property over any of the sons. But in our case the reason ceases: because by virtue of the statute the sons have all the property, whether she wills it or not, except for the fourth part, of which the woman can dispose at her discretion according to the tenor of that same statute. Hence it cannot happen, nor at least in our case did it happen, that the husband has more than any of the sons. Nor is what is said above impeded by the aforesaid statute alleged to the contrary, in that it provides that the husband gain nothing where sons survive: because I say that the husband is excluded by statutory disposition, since the statute in that addition did not intend to take away the gain it had granted to the husband. Whence I acknowledge that under statutory law he gains nothing. But in our case the husband claims by virtue of a common pact entered into between them at the time of the contract of marriage. This, however, the statute does not prohibit; indeed, it rather permits it, if it is carefully weighed at the end, where it says thus, namely: save that in the aforesaid case, where she has married a second time, the woman may dispose according to the laws and statutes of the commune of Siena, etc. As if to say that by disposition of the woman the husband will be able to gain, provided that the woman disposes according to the laws and statutes of Siena—for instance, that she does not give to the second husband more than any of the sons has. Likewise, that she does not dispose beyond the fourth part of her property. For the power of the woman is thus limited according to the laws and statutes of Siena. And by this, an answer is given to what was objected above, namely that it cannot be done by pact because it is prohibited by statute; on the contrary, it is permitted, given the disposition of the woman, which occurred in our case. Moreover, the statute prohibits the husband from gaining, but does not intervene to assist by giving the gain to the surviving sons over the husband; even if it did not permit it at the end, the pact is valid. For there is a great difference between prohibiting and not assisting, according to what was noted in a similar case by Bartolus in l. sed & si, §. scire, ff. de peti. haere. From all of which it is clearly evident that the husband ought to gain the antifactum by virtue of the pact entered into in the marriage contract, provided, as I said before, the gain does not exceed what falls to any of the sons of the said predeceased woman. But that this gain ought to be deducted from the fourth part of which the woman can dispose, and not from the three parts which must be left to the sons, is clearly proved from the disposition of the statute contained under the rubric, that women having sons may not leave beyond the fourth part. In which it is provided in effect, having regard to the statute itself and its addition, that a woman having sons or daughters, one or more, cannot leave, or donate, or sell, or alienate so that her children who remain can afterwards be deprived of their property, except for reason of necessity or sustenance, save that she may distribute a fourth part of her property at her discretion, etc. Which words, if carefully weighed, concern not only disposition in a last will, but also inter vivos; and thus the rule stands from that statute that a woman having children cannot, either inter vivos or in a last will, dispose of her property by alienating it beyond a fourth part. But it can come into doubt for no one that this gain accruing to the husband from the common pact entered into between them arises from the disposition of the woman: because if the woman had not so agreed, the husband would have gained nothing, as this is openly read and noted in the said l. hac edictali. Therefore it must be reckoned in her fourth. For if we were to say the opposite, it would follow that the woman could indirectly dispose of half of her property: for instance, because she could include a pact when contracting second nuptials that the surviving husband gain a fourth part of her property, and finally at death, or in life with the passage of time, she could dispose of another fourth part; which sounds absurd and would be expressly against the intention and words of the said statute, in which it is provided that she cannot dispose except for the cause of her sustenance, so that the sons would be deprived of three parts of the property. Nor, by the same reasoning, ought that gain of the antifactum to be deducted from the intact dowry: because according to this, three intact parts would not remain with the sons, and the woman would be found to have disposed beyond a fourth part of the whole. The end of that statute does not stand in the way where it says: Notwithstanding the disposition that she had first made, etc.; because it ought not to be understood so that the woman, by disposing multiple times, could leave beyond a fourth, since this would be openly against the intention of that statute; and an argument in l. sancimus, C. de dona. supports this; otherwise, the children could easily be deprived of their maternal property, and that statute could be circumvented, which must not be said; but it can be understood of a disposition, if any she had previously made, regarding the usufruct of the property. Or secondly, it can be understood, and better so, that the meaning of that clause is that three parts should pass to the sons notwithstanding any disposition the woman had first made of those assets. Hence it is that in the addition to that statute these words were appended, namely: Let the remaining three parts be divided pro rata among the sons. For the woman's disposition beyond a fourth part is of no moment, as is gathered from the intention of the statute; and what is read and noted on a similar point in the said l. hac edictali supports this. And further, in my judgment, it could be maintained that not only must this gain arising from the pact of the husband with the woman be deducted from the fourth part of which she can dispose, but I think the same even if that gain should accrue to the husband by disposition of the statute: because by her act half accrues to the husband, albeit by contracting marriage and giving him so great a dowry, since he who cannot alienate by pact must take care lest an alienation by operation of law arise from his act, as in l. codicillis, §. antepe., ff. de leg. 2. And this is what Iac. But., Bartolus, Fran. de Alber., and Baldus seem to have meant in a similar question on the said l. hac edictali, and Angelus on the Auth. de nup. in §. quia vero, where they say,

† that a second husband cannot gain more than one of the sons, not only if the gain arises from the woman's pact, but also if it arises from the disposition of the statute: because the woman herself is considered to leave it by giving cause for this gain, namely by contracting second nuptials. From these points, the answer to all arguments alleged above to the contrary is clear. Whence I conclude again that the husband ought to gain the antefactum from the agreement entered into with the woman, notwithstanding the survival of the sons, provided he does not have more than any of the sons. And such gain ought to be deducted from that fourth of which the woman was able to dispose, so that three parts may thus be left entirely to the sons. And let these remarks suffice.

consilium-panormitanus_cons_print_venice.argument:
1. Why positions have been admitted.
2. A position is said to be impertinent which does not serve to ground or aid the intention of the positioning party.
3. A sentence is said to be certain if it can be made certain in any part of the acts.
4. A confession does not require the fabric of a trial for its validity.
5. Although a general libel can be rejected, yet if it is answered, the answer holds, as does the judgment founded upon it.
body: IN the name of Christ, amen. In the cause or dispute which is presently pending between Lady Joanna of Modena on the one side, and Simone de Casonis on the other. Several points, conclusively however, must be examined in order. First, whether those positions, over which the present dispute turns, ought by law to have been answered. Second, assuming that they ought not to have been answered, whether—inasmuch as they have already been answered simply by the party—the confession prejudices the respondent. Third, assuming that the confession was valid to the prejudice of the respondent, whether the said vicar could declare all those answers to be null and of no effect, as having been made to positions concerning the act of another, and to positions that are captious and double. Fourth, if by law he could not so pronounce as he did pronounce, whether the said pronouncement is null ipso iure, or at least must be retracted by a judge's sentence; and on this account it will appear what the duties of the appellate judge ought to be in this dispute. I come in order to the first; and it seems that those positions did not ought to have been answered by law. For the first seems captious and double, since it contains several dwellings, etc., without any determination, which is contrary to what is noted in c. 1. and 2. de confes. in Sexto, and in l. 2. §. quod obseruari, C. de iura. cal. For the same reason, the same seems to be said of the second position, since in it it is said without determination that she found in the inheritance all the immovable goods, etc. Likewise, the third position seems captious to deceive the said Lady Joanna, since that confession to it would be directly contrary to the petition presented in court by the said Lady Joanna. The fourth position can also be quibbled at and rejected, as multiple, captious, and containing the act of another. But, notwithstanding these points, I consider that the contrary proceeds by law, namely, that the said positions proceed by law, and consequently they ought by law to have been answered. And first, I lay down this rule: that everything provable may be put as a position; which rule is excellently proved in my judgment in Clem. saepe, de uerbo. signi. in §. uerum, at the verse 'quia positiones', where it is said,

† 'long usage in causes has admitted positions for the easier dispatch of lawsuits on account of the confessions of the parties, and for clearer proof', etc.; and if so, it openly indicates that positions can be made concerning all matters touching the decision of the suit, so that the positioning party may be relieved of the burden of proof by the confession of the adverse party, and they may be made on the part of the defendant to weaken the intention of the plaintiff; and this the glossa intended more openly in cap. 1. de confes. in Sexto. The Lords of the Rota hold the same view in decisio 30. Nay more, I say that even that which cannot be proved, provided it comes to ground the intention of the party, can be positioned, as is evident in positions concerning a purely negative fact, as is proved in the previously cited c. 1. Baldus also openly held this rule in the previously cited l. 2. §. quod obseruari, where he says,

† that that position is called impertinent which does not serve to ground or aid the intention of the one putting it; otherwise it is called pertinent; and this is sufficiently clear from the examples given by the glossa in the said c. 1. and 2. de confes. in Sexto, and in Clem. saepe, de uerbo. signi., and by Innocent in c. dudum. 2. de elect. But the positions over which there is dispute most clearly come to weaken the intention of the plaintiff, and to relieve the defendant from the burden of proof; therefore they are legitimate, and they had to be answered by law. And that the said positions are such is most clearly apparent by weighing each one. For the first contains that the said Lady Joanna saw her natural brother possessing the dwellings with buildings, etc., which are contained in the petition of the same Lady Joanna. For this cannot be called impertinent, because it comes to weaken the intention of Lady Joanna herself. For from it there is inferred, at least obliquely and presumptively, that those goods claimed by Lady Joanna herself did not belong to her mother, as she narrated in her petition; therefore it ought to have been admitted, as appears from the aforesaid, and is noted by Baldus in the said §. quod obseruari. For from possession, ownership is consequentially inferred, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. ad probationem, C. locati. Nor can it be called captious or double, since it is lawful, very clear, and very certain even with respect to the goods, since it refers to the goods contained in the petition of Lady Joanna herself, of which she was most certain: both because she had described those goods in her libel, and thus is seen to know and confess everything, as is read and noted in l. cum precibus, C. de libe. cau. and by Antonius de Butrio in c. fin. de confes.; and because a position is sufficiently said to be certain from the fact that it refers to a certain writing produced in court.

† For a sentence is also in such a manner said to be certain, from the fact that it can be made certain in some part of the acts, as in l. pen. C. de sen. quae sine cer. quan., noted by Innocent in c. fin. de libe. obla.; and c. cum uenerabilis, near the end, de exce., and what is there noted, makes for this. Nor can it be impugned on the ground that it contains the act of another: for on the contrary, it contains the proper act of Lady Joanna herself, since it concerns her own senses, namely that she saw her natural brother possessing and holding; for this, see l. testium, C. de testi., and 3. q. 9. c. testes, with its glossa, and in c. de consue., and c. cum causam, de testi., and what is there noted. For this, see the glossa in the said c. 1. de confes. in Sexto, where by way of example that position is put: 'Item, that he knew such a one to be a cleric; Item, that he saw him wearing the tonsure and clerical dress'; and this seems undoubted, therefore I do not dwell on it. Nay, as I shall say below, even a position containing the act of another does not always not have to be answered. I say entirely the same with respect to the second position; for in it it is said that she found in the inheritance the goods contained in her said petition. For this position is made to aid the defendant and weaken the intention of the plaintiff herself, to infer, at least obliquely and presumptively, that those were not maternal goods, but paternal, or fraternal, etc.; and thus it was pertinent, nor was it double, nor captious: on the contrary, it is very simple, since it refers to the goods described in the petition of the plaintiff herself; nor does it contain the act of another, but on the contrary her own, as appears through that word, that she 'found' all the goods, etc. I say entirely the same with respect to the third, namely that she heard her mother saying, and let her answer concerning her own sense, namely that she heard, etc.; for this, see c. 2. de consue. For in things perceptible by the sense of hearing, deposition must be made through that sense, as is noted in the said c. cum causam, and in c. 2. de consue.; and this position most clearly came to weaken the intention of the plaintiff herself; therefore it ought to have been admitted, so that through her confession the defendant would be relieved from the burden of proving his exception. The same can be said of the fourth and last position, as appears there through the word 'heard'; for the article of common report greatly aids a party, according to what is noted by Bartolus in l. de minore. §. tormenta, ff. de quaestio., and c. ueniens, de testi., and 4. q. 3. c. si testes. §. item saepe, and c. licet ex quadam, de testi., with similar authorities. Nay, as I have said, even if a position contains entirely the act of another, it ought not on that account to be rejected, provided it serves for the decision of the case, and contains such a thing that a certain opinion can therefore fall upon the respondent, as Cino, Bartolus, and Baldus clearly held in the said l. 2. §. quod obseruari, C. de iur. cal.; and Butrio seems to follow this in l. pen. of the same title, and there openly held this in his lecture. The rule that I set out before makes for this, namely, that everything that comes into proof can be adduced in positions; and although the glossa seems to indicate otherwise in c. 1. and 2. de confes. in Sexto, and in the said §. quod obseruari, and Speculator in the title de posit. §. 5. at the verse 'et notanter': yet I say that those statements must be understood when the act of another is such that knowledge or opinion of it does not plausibly fall upon the one having to answer; this is clear through the laws cited in them: or it applies when someone would have to answer concerning the truth; in which case one is not bound to answer, since it is of such a nature that one cannot have certain knowledge of it. For he would undergo a double-edged perjury, as is said in l. Marcellus, ff. rer. amo.; Bartolus said this notably in the said l. Marcellus, near the end. And that this was the intention of those glossae, I prove through the examples that are placed in the same place. For the glossa in the said c. 1. in Sexto, among other positions that are made to prove someone to be excommunicated, places these two, namely: 'Item, that at that time that person struck was a cleric; Item, that he was in possession of the status of cleric', etc. For it is certain that these two positions contain the act of another, and nonetheless they are admitted; and this because knowledge or opinion of that fact can fall within the senses of the respondent, as I said above, according to Baldus. To the same effect is what the glossa notes in Clem. saepe, de uer. sig. on the word 'confessiones', which, in proving a loan against an heir, frames these two positions: 'Item, I position that I loaned one hundred to Titius; Item, that he promised to repay it to him on such a day; Item, that Titius instituted him heir', etc. Behold, therefore, that it was not the intention of Joannes Andreae to exclude all positions concerning the act of another simply. Without doubt, therefore, it must be concluded that in our case those positions were to be admitted by law, and consequently they had to be answered by law; and these points concerning the first question. I come now to the second, namely, assuming without prejudice to the truth that they ought not to have been answered by law, whether—from the fact that the said Lady Joanna answered—she created prejudice to herself? I firmly judge that she did. First, to this effect is the text cited in c. 1. de ac. in Sexto, where it is elegantly proved that although an exception is available to a party against the inquest framed against her, nevertheless, if, having passed it over, she answers the inquest, she creates prejudice to herself; to the same effect is what Innocent notes in c. qualiter et quando. 2. de ac.,

† where he says that even if, without any preceding web of a trial, someone comes to court and confesses against himself, he creates prejudice to himself, because a confession does not require the web of a trial for its validity. Hence we say that a confession is valid, although the process is found to be null from some defect, as is proved in c. Pisanis, de rest. spo., and there Innocent most openly affirms this, and others after him; to the same effect is the text with what is noted there in Clem. constitutionem, at the end, de ele., and what Bartolus notes there in l. si confessus, ff. de cust. reo., and better in l. maritus, ff. de quaestio. On this see the glossa in c. pen. de iur. cal., which says that although a party is not bound to answer except to an interrogation made at the petition of the adverse party alone, yet if he answers, he creates prejudice to himself, on the argument in l. si sine interrogatione, ff. de interro. ac.; and the Lords of the Rota hold the same in the previously cited decisio 30, where they say that although the interrogation was not to be answered because it was not made as it ought to have been made by law, yet if the party answered, he creates prejudice to himself; to the same effect is a good text in argument in l. si, C. de anna. exce., where it is clear

† that although a general libel can be rejected, yet if it is answered, the answer holds, and the judgment grounded upon it; and so Innocent intended in c. finali, de lib. ob.; and through these points it is briefly apparent what must be said concerning the second question. For I conclude that, assuming without prejudice to the truth that those positions ought not to have been answered, nevertheless, inasmuch as they were answered, the answer holds, and prejudices the confessant insofar as it tends to her prejudice. I come to the third, namely, assuming that the confession was valid, as proved above, whether the said vicar could pronounce the answer null, etc., as said above. And it is said without doubt that he could not: because, since a confession is part of the record of the proceedings, as in c. quoniam contra, de prob., and not simply of the record of the trial, but of the cause, since it pertains to the decision of the cause, the judge cannot, in the absence of a just cause, cut out the records of the cause, nor destroy them by his authoritative sentence; nay, they must be preserved with the notary of the cause against the false assertion of an unjust judge, as in the said c. quoniam. Likewise on this there is an open text in l. acta, ff. de re iud., where it is also proved most openly by the glossa and Bartolus that the judge cannot destroy the records of the cause without the consent of the parties; in support of this is that, even when the instance of the trial has expired, the records of the cause remain, such as confessions and depositions of witnesses and the like, as noted by Innocent and others in c. causam quae, de testi., and by Bartolus in l. cum lite mortua, ff. iud. sol. Furthermore, cite the most clear glossa in c. finali, de iureiu. in Sexto, which says that an answer made to the petition of a party cannot be revoked by the party, unless it is done immediately, for example before he leaves the sight of the judge, on the argument in c. praeterea, de testi. cog. and 32. q. 1. c. apud, where there is also a good glossa. The same must be said of the judge through the aforesaid, and because a confession is not revoked unless an error is shown. But error is proved by proving that the matter stands otherwise, as is read and noted in c. fin. de confes. and in l. error facti, C. de iur. et fac. igno.; and in our case no error was proved; therefore the judge could not pronounce the confession erroneous, or null. From these points I deduce the answer to the fourth and last question, whether that sentence of the judge was null; and I believe in that manner that it was, for many reasons. First, because it was delivered by a judge insufficiently informed, as in c. cum ex literis, de in integ. resti., noted by Bartolus in l. prolatam, C. de senten. et interlo. om. iu. Likewise it was notoriously unjust, as appears from the aforesaid; therefore it was null, as Innocent notes in cap. fraternitatis, de frigi.; see the text in cap. inter caetera, de re iu., and there Antonius confirms this.
